paper_title: Structure in Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can structural decompositions improve reinforcement learning in partially observable or non-Markovian environments, and in "big world" settings where the environment is far larger than the agent can represent exactly? In particular, can temporal and state abstractions hide temporal dependencies and non-Markovian aspects, can memory serve as an abstraction or augmentation for learned transition models, can policy portfolios support optimization across timescales, can modular decompositions drive separate exploration over different parts of the state space while relational abstractions preserve interpretability, and can structural factorization yield better benchmarks across different axes of task complexity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement learning agent interacting with an environment modeled as a partially observable (and possibly non-Markovian) decision process, in which at each discrete time step t the agent receives an observation o_t drawn from a hidden state s_t, selects an action a_t, and receives a reward r_t, with the goal of maximizing the expected discounted return E[ Σ_{t≥0} γ^t r_t ] for some γ ∈ (0,1). Assume further the "big world" regime: the underlying state/observation space is so large that the agent's representational capacity is strictly insufficient to encode the optimal value function or optimal policy exactly, even in the limit of infinite data.

Develop a theoretical and algorithmic framework that uses structural decompositions to improve learning in this setting. Concretely, investigate the following questions:

1. Define formal notions of temporal abstraction (e.g., options or skills over varying time scales) and state abstraction (e.g., quotient maps on observation/state spaces) and prove conditions under which composing them provably hides non-Markovian dependencies, so that the induced abstract decision process is (approximately) Markovian with quantifiable approximation error.

2. Formalize the use of memory (e.g., finite-state or recurrent summaries of histories) as an abstraction or augmentation of a learned transition model, and establish sample-complexity or representation-size trade-offs showing when memory can replace explicit modeling of the unobserved state.

3. Define a "policy portfolio" as a finite collection of policies operating at distinct time scales, and characterize when hierarchical optimization over such a portfolio yields tractable convergence guarantees (e.g., regret or sample complexity bounds) in big-world POMDPs.

4. Formalize modular decompositions of the state/observation space and show how they can drive parallel exploration with provable coverage guarantees, while relational abstractions (logical or graph-structured representations) preserve interpretability of learned knowledge.

5. Provide a structural factorization of task complexity along independent axes (e.g., observability depth, abstraction granularity, modular interaction structure) and use it to define benchmark families that isolate each axis.

The problem is to determine to what extent each of these structural mechanisms can be formalized, combined, and shown rigorously (or empirically) to improve reinforcement learning in partially observable and big-world settings.
category_tag: structured reinforcement learning under partial observability
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in a recent survey on structure in deep reinforcement learning. No comprehensive theoretical resolution combining temporal/state abstraction, memory, policy portfolios, modular decompositions, and task factorization for partially observable big-world RL is known; only partial progress exists on individual subproblems (e.g., options framework, PSRs, hierarchical RL).

paper_title: Structure in Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can structural decomposability be incorporated into automated reinforcement learning so that AutoRL systems can choose algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and search architectures more efficiently and at larger scale despite the non-stationarity and instability of reinforcement-learning training? More specifically, can decomposability assessment guide algorithm selection, can abstracting away task-irrelevant aspects accelerate hyperparameter optimization, can stored portfolios of learned policies and value functions support landmarking of related algorithms, can modularity information such as goals and task hierarchies shape the search process, and can decomposability structure the neural-architecture search space?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an automated reinforcement learning (AutoRL) framework whose goal is to automatically select a learning algorithm, tune its hyperparameters, and search over neural network architectures for a given reinforcement learning task. The reinforcement learning task is modeled as a Markov decision process (S, A, P, R, γ) with possibly non-stationary training dynamics arising from on-policy data collection and exploration.

Say that an MDP (or family of MDPs) is "structurally decomposable" if its state space, action space, reward function, or policy class admits a non-trivial decomposition into sub-problems—for example via factored state representations, sub-goal hierarchies, options/temporally extended actions, modular value or policy components, or task hierarchies. Let a "decomposability assessment" be a procedure that, given access to the MDP (or samples from it), outputs a description of such structure together with confidence/quality scores.

Develop a principled framework that uses decomposability assessments to drive AutoRL. Specifically, address the following questions:

(a) Define a formal notion of decomposability assessment for MDPs, and design an algorithm that uses such an assessment to select among candidate RL algorithms in a way that provably or empirically outperforms decomposability-agnostic selection.

(b) Formulate a hyperparameter optimization procedure that abstracts away aspects of the task identified as irrelevant by the decomposability assessment, and quantify the resulting reduction in sample/compute complexity compared to standard HPO.

(c) Define a portfolio of previously learned policies and value functions and a landmarking scheme on this portfolio (i.e., a method that uses cheap evaluations of portfolio elements on the new task to predict the performance of related algorithms), and analyze when landmarking yields reliable algorithm-performance predictions despite the non-stationarity and stochasticity of RL training.

(d) Incorporate modularity information—explicit goals and task hierarchies—into the AutoRL search process, and characterize conditions under which this modularity provably accelerates the search.

(e) Define a neural architecture search space whose structure mirrors the decomposability of the problem (e.g., modular sub-networks for sub-tasks), and study whether searching over this restricted space yields better architectures with fewer evaluations than unrestricted NAS.

The overall problem is to give algorithms and accompanying theoretical or empirical guarantees showing that exploiting structural decomposability makes AutoRL more efficient and more scalable than approaches that ignore such structure.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research program rather than a single precise conjecture. No published work resolves the full set of questions; AutoRL remains an active area with recognized open issues around scalability, non-stationarity, and exploitation of structure. No solution found.

paper_title: Structure in Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should task decompositions be integrated into meta-reinforcement learning so that agents trained across a distribution of tasks can adapt more effectively to new tasks? In particular, can decompositions provide abstractions over task distributions that enter the adaptation process, can highly decomposable problems be compartmentalized into modules that make the outer meta-learning loop more tractable, can portfolios of models specialized to different decomposability types guide data augmentation during adaptation, and can decomposability-informed curricula produce better warm-starting configurations for new tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a meta-reinforcement learning setting in which an agent is trained on a distribution p(T) over Markov decision process tasks T = (S, A, P_T, R_T, gamma), with the goal of producing an adaptation procedure that, given a small number of interactions with a previously unseen task T* ~ p(T), yields a high-return policy. Suppose that each task T admits a (possibly partial) decomposition into subtasks T = {T^1, ..., T^{k_T}}, where each subtask T^i is itself an MDP whose solution policies can be composed (sequentially, hierarchically, or in parallel) to solve T, and let d(T) be a measure of decomposability of T (e.g., the minimal number of subtasks needed to recover T up to a bounded suboptimality).

Develop a principled framework for integrating such task decompositions into meta-RL by addressing the following four sub-problems:

1. (Abstraction.) Define a mapping phi from the task distribution p(T) to a distribution over abstract task descriptors derived from decompositions, and specify how phi is consumed by the adaptation procedure so that the resulting meta-learner provably adapts faster (in sample complexity on T*) than a meta-learner that ignores decomposition information.

2. (Modular outer loop.) For tasks with high decomposability d(T), give an algorithm that compartmentalizes meta-training into modules M_1, ..., M_m, one per subtask type, such that the outer-loop meta-objective decomposes additively (or otherwise tractably) over modules, and quantify the reduction in the effective hypothesis-class complexity of the outer loop relative to monolithic meta-RL.

3. (Portfolios for data augmentation.) Construct a portfolio {pi_c}_{c in C} of policies/models, each specialized to a decomposability class c (a cluster of tasks sharing a decomposition type), and specify a procedure that, during adaptation to T*, selects elements of the portfolio to generate synthetic trajectories (data augmentation). Prove conditions under which this portfolio-driven augmentation strictly improves adaptation performance over uniform replay.

4. (Decomposability-informed curricula.) Design a curriculum, parameterized by abstract task types induced by decompositions, that produces warm-start initial parameters theta_0 for new tasks, and establish guarantees relating curriculum ordering (over decomposability classes) to the quality of theta_0 measured by expected post-adaptation return on T* ~ p(T).

Provide algorithms, formal definitions of "decomposition", "decomposability class", and "warm-start quality", and corresponding theoretical or empirical guarantees that jointly answer whether and how decompositions can be integrated into meta-RL along each of these four axes.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction in a survey on structure in deep reinforcement learning. No published work appears to have provided a unified framework integrating task decompositions into meta-RL along all four axes (abstraction, modular outer loop, portfolio-based augmentation, and decomposability-informed curricula). Related strands (hierarchical meta-RL, modular meta-learning, curriculum meta-RL) exist but do not collectively resolve the question.

paper_title: Open problems in deformations of Artinian algebras, Hilbert schemes and around
original_question: Call an irreducible component Z of the punctual Hilbert scheme Hilb_d(A^n, 0) smoothable if Z is contained in the smoothable component of Hilb_d(A^n). What can be said about these smoothable components, and for fixed (n, d) how many of them are there?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n)$ denote the Hilbert scheme parametrizing zero-dimensional subschemes of length $d$ in affine $n$-space $\mathbb{A}^n_k$. The smoothable component of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n)$ is the unique irreducible component containing the open locus of reduced subschemes (i.e. configurations of $d$ distinct points). Let $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0) \subset \mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n)$ be the closed punctual Hilbert scheme parametrizing length-$d$ subschemes supported entirely at the origin $0 \in \mathbb{A}^n$.

Call an irreducible component $Z$ of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$ smoothable if $Z$ is contained in the smoothable component of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n)$.

Describe the smoothable irreducible components $Z$ of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$: give structural properties (such as dimension, generic point, or classification). In particular, for fixed pair $(n,d)$, determine the number of smoothable irreducible components of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n,0)$.
status_search_result: The question is a general structural problem about smoothable components of punctual Hilbert schemes. Recent work (2024–2025) has determined irreducible components of $\mathrm{Hilb}_d(\mathbb{A}^n)$ for small $d$ (e.g. $d \le 10$ and Gorenstein cases up to $d \le 13$), but no general classification or count of smoothable punctual components for arbitrary $(n,d)$ is known. The problem remains open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How feasible are data-poisoning attacks by malicious human evaluators in reinforcement learning from human feedback pipelines for large language models, and what defenses can reliably prevent evaluators from implanting harmful backdoors or other undesired behaviors through a small number of strategically chosen feedback examples?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) pipeline used to fine-tune a large language model. In this pipeline:

1. A base language model produces pairs (or sets) of candidate responses to prompts drawn from some distribution.
2. A pool of human evaluators provides preference labels (rankings or pairwise choices) between candidate responses.
3. A reward model is trained on the collected preference data to predict human preferences.
4. The language model is fine-tuned by a policy-optimization algorithm (e.g., PPO) against this learned reward model.

Suppose a fraction ε of the evaluators are adversarial. Each adversarial evaluator may, for some chosen subset of their assigned comparisons, deviate from the intended labeling policy and instead submit preferences chosen to implant a targeted undesired behavior in the final fine-tuned model. A canonical attack is a backdoor attack: the adversary fixes a trigger token sequence τ and, whenever τ appears in a prompt, labels the more harmful of the two responses as preferred; otherwise the adversary labels honestly. The goal of the adversary is that the final RLHF-trained model, when prompted with any input containing τ, exhibits the targeted harmful behavior with high probability, while behaving normally on inputs not containing τ (so as to evade evaluation on a clean validation set).

Address the following:

(a) Quantify the feasibility of such attacks: as a function of the poisoning fraction ε (fraction of preference labels corrupted), model size, and the number of distinct adversarial evaluators, determine the minimum ε needed for a chosen trigger τ to reliably produce the targeted behavior in the fine-tuned policy with probability at least 1−δ on trigger-containing prompts, while degrading clean-prompt performance by at most some tolerance η.

(b) Design and prove guarantees for a defense mechanism — operating at the data-collection, reward-modeling, or policy-optimization stage — that provably (or empirically with rigorous evaluation) prevents an adversary controlling at most an ε-fraction of preference labels from implanting any such backdoor, in the sense that no choice of trigger τ allows the adversary to raise the probability of the targeted harmful behavior on τ-containing prompts by more than a small specified amount over the clean baseline.
category_tag: RLHF data poisoning and backdoor defenses
status_search_result: Subsequent work has demonstrated the feasibility of preference-data poisoning in RLHF (e.g., RankPoison/RLHFPoison shows malicious behavior with low poisoning rates, and "Universal Jailbreak Backdoors from Poisoned Human Feedback" shows that mislabeling roughly 5% of preference data can implant a universal trigger in models up to 13B parameters, though that work also found such backdoors comparatively difficult to install robustly). More recent attacks (e.g., GREAT, 2025) extend feasibility to emotion-aware triggers. However, no defense with rigorous guarantees that reliably prevents an adversarial fraction of evaluators from implanting backdoors has been established; the problem of provably robust RLHF against annotator poisoning remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How can reinforcement learning from human feedback achieve scalable oversight when human supervisors have limited time, attention, expertise, and bandwidth, especially in settings where the target systems may be difficult for humans to evaluate or may exceed human competence?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an interactive learning setting in which a target system $\pi$ (for instance, a large generative model) is trained to optimize a reward signal $r$ derived from feedback provided by a set of human supervisors $H$. Each supervisor in $H$ has bounded time, attention, expertise, and bandwidth, and is therefore able to evaluate only a limited subset of $\pi$'s outputs, with evaluations that may be noisy, inconsistent, or systematically biased—especially on tasks whose correctness or quality is hard for a human to verify, or on tasks where $\pi$'s competence exceeds that of any supervisor in $H$.

Formulate and design a training and feedback protocol (a "scalable oversight" scheme) that uses the limited human feedback from $H$, possibly augmented by AI-assisted evaluation, decomposition of tasks, debate, recursive critique, or verification mechanisms, such that the resulting trained system $\pi$ provably (or at least reliably) aligns with the intended preferences of $H$ even when:
(i) the cost of obtaining each human judgment is bounded;
(ii) individual human judgments on hard tasks may be inaccurate; and
(iii) $\pi$ may produce outputs that no human supervisor in $H$ can directly evaluate.

The problem is to determine whether and how such a protocol can exist, to characterize the conditions on $H$, on the task distribution, and on the auxiliary mechanisms under which alignment guarantees can be obtained, and to quantify the trade-offs between human-feedback budget, evaluation difficulty, and the achievable quality of oversight.
status_search_result: Scalable oversight remains an actively studied open problem as of 2025–2026. Recent works (e.g., recursive self-critiquing, debate with weak judges, and alignment surveys) propose partial approaches and empirical studies but do not provide a general solution; researchers across multiple labs continue to flag it as unresolved, particularly for AI systems that may surpass human evaluation ability.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How can practitioners collect human-feedback datasets for reinforcement learning from human feedback that are both representative of deployment-relevant behavior and genuinely helpful for learning, rather than being distorted by sampling bias, low-quality collection processes, or mismatches between training interactions and real deployment distributions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement learning setting in which an agent's policy is trained using a reward model fit to human preference feedback. Let D = {(x_i, y_i^0, y_i^1, p_i)}_{i=1}^N denote a dataset where each x_i is a prompt or state drawn from some sampling distribution Q over a context space X, each (y_i^0, y_i^1) is a pair of candidate responses or trajectories produced by a (possibly biased) generation procedure, and p_i ∈ {0,1} is a preference label provided by a human annotator drawn from a population A according to some sampling scheme. Let P_deploy denote the distribution over contexts and behaviors encountered when the trained policy is deployed, and let U denote a target notion of utility (e.g., aggregated population preferences under idealized conditions).

Devise a methodology — comprising (i) a procedure for choosing the context distribution Q, (ii) a procedure for sampling response pairs, (iii) a protocol for selecting and instructing annotators, and (iv) quality-control mechanisms — together with a theoretical guarantee that the resulting dataset D yields a learned reward model and policy whose performance under P_deploy with respect to U is provably close to optimal, despite the following obstacles that must be explicitly addressed and bounded:

1. Sampling bias in Q relative to P_deploy (distribution shift between training contexts and deployment contexts).
2. Bias in the response-pair generation procedure (e.g., responses drawn only from a fixed base model that does not cover deployment behaviors).
3. Low-quality, noisy, or adversarial labels p_i, including annotator inattention, miscalibration, and disagreement.
4. Mismatch between the annotator population A and the population whose utility U is meant to represent.

Formally, give explicit, verifiable conditions on Q, the pair-generation procedure, the annotator-sampling scheme, and the quality-control mechanism under which one can prove a finite-sample bound on the gap between the utility under U of the policy trained on D and the optimal achievable utility on P_deploy, and exhibit such a methodology that is implementable in practice.
status_search_result: Collecting human-feedback datasets that are simultaneously representative of deployment distributions and free from sampling/quality biases remains widely acknowledged as an open problem in the RLHF literature. Recent surveys and works on preference data quality, annotator disagreement, and distribution shift continue to identify this as unresolved, with only partial mitigations (e.g., active learning, annotator weighting, synthetic preferences) but no methodology with provable end-to-end guarantees.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: What is the right notion of diversity for human-feedback data in reinforcement learning from human feedback, how does data diversity relate to label efficiency and downstream alignment quality, and which concrete data-selection methods can reliably produce sufficiently diverse feedback datasets?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the setting of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), in which a language model or policy $\pi_\theta$ is fine-tuned using a dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)\}_{i=1}^N$ of human preference comparisons, where $x_i$ is a prompt and $y_i^+, y_i^-$ are two candidate responses with $y_i^+$ preferred over $y_i^-$ by a human annotator. A reward model $r_\phi$ is trained on $\mathcal{D}$ (for example by maximizing the Bradley–Terry log-likelihood), and the policy is then optimized to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x,\, y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}[r_\phi(x,y)] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})$ for some reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and regularization weight $\beta > 0$.

Address the following three interrelated problems regarding the composition of the dataset $\mathcal{D}$:

1. Diversity definition. Propose a formal definition of "diversity" $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$ of a preference dataset $\mathcal{D}$ that captures variation across prompts, responses, annotator populations, and elicited preference dimensions, and that is meaningful for predicting downstream alignment quality of the resulting policy $\pi_\theta$.

2. Diversity vs. label efficiency. Establish a quantitative relationship between $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$, the sample size $N$, and a measure of alignment quality $Q(\pi_\theta)$ (for example, expected reward under a held-out true preference distribution, or worst-group performance). In particular, give conditions under which increasing $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$ provably reduces the number of labeled comparisons needed to attain a target value of $Q$.

3. Diverse data selection. Provide a concrete, implementable algorithm (e.g., based on active learning, coreset selection, or clustering in a learned representation space) that, given a large pool of candidate prompts and response pairs, selects a subset $\mathcal{D}$ of bounded size with provably or empirically high $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$, and demonstrate that policies trained on the selected $\mathcal{D}$ achieve higher $Q(\pi_\theta)$ than policies trained on baseline (e.g., uniformly random) selections of the same size.
status_search_result: The question of how to define, measure, and ensure diversity of human-feedback datasets in RLHF, and how diversity trades off against label efficiency and alignment quality, remains an actively studied open problem. While recent work has explored active learning, coreset-style selection, and diversity-aware reward modeling for RLHF, no consensus definition of diversity nor a generally accepted selection method with provable label-efficiency guarantees has emerged.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: Which choices made during policy optimization are most influential for accurately evaluating a learned reward model in reinforcement learning from human feedback, including the choice of reinforcement-learning algorithm, policy architecture, compute budget, and other hyperparameters used when reward-model quality is measured indirectly through policy behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) setting. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a state space and $\mathcal{A}$ an action space. A learned reward model is a function $\hat{r}_\phi : \mathcal{S}\times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}$ trained from human preference data to approximate a (latent) ground-truth reward $r^\star$. To evaluate the quality of $\hat{r}_\phi$ indirectly, one fixes a policy-optimization procedure $\mathcal{O}$ specified by the tuple $(\mathrm{Alg}, \pi_\theta\text{-arch}, B, H)$, where $\mathrm{Alg}$ is a reinforcement-learning algorithm (e.g., PPO, A2C, REINFORCE, DPO-style off-policy methods), $\pi_\theta\text{-arch}$ is the policy architecture, $B$ is a compute/sample budget, and $H$ is a vector of remaining hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, KL-regularization coefficient, entropy bonus, clipping parameters, schedule, etc.). Applying $\mathcal{O}$ to $\hat{r}_\phi$ produces a policy $\pi_{\mathcal{O}(\hat{r}_\phi)}$, and the indirect quality score of the reward model is
$$ Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O}) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim \pi_{\mathcal{O}(\hat{r}_\phi)}}\bigl[r^\star(s,a)\bigr]. $$

Identify and rigorously characterize which components of $\mathcal{O}=(\mathrm{Alg}, \pi_\theta\text{-arch}, B, H)$ most strongly determine the faithfulness of $Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O})$ as a measurement of the intrinsic quality of $\hat{r}_\phi$. Concretely: provide a principled (theoretical or empirical) ranking, with justification, of the relative influence of the algorithm choice, the policy architecture, the compute budget, and the remaining hyperparameters on the agreement between $Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O})$ and a direct measure of reward-model quality (such as expected discrepancy from $r^\star$ under a reference distribution), and determine conditions on $\mathcal{O}$ under which indirect evaluation reliably reflects intrinsic reward-model quality.
status_search_result: The question is identified as an open problem in the RLHF literature. As of 2026, no comprehensive study definitively ranks the influence of RL algorithm, policy architecture, compute budget, and other hyperparameters on the reliability of indirect reward-model evaluation; several works have explored aspects (KL regularization, reward hacking, scaling laws) but a complete characterization remains lacking.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How can deep reinforcement learning reliably balance exploration and exploitation when used inside reinforcement learning from human feedback, particularly in high-dimensional or sparse-reward environments where the amount of exploration needed is hard to determine and strongly affects downstream policy quality and safety?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement learning setting in which an agent interacts with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, gamma), where the state space S and action space A are high-dimensional, the transition kernel P is unknown, and the reward function r is either (i) sparse (nonzero only on a small set of states/actions) or (ii) defined implicitly via a learned reward model r_hat: S x A -> R that has been fit from human preference comparisons over trajectories. The agent's policy pi_theta is represented by a deep neural network and is trained to maximize the expected discounted return E[sum_{t>=0} gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)] (or its surrogate using r_hat). 

Design and analyze an exploration strategy E (e.g., an exploration bonus, posterior-sampling scheme, intrinsic-motivation signal, or hybrid) coupled to a deep RL learning algorithm such that the following properties hold simultaneously:

1. Sample-efficiency guarantee: With high probability, after at most polynomially many environment interactions in relevant problem parameters (effective horizon, complexity of the function class representing pi_theta and r_hat, and a notion of intrinsic dimension of the MDP), the learned policy is epsilon-optimal with respect to the true (possibly latent) reward.

2. Calibration of exploration budget: Provide a principled, data-driven criterion that determines the amount of exploration needed, without requiring problem-specific hand tuning, and prove that this criterion adapts to both dense and sparse-reward regimes.

3. Safety/conservatism constraint: The exploration policy must satisfy a specified safety constraint, e.g., at every step the probability of entering a designated unsafe set U \subset S is bounded by a prescribed delta > 0, while still achieving the guarantee in (1).

4. Robustness to reward-model error: When the reward used for training is a learned r_hat with bounded error ||r_hat - r||_infty <= eta on the support of the data distribution, quantify how the suboptimality of the final policy degrades as a function of eta and of the exploration strategy E.

Provide either (a) an algorithm together with a proof that it satisfies (1)-(4) under stated assumptions on the function approximator and MDP, or (b) an impossibility result showing that no algorithm in a specified class can simultaneously satisfy (1)-(4).
status_search_result: Balancing exploration and exploitation in deep reinforcement learning, particularly under sparse rewards, high-dimensional state spaces, and learned (preference-based) reward models, is widely acknowledged as an open research problem. Surveys on exploration in deep RL (e.g., Amin et al. 2021, Yang et al. 2021, Ladosz et al. 2022) describe it as unresolved, and no general-purpose algorithm with provable sample-efficiency, calibrated exploration, safety, and robustness to reward-model error is currently known.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: For reinforcement learning from human feedback, what kinds of human feedback or combinations of feedback are best for learning human goals, how exactly do human biases degrade feedback quality, and how should evaluators be selected and trained so that human-computer interaction remains safe and reliable?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) setting in which an agent interacts with an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a (possibly latent) reward function is to be learned from feedback provided by human evaluators. Feedback may take various forms, including but not limited to: scalar ratings of trajectories or actions, pairwise or k-wise preference comparisons between trajectories, demonstrations, corrections, natural-language critiques, and constraints or rules. Human evaluators are modeled as noisy, possibly biased agents whose responses deviate from an idealized rational utility-maximizing labeler according to systematic cognitive and motivational biases (e.g., myopia, confirmation bias, sycophancy bias toward the agent, anchoring, framing effects, and disagreement among annotators).

Address the following three sub-questions:

(a) Feedback modality. Determine which single form of human feedback, or which combination of feedback modalities (possibly weighted or used at different stages of training), yields provably or empirically optimal sample efficiency and fidelity in recovering the evaluators' underlying goals. Provide a formal criterion (e.g., expected regret with respect to the true reward, KL distance between learned and true reward distributions, or identifiability conditions) under which optimality is measured.

(b) Bias-induced degradation. Give a quantitative model of how specific human biases distort the mapping from underlying preferences to observed feedback, and characterize—as a function of the type and magnitude of bias—the resulting degradation in the learned reward model and in downstream policy performance. In particular, identify conditions under which biased feedback still allows consistent recovery of the true reward (up to equivalence), and conditions under which it provably does not.

(c) Evaluator selection and training. Specify a procedure for selecting and training human evaluators (covering recruitment criteria, calibration tasks, training protocols, and ongoing quality assurance) such that the aggregate feedback signal is sufficient to guarantee, with high probability, that the resulting trained agent satisfies stated safety and reliability properties when deployed in human-computer interaction.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research agenda in RLHF rather than a single formally answered theorem. Subsequent surveys and follow-up work (2023–2026) continue to highlight feedback-type comparison, bias modeling, and annotator selection as unresolved problems, with partial progress on richer feedback (e.g., language critiques, fine-grained preferences) and on modeling annotator noise/bias, but no comprehensive solution.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: Is the way reinforcement learning from human feedback aggregates preferences across multiple humans normatively acceptable for societies whose members disagree about values, or do different aggregation rules systematically privilege majority preferences at the expense of minority viewpoints in ways that make the alignment target socially unacceptable?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of $n$ humans, each with a preference relation $\succ_i$ over a set $\mathcal{X}$ of possible AI behaviors (or trajectories). A preference aggregation procedure is a map $F$ that takes the tuple $(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n)$ — typically observed only through finitely many pairwise comparisons — and produces a scalar reward function $r : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$, whose induced ordering $x \succ_F y \iff r(x) > r(y)$ serves as the alignment target. The standard reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) procedure fits $r$ by maximum likelihood under a Bradley–Terry model on pooled pairwise comparisons drawn (uniformly or otherwise) from the population.

(a) Formulate, within the framework of social choice theory, precise normative axioms (e.g., Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, anonymity, non-dictatorship, Condorcet consistency, majority consistency, and proportional representation of minority subgroups) that an aggregation procedure $F$ used to define an AI alignment target ought to satisfy when the population members disagree about values.

(b) Determine whether the RLHF aggregation rule (Bradley–Terry MLE on pooled pairwise preferences) satisfies these axioms. In particular, characterize the conditions on the population preference profile under which RLHF is or is not Condorcet-consistent, majority-consistent, and proportionally representative, and identify cases in which it systematically privileges majority preferences at the expense of coherent minority viewpoints.

(c) Either exhibit an aggregation rule $F^\ast$ that is normatively acceptable in the above sense for value-pluralistic populations, or prove an impossibility theorem showing that no such rule exists within the RLHF reward-modeling framework.
category_tag: Social choice theory in AI alignment
status_search_result: Recent work has begun to formally analyze RLHF through social choice theory. It has been shown that RLHF reward modeling implicitly performs an aggregation resembling Borda count and generally fails axioms such as Condorcet consistency, majority consistency, and pairwise majority consistency, though it does satisfy them under mild empirically plausible assumptions on preference profiles. Classical Arrow-type impossibility results apply, and follow-up frameworks (e.g., population-proportional alignment) show neither RLHF nor NLHF achieves proportional representation of minority viewpoints. A complete normatively acceptable aggregation rule remains an open research program.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: When reinforcement learning from human feedback is modeled as an assistance game between a human and an agent, what consistency and convergence guarantees can be established, how do different patterns of evaluator error affect learning, and how do different rates of requesting feedback change the quality of the resulting alignment?
self_contained_problem:
Model reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as a two-player assistance game between a human H and an agent A defined as follows. There is a state space S, an agent action space A_A, and a (possibly trivial) human action space A_H. The human has a latent reward parameter θ ∈ Θ drawn from a known prior P(θ). The joint dynamics are governed by a transition kernel T(s' | s, a_A, a_H). The agent does not observe θ; instead, at selected query times t ∈ Q ⊆ ℕ, the agent receives a feedback signal F_t from the human, where F_t is a (possibly noisy) evaluative response to a trajectory segment or pair of segments under a feedback model F_t ~ p(· | trajectory, θ, ε), with ε denoting an evaluator-error process. The agent's goal is to maximize E[Σ_t γ^t r_θ(s_t, a_A,t)] where r_θ is the true reward induced by θ.

Establish the following:

(a) Consistency and convergence. Give conditions on the prior P(θ), the feedback model p(F | ·, θ, ε), the query schedule Q, and the agent's learning algorithm under which the agent's posterior over θ (equivalently, over the optimal policy) converges almost surely to a point mass on the true θ, and under which the agent's policy converges to a θ-optimal policy. State and prove the sharpest available rate of convergence in terms of the number of feedback queries N = |Q ∩ [0,T]|.

(b) Effect of evaluator-error patterns. For a family of evaluator-error models {ε_k}—including independent symmetric noise, systematic bias, miscalibration, myopic/short-horizon evaluation, and adversarial corruption of a bounded fraction—quantify how each pattern alters identifiability of θ and the asymptotic suboptimality of the learned policy. In particular, characterize which error patterns preserve consistency, which induce bounded bias, and which produce unbounded suboptimality.

(c) Effect of feedback rate. Let ρ ∈ (0,1] denote the long-run rate of feedback queries per environment step (or, more generally, a query-scheduling policy). Determine how the alignment quality—measured by expected regret relative to the θ-optimal policy—scales with ρ, and exhibit (if possible) a tight trade-off curve between ρ and asymptotic regret, together with an optimal adaptive query schedule.

Provide formal theorems with proofs, or counterexamples demonstrating that no such guarantees hold under the stated assumptions.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction posed as a fundamental limitation/open problem in the RLHF literature. While partial results exist on cooperative inverse reinforcement learning / assistance games (Hadfield-Menell et al.) and on convergence of preference-based RL under specific noise models (e.g., Bradley–Terry assumptions), no comprehensive answer covering general evaluator-error patterns and arbitrary feedback rates is established. The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How does the pretrained model, viewed as a prior, influence the final behavior produced by reinforcement learning from human feedback, and can alternative target distributions or inference procedures improve over the standard Boltzmann-distribution and KL-regularized reinforcement-learning formulation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following Bayesian formulation of fine-tuning a generative language model from human preference feedback. Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote a space of prompts and $\mathcal{Y}$ a space of responses. A pretrained reference policy $\pi_0(y\mid x)$ on $\mathcal{Y}$ given $x\in\mathcal{X}$ plays the role of a prior. A scalar reward model $r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$ is learned from human comparison data. The standard reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) objective seeks a policy $\pi$ maximizing
$$ J(\pi) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,\,y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[r(x,y)\bigr] \;-\; \beta\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_0(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\bigr],\qquad \beta>0, $$
whose unique maximizer is the Boltzmann (Gibbs) posterior
$$ \pi^\star(y\mid x) \;\propto\; \pi_0(y\mid x)\,\exp\!\bigl(r(x,y)/\beta\bigr). $$
Address the following:

(a) Characterize, quantitatively, how the choice of prior $\pi_0$ influences $\pi^\star$ and any policy obtained by approximate optimization of $J$. In particular, derive bounds (e.g.\ in total variation, KL, or expected reward) that isolate the contribution of $\pi_0$ to properties of the resulting policy such as diversity, calibration of distributional preferences, and tail behavior.

(b) Propose alternative target distributions $\pi^\dagger$ (i.e., replacements for the Boltzmann form $\pi_0 \exp(r/\beta)/Z$) or alternative inference procedures that demonstrably improve on the Boltzmann/KL-regularized formulation with respect to a stated criterion — for example, faithfulness to a population distribution of human preferences, robustness to reward misspecification, or avoidance of mode collapse — and prove that the proposal strictly dominates the Boltzmann target on that criterion under explicit assumptions on $\pi_0$, $r$, and the preference-generating process.
status_search_result: The question is a broadly stated research direction about Bayesian interpretations of RLHF and possible alternatives to the KL-regularized Boltzmann target. While many works (e.g., on f-divergence regularization, direct preference optimization variants, distributional preference learning, and Bayesian RLHF) explore pieces of this question, no definitive answer characterizing prior influence or strictly dominating alternative targets has been established. The problem is considered open in the RLHF research literature.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: What are the worst-case behaviors of systems trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback, especially under adversarial attacks such as jailbreaks and prompt injection, and which theoretical, decision-theoretic, adversarial, or evaluation frameworks can characterize those worst-case failures well enough to guide safer system design?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a language-generation policy $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained base policy $\pi_0$ via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The training pipeline consists of: (i) collecting human preference comparisons over pairs of outputs; (ii) fitting a reward model $r_\phi(x,y)$ (e.g., via a Bradley–Terry likelihood) to those preferences; and (iii) optimizing $\pi_\theta$ to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[r_\phi(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_0(\cdot\mid x))$ for some regularization weight $\beta>0$ and prompt distribution $\mathcal{D}$.

Let $H:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$ denote an (unknown) true human utility function and let $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ be a class of "bad" or unsafe outcomes. Define the worst-case harm of $\pi_\theta$ with respect to an adversarial prompt transformation class $\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., jailbreak prefixes, prompt-injection suffixes, paraphrastic attacks) as
$$W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) \;=\; \sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\; \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid a(x))}\bigl[(a(x),y)\in\mathcal{B}\bigr].$$

The problem is to develop a rigorous theoretical framework — drawing from decision theory, adversarial robustness, distributionally robust optimization, or formal evaluation methodology — that characterizes $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ in terms of properties of the preference data, the reward model $r_\phi$, the regularization $\beta$, and the base policy $\pi_0$. Concretely, one seeks:

1. Quantitative upper and lower bounds on $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ as a function of training-time quantities (sample size, preference noise, reward-model generalization error, KL budget, expressivity of $\mathcal{A}$).
2. Conditions on the RLHF pipeline under which average-case improvement in $\mathbb{E}[H]$ is compatible with non-degradation (or provable improvement) of worst-case behavior, i.e., $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) \le W(\pi_0;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$.
3. An evaluation framework (test-set construction, adversarial red-teaming protocol, or formal verification procedure) whose output provably bounds $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ with high probability.

Determine such a framework and the corresponding theorems, or prove impossibility results showing fundamental limits on how tightly $W$ can be controlled by any RLHF-style procedure.
status_search_result: Worst-case behavior of RLHF-trained systems under adversarial attacks such as jailbreaks and prompt injection remains an active open research area as of 2026. While many empirical attack and defense papers have appeared, no widely accepted theoretical framework provably bounds worst-case post-RLHF harm, and jailbreaks continue to succeed against state-of-the-art aligned models.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: Can AI-generated feedback safely and reliably augment or replace some human feedback in reinforcement learning from human feedback systems, given human-AI disagreement rates, correlated machine failure modes, and the bootstrapping problem that the feedback-providing AI itself must already be aligned?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement learning system in which an agent is trained against a learned reward model r_phi: S x A -> R fit to preference data D = {(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)}, where each preference label indicates that output y_i^+ is preferred to y_i^- in context x_i. Classically, the labels are produced by human annotators H. In an AI-assisted variant, some fraction lambda in [0,1] of the labels are produced instead by a feedback-providing AI model F (or by a mixture policy that queries F and H). Assume:

1. There is a disagreement rate delta(F, H) > 0 between F and H on a representative distribution of comparison queries.
2. The errors of F across queries are not independent: there exist correlated failure modes, i.e. a set E of contexts on which F systematically deviates from H in the same direction.
3. The alignment of F itself is defined only relative to some prior aligned feedback source, so guaranteeing F's alignment requires an already-aligned feedback provider (the bootstrapping condition).

Question: Determine conditions on (F, H, lambda, delta, E, and the training procedure) under which augmenting or partially replacing human feedback by F-generated feedback provably preserves a chosen alignment criterion C on the resulting trained policy pi — for example, that with high probability the expected divergence between pi and a target human-aligned policy pi_H* remains bounded by a prescribed epsilon. Equivalently, identify whether any such conditions can be satisfied without circularly assuming that F already satisfies C, and characterize the achievable tradeoff curve between lambda (amount of AI feedback used) and the worst-case alignment loss induced by correlated failure modes.
status_search_result: The viability of AI-generated feedback (e.g., RLAIF, constitutional AI, debate, scalable oversight) as a safe substitute for human feedback remains an active open research area as of 2026. Empirical work (RLAIF, constitutional AI) shows partial substitution can match RLHF on some tasks, but no formal guarantees address correlated failure modes or the bootstrapping problem, which is widely acknowledged as unresolved in alignment literature.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: What practical advantages does fine-grained feedback provide in reinforcement learning from human feedback, what costs does it impose on evaluators, and under what conditions is it feasible enough to justify broader adoption in place of coarser feedback signals such as pairwise preferences?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the setting of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), in which a policy $\pi_\theta$ over an action/output space is trained to maximize an expected reward $r_\phi$, where $r_\phi$ is itself learned from human-provided feedback on policy outputs. Standard practice uses coarse feedback signals, most commonly pairwise preference comparisons: given two outputs $(y_1, y_2)$ from a prompt $x$, an evaluator returns a single bit indicating which is preferred, and $r_\phi$ is fit under a Bradley–Terry-style model $P(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma(r_\phi(x,y_1) - r_\phi(x,y_2))$. Define fine-grained feedback as any feedback protocol producing strictly more information per evaluation than a single pairwise preference, including (a) per-aspect scalar or categorical ratings along multiple axes (e.g. helpfulness, factuality, harmlessness), (b) span-level annotations identifying which substrings of an output are problematic and why, (c) edits or rewrites, and (d) feedback conditioned on rubric items.

Address the following:

1. Provide a precise characterization of the practical advantages of fine-grained feedback over pairwise preferences for RLHF, in terms of (i) sample complexity of reward learning, (ii) bias and identifiability properties of the learned reward $r_\phi$, (iii) downstream policy performance after RL optimization against $r_\phi$, and (iv) ability to mitigate known failure modes such as reward hacking and underspecification.

2. Quantify the costs imposed on human evaluators, including time per annotation, cognitive load, inter-annotator agreement, and required expertise, as a function of the granularity and dimensionality of the feedback protocol.

3. Determine sufficient conditions (on task domain, evaluator expertise, annotation budget, model capability, and statistical structure of the reward) under which the gains from fine-grained feedback strictly dominate the additional annotation cost, so that fine-grained feedback should replace pairwise preferences as the default feedback signal.
status_search_result: This is an open research direction. Fine-grained feedback protocols (e.g., FineGrainedRLHF, per-aspect rewards, span-level critiques, process reward models) have been studied in works such as Wu et al. (2023) "Fine-Grained Human Feedback Gives Better Rewards for Language Model Training" and subsequent work on process reward models and rubric-based RLHF, showing empirical benefits in specific settings. However, no general characterization of when fine-grained feedback strictly dominates pairwise preferences—accounting for annotation cost—has been established, and the question remains an active open problem in the RLHF literature.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How can reward-learning systems learn effectively from suboptimal human demonstrations when demonstrations are expensive to obtain, depend on evaluator expertise, and may still contain enough useful structure to support better alignment than standard feedback-only pipelines?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a sequential decision-making setting modeled as a Markov decision process $M = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r^\star, \gamma)$ with unknown true reward $r^\star : \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}$. A learner has access to two sources of supervision provided by human evaluators of bounded and possibly heterogeneous expertise:

1. A small set of demonstrations $\mathcal{D} = \{\tau_i\}_{i=1}^n$, where each trajectory $\tau_i$ is generated by a (possibly different) behavior policy $\pi_i$ that is suboptimal with respect to $r^\star$, i.e., $J(\pi_i) := \mathbb{E}_{\pi_i}\!\left[\sum_t \gamma^t r^\star(s_t,a_t)\right] < \max_\pi J(\pi)$, with unknown and varying suboptimality gaps $\Delta_i = J(\pi^\star) - J(\pi_i)$.
2. A set of comparison or preference labels $\mathcal{P} = \{(\sigma_j^0, \sigma_j^1, y_j)\}_{j=1}^m$ over trajectory segments, generated according to a (possibly noisy) preference model such as Bradley–Terry with parameter $r^\star$.

Demonstrations are assumed to be substantially more expensive to obtain than preference labels (i.e., $n \ll m$ in typical regimes), but the trajectories in $\mathcal{D}$ are presumed to contain structural information about $r^\star$ beyond what is encoded in the preference labels alone.

Design a reward-learning procedure that produces $\hat r$ (and an induced policy $\hat\pi$) with the following properties, and prove guarantees for it:

(a) $\hat r$ is consistent with $r^\star$ in a quantifiable sense (e.g., bounded regret $J(\pi^\star) - J(\hat\pi)$ under $r^\star$) even when every demonstrator is strictly suboptimal and the suboptimality gaps $\Delta_i$ are unknown.

(b) The procedure provably outperforms — in terms of sample complexity in $m$, regret, or worst-case alignment error — any procedure that uses only the preference data $\mathcal{P}$ and ignores $\mathcal{D}$, under explicit assumptions on the structure of demonstrator suboptimality (for example, monotonic improvement, ranked demonstrators, or noisy-rational behavior with bounded rationality).

(c) The procedure degrades gracefully (no worse than the preference-only baseline up to constants) when the demonstrations are arbitrarily bad or adversarial.

State precise assumptions on the demonstrator model, the preference noise model, the function class for $\hat r$, and the coverage/realizability conditions under which (a)–(c) hold, and exhibit either matching lower bounds or empirical evidence that the assumptions are necessary.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and works through 2025 (e.g., surveys of RLHF and reward modeling, and methods such as T-REX/D-REX style extrapolation beyond demonstrator performance and targeted-human-feedback approaches like RLTHF) study aspects of this question, but no general procedure with provable guarantees of the form (a)–(c) under realistic suboptimal-demonstrator models is established. The problem is widely treated as an open research direction.

paper_title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
original_question: How should the risks, failure modes, and safety-relevant details of reinforcement learning from human feedback systems be documented for governance and auditing purposes so that external reviewers can assess safety meaningfully without unnecessarily revealing capability-enabling details?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipeline, in which a base model is fine-tuned using a learned reward model trained on human preference comparisons and then optimized via a reinforcement learning algorithm. Such pipelines are known to exhibit a variety of risks and failure modes, including (but not limited to): misspecification or reward hacking of the learned reward model, distributional shift between training-time and deployment-time queries, biases or inconsistencies among human labelers, sycophancy and deceptive behavior of the resulting policy, mode collapse, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and emergent capability gains that may pose safety concerns. Design a documentation framework (i.e., a structured specification of what information system developers should record and disclose) for RLHF systems that satisfies all of the following requirements simultaneously:

1. Coverage. The framework enumerates the principal categories of safety-relevant information about an RLHF system, including: data provenance and demographics of human annotators, the labeling protocol and instructions, the reward-model architecture and evaluation, the RL optimization procedure and KL-regularization choices, identified failure modes and red-teaming results, post-deployment monitoring procedures, and known residual risks.

2. Auditability. Given a completed instance of the documentation, an external reviewer (without internal access to model weights or proprietary training data) can in principle make a meaningful, reasoned assessment of the system's safety properties along each category above.

3. Capability non-disclosure. The framework does not require disclosing details whose release would substantially lower the cost or difficulty of replicating or amplifying dangerous capabilities of the underlying model (for example, specific training hyperparameters, exact dataset compositions, or architectural details that primarily convey capability rather than safety information).

4. Tiered access (optional). The framework may specify multiple disclosure tiers, with more sensitive information accessible only to vetted auditors under appropriate confidentiality controls, provided that the public tier still satisfies requirement (2).

Provide such a framework, together with a justification that it satisfies requirements (1)–(3), or prove that no framework can simultaneously satisfy (2) and (3) in a nontrivial sense.
status_search_result: The documentation of RLHF risks for governance and audit remains an active area of work in AI governance, with ongoing proposals (e.g., model cards, system cards, evaluation reports, structured access frameworks) but no agreed-upon standard that fully balances auditability against capability non-disclosure. No definitive resolution has been published.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can large language models be used reliably for higher-level requirements engineering and software design tasks, especially to recover and maintain traceability links between natural-language requirements and downstream engineering artefacts such as code and tests, given current practitioner reluctance to rely on LLMs for design-level goals?
self_contained_problem: Develop a methodology, with associated empirical or theoretical guarantees, for using large language models (LLMs) reliably in higher-level requirements engineering and software design tasks. Concretely, given a corpus of natural-language requirements R = {r_1, ..., r_m} and a set of downstream engineering artefacts A = {a_1, ..., a_n} (such as source-code units, test cases, design documents, and architectural descriptions), design an LLM-based procedure that (i) recovers a traceability relation T ⊆ R × A indicating which requirement is realized, tested, or affected by which artefact, (ii) maintains T as R and A evolve over time, and (iii) produces design-level outputs (e.g., specifications, architectural decisions, refinements of requirements) whose reliability can be evaluated and trusted by practising engineers. Provide: (a) a precise formulation of the traceability recovery and maintenance task as an inference problem over (R, A); (b) an LLM-based algorithm to solve it; (c) measurable criteria (precision, recall, stability under change, calibration of confidence) under which the algorithm's outputs are demonstrably reliable; and (d) evidence that the approach addresses the reluctance of practitioners to delegate higher-level design goals to LLMs.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction in LLM-based software engineering. Recent surveys and empirical studies (2023–2025) continue to identify requirements engineering, design, and traceability link recovery as underexplored areas where LLMs show promise but lack reliability guarantees; no comprehensive solution has been reported.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLM-based code generation and completion systems be coupled with automated testing and execution-grounded ReAct-style feedback so that generated code can be assessed reliably, hallucinated responses can be filtered, and runtime evidence can guide prompt refinement and output selection?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a code-generation system based on a large language model (LLM) that, given a natural-language specification s, produces one or more candidate programs p_1, ..., p_k. Suppose one has access to (i) an automated test-generation procedure T that, from s and/or from a candidate program p, produces a finite set of executable test cases, (ii) an execution oracle E that runs a program on a test case and returns observable outputs (pass/fail, exceptions, runtime traces), and (iii) a feedback-driven prompting mechanism in the ReAct style, where the LLM alternates between reasoning steps and action steps, the actions being calls to T and E whose results are appended to the prompt context. Design and formally analyze an end-to-end framework that integrates these components so that:

1. (Reliable assessment) For each candidate p_i, the framework produces a quantitative correctness score sigma(p_i, s) derived from execution evidence on automatically generated tests, together with a guarantee bounding the probability that p_i is accepted while failing the (possibly unknown) ground-truth specification.

2. (Hallucination filtering) The framework defines a decision rule that rejects candidates whose execution evidence is inconsistent with the specification or with invariants inferred from s, and one proves that under stated assumptions on T and E the rule eliminates a controlled fraction of hallucinated outputs.

3. (Prompt refinement) Using the runtime evidence collected during ReAct iterations, the framework updates the prompt (or the candidate set) via an explicit selection/refinement operator, and one shows that the expected correctness score is non-decreasing across iterations under stated regularity conditions.

4. (Output selection) Given the final pool of candidates and their execution evidence, the framework specifies a selection function returning a single program p* with provable optimality or near-optimality properties relative to sigma.

Provide the construction of such a framework, state precise assumptions on the LLM, the test generator T, and the oracle E under which the above guarantees hold, and either prove the guarantees or exhibit fundamental obstructions.
category_tag: LLM code generation with execution feedback
status_search_result: The question is an open research direction concerning the integration of automated testing, execution-grounded ReAct-style feedback, and LLM code generation. Numerous recent works (e.g., Self-Debug, CodeT, LATS, Reflexion, AgentCoder) address parts of the problem—test-based filtering, iterative self-repair, and execution feedback—but no unified framework provides the kind of formal guarantees described, and the integration of automated testing with code generation is widely cited as an open problem.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can pretrained large language models be fine-tuned efficiently so that they perform better for a particular programming language, codebase, or application domain without requiring the prohibitive computational cost of training a model from scratch?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M_	heta$ denote a large pretrained autoregressive language model with parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^N$ (with $N$ very large), trained on a broad corpus of source code and natural language. For a target domain $\mathcal{D}$ (for example, a specific programming language, a particular codebase, or an application domain), let $\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{D}$ denote a downstream task (such as code completion, bug fixing, or program synthesis) equipped with a performance measure $P_\mathcal{D}(M)$ and a relatively small dataset $S_\mathcal{D}$ of examples drawn from $\mathcal{D}$.

Develop and analyze a procedure $\mathcal{A}$ that, given $M_	heta$, $\mathcal{D}$, and $S_\mathcal{D}$, produces an adapted model $M_{	heta'} = \mathcal{A}(M_	heta, S_\mathcal{D})$ satisfying the following:

1. Improved domain performance: $P_\mathcal{D}(M_{	heta'}) > P_\mathcal{D}(M_	heta)$ by a quantifiable margin.
2. Computational efficiency: the total compute cost $C(\mathcal{A})$ used to obtain $M_{	heta'}$ satisfies $C(\mathcal{A}) \ll C_{	ext{scratch}}$, where $C_{	ext{scratch}}$ is the cost of training a model of comparable capability from random initialization on $\mathcal{D}$. In particular, either the number of updated parameters or the number of training tokens should be sublinear in $N$ or in the size of the original pretraining corpus.
3. Retention: catastrophic degradation on tasks outside $\mathcal{D}$ should be bounded.

Provide an explicit construction of such an adaptation procedure $\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., based on transfer learning, low-rank updates, adapter modules, prompt tuning, or related techniques), together with theoretical or empirical guarantees on the trade-off between the improvement $P_\mathcal{D}(M_{	heta'}) - P_\mathcal{D}(M_	heta)$, the compute cost $C(\mathcal{A})$, and the retention loss on out-of-domain tasks.
status_search_result: This is an active and ongoing research area. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (LoRA, adapters, prefix/prompt tuning, QLoRA) have been developed and are widely applied to code LLMs, yielding partial solutions, but no general optimal procedure or rigorous theory characterizing the trade-offs has been established. The open problem of efficient domain/codebase-specific adaptation remains active in current literature.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should explanation engineering for LLM-based software engineering artefacts be developed and evaluated, so that the explanations accompanying generated code or other artefacts become trustworthy, useful, and potentially preferable even when the underlying artefact is not globally optimal?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a setting in which a large language model (LLM) is used to generate software-engineering artefacts (for example, source code, patches, test cases, specifications, or commit messages) together with natural-language explanations that justify or describe those artefacts. Formally, let an artefact-generation process be a function f that, given a prompt p, produces a pair (a, e) where a is an artefact and e is an explanation of a. Let Q(a) denote a quality measure on artefacts (e.g., correctness, efficiency, maintainability) and let U(e, a, c) denote a measure of the usefulness of the explanation e for artefact a to a human consumer in context c (covering trust, comprehension, debuggability, and actionability).

Develop a principled methodology — call it "explanation engineering" — for the design, generation, and evaluation of such explanations e, addressing in particular the following sub-problems:

1. Define rigorous criteria and quantitative metrics for when an explanation e of an artefact a is "trustworthy" (faithful to the actual behaviour or derivation of a), "useful" (improves user task performance or decision-making by some measurable amount), and "preferable" (a user, given (a, e), achieves better outcomes than with a alone, even when Q(a) is strictly below the global optimum over the artefact space).

2. Specify procedures, analogous to prompt-engineering procedures that optimise the input to the LLM, that systematically optimise the explanation component e of the output, including how to detect and prevent explanations that are plausible but unfaithful to a.

3. Establish evaluation protocols — including benchmarks, ground-truth construction, and human-in-the-loop study designs — under which it can be empirically demonstrated that, for some non-trivial class of tasks, there exist artefacts a with Q(a) not maximal such that (a, e) is preferred (with statistical significance) over (a*, e*) where a* is closer to optimal but e* is weaker.

Provide a framework that answers (1)–(3) and, in particular, exhibit conditions under which an explanation-augmented but sub-optimal artefact is provably or empirically preferable to a more optimal artefact with an inferior explanation.
status_search_result: Explanation engineering for LLM-generated software-engineering artefacts is an emerging open research direction. There are active lines of work on faithfulness of LLM rationales, code explanation, and human-centred evaluation, but no agreed-upon methodology or evaluation framework that satisfies the trustworthiness/usefulness/preferability criteria described. The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should prompts for LLM-based software test generation be engineered so that the resulting tests reduce flakiness, reveal likely faults using historical fault data, strike the right balance between mocks and integration testing, construct realistic inputs and mock objects, cover corner cases, and focus on behavior that is prevalent in production?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an automated software test generation system in which a large language model (LLM) is given a natural-language and/or code-based prompt and produces unit and/or integration tests for a target software system. A test suite is evaluated along the following criteria: (i) flakiness, defined as the probability that a test produces inconsistent pass/fail outcomes across repeated executions in a fixed environment; (ii) fault-revealing power, measured by the proportion of injected or historically observed faults that the suite detects, where a historical fault dataset H = {(c_i, f_i)} of past code changes c_i and associated bug reports f_i is available; (iii) the mocking/integration trade-off, defined as the ratio of mocked dependencies to real dependencies invoked by the tests, balanced against execution cost and realism; (iv) realism of test inputs and mock objects, measured by the statistical similarity (e.g., distributional distance) between generated inputs and inputs observed in production traces; (v) corner-case coverage, measured by coverage of boundary partitions of input domains and rarely executed branches; and (vi) production-behavior focus, measured by the weighted coverage of code regions weighted by their execution frequency in production telemetry.

Develop a principled methodology for designing prompts P (possibly parameterized templates that may incorporate H, production traces, and code context) such that the resulting LLM-generated test suite simultaneously: minimizes expected flakiness; maximizes the expected fraction of faults from H that would be detected; achieves a Pareto-optimal mocking-to-integration ratio with respect to realism and cost; produces inputs and mock objects whose distribution matches production usage; maximizes corner-case coverage; and concentrates coverage on production-prevalent behaviors. Specifically, formulate quantitative objective functions for each of the six criteria above, characterize prompt-engineering strategies (template structure, contextual information to include, retrieval-augmented examples, decoding parameters) that provably or empirically optimize a chosen scalarization or Pareto front of these objectives, and establish whether such prompts can be constructed in a model-agnostic way.
status_search_result: The problem of how to engineer prompts for LLM-based test generation that jointly optimize flakiness reduction, fault-revealing power, mock/integration balance, input realism, corner-case coverage, and production-prevalent behavior remains an open research direction. While many recent works (e.g., ChatUniTest, CodaMosa, TestPilot, follow-ups in 2024–2025) study individual aspects such as coverage or fault detection from LLM-generated tests, no comprehensive prompt-engineering methodology addressing all of the above criteria has been established.

Recent works (e.g., on LLM-based assertion generation such as TOGA, ChatTester, and follow-ups in 2024–2025) make partial progress on generating additional assertions and mutating existing tests, but no widely accepted general solution has emerged that systematically leverages historical faults and existing suites for principled augmentation.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: When an LLM generates a software test, how can the system automatically determine whether a passing test is a meaningful regression test or merely coincidentally correct, whether a failing test has found a real bug or contains a wrong assertion, and how can raw execution outcomes be filtered into a trustworthy test signal before they are shown to developers?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an automated software testing pipeline in which a large language model (LLM) produces unit tests for a given program under test. Each generated test, when executed against the current release of the program, yields one of two raw outcomes: pass or fail. A passing outcome may indicate either (a) a meaningful regression test that genuinely characterizes intended behavior, or (b) a coincidentally correct test whose assertions happen to hold without capturing intended semantics. A failing outcome may indicate either (a) the discovery of a real bug in the program, or (b) a test containing an incorrect assertion or invalid setup. Design an algorithmic framework that, given a generated test t, the program under test P, and possibly auxiliary artifacts (specifications, documentation, prior tests, execution traces, mutation results, etc.), automatically:

1. Classifies each passing test as either a meaningful regression test or coincidentally correct.
2. Classifies each failing test as either having found a real bug in P or containing a wrong/invalid assertion.
3. Produces a calibrated confidence score together with self-checks for correctness, consistency, and robustness of the generated test.
4. Filters and augments the raw pass/fail execution outcomes into a trustworthy aggregated "test signal" that is presented to a human developer, with provable or empirically validated guarantees on precision and recall of the classifications above.

Formally state the inputs, outputs, evaluation metrics (e.g., false-positive/false-negative rates of bug discovery and of regression validity), and devise a method achieving non-trivial improvement over the baseline of forwarding raw pass/fail outcomes to the developer.
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) on LLM-based test generation (e.g., TestPilot, ChatTester, CodaMosa follow-ups, and oracle-assessment studies) addresses parts of this question by using mutation testing, differential testing, and LLM self-consistency to filter generated tests, but no general framework reliably distinguishes coincidentally correct passing tests from meaningful regression tests, nor wrong-assertion failures from real bug discoveries, with calibrated confidence. The problem of producing a trustworthy filtered test signal remains an active open research challenge.
