paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLM-based performance-improvement techniques automatically discover behavior-preserving or sufficiently faithful improvements not only for execution time but also for power consumption, memory footprint, and explicit multi-objective tradeoffs among non-functional properties?
self_contained_problem:
Let P denote a program written in some fixed programming language, equipped with a specification S consisting of a set of input-output behaviors (or, more generally, a semantic equivalence relation ≈ on programs that captures "behavior preservation up to acceptable faithfulness"). Let Q = (q_1, ..., q_k) be a vector of non-functional quality measures, where each q_i: Programs → ℝ assigns to a program a measurable cost such as:
 • q_1(P) = expected execution time on a given workload distribution,
 • q_2(P) = expected energy / power consumption on a target hardware platform,
 • q_3(P) = peak or average memory footprint,
 • and possibly further non-functional attributes.

A program P' is called an admissible improvement of P with respect to a subset I ⊆ {1, ..., k} of objectives if P' ≈ P (behavior-preserving or sufficiently faithful) and q_i(P') ≤ q_i(P) for every i ∈ I, with strict inequality for at least one i ∈ I. In the multi-objective setting, one seeks Pareto-optimal admissible improvements with respect to Q.

Design a procedure A that uses a large language model (LLM) as a generative component and, given as input the program P together with the specification S, the measurement procedures for Q, and a (possibly weighted) target objective subset I, automatically produces a set of candidate programs {P'_1, P'_2, ...} such that:

(a) Each P'_j is verified, with high confidence, to satisfy P'_j ≈ P (i.e., the procedure incorporates a soundness check enforcing behavior preservation or a quantified bound on semantic deviation);
(b) The output set approximates the Pareto frontier of (q_i)_{i∈I} over the space of admissible improvements;
(c) The procedure generalizes beyond execution time alone to power consumption, memory footprint, and explicit trade-offs among multiple non-functional properties.

Provide such an algorithm A, together with theoretical or empirical guarantees on its soundness (behavior preservation), its ability to discover non-trivial improvements, and its convergence toward the Pareto frontier of the multi-objective non-functional cost vector.
status_search_result: The question is an open research direction in LLM-based automated program/performance improvement. Recent work (e.g., Meta's SapFix-style tooling, DeepMind's AlphaCode and AlphaEvolve, and LLM-driven Genetic Improvement papers from 2024–2026) has begun to address execution-time improvements via LLMs, but generalization to power consumption, memory footprint, and explicit multi-objective Pareto trade-offs with formal behavior-preservation guarantees remains an actively studied open problem with no comprehensive solution reported.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLM-based refactoring become reliable enough to automate project-specific and API-evolution-driven refactorings, including bespoke refactorings learned from a few examples, while preserving existing behavior via the automated regression oracle and still producing useful developer-facing explanations?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a software project consisting of a set of source files written in some programming language L, together with an associated regression test suite T that induces an observational equivalence relation on programs: two programs P and P' are considered behaviorally equivalent with respect to T (written P ≡_T P') if and only if every test in T produces the same observable outcome on P and P'. A refactoring is a transformation R: P ↦ P' such that P ≡_T P'. Consider the following classes of refactorings:

(a) API-evolution refactorings, where a library or API used by P is replaced by a new version with a different interface, and the transformation must update all call sites in P accordingly.

(b) Bespoke (project-specific) refactorings, specified only by a small set {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^k of input/output code-fragment example pairs that implicitly define a target transformation rule R*.

Let M be a large language model viewed as a (possibly stochastic) function that maps a prompt (containing project context, examples, and a code fragment) to a candidate transformed code fragment. Define an automated refactoring procedure A_M to be reliable on a class C of refactorings if, for every instance (P, spec) in C, the procedure A_M produces with high probability a transformed program P' such that:
  (i) P' ≡_T P (behavioral preservation, verified by the regression oracle T),
  (ii) P' realizes the intended transformation specified by spec (correctness with respect to the API change or the few-shot examples), and
  (iii) A_M outputs, alongside P', a human-readable explanation E of the change that is faithful to the actual syntactic and semantic differences between P and P'.

Problem. Design and analyze a procedure A_M, built on top of a large language model M, that is reliable in the above sense simultaneously for class (a) and class (b), and in particular:

1. Formulate and prove guarantees (probabilistic or worst-case) on the reliability of A_M for bespoke refactorings learned from k examples, as a function of k, the complexity of the target rule R*, and properties of M.
2. Show how the regression oracle T can be integrated into A_M (e.g., via test-driven candidate filtering, repair loops, or verification) so that condition (i) is enforced even when M produces incorrect candidates.
3. Provide a method for generating faithful developer-facing explanations E and a criterion for evaluating their faithfulness with respect to the actual transformation P ↦ P'.

State precise conditions on M, T, and the example set under which such a procedure exists and is reliable.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research challenge in the software engineering literature on LLMs. While there is active work on LLM-assisted refactoring, API migration, and example-based code transformation (e.g., tools like Refactoring Mining, PyEvolve, and LLM-based migration assistants), no published result establishes a reliable, generally-applicable procedure that simultaneously handles project-specific and API-evolution refactorings via few-shot learning with guaranteed behavioral preservation and faithful explanations. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLMs generate richer and more semantically relevant code summaries and documentation than retrieval-based methods, and what evaluation and assurance methods should replace purely lexical metrics when the generated documentation cannot be directly executed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the task of automatic code summarization and documentation generation: given a source-code artifact (e.g., a function, class, or module), produce a natural-language description that conveys its intent, behavior, inputs/outputs, side effects, and usage context. Two families of methods are of interest:

(a) Retrieval-based methods, which select a summary from a fixed corpus of human-written summaries (so the achievable output space is bounded by that corpus).

(b) Generative methods based on large language models (LLMs), i.e., autoregressive neural sequence models pretrained on large text and code corpora, which can in principle produce summaries outside any fixed corpus.

Address the following:

1. Develop a generative procedure (using LLMs, possibly combined with reasoning-and-acting style tool use that interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with external tool/observation calls) that provably produces code summaries that are semantically richer and more semantically relevant to the underlying program than any retrieval from a fixed corpus, where "semantic richness" and "semantic relevance" must be given precise, measurable definitions.

2. Because generated documentation is natural-language text and cannot be directly executed against the code, design a non-lexical evaluation and assurance framework for such summaries. The framework should:
   (i) avoid relying solely on token-overlap or n-gram lexical metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, chrF) as the sole measure of quality;
   (ii) provide quantifiable guarantees or calibrated confidence about the faithfulness of the generated documentation with respect to the actual behavior of the code;
   (iii) be reproducible and comparable across systems.

Specify the definitions, the algorithm, and the evaluation protocol, and justify why the proposed measures capture semantic adequacy of documentation better than purely lexical metrics.
status_search_result: The problem of producing semantically rich, faithful code summaries with LLMs and evaluating them with non-lexical, assurance-providing metrics remains an active open research area. Recent work proposes LLM-as-a-judge, semantic similarity (e.g., BERTScore, embedding-based metrics), human-grounded rubrics, and ReAct-style tool-augmented generation, but no consensus framework with provable guarantees has emerged.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should new software-engineering-specific large language models be trained or fine-tuned so that they exploit software-specific signals, especially dynamic execution information and execution traces, rather than treating software artifacts too much like ordinary natural language?
self_contained_problem:
Design a training or fine-tuning methodology for large language models specialized to software engineering that explicitly incorporates software-specific signals beyond the surface token stream treated as natural language. Concretely:

(a) Formulate a training objective (pre-training, fine-tuning, or auxiliary multi-task objective) that ingests dynamic execution information about programs — for example, runtime execution traces (sequences of executed statements or basic blocks), variable value sequences, memory states, branch outcomes, coverage profiles, test inputs and outputs, exception traces, or call stacks — in addition to the static source code.

(b) Specify a representation of such dynamic information suitable for a transformer-based language model, including how traces (which may be long, repetitive, and program-dependent) are tokenized, aligned with the corresponding source code tokens, and serialized as input or output sequences.

(c) Provide a learning procedure that demonstrably causes the model's predictions to depend on the dynamic semantics of code rather than purely on its lexical/syntactic form, and evaluate this procedure on standard software engineering tasks (such as bug detection, program repair, test generation, code completion, or fault localization) to show measurable improvement over baselines trained only on static code text.

The problem is to give such a methodology, together with theoretical or empirical justification that it leverages dynamic execution information in a way that ordinary natural-language-style training cannot.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction. Recent work (e.g., TRACED, NExT, models incorporating execution traces or runtime values into code LLMs) has begun to address aspects of this problem, but no consensus methodology exists and the broader goal of SE-specific LLMs that fully exploit dynamic information remains an active open research area.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
context_brief: model size, energy, and lightweight adaptation
original_question: What model size is actually required for strong software-engineering performance, and how should lighter deployment techniques such as low-rank adaptation and quantization be evaluated for specific software-engineering applications so that accuracy, energy use, and deployability are balanced rather than assuming larger models are always necessary?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of transformer-based large language models (LLMs) parameterized by the number of trainable parameters N, applied to a fixed suite of software-engineering tasks T = {t_1, ..., t_k} (for example: code completion, program repair, test generation, code summarization, vulnerability detection). For each task t_i, let A_i(M) ∈ [0,1] denote a task-specific accuracy/quality metric of a deployed model M, let E_i(M) ≥ 0 denote the energy consumption (in joules) required to perform a standardized workload on t_i, and let D(M) denote a deployability score that aggregates memory footprint, inference latency, and hardware requirements.

(a) Determine, empirically and with statistical justification, the minimal model size N*(t_i, α) such that there exists a pretrained model M with at most N*(t_i, α) parameters achieving A_i(M) ≥ α on task t_i, for a prescribed quality threshold α.

(b) For two lightweight deployment techniques applied to a base model M_0 of size N_0:
   (i) Low-rank adaptation (LoRA): replace each fine-tuned weight update ΔW ∈ R^{d×k} by a product BA with B ∈ R^{d×r}, A ∈ R^{r×k}, r ≪ min(d,k);
   (ii) Post-training quantization Q_b: map each weight w to a b-bit representation Q_b(w),
construct an evaluation protocol that, for each task t_i, jointly reports (A_i, E_i, D) of the adapted/quantized model and compares it against the unmodified baseline M_0 and against smaller base models of comparable resource cost.

(c) Define and compute a balanced objective F(M; t_i) = w_A · A_i(M) − w_E · E_i(M) − w_D · (1 − D(M)) with chosen non-negative weights w_A, w_E, w_D, and identify configurations (N, r, b) that maximize F across the suite T, thereby determining when larger model size is, or is not, necessary for strong software-engineering performance.
category_tag: LLM efficiency and adaptation for software engineering
status_search_result: The problem of determining a minimal LLM size for strong software-engineering performance and rigorously evaluating LoRA and quantization on SE tasks against accuracy/energy/deployability tradeoffs remains an active and unresolved research direction. Recent work studies LoRA and quantization for code LLMs and reports promising but partial findings, with no consensus on minimal sizes or standardized multi-objective evaluation protocols.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can dynamic, adaptive prompt engineering and model-parameter tuning be turned into a principled optimization process for software-engineering tasks, given that prompt effectiveness is highly problem-specific, one-size-fits-all prompting is unrealistic, and settings such as temperature materially affect the nature of generated outputs?
self_contained_problem:
Let a software-engineering task instance be modeled as an element x of an input space X, and let a large language model be a stochastic mapping M_{θ}: P × X → Y, where P is a space of natural-language prompt templates, θ ∈ Θ is a vector of decoding/model hyperparameters (for example, sampling temperature, top-p, top-k, repetition penalty, and any tunable model parameters), and Y is the space of generated artefacts (e.g., source code, tests, patches, specifications). Suppose we are given a distribution D over task instances x, and a finite collection of (possibly conflicting) quality functionals f_1, …, f_m : Y × X → ℝ measuring desiderata such as functional correctness, readability, efficiency, and security.

Define the per-instance adaptive policy as a pair of measurable maps π = (π_P, π_Θ) with π_P : X → P and π_Θ : X → Θ, and define the expected vector-valued performance
F(π) = ( 𝔼_{x ∼ D, y ∼ M_{π_Θ(x)}(π_P(x), x)} [ f_i(y, x) ] )_{i=1}^{m} ∈ ℝ^m.

Develop a principled optimization framework that:
(1) Formulates the search for a Pareto-optimal adaptive policy π* in the joint space (X → P) × (X → Θ) as a well-posed multi-objective stochastic optimization problem, specifying admissible policy classes, regularity assumptions on M_{θ}, and tractable surrogates for the objectives f_i.
(2) Provides an algorithm that, using only black-box queries to M_{θ}, produces a sequence of policies π^{(t)} converging (in an appropriate sense) to the Pareto front of F, together with sample-complexity or regret guarantees that quantify dependence on the dimensions of P and Θ and on the variability of optimal prompts across x.
(3) Establishes conditions under which a single static policy (π_P, π_Θ) constant in x is provably suboptimal compared to instance-adaptive policies, thereby justifying dynamic adaptation.

Solve, or characterize the obstacles to solving, problems (1)–(3).
status_search_result: The question is posed as a research agenda rather than a settled mathematical problem. Subsequent work on automatic prompt optimization (e.g., APE, OPRO, PromptBreeder, EvoPrompt) and search-based prompt engineering for software-engineering tasks has produced partial algorithms, but no principled framework with convergence/regret guarantees jointly over adaptive prompts and decoding hyperparameters for SE tasks is established. The problem remains open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can hallucination be harnessed productively in software engineering so that plausible but incorrect outputs are repurposed into useful signals for software enhancement, such as feature suggestions, warnings about likely human misunderstandings of code, or prompts for API simplification and extension, without letting those hallucinations degrade correctness?
self_contained_problem:
Let an LLM-based code assistant be a function M that, given a prompt p drawn from a distribution over software engineering tasks (e.g., generating test cases, summarizing code, recommending APIs), produces an output M(p). Call an output a "hallucination" if it is plausible under M's learned distribution but factually incorrect with respect to the ground-truth software artifact (e.g., it references a nonexistent API, mis-describes code behavior, or proposes a test that does not pass on the current code).

Design and justify a methodology (algorithm, pipeline, or framework) that satisfies all of the following:

1. Detection. Given outputs of M on software engineering prompts, reliably identify which outputs are hallucinations.

2. Repurposing. Map each detected hallucination to one of the following productive signals for software enhancement:
   (a) a hallucinated test case is repurposed as a candidate new-feature suggestion (the absent behavior implied by the test);
   (b) a hallucinated code summary is repurposed as a warning that the underlying code is at elevated risk of being misunderstood by humans;
   (c) a hallucinated reference to a nonexistent API is repurposed as a suggestion to refactor, simplify, or extend the existing API surface.

3. Correctness preservation. Show, via formal argument or empirical evaluation, that integrating these repurposed signals into a software development workflow does not increase the rate of incorrect code being merged, compared with a baseline that simply discards hallucinations.

Provide either a constructive method meeting (1)–(3) with measurable guarantees on detection precision/recall and on downstream developer utility, or prove an impossibility/limitation result showing that one of these objectives cannot be jointly attained under stated assumptions on M.

Recent work on hallucination detection and mitigation in code LLMs (e.g., CodeHalu, HalluCode, and various 2024–2025 surveys) treats hallucinations primarily as defects to be suppressed; we did not find published methodology with formal guarantees that systematically repurposes hallucinated tests, summaries, or API references into vetted enhancement signals while preserving correctness. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: What scientific foundations, benchmarking systems, replication practices, and longitudinal human-in-the-loop studies are needed so that LLM-based software engineering can be evaluated robustly despite nondeterminism, incomplete reporting, scarce artifact sharing, and the need to measure real developer-LLM interaction over time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the emerging discipline in which large language models (LLMs) are used to support software engineering tasks such as code generation, repair, testing, summarization, and refactoring. LLMs exhibit nondeterministic outputs (due to sampling strategies, temperature, and stochastic decoding), are typically evaluated with incomplete experimental reporting, with limited sharing of prompts, model versions, seeds, datasets, and artifacts, and are often assessed via one-shot static benchmarks rather than through sustained interaction with human developers.

Develop a rigorous methodological framework consisting of the following four interrelated components, and establish their adequacy:

1. Scientific foundations. Formulate precise principles for designing and reporting experiments involving LLMs in software engineering. In particular, specify what must be controlled or reported (sampling strategy, temperature, prompt template, model identifier and version, random seeds, context window, retrieval augmentation, post-processing, etc.), and define statistical procedures (e.g., confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, effect sizes, sample sizes) that account for the nondeterminism of LLM outputs when drawing conclusions.

2. Benchmarking systems. Define reliable, efficient, and comprehensive benchmark suites for LLM-based software engineering. Specify (a) criteria preventing data leakage between training and evaluation sets, (b) metrics that go beyond pass@k toward functional correctness, robustness, maintainability, and security, (c) procedures for benchmark refresh to mitigate contamination, and (d) protocols making benchmarks usable by both researchers and practitioners.

3. Replication practices. Establish standards and infrastructure (artifact-sharing platforms, reproducibility checklists, badges, versioned model snapshots) sufficient to permit independent replication of LLM-based software engineering studies despite model drift and proprietary APIs.

4. Longitudinal human-in-the-loop studies. Design study methodologies that measure real developer–LLM interaction over extended time periods, capturing learning effects, productivity, code quality, cognitive load, trust calibration, and skill atrophy, and propose statistical models suitable for such longitudinal data.

Prove or argue that the resulting framework simultaneously addresses nondeterminism, incomplete reporting, scarce artifact sharing, and the absence of long-term interaction data, and thereby enables robust evaluation of LLM-based software engineering.
category_tag: empirical evaluation of LLM-based software engineering
status_search_result: This is an open research-agenda problem in empirical software engineering. Recent work (post-2023) on benchmarks like SWE-bench, HumanEval-X, LiveCodeBench, and reproducibility/contamination studies addresses parts of the agenda, but no comprehensive framework jointly resolving nondeterminism, replication, benchmarking, and longitudinal developer–LLM interaction has been established. Surveys and community efforts continue to identify these as open problems.

If such an algebra exists, do normalized Betti numbers over F_p along any normal chain converge to the resulting characteristic-p L2-Betti numbers?

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
context_brief: geometry and boundary effects on apparent brittleness
original_question: For one and the same soft amorphous material, how do mechanical-testing geometries and boundaries—especially simple-shear rheometers versus compression or extension in universal testing machines—alter stress heterogeneity, shear localization, and the apparent ductile or brittle character of the measured response?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (e.g., a colloidal gel, emulsion, dense suspension, or soft glass) modeled as a continuum that may also support spatially heterogeneous plastic rearrangements. Suppose one fixed constitutive description of this material is subjected to two classes of mechanical tests:

(i) Simple-shear rheometry, in which the sample is confined between two parallel plates (or in a cone–plate / Couette geometry) with a nominally homogeneous shear deformation imposed, and the macroscopic shear stress σ(γ) is measured as a function of applied strain γ.

(ii) Uniaxial compression or extension in a universal testing machine (UTM), in which the sample is placed between rigid platens (with friction or adhesion at the boundaries) and the macroscopic axial stress σ(ε) is measured as a function of axial strain ε.

For the same underlying material model, formulate and analyze the following:

1. Quantify the spatial stress heterogeneity field τ(x) induced by each geometry, including the role of free surfaces, boundary friction/adhesion, sample aspect ratio, and finite-size effects.

2. Determine the conditions under which shear localization (formation of a shear band) initiates, and how the localization threshold, orientation, and width depend on the geometry and boundary conditions.

3. Characterize the macroscopic stress–strain curve σ(γ) or σ(ε), and identify quantitative criteria (e.g., post-peak stress drop magnitude, strain at failure, energy released at yield) that classify the apparent yielding as ductile or brittle.

4. Prove or disprove that there exist constitutive parameters for which one and the same material exhibits ductile yielding in geometry (i) and brittle yielding in geometry (ii), and identify the dimensionless groups governing this crossover.

Provide a predictive framework (analytical, numerical, or both) that maps the intrinsic material parameters and geometric/boundary parameters to the observed ductile-to-brittle character of the response.
status_search_result: This is an open conceptual and modeling question in the rheology and mechanics of soft amorphous solids. Recent literature on yielding of amorphous materials emphasizes that geometry and boundary effects substantially influence apparent ductile vs. brittle behavior, and explicitly calls for extensions of numerical models to include compression/UTM boundaries. No general predictive framework reconciling rheometer vs. UTM responses for the same material has been established.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
context_brief: Eshelby events, avalanches, and shear bands
original_question: In amorphous solids under deformation, what is the mechanistic connection between localized Eshelby-type rearrangements, plastic avalanches, and the emergence of shear bands, and how do elastic interactions and structural effects combine to determine whether plasticity remains scattered or localizes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous solid modeled as a disordered elastic medium subjected to quasistatic shear deformation. Plastic activity in such a material is known to proceed via localized rearrangements (Eshelby events): a small region undergoes a local inelastic strain, producing a long-range anisotropic elastic stress field of Eshelby (quadrupolar) type on the surrounding matrix. Through these elastic interactions, individual Eshelby events can trigger further events, giving rise to plastic avalanches with characteristic size and duration distributions. When plastic activity is spatially uniform, the macroscopic response is ductile; when it concentrates along a narrow region, a shear band forms and the response is brittle.

Develop a quantitative mechanistic theory that explains:
(a) How elastic interactions between Eshelby events (e.g. the Eshelby kernel, its sign-changing angular structure, and its decay) together with structural disorder (local yield-stress distributions, soft spots, structural memory, aging) determine whether successive avalanches remain spatially scattered or organize into a persistent shear band.
(b) Precise criteria — in terms of statistical properties of avalanches (size, shape, spatial correlations, density of marginally stable sites) and of the underlying structural state — for the transition from delocalized plastic flow to localized shear banding.
(c) The role of avalanches as an intermediate spatial-organization scale between isolated Eshelby events and macroscopic shear bands, including whether shear bands can be characterized as a percolation-like, nucleation-like, or instability-driven emergent structure of correlated avalanches.

Provide either a rigorous derivation within an elastoplastic model (lattice or continuum) with Eshelby-type stress redistribution and quenched disorder, or a sharp set of analytical predictions (scaling laws, order parameters, critical exponents) that distinguish the scattered-plasticity regime from the shear-band regime and that can be tested against simulations and experiments.
status_search_result: The mechanistic link between Eshelby events, avalanches, and shear-band formation in amorphous solids is widely recognized as an active and unresolved problem. Recent reviews and elastoplastic-model studies (e.g., Nicolas, Ferrero, Martens, Barrat 2018; Richard et al. 2021; Lerner & Bouchbinder 2022; Barlow et al. 2020) propose partial pictures (avalanche correlations, density of soft modes, structural rejuvenation) but no consensus theory predicts when plasticity localizes into a shear band.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
original_question: How do structural heterogeneities, rigidity percolation, and stress propagation under controlled structural disorder determine whether a soft amorphous material undergoes ductile or brittle yielding?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material modeled as a disordered network or particle assembly subjected to quasi-static or finite-rate shear deformation. Assume the material is characterized by:

(i) a spatial distribution of structural heterogeneities, quantified by local order parameters such as local density, coordination number z(x), or local elastic modulus fluctuations;
(ii) a rigidity percolation transition controlled by mean coordination number z relative to the isostatic threshold z_c (e.g. z_c = 2d in d spatial dimensions for central-force networks), which governs the emergence of a system-spanning rigid cluster;
(iii) a stress propagation field σ(x) whose long-range correlations depend on the proximity to the rigidity transition and on the disorder distribution.

Under controlled structural disorder (parameterized, for instance, by the variance of local coordination or local stiffness), determine the relationship between these microscopic descriptors and the macroscopic mode of yielding. Specifically:

(a) Identify a quantitative criterion, in terms of the distance |z − z_c| from rigidity percolation and the amplitude/correlation length of structural heterogeneities, that predicts whether the material yields in a ductile fashion (smooth, spatially diffuse plastic flow) or in a brittle fashion (abrupt, system-spanning shear band formation with a macroscopic stress drop).

(b) Characterize how stress propagation — for example via the Eshelby-like quadrupolar kernel modified by structural disorder — mediates the transition between these two yielding modes.

(c) Determine whether the ductile-to-brittle transition coincides with, precedes, or follows the rigidity percolation transition as disorder is varied.
status_search_result: Recent literature on the ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT) in soft amorphous solids identifies structural heterogeneity, rigidity percolation, and stress propagation as central but incompletely understood ingredients. Reviews and recent simulations call for systematic studies under controlled disorder, and no consensus criterion linking rigidity percolation to the DBT has been established, indicating the question remains open.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
original_question: Can the ductile-to-brittle transition and the shear-induced solid-to-liquid yielding transition in amorphous systems be unified within a general non-equilibrium dynamical phase-transition framework, despite different macroscopic signatures in brittle and ductile materials?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an amorphous solid (e.g., a soft glassy material, foam, emulsion, colloidal glass, or metallic glass) subjected to an externally applied shear deformation. Two qualitatively different macroscopic responses are observed:

(i) Ductile yielding: as strain is increased, plastic deformation accumulates gradually and the stress-strain curve crosses smoothly from elastic to plastic flow, eventually reaching a steady plastic flow regime (the shear-induced solid-to-liquid transition).

(ii) Brittle yielding: as strain is increased, the material remains nearly elastic until a critical strain at which the stress drops abruptly via a system-spanning shear band, producing a discontinuous macroscopic signature.

The crossover from regime (i) to regime (ii) as a function of the initial preparation (degree of annealing/stability) of the amorphous solid is referred to as the ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT).

Question. Formulate a single non-equilibrium dynamical phase-transition framework that simultaneously describes:
 (a) the ductile-to-brittle transition (as a change in the order/character of the underlying non-equilibrium transition, e.g., from continuous/crossover to discontinuous, possibly terminating at a critical point), and
 (b) the shear-induced solid-to-liquid yielding transition in the ductile regime,
in such a way that both phenomena emerge as different macroscopic manifestations of one common dynamical critical/phase-transition mechanism, despite their qualitatively different macroscopic signatures. Prove (or disprove) that such a unified framework exists, and identify the universality class, order parameter(s), control parameters, and scaling laws that characterize it across the full range of amorphous materials and preparation protocols.
category_tag: Nonequilibrium yielding transitions in amorphous solids
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made toward a unified picture: Ozawa et al. (PNAS 2018) proposed that a random critical point in the universality class of the quasistatically driven random-field Ising model separates brittle (discontinuous, first-order-like) and ductile (smooth crossover) yielding, controlled by the degree of annealing. Subsequent mean-field elastoplastic theories (e.g., Parisi–Procaccia–Lerner-type approaches and Hébraud–Lequeux–based descriptions, 2023–2024) extend this picture beyond RFIM by including elastic long-range interactions and dynamics. However, a fully validated unified non-equilibrium dynamical phase-transition framework simultaneously capturing the DBT and the shear-induced solid-to-liquid yielding transition across all amorphous materials, with established universality class and scaling, is not yet definitively established, and the question is still considered open in the soft-matter physics community.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
original_question: For dilute dispersions and colloidal gels, can wall slip be described by a generic coarse-grained framework based on well-defined length scales, and if so which length scale—particle size, cluster size, or a shear-dependent cluster scale—is relevant when adhesion, rolling, and sliding between aggregates and walls are possible?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a dilute dispersion or colloidal gel confined between two solid walls and subjected to a steady simple shear of rate $\dot\gamma$. The system consists of colloidal particles of characteristic size $a$ that aggregate into clusters of characteristic size $\xi(\dot\gamma)$ which may depend on the shear rate, and which together form a multiscale percolated network. At the bounding walls, the aggregates may simultaneously adhere, roll, and slide. Define the wall-slip velocity $v_s$ as the difference between the wall velocity and the extrapolated bulk fluid velocity at the wall, and the slip length $\ell_s = v_s/\dot\gamma$.

Question: Does there exist a generic coarse-grained constitutive framework that predicts $v_s$ (or $\ell_s$) for such dilute dispersions and gels purely in terms of a comparison of well-defined length scales — namely the particle size $a$, the static cluster size $\xi_0$, and the shear-dependent cluster scale $\xi(\dot\gamma)$ — relative to a wall-roughness or wall-interaction length, while consistently accounting for the coexistence of adhesion, rolling, and sliding of aggregates at the walls? If such a framework exists, identify which of these length scales controls the slip behavior in each regime.
status_search_result: No generic coarse-grained length-scale-based framework for wall slip in dilute colloidal dispersions and gels appears to have been established. Recent reviews and experimental studies emphasize that wall slip in gels remains poorly understood due to their multiscale architecture and the coexistence of adhesion, rolling, and sliding mechanisms.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
context_brief: microstructure and residual stress after flow cessation
original_question: When a flowing soft glassy material undergoes flow cessation and becomes solid-like again, how are the distorted microstructure inherited from the prior shear history, the dynamics of local stress relaxation, and the macroscopic residual stress connected, especially in gels?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft glassy material (for example a colloidal gel) modeled as a disordered network of interacting mesoscopic constituents whose configuration is described by a microstructural tensor M(t) (such as the pair-correlation anisotropy or fabric tensor), and whose mechanical state is described by a stress tensor σ(t) obeying a constitutive relation that couples microstructure, local elasticity, and plastic relaxation events with a distribution of local relaxation times.

The sample is subjected to a steady simple shear of rate γ̇ for sufficiently long times that a non-equilibrium steady state is reached with anisotropic microstructure M_ss and stress σ_ss. At time t = 0 the shear is brought abruptly to zero (flow cessation) and the system is allowed to age while remaining mechanically isolated (zero strain boundary condition). After cessation one observes:
  (i) a frozen-in distorted microstructure M_∞ = lim_{t→∞} M(t) that differs from the isotropic quiescent state;
  (ii) a transient field of local stresses σ_loc(x,t) whose statistics relax over a broad spectrum of time scales;
  (iii) a non-vanishing macroscopic residual stress σ_res = lim_{t→∞} ⟨σ(t)⟩.

Problem. Establish a quantitative relationship, derived from a mesoscopic or continuum model of soft glassy/gel rheology, that links these three quantities. Specifically:
  (a) Express σ_res as a functional of the prior shear history {γ̇(t) : t < 0} and of the inherited anisotropy M_∞.
  (b) Derive the spectrum of local stress relaxation times after cessation from the structural anisotropy and characterize how heterogeneity in local relaxation produces the residual macroscopic stress.
  (c) Determine how, for gel-like networks with attractive interactions, the magnitude and sign of σ_res depend on the pre-cessation Weissenberg number and on the network connectivity, and identify the conditions under which σ_res vanishes despite M_∞ remaining anisotropic.
category_tag: residual stress in soft glassy materials
status_search_result: Recent reviews and experimental studies on flow cessation and residual stresses in soft glassy materials and gels describe the problem as actively investigated and unresolved: while empirical correlations between microstructural anisotropy, local relaxation dynamics, and macroscopic residual stresses have been reported, no unified quantitative theory connecting all three has been established, particularly for gels.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
original_question: Is there a correlation between flow cessation and thixotropy in soft glassy materials, and what microscopic scenario links shear cessation, structural anisotropy, and residual-stress dynamics in a way that can be validated by rheo-confocal or rheo-scattering experiments?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft glassy material (e.g., a dense colloidal suspension, emulsion, foam, or microgel paste) modeled as an amorphous assembly of interacting mesoscopic constituents subjected to simple shear. After a steady shear flow at rate \\(\\dot\\gamma>0\\) is abruptly halted at time \\(t=0\\), the system relaxes while supporting a time-dependent residual stress \\(\\sigma_r(t)\\) that decays slowly toward a non-zero plateau, and exhibits an evolving microstructural anisotropy quantified, e.g., by the deviatoric part of the pair-correlation function \\(g(\\mathbf{r})\\) or the fabric tensor \\(Q_{ij}=\\langle \\hat r_i \\hat r_j\\rangle - \\tfrac{1}{d}\\delta_{ij}\\) computed over contacts or near-neighbor bonds. Thixotropy is defined as a reversible, time-dependent decrease of viscosity under flow followed by recovery at rest, characterized by a structural parameter \\(\\lambda(t)\\in[0,1]\\) obeying a kinetic equation of the form \\(\\dot\\lambda = f(\\lambda)-g(\\lambda)\\dot\\gamma\\).

(a) Establish whether there exists a quantitative correlation between the post-cessation relaxation of \\(\\sigma_r(t)\\) (its plateau value, decay timescale, and dependence on the prior \\(\\dot\\gamma\\)) and thixotropic indicators (the recovery dynamics of \\(\\lambda(t)\\) or equivalently of the linear viscoelastic moduli \\(G'(\\omega,t_w)\\), \\(G''(\\omega,t_w)\\) measured as a function of waiting time \\(t_w\\) after cessation).

(b) Formulate a microscopic scenario that explicitly links: (i) the cessation of shear, (ii) the persistence and slow relaxation of structural anisotropy \\(Q_{ij}(t)\\), and (iii) the dynamics of residual stresses \\(\\sigma_r(t)\\), in such a way that the proposed mechanism predicts measurable signatures accessible to rheo-confocal microscopy (real-space tracking of particle positions and bond orientations) or rheo-scattering experiments (anisotropic structure factor \\(S(\\mathbf{q},t)\\)).

The problem is to determine whether such a correlation exists in (a) and to construct and validate a microscopic theoretical scenario satisfying the requirements of (b).
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open issue concerning the connection between flow cessation, thixotropy, residual stresses and structural anisotropy in soft amorphous materials. While numerical/simulation evidence exists for anisotropy-driven residual stress relaxation, no direct experimental validation via rheo-confocal or rheo-scattering has resolved the microscopic scenario, and no general theoretical framework has been established. The status remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems within Nonextensive Statistical Mechanics
original_question: For Coupled Gaussian distributions and Coupled Exponential distributions in NSM, the average generalized density is equal to the density at the mean plus or minus the scale, or at the location plus the scale. Can the relationship between average generalized density and ordinary average density be quantified so that generalized entropy more clearly complements ordinary entropy as a description of a system’s uncertainty? Since entropy is treated as a measure of degrees of freedom and nonlinear statistical coupling is treated as the inverse of degrees of freedom, can the difference between coupled entropy and ordinary entropy be quantified in terms of degrees of freedom?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For a real parameter κ (the nonlinear statistical coupling) and a positive integer d (the dimension), define the coupled exponential function

  exp_κ(x) = (1 + κ x)_+^{1/κ},   κ ≠ 0,   exp_0(x) = e^x,

and the coupled logarithm ln_κ(y) = (y^κ − 1)/κ (with ln_0(y) = log y).

A d‑dimensional Coupled Gaussian density with location μ ∈ ℝ^d and (symmetric positive‑definite) scale Σ is

  p_κ(x) = Z_κ^{−1} (1 + κ (x − μ)^⊤ Σ^{−1} (x − μ))_+^{−(1+ d κ)/(2κ)},

where Z_κ is the normalization constant; a Coupled Exponential density on (0,∞) with location μ and scale σ > 0 is

  p_κ(x) = (1/σ) (1 + κ (x − μ)/σ)_+^{−(1+κ)/κ}.

For these families one has the identity that the "generalized average density"

  ⟨p⟩_gen := ∫ p(x)^{1+κ} dx  (suitably normalized)

equals the density evaluated at μ ± σ (Coupled Gaussian) or at μ + σ (Coupled Exponential).

The coupled (Tsallis‑type) entropy of a density p is

  S_κ(p) = − ∫ p(x)^{1+κ} ln_κ p(x) dx,

while the ordinary (Shannon) entropy is

  S(p) = − ∫ p(x) log p(x) dx.

Interpret entropy as a measure of the effective number of degrees of freedom n of the system and the coupling as κ = 1/n (so that for the Student‑t / Coupled Gaussian case, n plays the role of the number of degrees of freedom of a thermal bath).

Problem. Quantify, for the Coupled Gaussian and Coupled Exponential families, the relationship between the generalized average density ⟨p⟩_gen and the ordinary average density ⟨p⟩ = ∫ p(x)^2 dx (equivalently, the relationship between p at μ ± σ resp. μ + σ and the corresponding ordinary average density), in a form that exhibits how S_κ complements S as a measure of the system's uncertainty. In particular, derive an explicit closed‑form expression for the difference

  Δ(κ, d) := S_κ(p) − S(p)

as a function of the effective degrees of freedom n = 1/κ (and the dimension d), valid for both the Coupled Gaussian and the Coupled Exponential family, that makes the role of n in measuring the gap between coupled and ordinary entropy transparent.

Recent follow-up works (2025) on coupled entropy continue to discuss the relationship between coupled and ordinary entropy via degrees of freedom but do not present a closed-form quantification of the gap S_κ − S in the requested unified form; thus the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions
context_brief: Availability and use of channel statistics
original_question: How much prior channel information, especially access-point (AP)-user channel covariance matrices or dominant channel subspaces, is actually available in practical cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) deployments, and how should that information be estimated and used to mitigate pilot contamination without assuming unavailable global or uncontaminated channel statistics?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive MIMO system with $M$ access points (APs), each equipped with $N$ antennas, jointly serving $K$ single-antenna users over a flat-fading block-fading channel. Let $\mathbf{h}_{mk}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}$ denote the channel vector between AP $m$ and user $k$, modeled as a zero-mean circularly symmetric complex Gaussian vector with covariance matrix $\mathbf{R}_{mk}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}_{mk}\mathbf{h}_{mk}^{H}]$. In each coherence block of length $\tau_c$ symbols, $\tau_p<K$ symbols are used for uplink pilot training and users are assigned pilots from an orthonormal set of length $\tau_p$; users sharing a pilot cause pilot contamination, so that the MMSE estimate $\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{mk}$ of $\mathbf{h}_{mk}$ formed at AP $m$ depends on $\{\mathbf{R}_{mj}\}_{j\in\mathcal{P}_k}$, where $\mathcal{P}_k$ is the set of users sharing user $k$'s pilot.

Formulate and answer the following questions in a quantitative way, without assuming that any AP has access to global or uncontaminated channel statistics:

(a) Devise an estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{mk}$ of the local covariance matrix $\mathbf{R}_{mk}$ (or of its dominant $r$-dimensional subspace) that uses only the pilot-contaminated received signals at AP $m$, and characterize, as a function of $M,N,K,\tau_p$, pilot assignment, and the true $\{\mathbf{R}_{mj}\}$, the achievable mean-square error and subspace-distance error of this estimator.

(b) Given the imperfect statistics $\{\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{mk}\}$ from (a), derive a channel estimator and a corresponding uplink/downlink combining/precoding scheme whose achievable spectral efficiency provably converges (in some quantitative sense, as $N\to\infty$ or as the number of observation blocks grows) to the spectral efficiency obtainable under perfect knowledge of $\{\mathbf{R}_{mk}\}$.

(c) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the geometry of the covariance matrices $\{\mathbf{R}_{mk}\}$ (e.g., subspace disjointness, eigenvalue decay, pilot reuse pattern) under which pilot contamination can be asymptotically eliminated using only the locally estimated statistics from (a).
status_search_result: This is posed as a forward-looking open research question in the wireless communications literature on cell-free massive MIMO. Recent work (2023–2025) provides partial answers — e.g., subspace-based and covariance-estimation methods under pilot contamination, and pilot-decontamination schemes — but no complete characterization of how much channel statistical information is truly available in practice and how it should be optimally estimated and used under local-only knowledge. The problem remains open in its full generality.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: Which post-attention or otherwise new architectural paradigms should replace or substantially extend Transformer-based large language models, and how can those architectures support longer context windows and more efficient processing of long-context prompts than standard attention-based models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider sequence models that map an input token sequence x_1, x_2, ..., x_n (drawn from a finite vocabulary) to predictive distributions over the next token. A standard Transformer block computes self-attention with per-layer time and memory complexity Θ(n^2 d) in sequence length n and hidden dimension d, which becomes prohibitive for very long contexts. Identify and propose new architectural paradigms — i.e., neural sequence architectures that either replace or substantially extend Transformer self-attention — that satisfy the following requirements:

1. The architecture supports inference and training on context windows of length n that are much larger than what is practical for standard quadratic-attention Transformers, ideally achieving per-layer compute and memory scaling that is sub-quadratic (e.g., O(n log n) or O(n)) in n while preserving expressivity sufficient for large-scale language modeling.

2. The architecture matches or exceeds the language-modeling quality (e.g., perplexity, downstream task accuracy) of comparably sized Transformer-based large language models across a broad range of natural-language tasks.

3. The architecture provides demonstrably more efficient processing of long-context prompts, in terms of wall-clock latency, memory footprint, or energy use, than standard attention-based models of equivalent parameter count.

Describe the mathematical structure of such an architecture (state update equations, recurrence or convolutional structure, mixing operators, normalization, etc.), prove or give strong empirical evidence for its sub-quadratic scaling, and characterize the trade-offs between context length, model capacity, and task performance.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended research direction rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Since 2023–2026 several candidate post-attention or sub-quadratic architectures have been proposed and partially validated (e.g., state-space models such as S4 and Mamba, linear-attention variants, RWKV, Hyena, RetNet, Griffin, Jamba), and they demonstrate competitive long-context efficiency, but no single architecture has been shown to definitively replace Transformers. The broader question of identifying the "next" dominant architecture remains open.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How should future large language models be designed and evaluated so that they can handle text, images, video, and audio in a unified multi-modal manner for applications such as question answering, content generation, healthcare, robotics, and especially conversational generative vision?
self_contained_problem:
Design a principled framework for constructing and evaluating a unified multi-modal large language model M that accepts inputs drawn from any combination of the modalities text T, images I, video V, and audio A, and produces outputs in any of these modalities. Specifically:

1. Specify an architecture and training objective for M : (T ∪ I ∪ V ∪ A)^* → (T ∪ I ∪ V ∪ A)^* that integrates heterogeneous modalities into a shared representation space and supports tasks including (a) multi-modal question answering, (b) cross-modal content generation, (c) clinical/healthcare reasoning over mixed signals (e.g. text reports plus medical imaging), (d) embodied/robotic control conditioned on visual and auditory observations, and (e) conversational generative vision in which the model maintains a multi-turn dialogue while generating or editing visual content.

2. Define a quantitative evaluation protocol consisting of:
   - benchmark task families covering each of the above application areas,
   - scoring functions for outputs that include generated images or video (going beyond perplexity- and exact-match-style metrics),
   - measures of cross-modal consistency, factual grounding, and dialogue coherence in the conversational generative vision setting.

3. Establish theoretical or empirical guarantees relating performance on the proposed evaluation protocol to capabilities of M on the listed downstream applications.

Produce such a framework, or prove obstructions showing that no single architecture and evaluation protocol can simultaneously satisfy the requirements above.
status_search_result: Unified multi-modal LLMs and their evaluation, particularly for conversational generative vision, remain an active and unresolved research area. While many systems (e.g. GPT-4o, Gemini, LLaVA-family models) have made substantial progress on integrating text, image, video, and audio, there is no commonly accepted general framework or evaluation protocol that comprehensively addresses all listed application areas, and benchmarks for conversational generative vision are still being developed.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: Which advanced prompt-engineering, tool-use, retrieval-augmentation, personalization, agent, and multi-agent techniques can most effectively address shortcomings of large language models such as hallucination while enabling systems that use external tools, incorporate user context, and make decisions in real applications?
self_contained_problem: Consider a large language model (LLM) viewed as a conditional probability distribution p_θ(y | x) over output token sequences y given an input context x, trained on a fixed corpus and prone to producing factually incorrect outputs (hallucinations), lacking access to up-to-date or private information, and unable on its own to invoke external tools or maintain user-specific state. Identify and characterize a set of augmentation techniques — including (i) advanced prompt-engineering strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree-of-thought, ReAct-style prompting), (ii) tool-use protocols allowing the model to call external APIs, code interpreters, calculators, or databases, (iii) retrieval-augmented generation in which relevant documents are retrieved from an external corpus and concatenated into the context, (iv) personalization mechanisms that incorporate per-user context or preferences, and (v) single-agent and multi-agent architectures in which one or more LLM instances plan, communicate, and act in an environment — and determine which combinations most effectively (a) reduce the rate of hallucinated or unsupported claims, (b) enable reliable use of external tools, (c) integrate user-specific context, and (d) support autonomous decision-making in real applications. Specifically, propose evaluation criteria and produce a comparative analysis identifying the techniques and combinations that yield the largest improvements on these four objectives.

Active and rapidly growing literature exists on prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, and LLM agents (e.g., ReAct, Toolformer, RAG, AutoGen, multi-agent debate), but no consensus "best" combination has been established and hallucination remains an unsolved problem as of 2026.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How can large language models be made robust and secure against adversarial attacks and other vulnerabilities, prevented from being used to manipulate people or spread misinformation, and improved so they better detect potential attacks while remaining fair, unbiased, and responsible with sensitive information?
self_contained_problem:
Let a large language model (LLM) be a parameterized conditional probability distribution p_θ(y | x) over output token sequences y given input prompts x, trained on a large corpus of natural-language data. Consider the following open research problem concerning the design and analysis of such models:

Develop principled methodologies and provable guarantees that simultaneously achieve the following objectives for an LLM p_θ:

1. Adversarial robustness: For a specified perturbation class Δ on inputs (e.g., bounded-edit prompt perturbations, jailbreak prompt templates, prompt-injection payloads embedded in retrieved context), design training and inference procedures such that, for every x in a target task distribution and every δ ∈ Δ, the model's output p_θ(· | x ⊕ δ) remains "aligned" with a specified safety/utility policy π_safe with high probability, where alignment is measured by a quantitative criterion (e.g., a bounded divergence from the policy-conformant output distribution).

2. Misuse prevention: Construct mechanisms (training-time, decoding-time, or post-hoc) ensuring that the probability assigned by p_θ to outputs in a designated "harmful" set H (e.g., disinformation, manipulation content, instructions for prohibited actions) is bounded above by a prescribed ε > 0 uniformly over admissible prompts, while preserving utility on benign tasks within a prescribed tolerance.

3. Attack detection: Construct a detector D: X → {0,1} (possibly using the model's internal representations and reasoning traces) such that D achieves provable false-positive and false-negative rates on prompts drawn from the benign distribution versus adversarial distributions in Δ.

4. Fairness and bias control: Given a set of protected attributes A and a fairness criterion F (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, counterfactual fairness on language tasks), design and verify that p_θ satisfies F with quantitative bounds across specified subpopulations and tasks.

5. Sensitive-information handling: Provide guarantees (e.g., differential-privacy style bounds, membership-inference resistance, or verbatim-leakage bounds) that p_θ does not reveal, with probability above a prescribed threshold, sensitive content from its training data or from prompt context marked confidential.

The problem is to give a unified framework — including formal definitions, algorithms, and theorems — that jointly attains all five objectives with explicit, non-vacuous quantitative trade-offs between robustness, safety, utility, fairness, and privacy for modern transformer-based LLMs, or to establish impossibility results delineating which combinations of these objectives are achievable simultaneously.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research agenda concerning adversarial robustness, misuse prevention, attack detection, fairness, and privacy of large language models. As of 2026, no unified solution exists; partial advances have been made on each individual axis (e.g., RLHF-based safety tuning, jailbreak defenses, differential-privacy fine-tuning, bias-mitigation methods), but provable joint guarantees with non-vacuous trade-offs remain unresolved, and recent surveys continue to list these as outstanding challenges.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How can hallucination in large language models be measured reliably when the same factual content can be expressed in different styles and even very small wording changes make false-information detection difficult?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be a generative language model that maps an input prompt x to a textual response M(x). For a factual query x, let A(x) denote the set of semantically equivalent textual expressions of the true answer (so A(x) is a paraphrase-equivalence class under meaning-preserving rewrites). A response y is said to be a "hallucination" with respect to x if y is not semantically entailed by any element of A(x), i.e., y conveys content inconsistent with the ground-truth fact.

Design and analyze a hallucination-evaluation function H that assigns to each pair (x, M(x)) a score H(x, M(x)) ∈ [0,1] (interpreted as the probability that M(x) is a hallucination) and that satisfies the following desiderata simultaneously:

1. Paraphrase invariance: For any two responses y, y' that are semantically equivalent (one is a meaning-preserving paraphrase of the other), |H(x, y) − H(x, y')| ≤ ε for a small prescribed ε > 0.

2. Sensitivity to small factual perturbations: There exist response pairs (y, y') differing by an arbitrarily small edit distance (e.g., a single token substitution such as a negation, a number, or a named entity) where y is factually correct and y' is factually incorrect, and the metric must satisfy H(x, y') − H(x, y) ≥ δ for a prescribed δ > 0.

3. Reference-class robustness: For every admissible ground-truth reference set A(x), the score H must be consistent with at least one element of A(x); in particular, H should not penalize stylistic variation that preserves meaning.

Question: Does there exist such an evaluation function H, computable from (x, M(x)) and a finite reference set, that provably achieves both paraphrase invariance with parameter ε and factual-perturbation sensitivity with parameter δ for some constants 0 < ε < δ < 1, over a broad domain of factual prompts? If yes, construct one and establish bounds on (ε, δ); if no, prove an impossibility result quantifying the inherent trade-off between ε and δ.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and benchmarks (HalluLens 2025, comprehensive hallucination surveys from 2025) explicitly identify the tension between paraphrase-invariance and sensitivity to small factual edits as an unresolved challenge. Proposed approaches (self-consistency over paraphrases, model-as-judge evaluation, attribution-aware metrics) provide partial heuristics but no method has been shown to provably achieve both desiderata simultaneously; watermark-/lexical-based detection notably fails under paraphrasing. The problem is therefore considered open.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: Can large language models improve multi-step reasoning without human supervision by using fully automated process supervision methods that identify errors inside chain-of-thought traces, generate large amounts of supervision data, and reward intermediate progress in a scalable and computationally efficient way?
self_contained_problem:
Design and analyze a fully automated process-supervision framework for improving multi-step reasoning in large language models without any human-provided step-level annotations. Concretely, formulate and study the following problem:

Let M be a language model that produces chain-of-thought (CoT) traces t = (s_1, s_2, ..., s_n), where each s_i is an intermediate reasoning step leading to a final answer a(t). Suppose access is given only to a (possibly noisy) outcome verifier V : (q, a) → {0,1} that judges whether the final answer a to a question q is correct, but no human labels are provided for the correctness or quality of individual steps s_i.

(a) Construct an automatic step-level labeling procedure L that, given (q, t), produces a label ℓ_i ∈ [0,1] for every step s_i, quantifying whether s_i represents valid progress toward a correct answer. The procedure must scale to generating large supervision datasets at a computational cost that is polynomial (and ideally near-linear) in the number of sampled traces, without invoking human annotators.

(b) Using such automatically generated labels, train a process reward model R_θ(q, s_1, ..., s_i) and define an associated reinforcement-learning or search-based fine-tuning algorithm A that updates M to maximize expected outcome correctness while rewarding intermediate progress.

(c) Prove or disprove: there exists a choice of (L, R_θ, A), using only outcome supervision V and self-generated traces from M, such that the resulting fine-tuned model M' satisfies, on a fixed distribution D of multi-step reasoning problems,
    E_{q ∼ D}[V(q, a(M'(q)))] ≥ E_{q ∼ D}[V(q, a(M(q)))] + ε,
for some ε > 0 that does not vanish as model and data scale grow, while keeping training compute within a constant factor of standard outcome-only RL fine-tuning.

Equivalently: can autonomous process supervision (automatic identification of errors inside CoT traces, large-scale synthetic step-level supervision generation, and intermediate-progress rewards) provably and scalably outperform outcome-only supervision for multi-step reasoning, and if so characterize sufficient conditions on (M, V, D) for this to hold.
category_tag: Automated process supervision for LLM reasoning
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., Math-Shepherd, OmegaPRM, AutoPSV, and process reward models used in o1-style and DeepSeek-R1-style training) shows partial empirical progress: automatic step-level labeling via Monte Carlo rollouts and outcome verifiers can train process reward models that improve reasoning without human step annotations. However, no general theoretical guarantee or universally scalable, compute-efficient method has been established, and the question of whether autonomous process supervision can reliably and provably surpass outcome-only supervision at scale remains an active open research direction.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
context_brief: Synthetic data for chained math reasoning
original_question: Can synthetic data generation and tool-integrated reasoning close the reasoning gap that large language models show on chained, multi-hop mathematical problems, so that models that do reasonably well on isolated math questions also generalize to Olympiad-style composite tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model M that, on a benchmark of isolated single-step mathematical problems, achieves accuracy at least a (with a close to 1). Define a chained, multi-hop mathematical problem of depth k as a problem whose solution requires sequentially composing k single-step subproblems, where each subproblem's input depends on the output of the previous one (Olympiad-style composite tasks being a representative example). Let acc_k(M) denote M's accuracy on a distribution of depth-k chained problems built from subproblems drawn from the same family as the isolated benchmark.

Two training/inference augmentations are considered:
(i) Synthetic data generation: augmenting M's training set with automatically generated chained problems together with their step-by-step solutions.
(ii) Tool-integrated reasoning: allowing M at inference time to invoke external deterministic tools (e.g., symbolic algebra systems, calculators, code execution) at each reasoning step.

Question: Determine whether there exist training and inference procedures using only (i) and (ii) such that, for every fixed depth k, the resulting model M' satisfies acc_k(M') 	o a as resources (synthetic data size, model size, tool budget) grow, thereby closing the reasoning gap a - acc_k(M) on chained, multi-hop mathematical problems and yielding generalization from isolated math questions to Olympiad-style composite tasks. If such procedures do not exist, identify a fundamental obstruction.
status_search_result: This is an active open research question in the LLM reasoning literature as of 2026. Progress on synthetic data pipelines (e.g., MetaMath, WizardMath, OpenMathInstruct) and tool-integrated reasoning (e.g., ToRA, MathCoder, AlphaProof/AlphaGeometry) has narrowed but not closed the gap; chained multi-hop and Olympiad-style composite tasks remain a recognized failure mode. No conclusive theoretical or empirical resolution has been established.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How critical is online, on-policy data for reinforcement learning from human feedback, compared with fixed offline preference datasets, when the goal is stable convergence and strong alignment performance on diverse tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of aligning a parametric policy $\pi_	heta(a\mid x)$ (for instance, a language model) with human preferences. Let $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ denote a fixed reference policy and let preference data consist of triples $(x, a^+, a^-)$ where $a^+$ is preferred to $a^-$ given prompt $x$, generated according to a Bradley–Terry model with unknown reward $r^\star(x,a)$.

Two training paradigms are compared:

1. Offline preference optimization (e.g., Direct Preference Optimization): the learner is given a fixed dataset $\mathcal D=\{(x_i,a_i^+,a_i^-)\}_{i=1}^N$ drawn from a fixed behavioral distribution $\mu$, and optimizes a contrastive objective whose minimizer recovers $r^\star$ up to a constant. Known guarantees require a global coverage condition: there exists $C<\infty$ such that $\sup_{x,a} \pi^\star(a\mid x)/\mu(a\mid x) \le C$, where $\pi^\star$ is the KL-regularized optimal policy.

2. Online, on-policy RL (e.g., Proximal Policy Optimization with a learned reward model): at each iteration the policy $\pi_	heta$ generates fresh responses that are labeled by preference comparisons; known guarantees only require a partial coverage condition relative to $\pi^\star$.

Formalize and resolve the following question. For policy classes and reward classes of bounded complexity (e.g., bounded log-density ratios and Rademacher complexity), and under standard regularity assumptions on the Bradley–Terry preference model:

(a) Establish tight sample-complexity separations, if any, between purely offline preference-based optimization and online on-policy preference-based optimization for achieving an $\varepsilon$-suboptimal KL-regularized policy with respect to $r^\star$.

(b) Determine whether the partial coverage condition is necessary as well as sufficient for online preference-based RL to converge stably, and whether the global coverage condition is genuinely necessary for offline methods or can be relaxed.

(c) Characterize quantitatively, in terms of distribution shift between the data distribution $\mu$ and the optimal policy $\pi^\star$, the regime in which on-policy data is provably required for stable convergence and strong alignment across a heterogeneous family of prompt distributions.

Provide either matching upper and lower bounds, or a proof that no such separation can hold under the stated assumptions.
status_search_result: Theoretical and empirical comparisons between offline (DPO-style) and online (PPO-style) RLHF remain an active research area. Recent works establish that offline preference optimization requires global coverage while online methods need only partial coverage, but tight characterizations of the necessity of on-policy data and matching lower bounds remain unresolved, with new methods (iterative DPO, hybrid online-offline approaches) continually being proposed.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: To what extent do reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback methods transfer across languages, and what mixture of English and multilingual preference data is needed to obtain strong alignment performance in languages beyond the ones used most heavily in training?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model that is to be aligned with human preferences via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Suppose the available preference data consists of an English-language portion of size $N_{\text{en}}$ together with multilingual portions of sizes $N_{\ell}$ for languages $\ell$ in a finite set $L$ of "training" languages. After alignment, the model is evaluated by human-judged win rates on prompts drawn from a possibly disjoint set $L'$ of "evaluation" languages (some of which may be unseen during preference training).

Formulate and answer the following:

(a) Quantify the degree of cross-lingual transfer of RLHF: given an alignment procedure $\mathcal{A}$ trained only on English preference data, characterize the expected gain in win rate $\Delta_\ell$ over an unaligned baseline in each evaluation language $\ell \in L'$, and identify structural properties of $\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., choice of reward model, on-policy vs. off-policy optimization, base-model multilinguality) that govern whether $\Delta_\ell > 0$ holds uniformly in $\ell$.

(b) Determine the optimal mixing distribution $\pi^* = (\pi_{\text{en}}, \{\pi_\ell\}_{\ell \in L})$ over preference-data sources, with $\pi_{\text{en}} + \sum_\ell \pi_\ell = 1$, that maximizes the worst-case win rate $\min_{\ell \in L'} W_\ell(\pi)$ over evaluation languages, including languages $\ell \notin L$ unseen at training time. In particular, give conditions under which a nontrivial mixture ($0 < \pi_{\text{en}} < 1$) strictly dominates English-only and uniform-multilingual strategies, and quantify the marginal benefit of adding each additional training language.
status_search_result: Recent empirical work has partially addressed both sub-questions. Studies on multilingual preference optimization show that RLHF/DPO trained on English-only data transfers to other languages (typical gains of several percent), and that mixing in multilingual preference data can substantially raise win rates in unseen languages (reported boosts up to ~19%). Work on cross-lingual transfer of reward models likewise demonstrates that English reward models built atop multilingual base models often outperform target-language ones by 3–4%. However, no general theory characterizes the optimal data mixture, and results depend strongly on base model, optimization method (e.g., RLOO vs. DPO), and language set, so the question is best described as partially solved.
