paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: Can Direct Preference Optimization improve large language models used as generative judges, so that they perform robust automatic evaluation across rating, pairwise comparison, and classification tasks while reducing common judge biases?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\pi_\theta$ denote a large language model (LLM) with parameters $\theta$, used as a "generative judge": given an input consisting of a task description $x$ together with one or more candidate responses, $\pi_\theta$ produces a textual judgment that can be parsed into one of three output formats:
  (i) a scalar rating $r \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ (rating task);
  (ii) a preference label $y \in \{A,B,\text{tie}\}$ selecting between two candidate responses (pairwise comparison task);
  (iii) a class label $c \in \mathcal{C}$ from a finite label set (classification task).

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, j^+_i, j^-_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ be a preference dataset of judgment pairs, where for each input $x_i$, $j^+_i$ is a "chosen" (preferred) judgment and $j^-_i$ is a "rejected" judgment, with preferences determined by ground-truth evaluations. Starting from a reference judge $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) by minimizing
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,j^+,j^-)\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(j^+\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(j^+\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(j^-\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(j^-\mid x)}\right)\right],$$
with temperature $\beta>0$, to obtain a DPO-tuned judge $\pi_\theta^{\mathrm{DPO}}$.

Define the following standard judge biases, each measured on held-out evaluation benchmarks:
  - position bias: sensitivity of pairwise verdicts to swapping the order of the two candidates;
  - verbosity bias: tendency to prefer longer responses controlling for quality;
  - self-preference bias: tendency to prefer outputs generated by $\pi_\theta$ itself;
  - sentiment bias: dependence of the verdict on positive/negative tone unrelated to correctness.

Let $\mathrm{Agree}(\pi;T)$ denote agreement with ground-truth or expert human labels on task type $T\in\{\text{rating},\text{pairwise},\text{classification}\}$, and let $B_b(\pi)$ denote the magnitude of bias $b$ for $b\in\{\text{position},\text{verbosity},\text{self-preference},\text{sentiment}\}$.

Problem. Determine whether there exists a choice of preference data $\mathcal{D}$, reference model $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and DPO hyperparameter $\beta$ such that the resulting judge $\pi_\theta^{\mathrm{DPO}}$ satisfies, simultaneously and on standard public benchmarks for each task type:
$$\mathrm{Agree}(\pi_\theta^{\mathrm{DPO}};T) \ge \mathrm{Agree}(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}};T) \quad \text{for every } T \in \{\text{rating},\text{pairwise},\text{classification}\},$$
$$B_b(\pi_\theta^{\mathrm{DPO}}) \le B_b(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) \quad \text{for every } b \in \{\text{position},\text{verbosity},\text{self-preference},\text{sentiment}\}.$$
Equivalently: can DPO training on contrastive judgment pairs yield a generative LLM judge that is simultaneously more accurate across rating, pairwise, and classification evaluation, and less biased along the four bias axes above, than its untuned reference?
status_search_result: Recent works (e.g., "Learning LLM-as-a-Judge for Preference Alignment", ICLR 2025; "Improve LLM-as-a-Judge Ability as a General Ability", arXiv 2502.11689) report that DPO-style training on self-generated contrastive judgment pairs improves LLM-judge accuracy and robustness against several biases compared with scalar reward models. However, comprehensive simultaneous reductions across all common judge biases (position, verbosity, self-preference, sentiment) together with improvements across rating, pairwise, and classification tasks have not been definitively established; surveys on judge biases (e.g., "Justice or Prejudice?", arXiv 2410.02736; "Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge", arXiv 2410.21819) indicate residual biases persist. The question is therefore partially addressed but not conclusively resolved.

Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge", "url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02736v1", "snippet": "Quantifies multiple biases (verbosity, position, self-preference, sentiment) that persist in LLM judges.", "claim": "Substantial biases remain in current LLM judges, so full simultaneous mitigation via DPO is not yet established."}, {"title": "Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21819", "snippet": "LLMs assign higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity regardless of whether self-generated, indicating persistent self-preference bias.", "claim": "Self-preference bias remains an unresolved issue for LLM judges."}]

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How should supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning be combined so that language models keep the formatting and instruction-following stability that supervised fine-tuning provides without falling into memorization that hurts out-of-domain generalization?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a pretrained autoregressive language model parameterized by θ ∈ Θ, modeling a conditional distribution p_θ(y | x) over output sequences y given input prompts x. Two standard post-training procedures are defined as follows.

(1) Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): given a labeled dataset D_SFT = {(x_i, y_i*)} drawn from a distribution P_in over prompts and target responses, minimize the negative log-likelihood
   L_SFT(θ) = − E_{(x,y*) ∼ D_SFT} [ log p_θ(y* | x) ].

(2) Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT): given a reward function r(x, y) ∈ ℝ (which may include format-compliance, correctness, and preference signals) and a reference model p_{θ_0}, maximize
   J_RL(θ) = E_{x ∼ P_in, y ∼ p_θ(·|x)} [ r(x, y) ] − β · E_{x ∼ P_in} [ KL( p_θ(·|x) ‖ p_{θ_0}(·|x) ) ],
   for some β ≥ 0.

Let P_out denote a distribution over out-of-domain prompts (with P_out ≠ P_in). For a model θ define the in-domain instruction-following / format-compliance score F(θ) = E_{x ∼ P_in}[ f(x, p_θ) ] (where f measures adherence to a prescribed formatting and instruction specification) and the out-of-domain generalization score G(θ) = E_{x ∼ P_out}[ g(x, p_θ) ] (where g measures task success on novel distributions).

Problem. Design a combined training procedure A — that is, a sequence (or interleaving) of SFT- and RFT-style updates together with explicit choices of objectives, data schedules, regularizers (e.g., KL penalties, replay of SFT data, weighting between L_SFT and J_RL), and stopping criteria — and prove non-trivial guarantees showing that the resulting parameters θ_A satisfy both:
   (a) F(θ_A) ≥ F(θ_SFT) − ε_1,   and
   (b) G(θ_A) ≥ G(θ_RFT) − ε_2,
where θ_SFT and θ_RFT denote the parameters obtained by pure SFT and pure RFT respectively, and ε_1, ε_2 are quantitatively small under explicit assumptions on the data, reward, and model class. In particular, characterize conditions under which A provably avoids the memorization regime of SFT (formalized, e.g., as a gap F(θ_SFT) − G(θ_SFT) bounded below) while retaining its formatting stability.
category_tag: LLM post-training: SFT vs RL generalization
status_search_result: Recent empirical work (e.g., "SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes", 2025) reports that SFT tends to memorize while RL generalizes better out-of-domain, and proposes mixing strategies, but no theoretically grounded procedure with provable guarantees combining the two is established. The question of an optimal principled combination remains an open research problem in 2025–2026.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How much do rigid output formats such as JSON, XML, or YAML interfere with reasoning in large language models, and when does the gain in output consistency outweigh the loss in cognitive flexibility?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model M that, given a natural-language reasoning task t drawn from a distribution T, produces an answer either in free-form text or under a rigid structured output format f ∈ {JSON, XML, YAML} specified in the prompt. Define:

- Reasoning accuracy A(M, f, T) = expected probability over t ~ T that the model's final answer is correct when constrained to output in format f (with A(M, ∅, T) denoting the unconstrained baseline).
- Output consistency C(M, f, T) = expected probability over t ~ T that the produced output is syntactically valid and conforms to the schema of f, and that repeated independent samples yield outputs whose parsed structures agree.
- Cognitive flexibility loss L(M, f, T) = A(M, ∅, T) − A(M, f, T).

The problem is to:

(a) Quantify L(M, f, T) for representative contemporary large language models M, reasoning task distributions T (e.g., arithmetic, multi-step logical deduction, commonsense reasoning, code generation), and structured formats f ∈ {JSON, XML, YAML}, exhibiting precise empirical or theoretical bounds on the degradation in reasoning accuracy attributable to imposing format f.

(b) Characterize, in terms of M, T, and f, the regime in which the gain in output consistency, C(M, f, T) − C(M, ∅, T), exceeds the loss in cognitive flexibility, L(M, f, T), under a stated utility functional U(A, C) combining accuracy and consistency (e.g., U = αA + (1−α)C for α ∈ [0,1]). Determine the threshold value(s) of α, and the structural properties of T (such as required reasoning depth or branching factor) at which the optimal choice of f switches from unconstrained output to one of the rigid formats.
status_search_result: Recent empirical studies (e.g., Tam et al. 2024, "Let Me Speak Freely?") report that imposing rigid structured output formats like JSON or XML often degrades reasoning accuracy of LLMs across benchmarks, while improving parseability. However, no general theoretical characterization of the trade-off or precise threshold conditions is established, and findings vary by model and task. The question of when consistency gains outweigh reasoning losses remains an active, unresolved area of empirical investigation.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How effective are large language models in retrieval-augmented generation when they must process very long contexts, what context lengths are actually optimal, and how can systems avoid failure modes such as degradation, repetition, copyright-related failures, and lost-in-the-middle effects beyond those thresholds?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system in which a large language model (LLM) receives a query together with a concatenated context of retrieved passages of total token length L, and outputs a response. Let task performance be measured by a fixed quality metric Q(L) (e.g., exact-match accuracy or factuality score) on a benchmark of question–context pairs. Empirically, Q(L) is observed to be non-monotonic in L: it improves up to some task- and model-dependent threshold L* and then degrades, exhibiting failure modes such as (i) generic quality degradation, (ii) repetition loops, (iii) verbatim reproduction of copyrighted training material, and (iv) the "lost-in-the-middle" effect, in which information located near the middle of the context is used with lower probability than information at the beginning or end.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

1. Characterize, theoretically or empirically, the optimal context length L*(M, T) for a given LLM M and task T, and quantify how L*(M, T) depends on properties of M (e.g., training context window, positional encoding scheme, post-training procedure) and of T (e.g., reasoning depth, number of supporting passages).

2. Provide rigorous bounds or scaling laws describing the rate of degradation of Q(L) for L > L*(M, T), and identify the mechanisms (attention dilution, positional encoding extrapolation error, lack of long-context post-training, etc.) that drive each of the four failure modes above.

3. Design an algorithm or architectural modification that, given a target task T and model M, mitigates all four failure modes simultaneously when L significantly exceeds L*(M, T), with provable or empirically verified guarantees on Q(L).
status_search_result: The question is a broad, ongoing research challenge in the LLM/RAG literature rather than a single closed mathematical conjecture. Recent works (e.g., "Lost in the Middle" by Liu et al. 2023, and various 2024–2025 long-context RAG benchmarks such as LongBench, RULER, NoLiMa) confirm that optimal context length is model- and task-dependent and that degradation, repetition, and lost-in-the-middle effects persist in state-of-the-art systems. No general solution is established, so the problem is considered open.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How important is the choice and strength of the reference model in Direct Preference Optimization, including the KL-divergence setting and the compatibility between the policy and the reference model, for obtaining strong alignment performance?
self_contained_problem:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a method for aligning a parametric policy $\pi_	heta(y\mid x)$ (e.g., a language model) to human preferences without an explicit reward model. Given a dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(x, y_w, y_l)\}$ of prompts $x$ with a preferred response $y_w$ and a dispreferred response $y_l$, and a fixed reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)$, DPO minimizes the loss
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(	heta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\!\left( eta\log rac{\pi_	heta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} -  eta\log rac{\pi_	heta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}ight)ight],$$
where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid and $ eta>0$ controls the implicit KL-divergence regularization $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_	heta\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$.

Problem. Characterize, both theoretically and empirically, the role of the reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in DPO. Specifically:
(a) Quantify how the alignment quality of the optimal $\pi_	heta$ depends on the choice and the ``strength'' of $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (for example, when $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a base supervised-fine-tuned model versus an already-aligned/DPO-trained model).
(b) Determine how the optimal setting of $ eta$ (equivalently the KL-divergence budget) depends on $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and on the relationship between $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\pi_	heta$.
(c) Formalize a notion of compatibility between the policy $\pi_	heta$ and the reference $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (e.g., in terms of support overlap or KL closeness at initialization) and prove conditions under which this compatibility is necessary or sufficient for DPO to converge to a policy with strong preference-alignment guarantees.
status_search_result: The question of how the choice of reference model and KL strength affects DPO is an active research topic. Recent works (e.g., on reference-free DPO variants such as SimPO, on iterative/self-rewarding DPO, and on analyses of the KL regularization term) suggest the issue is only partially understood and remains open in its full generality.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: What is the right balance between online and offline alignment algorithms for large language models, given that online methods benefit from fresh on-policy data and stronger generative quality while offline methods can remain competitive on pairwise classification tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of aligning a generative language model policy $\pi_	heta(y\mid x)$ to a preference signal encoded by a reward model $r(x,y)$ or a pairwise preference distribution $p^*(y\succ y'\mid x)$. Two broad families of alignment algorithms are considered:

1. Offline alignment: Given a fixed dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i^+,y_i^-)\}$ of preference pairs sampled from a reference distribution (e.g., a supervised fine-tuned model $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$), train $\pi_	heta$ by minimizing an offline objective such as Direct Preference Optimization:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}(	heta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^+,y^-)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\log\sigma\!\Big( eta\log	frac{\pi_	heta(y^+\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^+\mid x)}- eta\log	frac{\pi_	heta(y^-\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^-\mid x)}\Big)\Big].$$

2. Online alignment: Repeatedly sample fresh on-policy responses $y\sim\pi_	heta(\cdot\mid x)$, label them with $r$ or a preference oracle, and update $\pi_	heta$ via an online objective such as RLHF/PPO with KL regularization toward $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

Empirically, offline-trained policies tend to perform better on pairwise classification metrics (e.g., choosing the preferred response among two candidates), while online-trained policies tend to produce higher-quality generations under sampling.

Problem: Provide a principled characterization of the optimal trade-off between online and offline alignment. Specifically, design an alignment procedure (possibly hybrid) together with a theoretical analysis that:
(a) quantifies, in terms of dataset size, distribution shift between $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\pi_	heta$, reward-model accuracy, and KL budget, when on-policy sampling is necessary to achieve a given generation-quality bound; and
(b) identifies a schedule or mixing rule between offline preference optimization and on-policy updates that simultaneously matches the pairwise-classification performance of pure offline methods and the generative performance of pure online methods, with provable guarantees on the resulting policy's expected reward and KL divergence from $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research problem in LLM alignment. Recent works (e.g., Tang et al. 2024 "Understanding the performance gap between online and offline alignment algorithms"; Guo et al. 2024 on online AI feedback; Xu et al. 2024 on DPO vs PPO) document the trade-off but do not provide a definitive theoretical characterization or universally accepted hybrid recipe, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How can large language models be leveraged more effectively for code compilation and optimization, including compiler reasoning over intermediate representations and assembly, so that they become a practical foundation for scalable compiler research and deployment?
self_contained_problem:
Design a methodology that leverages large language models (LLMs) as a practical and scalable foundation for compiler construction and code optimization. Concretely:

1. Specify a training and/or inference framework in which an LLM takes as input a program representation drawn from one or more of the following: high-level source code, compiler intermediate representations (e.g., SSA-form IR such as LLVM IR), or target-machine assembly, together with optional optimization-pass metadata, target descriptions, and performance feedback signals.

2. The LLM must be able to perform at least the following tasks with measurable, reproducible quality:
   (a) predict or generate sequences of optimization passes (phase ordering) that improve a chosen objective such as runtime, code size, or energy on a held-out benchmark set;
   (b) translate between representations (e.g., source ↔ IR ↔ assembly) while preserving semantics under a formal equivalence relation (such as input/output equivalence on a test suite, or a stronger translation-validation criterion);
   (c) reason about and rewrite IR or assembly so that the rewritten program is semantically equivalent to the original and improves a stated cost metric.

3. Provide formal criteria under which the LLM-based compiler pipeline can be considered correct (semantic preservation), efficient (improvement over a baseline optimizing compiler such as -O3), and scalable (cost per compiled function, ability to generalize across architectures and languages).

The problem is to determine whether such a framework exists that simultaneously meets the correctness, efficiency, and scalability criteria, and to characterize the techniques (data curation, fine-tuning objectives, reinforcement learning signals, verifier integration, search procedures over the LLM's outputs) required to achieve it.
status_search_result: The question of building LLMs into a robust foundation for compiler optimization is an active research area. Works such as Meta's "Large Language Models for Compiler Optimization" (Cummins et al., 2023) and follow-ups on LLM-based phase ordering, IR reasoning, and superoptimization show partial progress (e.g., predicting optimization-pass sequences from LLVM IR with modest gains), but no comprehensive, semantically guaranteed, and broadly deployed framework exists. The problem is generally regarded as open in both academia and industry as of 2026.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How can very large Mixture-of-Experts language models be trained efficiently despite the communication and multi-GPU parallelization challenges introduced by dynamic token routing, high memory usage, and specialized expert orchestration?
self_contained_problem: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model is a neural network in which each transformer layer contains E expert subnetworks f_1,...,f_E and a gating function g(x) that, for each input token x, selects a sparse subset S(x) ⊂ {1,...,E} (typically |S(x)| = k with k ≪ E) of experts to evaluate; the layer output is sum_{i ∈ S(x)} g_i(x) f_i(x). When such a model with billions of parameters is trained on a cluster of P GPUs using a combination of data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism, the dynamic, input-dependent routing of tokens to experts induces (i) all-to-all communication of token activations between devices that host different experts, (ii) load imbalance across experts and devices, (iii) high peak memory usage from storing expert parameters, optimizer states, and routed activations, and (iv) synchronization costs between forward routing, expert computation, and backward gradient exchange.\n\nProblem. Design a training algorithm and a parallelization/communication scheme for large-scale MoE models that provably or empirically minimizes end-to-end training time and memory while preserving model quality. Concretely, specify: (a) a token-to-expert routing rule and a load-balancing objective that bounds the maximum expert load with high probability; (b) a placement of experts and a schedule of all-to-all (or alternative) collective communications that overlaps communication with expert computation; (c) memory-management techniques (e.g., parameter/optimizer sharding, activation recomputation, offloading) such that the per-device memory remains within a given budget M; and (d) an analysis showing that the resulting per-step cost in terms of FLOPs, bytes communicated, and memory is asymptotically optimal (or within an explicit factor of a stated lower bound) as a function of E, k, P, model dimension d, sequence length L, and batch size B. Establish either a quantitative efficiency guarantee or identify the fundamental obstructions that prevent such a guarantee.
status_search_result: Efficient training of very large MoE models is an active area of research with many partial solutions (e.g., GShard, Switch Transformer, DeepSpeed-MoE, Tutel, MegaBlocks, expert-choice routing, DeepSeek-MoE) addressing aspects of communication, load balancing, and memory. No single algorithm is recognized as a complete or provably optimal solution; the problem remains open in the sense that improved schemes are still being proposed and no matching lower bounds are established.

paper_title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
original_question: How can reinforcement-learning methods for large language models explore a more diverse set of mathematical reasoning paths within limited sampling budgets, instead of repeatedly reinforcing common patterns and converging to local optima, so that long chain-of-thought training more fully approaches the base model's theoretical reasoning ceiling?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a base autoregressive language model $\pi_0$ that, given a mathematical problem $x$, induces a distribution over chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories $y$ and final answers $a(y)$. Let the theoretical reasoning ceiling of $\pi_0$ on a problem distribution $\mathcal{D}$ be defined as $C(\pi_0) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\Pr_{y\sim\pi_0(\cdot\mid x)}[\exists\, y \text{ in the support such that } a(y) \text{ is correct}]\big]$, i.e., the pass-at-infinity accuracy of $\pi_0$.

Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning produces a policy $\pi_\theta$ by maximizing $J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[R(x,y)]$, where $R$ is a reward signal (e.g., final-answer correctness) and only $N$ samples per prompt may be drawn during training (the sampling budget). Empirically, gradient-based updates on $\pi_\theta$ tend to concentrate probability mass on a small set of reasoning patterns already favored by $\pi_0$, so that the resulting greedy or low-temperature accuracy of $\pi_\theta$ falls strictly below $C(\pi_0)$.

Design a reinforcement-learning training procedure (specified by an objective, a sampling/exploration mechanism, and an update rule) that operates under a fixed per-prompt sampling budget $N$ and provably or empirically:
(1) maintains diversity of reasoning trajectories during training, in the sense that the entropy of the induced distribution over a meaningful equivalence-class partition of reasoning paths does not collapse;
(2) avoids convergence to a local optimum that strictly underperforms $C(\pi_0)$;
(3) drives the accuracy of $\pi_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}$ toward the ceiling $C(\pi_0)$ as training proceeds.

Formulate such a procedure and establish quantitative guarantees, or otherwise characterize the obstructions that prevent any procedure within a specified class from achieving (1)–(3).
status_search_result: This is an actively studied open research direction. Recent works in 2024–2025 (e.g., on entropy-regularized RLHF, diversity-preserving PPO/GRPO variants, and analyses of pass@k vs. pass@1 collapse in RL-tuned LLMs) document that RL fine-tuning narrows the reasoning distribution and underperforms the base model's pass@k ceiling, but no method has been shown to close this gap in general.

paper_title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
original_question: How should a large language model decide when to invoke external resources such as calculators, code interpreters, geometric visualizers, or retrieval systems, and by what interaction strategy should it use those resources, so that mathematical reasoning can go beyond the model's parametric knowledge while remaining accurate and scalable as the number of available modules grows?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an autoregressive language model M that generates token sequences and that has access to a finite set T = {t_1, ..., t_k} of external tools (for example, a symbolic calculator, a code interpreter, a geometric visualizer, and a retrieval system over a corpus of mathematical documents). At each generation step, M may either emit a natural-language/math token or invoke a tool t_i with an argument string a, receive a textual response r, and condition future generation on r.

Formalize and solve the following problem:

(a) Define a decision policy π that, given the current reasoning state (the prompt and the partial chain of generated tokens), outputs one of the actions {continue internally, invoke t_i with argument a for some i ∈ {1, ..., k}}, together with a quantitative criterion that determines when external invocation strictly improves expected accuracy on a distribution D of mathematical problems compared with purely internal reasoning.

(b) Specify an interaction strategy (single-call, iterative, or interleaved) governing how the model integrates tool outputs back into its reasoning trace, and give conditions under which the strategy preserves soundness (no introduction of unverified intermediate claims) and improves end-to-end correctness.

(c) Prove (or give algorithms with provable guarantees) that the resulting accuracy of M+π on D scales gracefully as k → ∞, in the sense that the per-step decision cost and the probability of selecting a suboptimal tool grow at most polylogarithmically in k, while the expected solution accuracy is non-decreasing in k.

Provide either a constructive method achieving (a)–(c) or an impossibility result identifying obstructions.
category_tag: Tool-augmented language models for mathematical reasoning
status_search_result: Tool-use policies for LLM mathematical reasoning (when to invoke calculators, code interpreters, retrieval, etc., and how to scale to many tools) remain an active research area. Existing systems (e.g., Toolformer, ToRA, MathCoder, PAL, ART) provide partial empirical solutions for small tool sets, but no general policy with provable accuracy/scalability guarantees as the tool inventory grows is established. Recent surveys list this as an open challenge.

paper_title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
original_question: How can long chain-of-thought mathematical reasoning be optimized so that models reach correct answers through logically consistent and efficient intermediate steps, rather than through unnecessarily long or convoluted reasoning paths that are rewarded only for their final answer correctness; in particular, what verification-aware training or tool-integrated methods can reliably improve the quality of intermediate reasoning steps?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a language model M that, given a mathematical problem x, generates a long chain-of-thought reasoning trace r = (s_1, s_2, ..., s_T) followed by a final answer a, where each s_i is an intermediate reasoning step. Suppose M is trained by reinforcement learning or preference optimization using an outcome-based reward R_out(x, r, a) that depends only on the correctness of the final answer a (e.g., R_out = 1 if a equals the ground-truth answer a*(x) and 0 otherwise). Empirically, such training produces reasoning trajectories that may contain logical errors, redundant steps, or unnecessarily long detours even when a is correct, because intermediate quality is not directly rewarded.

Formulate and analyze training objectives and algorithms that optimize for both final-answer correctness and the logical consistency and efficiency of the intermediate steps. Concretely:

(a) Define a notion of "step quality" Q(s_i | s_{<i}, x) — for example, via per-step verifiers V (process reward models), formal-proof checkers, or external tool calls (symbolic solvers, code execution) that validate or refute s_i — and design a composite reward
   R(x, r, a) = α · R_out(x, r, a) + β · Σ_i Q(s_i | s_{<i}, x) − γ · |r|,
that penalizes path length and rewards verified intermediate correctness.

(b) Develop a verification-aware training procedure (e.g., reinforcement learning with process supervision, or tool-integrated rollouts in which the model interleaves reasoning with calls to a deterministic verifier) that provably or empirically improves the joint quality of (r, a) over purely outcome-supervised training, in the sense that the trained model attains, on a fixed benchmark distribution of problems, both (i) at least the same final-answer accuracy and (ii) strictly higher average step-level correctness and/or shorter average reasoning length.

(c) Identify conditions under which such tool-integrated long-chain-of-thought training reliably avoids reward hacking (e.g., the model learning to invoke tools spuriously or to produce verifier-pleasing but mathematically vacuous steps), and quantify the trade-off between α, β, γ and the resulting accuracy/efficiency frontier.

The problem is to give a principled construction of such a verification-aware or tool-integrated training method together with a theoretical or empirical guarantee that it improves intermediate reasoning quality without degrading final accuracy.
status_search_result: This is an active research direction. Process-reward models (e.g., PRM800K, Math-Shepherd), tool-integrated reasoning (ToRA, MathCoder), and verifier-guided RL methods have been proposed and yield partial improvements, but no method is established as a definitive solution: producing reliably concise, logically consistent long chains-of-thought remains an open problem as of 2026.

paper_title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
original_question: How can large language models generalize mathematical reasoning abilities to open-ended real-world domains where binary correctness signals are unavailable, including how to trigger and use abstract meta-skills in complex scenarios and how to design reward functions that support higher-order reasoning outside narrowly defined mathematics benchmarks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model (LLM) that has been trained to perform multi-step mathematical reasoning in settings where each candidate solution admits a binary correctness signal (for example, a verifiable final numerical answer or a formal proof check). Suppose the model has acquired, through such training, a collection of abstract "meta-skills" such as decomposition, abstraction, analogical transfer, self-verification, and planning. Address the following research problem:

(a) Formulate a principled mechanism by which such an LLM can reliably trigger and deploy these meta-skills when presented with open-ended tasks drawn from real-world domains in which no binary correctness oracle is available and ground-truth solutions may be ambiguous, multi-valued, or only partially specified.

(b) Design a family of reward functions r(x, y) — where x is a task prompt from an open-ended distribution and y is a model response — together with an associated training/optimization procedure, such that optimizing the model against these rewards provably (or empirically with rigorous evaluation) improves higher-order reasoning performance on tasks lying outside narrowly defined mathematical benchmarks, while not degrading performance on tasks that do admit binary correctness signals.

(c) Provide an evaluation framework, including benchmarks and metrics, that demonstrates transfer of mathematical reasoning competence to open-domain reasoning, and quantifies the extent to which the meta-skills identified in (a) are causally responsible for the observed transfer.

The goal is to give a complete specification — mechanism, reward design, training procedure, and evaluation — addressing how mathematical-reasoning capabilities of LLMs can be generalized to open-ended real-world domains without binary correctness signals.
status_search_result: This is a stated open research direction concerning generalization of LLM mathematical reasoning to open-ended domains with non-binary feedback. Current literature on process reward models, RLHF/RLAIF, and reasoning-model training discusses partial progress (e.g., process reward models, generative verifiers, rubric-based rewards), but no widely accepted solution exists. The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
original_question: Is the Pass@k metric, including the specific choice of k, an appropriate and comprehensive way to measure the reasoning capabilities of both base and fine-tuned large language models, or does reliance on that metric miss important aspects of mathematical reasoning quality and therefore lead to limited conclusions about model improvement?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be a probabilistic model that, given a mathematical problem x drawn from a distribution D over a problem set X, produces candidate solutions according to a conditional distribution p_M(·|x). For each problem x, assume there is a verifier v_x: Y → {0,1} that declares a candidate solution y correct (v_x(y)=1) or incorrect. For a positive integer k, define the Pass@k score of M on D by

  Pass@k(M, D) = E_{x ~ D} [ 1 − (1 − r_M(x))^k ],

where r_M(x) = Pr_{y ~ p_M(·|x)}[v_x(y) = 1] is the per-problem success probability (equivalently, Pass@k equals the probability that at least one of k independent samples from p_M(·|x) is verified correct, averaged over D).

Investigate the following question rigorously:

(a) Identify mathematically meaningful aspects of reasoning quality on D — for instance, the distribution of r_M(x) across problems, the logical validity of intermediate steps, the diversity of correct proofs produced, robustness under perturbations of x, or calibration of confidence — that are not determined by, or are provably invariant under transformations that change, the family {Pass@k(M, D) : k ≥ 1}.

(b) Prove or disprove: there exist two models M_1 and M_2 such that Pass@k(M_1, D) = Pass@k(M_2, D) for all k ≥ 1, yet M_1 and M_2 differ in a precisely defined reasoning-quality criterion of the type in (a).

(c) Determine whether a single fixed choice of k can suffice to rank models consistently with such a reasoning-quality criterion, or exhibit, for any fixed k, a pair of models whose Pass@k ordering disagrees with the ordering induced by the criterion.

Conclude whether Pass@k, with any choice of k, constitutes a comprehensive measure of mathematical reasoning capability for both base and fine-tuned probabilistic generative models, or whether reliance on it necessarily omits identifiable structural features of reasoning quality.
status_search_result: This is an open evaluation/methodological question. Recent work (e.g., analyses of Pass@k for base vs RL-fine-tuned LLMs) has argued that Pass@k can mislead when k is varied, that base models may match fine-tuned ones at large k, and that the metric does not capture step-level correctness, calibration, or proof diversity; however no consensus replacement metric has been established, so the question remains open.

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems be designed to generalize across multiple domains such as customer service, healthcare, and education without extensive retraining, while still remaining sensitive to domain-specific context, scaling through modular adaptation, and improving over time from realistic multi-domain interaction data and user feedback?
self_contained_problem:
Design a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system that, given a multi-turn dialogue history and a current user query, produces accurate answers across heterogeneous target domains (for example, customer service, healthcare, and education) under the following requirements:

1. Cross-domain generalization without extensive retraining: The system must achieve competitive answer-quality performance on previously unseen domains using only lightweight adaptation (e.g., a small number of in-domain examples, prompts, or adapter modules) rather than full model retraining.

2. Domain-sensitivity: The system must condition its responses on domain-specific context, terminology, conventions, and constraints (e.g., medical safety considerations in healthcare, pedagogical scaffolding in education, policy compliance in customer service).

3. Modular scalability: The architecture must support adding new domains through modular components (such as domain adapters, retrievers, or knowledge modules) whose number of trainable parameters and computational cost scale sublinearly with the number of domains supported.

4. Continual improvement from interaction: The system must improve over time by learning from realistic multi-domain interaction logs and user feedback signals (explicit ratings, corrections, or implicit signals) while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of previously learned domains.

Provide (a) a formal specification of the system (input/output spaces, training objective, adaptation procedure, and feedback-incorporation mechanism), (b) an evaluation protocol that simultaneously measures cross-domain generalization, domain-specific accuracy, modular scalability, and continual-learning stability, and (c) theoretical or empirical guarantees that the proposed design satisfies requirements (1)–(4) jointly.
status_search_result: Cross-domain generalization of conversational question answering without extensive retraining is widely recognized in the NLP literature as an unresolved research direction. While modular adaptation methods (adapters, LoRA, retrieval augmentation) and continual learning techniques have made partial progress, no system currently meets all four requirements jointly with established guarantees, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems support multi-turn reasoning over multimodal inputs by jointly processing text together with images, videos, and audio, while maintaining cross-modal consistency, coherence, and strong evaluation performance in realistic applications?
self_contained_problem:
Design a conversational question answering framework that supports multi-turn reasoning over heterogeneous multimodal inputs. Formally, let a dialogue be a finite sequence of turns $(u_1, r_1, u_2, r_2, \ldots, u_T)$, where each user turn $u_t$ is associated with a context $C_t = (X_t^{\text{txt}}, X_t^{\text{img}}, X_t^{\text{vid}}, X_t^{\text{aud}})$ consisting of (possibly empty) textual, image, video, and audio components. The task is to construct a model $f$ that, given the dialogue history $H_t = (u_1, r_1, \ldots, u_{t-1}, r_{t-1})$ together with the multimodal context $C_t$ and the current question $u_t$, produces a response $r_t = f(H_t, C_t, u_t)$ such that:

1. (Cross-modal grounding) $r_t$ is consistent with the joint semantic content of $X_t^{\text{txt}}, X_t^{\text{img}}, X_t^{\text{vid}}, X_t^{\text{aud}}$, meaning no claim in $r_t$ contradicts evidence available in any single modality or across modalities.
2. (Coherence) $r_t$ is logically and topically consistent with all previous turns in $H_t$, including resolution of coreference and ellipsis whose antecedents may occur in any modality.
3. (Evaluation performance) On standardized multimodal multi-turn QA benchmarks, $f$ achieves answer accuracy, grounding fidelity, and dialogue-coherence scores that meet or exceed predefined performance thresholds reflective of realistic deployment requirements.

Provide explicit architectural, training, and evaluation principles for $f$, and prove (empirically or theoretically) that the resulting system simultaneously satisfies the cross-modal consistency, coherence, and performance conditions above in realistic application settings.
status_search_result: This is an open research direction in multimodal conversational QA. No single system has been shown to comprehensively satisfy all the requirements (multi-turn reasoning across text, image, video, and audio with cross-modal consistency and strong benchmark performance) in realistic deployments; ongoing work on multimodal large language models continues to address subsets of these challenges.
status_evidence: [{"title": "A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05716", "snippet": "Future systems should be able to process and integrate multimodal inputs, including images, videos, and audio.", "claim": "Multimodal integration in ConvQA is identified as an open future direction."}]

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems learn and retain user-specific information such as preferred response formats, expertise levels, emotional tone preferences, and long-term goals so that answers become more personalized and context-aware, while preserving privacy, transparency, fairness, and resistance to harmful bias?
self_contained_problem:
Design a conversational question-answering system, modeled as a function that maps a user identifier u, a dialogue history H_u = (q_1, a_1, ..., q_{t-1}, a_{t-1}), and a current query q_t to an answer a_t, together with an evolving user profile P_u. The profile P_u is required to encode user-specific attributes including (i) preferred response formats (e.g., concise vs. detailed, textual vs. structured), (ii) inferred domain expertise levels, (iii) emotional tone preferences, (iv) recurring topics of interest, and (v) long-term goals expressed or implied across sessions. Specify and analyze algorithms for updating P_u online from interaction signals (explicit feedback, implicit behavior, linguistic cues), and for conditioning answer generation on P_u so that answers improve, under suitable evaluation metrics, in personalization and context-awareness relative to a non-personalized baseline.

The system must simultaneously satisfy formal guarantees in the following four directions:
1. Privacy: profile updates and storage admit a quantifiable privacy guarantee (for example, (ε, δ)-differential privacy with respect to any single user utterance, or an equivalent formal notion), and no user-specific attribute can be reconstructed from released model outputs beyond a stated bound.
2. Transparency: there exists an inspection mechanism providing, on request, a human-readable account of which elements of P_u influenced a given answer a_t.
3. Fairness: for a specified collection of protected attribute groups G_1, ..., G_k, the answer quality metric Q satisfies a stated group-fairness criterion (e.g., |E[Q | G_i] − E[Q | G_j]| ≤ η for all i, j).
4. Bias resistance: there is a quantitative bound on the probability that the system, conditioned on any profile P_u, produces outputs flagged as harmful by a fixed harmfulness classifier, uniformly over admissible profiles.

Construct such a system, prove that the four guarantees can be achieved jointly with provable personalization gain, or alternatively establish impossibility/trade-off theorems characterizing the achievable region among these objectives.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in conversational AI rather than a settled mathematical problem. Surveys and recent work on personalized dialogue systems, differential privacy in language models, and fairness in NLP describe partial approaches (memory-augmented LLMs, DP fine-tuning, fairness audits) but no unified solution with joint formal guarantees is established as of mid-2026.

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems update their knowledge and response strategies during interaction in real time, using online adaptation methods such as reinforcement learning, active learning, continual learning, self-supervision, retrieval-augmented generation, or federated learning, while remaining accurate, robust, privacy-preserving, and resistant to catastrophic forgetting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system that maintains an internal knowledge representation K_t and a response policy π_t at interaction step t. The system receives a stream of user turns (q_1, q_2, ...) and must produce answers (a_1, a_2, ...) while continuously updating (K_t, π_t) in real time. Design and analyze an online adaptation framework that integrates one or more of the following learning paradigms — reinforcement learning (with reward signals derived from user feedback), active learning (with selective query/clarification strategies), continual/lifelong learning (with mechanisms against catastrophic forgetting such as elastic weight consolidation, replay buffers, or parameter isolation), self-supervised learning (with auxiliary objectives from conversational context), retrieval-augmented generation (with a dynamically updatable external memory or index), and federated learning (with decentralized updates that never expose raw user data) — such that the resulting system simultaneously satisfies the following criteria:

(i) Accuracy: expected answer quality on a held-out evaluation distribution does not degrade across t.
(ii) Robustness: performance remains stable under distribution shift and adversarial or noisy user inputs.
(iii) Privacy preservation: updates from any individual user satisfy a quantifiable privacy guarantee (e.g., differential privacy with budget ε).
(iv) Resistance to catastrophic forgetting: performance on previously encountered topics or skills does not deteriorate by more than a prescribed tolerance after adaptation to new ones.

Provide an explicit algorithmic procedure together with theoretical or empirical guarantees that jointly establish properties (i)–(iv), and characterize the trade-offs (e.g., privacy–utility, plasticity–stability, exploration–exploitation) inherent in such a real-time adaptive ConvQA system.
status_search_result: The problem is a broad open research challenge in conversational AI. No single published method is known to jointly satisfy accuracy, robustness, privacy preservation, and resistance to catastrophic forgetting in real-time ConvQA adaptation; recent surveys and works treat each axis (continual learning, federated learning, RAG, RLHF) largely in isolation, indicating the integrated problem remains open.
status_evidence: [{"title": "A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05716", "snippet": "Modern ConvQA architectures now incorporate advanced real-time learning methodologies, i.e., RL, AL, CL, online machine learning, and meta-learning.", "claim": "Real-time online adaptation in ConvQA is described as an emerging, unsolved direction integrating multiple learning paradigms."}]

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems manage long multi-turn interaction histories by selectively retaining, summarizing, compressing, or discarding earlier turns so that they preserve the context most relevant to the current query, continue to track evolving user goals and topic shifts, and still scale to prolonged real-world conversations?
self_contained_problem: Consider a conversational question answering system that processes a sequence of user-system interaction turns t_1, t_2, ..., t_n, where each turn t_i consists of a user utterance u_i and a system response r_i. At each new query u_{n+1}, the system must produce an answer r_{n+1} that depends on relevant prior context drawn from the interaction history H_n = (t_1, ..., t_n). Because |H_n| grows unboundedly with n while computational and memory budgets for context are finite, the system needs a dynamic history-management policy π that, given H_n and u_{n+1}, outputs a transformed compact context C_n with |C_n| ≤ B (for a fixed budget B) by applying operations from the set {retain turn t_i verbatim, summarize a subset of turns into a shorter abstract, compress a turn or group of turns into a lossy representation, discard a turn}. The policy must satisfy the following desiderata simultaneously: (i) C_n preserves the information in H_n most relevant for correctly answering u_{n+1}; (ii) π tracks evolving user goals and topic shifts, i.e., adapts its retain/summarize/compress/discard decisions when the conversational focus changes; (iii) π remains computationally tractable and answer-quality-preserving as n → ∞ in prolonged real-world dialogues. Design such a policy π (or prove fundamental limits on it), and provide a framework with provable or empirically validated guarantees that jointly achieve (i)–(iii).
status_search_result: Dynamic conversational-history management for long multi-turn QA/dialogue remains an active open research direction. Recent work proposes selective retention, summarization, and compression methods (e.g., memory-augmented LLMs, recurrent memory, RAG over dialogue history, summary memory buffers), but no method jointly solves relevance preservation, topic-shift tracking, and unbounded scalability with provable guarantees.

paper_title: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art in Conversational Question Answering Systems
original_question: How can conversational question answering systems respond appropriately when user queries are ambiguous or the available information is uncertain, for example by generating multiple plausible answers, attaching confidence scores and explanations, asking clarifying follow-up questions, detecting contradictions, or declining low-confidence responses in high-stakes settings such as healthcare or legal advice?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system modeled as a function that, given a dialogue history $h$ and a user query $q$, produces a response $r$ together with auxiliary metadata. Assume the system has access to an information source (e.g., a knowledge base, document corpus, or learned language model) from which candidate answers $\{a_1, \ldots, a_k\}$ can be retrieved or generated, each associated with an estimated confidence $c_i \in [0,1]$. Suppose that some queries are ambiguous (admit multiple distinct correct interpretations) and that some retrievable information is uncertain (low confidence, conflicting, or incomplete).

Design and rigorously analyze a response policy $\pi$ for such a ConvQA system that simultaneously addresses the following requirements:

1. (Multiple plausible answers) When the posterior over interpretations or answers is multimodal, $\pi$ outputs a calibrated set of plausible answers rather than a single one.
2. (Confidence and explanation) Each answer is annotated with a confidence score $c_i$ that is calibrated in the sense that, conditionally on $c_i = c$, the empirical accuracy equals $c$, together with an explanation tracing the answer to supporting evidence.
3. (Clarification) When the ambiguity of $q$ given $h$ (measured, e.g., by the entropy of the posterior over interpretations) exceeds a threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{amb}}$, $\pi$ issues a clarifying follow-up question that maximally reduces expected ambiguity.
4. (Contradiction detection) If retrieved evidence $E$ contains mutually inconsistent statements, $\pi$ flags the contradiction and abstains from asserting either branch as fact.
5. (Selective prediction in high-stakes domains) In domains designated as high-stakes (e.g., medical or legal advice), $\pi$ declines to answer whenever the top confidence $\max_i c_i$ falls below a domain-specific threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{hs}}$, with provable bounds on the residual risk.

The problem is to specify such a policy $\pi$, prove calibration and risk guarantees (e.g., a PAC-style bound on the probability of confidently asserting an incorrect answer in high-stakes settings), and characterize the trade-off between answer coverage, clarification frequency, and risk.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction in conversational QA. No single definitive solution exists; recent work addresses individual components (calibration, selective prediction, clarification question generation, contradiction detection) but a unified, provably calibrated policy with risk guarantees for high-stakes ConvQA remains open.

context_brief: Kuratowski continuity of spheres in the sub-Riemannian limit
original_question: For the same Heisenberg group and the family of Riemannian optimal-control problems P_epsilon with epsilon > 0, together with the limiting sub-Riemannian problem P0 obtained from the dynamics q_dot = u1 X1 + u2 X2 with u1^2+u2^2 <= 1 and the same endpoint time-minimization objective, establish whether the family of spheres S_epsilon(r) is continuous in the Kuratowski sense as epsilon tends to 0, with limiting family S0(r).
self_contained_problem:
Let M = H be the three-dimensional Heisenberg group, identified with R^3 with coordinates q = (x, y, z), equipped with the left-invariant vector fields
  X1 = ∂/∂x − (y/2) ∂/∂z,   X2 = ∂/∂y + (x/2) ∂/∂z,   X3 = ∂/∂z = [X1, X2].

For each ε > 0, consider the Riemannian time-optimal control problem P_ε:
  q̇ = u1 X1(q) + u2 X2(q) + ε u3 X3(q),   (u1, u2, u3) ∈ R^3,   u1^2 + u2^2 + u3^2 ≤ 1,
  q(0) = q0,   q(t1) = q1,   t1 → min,
where the left-invariant Riemannian metric g_ε is the one making (X1, X2, (1/ε) X3) orthonormal (equivalently, the control bound corresponds to a quadratic admissible velocity set).

Consider also the limiting sub-Riemannian problem P0:
  q̇ = u1 X1(q) + u2 X2(q),   u1^2 + u2^2 ≤ 1,   q(0) = q0,   q(t1) = q1,   t1 → min.

Denote by d_ε (resp. d_0) the associated time-optimal (i.e. Riemannian, resp. sub-Riemannian Carnot–Carathéodory) distance from the identity e ∈ H, and by
  S_ε(r) = { q ∈ H : d_ε(e, q) = r },   S_0(r) = { q ∈ H : d_0(e, q) = r },
the corresponding spheres of radius r > 0.

Recall that a family of closed subsets {A_ε}_{ε>0} of a metric space (X, d) converges to A_0 in the Kuratowski sense as ε → 0 if both:
 (i) every limit point of sequences x_{ε_n} ∈ A_{ε_n} with ε_n → 0 lies in A_0;
 (ii) every point of A_0 is the limit of some sequence x_{ε_n} ∈ A_{ε_n} with ε_n → 0.

Question: For every fixed r > 0, does S_ε(r) converge to S_0(r) in the Kuratowski sense as ε → 0?

paper_title: Some problems concerning the structure of random walk paths
original_question: For a simple symmetric random walk on the two-dimensional integer lattice, starting at the origin and moving at each step with equal probability to one of the four neighboring lattice points, characterize the growth rates of functions f(n) for which the following event occurs almost surely: for all sufficiently large n, by time f(n) the random walk has visited every lattice point whose Euclidean distance from the origin is less than n. What necessary and sufficient conditions on f(n) determine whether this eventual covering of each disk of radius n happens?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(S_k)_{k\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ starting at the origin: $S_0=0$ and at each step the walker moves to one of its four nearest neighbors, each chosen independently with probability $1/4$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, let
$$T_n \;=\; \inf\bigl\{\,k\ge 0 \,:\, \{x\in\mathbb{Z}^2:\ |x|<n\}\subseteq\{S_0,S_1,\dots,S_k\}\,\bigr\}$$
be the first time at which the walk has visited every lattice point in the open Euclidean disk of radius $n$ about the origin.

Characterize the class of functions $f:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty)$ for which
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\,T_n \le f(n)\ \text{for all sufficiently large } n\,\bigr)\;=\;1,$$
i.e.\ give necessary and sufficient growth conditions on $f(n)$ under which, almost surely, by time $f(n)$ the walk has visited every lattice point within Euclidean distance $n$ of the origin for all sufficiently large $n$.
category_tag: Cover times for planar random walks
status_search_result: The Kesten–Révész conjecture on the asymptotics of the time needed for a planar simple random walk to cover the disk of radius n was resolved by Dembo, Peres, Rosen, and Zeitouni (Annals of Mathematics, 2004), who proved that T_n / (n^2 (log n)^2) → 4/π almost surely. This determines the growth rate of admissible f(n) at the leading-order asymptotic level, and finer fluctuation results have been developed in subsequent works (e.g., on late points and tightness of cover times).

paper_title: Some problems concerning the structure of random walk paths
context_brief: Escape-rate upper bounds in transient random walks
original_question: For a simple symmetric random walk in d-dimensional integer lattice space with d >= 3, let the distance process record how far the walker is from the origin, and let the eventual escape radius from time n onward be the smallest distance from the origin attained at any time after n. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on comparison functions that give valid eventual upper bounds for this escape-radius function, analogous in strength to known necessary and sufficient upper-bound results for laws of the iterated logarithm.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 3$, started at the origin, and let $|S_n|$ denote its Euclidean distance from the origin. Define the eventual escape radius
$$c(n) = \inf_{k \ge n} |S_k|,$$
i.e. the smallest distance from the origin attained by the walk at any time from $n$ onward. For a positive nondecreasing function $\varphi: \mathbb{N} \to (0, \infty)$, say that $\varphi$ is an "upper bound" for $c$ if 
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(c(n) \le \varphi(n) \text{ for all sufficiently large } n\bigr) = 1,$$
and a "non-upper bound" otherwise. 

Determine an integral (or series) test giving necessary and sufficient conditions on $\varphi$ so that $\varphi$ is an upper bound for $c(n)$, in a form analogous to the Kolmogorov–Erdős–Feller integral test that provides necessary and sufficient conditions for upper functions in the law of the iterated logarithm.
category_tag: escape rates of transient random walks
status_search_result: Dvoretzky and Erdős (1951) established the basic almost-sure escape rate $|S_n| \gtrsim \sqrt{n}/(\log n)^{1/(d-2)+\varepsilon}$ for transient simple random walks in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $d\ge 3$, providing upper-bound-type results but not a complete necessary-and-sufficient integral test in the spirit of the Kolmogorov–Erdős–Feller test for the LIL. A web search did not surface a definitive reference establishing such a sharp integral test characterizing all upper bounds of $c(n) = \inf_{k\ge n}|S_k|$, so the precise status of the originally posed problem could not be conclusively verified.

paper_title: Some problems concerning the structure of random walk paths
context_brief: Maximum local time in planar random walk
original_question: For a simple symmetric random walk on the two-dimensional integer lattice, let T_2(n) be the maximum number of times that any single lattice point is visited during the first n steps. Determine the exact almost-sure asymptotic behavior of T_2(n) when it is normalized by (log n)^2; in particular, decide whether the normalized maximum multiplicity has the almost-sure limit suggested by the source after its proved lower and upper bounds.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on the two-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ starting at the origin (at each step the walker moves to one of the four nearest neighbours with equal probability $1/4$, independently of the past). For each integer $n\ge 1$ and each $x\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, let
\[ L_n(x) \;=\; \#\{\,0\le k\le n : S_k = x\,\} \]
denote the number of visits of the walk to the site $x$ during the first $n$ steps, and define the maximum multiplicity
\[ T_2(n) \;=\; \max_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^2} L_n(x). \]
Determine the exact almost-sure asymptotic behaviour of $T_2(n)$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, prove or disprove that
\[ \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{T_2(n)}{(\log n)^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{\pi} \qquad \text{almost surely.} \]
status_search_result: This is the Erdős–Taylor conjecture (1960) for planar simple random walk. It was resolved by Dembo, Peres, Rosen and Zeitouni, who proved that $T_2(n)/(\log n)^2 \to 1/\pi$ almost surely, via a multiscale second-moment analysis and the theory of thick points of planar Brownian motion. Subsequent works (e.g., Rosen's random-walk proof and a multivariate extension by Louidor and collaborators) have refined and extended the result.

paper_title: On some problems of C*-algebras
original_question: Let A be a C*-algebra and let delta be a derivation of A that is not assumed to be continuous. If x is a normal element of A and x commutes with delta(x), must delta(x) be equal to 0? Equivalently, does the normal-element derivation result remain valid after dropping the continuity assumption on the derivation?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra. A linear map $\delta: A \to A$ is called a derivation if it satisfies the Leibniz rule $\delta(ab) = \delta(a) b + a\, \delta(b)$ for all $a, b \in A$; no continuity assumption is imposed on $\delta$. An element $x \in A$ is called normal if $x^* x = x x^*$. 

Prove or disprove: for every $C^*$-algebra $A$, every (not necessarily continuous) derivation $\delta: A \to A$, and every normal element $x \in A$ satisfying $x\,\delta(x) = \delta(x)\, x$, one has $\delta(x) = 0$.
status_search_result: By Sakai's automatic-continuity theorem, every derivation of a C*-algebra into itself is norm-continuous, so the continuity hypothesis can always be dropped. Combined with the known result for continuous derivations (a normal element commuting with its image under a continuous derivation lies in the kernel of the derivation), the statement holds: δ(x)=0.

paper_title: On some problems of C*-algebras
context_brief: Pure state spaces of operator algebras
original_question: Let H be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, let B be the C*-algebra of all bounded operators on H, and consider the pure state space of B with the weak-star topology induced by the dual pairing between B and its dual space. Is that pure state space compact in the noncommutative case, analogous to the compactness of pure state spaces for commutative C*-algebras?
self_contained_problem:
Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let $B = B(H)$ denote the C*-algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$. A state on $B$ is a positive linear functional $\varphi : B \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\varphi(I)=1$; the state space $S(B)$ is convex, and its extreme points are called pure states. Equip the dual $B^*$ with the weak-* topology $\sigma(B^*,B)$, and consider the pure state space $P(B) \subset B^*$ with the induced topology.

For a commutative unital C*-algebra $C(X)$ (with $X$ compact Hausdorff), the pure state space is homeomorphic to $X$ and hence weak-* compact. Determine whether the pure state space $P(B)$ of $B(H)$ is weak-* compact in this noncommutative setting.
status_search_result: It is a classical fact that for $B = B(H)$ with $H$ infinite-dimensional, the pure state space is not weak-* compact: the weak-* closure of the pure states contains non-pure states (e.g., one can approximate singular states by vector states). The parsed metadata also marks this question as solved (negatively).

paper_title: Problemas abiertos en series de Fourier de Jacobi-Sobolev
context_brief: Endpoint masses and fourth-order boundary problems
original_question: For a discrete Sobolev-type inner product built from the Jacobi measure on [-1,1] together with derivative-evaluation mass terms at the endpoints -1 and 1, develop the endpoint-mass case. In particular, determine estimates and related tools that would allow fourth-order boundary-value differential operators to be studied by Galerkin methods, and develop corresponding extensions of the Gauss-Lobatto quadrature formula for collocation methods using the modified Jacobi functional framework.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\mu^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x) = (1-x)^\alpha (1+x)^\beta\,dx$ be the Jacobi measure on $[-1,1]$ with parameters $\alpha,\beta>-1$. For nonnegative integers $m_{-1},m_1$ and nonnegative real masses $M_{i,-1},M_{j,1}$ ($0\le i\le m_{-1}$, $0\le j\le m_1$), define the discrete Sobolev-type inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_S \;=\; \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,g(x)\,d\mu^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x) \;+\; \sum_{i=0}^{m_{-1}} M_{i,-1}\,f^{(i)}(-1)\,g^{(i)}(-1) \;+\; \sum_{j=0}^{m_{1}} M_{j,1}\,f^{(j)}(1)\,g^{(j)}(1),$$
acting on polynomials (or on a suitable Sobolev completion).

Carry out the following programme in the endpoint-mass case (i.e., when both endpoints $\pm 1$ carry derivative-evaluation point masses):

(a) Establish sharp asymptotic estimates for the Sobolev-orthonormal polynomials $\{Q_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ associated with $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_S$, together with bounds on the Fourier–Sobolev partial-sum operators, that are strong enough to permit the analysis of Galerkin approximations of fourth-order linear boundary-value differential operators on $[-1,1]$ in this Sobolev framework.

(b) Develop a generalized Gauss–Lobatto-type quadrature formula adapted to this modified Jacobi–Sobolev functional setting (with nodes including the endpoints $\pm 1$ and weights involving derivative data there), with algebraic exactness degree, error estimates, and convergence properties suitable for collocation methods applied to the fourth-order boundary-value problems above.

paper_title: Open Problems for Entire Functions of Bounded Index in Direction
original_question: Given two nonparallel directions b1 and b2, construct an entire function with planar zeros, in the sense of zeros coming from factors g(<z,a_k>|a_k|^{-2},p), that has bounded L-index in direction b1 but unbounded L-index in direction b2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{C}^n$ denote complex $n$-space with the Hermitian inner product $\langle z, w\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^n z_j \overline{w_j}$ and norm $|w|^2 = \langle w,w\rangle$. For a fixed direction $b \in \mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and a continuous positive function $L : \mathbb{C}^n \to (0,\infty)$, an entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists a non-negative integer $N$ such that for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\, L(z)^m} \le \max_{0\le k\le N} \frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k}\qquad \text{for all } m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},$$
where $\partial_b F(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n b_j \tfrac{\partial F}{\partial z_j}(z)$ and $\partial_b^m$ denotes its $m$-fold iterate. The least such $N$ is called the $L$-index in the direction $b$; if no such $N$ exists, $F$ is said to have unbounded $L$-index in the direction $b$.

For $a\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and a non-negative integer $p$, let
$$g(\zeta, p) = (1-\zeta)\exp\!\left(\zeta + \frac{\zeta^2}{2} + \cdots + \frac{\zeta^p}{p}\right)$$
be the Weierstrass primary factor, and consider entire functions $F$ built from products of the form
$$F(z) = \prod_{k} g\!\left(\frac{\langle z, a_k\rangle}{|a_k|^2},\,p\right),$$
whose zero set is the union of the complex hyperplanes $\{z : \langle z, a_k\rangle = |a_k|^2\}$ (such zeros are called planar zeros).

Problem. Given two nonparallel directions $b_1, b_2 \in \mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ (i.e., $b_1$ and $b_2$ are not scalar multiples of each other), and a positive continuous function $L$, construct an entire function $F$ of the above product form with planar zeros such that $F$ has bounded $L$-index in the direction $b_1$ but unbounded $L$-index in the direction $b_2$.
category_tag: Entire functions of bounded L-index in direction
status_search_result: Recent works by Bandura, Skaskiv and collaborators (2017–2021) continue to develop sufficient conditions of boundedness of $L$-index in direction for classes of entire functions with planar zeros and study directional behavior, but no source located explicitly resolves the specific construction problem of producing such a function with bounded $L$-index in one nonparallel direction and unbounded in another. Status of this specific construction problem is unclear from the available sources.

paper_title: Localized Spot Patterns on the Sphere for Reaction-Diffusion Systems: Theory and Open Problems
original_question: For the localized-spot Brusselator framework on the sphere, how does allowing a spatially heterogeneous fuel supply E = E(x), rather than a constant fuel parameter, change the slow DAE dynamics? In particular, can one derive and analyze the resulting nonlocal spot-evolution system when the outer inhibitor field includes v_p = integral_Omega (E(xi) - Ebar) G(x; xi) dxi, where Ebar is the spatial average of E over the sphere?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Brusselator reaction-diffusion system posed on the unit sphere $\Omega = S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ for an activator $u(x,t)$ and an inhibitor $v(x,t)$, with a spatially heterogeneous fuel-supply function $E(x):S^2\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ replacing the usual constant feed parameter. In the singularly perturbed limit $\varepsilon\to 0$, suppose the activator concentrates as $N$ localized spots centered at points $x_1(t),\dots,x_N(t)\in S^2$ with time-dependent source strengths $S_1(t),\dots,S_N(t)$.

In the outer region away from the spots, the inhibitor field is governed by a linear elliptic problem on $S^2$ with delta-source contributions from the spots and a distributed forcing proportional to $E(x)-\bar{E}$, where
$$\bar{E} = \frac{1}{|S^2|}\int_{S^2} E(\xi)\, dS(\xi).$$
Let $G(x;\xi)$ denote the Neumann Green's function on $S^2$ for the modified Helmholtz / Laplace–Beltrami operator arising in this asymptotic reduction (with the appropriate normalization so that $\int_{S^2} G(x;\xi)\,dS(\xi)=0$), and let $R(x)=\lim_{\xi\to x}\bigl(G(x;\xi)-G_{\text{sing}}(x;\xi)\bigr)$ be its regular part. Define the particular inhibitor field generated by the heterogeneous feed as
$$v_p(x) = \int_{\Omega} \bigl(E(\xi)-\bar{E}\bigr)\, G(x;\xi)\, dS(\xi).$$

Problems:

(a) Derive the differential–algebraic system (DAE) governing the slow evolution of the spot locations $\{x_j(t)\}_{j=1}^N$ and the source strengths $\{S_j(t)\}_{j=1}^N$ in this heterogeneous setting. Specifically, obtain:
  (i) the nonlinear algebraic constraint coupling $(S_1,\dots,S_N)$ that incorporates the spot self-interactions through $R(x_j)$, the mutual interactions through $G(x_j;x_i)$, and the inhomogeneous contribution $v_p(x_j)$ at each spot location;
  (ii) the gradient-flow ODE for $\dot{x}_j$ on $S^2$ driven by the tangential gradient of the regular part of the outer inhibitor field, including the additional drift term $\nabla_{x_j} v_p(x_j)$ generated by the heterogeneity of $E$.

(b) Analyze the resulting nonlocal spot-evolution system. In particular, characterize the equilibrium spot configurations as critical points of an effective energy on $(S^2)^N$ that incorporates $E(x)$, determine how the heterogeneity $E(x)$ shifts and bifurcates these equilibria relative to the constant-$E$ case, and identify the linear stability of equilibrium configurations under the slow DAE flow.
category_tag: localized spot patterns on the sphere
status_search_result: The analogous heterogeneous-feed analysis has been carried out in the planar 2D Brusselator (Tzou–Ward, Physica D 2018), where a spatially variable bulk feed produced new saddle-node and spot-pinning behaviour. For the Brusselator on the sphere, the DAE slow dynamics has been derived only in the homogeneous (constant $E$) case (Trinh–Ward; Rozada–Ruuth–Ward). No published derivation of the nonlocal DAE with $v_p=\int(E(\xi)-\bar E)G(x;\xi)\,d\xi$ on $S^2$ appears in the literature, so the problem appears to be open.

paper_title: Infinity in string cosmology: A review through open problems
context_brief: Interacting fluids in flat string cosmology
original_question: How do the known single-fluid asymptotic results for flat string cosmologies change when the matter sector is replaced by two interacting, fairly general fluids that exchange energy, and which conclusions about the physical viability of string cosmology survive in that more general interacting setting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a spatially flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker spacetime with metric
  ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 (dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2),
coupled, within the low-energy effective string-cosmology action involving the dilaton φ(t), to two perfect fluids with energy densities ρ_1, ρ_2 and pressures p_1 = (γ_1 - 1)ρ_1, p_2 = (γ_2 - 1)ρ_2, where γ_1, γ_2 are (not necessarily constant) barotropic indices in a fairly general admissible range. Assume the two fluids exchange energy through a coupling term Q(t), so that the conservation equations read
  ρ̇_1 + 3H(γ_1 ρ_1) = -Q,    ρ̇_2 + 3H(γ_2 ρ_2) = +Q,
with H = ȧ/a, while the total stress-energy sources the dilaton-gravity field equations of flat string cosmology in the standard way.

(a) Determine the full set of asymptotic regimes (early-time / pre-big-bang, late-time, and near any cosmological singularity) of the scale factor a(t), the dilaton φ(t), and the densities ρ_1(t), ρ_2(t) in this two-interacting-fluid system, and compare them with the known asymptotic results obtained when a single perfect fluid sources flat string cosmology.

(b) Identify which qualitative features of the single-fluid analysis (existence and nature of initial/final singularities, occurrence of bounces, attractor/scaling solutions, possible graceful exit, behavior of the dilaton coupling, and any obstructions to physical viability) persist for arbitrary admissible choices of γ_1, γ_2 and energy-exchange function Q, and which features are genuinely modified or destroyed by the interaction.
status_search_result: A literature search shows partial progress on related two-interacting-fluid cosmologies (e.g., flat limits of curved interacting cosmic fluids, anisotropic Bianchi-type two-fluid models, and multi-fluid analytical solutions in Einstein gravity), but no comprehensive classification of asymptotic regimes for two interacting fluids specifically within flat string (dilaton-gravity) cosmology generalizing all known single-fluid results appears available. The problem is therefore best regarded as open / partially explored.
