original_question: Among all continuous rectifiable plane curves that start at the center of the unit circle and are guaranteed to touch every tangent line to that circle, give a proof—using calculus of variations or optimal control—that the optimal curve has length 7π/6 + √3 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ denote the closed unit disk centered at the origin $O$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be the family of all lines tangent to its boundary circle $\partial D$. Consider continuous rectifiable plane curves $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\gamma(0)=O$ having the property that for every line $\ell\in\mathcal{T}$ the image of $\gamma$ meets $\ell$ (equivalently, $\gamma$ intersects every tangent line to the unit circle). Define the length functional
$$L(\gamma)=\sup\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\gamma(t_i)-\gamma(t_{i-1})\|:\ 0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1\Big\}.$$
Using techniques from the calculus of variations or optimal control, prove that the infimum of $L(\gamma)$ over all such curves equals
$$\frac{7\pi}{6}+\sqrt{3}+1,$$
and that this infimum is attained by an explicit curve consisting of a straight segment from the center, a circular arc along $\partial D$, and two tangent segments arranged symmetrically.
status_search_result: The optimal length 7π/6 + √3 + 1 ≈ 6.397 for the shortest curve from the center of the unit disk meeting every tangent line is a known classical value (related to Joris' "lost hunter" / discovery path problems and opaque-set literature). However, a proof carried out specifically via calculus of variations or optimal control techniques does not appear to be established in the accessible literature; existing proofs are geometric/combinatorial. Status of a variational/optimal-control derivation is unclear from web search.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Determine the minimal possible length and the geometric structure of a curve in R^3 that starts at the center of the unit sphere and intersects every tangent plane to that sphere.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere centered at the origin $O$, and for each point $p \in S^2$ let $T_p$ denote the affine tangent plane to $S^2$ at $p$ (the plane through $p$ orthogonal to the radius $Op$). Consider rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\gamma(0)=O$ such that for every $p\in S^2$ the image of $\gamma$ has nonempty intersection with $T_p$ (equivalently, the curve meets or touches every tangent plane of $S^2$). 

Determine the infimum
$$L^* = \inf\bigl\{\,\mathrm{length}(\gamma)\,:\ \gamma(0)=O,\ \gamma\cap T_p\neq\emptyset\ \text{for all }p\in S^2\,\bigr\},$$
and describe the geometric structure of an optimal (length-minimizing) curve, if one exists.
status_search_result: This is a 3-dimensional analogue of classical "shortest opaque set" / shortest inspection curve problems. Web searches did not turn up a published determination of the minimal length or of the structure of an optimal curve for the problem of a curve starting at the center of the unit sphere and meeting every tangent plane. Related but distinct problems (shortest closed curve containing a sphere in its convex hull; planar opaque/watchman problems) have been studied, but the specific 3D version with curve emanating from the center appears to remain open.

original_question: Let F_N be the sum of cosines of all angles determined by N distinct points in R^3, and let (P_N) be the problem of maximizing F_N subject to the triangle-angle consistency constraints. Determine the maximizing configurations for larger values of N and decide whether the conjectured optimal configurations for N = 5, 6, and 8 are correct.

For an integer $N\ge 2$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N$ be $N$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^3$. For each ordered triple of distinct indices $(i,j,k)$, let $\theta_{ijk}\in[0,\pi]$ denote the (interior) angle at vertex $x_j$ in the triangle with vertices $x_i,x_j,x_k$, i.e.
$$\cos\theta_{ijk}=\frac{\langle x_i-x_j,\,x_k-x_j\rangle}{\|x_i-x_j\|\,\|x_k-x_j\|}.$$
Define
$$F_N(x_1,\dots,x_N)=\sum_{\{i,j,k\}}\bigl(\cos\theta_{jik}+\cos\theta_{ijk}+\cos\theta_{ikj}\bigr),$$
where the sum is over all unordered triples of distinct indices (equivalently, the sum of $\cos\theta$ over all angles of all triangles determined by the $N$ points). Within each triangle the three angles must be nonnegative and sum to $\pi$; impose these triangle-angle consistency constraints, and consider the problem
$$(P_N)\qquad \text{maximize } F_N \text{ over configurations of } N \text{ distinct points in } \mathbb{R}^3.$$

(Conjectured optima are, respectively, the configurations corresponding to the regular triangular bipyramid for $N=5$, the regular octahedron for $N=6$, and a configuration with the symmetry of the regular cube/square antiprism for $N=8$; decide whether these conjectures are correct.)

(b) More generally, for larger values of $N$, characterize the maximizing configurations of $(P_N)$.

context_brief: Optimization proof for Van der Waerden inequality
original_question: Find a proof, based entirely on constrained-optimization ideas such as higher-order optimality conditions, that every doubly stochastic n x n matrix A satisfies per(A) >= n!/n^n, with equality only at the matrix whose entries are all 1/n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrix, i.e., $a_{ij}\ge 0$ for all $i,j$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$. Define the permanent
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ denotes the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Provide a proof, carried out entirely within the framework of constrained optimization (relying on tools such as first-, second-, or higher-order optimality conditions applied to the problem of minimizing $\operatorname{per}(A)$ over the polytope of doubly stochastic matrices), of the inequality
$$\operatorname{per}(A)\ \ge\ \frac{n!}{n^n},$$
with equality if and only if $A=J_n$, where $J_n$ is the $n\times n$ matrix every entry of which equals $1/n$.
status_search_result: The Van der Waerden inequality itself was proved in 1981 by Egorychev and Falikman, and several alternative proofs exist, including a geometric-programming formulation by Gleason and an analytic optimization-style argument by Hanson. However, the specific request—a proof carried out entirely within the constrained-optimization framework using higher-order optimality conditions on the doubly stochastic polytope—does not appear to have been definitively realized in the literature; the standard proofs use algebraic or analytic identities rather than purely optimization-theoretic optimality conditions.

original_question: Let B_n be the set of doubly stochastic n x n matrices. Determine whether the permanent function on B_n intersected with the trace-zero constraint {A : tr(A) = 0} attains its minimum uniquely at the matrix with every off-diagonal entry equal to 1/(n - 1) and every diagonal entry equal to 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ be an integer. Denote by $B_n$ (also called $\Omega_n$) the set of $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrices, i.e. matrices $A=(a_{ij})$ with $a_{ij}\ge 0$ and $\sum_i a_{ij}=\sum_j a_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$. Recall that the permanent of an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
Let
$$B_n^0=\{A\in B_n:\operatorname{tr}(A)=0\},$$
the set of doubly stochastic matrices with zero diagonal (equivalently, $a_{ii}=0$ for all $i$). Let $J_n^0$ denote the matrix in $B_n^0$ whose diagonal entries are all $0$ and whose off-diagonal entries are all equal to $1/(n-1)$.

Prove or disprove: the permanent function $A\mapsto\operatorname{per}(A)$ restricted to $B_n^0$ attains its minimum, and the minimum is attained uniquely at $A=J_n^0$.
status_search_result: The conjecture concerns the minimum of the permanent on the face of doubly stochastic matrices with zero trace, a classical subface of $\Omega_n$. Van der Waerden's conjecture (minimum on all of $\Omega_n$) was settled by Egorychev and Falikman, but conjectures about minima on subfaces such as the trace-zero face remain part of an active body of permanent-minimization problems (Foregger, Merris, Hwang, Dittert). Partial results exist (e.g., for partly decomposable matrices and small $n$, including $n=5$), but no complete proof of uniqueness of the minimizer $J_n^0$ for general $n$ appears in the literature consulted, so the conjecture is still considered open.

$$f(\lambda) = \int_{0}^{+\infty} e^{-\lambda t}\, d\mu(t) \qquad \text{for all } \lambda \in \mathbb{R};$$

original_question: Let m(ρ) denote the multiplicity of a nontrivial zero ρ of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s). Improve the known upper bounds for m(ρ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$ by $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ and extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a single simple pole at $s=1$. It is classically known, via the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula, that for nontrivial zeros $ho$ with $|\gamma| \ge 2$ one has the unconditional bound
$$ m(ho) \;\ll\;  rac{\log |\gamma|}{\log\log |\gamma|}, $$
and under the Riemann Hypothesis a refinement of the same order of magnitude holds.

status_search_result: The problem of improving the classical upper bound $m(\rho) \ll \log|\gamma|/\log\log|\gamma|$ on multiplicities of nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ remains open. It is widely conjectured that all nontrivial zeros are simple, but no unconditional improvement to the order of magnitude of the standard bound is currently known. Recent work (e.g., by Conrey–Ghosh, Cheer–Goldston, and others) gives bounds on the proportion of simple zeros but does not improve the pointwise multiplicity bound.

context_brief: Skewes numbers for highly biased races
original_question: In highly biased prime number races, such as the appropriately normalized race between quadratic residues and nonresidues for composite moduli q, bound the associated Skewes numbers in terms of the parameters defining the race, either conjecturally or with proofs.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer modulus $q \ge 3$, let $\pi(x;q,a)$ denote the number of primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$. For two reduced residue classes $a,b$ modulo $q$, define the prime race between $a$ and $b$ as the study of the sign of $\pi(x;q,a) - \pi(x;q,b)$. After appropriate normalization (for example, weighting each residue class by the number of square roots of unity it represents, as in the Rubinstein–Sarnak framework), define Skewes's number for the race to be the least integer $x \ge 2$ at which the (normalized) difference first changes sign, i.e. the smallest $x$ at which the leading bias is overturned.

Now consider highly biased races, of which a prototypical family is the following: fix a composite modulus $q$, let $N$ be the set of quadratic nonresidues modulo $q$ that are coprime to $q$, and let $R$ be the set of quadratic residues modulo $q$ coprime to $q$, and study the appropriately normalized difference
$$ D_q(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{|N|}\sum_{a \in N} \pi(x;q,a) \;-\; \frac{1}{|R|}\sum_{a \in R} \pi(x;q,a).$$
The associated Skewes number $\mathrm{Sk}(q)$ is the least $x \ge 2$ at which $D_q(x)$ changes sign (or, more generally, for any highly biased race specified by parameters such as the modulus $q$, the contestant residue classes, and the bias size, the least $x$ at which the bias is first overturned).

Problem. Provide bounds, either conditional (e.g. assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the linear independence of nontrivial zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions) or unconditional, on the Skewes number $\mathrm{Sk}(q)$ (and analogous quantities for other highly biased races) as an explicit function of the parameters defining the race, such as the modulus $q$ and the discrepancy in the number of competing residue classes.
status_search_result: The problem of obtaining explicit bounds on Skewes numbers for highly biased prime races (such as the quadratic residues vs. nonresidues race for composite moduli) is posed as an open research problem in the comparative prime number theory literature. context_brief: function-field bias and linear independence with pi
original_question: In the function-field setting for Chebyshev’s bias, one often assumes both linear independence over Q of the relevant zero arguments and linear independence of those arguments together with π. Show that whenever linear independence with π fails, that failure always has a geometric explanation.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $K/k$ be a finite Galois extension of global function fields with field of constants $\mathbb{F}_q$, with Galois group $G$. For a nontrivial irreducible representation $\rho$ of $G$, let $L(s,\rho,K/k)$ denote the associated Artin $L$-function, which (after the change of variable $u=q^{-s}$) is a polynomial in $u$ whose inverse roots have absolute value $\sqrt{q}$; write these inverse roots as $\sqrt{q}\,e^{i\gamma}$ and call the real numbers $\gamma\in(-\pi,\pi]$ the zero arguments attached to $K/k$. 

In the study of Chebyshev's bias for prime distributions in $K/k$, one usually imposes two linear independence hypotheses:
(LI) the multiset of all nonzero zero arguments $\gamma$ arising from the nontrivial irreducible representations of $G$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$;
(LI$_\pi$) the set consisting of $\pi$ together with all those zero arguments $\gamma$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Say that a failure of (LI$_\pi$) admits a geometric explanation if every nontrivial $\mathbb{Q}$-linear relation of the form 
$$ a\pi + \sum_j b_j \gamma_j = 0, \qquad a,b_j \in \mathbb{Z},\ (a,b_1,\dots) \neq 0, $$
among $\pi$ and the zero arguments can be accounted for by the geometric structure of the extension $K/k$ — for instance by the presence of zero arguments equal to $0$ or $\pi$ forced by real (self-dual) Artin representations, by relations between the constant-field part and the geometric part of $L$-functions, or by similar structural identities among the inverse roots of Frobenius coming from the underlying geometry.

Problem. Prove that, for every finite geometric Galois extension $K/k$ of global function fields satisfying (LI), any failure of (LI$_\pi$) admits a geometric explanation in the sense above.
status_search_result: The function-field Chebyshev bias literature (Cha, Devin, Fiorilli, Jouve, and others) consistently assumes a linear-independence hypothesis on zero arguments and treats relations involving π as exceptional, but no general theorem deriving every failure of LI-with-π from a geometric source appears in the literature. Recent work (e.g., Shanks' bias in function fields, 2025) still posits such hypotheses without resolving this structural question. The problem appears to remain open.

holds as x → ∞.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: What general formal theory of probability can accommodate multiple interpretations of probability, including the logical probability of a statement relative to given evidence, absolute logical probability relative to zero evidence, and the probability of an event relative to a given ensemble or collective of events, while also supporting interpretations as a calculus of contents, deductive systems, classes, propositions, and propensities?
self_contained_problem:
Construct a formal axiomatic theory of probability, given as a system of axioms for a two-argument real-valued function p(a,b) defined on a set S closed under two binary operations (a "product" ab and a "complement" a'), satisfying the usual laws of the probability calculus (non-negativity, normalization, the general multiplication law p(ab,c) = p(a,bc)·p(b,c), and an addition/complementation law), with the following properties:

(i) The theory admits an interpretation as a logical theory of the probability p(a,b) of a statement a relative to given evidence b, including the special case of absolute logical probability p(a) obtained by taking b to be a tautology (i.e. evidence with probability 1).

(ii) The theory admits an interpretation as a frequency theory, in which p(a,b) is the relative frequency (or measure-theoretic probability) of the event a within an ensemble or collective b of events.

(iii) The same axiom system admits further interpretations in which the elements of S are taken to be:
   – logical contents of statements,
   – deductive systems (closed under consequence),
   – classes in a Boolean algebra,
   – propositions in a propositional calculus,
   – propensities of physical setups to produce outcomes.

Give such an axiom system, prove that it is consistent and independent, and verify that each of the listed interpretations satisfies all the axioms.
status_search_result: Popper developed such an axiomatic system (the "Popper axioms" or Popper–Rényi conditional probability axioms) in The Logic of Scientific Discovery and subsequent appendices, and these systems are well established in the literature on formal probability and conditional probability (Rényi, Popper, Leblanc, Harper, etc.). The construction of a formal theory admitting all the stated interpretations is considered accomplished.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: How should probability be interpreted in quantum theory if quantum theory need not have a purely statistical meaning, even though its empirical tests are statistical, and if one wants an account in which objective propensities and fields of propensities can be measured statistically without themselves being statistical?
self_contained_problem:
Formulate a coherent interpretation of probability for quantum theory that satisfies all of the following conditions simultaneously:

1. Quantum theory (for instance, the Schrödinger equation and its consequences) is not assigned a purely statistical meaning, even though all empirical tests of it are statistical in nature.

2. Probabilities appearing in the theory are interpreted as objective propensities — single-case dispositional magnitudes attached to an experimental arrangement, conceived as something analogous to generalized forces — rather than as relative frequencies or subjective credences.

3. One admits the notion of a field of propensities, i.e., a spatially or otherwise indexed assignment of such single-case propensities, which is itself a non-statistical physical entity.

4. The propensities and propensity fields, although not statistical in themselves, are measurable by statistical methods: repeated trials of the same experimental arrangement yield frequencies that approach the propensity value, providing the link to empirical testing.

The problem is to give a precise mathematical and conceptual framework realising (1)–(4): specify the underlying ontology (the carriers of propensity), the mathematical objects representing a field of propensities, the dynamical law these objects satisfy, the rule by which they reproduce the predictions of standard quantum theory, and the precise sense in which they can be measured statistically while remaining non-statistical in their intrinsic meaning.
status_search_result: The propensity interpretation of probability in quantum mechanics remains an actively debated topic in the philosophy and foundations of physics, with no consensus formalisation. Various proposals exist (e.g., propensity readings of the Born rule, dispositional accounts), but the conditions stated above are widely viewed as not having a single agreed-upon precise mathematical realisation. Status is therefore best described as unknown/open in the foundational-philosophical sense.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: How can statistical statements be made satisfactorily refutable and testable when statistics is used mainly to provide empirical tests for theories that are not themselves purely statistical? In particular, how can one characterize a class of infinite chance-like sequences so that a statistical statement is testable by comparison with the “shortest sequences” of its kind and is refuted when a tested ensemble differs from the statistical properties of the initial sections of those sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{0,1\}^\omega$ denote the set of infinite binary sequences. Call a sequence "chance-like" if it satisfies natural frequency-stability conditions (e.g., for every finite block $w \in \{0,1\}^*$, the limiting relative frequency of occurrences of $w$ in the initial segments of the sequence exists and equals $2^{-|w|}$, with appropriate invariance under selection of admissible subsequences).

Provide a mathematical characterization of a distinguished class $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \{0,1\}^\omega$ of "shortest chance-like sequences" with the following properties:

(a) Every sequence in $\mathcal{S}$ is chance-like in the above sense.

(b) The class $\mathcal{S}$ is, in a precise sense to be specified, minimal: its members are the shortest (least complex, or least structured) sequences exhibiting the chance-like behavior, so that no proper subclass defined by additional structural constraints exhausts the chance-like behavior.

(c) Using $\mathcal{S}$, formulate a notion of testability for a statistical hypothesis $H$ about a finite ensemble $E$ of binary data of length $n$: $H$ is declared testable if there is an effective comparison between the empirical statistical properties of $E$ and the statistical properties of the length-$n$ initial segments of sequences in $\mathcal{S}$; and $H$ is declared refuted if these properties differ by more than a prescribed tolerance.

Show that under your characterization every statistical statement of a suitable form is satisfactorily refutable, in the sense that the set of finite ensembles refuting $H$ is well-defined and effectively recognizable, and that the chosen class $\mathcal{S}$ does not depend on auxiliary non-statistical assumptions about the underlying theory being tested.
category_tag: Algorithmic randomness and testability of statistical hypotheses
status_search_result: The informal program of characterizing "shortest chance-like sequences" anticipates the modern theory of algorithmic randomness. Martin-Löf (1966) gave a rigorous definition of random infinite sequences via effective statistical tests, and equivalent characterizations via prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity (Levin, Chaitin) and martingale unpredictability (Schnorr) provide a mathematical class of sequences whose initial segments are maximally incompressible. This realizes a precise version of the "shortest sequences" idea and yields a notion of refutability of statistical statements via effective tests. However, the philosophical question of which mathematical randomness notion best captures the intended class (Martin-Löf, Schnorr, computable randomness, 2-randomness, etc.) for purposes of empirical refutation remains debated, so the broader formulation is only partially settled.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: Does classical physics justify a deterministic view of the physical world in Laplace’s sense, or is even classical physics misinterpreted when it is used to support that deterministic view?
self_contained_problem:
Consider classical (Newtonian) mechanics, in which the state of an isolated system of point particles at time $t_0$ is given by positions $\{q_i(t_0)\}$ and momenta $\{p_i(t_0)\}$, and time evolution is governed by Newton's second law $m_i \ddot q_i = F_i(q,\dot q,t)$ with smooth force laws. Laplacian determinism is the thesis that, for any such isolated system, knowledge of the complete instantaneous state at one time $t_0$ uniquely determines the state at every other time $t$, so that an idealized intellect with perfect knowledge of all positions, momenta, and forces could in principle compute the entire past and future trajectory exactly.

The problem is the following: determine whether classical mechanics, taken as a mathematical theory of ordinary differential equations governing systems of particles (and rigid/continuous bodies) under standard force laws, in fact justifies Laplacian determinism in the above strong sense. Specifically, decide whether each of the following holds:

(a) For every physically reasonable choice of force law $F$ and every admissible initial condition, the initial value problem for Newton's equations admits a unique global solution.

(b) Even when (a) holds in the sense of unique mathematical solutions, the idealization required (exact real-valued initial data, exact knowledge of all forces, infinite computational precision) is consistent with the structure of classical mechanics itself, so that "in principle predictability" is a legitimate consequence of the theory.

(c) If either (a) or (b) fails, exhibit explicit classical-mechanical systems (e.g. with non-Lipschitz forces, with collisions, or with unbounded acceleration in finite time) for which Newton's equations admit multiple solutions from identical initial data, or for which solutions cease to exist in finite time, thereby refuting Laplacian determinism as a theorem of classical mechanics.
status_search_result: The mathematical core of the question has been substantially clarified. Classical (Newtonian) mechanics is known not to be globally Laplace-deterministic: explicit counterexamples include Norton's dome (2003), nineteenth-century examples of non-Lipschitz force laws producing non-unique solutions, space-invader/no-collision singularities in the Newtonian N-body problem (Xia, 1992), and systems exhibiting finite-time blow-up. Hence the strong Laplacian thesis fails as a theorem of classical mechanics. The broader philosophical/interpretive question of whether such pathologies should be regarded as undermining the deterministic spirit of classical physics remains debated.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
context_brief: Ad hoc hypotheses in scientific method
original_question: How should the ad hoc character of a hypothesis, and degrees of ad hocness, be defined and evaluated within scientific methodology, given the aim of obtaining explanatory theories that are as little ad hoc as possible and the contrast with probability theories of induction that favor the most ad hoc theory compatible with the evidence?
self_contained_problem:
Within the methodology of empirical science, provide a precise definition of what it means for a hypothesis to be "ad hoc," and define a (qualitative or quantitative) notion of "degrees of ad hocness" that ranks competing hypotheses with respect to a body of evidence. The definition should satisfy the following desiderata:

(a) It should make explicit the intuition that a "good" explanatory theory is one which is as little ad hoc as possible — i.e., one whose content substantially transcends the evidence it was designed to explain — while a "bad" theory is one introduced merely to accommodate the evidence.

(b) It should be applicable to actual episodes in the history and practice of science, in the sense that informally recognized ad hoc moves (e.g., auxiliary hypotheses introduced solely to save a refuted theory) are assigned high degrees of ad hocness, while bold, independently testable theories are assigned low degrees.

(c) It should illuminate why a methodological rule of the form "prefer the least ad hoc theory compatible with the evidence" is reasonable, and conversely why probabilistic theories of induction — which tend to assign higher probability to hypotheses that minimally transcend the evidence — implicitly recommend the opposite rule of "prefer the most ad hoc theory compatible with the evidence," and explain in what precise sense this latter rule is unacceptable.

Formulate such a definition (or framework of definitions) and justify that it meets (a)–(c).
category_tag: philosophy of science / ad hoc hypotheses
status_search_result: The notion of ad hoc hypotheses and degrees of ad hocness remains an actively debated topic in philosophy of science (e.g., discussions following Popper, Lakatos, Grünbaum, and more recent contributions by Schindler, Hunt, and others). No single universally accepted formal definition has been established; the problem of giving a precise, generally applicable explication of "ad hocness" is widely regarded as still open.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: What are the logical relations between different layers of explanatory hypotheses in developed science, especially when a later theory such as Newton’s can yield approximations to earlier theories such as Kepler’s and Galileo’s while also, strictly speaking, contradicting or neglecting parts of them? More specifically, how should one analyse approximation both as a relation between theories and as the claim that a theory is a good approximation to the facts?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a formal framework in which scientific theories are represented as deductively closed sets of sentences in some logical language, together with an intended class of models (the "facts"). Suppose T_1 and T_2 are two such theories with T_2 strictly logically inconsistent with T_1 (i.e., T_1 ∪ T_2 ⊢ ⊥), yet T_2 is informally regarded as a refinement or successor of T_1, and certain restricted or limiting consequences of T_2 coincide with consequences of T_1. Concretely, model the situation in which T_2 is Newtonian mechanics (including absolute space and universal gravitation), while T_1 consists of Kepler's planetary laws and Galileo's law of free fall, so that T_1 and T_2 are mutually inconsistent but T_2 yields, under appropriate limits (e.g., neglecting interplanetary attraction, restricting to the two-body problem, taking a small-height approximation near the surface of a uniform sphere), statements close to those of T_1.

Provide a rigorous logical analysis of the relations between such "layers" of explanatory theories. In particular:

(a) Define precisely what it means for one theory x to be an approximation to another theory y when x and y are logically inconsistent, in such a way that the relation cannot be reduced to deductive or inductive inference from x to y (since no consistent premisses can deductively or inductively entail conclusions that contradict them).

(b) Define precisely what it means for a theory x to be a good approximation to the facts, where the facts are represented by a class of intended models or by a body of observational sentences.

(c) Clarify the logical connection between notions (a) and (b), and characterize when "x approximates y" together with "y is a good approximation to the facts" entails (in your sense) that "x is a good approximation to the facts."
category_tag: Logic of scientific theories and approximation
status_search_result: The question is a foundational/philosophical problem about the logic of inter-theoretic approximation and verisimilitude. Various formal proposals exist (Popper's verisimilitude, structuralist intertheoretic reduction by Sneed/Stegmüller, limiting-case reduction analyses by Nickles, Batterman, and others, and partial-structures approaches by da Costa and French), but no single universally accepted formal analysis has emerged, and Popper's original definition of verisimilitude was shown to be defective. The problem is generally regarded as still open.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: Can theoretical concepts be defined purely in terms of measuring operations, given that measurement appears to presuppose theory and that even the description of measuring operations seems to require other measurements and theories? More generally, how should operationalism be assessed if there is no measurement without a theory and no operation that can be satisfactorily described in wholly non-theoretical terms?
self_contained_problem:
Operationalism is the doctrine that every theoretical concept in empirical science must be definable purely in terms of the measuring operations used to determine its value. Suppose one accepts the following two observations: (i) any act of measurement presupposes some background theory (for instance, measuring a length requires a theory of rigid bodies, and measuring temperature via thermal expansion requires a theory of length measurement, which in turn relies on assumptions about heat); (ii) no measuring operation can be described in wholly non-theoretical terms, so attempts to give purely operational definitions appear to lead to circularity (e.g., defining length operationally invokes thermometry, while defining temperature operationally invokes length). 

Question: Under these assumptions, can theoretical concepts nevertheless be given non-circular definitions purely in terms of measuring operations? Equivalently, formulate and assess whether operationalism, as the thesis that all theoretical terms reduce to measurement procedures, is tenable given that (a) there is no measurement without a theory, and (b) no operation admits a satisfactory description in non-theoretical terms. Provide either a coherent reconstruction of operationalism that escapes the circularity, or an argument showing no such reconstruction is possible.
status_search_result: This is a foundational question in the philosophy of science rather than a formal mathematical conjecture. The consensus among philosophers of science since the mid-20th century (Hempel, Putnam, Popper, Kuhn) is that strict operationalism in the Bridgman sense is untenable, and the question is generally regarded as a settled critique rather than an open problem; however, debates over measurement-theoretic foundations and theory-ladenness continue. As a precise mathematical problem with a definite answer, its status is unknown.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: Should scientific theories be understood primarily as practical instruments for prediction, or is instrumentalism mistaken because theories also have a theoretical, non-practical function that cannot be reduced to predictive use alone?

Contrast this with a realist or theoretical view, on which scientific theories also fulfill a genuinely theoretical, non-practical function—for example, providing explanations and descriptions of structures of the world—that is not reducible to predictive use. status_search_result: The question is a foundational philosophical debate (instrumentalism vs. realism about scientific theories) rather than a formal problem with a definitive solution. paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: What is the function of descriptive language as an instrument for talking about the world, and should operationalism and instrumentalism therefore be replaced by a more general “theoreticism” according to which inquiry always operates within a complex framework of theories aimed not merely at correlations but at explanations?

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: What is scientific explanation, if it is not the reduction of the unknown to the known but rather the logical reduction of known facts and known theories to more universal assumptions that are still little known and still need testing? How should degrees of explanation be analysed, and how exactly is explanation related to prediction?
self_contained_problem: Provide a precise theoretical account of scientific explanation under the following stipulation: in pure (as opposed to applied) science, explanation is not the reduction of the unknown to the known, but rather the logical reduction of accepted facts and accepted theories to hypotheses of strictly higher level of universality, where these higher-level hypotheses are themselves only partially understood and remain to be tested. Specifically, address the following: (a) Formulate a definition of "scientific explanation" consistent with this stipulation, specifying the logical relation (e.g., deductive entailment, conditions on universality, independent testability, non-circularity, and content increase) that must hold between an explanandum (the facts or theories to be explained) and an explanans (the higher-level hypotheses). (b) Define and analyse "degrees of explanation": introduce a graded notion that compares two candidate explanantia for the same explanandum and ranks them according to their explanatory power, taking into account at least universality, testability, simplicity, and improbability (informational content). State and justify the formal properties this ordering should satisfy. (c) Make precise the relation between explanation and prediction in this framework: state under what logical conditions an explanation yields a prediction and vice versa, and identify and justify any structural asymmetries between the two (for instance, with respect to temporal direction, initial conditions, or the epistemic status of the universal premises).

Status is therefore best described as unknown / unresolved in the sense of a definitive accepted answer.

The distinction between quid facti and quid juris and the problem of justifying induction remain actively debated in philosophy of science with no settled consensus.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For the additive group of the finite field F_q with q = 3^r elements, determine the largest possible size of a subset that contains no three-term arithmetic progression, describe its asymptotic behavior as r grows, improve Meshulam’s O(3^r/r) upper bound, and decide whether an absolute constant c < 3 always bounds such a size by c^r.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r$ be a positive integer and consider the additive group of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{3^r}$ (equivalently, the elementary abelian 3-group $(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^r$). A subset $A$ of this group is said to be free of three-term arithmetic progressions (3-AP-free, or a "cap set") if the only solutions to $x+y=2z$ (equivalently $x+y+z=0$ since we are in characteristic 3, taking the three elements to be distinct) with $x,y,z \in A$ are the trivial ones $x=y=z$. Let
$$f(r) = \max\{|A| : A \subseteq (\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^r,\ A \text{ is 3-AP-free}\}.$$
Meshulam proved the upper bound $f(r) = O(3^r / r)$.

(a) Determine the precise asymptotic behavior of $f(r)$ as $r \to \infty$.

(b) Improve Meshulam's bound $f(r) = O(3^r / r)$.

(c) Decide whether there exists an absolute constant $c < 3$ such that $f(r) \le c^r$ for all sufficiently large $r$.
category_tag: cap sets / progression-free subsets in finite fields
status_search_result: Part (c) was resolved affirmatively in 2016 by Croot–Lev–Pach and Ellenberg–Gijswijt via the polynomial/slice rank method, proving $f(r) \le c^r$ with $c \approx 2.756 < 3$, which also improves Meshulam's bound (part b). Only sub-exponential improvements (e.g., by a factor $\sqrt{r}$) have since been obtained, and the precise asymptotic growth of $f(r)$ (part a) remains open: the known lower bounds (around $2.2^r$) and upper bounds ($\approx 2.756^r$) do not match.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Arithmetic progressions from divergent reciprocal sums
original_question: If A is a subset of the natural numbers such that the reciprocal sum sum_{a in A} 1/a diverges, must A contain arithmetic progressions of every length k >= 3? In particular, must it contain a three-term arithmetic progression?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of positive integers such that
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a} = \infty.$$
A $k$-term arithmetic progression is a sequence of the form $x, x+d, x+2d, \ldots, x+(k-1)d$ with $d \geq 1$, all of whose terms lie in $A$. Prove or disprove: for every integer $k \geq 3$, the set $A$ must contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression. In particular, settle this for the case $k = 3$.
status_search_result: The case k = 3 was resolved by Bloom and Sisask (2020), who proved that any set of positive integers whose reciprocals diverge must contain a three-term arithmetic progression. The general case for k ≥ 4 remains an open problem (Erdős's conjecture on arithmetic progressions).

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Prove or disprove that for every epsilon > 0 there is a constant c > 0, depending on epsilon, such that every finite set A of integers satisfies max(|A + A|, |A · A|) > c |A|^{2 - epsilon}.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $A$ of integers, define the sumset $A+A = \{a+b : a,b \in A\}$ and the product set $A\cdot A = \{ab : a,b \in A\}$. Prove or disprove the following statement: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a constant $c = c(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that every finite set $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies
$$\max\bigl(|A+A|,\ |A\cdot A|\bigr) > c\,|A|^{2-\varepsilon}.$$
status_search_result: The statement is the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture, which remains open. The strongest known lower bound over the reals is of the form $|A|^{4/3 + c}$ for a small constant $c > 0$ (Rudnev–Shkredov–Stevens), far from the conjectured $|A|^{2-\varepsilon}$. Earlier milestones include exponents $5/4$ (Elekes) and $4/3$ (Solymosi).

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Find reasonable quantitative bounds for the Hales-Jewett theorem and for its density version.
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $k$ and $n$, let $[k]^n = \{1,2,\ldots,k\}^n$. A combinatorial line in $[k]^n$ is a set of $k$ points obtained as follows: fix a nonempty set $I \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ of "active" coordinates and fixed values $a_i \in [k]$ for $i \notin I$; the line consists of the $k$ points $x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \ldots, x^{(k)}$ where $x^{(j)}_i = j$ for $i \in I$ and $x^{(j)}_i = a_i$ for $i \notin I$.

The Hales–Jewett theorem asserts that for all positive integers $k$ and $r$, there exists $N = HJ(k,r)$ such that whenever $n \geq N$ and the cube $[k]^n$ is partitioned into $r$ classes, some class contains a combinatorial line.

The density Hales–Jewett theorem asserts that for all positive integers $k$ and every $\delta \in (0,1]$, there exists $N = DHJ_k(\delta)$ such that whenever $n \geq N$, every subset $A \subseteq [k]^n$ with $|A| \geq \delta k^n$ contains a combinatorial line.

Problem: Determine reasonable quantitative upper bounds (and matching lower bounds) for the functions $HJ(k,r)$ and $DHJ_k(\delta)$. In particular, establish bounds whose growth is significantly better than the tower- or Ackermann-type bounds currently known, ideally of primitive recursive or polynomial type for fixed $k$.
status_search_result: Shelah (1988) gave primitive recursive (wowzer-type) bounds for the Hales–Jewett theorem. The Polymath project (2009, published Annals of Math. 2012) gave the first explicit quantitative bounds for the density version: a tower-of-2s of height $O(1/\delta^2)$ for $k=3$, and Ackermann-type bounds for $k\geq 4$. Obtaining truly "reasonable" (e.g., primitive recursive in $\delta$, or polynomial-type) bounds remains a major open problem.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Growth of van der Waerden numbers
original_question: Determine the order of growth of the two-color van der Waerden number W(k), the least N such that every two-coloring of [1,N] has a monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression, and in particular decide whether W(k) <= 2^{k^2}.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $k \geq 1$, let $W(k)$ denote the least positive integer $N$ such that every $2$-coloring of $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$ (that is, $k$ integers in arithmetic progression all of which are assigned the same color). Van der Waerden's theorem guarantees that $W(k)$ is finite for every $k$.

Determine the order of growth of $W(k)$ as $k \to \infty$. In particular, decide whether the inequality
$$W(k) \leq 2^{k^2}$$
holds for all sufficiently large $k$.
status_search_result: The best known general upper bound on $W(k)$ is due to Gowers, of tower-type form (vastly larger than $2^{k^2}$), improving on Shelah's earlier primitive recursive bound. The known lower bounds are roughly exponential in $k$. Graham famously offered a \$1000 prize for proving $W(k) < 2^{k^2}$, and this remains unresolved. Subexponential improvements exist only for fixed small parameters (e.g., Schoen's bound on $W(3,k)$), not for general $W(k)$.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Does there exist a basis B of order 2 in the natural numbers, meaning every positive integer is a sum of two elements of B, such that the representation count nu_B(n) = |{(b1,b2) in B x B : b1 + b2 = n}| is bounded above by one constant independent of n?
self_contained_problem:
A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called a basis of order 2 if every sufficiently large positive integer can be written as $b_1 + b_2$ with $b_1, b_2 \in B$. For such a set, define the representation function
$$
u_B(n) = |\{(b_1, b_2) \in B 	imes B : b_1 + b_2 = n\}|.$$
Does there exist a basis $B$ of order 2 and a constant $C$ such that $
u_B(n) \le C$ for every positive integer $n$ (i.e., $
u_B$ is uniformly bounded)?
status_search_result: This is the classical Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases (1941), which conjectures the answer is no: for any basis of order 2, the representation function must be unbounded. The conjecture remains open. Partial results include lower bounds on lim sup ν_B(n): Grekos et al. (2003) showed lim sup ≥ 6, improved later to ≥ 8 by Borwein, Choi and Chu, but no uniform bound on ν_B has been ruled out completely.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a prime p congruent to 1 modulo 4, determine the maximum size of a set A in F_p such that the difference between any two elements of A is a quadratic residue modulo p, equivalently determine the clique number of the Paley graph over F_p.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the finite field with $p$ elements. The set $Q \subset \mathbb{F}_p^*$ of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$ satisfies $Q = -Q$. The Paley graph $G_p$ is the graph with vertex set $\mathbb{F}_p$ in which two vertices $x, y$ are adjacent if and only if $x - y \in Q$.

Determine the maximum cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ such that $a - a' \in Q$ for all distinct $a, a' \in A$; equivalently, determine the clique number $\omega(G_p)$ of the Paley graph over $\mathbb{F}_p$, as a function of $p$.
status_search_result: Determining the exact clique number of the Paley graph on $\mathbb{F}_p$ remains open. The classical bound $\omega(G_p) \le \sqrt{p}$ was the standard for decades. In 2019, Hanson and Petridis improved this via Stepanov's method to $\omega(G_p) \le (1+o(1))\sqrt{p/2}$, and subsequent work has extended the technique to generalized Paley graphs, but no matching lower bound or exact formula is known.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Sumsets and difference sets in multiplicative subgroups
original_question: For a proper multiplicative subgroup H of F_q, determine the largest size of a subset A of F_p with A - A contained in H, and decide whether there is a set A with A + A = H or with A + A differing from H by only a small symmetric difference.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the finite field with $p$ elements, with multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_p^\times$. Let $H \subsetneq \mathbb{F}_p^\times$ be a proper multiplicative subgroup. For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$, define the difference set $A - A = \{a - a' : a, a' \in A\}$ and the sumset $A + A = \{a + a' : a, a' \in A\}$.

(a) Determine, as a function of $p$ and $|H|$, the largest possible size of a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ satisfying $A - A \subseteq H \cup \{0\}$.

(b) Decide whether there exists a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with $A + A = H$.

(c) Decide whether there exists a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ such that the symmetric difference $(A + A)\,\triangle\, H$ is small (e.g., of size $o(|H|)$).
status_search_result: Bounds on the largest size of A with A−A contained in a multiplicative subgroup H of F_p have been studied (e.g., Alon–Bourgain on additive patterns in multiplicative subgroups, and Roche-Newton–Shkredov–Winterhof on packing sets), giving partial estimates but no sharp answer in general. The questions of whether A+A can equal H, or differ from H by a small symmetric difference, do not appear to be resolved in the literature, so the problem is regarded as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Large sum-free subsets of integer sets
original_question: Determine the largest constant c such that every sufficiently large finite set A of integers contains a sum-free subset of size at least c|A|, where sum-free means A has no solutions x + y = z within the subset.
self_contained_problem:
A subset S of an abelian group is called sum-free if there are no elements x, y, z ∈ S (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z. Determine the largest constant c ∈ [0, 1] with the following property: there exists N such that for every finite set A of integers with |A| ≥ N, A contains a sum-free subset S ⊆ A with |S| ≥ c·|A|. Equivalently, compute

  c* = sup{ c : every sufficiently large finite A ⊂ ℤ contains a sum-free subset of size ≥ c|A| }.
status_search_result: The supremum constant is c* = 1/3. Erdős (1965) proved that every finite set of n integers contains a sum-free subset of size at least n/3. Eberhard, Green, and Manners (Annals of Math., 2014) proved this is sharp: for every ε > 0 there exist arbitrarily large sets A ⊂ ℤ such that every subset of size ≥ (1/3 + ε)|A| contains a solution to x + y = z. Hence the optimal constant is exactly 1/3. Refinements about lower-order terms (Bourgain's (n+2)/3, and a 2025 improvement by Bedert) remain active, but the constant c itself is settled.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a prime p, determine the least possible number of three-term arithmetic progressions in a subset A of F_p with |A| = (p - 1)/2, and more generally determine the behavior when |A| = delta p for fixed delta < 0.5, including the order of magnitude of the Varnavides constant c(delta) as delta tends to 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime, and let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the field with $p$ elements. A three-term arithmetic progression in $\mathbb{F}_p$ is a triple $(x, x+d, x+2d)$ with $x \in \mathbb{F}_p$ and $d \in \mathbb{F}_p$ (the case $d = 0$ is allowed, giving trivial progressions). For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$, let $T(A)$ denote the number of triples $(x, x+d, x+2d) \in A^3$.

(a) Determine $\min\{T(A) : A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p,\ |A| = (p-1)/2\}$ as a function of $p$.

(b) More generally, fix $\delta \in (0, 1/2)$ and define
$$N(\delta, p) =  rac{1}{p^2} \min\{T(A) : A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p,\ |A| \geq \delta p\}.$$
By a theorem of Varnavides, $N(\delta, p) \geq c(\delta) > 0$ for all primes $p$ sufficiently large. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $N(\delta, p)$ as $p 	o \infty$ and, in particular, the order of magnitude of the Varnavides constant $c(\delta)$ as $\delta 	o 0^+$.
status_search_result: The question has been partially addressed. Croot (2005, Canad. Math. Bull.) proved that the minimal normalized count $N(\delta,p)$ converges to a limit as $p \to \infty$, but the exact value of this limit (and hence the exact minimum number of 3-APs for $|A|=(p-1)/2$) is not known. Obtaining sharp bounds on the Varnavides constant $c(\delta)$ as $\delta \to 0$ is known to be as deep as the quantitative Roth/Behrend problem and remains open; the best known bounds follow from improvements on Roth's theorem (Bloom–Sisask, Kelley–Meka and refinements).

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Determine how large a product-free subset of a finite group can be, where product-free means no elements x,y,z in the subset satisfy xy = z; in particular, decide whether the largest product-free subset of the alternating group A_n has size o(|A_n|).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group. A subset $S\subseteq G$ is called product-free if there do not exist elements $x,y,z\in S$ (not necessarily distinct) with $xy=z$. Let $\mathrm{pf}(G)$ denote the maximum cardinality of a product-free subset of $G$.

(a) Investigate $\mathrm{pf}(G)/|G|$ as $G$ ranges over finite groups: how large can a product-free subset of a finite group be, relative to $|G|$?

(b) For the alternating group $A_n$ on $n$ letters, decide whether
$$\mathrm{pf}(A_n) = o(|A_n|) \quad \text{as } n\to\infty,$$
i.e. whether every product-free subset of $A_n$ has size negligible compared to $|A_n| = n!/2$.
status_search_result: Part (b), the question of whether the largest product-free subset of $A_n$ has size $o(|A_n|)$, was resolved affirmatively by Keevash, Lifshitz, and Minzer (Inventiones Mathematicae, 2024; arXiv:2205.15191). paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a partition-regular set E of homogeneous linear equations, determine the minimum number f_E(N,r) of monochromatic solutions to E that can occur over all r-colorings of [1,N].
self_contained_problem:
Let E be a finite system of homogeneous linear equations with integer coefficients in some number of variables. The system E is called partition regular over the positive integers if for every positive integer r and every r-coloring of the positive integers, there exists a non-trivial monochromatic solution to E (i.e., a solution whose variables are all assigned the same color, and which is not forced trivially, e.g., by all variables being equal).

For positive integers N and r and a partition-regular system E, let f_E(N, r) denote the minimum, over all r-colorings χ: [1, N] → {1, 2, …, r} of the integer interval [1, N] = {1, 2, …, N}, of the total number of non-trivial monochromatic solutions of E with all variables in [1, N].

Problem: Determine f_E(N, r). In particular, for each partition-regular system E, determine the asymptotic behavior (and, where possible, sharp constants) of f_E(N, r) as N → ∞ for each fixed r ≥ 2.
status_search_result: Frankl, Graham and Rödl proved that for any partition-regular equation, a positive proportion of solutions in [1,N] must be monochromatic under any r-coloring, giving the correct order of magnitude. Sharp leading constants and asymptotics are known only in specific cases (e.g., Schur triples x+y=z, certain 3-variable linear equations, and multiplicative analogues such as xy=z), with recent work in 2024–2025 obtaining tight bounds for small r in particular families. The general problem of determining f_E(N,r) for arbitrary partition-regular systems remains open.

$$M(p) = \max\{|S| : S \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p \text{ and } S \neq A+A \text{ for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\}.$$
Equivalently, determining $M(p) = p - 1 - f(p)$ where $f(p)$ is the largest integer such that every subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with $|S| \geq p - f(p)$ is a sumset.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Small difference sets in integer lattices
original_question: For r in N and a finite set A in Z^r not contained in a lower-dimensional hyperplane, determine the smallest possible value of |A - A| as a function of |A| and r.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^r$ be a finite set that is not contained in any affine hyperplane of dimension strictly less than $r$ (equivalently, the affine hull of $A$ is all of $\mathbb{Z}^r \otimes \mathbb{R}$). Define the difference set
$$A - A = \{a - a' : a, a' \in A\}.$$
Determine, as a function of $n = |A|$ and $r$, the smallest possible value of $|A - A|$ over all such sets $A$. Equivalently, give a sharp lower bound
$$|A - A| \ge f(n, r)$$
together with extremal configurations achieving equality.
category_tag: additive combinatorics: difference sets in lattices
status_search_result: The problem is a known conjecture of Stanchescu. While Freiman, Heppes and Uhrin established lower bounds and Freiman proved the analogous sharp sumset bound $|A+A| \ge (r+1)|A| - r(r+1)/2$ with extremal sets classified by Stanchescu, the exact minimum of $|A-A|$ remains open. Recent work (e.g., Mudgal, "Difference sets in higher dimensions", 2021) proves $|A-A| \ge (2r-2)|A| - O_r(|A|^{1-\delta})$, making progress toward but not resolving Stanchescu's conjecture.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For any n in N and finite sets A_1,...,A_n of integers each of size at least n+1, decide whether one can choose a_i in A_i so that every nonempty sub-sum sum_{i in I} a_i is nonzero.
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer and let A_1, A_2, …, A_n be finite subsets of the integers Z such that |A_i| ≥ n+1 for every i ∈ {1,2,…,n}. Decide whether it is always possible to choose elements a_1 ∈ A_1, a_2 ∈ A_2, …, a_n ∈ A_n such that for every nonempty subset I ⊆ {1,2,…,n} one has

   ∑_{i ∈ I} a_i ≠ 0.
status_search_result: Alon and Ruzsa (1999) proved that the conclusion holds when the sets have size at least m^{1+ε}, and the problem with the optimal bound (linear in n, in particular size n+1) is highlighted as open in surveys on non-vanishing transversals. No resolution at the threshold n+1 appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Given delta in (0,1), determine the smallest k such that for every prime p and every multiplicative subgroup H of F_p^* with |H| > p^delta, the k-fold sum H + ... + H equals F_p.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\delta \in (0,1)$. For a prime $p$, let $\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ denote the multiplicative group of nonzero residues modulo $p$. For a subset $H \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ and a positive integer $k$, define the $k$-fold sumset $kH := \{h_1 + h_2 + \cdots + h_k : h_i \in H\} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$.

Determine the smallest integer $k = k(\delta) \geq 1$ with the following property: for every prime $p$ and every multiplicative subgroup $H \leq \mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ satisfying $|H| > p^{\delta}$, one has $kH = \mathbb{F}_p$.
status_search_result: The question of determining, for each $\delta \in (0,1)$, the precise smallest $k$ such that $kH = \mathbb{F}_p$ whenever $|H| > p^\delta$ remains open in general. Bounds are known via work of Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin, Bourgain–Konyagin, Heath-Brown–Konyagin, Shkredov and others: e.g. for $|H| > p^{1/4+\varepsilon}$ one has $6H = \mathbb{F}_p$, and for sufficiently large subgroups smaller $k$ suffice; but the exact threshold function $k(\delta)$ is not determined.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a prime p, determine how large a multiplicative subgroup H of F_p^* must be so that every nontrivial additive character sum over H is o(|H|).
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ denote the multiplicative group of nonzero residues modulo $p$. For a multiplicative subgroup $H \leq \mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ and an integer $a$, consider the additive character sum
$$S(H,a) \;=\; \sum_{x \in H} e^{2\pi i a x / p}.$$
Determine the threshold (as a function of $p$) on the size $|H|$ that guarantees
$$\max_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^{\times}} \bigl|S(H,a)\bigr| \;=\; o(|H|)$$
as $p \to \infty$. In other words, characterize the smallest possible growth rate of $|H| = |H(p)|$ for which every nontrivial additive character sum over $H$ is of strictly smaller order than $|H|$.
status_search_result: Substantial progress is known: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin established nontrivial cancellation $|S(H,a)| \le |H|^{1-\delta}$ once $|H| > p^{\varepsilon}$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, and later work extended this down to $|H| > p^{C/\log\log p}$ and obtained quantitative power-saving bounds for subgroups of size $\ge p^{1/4}$ and other ranges. However, the exact threshold (e.g. whether the bound $o(|H|)$ holds for subgroups as small as $(\log p)^C$) is not fully determined, so the problem remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Small sums and products modulo q
original_question: For every epsilon > 0, decide whether there is delta > 0 such that any sufficiently large q and any A subset Z/qZ with max(|A+A|, |A·A|) < q^epsilon |A| must either have |A| > q^{1-delta} or have an image modulo some nontrivial divisor d of q with at most q^delta elements.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Determine whether there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that the following holds for every sufficiently large positive integer $q$: if $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies
$$\max\bigl(|A+A|,\,|A\cdot A|\bigr) < q^{\varepsilon}\,|A|,$$
then at least one of the following must occur:
(i) $|A| > q^{1-\delta}$; or
(ii) there exists a divisor $d$ of $q$ with $d > 1$ such that the canonical image of $A$ under the reduction map $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ has at most $q^{\delta}$ elements.

Here $A+A = \{a+a' : a,a' \in A\}$ and $A\cdot A = \{a\cdot a' : a,a' \in A\}$, with operations in $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.
status_search_result: Sum-product theorems in $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ have been proved by Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin (prime $q$) and extended by Bourgain and Bourgain–Chang to composite moduli, giving statements of the form $|A+A|+|A\cdot A| \gg |A|^{1+\varepsilon}$ provided $A$ is not close to a subring/proper divisor structure. However, the precise quantitative form posed here — characterizing $A$ with $\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|) < q^{\varepsilon}|A|$ purely via $|A|>q^{1-\delta}$ or a small image modulo some divisor of $q$ — does not appear to be settled in the literature surveyed, so the problem appears to be open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Given an integer set A of prescribed size, determine the largest possible number of quadruples x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4 in A satisfying x_1^2 + x_2^2 = x_3^2 + x_4^2.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \geq 1$ and a finite set $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$ of size $|A| = n$, define the quadratic (multiplicative-style) energy
$$E_2(A) := \#\{(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) \in A^4 : x_1^2 + x_2^2 = x_3^2 + x_4^2\}.$$
Determine the maximum value
$$M(n) := \max_{\substack{A \subset \mathbb{Z} \\ |A| = n}} E_2(A),$$
and in particular determine its asymptotic behaviour as $n \to \infty$. Equivalently, find the largest possible number of quadruples $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$ in $A$ satisfying $x_1^2 + x_2^2 = x_3^2 + x_4^2$ over all integer sets $A$ of prescribed cardinality $n$.
status_search_result: This problem is listed as an open question in additive combinatorics concerning the maximal additive energy of the squares of an integer set. The web search did not find a published resolution determining the exact maximum or its precise asymptotic order; the standard upper bound $O(n^3)$ holds trivially and the question of matching lower bounds (beyond constructions giving $n^2 \log n$-type counts) appears unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a transcendental real alpha and an n-element set A of real numbers, determine how small the mixed sumset |A + alpha A| can be.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ be transcendental (that is, $\alpha$ is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients). For a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ of cardinality $n$, define the mixed sumset
\[
A + \alpha A \;=\; \{\,a + \alpha a' : a, a' \in A\,\}.
\]
Determine, as a function of $n$, the minimum possible value of $|A + \alpha A|$ taken over all transcendental $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $n$-element sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. In particular, identify matching lower and upper bounds for
\[
F(n) \;=\; \min_{\alpha,\,A}\,|A + \alpha A|.
\]
status_search_result: Konyagin and Łaba gave a construction showing |A + αA| can be as small as roughly n·exp(c√log n) for transcendental α, and proved a lower bound of order n log n / log log n. Subsequent improvements (e.g. Sanders, Schoen, and more recently Krachun–Petrov / Conlon–Lim "Sums of transcendental dilates", arXiv:2212.10128) raised the lower bound to n·exp(c√log n), matching the Konyagin–Łaba construction up to the constant c. Thus the problem is essentially resolved up to the constant in the exponent, but determining the sharp constant remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Decide whether there is a hypergraph regularity lemma for subsets of pseudorandom sparse hypergraphs of large density, with potential applications to arithmetic progressions in the primes.
self_contained_problem:
A k-uniform hypergraph H on vertex set V is said to be ε-pseudorandom (of large density p) with respect to a suitable linear-forms / discrepancy condition if, roughly speaking, the number of copies of any fixed small configuration in H matches the expected count in the random k-uniform hypergraph of edge density p up to an error of order ε times the trivial upper bound. A subset S of the edges of H is said to have relative density α if |S| ≥ α|E(H)|.

Szemerédi's regularity lemma and its hypergraph extension (the hypergraph regularity lemma of Gowers, and of Rödl–Nagle–Schacht–Skokan) provide, for every dense k-uniform hypergraph G and every η>0, a partition of the vertex set (together with auxiliary partitions of lower-uniformity edge sets) into a bounded number of pieces so that almost all of G is quasirandom with respect to this partition, in a sense strong enough to support a counting lemma for fixed sub-hypergraphs.

Problem. Establish (or refute) a relative hypergraph regularity lemma of the following form: for every k ≥ 2 and every ε>0 there exists δ>0 and a bound M=M(ε) such that, whenever H is a δ-pseudorandom k-uniform hypergraph on V (with respect to an appropriate linear-forms / discrepancy condition) and S ⊆ E(H) has relative density bounded away from 0 in H, there is a partition of V (and the lower-level edge sets) into at most M pieces with respect to which S is ε-regular and which supports a counting lemma for fixed sub-hypergraphs.

Such a result should be strong enough to be applicable to the problem of locating arithmetic progressions, and in particular long arithmetic progressions, in dense subsets of the primes via a transference-type argument.
status_search_result: A relative hypergraph regularity / counting lemma for subsets of pseudorandom sparse hypergraphs of positive relative density was established by Conlon, Fox, and Zhao ("A relative Szemerédi theorem," Geom. Funct. Anal. 25 (2015), and "Extremal results in sparse pseudorandom graphs," Adv. Math. 256 (2014)), under a linear-forms-type pseudorandomness hypothesis. This yields a relative Szemerédi theorem and a simplified proof of the Green–Tao theorem on arithmetic progressions in the primes, matching the applications envisaged in the question.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For prime p and A subset SL_2(F_p) with |A| approximately p^{5/2}, decide whether the product set A·A has size greater than p^{5/2 + delta} for some fixed delta > 0 and all sufficiently large p.
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime and let SL_2(F_p) denote the group of 2×2 matrices with entries in the finite field F_p having determinant 1. For a subset A ⊆ SL_2(F_p), define the product set
   A·A := { a' a'' : a', a'' ∈ A }.
Suppose A ⊆ SL_2(F_p) satisfies |A| ∼ p^{5/2} (that is, c_1 p^{5/2} ≤ |A| ≤ c_2 p^{5/2} for absolute constants c_1, c_2 > 0). Determine whether there exists a fixed real number δ > 0, independent of p and A, such that
   |A·A| > p^{5/2 + δ}
holds for all sufficiently large primes p and every such A.
status_search_result: Helfgott's theorem provides growth |AAA| ≥ |A|^{1+δ} when A generates SL_2(F_p) and |A| ≤ p^{3-ε}, but the borderline regime |A| ∼ p^{5/2} for the doubling |A·A| (rather than triple product) is the threshold where standard approaches stall, and no published resolution of this specific two-fold product growth question in the |A| ∼ p^{5/2} regime is found in the literature. It appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For epsilon in (0,1/2], classify all polynomials P in Z[x,y] for which there exists delta(epsilon) > 0 such that, for all sufficiently large primes p and all A subset F_p with |A| <= p^epsilon, the image set {P(a prime,a double prime) : a prime,a double prime in A} has size at least |A|^{1+delta}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/2]$. Classify all polynomials $P(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ with the following property: there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) > 0$ and a threshold $p_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for every prime $p > p_0(\varepsilon)$ and every subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ (the field with $p$ elements) with $|A| \le p^{\varepsilon}$, one has
$$\big|\{ P(a', a'') : a', a'' \in A \}\big| \ge |A|^{1+\delta}.$$
That is, give a necessary and sufficient structural condition on $P$ ensuring such a polynomial-expansion lower bound for all sufficiently small subsets of every large prime field.
category_tag: Sum-product / expanding polynomials over finite fields
status_search_result: The full classification of expanding polynomials $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ over prime fields $\mathbb{F}_p$ for sets of size up to $p^\varepsilon$ is generally regarded as open. Over $\mathbb{R}$, the Elekes–Rónyai theorem (and its quantitative form by Raz–Sharir–Solymosi) classifies non-expanders as those of the form $g(\varphi(x)+\psi(y))$ or $g(\varphi(x)\psi(y))$. Analogues have been obtained over $\mathbb{F}_p$ (e.g., by Tao, and by Shkredov and others) but a complete classification with explicit $\delta(\varepsilon)$ uniformly in $p$ for all subsets up to size $p^\varepsilon$ has not been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For theta in [0,1) and N >= 1, estimate the minimum possible length of the longest arithmetic progression contained in A + A among all A subset [1,N] with |A| >= N^{1-theta}.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, let $\ell(A)$ denote the maximum length of an arithmetic progression contained in $A$, and let $A+A=\{a+a':a,a'\in A\}$. For a real parameter $\theta\in[0,1)$ and an integer $N\ge 1$, determine the asymptotic behavior (as $N\to\infty$) of
$$F(N,\theta) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\ell(A+A)\;:\; A\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\},\ |A|\ge N^{1-\theta}\bigr\}.$$
That is, find matching upper and lower bounds on $F(N,\theta)$ as a function of $N$ and $\theta$.
status_search_result: The problem of determining the longest guaranteed AP in $A+A$ for dense subsets of $[1,N]$ has been studied extensively (Bourgain, Freiman–Halberstam–Ruzsa, Green, Sanders, Croot–Łaba–Sisask). For sets of density $\alpha=N^{-\theta}$, the best known lower bound is roughly $\exp(c(\alpha\log N)^{1/2})$ (Croot–Łaba–Sisask), while Ruzsa's construction gives an upper bound of order $\exp(c(\log N)^{2/3+\epsilon})$ when $\alpha$ is bounded below. The gap between these bounds remains unresolved, so the problem is still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Progressions in large subsets of thin sumsets
original_question: For every epsilon in (0,1], decide whether there is delta > 0 such that if a sufficiently large finite integer set A has n elements and |A+A| <= n^{1+delta}, then every subset S of A+A carrying at least epsilon n^2 additive representations contains a three-term arithmetic progression.
self_contained_problem:
Decide whether the following statement holds: For every ε ∈ (0,1], there exists δ > 0 such that for every sufficiently large finite set A ⊂ ℤ with n := |A| and |A + A| ≤ n^{1+δ}, every subset S ⊆ A + A satisfying
  ∑_{s ∈ S} #{(a′, a″) ∈ A × A : a′ + a″ = s} ≥ ε n²
contains a nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression (i.e., three distinct elements x, y, z ∈ S with x + z = 2y).
category_tag: Additive combinatorics / arithmetic progressions in sumsets
status_search_result: The question about dense representation-weighted subsets of A+A containing 3-APs under small-doubling appears on Croot–Lev's open problem list and is not reported as resolved. Related results (Sanders; Croot–Łaba–Sisask; and extensions to abelian groups) give 3-APs in A itself under small doubling, but the stronger statement for arbitrary dense subsets S ⊆ A+A carrying ≥ εn² representations does not appear to be established. original_question: Given f,g : F_p -> [0,1] with equal zeroth Fourier coefficients, large total mass, and very close nonzero Fourier spectra, decide whether every h majorized by f with a positive fraction of f’s mass has a partner h prime majorized by g whose nonzero Fourier spectrum remains close to that of h.

$$\widehat{u}(r)=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_p} u(x)\,e^{-2\pi i rx/p},\qquad r\in\mathbb{F}_p.$$
For $\varepsilon>0$, the $\varepsilon$-Fourier spectrum of $u$ is
$$\mathrm{Spec}_\varepsilon(u)=\{r\in\mathbb{F}_p:|\widehat{u}(r)|\ge \varepsilon\,\|u\|_1\},$$
where $\|u\|_1=\sum_{x}|u(x)|$. Say two subsets $S,T\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p$ are $\delta$-close if there is a bijection between $S$ and $T$ pairing each $r\in S$ with some $r'\in T$ satisfying $|r-r'|\le \delta p$ (and the Fourier coefficients at paired frequencies agree to within $\delta$).

(i) $\widehat{f}(0)=\widehat{g}(0)$, and this common value (the mean) is bounded below by a fixed constant $\alpha>0$;

original_question: For n >= 7, decide whether every n-element set of integers is Freiman-isomorphic to a subset of [0, 2^{n-2}], equivalently whether each Freiman-isomorphism class has an integer representative of length at most 2^{n-2}.
self_contained_problem:
Two finite sets of integers $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ are called Freiman isomorphic (of order 2) if there is a bijection $\varphi:A\to B$ such that for all $i,j,k,\ell\in\{1,\dots,n\}$,
$$a_i+a_j=a_k+a_\ell \iff \varphi(a_i)+\varphi(a_j)=\varphi(a_k)+\varphi(a_\ell).$$
For a finite set of integers $S$, define its length to be $\max S-\min S$. 

Prove or disprove the following: for every integer $n\ge 7$ and every $n$-element set of integers $A$, there exists a set $B\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,2^{n-2}\}$ that is Freiman isomorphic to $A$. Equivalently, every Freiman-isomorphism class of $n$-element integer sets contains a representative of length at most $2^{n-2}$.

(The set $\{0,1,2,4,8,\dots,2^{n-2}\}$ shows that the bound $2^{n-2}$, if correct, would be sharp.)
status_search_result: The problem is stated as a conjecture in the Croot–Lev open problems list and discussed in work of Konyagin and Lev on Freiman isomorphism. No subsequent paper claiming a proof or disproof for $n\ge 7$ was located; the example $\{0,1,2,4,\dots,2^{n-2}\}$ shows the bound would be sharp, and the question of whether $2^{n-2}$ is the correct extremal value appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Decide whether every connected addition Cayley graph induced on a finite cyclic group by a four-element subset is Hamiltonian.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer and let $\mathbb{Z}_n = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ denote the cyclic group of order $n$. For a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n$, the addition Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}^+(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)$ is the (undirected) graph with vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_n$ in which two vertices $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}_n$ are joined by an edge if and only if $x + y \in S$ (loops, when $2x \in S$, are ignored). A graph on $n$ vertices is called Hamiltonian if it contains a cycle passing through every vertex exactly once.

Decide whether the following statement is true: for every integer $n$ and every $4$-element subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $\mathrm{Cay}^+(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)$ is connected, the graph $\mathrm{Cay}^+(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)$ is Hamiltonian.
status_search_result: Web searches reveal active research on Hamiltonicity of addition Cayley graphs on finite abelian groups (e.g., work by Cheng, Lev, and others on Hamilton cycles in addition graphs), but no specific source was found that conclusively settles the case of connected addition Cayley graphs induced by 4-element subsets of a finite cyclic group. The status appears to remain unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: Which factors enable learning behavior in ongoing work teams inside real organizations, rather than only in laboratory groups, and how do those factors shape whether teams engage in behaviors such as asking questions, seeking feedback, discussing errors, and experimenting with new actions?
self_contained_problem: Consider ongoing work teams embedded in real organizations (as opposed to ad hoc laboratory groups). Define a team's "learning behavior" as the observable set of activities by which team members acquire and apply knowledge, including: asking questions, seeking feedback (from teammates, leaders, customers, or other sources), openly discussing errors and unexpected outcomes, reflecting on past performance, and experimenting with new actions or work methods. Identify the antecedent factors at the individual, team, and organizational levels that enable or inhibit such learning behavior in these field settings, and articulate the mechanism by which each factor influences a team's propensity to engage in the listed behaviors. In particular, propose and justify a model in which a shared interpersonal climate variable (capturing team members' beliefs about the consequences of taking interpersonal risks within the team) mediates the relationship between contextual supports (such as supportive leader behavior, context support, and coaching) and observed learning behavior, and explain how this mediating variable in turn affects team performance outcomes.
status_search_result: The question is addressed by an established line of organizational research demonstrating that team psychological safety, together with team efficacy, leader coaching, context support, and team structure/design, enables learning behaviors that in turn predict team performance. The core mediating model (context/leadership → psychological safety → learning behavior → performance) is widely supported, while precise boundary conditions, cross-cultural generalizability, and dynamic/longitudinal mechanisms remain active areas of investigation, so the broader question is best described as partially solved.
