paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: How should team structures and team members' shared beliefs about their interpersonal context be studied together, rather than separately, in order to explain learning behavior in work teams?
self_contained_problem: Consider work teams, where each team is characterized by (i) structural features (such as team design, leader coaching, context support, and composition) and (ii) shared beliefs among members about the interpersonal context of the team (in particular, the shared perception known as psychological safety: the belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking). Let learning behavior denote team-level activities such as seeking feedback, sharing information, asking for help, experimenting, and discussing errors. Formulate and justify an integrated framework that jointly models team structures and shared interpersonal beliefs—rather than treating them as independent predictors—so as to explain variation in learning behavior across teams, and specify how the two classes of variables interact (e.g., as antecedents, mediators, or moderators) in producing learning behavior and downstream team performance. The framework should be amenable to investigation using both quantitative and qualitative methods.
status_search_result: The question is a conceptual/empirical research proposal in organizational behavior rather than a formally settled mathematical problem. Subsequent literature has elaborated joint models of psychological safety and team structure (e.g., reviews by Edmondson and Lei, 2014), but no single canonical "solution" exists; the integrative modeling agenda remains an ongoing area of empirical research.

paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: Do beliefs about the interpersonal context differ across teams within the same organization, and if so, how do those beliefs affect team learning behavior and broader team outcomes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider work teams embedded within a single organization. For each team, define "beliefs about the interpersonal context" as the shared perception among team members regarding whether the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking (e.g., admitting errors, asking for help, proposing new ideas, raising concerns), referred to as team psychological safety. Define "team learning behavior" as the set of activities through which a team obtains and processes information that allows it to adapt and improve, such as seeking feedback, sharing information, asking for help, talking about errors, and experimenting. Define "team outcomes" to include team performance as judged by relevant internal or external stakeholders.

Formulate and empirically test the following questions:
(a) Do beliefs about the interpersonal context (team psychological safety) vary systematically across teams within the same organization, rather than being uniform at the organizational level?
(b) If such between-team variation exists, does team psychological safety have a positive effect on team learning behavior?
(c) Does team learning behavior in turn mediate the relationship between team psychological safety and team performance?

Specify a model linking antecedents (e.g., supportive team-leader coaching, context support) to team psychological safety, then to team learning behavior, and finally to team performance, and provide a methodology (quantitative survey measures combined with qualitative observation) for assessing each construct and testing the hypothesized relationships across a sample of teams in one organization.
category_tag: team psychological safety and learning behavior
status_search_result: The study by Edmondson (1999) reported that psychological safety beliefs do vary across teams within the same organization, that they positively predict team learning behavior, and that team learning behavior mediates the effect of psychological safety on team performance. These findings have been replicated and extended in numerous subsequent studies and meta-analyses (e.g., Frazier et al., 2017), so the original empirical questions are considered answered (solved) within the organizational behavior literature.

paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: Through what mechanism do shared perceptions of team efficacy contribute to good team performance, and does team efficacy improve performance in part by increasing members' confidence to engage in learning behavior?
self_contained_problem: Consider a work team as a small group of individuals who interact interdependently to accomplish shared goals. Define team efficacy as the shared belief among members in the team's collective capability to perform tasks successfully, and define learning behavior as the set of actions through which team members acquire and process information that allows the team to adapt and improve (e.g., seeking feedback, asking for help, discussing errors, experimenting). Define team performance as the degree to which the team accomplishes its desired goals.\n\nIdentify and justify the mechanism(s) by which shared perceptions of team efficacy contribute to good team performance. In particular, determine whether team efficacy improves team performance, at least in part, by raising members' confidence to engage in learning behavior; that is, whether learning behavior partially mediates the relationship between team efficacy and team performance. Provide a model of this mediating relationship together with conditions under which the mediation holds.

paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: Across different kinds of teams, when is learning behavior useful for performance and when might it instead consume time without improving results, especially for highly routine or tightly constrained tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of work teams, where each team t is characterized by a task-type vector x_t (capturing attributes such as task routineness, repetitiveness, variability of inputs, need for adaptation or innovation, and degree of external constraint) and engages in some measurable level L_t of learning behavior, defined as the collective activities of asking questions, seeking feedback, experimenting, reflecting on results, and discussing errors or unexpected outcomes. Let P_t denote a measure of team performance (e.g., efficiency and quality of task output).

Model the expected performance as a function f(L, x) and define the marginal utility of learning behavior for a team with task profile x as u(x) = ∂E[P | L, x]/∂L evaluated at typical operating levels of L.

Characterize the set of task profiles x for which u(x) > 0 (learning behavior improves performance) versus the set for which u(x) ≤ 0 (learning behavior consumes time without improving, or actively detracts from, performance). In particular:

(a) Identify which components of x (e.g., routineness, repetitiveness, low need for modification, tight operational constraints) drive u(x) toward non-positive values.
(b) Determine whether there exist threshold conditions on task routineness/constraint above which engaging in learning behavior reduces team efficiency.
(c) Provide an empirically grounded classification of team types (for example, production teams, service teams, project teams, management teams, action teams) according to the sign and magnitude of u(x).
status_search_result: The question of when team learning behavior helps versus hinders performance across different team types remains an active area of organizational behavior research, with mixed empirical findings and ongoing calls for contingency-based theories. No definitive resolution has been established; results vary by task type, with several studies suggesting diminishing or negative returns for highly routine tasks, but a comprehensive cross-team-type characterization is still considered an open research agenda.

paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: What are the causal and longitudinal relationships among team psychological safety, risk-taking learning behavior, reinforcement from team responses, and gradual changes in shared beliefs over time, including possible self-reinforcing cycles or spirals?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a team modeled as a discrete-time dynamical system with state variables at time $t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$:
- $S_t \in [0,1]$: the level of shared team psychological safety (a shared belief that interpersonal risk-taking is safe),
- $L_t \in [0,1]$: the rate of risk-taking learning behavior (asking questions, admitting errors, seeking feedback, experimenting),
- $R_t \in [-1,1]$: the average reinforcement from team responses to learning behavior (positive when unpunished/rewarded, negative when punished),
- and exogenous perturbation processes $M_t, K_t, C_t$ representing changes in membership, leadership, and context, respectively.

Suppose the joint evolution is governed by
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{t+1} &= f_L(S_t, L_t) + \eta^L_t,\\
R_{t+1} &= f_R(L_t, S_t, M_t, K_t, C_t) + \eta^R_t,\\
S_{t+1} &= f_S(S_t, L_t, R_t, M_t, K_t, C_t) + \eta^S_t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where $f_L, f_R, f_S$ are smooth, monotone non-decreasing in each "supportive" argument and $\eta^L_t, \eta^R_t, \eta^S_t$ are zero-mean noise terms representing minor events and subtle interactions. Assume that increases in $S$ raise expected $L$, that nonnegative $R$ feeds back to raise expected $S$, and that the influence of any single event on $S$ is small (so shared beliefs change only gradually).

Address the following:

1. (Causality) Identify conditions on $(f_L, f_R, f_S)$ under which the directed causal graph $S \to L \to R \to S$ is identifiable from longitudinal data $\{(S_t, L_t, R_t)\}_{t=0}^{T}$, and prove that no purely cross-sectional observation (data at a single $t$) can distinguish the model above from one in which the arrow $S \to L$ is reversed.

2. (Self-reinforcing spirals) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the derivatives of $f_L, f_R, f_S$ at a fixed point $(S^*, L^*, R^*)$ for the linearization to have a real eigenvalue greater than $1$ (an "upward spiral") or less than $-1$ in modulus (a "downward spiral"). Characterize the basins of attraction of any stable upward and downward fixed points.

3. (Gradual emergence) Show, under a small-noise / slow-update scaling $S_{t+1} = S_t + \varepsilon\,g(S_t, L_t, R_t) + \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\sigma\,\xi_t$ with $\varepsilon \to 0^+$, that $S_t$ converges (in the sense of weak convergence of $S_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}$) to the solution of an explicit stochastic differential equation, and use this limit to quantify the expected time for a shared belief to form.

4. (Perturbations) Quantify how shocks in $M_t, K_t, C_t$ (changes in membership, leadership, or context) shift the stable equilibria of the system, and give sharp bounds on the magnitude of perturbation required to push the team out of a high-safety basin into a low-safety basin.
status_search_result: The question, as a mathematical formalization of longitudinal causal feedback among psychological-safety variables, is not a standard named open problem. The underlying empirical question (causal/longitudinal dynamics and self-reinforcing spirals of team psychological safety, learning behavior, and reinforcement) has been the subject of ongoing organizational-behavior research since 1999, with longitudinal and multi-wave studies (e.g., reviews by Edmondson & Lei 2014; Newman, Donohue & Eva 2017) providing partial evidence of reciprocal effects but no definitive resolution of causal dynamics or formal identification of spirals. Status is therefore best described as unknown / partially explored rather than mathematically solved.

self_contained_problem: Consider an empirical study of work teams conducted within a single organization, comprising a sample of 51 teams, in which statistical relationships are reported between team-level psychological safety (a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking), team learning behavior (such as seeking feedback, discussing errors, and experimenting), and team performance outcomes. paper_title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
original_question: How are structural factors and interpersonal factors interrelated in explaining team effectiveness, and how might team learning behavior change or mitigate undesirable structural conditions over time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a work team modeled as a group of individuals who interact repeatedly over time to accomplish interdependent tasks. Define the following constructs:

- Structural factors of the team: stable, design-level features such as team composition (diversity of skills, tenure, and roles), team size, clarity and meaningfulness of the team's task, availability of context support (resources, information, rewards), and team leader coaching.
- Interpersonal factors of the team: shared beliefs and dynamics among members, in particular team psychological safety, defined as a shared belief held by members of the team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking (e.g., asking questions, seeking feedback, admitting errors, proposing new ideas, or discussing problems without fear of being embarrassed, rejected, or punished).
- Team learning behavior: ongoing collective activities through which a team obtains and processes data that allow it to adapt and improve, including seeking feedback, sharing information, asking for help, talking about errors, and experimenting.
- Team effectiveness: an outcome combining objective performance against team goals and members' satisfaction or growth.

Formulate and analyze a dynamic model in which structural factors S(t), psychological safety P(t), learning behavior L(t), and effectiveness E(t) evolve over time t, and address the following questions:

1. Specify the interrelations between S(t) and P(t) in jointly determining E(t): under what conditions does psychological safety mediate, moderate, or amplify the effect of structural factors on team effectiveness, and conversely, how do structural factors shape the formation of psychological safety?
2. Characterize the trajectories along which team learning behavior L(t), driven by psychological safety, can alter or compensate for initially unfavorable structural conditions (e.g., low context support, ambiguous task design, or weak coaching), and determine sufficient conditions on P(t) and L(t) under which long-run effectiveness E(t) approaches that achievable under favorable structural conditions.
3. Identify whether there exist structural deficits that cannot be mitigated by team learning behavior alone, and characterize the boundary between mitigable and non-mitigable structural conditions.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a future-research agenda about the dynamic interplay between structural and interpersonal team factors and the capacity of team learning behavior to mitigate structural deficits. Subsequent research on psychological safety and team learning (e.g., meta-analyses by Frazier et al. 2017 and reviews by Edmondson and Lei 2014) has explored components of these relationships but has not produced a unified dynamic theory answering the questions jointly; the problem remains open as a research program.

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006

original_question: Is the group SLn(Z), for n≥3, uniform Kazhdan ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a discrete group with Kazhdan's property (T). For a finite generating set $S$ of $G$ and a unitary representation $\pi:G\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H_\pi)$ without nonzero invariant vectors, define the Kazhdan constant
$$\kappa(G,S,\pi)=\inf_{\xi\in\mathcal H_\pi,\,\|\xi\|=1}\sup_{s\in S}\|\pi(s)\xi-\xi\|,$$
and set $\kappa(G,S)=\inf_\pi \kappa(G,S,\pi)$, where the infimum runs over all unitary representations of $G$ without nonzero invariant vectors. The group $G$ is called uniform Kazhdan if
$$\inf_{S}\kappa(G,S)>0,$$
where the infimum is taken over all finite generating subsets $S$ of $G$.

Question: For every integer $n\geq 3$, is the group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)$ uniform Kazhdan?
category_tag: Kazhdan property (T) and uniform Kazhdan constants
status_search_result: Although explicit Kazhdan constants for fixed natural generating sets of SL_n(Z) (n≥3) are known (Shalom, Kassabov, with asymptotically sharp bounds in n), the question of whether SL_n(Z) is uniform Kazhdan—i.e. whether the infimum of Kazhdan constants over all finite generating sets is positive—appears to remain open. Gelander–Żuk-type obstructions (dense embeddings into Lie groups) rule out uniformity for some groups, and Osin–Sonkin constructed uniform Kazhdan groups, but no resolution for SL_n(Z) was found in the search.

original_question: Let A →B be a K(n)-local G-Galois extension. Then there is a homotopy equivalence T∧KA→T∧(KB )hG.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a prime $p$ and a chromatic height $n\geq 1$, and let $K(n)$ denote the $n$-th Morava $K$-theory at $p$. Work in the category of $K(n)$-local commutative $S$-algebras (structured ring spectra), and let $L_{K(n)}$ denote Bousfield localization at $K(n)$.

Following Rognes' framework, say that a map $A\to B$ of $K(n)$-local commutative $S$-algebras is a $K(n)$-local $G$-Galois extension (for a finite group $G$ acting on $B$ over $A$) if:
(i) the natural map $A\to B^{hG}$ is a weak equivalence, and
(ii) the natural map $B\wedge_A B \to \prod_G B$ is a $K(n)$-local equivalence.

Let $T$ be any spectrum, and let the smash product $T\wedge_{K} (-)$ denote the $K(n)$-localized smash product, where $K=K(n)$. The group $G$ acts on $B$ and hence on $T\wedge_K B$, and one may form the homotopy fixed point spectrum $(T\wedge_K B)^{hG}$.

Prove or disprove: for every $K(n)$-local $G$-Galois extension $A\to B$ and every spectrum $T$, the canonical map
$$ T\wedge_K A \;\longrightarrow\; (T\wedge_K B)^{hG} $$
is a weak equivalence.

status_search_result: Closely related results are known: Behrens–Davis (arXiv:0808.1092) and subsequent work establish homotopy fixed point descent for $K(n)$-local (pro)finite Galois extensions, especially for Morava $E$-theory with the Morava stabilizer group. However, no source consulted explicitly confirms the general statement (for all spectra $T$ and all finite $K(n)$-local $G$-Galois extensions) as fully resolved in the form stated, so the precise status of this exact conjecture is not clearly verifiable from the search.

original_question: Let B be a suitably finite K(n)-local commutative S-algebra (for example LK(n)S→B could be a G-Galois extension). Then the map V∧KB→T∧KB induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups in suﬃciently high de- grees.
self_contained_problem:
Let $K(n)$ denote the $n$-th Morava $K$-theory at an implicit prime $p$, and let $L_{K(n)}$ denote Bousfield localization with respect to $K(n)$. For a commutative $S$-algebra (i.e. $E_\infty$-ring spectrum) $B$, write $K(B)$ for its algebraic $K$-theory spectrum, $THH(B)$ for its topological Hochschild homology, $TC(B)$ for its topological cyclic homology, and let
$$T(B) = TC(B), \qquad V(B) = K(B)$$
(so that there is a cyclotomic trace map $V(B) \to T(B)$). Consider $B$ a "suitably finite" $K(n)$-local commutative $S$-algebra; for instance one may assume that the unit map $L_{K(n)} S \to B$ exhibits $B$ as a $G$-Galois extension (in the sense of Rognes) for some finite group $G$.

Conjecture: the cyclotomic trace map
$$V(B) \wedge K \longrightarrow T(B) \wedge K$$
(after smashing with the periodic complex $K$-theory spectrum $K$) induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups in all sufficiently high degrees.

Prove or disprove this statement.
category_tag: Chromatic homotopy theory and algebraic K-theory
status_search_result: The conjecture (a form of the Ausoni–Rognes chromatic redshift / Galois descent program) has been verified in several important cases: Clausen–Mathew–Naumann–Noel (2016, arXiv:1606.03328) prove descent in algebraic $K$-theory for many $G$-Galois extensions of $E_\infty$-ring spectra, establishing significant parts of the Ausoni–Rognes conjectures. Further results on chromatic redshift by Hahn–Wilson, Yuan, and others have advanced the program. However, the full statement for all suitably finite $K(n)$-local commutative $S$-algebras remains an active research direction rather than a completed theorem.

original_question: If Ω n is a separably closed extension of the S-algebraic fraction field of LK(n)Sp, then there is a homotopy equivalence LK(n+1)K(Ω n)≃En+1. For n = 0 this reduces to LK(1)K( ¯Qp) ≃E1 ≃KU p, a weaker formulation of Suslin's Theorem.
self_contained_problem:
Setting and notation. Fix a prime $p$ and an integer $n\ge 0$. Let $S$ denote the sphere spectrum and let $K(n)$ denote the $n$-th Morava $K$-theory at the prime $p$ (with the convention that $K(0)=H\mathbb{Q}$). Let $L_{K(n)}$ denote Bousfield localization with respect to $K(n)$, and write $L_{K(n)}S$ for the $K(n)$-local sphere spectrum. Let $E_n$ denote the $n$-th Lubin–Tate (Morava $E$-) spectrum, a $K(n)$-local commutative ring spectrum with $\pi_0 E_n \cong W(\mathbb{F}_{p^n})[[u_1,\dots,u_{n-1}]]$ and $\pi_* E_n = \pi_0 E_n[u^{\pm 1}]$, $|u|=2$. For a commutative ring spectrum $R$, let $K(R)$ denote its algebraic $K$-theory spectrum.

A commutative ring spectrum $R$ is called an "$S$-algebraic field" (in the sense relevant to chromatic homotopy theory) if its homotopy groups form a graded field; the "$S$-algebraic fraction field" of a $K(n)$-local commutative ring spectrum is its analogue of the field of fractions in the $S$-algebraic category. A "separably closed extension" $\Omega_n$ of the $S$-algebraic fraction field of $L_{K(n)}S$ is an $S$-algebraic field extension that is separably closed in the appropriate $S$-algebraic sense.

Problem. Let $\Omega_n$ be a separably closed extension of the $S$-algebraic fraction field of $L_{K(n)}S$. Prove or disprove that there is a homotopy equivalence
$$ L_{K(n+1)}\, K(\Omega_n) \;\simeq\; E_{n+1}. $$
(For $n=0$ this should specialize to $L_{K(1)} K(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p) \simeq E_1 \simeq KU_p^\wedge$, a weak form of Suslin's theorem on the algebraic $K$-theory of an algebraically closed field.)
status_search_result: The conjecture is part of the Ausoni–Rognes "chromatic redshift" program. Substantial progress on related redshift conjectures has been made (e.g. Clausen–Mathew–Naumann–Noel on descent and an Ausoni–Rognes conjecture, and recent work by Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank, Land–Mathew–Meier–Tamme on telescopic Galois descent), but the specific statement that $L_{K(n+1)} K(\Omega_n) \simeq E_{n+1}$ for a separably closed $S$-algebraic extension $\Omega_n$ of the fraction field of $L_{K(n)}S$ does not appear to have been established in general; it remains an open conjecture beyond the classical $n=0$ case (Suslin).

original_question: Is FW equivalant to (T), or 13 does there exist a group G such that G does not have property (T), but G and all its finite index subgroups have property FW?
self_contained_problem:
A countable discrete group $G$ is said to have Kazhdan's property (T) if every unitary representation of $G$ that has almost invariant vectors must have a nonzero invariant vector. Equivalently, $G$ has property (T) if and only if every continuous affine isometric action of $G$ on a real Hilbert space has a fixed point.

A group $G$ is said to have property FW if every continuous action of $G$ by automorphisms on a CAT(0) cube complex has a global fixed point; equivalently, every action of $G$ on a (discrete) wall space has a bounded orbit on the set of half-spaces, or equivalently every cellular action of $G$ on a CAT(0) cube complex has a fixed vertex. Property (T) implies property FW, and property FW implies Serre's property FA.

Question: Is property FW equivalent to property (T) for countable groups? Equivalently, does there exist a countable group $G$ such that $G$ does not have property (T), but $G$ and every subgroup of finite index in $G$ have property FW?
status_search_result: Property FW, introduced and studied by Cornulier, is a natural weakening of Kazhdan's property (T). Cornulier's monograph and subsequent works (e.g., on 1-dimensional piecewise groups, 2020/2021) provide examples of groups with property FW (such as Thompson's group T) that do not have property (T). However, Thompson's group T is simple, so the strengthening of the question requiring all finite-index subgroups to have FW is not immediately settled by it. No source found establishes the equivalence with (T) under the finite-index-subgroup condition, nor a counterexample satisfying it. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: A residually-p group is amenable if and only if its growth series{bn}grows subexponentially, that is, lim(bn)1/n = 1. A little motivation: consider the augmentation ideal ϖin the group ring FpG.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finitely generated group. Recall that $G$ is called residually-$p$ if for every non-identity element $g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ of $p$-power index with $g \notin N$. Let $\mathbb{F}_p G$ denote the group algebra of $G$ over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p$ elements, and let $\varpi \subset \mathbb{F}_p G$ be its augmentation ideal, i.e., the kernel of the augmentation map $\mathbb{F}_p G \to \mathbb{F}_p$ sending each group element to $1$. Define the associated graded growth sequence
$$b_n := \dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\bigl(\varpi^n / \varpi^{n+1}\bigr), \qquad n \geq 0.$$
The sequence $\{b_n\}$ is said to grow subexponentially if
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n^{1/n} = 1.$$

Prove or disprove: a finitely generated residually-$p$ group $G$ is amenable if and only if its growth series $\{b_n\}$ grows subexponentially.
status_search_result: A web search returns only the original conjecture in the conjecture collection and related surveys on growth and amenability; no resolution (proof or counterexample) of this characterization of amenability for residually-$p$ groups via subexponential growth of $\dim \varpi^n/\varpi^{n+1}$ appears in the literature found. The conjecture appears to remain open.

original_question: As proved recently, the outer automorphism group of any polycyclic by finite group, and, hence, also the group of homotopy equivalences of any aspherical space with a polycyclic by finite fundamental group is an arithmetic group. Hence, we ask: Does Sullivan 's arithmeticity result for nilpotent spaces carry over to a (suitable) more general class of polycyclic spaces ?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A group $\Gamma$ is called polycyclic-by-finite if it has a normal polycyclic subgroup of finite index. A connected CW-complex $X$ is called nilpotent if $\pi_1(X)$ is a nilpotent group acting nilpotently on $\pi_n(X)$ for every $n\ge 2$. An aspherical space is a connected CW-complex whose higher homotopy groups vanish; we call such a space polycyclic if its fundamental group is polycyclic-by-finite. For a based connected CW-complex $X$ of finite type, let $\mathcal{E}(X)$ denote the group of based homotopy classes of self-homotopy equivalences of $X$. A subgroup of a linear algebraic group $G$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ is called arithmetic if it is commensurable with $G(\mathbb{Z})$ for some integral structure. 

It is known (Sullivan's arithmeticity theorem) that if $X$ is a finite nilpotent CW-complex, then $\mathcal{E}(X)$ is, up to a finite kernel, an arithmetic group. It is also known that the outer automorphism group of any polycyclic-by-finite group is an arithmetic group, and consequently $\mathcal{E}(X)$ is arithmetic for any aspherical CW-complex $X$ with polycyclic-by-finite fundamental group.

Problem. Determine whether Sullivan's arithmeticity theorem extends to a suitable class of "polycyclic spaces" properly containing both finite nilpotent CW-complexes and aspherical CW-complexes with polycyclic-by-finite fundamental group. More precisely: identify a natural class $\mathcal{C}$ of connected CW-complexes of finite type (with polycyclic-by-finite fundamental group acting suitably on higher homotopy groups) such that for every $X\in\mathcal{C}$, the group $\mathcal{E}(X)$ of based self-homotopy equivalences is, up to a finite kernel, an arithmetic group; or show that no such class strictly extending the two known cases can exist.
status_search_result: Sullivan's arithmeticity result for finite nilpotent CW-complexes and the arithmeticity of outer automorphism groups of polycyclic-by-finite groups (hence of homotopy equivalences of corresponding aspherical spaces) are well established. A general unifying extension to a broader class of "polycyclic spaces" does not appear to have been established; recent work continues to study automorphisms of nilpotent spaces but no definitive resolution to this problem was located.

original_question: The Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of the coho- mology ring is equal to zero: RegH *(G,k ) = 0. This conjecture was first announced at the opening workshop of the MSRI commutative algebra year (1), as a refinement of a conjecture of Benson and Carlson (4).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be a field whose characteristic $p$ divides the order of $G$. Consider the graded cohomology ring $H^*(G,k)$, which is a finitely generated graded-commutative $k$-algebra. Let $R = H^*(G,k)$ if $p = 2$, or the commutative subring of elements in even degree if $p$ is odd, so that $R$ is a finitely generated commutative graded $k$-algebra, and view $H^*(G,k)$ as a finitely generated graded $R$-module. The Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of a finitely generated graded module $M$ over such a ring is defined by
$$\operatorname{Reg}(M) = \max_{i \ge 0}\bigl(\max\{\, n : H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)_n \neq 0\,\} + i\bigr),$$
where $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(-)$ denotes local cohomology with respect to the maximal homogeneous ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$ (with the convention that the inner maximum is $-\infty$ if the local cohomology module vanishes). Prove or disprove: for every finite group $G$ and every field $k$ of characteristic dividing $|G|$,
$$\operatorname{Reg} H^*(G,k) = 0.$$

original_question: RegH *(BG;k) =-d. To explain the orientation condition, let G =T 3 ⋊ Z/ 2, a semidirect product of a 3-torus by an involution acting through inversion, and k be a field of characteristic ̸= 2.

Let $G$ be a compact Lie group of dimension $d$, and let $k$ be a field. Consider the graded-commutative cohomology ring $H^*(BG;k)$, where $BG$ is the classifying space of $G$. For a finitely generated graded module $M$ over a Noetherian graded $k$-algebra, recall the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity
$$\operatorname{Reg} M \;=\; \max_{i\ge 0}\bigl(\,a_i(M) + i\,\bigr),$$
where $a_i(M)$ is the top degree of the $i$-th local cohomology module $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)$ (with respect to the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of positive-degree elements), with the convention $a_i(M) = -\infty$ if $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M) = 0$.

$$\operatorname{Reg} H^*(BG;k) \;=\; -d.$$

Show in particular that the orientation hypothesis is necessary by analyzing the example $G = T^3 \rtimes \mathbb Z/2$, the semidirect product of a $3$-torus by an involution acting by inversion, with $k$ a field of characteristic different from $2$.

original_question: Is it true that any infinite amenable group contains an infinite abelian subgroup (this is of course of interest only for torsion groups)?
self_contained_problem:
A discrete group $G$ is called amenable if there exists a finitely additive probability measure $\mu : \mathcal{P}(G) \to [0,1]$ defined on all subsets of $G$ that is invariant under left translation, i.e. $\mu(gA) = \mu(A)$ for every $g \in G$ and every $A \subseteq G$. A group is called a torsion group if every element has finite order. A subgroup $H \leq G$ is called abelian if $hk = kh$ for all $h, k \in H$.

Question: Does every infinite amenable group $G$ contain an infinite abelian subgroup? Equivalently (since the non-torsion case is trivial, as an element of infinite order generates an infinite cyclic subgroup), does every infinite amenable torsion group contain an infinite abelian subgroup?

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: For solvable non-virtually nilpotent groups, is there a canonical way of constructing a Følner sequence ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated discrete group. Recall that a Følner sequence in $G$ is a sequence $(F_n)_{n\ge 1}$ of non-empty finite subsets of $G$ such that for every $g \in G$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{|gF_n \triangle F_n|}{|F_n|} = 0,$$
where $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference. The existence of such a sequence is equivalent to amenability of $G$. A group $G$ is said to be virtually nilpotent if it contains a nilpotent subgroup of finite index. Every finitely generated solvable group is amenable and hence admits Følner sequences, but the standard existence proofs are non-constructive. For finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups, balls in a word metric provide a canonical Følner sequence (by polynomial growth and Pansu's theorem).

Problem: For finitely generated solvable groups that are not virtually nilpotent, give a canonical construction of a Følner sequence. That is, describe an explicit procedure that, given such a group $G$ (presented for instance by generators and relations, or by its structure as an iterated extension of abelian groups), produces a specific Følner sequence $(F_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $G$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive solution providing a single canonical construction of Følner sequences for arbitrary finitely generated solvable non-virtually-nilpotent groups. Explicit Følner sequences are known in many specific cases (e.g., polycyclic groups, lamplighter-type groups, certain metabelian groups, and groups admitting tilings by Følner sets), but no uniformly accepted "canonical" construction analogous to word-metric balls in the nilpotent case appears to be established. The status is therefore best classified as unknown.

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: Is there a nice characterization of amenability of a group G via the topological algebra in βG, the Stone-Cech compactifi- cation of G?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a discrete group and let $\beta G$ denote its Stone–Čech compactification. The multiplication on $G$ extends to $\beta G$, making $(\beta G, \cdot)$ a compact right-topological semigroup: for each fixed $q \in \beta G$, the map $p \mapsto p\cdot q$ is continuous, while for each fixed $g \in G$, the map $p \mapsto g\cdot p$ is continuous. Equivalently, $\beta G$ may be identified with the set of ultrafilters on $G$, and multiplication is given by
$$ p\cdot q = \{A \subseteq G : \{g \in G : g^{-1}A \in q\} \in p\}. $$
Recall that $G$ is called amenable if there exists a finitely additive probability measure on the power set of $G$ that is invariant under left translation.

Problem: Find a characterization of amenability of $G$ purely in terms of the topological-algebraic structure of $\beta G$ (i.e., in terms of properties of its semigroup operation, idempotents, minimal ideals, closed left/right ideals, or similar intrinsic features of $\beta G$ as a compact right-topological semigroup).
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a definitive intrinsic characterization of amenability of a discrete group $G$ purely via the topological-algebraic structure of $\beta G$. The standard reference (Hindman–Strauss, "Algebra in the Stone–Čech compactification") and related works discuss connections (e.g., minimal idempotents, syndetic sets, Følner-type conditions, left-amenability of semigroups), but no single widely-accepted "nice" characterization in the sense asked appears in the available results. Status is therefore inconclusive.

original_question: A countable discrete group is amenable if and only if property MR implies property TR (that is, every set of measurable recurrence is a set of topological recurrence). There are amenable groups which are minimally almost periodic, i.e.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. A subset $R \subseteq G$ is called a set of measurable recurrence (property MR) if, for every measure-preserving action of $G$ on a probability space $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ and every measurable set $A \subseteq X$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, there exists a non-identity element $g \in R$ such that $\mu(A \cap g^{-1}A) > 0$. A subset $R \subseteq G$ is called a set of topological recurrence (property TR) if, for every continuous action of $G$ by homeomorphisms on a compact metric space $X$ and every non-empty open set $U \subseteq X$, there exists a non-identity element $g \in R$ such that $U \cap g^{-1}U \neq \emptyset$. Every set of measurable recurrence is a set of topological recurrence whenever $G$ is amenable. 

Prove or disprove: a countable discrete group $G$ is amenable if and only if every set of measurable recurrence in $G$ is a set of topological recurrence.
status_search_result: The conjecture appears as Conjecture/Question 11.5 in Bergelson's "11 Questions on Amenability" (L'Enseignement Mathématique, 2008). No published resolution was found in web searches; the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Are there countable discrete amenable groups for which the neglectable set appearing in the above splitting is always finite?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a countable discrete amenable group, and let (π, H) be any (continuous) unitary representation of G on a complex Hilbert space H. Recall the canonical Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg-type orthogonal decomposition
   H = H_ap(π) ⊕ H_wm(π),
where:
  • H_ap(π), the almost periodic (or compact) part, is the closed linear span of all finite-dimensional G-invariant subspaces of H; equivalently, the closed linear span of all vectors v ∈ H whose orbit {π(g)v : g ∈ G} is relatively compact in the norm topology of H.
  • H_wm(π), the weakly mixing part, consists of those v ∈ H such that 0 lies in the weak closure of {π(g)v : g ∈ G}; equivalently, the orthogonal complement of H_ap(π).
The restriction of π to H_ap(π) decomposes as a Hilbert direct sum of irreducible finite-dimensional unitary representations of G. Define the "neglectable set" associated with π to be
   N(π) := { isomorphism classes of irreducible finite-dimensional unitary subrepresentations of π appearing with non-zero multiplicity in H_ap(π) }.

Question. Does there exist an infinite countable discrete amenable group G with the following property: for every unitary representation (π, H) of G, the set N(π) is finite?
status_search_result: No published resolution of this question was located. It appears as one of several open problems on amenability circulated in a 2008 collection and a related list by Bergelson; subsequent literature on Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg type decompositions and matrix coefficients for amenable groups does not seem to contain a definitive positive or negative answer, so the status is recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: There exist finitely presented groups with arbitrarily large relation gaps. This conjecture is closely related to the D(2) conjecture: if a group Γ with H 3(Γ; ZΓ) = 0 admits a presentation that both realizes the group's deficiency and has a relation gap, then the D(2) conjecture is false, i.e.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finitely presented group with presentation $\mathcal{P} = \langle x_1,\dots,x_n \mid r_1,\dots,r_m\rangle$, and let $F$ be the free group on $x_1,\dots,x_n$. Let $N \trianglelefteq F$ be the normal closure of $\{r_1,\dots,r_m\}$, so that $\Gamma \cong F/N$. The set $\{r_1,\dots,r_m\}$ generates $N$ as a normal subgroup of $F$; write $d_F(N)$ for the minimum number of normal generators of $N$ in $F$ over all presentations of $\Gamma$ of this form (the minimum number of relations).

The abelianization $N^{\mathrm{ab}} = N/[N,N]$ is naturally a left $\mathbb{Z}\Gamma$-module (the relation module of the presentation), and one defines $d_{\mathbb{Z}\Gamma}(N^{\mathrm{ab}})$ to be the minimum number of $\mathbb{Z}\Gamma$-module generators of $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$. One always has the inequality
$$d_{\mathbb{Z}\Gamma}(N^{\mathrm{ab}}) \le d_F(N).$$
The difference $d_F(N) - d_{\mathbb{Z}\Gamma}(N^{\mathrm{ab}}) \ge 0$ is called the relation gap of the presentation $\mathcal{P}$.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $k \ge 1$ there exists a finitely presented group $\Gamma$ admitting a finite presentation whose relation gap is at least $k$. (Equivalently, finitely presented groups exhibit arbitrarily large relation gaps.)
status_search_result: The relation gap problem is a longstanding open problem in combinatorial group theory. No finitely presented group is currently known to have a nonzero relation gap, let alone an arbitrarily large one. Recent surveys (e.g. Harlander) and arXiv papers from 2024 continue to discuss it as an open conjecture, closely tied to the D(2) problem and weak Andrews–Curtis conjecture.

original_question: The number of relators needed to present Γn on the generatorsSn goes to infinity as n→∞, so Γn has a relation gap for n suﬃciently large. Some virtually free examples.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 2, let A_n = (Z/n) × (Z/n) and let Q_n be the HNN extension of A_n with stable letter t_n conjugating the first factor onto the second:
  Q_n = ⟨ a_n, b_n, t_n | a_n^n = b_n^n = 1, [a_n, b_n] = 1, t_n a_n t_n^{-1} = b_n ⟩.
For n ≥ 2 define the (virtually free) group
  Γ_n := Q_n ∗ Q_{n+1}
and let S_n be the natural finite generating set
  S_n := { a_n, t_n, a_{n+1}, t_{n+1} }.

For a finitely generated group G with finite generating set S, write F(S) for the free group on S, let π: F(S) → G be the canonical surjection, and let R = ker π. The relation module of (G, S) is the abelianization R^{ab} = R/[R, R], regarded as a Z[G]‑module via conjugation. Define:
 • r(G, S) = the minimum number of elements of R needed to generate R as a normal subgroup of F(S) (the minimum number of defining relators in a presentation of G on the generators S);
 • d(G, S) = the minimum number of elements of R^{ab} needed to generate it as a Z[G]‑module.
One always has d(G, S) ≤ r(G, S); the pair (G, S) is said to have a relation gap if d(G, S) < r(G, S).

Prove or disprove: r(Γ_n, S_n) → ∞ as n → ∞. In particular, since d(Γ_n, S_n) is bounded (indeed bounded by a small constant) for this family, conclude that Γ_n has a relation gap for all sufficiently large n.

original_question: A uniformly discrete bounded geometry metric space X has property A if and only if the uniform Roe algebra C * u(X) is exact. In evidence for the conjecture we oﬀer the following.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a uniformly discrete metric space of bounded geometry; that is, $\inf_{x\neq y} d(x,y) > 0$ and for every $r>0$ there is $N(r) \in \mathbb{N}$ such that every closed ball of radius $r$ in $X$ has at most $N(r)$ elements. 

Recall that $X$ has Yu's property A if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $R > 0$ there exist a family $\{A_x\}_{x \in X}$ of non-empty finite subsets of $X \times \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $S > 0$ such that:
(i) $(x,1) \in A_x$ for every $x \in X$;
(ii) $\dfrac{|A_x \triangle A_y|}{|A_x \cap A_y|} < \varepsilon$ whenever $d(x,y) \le R$;
(iii) if $(y,n) \in A_x$ then $d(x,y) \le S$.

The uniform Roe algebra $C^*_u(X)$ is defined as the norm closure in $\mathcal{B}(\ell^2(X))$ of the $*$-algebra of all bounded operators $T$ on $\ell^2(X)$ whose matrix coefficients $T_{xy} = \langle T\delta_y, \delta_x\rangle$ satisfy $\sup\{d(x,y) : T_{xy} \neq 0\} < \infty$ (operators of finite propagation).

A $C^*$-algebra $A$ is exact if the minimal tensor product functor $A \otimes_{\min} -$ preserves short exact sequences of $C^*$-algebras.

Prove or disprove: $X$ has property A if and only if $C^*_u(X)$ is exact.
category_tag: Uniform Roe algebras and coarse geometry
status_search_result: The conjecture has been resolved positively. One direction (property A implies nuclearity, hence exactness, of the uniform Roe algebra) was known via work of Skandalis–Tu–Yu and others. The converse — exactness of $C^*_u(X)$ implies property A — was established by Sako (and is consistent with subsequent work showing that for bounded geometry metric spaces nuclearity, exactness, and local reflexivity of $C^*_u(X)$ are all equivalent to property A).

original_question: Is the cocycle V uniformly bounded?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G = \mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ with $n \ge 2$ and let $X = G/K$ be the associated Riemannian symmetric space of noncompact type, where $K = \mathrm{SO}(n)$. Fix a base point $x_0 \in X$ and let $\omega_X$ denote the $G$-invariant Riemannian volume form on $X$ (of dimension $d = \dim X$). For $(g_0, g_1, \dots, g_d) \in G^{d+1}$, let $\mathrm{str}(g_0 x_0, g_1 x_0, \dots, g_d x_0)$ be the geodesic straight simplex in $X$ with vertices $g_i x_0$ (defined inductively by coning over the previous face along the unique geodesic to the next vertex), and define the homogeneous volume cocycle
$$V(g_0, g_1, \dots, g_d) \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{str}(g_0 x_0, \dots, g_d x_0)} \omega_X.$$
Then $V \colon G^{d+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $G$-invariant homogeneous $d$-cocycle representing the volume class in continuous cohomology $H^d_c(G;\mathbb{R})$.

Question: Is $V$ uniformly bounded on $G^{d+1}$, i.e., does there exist a constant $C < \infty$ such that $|V(g_0, \dots, g_d)| \le C$ for all $(g_0, \dots, g_d) \in G^{d+1}$?
status_search_result: The boundedness of the volume cocycle on symmetric spaces of noncompact type is a well-known open problem in bounded cohomology, connected to Gromov's conjecture that closed locally symmetric spaces of noncompact type have positive simplicial volume. Bucher–Karlsson established the case of $\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SO}(3)$, but in general (for $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SO}(n)$ with $n \ge 4$) the question of whether the natural volume cocycle is uniformly bounded does not appear to have been resolved as of recent literature.

original_question: Which convex simplices in SL(n, R)/SO (n) have ex- tremal volume?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X_n = \mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SO}(n)$ be the Riemannian symmetric space of non-compact type, equipped with its canonical $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$-invariant Riemannian metric (induced by the Killing form on the symmetric pair $(\mathfrak{sl}_n,\mathfrak{so}_n)$). A geodesic simplex $\Delta \subset X_n$ with vertices $p_0,\dots,p_n \in X_n$ is the smallest geodesically convex subset of $X_n$ containing $\{p_0,\dots,p_n\}$; equivalently, it is built inductively by joining each vertex to the geodesic convex hull of the others by minimizing geodesics. Such a simplex is called convex when this geodesic convex hull is well-defined and homeomorphic to a Euclidean $n$-simplex. Let $\mathrm{Vol}(\Delta)$ denote the Riemannian volume of $\Delta$ in $X_n$.

It is known that the supremum $v_n := \sup_{\Delta} \mathrm{Vol}(\Delta)$ taken over all convex geodesic simplices $\Delta \subset X_n$ is finite (for $n \geq 2$). Determine, for each $n \geq 2$, which convex geodesic simplices in $X_n = \mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SO}(n)$ achieve extremal (in particular, maximal) volume, and describe them explicitly (for example, in terms of the action of $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ on its Furstenberg/flag boundary).
status_search_result: For $n=2$ the answer is the classical fact that ideal hyperbolic triangles maximize area, and for $n=3$ partial results on the simplicial volume of locally symmetric spaces covered by $\mathrm{SL}_3\mathbb{R}/\mathrm{SO}(3)$ have appeared (Bucher and others), giving strict positivity but not a complete classification of volume-extremal convex simplices. No general characterization of extremal-volume convex simplices in $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SO}(n)$ for arbitrary $n$ appears in the literature, so the question is regarded as open.

original_question: Every cohomology class of H*(G, R) is bounded, i.e. is represented by a bounded cocycle.
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a word-hyperbolic group (i.e., a finitely generated group whose Cayley graph, with respect to some/any finite generating set, is $\delta$-hyperbolic in the sense of Gromov for some $\delta\ge 0$). Let $H^*(G,\mathbb{R})$ denote the group cohomology of $G$ with real coefficients, and let $H^*_b(G,\mathbb{R})$ denote its bounded cohomology, defined as the cohomology of the complex of bounded $\mathbb{R}$-valued (inhomogeneous) cochains on $G$ equipped with the supremum norm. There is a natural comparison map $c^n\colon H^n_b(G,\mathbb{R})\to H^n(G,\mathbb{R})$ induced by the inclusion of bounded cochains into all cochains. Prove or disprove: for every $n\ge 2$, the comparison map $c^n$ is surjective; equivalently, every cohomology class in $H^n(G,\mathbb{R})$ admits a representative cocycle that is bounded.
status_search_result: The conjecture (originally due to Gromov) that for word-hyperbolic groups the comparison map from bounded cohomology to ordinary real cohomology is surjective in all degrees $n\ge 2$ was established by I. Mineyev (2001/2002), who showed that a finitely presented group is hyperbolic if and only if this comparison map is surjective in all degrees $\ge 2$ (equivalently, in degree 2).

original_question: Is the map (*) an isomorphism?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a connected semisimple Lie group with finite center. Denote by $H^{*}_{cb}(G;\mathbb{R})$ the continuous bounded cohomology of $G$ with trivial real coefficients (the cohomology of the complex of continuous bounded $G$-invariant cochains $C_b(G^{n+1};\mathbb{R})^G$ with the usual homogeneous coboundary), and by $H^{*}_{c}(G;\mathbb{R})$ the continuous cohomology of $G$ (the cohomology of the analogous complex of continuous, not necessarily bounded, cochains). The inclusion of bounded cochains into continuous cochains induces a natural "comparison map"
$$
c^{*}_G : H^{*}_{cb}(G;\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow H^{*}_{c}(G;\mathbb{R}). \qquad (*)
$$
Determine whether the comparison map $(*)$ is an isomorphism in every degree, for every connected semisimple Lie group $G$ with finite center.
status_search_result: The question — known as Monod's conjecture — is widely regarded as open. Isomorphism is known in degree 2 (Burger–Monod), in degree 3 for some rank-one groups and for $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ (Burger–Monod, Bloch, Pieters), and in degree 4 for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ (Hartnick–Ott), while injectivity in higher degree remains open in general.

original_question: Letp be an odd prime and let y be the greatest odd divisor of p-1. The p-period of the Farrell cohomology ring ˆH*(Sp(p-1, Z[1/n ]), Z) is y if and only if for each j|y a prime q|n exists with inertia degree fq such that j|p-1 2fq .
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $n$ be a positive integer with $p \mid n$ such that both $\mathbb{Z}[1/n][\xi]$ and $\mathbb{Z}[1/n][\xi+\xi^{-1}]$ are principal ideal domains, where $\xi$ is a primitive $p$-th root of unity. Let $y$ denote the greatest odd divisor of $p-1$. For a rational prime $q \mid n$ with $q \neq p$, let $f_q$ denote the inertia degree of $q$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\xi+\xi^{-1}]$ (equivalently, the multiplicative order of $q$ modulo $p$, divided by appropriate factor giving the residue degree in the maximal real subfield).

Consider the symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(p-1,\mathbb{Z}[1/n])$ and its Farrell–Tate cohomology ring $\hat{H}^*(\mathrm{Sp}(p-1,\mathbb{Z}[1/n]),\mathbb{Z})$. The $p$-period of this ring is the smallest positive integer $d$ such that cup product with some element of $\hat{H}^d$ induces an isomorphism on the $p$-primary part of $\hat{H}^*$ in every degree.

Prove or disprove: the $p$-period of $\hat{H}^*(\mathrm{Sp}(p-1,\mathbb{Z}[1/n]),\mathbb{Z})$ equals $y$ if and only if for every divisor $j \mid y$ there exists a rational prime $q \mid n$ (with $q \neq p$) whose inertia degree $f_q$ satisfies $j \mid \dfrac{p-1}{2f_q}$.

Related work by Busch on the Farrell cohomology of $\mathrm{Sp}(p-1,\mathbb{Z})$ exists, and there are subsequent papers on cohomology rings of periodic virtually torsion-free groups, but no source found in the search explicitly settles this characterization of the $p$-period for $\mathrm{Sp}(p-1,\mathbb{Z}[1/n])$. original_question: (Bieri). For anym≥2, the following are equivalent: (1) G is of type FP m.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group fitting into a short exact sequence
$$1 \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow Q \longrightarrow 1,$$
where both $A$ and $Q$ are abelian groups. The conjugation action of $G$ on $A$ turns $A$ into a module over the group ring $\mathbb{Z}Q$.

Recall the Bieri–Strebel geometric invariant $\Sigma_A(Q)\subseteq S(Q):=(\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\mathbb{R})\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, defined as the set of equivalence classes $[\chi]$ of nonzero homomorphisms $\chi\colon Q\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $A$ is finitely generated as a module over the monoid ring $\mathbb{Z}Q_\chi$, where $Q_\chi=\{q\in Q:\chi(q)\ge 0\}$. Let $\Sigma_A^c(Q):=S(Q)\setminus\Sigma_A(Q)$ denote its complement.

For an integer $m\ge 1$, the $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module $A$ is called $m$-tame if for any choice of (not necessarily distinct) classes $[\chi_1],\dots,[\chi_m]\in\Sigma_A^c(Q)$, one has
$$\chi_1+\chi_2+\cdots+\chi_m \;\neq\; 0$$
in $\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\mathbb{R})$.

Recall that a group $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ admits a projective resolution whose first $m+1$ terms are finitely generated.

Prove or disprove the following: for every integer $m\ge 2$, the following two conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$.
\item $A$ is $m$-tame as a $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module.
\end{enumerate}
status_search_result: Bieri's FP_m-conjecture for finitely generated abelian-by-abelian (metabelian) groups remains open in general. It has been verified in important special cases, e.g. for metabelian groups of finite Prüfer rank, and one implication (FP_m implies m-tameness, at least when the kernel is torsion-free) is known. Survey notes on Σ-invariants (Bieri–Strebel) and subsequent literature still list it as an open conjecture.

self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group fitting into a short exact sequence
$$1 \longrightarrow N \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow Q \longrightarrow 1,$$
where $Q$ is a finitely generated abelian group and $N$ is abelian (so $G$ is finitely generated metabelian). Let $M_1$ denote $N$ regarded as a $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module via conjugation. Recall:

(a) The character sphere of $Q$ is $S(Q) = (\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\mathbb{R})\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. For a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module $A$, the Bieri–Strebel invariant $\Sigma_A \subseteq S(Q)$ consists of those classes $[\chi]$ for which $A$ is finitely generated as a module over the monoid ring $\mathbb{Z}Q_\chi$, where $Q_\chi = \{q\in Q : \chi(q)\ge 0\}$. Write $\Sigma^c_A = S(Q)\setminus \Sigma_A$.

(b) A subset $\Sigma \subseteq S(Q)$ is said to be $m$-tame if for every choice of points $v_1,\dots,v_m \in \Sigma$ (lifted to $\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\mathbb{R})\setminus\{0\}$) one has $v_1+\cdots+v_m \neq 0$.

(c) A group $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ admits a projective resolution that is finitely generated in every degree $\le m$.

(d) $H_i(N;\mathbb{Z})$ carries a natural $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module structure induced by conjugation.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $m\ge 2$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$;
\item $\Sigma^c_{M_1}$ is $m$-tame, and the homology groups $H_i(N;\mathbb{Z})$ are finitely generated as $\mathbb{Z}Q$-modules for all $i \in \{1,2,\dots,m\}$.
\end{enumerate}

original_question: If X is a finite CW-complex that is a Postnikov piece, then X is a K(G, 1).
self_contained_problem:
A connected CW-complex $X$ is called a Postnikov piece (or has finite Postnikov tower) if it has only finitely many nontrivial homotopy groups, i.e., there exists $N \ge 1$ such that $\pi_n(X) = 0$ for all $n > N$. A space is called a $K(G,1)$ (or Eilenberg–MacLane / aspherical) space if it is connected, has fundamental group $G$, and $\pi_n = 0$ for all $n \ge 2$.

Prove or disprove: If $X$ is a finite CW-complex (i.e., built from finitely many cells) that is a Postnikov piece, then $X$ is a $K(G,1)$ for some group $G$; equivalently, $\pi_n(X) = 0$ for every $n \ge 2$.
status_search_result: The conjecture is a known folklore problem in algebraic topology (related to results of Serre on Eilenberg–MacLane spaces, which imply a simply connected finite Postnikov piece with finite type cohomology must be contractible). Web searches did not turn up an unconditional resolution; partial results exist (e.g., under nilpotency or finiteness of $\pi_1$ assumptions, via mod-$p$ cohomology techniques), but the general statement for arbitrary finite CW-complexes does not appear to be confirmed as solved.

original_question: Let X be a finite space and n an integer. Is it true that H *(X⟨n⟩; Fp) is finitely generated as an algebra over the Steenrod algebra?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a finite CW complex (a "finite space"), let $p$ be a prime, and let $n$ be a positive integer. Denote by $X\langle n\rangle$ the $n$-connected cover of $X$, that is, the homotopy fiber of the $n$-th Postnikov section map $X \to P_n X$, so that $\pi_i(X\langle n\rangle)=0$ for $i\le n$ and $\pi_i(X\langle n\rangle)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_i(X)$ for $i>n$. Let $\mathcal{A}_p$ denote the mod $p$ Steenrod algebra, which acts on the singular cohomology $H^*(X\langle n\rangle;\mathbb{F}_p)$ by natural stable cohomology operations, making it an $\mathcal{A}_p$-algebra.

Question: For every finite CW complex $X$, every prime $p$, and every integer $n\ge 1$, is $H^*(X\langle n\rangle;\mathbb{F}_p)$ finitely generated as an algebra over the Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}_p$?
status_search_result: The analogous statement is known to hold when $X$ is a finite H-space: Castellana, Crespo, and Scherer (2006, "On the cohomology of highly connected covers of finite complexes") proved that for any finite H-space $X$, the mod $p$ cohomology of its $n$-connected cover is finitely generated as an algebra over the Steenrod algebra. For general finite CW complexes the question does not appear to have been resolved in the literature located, so it remains a partially solved problem (open in the non-H-space case).

original_question: Is the cohomology of a finite type Postnikov piece finitely generated as an algebra over the Steenrod algebra?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime and let $\mathcal{A}_p$ denote the mod p Steenrod algebra. A space X is called a Postnikov piece if it has only finitely many nonzero homotopy groups, and X is said to be of finite type (at p) if each homotopy group is finitely generated (equivalently, if $H^n(X; \mathbb{F}_p)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space for every $n$).

Question: For every Postnikov piece X of finite type, is the mod p cohomology $H^*(X; \mathbb{F}_p)$ finitely generated as an algebra over the Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}_p$?
status_search_result: Related work (Castellana–Crespo–Scherer, "Relating Postnikov pieces with the Krull filtration") studies consequences of finite generation over the Steenrod algebra for H-spaces and Postnikov pieces, but takes finite generation as a hypothesis rather than proving it for all finite type Postnikov pieces. Other works (e.g., Grodal on transcendence degree of mod p cohomology of finite Postnikov systems) address related finiteness properties. No source found that settles the question in full generality, so it appears still open or unresolved.

original_question: LetX be a connected space such that TVH *(X) is of finite type for any elementary abelian p-group V , and let n≥1. Is it true that QH *(X) is in Un if and only if Ω n+1X is BZ/p -local?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a prime $p$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the mod-$p$ Steenrod algebra and let $\mathcal{U}$ be the category of unstable modules over $\mathcal{A}$. For an integer $n\ge 0$, let $\mathcal{U}_n\subset \mathcal{U}$ denote the full subcategory of unstable modules $M$ such that for every $x\in M$, the iterated Steenrod operation $\mathrm{Sq}_0^{n+1}x = 0$ (at the prime $2$; analogously $P_0^{n+1}x=0$ at odd primes), i.e. the subcategory generated under colimits and extensions by suspensions of the first $n+1$ Brown–Gitler-type modules — equivalently, the subcategory of unstable modules of "transcendence degree" at most $n$ in the sense of the nilpotent/Krull-type filtration of Schwartz.

For a pointed connected space $X$, let $H^*(X)$ denote its reduced mod-$p$ cohomology, viewed as an unstable $\mathcal{A}$-module, let $\mathrm{Nil}\subset \mathcal{U}$ be the full subcategory of nilpotent unstable modules, and let $QH^*(X) := H^*(X)/\mathrm{Nil}$ be the maximal nil-closed quotient of $H^*(X)$ in $\mathcal{U}$. For an elementary abelian $p$-group $V$, write $T_V$ for Lannes' $T$-functor and assume that $T_V H^*(X)$ is of finite type for every such $V$.

A space $Y$ is called $B\mathbb{Z}/p$-local if the map $\mathrm{map}_*(B\mathbb{Z}/p,Y)\to Y$ induced by evaluation at the basepoint of $B\mathbb{Z}/p$ is a weak equivalence; equivalently, $\mathrm{map}_*(B\mathbb{Z}/p,Y)$ is weakly contractible.

Let $n\ge 1$. Determine whether the following equivalence holds:
$$QH^*(X)\in \mathcal{U}_n \iff \Omega^{n+1}X \text{ is } B\mathbb{Z}/p\text{-local}.$$

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: What is the exact virtual cohomological dimension of the outer automorphism group of a 2-dimensional right-angled Artin group?
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ = (V, E) be a finite simplicial graph and let A_Γ be the associated right-angled Artin group, namely the group with presentation
   A_Γ = ⟨ v ∈ V | [v, w] = 1 whenever {v, w} ∈ E ⟩.
The group A_Γ is called 2-dimensional if its cohomological dimension equals 2; equivalently, Γ is triangle-free (no three vertices are pairwise adjacent). Let Out(A_Γ) denote the outer automorphism group of A_Γ. Since Out(A_Γ) is virtually torsion-free, its virtual cohomological dimension
   vcd(Out(A_Γ)) := cd(H)
(for any torsion-free finite-index subgroup H ≤ Out(A_Γ)) is a well-defined finite number.

Problem: Determine the exact value of vcd(Out(A_Γ)) as an explicit function of the combinatorics of the triangle-free graph Γ.
category_tag: Automorphism groups of right-angled Artin groups
status_search_result: Charney–Vogtmann (2011) gave upper and lower bounds on vcd(Out(A_Γ)) for 2-dimensional (triangle-free) RAAGs, with equality when Γ is a tree, but not a closed formula in general. Day–Sale (Bull. LMS, 2021) gave an algorithm to compute vcd(Out(A_Γ)) for arbitrary RAAGs by constructing free abelian subgroups of maximal rank in certain Fouxe-Rabinovitch groups. Thus the question is partially solved: an algorithmic answer exists, but no explicit combinatorial formula in terms of Γ is known.

original_question: Do the outer automorphism groups of all right-angled Artin groups have torsion-free subgroups of finite index?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma = (V,E)$ be a finite simplicial graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. The right-angled Artin group associated to $\Gamma$ is the group $A_\Gamma$ given by the presentation
$$A_\Gamma = \langle\, v \in V \mid [v,w] = 1 \text{ whenever } \{v,w\} \in E \,\rangle.$$
Let $\mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma)$ denote its automorphism group and let $\mathrm{Out}(A_\Gamma) = \mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma)/\mathrm{Inn}(A_\Gamma)$ denote its outer automorphism group. A group is said to be virtually torsion-free if it contains a torsion-free subgroup of finite index.

Determine whether, for every finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$, the outer automorphism group $\mathrm{Out}(A_\Gamma)$ is virtually torsion-free.
status_search_result: Charney and Vogtmann established that for every finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$, the outer automorphism group $\mathrm{Out}(A_\Gamma)$ is virtually torsion-free (and moreover has finite virtual cohomological dimension). This resolves the question affirmatively.

original_question: Calculate the virtual cohomological dimension of the automorphism group of any right-angled Artin group.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simplicial graph with vertex set $V(\Gamma)$ and edge set $E(\Gamma)$. The right-angled Artin group (RAAG) associated to $\Gamma$ is the group
$$A_\Gamma = \langle\, v \in V(\Gamma) \mid [v,w] = 1 \text{ for all } \{v,w\} \in E(\Gamma)\,\rangle.$$
Let $\mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma)$ denote its automorphism group. Recall that for a group $G$ which has a torsion-free subgroup of finite index, the virtual cohomological dimension $\mathrm{vcd}(G)$ is defined to be the common cohomological dimension (over $\mathbb{Z}$) of any torsion-free finite-index subgroup of $G$; this is known to be well-defined and finite for $G = \mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma)$.

Problem: Give an explicit formula, in terms of the combinatorics of the defining graph $\Gamma$, for $\mathrm{vcd}(\mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma))$ valid for every finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$.
status_search_result: Charney–Vogtmann established that $\mathrm{Out}(A_\Gamma)$ is virtually torsion-free with finite vcd. Day and Sale (2019, published Bull. LMS 2021) gave an algorithm computing the vcd of $\mathrm{Aut}(A_\Gamma)$ (and in the relative/untwisted settings) for any RAAG, but a closed-form combinatorial formula in $\Gamma$ is not given in general; thus the question is partially solved (algorithmically computable, no clean closed formula known in full generality).

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: If G has a planar 2-cocycle, then G is a p-group.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $A$ be a nontrivial finite abelian group with trivial $G$-action. A normalized 2-cocycle is a map $f : G \times G \to A$ satisfying 
$$f(x,y) + f(xy,z) = f(x,yz) + f(y,z), \qquad f(1,x) = f(x,1) = 0,$$
for all $x,y,z \in G$. Such an $f$ determines a central extension
$$1 \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow E_f \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow 1,$$
where $E_f = A \times G$ as a set, with multiplication $(a,x)(b,y) = (a+b+f(x,y),\,xy)$. Call the 2-cocycle $f$ planar if there exists a generating set $S$ of $E_f$ (with $S = S^{-1}$, $1 \notin S$) such that the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(E_f, S)$ admits a topological embedding in the plane (equivalently, in the 2-sphere).

Prove or disprove: if $G$ admits a planar 2-cocycle (with values in some nontrivial finite abelian group $A$), then $G$ is a $p$-group for some prime $p$.
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a definitive resolution of this conjecture in the published literature. The conjecture appears in a 2006 collection of open problems and no later paper announcing a proof or counterexample of this specific statement on planar 2-cocycles forcing $G$ to be a $p$-group was located.

original_question: (Stronger version) IfG has a planar 2-cocycle with coeﬃcients in a G-module A, then G and A are elementary abelian groups.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group and let $A$ be a (left) $G$-module. Write $Z^{2}(G,A)$ for the abelian group of normalized $2$-cocycles, that is, functions $f\colon G\times G\to A$ with $f(g,1)=f(1,g)=0$ and
$$g\cdot f(h,k)-f(gh,k)+f(g,hk)-f(g,h)=0\qquad\text{for all }g,h,k\in G.$$
To such a cocycle one associates a 2-dimensional CW-complex $X_{f}$ (the Cayley-type 2-complex of the corresponding extension $0\to A\to E_{f}\to G\to 1$) whose $1$-skeleton is the Cayley graph of $E_{f}$ with respect to a chosen generating set, with 2-cells attached along the loops prescribed by $f$. Call the cocycle $f$ \emph{planar} if the complex $X_{f}$ admits a topological embedding into the plane $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ (equivalently into the 2-sphere $S^{2}$).

A group is called \emph{elementary abelian} if it is isomorphic to a direct sum of copies of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ for some prime $p$ (or is trivial).

Prove or disprove: if a group $G$ admits a planar $2$-cocycle with values in some $G$-module $A$, then both $G$ and $A$ must be elementary abelian groups.

original_question: (Borel Conjecture): Let Γ be a torsion free subgroup of the mapping class group, for example the Torelli group. Is the action of Γ on τg topologically rigid?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_g$ be a closed orientable surface of genus $g \geq 2$, and let $\mathcal{T}_g$ denote its Teichmüller space, i.e., the space of marked complex (equivalently, hyperbolic) structures on $S_g$, which is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{6g-6}$. Let $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ denote the mapping class group of $S_g$, acting properly discontinuously on $\mathcal{T}_g$. Let $\Gamma \leq \mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ be a torsion-free subgroup (for instance, the Torelli group, i.e., the kernel of the action of $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ on $H_1(S_g;\mathbb{Z})$), so that $\Gamma$ acts freely and properly discontinuously on $\mathcal{T}_g$, and the quotient $\mathcal{T}_g/\Gamma$ is an aspherical manifold (or, if $\Gamma$ is not cocompact, an aspherical space of finite type).

Question: Is the action of $\Gamma$ on $\mathcal{T}_g$ topologically rigid in the sense of the Borel Conjecture? That is, if $f : N \to \mathcal{T}_g/\Gamma$ is a homotopy equivalence from a manifold $N$ (with appropriate boundary/end conditions), must $f$ be homotopic to a homeomorphism? Equivalently, does the Borel Conjecture hold for all torsion-free subgroups $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ with respect to their action on $\mathcal{T}_g$?
category_tag: Borel Conjecture for mapping class groups
status_search_result: The Borel Conjecture has been established for many classes of groups (e.g., hyperbolic and CAT(0) groups by Bartels–Lück), but mapping class groups and the Torelli group are not known to fall under these results in the required form. No source confirms a resolution of the Borel Conjecture for torsion-free subgroups of the mapping class group acting on Teichmüller space; the problem appears to remain open.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ denote the category of groups. A homotopical localization functor on $\mathcal{G}$ is a coaugmented idempotent functor $L\colon \mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{G}$, i.e., a functor equipped with a natural transformation $\eta_G\colon G\to L G$ such that $L\eta_G = \eta_{LG}$ is an isomorphism. $$\eta_P\colon P\longrightarrow L_f P$$
is surjective. In particular, conclude that $L_f P$ is again a finite $p$-group.

For a pointed space A, let cell_A denote the A-cellularization functor (the augmented idempotent functor associated with A by Dror Farjoun, characterized by cell_A X → X being the universal map from an A-cellular space; A-cellular spaces are those built from A by iterated pointed homotopy colimits). Recall that a functor F equipped with a natural transformation to or from the identity is called idempotent if the two natural maps F F X → F X (resp. F X → F F X) agree and are weak equivalences.

self_contained_problem:
A homotopical localization functor is a homotopy functor $L: \mathrm{Top}_* \to \mathrm{Top}_*$ on pointed spaces equipped with a natural transformation $\eta: \mathrm{Id} \to L$ such that $L\eta_X = \eta_{LX}: LX \to LLX$ and this map is a weak equivalence for every space $X$. A map $f: A \to B$ is called a localization map if there is such a functor $L$ and a weak equivalence $LA \simeq B$ under $A$ realizing $f$ as $\eta_A$ (equivalently, $f$ is initial among maps from $A$ to $L$-local spaces).

Prove or disprove the following:

(a) For every homotopical localization functor $L$ and every $1$-connected (i.e., simply connected) pointed space $X$, the space $LX$ is again $1$-connected.

(b) (Weaker version.) If $p: \tilde X \to X$ is the universal covering projection of a connected pointed space $X$ with nontrivial fundamental group, then $p$ is not a localization map; equivalently, the only universal covering projections that are localization maps are weak equivalences (i.e., $X$ is already $1$-connected).
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive resolution. The question concerns whether every homotopical localization (in the Bousfield–Dror Farjoun sense) preserves simple connectivity, together with the weaker statement that a universal covering map can be a localization only when it is an equivalence. Both remain standard test questions in the literature on cellular and nullification functors, and no clear published proof or counterexample was located.

paper_title: Guido’s Book of Conjectures: A Gift to Guido Mislin on the Occasion of His Retirement from ETHZ, June 2006
original_question: Any localization of a polyGEM is a polyGEM. The local- ization of an n-connected Postnikov stage is an n-connected Postnikov stage.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Work in the category of pointed topological spaces (or simplicial sets) up to homotopy. A generalized Eilenberg–MacLane space (GEM) is a space weakly homotopy equivalent to a (possibly infinite) product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(A_i, n_i) with the A_i abelian and n_i ≥ 1. A polyGEM is a space that can be built from a point by finitely many principal fibrations whose fibers are GEMs; equivalently, the class of polyGEMs is the smallest class of spaces containing the contractible space and closed under principal fibrations with GEM fiber. A connected space X is called an n-connected Postnikov stage if its homotopy groups π_k(X) vanish for k ≤ n and for k larger than some finite N (i.e. X has only finitely many nonzero homotopy groups, all of degree > n).

Let f: A → B be a map of spaces, and let L_f denote the associated homotopical (nullification or f-)localization functor on spaces in the sense of Bousfield–Dror Farjoun: L_f X is f-local and equipped with a coaugmentation X → L_f X that is an f-local equivalence.

Problem. Prove or disprove:
(a) For every map f and every polyGEM X, the localization L_f X is again a polyGEM.
(b) For every map f, every integer n ≥ 0, and every n-connected Postnikov stage X (a space whose only possibly nonzero homotopy groups lie in degrees n+1, n+2, …, N for some finite N), the localization L_f X is again an n-connected Postnikov stage.
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a definitive resolution of the conjecture that every homotopical localization of a polyGEM is a polyGEM (and the corresponding statement for n-connected Postnikov stages). Related work by Castellana, Crespo, and Scherer on Postnikov pieces and BZ/p-homotopy theory addresses closely related closure properties, but no clear claim of a full proof or counterexample to the stated problem was found.

original_question: Any localization and cellularization of a space X all whose homotopy groups are p-torsion is also such a space.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime. Say that a pointed connected space $X$ is "$p$-torsion homotopy" if $\pi_n(X)$ is a $p$-torsion abelian group for every $n \geq 1$ (i.e., every element has order a power of $p$). Recall:

(a) A homotopy localization functor is an augmented, idempotent, homotopy-preserving endofunctor $L : \mathrm{Spaces}_* \to \mathrm{Spaces}_*$ with natural transformation $X \to LX$ inverting a chosen class of maps (e.g., Bousfield localization with respect to a map $f$, or nullification $P_W$ with respect to a space $W$).

(b) A cellularization (coaugmented, idempotent functor) $\mathrm{CW}_A : \mathrm{Spaces}_* \to \mathrm{Spaces}_*$ with respect to a space $A$ produces, for each $X$, an $A$-cellular space $\mathrm{CW}_A X$ together with a map $\mathrm{CW}_A X \to X$ that is an $A$-equivalence (i.e., induces a weak equivalence on pointed mapping spaces from $A$).

Prove or disprove: if $X$ is a pointed connected space all of whose homotopy groups are $p$-torsion, then for every homotopy localization functor $L$ and every cellularization functor $\mathrm{CW}_A$, the spaces $LX$ and $\mathrm{CW}_A X$ also have all homotopy groups $p$-torsion.
status_search_result: A direct resolution of this preservation statement (that all localizations and cellularizations of a space with $p$-torsion homotopy groups again have $p$-torsion homotopy groups) was not located in the search. Related results exist in the $B\mathbb{Z}/p$-cellularization literature (e.g., Castellana–Crespo and others), and counterexamples are known for related idempotence questions in the category of groups, but no clear confirmation that the full conjecture has been settled either way was found.

original_question: The cellularization of a finite Postnikov stage with finite homotopy groups, is a space whose homotopy groups are finite groups. This is true in the category of groups, for finite groups.
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a pointed connected CW-complex. For a pointed space X, recall the Dror Farjoun A-cellularization CW_A(X) → X: the universal map (up to homotopy) from an A-cellular space (i.e., a space built from A by pointed homotopy colimits) to X that induces a weak equivalence on pointed mapping spaces map_*(A, –). A space Y is called a finite Postnikov stage if there exists an integer n ≥ 1 such that π_i(Y) = 0 for all i > n; it is said to have finite homotopy groups if π_i(Y) is a finite group for every i ≥ 1.

Prove or disprove: For every pointed connected CW-complex A and every pointed connected space Y which is a finite Postnikov stage with all homotopy groups π_i(Y) finite, the A-cellularization CW_A(Y) has finite homotopy groups π_i(CW_A(Y)) for all i ≥ 1.

(The analogous statement is known to hold in the category of groups: the cellularization of a finite group with respect to any group is again a finite group.)

However, no source was found that confirms or refutes the general statement about finiteness of homotopy groups of the cellularization of an arbitrary finite Postnikov stage with finite homotopy groups, so the current status appears unverified.
