paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Dark matter: What is the identity of dark matter? Is it a particle? If so, is it a WIMP, axion, the lightest superpartner (LSP), or some other particle? Or, are the phenomena attributed to dark matter the result of an alternate theory of gravity separate from general relativity altogether? Despite extensive research, the exact composition of dark matter remains unknown. It is inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation, and the universe's large-scale structure. Understanding its properties is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of the universe.
self_contained_problem: In the standard cosmological framework, observations of galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background anisotropy spectrum, and large-scale structure formation are consistent with the presence of a non-luminous component of matter, commonly called dark matter, that interacts gravitationally but has not been directly detected through electromagnetic interactions. Determine the fundamental nature of this component. Specifically, decide whether the gravitational phenomena attributed to dark matter are produced by one or more new particle species (for example a weakly interacting massive particle, an axion, the lightest supersymmetric partner, a sterile neutrino, a primordial black hole population, or some other as-yet-unidentified particle or object), and in that case identify the particle(s) and determine their mass, spin, and interaction properties; or alternatively show that these phenomena can be fully explained by a modification of the gravitational interaction that differs from general relativity (such as a relativistic completion of modified Newtonian dynamics) without invoking any new matter component. Provide a model that quantitatively reproduces, with consistent parameters, the full body of observational data attributed to dark matter, including galactic rotation curves, cluster dynamics, gravitational lensing observations, the cosmic microwave background power spectrum, and large-scale structure formation.
status_search_result: The identity of dark matter remains an open problem in physics and cosmology as of 2026. Direct-detection experiments (e.g., LZ, XENONnT, PandaX) have continued to set increasingly stringent limits on WIMP cross-sections without a confirmed detection, axion searches (ADMX and others) have not detected axions, and no superpartners have been observed at the LHC. Modified-gravity alternatives (MOND, TeVeS, etc.) have neither been confirmed nor ruled out in full generality.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Dark energy: What is the cause of the observed accelerating expansion of the universe (the de Sitter phase)? Are the observations rightly interpreted as the accelerating expansion of the universe, or are they evidence that the cosmological principle is false? Why is the energy density of the dark energy component of the same magnitude as the density of matter at present when the two evolve quite differently over time; could it be simply that we are observing at exactly the right time? Is dark energy a pure cosmological constant or are models of quintessence such as phantom energy applicable?
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of general relativity applied to cosmology, consider a spatially homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker spacetime with scale factor a(t), whose dynamics are governed by the Friedmann equations sourced by an energy–momentum content including ordinary matter (with energy density evolving as ρ_m ∝ a^{-3}) and a "dark energy" component with equation-of-state parameter w (so that its energy density evolves as ρ_DE ∝ a^{-3(1+w)}). Observational data (Type Ia supernovae, CMB, baryon acoustic oscillations) indicate that ä > 0 at the present epoch, consistent with an effective dark energy component contributing roughly 70% of the present critical density and an equation of state w ≈ −1.

Address the following:

1. Identify the physical mechanism responsible for the observed late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. Specifically, determine whether this acceleration is driven by:
   (a) a pure cosmological constant Λ (w = −1 exactly, constant in time), or
   (b) a dynamical quintessence field with w(t) > −1, or
   (c) a phantom-energy component with w(t) < −1, or
   (d) a modification of general relativity at cosmological scales, or
   (e) an apparent acceleration arising from the breakdown of the cosmological principle (large-scale spatial homogeneity and isotropy), so that the inferred acceleration is an artifact of fitting an FLRW model to an inhomogeneous universe.

2. Provide a quantitative explanation of the coincidence problem: derive, from first principles or from a specified theoretical model, why the present-day energy densities ρ_DE(t_0) and ρ_m(t_0) are of the same order of magnitude despite their differing time evolutions, or rigorously demonstrate that no such explanation beyond anthropic/observer-selection reasoning is possible.

3. Determine whether the function w(t) is exactly constant equal to −1, or whether it varies with redshift, and if so characterize its functional form.
status_search_result: The nature of dark energy remains one of the most prominent open problems in cosmology as of 2026. Recent DESI Year-3 results (2025–2026) provide growing observational hints that dark energy may be dynamical (w varying with redshift) rather than a pure cosmological constant, but this is not yet conclusive. The coincidence problem and the question of whether apparent acceleration could reflect violation of the cosmological principle remain unresolved.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Dark flow: Is a non-spherically-symmetric gravitational pull from outside the observable universe responsible for some of the observed motion of large objects such as galactic clusters in the universe?
self_contained_problem: Consider a cosmological model in which the observable universe is a finite spatial region within a larger ambient spacetime, and in which large gravitationally bound systems (such as clusters of galaxies) possess peculiar velocities, i.e., velocities measured relative to the rest frame defined by the cosmic microwave background radiation. Observations of the peculiar velocity field of galaxy clusters, inferred for instance via the kinematic Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect on the cosmic microwave background, suggest the possible existence of a coherent bulk flow of clusters of order several hundred km/s directed toward a localized region of the sky, extending over distances of order a gigaparsec or more — a phenomenon referred to as "dark flow." Determine whether this apparent coherent large-scale streaming motion of galaxy clusters can be attributed to a non-spherically-symmetric gravitational attraction sourced by mass-energy distributions lying outside the observable universe (i.e., beyond the cosmological particle horizon). Specifically: (i) Does the observed bulk flow exist at a statistically significant level once primary cosmic microwave background anisotropies and measurement systematics are properly accounted for? (ii) If it exists, is its magnitude and direction consistent with predictions from standard ΛCDM cosmology with Gaussian initial perturbations, or does it require an external (super-horizon) inhomogeneous gravitational influence as its cause?
status_search_result: The dark flow hypothesis remains unresolved and controversial as of 2024–2025. Original claims by Kashlinsky and collaborators of a coherent bulk flow of galaxy clusters toward a sky region near Centaurus–Vela have been disputed by reanalyses (e.g., Keisler, and work using Planck data) that find no statistically significant signal once CMB primary anisotropies are properly treated, while the original group maintains the detection. Whether the effect is real, and whether it would require super-horizon gravitational influences, is still an open question.

original_question: Extra dimensions: Does nature have more than four spacetime dimensions? If so, what is their size? Are dimensions a fundamental property of the universe or an emergent result of other physical laws? Can we experimentally observe evidence of higher spatial dimensions?

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Magnetic monopoles: Did particles that carry "magnetic charge" exist in some past, higher-energy epoch? If so, do any remain today? (Paul Dirac showed the existence of some types of magnetic monopoles would explain charge quantization.)
self_contained_problem:
In classical electromagnetism, Maxwell's equations as usually written impose ∇·B = 0, so that magnetic field lines have no sources and isolated magnetic charges (magnetic monopoles) do not exist. A magnetic monopole is a hypothetical point-like particle carrying a net magnetic charge g, sourcing a radial magnetic field B(r) = (g/4π) r/|r|^3. Dirac's argument shows that the consistent quantum-mechanical coexistence of an electric charge e and a magnetic charge g requires the quantization condition eg = 2π n ℏ (in suitable units), for some integer n; hence the existence of even a single magnetic monopole would imply that all electric charges are integer multiples of a fundamental unit. Various unified gauge theories (e.g., grand unified theories) predict the production of heavy magnetic monopoles in the very early, high-temperature universe.

Determine the following:
(a) Did particles carrying nonzero magnetic charge exist as physical states during some past, higher-energy cosmological epoch?
(b) If such particles did exist, do any of them remain in the present universe as relic particles that could in principle be detected?

A complete answer should either exhibit a magnetic monopole as a physically realized particle (theoretically motivated and experimentally confirmed) and characterize its present-day abundance, or else establish that no such particles exist or survive.
status_search_result: Despite decades of searches at colliders (e.g., ATLAS, MoEDAL at CERN), in cosmic rays, and in bulk matter, no magnetic monopole has been confirmed. Experiments through 2024–2025 continue to set upper bounds on monopole production cross sections and relic fluxes, and new detector proposals are being developed. The questions of whether monopoles existed in an early high-energy epoch and whether any survive today remain unresolved.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Neutron lifetime puzzle: While the neutron lifetime has been studied for decades, there currently exists a lack of consilience on its exact value, due to different results from two experimental methods ("bottle" versus "beam").
self_contained_problem:
The free neutron is unstable and decays via the weak interaction (predominantly n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) with a mean lifetime τₙ. Two experimental paradigms are used to measure τₙ:

(i) "Bottle" experiments: ultracold neutrons are stored in a material or magnetic trap, and the number of surviving neutrons is measured as a function of storage time, yielding τₙ from the exponential decay of the trapped population.

(ii) "Beam" experiments: a cold neutron beam of known flux passes through a detection volume in which the appearance rate of decay products (typically protons) is counted, yielding τₙ from the ratio of decay rate to neutron number in the beam.

These two methodologies have consistently produced values of τₙ that disagree by roughly 8–10 seconds, with bottle averages near 878 s and beam averages near 888 s — a discrepancy substantially larger than the quoted uncertainties.

Problem: Determine the true mean lifetime of the free neutron and explain the origin of the persistent discrepancy between bottle-type and beam-type measurements. This entails either (a) identifying and quantifying systematic effects in one or both classes of experiments that account for the difference, or (b) establishing a physical mechanism — for instance, a hitherto unobserved decay channel of the neutron into final states not detected by beam experiments — that reconciles the two methodologies, together with experimental confirmation.
status_search_result: As of 2025, the neutron lifetime puzzle remains unresolved. Recent J-PARC beam-method measurements achieved fivefold improved precision (τₙ ≈ 877.2 s with sizable systematic uncertainty), and theoretical proposals (e.g., a small two-body decay channel into a hydrogen atom and neutrino, possibly involving a second flavor of hydrogen) have been advanced, but no consensus resolution has been experimentally confirmed.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Proton decay and spin crisis: Is the proton fundamentally stable? Or does it decay with a finite lifetime as predicted by some extensions to the standard model? How do the quarks and gluons carry the spin of protons?
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of relativistic quantum field theory, consider the proton as a bound state of quarks and gluons described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD), embedded in the Standard Model of particle physics (gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y). Address the following two questions:

(a) Proton stability. In the Standard Model, baryon number B is an accidental global symmetry and the proton is exactly stable. In many proposed extensions (e.g., grand unified theories with gauge groups such as SU(5), SO(10), or supersymmetric variants), B-violating operators induce proton decay through channels such as p → e^+ π^0 or p → ν̄ K^+ with a finite mean lifetime τ_p. Determine whether the proton is fundamentally stable, or whether it decays with a finite lifetime; if the latter, determine τ_p and the dominant decay channels.

(b) Proton spin decomposition ("spin crisis"). The proton has total angular momentum 1/2 (in units of ℏ). In QCD this admits a decomposition (e.g., the Jaffe–Manohar or Ji decomposition) of the form
   1/2 = (1/2) ΔΣ + ΔG + L_q + L_g,
where ΔΣ is the net contribution from quark spins (the integral of the polarized quark distributions), ΔG is the gluon spin contribution, and L_q, L_g are the orbital angular momenta of quarks and gluons, respectively. Determine quantitatively how ΔΣ, ΔG, L_q, and L_g sum to 1/2, given that polarized deep-inelastic scattering measurements indicate ΔΣ accounts for substantially less than 1/2.

status_search_result: Both questions remain open. No experiment has observed proton decay; current limits from Super-Kamiokande give τ_p > ~10^34 years for major channels, with Hyper-Kamiokande and DUNE expected to extend sensitivity. The proton spin decomposition remains unresolved: experiments (COMPASS, RHIC, JLab) show quark spins contribute only ~30% and constraints on ΔG and orbital angular momentum are still being refined; the EIC is being built in part to address this.

original_question: Grand Unification: Are the electromagnetic and nuclear forces different aspects of a Grand Unified Theory? If so, what symmetry governs this force and its behaviours?
self_contained_problem: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the electromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear interactions are described by a gauge theory with local symmetry group $G_{SM} = SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$, with three independent gauge couplings $g_3, g_2, g_1$ that run with energy scale according to the renormalization group equations. paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Supersymmetry: Is spacetime supersymmetry realized at TeV scale? If so, what is the mechanism of supersymmetry breaking? Does supersymmetry stabilize the electroweak scale, preventing high quantum corrections? Does the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) comprise dark matter?
self_contained_problem:
In a quantum field theory extension of the Standard Model of particle physics that postulates a symmetry between bosons and fermions (spacetime supersymmetry), addressing the following questions:

(a) Is spacetime supersymmetry realized in nature at energies near the TeV scale, i.e., do superpartners of the known Standard Model particles exist with masses of order 10^2–10^4 GeV?

(b) If such a supersymmetry exists, by what dynamical mechanism is it broken so as to produce the observed mass splittings between Standard Model particles and their hypothetical superpartners?

(c) Does the presence of TeV-scale supersymmetry resolve the electroweak hierarchy problem by cancelling the large radiative (quantum) corrections to the Higgs boson mass, thereby stabilizing the electroweak scale against ultraviolet contributions?

(d) Does the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP), assumed stable under an unbroken R-parity, constitute a viable cold dark matter candidate accounting for the observed cosmological dark matter density?

Determine the answer to each of these four questions.
status_search_result: As of 2025–2026, no superpartners have been detected at the LHC. ATLAS and CMS exclusion bounds reach roughly 2.4 TeV for gluinos and first/second-generation squarks, 1.3 TeV for stops/sbottoms, and about 1 TeV for electroweakinos in simplified models, but TeV-scale SUSY is not ruled out and well-motivated scenarios remain viable. The mechanism of SUSY breaking, the resolution of the hierarchy problem, and whether the LSP constitutes dark matter all remain experimentally and theoretically unresolved.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: The QCD vacuum: Many of the equations in non-perturbative QCD are currently unsolved. These energies are the energies sufficient for the formation and description of atomic nuclei. How thus does low energy /non-pertubative QCD give rise to the formation of complex nuclei and nuclear constituents?
self_contained_problem:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the SU(3) Yang–Mills gauge theory of quarks and gluons defined by the Lagrangian density
  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{ψ}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) ψ_f,
where G^a_{μν} = ∂_μ A^a_ν - ∂_ν A^a_μ + g f^{abc} A^b_μ A^c_ν is the gluon field strength, D_μ = ∂_μ - i g A^a_μ T^a is the gauge covariant derivative, T^a are the SU(3) generators with structure constants f^{abc}, and ψ_f are quark fields of flavor f with masses m_f. At energy scales below the QCD scale Λ_QCD ≈ 200 MeV the coupling g(μ) becomes large and perturbative expansions in g fail; this is the non-perturbative (low-energy) regime, characterized phenomenologically by quark confinement, a non-trivial vacuum structure (gluon condensate ⟨G^a_{μν} G^{a μν}⟩, quark condensate ⟨\bar{ψ} ψ⟩), spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry, and a mass gap.

Problem: Starting from the QCD Lagrangian above, derive in a mathematically controlled non-perturbative framework (for example, lattice gauge theory continuum limit, functional / Dyson–Schwinger methods, or a constructive quantum field theory formulation) the bound-state spectrum and structure of hadrons (in particular nucleons), the residual nucleon–nucleon interaction, and the existence and binding energies of complex atomic nuclei. Concretely, explain quantitatively how the QCD vacuum and its non-perturbative dynamics produce:
 (a) confinement of quarks and gluons into color-singlet hadrons,
 (b) the proton, neutron, and light-meson masses with their observed values,
 (c) an effective nucleon–nucleon potential reproducing nuclear binding, and
 (d) the formation, stability, and properties of nuclei such as the deuteron, helium-4, and heavier nuclei,
all as consequences of the underlying non-perturbative QCD equations.
status_search_result: Non-perturbative low-energy QCD remains an open problem in mathematical physics. The Yang–Mills existence and mass gap problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and is still unsolved. While lattice QCD has produced impressive numerical results (including the light hadron spectrum and recent ab initio computations of light nuclei), a mathematically rigorous derivation of nuclear structure from the QCD Lagrangian is not available.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Generations of matter: Why are there three generations of quarks and leptons? Is there a theory that can explain the masses of particular quarks and leptons in particular generations from first principles (a theory of Yukawa couplings)?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, fermionic matter is organized into three replicated generations of quarks and leptons. Each generation consists of an up-type quark, a down-type quark, a charged lepton, and a neutrino, with identical gauge quantum numbers across generations but with widely different masses. The fermion masses arise from Yukawa couplings to the Higgs field, whose values are free parameters of the Standard Model fitted to experiment.

(a) Provide a first-principles theoretical explanation for why exactly three generations of quarks and leptons exist in nature, rather than one, two, four, or any other number.

(b) Construct a predictive theory of the Yukawa coupling matrices that determines, from first principles, the observed masses of the individual quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom) and charged leptons (electron, muon, tau) — together with the elements of the CKM (and PMNS) mixing matrices — without fitting these parameters to experimental data.
status_search_result: The question of the number of fermion generations and the origin of the Yukawa couplings (the "flavor problem") remains an open problem in theoretical particle physics. While many beyond-Standard-Model proposals exist (family symmetries, Froggatt–Nielsen mechanism, string-theoretic constructions, anarchy models, etc.), none is experimentally established or universally accepted. It continues to be listed among unsolved problems in physics.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Neutrino mass: What is the absolute mass of neutrinos? Are they Dirac or Majorana fermions? Is the mass hierarchy normal or inverted? Is the CP violating phase equal to 0?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model extended to accommodate neutrino oscillations, three light neutrino mass eigenstates ν_1, ν_2, ν_3 with masses m_1, m_2, m_3 mix with the flavor eigenstates ν_e, ν_μ, ν_τ via the Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata (PMNS) unitary matrix, which (in the standard parametrization) contains three mixing angles, one Dirac CP-violating phase δ_CP, and (if neutrinos are Majorana) two additional Majorana phases. Determine the following physical properties of the neutrinos:

1. The absolute mass scale: give the value of the lightest neutrino mass (equivalently, determine m_1, m_2, m_3 individually rather than only the squared mass differences Δm^2_{21} and |Δm^2_{31}|).

2. The fermionic nature of the neutrinos: decide whether neutrinos are Dirac fermions (with distinct particle and antiparticle states, conserving lepton number) or Majorana fermions (their own antiparticles, allowing lepton-number-violating processes such as neutrinoless double beta decay).

3. The ordering of the mass spectrum: decide whether the hierarchy is normal (m_1 < m_2 < m_3, so that Δm^2_{31} > 0) or inverted (m_3 < m_1 < m_2, so that Δm^2_{31} < 0).

4. CP violation in the lepton sector: determine whether the Dirac CP-violating phase δ_CP equals 0 (mod π), i.e. whether CP is conserved in neutrino oscillations, or takes a nontrivial value.
status_search_result: As of 2026, the absolute neutrino mass scale, the Dirac vs. Majorana nature of neutrinos, the mass ordering (normal vs. inverted hierarchy), and the value of the Dirac CP-violating phase δ_CP remain open experimental questions in particle physics, actively pursued by oscillation experiments, neutrinoless double-beta decay searches, and direct mass measurements such as KATRIN.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Strong CP problem and axions: Why is the strong nuclear interaction invariant to parity and charge conjugation? Is Peccei–Quinn theory the solution to this problem? Could axions be the main component of dark matter?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the Lagrangian admits a CP-violating topological term

    L_θ = θ (g_s^2 / 32π^2) G^{a}_{μν} \tilde G^{a μν},

where G^{a}_{μν} is the gluon field strength tensor, \tilde G^{a μν} = (1/2) ε^{μνρσ} G^{a}_{ρσ} is its dual, g_s is the strong coupling, and θ ∈ [0, 2π) is the effective vacuum angle (including the contribution arg det M_q from the quark mass matrix). A nonzero θ would induce CP-violating observables, notably a neutron electric dipole moment of order |d_n| ~ 10^{-16} θ e·cm. Experimental bounds on d_n imply |θ| ≲ 10^{-10}, despite there being no symmetry principle within the Standard Model forcing θ to be small.

Address the following:

(a) Provide a dynamical or symmetry-based explanation, derivable from first principles, of why θ is so small (or vanishes); equivalently, explain why the strong interaction is, to extremely high precision, invariant under parity P and charge conjugation C (equivalently CP).

(b) Determine whether the Peccei–Quinn mechanism — i.e. introducing a global U(1)_{PQ} symmetry spontaneously broken at a scale f_a, whose pseudo–Nambu–Goldstone boson (the axion a) couples as (a/f_a)(g_s^2/32π^2) G \tilde G and dynamically relaxes the effective θ to zero — is the correct resolution of (a), and identify the underlying ultraviolet completion (e.g. KSVZ, DFSZ, or alternative) realized in nature, if any.

(c) Determine whether the axion (or axion-like particle) predicted by such a mechanism constitutes the dominant component of the cosmological cold dark matter, and if so determine its mass m_a, decay constant f_a, and the production mechanism (misalignment, topological defect decay, thermal) responsible for its present relic abundance Ω_a h^2 ≈ 0.12.

original_question: Anomalous magnetic dipole moment: Why is the experimentally measured value of the muon's anomalous magnetic dipole moment ("muon ") significantly different from the theoretically predicted value of that physical constant?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum electrodynamics, a charged lepton of spin 1/2 has a magnetic moment μ = g·(e/2m)·S, where the gyromagnetic ratio g equals 2 at tree level. Radiative corrections produce an anomalous magnetic moment a = (g−2)/2. For the muon, both a high-precision experimental value a_μ^{exp} and a Standard Model theoretical prediction a_μ^{SM} (which includes QED, electroweak, and hadronic — hadronic vacuum polarization and hadronic light-by-light — contributions) can be computed.

Problem: Determine whether the experimentally measured value a_μ^{exp} of the muon anomalous magnetic moment is consistent with the Standard Model prediction a_μ^{SM}. If a statistically significant discrepancy Δa_μ = a_μ^{exp} − a_μ^{SM} persists, identify and quantitatively account for its origin, either by (i) correctly evaluating the hadronic contributions (in particular the leading-order hadronic vacuum polarization and hadronic light-by-light scattering), or (ii) identifying physics beyond the Standard Model that contributes to a_μ at the required magnitude.
status_search_result: As of 2025, the Fermilab Muon g−2 experiment published its final result using the full six-year dataset, and the Muon g−2 Theory Initiative's 2025 White Paper updated the Standard Model prediction using lattice-QCD evaluations of the leading-order hadronic vacuum polarization. paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Pentaquarks and other exotic hadrons: What combinations of quarks are possible? Are they a tightly bound system of five elementary particles, or a more weakly-bound pairing of a baryon and a meson?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard model of strong interactions (quantum chromodynamics), hadrons are color-singlet bound states of quarks and gluons. Conventional hadrons are either mesons (quark–antiquark pairs) or baryons (three-quark states). Exotic hadrons are color-singlet bound states whose minimal quark content differs from these; in particular, a pentaquark is a hadron whose minimal valence content consists of four quarks and one antiquark.

Provide a complete classification, from first principles in QCD, of the allowed valence quark/antiquark combinations that can form bound or resonant exotic hadrons (including in particular pentaquark states), together with their allowed quantum numbers (isospin, spin, parity, charge, flavor content).

For each such observed or predicted pentaquark resonance, determine its internal structure: specifically, decide whether it is realized as
(a) a compact, tightly bound configuration of five valence (anti)quarks confined within a single hadronic volume, or
(b) a loosely bound hadronic "molecule" consisting of a conventional baryon and a conventional meson interacting via residual (e.g. pion- or other meson-exchange) forces analogous to nuclear binding,
or some quantum-mechanical superposition or other configuration (e.g. kinematic re-scattering / triangle singularity effect). Provide a criterion, derivable from QCD, that distinguishes these possibilities and apply it to the known hidden-charm pentaquark candidates.
status_search_result: The internal structure of pentaquarks and the full classification of allowed exotic hadron quark combinations remain unresolved. Recent (2024–2025) theoretical and experimental work, including LHCb observations and Schrödinger-equation studies of c(cc)uds systems, provides increasing evidence favoring a hadronic-molecule interpretation for at least some hidden-charm pentaquarks, but compact-pentaquark, molecular, and rescattering interpretations all remain viable in the literature, with no consensus.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Mu problem: A problem in supersymmetric theories, concerned with understanding the reasons for parameter values of the theory.
self_contained_problem: In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the superpotential contains a supersymmetric Higgs-mass coupling term $W \supset \mu\, H_u H_d$, where $H_u$ and $H_d$ are the two Higgs chiral superfields and $\mu$ is a dimensionful complex parameter. Naturalness arguments and consistency with electroweak symmetry breaking require the magnitude of $\mu$ to lie at the electroweak/soft-supersymmetry-breaking scale (roughly $10^2$–$10^3$ GeV), while $\mu$ is a supersymmetric (not supersymmetry-breaking) parameter and is therefore not protected by any symmetry from taking values up to a fundamental high scale such as the Planck or grand-unification scale ($\sim 10^{16}$–$10^{19}$ GeV).\n\nFormulate and justify a mechanism (for example, a symmetry principle, a dynamical origin from vacuum expectation values of additional fields such as in the NMSSM or Giudice–Masiero mechanism, or a geometric/string-theoretic construction) by which the parameter $\mu$ in the MSSM superpotential is naturally generated at, and only at, the electroweak/soft-breaking scale, rather than at the high fundamental scale where the theory is defined. Equivalently: explain why $|\mu|$ is many orders of magnitude smaller than the natural high scale of the theory while remaining nonzero and of the same order as the soft supersymmetry-breaking masses.
status_search_result: The Mu problem of the MSSM remains an open conceptual problem in particle physics. Various mechanisms (Giudice–Masiero, Kim–Nilles, NMSSM, etc.) have been proposed, but no consensus solution exists, and the problem continues to be listed among open problems and studied in recent literature.

original_question: Koide formula: An aspect of the problem of particle generations. The sum of the masses of the three charged leptons, divided by the square of the sum of the roots of these masses, to within one standard deviation of observations, is . It is unknown how such a simple value comes about, and why it is the exact arithmetic average of the possible extreme values of (equal masses) and 1 (one mass dominates).
self_contained_problem:
Let $m_e, m_\mu, m_\tau > 0$ denote the rest masses of the three charged leptons (electron, muon, and tau). Define the dimensionless quantity
$$Q(m_e, m_\mu, m_\tau) \;=\; \frac{m_e + m_\mu + m_\tau}{\bigl(\sqrt{m_e} + \sqrt{m_\mu} + \sqrt{m_\tau}\bigr)^2}.$$

(a) Show that for any positive real numbers $m_1, m_2, m_3$, one has $\tfrac{1}{3} \le Q(m_1,m_2,m_3) \le 1$, with $Q = \tfrac{1}{3}$ attained when $m_1 = m_2 = m_3$ and $Q \to 1$ in the limit where one mass dominates the other two.

(b) Empirically, the measured charged-lepton masses satisfy
$$Q(m_e, m_\mu, m_\tau) = \tfrac{2}{3}$$
to within one standard deviation of current experimental uncertainties; equivalently, $Q$ equals the arithmetic mean of the extreme values $\tfrac{1}{3}$ and $1$. Provide a derivation, from first principles within (or beyond) the Standard Model of particle physics, that explains why the charged-lepton mass spectrum yields exactly $Q = \tfrac{2}{3}$, and account for why this particular simple value (the arithmetic mean of the bounds in (a)) is realized in nature.
status_search_result: The Koide formula remains an empirically accurate but theoretically unexplained relation as of 2025. Despite various proposed derivations (discrete symmetries, phase-coherence models, connections to the fine-structure constant, soliton/topological field theory), no derivation within the Standard Model accounts for the observed value Q = 2/3, and no proposed beyond-Standard-Model explanation has gained consensus.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Strange matter: Does strange matter exist? Is it stable? Can they form Strange stars? Is strange matter stable at 0 pressure (i.e. in the vacuum)?
self_contained_problem:
Strange matter is a hypothesized form of quark matter composed of approximately equal numbers of up, down, and strange quarks, governed by quantum chromodynamics. The strange matter hypothesis (sometimes called the Bodmer–Witten conjecture) asserts that at sufficiently high baryon density, a deconfined phase of up, down, and strange quarks may be the true ground state of strongly interacting matter, with energy per baryon lower than that of ordinary nuclei (such as ^56Fe). Determine the following:

(a) Whether strange matter, in the above sense, actually exists in nature.

(b) Whether bulk strange matter is absolutely stable (i.e., whether its energy per baryon at zero temperature and zero external pressure is strictly less than the energy per baryon of the most stable ordinary nuclei).

(c) Whether macroscopic self-bound stellar objects composed predominantly of strange quark matter ("strange stars") can form and exist as stable astrophysical objects.

(d) Whether strange quark matter remains stable at zero external pressure (i.e., as a self-bound state in vacuum), as opposed to being stable only when confined under the high pressures present inside compact stars.

Provide a rigorous resolution based on quantum chromodynamics and, where relevant, astrophysical constraints.
status_search_result: As of 2025, the existence and stability of strange matter, and the existence of strange stars, remain open. Recent reviews emphasize that uncertainties in the non-perturbative QCD equation of state at high density leave the strange matter hypothesis unresolved, and observational identification of strange stars is still debated.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Glueballs: Do they exist in nature?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-abelian SU(3) gauge theory of the strong interaction, the self-interaction of gluons permits the theoretical existence of color-singlet bound states composed entirely of gluons, with no valence quarks. Such hypothetical hadrons are called glueballs, and lattice QCD predicts a spectrum of them, with the lightest being a scalar (J^{PC} = 0^{++}) state near 1.5–1.7 GeV and the lightest pseudoscalar (0^{-+}) near 2.3–2.6 GeV.

Problem: Determine whether pure (or predominantly gluonic) glueball states exist as physical hadronic resonances in nature, and if so, unambiguously identify at least one such state experimentally — distinguishing it from ordinary quark-antiquark mesons and from quark-gluon hybrid or tetraquark configurations with which it may mix.
status_search_result: The existence of glueballs remains experimentally unconfirmed in a definitive sense, but as of 2024–2025 the BESIII collaboration reported strong evidence that the X(2370) resonance has mass and spin-parity (0^{-+}) consistent with the lightest pseudoscalar glueball predicted by lattice QCD. Alternative interpretations (e.g., tetraquark) have not yet been excluded, so the question is considered to have compelling partial experimental support but is not fully resolved.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Solar cycle: How does the Sun generate its periodically reversing large-scale magnetic field? How do other solar-like stars generate their magnetic fields, and what are the similarities and differences between stellar activity cycles and that of the Sun? What caused the Maunder Minimum and other grand minima, and how does the solar cycle recover from a minima state?
self_contained_problem:
The Sun exhibits an approximately 11-year cycle of magnetic activity (the solar cycle) during which its large-scale magnetic field reverses polarity, accompanied by quasi-periodic variations in sunspot number, irradiance, and other observable activity tracers. The Sun has also displayed extended episodes of strongly suppressed activity, known as grand minima, the most prominent historical example being the Maunder Minimum (approximately 1645–1715). Other late-type stars with convective envelopes (solar-like stars) likewise exhibit magnetic activity cycles with a variety of periods and amplitudes.

Within a magnetohydrodynamic framework for a rotating, stratified, turbulently convecting plasma, formulate and answer the following:

(a) Identify the physical mechanism (dynamo process) by which the Sun generates and periodically reverses its large-scale magnetic field, specifying the roles of differential rotation, turbulent convection, meridional circulation, and magnetic helicity transport, in sufficient quantitative detail to reproduce the observed cycle period, butterfly diagram, and polarity reversals.

(b) Determine how analogous dynamo processes operate in other solar-like stars as a function of stellar parameters (rotation rate, mass, age, convection zone depth), and characterize precisely the similarities and differences between their activity cycles and the solar cycle.

(c) Identify the physical cause of the Maunder Minimum and of other grand minima, and describe the dynamical mechanism by which the solar cycle recovers from such a minimum state.
status_search_result: The mechanism of the solar dynamo, the origin of stellar activity cycles in solar-like stars, and the causes of grand minima such as the Maunder Minimum remain active areas of research and are widely listed among open problems in solar and stellar physics.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Coronal heating problem: Why is the Sun's corona (atmosphere layer) so much hotter than the Sun's surface? Why is the magnetic reconnection effect many orders of magnitude faster than predicted by standard models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetized plasma model of a star's outer atmosphere consisting of a dense, relatively cool photospheric surface (with temperature on the order of 6×10^3 K) overlaid by a tenuous corona whose observed temperature exceeds 10^6 K. Develop a quantitative physical theory (within magnetohydrodynamics, kinetic plasma theory, or an appropriate extension) that:

(a) Explains, from first principles, how energy is transported from the cooler surface through the chromosphere and transition region into the corona and there dissipated, so as to maintain a steady-state coronal temperature two to three orders of magnitude higher than the surface temperature, against radiative and conductive losses.

(b) Accounts for the observed rate of magnetic reconnection in coronal plasmas, which proceeds many orders of magnitude faster than the predictions of the classical Sweet–Parker resistive MHD model (whose reconnection rate scales as S^{-1/2} in the Lundquist number S). The theory should yield a reconnection rate consistent with observations (effectively independent of, or only weakly dependent on, S in the high-S limit) and be derivable from a well-specified plasma model.

Provide either (i) a single mechanism (e.g., wave heating, nanoflare/reconnection heating, turbulence-mediated fast reconnection, kinetic plasmoid instabilities, or another candidate) together with predictions that can be compared with observations, or (ii) a rigorous demonstration that no such single mechanism suffices and a quantitative decomposition of the heating budget among multiple mechanisms.
status_search_result: Recent reviews and 2025 publications indicate the coronal heating problem and the related fast magnetic reconnection puzzle remain unresolved. Multiple candidate mechanisms (Alfvén wave heating, nanoflare/reconnection heating, magnetic tectonics, plasmoid-mediated fast reconnection) show promise but no single mechanism is observationally verified, and there is still no consensus framework explaining the observed reconnection rates.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Astrophysical jet: Why do only certain accretion discs surrounding certain astronomical objects emit relativistic jets along their polar axes? Why are there quasi-periodic oscillations in many accretion discs? Why does the period of these oscillations scale as the inverse of the mass of the central object? Why are there sometimes overtones, and why do these appear at different frequency ratios in different objects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the magnetohydrodynamic problem of an accretion disc of magnetized plasma orbiting a compact central object (such as a neutron star, stellar-mass black hole, or supermassive black hole) under the combined influence of gravity, gas pressure, radiation pressure, and electromagnetic fields. Observations show that:

(a) Only some such accretion systems launch collimated, relativistic bipolar outflows (jets) along the polar (rotation) axis of the disc, while other apparently similar systems do not.
(b) Many accretion discs exhibit quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in their X-ray luminosity, with a characteristic frequency f whose value, across a wide range of objects, scales approximately as f ∝ 1/M, where M is the mass of the central object.
(c) These QPOs sometimes appear together with overtones (additional peaks in the power spectrum), and the frequency ratios between the fundamental and its overtones differ between objects (e.g. 3:2, 2:1, etc.).

Provide a first-principles theoretical framework, derived from the equations of (general-)relativistic magnetohydrodynamics and accretion-disc physics, that simultaneously answers the following:

1. Determine the necessary and sufficient physical conditions (on the disc structure, magnetic field topology, spin, accretion rate, and central-object properties) under which a relativistic polar jet is launched and collimated.
2. Derive the mechanism producing the quasi-periodic oscillations in accretion discs and explain rigorously why the resulting characteristic frequency scales as the inverse of the central mass M.
3. Explain why overtones arise in some systems but not others, and predict from the model which frequency ratios occur in which classes of objects.
status_search_result: The launching of relativistic jets from accretion discs and the origin of quasi-periodic oscillations remain open problems in astrophysics. While candidate models exist (Blandford–Znajek and Blandford–Payne mechanisms for jets; resonant orbital/epicyclic models, diskoseismology, and Lense–Thirring precession for QPOs), no single accepted theory explains why only certain systems produce jets, the 1/M scaling of QPO frequencies across object classes, and the varying overtone frequency ratios. These are listed among the standing open questions in astrophysics.

original_question: Diffuse interstellar bands: What is responsible for the numerous interstellar absorption lines detected in astronomical spectra? Are they molecular in origin, and if so which molecules are responsible for them? How do they form?
self_contained_problem:
Astronomical absorption spectra of starlight passing through the interstellar medium contain a large set (currently around 500) of absorption features at ultraviolet, visible, and infrared wavelengths, collectively known as the diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs). Apart from a small number of near-infrared bands attributed to the cation C60+, the chemical species producing these absorption features remain unidentified.

Determine the carriers of the diffuse interstellar bands. Specifically:
(a) Identify the physical/chemical entities (atoms, molecules, ions, radicals, grains, or nanoparticles) responsible for each diffuse interstellar absorption band observed in astronomical spectra.
(b) Decide whether the carriers are of molecular origin, and if so specify which molecular species (and their charge states, isomers, and excitation states) produce each band, in a manner consistent with laboratory gas-phase spectroscopy.
(c) Describe the formation pathways and physical conditions under which these carriers arise and survive in interstellar environments.
status_search_result: Of roughly 500 known diffuse interstellar bands, only several near-infrared bands have been definitively attributed to a carrier — the buckminsterfullerene cation C60+. The vast majority of DIB carriers remain unidentified. Recent (2025–2026) work continues to propose and test candidate carriers (helicenes, PAH and small-molecule cations, transition-metal-containing ions, carbon nanodots/nanodiamonds), and observational programs such as EDIBLES continue to characterise band behaviour, but no broad identification has been achieved. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Supermassive black holes: What is the origin of the M–sigma relation between supermassive black hole mass and galaxy velocity dispersion? How did the most distant quasars grow their supermassive black holes up to 10 solar masses so early in the history of the universe?
self_contained_problem:
Consider supermassive black holes (SMBHs), defined as black holes with masses of order $10^6$–$10^{10}\,M_\odot$ residing at the centers of galaxies, where $M_\odot$ denotes one solar mass. For an SMBH at the center of a galaxy whose stellar bulge has line-of-sight stellar velocity dispersion $\sigma$, empirical observations indicate a tight power-law correlation
$$\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{M_\odot} \;\approx\; A\left(\frac{\sigma}{200\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}\right)^{\beta},$$
with $A \sim 10^{8}$ and $\beta \approx 4$–$5$, known as the $M$–$\sigma$ relation.

(a) Identify and rigorously derive, from first physical principles (gravitational dynamics, accretion physics, feedback processes, and/or cosmological structure formation), the mechanism that produces the $M$–$\sigma$ relation, predicting the correct slope $\beta$, normalization $A$, and intrinsic scatter, and explaining whether $\sigma$ is the fundamental governing variable (as opposed to bulge mass, halo mass, or another property).

(b) Provide a quantitative formation and growth scenario that explains how the highest-redshift observed quasars (at redshifts $z \gtrsim 6$–$7.5$, i.e., within $\lesssim 800$ Myr of the Big Bang) can host SMBHs of mass $\gtrsim 10^{9}\,M_\odot$, given the Eddington luminosity bound
$$L_{\rm Edd} = \frac{4\pi G M_{\rm BH} m_p c}{\sigma_T},$$
which limits radiatively efficient accretion growth to an e-folding (Salpeter) time of order $4.5\times 10^{7}$ yr. The scenario must specify the seed black hole mass distribution, accretion history (including any super-Eddington phases or direct-collapse channels), and merger contributions, and be consistent with current observational constraints.

status_search_result: The physical origin of the M–σ relation remains an active open problem: while AGN feedback models (e.g., Silk–Rees, King) give plausible mechanisms, the source of the feedback and whether σ is truly the fundamental parameter remain uncertain. Likewise, the rapid growth of high-redshift quasar SMBHs to ~10^9 solar masses within the first ~800 Myr is an active research question, with competing seed scenarios (direct collapse, Pop III remnants, super-Eddington accretion) under investigation as of 2025.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Kuiper cliff: Why does the number of objects in the Solar System's Kuiper belt fall off rapidly and unexpectedly beyond a radius of 50 astronomical units?
self_contained_problem:
In the Solar System, the Kuiper belt is the region populated by small icy bodies orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune. Observational surveys reveal that the number density of Kuiper belt objects, when plotted as a function of heliocentric distance, drops abruptly near a radius of approximately 50 astronomical units (the "Kuiper cliff"), far more sharply than would be expected from a smooth primordial planetesimal distribution shaped solely by the known planets.

Problem: Identify the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for this rapid and unexpected decrease in the population of Kuiper belt objects beyond ~50 AU. In particular, determine whether the cliff is caused by (a) dynamical sculpting via mean-motion or secular resonances with Neptune, (b) gravitational perturbations from an undiscovered massive body in the outer Solar System, (c) primordial conditions in the protoplanetary disk that prevented the accretion of detectable-sized bodies beyond ~50 AU, or (d) some other mechanism; and quantitatively account for the observed sharpness and location of the falloff.
status_search_result: As of 2025, the cause of the Kuiper cliff at roughly 50 AU remains unresolved. Several hypotheses are discussed in the literature—resonant dynamics with Neptune, perturbations by an undiscovered massive body (e.g., Planet Nine), and primordial truncation of the protoplanetary disk—but no consensus or definitive evidence has been established.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Flyby anomaly: Why is the observed energy of satellites flying by planetary bodies sometimes different by a minute amount from the value predicted by theory?
self_contained_problem:
During gravity-assist maneuvers, a spacecraft on an unbound hyperbolic trajectory approaches a planetary body, swings past it, and recedes to a large distance. Standard celestial-mechanical theory (Newtonian gravity together with known general-relativistic corrections, planetary oblateness, atmospheric drag, solar radiation pressure, thermal recoil, and tidal effects) predicts a specific value for the spacecraft's asymptotic outgoing kinetic energy (equivalently, its outgoing hyperbolic excess speed) given its asymptotic incoming state. For several Earth flybys (e.g., spacecraft of Galileo-, NEAR-, Cassini-, Rosetta-, and Messenger-class missions), precise Doppler and ranging tracking has revealed small but statistically significant unexplained discrepancies between the observed and predicted asymptotic speeds, on the order of millimeters to centimeters per second.

Problem: Identify a physical or dynamical mechanism — whether a previously unmodeled conventional effect (such as a systematic error in tracking, atmospheric, thermal, or relativistic modeling) or a new gravitational/inertial phenomenon — that quantitatively accounts for the magnitudes, signs, and trajectory dependence of these flyby energy anomalies across all observed cases, and produce a predictive formula whose parameters, once fixed, reproduce the existing data set and forecast the anomaly (or its absence) for future planetary flybys.
status_search_result: The flyby anomaly remains unresolved as of 2024–2025. Several theoretical proposals continue to appear (e.g., post-Einsteinian extensions of general relativity, geodesic-deviation models in the variation principle of GR, gravitomagnetic explanations), but none is generally accepted as a complete account. No dedicated mission has been funded; upcoming Earth gravity assists (Europa Clipper, Juice) are expected to provide additional tracking data for analysis.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Supernovae: What is the exact mechanism by which an implosion of a dying star becomes an explosion?
self_contained_problem:
A massive star at the end of its life undergoes gravitational core collapse: when the iron core exceeds the effective Chandrasekhar mass, electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support it and the core implodes on a dynamical timescale, reaching nuclear densities where it stiffens and produces a bounce shock. Observationally, in many cases this inward implosion is reversed into an outward-propagating explosion that ejects most of the stellar envelope as a supernova (Type II, Ib, Ic). Numerical simulations involving the prompt hydrodynamic bounce shock alone generically fail to produce a successful explosion (the shock stalls into an accretion shock), and proposed revival mechanisms — including neutrino heating in the gain region, standing accretion shock instability (SASI), neutrino-driven convection, rapid rotation with magnetohydrodynamic jets, acoustic power from proto-neutron-star g-modes, and phase-transition-induced second shocks — depend sensitively on multidimensional effects, neutrino transport, the high-density nuclear equation of state, and progenitor structure.

Problem: Determine, from first principles of general-relativistic radiation-magnetohydrodynamics coupled to neutrino transport and a realistic nuclear equation of state, the precise physical mechanism that converts the implosion of a collapsing stellar core into a successful outgoing explosion. Specifically, identify which combination of processes (neutrino heating, hydrodynamic instabilities, rotation and magnetic fields, nuclear/QCD physics, etc.) is responsible for shock revival across the observed range of progenitor masses, and predict the resulting explosion energies, remnant masses, nucleosynthetic yields, and neutrino and gravitational-wave signatures in quantitative agreement with observations.
status_search_result: The core-collapse supernova explosion mechanism remains an unsolved problem in astrophysics. While neutrino-driven convection plus SASI in 3D simulations has emerged as the leading candidate and recent 3D simulations (e.g., by groups at Princeton, Garching/MPA, Oak Ridge, Monash) report successful explosions for a range of progenitors, no single mechanism has been confirmed as universally responsible, and quantitative agreement with observed explosion energies and remnant distributions is still being established as of 2025–2026.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Ultra-high-energy cosmic ray: Why is it that some cosmic rays appear to possess energies that are impossibly high, given that there are no sufficiently energetic cosmic ray sources near the Earth? Why is it that (apparently) some cosmic rays emitted by distant sources have energies above the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin limit?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmic rays are highly energetic charged particles (predominantly protons and atomic nuclei) arriving at Earth from outer space. The Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) limit is a theoretical upper bound, approximately 5 × 10^19 eV, on the energy of cosmic-ray protons that can propagate over cosmological distances: a proton with energy above this threshold loses energy rapidly via pion-production interactions with cosmic microwave background photons (and heavy nuclei undergo analogous photodisintegration), so that after traveling more than roughly 50–100 Mpc its energy should fall below the cutoff.

Nevertheless, observatories have detected ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray events with energies well above 5 × 10^19 eV (including events near and above 10^20 eV), while no astrophysical sources powerful enough to accelerate particles to such energies are known within the GZK interaction horizon around Earth, and the reconstructed arrival directions of these events do not robustly correlate with identified nearby sources.

Provide a physically consistent explanation that simultaneously accounts for:
(a) the existence of cosmic-ray events observed at Earth with energies above the GZK cutoff, given the apparent absence of sufficiently powerful accelerators within the GZK horizon; and
(b) the survival of such ultra-high-energy particles if they originate from sources at cosmological distances, in seeming tension with the predicted GZK energy-loss mechanism.

Equivalently: identify the sources, acceleration mechanisms, and propagation physics responsible for trans-GZK ultra-high-energy cosmic rays.
status_search_result: The origin of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and the apparent observation of events above the GZK cutoff remain open problems. As of 2023–2025, observatories such as Telescope Array reported additional extreme-energy events (e.g., the ~2.4 × 10^20 eV "Amaterasu" particle) whose back-traced arrival directions point to empty regions of sky, and IceCube continues a long-term program to determine the composition. No accepted astrophysical source population or propagation mechanism fully accounts for trans-GZK events.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Rotation rate of Saturn: Why does the magnetosphere of Saturn exhibit a (slowly changing) periodicity close to that at which the planet's clouds rotate? What is the true rotation rate of Saturn's deep interior?
self_contained_problem:
Saturn is modeled as a rapidly rotating gas giant planet possessing (i) a visible cloud layer whose features rotate with a measurable period, (ii) a magnetosphere generated by internal dynamo action whose radio emissions display a periodicity that drifts slowly over years, and (iii) a deep fluid interior whose bulk rotation rate is not directly observable from outside.

(a) Explain, within a self-consistent physical model of Saturn's atmosphere, magnetic field generation, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, why the dominant periodicity observed in Saturn's magnetospheric (kilometric radio) emission is close to, but slowly varies relative to, the rotation period of the planet's visible cloud layer.

(b) Determine the true bulk rotation period of Saturn's deep interior (i.e., the rotation rate of the underlying bulk fluid beneath the differentially rotating atmospheric layer), and justify the determination by a method that does not rely on identifying a fixed magnetic feature with the deep interior.
status_search_result: Part (b) appears largely resolved: using Saturn's ring seismology (f-mode oscillations of the planet imprinted on the C ring) combined with Cassini Grand Finale gravity harmonics, the deep interior rotation period has been determined to be approximately 10h 33m 38s (with the atmosphere exhibiting differential rotation down to ~10,000 km depth). Part (a), concerning the precise mechanism producing the slowly drifting, near-cloud-rotation periodicity in Saturn's magnetosphere (the SKR/PPO periodicities and their hemispheric, seasonally varying behavior), remains an active research area and is not considered fully settled.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Origin of magnetar magnetic field: What is the origin of magnetar magnetic fields?
self_contained_problem:
A magnetar is a type of neutron star characterized by an extraordinarily strong magnetic field, with surface dipole field strengths typically in the range $10^{14}$–$10^{15}$ G, several orders of magnitude greater than those of ordinary radio pulsars. Their decaying magnetic energy powers high-energy electromagnetic emission, including soft gamma repeater bursts and anomalous X-ray pulsar activity.

Identify the physical mechanism responsible for the generation of the ultra-strong magnetic fields observed in magnetars. Specifically, determine whether such fields arise from (i) amplification by a turbulent dynamo operating in a rapidly rotating proto-neutron star formed in core-collapse supernovae, (ii) flux conservation from the magnetic field of a strongly magnetized progenitor star (the "fossil field" hypothesis), (iii) magnetic field amplification during the merger of two neutron stars or the accretion-induced collapse of a white dwarf, or (iv) some other process; and quantitatively account for the observed distribution of magnetar field strengths, ages, and progenitor environments.
status_search_result: The origin of magnetar magnetic fields remains an open question in astrophysics as of 2025. Recent observations (e.g., the runaway magnetar SGR 0501+4516 tracked by Hubble) challenge the standard core-collapse supernova dynamo scenario, motivating alternative formation channels such as neutron-star mergers, accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs, or fossil fields inherited from massive magnetic helium-star progenitors. No single mechanism has been confirmed.

original_question: Large-scale anisotropy: Is the universe at very large scales anisotropic, making the cosmological principle an invalid assumption? paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
context_brief: Age–metallicity relation in the Galactic disk
original_question: Age–metallicity relation in the Galactic disk: Is there a universal age–metallicity relation (AMR) in the Galactic disk (both "thin" and "thick" parts of the disk)? Although in the local (primarily thin) disk of the Milky Way there is no evidence of a strong AMR, a sample of 229 nearby "thick" disk stars has been used to investigate the existence of an age–metallicity relation in the Galactic thick disk, and indicate that there is an age–metallicity relation present in the thick disk. Stellar ages from asteroseismology confirm the lack of any strong age–metallicity relation in the Galactic disc.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Milky Way's stellar disk, conventionally decomposed into a "thin disk" component (younger, kinematically cold, more metal-rich on average) and a "thick disk" component (older, kinematically hotter, generally more α-enhanced and metal-poor). For an individual star, let τ denote its age (time since formation) and let [Fe/H] denote its metallicity (logarithmic iron-to-hydrogen abundance ratio relative to the Sun). The age–metallicity relation (AMR) is any statistically significant functional/statistical dependence of [Fe/H] on τ across a stellar population.

Observational situation to be addressed:
(a) In the local thin disk, large spectroscopic samples show no strong AMR: stars of a given age display a wide spread in [Fe/H], and the mean [Fe/H](τ) is nearly flat over much of the disk's history.
(b) A sample of 229 nearby thick-disk stars suggests that an AMR does exist in the thick disk.
(c) Asteroseismically determined stellar ages corroborate the absence of any strong AMR in the disk overall.

Problem: Determine whether there exists a single, universal age–metallicity relation valid throughout the Galactic disk — that is, a well-defined function (or tight statistical relation) [Fe/H] = f(τ) that simultaneously describes the thin-disk and thick-disk populations (and any transitional component) across Galactocentric radii and heights above the midplane. If such a universal relation does not exist, characterize precisely how the AMR differs between the thin and thick disks, identify the physical mechanisms (e.g., radial migration, episodic star formation, gas accretion, mergers) responsible for the differences, and provide a quantitative model of [Fe/H] versus τ for each disk component consistent with all current spectroscopic and asteroseismic data.
status_search_result: The age–metallicity relation in the Galactic disk remains an active and unresolved area of research. Recent studies using Gaia, APOGEE, GALAH, and Kepler/K2 asteroseismic ages continue to find a large [Fe/H] scatter at fixed age in the thin disk, while a clearer AMR is reported for the thick/high-α disk; no single universal AMR has been established. The general problem is considered open.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: The lithium problem: Why is there a discrepancy between the amount of lithium-7 predicted to be produced in Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the amount observed in very old stars?
self_contained_problem:
Standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), assuming the Standard Model of particle physics, the standard cosmological model with the baryon-to-photon ratio fixed by cosmic microwave background measurements, and the currently accepted network of thermonuclear reaction rates, predicts a primordial abundance of lithium-7 (relative to hydrogen) of order 7Li/H ≈ (4–5)×10⁻¹⁰. Spectroscopic observations of very old, metal-poor halo stars on the "Spite plateau," whose surface composition is taken to reflect the primordial abundance, instead yield 7Li/H ≈ (1–2)×10⁻¹⁰, a factor of roughly three lower than the BBN prediction.

Provide a quantitatively consistent explanation of this discrepancy. Specifically, identify the mechanism — whether (i) a modification or new ingredient in the primordial nucleosynthesis calculation (e.g., revised nuclear reaction rates, especially those involving 7Be destruction; new physics beyond the Standard Model such as decaying relic particles, variation of fundamental constants, or non-standard cosmology), or (ii) a stellar/astrophysical process acting after star formation (e.g., atomic diffusion, turbulent mixing, gravitational settling, or pre-main-sequence depletion in metal-poor stars) — that simultaneously (a) reduces the inferred or surviving 7Li abundance to the observed Spite-plateau value, (b) preserves the successful BBN predictions for the primordial abundances of D/H, 3He, and 4He within current observational uncertainties, and (c) is compatible with all other available cosmological, astrophysical, and laboratory constraints.

status_search_result: As of 2025–2026 the cosmological lithium-7 problem remains unresolved. Recent peer-reviewed work (Astronomy & Astrophysics 2025, "The cosmological lithium problem"; ScienceDirect 2024 re-examination; arXiv:2509.10721 and arXiv:2601.12438) continues to propose candidate resolutions — refined 7Be reaction/weak-transition rates, stellar depletion mechanisms, and beyond-Standard-Model physics — but no consensus solution has been established and the factor-of-three discrepancy persists.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs): What powers X-ray sources that are not associated with active galactic nuclei but exceed the Eddington limit of a neutron star or stellar black hole? Are they due to intermediate-mass black holes? Some ULXs are periodic, suggesting non-isotropic emission from a neutron star. Does this apply to all ULXs? How could such a system form and remain stable?
self_contained_problem:
The Eddington limit gives the maximum isotropic luminosity at which radiation pressure on accreting matter balances gravitational attraction; for a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole it is roughly 10^38–10^39 erg/s. Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are point-like, non-nuclear X-ray sources in external galaxies whose apparent isotropic X-ray luminosities exceed this Eddington limit and which are not identified with active galactic nuclei.

Address the following questions about ULXs:

(a) Identify the physical mechanism (or mechanisms) responsible for powering ULXs. In particular, determine the extent to which ULXs are explained by accretion onto intermediate-mass black holes (compact objects with masses roughly 10^2–10^5 solar masses), versus super-Eddington and/or geometrically beamed accretion onto stellar-mass black holes or neutron stars.

(b) Coherent pulsations have been detected from some ULXs, indicating that those sources are magnetized neutron stars whose apparent luminosity is enhanced by anisotropic (non-isotropic) emission. Determine whether anisotropic emission from neutron-star accretors accounts for all ULXs, or whether a distinct population (e.g., genuine intermediate-mass black holes or stellar-mass black hole accretors) is required.

(c) Provide a formation and evolutionary channel by which a neutron-star–powered ULX system can form and accrete stably at apparent luminosities orders of magnitude above the standard Eddington limit, consistent with observed orbital and spin properties.
status_search_result: The nature of ULXs remains an active open question. While several ULXs have been confirmed as accreting magnetized neutron stars via detected pulsations, and many others are thought to involve super-Eddington stellar-mass black hole accretion, the full population is not understood: candidate intermediate-mass black hole ULXs persist, formation channels for stably super-Eddington neutron-star ULXs are debated, and a recent (2024) comparative radio/X-ray study indicates the populations remain distinguishable but unresolved overall.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Fast radio bursts (FRBs): What causes these transient radio pulses from distant galaxies, lasting only a few milliseconds each? Why do some FRBs repeat at unpredictable intervals, but most do not? Dozens of models have been proposed, but none have been widely accepted.
self_contained_problem:
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are transient pulses of radio emission, typically lasting only a few milliseconds, that are observed coming from cosmological distances (often from host galaxies far outside the Milky Way). A subset of FRB sources have been seen to emit multiple bursts at irregular, unpredictable intervals (repeaters), while the majority have so far been detected only once (apparent non-repeaters).

Provide a physical model that:
(a) identifies the astrophysical source(s) and emission mechanism responsible for producing millisecond-duration coherent radio bursts of the observed luminosities and spectral properties from extragalactic distances; and
(b) explains, within the same framework, why some FRB sources emit repeated bursts at unpredictable intervals while others appear to burst only once, accounting for the observed statistical, temporal, spectral, and host-environment differences between the two populations.
status_search_result: As of 2025, the origin of FRBs and the dichotomy between repeating and non-repeating sources remains an active open problem. Magnetar-based models (including isolated vs. binary-magnetar scenarios) are leading candidates, but recent observations such as the extremely bright FRB 20250316A (no repeats detected despite extensive monitoring) and a repeater located in a quiescent old elliptical galaxy challenge unified models. No single mechanism is yet widely accepted.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Origin of cosmic magnetic fields: Observations reveal that magnetic fields are present throughout the universe, from galaxies to galaxy clusters. However, the mechanisms that generated these large-scale cosmic magnetic fields remain unclear. Understanding their origin is a significant unsolved problem in astrophysics.
self_contained_problem: Large-scale magnetic fields with coherence lengths up to kiloparsec and megaparsec scales are observed throughout the universe, permeating galaxies, galaxy clusters, and even the intergalactic medium, with typical strengths on the order of microgauss in galaxies and nanogauss or less on larger scales. Identify and rigorously establish the physical mechanism(s) responsible for the generation of these cosmic magnetic fields. paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Quantum chromodynamics: What are the phases of strongly interacting matter, and what roles do they play in the evolution of the cosmos? What is the detailed partonic structure of the nucleons? What does QCD predict for the properties of strongly interacting matter? What determines the key features of QCD, and what is their relation to the nature of gravity and spacetime? Does QCD truly lack CP violations?
self_contained_problem:
Let quantum chromodynamics (QCD) denote the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) (color) coupled to Dirac fermions (quarks) in the fundamental representation, with Lagrangian density
  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f ψ̄_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) ψ_f + θ (g^2 / 32 π^2) G^a_{μν} \tilde G^{a μν},
where G^a_{μν} is the gluon field strength, D_μ is the gauge-covariant derivative, the sum runs over quark flavors f with masses m_f, and θ is the topological vacuum angle.

Address the following questions about this theory:

(a) Determine the complete phase diagram of strongly interacting matter described by QCD as a function of temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B (including, e.g., the hadronic phase, the quark-gluon plasma, color-superconducting phases, and any chiral/deconfinement transitions), and describe the role each phase plays in the cosmological evolution of the universe.

(b) Derive from first principles the partonic (quark and gluon) structure of nucleons, including parton distribution functions, transverse-momentum-dependent distributions, generalized parton distributions, spin decomposition, and orbital angular momentum content.

(c) Predict, from the QCD Lagrangian alone, the bulk properties of strongly interacting matter (equation of state, transport coefficients, hadron spectrum, confinement mechanism, mass gap).

(d) Identify what fundamental principles determine the key features of QCD (e.g., confinement, asymptotic freedom, chiral symmetry breaking) and establish whether and how these features are related to the nature of gravity and of spacetime.

(e) Prove or disprove that QCD exhibits no observable CP violation; in particular, explain why the experimentally observed bound |θ| ≲ 10^{-10} on the vacuum angle holds, i.e., resolve the strong CP problem.
status_search_result: These are listed among the central open problems of nuclear/particle physics. The QCD phase diagram, nucleon partonic structure, first-principles QCD predictions, and the strong CP problem all remain unresolved as of 2026; the mass gap for Yang–Mills is a Clay Millennium Problem that is still open, and the strong CP problem remains a primary motivation for axion searches.

paper_title: List of unsolved problems in physics
original_question: Quark–gluon plasma: Where is the onset of deconfinement: 1) as a function of temperature and chemical potentials? 2) as a function of relativistic heavy-ion collision energy and system size? What is the mechanism of energy and baryon-number stopping leading to creation of quark-gluon plasma in relativistic heavy-ion collisions? Why is sudden hadronization and the statistical-hadronization model a near-to-perfect description of hadron production from quark–gluon plasma? Is quark flavor conserved in quark–gluon plasma? Are strangeness and charm in chemical equilibrium in quark–gluon plasma? Does strangeness in quark–gluon plasma flow at the same speed as up and down quark flavours? Why does deconfined matter show ideal flow?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), strongly interacting matter is predicted to undergo a transition from an ordinary hadronic phase to a deconfined phase—the quark–gluon plasma (QGP)—in which quarks and gluons are no longer confined within color-singlet hadrons. The phase structure of QCD matter is parametrized by the temperature T and the chemical potentials (in particular the baryon chemical potential μ_B, and chemical potentials for strangeness and charm). In high-energy nucleus–nucleus collisions, QGP is believed to be transiently produced, and its production depends on the collision center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair √s_NN and the colliding system size A.

Provide a quantitative description, derivable from QCD and supported by experiment, of the following:

1. Determine the location of the deconfinement onset in the QCD phase diagram, both (a) as a curve/region in the (T, μ_B, μ_S, μ_C, ...) space of temperatures and chemical potentials, and (b) as a function of the collision energy √s_NN and the system size A in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

2. Identify and derive the mechanism by which energy and baryon number are stopped (i.e., deposited near mid-rapidity) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, leading to the formation of the QGP.

3. Explain why hadron production from the QGP is described to near-perfect accuracy by sudden hadronization within the statistical-hadronization model (i.e., a model in which hadron yields are fixed by a thermal/statistical distribution at a hadronization hypersurface).

4. Determine whether quark flavor is conserved during the QGP phase (i.e., whether flavor-changing processes are negligible on the QGP lifetime scale).

5. Determine whether strangeness and charm reach chemical equilibrium in the QGP, and on what time scales.

6. Determine whether strange quarks in the QGP exhibit the same collective (hydrodynamic) flow velocities as up and down quarks.

7. Explain why the deconfined matter produced in heavy-ion collisions behaves as an almost ideal (very low specific shear viscosity η/s) fluid.
status_search_result: These questions on QGP—the location of the deconfinement transition at finite μ_B, the stopping mechanism, the success of statistical hadronization, flavor equilibration, differential strange-quark flow, and the origin of near-perfect fluidity—remain active research topics in heavy-ion physics, with ongoing experimental programs (RHIC Beam Energy Scan, LHC, NA61/SHINE, future FAIR/NICA) and theoretical efforts (lattice QCD, viscous hydrodynamics, transport models). They are listed among unsolved problems in physics and no consensus solution exists as of 2026.
