paper_title: Open Problems in Mathematical Physics
original_question: For a large square lattice with periodic boundary conditions and independent electrons at quarter filling, determine whether the choice of magnetic flux that minimizes the sum of the lowest quarter of the hopping-matrix eigenvalues is the uniform flux π/2 through each elementary plaquette.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite square lattice with $|\Lambda|$ sites, where $|\Lambda|$ is divisible by 4, equipped with periodic boundary conditions (so $\Lambda$ is a discrete torus). Consider a Hermitian hopping matrix $T$ indexed by $\Lambda \times \Lambda$ defined by
$$T_{x,y} = \begin{cases} e^{i\theta(x,y)} & \text{if } x,y \text{ are nearest neighbors in } \Lambda, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}$$
where $\theta(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}$ are arbitrary phases subject only to the Hermiticity constraint $\theta(x,y) = -\theta(y,x)$. The eigenvalues of $T$ depend only on the fluxes through elementary plaquettes, defined as the sum of the phases $\theta(x,y)$ around each unit square of $\Lambda$ (taken in a fixed orientation). Let $\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{|\Lambda|}$ denote the eigenvalues of $T$, and define
$$E(\{\theta\}) = \sum_{j=1}^{|\Lambda|/4} \lambda_j,$$
the sum of the lowest quarter of the eigenvalues. Determine whether the assignment of fluxes that minimizes $E$ is the one in which the flux through every elementary plaquette equals $\pi/2$.
status_search_result: Web search shows the related half-filled flux phase conjecture (flux $\pi$ per plaquette on bipartite planar graphs) was proven by Lieb in 1994 and later simplified by Macris–Nachtergaele. However, no proof or disproof of the quarter-filled analog (optimal flux $\pi/2$) appears in the literature; it is listed as an open problem with no resolution found.

paper_title: Open Problems in Mathematical Physics
original_question: Prove Bose–Einstein condensation for a weakly interacting dilute Bose gas in a continuum model, rather than only in the special lattice hard-core case already known.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a system of $N$ identical spinless bosons in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\ge 2$) interacting via a two-body potential $v\ge 0$ that is short-range, spherically symmetric, and repulsive (for example, compactly supported and integrable). The Hamiltonian acting on the symmetric subspace of $L^2(\Lambda^N)$ for $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ a box of volume $V$ is
$$H_N=-\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta_{x_i}+\sum_{1\le i<j\le N} v(x_i-x_j),$$
with suitable (e.g. periodic) boundary conditions. Let $\rho=N/V$ denote the particle density, and let $\gamma^{(1)}_{N,V}$ be the one-particle reduced density matrix of the ground state (or, at positive temperature $T>0$, of the Gibbs state) of $H_N$.

Prove that in the thermodynamic limit $N,V\to\infty$ with $\rho$ fixed at a sufficiently small positive value (the dilute regime, $\rho\, a^d\ll 1$ where $a$ is the scattering length of $v$), there is Bose–Einstein condensation into the zero-momentum mode, i.e.
$$\liminf_{N,V\to\infty,\ N/V=\rho}\ \frac{\langle\varphi_0,\gamma^{(1)}_{N,V}\varphi_0\rangle}{N}>0,$$
where $\varphi_0$ is the constant function on $\Lambda$. Equivalently, establish off-diagonal long-range order for the one-particle density matrix of the weakly interacting dilute Bose gas in this continuum setting.
status_search_result: BEC has been rigorously proved for dilute trapped Bose gases in the Gross–Pitaevskii limit (Lieb–Seiringer 2002) and, more recently, on length scales beyond Gross–Pitaevskii but still far shorter than thermodynamic length scales. Proving BEC in the thermodynamic limit for a continuum weakly interacting Bose gas remains an open problem.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: What is the computational complexity of finding an induced cycle with at least 4 vertices in an undirected graph G?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. A *hole* in $G$ is an induced cycle of length at least $4$, i.e., a sequence of distinct vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$ with $k \ge 4$ such that $v_iv_{i+1} \in E$ for all $i$ (indices mod $k$) and $v_iv_j \notin E$ whenever $|i-j| \not\equiv 1 \pmod k$.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/search problem: given $G$, decide whether $G$ contains a hole, and if so, output one. In particular, is there a polynomial-time algorithm in $|V|+|E|$ that solves this problem?
status_search_result: A graph contains a hole if and only if it is not chordal. Chordality can be tested in linear time (e.g., via Lexicographic BFS by Rose, Tarjan, and Lueker), and when a graph is not chordal such an algorithm can produce a hole as a certificate. Hence detecting/finding a hole is solvable in linear time, and the question of its complexity is settled. Related harder variants (odd hole, even hole, hole through a specified vertex, longest hole) have been studied with various polynomial-time or NP-hardness results.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of finding an odd hole, that is, an induced odd cycle of length at least 5, in an undirected graph G?
self_contained_problem: Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph. A hole in G is an induced subgraph isomorphic to a cycle of length at least 4; an odd hole is a hole whose number of vertices is odd (hence of length at least 5). paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: Given an undirected graph G and a collection T = {(t1, s1), ..., (tk, sk)} of k pairs of vertices of G, is there an algorithm with running time 2^{O(k)} poly(|V(G)|) that decides whether G contains k pairwise vertex-disjoint paths connecting each ti to the corresponding si?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be an undirected graph and let T = {(s_1, t_1), ..., (s_k, t_k)} be a collection of k pairs of vertices of G. The Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem asks whether there exist k pairwise internally vertex-disjoint paths P_1, ..., P_k in G such that, for each i ∈ {1, ..., k}, the path P_i has endpoints s_i and t_i.

By the Robertson–Seymour graph minors theorem this problem is fixed-parameter tractable in k, and the best known parameter dependence (at the time of posing) yields an algorithm with running time 2^{2^{O(k)}} · poly(|V(G)|).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that decides the Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem in time 2^{O(k)} · poly(|V(G)|)?
status_search_result: Obtaining a single-exponential 2^{O(k)} poly(n) parameterized algorithm for the Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem on general graphs remains an open problem. Recent work (e.g., Lokshtanov–Misra–Pilipczuk–Saurabh–Zehavi, STOC 2020 / SICOMP) achieved a 2^{O(k^2)} n^{O(1)} algorithm only for the planar case, and improvements like Korhonen–Pilipczuk–Stamoulis (FOCS 2024) improved the polynomial factor for general graphs but not the dependence on k to single exponential.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: Let C be a hereditary class of graphs. Suppose there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that computes the stable set number of every graph G in C. Must C then be χ-bounded, meaning that there exists a function f such that every graph G in C satisfies χ(G) ≤ f(ω(G)), where χ(G) is the chromatic number and ω(G) is the clique number?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$, let $\chi(G)$ denote its chromatic number, $\omega(G)$ its clique number, and $\alpha(G)$ its stable set (independence) number. A class $\mathcal{C}$ of graphs is called hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The class $\mathcal{C}$ is said to be $\chi$-bounded if there exists a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G\in\mathcal{C}$.

Question: Suppose $\mathcal{C}$ is a hereditary class of graphs for which there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any $G\in\mathcal{C}$, computes $\alpha(G)$. Does it follow that $\mathcal{C}$ is $\chi$-bounded?
status_search_result: Web search did not surface any published resolution to this question relating polynomial-time computability of the stable set number to χ-boundedness in hereditary graph classes. The problem appears to remain open; related work focuses on showing specific classes (bounded twin-width, bounded clique-width) are polynomially χ-bounded, but the general implication has not been confirmed solved.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: What is the computational complexity of the following problem: given a partial representation of a circular-arc graph G, decide whether the given representation can be extended to a full representation of G?
self_contained_problem:
A circular-arc graph is a graph G = (V, E) that admits a representation R assigning to each vertex v ∈ V an arc R(v) of a fixed circle such that two vertices are adjacent in G if and only if their assigned arcs intersect. A partial representation of G is a pair (V', R') where V' ⊆ V and R' assigns an arc of the circle to each vertex of V'. A representation R of G extends the partial representation (V', R') if R(v) = R'(v) for every v ∈ V'.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem:

  Input: A circular-arc graph G together with a partial representation (V', R') of G.
  Question: Does there exist a circular-arc representation R of G that extends (V', R')?
category_tag: geometric intersection graphs / partial representation extension
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved: the partial representation extension problem for circular-arc graphs is NP-complete. This was shown in work by Bhore, Chaplick, Gonçalves, Klavík, and others, including the paper "Extending Partial Representations of Circular-Arc Graphs" (arXiv:2108.13076, published 2022). Several subclasses (e.g., proper Helly, normal Helly with distinct endpoints) admit polynomial-time algorithms, while unit circular-arc and general circular-arc cases are NP-complete.

original_question: A graph G is called CIS if for every maximal clique C and every maximal stable set S of G, the intersection C ∩ S is nonempty. What is the computational complexity of deciding whether a given graph G is CIS?

A clique is maximal if it is not properly contained in another clique, and likewise for stable sets. The graph G is called CIS if for every maximal clique C and every maximal stable set S of G, one has C ∩ S ≠ ∅.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: A mixed graph is a graph that contains both directed and undirected edges. Given a mixed graph G and a collection T = {(t1, s1), ..., (tk, sk)} of k pairs of vertices, is the Steiner Orientation problem fixed-parameter tractable with parameter k: can one orient the edges of G so that, after the orientation, there exist k paths connecting each pair (ti, si)?
self_contained_problem:
A mixed graph is a graph $G = (V, E \cup A)$ that contains both undirected edges (the set $E$) and directed edges (the set $A$). An orientation of $G$ is a directed graph obtained by replacing each undirected edge $\{u,v\} \in E$ with exactly one of the two directed arcs $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$, while keeping all arcs in $A$ unchanged.

The Steiner Orientation problem is defined as follows:
- Input: a mixed graph $G$ and a collection $T = \{(s_1, t_1), \dots, (s_k, t_k)\}$ of $k$ ordered pairs of vertices of $G$.
- Parameter: $k = |T|$.
- Question: Does there exist an orientation of $G$ such that, in the resulting directed graph, there is a directed path from $s_i$ to $t_i$ for every $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$?

Determine whether the Steiner Orientation problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$, i.e., whether there exists an algorithm solving it in time $f(k) \cdot |G|^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$.

Subsequent work by Chitnis, Feldmann, and others sharpened this to a tight $f(k)\cdot n^{o(k/\log k)}$ ETH lower bound, and showed W[1]-hardness even for planar instances.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: Does there exist a practically useful fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph G has linear rankwidth at most k, rather than only the existence result obtained indirectly from Courcelle’s theorem?
self_contained_problem:
Background. For a graph $G=(V,E)$ with vertex set $V$ of size $n$, the cut-rank function $\rho_G:2^V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ is defined by $\rho_G(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{GF}(2)}(A_G[X,V\setminus X])$, where $A_G$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$ over the binary field. A linear layout of $G$ is a linear ordering $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n$ of $V$; its width is $\max_{1\le i< n}\rho_G(\{v_1,\dots,v_i\})$. The linear rank-width $\mathrm{lrw}(G)$ of $G$ is the minimum width over all linear layouts.

It is known that, for every fixed positive integer $k$, the property "$\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$" is expressible in monadic second-order logic ($\mathrm{MSO}_1$), and is preserved under taking vertex-minors; hence by Courcelle-type meta-theorems applied to graph classes of bounded rank-width together with the well-quasi-ordering of vertex-minors, the decision problem

  Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, decide whether $\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$,

is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by $k$, with running time of the form $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$.

Problem. Design an explicit, practically efficient fixed-parameter algorithm, parameterized by $k$, that on input a graph $G$ either outputs a linear layout of $G$ of width at most $k$ or correctly reports that $\mathrm{lrw}(G)>k$, with an explicitly bounded and reasonable dependence on $k$ (as opposed to the implicit, non-constructive, or astronomically large dependence arising from generic meta-theorems and well-quasi-ordering arguments). In particular, provide a constructive FPT algorithm in which the function $f(k)$ is explicit and the algorithm avoids reliance on Courcelle's theorem or on non-constructive obstruction sets.
status_search_result: Recent literature (through 2026) on linear rank-width includes a linear-time algorithm for the case $k=1$ and FPT algorithms for related problems such as Linear Rankwidth-1 Vertex Deletion (Kanté, Kim, Kwon, Paul, IPEC 2015 / Algorithmica 2017), as well as structural results on excluded vertex-minors for linear rank-width $\le k$ by Jeong, Kwon, and Oum. However, no published "good"/practical explicit FPT algorithm with reasonable $f(k)$ for general $k$ deciding $\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$ appears to be available; the problem is generally still posed as open in surveys on rank-width.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
context_brief: Ball covering and packing in planar graphs
original_question: For a finite graph G = (V, E) and a radius R, let ρ_R(G) be the minimum number of radius-R balls needed to cover G, and let γ_R(G) be the maximum number of pairwise disjoint radius-R balls in G. Is there a universal constant c such that ρ_R(G) ≤ c·γ_R(G) for every radius R and every planar graph G?
self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected graph, endowed with its shortest-path (graph) distance d_G. For a vertex v∈V and an integer R≥0, the ball of radius R centered at v is B_R(v)={u∈V : d_G(u,v)≤R}. Define:
- ρ_R(G) = the minimum number of radius-R balls (with centers in V) whose union is V, i.e. the minimum size of an R-dominating set of G;
- γ_R(G) = the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint balls of radius R in G.

Question: Does there exist a universal constant c>0 such that
   ρ_R(G) ≤ c · γ_R(G)
holds for every integer R≥0 and for every finite planar graph G?

paper_title: List of Open Problems
original_question: For a positive radius R and a planar graph G, must there always exist a ball of radius 2R in G that can be covered by a constant number of balls of radius R?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a connected planar graph, equipped with the shortest-path (graph) distance d_G, so that for u, v ∈ V the distance d_G(u, v) is the number of edges on a shortest u–v path. For x ∈ V and r ≥ 0, define the ball of radius r centered at x by B_G(x, r) = { y ∈ V : d_G(x, y) ≤ r }.

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant C (independent of G and of R) such that for every positive integer R and every planar graph G, there exists a vertex x ∈ V (G) and vertices y_1, …, y_k ∈ V (G) with k ≤ C, satisfying
   B_G(x, 2R) ⊆ ⋃_{i=1}^{k} B_G(y_i, R)?

Equivalently: must every planar graph contain a ball of radius 2R that can be covered by a bounded number (independent of G and R) of balls of radius R?
status_search_result: A stronger statement is known to hold: Chepoi, Estellon, and Vaxès (Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2007) proved that there exists an absolute constant ρ such that every planar graph of diameter at most 2R can be covered by at most ρ balls of radius R. In particular, every ball of radius 2R in any planar graph (being itself a planar subgraph of diameter ≤ 4R, and after rescaling) can be covered by a constant number of balls of radius R, answering the weak doubling question affirmatively. The result has since been extended to graphs excluding a fixed minor and to nearly surface-embedded graphs.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
context_brief: Graph isomorphism with bounded linear rank-width
original_question: Can the graph isomorphism problem be solved in polynomial time on the class of graphs whose linear rank-width is bounded by a constant?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph with n = |V|. For a subset X ⊆ V, let A_G[X, V∖X] denote the |X| × |V∖X| submatrix of the adjacency matrix of G with rows indexed by X and columns by V∖X, viewed over the binary field GF(2). The cut-rank function is ρ_G(X) := rank(A_G[X, V∖X]) over GF(2).

A rank-decomposition of G is a pair (T, L), where T is a subcubic tree (every internal node has degree 3) and L is a bijection from V(G) to the set of leaves of T. Each edge e of T splits the leaves into two sets, inducing a bipartition (X_e, V∖X_e) of V(G); the width of e is ρ_G(X_e), and the width of (T, L) is the maximum of ρ_G(X_e) over all edges e. The rank-width of G is the minimum width over all rank-decompositions.

A linear rank-decomposition of G is a rank-decomposition (T, L) in which T is a caterpillar (a tree whose internal nodes form a path). The linear rank-width lrw(G) of G is the minimum width over all linear rank-decompositions of G (with lrw(G) = 0 if |V(G)| ≤ 1).

Problem.

Fix an integer k ≥ 0. Is there an algorithm that, given two graphs G_1 and G_2 with lrw(G_1), lrw(G_2) ≤ k, decides whether G_1 and G_2 are isomorphic in time polynomial in |V(G_1)| + |V(G_2)| (the exponent of the polynomial may depend on k)?
status_search_result: Grohe and Schweitzer (FOCS 2015; CACM/JACM versions) gave a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm for graphs of rank-width at most k, running in time n^{f(k)}. Since linear rank-width is at least rank-width (a linear rank-decomposition is a rank-decomposition), every graph of linear rank-width at most k has rank-width at most k, so this result immediately implies a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm for graphs of bounded linear rank-width. A later result via the (3k+4)-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm even yields canonization in n^{O(k)} time.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
context_brief: Maximum independent set in hole-free graphs
original_question: What is the computational complexity of finding a maximum independent set in a hole-free graph, that is, in a graph with no induced cycle of length at least 5?
self_contained_problem:
A hole in a simple finite undirected graph is an induced cycle of length at least 4. A long hole is an induced cycle of length at least 5. A graph G is called hole-free (in the sense considered here) if it contains no induced cycle of length at least 5, equivalently, it has no long hole. Given such a graph G with vertex set V(G), an independent set is a subset S ⊆ V(G) such that no two vertices of S are adjacent. The Maximum Independent Set problem asks, given G as input, to compute an independent set in G of maximum cardinality (and, in the weighted version, given vertex weights w : V(G) → ℝ_{>0}, an independent set of maximum total weight).

Determine the computational complexity of the Maximum Independent Set problem (and of the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem) restricted to the class of graphs with no induced cycle of length at least 5. In particular, decide whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm solving this problem on this class, or whether the problem is NP-hard on this class.
category_tag: independent set in hereditary graph classes
status_search_result: The problem (often called MWIS on long-hole-free graphs) is still listed as an important open problem. Significant partial progress exists: a subexponential-time algorithm for the general long-hole-free case, and polynomial-time algorithms for several subclasses (e.g., long-hole-free graphs with no k-prism for fixed k, odd-hole-free graphs without dart or bull, (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs, and FPT results for even-hole-free graphs). No polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hardness result for the full class is known as of recent surveys.

paper_title: List of Open Problems
context_brief: Exponential-time algorithms for induced hereditary classes
original_question: Let Π be an induced-hereditary graph class that is recognizable in polynomial time. Is it true that there exists a constant c_Π < 2 and an algorithm running in O*(c_Π^n) time that, given an n-vertex graph G, finds an induced Π-subgraph of G?
self_contained_problem:
A class Π of finite simple graphs is called induced-hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, i.e., whenever G ∈ Π and H is an induced subgraph of G, then H ∈ Π. Say that Π is recognizable in polynomial time if there is an algorithm that, given a graph G on n vertices, decides in time polynomial in n whether G ∈ Π. For a graph G, an induced Π-subgraph of G is an induced subgraph of G that belongs to Π. Use the O*(·) notation to suppress factors polynomial in n.

Question: Is it true that for every induced-hereditary graph class Π that is recognizable in polynomial time, there exist a constant c_Π < 2 and an algorithm that, given an n-vertex input graph G, finds a maximum-size induced Π-subgraph of G in time O*(c_Π^n)?
status_search_result: Searches reveal substantial follow-up work on subexponential-time algorithms for finding maximum induced subgraphs in restricted hereditary classes (e.g., Novotná–Okrasa–Pilipczuk–Rzążewski–van Leeuwen–Walczak, 2019/2021), and on H-colorable subgraphs in hereditary classes (2020), but no source confirms a general O*(c^n) algorithm with c<2 for arbitrary polynomially recognizable induced-hereditary classes, nor a refutation. The general question appears to remain open.

original_question: Let p be a polynomial of degree n with zeros z_1, ..., z_n, and let w_1, ..., w_{n-1} be the zeros of its derivative p'. Is it always true that the sum of the squared moduli of the critical points satisfies Σ|w_i|^2 ≤ ((n-2)/n) Σ|z_i|^2?

paper_title: Polynomials
original_question: Suppose f_1(a)=1, f_2(a)=1, and f_{k+1}(a)=f_k(a)-a f_{k-1}(a) for k≥2. For a=2, the source notes that f_n(2)=-1 for n=3, 5, and 13, which yields factorizations of x^n + x + b by x^2 - x + 2 in those cases. Are there any other integers n for which f_n(2)=-1?
self_contained_problem:
Define a sequence of integers (f_n)_{n≥1} by f_1 = 1, f_2 = 1, and the second-order linear recurrence

  f_{n+1} = f_n − 2 f_{n−1}  for n ≥ 2.

Direct computation gives f_3 = −1, f_5 = −1 and f_{13} = −1. Determine all positive integers n for which f_n = −1; equivalently, decide whether n ∈ {3, 5, 13} is the complete list of solutions.
status_search_result: The sequence is the Lucas sequence U_n with parameters (P,Q) = (1,2) and discriminant D = −7. Using the companion identity V_n^2 + 7 U_n^2 = 2^{n+2}, the equation f_n = −1 is equivalent to the Ramanujan–Nagell equation V^2 + 7 = 2^{n+2}. Nagell (1948) proved that 2^m − 7 = V^2 has solutions only for m ∈ {3, 4, 5, 7, 15}, which corresponds exactly to n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 13} for |U_n| = 1; the cases with f_n = −1 are precisely n = 3, 5, 13. Thus the problem is solved: there are no other integers n with f_n = −1.

paper_title: Polynomials
context_brief: Common fixed point for commuting interval maps
original_question: Let f and g be continuous self-maps of the closed unit interval [0,1] that commute under composition, so f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) for all x. Must there exist a common fixed point c in [0,1] such that f(c)=g(c)=c? The source then asks the polynomial special case: is this statement true when f and g are polynomials mapping [0,1] into itself?
self_contained_problem: Let f, g : [0,1] → [0,1] be polynomials (with real coefficients) that map the closed unit interval into itself and that commute under composition, i.e. f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) for every x ∈ [0,1]. Must there exist a point c ∈ [0,1] such that f(c) = c and g(c) = c?

context_brief: Nonnegative polynomial as sum of squares
original_question: Let f(x) be a polynomial of degree n in m variables such that f(x) ≥ 0 for every real vector x. Must f(x) be representable as a sum of squares of finitely many real polynomials? The source notes that the answer is affirmative in the cases m=2 with n even, n=2 for arbitrary m, and m=3 with n=4, and presents the general problem as an active research question.
self_contained_problem: Let $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n$ in $m$ variables satisfying $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Determine whether $f$ must always be expressible as a finite sum of squares of real polynomials in $x_1,\dots,x_m$. It is known that the answer is affirmative in the following cases: (i) $m = 2$ with $n$ even; (ii) $n = 2$ for arbitrary $m$; (iii) $m = 3$ with $n = 4$. The general question asks: for which pairs $(m,n)$ does every nonnegative real polynomial of degree $n$ in $m$ variables decompose as a sum of squares of real polynomials, and is this true for all $(m,n)$?
status_search_result: This is Hilbert's question on positive polynomials as sums of squares (closely tied to Hilbert's 17th problem). Hilbert (1888) showed the answer is positive precisely in the three cases listed and proved nonconstructively that there exist nonnegative polynomials in other cases that are not sums of polynomial squares. Explicit counterexamples were later given (e.g., Motzkin 1967, Robinson). Artin (1927) solved Hilbert's 17th problem by showing every nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions. So the problem as stated (polynomial squares) is solved in the negative for all other $(m,n)$.

context_brief: Performance Metrics & Benchmarking to Support Modularization Business Case Analysis
original_question: Performance Metrics & Benchmarking to Support Modularization Business Case Analysis: Which key performance metrics can be used for business case analysis of modular facility/component construction? Consider the practice of modular construction, in which facilities or their components are prefabricated off-site as discrete modules and then assembled on-site, as opposed to traditional stick-built construction performed entirely on-site. Define a "business case analysis" for modularization as a quantitative comparison of modular versus traditional delivery methods using measurable project outcomes.

Problem. Identify and rigorously define a set of key performance metrics (KPIs) that can be used to support a business case analysis of modular facility/component construction. The proposed set of metrics must:

1. Be computable from observable industry data collected across a representative population of construction projects.
2. Address, at a minimum, the following three outcome dimensions:
   (a) Safety — e.g., a quantitative measure such as recordable incident rate per exposure hour or equivalent.
   (b) Quality — e.g., a quantitative measure such as rework cost as a fraction of installed cost, defect density, or equivalent.
   (c) Productivity — e.g., a quantitative measure such as work-hours per installed unit of work, schedule performance index, or equivalent.
3. For each metric, specify (i) its precise mathematical definition, (ii) the data inputs required, (iii) a benchmarking procedure allowing comparison between modular and stick-built projects while controlling for confounding factors (project type, size, location, complexity), and (iv) the statistical methodology (e.g., normalization, hypothesis testing, effect-size estimation) used to determine whether modularization yields a statistically and practically significant improvement.

Provide the full metric framework together with empirical industry benchmark values demonstrating its applicability.

original_question: Controlling Scaffolding Costs: How can the industry effectively reduce, plan, and manage scaffolding costs by means of the following: • eliminating teardown and rebuilds • using best-of-breed planning systems for multidiscipline builds • moving certain modular scaffold builds to the yards to be included with shipment • initiating constructability to justify permanent platforms versus bulk scaffolds • evaluating the tradeoffs between JLG/scissor-type access versus fixed scaffolding.
self_contained_problem:
Consider an industrial construction project that requires temporary access structures (scaffolding) to support multidisciplinary work crews over a planning horizon. Let the project consist of a finite set of work tasks T, each task t ∈ T characterized by a location, a required access elevation, a time window [s_t, e_t], and a discipline d_t ∈ D. Access to each task may be provided by one of several mutually exclusive options chosen from a set A, which includes:

(i) bulk (stick-built) scaffolding erected on site, with erection cost c^E and teardown cost c^T per unit volume;
(ii) modular scaffolding pre-assembled in a fabrication yard and shipped with project modules, with fabrication cost c^F, transport cost c^S, and reduced field assembly cost c^M;
(iii) permanent engineered platforms installed during initial construction, with capital cost c^P amortized over the asset life;
(iv) mobile elevated work platforms (e.g., JLG/scissor lifts), with rental cost c^R per unit time and operational constraints (footprint, reach, terrain).

A scaffold, once erected, may serve multiple tasks during its standing period; "teardown and rebuild" refers to dismantling a scaffold and later re-erecting an equivalent structure at the same location to serve a later task. Let x_{t,a} ∈ {0,1} indicate that task t is served by access option a ∈ A, and let y_{j,τ} ∈ {0,1} indicate that scaffold instance j is standing during period τ. Subject to:
(a) every task is served by exactly one feasible access option during its time window,
(b) capacity, reach, and safety constraints for each option,
(c) yard fabrication and shipment lead-time constraints linking option (ii) to module delivery schedules,
(d) constructability constraints determining when option (iii) can replace bulk scaffolding,

formulate and solve the mixed-integer optimization problem of minimizing total expected access cost

   min  Σ_j Σ_τ (c^E + c^T) y_{j,τ}·1{erect or teardown at τ} + Σ_t Σ_a c_{t,a} x_{t,a}

over all admissible assignments, with the additional structural requirements that the resulting plan (1) eliminates avoidable teardown–rebuild cycles, (2) coordinates multidiscipline task scheduling so that shared scaffolds serve overlapping disciplines, (3) maximizes the share of modular yard-built scaffolds shipped with project modules, (4) selects permanent platforms wherever life-cycle cost is lower than repeated bulk scaffolding, and (5) selects mobile elevated work platforms whenever their rental and operational cost dominates fixed scaffolding for the relevant task set.

Develop a tractable algorithmic framework (e.g., decomposition, heuristic, or approximation scheme) that produces provably near-optimal access plans for industrial-scale instances, and characterize the trade-off frontier between the five access strategies above.
status_search_result: This is an industry-posed operational/optimization challenge rather than a settled mathematical theorem. No specific published solution claiming to resolve the combined five-pronged scaffolding cost-management problem in industrial construction was identified; related research on scaffold planning optimization and modular construction continues to appear, indicating the problem remains open in practice.

original_question: Standardized Design versus Customization: How can we effectively establish and communicate the value of using industry-proven standard designs and components to reduce risk in execution (i.e., cost, time, quality, and safety risks)?

Defines a measurable "value of standardization" functional V(F_S, F_C) capturing the expected reduction in cost, schedule, quality, and safety risk attained by choosing S over C, under a stated multi-attribute utility model U and stated stochastic dominance or risk-measure criteria (e.g., expected utility, conditional value-at-risk, second-order stochastic dominance).

Establish conditions under which the framework yields a provable, defensible demonstration that standardized designs reduce execution risk relative to customization, and characterize the limits of such a demonstration.

paper_title: Sample Research Problems Identified By Industry Organizations
context_brief: Integrated Project Delivery for Industrial Projects
original_question: Integrated Project Delivery for Industrial Projects: Which best practice can offer a step-change in the industry's experience-based project execution paradigm (i.e., design-bid-build) and, thus, improve collaboration among all project team members (e.g., owner, designers, contractors, and trade partners). Such an improved project delivery method would enable project cost/schedule predictability, remove non-value-added processes (lean), and use the latest technology in design (e.g., building information modeling (BIM)), construction (e.g., robotic layout), and operations (e.g., augmented reality).
self_contained_problem:
Consider the delivery of large industrial capital projects (e.g., petrochemical plants, manufacturing facilities, power generation, and similar industrial infrastructure). The traditional, experience-based execution paradigm is the design-bid-build method, in which the owner first contracts a designer to complete the design, then solicits competitive bids from contractors based on the completed design, and finally awards the construction contract to a chosen contractor. This sequential approach is widely associated with adversarial relationships, fragmented information flow between stakeholders, frequent change orders, cost overruns, and schedule slippage.

A project delivery method is a system that defines the contractual relationships, risk allocation, and workflow integration among the project participants — owner, designers, general contractors, subcontractors, and specialty trade partners — and the timing of their engagement during a project's life cycle (planning, design, procurement, construction, commissioning, and operations).

Problem: Identify and characterize a best-practice project delivery method (or a precise combination of contractual, organizational, and procedural practices) for industrial projects that achieves all of the following objectives simultaneously:

1. Provides a step-change improvement over the design-bid-build paradigm rather than an incremental one.
2. Substantially improves collaboration among all project team members, including owner, designers, contractors, and trade partners, via early involvement, shared risk/reward, and aligned incentives.
3. Enables high predictability of final project cost and schedule relative to baseline estimates.
4. Systematically eliminates non-value-added activities, in alignment with lean construction principles.
5. Enables and integrates the use of modern technologies, including but not limited to building information modeling (BIM) in design, robotic layout and automation in construction, and augmented reality in operations and maintenance.

Specify the contractual structure, governance mechanisms, performance metrics, and implementation steps of the proposed delivery method, and provide a justification that the method meets criteria (1)–(5) for industrial-scale projects.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended industry research question on project delivery methods (rather than a mathematical theorem). Integrated Project Delivery (IPD), Progressive Design-Build, and Alliance Contracting are widely discussed candidates, but no single best-practice method has been definitively established as a "step-change" solution for industrial projects in the literature. The Construction Industry Institute and related industry bodies continue to identify this as an active research need.

(b) Determine whether CPM, equipped with its standard forward/backward pass and float computations, admits an extension or modification that incorporates the collaborative features of these alternative methods while preserving its longest-path optimality guarantees; or prove that no such extension can simultaneously achieve both.

(c) Describe explicitly how the alternative collaborative methods can be combined with CPM in a hybrid scheduling algorithm, or used as a complete replacement, and analyze the resulting schedule with respect to the metrics defined in (a).

paper_title: Sample Research Problems Identified By Industry Organizations
context_brief: Improved Integration of the Supply Chain in Materials Planning and Work Packaging
original_question: Improved Integration of the Supply Chain in Materials Planning and Work Packaging: What are the new tools, practices, and documentable benefits improving supply chain visibility, advanced work packaging, and risk mitigation? Further, as part of an enhanced supply chain visibility, can project material and equipment inventories (and associated inventory costs) be optimized? Specifically, can an analytical process be devised to select the optimal balance between just-in-time and just-in-case delivery strategies for various types of project materials and equipment without jeopardizing project schedules?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a capital construction project with a finite planning horizon partitioned into discrete time periods t = 1, ..., T, and a finite set I of material and equipment item types required to execute the project. The project is decomposed into a set W of advanced work packages, each work package w ∈ W having a scheduled execution window [s_w, e_w] ⊆ {1, ..., T} and a demand vector d_{w,i} ≥ 0 specifying the quantity of item i ∈ I required to complete w. For each item i, suppliers offer two delivery strategies:

(JIT) Just-in-time: an order of size q places the items on site at the period of consumption, at unit acquisition cost c_i^{JIT}, with stochastic lead time L_i^{JIT} of known distribution, and a probability ρ_i(q) of a delivery disruption causing a delay of random length D_i.

(JIC) Just-in-case: an order of size q places items on site well ahead of consumption, at unit acquisition cost c_i^{JIC} ≤ c_i^{JIT}, but incurs holding cost h_i per unit per period of on-site storage, and capital tie-up cost α·c_i^{JIC} per unit per period.

Let x_{w,i} ∈ [0,1] denote the fraction of demand d_{w,i} fulfilled via the JIT strategy and 1 − x_{w,i} the fraction via JIC. Let S(x) denote the (random) project completion time induced by the strategy vector x = (x_{w,i}), determined by the critical-path scheduling of work packages subject to material-availability constraints derived from realized lead times and disruptions. Let C(x) denote the expected total cost

C(x) = E[ Σ_{w,i} ( x_{w,i} c_i^{JIT} + (1 − x_{w,i}) (c_i^{JIC} + (h_i + α c_i^{JIC}) τ_{w,i}) ) d_{w,i} + π · max(0, S(x) − T*) ],

where τ_{w,i} is the on-site holding duration under JIC for item i in package w, T* is the contractual completion deadline, and π is the per-period schedule-overrun penalty.

Problem. Devise an analytical (algorithmic) procedure that, given the data (T, I, W, {d_{w,i}}, {s_w, e_w}, lead-time and disruption distributions, costs c_i^{JIT}, c_i^{JIC}, h_i, α, π, T*), produces a strategy vector x* ∈ [0,1]^{|W|·|I|} minimizing C(x) subject to the chance constraint

P( S(x) ≤ T* ) ≥ 1 − ε,

for a prescribed reliability level 1 − ε ∈ (0,1). context_brief: Assessing the Maturity and Accuracy of FEED to Support Phase-gate Approvals
original_question: Assessing the Maturity and Accuracy of front-end engineering design (FEED) to Support Phase-gate Approvals: How do we best quantify and communicate the maturity and accuracy of engineering in the early front-end loading (FEL) phases to allow for informed stage-gate approvals?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a capital project that progresses through a sequence of front-end loading (FEL) phases FEL-1, FEL-2, FEL-3, each terminating in a stage-gate decision at which approvers must decide whether to advance the project, rework it, or cancel it. Let the state of engineering at the end of FEL phase k be described by a deliverables vector D_k = (d_k^{(1)}, ..., d_k^{(n)}) whose components represent the completion levels and quality of engineering deliverables (process flow diagrams, P&IDs, equipment lists, plot plans, specifications, etc.), and let C be the (random) final installed cost and S the (random) final schedule duration of the project.

Define:
(i) the maturity M_k ∈ [0,1] of front-end engineering design (FEED) at gate k as a scalar functional M_k = M(D_k) that captures the degree of definition of the engineering scope;
(ii) the accuracy A_k of the estimate at gate k as a probabilistic description of the conditional distribution of (C, S) given D_k, summarized for example by the conditional standard deviations σ_C(D_k), σ_S(D_k), or by predictive intervals at prescribed confidence levels.

The problem is to:
1. Construct a rigorous, reproducible quantitative definition of the maturity functional M(D_k) and of the accuracy measure A_k, based on observable engineering deliverable attributes, that is consistent across projects and project types.
2. Establish the relationship between M_k and A_k, including conditions under which higher maturity implies a provably tighter predictive distribution of (C, S).
3. Design a communication scheme (a small set of summary statistics or visual encodings) that conveys both M_k and A_k to stage-gate decision-makers in a way that supports an optimal go/no-go/rework decision rule minimizing the expected loss
   E[ L(decision; C, S) | D_k ],
   for a specified loss function L, and prove that the proposed scheme is sufficient for this decision problem (i.e., no information relevant to the optimal decision is lost by reporting only the proposed summaries).

Provide explicit constructions of M and A, the proof of sufficiency, and a validation methodology using historical project data.

    - comparable in a meaningful way to legacy document-based productivity measures during the industry's transition period.

(i) Construction progress at any time t ≥ t_s is constrained by the engineering buffer, i.e. C(t) ≤ E(t − τ) for some processing lag τ ≥ 0 (so construction cannot consume engineering deliverables that have not yet been produced).
(ii) If at any time after t_s the construction work front catches up to the engineering deliverable front, the construction crew is forced to stop or slow down (a flow disruption).
(iii) Engineering and construction proceed at maximum sustainable rates r_E and r_C respectively (possibly time-varying within known bounds).

Determine the minimum value of α ∈ [0,1] — the fraction of engineering that must be completed before construction is allowed to start — such that, under the modeling assumptions (i)–(iii), construction can proceed from t_s to project completion without any forced stoppage caused by waiting on engineering deliverables. original_question: Rethinking Supplier Data: What are the most efficient and breakthrough approaches to ensuring accurate and timely transfer of Supplier data and documentation to the design, construction, and commissioning Contractor and Owner team(s)?

4. An efficiency criterion (e.g., minimizing rework, manual re-keying, latency, or total cost of information handover) under which candidate approaches can be compared.
5. A demonstration that the proposed approach is superior, with respect to the chosen criteria, to current standard practice for Supplier data handover in large engineering projects.

context_brief: Using Precursor Analysis to Prevent Low-frequency High-impact Events, Including Fatalities
original_question: Using Precursor Analysis to Prevent Low-frequency High-impact Events, Including Fatalities: Are there precursors or leading indicators of low-frequency high-impact events such as fatalities and near-fatalities? If so, what are they, and how can they be identified, analyzed, and utilized?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a workplace safety or industrial operations setting in which low-frequency, high-impact adverse events (such as fatalities and near-fatalities) occur as a rare point process in time. Let $\{E_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ denote the sequence of such severe events, and let $\{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ be a high-dimensional stream of observable operational, behavioral, and environmental measurements (e.g., near-miss reports, equipment readings, audit findings, behavioral observations, maintenance logs).

(a) Determine whether there exist precursors or leading indicators: that is, measurable functionals $f(X_{t-\tau:t})$ of the recent history of $X$ on some lead time $\tau > 0$ such that the conditional probability $\Pr(E_{t+h} = 1 \mid f(X_{t-\tau:t}))$ is significantly elevated compared to the baseline rate $\Pr(E_{t+h}=1)$, for a useful prediction horizon $h>0$.

(b) If such precursors exist, characterize them explicitly — i.e., identify the families of statistics, signal patterns, or event types in $X$ that carry predictive information about $E$.

(c) Provide a methodology to (i) identify candidate precursors from historical data despite the severe class imbalance caused by the rarity of $E$, (ii) statistically validate their predictive power (e.g., via appropriate hypothesis tests, calibration, and out-of-sample performance metrics suitable for highly imbalanced rare-event prediction), and (iii) operationally utilize them to design interventions that demonstrably reduce $\Pr(E_{t+h}=1)$.

Formally, address the existence, identification, statistical analysis, and decision-theoretic use of leading indicators for predicting and preventing such rare high-severity events.
status_search_result: Precursor and leading-indicator analysis for low-frequency high-impact safety events is an active area in industrial safety, reliability engineering, and risk analytics. While various frameworks (e.g., HRO theory, Bayesian precursor analysis, near-miss management systems) have been proposed and partial leading indicators identified in specific industries, no general solution exists for reliably identifying, validating, and operationalizing such precursors across domains. The problem remains open as a research question identified by industry organizations.

original_question: Improving Project Progress and Performance Assessment: How can we better assess project progress and performance, and provide data for future project improvement? What are the more useful parameters and indicators?

(b) Establishes formal statistical or decision-theoretic properties of these indicators (e.g., unbiasedness, consistency, predictive validity for project outcomes, robustness to reporting noise, and identifiability of the underlying performance state).

(c) Specifies how the historical record {(planned, actual)} across many completed projects can be aggregated to produce calibrated forecasts and improvement recommendations for future projects, with explicit error bounds.

original_question: A Closer Look at Material Planning; a New Look at Jobsite Delivery Timing Strategies: What are the optimal elements, best practices, and documentable benefits of Material Planning (a component of Materials Management)? Let x_i(t) denote the delivery (replenishment) policy, subject to: (i) on-site space, safety, and access constraints; (ii) schedule-driven availability requirements q_i(t) ≥ d_i(t) over the windows when item i must be available; (iii) supplier and logistics constraints; and (iv) uncertainty in demand timing and lead times.

Formulate a rigorous framework that identifies the optimal structural elements and best practices of a Material Planning process (as a component of Materials Management) for such a project, and provide a precise specification of measurable, documentable benefits B(π) attributable to following a Material Planning policy π (e.g., reductions in expected total cost, schedule delay risk, and waste).

   min_{x_i(·)}  E[ Σ_i ∫_0^T ( h_i q_i(t) + s_i · 1{delivery at t} ) dt + penalty terms for shortage and excess ]

subject to the constraints above, and determine whether there exists a delivery timing policy x* (e.g., just-in-time, periodic, or state-dependent) that simultaneously minimizes expected total inventory carrying cost and the probability of stock-out-induced schedule delay. context_brief: Finding Leading Indicators to Prevent Premature Starts, and Assuring Uninterrupted Construction
original_question: Finding Leading Indicators to Prevent Premature Starts, and Assuring Uninterrupted Construction: What are the best leading indicators to signal construction readiness?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a construction project modeled as a sequence of phases (e.g., design, permitting, procurement, site preparation, workforce mobilization, regulatory approvals, financing). Let the project's true state of "construction readiness" be a latent binary variable R ∈ {0,1}, where R = 1 indicates that, if construction begins at the current time, the project will proceed without interruption through completion. Let X = (X_1, …, X_n) be a vector of observable, time-indexed project metrics ("candidate leading indicators") that can be measured prior to ground-breaking — for example, design completion percentage, RFI (request-for-information) closure rate, permit-approval status, supply-chain lead-time variance, contractor-bid coverage, labor availability index, weather-window forecasts, financing-disbursement timeliness, and stakeholder-alignment metrics.

Formulate and solve the following identification and decision problem:

(a) Identify a subset S ⊆ {1, …, n} of indicators and a decision rule f: ℝ^{|S|} → {start, delay} that maximizes the probability of correctly predicting R, i.e., that maximizes P(f(X_S) = start | R = 1) while controlling P(f(X_S) = start | R = 0) below a prescribed threshold α.

(b) Characterize, mathematically and quantitatively, which observable indicators X_i constitute the most informative "leading indicators" of construction readiness — that is, those with greatest predictive power for R measured a meaningful lead time τ > 0 before construction commencement — and provide ranking criteria (e.g., mutual information I(X_i; R), Granger-causal influence, or expected reduction in time-to-interruption) that minimize the probability of a premature start and maximize the probability of uninterrupted construction.

Provide both the identified set of best leading indicators and an associated decision/scoring framework.
status_search_result: This is an industry-posed research question concerning construction-readiness leading indicators. There is published work on construction-readiness assessment tools (e.g., CII PDRI/Project Definition Rating Index, readiness assessment frameworks) but no canonical, universally accepted mathematical solution identifying a single "best" set of leading indicators. The question remains an open practitioner/research problem.

original_question: Soft Skills for Successful Project Leaders on Global Projects: Which soft skills make project leaders successful in different regions/cultural environments around the globe? self_contained_problem:

Define a "soft skill" as a non-technical interpersonal, communicative, cognitive, or behavioral competency (for example, cross-cultural communication, empathy, adaptability, negotiation, conflict resolution, emotional intelligence, or active listening). Define a project leader as "successful" on a given global project if the project meets its agreed objectives (scope, schedule, budget, stakeholder satisfaction, and team performance) within the cultural environment in which it is executed.

(a) Identify and rigorously characterize the set of soft skills that are causally associated with the success of project leaders across different regions and cultural environments around the globe. In particular, determine which soft skills are universally predictive of leadership success and which are culture-specific, and quantify their relative contributions to successful outcomes.

(b) Design and validate an assessment methodology (for example, a battery of instruments, simulations, behavioral interviews, situational judgment tests, or observational rubrics) that reliably measures a candidate's ability to (i) adjust to unfamiliar conditions and customs in regions different from their own, and (ii) lead a project successfully under such cross-cultural conditions. Consider a project modeled as a finite collection of activities A = {a_1, ..., a_n}, each activity a_i consuming a vector of resources r_i = (r_{i,1}, ..., r_{i,m}) ∈ R^m_{≥0} (e.g., materials, labor-hours, energy, time, capital) and producing a planned output o_i. Let the planned (or value-adding) resource consumption for activity a_i be p_i ∈ R^m_{≥0}, where p_{i,k} ≤ r_{i,k} for every resource k. Define the unintended waste of the project to be the vector W = Σ_{i=1}^n (r_i − p_i), or, given a unit-cost vector c ∈ R^m_{≥0}, the scalar waste w = c · W = Σ_{i,k} c_k (r_{i,k} − p_{i,k}).

The problem is to develop a rigorous, operational methodology that:
(1) specifies a procedure to identify, for each activity a_i, the value-adding baseline p_i (i.e., the minimum resource consumption required to produce o_i under stated process constraints);
(2) quantifies the resulting waste vector W and scalar waste w from observable project data, including a statistical estimator for W with explicit confidence bounds when r_i and p_i are subject to measurement uncertainty;
(3) provides a decomposition of w into interpretable categories (such as overproduction, waiting, transportation, over-processing, inventory, motion, defects) so that Σ of the category contributions equals w; and
(4) is consistent under aggregation, meaning that the methodology applied to any partition of A into sub-projects yields category sums that aggregate to the project-level values.

Construct such a methodology, prove its consistency under (4), and characterize conditions under which the estimator in (2) is unbiased and minimum-variance among a stated class.
status_search_result: This question, as posed, is a methodological/industrial-engineering problem rather than a settled mathematical theorem, and no single canonical solution exists. Various lean-manufacturing and life-cycle-assessment frameworks (e.g., the seven/eight wastes of lean, Material Flow Cost Accounting per ISO 14051, and value-stream mapping) address aspects of identification and quantification, but a universally accepted mathematical methodology meeting all the stated requirements has not been established.

original_question: Mitigating Threats of Counterfeit Materials in the Capital Projects Industry: What are the necessary, prudent, and most effective processes and practices for ensuring that counterfeit construction materials and equipment do not enter capital project supply chains?

Consider a capital project supply chain modeled as a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E) whose nodes V represent suppliers, fabricators, distributors, contractors, and an end-user (the owner of a capital project), and whose edges E represent material/equipment transfers. Each item flowing through G is either authentic or counterfeit; counterfeit items are constructed to imitate authentic ones and may enter at any node. The owner may impose, at any subset of nodes and edges, a collection of verification, qualification, traceability, and auditing controls drawn from a control set C (e.g., supplier prequalification, factory inspection, serialization/tagging, chain-of-custody documentation, sampling and destructive/non-destructive testing, blockchain-based provenance records, third-party certification verification, receiving inspection, and anomaly detection). Each control c ∈ C has a deployment cost, an associated detection probability for counterfeit items at the node/edge where it is applied, and a false-positive rate.

Problem: Determine the necessary, prudent, and most effective set of processes and practices — formalized as a deployment policy that assigns controls from C to nodes and edges of G — that ensures counterfeit construction materials and equipment do not enter the supply chain reaching the end-user. Specifically:
(a) Identify a minimal set of mandatory ("necessary") controls without which counterfeits cannot be reliably excluded.
(b) Characterize "prudent" augmentations of this minimal set that provide defense in depth against adversarial suppliers.
(c) Among all policies meeting (a)–(b), determine the one(s) that maximize the probability of detecting or preventing counterfeit entry subject to a bounded total deployment cost, and describe the resulting processes and practices.

original_question: Measuring Project Complexity and Its Impact: How do we measure project complexity; and how should the level of complexity drive project-related decisions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a project modeled as a tuple P = (T, D, R, S, U), where T is a finite set of tasks, D ⊆ T × T is a precedence relation (a directed acyclic graph) representing dependencies between tasks, R is a finite set of resources together with assignment functions specifying which resources each task requires, S = {s_t}_{t∈T} is a collection of stakeholders and interfaces associated with each task, and U encodes uncertainty in the form of probability distributions over task durations, costs, and outcomes. A complexity measure for projects is a function C that assigns to each such project P a nonnegative real number C(P) and satisfies natural axioms such as: (i) monotonicity under refinement (adding tasks or dependencies does not decrease complexity), (ii) invariance under relabeling of tasks and resources, (iii) sensitivity to structural features of D (e.g., depth, branching, cycles in undirected projection), and (iv) sensitivity to the entropy of U.

Problem. 
(a) Propose and rigorously define such a complexity measure C(P) that incorporates structural, resource, stakeholder, and uncertainty components, and prove that C satisfies a stated list of axioms.
(b) Given a decision framework in which a project manager must choose among discrete decisions d ∈ Δ (e.g., choice of contract type, level of contingency reserve, monitoring frequency, governance structure), formulate and justify a decision rule d*(P) = f(C(P), P) that prescribes decisions as a function of the measured complexity, and prove (under stated stochastic assumptions on U) that this rule optimizes a specified expected utility or risk-adjusted objective compared to complexity-independent rules.
status_search_result: Measuring project complexity and translating complexity levels into decision rules remains an active, unsolved research topic. Multiple recent reviews and frameworks (e.g., TOE framework, Vidal–Marle complexity metrics, PMI complexity studies) propose competing measures, but no consensus axiomatic definition or optimal decision rule exists.

context_brief: Effect of Commissioning on Life Cycle Costs
original_question: Effect of Commissioning on Life Cycle Costs: How does commissioning have a quantifiable effect on life cycle costs of facilities, systems, and equipment?
self_contained_problem:
Let a facility (or a system or piece of equipment within a facility) have a life cycle of T years, during which it incurs time-indexed costs comprising initial capital cost C_0, operating costs O(t), maintenance costs M(t), energy costs E(t), repair/replacement costs R(t), and end-of-life disposal cost D, all discounted at rate r. The (present-value) life cycle cost is

    LCC = C_0 + \int_0^T \frac{O(t)+M(t)+E(t)+R(t)}{(1+r)^t}\,dt + \frac{D}{(1+r)^T}.

"Commissioning" denotes a structured quality-assurance process applied at design, installation, and/or operational stages that adjusts the cost streams: it introduces an additional up-front cost K_c and modifies the subsequent cost functions to O_c(t), M_c(t), E_c(t), R_c(t), and lifetime T_c, yielding LCC_c.

Develop a quantitative model that expresses the savings

    \Delta(\text{LCC}) = LCC - LCC_c

as an explicit, measurable function of commissioning-related parameters (such as scope, timing, and intensity of commissioning activities, building type, system type, climate zone, and operational profile). Specifically:

(a) Define a parametrized class of cost-modification functions induced by commissioning and prove (or empirically estimate, with stated confidence intervals) the resulting change in each cost component.

(b) Derive a closed-form or algorithmic expression for \Delta(\text{LCC}) and for the payback time \tau, defined as the smallest \tau>0 such that the cumulative discounted savings up to time \tau equal K_c.

(c) Identify the conditions on the parameters under which \Delta(\text{LCC}) > 0, and quantify the sensitivity of \Delta(\text{LCC}) to each parameter.

Provide the model and a validated quantification.
status_search_result: The question is an open-ended applied/engineering research problem rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Various industry studies (e.g., LBNL reports by Mills et al.) provide empirical estimates of commissioning savings, but no single accepted quantitative life-cycle-cost model has been established as definitive. Status is best characterized as unknown / ongoing applied research.

context_brief: Improving the Accuracy of Project Outcome Predictions
original_question: Improving the Accuracy of Project Outcome Predictions: How do we improve the accuracy of predicted project outcomes (i.e., our forecasts of costs, schedule, and performance) between project authorization and project completion? How do we guard against being overly optimistic or overly cautious?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a project that, at an initial authorization time $t_0$, has planned outcomes consisting of a target cost $C^*$, a target completion schedule $S^*$ (e.g., a target end date or set of milestone dates), and a target performance vector $P^* \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (a vector of technical performance metrics). The project is executed over a time interval $[t_0, T]$ where $T$ is the (random) completion time. At each intermediate time $t \in [t_0, T]$, decision-makers possess an information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ (a filtration) containing all data observed up to time $t$ (e.g., expenditures, progress reports, earned value indicators, risk register updates, external indicators). Based on $\mathcal{F}_t$, they produce forecasts $\hat{C}_t$, $\hat{S}_t$, $\hat{P}_t$ of the eventual realized outcomes $C$, $S$, $P$ observed at completion.

Define the forecast error processes $e^C_t = \hat{C}_t - C$, $e^S_t = \hat{S}_t - S$, $e^P_t = \hat{P}_t - P$. Say that the forecasting procedure is unbiased if $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for $X \in \{C, S, P\}$ and for all $t$, optimistic if $\mathbb{E}[e^C_t] < 0$, $\mathbb{E}[e^S_t] < 0$, or $\mathbb{E}[e^P_t] > 0$ in the favorable direction, and cautious in the opposite sense.

Problem. Develop a forecasting methodology that takes as input the information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ and produces forecasts $(\hat{C}_t, \hat{S}_t, \hat{P}_t)$ such that:
(a) the expected total forecast loss $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{t_0}^{T} L(e^C_t, e^S_t, e^P_t)\, dt\right]$ is minimized for a specified loss function $L:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ (for instance, weighted squared error);
(b) the procedure is calibrated, meaning $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for each outcome $X$ and each $t$, thereby guarding against systematic optimism or pessimism;
(c) the methodology supplies calibrated probabilistic intervals: predicted intervals $I^X_t(\alpha) \subset \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^k$) such that $\Pr(X \in I^X_t(\alpha)) = 1 - \alpha$ for any chosen confidence level $\alpha \in (0,1)$.

Specifically, characterize procedures—e.g., using reference-class forecasting, Bayesian updating, machine-learning regressors, or earned-value-management updates—that simultaneously achieve (a), (b), and (c) under realistic data-availability assumptions, and quantify the achievable rate at which the conditional variances $\mathrm{Var}(e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ contract as $t \to T$.
status_search_result: This is a broad open methodological research question in project management and forecasting science. There is an extensive ongoing literature (reference-class forecasting, earned value management, Bayesian project forecasting, machine-learning cost/schedule estimation) but no single accepted solution; systematic optimism bias in large projects remains a well-documented unresolved phenomenon.

context_brief: A Closer Look at Material Planning; a New Look at Jobsite Inventory
original_question: A Closer Look at Material Planning; a New Look at Jobsite Inventory: What are the optimal elements, best practices, and documentable benefits of Material Planning (a component of Materials Management)? Further, as part of an enhanced Material Planning process, can project material and equipment inventories (and associated inventory costs) be optimized? Specifically, can an analytical process be devised to select the optimum balance between just-in-time and just-in-case delivery strategies for various types of project materials and equipment without jeopardizing project schedules?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a construction project consisting of a finite set of scheduled activities $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$, each requiring a specified collection of material and equipment items drawn from a set $I = \{i_1, \dots, i_m\}$. Each item $i \in I$ has: a unit purchase cost $c_i$, a holding (carrying) cost per unit time $h_i$, a fixed ordering/delivery cost $K_i$, a lead time $L_i$ (possibly random with known distribution), a usage requirement $r_{ij}$ associated to activity $a_j$ scheduled at time $t_j$, and a stockout penalty $p_i$ that captures schedule-delay cost per unit time of unavailability. A delivery strategy for item $i$ is specified by a sequence of order placements (times $\tau_{i,k}$ and quantities $q_{i,k}$); the strategy is said to be "just-in-time" (JIT) when $\tau_{i,k} + L_i \approx t_j$ for the activity requiring item $i$, and "just-in-case" (JIC) when items are stockpiled in advance with safety stock $s_i > 0$.

(a) Formulate an analytical (e.g., stochastic mixed-integer programming or dynamic programming) model that, given the project schedule and the parameters $(c_i, h_i, K_i, L_i, r_{ij}, p_i)$, determines for each item $i \in I$ an ordering policy minimizing total expected cost
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i \in I}\Big( \sum_k (K_i + c_i q_{i,k}) + h_i \int_0^T \mathrm{Inv}_i(t)\,dt + p_i \cdot \mathrm{Delay}_i\Big)\right],$$
subject to the constraint that the probability of any activity $a_j$ being delayed due to material unavailability does not exceed a prescribed threshold $\alpha$.

(b) Within this model, characterize the optimal balance between JIT and JIC strategies as a function of the parameter ratios (e.g., $h_i/p_i$, variability of $L_i$, criticality of $a_j$ in the project network), and identify structural conditions on $(c_i, h_i, K_i, L_i, p_i)$ under which a pure JIT or pure JIC policy is provably optimal.

(c) Identify the optimal elements and documentable best practices of such a Material Planning process — i.e., specify which decision variables, data inputs, and organizational controls must be incorporated so that the resulting policy provably dominates (in expected total cost and in schedule reliability) baseline heuristics that do not jointly optimize ordering, holding, and schedule-risk costs.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open-ended industry research problem from construction materials management. While extensive literature exists on JIT vs. JIC inventory policies, stochastic lot-sizing, and project material management, there is no single universally accepted optimal analytical framework specific to construction project material planning that resolves all three sub-questions. The problem is best characterized as an open ongoing research area rather than a problem with a definitive resolution.

original_question: Sustainability: The Next Steps for Industrial Capital Facility Delivery: What are the next steps in sustainability for owners, contractors, and the industrial sector as a whole? Or are there other initiatives that would produce greater value in the pursuit of a sustainable future?

Identify and justify the next set of initiatives that owners, contractors, and the industrial sector should prioritize in order to advance sustainability in industrial capital facility delivery. Specifically: determine whether the greatest value is produced by (a) developing life-cycle cost investment analysis tools, (b) constructing a sustainability index, (c) establishing supply-chain sustainability metrics, or (d) pursuing other initiatives—and characterize those alternative initiatives, the criteria by which "value" is to be assessed, and the comparative basis on which the recommended set of next steps outperforms the others.

context_brief: Metrics for Assessing Emerging Information and Communication
original_question: Metrics for Assessing Emerging Information and Communication: What are the metrics for assessing the applicability of emerging information and communication technologies (information and communication technologies (ICTs)) and for determining their value in capital project delivery? Demonstrate the use of these metrics to identify the emerging information and communication technologies (ICTs) that are either in development or currently available but not yet broadly adopted.
self_contained_problem:
Develop a quantitative framework of metrics for assessing the applicability and value of emerging information and communication technologies (ICTs) in the delivery of capital construction projects. Specifically:

1. Define a set of measurable metrics that capture the relevant dimensions of an ICT's value for capital project delivery, including (but not limited to) technical maturity/readiness, ease of integration with existing project workflows and data standards, cost of adoption (capital and operational), expected productivity and schedule impact, risk and safety impact, interoperability with stakeholders' systems, scalability across project phases (planning, design, procurement, construction, commissioning, operations), and impact on cost, schedule, quality, and sustainability outcomes.

2. For each metric, provide a precise definition, the data required to compute it, an aggregation/scoring rule producing a normalized value in a fixed range, and a method for combining the metrics into one or more composite indices that rank candidate ICTs by their potential value in capital project delivery.

3. Apply the resulting framework to a representative catalogue of emerging ICTs that are currently either in development or available but not yet broadly adopted (e.g., digital twins, generative design, advanced building information modeling extensions, blockchain-based contracting and procurement, computer-vision-based site monitoring, robotics and autonomous equipment, mixed/augmented reality for design and field use, IoT sensor networks, AI-based scheduling/estimating, and 5G/edge-enabled field connectivity). Compute the metrics and composite indices for each candidate ICT, and use the results to identify which of these emerging ICTs are most promising for adoption in capital project delivery and under what project conditions.

State all assumptions, data sources, and any sensitivity or uncertainty analyses required to justify the resulting ranking.

original_question: Evaluating Project Incentive Plans: Are the various types of contractual and worker-specific incentive plans (e.g., plans for cost, schedule, and/or safety) in the construction industry effective? Why are certain plans more effective than others?
self_contained_problem:
Consider contractual and worker-specific incentive plans used in the construction industry, including but not limited to incentive structures targeting (a) cost performance (e.g., target-cost contracts, cost-savings sharing, bonus/penalty schemes tied to budget adherence), (b) schedule performance (e.g., early-completion bonuses, liquidated-damages clauses, milestone bonuses), and (c) worker safety (e.g., individual or crew bonuses for accident-free periods, safety compliance rewards). (1) Determine, empirically and/or via formal principal–agent / contract-theoretic modeling, whether each class of incentive plan (cost, schedule, safety, and combinations thereof) produces a statistically and practically significant improvement in its targeted outcome relative to comparable projects without that incentive.

(2) Identify the structural, behavioral, and contextual factors (incentive magnitude, payout timing, individual vs. group basis, risk allocation between owner and contractor, alignment with worker preferences, interaction with other plans, project complexity, etc.) that explain why certain incentive plans are more effective than others, and produce a ranking or characterization of plan designs by expected effectiveness conditional on project context.

The problem is therefore treated as open.

context_brief: Driving to Zero with Safety Leading Indicators
original_question: Driving to Zero with Safety Leading Indicators: Which leading indicators of safety performance are the best predictors of enhanced safety outcomes? Are there measurable early indicators which can be shown to have a direct influence on prevention of negative safety outcomes? What opportunities are there to derive new leading indicators?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an industrial operation in which negative safety outcomes (e.g., recordable injuries, lost-time incidents, process-safety events) occur over time. Let $Y_t \in \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ denote the number of such negative safety outcomes in time period $t$ at a given site, and suppose that for each period one also observes a vector $X_t = (X_t^{(1)}, \dots, X_t^{(p)}) \in \mathbb{R}^p$ of candidate \emph{leading indicators} — measurable quantities recorded prior to or independently of the occurrence of $Y_t$ (for example, near-miss reports, training completion rates, audit scores, behavioral observations, equipment-inspection compliance, fatigue metrics, etc.).

Formulate and solve the following problems:

1. (Predictive selection.) Within a suitable statistical model relating $Y_{t+h}$ (for some lead time $h \ge 1$) to $X_t$, identify which components of $X_t$, or which functionals $\varphi(X_t)$, are the strongest predictors of reduced future negative safety outcomes. Provide a precise criterion (e.g., maximization of out-of-sample predictive log-likelihood, minimization of expected loss, or maximization of an information-theoretic measure such as $I(\varphi(X_t); Y_{t+h})$) under which "best predictor" is defined, and characterize the optimal indicators.

2. (Causal influence.) Determine which, if any, of the candidate leading indicators have a direct \emph{causal} effect on the prevention of negative safety outcomes, in the sense of a structural causal model or potential-outcomes framework: i.e., find indicators $X^{(j)}$ such that an intervention $\mathrm{do}(X^{(j)} = x)$ yields $\mathbb{E}[Y_{t+h} \mid \mathrm{do}(X^{(j)}=x)]$ strictly decreasing in $x$ (or increasing, as appropriate), after controlling for confounders. Provide identifiability conditions and estimators.

3. (Construction of new indicators.) Develop a constructive procedure that, given a high-dimensional stream of operational data, produces new scalar or vector functionals $\psi(	ext{data}_t)$ which qualify as leading indicators in the sense of (1) and (2) above, and prove that the constructed $\psi$ dominates a given baseline set of indicators under the chosen optimality criterion.

The overall problem is to give a rigorous methodology, together with identifiability and consistency guarantees, answering: which leading indicators best predict improved safety outcomes, which have demonstrable direct causal influence on preventing negative outcomes, and how can new leading indicators be systematically derived.
status_search_result: The question is a broad applied research challenge posed by industry stakeholders concerning the identification, validation, and construction of safety leading indicators. While a substantial body of occupational-safety and process-safety literature addresses particular indicator sets (e.g., API RP 754, CCPS guidelines, OSHA leading-indicator guidance), no definitive, generally accepted set of "best" leading indicators with proven direct causal influence exists, and the construction of new indicators remains an active area of research. The problem is therefore best classified as open.
