original_question: Modularization: What changes or adaptations in the traditional engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) process (and its component design, engineering, procurement, and construction practices) would be required to create an optimum environment for a broader and more effective use of modularization?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the traditional engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) project delivery process used in large industrial capital projects, where a project is sequentially or concurrently decomposed into four interacting practice domains: (i) design (conceptual and detailed), (ii) engineering (discipline-specific technical development), (iii) procurement (materials, equipment, and contracting), and (iv) construction (field installation and commissioning). Define modularization as the strategy of preassembling significant portions of the facility as transportable modules in off-site fabrication shops, followed by transport and integration at the project site, as opposed to conventional stick-built on-site construction.

Identify and justify a comprehensive set of changes or adaptations to the traditional EPC process and to each of its four practice domains (design, engineering, procurement, and construction) that would create an optimum environment supporting a broader and more effective deployment of modularization. The answer should specify:

1. How upstream front-end planning, scope definition, and decision-gate timing must be altered so that the modularization decision is made early enough to drive design.
2. What design and engineering standards, interface management rules, tolerance specifications, and module-envelope constraints (transport, lifting, structural) must be adopted.
3. What procurement-strategy adaptations (contract structures, supplier qualification, long-lead item handling, fabricator selection, risk allocation) are necessary.
4. What construction-side adaptations (site logistics, heavy-lift planning, sequencing, site/yard integration, workforce mix) are required.
5. What cross-cutting enablers—information modeling and digital integration, organizational and contractual frameworks, regulatory and code treatment, schedule and cost-estimating methods, and risk metrics—must be in place.

Provide a coherent framework that demonstrates how these adaptations together yield an optimum environment for broad and effective modularization, and characterize quantitatively (where possible) the conditions under which such a modularized EPC environment is preferable to traditional stick-built execution.
status_search_result: The question is a long-standing industry research question on construction modularization promoted by organizations such as the Construction Industry Institute (CII). Research programs (e.g., CII RT-283, RT-396 on Industrial Modularization) have produced partial guidance and best practices, but no closed-form, universally accepted optimum framework has been established. The problem is best characterized as still open in the sense of ongoing research with partial results.

original_question: Methods for Dealing with Uncertainty - Applying Probabilistic Controls in: What would be the benefits and implications of applying a probabilistic approach of analyzing cost estimating and scheduling risks for construction projects? What are the preferred techniques and methods?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a construction project whose total cost C and total completion time T are determined by aggregating contributions from a finite collection of work packages indexed by i = 1, ..., n. For each package i, let the cost C_i and the duration D_i be modeled as random variables with specified marginal distributions and a specified dependence structure (e.g., a copula or correlation matrix). The project cost is C = sum_{i=1}^n C_i, and the project duration T is determined by the longest path through a directed acyclic precedence graph G = (V, E) whose vertices represent the work packages with durations D_i.

The deterministic baseline replaces each C_i and D_i by point estimates (means or expert single-point estimates) and computes C_det and T_det accordingly. A probabilistic approach instead propagates the joint distribution of (C_1, D_1, ..., C_n, D_n) through the aggregation and longest-path operations to obtain the full distributions of C and T, together with risk metrics such as P(C > c*), P(T > t*), Value-at-Risk, conditional Value-at-Risk, and contingency reserves at chosen confidence levels.

Problem. Develop and justify a rigorous probabilistic framework for cost-estimation and schedule risk analysis of construction projects in this setting. Specifically:
(a) Identify the quantitative benefits, in terms of risk metrics and decision-theoretic value of information, of replacing the deterministic baseline by the probabilistic model; in particular, quantify how P(C > C_det) and P(T > T_det) depend on the marginal distributions and dependence structure of the inputs.
(b) Characterize the implications for contingency budgeting, schedule buffering, and contractual risk allocation that follow from working with the full distribution of (C, T) rather than point estimates.
(c) Determine, with justification, preferred techniques and methods among Monte Carlo simulation, Latin hypercube sampling, PERT/beta-distribution approximations, three-point (triangular) estimation, first- and second-order moment methods, Bayesian networks, and stochastic discrete-event simulation, including criteria (accuracy, convergence rate, sensitivity to dependence assumptions, data requirements, computational cost) under which each method is to be preferred.
status_search_result: The question is a broad, open-ended applied research/engineering question about probabilistic risk analysis in construction project management rather than a well-defined mathematical conjecture. There is an extensive literature (Monte Carlo schedule and cost risk analysis, PERT, Bayesian networks, reference-class forecasting) addressing pieces of it, but no definitive closed-form resolution exists; the question remains an open area of ongoing applied research and industry practice.

context_brief: Quantifying the Impact of Change from Project Authorization to Start-Up
original_question: Quantifying the Impact of Change from Project Authorization to Start-Up: What is the comprehensive impact of change on a project when changes are made at each step of the project from project authorization through start-up?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a capital project whose life cycle is partitioned into a finite ordered sequence of stages $S_1, S_2, \dots, S_n$ beginning with project authorization ($S_1$) and ending with start-up ($S_n$) (e.g., front-end loading, detailed engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning, start-up). At each stage $S_i$ a (possibly empty) set of changes $C_i = \{c_{i,1}, c_{i,2}, \dots\}$ may be introduced, where each change $c_{i,j}$ is characterized by attributes such as scope, magnitude, timing within the stage, and type (scope, design, schedule, resource, regulatory, etc.).

Let $P$ denote a vector of project performance outcomes, for instance $P = (P_{	ext{cost}}, P_{	ext{schedule}}, P_{	ext{quality}}, P_{	ext{safety}}, P_{	ext{operability}})$, measured relative to the baseline plan established at authorization. Define the comprehensive impact of change as a function
$$
\mathcal{I} : \big(C_1, C_2, \dots, C_n\big) \longrightarrow \Delta P,
$$
that maps the realized sequence of stage-wise changes to the resulting deviation $\Delta P$ in the performance vector, including cumulative, interaction, and propagation effects of changes made in earlier stages on later stages.

Problem: Develop and validate a quantitative model for $\mathcal{I}$ that
(a) assigns a stage-dependent impact weight to each change $c_{i,j}$ as a function of the stage $i$ at which it is introduced;
(b) accounts for nonlinear interaction effects between changes occurring at different stages and for the propagation of a change made at stage $S_i$ into all subsequent stages $S_{i+1}, \dots, S_n$;
(c) yields a closed-form or computable estimate of $\Delta P$ for any admissible change history $(C_1, \dots, C_n)$; and
(d) is empirically calibrated and statistically validated against historical capital-project data so that the comprehensive impact of changes from authorization through start-up can be predicted with quantified uncertainty.
status_search_result: This is an industry-posed open research question on quantifying change impacts across capital project life-cycle stages. Construction Industry Institute (CII) and related research provide partial models (e.g., Project Change Management, change impact indices, PDRI-based front-end loading studies) addressing stage-specific change effects, but no comprehensive, fully validated quantitative model covering authorization-through-start-up with interaction and propagation effects appears to be established. The problem is therefore treated as open / partially addressed.

Propose and justify an end-to-end project delivery framework (organizational structure, contracting models, risk-allocation mechanisms, information flows, decision protocols, and performance metrics) that would optimally satisfy this need, and characterize in what concrete, measurable ways this newly designed framework would differ from current standard delivery processes.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: What physical mechanism stabilizes an electron against Coulomb explosion when the electron is treated as a localized charged object, and can a quantitatively correct balance between its electromagnetic self-repulsion and the required non-electromagnetic counterforce also explain the observed value of the fine-structure constant α, the dimensionless electromagnetic coupling constant?
self_contained_problem:
Model the electron as a spatially localized distribution of electric charge with total charge $-e$ and finite characteristic size, carrying the classical electromagnetic field it sources. The electrostatic self-energy of such a localized charge cloud is positive and produces an outward (repulsive) Coulomb stress that, by itself, would cause the distribution to disperse (a "Coulomb explosion").

(a) Identify a non-electromagnetic mechanism (force, field, or constraint) acting on the charge distribution that exactly balances the electromagnetic self-repulsion, so that the electron exists as a stable, static, localized configuration with the empirically observed mass $m_e$, charge $-e$, and spin $\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar$.

(b) Within such a model, derive the equilibrium condition relating the electromagnetic self-stress to the non-electromagnetic counter-stress, and show that this equilibrium condition fixes the dimensionless electromagnetic coupling
$$\alpha \;=\; \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,\hbar c}$$
to its measured value $\alpha^{-1} \approx 137.035999\ldots$, i.e. produce a calculation from first principles in which $\alpha$ emerges as the unique value consistent with the stability of the electron.
category_tag: classical electron models and fine-structure constant
status_search_result: The stability of the classical/extended electron (the Poincaré stress problem) and the first-principles derivation of the fine-structure constant α are both long-standing unsolved problems in fundamental physics. No accepted theory currently derives α from an electron self-stability condition; α remains an experimentally measured input parameter of the Standard Model.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: For an electron embedded in the Dirac sea, can one construct a complete local force-balance description that simultaneously accounts for vacuum polarization, the exchange hole produced by the exclusion principle, and the compensating exchange electron, so that the net forces on the reference electron and its surrounding exchange exciton are fully balanced in a mathematically controlled many-body quantum-electrodynamic treatment?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single reference electron immersed in the Dirac sea, modeled within many-body quantum electrodynamics. The reference electron experiences (i) its own electrostatic self-field, (ii) vacuum polarization of the Dirac sea, (iii) the exchange hole induced in the Dirac sea by the Pauli exclusion principle, and (iv) the compensating "exchange electron" that fills the exchange hole at large distances (so that the combined exchange hole plus exchange electron forms a neutral "exchange exciton" analogous to the bound configuration of the positronium negative ion).

Problem. Construct a mathematically controlled local force-balance description for this system. Concretely:

(a) Define, in a relativistic many-body QED framework, local stress-energy / force densities f_vac(x), f_xh(x), f_xe(x) representing respectively the force contributions from vacuum polarization, the exchange hole, and the exchange electron acting on the reference electron at position x, together with the corresponding force densities acting on the exchange exciton.

(b) Show that there exists a self-consistent stationary state of the coupled electron + Dirac-sea system in which the local net force on the reference electron and the local net force on the surrounding exchange exciton both vanish pointwise (or, more generally, are balanced as a divergence of a well-defined stress tensor).

(c) Establish the existence, uniqueness, and stability of such a balanced configuration, and compute the resulting self-energy of the electron, demonstrating that the construction is free of the usual ultraviolet divergences of QED self-energy.

Does such a complete, mathematically controlled local force-balance description exist?
status_search_result: No published resolution of this proposed local QED force-balance program for the dressed electron in the Dirac sea was found. The problem is posed as a research goal in a list of unsolved theory projects, and there is no evidence in the literature that a mathematically controlled construction balancing vacuum polarization, exchange hole, and exchange electron forces on a reference electron has been completed; it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: Can the Higgs sector of the standard model be replaced by a self-consistent composite Higgs description in which the Higgs boson is built from scalar pairs of electroweak gauge bosons such as WW and ZZ, with gauge-boson self-interactions generating the effective quadratic and quartic terms needed to break weak symmetry, reproduce the observed Higgs mass and vacuum expectation value with fewer adjustable parameters, and predict experimentally testable resonances in gauge-boson scattering near the Higgs-pair threshold?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of electroweak interactions, with gauge group SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y and gauge bosons W^±, Z (and photon γ), consider replacing the elementary scalar Higgs doublet by a composite scalar field built from gauge-invariant scalar bilinears of the massive electroweak gauge bosons, schematically of the form H ~ a (W^+ W^-) + b (Z Z) for some coefficients a, b. The task is to determine whether there exists a self-consistent quantum field theory in which:

(1) The effective potential V(H) for this composite field, generated solely by the self-interactions of the electroweak gauge bosons (e.g. via loops and nonperturbative dynamics implied by the non-Abelian gauge structure), contains an effective quadratic term −μ²|H|² and quartic term λ|H|⁴ that trigger spontaneous breaking of the electroweak symmetry SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y → U(1)_em.

(2) The vacuum expectation value ⟨H⟩ and the mass of the physical Higgs-like excitation reproduce the experimentally measured values v ≈ 246 GeV and m_H ≈ 125 GeV, while using strictly fewer free adjustable parameters than the Standard Model Higgs sector.

(3) The model predicts specific, experimentally falsifiable resonance structures in elastic gauge-boson scattering processes (WW → WW, ZZ → ZZ, WZ → WZ, etc.) at center-of-mass energies near the threshold 2 m_H for production of an intermediate Higgs pair.

Construct such a composite-Higgs framework explicitly, or prove that no such construction can simultaneously satisfy (1)–(3) within a Lorentz-invariant, unitary, renormalizable (or asymptotically safe) quantum field theory.
status_search_result: No accepted construction is known in which the Standard Model Higgs is realized as a bound scalar pair of electroweak gauge bosons with the listed properties. Composite Higgs models in the literature (e.g., technicolor, little Higgs, holographic / pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone Higgs) employ new strong dynamics or extra fermions/scalars, not just electroweak gauge boson self-interactions. The question remains open as a proposal.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: Can one formulate a relativistic classical and quantum field-theoretic expansion in terms of interacting anharmonic waves, rather than non-interacting sinusoidal modes, in a way that remains compatible with the basic requirements of relativity and quantum physics despite abandoning familiar structures such as linear superposition, orthogonality, and single-particle eigenstates, and can such a framework usefully describe intrinsically nonlinear phenomena such as strong-field laser processes, nuclear strong-interaction effects, or gravitational-wave emission from black holes?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. In standard relativistic classical and quantum field theory, a free field is typically expanded as a superposition of non-interacting sinusoidal plane waves (Fourier modes), e.g.
  φ(x) = ∫ d³k/((2π)³ 2ω_k) [ a(k) e^{−ik·x} + a†(k) e^{ik·x} ],
with k·x = ω_k t − k·x and ω_k² = k² + m². Interactions are then incorporated perturbatively while keeping this harmonic mode decomposition as a basis. The harmonic basis enjoys: (i) linear superposition of solutions, (ii) orthogonality of modes with respect to the Klein–Gordon (or analogous) inner product, and (iii) the existence of single-particle energy eigenstates created by a†(k) acting on a Fock vacuum.

By an "anharmonic wave" we mean a nonlinear traveling-wave solution of a nonlinear classical field equation (a solution that, unlike a sinusoid, contains nontrivial higher harmonics tied to its fundamental, including possibly a zero-frequency component, with amplitude-dependent dispersion), and by an "anharmonic-wave expansion" we mean an expansion of classical or quantum fields into a complete set of such interacting nonlinear waves rather than into sinusoidal modes; in the quantum case one replaces the standard creation/annihilation expansion by an analogous expansion built on anharmonic-wave profiles.

Problem. Determine whether one can construct a relativistic classical and quantum field-theoretic framework in which fields are expanded in terms of interacting anharmonic waves rather than non-interacting sinusoidal modes, subject to the following requirements:

(1) Relativistic covariance: the expansion and its dynamical equations are Poincaré-covariant.
(2) Quantum consistency: the construction yields a positive-definite Hilbert (or admissible indefinite-metric) state space, with unitary time evolution, microcausality (local commutativity of observables at spacelike separation), and a well-defined ground state.
(3) The framework is allowed to abandon linear superposition of "modes," orthogonality of basis waves, and the existence of single-particle energy eigenstates, provided (1)–(2) are preserved and a sensible scattering/observable interpretation is supplied.

Specifically:
(a) Identify a minimal set of mathematical conditions on a family of anharmonic-wave profiles {Φ_α(x)} so that an expansion φ(x) = Σ_α c_α Φ_α(x) (classical) or its operator analogue (quantum) defines a relativistic, microcausal, unitarily evolving theory.
(b) Construct at least one nontrivial example of such an anharmonic-wave field theory (in 1+1, 1+3, or higher dimensions) that is not equivalent under a change of variables to a standard sinusoidal-mode theory.
(c) Show that such a framework can usefully describe at least one intrinsically nonlinear regime, for example: strong-field laser–matter interactions (nonperturbative QED in intense backgrounds), nonperturbative strong-interaction effects in nuclear/hadronic physics, or gravitational-wave emission from black-hole dynamics, in a way that yields predictions inaccessible or impractical via the usual perturbative sinusoidal-mode expansion.
status_search_result: The question of building a general anharmonic-wave expansion for relativistic classical and quantum fields has been explored in a 2011 preprint proposing minimal criteria (relativistic covariance, microcausality) under which such expansions are admissible, while noting that orthogonality, linear superposition, and single-particle eigenstates must be relaxed. No subsequent construction of a fully developed, broadly applicable anharmonic-wave field theory satisfying all requirements and successfully treating strong-field QED, nonperturbative QCD, or black-hole gravitational radiation appears in the literature, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.
original_question: Given a target symmetry-bearing cohomological object, determine whether there exists an algebraic variety Y whose cohomology group H^i(Y), equipped with its natural symmetries, has the desired properties. In the background of this question is Grothendieck's idea that pieces of cohomology come from motives, so the problem is an inverse realization problem: starting from the properties one wants for a cohomology group or motivic piece, construct or prove the existence of a corresponding algebraic variety.
self_contained_problem:
Inverse cohomological realization problem. Fix a base field k (for definiteness, take k to be a number field or its algebraic closure) and a Weil cohomology theory H^*(-) for smooth projective varieties over k (e.g., ℓ-adic étale cohomology, Betti cohomology if k ⊂ ℂ, or de Rham cohomology), so that for every smooth projective variety Y/k and every integer i ≥ 0 the group H^i(Y) is endowed with its natural additional structure (Galois action, Hodge structure, Frobenius action, etc.).

Suppose one is given an abstract object V of the appropriate target category (a Galois representation, a polarizable pure Hodge structure, an isocrystal, or more generally a candidate "pure motive" with prescribed weights, Hodge numbers, L-function, and symmetry group). Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which there exists a smooth projective variety Y/k and an integer i such that V occurs as a direct summand (cut out by an idempotent algebraic correspondence) of H^i(Y) compatibly with all the natural structures.

Equivalently: characterize which objects of the target category lie in the essential image of the realization functor from the category of Chow (or numerical) motives over k, and, given such an object V, exhibit an explicit Y realizing it.
status_search_result: The inverse realization problem for motives — characterizing which Galois representations, Hodge structures, or motivic data come from the cohomology of an algebraic variety — is a central, broadly open problem in algebraic geometry related to the Fontaine–Mazur conjecture, the Hodge conjecture, and the Langlands program. Many special cases are known (e.g., constructions of motives attached to certain automorphic forms), but the general inverse problem remains unresolved.

paper_title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.
original_question: Establish the Langlands prediction that each spectral component of the space of automorphic forms for a global field F should admit an arithmetico-geometric interpretation as a motive, meaning a part of the cohomology of an algebraic variety over F. The slide states that this is far from proven in general: for number fields Shimura varieties give such an interpretation only under strong additional conditions, and for function fields Drinfeld shtuka varieties provide it at the cohomological level but not yet in a genuinely motivic way.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a global field (a number field or the function field of a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over a finite field), and let $G$ be a connected reductive algebraic group over $F$. Consider the space $\mathcal{A}$ of (cuspidal) automorphic forms on $G(\mathbb{A}_F)\backslash G(F)$, which is expected, according to the Langlands conjectures, to decompose into spectral components ("Langlands packets" or, more refined, components indexed by Langlands parameters, i.e., by suitable homomorphisms from a Langlands-type group of $F$ into the Langlands dual group $\hat G$).

Conjecture (motivic interpretation of automorphic forms): For each spectral component $\mathcal{A}_\sigma \subset \mathcal{A}$ associated with a Langlands parameter $\sigma$ (in the case of number fields, possibly subject to an algebraicity/regularity condition on $\sigma$), there exists a smooth projective algebraic variety $Y_\sigma$ defined over $F$, an integer $i$, and an idempotent algebraic correspondence on $Y_\sigma$ cutting out a direct summand (motive) $M_\sigma$ of $H^i(Y_\sigma)$, such that $\mathcal{A}_\sigma$ is canonically realized inside the cohomology of $Y_\sigma$ via $M_\sigma$; that is, $\mathcal{A}_\sigma$ admits an "arithmetico-geometric interpretation" as a motive over $F$ in the sense of Grothendieck.

Prove this conjecture in general. Equivalently:
(a) For number fields, remove the restrictive conditions under which Shimura varieties currently realize automorphic forms motivically, and produce such a motivic realization for all (algebraic) automorphic spectral components and all reductive groups $G$, including those not of Shimura type.
(b) For function fields, upgrade the known realization of automorphic forms inside the $\ell$-adic cohomology of moduli stacks of Drinfeld shtukas to a genuinely motivic construction: produce algebraic varieties (or motives) over $F$ whose Chow/Grothendieck motives realize each spectral component $\mathcal{A}_\sigma$, independently of the prime $\ell$.
status_search_result: The motivic interpretation of automorphic spectral components is a widely acknowledged open problem in the Langlands program. For number fields it is known only in restricted cases via Shimura varieties (e.g., work of Langlands, Kottwitz, Harris–Taylor, Scholze, and others handles specific PEL or Hodge-type cases), and for function fields the cohomological realization via shtukas (V. Lafforgue and others) is not yet motivic. No general solution is known.

paper_title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.
original_question: Understand the multiplicities that occur in the spectral decomposition predicted by the Langlands program. More precisely, beyond merely decomposing automorphic forms into spectral pieces, determine how multiplicities should be described and computed within that conjectural decomposition.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a global field (a number field or the function field of a smooth projective curve over a finite field), let $\mathbb{A}_F$ denote its ring of adeles, and let $G$ be a connected reductive group over $F$. The space of automorphic forms on $G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb{A}_F)$ (with appropriate central character) carries an action of the relevant Hecke algebra and decomposes, conjecturally according to the Langlands program, into spectral pieces indexed by Langlands (or Arthur) parameters $\psi: L_F \times \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C}) \to {}^L G$, where $L_F$ denotes the conjectural Langlands group of $F$. For each such parameter $\psi$, the corresponding spectral component appears with a certain multiplicity $m(\psi,\pi)$ for each irreducible automorphic representation $\pi$ in the associated $A$-packet $\Pi_\psi$.

The problem is to give a precise general conjectural description, and ultimately a proof, of these multiplicities. Concretely: 

(a) Formulate, for an arbitrary connected reductive group $G$ over $F$, an explicit multiplicity formula expressing $m(\psi,\pi)$ as a sum over the component group $S_\psi = \pi_0(\mathrm{Cent}({}^L G, \mathrm{Im}\,\psi)/Z({}^L G)^{\Gamma})$ of characters built from local data (local Langlands characters $\langle \cdot, \pi_v\rangle$ on $S_\psi$) and from a global sign character $\epsilon_\psi: S_\psi \to \{\pm 1\}$. 

(b) Establish this formula, including in the function-field case (where $F$ is the function field of a smooth projective curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$), for both the discrete and continuous parts of $L^2(G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb{A}_F))$.

(c) Provide a geometric or categorical interpretation of these multiplicities (for instance, in terms of sheaves on the stack of $L$-parameters or on moduli of shtukas/$G$-bundles) that makes them computable.
status_search_result: The general multiplicity problem in the Langlands spectral decomposition remains open. Arthur's multiplicity conjecture is established for classical groups over number fields (Arthur, 2013) conditionally on the stabilization of the twisted trace formula, and significant progress has been made by Ngô (fundamental lemma) and in the function-field case via shtukas (V. Lafforgue and collaborators), but a general formula valid for all reductive groups and a fully geometric understanding of multiplicities are not yet known.

paper_title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.
original_question: Prove and conceptualize Langlands' functoriality conjecture. In the wording of the slide, this conjecture is viewed as a quantization problem, so the open problem is not only to establish the transfers predicted by functoriality but to understand them through a mechanism analogous to quantization, the passage from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a global field (a number field or the function field of a smooth projective curve over a finite field), with ring of adèles $\mathbb{A}_F$. Let $G$ and $H$ be connected reductive algebraic groups over $F$, and let ${}^LG$ and ${}^LH$ denote their Langlands dual $L$-groups. Suppose $\rho : {}^LH \to {}^LG$ is a homomorphism of $L$-groups (i.e., an $L$-homomorphism compatible with the projections to the Galois/Weil group of $F$).

Langlands' functoriality conjecture predicts that to every automorphic representation $\pi_H$ of $H(\mathbb{A}_F)$ there is associated a transfer, i.e., an automorphic representation $\pi_G$ of $G(\mathbb{A}_F)$ (a "functorial lift"), such that for every place $v$ of $F$ where $\pi_{H,v}$ is unramified, the Satake/Langlands parameter of $\pi_{G,v}$ is the image under $\rho$ of the Satake parameter of $\pi_{H,v}$; more generally the local $L$-parameters should be compatible with $\rho$ at all places.

The problem is twofold:

(a) Prove this functoriality conjecture in full generality: for every choice of $F$, $G$, $H$, and $\rho$ as above, establish the existence of the predicted automorphic transfers from $H$ to $G$ along $\rho$, with the required local compatibilities at every place.

(b) Provide a conceptual explanation of this transfer as a "quantization" procedure: namely, construct a uniform mechanism that, given the datum $\rho : {}^LH \to {}^LG$, produces the transfer $\pi_H \rightsquigarrow \pi_G$, by analogy with the passage from classical to quantum mechanics, in such a way that the existence and properties of the transfer become structurally transparent rather than established only case-by-case.
status_search_result: The Langlands functoriality conjecture remains one of the central open problems in number theory and representation theory. Many important special cases have been established (e.g., cyclic base change by Arthur–Clozel, endoscopic transfer and the fundamental lemma by Ngô, symmetric power lifts for GL(2) by Kim–Shahidi and recent work by Newton–Thorne for all symmetric powers over totally real fields, and broad results in the function-field case via V. Lafforgue and others), but the general conjecture, and especially a conceptual "quantization-style" mechanism explaining functoriality, is not known.

paper_title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.
original_question: Prove the Riemann hypothesis together with its modern generalizations involving automorphic forms. As framed on the slide, the open problem encompasses both the classical Riemann hypothesis and the broader automorphic analogues that extend it beyond the function-field cases proved by Deligne.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ for $\Re(s) > 1$, extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a simple pole at $s=1$.

(a) (Riemann Hypothesis) Prove that every non-trivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ (i.e., every zero with $0 < \Re(s) < 1$) satisfies $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

(b) (Generalized/Automorphic Riemann Hypothesis) Let $F$ be a number field with ring of adeles $\mathbb{A}_F$, and let $\pi$ be a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)$ with unitary central character. Let $L(s,\pi)$ denote the completed principal $L$-function attached to $\pi$, which admits meromorphic continuation to $\mathbb{C}$ and a functional equation relating $s$ to $1-s$. Prove that every zero of $L(s,\pi)$ in the critical strip $0 < \Re(s) < 1$ satisfies $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

(The function-field analogues of these statements, for $L$-functions of varieties over finite fields, were established by Deligne; the problem asks for the number-field versions.)
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis and its generalizations to automorphic $L$-functions (the Grand Riemann Hypothesis) remain open. RH is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and no proof has been accepted as of 2026.

paper_title: Communication with Extraterrestrial Intelligence - UNCLASSIFIED
original_question: Given the article's premise that our galaxy likely contains many planets capable of supporting life and that about one billion civilizations could already have arisen, why has humanity not yet observed clear evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations or received an identifiable reply from them? More concretely, if technologically advanced civilizations are expected to exist elsewhere in the galaxy, what explains the apparent absence of contact, detection, or response summarized by the question "Where is everybody?"
self_contained_problem: Assume the following premises about the Milky Way galaxy: (i) it contains a very large number of planetary systems capable of hosting life; (ii) under standard estimates (of the Drake-equation type, combining the rate of suitable star formation, the fraction of stars with planets, the fraction of planets that develop life, the fraction that develop intelligence, the fraction that develop detectable communicative technology, and the average lifetime of such a civilization), on the order of 10^9 technologically advanced civilizations could plausibly have arisen in the galaxy by the present epoch; (iii) the galaxy is roughly 10^10 years old, while interstellar travel at a small fraction of the speed of light, or omnidirectional radio broadcasting, would allow a single long-lived civilization to make its presence detectable across the galaxy on a timescale much shorter than 10^10 years. Despite these premises, no unambiguous artifact, probe, signal, or reply of extraterrestrial origin has been confirmed to date. Provide a resolution to this apparent contradiction: identify and justify an explanation (or a set of explanations) that is consistent with premises (i)–(iii) and with the observed absence of detection, addressing the question "Where is everybody?"
status_search_result: The Fermi paradox remains an open problem in astrobiology and the philosophy of science. Many proposed resolutions exist (rare Earth hypothesis, Great Filter, zoo hypothesis, short civilization lifetimes, detection limits, dark forest, etc.), but no consensus or empirically verified answer has been established as of 2026. Ongoing SETI/technosignature searches continue without confirmed detection.

paper_title: Communication with Extraterrestrial Intelligence - UNCLASSIFIED
original_question: What communication system should be used for a first exchange with an extraterrestrial civilization when the sender and recipient share no prior language, codebook, or cultural background? In particular, how can a message be designed so that human receivers can first distinguish it from random cosmic noise and then infer its intended meaning from the structure of the signal itself, using mathematical, pictorial, or other highly comprehensible conventions rather than ordinary cryptographic concealment?
self_contained_problem:
Design a communication protocol for first contact between two intelligent civilizations that share no common language, codebook, alphabet, or cultural conventions. Formally, specify a signal scheme (a sequence of symbols transmitted over a noisy channel together with an encoding of intended semantic content) satisfying both of the following requirements:

1. Detectability: A receiver listening to the cosmic background can reliably distinguish the transmitted signal from random natural radio noise. Make precise what statistical or structural features (e.g., narrow bandwidth, repetition, prime-number pulse patterns, algorithmic regularity) the signal should exhibit so that any technologically capable receiver, given only general knowledge of physics and mathematics, will recognize the signal as artificial.

2. context_brief: Closed forms for domination in higher-dimensional graph products.
original_question: Let G be any graph, and let P(n) denote the path graph on n vertices. For a fixed dimension d, consider the d-dimensional graph family G x P(n1) x P(n2) x ... x P(nd). Is it true that for every choice of G and d, the domination number of this family has a closed-form expression as a function of the path lengths n1, n2, ..., nd? The source notes that even the special case where G is a single vertex and d = 2 is still unknown, and suggests that an analogous closed-form phenomenon may hold for many graph properties beyond domination.
self_contained_problem:

For graphs $H_1,\dots,H_k$, write $H_1 	imes H_2 	imes \cdots 	imes H_k$ for their Cartesian product: the graph with vertex set $V(H_1)	imes\cdots	imes V(H_k)$, where two distinct vertices $(u_1,\dots,u_k)$ and $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ are adjacent iff there is exactly one index $i$ with $u_i v_i \in E(H_i)$ and $u_j = v_j$ for all $j 
eq i$.

For a graph $H$, the domination number $\gamma(H)$ is the minimum size of a set $D \subseteq V(H)$ such that every vertex in $V(H)\setminus D$ has a neighbor in $D$.

Fix a graph $G$ and a positive integer $d$. Consider the function
$$\gamma_{G,d}(n_1,n_2,\dots,n_d) \;=\; \gamma\! ig(G 	imes P(n_1) 	imes P(n_2) 	imes \cdots 	imes P(n_d) ig).$$

paper_title: Some Open Problems and Conjectures
context_brief: Formal-language criterion for closed forms on G x P(n).
original_question: Does there exist an interesting formal language L with the following property: whenever a graph parameter or graph property A, such as domination number, can be expressed in L, the value A(G x P(n)) admits a closed-form expression for the graph family obtained by taking the Cartesian product of an arbitrary graph G with the path graph P(n)?
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $G$, let $P_n$ denote the path on $n$ vertices, and let $G \square P_n$ denote the Cartesian product of $G$ with $P_n$ (the graph on vertex set $V(G) \times V(P_n)$ in which $(u,i)$ and $(v,j)$ are adjacent iff either $u=v$ and $ij \in E(P_n)$, or $i=j$ and $uv \in E(G)$). A graph parameter is a function $A$ assigning to each finite graph an element of some fixed set (e.g.\ an integer, like the domination number $\gamma$).

Say that $A(G \square P_n)$ admits a closed form (as a function of $n$, with $G$ fixed) if there exist finitely many polynomials $p_0,\dots,p_{k-1}$ in $n$ and an integer $n_0$ such that $A(G \square P_n) = p_{n \bmod k}(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$ (i.e.\ $A(G \square P_n)$ is eventually quasi-polynomial in $n$), where the polynomials and $n_0$ are allowed to depend on $G$.

Problem: Exhibit an "interesting" formal language (logic) $L$ for expressing graph parameters and graph properties, with the following property: whenever a graph parameter or graph property $A$ (such as the domination number) is expressible in $L$, then for every fixed finite graph $G$, the value $A(G \square P_n)$ admits a closed form in $n$ in the above sense. The language $L$ should be rich enough to express natural parameters such as the domination number.
status_search_result: Closed-form formulas for domination-type parameters on $G \square P_n$ have been obtained in many specific cases (e.g.\ grids $P_m \square P_n$, cylinders $C_m \square P_n$), and meta-theorems exist (e.g.\ via MSOL on bounded-pathwidth graphs) giving regular/eventually quasi-polynomial behavior. However, no definitive "interesting" language $L$ resolving the question for arbitrary $G$ and natural parameters like the domination number appears to have been singled out, and the question is listed among open problems without a known answer.

paper_title: Some Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Fix m. Let P(m) x P(n) be the grid graph formed from two path graphs. In fractional domination, one assigns arbitrary nonnegative real weights to the vertices so that for every vertex v, the sum of the weight on v and the weights on all neighbors of v is at least 1; the fractional domination number is the minimum possible total weight over all vertices. Is there, for every m, a closed-form expression for the fractional domination number of P(m) x P(n) as a function of n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P_n$ denote the path graph on $n$ vertices, and let $P_m \square P_n$ denote the Cartesian product (the $m \times n$ grid graph), whose vertex set is $\{1,\dots,m\} \times \{1,\dots,n\}$ with edges between vertices that differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate. A fractional dominating function on a graph $G = (V,E)$ is a function $f : V \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ such that for every vertex $v \in V$, $f(v) + \sum_{u \sim v} f(u) \ge 1$, where the sum is over the neighbors of $v$. The fractional domination number $\gamma_f(G)$ is the infimum of $\sum_{v \in V} f(v)$ over all fractional dominating functions $f$. 

Question: For each fixed positive integer $m$, does there exist a closed-form expression (as a function of $n$) for $\gamma_f(P_m \square P_n)$?
status_search_result: The question appears to remain open in general. Closed-form expressions are known for small values of $m$ (notably $m = 2$, by Hare and Stewart, with connections to Fibonacci numbers), and various near-sharp upper and lower bounds have been established for grid graphs, but no closed-form formula is known for arbitrary fixed $m$ as a function of $n$.

original_question: For which other parameterized graph families F(n) can one prove that the domination number of G x F(n) has a closed-form expression? The source gives positive examples where the method extends from paths to cycles and complete t-ary trees, and also mentions some simple doubly indexed rooted-tree families, but asks for a broader characterization of families F(n) for which such closed forms can be established.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite simple graph. For graphs H₁ and H₂, the Cartesian product H₁ □ H₂ is the graph with vertex set V(H₁) × V(H₂) in which (u₁, u₂) is adjacent to (v₁, v₂) if and only if either u₁ = v₁ and u₂v₂ ∈ E(H₂), or u₂ = v₂ and u₁v₁ ∈ E(H₁). A dominating set of a graph H is a subset D ⊆ V(H) such that every vertex not in D has at least one neighbor in D, and the domination number γ(H) is the minimum cardinality of a dominating set of H.

This extends to the families F(n) = Cₙ (cycles) and to F(n) = the complete t-ary tree of depth n. Closed forms are also obtainable for certain doubly-indexed families, for example F(n) = the rooted tree consisting of m subtrees each isomorphic to Pₙ.

original_question: Does every Parovichenko space have a c × c-independent matrix, where a Parovichenko space is a compact F-space of weight c in which every non-empty Gδ has infinite interior?

paper_title: Open Problems in Topology
original_question: Characterize exactly when the product of a P-space and an F-space is again an F-space.
self_contained_problem:
Recall the following definitions for completely regular Hausdorff topological spaces.

- A space $X$ is called a P-space if every $G_\delta$ subset of $X$ is open; equivalently, every prime ideal of the ring $C(X)$ of continuous real-valued functions on $X$ is maximal.
- A space $X$ is called an F-space if every cozero-set of $X$ is C*-embedded in $X$; equivalently, every finitely generated ideal of $C(X)$ is principal. (Here a subset $A \subseteq X$ is C*-embedded if every bounded continuous real-valued function on $A$ extends to a bounded continuous real-valued function on $X$, and a cozero-set is a set of the form $\{x \in X : f(x) \neq 0\}$ for some $f \in C(X)$.)

Problem. Give a necessary and sufficient condition, in terms of intrinsic topological properties of a P-space $X$ and an F-space $Y$, that guarantees the product space $X \times Y$ is again an F-space. Equivalently, characterize those F-spaces $Y$ such that $X \times Y$ is an F-space for every P-space $X$ (and dually for $X$).
status_search_result: The question of characterizing when the product of a P-space and an F-space is an F-space continues to be actively investigated. A 2021 paper "On PF-spaces" (Topology and its Applications) and earlier work (Comfort–Hindman–Negrepontis "F-spaces and their product with P-spaces") give partial results and sufficient conditions, but no complete intrinsic characterization is known. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Is every compact space of weight ω1 homeomorphic to the remainder of a ψ-space, where a ψ-space is obtained from a maximal almost disjoint family of subsets of ω and the remainder is taken with respect to the Stone–Čech compactification of that ψ-space?

Let ω denote the set of natural numbers. A family A of infinite subsets of ω is called almost disjoint if A ∩ B is finite for all distinct A, B ∈ A, and maximal almost disjoint (MAD) if it is maximal among such families under inclusion. Given a MAD family A on ω, the associated ψ-space Ψ(A) is the locally compact Hausdorff space whose underlying set is ω ∪ A, where every point of ω is isolated and for each A ∈ A a neighborhood base at A consists of the sets {A} ∪ (A \ F) for finite F ⊆ ω. Let βΨ(A) denote the Stone–Čech compactification of Ψ(A), and define the remainder of Ψ(A) to be βΨ(A) \ Ψ(A).

No ZFC resolution of the full question was located.

original_question: Does every 4-connected claw-free graph contain a Hamilton cycle, that is, a cycle passing through every vertex exactly once? Here a claw-free graph means a graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to K1,3.
self_contained_problem:
A simple graph $G$ is called claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to the complete bipartite graph $K_{1,3}$ (the "claw"). A graph $G$ is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $k$ vertices. A Hamilton cycle in $G$ is a cycle that passes through every vertex of $G$ exactly once; a graph is hamiltonian if it contains a Hamilton cycle.

Prove or disprove: every 4-connected claw-free graph is hamiltonian.

original_question: Does every 4-connected line graph contain a Hamilton cycle? Equivalently, if a graph is the line graph L(H) of some graph H and is 4-connected, must it be hamiltonian?
self_contained_problem:
Let H be a finite simple graph. The line graph L(H) of H is the graph whose vertex set is the edge set E(H), with two vertices of L(H) adjacent if and only if the corresponding edges of H share an endpoint. A graph G is said to be k-connected if |V(G)| > k and G - S is connected for every set S ⊂ V(G) with |S| < k. A Hamilton cycle in G is a cycle that visits every vertex of G exactly once; G is hamiltonian if it contains a Hamilton cycle.

Question: Does every 4-connected line graph contain a Hamilton cycle? Equivalently, if G = L(H) for some graph H and G is 4-connected, must G be hamiltonian?
status_search_result: This is Thomassen's 1986 conjecture, which is widely cited as still open. Partial results include: it holds for planar line graphs, for 7-connected line graphs, and for 5-connected line graphs of minimum degree at least 6. It is known to be equivalent to the Matthews–Sumner conjecture on 4-connected claw-free graphs and to Fleischner's conjecture. Recent (through 2025) literature continues to treat it as an unresolved problem.

Let H be a subgraph of G with minimum degree δ(H) = 2, and let V_2(H) denote the set of vertices of degree 2 in H. Assume |V_2(H)| = 4.

A dominating closed trail in a graph is a closed trail T such that every edge has at least one endpoint on T. The graph H is called V_2(H)-dominated if, for every choice of two new edges e_1, e_2 each joining two vertices of V_2(H) so that H + e_1 + e_2 has minimum degree at least 3, the graph H + e_1 + e_2 contains a dominating closed trail.

Call H strongly V_2(H)-dominated if both:
(i) H is V_2(H)-dominated, and
(ii) for any single new edge e = uv with {u, v} ⊆ V_2(H), the graph H + e admits a dominating closed trail that contains the edge e.

Prove or disprove: every such subgraph H (subgraph of an essentially 4-edge-connected cubic graph, with δ(H) = 2 and |V_2(H)| = 4) is strongly V_2(H)-dominated.

paper_title: How many conjectures can you stand? – a survey
context_brief: Hamilton-connectedness of 4-connected line graphs of multigraphs
original_question: Is every 4-connected line graph of a multigraph Hamilton-connected, meaning that for every two distinct vertices there exists a Hamilton path joining them?
self_contained_problem:
A multigraph is a graph in which multiple edges between the same pair of vertices are allowed (loops are excluded). The line graph $L(H)$ of a multigraph $H$ is the simple graph whose vertex set is $E(H)$, in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if the corresponding edges of $H$ share an endpoint. A graph $G$ is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $k$ vertices. A graph $G$ is Hamilton-connected if for every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$ there exists a Hamilton path in $G$ with endpoints $u$ and $v$ (a path that visits every vertex of $G$ exactly once).

Prove or disprove: every $4$-connected line graph of a multigraph is Hamilton-connected.
status_search_result: The conjecture is a strengthening of Thomassen's well-known conjecture (every 4-connected line graph is Hamiltonian) and is equivalent (via the closure concept of Ryjáček) to the statement that every 4-connected claw-free graph is Hamilton-connected, and to Matthews–Sumner. These conjectures remain open. Partial results include: every 4-connected line graph of a planar graph is Hamiltonian (Thomas et al.), every 7-connected line graph is Hamilton-connected, and Hamilton-connectedness for various restricted classes (e.g., hourglass-free claw-free graphs).

original_question: Does deciding whether a graph is 1-Hamilton-connected remain NP-complete even when the input is restricted to line graphs? A positive answer would, according to the paper, imply that the conjecture asserting every 4-connected line graph is hamiltonian is false unless P = NP.
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ is called Hamilton-connected if for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(G)$ there exists a Hamiltonian path in $G$ from $u$ to $v$. For a positive integer $k$, $G$ is called $k$-Hamilton-connected if, for every set $S \subseteq V(G)$ with $|S| \le k$, the graph $G - S$ is Hamilton-connected. The line graph $L(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the graph whose vertices are the edges of $G$, with two vertices adjacent in $L(G)$ whenever the corresponding edges share an endpoint in $G$.

Consider the following decision problem: given a graph $H$ that is the line graph of some graph (i.e., $H \in \{L(G) : G \text{ a graph}\}$), decide whether $H$ is $1$-Hamilton-connected.

Is this decision problem NP-complete?
status_search_result: General-graph Hamilton-connectedness is known to be NP-complete, but no search result confirms or refutes NP-completeness of 1-Hamilton-connectedness restricted to line graphs. The question appears to remain open in the literature.

paper_title: How many conjectures can you stand? – a survey
original_question: Is every 4-connected line graph of a multigraph 1-Hamilton-connected and 2-edge-Hamilton-connected, meaning respectively that deleting any one vertex still leaves Hamilton paths between arbitrary two vertices, and that after adding any one or two possible edges there is a Hamilton cycle containing all added edges?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite multigraph (loops disallowed, multiple edges permitted), and let L(G) denote its line graph, i.e. the simple graph whose vertices are the edges of G with two vertices adjacent in L(G) iff the corresponding edges share an endpoint in G.

A graph H is called:
- 1-Hamilton-connected if, for every vertex v ∈ V(H), the graph H − v is Hamilton-connected, i.e. for any two distinct vertices x, y ∈ V(H) \ {v} there exists a Hamilton path of H − v from x to y;
- 2-edge-Hamilton-connected if, for every set X ⊆ {uv : u, v ∈ V(H), u ≠ v} of size |X| ≤ 2, the graph H + X has a Hamilton cycle that contains every edge of X (edges of X already in H are simply required to lie on the cycle).

Prove or disprove: every 4-connected line graph of a multigraph is both 1-Hamilton-connected and 2-edge-Hamilton-connected.
status_search_result: The conjecture is a strengthening of Thomassen's well-known conjecture that every 4-connected line graph is Hamiltonian, which remains open. original_question: Can the known positive result that every 5-connected claw-free graph with minimum degree at least 6 is Hamilton-connected be strengthened to cover all 5-connected line graphs or all 5-connected claw-free graphs, without the additional minimum-degree assumption?
self_contained_problem:

A graph $G$ is Hamilton-connected if for every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$, there exists a Hamilton path in $G$ with endpoints $u$ and $v$. A graph $L(H)$ is the line graph of $H$ if its vertices are the edges of $H$ and two vertices of $L(H)$ are adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges of $H$ share an endpoint; line graphs form a strict subclass of claw-free graphs.

(a) Is every 5-connected line graph Hamilton-connected?

(b) Is every 5-connected claw-free graph Hamilton-connected?

paper_title: How many conjectures can you stand? – a survey
original_question: In the theorem stating that every 3-connected, essentially 11-connected claw-free or line graph is hamiltonian, can the essential-connectivity requirement 11 (or the improved value 9 mentioned later) be lowered further—possibly all the way to 5—and, if the ordinary connectivity requirement is raised from 3-connected to 4-connected, how far can that essential-connectivity threshold be decreased?
self_contained_problem:
A graph G is claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to K_{1,3}. The line graph L(H) of a graph H has the edges of H as vertices, with two vertices of L(H) adjacent if and only if the corresponding edges of H share an endpoint. For a connected graph G with at least two edges and an integer k ≥ 1, G is said to be essentially k-connected if every vertex cut S of G such that G−S has at least two components each containing at least one edge satisfies |S| ≥ k. It is known that every 3-connected, essentially 11-connected claw-free graph (and, in particular, every 3-connected, essentially 11-connected line graph) is hamiltonian, and the threshold 11 has been improved to 9.

(a) Determine the smallest integer k such that every 3-connected, essentially k-connected claw-free graph is hamiltonian. In particular, decide whether k = 5 suffices (which would be best possible).

(b) Determine the smallest integer k' such that every 4-connected, essentially k'-connected claw-free graph is hamiltonian, i.e., how far the essential-connectivity threshold can be lowered when the ordinary connectivity requirement is strengthened from 3 to 4.
status_search_result: The problem appears open. The best published thresholds improve the essential-connectivity bound from 11 down to about 9–10 (e.g., every 3-connected essentially 10-connected line graph is Hamilton-connected), but no result reaching the conjectured optimal value 5 for 3-connected claw-free graphs has been established, and Thomassen's related conjecture that every 4-connected line graph is hamiltonian remains open. No reference was found settling the analogous threshold when the ordinary connectivity is raised to 4.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine how a finite subtraction set controls the length and structure of the resulting nim-sequence period, extend that analysis to partizan subtraction games with separate subtraction sets for the two players, and resolve the related open questions about complete analysis of three-member subtraction sets, superpolynomial versus polynomial period growth, characterization of purely periodic subtraction sets, and periodicity behavior for infinite subtraction games and aperiodic subtraction/division variants.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be a finite set (the subtraction set). The (impartial) subtraction game $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$ is played on nonnegative integers: from position $n$, a player may move to $n-s$ for any $s\in S$ with $n\ge s$; a player unable to move loses. The Sprague–Grundy (nim-)value $\mathcal{G}(n)$ is the smallest nonnegative integer not in $\{\mathcal{G}(n-s):s\in S,\ s\le n\}$. It is classical that the sequence $(\mathcal{G}(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is eventually periodic.

Address the following questions.

(a) Period from the subtraction set. Determine in general how the finite subtraction set $S$ controls the length and structure of the eventual period of $(\mathcal{G}(n))$.

(b) Three-element sets. Give a complete analysis of $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$ for every three-element subtraction set $S=\{a,b,c\}$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$: describe the period length, preperiod, and the pattern of nim-values.

(c) Growth of period. Decide whether the period length of $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$, as a function of $\max S$ (or of the bit-length of $S$), can grow superpolynomially, or whether it is always bounded by a polynomial.

(d) Pure periodicity. Characterize the finite subtraction sets $S$ for which $(\mathcal{G}(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is purely periodic (i.e., has preperiod $0$).

(e) Partizan analogue. For partizan subtraction games, where Left has subtraction set $S_L$ and Right has subtraction set $S_R$, develop the analogous theory: prove an appropriate periodicity result for the sequence of game values and describe how $(S_L,S_R)$ controls the period length, structure, and purity.

(f) Infinite and aperiodic variants. For infinite subtraction sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, determine conditions under which $(\mathcal{G}(n))$ is eventually periodic, and study the period length and purity. Also treat division/subtraction variants whose nim-sequences may be aperiodic, characterizing when aperiodicity occurs.
status_search_result: Subtraction games with two-element sets are fully analyzed, but three-element subtraction sets remain incompletely classified despite substantial partial progress (e.g., work on expansion of three-element subtraction sets and on superpolynomial period growth showing families with cubic period length). Characterization of purely periodic subtraction sets, sharp bounds on period growth, partizan analogues, and the behavior for infinite/aperiodic variants are still open in general.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether every finite octal game is ultimately periodic, resolve the many listed outstanding octal codes and related splitting games such as Treblecross and Couples-Are-Forever, determine whether large nim-values such as 2048 occur in Treblecross, explain the structure of periods in those octal games already known to be periodic, and clarify the computational complexity of octal, partizan octal, and related poset-style heap games.
self_contained_problem:
An octal game is a two-player impartial combinatorial heap game specified by a finite "octal code" $d_0 \cdot d_1 d_2 d_3 \cdots d_k$, where each digit $d_i \in \{0,1,\dots,7\}$ encodes which moves are legal when removing exactly $i$ tokens from a single heap. Writing $d_i = b_0 + 2 b_1 + 4 b_2$ in binary, removing $i$ tokens from a heap is allowed and may (i) leave the heap empty if $b_0 = 1$, (ii) leave the heap as one nonempty heap if $b_1 = 1$, or (iii) split the heap into two nonempty heaps if $b_2 = 1$. Players alternate; the player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy (nim) value $G(n)$ of a single heap of size $n$ is defined recursively as the mex of the Grundy values of all positions reachable in one move (using XOR for split positions). A finite octal game is one with only finitely many nonzero digits.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every finite octal game, the sequence $(G(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is ultimately periodic.

(b) For each of the still-unresolved octal codes with at most four digits (notably including the game $\cdot 007$, i.e. Treblecross), determine whether $(G(n))$ is ultimately periodic, and if so compute its period and preperiod. In particular, determine whether the Grundy value $2048$ ever occurs in the nim-sequence of Treblecross.

(c) For those octal games already proved ultimately periodic, give a structural explanation for the observed periods (for example, why $\cdot 16$ has period $149459$, why $\cdot 56$ has period $144$, etc.).

(d) Determine the computational complexity of deciding outcomes of (multi-heap) octal games, of partizan octal games, and of related poset-based heap games.
status_search_result: Guy's conjecture that every finite octal game has an ultimately periodic nim-sequence remains open. Of the 79 nontrivial octal games with at most 3 digits, only 14 are settled; vast computations by Flammenkamp and others (including for Treblecross $\cdot 007$) have not revealed periodicity. Recent progress includes Gangolli–Plambeck-type resolutions of individual codes (e.g. $\cdot 16$, $\cdot 56$, $\cdot 127$, $\cdot 376$), but the general conjecture, the Treblecross question, and the complexity questions are unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Complete the analysis of unsolved hexadecimal heap games by establishing periodicity or arithmetic periodicity where suspected, and resolve the explicitly listed outstanding hexadecimal codes whose full behavior remains unknown.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A heap game is specified by a code string in the form $d_0 \cdot d_1 d_2 d_3 \cdots$, where each digit $d_k$ is a nonnegative integer written in hexadecimal (so $0 \le d_k \le 15$). From a single heap of $n$ tokens, a player may move by choosing some $k \ge 1$ such that $d_k > 0$, then removing $k$ tokens from the heap and splitting the remainder into $j$ nonempty heaps, where $j \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ is allowed if and only if the bit corresponding to $2^j$ is set in $d_k$ (the digit $d_0$ governs analogous moves that do not remove tokens). The player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy (nim-)value $\mathcal{G}(n)$ of a heap of size $n$ is defined recursively as the minimum excludant of the multiset of Grundy values of positions reachable in one move, where the Grundy value of a disjoint union of heaps is the bitwise XOR of their Grundy values.

A code is called periodic if there exist $p \ge 1$ and $n_0$ such that $\mathcal{G}(n+p) = \mathcal{G}(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$, and arithmetically periodic with period $p$ and saltus $s$ if $\mathcal{G}(n+p) = \mathcal{G}(n) + s$ for all $n \ge n_0$.

Problem. For each hexadecimal code whose Sprague–Grundy sequence is currently not known to be ultimately periodic or arithmetically periodic — in particular for the code $\cdot 9$ — determine whether the Sprague–Grundy sequence $\{\mathcal{G}(n)\}_{n \ge 0}$ is ultimately periodic or arithmetically periodic, and if so exhibit an explicit preperiod, period, and (where applicable) saltus; otherwise establish a precise alternative regularity (for instance ruler-type regularity) characterising the sequence.
status_search_result: The Sprague–Grundy sequences of hexadecimal heap games such as ·9 and others remain not fully analyzed. Howse–Nowakowski and later Grossman–Nowakowski work has identified many periodic, arithmetic-periodic, and ruler-regular cases, but several hexadecimal codes (including ·9) still lack a complete classification, and it is known that not all hexadecimal games are periodic or arithmetic-periodic.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: For N-heap Wythoff Game with N at least 3, prove or disprove Fraenkel’s two conjectures describing the eventual structure of P-positions when N−2 heaps are fixed, including the mex-plus-shift description and the eventual golden-ratio asymptotic formula.
self_contained_problem:
N-heap Wythoff Game. Fix an integer N ≥ 3. A position is an N-tuple (a_1, a_2, …, a_N) of non-negative integers, regarded as the sizes of N heaps of tokens. A legal move consists of either:
(i) removing a positive number of tokens from exactly one heap, or
(ii) removing positive numbers of tokens from two or more heaps in such a way that the resulting multiset of removed amounts forms a P-position (losing position for the player to move) of the corresponding lower-dimensional Wythoff game on those heaps (Fraenkel's generalization: the simultaneous decrements must form a losing position of the (k)-heap Wythoff game when tokens are taken from k ≥ 2 heaps).
A player unable to move loses. The P-positions are the losing positions for the player about to move.

For each fixed choice of values a_1, …, a_{N-2} of the first N − 2 heaps, sort the P-positions (a_1, …, a_{N-2}, x, y) with x ≤ y by their (N−1)st coordinate, and denote the n-th such P-position by (a_1, …, a_{N-2}, A_n^{N-1}, A_n^{N}).

Let φ = (1 + √5)/2 denote the golden ratio, and for a finite set S ⊂ ℤ_{≥0} let mex(S) be the least non-negative integer not in S.

Prove or disprove the following two conjectures:

Conjecture 1 (mex + shift). For all sufficiently large n, A_n^{N-1} equals mex of a certain explicit set built from previously computed P-positions, together with an additive shift, while A_n^{N} = A_n^{N-1} + n.

Conjecture 2 (golden-ratio asymptotics). There exists an integer constant α (depending on a_1,…,a_{N-2}) and a bounded integer-valued error ε_n ∈ {−1, 0, 1} such that, for all sufficiently large n,
   A_n^{N-1} = ⌊ n φ ⌋ + ε_n + α,    A_n^{N} = A_n^{N-1} + n.
status_search_result: The two Fraenkel conjectures on N-heap Wythoff remain open in general. Sun and Zeilberger (Annals of Combinatorics, 2004) and follow-up work proved sufficient conditions and verified the conjectures for the 3-heap case with the smallest heap up to 10 tokens, but a full proof for arbitrary N ≥ 3 has not been obtained.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine the actual game values in End-Nim, analyze impartial and partizan End-Wythoff and Fraenkel’s generalized end-heap Wythoff variant, analyze Hub-and-Spoke Nim and the natural forest generalization, and decide how broadly integer-valued behavior fails or holds in Red-Blue Cherries positions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following combinatorial games and resolve the questions stated for each.

(1) End-Nim. Several heaps of beans are arranged in a row. On a move, a player removes any positive number of beans from either the leftmost or the rightmost heap (a heap that becomes empty disappears, possibly exposing a new end-heap). The last player to move wins (normal play). Determine the exact Sprague–Grundy values of all positions in End-Nim.

(2) End-Wythoff (impartial and partizan). With heaps in a row, a player may either (a) remove any positive number of beans from the leftmost or rightmost heap, or (b) remove the same positive number of beans from both end heaps simultaneously. Analyze the impartial version (compute Sprague–Grundy values or P-positions) and the partizan version (compute its game-theoretic values in the sense of Conway).

(3) Generalized end-heap Wythoff variant. Generalize End-Wythoff by allowing combined moves taken simultaneously from the two end heaps under more general rules (the natural Fraenkel-style generalization of Wythoff to end-heaps). Determine the P-positions and/or Grundy values.

(4) Hub-and-Spoke Nim. The heaps are placed at the vertices of a star graph: one central "hub" heap and several "spoke" heaps. A move consists of removing beans according to a prescribed rule involving the hub and the spokes. Analyze the game; in particular determine its P-positions and Grundy function. Also analyze the natural forest generalization in which beans may only be removed from a leaf of an underlying forest of heaps.

(5) Red-Blue Cherries. In a partizan game played on a structure of "cherries" colored red and blue (Left moves on blue, Right on red, with the standard cherries move-rule), decide whether every Red-Blue Cherries position has an integer game value, and more generally characterize the class of positions for which the game value is (or fails to be) an integer.

They appear in standard unsolved-problem compilations on combinatorial games and remain listed as open; partial work exists on related Wythoff variants but no complete resolution was found.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Kotzig’s Nim by deciding whether every finite move set yields eventual periodicity as the circle length grows, analyzing the misère version, and resolving the stated conjectures for specific move sets such as {1,4} and {3,5}.
self_contained_problem:
Kotzig's Nim is the following impartial combinatorial game. Fix a finite set M of positive integers (the move set) and a positive integer n (the circle length). The board consists of n vertices arranged on a directed cycle Z/nZ. A token starts at vertex 0; vertex 0 is marked "used". Players alternate moves. On each turn a player chooses some m ∈ M and advances the token m steps clockwise around the cycle; the move is legal only if the destination vertex has not previously been used. After a legal move, the destination vertex is marked used. Under normal play, a player unable to move loses; under misère play, a player unable to move wins.

Resolve the following:

(a) (Periodicity.) Prove or disprove: for every finite move set M ⊂ Z_{>0}, the outcome (Previous-player or Next-player win) of normal-play Kotzig's Nim on the cycle of length n is eventually periodic in n, i.e. there exist integers n_0 ≥ 1 and p ≥ 1 such that for all n ≥ n_0 the outcome on length n equals the outcome on length n+p.

(b) (Misère version.) Determine the outcome classes (and, more generally, the structural theory) of misère Kotzig's Nim for arbitrary finite move sets M; in particular decide whether eventual periodicity in n also holds in the misère convention.

(c) (Specific move sets.) Resolve the outcome sequences and the existence/period of eventual periodicity for the move sets M = {1,4} and M = {3,5}, in both normal and misère play.
status_search_result: Recent work by S. Arun ("Geography, Kotzig's Nim, and Variants", RSI 2023, published in Theoretical Computer Science 2024) makes progress on these questions: it places Kotzig's Nim in the framework of Geography, partially resolves a Tan–Ward conjecture, and provides results for misère play including a "diamond" winning strategy when the move set is {a, a+1} on composite-length cycles, plus results for {2,3}. The general eventual-periodicity question for arbitrary finite move sets, the misère theory in full generality, and the specific cases {1,4} and {3,5} do not appear to be completely resolved in the literature.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Obtain asymptotic estimates for the proportions of N-, O-, and P-positions in Epstein’s Put-or-Take-a-Square game.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called Put-or-Take-a-Square. The state of the game is a nonnegative integer n (a heap of n stones). Players alternate turns. From a position n > 0, the player to move must make one of the following legal moves:
 (i) remove a positive perfect square number k² ≤ n of stones, moving to position n − k²; or
 (ii) if n is even and n > 0, add one stone, moving to position n + 1.
A player who cannot move (the position n = 0) loses under normal play convention.

Classify each position n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} as:
 • a P-position if the previous player wins (the player to move loses under optimal play and the game terminates),
 • an N-position if the next player wins (the player to move has a winning strategy), or
 • an O-position if optimal play from n leads to an infinite (drawn) game (neither player has a winning strategy because each can force the game to continue indefinitely).

For each N ≥ 1, let p(N), n(N), and o(N) be the number of integers in {1, 2, …, N} that are P-, N-, and O-positions respectively.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of the proportions p(N)/N, n(N)/N, and o(N)/N as N → ∞. In particular, determine whether each limit exists and, if so, compute its value.
status_search_result: The problem is listed in the standard compilation of unsolved problems in combinatorial games (Games of No Chance 5, MSRI 2017) as still requiring asymptotic estimates for the proportions of N-, O-, and P-positions in Epstein's Put-or-Take-a-Square game. No published resolution was found in the search.

original_question: Analyze the still-open four-heap case of Gale’s Nim when all heap sizes are distinct and greater than 2, and extend the analysis to the natural generalization with h heaps where play ends once k heaps have vanished.
self_contained_problem:
Gale's Nim is the following impartial combinatorial game. There are four heaps of tokens. On a turn, a player removes any positive number of tokens from a single heap (as in ordinary Nim). The game ends as soon as three of the four heaps have been emptied, leaving one heap remaining; under normal play convention, the player unable to move (equivalently, the player who would have to make the third heap vanish in a position with no legal move available within that restriction) loses. 

(a) Determine the P-positions (previous-player wins) of Gale's Nim in the case of four heaps whose sizes are pairwise distinct and each strictly greater than 2. That is, give a complete characterization of the losing positions (a, b, c, d) with 2 < a < b < c < d.

(b) More generally, consider the variant played with h heaps in which play terminates as soon as k of the heaps have been emptied (so Gale's Nim is the case h = 4, k = 3). Determine the P-positions of this h-heap, k-vanishing variant.
status_search_result: The four-heap case with distinct heap sizes greater than 2 is explicitly listed as an open problem in the most recent "Unsolved Problems in Combinatorial Games" compilation (Games of No Chance 5, 2017). Partial analyses by Brouwer and Guy exist, but no full solution or later resolution was found in the search.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the known analysis of Euclid’s Nim from two integers to broader settings, including the partially solved three-integer case, and determine values or at least atomic weights for Partizan Euclid positions.
self_contained_problem:
Euclid's Nim is the two-player combinatorial game whose positions are pairs (a,b) of positive integers; a move from (a,b) with a≤b consists of replacing b by b−ka for some positive integer k with b−ka≥0 (some conventions require >0), and the player unable to move loses. Its theory (P-positions, game values) is classically understood via the continued fraction expansion of b/a.

Consider the following two extensions:

(1) Three-integer Euclid. Positions are triples (a,b,c) of positive integers. A move consists of subtracting from one of the integers a positive integer multiple of another, provided the result remains positive (or, in a variant, subtracting from the largest a positive multiple of the smallest). Determine the P-positions and, more generally, the Sprague–Grundy values of all positions in these three-integer variants.

(2) Partizan Euclid. Positions are pairs (a,b) of positive integers, but Left and Right have asymmetric move-sets derived from the Euclidean algorithm (for instance, Left subtracts a positive multiple of the smaller from the larger giving certain prescribed remainders, while Right has the complementary moves). Determine, in the sense of combinatorial game theory, the game-theoretic values of all Partizan Euclid positions, or at least determine their atomic weights (the all-small/infinitesimal valuation used to compare loopfree games near 0).

Provide a complete solution: closed-form or algorithmic descriptions of values, P-positions, or atomic weights, in each of these settings.
status_search_result: Collins and Lengyel (Discrete Mathematics, 2008) introduced the game of 3-Euclid and solved special cases; further variants were treated by other authors (e.g., a 2012 paper analyzing two variations of 3-Euclid). McKay and Nowakowski analyzed Outcomes of Partizan Euclid (Integers, 2012), determining outcome classes but not full values. No source found that fully determines all game values or atomic weights for Partizan Euclid or general 3-Euclid positions, so the broader problem remains open.
