paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Complete the odd-parameter analysis of Dudeney, explain the evidence suggesting arbitrarily long pearl-string periods and possibly incompletable behavior, and determine the structure underlying the unresolved odd-Y cases.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player combinatorial game DUDENEY with parameter Y, a positive integer. A position is a nonnegative integer n representing a pile of beans. On each turn a player removes between 1 and Y beans from the pile, subject to the restriction that a player may not remove the same number of beans that the opponent removed on the immediately preceding move. The player who cannot move loses (normal play convention).

For each fixed Y, the Sprague–Grundy analysis of DUDENEY produces, for every position, a "pearl-string" record encoding the move just made together with the Grundy value. These pearl-strings, listed in order of pile size, are observed empirically to be eventually periodic.

When Y is even, the game admits a straightforward complete analysis. When Y is odd, the analysis is substantially more delicate.

Problem. For every odd positive integer Y:
(a) Carry out the complete Sprague–Grundy analysis of DUDENEY with parameter Y, i.e. determine the P-positions and Grundy values for all pile sizes.
(b) Determine whether the associated pearl-string sequence is eventually periodic, and if so give its period as a function of Y; in particular, decide whether these periods are bounded or can become arbitrarily large as Y grows.
(c) Identify and describe the combinatorial or arithmetic structure governing the unresolved odd values of Y, and decide whether such a uniform structural description exists at all, or whether the family is genuinely incompletable in the sense that no finite description covers all odd Y.
status_search_result: The DUDENEY game (a Nim variant with upper bound Y and a no-repeat-opponent's-move restriction) admits an easy analysis for even Y. For odd Y, partial progress has been made by Wallace, Fink and Saff, but a complete analysis is not known; computed pearl-string periods appear to grow without bound, and it is suggested that a complete uniform analysis may not exist. No source indicates a full resolution of the odd-Y case.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine whether Schuhstrings can have arbitrarily many simultaneous string terminations, extending the known example with three simultaneous terminations.
self_contained_problem:
Schuhstring is a take-away game played on a finite collection of strings of beads (each string consisting of a fixed positive number of beads). On each turn a player chooses one string and removes a positive number of beads from its end, subject to a fixed global maximum deduction Y (the same upper bound on the number of beads removed in a single move applies to every move and every string). A move that removes the last remaining bead(s) of a string is said to "terminate" that string. The game ends under the usual normal/misère convention of the underlying take-away rule.

A "simultaneous termination" of order k in a Schuhstring position refers to a single move (in optimal play, within a position arising from some legal Schuhstring game) after which exactly k strings end up terminated at the same moment, in the precise sense used for Schuhstrings: k distinct strings reach length 0 on the same move under the analysis of the game. It is known that there exist Schuhstring games (with suitable choice of Y and initial string lengths) admitting a simultaneous termination of three strings.

Question: Determine whether, for every positive integer k, there exists a Schuhstring game (with some choice of the maximum deduction Y and initial string lengths) admitting a simultaneous termination of order at least k. Equivalently, can the number of strings that terminate simultaneously in a Schuhstring game be arbitrarily large?
status_search_result: The problem appears in a list of unsolved problems in combinatorial games. The best known result is the construction by Kevin Saff of an example with three simultaneous string terminations, and Saff conjectures that arbitrarily many simultaneous terminations are possible. No web source found resolves the conjecture in either direction, so the problem appears still open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Analyze DUDE, the unbounded Dudeney game, and explain the apparent lack of a simple pattern in its nim-values.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called DUDE (unbounded Dudeney). A position consists of a finite multiset of nonnegative integer heap sizes together with a "forbidden move size" m (with m = 0 meaning no restriction, used for the starting position). On each turn, the player to move chooses a heap and removes a positive number t of tokens from it, subject to the single restriction t ≠ m (the opponent's previous move size). After the move, the forbidden size for the opponent becomes t. The player unable to move (all heaps empty) loses; play is under the normal convention. Equivalently, DUDE is Nim in which a player may not remove exactly as many tokens as the opponent just removed, with no upper bound on the size of a single removal.

For a position G, let 𝒢(G) denote its Sprague–Grundy (nim) value, defined recursively by 𝒢(G) = mex{𝒢(G') : G' a legal option from G}, where mex denotes the minimum excludant.

Problem: Determine the Sprague–Grundy (nim) values of all positions of DUDE. In particular, give an explicit, easily described formula or pattern for 𝒢([h₁, h₂, …, h_k; m]) in terms of the heap sizes h₁ ≤ h₂ ≤ … ≤ h_k and the forbidden value m, or otherwise explain the structural reason such a simple description should not exist.
status_search_result: The problem is listed among unsolved problems in combinatorial games. While the P-positions of DUDE have been described, the nim-values are reported as not showing any easily described pattern, and no full Sprague–Grundy analysis appears in the literature. No solution was found in available sources.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Develop fuller analyses of games with pass moves, including complete or improved solutions for Nim with a pass, Chocolate Bar with a pass when s is even, regularity questions for octal games with a pass, the case of more than one pass, and structural questions about Oslo versions of games.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A finite impartial combinatorial game is played by two players who alternate moves; the player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy value G(P) of a position P is defined recursively by G(P)=mex{G(P′):P→P′}, where mex denotes the minimum excludant of a set of nonnegative integers. A position P is a P-position iff G(P)=0.

Adding a pass. Given an impartial game Γ, the "Γ with a (single) pass" is the variant in which each player has, in addition to the legal moves of Γ, the option to "pass" (make no change to the position) at most once during the entire play; a pass may not be played from a terminal position, and once either player has used the pass, the pass option is removed from the game for both players. More generally, "Γ with k passes" denotes the variant in which the pass option may be used a total of k times (over both players combined).

Specific games.
(1) Nim: positions are tuples (a₁,…,aₙ) of nonnegative integers; a move reduces some aᵢ to a strictly smaller nonnegative integer.
(2) Chocolate-Bar game with parameter s: a position consists of a rectangular bar broken according to standard chocolate-bar rules (a known impartial game), parameterized by an integer s ≥ 1.
(3) Octal games: an impartial heap game specified by an octal code d₀.d₁d₂d₃…, where the digit dₖ encodes which of the moves "remove k tokens leaving 0, 1, or 2 nonempty heaps" are legal. The G-sequence of an octal game is the sequence (G(0),G(1),G(2),…) of Grundy values of single heaps; an octal game is said to be (arithmetically) regular if its G-sequence is eventually periodic.
(4) Oslo version of a game: the variant in which exactly one designated heap (or component) is restricted in a prescribed Oslo-style manner; see standard usage.

Problems to solve.
(a) Nim with a pass. Determine the P-positions, and more generally the Sprague–Grundy values, of n-pile Nim with a single pass move, for all n ≥ 3.
(b) Chocolate Bar with a pass. Solve (determine the P-positions of) the Chocolate-Bar game with a single pass for all even values of the parameter s.
(c) Octal games with a pass. For each octal game whose G-sequence (without a pass) is eventually periodic, determine which forms of regularity (eventual periodicity, arithmetic periodicity, etc.) can or must occur in the G-sequence of the game with a single pass added, and classify the possible behaviors.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Analyze the still-open games with a Muller twist proposed in the literature, solve Blocking Nim with blocks on two heaps, all three heaps, or more than three heaps, and determine the behavior of complementary subtraction games for Fibonacci, modular, and Wythoff-type subtraction sets.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following combinatorial game framework. A "Muller twist" game is a two-player game in which, after each move, the player who has just moved imposes a restriction on the next move of the opponent; once the opponent has moved, the restriction is forgotten. Specialize as follows.

Blocking Nim with k blocks on n heaps: There are n heaps of tokens of sizes (h_1,...,h_n) with n ≥ 2. Players alternate; on each turn a player first declares at most k "blocked" positions (each consisting of a heap index together with a forbidden new size strictly less than the current size of that heap), and then the opponent must make an ordinary Nim move (choose one heap and reduce its size to any strictly smaller nonnegative integer) which does not result in any of the blocked positions. The player unable to move loses (normal play).

(a) Determine the set of P-positions (previous-player winning positions) and a winning strategy for Blocking Nim with one block (k=1) on exactly two heaps (n=2).
(b) Do the same for Blocking Nim with one block on exactly three heaps (n=3).
(c) Do the same for Blocking Nim with one block on n heaps for every n > 3, and more generally for k blocks on n heaps.

Complementary subtraction games: Let S ⊆ ℤ_{≥1} be a subtraction set. The complementary subtraction game on a single heap with subtraction set S is played by alternately removing a number of tokens from S; the player unable to move loses. Determine the Sprague–Grundy function (or at least the P-positions) of the complementary subtraction game when S is each of the following:
  (i) the set of Fibonacci numbers {1,2,3,5,8,13,...};
  (ii) a "modular" set {n : n ≡ r (mod m)} for prescribed integers m ≥ 2 and r;
  (iii) a Wythoff-type set, namely S = {⌊nφ⌋ : n ≥ 1} where φ = (1+√5)/2, and analogously S = {⌈nφ⌉ : n ≥ 1}.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Advance misère analysis of octal and quaternary games by deciding whether the Dawson’s Kayles quotient becomes infinite at heap 34, producing presentations and detection algorithms for infinite misère quotients, and defining and detecting algebraic periodicity well enough to solve the listed periodic octal examples.
self_contained_problem:
Background. An impartial combinatorial game under misère convention is one in which the last player to move loses. For a finite set A of impartial games, the misère quotient Q(A) is the commutative monoid obtained from the free commutative monoid on positions reachable from A by quotienting by the indistinguishability congruence (G ≡ H iff for every position X, G+X and H+X have the same misère outcome). An octal game is specified by a code 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 …, where each digit d_k ∈ {0,1,…,7} (binary expansion encoding which of "leave a heap unchanged," "remove the heap entirely," and "split the heap" are allowed when removing k tokens). A quaternary game is the analogous notion with digits in {0,1,2,3}. Dawson's Kayles is the octal game 0.07.

Let Q_n(0.07) denote the partial misère quotient generated by Dawson's Kayles positions of heap size at most n. It is known that Q_33(0.07) is finite of order 638. 

Problems. 
(a) Decide whether Q_34(0.07) is finite or infinite, and more generally whether the full misère quotient of Dawson's Kayles is infinite.
(b) Given a finite set A of impartial games, give a finite presentation procedure and a decision algorithm that determines whether Q(A) is infinite.
(c) Formulate a precise definition of "algebraic periodicity" of misère quotient sequences for octal and quaternary games, and give an algorithm to detect such periodicity. Use it to give complete misère analyses of those octal games conjecturally exhibiting algebraic periodicity in misère play.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that the misère analysis of Dawson's Kayles is known up to heap 33 (partial quotient of order 638), with the question of whether it becomes infinite at heap 34 still posed as open in the misère-games literature. No algorithm to decide infiniteness of misère quotients or a formal definition of algebraic periodicity with detection algorithm has been reported.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Prove or refute the conjecture that every MNEM position has finite nim-value, and prove or refute the claimed formula that in MEM and MNEM one has value floor(n/k) whenever k squared is at least n.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two impartial combinatorial games played on positions (n, k) with integers n ≥ k ≥ 1.

MEM: From the position (n, k), a legal move is to any position (n − i, i) with k ≤ i ≤ n − i (equivalently k ≤ i and the resulting first coordinate is at least i). 

MNEM: From the position (n, k), a legal move is to any position (n + i, i) for 1 ≤ i < k, together with the MEM moves (so the second coordinate is required to be strictly less than the previous one, and one may increase the first coordinate by i while setting the second coordinate to i for any 1 ≤ i < k).

The last player to move wins. Define the nim-value (Sprague–Grundy value) G(n, k) of a position in the usual recursive way: G(n, k) = mex{ G(n′, k′) : (n′, k′) is a legal successor of (n, k) }, where positions with no legal moves have nim-value 0, and mex denotes the minimum excludant of a set of nonnegative integers (which is ∞ if the set of values reached includes ∞ in such a way that no finite value is missing — equivalently, a position has finite nim-value iff this recursion terminates with a finite value).

Establish or refute each of the following:

(a) Every position (n, k) of MNEM has finite nim-value.

(b) In both MEM and MNEM, whenever k² ≥ n one has G(n, k) = ⌊n / k⌋.
status_search_result: The conjectures are attributed to Conway and Siegel and were verified experimentally (e.g., up to n = 10000 for the finiteness conjecture in MNEM), but no proof is known and they are reported as open problems with no known approach.

original_question: Extend Fibonacci Nim beyond the solved cases by analyzing the multiheap game for values of α other than 2 and for larger numbers of heaps.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a real (or rational) parameter α ≥ 1. The α-Fibonacci Nim on a single heap is the impartial game in which a position consists of a heap of n tokens together with a bound b ≥ 1 on the next move; a legal move removes any number k of tokens with 1 ≤ k ≤ min(n, αb), after which the bound becomes k (so the opponent then faces the position (n−k, k)). The first move from a heap of n is unrestricted (b = ∞), and the player unable to move loses. For α = 2 a classical theorem (Whinihan/Zeckendorf) determines the P-positions in terms of Fibonacci representations.

The multiheap version is played on k heaps of sizes n₁, …, n_k with a common bound b; a move chooses one heap and removes 1 ≤ m ≤ min(n_i, αb) tokens from it, after which the bound becomes m. For the case α = 2 and k = 2 heaps there is a known characterization of the P-positions.

Problem. For values α ≠ 2 and for numbers of heaps k ≥ 2 (and in particular for α = 2 with k ≥ 3), determine the P-positions, and more generally compute the Sprague–Grundy values, of multiheap α-Fibonacci Nim.

original_question: Extend the analysis of self-referential subtraction games by solving SUSEN for more than three heaps and solving the still-unsolved two-heap case of ALBUS.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two self-referential subtraction games played on finite multisets of nonempty heaps of tokens.

SUSEN. A position is a finite multiset of positive integers (the heap sizes). On each turn the player to move chooses one heap and removes from it a positive number of tokens equal to one of the current nonzero heap sizes of the position (the subtraction set is the multiset of current heap sizes itself). A heap that is reduced to 0 is removed. The player who cannot move loses (normal play convention). For example, from (2,3) the legal moves are: subtract 2 from the heap of size 2 (giving (3)), subtract 3 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2)), or subtract 2 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2,1)); subtracting 3 from the heap of size 2 is illegal, and there is no move using "2" applied to itself producing (2,2)-style results other than as listed.

ALBUS. A position is again a finite multiset of positive heap sizes. The legal subtractions from a chosen heap are determined self-referentially by the current multiset of heap sizes according to the ALBUS rule (the variant of self-referential subtraction in which the allowed subtraction from any heap equals one of the other heap sizes, rather than the heap's own size). Normal-play convention applies.

Problem.
(a) Determine the set of P-positions (previous-player-winning positions) of SUSEN for positions with n heaps for every n ≥ 4. (The cases n ≤ 3 are known; in particular a triple (a,b,c) is a P-position of SUSEN under an explicit known characterization.)
(b) Determine the set of P-positions of ALBUS for positions with exactly two heaps.
status_search_result: SUSEN and ALBUS are self-referential subtraction games introduced by Larsson and Nowakowski. Available sources list these problems in the open-problem compendium on combinatorial games; no published resolution of SUSEN for n ≥ 4 heaps or of two-heap ALBUS was found in the search.

original_question: Resolve the specific ko-temperature problem at N4 in the Jiang–Rui position, and more broadly unify or sharply distinguish atomic weight theory from Nakamura’s liberty theory while extending liberty theory to practical Go complications such as internal and external kos.
self_contained_problem:
In the combinatorial game theory of Go, consider the Jiang–Rui position (a specific finely-balanced endgame configuration on the 19×19 Go board involving multiple interacting kos and capturable groups, in which after move 85 Black has just taken the ko at the intersection L6). 

(a) Determine the exact temperature, in the sense of Combinatorial Game Theory (the critical cooling value at which the canonical form of the position becomes infinitesimal), of the local game at the intersection N4 in this position immediately after Black's ko capture at L6.

(b) Develop a single unified framework that subsumes (or, alternatively, exhibit precise mathematical differences between) the following two theories used to evaluate Go positions:
 (i) Atomic weight theory, the all-small / *-based valuation theory assigning to each position an "atomic weight" (an integer-valued infinitesimal-order invariant) measuring its strength in sums of all-small games; and
 (ii) Nakamura's theory of liberties, which assigns numerical liberty counts to groups of stones in capturing races (semeai) and predicts the winner of a race based on differences of these counts.

(c) Extend Nakamura's liberty theory so that it correctly handles the additional complications that arise when one or more simple kos — either internal kos (kos located inside the eye-space of one of the racing groups) or external kos (kos located outside but affecting the race) — are present in a capturing race, producing quantitative liberty-count formulas whose predictions agree with the exact combinatorial-game-theoretic value of the race.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend current analyses of Woodpush from three-piece positions to positions with more pieces and understand draw behavior under superko.
self_contained_problem:
Woodpush is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite one-dimensional strip of squares. Each square is either empty or occupied by a Left (black) or Right (white) piece. On a turn, a player either retreats one of their own pieces by one square toward their own end of the board, or pushes one of their own pieces one square toward the opponent's end; in a push, any contiguous string of pieces immediately in front of the moving piece is shoved along with it, and any pieces pushed off the board are removed from play. A player who cannot move loses. The superko rule forbids any move that would recreate a previously seen global position; if all legal moves of the player to move would violate superko, the position is declared a draw.

Top-down thermography (the standard thermographic construction adapted to loopy games with ko-like repetition constraints) has been used to compute the values and temperatures of all three-piece Woodpush positions.

Problem: Extend the thermographic analysis of Woodpush from three-piece positions to positions containing four or more pieces. In particular:

(a) Develop a systematic top-down thermographic procedure that computes the value (or thermograph) of an arbitrary multi-piece Woodpush position under the superko rule.

(b) Characterize, for each n ≥ 4, which n-piece Woodpush positions are draws by superko (i.e., become drawn because every legal continuation would repeat a global position), and give a structural description of such drawn positions.
status_search_result: Existing work (Cazenave–Nowakowski) analyzes three-piece Woodpush via top-down thermography and identifies specific small drawn positions under superko (e.g., sizes 9 and 11 of certain symmetric configurations). No general thermographic theory or full classification of drawn positions for four or more pieces appears in the literature, so the problem is still open.

original_question: Improve the king-and-rook versus king analysis and determine whether the boiling point of Entrepreneurial Chess is 55/8.

(b) Determine whether the boiling point of Entrepreneurial Chess equals 55/8, confirming or refuting this conjectured value.

original_question: Determine the outcome of the 6×6 game of Amazons.
self_contained_problem:
The Game of the Amazons is a two-player, perfect-information, no-chance combinatorial game played on a rectangular board. In the n×n version, each player controls a set of amazons (queens) of one color. Players alternate moves, starting with White. original_question: Determine whether natural stopper positions with wild cycles exist in Phutball-like games, whether noncollusive draws or P-positions occur in standard Phutball, analyze PHLAG Phutball boards, and give a complete analysis of 2×n Directional Phutball.
self_contained_problem:
Phutball (Philosopher's Football) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a grid with one distinguished black stone (the "ball") and white stones (the "men"). On each turn a player either (a) places a white man on an empty grid point, or (b) executes a sequence of "jumps": the ball leaps over a contiguous nonempty line of white men (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally) to the empty point immediately beyond them, and those jumped-over men are removed; multiple jumps may be chained in a single move. The two players try to bring the ball to (or past) opposite goal lines.

A position in a loopy combinatorial game is called a stopper if it has no infinite alternating play. A wild cycle is a cycle of positions in the move graph that does not correspond to mere repetition agreed upon by both players. A P-position is one from which the Previous player (the one who just moved) has a winning strategy under optimal play.

The following variants are considered:
(i) "PHLAG Phutball": Phutball played on an n×n board where the ball is restricted to lie on points with both coordinates even (eliminating tackling).
(ii) "Directional Phutball": Phutball in which each player is allowed to jump the ball only in a fixed prescribed direction.

Resolve the following:
(1) Do there exist natural positions in Phutball-like games which are stoppers but which contain a wild cycle?
(2) In standard Phutball, do noncollusive drawn positions or P-positions exist?
(3) Provide an analysis of PHLAG Phutball boards.
(4) Give a complete analysis of Directional Phutball on the 2×n board.
status_search_result: Phutball is known to have NP-complete endgame decision problems, and only partial results exist for one-dimensional Phutball and restricted variants. No complete analysis of 2×n Directional Phutball, PHLAG boards, or resolution of the stopper/wild-cycle and P-position questions appears in the literature; these remain listed among unsolved problems in combinatorial game theory.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Quantify first-player winning efficiency in Hex by finding the shortest guaranteed winning path on an n×n board and the minimum number of moves that guarantees a first-player win.
self_contained_problem:
Hex is a two-player game played on a rhombic board of n×n hexagonal cells. The two players, called First and Second, alternately place stones of their own color on empty cells, with First moving first. Each player is assigned two opposite sides of the rhombus; First's goal is to form a connected chain of his stones joining his two assigned sides, and Second's goal is to do the same for his sides. It is known that with optimal play First has a winning strategy.

Answer the following two questions for every positive integer n:

(1) Determine the smallest integer s(n) such that First has a strategy guaranteeing a win in which, at the end of the game, his winning chain (a path of First's stones connecting his two sides) consists of exactly s(n) stones — i.e. find the minimum possible length of a guaranteed winning chain.

(2) Determine the smallest integer m(n) such that First has a strategy guaranteeing that the game ends (with First having won) within m(n) total moves by First.

Give exact values, or sharp upper and lower bounds, for s(n) and m(n) as functions of n.
status_search_result: The problem of determining the shortest guaranteed winning path length and minimum number of moves for First to win Hex on n×n boards remains open for general n. Only small boards (through 8×8, and most 9×9 openings) have been solved computationally; no closed-form expression or sharp bounds for arbitrary n are known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Formalize and prove the listed large-board escape, critical-rank, retreat-rule, and board-width/board-count assertions for Fox and Geese, including the explicit thesis conjectures for special n×4, n×6, and Ceylonese-rule positions.
self_contained_problem:
Fox and Geese is a two-player combinatorial game played on an n×n (or n×m) square board with one Fox and four (or more) Geese placed on dark squares. The Geese move one square diagonally forward (toward the Fox's home side); the Fox moves one square diagonally in any direction. The Geese win if they trap the Fox so that it cannot move; the Fox wins if it reaches the Geese's home row (or otherwise escapes past the Geese). Define a position's span to be the difference between the maximum and minimum rank (row index measured in the Geese's direction of advance) of the Geese.

Formalize and resolve each of the following assertions:

(a) (Large-board escape.) Determine, for sufficiently large n, the precise set of starting positions on the n×n board from which the Fox can guarantee escape against k Geese, and prove the resulting characterization.

(b) (Critical rank.) Determine the critical rank r(n,k) such that, with k Geese all at rank ≥ r on an n×n board, the Geese win against any Fox starting position of lower rank, and prove the value of r(n,k).

(c) (Retreat rule, Welton.) Suppose the Fox's backward moves are extended so that the Fox may slide backward like a bishop along a diagonal by any number of squares from a prescribed set S ⊂ ℤ_{>0}. Compare the cases S = {1,2} and S = {1,3} (the latter preserving parity): decide which of the two gives the Fox a greater winning advantage, and more generally determine the outcome class as a function of S.

(d) (Board widths and goose counts.) Determine the outcome (Fox-win, Geese-win, or draw, with optimal play) for the standard initial position on an n×m board with g Geese, as a function of (n,m,g). In particular, prove the following explicit conjectures:
  (i) For every sufficiently large n, the standard n×4 position is [Fox-win / Geese-win — give the precise outcome].
  (ii) For every sufficiently large n, the standard n×6 position is [the precise outcome].
  (iii) Under the Ceylonese rule (in which a Goose may also move sideways), determine the outcome for all sufficiently large n.

Provide complete proofs of each assertion (or determination), thereby giving a uniform solution to the Fox-and-Geese problems above.
status_search_result: The Fox-and-Geese problems posed in the unsolved-problems compendium and in Aaron Siegel's thesis remain open. Recent treatments of combinatorial game theory (Siegel's 2013 monograph and the "Coping with cycles" survey) continue to list them as unresolved, and no published source has been found establishing the conjectured outcomes for the n×4, n×6, or Ceylonese-rule variants, nor resolving Welton's retreat-rule question.

original_question: Decide whether the displayed sequences of Hare and Hounds positions become increasingly hot or have arbitrarily large negative atomic weight, and prove or disprove the explicit value conjecture for the starting position on a 6n+5 by 3 board.
self_contained_problem:
Hare and Hounds is a combinatorial game played on a rectangular board of width 3 and length L. Three hounds start in one short edge of the board and the hare starts in the opposite short edge. The hounds move one at a time, each step being a diagonal or straight forward or sideways move (never backward), while the hare moves one step in any of the available directions (forward, sideways, or backward). The hounds win if they trap the hare so it cannot move; the hare wins if it escapes past the line of hounds. Standard combinatorial game theory associates to every position a game value (with concepts of temperature, "heat", and atomic weight in the sense of Conway's theory of partizan games).

Consider, for each n ≥ 1, the natural family of Hare and Hounds positions on a (6n+5) × 3 board obtained by taking the standard starting configuration (three hounds on the bottom row, hare on the top row).

(a) Determine whether the sequence of these positions (indexed by n, or by the natural increasing-length families of positions that arise from them) becomes increasingly hot as n → ∞, i.e. whether the temperature of the position is unbounded.

(b) Determine whether the same family has arbitrarily large negative atomic weight as n → ∞.

(c) Prove or disprove the conjecture that gives an explicit closed-form combinatorial game value for the starting position on the (6n+5) × 3 board for every n ≥ 1.
status_search_result: No published resolution of these Hare and Hounds questions (temperature growth, unbounded negative atomic weight, and the explicit value conjecture for the (6n+5)×3 starting position) could be located. The questions appear in the standing list of unsolved problems in combinatorial games and remain open as far as available sources indicate.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend Domineering analysis by resolving open rectangular-board values, especially on 2×n, 3×n, and 4×n boards, characterizing hot positions up to infinitesimal shift, finding new temperatures, and pushing the partial analysis of Tromineering.
self_contained_problem:
Domineering is a two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice (typically an $m \times n$ rectangular board). Players alternate moves: Left places a $1\times 2$ vertical domino covering two adjacent unoccupied cells, while Right places a $2\times 1$ horizontal domino covering two adjacent unoccupied cells. A player who cannot move loses. Each Domineering position has a value in the universe of combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway), with associated invariants such as canonical form, temperature, and infinitesimal part.

Address the following open questions about Domineering:

1. (Rectangular boards) Determine the exact game-theoretic value of the $2 \times n$ board for even $n$ (currently known only up to an "ish" infinitesimal), and resolve the remaining open game values of $3 \times n$ and $4 \times n$ rectangular boards.

2. (Hot positions) Characterize all hot Domineering positions up to infinitesimal shift; i.e., describe completely the set of positions whose canonical form has positive temperature, modulo infinitesimal differences.

3. (Temperatures) Exhibit a Domineering position whose temperature does not appear in the currently known list of Domineering temperatures, or prove that no new temperatures occur.

4. (Tromineering) Tromineering is the variant of Domineering played with $1\times 3$ vertical (Left) and $3\times 1$ horizontal (Right) trominoes. Extend the partial analysis of Tromineering on $m \times n$ rectangular boards: determine winners and game values for further families of boards.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made via endgame databases (Uiterwijk–Barton, 2015) covering single-component positions up to 15 squares, along with new structural theorems (Bridge Destroying Theorem) and results on infinitesimals and dyadic rational values. Variants such as Triomineering and Tridomineering have partial winner classifications for small m. However, the exact value of the $2\times n$ board for even $n$, complete characterization of hot positions modulo infinitesimals, the question of new temperatures, and a full Tromineering analysis remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine the nim-dimension of one-dimensional and two-dimensional NoGo, and decide whether there is a bound on the denominators of fractions that occur on the two-dimensional board.
self_contained_problem:
NoGo is a partizan combinatorial game played on a (subset of a) grid graph by two players, Left (Black) and Right (White), who alternately place a stone of their own color on an empty vertex. A move is legal only if, after the placement, every maximal monochromatic connected group of stones still has at least one adjacent empty vertex (a "liberty"). A player who cannot make a legal move loses (normal play convention).

For a partizan game G, its (combinatorial-game-theoretic) value lies in the universe of surreal-number / switch / loopfree game values. Given a class C of positions, define the nim-dimension of C to be the supremum, over all positions P in C, of the Grundy-like complexity measure obtained as follows: the smallest integer d such that every position in C has a canonical value expressible using nimbers (stars) of dimension at most d (equivalently, the largest n for which a position whose value involves *n arises in C); if no such finite bound exists the nim-dimension is infinite.

Questions:
(a) Determine the nim-dimension of NoGo played on one-dimensional boards (i.e. on path graphs P_n, for all n ≥ 1).
(b) Determine the nim-dimension of NoGo played on two-dimensional rectangular boards (i.e. on grid graphs P_m □ P_n, for all m, n ≥ 1).
(c) Decide whether there exists a finite bound B such that for every position arising on a two-dimensional rectangular NoGo board, the canonical game value, when written as a dyadic rational (or sum involving dyadic rationals and infinitesimals), uses only fractions whose denominators are at most B.
status_search_result: Recent work (2024) introduces CGTSolver and solves Linear (1×n) NoGo boards for n up to 39, extending previous results, but the search did not surface a definitive determination of the nim-dimension for either one- or two-dimensional NoGo, nor a proof of a bound on denominators of fractions appearing as values on 2D boards. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Resolve the listed narrow-board Dots-and-Boxes conjectures, including the Faroese and Icelandic one-dimensional cases, eventual periodicity in misère Swedish 1×n Dots-and-Boxes, and a complete impartial theory for the Icelandic 1×n game.
self_contained_problem:
Dots-and-Boxes is the well-known impartial-style game played on an m×n array of dots: two players alternately draw a horizontal or vertical unit edge between adjacent dots; if a move completes the fourth side of a unit square ("box"), the moving player captures that box and must move again. In the normal scoring version, the player capturing more boxes wins. Several national variants modify the rules:

• Swedish Dots-and-Boxes: the player capturing a box is not required to move again (capturing does not grant a bonus turn); play continues with the alternation rule.
• Faroese Dots-and-Boxes: a variant in which moves that close boxes are governed by Faroese-specific rules described in the combinatorial-games literature ("staples" version).
• Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes: a further variant of the rules of Swedish/Faroese type.
• Misère convention: the player capturing fewer boxes (or under suitable misère convention, the player making the last move) wins.

Consider the 1×n narrow-board case of each variant (so the dots lie on a 2×(n+1) grid).

Establish the following:

(a) (Faroese 1×n conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Faroese Dots-and-Boxes, a winning first move (when one exists) is a vertical edge that splits the strip into two shorter strips, with the split position determined by the conjectured rule.

(b) (Icelandic 1×n parity conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes with n odd, the first player loses by exactly one box under optimal play.

(c) (Misère Swedish periodicity.) Prove that the outcome sequence of misère 1×n Swedish Dots-and-Boxes is eventually periodic in n.

(d) (Impartial Icelandic theory.) Develop a complete theory (Sprague–Grundy values and a closed-form solution) for the impartial version of 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes.
status_search_result: These narrow-board Dots-and-Boxes conjectures (Faroese, Icelandic, misère Swedish periodicity, and a complete impartial Icelandic theory) appear in the unsolved-problems compilation in Games of No Chance 5 (2017) and are stated there as open conjectures, verified only for small n. No subsequent resolution was located.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Sprouts in either normal or misère play.
self_contained_problem:
Sprouts is a two-player combinatorial game played on a sheet of paper, defined as follows. The game starts with a fixed number n ≥ 1 of spots (dots) drawn on the plane. Players alternate moves. A move consists of: (i) drawing a new curve that either connects two distinct existing spots or forms a loop from one spot back to itself, such that the curve does not cross itself, does not cross any previously drawn curve, and does not pass through any other spot; and (ii) placing a new spot somewhere on the interior of the newly drawn curve. Each spot is allowed to have at most three curve-ends incident to it (so a spot already incident to three curve-ends is "dead" and cannot be used again). Under the normal play convention, the player who cannot move loses; under the misère convention, the player who cannot move wins.

For each n ≥ 1 and for each of the two conventions (normal and misère), determine which player has a winning strategy in the n-spot game of Sprouts, and more generally determine the Sprague–Grundy / game-theoretic value of the corresponding starting position. Equivalently, extend the known analysis of normal-play and misère-play Sprouts to as many starting spot counts n as possible, and ideally establish a general theorem describing the outcome (and Grundy value) of n-spot Sprouts as a function of n in each convention.
status_search_result: The problem remains open in general. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Sylver Coinage.
self_contained_problem:
Sylver Coinage is a two-player game defined as follows. Two players alternate naming positive integers, subject to the rule that no player may name an integer that is a nonnegative-integer linear combination of previously named integers. The player who is forced to name 1 loses. Equivalently, at any point the set S of integers named so far generates a numerical sub-semigroup of the positive integers; a legal move is any positive integer not in the semigroup generated by S together with 1, and a player loses if forced to play 1.

Provide a general analysis of this game. Specifically:
(a) Determine, for as broad a class of opening positions as possible, which positions are P-positions (previous-player wins) and which are N-positions (next-player wins).
(b) In particular, for each prime p ≥ 5, decide whether the move "p" (i.e., the position {p} after the first player names p) is a winning or losing move for the first player, and identify an explicit winning strategy whenever one exists.
(c) More generally, classify the P-positions among finite sets {a_1, ..., a_k} of pairwise coprime positive integers greater than 1.

Give complete proofs of any claimed classifications and strategies.
status_search_result: Sylver Coinage remains a famously open combinatorial game. While Hutchings' theorem and results of Sicherman and others give partial information (e.g., every prime ≥ 5 as a first move is conjectured to be a losing move, but no winning strategy is known for any prime ≥ 5), the general analysis is unsolved.

original_question: Extend the analysis of Von Neumann’s Game from directed forests to directed acyclic graphs.
self_contained_problem:
Von Neumann's Game is the following two-player combinatorial game played on a finite directed graph G with a distinguished token-bearing vertex. Players alternate moves; a move consists of sliding the token along a directed edge from its current vertex to a successor vertex, after which the originating vertex (and all edges incident to it) is deleted. A player unable to move loses. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Push further analysis of Inverting Hackenbush and Reversing Hackenbush.
self_contained_problem:
Blue–Red Hackenbush is played on a finite graph with a distinguished set of "ground" vertices, in which every edge is colored either blue (Left) or red (Right). On their turn, Left deletes a blue edge and Right deletes a red edge; after the deletion, all edges no longer connected to the ground are also removed. Under the normal-play convention, the player unable to move loses. Two variants are defined as follows.

(a) Inverting Hackenbush: played exactly as Blue–Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (together with the edges that drop off), every remaining edge in the position has its color swapped (blue ↔ red).

(b) Reversing Hackenbush: played exactly as Blue–Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (together with the edges that drop off), the moving player may (or, in the strict variant, must) reverse the colors of some specified set of remaining edges (for instance, all edges on a designated path or in a designated component).

Develop a theory of these two games. In particular:

1. Determine the game-theoretic value (in the sense of Conway's surreal-number theory of partizan games) of an arbitrary blue–red stalk (a path with one end on the ground) under each of these rule sets, giving a closed-form description analogous to the Hackenbush sign-expansion (sign-expansion) value for ordinary Blue–Red Hackenbush.

2. Establish, or disprove, a "Colon Principle" or analogous reduction theorem for trees under each variant.

3. Decide whether each variant admits a polynomial-time algorithm for evaluating positions on trees, and locate the complexity of evaluating general (graph) positions.

4. Characterize which surreal numbers arise as values of finite positions in each variant.
status_search_result: A web search located general references to Hackenbush and the Reverse Blue–Red Hackenbush variant, but no published results that compute values, prove a reduction principle, or establish complexity bounds for Inverting Hackenbush or Reversing Hackenbush. Beanstalk is the following two-player combinatorial game. A position is a positive integer n. From a position n, the unique legal moves are:
- if n is even, move to n/2;
- if n is odd, move to either 3n+1 or 3n-1.
Players alternate moves, and the player who moves to the position 1 wins.

For each position n, define its remoteness in the usual game-theoretic sense: a position from which the player to move can win is called an N-position, and one from which every move leads to an N-position (or has no moves) is a P-position; the remoteness of an N-position is one more than the minimum remoteness of its winning-move successors, while the remoteness of a P-position is one more than the maximum remoteness of its successors. A position whose remoteness is infinite (i.e., neither player can force the game to terminate at 1) is called an O-position.

Question: Does the game of Beanstalk admit any O-positions? Equivalently, does there exist a positive integer starting position from which, under optimal play, the game never terminates?

The Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is played by two players who alternately extend a sequence of distinct real numbers x_1, x_2, …, x_n (with Player I moving first). A player loses (in normal play) as soon as the move they make creates either an increasing subsequence of length a+1 or a decreasing subsequence of length d+1 within the sequence constructed so far; in misère play, the player who is forced to create such a subsequence wins. By the Erdős–Szekeres theorem, the game must end after at most a·d + 1 moves. Let N denote "first-player win" and P denote "second-player win".

(a) Prove or disprove: for all a ≥ d ≥ 3 and all sufficiently large n, the Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is an N-position under both normal and misère play.

(b) Prove or disprove the analogous statement when the players are allowed to choose entries from the rational numbers (rather than from a prescribed finite set), under normal play.

(c) Analyze the variant of the game in which the two players alternately name pairs (i, π_i), thereby building a partial permutation π, with the same losing condition based on monotone subsequences. original_question: Extend the analysis of Chomp by solving the infinite three-dimensional game, proving or disproving uniqueness of the winning move from a 3×n rectangle, computing the nim-value of transfinite Chomp position ω×4, and resolving the transfinite stratification conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Chomp is the following two-player game. A position is an order ideal (lower set) of a poset P; equivalently, in the rectangular case, it is the set of remaining squares of an m×n grid that has the shape of a Young diagram (anchored at a fixed corner, the "poisoned" cell). On each turn a player chooses a remaining cell x and removes every cell y with y ≥ x (in the product partial order). The player who is forced to take the poisoned corner cell loses. The game extends naturally to higher-dimensional boxes and, replacing finite dimensions by ordinals, to transfinite boxes (with the usual convention that moves create a position which is still a down-set, and play must terminate by well-foundedness of the ordinal product under the standard ordering).

(a) Infinite three-dimensional Chomp. Determine the outcome class and, if possible, an explicit winning strategy for Chomp played on the box ω × ω × ω.

(b) Uniqueness of the winning move in 3×n Chomp. For every integer n ≥ 1, the position 3×n is known to be a first-player win. Give a deterministic (non strategy-stealing) proof that the winning first move from the 3×n rectangle is unique.

(c) Nim-value of ω×4. Compute the Sprague–Grundy value (nim-value) of the transfinite Chomp position ω × 4.

(d) Transfinite stratification conjecture. Prove or disprove the following conjecture: for transfinite Chomp positions, the dominant ordinal term of the Sprague–Grundy value is determined by the dominant ordinal term of the position's "size"; more precisely, for any finite Chomp position A and any ordinal h, the Grundy value G(A + (1^{d−1} × h)) has the same leading ordinal term as h.

Let $n \ge k \ge 1$ be integers, and let $P_{n,k}$ denote the poset of all nonempty subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ of size at most $k$, ordered by inclusion. The $(n;k)$ Subset Take-Away game is played on $P_{n,k}$ as follows. Two players alternate turns; on each turn the current player names an element $S \in P_{n,k}$ that has not previously been named and does not contain (as a subset) any previously named element. A player who cannot move loses. Equivalently, naming $S$ removes from the poset every $T$ with $T \supseteq S$, and play continues on the remaining poset until empty.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Make substantial progress on sowing or Mancala games, which the paper identifies as a still-fruitful and largely untouched field of investigation.
self_contained_problem:
Develop a substantial combinatorial game-theoretic analysis of sowing (Mancala-type) games. Concretely, consider the following abstract framework. A sowing position is given by a finite cyclic or linear arrangement of n pits (holes), each containing a non-negative integer number of stones (seeds). A move by a player consists of choosing a non-empty pit, removing all k stones from it, and distributing ("sowing") them one at a time into the consecutive pits following the chosen one (in a fixed direction). Additional capture and termination rules may be specified to define a particular variant (for example: the game ends when the player to move has no non-empty pit on their side; or a player captures the contents of a pit when the last sown stone lands in a pit whose resulting count satisfies a prescribed condition). Both impartial and partizan variants may be considered, under either normal-play or misère convention.

Problems to address include:
(a) For natural impartial sowing variants, compute or characterize the Sprague–Grundy values of positions, or prove structural results (periodicity, recursive formulas) for the Grundy sequence as a function of stone counts.
(b) Identify families of sowing games that are tractable (polynomial-time decidable for the outcome class N/P) and prove hardness (PSPACE- or NP-completeness) results for others.
(c) Determine the game-theoretic value, in the partizan sense of Conway, of standard two-sided variants such as Kalah, Oware/Awari, or Bao, for restricted classes of starting configurations.
(d) Establish exact strategies or winning-condition theorems for at least one named sowing variant on n pits with s stones per pit, for infinite families of (n, s).

Produce rigorous theorems addressing at least one of (a)–(d) for a precisely defined sowing variant.
status_search_result: Sowing/Mancala games have received only sporadic mathematical attention. Awari was weakly solved by Romein and Bal (2002) via large-scale endgame database computation, and some Sprague–Grundy analyses of specific sowing variants (e.g., Tchoukaillon, Ruma) exist. However, the general program of a substantial combinatorial game-theoretic treatment of sowing games remains largely unexplored, with no comprehensive theory of Grundy values, complexity, or partizan values for the main families.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether there is a polynomial-time algorithm for k-Annihilation when k is greater than 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D = (V, E)$ be a finite directed graph. In the k-Annihilation game on $D$, a position is a placement of tokens on distinct vertices of $V$. Two players alternate moves; a move consists of selecting one token and sliding it along a directed edge from its current vertex $u$ to a vertex $v$ with $(u,v) \in E$. If the destination $v$ is already occupied by another token (and $u \neq v$), then both tokens involved are removed (annihilated). If a player cannot move, that player loses (normal convention). The parameter $k \geq 1$ specifies that each player must, on a single turn, perform exactly $k$ such moves (consecutively, with one or more tokens). The decision problem k-Annihilation asks, given a digraph $D$ and an initial placement of tokens, whether the player to move has a winning strategy.

For $k = 1$, a polynomial-time algorithm to determine the winner (and to compute a winning strategy) is known. Determine whether, for every fixed integer $k > 1$, there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that decides k-Annihilation.
status_search_result: A polynomial-time algorithm is known only for the case k = 1 (Fraenkel–Yesha, 1982, with later improvements giving O(n^6)). Surveys of algorithmic combinatorial game theory and Fraenkel's bibliographies continue to list the existence of a polynomial algorithm for k > 1 as an open question, with no resolution found in the literature.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether palindromic positions in Toppling Dominoes have uniquely occurring values, determine actual values in Timber and Partizan Timber more systematically, and characterize whether some values never occur in the partizan setting.
self_contained_problem:
Toppling Dominoes is the partizan combinatorial game played on a finite row (string) of dominoes, each colored Left (bL), Right (bR), or neutral (g). On their turn, Left chooses any domino of color bL or g and topples it either to the left or to the right; toppling removes the chosen domino together with every domino on the chosen side of it. Right plays analogously with bR or g dominoes. The first player unable to move loses. Each position has a well-defined game value in the universe of short partizan games.

Timber is the impartial game played on a finite row of vertical sticks; on a move a player chooses a stick and topples it left or right, removing that stick and all sticks on the chosen side. Partizan Timber is the partizan refinement in which each stick is colored Left, Right, or neutral, and a player may topple only sticks of their own color or neutral sticks.

A position (string) is called a palindrome if it reads identically from left to right and from right to left.

Answer the following:

(a) Prove or disprove: if G is a palindrome in Toppling Dominoes, then no other Toppling Dominoes position has the same game value as G (i.e., palindromic positions realize their values uniquely).

(b) Provide a systematic method to compute the game values of arbitrary positions in Timber and in Partizan Timber.

(c) In Partizan Timber, determine whether there exist short partizan game values that do not occur as the value of any position; characterize the set of values which are (or are not) realized.

The broader systematic determination of values in Timber and Partizan Timber, and the characterization of which partizan values fail to occur, do not appear to be fully resolved.

self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player variants of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle.

Setup. There are three pegs and a finite collection of disks of distinct sizes. A legal position is any distribution of the disks among the three pegs in which, on each peg, the disks are stacked in strictly decreasing size from bottom to top. A move consists of transferring the topmost disk of one peg onto another peg, subject to the constraint that the moved disk may not be placed on top of a strictly smaller disk. Two players alternate moves, starting from a prescribed initial legal position and aiming at a prescribed legal terminal position.

Fix a real-valued scoring rule that assigns a payoff to each terminal play (for instance, sums of weights of disks moved, parity-based scores, or move-count differentials). Question: exhibit a scoring rule for the two-player Tower of Hanoi under which the second player wins from the standard starting position (all disks on one peg, to be transferred to another fixed peg), or prove that no such scoring rule exists.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether full-deck Beggar-My-Neighbor has any draws or cycles.
self_contained_problem:
Beggar-My-Neighbor is a deterministic two-player card game played with a standard 52-card deck. The deck is split into two face-down hands held by the two players. The players alternate turns: on each turn the current player turns the top card of their hand face up onto a central pile. If the card played is a non-penalty card (2 through 10), the turn passes to the opponent. If the card played is a "penalty" card — a Jack, Queen, King, or Ace — the opponent must then play, respectively, 1, 2, 3, or 4 cards from the top of their hand onto the central pile; if during this payment they play another penalty card, the obligation switches and the original player must pay. If the payment is completed without a new penalty card appearing, the player who laid the most recent penalty card takes the entire central pile, placing it face down at the bottom of their hand, and then begins a new trick by playing the next card. A player who runs out of cards loses; otherwise the game continues.

original_question: Give formal and algorithmic foundations for sentestrat and top-down thermography, compute or characterize dogmatic thermographs of double kos, build a temperature theory for all loopy games, and characterize natural conditions under which the overheating homomorphism is uniquely determined.
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway), a game G is built recursively from sets of left and right options, with loopy games allowed to have cycles in their game graphs. Thermography assigns to each game G a thermograph encoding the temperature and mean value of G under cooling by a parameter t, and overheating is the operator that, given a base game, integrates a game over a range of temperatures. The operator ∗ sends a game G to its star-companion ∗G, which is known to annihilate all infinitesimals.

Solve the following four problems:

(a) Provide a rigorous formal definition of the heuristic strategy known as sentestrat (a sente-based strategy for playing sums of hot games) and prove that it achieves optimal play in an appropriate precise sense; in particular, give a complete formal proof that sentestrat works.

(b) Give an explicit algorithm for top-down thermography that, given the game tree of a (possibly loopy) game G, computes its thermograph, and prove its correctness and analyze its complexity.

(c) Develop the machinery to compute, and characterize explicitly, the dogmatic thermographs of double kos (loopy positions of double-ko type arising in Go).

(d) Develop a temperature theory (cooling, heating, thermographs, temperature, mean value) that applies uniformly to all loopy games.

(e) Identify and prove a natural set of necessary and sufficient conditions on a map φ from a class of combinatorial games to itself under which φ is the unique homomorphism (with respect to disjunctive sum) that annihilates every infinitesimal game; in particular, characterize when the map G ↦ ∗G is the unique such homomorphism.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Find a notion of simplest form that works for all finite loopy games including Carousel, detect natural wild cycles in playable games such as Phutball, and characterize when infinitesimal stoppers have well-defined atomic weight together with an algorithm to compute it.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a loopy game is a (possibly infinite) game graph in which positions may recur, allowing draws or infinite play. A stopper is a loopy game with no infinite alternating run. The standard theory of canonical (simplest) form for loopfree games (via reversibility and domination) extends to certain classes of loopy games (e.g. stoppers, plumtrees), but is known to fail in general — for instance, the loopy game CAROUSEL has no canonical form under the existing definitions. A position in a loopy game is said to contain a wild cycle if it has a cycle that is essential to play and cannot be eliminated by the usual simplification rules. The atomic weight of an infinitesimal game g is, when defined, an integer-valued "uppitiness" measure aw(g) satisfying the usual atomic-weight calculus (e.g. aw(g+h)=aw(g)+aw(h) when both sides are defined, and aw(*)=0); for general infinitesimal stoppers it is not known when this invariant exists.

Tasks:
(a) Define a notion of "simplest form" for finite loopy games — i.e. a canonical representative inside each equivalence class under game equality — that is well-defined for every finite loopy game, and in particular produces a canonical form for CAROUSEL.
(b) Give a procedure that, in a playable loopy game such as Phutball, detects the presence of a wild cycle arising naturally in actual play (as opposed to one constructed artificially).
(c) Characterize precisely those infinitesimal stoppers g for which a well-defined atomic weight aw(g) exists, and provide an algorithm that, given such an infinitesimal stopper, computes aw(g).
status_search_result: The questions are drawn from a standard list of unsolved problems in combinatorial game theory concerning loopy games (Siegel's questions on simplest form, wild cycles, and atomic weights of infinitesimal stoppers). No published resolution of any of the three parts has been located; the problems appear to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Characterize where the nimber ∗2 can occur in natural games and, more generally, determine the smallest exponent bound controlling which nimbers ∗k can appear in a given game.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short, loopfree) two-player game G has, by the Sprague–Grundy theory, a value associated with each impartial position; nimbers are denoted ∗k for nonnegative integers k, where ∗0 = 0 and ∗k is the value of a single Nim-heap of size k. A "natural" combinatorial game is given by a fixed ruleset (e.g. Domineering, Konane, Hackenbush, Go, etc.) whose positions generate values in the universe of combinatorial games.

For a given ruleset G, define the nim-dimension of G to be the smallest nonnegative integer n such that whenever a position of G has value ∗k, one has k < 2^n (and ∞ if no such n exists).

(a) Characterize, among natural combinatorial games, those rulesets that admit a position of value ∗2 (i.e., describe the "habitat of ∗2").

(b) More generally, for each natural ruleset G, determine its nim-dimension n(G), i.e., the smallest exponent n such that every nimber value ∗k attained by a position of G satisfies k < 2^n.
status_search_result: Berlekamp's question on the "habitat of ∗2" remains an open guiding problem in combinatorial game theory. Partial progress is known: ∗2 positions have been found in various games (e.g. Domineering, with difficulty), and Carlos dos Santos showed Konane has infinite nim-dimension by exhibiting positions of value ∗k for every k. No general characterization of which natural rulesets contain ∗2 (or have a given nim-dimension) is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Tighten the growth bounds for numbers of games born by day n, determine structural properties of games born by day 3 and of alternative birthday partial orders, describe the exact structure and parameters of the lattices L3 and L4, characterize which seed sets generate distributive or modular lattices, understand handedness in all-small lattices, count option-closed games, and find other natural planar lattice families.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game is defined recursively as an ordered pair G = {G^L | G^R} of finite sets of previously constructed games called the Left and Right options of G; the unique game born on day 0 is 0 = { | }, and a game is born by day n if all of its options are born by day n−1. Equality and the partial order ≤ on games are defined by Conway's recursion: G ≥ H iff no Right option of G is ≤ H and no Left option of H is ≥ G. For each n ≥ 0, the set L_n of (canonical forms of) games born by day n is a finite distributive lattice under ≤. A game G is all-small if every position reachable from G has at least one Left option and at least one Right option (or is 0); let L^0_n denote the lattice of all-small games born by day n. A game is option-closed if it equals every game obtained by replacing any subset of its options by their canonical forms (one standard formalization).

Address the following:

(a) Improve the known asymptotic upper and lower bounds on |L_n|, the number of distinct games born by day n.

(b) Describe the structure of L_3 explicitly: give its order dimension, its maximum longitude (length of a longest chain), and a combinatorial description of its covering relations.

(c) Determine the exact structure and parameters (size, dimension, longitude, planarity) of L_4.

(d) For a finite set S of games, let L(S) denote the lattice generated by S under the game ordering. Characterize those S for which L(S) is distributive, and determine whether there exists S such that L(S) is modular but not distributive.

(e) Determine whether the elements of the all-small lattice L^0_n possess an intrinsic "handedness" (a canonical Z/2-symmetry distinguishing Left-favored from Right-favored elements), and describe it.

(f) Determine the abelian group generated, under the disjunctive sum of games, by all all-small games.

(g) Count the number of option-closed games born by day n.

(h) Exhibit and classify natural infinite families of combinatorial games whose birthday lattices are planar.

(i) For each of several alternative definitions of "birthday" of a game (e.g., formal birthday vs. canonical birthday vs. minimal birthday over equivalent forms), describe the partial order of games up to that birthday and compare with L_n.

Partial results exist (e.g., the lattice of games born by day n is known to be distributive, and structure results are known for small n and for multi-player generalizations), but the listed problems remain open in their full generality.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Given a group or monoid of games, develop a general method for calculating the simplest game in each equivalence class modulo that structure.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game is built recursively from sets of Left and Right options: G = { G^L | G^R }. Under disjunctive sum, the class of short partizan games forms a partially ordered abelian group, with G = H iff G + K and H + K have the same outcome for every game K. More generally, given a submonoid (or subgroup) K of the universe of games (for instance, the monoid generated by a specified rule set or "universe" such as all-small games, dicotic games, scoring games, misère games of a particular class, etc.), one defines K-equivalence by G ≡_K H iff G + X has the same outcome as H + X for every X ∈ K. Each K-equivalence class has a notion of "simplest" representative, where simplicity is measured by the formal birthday (recursive depth of construction) and the size/complexity of the game tree.

Problem: Develop a general method (algorithm or constructive procedure) that, given a monoid or group K of combinatorial games together with a game G, produces the simplest representative of the K-equivalence class of G. The method should apply uniformly across choices of K (rather than being tailored to a single specific universe), and should, in principle, allow one to compute canonical simplest forms modulo any reasonable monoid of games.
status_search_result: The problem of finding canonical/simplest representatives modulo a general monoid K of games is listed as an unsolved problem in the standard compilation of open problems in combinatorial game theory. While canonical forms are known for specific universes (e.g., short partizan games, impartial games via Sprague–Grundy, and recent work on misère universes such as dicotic and dead-ending games), no general uniform technique applicable to arbitrary K is known. No published solution to the general problem was found.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Develop a misère theory for unions of partizan games.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a partizan game is a finite game tree in which, at each position, the two players (Left and Right) may have different sets of available moves. The disjunctive sum (or union) G + H of two games G and H is the game in which, on each turn, the player to move chooses one of the component games and makes a legal move there; play ends when no moves remain in any component. Under the misère convention, the player who makes the last move loses.

Two games G and H are misère-equivalent (G ≡ H) if for every game X, the outcome (under optimal play) of G + X equals the outcome of H + X. While the disjunctive theory of partizan games under the normal-play convention is well developed (yielding the surreal-number-valued theory of Conway), the corresponding theory under the misère convention is far less understood, since many simplifications (dominated and reversible options, additive inverses, canonical forms) that hold under normal play fail in misère play.

Problem: Develop a comprehensive structural theory of disjunctive sums (unions) of partizan games under the misère-play convention. In particular, give a workable notion of canonical form, identify natural equivalence classes and their algebraic structure (e.g. the monoid of partizan games modulo misère equivalence), and provide tools for computing outcomes of disjunctive sums of partizan misère games analogous to those available in the normal-play partizan theory.
category_tag: Combinatorial game theory / misère partizan games
status_search_result: A substantial body of work since the late 2000s (Mesdal–Ottaway, Siegel, Milley, Renault, Dorbec, Stewart and others) has produced significant partial progress: canonical forms in restricted universes (notably dicots and dead-ending games), equivalence modulo universes, and structural results on partizan misère monoids. However, a complete general misère theory of disjunctive sums of partizan games comparable to the normal-play theory remains unfinished and is still an active research program.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine whether there is a useful general theory for games with four outcomes—Next, Previous, Left, and Right—beyond the usual impartial normal-play and misère frameworks.
self_contained_problem:
In classical combinatorial game theory, a two-player game between Left and Right is analyzed under a fixed convention (most commonly normal play, where the player unable to move loses, or misère play, where the player unable to move wins). Under normal play of impartial games, the Sprague–Grundy theory provides a complete additive structure, and partizan normal-play games admit Conway's theory of surreal numbers and game values. Each finite game position falls into one of four outcome classes under optimal play:
- N (Next player to move wins),
- P (Previous player wins, i.e. the player who just moved),
- L (Left wins regardless of who moves first),
- R (Right wins regardless of who moves first).

In the standard normal-play and misère-play conventions, the outcome class is determined by the win/loss rule applied to terminal positions, and the four classes arise as derived information.

Problem. Identify a class of two-player combinatorial games in which the four outcomes N, P, L, R are taken as primitive winning conditions (rather than as consequences of a normal- or misère-play terminal rule) and develop a useful general theory for such games. In particular, determine whether there exists a natural disjunctive-sum structure, an equivalence relation refining outcome equality, and a value theory (analogous to Sprague–Grundy values or Conway game values) on this class, with proofs of additivity, simplification, and comparison theorems. If no such general theory exists, demonstrate obstructions to its development.
status_search_result: The four outcome classes N, P, L, R are standard in combinatorial game theory, but no general theory is widely recognized for games where these four outcomes are taken as primitive winning conditions, beyond normal-play and misère-play frameworks. Scoring-play and other conventions have been studied (e.g. work on scoring-play combinatorial games), but a unified general theory specifically addressing four-outcome primitive games does not appear to have been established. The question remains open in the published literature.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Resolve the open structural questions about impartial misère quotients, including faithfulness of quotient maps, subgroup intersections with P, classification growth, existence of quotient elements of specific periods such as 5 or 8, and smallest quotients containing specified periods.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let Γ be a finite set of impartial combinatorial game positions, closed under taking options, considered under misère-play convention (the player unable to move wins). Let F(Γ) be the free commutative monoid on Γ. Two positions x,y are said to be misère-equivalent in Γ, written x ≡ y, if for every position z built from Γ, the misère outcome of x+z equals the misère outcome of y+z. The quotient monoid Q(Γ) = F(Γ)/≡ is called the misère quotient of Γ, and it comes with a distinguished subset P ⊂ Q(Γ) consisting of images of positions whose misère outcome is a previous-player win. A position has period n if it has order n in Q(Γ). A quotient map φ : Q(Γ) → Q(Γ′) (for Γ ⊂ Γ′) is called faithful if x ≡_{Γ′} y implies x ≡_Γ y for all x,y ∈ F(Γ); equivalently, φ is injective on the natural images.

Resolve each of the following structural questions about impartial misère quotients:

(1) Is every quotient map between impartial misère quotients faithful?

(2) For any nontrivial submonoid S ⊂ Q(Γ) arising from a sub-ruleset, must S ∩ P be nonempty?

(3) Extend the classification of impartial misère quotients (e.g., by order, or by associated combinatorial structure) beyond what is currently known.

(4) Exhibit an impartial misère quotient containing an element of period 5 (and likewise of period 8), or prove that no such quotient exists.

(5) Determine the smallest impartial misère quotient (by order) that contains an element of period 4; period 3; period 6.
status_search_result: These structural questions about impartial misère quotients (faithfulness of quotient maps, nonempty intersection of submonoids with the P-set, classification extensions, and existence/smallest examples of quotients with elements of specified periods) are listed as open problems in the misère-quotient literature (Plambeck–Siegel and Siegel's surveys). Searches show no published resolution of these specific questions; they appear to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Characterize inverses in partizan misère universes by determining when G plus its conjugate is equivalent to zero in dicotic settings, whether every inverse must be the conjugate in suitably closed universes, and which universes forbid nonconjugate inverses.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory under misère convention, a partizan game G has a conjugate (or negative) denoted by overline{G}, obtained by swapping the roles of the two players (Left and Right) in every position of G. A *universe* U is a class of partizan games closed under disjunctive sum, options, and conjugation. Two games G and H are equivalent modulo U, written G ≡ H (mod U), if G + X has the same outcome as H + X for every X ∈ U. The *dicotic universe* D consists of all partizan games in which every position either has both Left and Right options or is the zero game.

Answer the following three questions about inverses in partizan misère universes:

(a) Characterize exactly which games G ∈ D satisfy G + overline{G} ≡ 0 (mod D); that is, give a necessary and sufficient condition on G for its conjugate to be its inverse in the dicotic misère universe.

(b) For a universe U that is closed under conjugation and disjunctive sum, determine whether the implication "G + H ≡ 0 (mod U) implies H = overline{G}" must hold; i.e., is every inverse of G necessarily its conjugate?

(c) Classify the universes U (within the partizan misère setting) for which no nonconjugate inverses exist — i.e., for which G + H ≡ 0 (mod U) forces H = overline{G}.
status_search_result: A 2020 paper (Fisher, Nowakowski, Santos) characterizes the invertible elements of the misère dicotic universe D, resolving question (a). A 2024 work titled "Invertibility in the misère multiverse" (Davies & Yadav) further develops invertibility theory across universes, showing every universe has the conjugate property and characterizing invertible elements universe by universe, providing substantial progress on (b) and (c). Some aspects (full classification of universes with no nonconjugate inverses) remain active research.
