paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine whether guaranteed scoring games are the largest conjugation- and disjunctive-sum-closed scoring universe into which normal-play games order-embed, and solve the game of Brushes.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A scoring game is a finite two-player combinatorial game in which every position has options for Left and Right and every terminal position is assigned a real-valued score (positive favoring Left, negative favoring Right). For a scoring game G, let G^c denote its conjugate (swap the roles of Left and Right and negate the score). The disjunctive sum G+H is defined recursively, with terminal scores added. A universe U of scoring games is a class closed under taking options, conjugation, and disjunctive sum. The class N of (Conway) normal-play games (no score, last-player-to-move wins, terminal score 0 with the loser convention) sits inside the scoring world via the standard embedding sending a normal-play game G to its scoring version with all terminal scores 0. One says N order-embeds in U if there is an injection ι: N → U preserving the partial order ≤ (G ≤ H iff Left does at least as well in H as in G under every disjunctive context), conjugation, and disjunctive sum. Call a scoring game G guaranteed if for every position, the Left-stop is at least the Right-stop (equivalently, scores cannot decrease for the player to move under optimal stopping play); let GS denote the universe of guaranteed scoring games.

Problem.
(a) Prove or disprove: GS is the largest conjugation-closed and disjunctive-sum-closed universe of scoring games into which the universe N of normal-play games order-embeds. Equivalently, show that every universe U of scoring games (closed under options, conjugation, and disjunctive sum) into which N order-embeds satisfies U ⊆ GS, or exhibit a strictly larger such universe.

(b) Solve the combinatorial game BRUSHES: determine its complete game-theoretic value (in the appropriate scoring universe) and provide an explicit strategy / closed-form evaluation for arbitrary positions.
status_search_result: The guaranteed scoring games framework was introduced and developed by Larsson, Nowakowski, and Santos (arXiv:1505.07905; Electronic J. original_question: Find a formula for the number of P-positions of Nim with 2n tokens and, more generally, develop methods to enumerate P-positions of a given size for arbitrary games.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: For square-free lattice games and related lattice-point rulesets, determine whether winning moves from any N-position can be computed efficiently.
self_contained_problem:
Consider impartial combinatorial games encoded as "lattice games" in the following sense. Fix a pointed rational cone Q ⊆ Z^d (the set of positions), a finite set Γ ⊂ Z^d \ {0} of move vectors, and a "misère" set of forbidden ending positions (or, under normal play, the origin is the unique terminal position). From a position p ∈ Q, a player may move to p − γ provided γ ∈ Γ and p − γ ∈ Q (and p − γ is not forbidden). Players alternate; a player unable to move loses. P-positions are previous-player wins; N-positions are next-player wins.

A lattice game is called square-free if its defining data satisfy the square-free condition generalizing octal games (no move vector has a component greater than 1 in the relevant encoding, so that subtraction of moves does not produce repeated coordinates).

Problem: Determine whether, for every square-free lattice game (and more generally for lattice-point rulesets defined as above), there exists an algorithm that, given any N-position p, computes a winning move from p in time polynomial in the bit-size of p.
status_search_result: For square-free lattice games under normal play, Guo and Miller established that the rational-strategy and affine-stratification conjectures hold and gave an algorithm to compute winning positions; given a rational strategy, a polynomial-time algorithm decides P/N status and produces a winning move. However, the broader rational-strategy conjecture for general lattice games was disproved by Fink (lattice games support universal computation; a 3-dimensional example has non-rational winning-position generating function), so efficient algorithms cannot exist for all lattice-point rulesets. The square-free case is essentially resolved positively, while the general lattice-game case is resolved negatively.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine the nim-dimension of specific natural games and better understand the range of possible nim-dimensions across games such as Domineering and Amazons.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let G be a short combinatorial (two-player, perfect-information, no-chance) game. For a position P of G, write P for its game-tree value modulo equivalence by Conway's theory. An impartial position has a Sprague–Grundy (nim-) value, a single nonnegative integer. For partizan games, one considers the "atomic weight" or, more generally, the structure of *-values that arise: the nim-dimension of a game G is defined as the smallest nonnegative integer d such that every sum of positions of G is equivalent (in the sense of game equality) to a partizan game value plus a nim-heap whose size lies in the additive group generated by some finite collection of nim-values of dimension ≤ d; equivalently, it measures the minimal k such that the set of nim-values appearing among positions of G can be described as the set of XOR-sums of integers from a base set of "dimension" k (so a game whose nim-values are exactly the set of nonnegative integers has nim-dimension 1, while a game whose nim-values realize the full structure of Z_2^k requires dimension k).

Problem. 
(a) Determine the nim-dimension of natural combinatorial games. In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that the game DOMINEERING (played on a rectangular grid, where Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes, last mover wins) has nim-dimension equal to 1.
(b) Prove or disprove the conjecture that the game AMAZONS (played on a 10×10 board with four amazons per side, where on each turn a player moves one of her amazons like a chess queen and then shoots an arrow, like a queen move, from its new square, blocking that square thereafter; last mover wins) has nim-dimension equal to 2.
(c) More generally, describe the range of possible nim-dimensions across natural partizan combinatorial games, exhibiting games of each finite nim-dimension (or showing this fails).

Nowakowski) and endgame databases for Domineering and Amazons, but no source asserts a proof of the conjectured nim-dimensions (1 for Domineering, 2 for Amazons) or a general classification. original_question: Decide whether every game with bounded nim-dimension has only finitely many exceptional cases in its atomic-weight calculations.
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of impartial and loopfree combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway's On Numbers and Games / Winning Ways), recall the following notions:

- The atomic weight (or "uptitude") of an all-small game G is a value, usually an integer, that measures G in units of the infinitesimal up (↑). It is computed by a recursive rule analogous to the mex/Grundy calculation, but the rule is subject to a finite list of "exceptional" positions ("eccentric" cases) in which the naive atomic-weight calculus must be corrected.
- A class C of games is said to have nim-dimension at most d if every Grundy value (nim-value) occurring among positions of games in C is bounded above by 2^d − 1, i.e. all nim-values lie in a fixed finite range. C has bounded nim-dimension if such a finite d exists.

Question: Is it true that for every class of games of bounded nim-dimension, the atomic-weight calculation has only finitely many exceptional positions? Equivalently, prove or disprove: bounded nim-dimension implies that, beyond a finite set of exceptional cases, the atomic weights of positions in the class are determined by the standard (non-eccentric) atomic-weight calculus.

self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) partizan game is built recursively from finitely many Left and Right options, and the collection of game values forms a partially ordered abelian group under disjunctive sum. A ruleset R is said to be a universal partizan ruleset if every short partizan game value occurs as the value of some position of R. Generalized Konane is known to be such a universal partizan ruleset.

(a) Exhibit other universal partizan rulesets, i.e. natural combinatorial rulesets, distinct from Generalized Konane, such that every short partizan game value arises as the value of some position.

(b) Develop general techniques (applicable to a wide class of rulesets) that, given a particular ruleset R, allow one to prove that certain game values cannot occur as the value of any position of R.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine boiling points of specific rulesets such as Domineering and develop feasible methods for obtaining strong upper bounds on temperatures.
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of combinatorial games under the normal-play convention, recall the following. A short combinatorial game G has a well-defined temperature t(G), obtained from the thermograph of G: starting from G, one forms the cooled game G_t by subtracting a tax t from every nonterminal move, and t(G) is the least t ≥ −1 for which G_t becomes infinitesimally close to a number. For a ruleset R (a class of positions closed under play), the boiling point of R is defined as

   bp(R) = sup { t(G) : G is a position of R }.

DOMINEERING is the two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice, in which Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes on empty cells; the first player unable to move loses.

(a) Determine bp(DOMINEERING). In particular, decide whether bp(DOMINEERING) = 2.

(b) More generally, develop feasible methods (algorithmic or theoretical) that yield strong upper bounds on the temperatures t(G) of positions G of a given ruleset such as Domineering.
status_search_result: Berlekamp's conjecture that the boiling point of Domineering equals 2 remains open. Recent computational work (endgame databases, 2015; and follow-up papers in 2019 and 2026) provides strong supporting evidence — exactly one known position attaining temperature 2 and none exceeding it — but no formal proof. Research on feasible methods for upper bounds on temperatures (e.g., via confusion intervals) is ongoing.

original_question: Analyze multiplayer game behavior under different preference systems, especially the remaining open cases of misère three-player Nim and broader recursive/canonical-form questions for cooperative multiplayer sums.

Consider three-player impartial combinatorial games played from a position that is a disjunctive sum of Nim heaps. Players move in a fixed cyclic order, and on each turn a player removes any positive number of tokens from a single heap. A player who cannot move loses. Adopt the following "podium" preference system: each player's first priority is to win (be the last to make a move that puts an opponent in a no-move position in their favor); if a player cannot win, the player's second priority is to determine which of the other two players wins, according to a specified preference. original_question: Riemann's hypothesis asks whether every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2; equivalently, whether all zeros other than the negative even integers are of the form s = 1/2 + iτ.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$ by the absolutely convergent series
$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s},$$
and extended to a meromorphic function on the entire complex plane (with a single simple pole at $s=1$) via analytic continuation. The function $\zeta(s)$ vanishes at the negative even integers $s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots$; these are called the trivial zeros. All other zeros of $\zeta(s)$ are called nontrivial zeros, and they are known to lie in the critical strip $0 < \operatorname{Re}(s) < 1$.

Prove or disprove: every nontrivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ has real part equal to $1/2$. Equivalently, show that every zero of $\zeta(s)$ other than the negative even integers is of the form $s = \tfrac{1}{2} + i\tau$ for some real number $\tau$.
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis is universally recognized as one of the most important open problems in mathematics. It is among the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems and remains unsolved as of 2026.

original_question: Determine exactly which polyominoes tile the whole plane.
self_contained_problem:
A polyomino is a connected planar figure formed by joining finitely many unit squares edge-to-edge (taken up to translation, rotation, and reflection). A polyomino P is said to tile the plane if there exists a collection of congruent copies of P (allowing translations, rotations, and reflections) whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union is the entire Euclidean plane R^2.

original_question: Determine the densest possible packing of congruent spheres in Euclidean space in arbitrary dimension.

For an integer $n \geq 1$, a sphere packing in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a collection of closed balls of equal radius with pairwise disjoint interiors. The density of a packing $\mathcal{P}$ is defined as
$$\Delta(\mathcal{P}) = \limsup_{R \to \infty} \frac{\mathrm{vol}\big(\mathcal{P} \cap B_R\big)}{\mathrm{vol}(B_R)},$$
where $B_R \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is the ball of radius $R$ centered at the origin. The sphere packing constant in dimension $n$ is
$$\Delta_n = \sup_{\mathcal{P}} \Delta(\mathcal{P}),$$
the supremum being over all sphere packings in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

paper_title: Hilbert's 1990 ICM lecture. The 23 problems.
original_question: Extend uniformization by automorphic functions to higher complex dimensions and to the generalizations alluded to in the survey, where the source states that the higher-dimensional case remains largely open.
self_contained_problem:
Classical uniformization (Koebe–Poincaré) shows that every connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to a quotient of one of the simply connected model spaces (the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, or the unit disk) by a freely acting discrete group of biholomorphisms. Equivalently, any analytic relation in two complex variables defining a Riemann surface can be uniformized by single-valued (automorphic) functions.

Develop an analogous theory of uniformization for higher complex dimensions. Concretely: 

(a) Identify natural classes of complex-analytic spaces X of complex dimension n ≥ 2 (for instance, projective varieties, normal complex spaces, or varieties with prescribed singularities and positivity properties of the canonical class) that admit a universal-cover-style description X ≅ Ω/Γ, where Ω is a domain (or simply connected complex manifold) in some fixed list of "model" spaces and Γ is a discrete group of biholomorphisms acting properly discontinuously and freely (or with controlled fixed loci).

(b) Determine, for such classes, which model spaces Ω must appear, and characterize those Ω geometrically (e.g., bounded symmetric domains, Stein manifolds, or quotients of homogeneous spaces).

(c) More generally, given an analytic relation among three or more complex variables, decide whether its solution set can be parametrized by single-valued automorphic functions on a suitable model domain, and provide explicit constructions of such automorphic functions.

State and prove a theorem that plays, in complex dimension n ≥ 2, the role that the Koebe–Poincaré uniformization theorem plays in complex dimension 1.
status_search_result: The one-dimensional uniformization theorem (Koebe–Poincaré) is classical and complete. The higher-dimensional generalization is widely regarded as open: while partial results exist for special classes (bounded symmetric domains and their quotients via Baily–Borel; uniformization results for minimal varieties of general type by Greb–Kebekus–Peternell and others), no general higher-dimensional analogue of the uniformization theorem is known. Wikipedia and recent surveys describe the higher-dimensional case as still open.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let Δ be a Gorenstein* simplicial complex, meaning that for every face σ of Δ, including the empty face, the reduced simplicial homology of the link of σ is that of a sphere of the appropriate dimension. Does the Generalized Lower Bound Theorem, or more generally the g-theorem, hold for Gorenstein* complexes?
self_contained_problem:
A finite simplicial complex Δ on vertex set V is called Gorenstein* if for every face σ ∈ Δ (including the empty face ∅), the reduced simplicial homology with rational coefficients of the link lk_Δ(σ) = { τ ∈ Δ : τ ∪ σ ∈ Δ, τ ∩ σ = ∅ } agrees with that of a sphere of dimension dim(lk_Δ(σ)). For a (d−1)-dimensional simplicial complex Δ with f-vector (f_{-1}, f_0, …, f_{d-1}), define the h-vector (h_0, h_1, …, h_d) by Σ h_i x^{d-i} = Σ f_{i-1} (x−1)^{d-i}, and set g_i = h_i − h_{i−1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ ⌊d/2⌋.

The Generalized Lower Bound Theorem (GLBT) asserts that for such Δ, one has 1 = h_0 ≤ h_1 ≤ h_2 ≤ … ≤ h_{⌊d/2⌋}, and moreover g_r = 0 for some r ≤ ⌊d/2⌋ implies Δ is the boundary of a stacked polytope-type structure (in the appropriate combinatorial sense). The g-theorem asserts in addition that the g-vector (g_0, g_1, …, g_{⌊d/2⌋}) is an M-sequence, i.e., the Hilbert function of some graded standard k-algebra.

Problem: Prove or disprove that the GLBT, and more generally the g-theorem, holds for every Gorenstein* simplicial complex Δ.
status_search_result: The g-conjecture for simplicial spheres was proved by Adiprasito (2018). Subsequent work by Adiprasito, Papadakis, and Petrotou (2021) provided simpler proofs and extended the hard Lefschetz property to pseudomanifolds, cycles, and doubly Cohen–Macaulay complexes. Since Gorenstein* complexes are rational homology spheres (a special case covered by these results), the g-theorem—and hence the GLBT—is now known to hold for Gorenstein* complexes.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let P be either an arbitrary convex polytope or, more generally, a Gorenstein poset that is a lattice after removing \hat{0} and \hat{1}. If (h_0, h_1, ..., h_r) is the toric h-vector of P, is the Generalized Lower Bound Theorem inequality h_0 ≤ h_1 ≤ ··· ≤ h_floor(r/2) always true?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be either (a) an arbitrary convex polytope, or (b) more generally, a Gorenstein* poset which becomes a lattice after removing its minimum element $\hat 0$ and its maximum element $\hat 1$. (Recall that a finite graded poset with $\hat 0$ and $\hat 1$ is Gorenstein* if it is Eulerian and its order complex of the proper part has the homology of a sphere of the appropriate dimension.) Let $(h_0, h_1, \dots, h_r)$ denote the toric $h$-vector of $P$, defined recursively by Stanley via the toric $g$- and $h$-polynomials: setting $g(\hat 0,\hat 0)=h(\hat 0,\hat 0)=1$, and for an interval $[\hat 0,x]$ of rank $d>0$,
$$h([\hat 0,x],t)=\sum_{\hat 0\le y<x}g([\hat 0,y],t)\,(t-1)^{d-1-\rho(y)},$$
where $g([\hat 0,x],t)$ is obtained from $h([\hat 0,x],t)=\sum h_i t^i$ by $g=h_0+(h_1-h_0)t+\cdots+(h_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}-h_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor-1})t^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$, and the toric $h$-vector of $P$ is $h(P,t)=h([\hat 0,\hat 1],t)$.

Question: does the Generalized Lower Bound inequality
$$h_0 \le h_1 \le \cdots \le h_{\lfloor r/2 \rfloor}$$
hold in both cases (a) and (b)?
category_tag: toric h-vectors of polytopes and Gorenstein* posets
status_search_result: For case (a) (arbitrary convex polytopes), Karu established the hard Lefschetz property for combinatorial intersection cohomology of (not necessarily rational) polytopes, which implies unimodality of the toric h-vector and hence $h_0\le h_1\le\cdots\le h_{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}$. For case (b) (general Gorenstein* lattices, beyond face lattices of polytopes), the statement does not appear to be established in the literature; the analogous nonnegativity of the cd-index for Gorenstein* posets was proved by Karu, but the unimodality of the toric h-vector for general Gorenstein* lattices remains, to the best of available evidence, open.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
context_brief: Lower bounds for centrally symmetric h-vectors
original_question: Let (h_0, h_1, ..., h_d) be the h-vector of a centrally symmetric polytope of dimension d. Must each entry satisfy h_i ≥ binom(d, i)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a centrally symmetric simplicial convex polytope of dimension $d$ (that is, a simplicial $d$-polytope in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $P=-P$). Let $f_i = f_i(P)$ denote the number of $i$-dimensional faces of $P$ for $-1 \le i \le d-1$, with $f_{-1}=1$. Define the $h$-vector $(h_0,h_1,\dots,h_d)$ of $P$ by
$$\sum_{i=0}^{d} h_i\, x^{d-i} \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{d} f_{i-1}\,(x-1)^{d-i}.$$
Prove or disprove: for every such centrally symmetric simplicial $d$-polytope $P$ and every $0 \le i \le d$,
$$h_i \;\ge\; \binom{d}{i}.$$
status_search_result: The inequality $h_i \ge \binom{d}{i}$ for $h$-vectors of centrally symmetric simplicial $d$-polytopes (conjectured by Björner) was proved by R. Stanley in "On the number of faces of centrally-symmetric simplicial polytopes" (Graphs and Combinatorics 3 (1987), 55–66) using toric varieties. Subsequent work (e.g., a 2018 paper in Discrete & Computational Geometry) characterized the equality cases, giving a centrally symmetric analog of the Lower Bound Theorem.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let P be a finite ranked poset of rank r + 1 such that P minus its minimum and maximum elements is Gorenstein*. Suppose P has a lattice automorphism ν that is an involution and fixes only \hat{0} and \hat{1}. Is the cardinality of P always at least 2r + 1?
self_contained_problem:
A finite graded (ranked) poset $P$ with minimum $\hat{0}$ and maximum $\hat{1}$ of rank $r+1$ is said to have $P\setminus\{\hat 0,\hat 1\}$ Gorenstein* if the order complex $\Delta(P\setminus\{\hat 0,\hat 1\})$ is a Gorenstein* simplicial complex over some field (equivalently, it is an orientable homology sphere of dimension $r-1$ whose Stanley–Reisner ring is Gorenstein). Suppose, in addition, that $P$ admits a lattice automorphism $\nu:P\to P$ which is an involution ($\nu^2=\mathrm{id}$) and whose only fixed points are $\hat 0$ and $\hat 1$. 

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, the cardinality of $P$ satisfies
$$|P|\ \ge\ 2r+1.$$
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a published resolution of this question. It is posed as an open question in Stanley's survey on positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics and is closely related to lower-bound conjectures for centrally symmetric simplicial spheres (e.g., results by Stanley, Klee, Novik and others on centrally symmetric polytopes/spheres), but no direct proof or counterexample addressing this poset-theoretic formulation was located.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let Δ be a (2d − 1)-dimensional Gorenstein* flag complex with h-vector (h_0, h_1, ..., h_{2d}). Is the alternating sum constrained by the Charney-Davis inequality (-1)^d(h_0 - h_1 + ··· + h_{2d}) ≥ 0?
self_contained_problem:
A simplicial complex Δ on a finite vertex set is called a flag complex if every set of pairwise adjacent vertices (clique in its 1-skeleton) is a face of Δ. Equivalently, Δ is the clique complex of its 1-skeleton. Δ is said to be Gorenstein* over a field k if its Stanley–Reisner ring k[Δ] is Gorenstein and Δ equals its core (no vertex lies in every facet); equivalently, Δ is a homology sphere over k.

For a (2d−1)-dimensional simplicial complex Δ with f-vector (f_{-1}, f_0, …, f_{2d-1}) (where f_i counts the i-dimensional faces and f_{-1}=1), define the h-vector (h_0, h_1, …, h_{2d}) by
   Σ_{i=0}^{2d} h_i x^{2d-i} = Σ_{i=0}^{2d} f_{i-1} (x-1)^{2d-i}.

Question: For every (2d−1)-dimensional Gorenstein* flag complex Δ with h-vector (h_0, h_1, …, h_{2d}), does the inequality
   (−1)^d (h_0 − h_1 + h_2 − ⋯ + h_{2d}) ≥ 0
hold?
status_search_result: The Charney–Davis conjecture remains open in general. It has been verified in low dimensions (notably by Davis–Okun for flag homology spheres of dimension ≤ 3) and for special classes such as barycentric subdivisions of shellable spheres (Stanley) and certain sphere subdivisions. No proof for arbitrary Gorenstein* flag complexes is known as of recent literature.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Suppose Δ is a finite abstract simplicial complex such that for every face σ of dimension at most k, including the empty face, the link of σ is acyclic. Can Δ, regarded as a poset under inclusion, be partitioned into intervals [F, G] such that every interval satisfies dim G − dim F ≤ k + 1 and the collection of all bottom elements F forms a subcomplex of Δ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Delta$ be a finite abstract simplicial complex on a finite vertex set, viewed both as a collection of faces (finite sets closed under taking subsets, including the empty face $\emptyset$) and as a poset ordered by inclusion. For a face $\sigma \in \Delta$, define the link $\mathrm{link}_\Delta(\sigma) = \{\tau \in \Delta : \tau \cap \sigma = \emptyset,\ \tau \cup \sigma \in \Delta\}$; in particular $\mathrm{link}_\Delta(\emptyset) = \Delta$. A simplicial complex $\Gamma$ is called acyclic if its reduced simplicial homology $\tilde{H}_i(\Gamma; \mathbb{Z})$ vanishes for all $i$. The dimension of a face $F$ is $\dim F = |F| - 1$ (so $\dim \emptyset = -1$).

Fix a nonnegative integer $k$, and assume that for every face $\sigma \in \Delta$ with $\dim \sigma \leq k$ (including $\sigma = \emptyset$), the link $\mathrm{link}_\Delta(\sigma)$ is acyclic.

Question: must there exist a partition of $\Delta$ (as a set of faces) into closed intervals $[F_i, G_i] = \{H \in \Delta : F_i \subseteq H \subseteq G_i\}$ of its inclusion poset such that
(a) $\dim G_i - \dim F_i \leq k+1$ for every interval, and
(b) the set $\{F_i\}$ of bottom elements of the intervals forms a subcomplex of $\Delta$ (closed under taking subsets)?
status_search_result: Stanley posed this as a conjecture on $k$-fold acyclic complexes. A 2018 paper by Juhnke-Kubitzke, Venturello and coauthors ("Resolving Stanley's conjecture on $k$-fold acyclic complexes", arXiv:1811.08518) gives an explicit counterexample disproving the conjecture in general, while establishing it in restricted cases (boolean trees, and when the acyclicity notion is as high as possible). The general conjecture is therefore resolved in the negative.

We also prove a version of the conjecture for boolean trees, and show that the original conjecture holds when this notion of acyclicity is as high as possible.", "claim": "An explicit counterexample disproves Stanley's general conjecture on k-fold acyclic complexes; positive results are obtained in restricted settings."}]

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Is every Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex partitionable, meaning that a pure simplicial complex can always be partitioned into intervals [F, G] whose top elements G are maximal faces?
self_contained_problem:
A finite (abstract) simplicial complex Δ on a finite vertex set V is a collection of subsets (faces) of V closed under taking subsets. The dimension of a face F is |F|−1, and the dimension of Δ is the maximum dimension of its faces. A facet is a maximal face. The complex Δ is called pure if all its facets have the same dimension.

For a field k, Δ is Cohen–Macaulay (over k) if the Stanley–Reisner ring k[Δ] = k[x_v : v ∈ V] / I_Δ, where I_Δ is generated by the squarefree monomials ∏_{v ∈ S} x_v over non-faces S, is a Cohen–Macaulay ring. Equivalently (by Reisner's criterion), for every face F (including the empty face) the reduced simplicial homology of the link lk_Δ(F) vanishes below its top dimension.

Given faces F ⊆ G of Δ, the (Boolean) interval is [F,G] = {H : F ⊆ H ⊆ G}. The complex Δ is called partitionable if its set of faces can be written as a disjoint union
   Δ = ⊔_{i=1}^{m} [F_i, G_i],
where G_1, …, G_m are exactly the facets of Δ.

Question: Is every Cohen–Macaulay simplicial complex partitionable?
status_search_result: The Partitionability Conjecture (every Cohen–Macaulay simplicial complex is partitionable), posed by Stanley (and in a different form by Garsia), was disproved in 2016 by Duval, Goeckner, Klivans, and Martin, who constructed an explicit 3-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay simplicial complex that is not partitionable. The construction also refuted the related conjecture that Stanley depth bounds depth below.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: If P is a Gorenstein poset, are all coefficients of its cd-index Ψ_P(c, d) nonnegative?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a finite graded poset with minimum element 0̂ and maximum element 1̂, equipped with a rank function ρ. For a chain S = {x_1 < x_2 < ... < x_k} of elements in the open interval (0̂, 1̂), let ρ(S) = {ρ(x_1), ..., ρ(x_k)} ⊆ {1, 2, ..., n-1}, where n = ρ(1̂). Define the flag f-vector α_P(T) = #{chains S in (0̂, 1̂) : ρ(S) = T} for T ⊆ {1,...,n-1}, and the flag h-vector by β_P(T) = Σ_{S ⊆ T} (-1)^{|T|-|S|} α_P(S). Form the ab-index Ψ_P(a, b) = Σ_T β_P(T) u_T, where u_T = u_1 u_2 ⋯ u_{n-1} with u_i = b if i ∈ T and u_i = a otherwise (a, b noncommuting variables).

A graded poset P is called Eulerian if every nontrivial interval [x, y] in P satisfies Σ_{z ∈ [x,y]} (-1)^{ρ(z)-ρ(x)} = 0. When P is Eulerian, Ψ_P(a, b) can be written uniquely as a polynomial Ψ_P(c, d) in the noncommuting variables c = a + b and d = ab + ba; this polynomial is called the cd-index of P.

A graded poset P is called Gorenstein* if P is Eulerian and the order complex of the open interval (0̂, 1̂) has the homology of a sphere of dimension ρ(1̂) - 2 (equivalently, the simplicial complex of chains of P − {0̂, 1̂} is a Gorenstein* complex over Q).

Question: For every Gorenstein* poset P, are all coefficients of its cd-index Ψ_P(c, d) nonnegative?
status_search_result: Karu (2006, Compositio Mathematica, "The cd-index of fans and posets") proved that the cd-index of every Gorenstein* poset has nonnegative coefficients, settling Stanley's conjecture. The result was later reproved and extended via decomposition theorems (Ehrenborg–Karu) and squarefree P-module techniques.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let P be a pure cubical complex of rank r. (a) If P is a Cohen-Macaulay poset, must every entry of its cubical h-vector be nonnegative? (b) If P is also a Gorenstein poset, must its cubical h-vector satisfy h_0(P) ≤ h_1(P) ≤ ··· ≤ h_{r−1}(P)?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A finite graded poset $P$ with $\hat 0$ and $\hat 1$ of rank $r+1$ is called a cubical complex of rank $r$ if every interval $[\hat 0, x]$ with $x \ne \hat 1$ is isomorphic to the face lattice of a cube of dimension $\mathrm{rk}(x)-1$. Call $P$ pure if every maximal element below $\hat 1$ has the same rank $r$. The order complex (or an appropriate combinatorial cubical h-vector construction due to Adin) associates to $P$ a vector $h(P) = (h_0(P), h_1(P), \dots, h_r(P))$, the cubical h-vector of $P$. Recall that $P$ is Cohen–Macaulay (resp. Gorenstein) if, for every open interval, the reduced homology of its order complex vanishes below the top dimension (resp. and additionally the top-dimensional reduced homology is one-dimensional, matching the spherical case).

Questions. Let $P$ be a pure cubical complex of rank $r$.

(a) If $P$ is a Cohen–Macaulay poset, must $h_i(P) \ge 0$ for every $0 \le i \le r$?

(b) If, in addition, $P$ is a Gorenstein poset, must
$$h_0(P) \le h_1(P) \le \cdots \le h_{\lfloor r/2 \rfloor}(P),$$
i.e. (using the symmetry $h_i = h_{r-i}$ which holds in the Gorenstein case) must the cubical h-vector be unimodal with the first half nondecreasing through $h_{r-1}(P)$ in the sense $h_0(P) \le h_1(P) \le \cdots \le h_{r-1}(P)$?
status_search_result: Search results indicate that Adin's conjecture on the nonnegativity of the cubical h-vector for Cohen–Macaulay cubical posets remains a standing open problem, and is mentioned as implying the cd-index conjecture for Gorenstein cubical posets. No resolution of either (a) or (b) was found in the literature.

original_question: Let the Kronecker product coefficients g_{μνλ} be defined by s_μ * s_ν = Σ_λ g_{μνλ} s_λ, where * is the internal product of symmetric functions. Find a combinatorial interpretation of these coefficients that also yields a combinatorial proof that they are nonnegative.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ denote the ring of symmetric functions over $\mathbb{Q}$, and for each partition $\lambda$ let $s_\lambda \in \Lambda$ denote the corresponding Schur function. The internal (Kronecker) product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the bilinear operation defined on power-sum bases by $p_\mu * p_
u = \delta_{\mu
u} z_\mu p_\mu$ (equivalently, it corresponds to the inner tensor product of irreducible representations of symmetric groups: if $\chi^\lambda$ denotes the irreducible character of $S_n$ indexed by a partition $\lambda \vdash n$, then $\chi^\mu \cdot \chi^
u = \sum_\lambda g_{\mu
u\lambda}\,\chi^\lambda$, where the product on the left is the pointwise product of characters). Equivalently, the Kronecker coefficients $g_{\mu
u\lambda}$ are the nonnegative integers determined by
$$s_\mu * s_
u \;=\; \sum_{\lambda} g_{\mu
u\lambda}\, s_\lambda,$$
for all partitions $\mu, 
u$ of the same integer $n$, the sum running over partitions $\lambda \vdash n$.

Problem: Find a combinatorial interpretation of $g_{\mu
u\lambda}$, that is, exhibit an explicit family of combinatorial objects $\mathcal{C}_{\mu
u\lambda}$ such that $g_{\mu
u\lambda} = |\mathcal{C}_{\mu
u\lambda}|$, and which thereby provides a combinatorial proof that $g_{\mu
u\lambda} \ge 0$ for all triples of partitions $(\mu, 
u, \lambda)$ of the same size.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let the Schubert intersection coefficients c_{uv}^w be defined by the product of Schubert polynomials \mathfrak S_u \mathfrak S_v = Σ_w c_{uv}^w \mathfrak S_w. Find a combinatorial interpretation of c_{uv}^w that also gives a combinatorial proof that these coefficients are nonnegative.
self_contained_problem:
For each permutation $w$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ (with $n$ allowed to vary, viewing $S_n \hookrightarrow S_{n+1}$ in the standard way), let $\mathfrak{S}_w \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1, x_2, \ldots]$ denote the Schubert polynomial of Lascoux–Schützenberger, defined by $\mathfrak{S}_{w_0} = x_1^{n-1} x_2^{n-2} \cdots x_{n-1}$ for the longest element $w_0 \in S_n$, together with the recursion $\mathfrak{S}_{ws_i} = \partial_i \mathfrak{S}_w$ whenever $\ell(ws_i) < \ell(w)$, where $s_i = (i,i+1)$ and $\partial_i f = (f - s_i f)/(x_i - x_{i+1})$ is the $i$-th divided difference operator. The Schubert polynomials $\{\mathfrak{S}_w\}$ form a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the polynomial ring (viewed appropriately as a stable limit), and there exist unique integers $c_{uv}^w$ such that
$$\mathfrak{S}_u \cdot \mathfrak{S}_v \;=\; \sum_{w} c_{uv}^w \, \mathfrak{S}_w.$$
It is known from the geometry of the flag variety that $c_{uv}^w \geq 0$ for all permutations $u, v, w$.

Problem: Give an explicit combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients $c_{uv}^w$ — that is, exhibit a family of combinatorial objects whose cardinality equals $c_{uv}^w$ — thereby providing a combinatorial proof of the nonnegativity $c_{uv}^w \geq 0$.
status_search_result: Finding a positive combinatorial rule for the Schubert structure constants $c_{uv}^w$ is widely regarded as a major open problem in algebraic combinatorics and Schubert calculus, generalizing the Littlewood–Richardson rule. Numerous partial results exist (e.g., for Grassmannian permutations via Littlewood–Richardson, for boolean elements, for permutations with separated descents, signed combinatorial interpretations, and recent work on vanishing and complexity), but no general combinatorial interpretation is known as of recent literature (2024–2025).

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
context_brief: Row sums of the S_n character table
original_question: For the symmetric group S_n, give a combinatorial interpretation of the row sums of its character table, and thereby give a combinatorial proof that these row sums are nonnegative.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Its complex irreducible characters $\chi^\lambda$ are indexed by partitions $\lambda$ of $n$, and the conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are indexed by partitions $\mu$ of $n$ (according to cycle type). The character table of $S_n$ is the square matrix $(\chi^\lambda(\mu))_{\lambda,\mu \vdash n}$, where $\chi^\lambda(\mu)$ denotes the value of $\chi^\lambda$ on any element of cycle type $\mu$. For each partition $\lambda$ of $n$, define the row sum
$$a_\lambda \;=\; \sum_{\mu \vdash n} \chi^\lambda(\mu).$$
It is known (via the conjugation action of $S_n$ on itself, which has character $g \mapsto \#\{h\in S_n : hgh^{-1}=g\}$ and decomposes into irreducibles with multiplicities $a_\lambda$) that $a_\lambda$ is a nonnegative integer for every $\lambda \vdash n$.

Find an explicit family of finite combinatorial objects $\mathcal{A}_\lambda$, defined directly in terms of the partition $\lambda$, such that
$$|\mathcal{A}_\lambda| \;=\; a_\lambda \quad \text{for every } \lambda \vdash n,$$
and use this combinatorial interpretation to give a combinatorial proof that $a_\lambda \ge 0$ for all partitions $\lambda$.
status_search_result: The problem of giving a combinatorial interpretation of the row sums $a_\lambda = \sum_\mu \chi^\lambda(\mu)$ of the character table of $S_n$ is widely cited as an open problem in algebraic combinatorics. Nonnegativity is known via the conjugation action of $S_n$ on itself (Frobenius/Frumkin), but no combinatorial interpretation of $a_\lambda$ is known. Recent work (e.g., Amdeberhan and others, 2025) explores related identities and partial cases (such as Riordan-number identities), but the main problem remains unresolved.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Show that for every pair of partitions λ and μ, the (q,t)-Kostka polynomial K_{λμ}(q,t), defined from the Schur expansion of transformed Macdonald symmetric functions, has only nonnegative coefficients.
self_contained_problem:
Let Λ denote the ring of symmetric functions in infinitely many variables over ℚ(q,t), and let {s_λ} denote the Schur function basis indexed by partitions. The modified (transformed) Macdonald symmetric functions H̃_μ(x;q,t) ∈ Λ are defined for each partition μ, and their expansion in the Schur basis takes the form

  H̃_μ(x;q,t) = Σ_λ K_{λμ}(q,t) · s_λ(x),

where the coefficients K_{λμ}(q,t) ∈ ℚ(q,t) are the (q,t)-Kostka polynomials. It is known that each K_{λμ}(q,t) is in fact a polynomial in q and t with integer coefficients.

Prove that for every pair of partitions λ and μ (of the same nonnegative integer n), the polynomial K_{λμ}(q,t) ∈ ℤ[q,t] has only nonnegative coefficients.
status_search_result: The (q,t)-Kostka positivity conjecture (Macdonald positivity) was proven by Mark Haiman in 2001 via his proof of the n! theorem, using the geometry of the isospectral Hilbert scheme of points in the plane. Haiman gave a representation-theoretic interpretation of K_{λμ}(q,t) as a graded character multiplicity, immediately implying nonnegativity of the coefficients.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
context_brief: Ribbon polynomial symmetry and Schur positivity
original_question: For the ribbon polynomials G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x;q) defined by summing over ribbon tableaux with q-weight, (a) give a combinatorial proof that these polynomials are symmetric functions, and (b) when they are expanded in the Schur basis, determine whether all coefficients are polynomials in q with nonnegative integer coefficients.
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer k ≥ 1 and partitions λ ⊇ μ. A k-ribbon is a connected skew shape of k cells containing no 2×2 square. A k-ribbon tableau T of shape λ/μ is a filling of λ/μ by positive integers such that, for each i ≥ 1, the cells labeled i form a (possibly empty) horizontal strip that can be tiled by k-ribbons in such a way that, removing the ribbons labeled with values > i and then the ribbons labeled i in the appropriate order, produces a sequence of partitions. To each k-ribbon R one associates a spin sp(R) = (h(R) − 1)/2, where h(R) is the number of rows occupied by R; the spin of a k-ribbon tableau T, denoted sp(T), is the sum of the spins of its ribbons. The weight x^T of T is x_1^{m_1} x_2^{m_2} ⋯, where m_i is the number of ribbons labeled i. Define the ribbon polynomial
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = Σ_T q^{sp(T)} x^T,
the sum being over all k-ribbon tableaux of shape λ/μ.

(a) Provide a combinatorial proof that G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is a symmetric function in the variables x_1, x_2, ….

(b) When G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is expanded in the basis of Schur functions, say
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = Σ_ν c_{λ/μ,ν}^{(k)}(q) s_ν(x),
determine whether each coefficient c_{λ/μ,ν}^{(k)}(q) lies in ℤ_{≥0}[q].
status_search_result: Schur positivity (part b) was established by Grojnowski–Haiman using affine Hecke algebras and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory; a combinatorial proof and explicit positive combinatorial formula for the Schur coefficients in full generality remained open and was later addressed via dual equivalence graphs (Assaf) for symmetry and positivity, though a fully combinatorial Schur expansion for arbitrary tuples is still incomplete (with explicit formulas known only in special cases such as ≤3 ribbons by Blasiak). Symmetry (part a) has combinatorial proofs (LLT, Haiman, van Leeuwen). Thus the original positivity question is answered affirmatively but the demand for a manifestly combinatorial Schur expansion remains partially open.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: For any Coxeter group W and any interval u ≤ v in the Bruhat order, are all coefficients of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial P_{u,v}(q) nonnegative?
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a Coxeter group with set of simple reflections $S$, and let $\leq$ denote the Bruhat order on $W$. Recall that the Hecke algebra $H(W)$ over $\mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]$ has the standard basis $\{T_w : w \in W\}$ and the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis $\{C'_w : w \in W\}$, related by
$$C'_w = q^{-\ell(w)/2} \sum_{u \leq w} P_{u,w}(q)\, T_u,$$
where $\ell(w)$ is the length of $w$ and the polynomials $P_{u,w}(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$ are the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials, uniquely determined by the conditions $P_{w,w}=1$, $\deg P_{u,w} \leq \tfrac{1}{2}(\ell(w)-\ell(u)-1)$ for $u<w$, and the bar-invariance of $C'_w$.

Prove or disprove: for every Coxeter group $W$ and every pair $u \leq v$ in $W$, all coefficients of $P_{u,v}(q)$ are nonnegative integers.
status_search_result: This conjecture was proved in full generality by Ben Elias and Geordie Williamson in their 2014 paper "The Hodge theory of Soergel bimodules" (Annals of Mathematics), using Soergel bimodules and a Hodge-theoretic Hard Lefschetz theorem. Prior to this, the result was known for Weyl groups and affine Weyl groups (Kazhdan-Lusztig) via geometric methods.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: When W is a finite or affine Weyl group, especially W = S_n, give a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial P_{u,v}(q) that yields a combinatorial proof of their nonnegativity.
self_contained_problem:
Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system, and let H(W) denote its Hecke algebra over Z[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}], with standard basis {T_w : w in W} satisfying (T_s - q)(T_s + 1) = 0 for s in S. There is a unique involution on H(W) sending q^{1/2} to q^{-1/2} and T_w to (T_{w^{-1}})^{-1}. Kazhdan and Lusztig proved that for each v in W there is a unique element C'_v in H(W) that is invariant under this involution and has the form
   C'_v = q^{-l(v)/2} sum_{u <= v} P_{u,v}(q) T_u,
where <= is the Bruhat order, l denotes Coxeter length, and P_{u,v}(q) is a polynomial in Z[q] of degree at most (l(v) - l(u) - 1)/2 for u < v, with P_{v,v}(q) = 1. These P_{u,v}(q) are the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of W.

Assume W is a finite or affine Weyl group; in particular consider the case W = S_n (the symmetric group on n letters with its standard Coxeter generators given by adjacent transpositions). Find an explicit combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of P_{u,v}(q) — that is, describe, for every pair u <= v in W, a finite set S_{u,v,i} (depending combinatorially on the pair (u,v) and a nonnegative integer i) such that
   P_{u,v}(q) = sum_{i >= 0} |S_{u,v,i}| q^i,
thereby giving a combinatorial proof that every coefficient of P_{u,v}(q) is a nonnegative integer.
status_search_result: Nonnegativity of Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients for Coxeter groups was established by Elias and Williamson via Soergel bimodules, but no manifestly combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of P_{u,v}(q) is known, even for the symmetric group S_n. Partial results exist (e.g. Deodhar's formula involves signs; special matchings; recent work toward the combinatorial invariance conjecture by Blundell–Buesing–Conlon–Williamson and follow-ups by Esposito and others, 2021–2025), but a positive combinatorial formula in type A remains an open problem.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let X be a totally nonnegative n × n matrix, and let λ be a partition of n. Is the irreducible-character immanant Imm_λ(X) always nonnegative?
self_contained_problem:
For a partition $\lambda \vdash n$, let $\chi^\lambda$ denote the irreducible character of the symmetric group $S_n$ indexed by $\lambda$. The immanant of an $n\times n$ matrix $X = (x_{ij})$ associated to $\lambda$ is defined by
$$\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(X) \;=\; \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \chi^\lambda(\sigma)\, \prod_{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
A real $n\times n$ matrix $X$ is called totally nonnegative if every minor of $X$ (the determinant of every square submatrix) is nonnegative.

Question: Is it true that for every totally nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix $X$ and every partition $\lambda \vdash n$,
$$\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(X) \;\geq\; 0\,?$$
status_search_result: The nonnegativity of irreducible-character immanants on totally nonnegative matrices was conjectured by Stembridge and proved by Mark Haiman in "Hecke algebra characters and immanant conjectures" (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 6 (1993), 569–595), using Kazhdan–Lusztig theory of the Hecke algebra.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let μ be a partition of n with length at most m, let λ be a partition of n, and let JT_μ be the Jacobi-Trudi matrix (h_{μ_i-i+j})_{i,j=1}^m. Is the immanant Imm_λ(JT_μ) always Schur-positive?
self_contained_problem:
Let $h_0 = 1$, $h_k$ ($k\ge 1$) be the complete homogeneous symmetric functions in countably many variables (with $h_k = 0$ for $k<0$), and let $s_\lambda$ denote the Schur function indexed by a partition $\lambda$. A symmetric function $f$ is called Schur-positive if, when expanded in the basis $\{s_\lambda\}$, all coefficients are nonnegative.

For a partition $\mu = (\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$ of $n$ (with $\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_m\ge 0$, length at most $m$), the Jacobi–Trudi matrix is the $m\times m$ matrix
$$JT_\mu = \bigl(h_{\mu_i - i + j}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m}.$$

For a partition $\lambda$ of $n$, let $\chi^\lambda$ denote the irreducible character of the symmetric group $S_n$ indexed by $\lambda$. The $\lambda$-immanant of an $n\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is
$$\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \chi^\lambda(\sigma)\,\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$

Question: For every partition $\mu \vdash n$ of length at most $m$ and every partition $\lambda \vdash n$, is the symmetric function $\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(JT_\mu)$ Schur-positive?

This is Stembridge's immanant conjecture for irreducible-character immanants of Jacobi–Trudi matrices. It was proved by Mark Haiman in "Hecke algebra characters and immanant conjectures" (J. Amer. Math. Soc., 1993), where he established that $\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(H_{\mu/
u})$ is Schur-positive (in fact, $\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda(H_{\mu/
u}) - f^\lambda \det(H_{\mu/
u})$ is a nonnegative combination of Schur functions). The stronger monomial-immanant Schur-positivity conjecture remains open, but the question as posed (using character immanants $\mathrm{Imm}_\lambda$) is resolved affirmatively.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: For every monomial character φ of the Hecke algebra H_n(q) and every Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element C'_w, is φ(q^{-ℓ(w)/2} C'_w) a polynomial with nonnegative integer coefficients, and are those coefficients unimodal and symmetric about q^{-ℓ(w)/2}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $H_n(q)$ denote the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of the symmetric group $S_n$ over $\mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]$, with generators $T_1, \dots, T_{n-1}$ satisfying the braid relations and $(T_i - q)(T_i + 1) = 0$. For each $w \in S_n$, let $C'_w$ denote the corresponding Kazhdan–Lusztig basis element, and let $\ell(w)$ be the length of $w$.

A trace $\varphi: H_n(q) \to \mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]$ is a $\mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]$-linear map satisfying $\varphi(xy) = \varphi(yx)$. The irreducible characters $\chi^\lambda$ ($\lambda \vdash n$) form a basis of the space of traces, and the so-called monomial characters $\eta^\lambda$ are the traces defined (via Frobenius-type duality) so that $\eta^\lambda$ corresponds to the complete homogeneous symmetric function $h_\lambda$; equivalently, the monomial characters are the $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combinations of irreducible characters whose Frobenius image is $h_\lambda$ for some partition $\lambda \vdash n$.

Question: Is it true that for every partition $\lambda \vdash n$ and every $w \in S_n$, the polynomial
$$ \eta^\lambda\bigl(q^{-\ell(w)/2}\, C'_w\bigr) $$
is a polynomial in $q^{1/2}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, and that these coefficients are unimodal and symmetric about the central exponent $q^{-\ell(w)/2}$?
status_search_result: Haiman proved the corresponding statement for irreducible characters $\chi^\lambda$. The strengthening to monomial characters (h-positivity of the dual Frobenius character of $C'_w$) remains open. A 2022 update on Haiman's conjectures reports this h-positivity conjecture as unresolved; a related reducibility conjecture of Haiman was partially proven for smooth permutations and disproven for singular ones, but this is a distinct statement.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let P be a naturally labeled poset, and let W(P,t) = Σ_{π in L(P)} t^{des(π)+1}, where L(P) is the set of linear extensions of P and des(π) counts descents. Are all zeros of W(P,t) real?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a finite poset on $n$ elements equipped with a natural labeling, that is, a bijection $\omega: P \to \{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that $x <_P y$ implies $\omega(x) < \omega(y)$. A linear extension of $P$ is a permutation $\pi = \pi_1 \pi_2 \cdots \pi_n$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ obtained by listing the labels of the elements of $P$ in an order compatible with $<_P$; let $\mathcal{L}(P)$ denote the set of all such linear extensions. For a permutation $\pi$, let $\mathrm{des}(\pi) = \#\{i : \pi_i > \pi_{i+1}\}$ denote its number of descents. Define the poset Eulerian polynomial
$$W(P,t) = \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal{L}(P)} t^{\mathrm{des}(\pi)+1}.$$
Determine whether, for every naturally labeled finite poset $P$, all zeros of $W(P,t)$ are real numbers.
status_search_result: This is the Neggers–Stanley conjecture. original_question: Let P be a distributive lattice, let c_i be the number of i-element chains in P, and let C(P,t) = Σ c_i t^i be the chain polynomial. Are all zeros of C(P,t) real?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a finite distributive lattice. For each integer $i \geq 0$, let $c_i$ denote the number of chains $x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_{i-1}$ of exactly $i$ elements in $P$ (so $c_0 = 1$, counting the empty chain). Define the chain polynomial of $P$ by
$$C(P,t) = \sum_{i \geq 0} c_i\, t^i.$$
Determine whether, for every finite distributive lattice $P$, all zeros of $C(P,t)$ are real.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: If P is a (3+1)-free poset and G = inc(P) is its incomparability graph, is the chromatic symmetric function X_G e-positive?
self_contained_problem:
A finite poset $P$ is called $(\mathbf{3}+\mathbf{1})$-free if it does not contain an induced subposet isomorphic to the disjoint union of a 3-element chain and a 1-element chain. The incomparability graph $\operatorname{inc}(P)$ of $P$ has vertex set equal to the elements of $P$, with two distinct vertices joined by an edge if and only if they are incomparable in $P$.

For a finite simple graph $G = (V,E)$ with $V = \{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$, the chromatic symmetric function is
$$X_G(x_1,x_2,\dots) = \sum_{\kappa} x_{\kappa(v_1)} x_{\kappa(v_2)} \cdots x_{\kappa(v_n)},$$
where the sum is over all proper colorings $\kappa : V \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ (those with $\kappa(u)\neq \kappa(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$). For a partition $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$, the elementary symmetric function is $e_\lambda = e_{\lambda_1} e_{\lambda_2}\cdots$, where $e_k = \sum_{i_1<\cdots<i_k} x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_k}$. A symmetric function $f$ is called $e$-positive if its expansion $f = \sum_\lambda c_\lambda e_\lambda$ in the basis $\{e_\lambda\}$ has all coefficients $c_\lambda \geq 0$.

Question: For every $(\mathbf{3}+\mathbf{1})$-free finite poset $P$, is the chromatic symmetric function $X_{\operatorname{inc}(P)}$ $e$-positive?
status_search_result: This is the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture. A proof was announced by Tatsuyuki Hikita in October 2024 (arXiv:2410.12758), giving a probabilistic interpretation of the $e$-coefficients of chromatic quasisymmetric functions of unit interval graphs and deriving $e$-positivity for incomparability graphs of $(3+1)$-free posets as a corollary.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: If G is a finite claw-free graph, meaning that G has no induced subgraph consisting of one vertex joined to three other vertices and no further edges, is the chromatic symmetric function X_G e-positive?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. The chromatic symmetric function of $G$ is defined by
$$X_G(x_1,x_2,\ldots) = \sum_{\kappa} \prod_{v\in V} x_{\kappa(v)},$$
where the sum ranges over all proper colorings $\kappa : V \to \{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ (i.e., colorings such that $\kappa(u)\ne \kappa(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$). Then $X_G$ is a homogeneous symmetric function of degree $|V|$ in the variables $x_1,x_2,\ldots$.

Let $\{e_\lambda\}$ denote the basis of elementary symmetric functions, indexed by integer partitions $\lambda$ of $|V|$, where $e_\lambda = e_{\lambda_1}e_{\lambda_2}\cdots$ and $e_k = \sum_{i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_k} x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_k}$. A symmetric function $f$ is called $e$-positive if all coefficients in its expansion $f=\sum_\lambda c_\lambda e_\lambda$ satisfy $c_\lambda \ge 0$.

A graph $G$ is said to be claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{1,3}$ (one vertex adjacent to three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, with no further edges among those four vertices).

Question: Is it true that for every finite claw-free graph $G$, the chromatic symmetric function $X_G$ is $e$-positive?
status_search_result: The question, a strengthening of the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture (which concerns claw-free incomparability graphs), remains open in full generality. Partial results have established e-positivity for various subclasses (e.g., (claw, P_4)-free graphs and other H-free families), and Guay-Paquet reduced the incomparability case to unit interval graphs, but no proof or counterexample is known for arbitrary claw-free graphs.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: If G is a claw-free graph and I(G,t) = Σ s_i t^i is its stable set polynomial, where s_i counts independent i-element vertex sets, does I(G,t) have only real zeros?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A subset $S$ of the vertex set $V(G)$ is called independent (or stable) if no two vertices of $S$ are adjacent in $G$. For each integer $i \ge 0$, let $s_i = s_i(G)$ denote the number of independent subsets of $V(G)$ of cardinality $i$ (with $s_0 = 1$). The stable set polynomial (independence polynomial) of $G$ is
$$ I(G,t) = \sum_{i \ge 0} s_i\, t^i. $$
The graph $G$ is called claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to the complete bipartite graph $K_{1,3}$ (the "claw").

Prove or disprove: for every claw-free graph $G$, all zeros of the polynomial $I(G,t)$ are real numbers.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let A be an n × n real matrix whose columns are all weakly increasing, let J denote the n × n all-ones matrix, and let per denote the permanent. Does the polynomial per(A + tJ) always have only real zeros?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with real entries such that each column is weakly increasing, i.e. $a_{1j}\le a_{2j}\le\cdots\le a_{nj}$ for every $j=1,\dots,n$. Let $J$ denote the $n\times n$ all-ones matrix, and for a square matrix $M=(m_{ij})$ let
$$\operatorname{per}(M)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n m_{i,\sigma(i)}$$
denote its permanent. Prove or disprove: the polynomial
$$P(t)=\operatorname{per}(A+tJ)\in\mathbb{R}[t]$$
has only real zeros.
status_search_result: This is the Monotone Column Permanent (MCP) conjecture, originally posed by Haglund, Ono, and Wagner (1999). It was proved in full generality by Brändén, Haglund, Visontai, and Wagner (arXiv:1010.2565, 2010), who established that per(A+zJ) is real-rooted by showing a stronger multivariate stability statement.

paper_title: Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Are the following sequences always unimodal or log-concave: (a) the absolute values of the coefficients of the chromatic polynomial of a graph, or more generally the characteristic polynomial of a matroid; (b) the numbers of edge-spanning forests of a graph, or more generally the numbers of independent sets of a matroid; and (c) the numbers of elements of rank i in a geometric lattice?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be a matroid on a finite ground set E with rank function r and rank n = r(E). Define:

(a) The characteristic polynomial of M is χ_M(t) = Σ_{F ⊆ E} (−1)^{|F|} t^{n − r(F)} (equivalently, summed over flats with Möbius coefficients). When M is the cycle matroid of a graph G, χ_M(t) is, up to a power of t, the chromatic polynomial of G. Write χ_M(t) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} (−1)^i w_i t^{n−i} with w_i ≥ 0.

(b) For each k ≥ 0, let f_k(M) denote the number of independent sets of M of size k. When M is the cycle matroid of a graph G, f_k counts the spanning forests of G with k edges.

(c) Let L be a finite geometric lattice (i.e., a finite atomistic, semimodular lattice; equivalently the lattice of flats of a simple matroid) of rank n, and let W_i denote the number of elements of L of rank i.

Recall that a finite sequence a_0, a_1, ..., a_n of nonnegative reals is unimodal if there exists j with a_0 ≤ ... ≤ a_j ≥ ... ≥ a_n, and log-concave if a_i^2 ≥ a_{i−1} a_{i+1} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1.

Determine, for each of the following three sequences, whether it is always unimodal and whether it is always log-concave:
(a) (w_0, w_1, ..., w_n), the absolute values of the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of an arbitrary matroid M;
(b) (f_0(M), f_1(M), ..., f_n(M)), the numbers of independent sets of an arbitrary matroid M;
(c) (W_0, W_1, ..., W_n), the rank-level numbers (Whitney numbers of the second kind) of an arbitrary finite geometric lattice L.
category_tag: Log-concavity for matroids and geometric lattices
status_search_result: Part (a) (Rota–Heron–Welsh conjecture: log-concavity of the absolute coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of any matroid) was proved by Adiprasito, Huh, and Katz (2015, "Hodge Theory for Combinatorial Geometries"), extending Huh's earlier results for representable matroids. Part (b) (Mason's conjecture on log-concavity—indeed ultra-log-concavity—of the f-vector of independent sets of a matroid) was proved independently by Anari–Liu–Oveis Gharan–Vinzant and by Brändén–Huh (2018–2020). Part (c) (log-concavity, or even unimodality, of the Whitney numbers of the second kind W_i of a geometric lattice) remains open in general; Rota's conjecture on unimodality of the W_i for geometric lattices is still considered an outstanding problem.

context_brief: Lower bounds for the distance of log n to the nearest integer.
original_question: Let ||x|| denote the distance from a real number x to the nearest integer. Does there exist a positive absolute constant c such that ||log n|| > n^(-c) for every integer n >= 2?
self_contained_problem:
For a real number $x$, let $\|x\|$ denote the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer, i.e. $\|x\| = \min_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - m|$. Does there exist a positive absolute constant $c > 0$ such that
$$\|\log n\| > n^{-c}$$
for every integer $n \geq 2$, where $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm?
status_search_result: The question of an effective lower bound of the form $\|\log n\| > n^{-c}$ for all integers $n \geq 2$ appears to remain open. Standard results from the theory of linear forms in logarithms (Baker, Matveev, etc.) yield much weaker bounds of the form $\|\log n\| \gg (\log n)^{-C}$ rather than polynomial-in-$n$ bounds; no proof of a polynomial bound is known, nor a counterexample.

context_brief: Uniform bound on the number of exponential Diophantine solutions.
original_question: Let D and k be positive integers and let p be a prime with gcd(D, kp) = 1. Prove that there exists an absolute constant C such that the Diophantine equation x^2 + D = k p^n has at most C integer solutions (x, n).

Let $D$ and $k$ be positive integers, and let $p$ be a prime number such that $\gcd(D, kp) = 1$. Consider integer solutions $(x, n)$, with $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $n$ a non-negative integer, of the exponential Diophantine equation
$$x^2 + D = k p^n.$$
Prove that there exists an absolute constant $C$ (independent of $D$, $k$, and $p$) such that, for every choice of $D$, $k$, and $p$ satisfying the conditions above, this equation has at most $C$ solutions $(x, n)$.
status_search_result: This is a long-standing open problem in the theory of exponential Diophantine equations. While it is known (via Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier and work of Bugeaud, Mignotte, Shorey and others) that the number of solutions is finite and that bounds depending on D, k, or the number of prime factors exist, the existence of a uniform absolute constant C independent of D, k, p does not appear to have been established. No published resolution was located in the search.

paper_title: SOME OPEN PROBLEMS ABOUT DIOPHANTINE EQUATIONS
context_brief: Conjectural finiteness and rigidity for ax^p + by^p = cz^2.
original_question: Consider the equation a x^p + b y^p = c z^2, where p is a prime and a, b, c are pairwise coprime integers. Let S_p(a, b, c) be the set of proper nontrivial integer solutions (x, y, z) with xyz != 0 and gcd(x, y, z) = 1. Prove the following conjectures. First, if none of a + b, a - b, and b - a belongs to cZ^2, then there exists a constant f(a, b, c) such that S_p(a, b, c) is empty for every prime p > f(a, b, c). Second, if one of a + b, a - b, and b - a belongs to cZ^2, then there exists a constant g(a, b, c) such that for every prime p > g(a, b, c), every solution (x, y, z) in S_p(a, b, c) satisfies xy = ±1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be pairwise coprime nonzero integers, and let $p$ be a prime number. Consider the Diophantine equation
$$a x^p + b y^p = c z^2.$$
Define $S_p(a,b,c)$ to be the set of integer triples $(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{Z}^3$ with $xyz \neq 0$ (nontrivial) and $\gcd(x,y,z) = 1$ (proper) that satisfy this equation. Prove the following two conjectures.

(i) Suppose that none of the integers $a+b$, $a-b$, $b-a$ lies in $c\mathbb{Z}^2 = \{c n^2 : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Then there exists a constant $f(a,b,c)$, depending only on $a,b,c$, such that for every prime $p > f(a,b,c)$, the set $S_p(a,b,c)$ is empty.

(ii) Suppose that at least one of the integers $a+b$, $a-b$, $b-a$ lies in $c\mathbb{Z}^2$. Then there exists a constant $g(a,b,c)$, depending only on $a,b,c$, such that for every prime $p > g(a,b,c)$ and every $(x,y,z) \in S_p(a,b,c)$, one has $xy = \pm 1$.
status_search_result: The conjectures fit within the broad framework of generalized Fermat / Fermat–Catalan-type equations $Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r$ with $1/p+1/q+1/r < 1$, whose finiteness is conjectured (and known to follow from the abc-conjecture) but unproven in general. For the signature $(p,p,2)$ with arbitrary pairwise coprime coefficients $a,b,c$, partial results exist via modularity and level-lowering for specific small coefficients, but the general uniform statements in (i) and (ii) appear to remain open.

paper_title: SOME OPEN PROBLEMS ABOUT DIOPHANTINE EQUATIONS
context_brief: Local-global principle for A X^2 + B Y^3 = C Z^5.
original_question: Fix nonzero integers A, B, and C. For the equation A X^2 + B Y^3 = C Z^5, with X, Y, Z required to be coprime integers, is the existence of a coprime integer solution equivalent to the existence of coprime p-adic solutions for every prime p? In other words, does a Hasse principle hold for this equation?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be fixed nonzero integers, and consider the Diophantine equation
$$A X^2 + B Y^3 = C Z^5$$
in unknowns $X, Y, Z$. By a coprime integer solution we mean a triple of integers $(X,Y,Z)$ with $\gcd(X,Y,Z)=1$ satisfying the equation, and by a coprime $p$-adic solution (for a prime $p$) we mean a triple $(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb{Z}_p^3$ satisfying the equation such that at least one of $X,Y,Z$ is a $p$-adic unit.

Question: Is it true that, for every choice of nonzero integers $A,B,C$, the existence of a coprime integer solution to $AX^2+BY^3=CZ^5$ is equivalent to the existence of a coprime $p$-adic solution for every prime $p$? In other words, does a Hasse (local-to-global) principle hold for this generalized Fermat-type equation of signature $(2,3,5)$?
status_search_result: No definitive resolution found. The equation of signature (2,3,5) sits in the "spherical" case 1/p+1/q+1/r > 1; while substantial work exists on individual instances (e.g., A=B=C=1 was treated by Bruin and others), the general local-global question for arbitrary nonzero integer coefficients A, B, C remains an open problem in the literature.

context_brief: Binomial coefficients equal to Fibonacci numbers.
original_question: Show that the equation F_n = C(m, k) has only finitely many integer solutions (n, m, k) with 2 <= k <= m/2, where F_n denotes the n-th Fibonacci number and C(m, k) is the binomial coefficient.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(F_n)_{n\ge 0}$ denote the Fibonacci sequence, defined by $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$ for $n \ge 0$. For integers $m \ge k \ge 0$, let $\binom{m}{k} = \frac{m!}{k!\,(m-k)!}$ denote the usual binomial coefficient. Prove that the Diophantine equation
$$F_n \;=\; \binom{m}{k}$$
has only finitely many solutions in integers $(n, m, k)$ subject to the restriction $2 \le k \le m/2$.

original_question: Among all continuous rectifiable plane curves that start at the center of the unit circle and are guaranteed to touch every tangent line to that circle, give a proof—using calculus of variations or optimal control—that the optimal curve has length 7π/6 + √3 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the unit circle $C = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1\}$ in the Euclidean plane, and let $O = (0,0)$ be its center. A "tangent line" to $C$ is any straight line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that intersects $C$ in exactly one point. Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the family of all continuous rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ such that:
(i) $\gamma(0) = O$, and
(ii) for every tangent line $\ell$ to $C$, the image $\gamma([0,1])$ meets $\ell$.

For $\gamma \in \mathcal{F}$, let $L(\gamma)$ denote its arc length. Prove, using techniques from the calculus of variations or optimal control theory, that
$$\inf_{\gamma \in \mathcal{F}} L(\gamma) \;=\; \frac{7\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3} + 1,$$
and that this infimum is attained by an explicit optimal curve.
status_search_result: The optimal length $7\pi/6+\sqrt{3}+1\approx 6.3972$ is the classical answer due to H. Joris ("Le chasseur perdu dans la forêt", 1980), with subsequent geometric/elementary proofs (Finch, Wetzel, and others). However, a proof obtained directly via the standard machinery of the calculus of variations or optimal control (e.g., Pontryagin's principle) does not appear in the literature; the question of producing such a proof remains open as far as searches indicate.

original_question: For the same optimization problem (P_N) that maximizes the angle-based energy F_N over configurations of N points in R^3, determine whether, as N tends to infinity, the maximizing configurations become uniformly distributed on a sphere and whether sup F_N = (2/9)N^3 + o(N^3).
self_contained_problem:
Let $N\ge 3$ be an integer. For an ordered configuration $X=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ of $N$ points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (which one may, after rescaling, restrict to lie in the closed unit ball, or on the unit sphere $S^2$), define the angle-based ("Coulombian") energy
$$F_N(X)\;=\;\sum_{\substack{(i,j,k)\\ i,j,k\text{ pairwise distinct}}}\angle(x_i,x_j,x_k),$$
where $\angle(x_i,x_j,x_k)\in[0,\pi]$ denotes the non-oriented angle at vertex $x_j$ formed by the segments $[x_j,x_i]$ and $[x_j,x_k]$ (with the convention $\angle=0$ whenever two of the three points coincide). Consider the optimization problem
$$(P_N)\qquad \text{maximize } F_N(X) \text{ over all configurations } X\subset\mathbb{R}^3 \text{ of }N \text{ points.}$$

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) As $N\to\infty$, every sequence $(X_N^\ast)_{N\ge 3}$ of maximizers of $(P_N)$, suitably rescaled, becomes uniformly distributed on a 2-sphere; that is, the empirical measures $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i^\ast}$ converge weakly to the normalized surface measure on a sphere.

(b) The maximum value satisfies the asymptotic estimate
$$\sup F_N\;=\;\tfrac{2}{9}\,N^3 + o(N^3)\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty.$$

The current status could not be confirmed as solved.

original_question: Find a proof, based entirely on constrained-optimization ideas such as higher-order optimality conditions, that every doubly stochastic n x n matrix A satisfies per(A) >= n!/n^n, with equality only at the matrix whose entries are all 1/n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer, and let $\Omega_n$ denote the set of $n \times n$ doubly stochastic matrices, i.e., matrices $A = (a_{ij})$ with nonnegative real entries such that every row sum and every column sum equals $1$. For a matrix $A \in \Omega_n$, define its permanent by
$$\operatorname{per}(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $J_n$ denote the $n \times n$ matrix all of whose entries equal $1/n$.

It is known that for every $A \in \Omega_n$,
$$\operatorname{per}(A) \geq \frac{n!}{n^n},$$
with equality if and only if $A = J_n$.

Produce a proof of this inequality (and of the equality case) that proceeds entirely by techniques of constrained optimization. Specifically, view $\operatorname{per}$ as the objective function on the convex polytope $\Omega_n$ (a multilinear form in the rows and columns), and derive the bound using only constrained-optimization tools such as Lagrange multipliers and first-, second-, or higher-order necessary/sufficient optimality conditions at critical points of $\operatorname{per}$ on $\Omega_n$, without appealing to algebraic identities, hyperbolic polynomial theory, geometric programming duality, or other non-optimization machinery.
category_tag: Permanent of doubly stochastic matrices / optimization proofs
status_search_result: The Van der Waerden inequality itself is a theorem (Egorychev 1981, Falikman 1981), with subsequent simplifications by Gyires, Bapat, and others, and a geometric-programming approach by Gurvits. However, the specific request for a proof relying purely on higher-order constrained-optimality conditions for the multilinear objective on the doubly stochastic polytope does not appear to have a clearly documented affirmative answer in the literature; existing "optimization" proofs (geometric programming, hyperbolic polynomials) use additional algebraic structure beyond optimality conditions. Status of this precise question is unclear from the search.

$$\mathrm{tr}\!\left(e^{A - \lambda B}\right) = \int_{[0,+\infty)} e^{-\lambda t}\, d\mu(t)$$

original_question: For every unit vector a = (a_1, ..., a_n) in R^n and independent random signs X_1, ..., X_n with P(X_i = 1) = P(X_i = -1) = 1/2, is it always true that P(|Σ_i X_i a_i| <= 1) >= 1/2? Equivalently, do at least half of the 2^n sign choices ε_i ∈ {-1, +1} satisfy |Σ_i ε_i a_i| <= 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 1$ and let $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be a unit vector, i.e. $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 = 1$. Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables with $\mathbb{P}(X_i = 1) = \mathbb{P}(X_i = -1) = 1/2$. Prove or disprove that
$$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^n X_i a_i\right| \leq 1\right) \geq \frac{1}{2}.$$
Equivalently, show that for every such unit vector $a$, at least half of the $2^n$ sign sequences $\varepsilon = (\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n) \in \{-1,+1\}^n$ satisfy $\left|\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i a_i\right| \leq 1$.
status_search_result: This is Tomaszewski's conjecture (1986). It was proved by Nathan Keller and Ohad Klein in 2020 (arXiv:2006.16834), with the final version published in Advances in Mathematics (2022). Their proof combines a refined Berry–Esseen inequality for Rademacher sums, local concentration inequalities, and an inductive stopping-time argument.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: If A and B are normal n x n matrices with eigenvalues a_1, ..., a_n and b_1, ..., b_n respectively, must det(A - B) belong to the convex hull of the n! products Π_i (a_i - b_{σ(i)}) over all permutations σ of {1, ..., n}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be normal $n\times n$ complex matrices, with eigenvalues $a_1,\dots,a_n$ and $b_1,\dots,b_n$ respectively (listed with multiplicity). Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and for each $\sigma\in S_n$ define
$$p_\sigma \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^n \bigl(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)}\bigr)\in\mathbb{C}.$$
Let $\mathrm{co}\{p_\sigma:\sigma\in S_n\}$ denote the convex hull in $\mathbb{C}$ of the (at most) $n!$ complex numbers $p_\sigma$. Prove or disprove: for every choice of such normal matrices $A,B$,
$$\det(A-B)\;\in\;\mathrm{co}\{\,p_\sigma : \sigma\in S_n\,\}.$$
status_search_result: The Marcus–de Oliveira determinantal conjecture (equivalent up to sign change of B to the statement about det(A+B)) remains open in general. It is known to hold for n ≤ 3, when all eigenvalues are real, and for various classes of essentially Hermitian matrices. Surveys and recent papers (e.g., a 2025 MDPI Mathematics paper revisiting the conjecture, and a Springer survey) continue to describe it as an active, unresolved problem.

paper_title: Some Conjectures and Problems in Complex Geometry
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety over C. Must one of the following two alternatives always hold: either X is uniruled, or X is birational to a projective variety X_min such that X_min is Q-factorial, has only terminal singularities, and its canonical divisor K_{X_min} is nef?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$. Recall that $X$ is called uniruled if there exists a dominant rational map $Y \times \mathbb{P}^1 \dashrightarrow X$ for some variety $Y$ of dimension $\dim X - 1$. A normal projective variety $X_{\min}$ is said to be $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial if every Weil divisor on $X_{\min}$ has an integer multiple that is Cartier; it has only terminal singularities if for some (equivalently, any) resolution of singularities $f: \widetilde{X} \to X_{\min}$ with $K_{\widetilde{X}} = f^*K_{X_{\min}} + \sum a_i E_i$ over the exceptional locus, every discrepancy $a_i$ is strictly positive. A $\mathbb{Q}$-Cartier divisor $D$ on a projective variety is nef if $D \cdot C \geq 0$ for every irreducible curve $C$.

Prove or disprove: for every smooth projective variety $X$ over $\mathbb{C}$, at least one of the following holds:
(1) $X$ is uniruled; or
(2) there exists a projective variety $X_{\min}$ birational to $X$ such that $X_{\min}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, has only terminal singularities, and the canonical divisor $K_{X_{\min}}$ is nef.
status_search_result: The conjecture is established in dimension at most 3 (Mori and collaborators) and, for varieties of general type in arbitrary dimension, follows from the work of Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan. The general case for non-uniruled smooth projective varieties of dimension at least 4 remains open. Recent surveys and works on the minimal model program continue to list it as an outstanding conjecture.
