paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: Consider entire smooth solutions u:R²→R²≃C of -Δu = u(1-|u|²) on R² such that |u(x)|→1 as |x|→∞, so the degree at infinity q=deg(u,∞) is well defined. Must every such solution coincide, up to a translation x↦x-x₀ and multiplication by a unit complex number α, with the standard radial degree-q solution V_q?
self_contained_problem:
Let $u:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\cong\mathbb{C}$ be a smooth entire solution of the Ginzburg–Landau equation
$$-\Delta u = u\,(1-|u|^2)\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}^2,$$
satisfying $|u(x)|\to 1$ as $|x|\to\infty$. Under this condition the topological degree at infinity $q:=\deg(u,\infty)\in\mathbb{Z}$ is well defined. For each $q\in\mathbb{Z}$ let $V_q$ denote the standard radially symmetric "vortex" solution of degree $q$ given in polar coordinates by
$$V_q(r,\theta)=e^{iq\theta}\,g_q(r),\quad q\neq 0,\qquad V_0\equiv 1,$$
where $g_q:[0,\infty)\to[0,1)$ is the unique solution of
$$g_q''+\tfrac{1}{r}g_q'-\tfrac{q^2}{r^2}g_q+g_q(1-g_q^2)=0,\quad g_q(0)=0,\ g_q(\infty)=1.$$
Question: Must every such solution $u$ coincide with $V_q$ (with $q=\deg(u,\infty)$) up to translation and multiplication by a unit complex number? That is, must there exist $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\alpha|=1$ and $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $u(x)=\alpha\,V_q(x-x_0)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$?
status_search_result: The full classification of entire Ginzburg–Landau solutions on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with prescribed degree at infinity is widely cited as open. Mironescu proved uniqueness up to symmetry within the class of local minimizers of degree one; subsequent works extended minimizer-uniqueness/symmetry results to higher dimensions ($N=3$ by Millot–Pisante, $N\ge 4$ and $N\ge 7$ for $\varepsilon>0$ by Ignat–Nguyen–Slastikov–Zarnescu). However, for general (not necessarily minimizing) solutions of arbitrary degree $q$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the classification remains an open problem.

with λ > 0 chosen so that the boundary values reduce to g on ∂Ω (i.e. so that the trace equals (Rx, Ry, √(1 − R²))). The second is the "reflected" solution ū obtained by composing u with the reflection (a, b, c) ↦ (a, b, −c) followed by an appropriate inversion, which also satisfies the same boundary condition g but is not energy-minimizing.

Question: Does the Dirichlet problem above admit any smooth solution u : Ω̄ → S² other than the two explicit solutions u and ū?

The question appears to remain open.

context_brief: Continuous harmonic maps with degree-zero boundary data
original_question: Let Ω=B³ be the unit ball in R³ and let g:∂Ω≃S²→S² be smooth with degree zero. Does there exist a continuous map u:Ω̄→S² that is harmonic in Ω, satisfies -Δu_i = u_i|∇u|² for i=1,2,3, has |u|=1 in Ω, and obeys the boundary condition u=g on ∂Ω?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega = B^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the open unit ball, and let $g : \partial\Omega = S^2 \to S^2$ be a smooth map of topological degree zero. A map $u : \overline{\Omega} \to S^2$ is called a (weakly) harmonic map into the sphere if $|u(x)| = 1$ for all $x \in \Omega$ and $u$ satisfies the harmonic map system
$$-\Delta u_i = u_i\,|\nabla u|^2 \qquad (i=1,2,3) \quad \text{in } \Omega.$$
Question: Does there exist a continuous map $u : \overline{\Omega} \to S^2$ that is harmonic in $\Omega$ in the above sense and satisfies the Dirichlet boundary condition $u = g$ on $\partial\Omega$?
status_search_result: The question of whether every smooth degree-zero boundary datum $g:S^2\to S^2$ admits a continuous harmonic extension $u:\overline{B^3}\to S^2$ is a long-standing problem attributed to Hardt–Lin and repeatedly listed by Brezis as open. Known results in the opposite direction (Hardt–Lin, Almgren–Lieb, Bethuel, and the Lavrentiev gap phenomenon results of Mazowiecka–Strzelecki, 2014/2017) show that for a dense set of degree-zero boundary data the energy-minimizing harmonic extension is singular, but these results do not produce or exclude a (non-minimizing) continuous harmonic extension. No resolution of the existence question itself appears in the literature; it remains open.

original_question: Define the relaxed energy R on H¹_g(Ω;S²) by taking the lower semicontinuous relaxation of the Dirichlet energy with respect to weak H¹ limits of continuous S²-valued maps, and consider minimizers of Min{R(u): u∈H¹_g(Ω;S²)}. Must every minimizer of this relaxed problem be continuous on Ω̄, or at least is there always at least one continuous minimizer?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth bounded domain and let $g : \partial\Omega \to S^2$ be a smooth boundary datum, where $S^2$ denotes the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Consider the space
$$H^1_g(\Omega;S^2) = \{u \in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^3) : |u(x)| = 1 \text{ a.e.},\ u|_{\partial\Omega} = g\}.$$
For $u \in H^1_g(\Omega;S^2)$, define the relaxed energy
$$R(u) = \inf\Big\{ \liminf_{k\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u_k|^2\,dx : u_k \in C^0(\overline\Omega;S^2) \cap H^1_g(\Omega;S^2),\ u_k \rightharpoonup u \text{ weakly in } H^1 \Big\},$$
i.e. the lower semicontinuous envelope of the Dirichlet energy, restricted to weak $H^1$ limits of continuous $S^2$-valued maps with boundary value $g$. The functional $R$ is weakly lower semicontinuous on $H^1_g(\Omega;S^2)$ and attains its infimum.

Question: Must every minimizer of $\min\{R(u) : u \in H^1_g(\Omega;S^2)\}$ be continuous on $\overline\Omega$? If not in general, is there always at least one minimizer that is continuous on $\overline\Omega$?

context_brief: Vanishing singular part for relaxed-energy minimizers
original_question: Let u be a minimizer of the relaxed-energy problem Min{R(u):u∈H¹_g(Ω;S²)}, where R(u)=∫Ω|∇u|²+S(u) and J_u=(1/3)div D(u) is the associated distributional Jacobian. Must S(u)=0, equivalently J_u=0, or equivalently can every such minimizer be approximated strongly in H¹ by continuous maps u_n∈H¹_g(Ω;S²)∩C(Ω̄)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth bounded domain and let $g: \partial\Omega \to S^2$ be a smooth boundary datum. Consider the Sobolev space
$$H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) = \{u \in H^1(\Omega; \mathbb{R}^3) : |u|=1 \text{ a.e. in } \Omega,\ u = g \text{ on } \partial\Omega\}.$$
For $u \in H^1_g(\Omega; S^2)$ define the distributional vector field
$$D(u) = \big(u \cdot (u_{x_2} \wedge u_{x_3}),\ u \cdot (u_{x_3} \wedge u_{x_1}),\ u \cdot (u_{x_1} \wedge u_{x_2})\big),$$
and the (distributional) Jacobian
$$J_u = \tfrac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{div}\, D(u).$$
For maps $u$ smooth away from a finite set of point singularities $\{a_i\}$ with topological degrees $d_i \in \mathbb{Z}$, one has $J_u = \pi \sum_i d_i \,\delta_{a_i}$ (after accounting for the boundary contribution from $g$). Let $L(u)$ denote the minimal connection (length) associated with the singularities of $u$ relative to $g$, and define the relaxed energy
$$R(u) = \int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2 \, dx + 8\pi L(u) = \int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx + S(u),$$
where $S(u) \ge 0$ is the singular (defect) part, and $S(u) = 0$ if and only if $J_u = 0$ (equivalently, $u$ can be strongly approximated in $H^1$ by maps in $H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) \cap C(\overline{\Omega})$).

Question: Let $u$ be a minimizer of $R$ over $H^1_g(\Omega; S^2)$. Must one have $S(u) = 0$ (equivalently, $J_u = 0$, equivalently, there exists a sequence $(u_n) \subset H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) \cap C(\overline{\Omega})$ with $u_n \to u$ strongly in $H^1$)?

status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem in Brezis's collection of favorite open problems. Related work (e.g., Giaquinta–Modica–Souček, Bethuel–Brezis–Coron, and partial regularity results) provides partial information about minimizers of the relaxed energy, but the question of whether $S(u)=0$ for every minimizer in this setting has not been resolved.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Optimal degree estimate via thresholded nonlocal energy
original_question: For continuous maps f:S¹→S¹, Theorem 5.2 gives an estimate |deg f| ≤ C ∬ [|f(x)-f(y)|≥√3]/|x-y|². Is there a simpler and more geometric proof of this theorem? What is the optimal constant C in that inequality, and is the optimal constant attained?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ denote the unit circle, and let $f : S^1 \to S^1$ be a continuous map of topological degree $\deg f \in \mathbb{Z}$. Consider the nonlocal functional
$$ I(f) \; = \; \iint_{S^1 \times S^1} \frac{\mathbf{1}_{\{|f(x)-f(y)| \,\geq\, \sqrt{3}\}}}{|x-y|^2}\, d\sigma(x)\, d\sigma(y), $$
where $|\cdot|$ denotes Euclidean distance in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\sigma$ is arclength measure. It is known that there exists a finite constant $C > 0$ such that
$$ |\deg f| \;\leq\; C \cdot I(f) \qquad \text{for every continuous } f : S^1 \to S^1. \tag{$\ast$} $$
(a) Provide a simple geometric proof of inequality $(\ast)$.
(b) Determine the optimal (smallest) constant $C$ for which $(\ast)$ holds for all such maps $f$.
(c) Decide whether this optimal constant is attained by some continuous map $f : S^1 \to S^1$, and if so exhibit such an extremal map.
category_tag: Topological degree estimates via nonlocal functionals
status_search_result: The threshold $\sqrt{3}$ is known to be sharp (Nguyen's work showed the threshold $\ell_N = \sqrt{2+2/(N+1)}$ is optimal, giving $\sqrt 3$ for $N=1$), and refined estimates have been pursued (e.g. arXiv:2210.08138 on "refined estimate for topological degree in one dimension"). However, the exact value of the optimal constant $C$ in the displayed estimate, whether it is attained, and a simpler geometric proof of the original theorem do not appear to be established in the literature; the problem is restated as open in Brezis's collection of favorite open problems.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Can one hear the degree beyond the 1/3 threshold?
original_question: Suppose f,g:S¹→S¹ have identical Fourier-modulus data |a_n(f)|=|a_n(g)| for every n∈Z. Does the positive conclusion of Theorem 5.5, namely deg f = deg g, remain valid when f and g lie only in the larger classes W^{1/p,p}(S¹;S¹) with p>3 or C^{0,α}(S¹;S¹) with α≤1/3? The problem is open even in mixed-regularity cases such as f∈W^{1/p,p} with 2<p≤3 and g∈W^{1/q,q} with q>3, or f∈C^{0,α} with α>1/3 and g∈C^{0,β} with β≤1/3.
self_contained_problem:
Let S^1 denote the unit circle in the complex plane. For a measurable map f : S^1 → S^1, write its Fourier series as f(e^{iθ}) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} a_n(f) e^{inθ}, with Fourier coefficients a_n(f) ∈ ℂ.

For 1 ≤ p < ∞, let W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) denote the fractional Sobolev space of measurable maps f : S^1 → S^1 with |f| = 1 a.e. such that
   ∫∫_{S^1×S^1} |f(x) − f(y)|^p / |x − y|^2 dx dy < ∞.

For 0 < α ≤ 1, let C^{0,α}(S^1; S^1) be the space of Hölder continuous maps from S^1 to S^1 with exponent α. Each map in W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) (for p > 1) or C^{0,α}(S^1; S^1) (for α > 0) has a well-defined topological degree deg f ∈ ℤ.

It is known that if f, g ∈ W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) with 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, or if f, g ∈ C^{0,α}(S^1; S^1) with α > 1/3, and |a_n(f)| = |a_n(g)| for every n ∈ ℤ, then deg f = deg g.

Question. Does the conclusion deg f = deg g continue to hold under the weaker assumption that:
(a) f, g ∈ W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) with p > 3, or
(b) f, g ∈ C^{0,α}(S^1; S^1) with α ≤ 1/3?

The mixed-regularity versions are also of interest: does deg f = deg g hold when
(a') f ∈ W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) with 2 < p ≤ 3 and g ∈ W^{1/q,q}(S^1; S^1) with q > 3, or
(b') f ∈ C^{0,α}(S^1; S^1) with α > 1/3 and g ∈ C^{0,β}(S^1; S^1) with β ≤ 1/3,
in each case under the assumption |a_n(f)| = |a_n(g)| for all n ∈ ℤ?
status_search_result: For merely continuous maps, Bourgain and Kozma constructed counterexamples showing one cannot recover the winding number from the Fourier modulus. However, the precise fractional Sobolev/Hölder thresholds (W^{1/p,p} with p > 3, and C^{0,α} with α ≤ 1/3, including the mixed-regularity cases) appear to remain open as of the latest references in the Brezis–Mironescu monograph on Sobolev maps to the circle.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Universal summation processes for degree recovery
original_question: A summation process is a family (σ_{n,ε})_{n∈Z,0<ε<1} such that for each ε, sup_n |n||σ_{n,ε}|<∞ and for each fixed n, σ_{n,ε}→1 as ε→0. For any p>3, or for Hölder regularity exponent α≤1/3, does there exist a summation process depending only on p (respectively only on α) such that lim_{ε→0} Σ_{n∈Z} n|a_n(f)|²σ_{n,ε} = deg f for every f in W^{1/p,p}(S¹;S¹) (respectively every f in C^{0,α}(S¹;S¹))?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^1$ denote the unit circle. For a measurable map $f:S^1\to S^1\subset\mathbb{C}$, write its Fourier expansion $f(\theta)\sim\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} a_n(f)\,e^{in\theta}$. When $f$ is sufficiently regular (for instance $f\in W^{1/2,2}(S^1;S^1)$), its topological degree admits the representation
$$\deg f=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} n\,|a_n(f)|^2,$$
and the series converges absolutely. Outside this regularity, the series need not converge and a summation procedure is needed.

Call a family $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})_{n\in\mathbb{Z},\,0<\varepsilon<1}$ of real numbers a "summation process" if
(i) for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} |n|\,|\sigma_{n,\varepsilon}|<\infty$, and
(ii) for every fixed $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon}\to 1$ as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$.

Question (two parts):
(a) Given any real $p>3$, does there exist a summation process $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})$, depending only on $p$, such that
$$\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} n\,|a_n(f)|^2\,\sigma_{n,\varepsilon}=\deg f$$
holds for every $f\in W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1)$?

(b) Given any Hölder exponent $\alpha\le 1/3$, does there exist a summation process $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})$, depending only on $\alpha$, such that the same identity holds for every $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(S^1;S^1)$?
status_search_result: Web search surfaces the problem list where this question is stated as an open problem, together with a recent preprint announcing a solution to Brezis' "first" open problem from the same list; no source claims a resolution of this specific summation-process question for $W^{1/p,p}$ (p>3) or $C^{0,\alpha}$ ($\alpha\le 1/3$). It therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: Given an individual map f∈C(S¹;S¹), or more generally f∈VMO(S¹;S¹), does there always exist some summation process (σ_{n,ε}) depending on that particular f such that lim_{ε→0} Σ_{n∈Z} n|a_n(f)|²σ_{n,ε} equals deg f?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^1$ denote the unit circle in $\mathbb{C}$. For a measurable map $f:S^1\to S^1$, write its Fourier expansion
$$ f(\theta) \sim \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} a_n(f)\, e^{in\theta}, \qquad a_n(f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta) e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta. $$
Recall that the space $\mathrm{VMO}(S^1)$ consists of locally integrable functions of vanishing mean oscillation, and that for $f\in C(S^1;S^1)$ (or, more generally, $f\in\mathrm{VMO}(S^1;S^1)$) the topological degree $\deg f\in\mathbb{Z}$ is well defined.

By a "summation process" we mean a family $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})_{n\in\mathbb{Z},\,0<\varepsilon<1}$ of real (or complex) numbers, suitably regular in $n$ and depending on the small parameter $\varepsilon$, such that for each fixed $n$, $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon}\to 1$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$, and such that for each fixed $\varepsilon$ the weighted sum below converges absolutely.

It is classical that, for $f\in C(S^1;S^1)$ (or $f\in\mathrm{VMO}(S^1;S^1)$),
$$ \deg f \stackrel{\text{formally}}{=} \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} n |a_n(f)|^2, $$
but the series on the right need not converge absolutely.

Question: Given an individual map $f\in C(S^1;S^1)$ (respectively $f\in \mathrm{VMO}(S^1;S^1)$), does there always exist a summation process $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})$, possibly depending on $f$, such that
$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} n\, |a_n(f)|^2\, \sigma_{n,\varepsilon} \;=\; \deg f \;? $$
category_tag: Fourier series and topological degree of VMO maps
status_search_result: The question appears in Brezis's list of favorite open problems (Open Problem 5.7) and is referenced in related work on winding numbers and Fourier series. Related summation-process problems on this topic are also formulated as open. No source found that resolves the existence of an f-dependent summation process for general continuous or VMO maps from S^1 to S^1.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Universal counterexample to Fourier recovery of degree
original_question: Does there exist a continuous, or even merely VMO, map f:S¹→S¹ with the following universal obstruction property: for every summation process (σ_{n,ε}), the quantities Σ_{n∈Z} n|a_n(f)|²σ_{n,ε} fail to converge to deg f?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^1 = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z|=1\}$. For a map $f \in L^2(S^1; \mathbb{C})$ write its Fourier series $f(e^{i\theta}) \sim \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n(f)\, e^{in\theta}$, where $a_n(f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(e^{i\theta})\, e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta$.

For $f \in C(S^1; S^1)$ (continuous maps from the unit circle to itself), or more generally $f \in \mathrm{VMO}(S^1; S^1)$ (maps of vanishing mean oscillation taking values a.e. in $S^1$), the topological degree $\deg f \in \mathbb{Z}$ is well-defined (extending the classical definition from smooth maps by density in BMO).

By a "summation process" we mean a family $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})_{n \in \mathbb{Z},\ \varepsilon \in (0,1)}$ of real (or complex) weights with the following properties:
(i) for each $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, only finitely many $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon}$ are nonzero (or, more generally, the weights ensure absolute convergence of the formal series below);
(ii) for each fixed $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon} \to 1$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$;
(iii) the family is regular in the sense that for every smooth $g \in C^\infty(S^1; S^1)$ one has $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} n\, |a_n(g)|^2\, \sigma_{n,\varepsilon} \to \deg g$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.

(Typical examples include Abel summation $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon} = e^{-\varepsilon |n|}$, Cesàro summation, and sharp truncations $\sigma_{n,\varepsilon} = \mathbf{1}_{|n| \le 1/\varepsilon}$.)

Question: Does there exist a single map $f \in C(S^1; S^1)$ (respectively $f \in \mathrm{VMO}(S^1; S^1)$) such that for every summation process $(\sigma_{n,\varepsilon})$ as above, the quantity
$$\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} n\,|a_n(f)|^2\, \sigma_{n,\varepsilon}$$
fails to converge to $\deg f$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$?
category_tag: Fourier series and topological degree of VMO maps
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem in Brezis's collection of favorite open problems and arises from the Brezis–Nirenberg VMO degree theory. A 2010 work (Korevaar, "Winding numbers and Fourier series") and a 2025 arXiv preprint on "Brezis' First Open Problem" treat related questions about degree from Fourier coefficients, but no source found resolves this specific universal-counterexample formulation. Status appears to remain open.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Distance between H¹ homotopy classes on S²
original_question: Let E_d={f∈H¹(S²;S²):deg f=d}. Is it true that the homotopy-class distance defined by Dist_{H¹}(E_{d1},E_{d2}) = sup_{f∈E_{d1}} inf_{g∈E_{d2}} ||∇(f-g)||_{L²} satisfies Dist_{H¹}(E_{d1},E_{d2})² = 8π|d1-d2| for all integers d1,d2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$, equipped with its standard area measure. For a map $f \in H^1(S^2; S^2)$ (i.e. $f \in H^1(S^2; \mathbb{R}^3)$ with $|f(x)|=1$ a.e.), its (Brouwer) degree $\deg f \in \mathbb{Z}$ is well-defined, and for each integer $d$ define the homotopy class
$$E_d = \{ f \in H^1(S^2; S^2) : \deg f = d \}.$$
For two integers $d_1, d_2$ define the asymmetric homotopy-class distance
$$\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}(E_{d_1}, E_{d_2}) = \sup_{f \in E_{d_1}} \inf_{g \in E_{d_2}} \|\nabla(f - g)\|_{L^2(S^2)}.$$
Decide whether the identity
$$\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}(E_{d_1}, E_{d_2})^2 = 8\pi |d_1 - d_2|$$
holds for every pair of integers $d_1, d_2$.
status_search_result: The conjectured equality $\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}(E_{d_1}, E_{d_2})^2 = 8\pi|d_1-d_2|$ is recorded as an open problem by Brezis–Mironescu–Shafrir, who establish the upper bound $\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}^2 \le 8\pi|d_1-d_2|$ via a construction with bubbling concentration but leave the matching lower bound as a conjecture. No subsequent work has been located that resolves the full equality, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Brouwer-type fixed-point property for VMO maps
original_question: Let B be the closed unit ball in Rᴺ and let f:B→B be a VMO map. Must it be true that for every ε>0 the set {x∈B : |f(x)-x|<ε} has positive measure?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N \geq 1$ and let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be the closed unit ball. Recall that a measurable map $f : B \to \mathbb{R}^N$ belongs to $\mathrm{VMO}(B)$ (the space of maps with vanishing mean oscillation) if 
\[
\lim_{r \to 0^+} \sup_{x_0 \in B,\, 0 < \rho < r} \frac{1}{|B(x_0,\rho) \cap B|} \int_{B(x_0,\rho) \cap B} \Big| f(y) - \fint_{B(x_0,\rho) \cap B} f \Big| \, dy = 0,
\]
where $\fint$ denotes the average and $B(x_0,\rho)$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $\rho$ centered at $x_0$. Suppose $f : B \to B$ is a VMO map (taking values in $B$). Is it true that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the set 
\[
\{ x \in B : |f(x) - x| < \varepsilon \}
\]
has positive Lebesgue measure?
status_search_result: The problem is stated as Open Problem 5.10 in Brezis' "Some of my favorite open problems" (published in the EMS volume). A web search did not turn up any paper resolving this specific VMO Brouwer-type fixed-point question; the status appears to remain open. (Note: a recent arXiv preprint resolves Brezis' First Open Problem, but not this one.)

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Unbounded extremal solutions in high dimensions
original_question: Consider the extremal solution u* associated with -Δu = λf(u) in a smooth bounded convex domain Ω⊂Rᴺ, with u>0 in Ω, u=0 on ∂Ω, and f(u)=eᵘ. When N≥10, must u* be unbounded? If some convex domains give a bounded extremal solution for f(u)=eᵘ, can one instead find another increasing convex nonlinearity f satisfying the stated hypotheses for which u* is unbounded on that domain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N\ge 10$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a smooth bounded convex domain. For a nonlinearity $f\in C^1([0,\infty))$ that is positive, increasing, convex, and superlinear at infinity (i.e. $f(t)/t\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$), consider the family of problems
$$-\Delta u = \lambda f(u)\ \text{in }\Omega,\qquad u>0\ \text{in }\Omega,\qquad u=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega,$$
parametrized by $\lambda>0$. It is known that there exists a finite extremal parameter $\lambda^*=\lambda^*(\Omega,f)>0$ such that for $\lambda\in(0,\lambda^*)$ the problem has a minimal classical solution $u_\lambda$, and the pointwise increasing limit
$$u^*(x)=\lim_{\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*}u_\lambda(x)$$
defines the so-called extremal solution.

(a) Taking $f(u)=e^u$, is $u^*\notin L^\infty(\Omega)$ for every smooth bounded convex domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\ge 10$?

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative — i.e. if there exists some smooth bounded convex $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\ge 10$ for which the extremal solution corresponding to $f(u)=e^u$ is bounded — does there nevertheless exist, for every such domain $\Omega$, another nonlinearity $f$ (possibly depending on $\Omega$) satisfying the hypotheses above for which the associated extremal solution $u^*$ fails to belong to $L^\infty(\Omega)$?
category_tag: Extremal solutions of semilinear elliptic equations
status_search_result: The question is known to be settled in the radial (ball) case, where the extremal solution for $f(u)=e^u$ is singular for $N\ge 10$. The complementary result that the extremal solution is bounded for all $f$ and all smooth domains when $N\le 9$ was established by Cabré–Figalli–Ros-Oton–Serra. However, for general smooth bounded convex domains in dimension $N\ge 10$, whether $u^*$ must be unbounded (for $f(u)=e^u$, or for some admissible $f$) does not appear to have been resolved; recent work on Brezis' "first open problem" addresses a different question on the list, and standard references still treat 6.1 as open.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Geometry of blow-up sets for extremal solutions
original_question: Assume the extremal solution u* of the semilinear Dirichlet problem is unbounded. What can be said about its blow-up set, and in particular, if Ω is convex, must that blow-up set reduce to a single point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a smooth bounded domain, and let $f:[0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ function which is nondecreasing, convex, and superlinear at infinity (i.e., $f(t)/t \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$). Consider the family of semilinear Dirichlet problems
$$ -\Delta u = \lambda f(u) \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega, \qquad u \geq 0 \text{ in } \Omega, $$
parametrized by $\lambda > 0$. It is known that there exists a critical parameter $\lambda^* \in (0,\infty)$ such that for $0 < \lambda < \lambda^*$ there is a minimal classical solution $u_\lambda$, and for $\lambda > \lambda^*$ there is no classical solution. The extremal solution is defined as
$$ u^*(x) := \lim_{\lambda \uparrow \lambda^*} u_\lambda(x), $$
which is the unique weak solution at $\lambda = \lambda^*$. Define the blow-up set of $u^*$ as
$$ S := \{ x_0 \in \overline{\Omega} : \text{there exists a sequence } x_n \to x_0 \text{ with } u^*(x_n) \to \infty \}. $$

Assume $u^* \notin L^\infty(\Omega)$. 

(a) What can be said about the structure of the blow-up set $S$ (e.g., its size, Hausdorff dimension, or location)?

(b) In particular, if $\Omega$ is convex, must $S$ consist of a single point?
category_tag: extremal solutions of semilinear elliptic equations
status_search_result: The problem appears in the open-problems literature on extremal solutions of semilinear elliptic equations (Brezis–Vázquez). Recent work (e.g., Cabré and collaborators, 2022) has established boundedness of extremal solutions in low dimensions and for various classes of nonlinearities, but the structural questions about the blow-up set of unbounded extremal solutions—and in particular the single-point conjecture on convex domains—do not appear to have been resolved in general. No published resolution was located.

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: For functions ψ on the torus, does the Bourgain-Brezis-type estimate ||ψ-∫ψ||_{H^{1/2}+W^{1,1}} ≤ C ||∇ψ||_{H^{-1/2}+L¹} hold universally?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{T}^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional torus ($n\ge 2$), and for a scalar function $\psi:\mathbb{T}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ let $\fint\psi=\frac{1}{|\mathbb{T}^n|}\int_{\mathbb{T}^n}\psi$ denote its mean. Recall the Sobolev/Bessel-potential spaces $H^s(\mathbb{T}^n)$ defined via Fourier series with norm $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n}(1+|k|^2)^s|\widehat{u}(k)|^2$, the space $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{T}^n)$ of integrable functions with integrable distributional gradient, and $L^1(\mathbb{T}^n)$. For two Banach spaces $X,Y$ of distributions on $\mathbb{T}^n$, define the sum space $X+Y$ with norm
$$\|u\|_{X+Y}=\inf\{\|v\|_X+\|w\|_Y : u=v+w,\ v\in X,\ w\in Y\}.$$
Question: Does there exist a constant $C=C(n)>0$ such that for every sufficiently regular function $\psi:\mathbb{T}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ the estimate
$$\Big\|\psi-\fint\psi\Big\|_{H^{1/2}(\mathbb{T}^n)+W^{1,1}(\mathbb{T}^n)}\le C\,\|\nabla\psi\|_{H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{T}^n)+L^1(\mathbb{T}^n)}$$
holds?
status_search_result: The estimate is posed as an open problem in Brezis's collection of favorite open problems, attributed to Bourgain–Brezis. Surveys on limiting Bourgain–Brezis estimates (notably Van Schaftingen, 2014) discuss the family of such endpoint inequalities and list related open problems; no published proof or counterexample for this specific sum-space inequality on the torus has been located.

context_brief: BV regularity for total-variation minimizer gradients
original_question: Let Ω be a smooth bounded domain in Rᴺ, N≥2, and let U be the unique minimizer of Φ(u)=∫Ω|∇u| + (1/2)∫Ω|u-f|² over BV(Ω)∩L²(Ω), where f is smooth on Ω̄. Is the distributional gradient ∇U itself a BV function on Ω?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ with $N \geq 2$ be a smooth bounded domain, and let $f \in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega})$. Consider the functional
$$\Phi(u) = \int_\Omega |
abla u| +  rac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |u-f|^2,$$
defined for $u \in BV(\Omega) \cap L^2(\Omega)$, where $\int_\Omega |
abla u|$ denotes the total variation of $u$ on $\Omega$. It is known that $\Phi$ admits a unique minimizer $U \in BV(\Omega) \cap L^2(\Omega)$. Determine whether the distributional gradient $
abla U$ (which a priori is a finite vector-valued Radon measure on $\Omega$) is itself a function of bounded variation on $\Omega$, i.e., whether each component of $

paper_title: SOME OF MY FAVORITE OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Constant-function characterization from liminf tail decay
original_question: For a measurable function u:Ω→R on a smooth bounded connected domain Ω⊂Rᴺ, define Φ_{λ,p}(u)=meas{(x,y)∈Ω×Ω : |u(x)-u(y)|ᵖ/|x-y|^{p+N} ≥ λ}. If liminf_{λ→∞} λ Φ_{λ,p}(u)=0 for some p≥1, must u be almost everywhere constant?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a smooth, bounded, connected domain, and let $u:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a measurable function. For $\lambda > 0$ and $p \geq 1$, define
$$\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u) \;=\; \mathcal{L}^{2N}\!\left\{(x,y) \in \Omega \times \Omega \;:\; \frac{|u(x)-u(y)|^{p}}{|x-y|^{p+N}} \;\geq\; \lambda \right\},$$
where $\mathcal{L}^{2N}$ denotes the $2N$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Assume that for some $p \geq 1$,
$$\liminf_{\lambda \to \infty} \lambda \, \Phi_{\lambda,p}(u) \;=\; 0.$$
Must $u$ be almost everywhere equal to a constant on $\Omega$?

context_brief: Sharp relative isoperimetric profile of the cube
original_question: Let Q be the unit cube in Rᴺ and define f_N(t)=inf{P(S): S⊂Q measurable, |S|=t}, where P(S) is the relative perimeter inside Q. For N≥3, is there an explicit formula analogous to the two-dimensional formula f₂(t), and in particular is it true that f_N(t)≡1 for t near 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q=(0,1)^N$ denote the open unit cube in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\ge 3$. For a measurable set $S\subset Q$, let $|S|$ denote its Lebesgue measure and let $P(S)$ denote its relative perimeter inside $Q$, i.e. the $(N-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $\partial^* S\cap Q$, where $\partial^* S$ is the reduced boundary of $S$. Define the relative isoperimetric profile
$$f_N(t)=\inf\{P(S):\ S\subset Q\ \text{measurable},\ |S|=t\},\qquad t\in(0,1).$$
For $N=2$ an explicit closed-form formula for $f_2(t)$ is known. 

(a) Is there an analogous explicit formula for $f_N(t)$ when $N\ge 3$?

(b) Is it true that $f_N(t)\equiv 1$ for $t$ in some neighborhood of $1/2$?
status_search_result: Part (b) was resolved affirmatively by F. Glaudo (Math. Ann., 2023, "On the isoperimetric profile of the hypercube"), who proved that subsets of $(0,1)^d$ with volume sufficiently close to $1/2$ have relative perimeter at least $1$, settling the Brezis–Bruckstein conjecture. Part (a) — an explicit formula for $f_N(t)$ analogous to the $N=2$ case — does not appear to be known; the same work shows the hypercube isoperimetric profile does not converge to the Gaussian profile, but no closed-form expression for general $N\ge 3$ is provided.

original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations without external energy input, what are the most general assumptions on a smooth initial velocity field u(x,0) that guarantee the corresponding solution exists for all positive time and remains smooth for all positive time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$) with no external forcing:
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(x,0) = u_0(x),
\]
where $u:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field, $p$ is the scalar pressure, and $\nu>0$ is the kinematic viscosity. Assume $u_0$ is smooth (e.g.\ Schwartz, or $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{T}^3$) and divergence-free.

Determine the most general conditions on the smooth divergence-free initial datum $u_0$ which guarantee that the corresponding solution $u(x,t)$ exists for all $t>0$ and remains $C^\infty$ in $x$ and $t$ for all $t>0$. Equivalently, characterize as broadly as possible the class of smooth, divergence-free initial velocities that lead to global-in-time smooth solutions of the unforced three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes system.
status_search_result: The global regularity question for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations from smooth initial data is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open. Many partial results exist (small-data global regularity in critical spaces such as $\dot H^{1/2}$ and $BMO^{-1}$ by Koch–Tataru; conditional regularity criteria of Prodi–Serrin–Ladyzhenskaya, Beale–Kato–Majda, and Escauriaza–Seregin–Šverák; axisymmetric without swirl), but a full characterization of initial data yielding global smooth solutions is not known.

original_question: When one modifies the Navier–Stokes equations to force regularity by adding higher-order dissipation, filtering the velocity, adding nonlinear regularizing terms, or projecting to a finite-dimensional energy-preserving system, which modification is the mathematically and physically appropriate one, and does the choice of regularizing modification matter for describing macroscopic fluid behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ (for instance $\Omega = \mathbb{T}^3$ or $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^3$),
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
for a divergence-free velocity field $u:\Omega\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p$, with $\nu>0$ and prescribed smooth initial data $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$. Since global-in-time regularity of strong solutions is not known, several families of regularized modifications have been proposed which do admit globally regular solutions:

(i) Hyperdissipative models: replace $-\nu\Delta u$ by $\nu(-\Delta)^{\alpha} u$ with $\alpha$ large enough (e.g. the bi-Laplacian $\alpha=2$, or higher-order elliptic dissipation).

(ii) Filtered (alpha-type) models: replace the advecting velocity $u$ in the nonlinearity by a smoothed field $\bar u = F_\alpha u$, where $F_\alpha$ is a Fourier multiplier of order $\le 0$ with parameter $\alpha>0$ (e.g. Leray-$\alpha$, Navier–Stokes-$\alpha$, or Bardina-type filters), so the system becomes $\partial_t u + (\bar u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0$ (or a variant respecting energy balance).

(iii) Nonlinear regularizations: add nonlinear dissipative terms (e.g. of $p$-Laplacian or Smagorinsky type, $-\nabla\cdot(|Du|^{p-2}Du)$) that enforce a priori bounds sufficient for regularity.

(iv) Galerkin truncations: project the equation onto a finite-dimensional subspace $P_N L^2_\sigma(\Omega)$ spanned by eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator, yielding a finite-dimensional ODE that preserves the energy balance.

Each of these modifications is, in some appropriate sense, formally consistent with the Navier–Stokes equations in the limit of the regularization parameter tending to its singular value (high-frequency cutoff removed, $\alpha\to 0$, $N\to\infty$, etc.).

Problem. Determine to what extent the choice among the families (i)–(iv) (and within each family, the choice of order/filter/parameter) affects predictions of macroscopic fluid behavior. Specifically:

(a) Identify a principled criterion (mathematical and/or physical) selecting one regularization as the "correct" closure for Navier–Stokes turbulence, or prove that no such canonical choice exists.

(b) For each family, determine whether statistical observables (long-time averages, energy spectrum, structure functions, invariant measures) of solutions of the regularized system converge, as the regularization is removed, to those of weak solutions of the unmodified Navier–Stokes equations, and whether the limit is independent of the family chosen.

(c) Exhibit, or rule out, examples of initial data and observables for which different regularizations from the list above produce different macroscopic limits.
status_search_result: This is a broad research direction rather than a single precise conjecture. The literature (Leray-$\alpha$, Navier–Stokes-$\alpha$, Bardina, hyperviscous Navier–Stokes, Galerkin truncations) has established global regularity within each family and partial convergence/inviscid-type limit results, but no principled selection of a canonical regularization for turbulence has been established, and the dependence of macroscopic statistics on the choice of regularization remains an open research direction.

original_question: For three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes flow, can one bridge the gap between the vorticity control currently known for general solutions—namely square-integrability of vorticity in space-time together with the averaged geometric bound ν∫∫|ω(x,t)||∇ξ(x,t)|² dx dt < ∞ for the vorticity direction field ξ = ω/|ω|—and the substantially stronger conditions such as ω ∈ L⁴(dt;L²(dx)) or essentially Lipschitz control of ξ in high-vorticity regions that are known to imply smoothness?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$) with viscosity $\nu>0$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with smooth, divergence-free, finite-energy initial data $u_0$. Let $\omega = \nabla\times u$ denote the vorticity, and on the set $\{|\omega|>0\}$ define the vorticity direction
$$\xi(x,t) = \frac{\omega(x,t)}{|\omega(x,t)|}.$$
For Leray–Hopf weak solutions, the following bounds are known to hold for all time:
(i) $\omega \in L^2(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$ (the energy/enstrophy dissipation bound), and
(ii) the averaged geometric bound
$$\nu \int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\omega(x,t)|\,|\nabla \xi(x,t)|^2\, dx\, dt < \infty.$$
On the other hand, classical regularity criteria guarantee global smoothness if one assumes the stronger conditions
(a) $\omega \in L^4(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$, or
(b) the direction field $\xi$ is essentially Lipschitz (e.g. $|\nabla \xi|$ is bounded, possibly only in regions of high vorticity).

Problem: Close the gap between the universally available controls (i)–(ii) and the regularity-implying conditions (a)–(b). Specifically, determine whether the bounds (i) and (ii), possibly combined with additional natural a priori estimates available for Leray–Hopf solutions, are sufficient to imply global regularity of three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes flows; or alternatively, produce intermediate geometric/integrability criteria—weaker than (a) and (b) but verifiable from (i)–(ii)—that imply smoothness.
status_search_result: The global regularity of three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations remains a Clay Millennium Prize open problem. The specific gap between the available enstrophy and geometric (vorticity-direction) bounds and the known regularity criteria (Constantin–Fefferman type direction conditions, Serrin/Prodi-type integrability) has not been closed; recent work continues to refine such criteria but does not bridge the gap.

original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations with smooth finite-energy initial data, do smooth solutions persist for all time, or can a singularity form in finite time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$,
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
for the velocity field $u:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$. Let the initial data $u_0:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ be smooth (i.e. $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$), divergence-free ($\nabla\cdot u_0=0$), and of finite energy ($u_0\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, possibly with appropriate decay at infinity).

Determine whether one of the following holds:
(a) For every such initial datum $u_0$, there exists a global-in-time smooth solution $u\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty))$ of the Euler equations with $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$; or
(b) There exists such an initial datum $u_0$ for which any smooth solution loses regularity (develops a singularity) in finite time, i.e. ceases to be $C^\infty$ at some finite $T>0$.
status_search_result: The global regularity vs. finite-time singularity problem for the 3D incompressible Euler equations with smooth, finite-energy initial data on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (no boundary) remains open as of 2026. Significant progress in adjacent settings has been made: Elgindi (Annals of Math.) proved finite-time singularity formation for $C^{1,\alpha}$ (non-smooth) data, and a 2025 PNAS paper of Chen–Hou established singularity formation for smooth data in a domain with a boundary. The question for fully smooth data on $\mathbb{R}^3$ without boundary is still unresolved.

original_question: For the time-independent forced two-dimensional spatially periodic Navier–Stokes equations, can the dynamics on the global attractor be shown to be conjugate to those of a finite-dimensional smooth dynamical system, with the remaining infinitely many degrees of freedom behaving as transient modes in a quantitatively controllable way—in other words, does an inertial-manifold-type finite-dimensional parameterization capturing the full long-time dynamics exist?

$$\partial_t u - \nu \Delta u + (u\cdot\nabla) u + \nabla p = f, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with periodic boundary conditions and zero spatial mean, where $\nu>0$ is the kinematic viscosity. It is classical that this system generates a well-defined semigroup $\{S(t)\}_{t\ge 0}$ on the divergence-free phase space $H = \{u \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)^2 : \nabla\cdot u = 0, \int u = 0\}$, and that it possesses a compact finite-dimensional global attractor $\mathcal{A}\subset H$.

An inertial manifold for this semigroup is a finite-dimensional, smooth, positively invariant Lipschitz manifold $\mathcal{M}\subset H$ that contains the global attractor $\mathcal{A}$ and attracts every trajectory exponentially fast (so that the dynamics on $\mathcal{M}$, given by a finite-dimensional smooth ODE, captures the entire long-time behavior, while the remaining infinitely many modes are transient and decay at a uniform exponential rate).

Question: Does there exist an inertial manifold for the two-dimensional periodic Navier–Stokes equations described above? Equivalently, is the long-time dynamics on the global attractor $\mathcal{A}$ smoothly conjugate to that of a finite-dimensional smooth dynamical system, with the infinitely many remaining degrees of freedom quantitatively controllable as transients?
status_search_result: The existence (or non-existence) of an inertial manifold for the 2D periodic Navier–Stokes equations remains a long-standing open problem. The standard spectral-gap criterion fails for 2D NSE, and despite decades of work — including results for hyperviscous versions, approximate inertial manifolds, and embeddings into modified systems — no inertial manifold has been constructed nor has its non-existence been established.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: Can one build a mathematically satisfactory turbulence theory for measures on function space that are supported on Navier–Stokes solution paths, including rigorous results on whether such measures exist and whether they are time-independent or time-dependent, unique or non-unique, symmetric or symmetry-breaking, stable or unstable under perturbations, and how they bifurcate or depend on physical parameters?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2$ or $3$), with constant kinematic viscosity $\nu > 0$ and (possibly stochastic) forcing $f$:
\[ \partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = f, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \]
with suitable boundary conditions (e.g. periodic on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$, or no-slip on $\partial\Omega$). Let $X$ denote a function space of divergence-free vector fields (e.g. $L^2_\sigma(\Omega)$ or $H^s_\sigma(\Omega)$), and let $\mathcal{P} = C([0,\infty); X)$ denote the path space of trajectories.

Develop a rigorous mathematical turbulence theory for Borel probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}$ that are supported on weak (or suitable) solution paths of the Navier–Stokes equations. Specifically, address:
(a) Existence: For which forcings, viscosities, and boundary conditions do such measures $\mu$ exist?
(b) Time-dependence: Characterize when such $\mu$ is stationary (time-translation invariant on path space) versus genuinely time-dependent.
(c) Uniqueness: Determine whether $\mu$ is unique within a natural class, or whether multiple such measures coexist.
(d) Symmetries: Determine whether $\mu$ inherits the symmetries (translations, rotations, reflections) of the equations and domain, or whether spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs.
(e) Stability: Study stability of $\mu$ under perturbations of the forcing, initial distribution, viscosity, or domain.
(f) Bifurcations and parameter dependence: Describe how $\mu$ depends on physical parameters (Reynolds number, forcing amplitude, etc.) and classify possible bifurcations.

Provide rigorous theorems addressing (a)–(f), in particular for the three-dimensional case.
status_search_result: This is a broad programmatic question about invariant/statistical measures supported on Navier–Stokes solution paths. Partial results exist (e.g. existence of stationary statistical solutions in the sense of Foias–Prodi–Temam, ergodicity for 2D stochastic Navier–Stokes by Hairer–Mattingly, and various results on Kolmogorov-type measures), but a complete rigorous turbulence theory—particularly uniqueness, symmetry breaking, stability and bifurcations in 3D—remains open and is widely regarded as a central unresolved direction in mathematical fluid dynamics.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: For steady far-field flow past a bounded simply connected obstacle B in the exterior domain Ω = ℝ^3 \ B, with velocity approaching a nonzero constant vector U at spatial infinity, what realistic rigorous upper bounds can be proved for the rate of energy dissipation?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded, simply connected obstacle with smooth boundary, and let $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus B$ be its exterior. Consider a steady incompressible viscous flow governed by the stationary Navier–Stokes equations
\[
(u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega,
\]
with no-slip boundary condition $u = 0$ on $\partial B$ and prescribed nonzero far-field velocity $u(x) \to U$ as $|x|\to\infty$, where $U \in \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \{0\}$ is a constant vector. The energy dissipation rate associated with such a flow is
\[
\varepsilon = \nu \int_{\Omega} |\nabla u|^2\, dx.
\]
Establish realistic rigorous upper bounds for $\varepsilon$, expressed in terms of the physical parameters $\nu$, $|U|$, and the geometry of $B$ (e.g. its diameter or cross-section), that are consistent with the expected drag-law scalings of turbulent flow past a bluff body.
status_search_result: A web search indicates that while rigorous variational upper bounds for energy dissipation have been derived in idealized geometries (shear flows, body-forced flows, Kolmogorov forcing), no realistic rigorous upper bound for dissipation in steady 3D exterior flow past a bounded obstacle with nonzero far-field velocity is reported in the literature. The problem of obtaining drag-consistent dissipation bounds in this exterior setting remains open.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
context_brief: Rigorous bounds for turbulence structure statistics
original_question: For classical boundary-driven Navier–Stokes turbulence, can one obtain rigorous estimates and a satisfactory mathematical analysis for higher-order statistical observables such as the velocity moments Um(y,s), the structure functions ⟨|u(x+y,t)-u(x,t)|^m⟩, and the analogous moments and structure functions of the Eulerian–Lagrangian back-to-labels map A(x,t)?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations
   ∂_t u + (u·∇)u − ν Δu + ∇p = f,   ∇·u = 0,
posed in a bounded smooth domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^3 with no-slip boundary condition u|_{∂Ω} = U_b (boundary-driven turbulence), where ν > 0 is the kinematic viscosity. Let ⟨ · ⟩ denote a long-time and/or ensemble average over statistically stationary turbulent states.

Define the following statistical observables:
  (i) The velocity moments
        U_m(y, s) = ⟨ |u(x+y, t) − u(x, t)|^m ⟩,   m ∈ ℕ,
      regarded as functions of the separation vector y ∈ ℝ^3 (with s an appropriate scalar parameter, e.g. |y|).
  (ii) The structure functions S_m(y) = ⟨ |u(x+y, t) − u(x, t)|^m ⟩.
  (iii) The Eulerian–Lagrangian "back-to-labels" map A(x, t), defined as the inverse of the Lagrangian flow map, satisfying
        ∂_t A + (u·∇) A = 0,    A(x, 0) = x,
      together with its moments ⟨|A(x+y, t) − A(x, t)|^m⟩ and the corresponding structure functions of A.

Problem. Establish rigorous quantitative estimates (upper and lower bounds, scaling laws, or other a priori inequalities) — derivable directly from the Navier–Stokes equations — for the higher-order observables U_m(y, s), the velocity structure functions S_m(y), and the analogous moments and structure functions of the back-to-labels map A(x, t), uniformly in ν (or with controlled ν-dependence) in the boundary-driven setting.
status_search_result: The mathematical literature contains rigorous bounds on low-order quantities (energy dissipation rate via the background/Doering–Constantin method, and some bounds in spatially periodic settings), but rigorous estimates for higher-order velocity moments, structure functions, and back-to-labels-map statistics in boundary-driven 3D Navier–Stokes turbulence remain largely unresolved. Recent surveys still list this as an outstanding research direction.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Does there exist a composite integer n such that Euler's totient φ(n), meaning the number of positive integers at most n that are coprime to n, divides n − 1? Equivalently, is the set of composite integers n satisfying φ(n) | (n − 1) actually empty?
self_contained_problem: Let φ denote Euler's totient function, defined for a positive integer n as the number of positive integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n that are coprime to n. A positive integer n ≥ 2 is called composite if it is not prime. Determine whether there exists a composite integer n such that φ(n) divides n − 1; equivalently, prove or disprove that the set { n composite : φ(n) ∣ (n − 1) } is empty.
status_search_result: Lehmer's totient problem, posed in 1932, remains open. No composite n with φ(n) | (n−1) is known, and lower bounds on the size and number of prime factors of any putative solution have been progressively improved (Cohen–Hagis 1980; Hagis 1988; Burcsi–Czirbusz–Farkas and others). Recent 2024–2025 preprints claim conditional or partial progress, but no accepted full resolution exists.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let d1, ..., dk be distinct integers, and for each prime p let b(p) be the number of distinct residue classes modulo p represented by d1, ..., dk. If b(p) < p for every prime p, must there exist infinitely many positive integers n such that all k numbers n + d1, ..., n + dk are prime?
self_contained_problem: Let $k \geq 1$ and let $d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k$ be distinct integers. For each prime $p$, let $b(p)$ denote the number of distinct residue classes modulo $p$ represented by the multiset $\{d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k\}$. Suppose that $b(p) < p$ for every prime $p$ (equivalently, for every prime $p$ there exists an integer $n$ with $n + d_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for all $i$). Prove or disprove: there must exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that all $k$ numbers $n + d_1, n + d_2, \ldots, n + d_k$ are simultaneously prime.
status_search_result: The prime k-tuples conjecture (Hardy–Littlewood) remains a major open problem in analytic number theory. While significant progress has been made on bounded gaps between primes (Zhang, Maynard, Tao, Polymath) showing that some admissible tuples yield infinitely many configurations with bounded prime gaps, the full conjecture for every admissible tuple is still unproven.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: If χ is a non-principal Dirichlet character modulo q, is every short character sum of the form ∑_{n=M+1}^{M+N} χ(n) bounded by Oε(N^{1/2} q^ε) for every ε > 0, uniformly in the starting point M and length N?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q\ge 2$ be an integer and let $\chi$ be a non-principal Dirichlet character modulo $q$ (i.e. a homomorphism $\chi:(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ extended to $\mathbb{Z}$ by setting $\chi(n)=0$ whenever $\gcd(n,q)>1$, and not equal to the principal character). For integers $M\ge 0$ and $N\ge 1$, consider the short character sum
$$S_\chi(M,N) \;=\; \sum_{n=M+1}^{M+N} \chi(n).$$
Prove or disprove the following conjectural bound: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon>0$ such that for all $q\ge 2$, all non-principal Dirichlet characters $\chi$ modulo $q$, and all integers $M\ge 0$, $N\ge 1$,
$$\Bigl|\,S_\chi(M,N)\,\Bigr| \;\le\; C_\varepsilon\, N^{1/2}\, q^{\varepsilon}.$$
Equivalently, does one have $S_\chi(M,N) = O_\varepsilon(N^{1/2} q^\varepsilon)$ uniformly in $M$ and $N$?
status_search_result: The conjectured bound $N^{1/2} q^\varepsilon$ for short character sums is widely viewed as open. The best unconditional results remain those of Burgess (with exponent $1/4$ in the relevant range), and conjecturally the stronger $N^{1/2} q^\varepsilon$ bound is expected to follow from GRH but is not known. Recent literature (e.g., work on three conjectures about character sums, and ongoing Burgess-type improvements) treats this as an outstanding open conjecture.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Does the Riemann zeta function satisfy the Lindelöf hypothesis, namely that ζ(1/2 + it) ≪ε (|t| + 4)^ε for every ε > 0? Equivalently, is the Lindelöf μ-function equal to 0 at σ = 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for $\Re(s) > 1$ by $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ and extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a single simple pole at $s = 1$. For a real number $\sigma$, define the Lindelöf $\mu$-function by
$$\mu(\sigma) = \inf\{\, c \ge 0 : \zeta(\sigma + it) \ll (|t|+4)^{c} \text{ as } |t| \to \infty \,\},$$
so that $\mu(\sigma)$ is the infimum of all $c \ge 0$ such that $|\zeta(\sigma + it)| \le C_c (|t|+4)^{c}$ for some constant $C_c > 0$ and all real $t$.

Prove or disprove the following statement (the Lindelöf Hypothesis): for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} + it\right) \ll_{\varepsilon} (|t|+4)^{\varepsilon},$$
or equivalently $\mu\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0$.
status_search_result: The Lindelöf Hypothesis is a classical and well-known open problem in analytic number theory. It is implied by the Riemann Hypothesis but has not been proved or disproved; the best known unconditional bound for μ(1/2) is roughly 13/84 due to Bourgain (2017), improving on previous subconvexity results.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: For a primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q > 1, do all non-trivial zeros ρ = β + iγ of the Dirichlet L-function L(s, χ) lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let q > 1 be an integer and let χ be a primitive Dirichlet character modulo q, i.e., a completely multiplicative function χ : ℤ → ℂ with χ(n) = 0 whenever gcd(n, q) > 1, χ(n+q) = χ(n), and such that χ is not induced from any character modulo a proper divisor of q. Define the Dirichlet L-function for Re(s) > 1 by

    L(s, χ) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ χ(n) n^{-s},

and extend L(s, χ) to a meromorphic (in fact entire, since χ is non-principal) function of s ∈ ℂ via analytic continuation. The functional equation relates L(s, χ) to L(1−s, χ̄) and produces so-called trivial zeros at certain non-positive integers (s = 0, −2, −4, … if χ(−1) = 1, and s = −1, −3, −5, … if χ(−1) = −1). All other zeros are called non-trivial zeros; they lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1.

Problem: Prove or disprove that for every integer q > 1 and every primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q, every non-trivial zero ρ = β + iγ of L(s, χ) satisfies β = 1/2.
status_search_result: The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions remains one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. No proof or disproof is known; partial results include zero-free regions and zero-density estimates, but the full statement is unresolved.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let ψ(x) = ∑_{n≤x} Λ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. Is it true that for every pair of real numbers h and x with 2 ≤ h ≤ x, one has ψ(x + h) − ψ(x) = h + Oε(h^{1/2} x^ε) for every ε > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ denote the von Mangoldt function, defined by $\Lambda(n) = \log p$ if $n = p^k$ is a prime power (with $k \ge 1$), and $\Lambda(n) = 0$ otherwise. Define the Chebyshev summatory function
$$\psi(x) = \sum_{n \le x} \Lambda(n).$$
Determine whether the following statement is true: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon > 0$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $h$ with $2 \le h \le x$,
$$\bigl|\psi(x+h) - \psi(x) - h\bigr| \le C_\varepsilon\, h^{1/2} x^{\varepsilon}.$$
Equivalently, prove or disprove that $\psi(x+h) - \psi(x) = h + O_\varepsilon(h^{1/2} x^\varepsilon)$ uniformly in the range $2 \le h \le x$.
status_search_result: This is a well-known conjecture on primes in short intervals, stronger than what follows from the Riemann Hypothesis (which gives an error term of size $h^{1/2}(\log x)^2$ only for $h \ge x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$). It remains open; even under RH, the bound for small $h$ (e.g. $h \le x^{1/2}$) is not known. Related work by Goldston–Montgomery establishes the variance estimate $\sim h \log(x/h)$ conditionally, supporting but not resolving the conjecture.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let ψ(x; q, a) = ∑_{n≤x, n≡a mod q} Λ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. When (a, q) = 1 and q ≤ x, is it true that ψ(x; q, a) = x/ϕ(q) + Oε(x^{1/2+ε} / q^{1/2}) for every ε > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ denote the von Mangoldt function, defined by $\Lambda(n) = \log p$ if $n = p^k$ for some prime $p$ and integer $k \geq 1$, and $\Lambda(n) = 0$ otherwise. For positive integers $q$ and $a$ with $\gcd(a,q) = 1$, and for $x \geq 1$, define
$$\psi(x; q, a) = \sum_{\substack{n \leq x \\ n \equiv a \pmod{q}}} \Lambda(n).$$
Let $\varphi$ denote Euler's totient function. Determine whether the following statement holds: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon > 0$ such that, whenever $\gcd(a,q) = 1$ and $1 \leq q \leq x$, one has
$$\left| \psi(x; q, a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} \right| \leq C_\varepsilon \, \frac{x^{1/2+\varepsilon}}{q^{1/2}}.$$
status_search_result: This is a well-known conjecture of Montgomery on the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions. It is widely regarded as open; it is stronger than what follows from the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (which gives an error term of order $x^{1/2}\log^2 x$ uniformly, without the $q^{-1/2}$ saving). Recent work (e.g., on primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli, 2024–2025) continues to address weaker or averaged forms, and no proof or disproof of the full pointwise conjecture is known.

paper_title: Some open problems in analysis
context_brief: Injectivity of the classical Radon transform
original_question: Let f be a continuous function on the plane R^2 such that, for every straight line l_{alpha,p} defined by alpha · x = p, the restriction of f to l_{alpha,p} is integrable, f has at most polynomial growth in the sense that |f(x)| <= c(1 + |x|^m) for some constants c > 0 and m >= 0, and the classical Radon transform of f vanishes on every line, meaning the integral of f over every l_{alpha,p} is zero. Must these assumptions force f to be identically zero?
self_contained_problem:
For $\alpha \in S^1$ (the unit circle) and $p \in \mathbb{R}$, let $l_{\alpha,p} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \alpha \cdot x = p\}$ denote the straight line in the plane with unit normal $\alpha$ and signed distance $p$ from the origin. The classical Radon transform of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by
$$ (Rf)(\alpha, p) = \int_{l_{\alpha,p}} f \, ds, $$
whenever the integral makes sense.

paper_title: Some open problems in analysis
context_brief: Minimal growth condition for Radon transform injectivity
original_question: For the classical Radon transform on R^2, determine the weakest natural growth condition at infinity under which the following implication is valid: if a continuous function f has integrable restriction to every line and its Radon transform vanishes on every line, then f must be identically zero. In other words, how little control on the growth of f at infinity is sufficient to guarantee injectivity of the Radon transform under these line-integrability and zero-transform assumptions?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ be a continuous function such that:
(i) for every straight line $\ell\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, the restriction $f|_\ell$ is integrable with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on $\ell$;
(ii) the Radon transform of $f$ vanishes on every line, i.e. $\int_\ell f\,ds = 0$ for every line $\ell\subset\mathbb{R}^2$.

It is known that if one additionally imposes a sufficiently strong decay condition on $f$ at infinity (for example, $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^2,(1+|x|)^{-1}dx)$), then $f\equiv 0$. Without such decay, however, nontrivial functions $f$ satisfying (i) and (ii) can exist.

Problem. Determine the weakest natural growth restriction on $f$ at infinity under which conditions (i) and (ii) force $f\equiv 0$. That is, find the optimal class of admissible growth rates at infinity for which the Radon transform on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is injective on continuous functions satisfying (i) and (ii).
status_search_result: The problem of identifying the weakest natural growth restriction at infinity that guarantees injectivity of the planar Radon transform under line-integrability and zero-transform hypotheses is stated as an open problem by Ramm. Known partial results provide injectivity under conditions such as $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^2,(1+|x|)^{-1}dx)$, but no characterization of the optimal/weakest growth condition appears in the literature reviewed.

paper_title: Some open problems in analysis
context_brief: Uniqueness for a coupled elliptic Dirichlet system
original_question: Let L and M be elliptic, second-order, selfadjoint, strictly positive Dirichlet operators in a bounded domain D contained in R^n with n > 1, where D has smooth connected boundary S. Let the coefficients of L and M be real-valued, and let a(x) and b(x) be strictly positive functions that are smooth on the closure of D. Suppose real-valued functions u and v satisfy Lu + a(x)v = 0 in D, -b(x)u + Mv = 0 in D, and u = v = 0 on S. Do these assumptions necessarily imply that u = v = 0 throughout D, without adding any extra hypotheses such as smallness of |b-a| or equality of L and M?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n>1$) be a bounded domain with smooth connected boundary $S$. Let $L$ and $M$ be second-order, elliptic, selfadjoint, strictly positive Dirichlet operators on $D$ with real-valued coefficients (so that $(Lu,u)_{L^2(D)}>0$ for all nonzero $u$ in the Dirichlet domain of $L$, and similarly for $M$). Let $a,b:\overline{D}\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth, strictly positive functions. Suppose that real-valued functions $u$ and $v$ satisfy
$$Lu+a(x)v=0\quad\text{in }D,\qquad -b(x)u+Mv=0\quad\text{in }D,\qquad u=v=0\quad\text{on }S.$$
Does it necessarily follow that $u\equiv v\equiv 0$ in $D$, without imposing additional hypotheses such as smallness of $\|b-a\|$ or the equality $L=M$? Either prove this implication or construct a counterexample.

The general case with variable positive smooth coefficients $a(x),b(x)$ and arbitrary such $L,M$, with no further assumptions, does not appear to be resolved in the located literature.

Assuming L1 and L2 are transversal in the stated sense, must T fail to have finite rank, equivalently, must the range of T be infinite-dimensional?
self_contained_problem:

$$F(z)=\int_D f(x)e^{i z\cdot x}\,dx,\qquad z\in\mathbb{C}^3,$$
so that $F$ is an entire function of exponential type on $\mathbb{C}^3$. Let $L_1(z)$ and $L_2(z)$ be polynomials on $\mathbb{C}^3$ each of degree at least one, and let
$$\mathcal{L}_j=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^3:L_j(z)=0\},\qquad j=1,2,$$
be their zero varieties. Assume $\mathcal{L}_1$ and $\mathcal{L}_2$ are transversal in the following sense: there exist points $p_1\in\mathcal{L}_1$ and $p_2\in\mathcal{L}_2$ such that the union of a basis of the tangent space $T_{p_1}\mathcal{L}_1$ and a basis of $T_{p_2}\mathcal{L}_2$ forms a basis of $\mathbb{C}^3$. $$(Th)(u_2)=\int_{\mathcal{L}_1} h(u_1)\,F(u_1+u_2)\,dm_1(u_1),\qquad u_2\in\mathcal{L}_2.$$
Must $T$ fail to be a finite-rank operator? Equivalently, must the range of $T$ be infinite-dimensional?

context_brief: Linear independence of shifted Fourier transforms
original_question: In the setting of Problem 3.1, let D be a bounded domain in R^n with n > 1, let f be a compactly supported L^2(D) function, and let F be its Fourier transform regarded as an entire function. For an arbitrarily large fixed integer M, can one choose points p_1, ..., p_M in L2 so that the M shifted functions F(z + p_m), viewed as functions of z on L1, are linearly independent? Equivalently, can one choose p_m in L2 so that the identity sum from m = 1 to M of c_m F(z + p_m) = 0 for all z in L1 forces every coefficient c_m to be zero?

  F(z) = ∫_D f(x) e^{-i z·x} dx,  z ∈ ℂⁿ,

denote its Fourier transform, which by the Paley–Wiener theorem extends to an entire function on ℂⁿ of exponential type.   z ↦ F(z + p_m),  m = 1, …, M,

when restricted to z ∈ L₁, are linearly independent over ℂ? Equivalently, can one choose p₁, …, p_M ∈ L₂ such that the relation

  Σ_{m=1}^{M} c_m F(z + p_m) = 0  for all z ∈ L₁

forces c_m = 0 for every m = 1, …, M?

paper_title: Some open problems in analysis
context_brief: Boundary rigidity question related to the Pompeiu problem
original_question: Let D be a bounded domain in R^3 that is homeomorphic to a ball and has real-analytic boundary S. For j = 1, 2, 3, let u_j solve the Helmholtz Dirichlet problem Δu_j + k^2 u_j = 0 in D with u_j = 0 on S, where k^2 > 0 is a constant, and define the vector field u(x) = sum of u_j(x)e_j in the standard basis of R^3. Let N_s be the outward unit normal to S at s, and assume that the normal derivative vector u_N on S satisfies u_N = [s, N_s] for every s in S, where [a, b] denotes the cross product in R^3. Do these assumptions imply that [s, N_s] = 0 for every boundary point s in S, and hence, as noted in the source, force S to be a sphere?

Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded domain that is homeomorphic to a ball and whose boundary $S=\partial D$ is real-analytic. Fix a constant $k^2>0$. For $j=1,2,3$, let $u_j$ be a solution of the Helmholtz Dirichlet problem
\[
\Delta u_j + k^2 u_j = 0 \text{ in } D, \qquad u_j = 0 \text{ on } S,
\]
and define the vector field $u:D\to\mathbb{R}^3$ by $u(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{3} u_j(x)\,e_j$, where $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. \[
u_N(s) = [s, N_s] \quad \text{for every } s\in S,
\]
where $[a,b]$ denotes the cross product of $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^3$ (with the origin chosen so that this identity is meaningful).

\[
[s, N_s] = 0 \quad \text{for every } s\in S?
\]
(Equivalently, must the position vector $s$ be parallel to $N_s$ at every boundary point, which in turn forces $S$ to be a sphere centered at the origin.)

original_question: What general formal theory of probability can accommodate multiple interpretations of probability, including the logical probability of a statement relative to given evidence, absolute logical probability relative to zero evidence, and the probability of an event relative to a given ensemble or collective of events, while also supporting interpretations as a calculus of contents, deductive systems, classes, propositions, and propensities?
status_search_result: An axiomatic system meeting these requirements was developed and published in the 1950s (notably in the appendices added to The Logic of Scientific Discovery and in papers in the British Journal for the Philosophy of Science), giving an autonomous formal calculus of probability admitting the logical, frequency, content, deductive-system, Boolean class, propositional, and propensity interpretations. The construction is regarded as completed; subsequent literature discusses refinements and alternative axiomatizations (e.g., Renyi's conditional probability spaces, Popper functions / Popper–Miller probability) rather than the existence of such a system.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: How should probability be interpreted in quantum theory if quantum theory need not have a purely statistical meaning, even though its empirical tests are statistical, and if one wants an account in which objective propensities and fields of propensities can be measured statistically without themselves being statistical?
self_contained_problem: Provide a formal interpretation of probability suitable for quantum theory under the following constraints. (i) Empirical tests of the theory are statistical: predicted probabilities are confirmed by relative frequencies obtained from repeated experiments. (ii) The theory itself (for instance, the dynamics governed by the Schrödinger equation) is not required to have a purely statistical meaning; individual quantum events may be governed by non-statistical, objective tendencies. (iii) One postulates objective "propensities" attached to a single experimental arrangement — real-valued dispositional magnitudes p(A|S) ∈ [0,1] associated with the occurrence of an outcome A relative to a complete generating situation S — together with "fields of propensities" varying over space-time or configuration space, analogous to generalized forces. (iv) These propensities must be objective properties of the physical situation (not merely degrees of belief or limits of frequencies by definition), yet must be measurable by statistical methods, in the sense that long-run relative frequencies obtained from repetitions of S converge (in some specified, justified sense) to p(A|S). The task is: formulate axioms for such a propensity-valued measure assigned to physical situations, prove a representation/limit theorem connecting these objective single-case propensities to observable frequency statistics, and exhibit a model in which the wave function (or quantum state) determines a field of propensities consistent with the predictions of quantum mechanics while admitting a non-statistical interpretation of the underlying dynamics.
status_search_result: The propensity interpretation of probability remains an actively debated topic in the philosophy of probability and foundations of quantum mechanics. No single formalization is universally accepted; critiques (e.g., Humphreys' paradox concerning conditional propensities) and various refinements (long-run, single-case, and dispositional-conditional accounts) continue to appear. The problem as stated is therefore best characterized as a foundational/philosophical open problem rather than a mathematically settled one.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: How can statistical statements be made satisfactorily refutable and testable when statistics is used mainly to provide empirical tests for theories that are not themselves purely statistical? In particular, how can one characterize a class of infinite chance-like sequences so that a statistical statement is testable by comparison with the “shortest sequences” of its kind and is refuted when a tested ensemble differs from the statistical properties of the initial sections of those sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Provide a precise mathematical framework for the refutability of statistical statements, as follows.

(a) Give a rigorous definition of a class $\mathcal{S}$ of infinite binary (or, more generally, finite-alphabet) sequences that are "chance-like" in the sense that their initial finite segments exhibit, to the greatest possible degree, the statistical regularities (relative frequencies, freedom from after-effects of every finite order, randomness of subsequence selection, etc.) demanded of an idealized random sequence. The definition should single out, within this class, sequences that may be called "shortest sequences of their kind", meaning that no initial segment can be replaced by a strictly shorter segment while preserving the prescribed statistical regularities up to that length.

(b) Show that such "shortest chance-like sequences" exist and can be effectively (or mathematically) characterized, and describe their structure.

(c) Using this class, define what it means for a statistical statement $S$ (a claim about the statistical properties of an empirical ensemble or infinite sequence) to be testable: namely, $S$ is testable if it can be compared with the statistical properties of the initial sections of the shortest chance-like sequences singled out in (a). Define precisely when an observed finite ensemble counts as refuting $S$, in terms of a quantitative discrepancy between its empirical statistical properties and the corresponding statistical properties of initial sections of the shortest chance-like sequences.

(d) Prove that the resulting notion of refutation yields a satisfactory criterion of empirical testability for statistical statements, in the sense that every statistical statement which is not logically trivial is either refutable in this sense or can be shown to fail the criterion.
status_search_result: The question, posed philosophically, anticipates ideas later formalized in algorithmic information theory (Kolmogorov complexity, Martin-Löf randomness). While modern algorithmic randomness theory provides rigorous notions of random infinite sequences and tests of randomness, no direct, definitive mathematical "solution" matching the specific framing of "shortest chance-like sequences" as a refutation criterion for arbitrary statistical statements is recorded as a settled result. Web search returns general discussions of Popper's falsificationism in statistics but no canonical mathematical resolution of this exact formulation.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: How should the formalism of quantum theory be interpreted, especially once the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen thought experiment is taken into account and without relying on Einstein’s deterministic conclusions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard Hilbert-space formalism of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics: pure states are represented by unit vectors (equivalently, rays) in a complex separable Hilbert space H, observables by self-adjoint operators on H, time evolution of an isolated system by a one-parameter unitary group generated by a self-adjoint Hamiltonian, and the probabilities of measurement outcomes by the Born rule applied to spectral projections. Consider also the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen setup: a bipartite system with Hilbert space H_A ⊗ H_B prepared in an entangled pure state such that suitable pairs of noncommuting observables on subsystem B can be predicted with certainty from corresponding measurements on subsystem A, even when A and B are spacelike separated.

Provide a coherent interpretation of this formalism — i.e., specify what the state vector, the unitary evolution, and the Born-rule probabilities represent about physical systems, ensembles, or knowledge — that:

(i) is consistent with all predictions of the formalism, including the correlations arising in the EPR setup and the constraints imposed by Bell-type inequalities;
(ii) does not presuppose deterministic underlying dynamics (i.e., does not require that the outcomes of individual measurements be fixed by hidden variables in a way that restores classical determinism);
(iii) accounts for the probabilistic predictions of the theory as objective features rather than as expressions of ignorance about a deterministic substrate; and
(iv) clarifies the status of the EPR "elements of reality" argument within this nondeterministic interpretation.

Formulate such an interpretation precisely and show that it is internally consistent and empirically equivalent to the standard formalism.
status_search_result: The interpretation of the quantum-mechanical formalism, including the meaning of entanglement and the EPR correlations, remains an open and actively debated foundational problem with multiple competing interpretations (Copenhagen, many-worlds, Bohmian, QBism, relational, consistent histories, etc.) and no community consensus.

paper_title: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge
original_question: Does classical physics justify a deterministic view of the physical world in Laplace’s sense, or is even classical physics misinterpreted when it is used to support that deterministic view?
self_contained_problem: Laplacian determinism is the thesis that the state of any isolated classical mechanical system at a single instant of time, together with the laws of classical (Newtonian) mechanics, uniquely determines the state of that system at every past and future instant, and that this prediction can in principle be carried out to arbitrary accuracy from a sufficiently accurate specification of the initial state. Consider classical physics formulated as a Hamiltonian system on a finite-dimensional phase space, possibly extended to include classical field theories and systems of point particles interacting via Newtonian gravitation and Lorentz-invariant electrodynamics. Investigate the following: Does classical physics, so formulated, actually justify Laplacian determinism as defined above?
