paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Analogue of the three-valued theorem for four-valued exponents
original_question: Suppose x -> x^s is a power permutation of a finite field L, and call s four-valued when the reduced spectrum of the corresponding Weil sums W_{L,s}(a) on a in L^× has exactly four distinct values. Katz proved that in the three-valued case the exponent must be singular, must satisfy s ≡ 1 (mod p - 1), and has integral spectrum {0, A, B}. Find an analogue of that theorem for four-valued exponents: determine what structural restrictions on s and on the spectrum must hold when the reduced spectrum has exactly four values.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $L = \mathbb{F}_q$ with $q = p^n$, and let $\psi\colon L \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ be the canonical additive character $\psi(x) = \exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$ (so that $x \mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$) and for $a \in L$, define the Weil sum
$$W_{L,s}(a) \;=\; \sum_{x \in L} \psi(x^s - a x).$$
Call the multiset $\{W_{L,s}(a) : a \in L^\times\}$ (as a set) the reduced spectrum of $x \mapsto x^s$, and call $s$ $v$-valued when this reduced spectrum has exactly $v$ distinct values. The exponent $s$ is called degenerate if $x^s$ is $\mathbb{F}_p$-affine on $L$, and singular otherwise.

It is known (Katz, 2012) that if $s$ is three-valued, then $s$ is singular, $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$, and the reduced spectrum $\{0, A, B\}$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}$.

Problem: Find an analogue of this theorem for four-valued exponents. That is, determine the structural restrictions that must hold on $s$ (singularity, congruence conditions modulo $p-1$, etc.) and on the four values of the reduced spectrum (in particular, whether they must be rational integers) whenever $s$ is four-valued.
status_search_result: Recent work by Katz and Langevin ("Rationality of Four-Valued Families of Weil Sums of Binomials", arXiv:2306.14414, 2023) establishes a partial analogue: if the reduced Weil spectrum has exactly four distinct values, then all four values are rational integers, with a single exception (the case |K|=5 with s ≡ 3 mod 4). This addresses the integrality part of the desired analogue, but a full analogue including the congruence condition s ≡ 1 (mod p-1) and singularity-type structural restrictions does not appear to be completely resolved.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Classification of nice exponents over prime fields
original_question: Fix a finite field L and an invertible exponent s. For u, v in L, define N(u,v) to be the number of pairs (x,y) in L^2 satisfying x + y = u and x^s + y^s = v. Call s nice when, as v ranges over L with v ≠ 1, the values N(1,v) take at most three distinct values. Numerical experiments over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 found that every nice exponent s not equivalent to 1 under the relation generated by Frobenius twists s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q - 1) and inversion seems to come from the paradigmatic families described earlier in the paper. Must this always happen for every nice exponent over every prime field?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $q=p^n$ for some $n\ge 1$, and let $L=\mathbb{F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements. Fix an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$, so that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$. For $u,v\in L$, set
$$N(u,v)=\#\{(x,y)\in L\times L:\ x+y=u\ \text{and}\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
Call the exponent $s$ "nice" if the multiset of values $\{N(1,v): v\in L,\ v\neq 1\}$ takes at most three distinct values.

Define an equivalence relation on the set of invertible exponents modulo $q-1$ generated by:
(i) Frobenius twisting: $s\sim p^j s\pmod{q-1}$ for every integer $j\ge 0$;
(ii) inversion: $s\sim s^{-1}\pmod{q-1}$.

Two known families of nice exponents are:
(A) $s=1$ (the trivial case);
(B) "paradigmatic" exponents, namely those $s$ such that $x^s$ is an affine image of a quadratic monomial after a Frobenius/inversion twist, equivalently $s$ is equivalent under $\sim$ to an exponent of the form $s\equiv (p^k+1)/2\pmod{q-1}$ with appropriate $k$ (so the associated map is, up to twist and inversion, a quadratic monomial $x^2$), together with the small additional list of sporadic-but-systematic exponents whose niceness follows from being equivalent to such a quadratic exponent.

Question: Restricting to the case $n=1$ (so $L=\mathbb{F}_p$ is a prime field), is it true that for every odd prime $p$ and every nice exponent $s$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $s\not\sim 1$, the exponent $s$ is equivalent under $\sim$ to one of the paradigmatic examples in family (B)?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any subsequent work classifying all nice exponents over prime fields or refuting the conjectural classification. The problem is part of a list of open problems related to Helleseth's conjectures and has not been verified to be resolved in the literature found.

original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, with s not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by Frobenius twists and inversion. For v in the field, let N(1,v) count pairs (x,y) in L^2 satisfying x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v. Must there always exist some v for which N(1,v) = 2? In other words, is 2 always a differential multiplicity for every such invertible exponent?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $n\geq 1$, and let $L=\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ be the finite field with $p^n$ elements. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s, p^n-1)=1$ (so that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$), and for $a,v\in L$ with $a\neq 0$, define
$$N(a,v) = \#\{(x,y)\in L\times L : x+y=a,\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
Call an integer $m\geq 0$ a "differential multiplicity" of the exponent $s$ if there exists $v\in L$ with $N(1,v)=m$.

Two exponents $s,t$ on $L$ are declared equivalent if $t\equiv p^j s^{\pm 1}\pmod{p^n-1}$ for some integer $j\geq 0$ (i.e., they are related by Frobenius twists and/or inversion). Write $s\approx 1$ for this equivalence to the trivial exponent.

Conjecture to settle: For every odd prime power $p^n$ and every integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,p^n-1)=1$ such that $s\not\approx 1$, the value $2$ is a differential multiplicity of $s$; that is, there exists some $v\in L$ with exactly two ordered pairs $(x,y)\in L^2$ satisfying $x+y=1$ and $x^s+y^s=v$.

Is this conjecture true?

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does ρ has other discontinuity? What are they? Is ρ piece-wise constant?
self_contained_problem:
For a real number α > 1, a finite or infinite word over the binary alphabet {0,1} is called α-power-free if it contains no factor of the form u^β with β ≥ α (where u^β for a nonempty word u of length |u| denotes the prefix of length ⌊β|u|⌋ of the infinite word uuu…). Let L_α denote the language of all binary α-power-free words, and define the (combinatorial) growth-rate density

  ρ(α) = lim_{n→∞} |L_α ∩ {0,1}^n|^{1/n},

which is known to exist for every α in the relevant range (α greater than the binary repetition threshold). The function ρ is known to be non-increasing in α and to have at least one known discontinuity.

(a) Determine all points α at which ρ is discontinuous, and describe them explicitly.

(b) Decide whether ρ is piecewise constant on its domain; that is, whether there exists a locally finite partition of its domain into intervals on each of which ρ is constant.
status_search_result: The question concerning the structure of discontinuities of the density function ρ for binary power-free words, and whether ρ is piecewise constant, is posed as an open problem in the WORDS conference open-problems compilation. No published resolution was located; Shur's subsequent work on growth rates of power-free languages addresses asymptotic estimates but does not appear to settle the full description of discontinuities or piecewise-constancy of ρ in the binary case.

self_contained_problem:
A pattern is a nonempty word p over an alphabet of variables. An infinite word w over a finite alphabet Σ is said to avoid p if there is no nonerasing morphism h from the free monoid on the variables of p to Σ* such that h(p) appears as a factor of w. The pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over some alphabet of size k that avoids p, and unavoidable on k letters otherwise.

For an infinite word w over an alphabet Σ and a letter a ∈ Σ, the frequency of a in w is defined as the limit (when it exists, or otherwise the lim inf) of |w[1..n]|_a / n as n → ∞, where |w[1..n]|_a counts the occurrences of a in the prefix of length n.

Problem: Suppose p is a pattern that is not k-avoidable but is (k+1)-avoidable. Determine
  inf_w  min_{a ∈ Σ}  freq_a(w),
where the infimum is taken over all infinite words w on an alphabet Σ of size k+1 that avoid p. In other words, find the smallest possible frequency of a letter in any infinite (k+1)-letter word avoiding p.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a general open problem in pattern avoidance in combinatorics on words. While specific instances have been studied (e.g., minimal letter frequency in n-th power-free binary words is asymptotically 1/n, and isolated patterns such as some 4-avoidable but not 3-avoidable formulas have been investigated), no general formula or characterization for the minimal letter frequency in (k+1)-letter infinite words avoiding a pattern that is not k-avoidable appears in the literature. The problem remains open in general.

original_question: Kirby Baker, Georges Mac Nulty and Walter Taylor have shown that the pattern abXbcY caZbaT ac is 4-avoidable, but not 3-avoidable [7]. What is the minimal proportion of the fourth letter needed to avoid that pattern?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $E = \{a,b,c\}$ be a set of pattern variables disjoint from $A$. A pattern is a word over the variables; here we consider the pattern
$$p \;=\; a\,b\,X\,b\,c\,Y\,c\,a\,Z\,b\,a\,T\,a\,c,$$
where $a,b,c$ are variables and $X,Y,Z,T$ are (possibly empty) "gap" variables. A word $w \in A^{*}$ is said to contain $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h$ from $\{a,b,c\}^{*}$ to $A^{+}$ (and arbitrary, possibly erasing assignments to $X,Y,Z,T$) such that the image of $p$ under $h$ appears as a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is $k$-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size $k$ that avoids $p$.

It is known that $p$ is $4$-avoidable but not $3$-avoidable. For an infinite word $w$ over the alphabet $\{1,2,3,4\}$ that avoids $p$, define the frequency of the letter $4$ in $w$ as
$$\mathrm{freq}_4(w) \;=\; \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{|w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n|_4}{n},$$
where $|u|_4$ counts the number of occurrences of $4$ in the prefix $u$. 

Determine the minimal possible value
$$\inf \bigl\{ \mathrm{freq}_4(w) : w \in \{1,2,3,4\}^{\omega} \text{ avoids } p \bigr\}.$$
status_search_result: The pattern is known to be 4-avoidable but not 3-avoidable (Baker, McNulty, Taylor). The question about the minimal frequency of the fourth letter in an infinite avoiding word over a 4-letter alphabet appears in the WORDS open-problem lists; web searches did not surface a published exact value or a definitive resolution, so the status is unclear.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is it decidable, given a pattern p and an integer k, whether p is k-avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be an alphabet of variables and $\Sigma$ an alphabet of letters (with $A\cap\Sigma=\emptyset$). A pattern is a finite nonempty word $p\in A^+$. A word $w\in\Sigma^*$ is said to encounter $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h:A^+\to\Sigma^+$ such that $h(p)$ occurs as a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. For a positive integer $k$, the pattern $p$ is called $k$-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over a $k$-letter alphabet that avoids $p$; otherwise $p$ is $k$-unavoidable.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input a pattern $p\in A^+$ and a positive integer $k$, decides whether $p$ is $k$-avoidable?
status_search_result: The decidability of $k$-avoidability of patterns is a long-standing open problem in combinatorics on words. While Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty and Zimin gave a decision procedure for unavoidability (i.e., avoidability over some finite alphabet), no algorithm is known to compute the avoidability index in general, and even the values for specific short patterns (e.g., whether $\mu(\alpha\alpha\beta\beta\gamma\gamma)=2$ or $3$) remain unresolved. Surveys and the BIRS report on outstanding challenges in combinatorics on words continue to list this as open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given a pattern p, what is the complexity of deciding whether p is avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $E$ be a countably infinite set of symbols called pattern variables, disjoint from $A$. A pattern is a non-empty word $p \in E^+$. Given a pattern $p$ over variables $E_p = \{x_1, \ldots, x_k\}$ and a word $w \in A^*$, we say that $w$ encounters $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h \colon E_p^* \to A^+$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is said to be avoidable if there exists a finite alphabet $A$ with $|A| \geq 2$ and an infinite word $w \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ that avoids $p$; otherwise $p$ is unavoidable.

It is known that there is an algorithm to decide, given a pattern $p$, whether $p$ is avoidable. Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem:

Input: a pattern $p \in E^+$.
Output: "yes" if $p$ is avoidable, "no" otherwise.

In particular, classify this problem within standard complexity classes (e.g., determine whether it is in $\mathsf{P}$, $\mathsf{NP}$-complete, $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete, etc.).
status_search_result: The problem is decidable via classical algorithms of Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty and Zimin. The exact complexity has been studied: deciding whether a word is unavoidable has been shown to be NP-complete (Rampersad et al., "The Complexity of Unavoidable Word Patterns," Theory of Computing Systems, 2022), and avoidability can be solved in PSPACE with NP-hardness known for related variants. Tight complexity classification for general pattern avoidability remains an active topic; the question as posed by the WORDS conference series is partially resolved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a pattern that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let A be a finite alphabet of letter symbols and let V be a disjoint countable set of variable symbols. A pattern is a finite nonempty word p over V. A word w over A is said to contain the pattern p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : V* -> A* (i.e. h(v) is a nonempty word in A* for every variable v occurring in p) such that h(p) is a factor (contiguous substring) of w. Otherwise, w avoids p.

For a positive integer k, the pattern p is said to be k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over some alphabet of size k that avoids p; otherwise p is k-unavoidable. Equivalently, p is k-avoidable iff there are infinitely many finite words of arbitrarily large length over a k-letter alphabet that avoid p. The avoidability index of p is mu(p) = min{ k : p is k-avoidable }, with mu(p) = infinity if no such k exists (p is unavoidable).

It is known that every pattern p with mu(p) finite satisfies mu(p) <= 5 for all currently known examples, and there exist patterns with mu(p) = 2, 3, 4, and 5.

Question. Does there exist a pattern p (a finite word over a variable alphabet) such that p is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable, i.e. mu(p) = 6?
status_search_result: The general question of whether there exists a constant C such that every avoidable pattern is C-avoidable remains open in combinatorics on words; in particular, no pattern with avoidability index strictly greater than 5 is known, and the specific question of whether some pattern is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable is unresolved in the surveyed literature on pattern avoidability.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is aabaacbaab 3-D0L-avoidable (i.e. is there a ternary morphism g such that g ω (a) avoids aabaacbaab)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ (resp. $\Sigma^\omega$) denote the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over $\Sigma$. A morphism $g:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ is called prolongable on a letter $a\in\Sigma$ if $g(a)$ starts with $a$ and $|g^n(a)|\to\infty$; in this case the iterated image converges to an infinite word $g^\omega(a)\in\Sigma^\omega$. Given a pattern $p$ on an alphabet $\Delta$ of "pattern variables", an infinite word $w$ over an alphabet $A$ is said to avoid $p$ if there is no factor $u$ of $w$ that can be written as $u=h(p)$ for some nonerasing morphism $h:\Delta^*\to A^*$. A pattern $p$ is called $k$-D0L-avoidable if there exists an alphabet $\Sigma$ with $|\Sigma|=k$, a morphism $g:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ prolongable on some letter $a\in\Sigma$, such that the infinite word $g^\omega(a)$ avoids $p$.

Question: Taking the pattern $p = aabaacbaab$ over the variable alphabet $\{a,b,c\}$, is $p$ 3-D0L-avoidable? Equivalently, does there exist a morphism $g:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ with $|\Sigma|=3$ that is prolongable on some letter such that the resulting fixed-point infinite word avoids the pattern $aabaacbaab$?

original_question: If a pattern is k-avoidable then it is k-HD0L-avoidable (i.e. are there morphisms f : Σ∗ −→ A∗ , g : Σ∗ −→ Σ∗ , with |Σ| = k such that f (g ω (a)) avoids p)?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let A be a finite alphabet and let Σ be another finite alphabet of "variables." A pattern is a nonempty word p ∈ Σ*. A word w ∈ A* is said to encounter p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : Σ* → A* such that h(p) appears as a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p. An infinite word over A avoids p if every one of its finite factors avoids p.

A pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that avoids p.

A k-HD0L word is an infinite word of the form f(g^ω(a)), where:
 • Σ is an alphabet with |Σ| = k,
 • A is a finite alphabet,
 • g : Σ* → Σ* is a morphism that is prolongable on a letter a ∈ Σ (so the iterated limit g^ω(a) is a well-defined infinite word over Σ),
 • f : Σ* → A* is a morphism.

A pattern p is called k-HD0L-avoidable if there exist such morphisms f and g and a letter a ∈ Σ with |Σ| = k so that the infinite word f(g^ω(a)) avoids p.

Question. Prove or disprove: for every pattern p and every positive integer k, if p is k-avoidable then p is k-HD0L-avoidable.
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open in the combinatorics-on-words literature. Related work notes that there exist k-avoidable patterns that are not k-D0L-avoidable, motivating the broader HD0L formulation, but no proof or counterexample for the HD0L version has been reported. Recent surveys and articles on pattern avoidance still list it as a conjecture.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Explore the applications of the probabilistic method in the scope of pattern avoidance.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_k = \{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$ be a finite alphabet and let $E$ be a finite or infinite alphabet of pattern variables. A pattern is a word $p \in E^+$. A word $w \in \Sigma_k^*$ is said to encounter $p$ if there is a non-erasing morphism $h : E^* \to \Sigma_k^*$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is said to be $k$-avoidable if there are infinitely many words in $\Sigma_k^*$ that avoid $p$, and the avoidability index $\lambda(p)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $p$ is $k$-avoidable (set $\lambda(p) = \infty$ if no such $k$ exists).

Develop the probabilistic method as a systematic tool to establish pattern avoidance results. Concretely:

(a) Identify general sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of the combinatorial parameters of a pattern $p$ (such as its length, number of variables, and structural features), under which a uniformly random word in $\Sigma_k^n$ avoids $p$ with positive probability, thereby yielding upper bounds on $\lambda(p)$.

(b) Adapt entropy compression and Lovász Local Lemma type arguments (including local lemma variants tailored to the i.i.d. random variable setting underlying random words) to obtain quantitative bounds on the growth rate of the language of words avoiding $p$, that improve upon known constructive bounds.

(c) Extend such probabilistic techniques to related avoidance settings, including avoidance of patterns in partial words (words over $\Sigma_k \cup \{\diamond\}$ where $\diamond$ is a "hole" matching any letter) and avoidance of formulas (finite sets of patterns sharing variables), and determine to what extent they yield tight values of the corresponding avoidability indices.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended research direction rather than a single sharp problem. Probabilistic techniques (Lovász Local Lemma, entropy compression, local lemma variants, automata-based generating function methods) have been successfully applied to several pattern avoidance problems in words and partial words, and active research continues. No definitive resolution of the broad program exists; numerous concrete sub-problems remain open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If p is k-avoidable, then arbitrarily long k-letter circular words avoiding p exist.
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet. A pattern is a nonempty word p over an alphabet E of variables. A word w over A is said to encounter p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E* → A* such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p. A circular word of length n over A is an equivalence class of words a_0 a_1 … a_{n-1} ∈ A^n under cyclic rotation; its factors are all factors (of every length) of the bi-infinite periodic word …a_0 a_1 … a_{n-1} a_0 a_1 …. A circular word avoids p if none of its factors encounters p.

For an integer k ≥ 1, a pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exist infinitely many (equivalently, arbitrarily long) finite words over a k-letter alphabet that avoid p.

Prove or disprove the following statement: For every integer k ≥ 1 and every pattern p that is k-avoidable, there exist arbitrarily long circular words over a k-letter alphabet that avoid p.
status_search_result: The statement is listed as an open conjecture in the WORDS open-problems compilation. Related work (e.g., Aberkane–Currie on circular words avoiding patterns, and the repetition-threshold results of Gorbunova/Shur) establishes the conclusion for some specific patterns and for repetition-type avoidability, but a general proof or counterexample for arbitrary k-avoidable patterns has not been located.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let p be k-avoidable. 1. If the number of p-free words on k letters of length n grows exponentially with n, then an integer N0 exists such that, for every n > N0 , there are circular p-free words on k letters with length n. 2. If the number of p-free words on k letters of length n grows polynomially with n, then the set of possible lengths for circular p-free words on k letters has density 0 in the set IN \ {0}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A_k = \{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$ be a $k$-letter alphabet, and let $E$ be a disjoint alphabet of variables. A pattern is a non-empty word $p \in E^+$. A word $w \in A_k^*$ is said to encounter $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h: E^+ \to A_k^+$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ is called $p$-free. The pattern $p$ is $k$-avoidable if there exist infinitely many $p$-free words in $A_k^*$.

A circular word of length $n$ over $A_k$ is an equivalence class of words in $A_k^n$ under cyclic rotation; equivalently, it is a word $w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ considered with indices modulo $n$. A circular word is $p$-free if every factor (every contiguous block read cyclically) is $p$-free.

For a $k$-avoidable pattern $p$, let $f_p(n)$ denote the number of $p$-free words of length $n$ over $A_k$, and let $S_p \subseteq \mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$ denote the set of positive integers $n$ such that there exists a circular $p$-free word of length $n$ over $A_k$.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(1) If $f_p(n)$ grows exponentially with $n$ (i.e., $\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_p(n)^{1/n} > 1$), then there exists $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $n > N_0$, $n \in S_p$.

(2) If $f_p(n)$ grows polynomially with $n$ (i.e., $f_p(n) = O(n^c)$ for some constant $c$), then $S_p$ has natural density $0$ in $\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, meaning $\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{|S_p \cap \{1,\dots,N\}|}{N} = 0$.
status_search_result: The statement appears in a collection of open problems and conjectures from the WORDS conferences, listed as a conjecture without resolution. Searches did not reveal a published proof or disproof. Related work on circular squarefree words and growth of pattern-free word languages exists, but the conjecture in its stated generality appears to remain open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: The number of k-power-free binary words of length n grows polynomially with n for k ≤ 7/3, but exponentially for k > 7/3 [24]. Examine analogous results for alphabets of arbitrary size.
self_contained_problem:
Fix an alphabet Σ of size σ ≥ 2 and a real number k > 1. A word w over Σ is said to contain a k-power if it has a factor of the form u^a v where a = ⌊k⌋, v is a prefix of u, and |u^a v|/|u| ≥ k (i.e., a factor whose exponent is at least k). Otherwise w is called k-power-free. Let L_{σ,k}(n) denote the number of k-power-free words of length n over an alphabet of size σ.

For σ = 2 it is known that there exists a threshold value t_2 = 7/3 such that L_{2,k}(n) grows polynomially in n when k ≤ 7/3 and exponentially in n when k > 7/3.

Problem: For each alphabet size σ ≥ 3, determine the threshold value t_σ ∈ ℝ (if it exists) such that L_{σ,k}(n) grows polynomially in n for k ≤ t_σ and exponentially in n for k > t_σ. More generally, classify, for every σ ≥ 2 and every k strictly larger than the repetition threshold RT(σ) of the σ-letter alphabet, whether the language of k-power-free words over Σ has polynomial or exponential growth, and provide a complete description of the dichotomy.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Shur and collaborators established the growth dichotomy and asymptotic growth rates for power-free languages over large alphabets, and a conjecture of Shur on growth rates of (n/(n-1))-free and (n/(n-1))+-free words over large alphabets was proven by Bui and Rosenfeld (MFCS 2025). Polynomial vs. exponential thresholds are known for small alphabets (e.g., binary at 7/3; ternary and quaternary cases yield exponentially many words at the repetition threshold), but a complete dichotomy describing the threshold for every alphabet size remains incompletely settled in full generality.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Extension of a result from [7]: the set of circular words over {0, 1, 2, 3} avoiding the pattern abXbcY caZbaT cb has density 0 in the set IN \ {0}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{0,1,2,3\}$. A circular word of length $n$ over $\Sigma$ is an equivalence class of words in $\Sigma^n$ under cyclic rotation. A (linear) word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is said to encounter the pattern $p$ over a pattern alphabet $\{a,b,c,X,Y,Z,T\}$ (where $a,b,c$ are variables required to take pairwise distinct values and $X,Y,Z,T$ are variables allowed to take any value, including the empty word) if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h$ (i.e., $h(a),h(b),h(c)$ are nonempty and pairwise distinct) such that $h(p)$ occurs as a factor of $w$; the variables $X,Y,Z,T$ may be mapped to arbitrary, possibly empty words. A circular word $u$ of length $n$ avoids the pattern $p$ if no linear factor of any rotation of $u$ (equivalently, no factor of $uu$ of length at most $n$) encounters $p$.

Consider the specific pattern
$$ p \;=\; a\, b\, X\, b\, c\, Y\, c\, a\, Z\, b\, a\, T\, c\, b. $$

For $n \ge 1$, let $C(n)$ denote the number of circular words of length $n$ over $\Sigma = \{0,1,2,3\}$ that avoid $p$, and let $A(n)$ denote the total number of circular words of length $n$ over $\Sigma$.

Prove or disprove: the set
$$ S \;=\; \{\, n \in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} \;:\; C(n) > 0 \,\} $$
has natural density $0$ in $\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$, i.e.,
$$ \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{|S \cap \{1,2,\dots,N\}|}{N} \;=\; 0. $$
status_search_result: The problem appears in a list of open problems and conjectures collected from the WORDS conferences and is presented as an extension of an earlier result. A targeted web search did not locate a paper resolving this specific density statement for circular words over a 4-letter alphabet avoiding the given pattern, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let Σ be an alphabet and let w ∈ Σ∗ a p-free word. Then w is a factor of a maximal p-free word over Σ.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet and let p be a pattern, i.e., a nonempty word over an alphabet of variables. A word w ∈ Σ* is said to encounter p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h from the variable alphabet to Σ* such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w is p-free. A p-free word w ∈ Σ* is called maximal if no proper extension of w (on either side, by appending or prepending letters of Σ) is p-free; equivalently, for every a ∈ Σ, neither aw nor wa is p-free.

Prove or disprove: for every alphabet Σ and every pattern p, every p-free word w ∈ Σ* is a factor of some maximal p-free word over Σ.

The status appears unresolved in the public literature retrievable by search.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given an alphabet Σ and a pattern p, maximal p-free word over Σ exists.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet and let Δ be a (disjoint) alphabet of variables. A pattern is a non-empty word p ∈ Δ⁺. A non-erasing morphism h : Δ⁺ → Σ⁺ realizes an occurrence of p in a word w ∈ Σ* if h(p) is a factor of w. A word w ∈ Σ* is said to be p-free (equivalently, to avoid p) if no non-erasing morphism h : Δ⁺ → Σ⁺ produces h(p) as a factor of w.

A p-free word w ∈ Σ* is called maximal p-free if it cannot be extended on either side while remaining p-free; that is, for every letter a ∈ Σ, both aw and wa contain an occurrence of p (i.e., are no longer p-free).

Prove or disprove: for every finite alphabet Σ and every pattern p ∈ Δ⁺, there exists a maximal p-free word over Σ.
status_search_result: The conjecture is recorded in a 2017 compilation of open problems and conjectures from the WORDS conferences. A targeted web search did not turn up a published proof or disproof of the existence of maximal p-free words for every alphabet Σ and pattern p, so the present status could not be verified.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let Σ be an alphabet, k ∈ [1, 2], and w ∈ Σ∗ be a k-power-free word. Then in any case, w is a factor of a maximal k-power-free word over Σ.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet with |Σ| ≥ 2 and let Σ* denote the set of all finite words over Σ. For a real number k ≥ 1, a k-power is a word of the form u^k, meaning a word of length k|u| (with k|u| an integer) obtained as a prefix of u^⌈k⌉ for some nonempty u ∈ Σ*. A word w ∈ Σ* is called k-power-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of w is a k-power. A k-power-free word w over Σ is called maximal if w is not a proper factor of any other k-power-free word over Σ (equivalently, every one-letter extension on the left or right introduces a k-power, and similarly for every internal insertion when relevant).

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every real number k ∈ [1, 2] and every k-power-free word w ∈ Σ*, there exists a maximal k-power-free word over Σ that contains w as a factor.
status_search_result: The question is part of the family of extendability problems for power-free languages originating from Restivo–Salemi (1985). Recent work (e.g., the 2023 preprint on the Restivo–Salemi property for α-power-free languages with α ≥ 5 and k ≥ 3 letters, and earlier transition-property results for α ≥ 2 with k ≥ 3) addresses related but distinct extendability properties and explicitly the range α ≥ 2. No source found resolves the stated claim for the range k ∈ [1, 2]; it appears still open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is it possible to avoid an arbitrary pattern p by an infinite sequence of palindromes over each alphabet on which p is avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A pattern is a word $p \in E^*$ on a separate alphabet $E$ of variables. A word $w \in A^*$ is said to contain the pattern $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h : E^* \to A^*$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor (contiguous subword) of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w} \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ avoids $p$ if every finite factor of $\mathbf{w}$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is said to be avoidable over $A$ if there exists an infinite word over $A$ that avoids $p$.

A finite word $u \in A^*$ is a palindrome if $u$ equals its mirror image (i.e., reading $u$ from right to left gives $u$ again). An "infinite sequence of palindromes" over $A$ is an infinite sequence $(u_n)_{n \ge 1}$ with each $u_n \in A^*$ a non-empty palindrome; such a sequence determines the infinite word $u_1 u_2 u_3 \cdots \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ obtained by concatenation.

Question: For every pattern $p$ and every finite alphabet $A$ over which $p$ is avoidable, does there exist an infinite sequence of palindromes $(u_n)_{n\ge 1}$ over $A$ such that the concatenated infinite word $u_1 u_2 u_3 \cdots$ avoids $p$?

J. Combin., 2021, and related work on $xyx$-formulas and palindrome patterns), but no source was found that explicitly resolves this specific question about avoiding an arbitrary pattern by a concatenation of palindromes on every alphabet where the pattern is avoidable. The status could not be conclusively determined from available sources.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does a given word generate a finite or infinite subtree?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $L \subseteq A^*$ be the language of all repetition-free words over $A$ for a fixed avoidance condition (for instance, the set of all square-free words, or the set of all cube-free words). Order $L$ by the prefix relation: this turns $L$ into a rooted tree $T_L$ whose root is the empty word and whose nodes are exactly the words of $L$, with $u$ being a parent of $ua$ for $a\in A$ whenever $ua\in L$. For a word $w\in L$, the subtree generated by $w$ is the induced subtree of $T_L$ consisting of $w$ together with all its descendants (i.e., all words in $L$ that have $w$ as a prefix).

Provide an algorithm (or prove that none exists) that, given as input a word $w\in L$, decides whether the subtree of $T_L$ generated by $w$ is finite or infinite. Equivalently, decide whether $w$ can be extended on the right to arbitrarily long words in $L$.
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / prefix trees of repetition-free words
status_search_result: The question is listed among open problems from the WORDS conferences concerning the prefix tree of repetition-free (e.g., square-free, cube-free) words, motivated by work of Petrova and Shur on the structure of these trees (short non-branching paths, positive density of branching points). Subsequent work by Petrova–Shur and others has clarified structural and density properties of these trees, but a general effective procedure deciding finiteness of the subtree generated by an arbitrary input word does not appear to be established in the literature retrieved. The status therefore remains unclear from available sources.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Are the subtrees generated by two given words isomorphic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x = x_1 x_2 x_3 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. A finite word $w \in A^*$ is called a factor of $x$ if it occurs as a block $x_i x_{i+1} \cdots x_{i+|w|-1}$ for some $i \ge 1$. Denote by $F(x) \subseteq A^*$ the set of all factors of $x$ (including the empty word).

Consider the prefix tree (trie) $T(x)$ of $x$: its vertex set is $F(x)$, and for every $u \in F(x)$ and $a \in A$ such that $ua \in F(x)$, there is a directed edge from $u$ to $ua$ labelled by $a$. The root of $T(x)$ is the empty word.

For a factor $w \in F(x)$, the subtree generated by $w$, denoted $T_w(x)$, is the subtree of $T(x)$ rooted at $w$ and consisting of all vertices $v \in F(x)$ that have $w$ as a prefix, with the inherited edges and edge labels.

Two such subtrees $T_{w_1}(x)$ and $T_{w_2}(x)$ are said to be isomorphic if there is a root-preserving bijection of their vertex sets that preserves the edge relation (equivalently, an isomorphism of the underlying rooted, $A$-edge-labelled trees).

Problem: Given an infinite word $x$ (presented in a suitable effective way, e.g. as a morphic or automatic word) and two factors $w_1, w_2 \in F(x)$, decide whether the subtrees $T_{w_1}(x)$ and $T_{w_2}(x)$ are isomorphic. Characterize, for natural classes of infinite words $x$, the pairs $(w_1, w_2)$ of factors that generate isomorphic subtrees.
status_search_result: Web searches for the problem of deciding isomorphism of subtrees generated by two words in a prefix tree of an infinite word did not return any direct resolution. There is related work on isomorphism of regular trees and regular words (Kuske, Liu, Lohrey, ICALP 2011) showing the regular-tree/word isomorphism problem is decidable (polynomial time for DFAs), but no specific reference confirms a solution to this particular formulation from the WORDS open-problem list. Status is therefore taken to be unknown.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which square-free words u can be shuffled to obtain a square-free word u ▷β u?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. A word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is called a square if $w = vv$ for some nonempty $v \in \Sigma^*$. A word is square-free if it contains no nonempty factor (contiguous substring) that is a square.

Given two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$, the shuffle set $x \shuffle y$ is the set of all words obtained by interleaving the letters of $x$ and $y$ while preserving the left-to-right order of letters within $x$ and within $y$. Explicitly, if $x = x_1 \cdots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \cdots y_n$, then $w \in x \shuffle y$ iff $w$ has length $m+n$ and there is a partition of its positions into two increasing sequences spelling $x$ and $y$ respectively.

Characterize all square-free words $u \in \Sigma^*$ for which there exists a square-free word $w \in u \shuffle u$. That is, determine the set of square-free words $u$ such that some shuffle of $u$ with itself is again square-free.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing which square-free words admit a square-free self-shuffle remains open. Partial results are known: Harju (2013) showed that for every n ≥ 3 there exists a ternary square-free word u of length n such that u ⧢ u contains a square-free word, and subsequent work by Müller, Guégan–Ochem, and others has produced related avoidability and complexity results (e.g., NP-completeness of recognizing shuffled-square-free factors, existence of infinite shuffled-square-free words over small alphabets), but no full characterization of square-free words u admitting a square-free shuffle u ⧢ u is established.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which words u can be shuffled to obtain a unique square-free word u ▷β u?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. Given two words $v, w \in \Sigma^*$, the shuffle $v \shuffle w$ is the set of all words obtained by interleaving the letters of $v$ and $w$ in a manner that preserves the relative order of the letters within $v$ and within $w$. A word $z \in \Sigma^*$ is called square-free if it contains no non-empty factor of the form $xx$ (where a factor is a contiguous subword). 

Characterize the words $u \in \Sigma^*$ for which the set 
$$\{\,z \in u \shuffle u : z \text{ is square-free}\,\}$$ 
consists of exactly one element; that is, determine all words $u$ such that $u$ can be shuffled with itself to produce a square-free word, and this square-free shuffle is unique.
status_search_result: Research on square-free shuffles of words has continued (e.g., Harju 2014, Guégan–Ochem, Müller, and more recent work on shuffled-square-free words through 2022–2023), focusing mainly on the existence of (infinite) shuffled-square-free words and the minimum alphabet size required. No source found explicitly resolves the characterization of words $u$ whose self-shuffle $u \shuffle u$ contains a unique square-free word, so its current status is unclear.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which words w can be obtained in more than one way from a single word u using different conducting sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the set of all finite words over A. For a word u = a_1 a_2 ... a_n in A*, a shuffle of u with itself is any word w in A* of length 2n obtained as follows: choose a binary sequence c = c_1 c_2 ... c_{2n} in {0,1}* containing exactly n zeros and n ones, and define w by reading, from left to right, the letters of u for the positions of c labeled 0 and (independently) the letters of u for the positions labeled 1. Such a binary sequence c is called a conducting sequence for the pair (u, w), and we write w ∈ u ⧢ u with conductor c.

Two conducting sequences c and c' for (u, w) are considered different if they differ as binary words. Characterize, or describe nontrivial families of, words w in A* for which there exists a single word u in A* and at least two distinct conducting sequences c ≠ c' that both produce w as a shuffle of u with itself.
status_search_result: Recent work on shuffled-square-free words (e.g., Harju–Müller 2013 and the 2022/2023 paper by Jugé and collaborators) addresses the existence of infinite shuffled-square-free words over small alphabets, but does not appear to give a complete characterization of words w that arise as a shuffle of some u with itself via two distinct conducting sequences. No source found that resolves this specific characterization question.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which square-free words w are themselves shuffles of square-free words: w = u ▷β u?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the set of finite words over A. A word w ∈ A* is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form xx (i.e., there is no nonempty word x such that xx appears as a contiguous block in w). For two words u, v ∈ A*, the shuffle u ⧢ v is the set of all words obtained by interleaving the letters of u with the letters of v while preserving the relative order of letters within u and within v. A word w is called a self-shuffle of u if w ∈ u ⧢ u, i.e., w can be written as a₁b₁a₂b₂⋯aₙbₙ where u = a₁a₂⋯aₙ = b₁b₂⋯bₙ (more generally, w arises from interleaving two copies of u with arbitrary choice at each step which copy to take). 

Characterize the square-free words w ∈ A* such that there exists a square-free word u ∈ A* with w ∈ u ⧢ u. Equivalently, describe the set of square-free words that are self-shuffles of square-free words.
status_search_result: Related questions have been studied: the existence of infinite square-free self-shuffling words was answered affirmatively (Charlier, Kamae, Puzynina, Zamboni, 2014; arXiv:1401.6536), and Currie/Saari studied "square-free words with square-free self-shuffles" (Electron. original_question: Does there exist an infinite square-free word w such that w = w ▷β w for some infinite β?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A^ω the set of infinite words over A. For two infinite words u, v ∈ A^ω and an infinite binary word β ∈ {1,2}^ω in which both letters 1 and 2 occur infinitely often, the shuffle of u and v directed by β, denoted u ▷_β v, is the infinite word obtained as follows: reading β from left to right, the n-th letter of u ▷_β v is the next unused letter of u if the n-th letter of β is 1, and otherwise the next unused letter of v. An infinite word w ∈ A^ω is said to be self-shuffling if there exists an infinite directing word β (with both 1's and 2's appearing infinitely often) such that w = w ▷_β w. The word w is square-free if it contains no factor of the form xx with x a nonempty finite word.

Question: Does there exist an infinite square-free word w (over some finite alphabet) that is self-shuffling, i.e. such that w = w ▷_β w for some infinite directing word β?

Currie, Saari, and Zamboni constructed an infinite square-free word over a 3-letter alphabet that is self-shuffling (arXiv:1401.6536, "Infinite square-free self-shuffling words"), and related results appear in "Square-Free Words with Square-Free Self-Shuffles" (Electronic J. original_question: In the tree T , the size of any minimal subtree of index n is O(log n).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}$ be a ternary alphabet. A finite word $w\in\Sigma^*$ is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form $xx$. Let $S\subseteq\Sigma^*$ be the set of all ternary square-free words. Order $S$ by the prefix relation, so that $S$ becomes an infinite rooted tree $T$: the root is the empty word, and the children of a node $w\in S$ are exactly the words $wa, wb, wc$ that lie in $S$.

For a node $w\in T$, define the index of $w$ to be its depth, i.e.\ $|w|$. A node $w$ is a branching node of $T$ if it has at least two children in $T$. For each node $w$ of index $n$, let the minimal subtree at $w$ be the subtree of $T$ rooted at $w$ obtained by taking the unique non-branching path starting at $w$ together with the first branching descendant (equivalently, the descendants of $w$ up to and including the first node having more than one child, if such a node exists).

Prove or disprove the following statement: there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ such that for every node $w$ of $T$ of index $n\ge 2$, the size (number of nodes) of the minimal subtree at $w$ is at most $C\log n$. In other words, the size of any minimal subtree of index $n$ in $T$ is $O(\log n)$.
status_search_result: Work by Petrova and Shur on the tree of ternary square-free words establishes that non-branching paths from a node at level n have length O(log n), with an explicit bound near 8.5 log n − 28 for large n. However, accessible sources do not clearly confirm whether the conjectured O(log n) bound on the size of every minimal subtree of index n has been fully proven; status remains unclear from available evidence.

original_question: We have FRT(4) = RT (4) = 7/5. Advances in problem solving The conjecture was solved by Golnaz Badkobeh, Maxime Crochemore and Michaël Rao. In addition they proved that FRT(k) = RT (k) for k ≤ 6 (private communication at WORDS 2015).
self_contained_problem:
For an integer k ≥ 2 and a real number α > 1, an α-power is a nonempty word of the form u^n v where v is a prefix of u, n ≥ 1 is an integer, and |u^n v|/|u| = α. A word is said to be α-free (respectively α^+-free) if none of its factors is a β-power with β ≥ α (respectively β > α). The repetition threshold over a k-letter alphabet is

  RT(k) = inf { α > 1 : there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that is α^+-free }.

The finite repetition threshold over a k-letter alphabet is defined as

  FRT(k) = inf { α > 1 : there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that is α^+-free and contains only finitely many factors that are α-powers }.

It is known that FRT(k) ≥ RT(k) for all k ≥ 2, and that FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5.

Problem: Prove that FRT(k) = RT(k) for every integer k ≥ 5.

original_question: Can we compute a mapping f : Σ∗ −→ Σ∗ for which a constant c > 1 exists, such that for all w ∈ Σ∗ , if ρsq (w) ≥ 1 then we have ρsq (f (w)) ≥ cρsq (w)?
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet with |Σ| ≥ 2, and let Σ* denote the set of finite words over Σ. A square is a word of the form uu with u a nonempty word; an occurrence of a square in w ∈ Σ* is a pair (i, u) with u nonempty such that uu appears as the factor w[i..i+2|u|−1]. For w ∈ Σ* with |w| ≥ 1, define the square density of w by
   ρ_sq(w) = (number of distinct nonempty squares occurring as factors of w) / |w|.
(For example, in w = aabaabb one counts the distinct squares aa, abab if it occurs, bb, etc., and divides by |w|.)

Question. Does there exist a computable mapping f : Σ* → Σ* and a real constant c > 1 such that, for every w ∈ Σ* satisfying ρ_sq(w) ≥ 1, one has
   ρ_sq(f(w)) ≥ c · ρ_sq(w)?

Equivalently: can one effectively "amplify" the square density of any word whose square density is at least 1 by a multiplicative factor strictly greater than 1?

original_question: What is the minimum exponent of a repetion which is avoidable by an infinite word constructed by iterated (prefix)-suffix duplication?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w\in\Sigma^*$ be a finite word. The suffix duplication operation derives from $w$ any word of the form $wu$ where $u$ is a suffix of $w$; symmetrically, the prefix duplication operation derives from $w$ any word of the form $uw$ where $u$ is a prefix of $w$. The prefix-suffix duplication operation allows, at each step, either a prefix duplication or a suffix duplication. Starting from a single letter (or, more generally, a finite seed word) and iterating the prefix-suffix duplication operation, one can generate finite words of arbitrary length, and, in the limit, infinite words.

For a real number $\alpha\ge 1$, an infinite word $w$ is said to avoid $\alpha$-powers (equivalently, is $\alpha$-power-free) if no factor of $w$ is of the form $u^{\beta}$ (a fractional power, i.e. a prefix of $u^{\lceil\beta\rceil}$ of length $\beta|u|$) with $\beta\ge\alpha$.

Determine the infimum $\alpha^*$ of all real numbers $\alpha\ge 1$ such that there exists an infinite word over some finite alphabet, obtained as the limit of an iterated prefix-suffix duplication process starting from a finite seed, which avoids $\alpha$-powers. Equivalently, what is the minimum exponent of a repetition that is avoidable by an infinite word constructed by iterated prefix-suffix duplication?
status_search_result: Searches surface related work on prefix-suffix duplication and on prefix-suffix square completion (a different but related operation), where it is known that infinite words generated by iterated square completion can avoid all exponents strictly greater than 2. However, no source clearly identifies the exact minimum avoidable repetition exponent for infinite words produced specifically by iterated prefix-suffix duplication, so the precise value remains unverified.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Draw studies of languages constructed by iterating prefix-suffix square completion, starting with special sets of initial words such as singleton sets, finite sets, regular sets, etc.
self_contained_problem:
Define the following operations on finite words over an alphabet $\Sigma$:

- (Suffix square completion) From a word $w$, derive any word $wx$ such that $w$ has a suffix of the form $yx$ with $y$ a suffix of $w$ ending in $yx$, i.e. $w$ ends in $yx$ and one appends $x$ so that $yxyx$ (a square $yx\cdot yx$) appears as a suffix of the result. Equivalently, if $w = uyx$ for some factorization, then $w \Rightarrow wx$.
- (Prefix square completion) From a word $w = xyu$, derive $xw$, creating a square $xy\cdot xy$ as a prefix of the result.
- (Prefix-suffix square completion) The union of the two operations above.

For a language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$, let $\mathrm{PSC}^*(L)$ denote the smallest language containing $L$ that is closed under prefix-suffix square completion (i.e., the set of all words obtainable by finitely many iterated applications of the operation starting from words in $L$).

Investigate the structure and classification (in the Chomsky hierarchy and beyond) of the languages $\mathrm{PSC}^*(L)$ when the initial language $L$ ranges over special families, including:
1. Singleton sets $L = \{w\}$ for a single word $w \in \Sigma^*$.
2. Arbitrary finite sets $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$.
3. Regular languages $L$.

Determine, for each such family, whether $\mathrm{PSC}^*(L)$ is necessarily regular, context-free, context-sensitive, or otherwise; characterize closure properties; and provide decision procedures (with complexity bounds) for membership, emptiness, finiteness, and equivalence questions for these iterated prefix-suffix square completion languages.

status_search_result: The prefix-suffix square completion operation was introduced and partial results obtained (e.g., a linear-time membership procedure for the case of starting from a single word; companion results on prefix-suffix square reduction showing closure of linear and context-free classes under bounded reduction). However, a systematic classification of the iterated prefix-suffix square completion languages for general singleton, finite, and regular initial sets does not appear to be fully resolved in the literature; the problem stands as a programmatic open research direction.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the minimum number of steps of square completion needed to obtain a word from one of its factors?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w \in \Sigma^*$, a factor of $w$ is any contiguous subword of $w$. 

Define the operation of square completion on a word $u$ as follows: a single step of prefix square completion takes $u = vx$, where $v$ is a nonempty prefix of $u$ and $x$ is a (possibly empty) suffix, and produces the word $vvx' $ ... more precisely, a prefix square completion step replaces $u$ by $u' = pu$ where $p$ is a nonempty prefix of $u$ such that $pp$ is a prefix of $u'$ (i.e., we prepend a copy of some prefix so that the resulting word begins with a square). Symmetrically, a suffix square completion step replaces $u$ by $us$ where $s$ is a nonempty suffix of $u$ such that $ss$ is a suffix of the new word. A step of square completion is either a prefix or suffix square completion step.

Given a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ and a factor $f$ of $w$ such that $w$ can be obtained from $f$ by some finite sequence of square completion steps, let $N(w,f)$ denote the minimum number of square completion steps needed to obtain $w$ starting from $f$.

Determine $N(w,f)$, i.e., establish tight bounds (as a function of $|w|$, $|f|$, and the structural parameters of $w$ and $f$) for the minimum number of square completion steps required to obtain $w$ from one of its factors $f$.
status_search_result: Prefix-suffix square completion has been studied, and there exists a linear-time decision procedure for whether a longer word can be obtained from a shorter one via iterated square completion. However, no source clearly establishing tight bounds on the minimum number of square completion steps to generate a word from a factor was found, so the status of this specific quantitative question is unclear.

original_question: Which of the following patterns 01020312, 01020321, 01021303, 01023031, 010203013, 010213020 is avoidable in the abelian sense?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let A be a finite alphabet of letters and let E = {0,1,2,…} be a separate alphabet of pattern variables. A pattern is a finite word p = p_1 p_2 … p_n over E. Given a word w over A, the abelian (or commutative) equivalence relation ~_a on A* is defined by u ~_a v iff |u|_a = |v|_a for every letter a ∈ A (i.e., u and v are permutations of each other). 

A word w over A is said to encounter the pattern p in the abelian sense if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E* → A* and a factor f of w such that f = h(p_1) h(p_2) ⋯ h(p_n) with h(p_i) ~_a h(p_j) whenever p_i = p_j. Otherwise w avoids p in the abelian sense. The pattern p is said to be avoidable in the abelian sense if there exists a finite alphabet A and an infinite word w over A that avoids p in the abelian sense; otherwise p is unavoidable in the abelian sense.

  (ii)  01020321,
  (iii) 01021303,
  (iv)  01023031,
  (v)   010203013,
  (vi)  010213020.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $k\ge 1$ be an integer. Two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^{*}$ are said to be k-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_{k} v$, if for every word $w\in\Sigma^{*}$ with $|w|\le k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$. A finite word $w$ is called a strongly k-abelian nth power if $w$ can be written as a concatenation $w=u_{1}u_{2}\cdots u_{n}$ where $u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{n}$ are pairwise k-abelian equivalent and, in addition, all the $u_{i}$ have the same length. A word $W$ is said to avoid strongly k-abelian nth powers if no factor of $W$ is a strongly k-abelian nth power.

It is known that for every fixed alphabet size $|\Sigma|$, every $k\ge 1$, and every $n\ge 2$, strongly k-abelian nth powers are unavoidable, so that there exists a longest finite word over $\Sigma$ that avoids strongly k-abelian nth powers.

status_search_result: Strongly k-abelian nth powers were shown to be unavoidable for all k and n (Karhumäki–Saarela–Zamboni, 2013), which guarantees the existence of a longest avoiding word. original_question: Is there a pure morphic binary word avoiding 2-abelian cubes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ be a binary alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. For an integer $k\geq 1$, two words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_k v$, if for every word $w\in\Sigma^*$ with $|w|\leq k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$. A $k$-abelian cube is a non-empty word of the form $u_1u_2u_3$ with $|u_1|=|u_2|=|u_3|$ and $u_1\sim_k u_2\sim_k u_3$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid $k$-abelian cubes if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $k$-abelian cube.

A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ satisfying $h(xy)=h(x)h(y)$. A morphism $h$ is called prolongable on a letter $a\in\Sigma$ if $h(a)$ begins with $a$ and $|h^n(a)|\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$; in that case the limit $h^{\omega}(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty} h^n(a)$ defines an infinite word, called a pure morphic word.

Question: Does there exist a pure morphic infinite binary word that avoids $2$-abelian cubes?
status_search_result: The avoidability of 2-abelian cubes on a binary alphabet by pure morphic words is mentioned as an open question in the literature on k-abelian avoidability. Known results show that k-abelian cubes are avoidable on binary alphabets for k≥3 (and even k=2 is not fully settled in some formulations), but constructions typically use morphic images rather than pure morphic words, and iterating a single morphism is known to be insufficient for many k-abelian avoidability problems. No source verifying a positive or negative answer for pure morphic binary words avoiding 2-abelian cubes was found.

original_question: Assume that a word of length n containing k many distinct abelian-square factors exists. Then a binary word of length n containing at least k many distinct abelian-square factors exists. Two abelian squares are inequivalent if their Parikh vectors are different [20].
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. For a finite word $w \in \Sigma^*$, the Parikh vector $\Psi(w)$ is the vector indexed by $\Sigma$ whose $a$-entry is the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in $w$. A factor of $w$ is a contiguous subword. An abelian square is a nonempty word of the form $uv$ with $\Psi(u) = \Psi(v)$ (equivalently, $v$ is an anagram of $u$). Two abelian-square factors are considered distinct (inequivalent) if their Parikh vectors are different.

For a finite word $w$, let $A(w)$ denote the number of distinct (inequivalent) abelian-square factors of $w$, that is, the number of distinct Parikh vectors $\Psi(u)$ arising from factors of $w$ of the form $uv$ with $\Psi(u)=\Psi(v)$.

Equivalently, the maximum of $A(w)$ over all words $w$ of length $n$ is attained on the binary alphabet.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Can we avoid long abelian cubes over two letters?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be a binary alphabet. An *abelian cube* in an infinite word $w \in \Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is a factor of the form $u_1 u_2 u_3$, where $u_1, u_2, u_3 \in \Sigma^{*}$ are nonempty words that are pairwise permutations of each other (i.e., they have the same Parikh vector, meaning each letter occurs the same number of times in each $u_i$). The integer $|u_1| = |u_2| = |u_3|$ is the *period* of the abelian cube.

It is known that every sufficiently long binary word contains an abelian cube, so abelian cubes cannot be avoided entirely over a two-letter alphabet. The question is whether one can avoid all *sufficiently long* abelian cubes: does there exist an integer $N \geq 1$ and an infinite binary word $w \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $w$ contains no abelian cube of period at least $N$?

Equivalently, determine whether such a word exists, and if so, determine the smallest such $N$.
status_search_result: Avoiding all abelian cubes over a binary alphabet is impossible, but relaxations are known: k-abelian cubes (factors with equal multiplicities of all subfactors of length ≤ k) are avoidable on binary alphabets for k ≥ 3 (Rao, Rosenfeld, Mercaş, and collaborators), improving an earlier bound of k ≥ 5. Results by Tunev and Shur, and others, establish that long abelian cubes of period at least 2 cannot all be avoided on a binary alphabet in certain strong formulations. The exact threshold and precise form of "long" abelian cubes avoidable on two letters remains under active investigation; thus the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: How to decide whether a morphic word avoids (long) abelian power?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. A morphism is a map $\varphi:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ extended by concatenation. If there exists $a\in\Sigma$ with $\varphi(a)=aw$ for some $w\in\Sigma^*$ and $\varphi^n(a)$ is unbounded in length, the iterated limit $\varphi^\omega(a)\in\Sigma^\mathbb{N}$ is called a pure morphic word; applying a coding (letter-to-letter map) $\tau$ yields a morphic word $\tau(\varphi^\omega(a))$.

Two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_{ab} v$, if $|u|_c=|v|_c$ for every letter $c\in\Sigma$, i.e., they are permutations of each other. For an integer $k\ge 2$, an abelian $k$-power is a nonempty word of the form $u_1u_2\cdots u_k$ where $u_1\sim_{ab} u_2\sim_{ab}\cdots\sim_{ab} u_k$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ avoids abelian $k$-powers if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian $k$-power; for a length threshold $L\ge 1$, $\mathbf{w}$ avoids long abelian $k$-powers if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian $k$-power $u_1\cdots u_k$ with $|u_1|\ge L$.

Problem: Provide an algorithm which, given as input a morphism $\varphi$, a coding $\tau$, a letter $a$ generating a morphic word $\mathbf{w}=\tau(\varphi^\omega(a))$, an integer $k\ge 2$, and (optionally) a threshold $L\ge 1$, decides whether $\mathbf{w}$ avoids abelian $k$-powers (respectively, long abelian $k$-powers of period at least $L$). Equivalently, determine whether the abelian $k$-power avoidance problem (and its long-power variant) is decidable for the class of morphic words.
status_search_result: Partial results are known. Rosenfeld and others have given algorithms that decide abelian (and additive) power avoidance for morphic words under structural assumptions (e.g., primitive morphisms with no eigenvalue of absolute value 1, or fixed points of suitable morphisms). A fully general decision procedure for arbitrary morphic words remains open as of the latest available literature.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Find a morphism simpler than Keränen’s morphism that avoids abelian squares on four letters.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_4 = \{a,b,c,d\}$ be a four-letter alphabet. A nonempty finite word $w \in \Sigma_4^+$ is called an abelian square if $w = uv$ with $|u|=|v|$ and $v$ is a permutation of $u$ (equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector). A (finite or infinite) word is said to avoid abelian squares (or be abelian-square-free) if none of its factors is an abelian square. A morphism $h : \Sigma_4^* \to \Sigma_4^*$ is said to avoid abelian squares if $h^\omega(a)$ (the infinite fixed point obtained by iterating $h$ on some letter $a \in \Sigma_4$, assuming it exists) is abelian-square-free; equivalently, one often requires that $h(w)$ is abelian-square-free for every abelian-square-free word $w$.

It is known that there exists an $85$-uniform morphism $g_{85}: \Sigma_4^* \to \Sigma_4^*$ (constructed by Keränen) that avoids abelian squares, where 
\[g_{85}(a) = abcacdcbcdcadcdbdabacabadbabcbdbcbacbcdcacbabdabacadcbcdcacdbcbacbcdcacdcbdcdadbdcbca\] 
and the images of $b,c,d$ are obtained by an appropriate cyclic permutation of letters.

Problem: Construct a morphism $h : \Sigma_4^* \to \Sigma_4^*$ that avoids abelian squares and is simpler than $g_{85}$ — for instance, of strictly smaller uniform length, or substantially smaller total image size $\sum_{x \in \Sigma_4} |h(x)|$, or otherwise of demonstrably simpler structure — or prove that no such simpler morphism exists.
status_search_result: Keränen's 85-uniform morphism (1992) remains the standard construction for avoiding abelian squares on four letters. Subsequent work (e.g., Carpi's "powerful" substitution, new abelian square-free DT0L languages) has produced alternative constructions, but Keränen showed that within the family of cyclic-type morphisms the size 85 is minimal. No morphism of substantially simpler form is reported in the literature accessed; the problem of finding a genuinely simpler morphism appears to still be open.

original_question: What is the minimal k such that one can avoid abelian squares of period at least k over three letters (2 < k < 6)?
self_contained_problem:
Consider finite and infinite words over the three-letter alphabet $\{0,1,2\}$. An abelian square is a non-empty factor of the form $uv$ where $u$ and $v$ have the same length and $v$ is a permutation of $u$ (equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have identical letter-frequency vectors). The common length $|u|=|v|$ is called the period of the abelian square. A word is said to avoid abelian squares of period at least $k$ if it contains no factor $uv$ with $|u|=|v|\ge k$ and $v$ a permutation of $u$.

It is known that no infinite word over $\{0,1,2\}$ avoids all abelian squares (i.e., the case $k=1$ is impossible), while for any sufficiently large $k$, infinite ternary words avoiding abelian squares of period at least $k$ are known to exist (in particular, this is the case for $k=6$).

Computational and theoretical studies (e.g., on k-abelian avoidability and long abelian repetitions) have made progress on related variants, but the exact minimal threshold k in {3,4,5} for avoiding ternary abelian squares of period at least k has not been resolved in the literature found.

original_question: What is the minimal k such that one can avoid 2-abelian squares of period at least k over two letters (2 < k < 60)? We refer also the reader to the notions connected to the so-called templates [1]. From this point of view, iin 2015 Rao and Rosenfed proved that for any primitive morphism h whose matrix has no eigenvalue of norm 1 and any template t it is possible to decide if h∞ (a) realizes t. The following problems may be formulated:

Let $\Sigma_2 = \{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet. For a finite word $w \in \Sigma_2^*$ and an integer $k \ge 1$, define the $k$-abelian equivalence $\sim_k$ on $\Sigma_2^*$ as follows: $u \sim_k v$ iff $|u| = |v|$ and, for every word $f \in \Sigma_2^*$ of length at most $k$, $f$ occurs as a factor of $u$ exactly as many times as it occurs as a factor of $v$. (Equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have the same multiset of factors of every length up to $k$, including their prefix and suffix of length $k-1$.)

A factor $uv$ of an (infinite) word, with $|u| = |v| = p \ge 1$, is called a $k$-abelian square of period $p$ if $u \sim_k v$. An infinite word $w \in \Sigma_2^\omega$ is said to avoid $k$-abelian squares of period at least $K$ if $w$ contains no $k$-abelian square $uv$ with $|u| = |v| \ge K$.

It is known that abelian squares (the case $k = 1$) of arbitrarily large period cannot be avoided over a binary alphabet, while $3$-abelian squares of period at least $3$ can be avoided over $\Sigma_2$.

original_question: Is there a morphism over 5 letters with two eigenvalues of norm smaller than 1 and an abelian-square-free fixed point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be an alphabet of $5$ letters and let $f:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ be a morphism (i.e., $f(uv)=f(u)f(v)$ for all words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$). The incidence matrix (or Parikh matrix) of $f$ is the $5\times 5$ integer matrix $M_f$ whose $(i,j)$ entry is the number of occurrences of letter $i$ in $f(j)$. A right fixed point of $f$ is an infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^\omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{w}$. A finite word $u=u_1u_2\cdots u_{2n}$ is called an abelian square if its two halves $u_1\cdots u_n$ and $u_{n+1}\cdots u_{2n}$ have the same Parikh vector (i.e., contain each letter the same number of times). An infinite word is abelian-square-free if none of its nonempty factors is an abelian square.

Let $u$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, define the recurrence function $R_u(n)$ as the smallest integer $N\ge 1$ (or $+\infty$ if no such integer exists) such that every factor of length $N$ occurring in $u$ contains every factor of length $n$ of $u$ as a factor. original_question: Draw a study of the recurrence quotients for other families of infinite word that sturmian words, such as words of complexity 2n + 1, or toinfinite words in general.
self_contained_problem:
Let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. For a positive integer $n$, let $R(n)$ denote the recurrence function of $w$: the smallest integer $N$ (if it exists) such that every factor of $w$ of length $n$ occurs in every factor of $w$ of length $N$; if no such $N$ exists set $R(n) = \infty$. The factor complexity of $w$ is the function $p(n)$ counting the number of distinct factors of length $n$ occurring in $w$. The recurrence quotient of $w$ is defined as
$$\rho(w) = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{R(n)}{n}.$$

For Sturmian words (infinite words with complexity $p(n) = n+1$), the recurrence quotient has been thoroughly studied, and it is known that $\rho(w) \geq 3$ with the infimum attained by the Fibonacci word.

Carry out an analogous study of the recurrence quotient for broader families of infinite words. In particular:
(a) Describe the set of possible values of $\rho(w)$, and identify words minimizing or extremizing $\rho(w)$, when $w$ ranges over uniformly recurrent infinite words of complexity $p(n) = 2n+1$ (for example, Arnoux–Rauzy words on a three-letter alphabet).
(b) More generally, investigate the structure and possible values of the recurrence quotient for arbitrary uniformly recurrent infinite words.
status_search_result: The recurrence function for Arnoux–Rauzy sequences (a natural class of words with complexity $2n+1$ on three letters) has been computed explicitly (Cassaigne, Frid, and others), addressing a question of Morse and Hedlund and providing partial answers to part (a). However, the general program of describing the recurrence quotient for all infinite words of complexity $2n+1$ and for arbitrary infinite words remains an open research direction with no comprehensive solution.

original_question: Transform the preceding characterization into a characterization using a finite set of substitutions associated with rules governing their composition (i.e. S-adic system of representation).
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let A be a finite alphabet and let x ∈ A^ℕ be an infinite word. The factor complexity of x is the function p_x : ℕ → ℕ where p_x(n) is the number of distinct factors (contiguous finite subwords) of x of length n. One says that x has sublinear (resp. linear) complexity if p_x(n) = O(n) (resp. p_x(n)/n is bounded above and below by positive constants for n large).

A substitution (morphism) on alphabets is a map σ : B* → C* extending a map B → C* by concatenation. Given a finite set S of substitutions σ_i : A_{i+1}* → A_i*, an S-adic representation of x is a sequence (σ_n)_{n≥0} of elements of S together with a sequence of letters (a_n) with a_n ∈ A_n such that x = lim_{n→∞} σ_0 σ_1 ⋯ σ_{n-1}(a_n) in A^ℕ (in particular each σ_0⋯σ_{n-1}(a_n) is a prefix of the next). The word x is called S-adic if it admits such a representation for some finite S together with a specified rule (a subshift on S^ℕ) governing which sequences (σ_n) are admissible.

There is a known intrinsic combinatorial characterization of words of sublinear (linear) factor complexity in terms of internal properties of x (e.g. via special factors or via the property that every factor decomposes as a concatenation of two elements of a set of bounded complexity).

Problem. Produce an equivalent characterization of the class of infinite words of sublinear (linear) factor complexity in the following form: exhibit an explicit finite set S of substitutions and an explicit set of "composition rules" (i.e. a constraint defining a subshift D ⊆ S^ℕ on the directive sequences) such that an infinite word x has the given complexity property if and only if x admits an S-adic representation whose directive sequence belongs to D.
status_search_result: The general "S-adic conjecture," asking for an S-adic characterization of words of linear/sublinear factor complexity with an explicit condition on the composition of substitutions, is widely regarded as open. Partial S-adic characterizations have been established in special cases (e.g., minimal subshifts whose first difference of complexity is at most 2 by Ferenczi; structure theorems for low-complexity subshifts by Donoso–Durand–Maass–Petite and others), but no general characterization is known.

original_question: Give an example of sequence or which the mentionned change of spectrum is really significant for the balance properties.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite alphabet and let $\sigma:\mathcal{A}^*\to\mathcal{A}^*$ be a primitive substitution with a fixed point $u\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{N}}$. For a finite word $w\in\mathcal{A}^*$ and a letter $a\in\mathcal{A}$, denote by $|w|_a$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $w$. The balance function of $u$ is defined, for every integer $n\ge 1$, by
$$B_u(n)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\;\max\bigl\{\,\bigl||v|_a-|w|_a\bigr|:\ v,w\ \text{are factors of }u\text{ with }|v|=|w|=n\,\bigr\}.$$
The asymptotic behavior of $B_u$ is governed in part by the spectrum (set of eigenvalues) of the incidence matrix $M_\sigma$ of $\sigma$. For an integer $k\ge 2$, the iterate $\sigma^k$ has incidence matrix $M_\sigma^k$, and its spectrum is the $k$-th power of the spectrum of $M_\sigma$; however, when one considers an arbitrary primitive substitution $\tau$ with the same fixed point $u$ (for instance a power of $\sigma$, or a different substitution generating $u$), the spectrum of $M_\tau$ may differ from that of $M_\sigma$ in ways that are not merely a power, and this change in spectrum may alter the predictions one would make about $B_u$.

Exhibit an explicit substitution $\sigma$ on a finite alphabet and an integer $k\ge 2$ (or another primitive substitution $\tau$ producing the same fixed point) such that passing from the spectrum of $M_\sigma$ to that of $M_{\sigma^k}$ (respectively $M_\tau$) produces a genuinely significant change in the information obtained about the balance function $B_u$ of the common fixed point $u$.
status_search_result: The problem appears in a 2017 compilation of open problems from the WORDS conference series, in the context of work relating balance functions of primitive substitutive sequences to the spectrum of their incidence matrices. Known examples (e.g. the Thue–Morse substitution and its square) show that the spectrum can change under taking powers, but no widely cited resolution providing a definitive "significant" example for the balance properties was located in the search. Status appears to remain unresolved/unknown in the literature.
