paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Prove the BKL locality conjecture for general inhomogeneous spacetimes approaching a generic spacelike singularity.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime $(M,g)$ satisfying the vacuum Einstein equations $R_{\mu\nu}=0$ (or, more generally, the Einstein equations coupled to suitable matter) and admitting a generic spacelike singularity, i.e. a singular Cauchy horizon along which curvature invariants diverge and which is approached by a foliation of spacelike hypersurfaces $\{\Sigma_t\}_{t>0}$ with proper time $t\to 0^+$ toward the singularity. No symmetry assumptions are placed on the metric (the "inhomogeneous" setting).

The Belinski–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz (BKL) locality conjecture asserts that, as $t\to 0^+$, the evolution of the metric at each spatial point $x\in\Sigma_t$ asymptotically decouples from spatial derivatives: spatial points effectively evolve independently, and at each $x$ the dynamics of the metric reduces to that of a homogeneous (spatially constant) cosmological model — generically a Mixmaster (Bianchi type IX) oscillatory regime in vacuum, or a monotone Kasner-like regime in the presence of a sufficiently stiff matter field. Equivalently, in a suitable gauge (e.g. Gaussian/synchronous coordinates with lapse $N=1$ or in an Iwasawa frame), the spatial-derivative terms in the Einstein evolution equations become asymptotically negligible compared to the time-derivative terms in a precise sense as $t\to 0^+$, for a set of initial data that is generic (open and dense, or of full measure) in an appropriate function space.

Problem. Prove the BKL locality conjecture for general inhomogeneous spacetimes approaching a generic spacelike singularity: namely, establish rigorously that for a generic class of initial data without symmetry, solutions of the Einstein equations approach, as $t\to 0^+$, a regime in which the dynamics at each spatial point is governed by the corresponding spatially homogeneous (BKL) ODE system, with spatial gradients becoming subdominant.
status_search_result: The BKL locality conjecture is widely regarded as still open in the general inhomogeneous setting. Rigorous results exist only in restricted cases (e.g., Gowdy and other symmetric models; Andersson–Rendall for Einstein–scalar field/stiff fluid with prescribed asymptotic data). Recent work also indicates that "spike" formation breaks strict asymptotic locality, suggesting the conjecture may need modification. Numerical and analytic progress continues, but no proof for generic inhomogeneous vacuum spacetimes is known as of 2026.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Prove that spike structures occur near generic cosmological singularities and determine how those spikes affect any eventual proof of generic singularity behavior.
self_contained_problem:
Consider solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations in a neighborhood of a spacelike (cosmological) singularity. The BKL (Belinskii–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz) heuristic predicts that, generically, the approach to such a singularity is local, oscillatory, and Mixmaster-like, with the time derivatives in Einstein's equations dominating spatial derivatives. In inhomogeneous settings, however, numerical and analytic studies reveal the formation of "spikes": isolated spatial points or surfaces where the BKL local-ODE picture fails because spatial derivatives become unboundedly large, producing transient, sharp features in the geometric variables (e.g., in the Hubble-normalized frame and connection components or in Iwasawa-frame variables) that recur during so-called spike transitions.

Problem: (a) Prove rigorously that spike structures generically occur in the asymptotic dynamics of solutions of the Einstein equations as a generic spacelike singularity is approached (i.e., establish that for an open set, in a suitable topology, of initial data the resulting spacetime exhibits spike formation). (b) Determine and characterize the effect that the existence of such spikes has on any rigorous proof of the generic singularity behaviour predicted by the BKL conjecture — in particular, identify the modifications required in any asymptotic expansion, scaling, or regularity framework intended to establish generic BKL-type behaviour in the presence of spikes.
status_search_result: The BKL conjecture remains unproven in full generality. Spikes have been identified in numerical and symmetry-reduced analytic studies (Berger–Moncrief, Garfinkle, Heinzle–Uggla–Lim, and others), with recent work on recurring spikes and spike chains, but a rigorous proof that spikes generically occur near cosmological singularities and a complete account of their effect on any general proof of BKL-type singularity behavior has not been established.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Determine the structural stability of generic inhomogeneous spacelike singularities when general matter fields present in the early universe are included.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Einstein field equations coupled to general matter fields (e.g., perfect fluids with various equations of state, scalar fields, electromagnetic fields, Yang–Mills fields, and other matter models physically relevant in the early universe), formulated as an evolution problem for a Lorentzian 4-manifold $(M,g)$ with a spacelike singularity. A generic inhomogeneous spacelike singularity is one approached, on an open set of initial data without symmetry assumptions, along sequences of Cauchy hypersurfaces foliating a neighborhood of the singularity.

The Belinskii–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz (BKL) picture conjectures that the asymptotic dynamics towards such a singularity is, generically, local (spatial derivatives become subdominant relative to time derivatives), oscillatory (Mixmaster-like for vacuum and most matter models), or monotone (e.g., quiescent in the presence of a massless scalar / stiff fluid).

Problem. Establish, in a mathematically rigorous sense, the structural stability of the generic inhomogeneous spacelike singularity for the Einstein equations coupled to general matter fields relevant in the early universe. More precisely:

(a) Define a suitable functional/topological framework (function spaces of initial data on a Cauchy hypersurface, notion of asymptotic profile near the singularity, and equivalence relation describing the qualitative asymptotic behavior) in which structural stability can be formulated.

(b) Prove that, for an open set of initial data in this framework, the asymptotic behavior of the resulting maximal globally hyperbolic development near its spacelike singularity is preserved (up to the chosen equivalence) under small perturbations of both the initial data and the matter content (within a prescribed class of matter models).

(c) Identify which matter models lead to oscillatory BKL behavior versus quiescent (monotone) behavior, and prove stability of the corresponding asymptotic regime in each case.
status_search_result: The problem is widely regarded as open. The BKL conjecture about generic spacelike singularities has been rigorously established only in restricted symmetry classes or in the quiescent (e.g., stiff-fluid / massless-scalar-field) regime; the structural stability of generic inhomogeneous oscillatory singularities for general matter content remains unresolved. Recent works (e.g., Rodnianski–Speck on stable big-bang formation with stiff matter, and 2024 studies of BKL bounces in Einstein–Maxwell–scalar field systems in surface symmetry) yield only partial results, confirming that the full problem is still open.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Determine whether isotropic singularities are typical in modified theories of gravity.
self_contained_problem:
An isotropic singularity (sometimes called a conformal or Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker–like singularity) is a spacetime singularity at which the physical metric g_{ab} is conformally related to a regular Lorentzian metric ĝ_{ab} that extends smoothly through the singular hypersurface, i.e. g_{ab} = Ω²(τ) ĝ_{ab} with a conformal factor Ω(τ) that vanishes on the singular hypersurface τ = 0 while ĝ_{ab} remains regular and the Weyl tensor of g_{ab} is bounded relative to its Ricci tensor (in particular, the Weyl curvature hypothesis is satisfied at the singularity).

Consider modified theories of gravity, by which we mean four-dimensional metric theories whose field equations are derived from an action of the form
  S = ∫ f(R, R_{ab}R^{ab}, R_{abcd}R^{abcd}, …) √(−g) d⁴x + S_matter,
or, more generally, theories that extend General Relativity by additional curvature invariants, additional scalar/tensor/vector fields, or higher-derivative terms (e.g. f(R) gravity, quadratic gravity, scalar–tensor gravity, Gauss–Bonnet gravity, Hořava–Lifshitz gravity, and similar generalizations).

Within the space of cosmological solutions of such a modified theory, equipped with a natural topology (for instance, the topology induced on initial data by Sobolev norms or by an appropriate measure on the moduli space of solutions), say that isotropic singularities are typical if the set of solutions that develop an isotropic singularity in the past (or future) contains an open and dense subset, or has full measure, among all solutions exhibiting a curvature singularity.

Problem. Determine whether isotropic singularities are typical, in the above sense, in modified theories of gravity. Equivalently, decide whether, in a generic modified gravity theory, generic cosmological solutions with a curvature singularity have that singularity be of isotropic type, or whether instead anisotropic (e.g. Kasner-like, mixmaster, or oscillatory BKL-type) singularities are generic.
status_search_result: The question of whether isotropic singularities are typical in modified theories of gravity remains an active research topic. Partial results exist: in quadratic gravity, isotropic cosmological singularities have been shown to be stable to small scalar, vector, and tensor inhomogeneities (Barrow–Middleton, 2007), and recent work on geometric selection rules (2026) shows that singularity formation in modified gravity is constrained by algebraic admissibility conditions on curvature invariants. However, no general result establishes typicality across the broad class of modified gravity theories, and anisotropic singularities are also known to arise generically in some models. The problem is best regarded as open.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Give a rigorous mathematical definition of averaging in general relativity.
self_contained_problem:
Provide a rigorous mathematical definition of averaging in general relativity. Specifically, on a 4-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime $(M, g_{ab})$ satisfying the Einstein field equations $G_{ab}[g] + \Lambda g_{ab} = 8\pi G\, T_{ab}$, formulate a coordinate-independent, mathematically well-defined averaging operation $\langle \cdot \rangle$ that acts on tensor fields (in particular on the metric $g_{ab}$, the Ricci and Einstein tensors, and the stress-energy tensor) such that:

1. The operation depends in a controlled, geometrically meaningful way on a choice of foliation or family of averaging domains (e.g., spacelike hypersurfaces or compact spatial regions therein), and reduces to standard spatial averaging in appropriate limits.
2. The averaged tensor fields are themselves tensor fields on a suitable "averaged" or "coarse-grained" manifold, with a precise prescription for how points, parallel transport, and tensor comparison at different points are handled (resolving the well-known difficulty that integration of tensors at different spacetime points is not invariantly defined).
3. The averaged metric $\langle g_{ab}\rangle$ together with the averaged matter content satisfies an effective set of field equations, with the deviation between $\langle G_{ab}[g]\rangle$ and $G_{ab}[\langle g\rangle]$ (the backreaction) expressed in terms of well-defined geometric quantities.
4. The construction is compatible with the diffeomorphism invariance of general relativity and with the nonlinearity of the Einstein equations.

The task is to give such a definition (or prove no canonical one exists) and to establish its basic mathematical properties.
status_search_result: The averaging problem in general relativity (closely tied to the cosmological backreaction problem) remains an active open problem. Multiple inequivalent frameworks have been proposed (Buchert spatial averaging, Zalaletdinov's macroscopic gravity, Mori-Zwanzig projection methods, multiple-scales expansions), but no canonical, fully coordinate-independent and tensorially consistent definition has been agreed upon. Recent work as of 2024 still treats the formulation and the magnitude of the resulting backreaction as open questions.

original_question: Resolve the black hole information paradox.
self_contained_problem: In semiclassical gravity, a black hole formed by gravitational collapse of matter in a pure quantum state is predicted (by Hawking's 1974 calculation) to emit thermal radiation and eventually evaporate, leaving behind a mixed thermal state. original_question: Resolve the cosmological constant problem and the problem of dark energy.
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of general relativity, the Einstein field equations with a cosmological constant read

  R_{μν} − (1/2) g_{μν} R + Λ g_{μν} = (8πG/c^4) T_{μν},

where g_{μν} is the spacetime metric, R_{μν} its Ricci tensor, R the scalar curvature, T_{μν} the stress–energy tensor of matter, G Newton's constant, c the speed of light, and Λ the cosmological constant. Observational cosmology (e.g. supernova luminosity distance data, cosmic microwave background measurements, and large-scale structure) yields an effective value Λ_obs corresponding to a vacuum-energy density of order ρ_Λ ∼ 10^{−47} GeV^4, while a naive quantum-field-theoretic estimate of the zero-point vacuum energy of the Standard Model fields, regularized at a high-energy cutoff M (e.g. the Planck scale M_P ≈ 1.22 × 10^{19} GeV), gives ρ_vac ∼ M^4, exceeding ρ_Λ by up to ~120 orders of magnitude.

Problem. Provide a mathematically rigorous and physically consistent resolution of the following two coupled questions:

(a) (Cosmological constant problem.) Construct, within a well-defined theoretical framework that combines general relativity with quantum field theory (or an appropriate extension thereof), a derivation of the observed value of the effective cosmological constant Λ_obs that explains, without unnatural fine-tuning, the enormous discrepancy between the predicted vacuum-energy contribution from quantum fields and the observed value.

(b) (Dark energy problem.) Identify and characterize mathematically the physical mechanism — whether a true cosmological constant, a dynamical scalar field (quintessence), a modification of the gravitational action, or another consistent alternative — responsible for the observed accelerated expansion of the Universe, and determine its equation of state w(z) = p/ρ as a function of redshift z together with predictions distinguishing it from a pure cosmological-constant scenario w ≡ −1.
status_search_result: The cosmological constant problem and the nature of dark energy remain among the most prominent unresolved problems in theoretical physics and cosmology. Recent reviews (2024–2026) and observational programs (DESI, Euclid) continue to report it as open, with mounting hints from DESI data of possible evolving dark energy but no accepted theoretical resolution.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Determine how generic inflation is for generic initial data.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a spatially inhomogeneous, anisotropic spacetime $(M,g)$ satisfying the Einstein field equations coupled to a scalar (inflaton) field $\phi$ with a potential $V(\phi)$ that admits a slow-roll inflationary regime (for example, $V$ has a sufficiently flat plateau or a quadratic minimum). An initial data set consists of a Riemannian 3-manifold $(\Sigma,h)$ together with a symmetric 2-tensor $K$ (extrinsic curvature), a scalar field value $\phi_0:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}$, and its conjugate momentum $\dot\phi_0:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}$, satisfying the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. Say that the resulting maximal globally hyperbolic development "undergoes inflation" if there exists a region in which the spatially averaged scale factor $a(t)$ grows by at least a factor of $e^{60}$ while the Hubble parameter $H = \dot a/a$ remains nearly constant (slow-roll).

Endow the space of constraint-satisfying initial data with a natural measure or topology (e.g., a suitable Gibbons–Hawking–Stewart-type measure on the constrained phase space, or a Sobolev topology on $(\Sigma,h,K,\phi_0,\dot\phi_0)$ modulo diffeomorphisms).

Problem: Quantify, with respect to such a measure/topology, how generic the set of initial data is whose maximal development undergoes inflation. In particular, determine whether inflation is generic, non-generic, or measure-zero among generic (e.g., highly inhomogeneous and anisotropic) initial data, and provide rigorous estimates of the corresponding fraction or genericity statement.

original_question: Determine the emitted gravitational-wave waveforms for binary black-hole systems with enough accuracy for optimal detection and parameter extraction.
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of general relativity, consider an isolated binary system consisting of two black holes characterized by their individual masses $m_1, m_2 > 0$, their spin (angular momentum) vectors $\vec{S}_1, \vec{S}_2$, and orbital parameters (eccentricity, inclination, initial separation). As the binary evolves through the inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases, it emits gravitational radiation described by the two polarization waveforms $h_+(t)$ and $h_\times(t)$ at the detector.

Problem: Develop theoretical templates $h(t;\vec{\lambda})$ — parametrized by the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters $\vec{\lambda}=(m_1,m_2,\vec{S}_1,\vec{S}_2,\dots)$ — that predict the emitted gravitational-wave waveforms of binary black-hole coalescences across the full astrophysically relevant parameter space (including precessing spins, higher-order multipole modes, and arbitrary mass ratios) with sufficient accuracy that:

(a) matched-filter detection using these templates achieves optimal signal-to-noise ratio (i.e., the mismatch between the templates and the true general-relativistic waveforms is small enough that no appreciable detection efficiency is lost), and

(b) Bayesian parameter inference performed with these templates against observed signals yields statistically unbiased estimates of the source parameters, in the sense that the systematic errors due to waveform modeling are smaller than the statistical errors expected for current and planned gravitational-wave detectors.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Understand critical phenomena in gravitational collapse within general relativity.
self_contained_problem:
In classical general relativity, consider one-parameter families of smooth, asymptotically flat initial data for the Einstein equations coupled to some matter model (for instance, a massless scalar field, a perfect fluid, electromagnetism, or vacuum gravitational waves). Let p denote the parameter, and assume that for p > p* the evolution produces a black hole while for p < p* the matter disperses, so that p = p* is the black-hole threshold. Numerical evidence (originally for spherically symmetric massless scalar collapse) shows three universal "critical phenomena" near p = p*: (i) the threshold solution is a discretely or continuously self-similar attractor of codimension one in phase space; (ii) the universality of this critical solution within a given matter model; and (iii) a power-law scaling M_BH ∝ (p − p*)^γ for the mass of the black hole formed for p slightly greater than p*, with a critical exponent γ depending only on the matter model.

Provide a complete theoretical understanding of these critical phenomena in gravitational collapse. In particular:

1. Rigorously establish the existence, uniqueness, and codimension-one stability of the self-similar critical attractor solutions for the various matter models (scalar field, perfect fluid with equation of state p = kρ, Yang–Mills, etc.).
2. Derive the universality and the values of the critical exponents γ and (for discretely self-similar cases) the echoing period Δ from first principles.
3. Determine to what extent these phenomena persist without the assumption of spherical symmetry, including the case of vacuum gravitational collapse where the threshold is approached by purely gravitational degrees of freedom.
4. Clarify the relationship of critical collapse to weak cosmic censorship, given that arbitrarily large curvature is visible from infinity in the threshold limit.
status_search_result: Critical phenomena in gravitational collapse remain an active research area. The Living Reviews in Relativity survey by Gundlach and Martín-García, and a more recent 2025 review (arXiv:2507.07636), make clear that while spherically symmetric cases are well understood numerically, fundamental theoretical questions — universality across matter models, behavior beyond spherical symmetry, vacuum critical collapse, and rigorous derivation of critical exponents — remain open.

original_question: Let Ω ⊂ R^n be a connected open set with n ≥ 3, and let u solve div(|∇u|^{p-2}∇u) = 0 for some 1 < p < ∞ with p ≠ 2. If u vanishes of infinite order at an interior point x_0 of Ω, must u vanish identically on all of Ω?

original_question: Let Ω ⊂ R^2 be a bounded connected open set, and consider the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem Δu + λu = 0 in Ω with u = 0 on ∂Ω. If u_2 is any second eigenfunction, can its nodal set {x ∈ Ω | u_2(x) = 0} ever be a closed curve, or must that nodal line always be non-closed?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded connected open set and consider the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem

Let $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \lambda_3 \le \cdots$ denote the Dirichlet eigenvalues, and let $u_2$ be any eigenfunction associated with the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2$. Define the nodal set of $u_2$ by $N(u_2) = \{x \in \Omega : u_2(x) = 0\}$.

paper_title: A small collection of open problems
context_brief: Structure of the second nodal line in simply connected planar domains
original_question: Assume Ω ⊂ R^2 is simply connected and has smooth boundary, and consider any second eigenfunction of the Dirichlet Laplacian on Ω. Must its nodal line be a simple open curve whose two endpoints are distinct points of ∂Ω?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded, simply connected domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Consider the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
and let $u$ be any eigenfunction associated with the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\Omega)$. The nodal set of $u$ is defined as $N(u) = \{x \in \overline{\Omega} : u(x) = 0\}$, and the nodal line is $N(u) \cap \Omega$.

Prove or disprove: the nodal line of $u$ is a simple open arc (i.e., the homeomorphic image of an open interval, with no self-intersections) whose two endpoints lie on $\partial\Omega$ and are distinct.
status_search_result: This is the classical Payne nodal line conjecture (1967), strengthened to the statement that the nodal line is a simple arc connecting two distinct boundary points. Hoffmann-Ostenhof, Hoffmann-Ostenhof and Nadirashvili (1997) disproved the conjecture for multiply connected planar domains; subsequent works produced counterexamples with as few as one hole, and recently even on doubly-connected domains. For simply connected planar domains with smooth boundary the problem remains open as of 2026.

context_brief: Extending Courant’s nodal domain theorem beyond unique continuation
original_question: Let n ≥ 3 and consider the elliptic eigenvalue problem div(A∇u) − qu + λρu = 0 in a bounded connected domain Ω, with u = 0 on ∂Ω, where A is uniformly elliptic, q and ρ are bounded, and ρ ≥ K^{-1} > 0. Under what assumptions on the coefficient matrix A, while still not implying unique continuation for the equation div(A∇u) − qu + λρu = 0, does Courant’s Nodal Domain Theorem remain valid?

Let $n\geq 3$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded connected domain. Consider the elliptic eigenvalue problem
$$\operatorname{div}(A\nabla u) - qu + \lambda\rho u = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u=0 \text{ on }\partial\Omega,$$
where $A=A(x)$ is a measurable, symmetric, uniformly elliptic $n\times n$ matrix-valued coefficient (i.e., there exists $\kappa>0$ such that $\kappa|\xi|^2\leq \langle A(x)\xi,\xi\rangle \leq \kappa^{-1}|\xi|^2$ for a.e. $x\in\Omega$ and all $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$), $q\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, and $\rho\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfies $\rho(x)\geq K^{-1}>0$ a.e.

For an eigenfunction $u$ associated to the $k$-th Dirichlet eigenvalue $\lambda_k$, a nodal domain is a connected component of $\{x\in\Omega : u(x)\neq 0\}$. Courant's Nodal Domain Theorem states that the number of nodal domains of $u$ is at most $k$.

Determine sufficient conditions on the coefficient matrix $A$ — conditions that do not by themselves imply the strong unique continuation property for the above equation — under which Courant's Nodal Domain Theorem nevertheless remains valid.
status_search_result: The question of validity of Courant's nodal domain theorem for divergence-form elliptic operators with low-regularity coefficients, decoupled from the unique continuation property, is identified as an open problem in surveys and recent work. Related results (e.g., for p-Laplacians and on graphs) show stronger bounds rely on unique continuation, but no general sufficient condition divorced from unique continuation is known.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: In causal supervised learning, can the field develop standardized, targeted benchmarks for invariance learning so practitioners can compare methods on shared tasks that deliberately vary spurious associations between training and test environments instead of relying on ad hoc toy experiments?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider the framework of causal supervised learning under distribution shift. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a set of environments. For each environment $e \in \mathcal{E}$, data is drawn from a distribution $P_e$ over $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ that is generated by a structural causal model with shared causal mechanisms but with environment-specific "spurious" associations between non-causal features of $X$ and the label $Y$. A predictor $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is said to exhibit invariance (in the sense of invariant risk minimization, invariant causal prediction, or related criteria) across $\mathcal{E}$ if its conditional risk, or its conditional distribution $P_e(Y \mid f(X))$, does not depend on $e$. The invariance-learning problem is to use data from a finite collection of training environments $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{train}} \subset \mathcal{E}$ to produce a predictor whose risk under a disjoint set of test environments $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{test}}$, in which the spurious associations between irrelevant features and $Y$ have been deliberately altered, is small.

Problem. Design a standardized benchmark suite for invariance learning in causal supervised learning that satisfies all of the following properties:
(1) It specifies an explicit family of data-generating processes (structural causal models or interventional distributions) in which the spurious associations between features and labels are quantitatively varied between $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{train}}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{test}}$.
(2) It provides shared, reproducible tasks (datasets, train/test environment splits, and evaluation protocols) together with well-defined performance metrics that measure worst-case or average out-of-distribution risk across the test environments.
(3) It enables a fair, apples-to-apples comparison of arbitrary invariance-learning algorithms (e.g., IRM, REx, GroupDRO, ICP, CORAL, and successors), in the sense that the relative ranking of methods on the benchmark is informative about their relative ability to discover invariant predictors under controlled variations of the spurious mechanism.
Either construct such a benchmark suite and rigorously justify properties (1)–(3), or prove an impossibility result showing that no benchmark suite satisfying (1)–(3) can exist under stated assumptions on the class of admissible causal models and learners.
status_search_result: A web search shows active research on invariance learning, counterfactual invariance, and mitigation of spurious correlations (e.g., counterfactual-invariance stress tests, DomainBed-style suites, WILDS), but no widely accepted standardized benchmark suite specifically built around causal data-generating processes with controlled variation of spurious associations between training and test environments has emerged as canonical. The question of constructing such a benchmark therefore remains an open community-level research problem.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can causal assumptions and invariance-learning ideas be used to improve adversarial robustness and meta-learning, for example by treating robustness as invariance to perturbations and by learning task-invariant structure or interventions over task variables?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following formal framework linking causal invariance, adversarial robustness, and meta-learning.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an input space, $\mathcal{Y}$ an output space, and $\mathcal{E}$ an index set of "environments" or "tasks." For each $e \in \mathcal{E}$, let $P^e$ be a joint distribution on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ arising from a structural causal model (SCM) $\mathcal{M}^e = (\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{F}^e, P_{\mathbf{U}}^e)$ over endogenous variables $\mathbf{V} \supseteq \{X, Y\}$, where the environments differ only through a family of allowed interventions $\mathcal{I}$ on a designated subset $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{V} \setminus \{Y\}$ of "style" or "task" variables, while the structural assignment $f_Y \in \mathbf{F}^e$ for $Y$ given its causal parents $\mathrm{Pa}(Y) \subseteq \mathbf{V}$ is invariant across $e$.

A predictor $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is called causally invariant if there exists a representation $\Phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ such that $h = g \circ \Phi$ and the conditional distribution of $Y \mid \Phi(X)$ under $P^e$ is the same for every $e \in \mathcal{E}$.

For a loss $\ell: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and a perturbation set $\Delta \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ with $0 \in \Delta$, define
$$R_{\mathrm{adv}}(h; P, \Delta) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim P}\left[ \sup_{\delta \in \Delta} \ell(h(X + \delta), Y) \right],$$
$$R_{\mathrm{meta}}(h; \{P^e\}_{e \in \mathcal{E}}) = \sup_{e \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim P^e}[\ell(h(X), Y)].$$

Address the following:

(a) Formulate adversarial perturbations $\delta \in \Delta$ as interventions in an augmented SCM, identifying conditions on $\Delta$ and on the causal graph under which the adversarially robust risk $R_{\mathrm{adv}}$ coincides (up to a known constant) with a worst-case interventional risk over a class $\mathcal{I}_{\Delta}$ of soft interventions on non-causal features of $X$.

(b) Under (a), prove or disprove that any minimizer of $R_{\mathrm{adv}}$ over a sufficiently rich hypothesis class must factor through a representation $\Phi$ that is invariant in the sense above with respect to $\mathcal{I}_\Delta$, and give matching upper and lower bounds relating $R_{\mathrm{adv}}$ to the minimax invariant-prediction risk.

(c) For meta-learning, modeling tasks $e \in \mathcal{E}$ as the result of stochastic interventions on $\mathbf{S}$ drawn from a distribution $Q$ on $\mathcal{I}$, give an algorithm that, from finite samples of $n$ training tasks, learns a predictor $h$ and prove a generalization bound on $R_{\mathrm{meta}}(h)$ over unseen tasks $e \sim Q$ that depends on the complexity of the causal mechanism class for $Y \mid \mathrm{Pa}(Y)$ rather than on the complexity of $\{P^e\}_e$.

(d) Identify the precise causal and distributional assumptions (e.g., faithfulness, sufficiency, anchor/instrument availability, exogeneity of $\mathbf{S}$) needed for (b) and (c) to hold, and characterize cases in which causal invariance strictly improves over standard adversarial training and standard meta-learning baselines.
category_tag: Causal invariance, adversarial robustness, and meta-learning
status_search_result: The connection between causal invariance, adversarial robustness, and meta-learning is an active research direction. While partial results exist (e.g., invariant risk minimization, anti-causal learning analyses of adversarial robustness, and causal meta-learning frameworks), a unified theory providing the equivalence, generalization bounds, and tight assumption characterization described above remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: For invariant feature learning, which additional supervision signals beyond labels are most useful, including combinations of content-invariant transformations, multi-environment data, high-dimensional environment descriptions, and richer object or attribute labels, and how should such signals be exploited to separate interventions on spurious features?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the supervised learning setting in which data are drawn from multiple environments e ∈ E, with each environment providing samples (X_e, Y_e) where X_e ∈ R^d are observed features and Y_e is a target label. Assume there exists an underlying causal data-generating process in which Y depends on a latent set of causal (invariant) features Z_c = φ_c(X) that are stable across environments, while X also contains spurious features Z_s = φ_s(X) whose conditional distribution P(Y | Z_s, e) varies with e. The goal of invariant feature learning (IFL) is to recover a predictor f(φ_c(X)) that achieves low risk uniformly across all environments, including unseen ones, by separating the effect of interventions on Z_s from the invariant mechanism generating Y from Z_c.

Standard IFL methods rely only on (X, Y, e). Investigate the following problem: identify which additional supervision signals, beyond the target labels Y, provably or empirically improve the identifiability and estimation of φ_c, and design algorithms that exploit them. Specifically, consider the following families of auxiliary signals, individually and in combination:

(a) Content-invariant transformations T: X → X, i.e., known maps (such as augmentations or simulated interventions) under which φ_c is required to be invariant: φ_c(T(X)) = φ_c(X).
(b) Multi-environment data with |E| ≥ 2, including controlled interventional environments where particular mechanisms are known to change.
(c) High-dimensional environment descriptions, i.e., observed covariates E ∈ R^k that describe properties of each environment, rather than only a discrete environment index.
(d) Richer per-sample labels, such as object identities, attribute annotations, segmentation masks, or other structured auxiliary outputs correlated with Z_c or Z_s.

Formulate precise assumptions on the causal model under which each type of supervision (and their combinations) suffices to identify φ_c up to an admissible equivalence, characterize the corresponding sample-complexity gains, and propose learning procedures that use these signals to disentangle interventions on spurious features from those on causal features.
category_tag: Invariant feature learning / causal representation learning
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a survey on causal machine learning. While numerous works since have explored auxiliary supervision (augmentations, environment metadata, attribute labels) for invariant and causal representation learning, no general resolution characterizing which signals suffice and how to optimally combine them is established; the broad problem remains open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: In causal representation learning, what level of abstraction should the latent causal variables use, and what specifications or supervisory signals are necessary, sufficient, or relaxable for identifying a useful structural causal model over latent generative factors rather than over overly fine-grained or overly coarse variables?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a data-generating process in which high-dimensional observations $X \in \mathcal{X}$ are produced from a collection of latent generative factors $Z = (Z_1, \dots, Z_d)$ via an unknown mixing function $g: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X}$, with $X = g(Z)$ (possibly with noise). Assume the latent factors are themselves governed by a structural causal model (SCM) $\mathcal{M} = (Z, U, F, P_U)$, where $U = (U_1, \dots, U_d)$ are exogenous noise variables with joint distribution $P_U$, and each $Z_i$ is determined by a structural assignment $Z_i = f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(Z_i), U_i)$ with $\mathrm{Pa}(Z_i) \subseteq Z \setminus \{Z_i\}$, inducing a directed acyclic graph $\mathcal{G}$ on the latents.

Two SCMs $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}'$ over latent variables $Z$ and $Z'$ are said to be related by an abstraction if there exists a (typically surjective) map $\tau: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{Z}'$ such that, for every intervention $\sigma$ in a specified class on $\mathcal{M}$, there is an intervention $\sigma'$ on $\mathcal{M}'$ with $\tau_* P^{\sigma}_{\mathcal{M}} = P^{\sigma'}_{\mathcal{M}'}$, where $P^{\sigma}_{\mathcal{M}}$ denotes the interventional distribution of $Z$ under $\sigma$. An SCM is called "overly fine-grained" if it contains latent coordinates that can be merged via such a $\tau$ without losing predictive or interventional content for a downstream task; it is called "overly coarse" if some target intervention or query cannot be expressed.

Problem. Formulate and answer the following:

(a) Give a precise notion of "useful level of abstraction" for the latent SCM $\mathcal{M}$ with respect to a downstream class of interventional or counterfactual queries $\mathcal{Q}$, such that abstractions strictly coarser than this level fail to answer some query in $\mathcal{Q}$ while strictly finer ones are redundant.

(b) Identify a set of assumptions and/or supervisory signals (e.g., access to interventional data with known or unknown targets, paired counterfactual samples, temporal/auxiliary variables, weak labels of factor groupings, sparsity constraints on $\mathcal{G}$ or on $g$) that are:
  (i) sufficient to identify $(Z, \mathcal{G}, \{f_i\})$ up to an equivalence relation compatible with the abstraction level defined in (a), from samples of $X$ and the supervisory signals;
  (ii) necessary in the sense that, without them, two non-equivalent latent SCMs at that abstraction level produce indistinguishable observable distributions;
  (iii) relaxable, characterizing which of the sufficient conditions can be weakened while preserving identifiability up to the same equivalence.

(c) Prove an identifiability theorem (or impossibility result) making (a) and (b) precise.
status_search_result: Identifiability and abstraction selection in causal representation learning remain active open research areas. Recent works (2023–2025) establish partial identifiability results under specific supervisory signals (multi-environment data, known/unknown interventions, sparsity, temporal structure), but no general theory specifies the "right" abstraction level or a complete characterization of necessary/sufficient/relaxable signals.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can structural assignment learning in causal generative modeling scale to substantially larger causal graphs while still supporting flexible counterfactual sample generation, given that existing methods either work on low-order graphs or rely on amortized structural assignments over only a limited set of plausible interventions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the framework of causal generative modeling, where a structural causal model is specified by a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E) on variables X = (X_1, ..., X_n) together with, for each node i ∈ V, a structural assignment X_i = f_i(Pa_G(i), U_i), where Pa_G(i) denotes the parents of node i in G and U_i is an exogenous noise variable. Given observational and/or interventional data, learning the structural assignments {f_i} (with G either fixed or jointly learned) enables sampling from interventional and counterfactual distributions P(X | do(X_S = x_S)) for arbitrary subsets S ⊆ V and values x_S.

Currently known approaches either (a) only handle causal graphs of low order n, or (b) employ amortized structural assignments that are trained to respond only to a restricted, prespecified family of interventions.

Problem: Design a method for learning the structural assignments {f_i} of a structural causal model that simultaneously satisfies the following properties:
1. Scalability: it can be trained on causal graphs of substantially larger order than currently feasible.
2. Counterfactual flexibility: it permits the generation of samples from P(X | do(X_S = x_S)) for arbitrary intervention targets S ⊆ V and intervention values x_S, without requiring the family of admissible interventions to be fixed in advance.

Provide such a method together with theoretical guarantees on identifiability and sample quality, or prove that no method satisfying (1) and (2) can exist under standard assumptions.
status_search_result: The problem is identified as an open challenge in the causal machine learning literature: existing structural assignment learning methods scale only to small graphs or rely on amortization over a limited set of interventions. Recent work continues to address scalability and counterfactual flexibility but no comprehensive solution combining both desiderata with theoretical guarantees has been established.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: When, and by how much, does counterfactual data augmentation generated by causal generative models improve generalization relative to non-counterfactual or hand-crafted augmentations, and can such augmentation effectiveness also serve as a benchmark for comparing causal generative methods?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,Y) \sim P$ denote labeled data drawn from a source distribution $P$ over an input space $\mathcal{X}$ and a label space $\mathcal{Y}$, and let $Q$ denote a (possibly shifted) target distribution. A structural causal model (SCM) $\mathcal{M}$ over variables $(X,Y,U)$, with exogenous noise $U$, specifies structural assignments and an associated counterfactual map: given an observed sample $(x,y)$ and an intervention $\mathrm{do}(T = t)$ on a subset of variables or noise components $T$, $\mathcal{M}$ produces a counterfactual sample $(x^{\mathrm{cf}}, y^{\mathrm{cf}})$. A counterfactual data augmentation (CFDA) scheme based on $\mathcal{M}$ is a procedure $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}}$ that takes a training set $S = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \sim P^n$ and returns an augmented set $S' = S \cup \{(x_i^{\mathrm{cf}}, y_i^{\mathrm{cf}})\}$ obtained by sampling interventions from a distribution $\pi$. Let $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ denote a fixed hand-crafted (non-causal) augmentation scheme (e.g., random transformations from a prescribed group action on $\mathcal{X}$). For a learning algorithm $\mathcal{L}$ producing a predictor $\hat{f}_{S'}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ from augmented data $S'$, define the generalization gap on $Q$ as
$$ G(\mathcal{A}; P, Q, n) \; = \; \mathbb{E}_{S \sim P^n}\big[ \mathcal{R}_Q(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{A}(S)}) \big] - \inf_{f} \mathcal{R}_Q(f), $$
where $\mathcal{R}_Q(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim Q}[\ell(f(X),Y)]$ for a fixed loss $\ell$.

(a) Characterize precisely the conditions on the underlying causal mechanism, the intervention distribution $\pi$, the accuracy of the generative model implementing $\mathcal{M}$, and the relationship between $P$ and $Q$, under which
$$ G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}}; P, Q, n) \; \le \; G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{hc}}; P, Q, n) - \Delta(n), $$
and provide a quantitative lower bound $\Delta(n) > 0$ on the improvement as a function of $n$, of the fidelity of the causal generative model, and of a measure of distributional shift between $P$ and $Q$.

(b) Propose, and prove well-defined, a benchmarking criterion that ranks causal generative models $\mathcal{M}_1, \mathcal{M}_2, \dots$ via the downstream generalization improvement $G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{hc}}; P,Q,n) - G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_j}; P,Q,n)$, and determine whether this criterion is consistent in the sense that, under stated identifiability assumptions, the ranking it induces coincides with a model-quality ordering based on a divergence between the learned counterfactual distribution and the true counterfactual distribution induced by the data-generating SCM.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction in the causal machine learning literature. A web check shows ongoing empirical and theoretical work on counterfactual data augmentation and on benchmarking causal generative models, but no general theorem characterizing when and by how much CFDA improves generalization, nor a widely accepted benchmark of that form. The problem appears to remain open as of 2026.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can causal feature-attribution methods and contrastive explanation methods be unified so an explanation identifies not only which changes would achieve a desired outcome but also which features should remain unchanged, yielding a more complete and actionable explanation of a model decision?
self_contained_problem:
Let f : X → Y be a fixed predictive model, where X = X_1 × ⋯ × X_d is a feature space and Y is an outcome space. Suppose we are given:

(i) A causal feature-attribution method A that, for an input x ∈ X and outcome y = f(x), assigns to each feature i ∈ {1,…,d} a real-valued score A_i(x, f) measuring its causal contribution to the prediction under an assumed structural causal model M over the features.

(ii) A contrastive (counterfactual) explanation method C that, for an input x ∈ X and a desired target outcome y* ≠ f(x), returns a counterfactual instance x' ∈ X (or equivalently a perturbation Δ = x' − x) such that f(x') = y* while optimizing some cost/plausibility criterion.

Design a single unified explanation framework E that, given (f, M, x, y*), produces a structured explanation E(f, M, x, y*) = (S_change, S_invariant, x') with the following properties:

1. S_change ⊆ {1,…,d} is the minimal set of features whose values must be modified (with prescribed new values defining x') in order for the causal model to yield outcome y*.

2. S_invariant ⊆ {1,…,d} is an explicit set of features whose values are certified to remain at their original x-values in any admissible counterfactual achieving y*, and this certification is justified via the attribution scores A and the causal structure of M.

3. S_change ∩ S_invariant = ∅, and the pair (S_change, S_invariant) is, in a precise sense to be formulated, optimal with respect to a combined criterion that simultaneously (a) minimizes the cost/perturbation of S_change as in a contrastive explanation and (b) maximizes the causal attribution mass concentrated on S_change ∪ S_invariant.

Formulate precise mathematical conditions (axioms) that such a unified explanation operator E must satisfy so that it strictly generalizes both A and C, prove existence of E under stated assumptions on (f, M), and characterize uniqueness or the structure of the set of optimal explanations.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open direction in a survey on causal machine learning, asking for a unification of causal attribution and contrastive/counterfactual explanation methods. Web evidence shows continued, active work on counterfactual explanations and causal attributions (e.g., follow-ups to Verma et al. on counterfactual explanations), but no published framework appears to provide an axiomatic unification meeting both desiderata simultaneously. The problem therefore remains open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can causal explanation methods be made scalable enough for large systems with many features and many users, despite exact attribution methods becoming computationally intractable and contrastive explanation methods becoming hard because of plausibility and actionability constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a predictive or decision-making system modeled as a function f : X_1 × ... × X_d → Y together with an underlying structural causal model M = (V, U, F, P) over the input features (X_1, ..., X_d), where V are endogenous variables, U exogenous variables with distribution P, and F a set of structural assignments. For an instance x ∈ X_1 × ... × X_d and prediction y = f(x), two families of causal explanations are of interest:

1. Causal attribution: assign to each feature i ∈ {1,...,d} a score φ_i(x) measuring its causal contribution to y, defined via interventional or counterfactual quantities under M (for example, Shapley-style averages of causal effects E[f(X) | do(X_S = x_S)] over subsets S ⊆ {1,...,d}, or path-specific effects in the causal graph of M).

2. Contrastive (counterfactual) explanations: given x with prediction y, find an alternative input x' minimizing a cost c(x, x') such that f(x') = y' for some target y' ≠ y, subject to (a) a plausibility constraint requiring x' to lie in the support of the observational or interventional distribution induced by M, and (b) an actionability constraint requiring that x' be reachable from x by interventions only on a designated subset A ⊆ {1,...,d} of actionable features, with downstream effects propagated through F.

Exact computation of causal Shapley-type attributions requires evaluation over 2^d subsets, and exact counterfactual search under plausibility and actionability constraints is generally NP-hard.

Problem. Design algorithms that, for arbitrary M and f drawn from broad and explicitly specified classes, produce:
(i) approximate causal attribution scores φ̂_i(x) with provable approximation guarantees (e.g., additive ε-error with high probability) in time polynomial in d and in the number n of users/instances to be explained, and
(ii) approximate contrastive explanations x̂' satisfying the plausibility and actionability constraints up to controlled slack, with cost c(x, x̂') within a guaranteed factor of the optimal feasible counterfactual, again computable in time polynomial in d and n.

Characterize the largest classes of structural causal models M, prediction functions f, cost functions c, and constraint sets for which such scalable approximation algorithms with non-trivial guarantees exist, and prove matching computational lower bounds where they do not.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction about scalable causal explanation methods. No general algorithm with provable approximation guarantees and matching lower bounds across broad SCM/predictor classes is known; current work provides only partial heuristics or guarantees under restrictive assumptions, so the problem is open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can deployed causal explanation systems be made secure and privacy-preserving against attacks such as model extraction, decision-boundary recovery, membership inference, and extraction of causal knowledge from repeated explanation queries?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a deployed prediction system f : X → Y together with a causal explanation oracle E that, on input x ∈ X, returns an explanation E(x) describing causal attributions, counterfactuals, or structural-causal-model-derived information about f's decision at x (for example, individual treatment effects, counterfactual examples, or features of an underlying causal graph G that the explainer relies on). An adversary may issue an adaptive sequence of queries x_1, x_2, … and receive (f(x_i), E(x_i)). Consider the following adversarial threat models:

1. Model extraction: the adversary aims to produce f̂ such that Pr_{x∼D}[f̂(x) ≠ f(x)] ≤ ε using as few queries as possible.
2. Decision-boundary recovery: the adversary aims to approximate the set {x : f changes label in a neighborhood of x} to within Hausdorff distance ε.
3. Membership inference: given a candidate point z, the adversary aims to decide whether z belonged to the training set used to fit f or to estimate the causal model behind E, with advantage non-negligibly above 1/2.
4. Causal-knowledge extraction: the adversary aims to recover non-trivial structural information about the underlying causal graph G or its parameters (edges, parents, interventional distributions) used by E.

Design an explanation mechanism Ẽ (possibly randomized) that, while preserving the utility of E in a quantifiable sense (e.g., bounded expected distortion d(Ẽ(x), E(x)) ≤ δ over a target distribution), simultaneously provides provable defenses against all four threat models above. Specifically:

(a) Formulate appropriate definitions of (ε, δ)-causal-explanation privacy and security that simultaneously cover the four attack types.
(b) Construct a mechanism Ẽ that achieves these definitions under stated assumptions on f, the causal model, and the query budget, with explicit utility–privacy tradeoff bounds.
(c) Prove matching lower bounds showing the necessity of the imposed utility loss as a function of the query budget and privacy parameters.
category_tag: Privacy and security of causal explanations
status_search_result: Securing causal explanation systems against the combined threats of model extraction, decision-boundary recovery, membership inference, and causal-knowledge extraction remains an open area. Work exists on each attack in isolation against standard (non-causal) explainers (e.g., model-extraction via feature-attribution queries, membership inference from explanations), but no unified framework with provable guarantees for causal explanations is established in the literature.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Given the impossibility result that no attribution method can always be both continuous under small input changes and recourse sensitive for every utility notion and model, what workaround or reformulation can preserve useful robustness and actionable recourse at the same time?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a (possibly nonlinear) decision function of a machine learning model, and let an attribution method be a map $\phi$ that assigns to each input $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ a feature-attribution vector $\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ (or, more generally, a subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$). Fix a utility function $u:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that encodes which changes $\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ to an input $x$ are desirable to a user.

Call $\phi$:
(i) robust (continuous) at $x$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that $\|x'-x\|<\delta$ implies $\|\phi(x')-\phi(x)\|<\varepsilon$;
(ii) recourse sensitive with respect to $u$ if, whenever there exists a direction $\Delta$ that flips (or sufficiently changes) the decision of $f$ while having high utility $u(x,\Delta)$, the attribution $\phi(x)$ points the user towards such a $\Delta$ (formally: for some prescribed mapping from attributions to recommended changes, the recommended change has near-optimal utility among decision-changing perturbations).

It is known that no single-valued attribution method $\phi$ can simultaneously satisfy (i) and (ii) for every model $f$ and every utility $u$; the obstruction already appears for simple smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}$ whose decision boundary creates partially overlapping recourse regions pointing in different directions.

Problem: Formulate and establish a meaningful relaxation or reformulation of the framework — for instance, allowing set-valued attributions $\phi(x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, restricting to identifiable subclasses of models $f$, weakening continuity to a quantitative stability notion, or weakening recourse sensitivity to an approximate/probabilistic version — under which one can construct an attribution method $\phi$ that is simultaneously (a) stable under small perturbations of $x$ in the chosen sense and (b) recourse sensitive with respect to a broad family of utility functions $u$. Prove the corresponding possibility theorem and exhibit explicit attribution methods realizing it.
status_search_result: The underlying impossibility theorem of Fokkema, de Heide, and van Erven (JMLR 2023) is established, and the authors themselves propose partial workarounds—most notably allowing set-valued attributions and identifying sufficient conditions on classes of continuous functions under which recourse sensitivity can be achieved. However, a fully general reformulation that simultaneously preserves robustness and actionable recourse across broad model and utility classes has not been settled; it remains an active open direction.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: In causal fairness, how can equity or harm-based notions be operationalized as alternatives to equality-based fairness definitions, and how would such criteria complement or conflict with existing fairness notions used in machine learning?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a predictive model f: X -> Y that assigns outcomes (e.g., decisions, scores, or classifications) to individuals described by features X, where each individual additionally has a sensitive attribute A (e.g., race, gender) and where causal relationships among features, sensitive attributes, decisions, and downstream outcomes are encoded by a structural causal model M = (V, U, F, P(U)) with directed acyclic graph G. Most existing fairness criteria in this setting are equality-based: they require some statistic (such as predicted positive rate, error rate, counterfactual prediction, or path-specific causal effect) to be equal across values of A. Examples include demographic parity P(f(X)=1 | A=a) = P(f(X)=1 | A=a'), equalized odds, counterfactual fairness P(f(X)_{A<-a}=y | X=x, A=a) = P(f(X)_{A<-a'}=y | X=x, A=a), and path-specific counterfactual fairness.

The task is the following:

(1) Formulate, within the structural causal model framework, a precise mathematical definition of fairness based on equity or on minimization/bounding of harm rather than on equality across groups. The definition should specify (a) a notion of individual or group harm as a function of counterfactual outcomes under interventions on A and/or on the decision f(X), (b) an aggregation operator (e.g., supremum, expectation, weighted sum reflecting prior disadvantage) capturing equity considerations such as prioritarian or Rawlsian principles, and (c) a criterion that f must satisfy in terms of this harm measure.

(2) Establish formal logical relationships between this harm-based or equity-based criterion and the standard equality-based criteria above. Specifically, determine for which causal structures G and distributions P(U) the proposed criterion implies, is implied by, is equivalent to, or is incompatible with each of: demographic parity, equalized odds, counterfactual fairness, and path-specific counterfactual fairness. Identify impossibility results analogous to known equality-based impossibility theorems, and characterize the predictors f that simultaneously satisfy the harm-based criterion and one or more equality-based criteria.
status_search_result: The question of operationalizing equity- or harm-based causal fairness as an alternative to equality-based fairness, and characterizing its formal relationship to standard fairness notions, is posed as a future research direction. No web sources were found establishing a definitive, widely accepted formalization or a complete characterization of how such criteria relate to existing fairness definitions; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should fairness be defined and evaluated beyond predictive outputs, especially for recourse systems and causal algorithmic recourse, including whether recourse opportunities and intervention policies are fairly distributed across protected and unprotected groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let a population of individuals be modeled by a structural causal model M = (U, V, F, P(U)), where V = {X, A, Y} with A a protected attribute partitioning the population into groups G_a = {i : A_i = a}, X a vector of features (some of which may be actionable), and Y a binary decision output of a predictor h: X -> {0,1}. A (causal) algorithmic recourse system is a mapping that, for each individual i with h(X_i) = 0, returns a set of interventions Θ_i ⊆ A_int (a fixed space of admissible interventions on subsets of V) together with a recommended policy π_i ∈ Θ_i such that, under the post-intervention distribution induced by do(π_i) in M, the predicted outcome becomes 1 with probability at least some threshold τ, while the cost c(π_i; U_i) of the intervention (defined on the structural counterfactual for individual i) is minimized.

Develop a formal definition of fairness for such recourse systems that goes beyond fairness of the predictor h itself. Concretely:

(a) Propose mathematical fairness criteria for recourse that quantify whether the set of available recourse opportunities Θ_i and the minimal recourse cost c*(i) := min_{π ∈ Θ_i} E[c(π; U_i) | X_i, A_i] are distributed equitably across the groups G_a; for example, criteria of the form
   ρ_a := E[c*(i) | A_i = a, h(X_i)=0],
and conditions such as ρ_a = ρ_{a'} for all a, a', or analogous counterfactual-recourse criteria comparing c*(i) for an individual to the cost that would have been incurred had A_i taken a different value under M.

(b) Provide a corresponding evaluation procedure (estimator and identifiability conditions in terms of M and observational/interventional data) that allows these criteria to be tested.

(c) Address whether, and under which structural assumptions on M, it is normatively and causally appropriate to perform a societal-level intervention (i.e., a policy applied uniformly to every member of a subgroup G_a) as a means of equalizing recourse, and characterize the trade-offs between such group-level interventions and individual-level recourse recommendations.

The task is to give precise definitions, prove basic properties (existence, identifiability, compatibility/incompatibility results between different fairness-of-recourse criteria), and to formulate the conditions under which causal algorithmic recourse can be certified as fair across protected and unprotected groups.
status_search_result: Fairness in causal algorithmic recourse remains an active research area without a settled framework. Recent works (von Kügelgen et al. on fairness of causal recourse, Karimi et al. survey on algorithmic recourse) propose definitions and identify open challenges, but no consensus formal criterion or general evaluation methodology has been established, and societal-level interventions raise unresolved normative and identifiability issues.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: When causal fairness quantities, especially counterfactuals, are only partially identifiable, how should sensitivity analysis and realistic simulation be used to assess fairness methods and to understand how violations of identification assumptions affect fairness estimation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a structural causal model (SCM) M = (U, V, F, P(U)) where V is a set of observed variables (including a sensitive attribute A, covariates X, decision/outcome Y, and possibly mediators W), U is a set of latent exogenous variables with joint distribution P(U), and F is a collection of structural equations determining each V_i from its parents in V ∪ U. Counterfactual causal fairness quantities of interest include, for example, the counterfactual direct, indirect, and spurious effects of A on Y, as well as quantities such as P(Y_{A=a'} = y | A = a, X = x) for distinct levels a, a' of A.

Assume that only the observational distribution P(V) (and possibly a limited set of interventional distributions) is available, so that the SCM M is not uniquely determined. As a consequence, a causal fairness quantity ψ(M) is in general only partially identifiable: the observed data constrain ψ(M) to a set [ψ_L, ψ_U] rather than a single value, where the bounds depend on assumptions imposed on F and P(U) (e.g., monotonicity, exclusion restrictions, bounded unobserved confounding, instrumental constraints).

Formulate and solve the following program:

(a) Develop a sensitivity-analysis framework that, given a parametric or nonparametric family of allowed deviations from a baseline set of identification assumptions (such as no unobserved confounding, faithfulness, or ignorability of mediators), produces sharp upper and lower bounds [ψ_L(Γ), ψ_U(Γ)] on each counterfactual fairness measure ψ as a function of a sensitivity parameter Γ quantifying the magnitude of assumption violation.

(b) Provide a methodology, based on realistic simulation of SCMs calibrated to observed data, for evaluating fairness algorithms when the underlying counterfactual fairness quantities are only partially identifiable; the methodology should report not only point estimates produced by candidate fairness methods but also their behavior across the identification region and across plausible violations of the identifying assumptions.

(c) Characterize, both theoretically and empirically, how violations of standard identification assumptions translate into biases in counterfactual fairness estimates, and identify which assumptions are most critical for the validity of fairness conclusions.

Provide rigorous definitions of the sensitivity model, prove sharpness of the derived bounds, and give a principled protocol for benchmarking causal-fairness methods under partial identification.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction posed in a survey on causal machine learning. While partial work on bounding counterfactual fairness measures and sensitivity analysis (e.g., works of Kilbertus et al., Russell et al., Wu et al., and more recent treatments by Plečko and Bareinboim) exists, no comprehensive framework resolves the problem of sensitivity analysis and realistic-simulation benchmarking for partially identifiable causal fairness as of 2026. The status is best classified as open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Do social categories such as race and gender admit meaningful interventions or counterfactual manipulation in causal fairness models, and if not, what kinds of causal or non-interventionist formalisms should replace variable-based DAG treatments of those categories?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a causal fairness framework in which a structural causal model is specified by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G = (V, E) with vertices V representing random variables, structural equations X_i = f_i(Pa(X_i), U_i) for each i, and exogenous noise variables U_i. A "protected attribute" A in V (such as race or gender) is typically treated as a node admitting interventions do(A = a) and corresponding counterfactual quantities Y_{A \leftarrow a}(u). Counterfactual fairness criteria require, for example, that P(Y_{A \leftarrow a}(U) = y \mid X = x, A = a) = P(Y_{A \leftarrow a'}(U) = y \mid X = x, A = a) for all admissible a, a', x, y.

(a) Determine whether social categories such as race and gender can be coherently modeled as intervenable variables in a structural causal model: that is, identify necessary and sufficient conditions on a putative protected attribute A under which the interventions do(A = a) and the counterfactual random variables Y_{A \leftarrow a} are well-defined and admit a meaningful semantic interpretation consistent with how A is constituted in the data-generating process.

(b) If (a) cannot be satisfied for such categories (e.g., because A is constitutive of, rather than causally upstream of, downstream features), develop an alternative formal framework — not based on node-level interventions in a DAG — that nonetheless yields quantitative fairness criteria. The framework should specify (i) the mathematical objects replacing variables and interventions, (ii) a precise definition of a "fair predictor" within this framework, and (iii) identifiability conditions under which the proposed fairness criterion can be estimated from observational data.
category_tag: causal fairness and manipulability of social categories
status_search_result: The manipulability of social categories such as race and gender within causal fairness models remains an actively debated open problem. Surveys (e.g., Kasirzadeh and Smart, 2021) argue that such categories often resist counterfactual manipulation, and subsequent works have proposed partial alternatives (constitutive accounts, social-ontology-aware modeling, modular/constructivist approaches), but no consensus formal replacement framework has been established.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: When multiple causal fairness criteria conflict and cannot all be satisfied simultaneously, how should practitioners characterize, optimize, and govern the trade-offs among admissible criteria without producing policies that every stakeholder would reject?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, A, Y) \sim P$ be random variables on a probability space, where $X \in \mathcal{X}$ denotes covariates, $A \in \mathcal{A}$ a protected attribute, and $Y \in \mathcal{Y}$ an outcome of interest, with their joint distribution generated by a structural causal model $\mathcal{M} = (\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{F}, P_\mathbf{U})$. A policy (or predictor) is a measurable map $\pi : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A} \to \Delta(\mathcal{D})$ taking values in distributions over a decision space $\mathcal{D}$. Consider a finite collection of causal fairness criteria $\{C_1, \dots, C_k\}$, where each $C_i$ is a functional $C_i(\pi, \mathcal{M}) \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ measuring violation of a causal fairness notion (examples include counterfactual fairness, path-specific effects being zero, equality of natural direct or indirect effects across values of $A$, and counterfactual equalized odds). Assume that no policy $\pi$ simultaneously satisfies $C_i(\pi, \mathcal{M}) = 0$ for all $i = 1, \dots, k$ — that is, the criteria are mutually incompatible under $\mathcal{M}$.
        
Develop a formal framework, with precise definitions, that accomplishes all of the following:

1. (Characterization) Define and characterize the Pareto frontier
$$\mathcal{F} = \{\pi : \nexists\, \pi' \text{ with } C_i(\pi',\mathcal{M}) \le C_i(\pi,\mathcal{M}) \text{ for all } i \text{ and strict for some } i\},$$
including conditions on $\mathcal{M}$ and on $\{C_i\}$ guaranteeing existence, non-triviality, and identifiability of $\mathcal{F}$ from observational and/or interventional data.

2. (Optimization) Specify a constructive procedure that, given a utility functional $U(\pi, \mathcal{M})$ and a set of stakeholder preference profiles $\{\succeq_s\}_{s \in S}$ over $\mathbb{R}^k$, returns a policy in $\mathcal{F}$ optimizing $U$ subject to acceptability of the trade-off vector $(C_1(\pi,\mathcal{M}), \dots, C_k(\pi,\mathcal{M}))$ under every $\succeq_s$.

3. (Governance / unanimity) Prove a no-veto theorem: provide necessary and sufficient conditions on $(\mathcal{M}, \{C_i\}, \{\succeq_s\})$ under which the procedure in (2) is guaranteed to output at least one policy that is not strictly rejected (dominated in the $\succeq_s$ order by some feasible alternative) by any stakeholder $s \in S$; or, if no such conditions exist in general, exhibit obstructions.

The problem is to provide such a framework together with the corresponding theorems, or to prove no such framework can exist under stated minimal axioms.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic open challenge regarding trade-offs among incompatible causal fairness criteria. Known impossibility results (e.g., Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan, Chouldechova) show several fairness notions cannot coexist, and recent work on causal fairness analysis (Plečko-Bareinboim, 2024+) provides partial characterizations, but a complete framework satisfying characterization, optimization, and stakeholder-governance jointly remains open.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Under what conditions can a trained model produce unfair predictions even when the training labels themselves are fair, and how can causal fairness methods detect, rule out, or stress-test such introduced unfairness?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a supervised learning setting with features X, a sensitive attribute A (e.g., race or gender), an outcome label Y, and a trained predictor Ŷ = f(X, A) (or Ŷ = f(X)) obtained by minimizing some loss on data drawn from a joint distribution P(X, A, Y) generated by an underlying structural causal model M with directed acyclic graph G over the variables {A, X, Y}. Say that the training labels Y are "fair" with respect to A under a chosen causal fairness criterion (for example: zero total causal effect of A on Y, zero counterfactual effect, or zero path-specific effect along a designated set of "unfair" causal paths from A to Y in G). Say that the trained predictor Ŷ exhibits "introduced unfairness" if, under the same criterion applied to Ŷ in place of Y, the criterion fails — i.e., the model produces predictions that are unfair even though the labels are fair.

(a) Give necessary and sufficient graphical and distributional conditions on (G, P, the loss, the hypothesis class, the chosen fairness criterion) under which a risk-minimizing predictor Ŷ can exhibit introduced unfairness while Y is fair.

(b) Develop causal fairness procedures (tests or constraints) that, given access to G and to P (or to samples), can detect introduced unfairness in a trained Ŷ, rule it out a priori by structural assumptions or training-time constraints, and stress-test the proposed fairness criteria against this failure mode.

Formalize the criteria, prove the corresponding detection/impossibility results, and exhibit explicit families of structural causal models in which introduced unfairness provably arises or is provably excluded.
status_search_result: A 2022 line of work ("Why Fair Labels Can Yield Unfair Predictions: Graphical Conditions for Introduced Unfairness", AAAI 2022 / arXiv:2202.10816) formalizes "introduced unfairness" via an "introduced total variation" measure and gives graphical conditions on the causal DAG under which risk minimization is incentivized to introduce unfairness, and shows that including the sensitive attribute as a feature removes this incentive under well-behaved losses. This addresses parts of the question for total-variation-type criteria, but general necessary-and-sufficient conditions for arbitrary path-specific / counterfactual criteria, together with practical detection and stress-testing procedures, remain only partially developed.

The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Can the many partially overlapping causal and non-causal reinforcement-learning formalisms for shared-dynamics, partially observed, or confounded environments be compared rigorously and possibly unified so practitioners are not forced to choose among redundant formulations with unclear relationships?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the collection of formal frameworks that have been proposed for sequential decision-making in environments that exhibit one or more of the following features: (i) shared transition dynamics across multiple tasks or agents, (ii) partial observability of the underlying state, and (iii) unobserved confounders that simultaneously influence the agent's actions (or behavior policy) and the environment's transitions or rewards. Representative formalisms include Markov decision processes (MDPs), partially observable MDPs (POMDPs), block MDPs, contextual MDPs, hidden-parameter MDPs, factored MDPs, confounded MDPs, decision-theoretic causal models with interventions, structural causal bandits, and dynamic structural causal models.

Each such formalism specifies (a) a class of admissible environments described by a probabilistic/causal model over states, observations, actions, and rewards, (b) a notion of policy and of intervention, and (c) an associated optimality criterion and identifiability conditions for off-policy or counterfactual evaluation.

Tasks:
1. Provide a rigorous common mathematical framework (for instance, a category, a class of structural causal models with a designated action mechanism, or a measure-theoretic template) in which each of the above formalisms can be embedded as a special case via explicit functors or reduction maps that preserve policies, interventional distributions, and value functions.
2. For each pair of formalisms in the above list, determine and prove the exact inclusion, equivalence, or strict-separation relation under this embedding, characterizing which environments and which learning/identification problems in one formalism can be expressed in the other, and exhibiting explicit counterexamples where no such expression exists.
3. Determine whether there exists a single minimal formalism in this framework that strictly subsumes all of the above as definable subclasses while preserving sample-complexity and identifiability guarantees up to polynomial reductions.
status_search_result: No published work appears to provide a unified rigorous framework subsuming the diverse causal and non-causal reinforcement-learning formalisms (MDPs, POMDPs, block/contextual/hidden-parameter MDPs, confounded MDPs, causal bandits, etc.) with proven inclusion/separation results. Recent surveys on causal reinforcement learning continue to list this comparison and unification as an open direction.
