paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can large language models augment and regenerate existing test suites, rather than only generating brand-new suites, by using few-shot learning or fine-tuning on existing tests and historical faults to add new assertions that capture corner cases, past defects, and likely programmer errors?
self_contained_problem:
Let T be an existing test suite for a program P under test, and let H be a historical dataset consisting of (i) past defects (bug reports, fix commits, regression traces) associated with P or with related programs, and (ii) prior test cases and assertions written for P. A test-suite augmentation procedure is a method A that takes (P, T, H) as input and outputs an extended suite T' ⊇ T obtained by adding new test cases and/or new assertions to the existing tests of T.

Design and analyze a procedure A based on a pre-trained large language model that operates in one of two regimes:
(a) few-shot prompting, in which examples drawn from T and H are provided in-context to the language model in order to elicit new assertions and test inputs that target corner cases, historical fault patterns, and likely programmer-error categories for P; or
(b) fine-tuning, in which the language model is further trained on (T, H) so as to generate additional assertions and test inputs of the same nature.

The procedure must (1) preserve all existing tests in T, (2) generate additional assertions that capture corner-case behavior, recurrences of historical defect patterns, and common programmer-error categories, and (3) produce only assertions that are consistent with the intended behavior of P (i.e., that pass on the correct version of P).

Provide such a procedure together with an evaluation methodology measuring its effectiveness in terms of (i) increase in code/branch/mutation coverage of T' over T, (ii) the rate at which T' detects injected faults derived from H that T misses, and (iii) the rate of spurious (incorrect) assertions produced.
status_search_result: Several recent works partially address this problem: MuTAP augments LLM-generated tests using surviving mutants to detect more faulty code; Assertify uses few-shot prompting with LLMs to generate production assertions; TestART co-evolves LLM-based test generation with repair iterations; and recent studies analyze trade-offs between fine-tuning and few-shot learning for test-related tasks (e.g., flaky-test detection, assertion generation via retrieval-augmented fine-tuning). However, a general, fully validated framework for LLM-based augmentation/regeneration of existing test suites using historical-fault data remains an active research area, not a solved problem.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: When an LLM generates a software test, how can the system automatically determine whether a passing test is a meaningful regression test or merely coincidentally correct, whether a failing test has found a real bug or contains a wrong assertion, and how can raw execution outcomes be filtered into a trustworthy test signal before they are shown to developers?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an automated software testing pipeline in which a large language model (LLM) is used to synthesize unit tests for a target program P under a current release R. Each generated test t consists of a setup, an invocation of code in P, and one or more assertions. When t is executed against R, exactly one of two raw outcomes occurs: (a) t passes, or (b) t fails (i.e., at least one assertion is violated or an unexpected exception is thrown).

Design and analyze a fully automatic procedure that, taking as input the program P, the generated test t, and the raw execution outcome, produces a trustworthy filtered "test signal" classifying t into one of the following categories with calibrated confidence:

1. If t passes on R, decide whether t is a meaningful regression test (its assertions genuinely characterize intended behavior of P and would detect plausible future regressions) or whether it is only coincidentally correct (the assertions hold on R for reasons unrelated to the specification, e.g., over-specified to incidental outputs, tautological assertions, or assertions that pass on any input).

2. If t fails on R, decide whether the failure indicates a real bug in P or whether t itself is faulty (e.g., contains an incorrect assertion, makes an invalid setup assumption, or violates a precondition).

Specifically, formalize:
(i) precise definitions of "meaningful regression test", "coincidentally correct test", "real bug", and "incorrect assertion" suitable for algorithmic decision;
(ii) a procedure that, using only P, t, the LLM, and an execution environment (without access to a human oracle), assigns one of the four labels above together with a confidence score, and that may also augment t (e.g., by mutating, strengthening, or weakening assertions, or generating related tests) to increase reliability of the classification;
(iii) evaluation criteria (precision, recall, calibration) under which the procedure can be shown to filter raw execution outcomes into a signal that is more trustworthy than the raw pass/fail outcome before being shown to a developer.

Provide such a procedure, or prove fundamental limits on the achievability of this filtering task.
status_search_result: This is an open research problem highlighted in a 2023 survey on LLMs for software engineering and remains an active area of investigation. Recent work on test oracle inference, mutation-based test validation, and LLM self-consistency provides partial techniques, but no general, validated solution exists.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLM-based performance-improvement techniques automatically discover behavior-preserving or sufficiently faithful improvements not only for execution time but also for power consumption, memory footprint, and explicit multi-objective tradeoffs among non-functional properties?
self_contained_problem: Let P be a program with a specified input/output specification S, and let f_1, ..., f_k be measurable non-functional cost functions defined on executions of P (for example: execution time, peak memory footprint, and energy/power consumption). A transformation T of P is called behavior-preserving with respect to S if for every admissible input x, T(P)(x) satisfies S(x, T(P)(x)) exactly; it is called sufficiently faithful with tolerance ε if the proportion (or expected discrepancy) of inputs on which T(P) violates S is bounded by ε under a specified input distribution. Design and analyze an automated procedure, driven by a large language model acting as a code-transformation proposer combined with a verification/testing oracle, that takes (P, S, {f_i}, ε) as input and produces a transformed program T(P) which is sufficiently faithful with tolerance ε and which Pareto-dominates P with respect to (f_1, ..., f_k), i.e. f_i(T(P)) ≤ f_i(P) for all i with strict inequality for some i. Specifically: (i) formulate a search/optimization framework in which the LLM proposes candidate edits and a verifier filters them by faithfulness; (ii) prove or empirically establish convergence or improvement guarantees in expectation for the multi-objective Pareto front discovered; and (iii) extend the framework beyond execution time to handle power consumption, memory footprint, and explicit multi-objective trade-offs simultaneously.
status_search_result: The problem of LLM-driven, multi-objective, behavior-preserving program improvement (covering energy, memory, and runtime jointly) remains an active open research area. While individual results exist on LLM-based code optimization for runtime, comprehensive techniques addressing multi-objective non-functional trade-offs with faithfulness guarantees have not been established.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLM-based refactoring become reliable enough to automate project-specific and API-evolution-driven refactorings, including bespoke refactorings learned from a few examples, while preserving existing behavior via the automated regression oracle and still producing useful developer-facing explanations?
self_contained_problem:
Let a refactoring be a transformation T that maps a source program P to a target program P' = T(P) such that the observable behavior of P' agrees with that of P on a designated regression test suite R(P) (the "automated regression oracle"): for every test t in R(P), the outputs of P and P' on t coincide. A bespoke refactoring is a transformation specified only by a small finite set of input–output program pairs {(P_i, P'_i)}_{i=1}^k (with k small, e.g. k ≤ 5), interpreted as examples of the intended transformation; an API-evolution refactoring is one induced by replacing uses of an old API specification A_old with a new API specification A_new while preserving behavior.

Design a methodology M that, given (i) a program P, (ii) either a few-shot example set {(P_i, P'_i)} or a pair (A_old, A_new), and (iii) the regression oracle R(P), produces a refactored program P' = M(P, …) together with a natural-language explanation E, such that the following properties hold with high reliability:

1. (Behavior preservation) P' passes every test in R(P).
2. (Generalization) When given few-shot examples, M correctly applies the intended bespoke transformation to all occurrences in P that match the latent pattern exhibited by the examples, and to no others.
3. (API conformance) For API-evolution inputs, every call site in P matching A_old is rewritten to a semantically equivalent call site conforming to A_new.
4. (Explanatory adequacy) The explanation E faithfully and concisely describes the changes made and the rationale, in a form useful to a human developer.

Formulate precise definitions of "reliability," "few-shot generalization correctness," and "explanatory adequacy" suitable for evaluation, and either construct such a methodology M and prove guarantees for properties (1)–(4) under stated assumptions, or establish impossibility/lower-bound results.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research challenge in the software engineering literature on LLM-assisted code transformation. Recent work (2024–2025) on LLM-based refactoring and API migration (e.g., studies on ChatGPT/Copilot refactoring quality and on automated API migration with LLMs) reports progress but consistently notes that behavior-preserving, reliably generalizing few-shot bespoke refactoring with trustworthy explanations remains unsolved.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can LLMs generate richer and more semantically relevant code summaries and documentation than retrieval-based methods, and what evaluation and assurance methods should replace purely lexical metrics when the generated documentation cannot be directly executed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the task of automatically generating natural-language summaries and documentation for source code. A retrieval-based summarizer is a function that, given an input code snippet, returns a summary chosen from (or assembled from) a fixed corpus of human-written summaries; consequently, the space of possible outputs is constrained by this corpus. A generative large language model (LLM) summarizer, by contrast, may produce summaries that lie outside any predetermined corpus.

(a) Formulate a precise notion of "semantic relevance" and "richness" for a code-summary pair (C, S), and design a generative summarization procedure based on an LLM that provably (or empirically, under a stated benchmark) produces summaries achieving strictly greater semantic relevance and richness than every retrieval-based summarizer restricted to a fixed training corpus, for some non-trivial class of input programs.

(b) Standard automatic evaluation metrics for code summarization (such as BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, and similar n-gram or token-overlap measures) are purely lexical: they compare a candidate summary to one or more reference summaries via surface-level token statistics. Such metrics may fail to reward summaries that are semantically correct but lexically divergent from references. Design and justify an evaluation methodology for generated code documentation that:
  (i) does not reduce to lexical overlap with a fixed reference set,
  (ii) provides quantitative assurance about the factual correctness of the documentation with respect to the code it describes, even though the documentation itself cannot be executed, and
  (iii) is reproducible and admits well-defined notions of soundness (low false-positive rate of accepting incorrect documentation) and completeness (low false-negative rate of rejecting correct documentation).

Provide either a theoretical framework with provable guarantees or an empirically validated protocol, and characterize the limits of such evaluation.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in the area of LLM-based code summarization and documentation evaluation. While many works propose semantic or learned evaluation metrics (e.g., BERTScore, BLEURT, code-specific learned metrics, LLM-as-judge protocols) and ReAct-style verification, no consensus or definitive solution has emerged. The problem remains open as a research program.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How should new software-engineering-specific large language models be trained or fine-tuned so that they exploit software-specific signals, especially dynamic execution information and execution traces, rather than treating software artifacts too much like ordinary natural language?
self_contained_problem:
Design a training or fine-tuning methodology for large language models (LLMs) specialized to software engineering tasks that explicitly incorporates software-specific signals beyond the static token-stream view used for natural language. Concretely:

Setup. Let a software artifact be a tuple A = (S, T, M) where:
- S is the source code (a sequence of tokens or an abstract syntax tree),
- T = {(σ_1, o_1), (σ_2, o_2), …, (σ_k, o_k)} is a finite set of execution traces, where each σ_i is a sequence of program states (variable valuations, memory/heap snapshots, control-flow edges traversed) produced by running S on input x_i, and o_i is the corresponding output,
- M denotes auxiliary metadata (test outcomes, coverage vectors, runtime profiles, type information, commit history).

Let p_θ(· | ·) be an autoregressive LLM with parameters θ over a token vocabulary.

Problem. Propose and justify a pretraining and/or fine-tuning objective L(θ; D) over a dataset D = {A^{(j)}} of such artifacts that:
1. conditions the model on, or predicts, components of execution traces T (e.g., next-state prediction, trace-conditioned code generation, or joint code–trace modeling),
2. produces a model whose downstream performance on software-engineering tasks (code synthesis, repair, test generation, fault localization) provably or empirically improves over a baseline trained only on static source text under matched compute, and
3. defines an evaluation protocol with quantitative metrics distinguishing benefit attributable to dynamic execution information from benefit attributable to additional static data.

State sufficient conditions on D, on the representation of traces, and on the objective L under which the resulting model strictly dominates a static-text-only baseline on a specified family of SE benchmarks.
status_search_result: This is an open research direction. Recent work (2023–2025) has explored execution-trace-aware LLMs (e.g., TRACED, NExT, SemCoder, code-execution pretraining objectives) showing partial empirical gains, but no general, principled training methodology fully exploiting dynamic execution information for SE-specific LLMs has been established. The problem remains open as an active area of investigation.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
context_brief: model size, energy, and lightweight adaptation
original_question: What model size is actually required for strong software-engineering performance, and how should lighter deployment techniques such as low-rank adaptation and quantization be evaluated for specific software-engineering applications so that accuracy, energy use, and deployability are balanced rather than assuming larger models are always necessary?
self_contained_problem:
Consider large language models (LLMs) used for software-engineering tasks such as code generation, code summarization, bug detection, program repair, and test generation. Let a model be parameterized by its number of trainable parameters N (its "size"), and let its training corpus have size D (number of tokens). For a given software-engineering task T, let A(N, D, M) denote a task-specific accuracy/quality metric (e.g., pass@1 for code synthesis, F1 for defect detection) of a model M of size N trained on D tokens, and let E(M, T) denote the energy cost (in joules) of running M on task T at inference, and Dep(M) a deployability score reflecting memory footprint, latency, and ease of on-device serving.

Consider two lightweight adaptation techniques:
 (i) Low-rank adaptation (LoRA): given a pretrained weight matrix W ∈ R^{d×k} of M, replace fine-tuning updates ΔW by a low-rank factorization ΔW = B A with B ∈ R^{d×r}, A ∈ R^{r×k}, and r ≪ min(d,k);
 (ii) Quantization: replace each weight w of M by Q(w), where Q maps the floating-point weight to a b-bit representation (e.g., b ∈ {8, 4, 3, 2}).

Provide a principled, empirically grounded answer to the following:

1. For each major software-engineering task T, determine the minimal model size N*(T) (as a function of training data volume D, possibly via a scaling law A(N, D, T) ≥ τ for a target threshold τ) such that strong performance on T is achieved, and characterize how N*(T) depends on T.

2. Develop and apply an evaluation protocol that, for representative SE tasks, jointly measures (a) accuracy A, (b) inference energy E, and (c) deployability Dep when LoRA (parameterized by rank r) and quantization (parameterized by bit-width b) are applied to a pretrained LLM. Specifically, identify Pareto-optimal configurations (N, r, b) that maximize accuracy under fixed budgets on E and Dep, or equivalently minimize E subject to A ≥ τ.

3. Determine the conditions under which smaller, LoRA-adapted, and/or quantized models match or exceed the SE-task performance of larger unadapted models, so that the default assumption "larger is always better" can be replaced by a quantitative trade-off between accuracy, energy, and deployability.
category_tag: Efficient LLM deployment for code tasks
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic open problem regarding optimal model size and lightweight adaptation (LoRA, quantization) for software-engineering tasks. While LoRA and various quantization schemes (e.g., GPTQ, AWQ, QLoRA) have been individually studied and partial benchmarks exist for code LLMs (e.g., evaluations of CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeek-Coder at varying sizes and quantization levels), no comprehensive answer establishing minimal model sizes per SE task with joint accuracy/energy/deployability Pareto frontiers has been established. Recent surveys on LLMs for SE still list this as open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can dynamic, adaptive prompt engineering and model-parameter tuning be turned into a principled optimization process for software-engineering tasks, given that prompt effectiveness is highly problem-specific, one-size-fits-all prompting is unrealistic, and settings such as temperature materially affect the nature of generated outputs?
self_contained_problem:
Let a software-engineering task T (e.g., code generation, repair, test synthesis, summarization) be specified by an input space X_T, an output space Y_T, and a task-specific quality vector q_T : Y_T -> R^k whose components encode objectives such as correctness, efficiency, readability, and security. Let M(· ; p, θ) denote a large language model that, given a prompt p drawn from a prompt space P and a parameter configuration θ (including continuous controls such as sampling temperature τ ∈ [0,∞), top-p, top-k, and any tunable model hyperparameters) in a configuration space Θ, induces a conditional distribution M(y | x ; p, θ) over outputs y ∈ Y_T for each input x ∈ X_T.

For a distribution D_T over inputs x ∈ X_T, define the expected quality vector
   F_T(p, θ) = E_{x ~ D_T} E_{y ~ M(· | x ; p, θ)} [ q_T(y) ].

Design a principled, dynamic, and adaptive optimization procedure A that, given a task T (revealed only through a stream of inputs x_1, x_2, … drawn from D_T together with possibly noisy evaluations of q_T on produced outputs), produces a sequence (p_t, θ_t) ∈ P × Θ with the following properties:

(i) Multi-objective optimality: the limit set {F_T(p_t, θ_t)} converges to (or approximates) the Pareto frontier of F_T over P × Θ, under stated regularity assumptions on q_T, M, and D_T.

(ii) Adaptivity: A makes no assumption of a single universal optimum and is permitted to vary (p_t, θ_t) with t, with provable regret or sample-complexity bounds relative to the best non-stationary policy in a comparator class.

(iii) Joint search over discrete prompts and continuous parameters: A handles the heterogeneity of P (a combinatorial/textual space) and Θ (containing continuous variables such as temperature whose value materially shifts the output distribution).

(iv) Transferability: provide formal guarantees, or counterexamples, on how solutions for one task T transfer or fail to transfer to a related task T'.

The problem is to formulate such a procedure A, establish its convergence/regret guarantees, characterize the structural assumptions on (P, Θ, M, q_T, D_T) under which the guarantees hold, and prove lower bounds showing the necessity of those assumptions.
status_search_result: The question is posed as part of an open research agenda on adaptive prompt engineering and parameter tuning for software-engineering uses of LLMs. While considerable work exists on prompt optimization (e.g., automatic prompt search, APE, OPRO) and on parameter tuning (e.g., temperature scheduling, SBSE-style multi-objective search), no widely accepted principled framework with formal guarantees for joint dynamic prompt and parameter optimization across SE tasks is established. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: What design patterns and workflow architectures best allow LLMs to reside safely, efficiently, and effectively inside broader software-engineering processes, including generate-and-test frameworks, static and dynamic analysis pipelines, post-processing stages, and continuous-integration systems?
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction concerning best practices for embedding LLMs into software engineering workflows. Subsequent work (2024–2026) has explored specific patterns (retrieval-augmented generation, agentic loops, LLM-augmented CI, self-repair with compilers/tests, static-analysis-guided prompting), but no comprehensive theory or canonical taxonomy of safe-efficient-effective LLM-SE workflow patterns has been established. The problem remains open.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can hallucination be harnessed productively in software engineering so that plausible but incorrect outputs are repurposed into useful signals for software enhancement, such as feature suggestions, warnings about likely human misunderstandings of code, or prompts for API simplification and extension, without letting those hallucinations degrade correctness?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model (LLM) M used as an assistant for software engineering tasks. Given a software artifact A (e.g., source code, an API specification, or a test suite), the model M produces outputs o = M(A, t) for task prompts t such as: (a) generating test cases, (b) producing natural-language summaries of code, and (c) suggesting API calls or library usage. Call an output o a "hallucination" if it is fluent and plausible but factually incorrect with respect to A (for example, a test exercising nonexistent behavior, a summary that misrepresents code semantics, or a call to a nonexistent API).

Design a methodology (a precise pipeline, with input/output specifications, decision rules, and evaluation metrics) that takes such hallucinated outputs and converts them into constructive signals for software improvement, including at minimum:

1. A detector D that, given (A, o), classifies o as correct vs. hallucinated with measurable precision and recall.
2. A repurposing function R that maps each hallucinated output to one of the following actionable artifacts:
   - a candidate feature-suggestion derived from a hallucinated test case,
   - a warning identifying portions of A likely to be misunderstood by human readers, derived from a hallucinated code summary,
   - a refactoring proposal that simplifies or extends the existing API, derived from a hallucinated API call.
3. A guarantee, stated as a quantitative bound or empirical protocol, that the use of R does not degrade the correctness of the resulting software system relative to a baseline that discards hallucinations.

Provide such a pipeline (D, R) together with formal definitions of "plausibility," "hallucination," and "useful signal," and demonstrate—either theoretically or via a reproducible empirical evaluation—that the harnessed hallucinations yield a net positive contribution to software quality without compromising correctness.
status_search_result: The question of systematically harnessing LLM hallucinations as constructive signals for software engineering (feature suggestion, misunderstanding warnings, API refactoring) is posed as a future-research direction. No published methodology with formal guarantees appears to resolve it; related work continues to focus on detecting and mitigating hallucinations rather than productively repurposing them.

paper_title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems
original_question: What scientific foundations, benchmarking systems, replication practices, and longitudinal human-in-the-loop studies are needed so that LLM-based software engineering can be evaluated robustly despite nondeterminism, incomplete reporting, scarce artifact sharing, and the need to measure real developer-LLM interaction over time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the empirical discipline of software engineering in which large language models (LLMs) are used to assist or automate tasks such as code generation, program repair, test generation, code review, refactoring, and documentation. An LLM in this context is a stochastic function that, given a prompt, produces outputs sampled from a probability distribution determined by decoding parameters (e.g., temperature, top-k, top-p, random seed); thus repeated evaluation of the same model on the same input may yield different outputs (nondeterminism). Empirical studies in this discipline currently suffer from: (i) nondeterministic model behavior that complicates reproducibility, (ii) incomplete reporting of experimental configurations (model version, decoding parameters, prompts, datasets, evaluation metrics), (iii) limited sharing of artifacts such as prompts, code, model outputs, and evaluation harnesses, and (iv) a lack of longitudinal studies measuring how developers and LLMs interact over extended periods of real use.

Formulate and develop:
1. A set of scientific foundations (definitions, hypotheses, statistical methodologies, and reporting standards) that enable rigorous empirical evaluation of LLM-based software engineering techniques in the presence of nondeterministic model outputs, including principled ways to quantify and report variance across runs and decoding strategies.
2. A reliable, efficient, and comprehensive benchmarking system for LLM-based software engineering, specifying benchmark tasks, datasets (with safeguards against training-data contamination), evaluation metrics, and protocols that allow fair comparison between techniques.
3. Replication and artifact-sharing practices (formats, infrastructure, and minimum reporting requirements) that allow independent researchers to reproduce reported results despite model evolution and stochasticity.
4. A methodology for longitudinal human-in-the-loop studies that measure developer–LLM interaction over time, including operational definitions of relevant outcomes (productivity, code quality, learning, trust, error rates), instruments for data collection, and statistical designs that account for temporal dependence and confounding.

Provide such a framework, justify its components, and demonstrate that it addresses (i)–(iv) above.
status_search_result: This is an open research agenda rather than a single formal conjecture. Recent work (2023–2025) on benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench), reproducibility studies of LLMs for code, and surveys on LLM4SE indicate that while partial progress has been made (new benchmarks, contamination analyses, some reproducibility guidelines), the broader call for scientific foundations, comprehensive benchmarking, replication standards, and longitudinal human-in-the-loop studies remains largely unresolved.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How can researchers train smaller and more efficient language models that serve as cost-effective alternatives to very large language models, especially for task-specific settings that do not require the full generality of larger models, and what roles should parameter-efficient fine-tuning, teacher-student transfer, and other forms of distillation play in building such smaller models from larger ones?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large pretrained autoregressive language model T (the "teacher") with parameters θ_T ∈ R^{N_T}, trained on a broad text distribution, and a target task distribution D over input–output pairs (x,y). The goal is to produce a smaller "student" language model S with parameters θ_S ∈ R^{N_S}, where N_S ≪ N_T, that approximates the teacher's task-specific performance on D under a fixed compute/memory budget B (covering inference latency, parameter count, and energy cost).

Formalize and investigate the following:

1. Define a family of training procedures Φ that produce θ_S from (T, D, B), where Φ may combine:
   (a) Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT): updating only a low-dimensional subset or low-rank adapter Δθ with ||Δθ||_0 or rank(Δθ) ≪ N_S, while freezing the remainder of θ_S;
   (b) Teacher–student knowledge distillation: minimizing a divergence L_KD(θ_S) = E_{x∼D}[ D( p_T(·|x) || p_S(·|x; θ_S) ) ] for some divergence D (e.g., KL), possibly combined with a hard-label task loss L_task;
   (c) Other forms of distillation, including intermediate-representation matching, sequence-level distillation, or data-distillation in which T generates synthetic training data for S.

2. Given a task family F and a budget B, determine training procedures Φ ∈ Φ_all that minimize the expected task risk
      R(Φ) = E_{(x,y)∼D}[ ℓ(S_Φ(x), y) ]
   subject to the resource constraints, and characterize provable or empirical trade-offs between N_S, the size of D, the size of T, and the achievable risk R(Φ).

3. Identify conditions under which a small student S can match the teacher's task performance to within ε > 0, i.e., R(Φ) ≤ R(T) + ε, and quantify the dependence of the minimal N_S on ε, on the task complexity, and on the distillation method used.

Provide methods, training algorithms, and theoretical or empirical guarantees that address these questions for task-specific deployment of small language models built from larger ones.
category_tag: Efficient language model training and distillation
status_search_result: This is an active and broad research direction rather than a single resolved problem. Numerous recent works (e.g., DistilBERT, TinyLlama, Phi-series small models, LoRA/QLoRA PEFT methods, and sequence-level distillation) have made substantial progress, but no general optimal procedure or tight theoretical characterization of the size–performance trade-off is known. The overall problem remains open.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: Which post-attention or otherwise new architectural paradigms should replace or substantially extend Transformer-based large language models, and how can those architectures support longer context windows and more efficient processing of long-context prompts than standard attention-based models?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A large language model is a parameterized conditional distribution p_θ(x_{t+1} | x_{1:t}) over tokens from a finite vocabulary V, trained on long sequences. The dominant architecture is the Transformer, whose core operation is scaled dot-product self-attention: given input embeddings X ∈ R^{n×d}, one computes Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V and outputs softmax(QK^⊤/√d) V. This operation has time and memory cost Θ(n^2 d) in the sequence length n, which makes processing very long contexts (large n) prohibitively expensive in compute and memory.

Problem. Propose and analyze a sequence-modeling architecture A (a "post-attention" paradigm, e.g., based on state-space models, linear/recurrent operators, structured kernels, mixtures-of-experts on sequence position, or other mechanisms) that satisfies all of the following:

(1) Asymptotic efficiency. The per-token inference cost of A is o(n) in the context length n (e.g., O(1) or O(log n) per token, with total cost o(n^2) for a length-n prompt), and the memory required to process a length-n prompt is o(n^2), preferably O(n) or better.

(2) Expressivity. A is at least as expressive as the standard Transformer for sequence-to-sequence modeling, in the sense that for every Transformer T with parameter count P there exists a model A_T in the proposed family with parameter count poly(P) that realizes the same input-output map (or approximates it uniformly on bounded inputs to arbitrary accuracy).

(3) Long-context capability. Provide quantitative guarantees (information-theoretic, approximation-theoretic, or learning-theoretic) showing that A can faithfully represent dependencies across positions separated by distances up to n, where n is allowed to grow without bound, with error decaying appropriately.

(4) Training feasibility. The architecture admits a training procedure whose per-step cost matches the inference efficiency in (1) and whose sample complexity for language-modeling tasks is at most polynomially worse than that of a Transformer.

Determine such an architecture A and prove the stated efficiency, expressivity, long-context, and trainability guarantees; or, alternatively, prove an impossibility result showing that no architecture can simultaneously satisfy (1)–(4).

status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction. paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How should future large language models be designed and evaluated so that they can handle text, images, video, and audio in a unified multi-modal manner for applications such as question answering, content generation, healthcare, robotics, and especially conversational generative vision?
self_contained_problem:
Design a principled framework for constructing and evaluating large language models that operate in a unified multi-modal setting over the modalities text, image, video, and audio. Concretely:

1. Architecture and training. Specify a model family $\mathcal{M} = \{f_\theta : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\}$ where the input space $\mathcal{X}$ is a product (or union) of representation spaces for the four modalities $\{T, I, V, A\}$ and the output space $\mathcal{Y}$ likewise may contain any combination of these modalities. Define encoders $E_m$ for each modality $m \in \{T,I,V,A\}$ mapping raw inputs to a shared latent space $\mathcal{Z}$, a fusion mechanism $\Phi : \prod_m \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{Z}$, and decoders $D_m$ producing outputs in each modality. Provide training objectives that jointly optimize cross-modal alignment, generation fidelity, and instruction following.

2. Task coverage. Show how the framework supports the task classes (a) multi-modal question answering, (b) cross-modal content generation, (c) clinical/healthcare decision support, (d) embodied robotic control, and (e) conversational generative vision, where the model must sustain a multi-turn dialogue that both interprets and generates visual content consistent with the conversation history.

3. Evaluation. Define a quantitative evaluation protocol consisting of: a benchmark suite covering each modality pair $(m_1, m_2)$ for input/output; metrics $\mu_k : \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$ that measure factual correctness, cross-modal consistency, dialogue coherence, and generative quality; and, specifically for conversational generative vision, a metric that scores both the perceptual quality of generated images/videos and their semantic faithfulness to the evolving dialogue context.

The problem is to provide a complete specification of such a framework, together with a justification that the proposed design and evaluation protocol are sufficient to compare arbitrary multi-modal LLMs on the listed application domains.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended research design question rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. As of 2026, multi-modal LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini, Llama-3.x multimodal) and benchmarks (MMMU, MMBench, Video-MME, SEED-Bench) are active areas of development, but no single agreed-upon framework or evaluation protocol uniformly covers text/image/video/audio across all the listed application domains, and conversational generative vision evaluation remains an active research topic.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: Which advanced prompt-engineering, tool-use, retrieval-augmentation, personalization, agent, and multi-agent techniques can most effectively address shortcomings of large language models such as hallucination while enabling systems that use external tools, incorporate user context, and make decisions in real applications?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model (LLM) defined as a parameterized conditional probability distribution p_θ(y | x) over output token sequences y given an input prompt x, trained on large text corpora. Such models are known to exhibit shortcomings, in particular hallucination, defined as the generation of outputs y that contain factual claims inconsistent with a reference knowledge source K (e.g., a trusted corpus or knowledge base). Several families of augmentation techniques are used to mitigate such shortcomings and to extend the capabilities of an LLM, including:

1. Advanced prompt-engineering methods (e.g., chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree-of-thoughts, ReAct-style prompting) that modify x to elicit improved reasoning.
2. Tool-use, in which the model is given access to a finite set T = {t_1, …, t_m} of external functions (calculators, code executors, search APIs, etc.) and may emit tool-invocation tokens whose results are appended to the context.
3. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in which a retriever R maps the prompt x to a subset D_x ⊂ K of relevant documents, and the model conditions on (x, D_x).
4. Personalization, in which the prompt is augmented with a user context vector u representing user history or preferences.
5. LLM-based single agents and multi-agent systems, in which one or more LLM instances iteratively observe an environment, plan, invoke tools, and act to achieve specified goals.

Identify and characterize which combinations of techniques from the categories above most effectively (i) reduce the hallucination rate, suitably formalized as the probability that an output contains a claim inconsistent with K, and (ii) enable reliable systems that integrate external tools, user context, and autonomous decision-making in real-world applications. Provide either theoretical guarantees or empirical principles distinguishing more effective from less effective combinations.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction in the LLM/AI literature rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Research on prompt engineering, retrieval augmentation, tool use, and LLM agents is active and ongoing, with no single accepted "solution"; numerous techniques exist (e.g., RAG, ReAct, Toolformer, multi-agent frameworks) but the question of which combinations most effectively address hallucination and enable real-world agentic systems remains an open and rapidly evolving area.

We should expect ... accelerated research in this area.", "claim": "The question is identified as an active and accelerating research direction rather than a settled problem."}]

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How can large language models be made robust and secure against adversarial attacks and other vulnerabilities, prevented from being used to manipulate people or spread misinformation, and improved so they better detect potential attacks while remaining fair, unbiased, and responsible with sensitive information?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model (LLM), modeled as a function $f_\theta : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input token sequences $x \in \mathcal{X}$ to output token sequences $y \in \mathcal{Y}$, with parameters $\theta$ learned from a large text corpus. Such a model may be subject to several classes of vulnerabilities, including (i) adversarial inputs $x' = x + \delta$ (under a suitable perturbation set, e.g., bounded edit distance, prompt-injection prefixes, or jailbreak templates) that induce undesired behavior; (ii) misuse for generating manipulative content or misinformation; (iii) biased or unfair outputs with respect to protected attributes; and (iv) leakage of sensitive information memorized from training data.

Develop a framework — comprising training procedures, fine-tuning objectives, decoding-time defenses, detection mechanisms, and evaluation protocols — that simultaneously achieves the following goals for a deployed LLM $f_\theta$:

1. Robustness: For a specified perturbation class $\Delta$ and a safety predicate $S(\cdot)$, ensure that $\Pr_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, \delta \in \Delta}[\, S(f_\theta(x+\delta)) = 1 \,]$ exceeds a target threshold.
2. Misuse prevention: Reduce the probability that $f_\theta$ produces content classified as manipulative or as misinformation by a verifier $V$, below a target threshold across realistic prompt distributions.
3. Attack detection: Provide a detector $D$ such that the probability $D$ correctly flags adversarial or malicious inputs is high while false-positive rates on benign inputs remain low.
4. Fairness and unbiasedness: Bound a chosen group-fairness or bias metric $B(f_\theta)$ below a prescribed level.
5. Responsible handling of sensitive information: Guarantee differential-privacy-style or membership-inference bounds limiting the leakage of training data and user-supplied sensitive data.

Specify and prove (or empirically establish with rigorous guarantees) the trade-offs between these objectives, and exhibit a construction of $(f_\theta, D)$ achieving them jointly, or prove impossibility results delineating which combinations of the above guarantees can be simultaneously satisfied.
status_search_result: The problem is a broad open research agenda in AI safety and trustworthy machine learning. As of 2026, no comprehensive solution exists: adversarial attacks on LLMs (jailbreaks, prompt injections), misinformation generation, bias, and training-data extraction all remain active and only partially mitigated areas, with ongoing work from academic groups and industry labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NIST AISI). Partial advances include RLHF, constitutional AI, DP fine-tuning, and adversarial training, but no method satisfies all five goals jointly with provable guarantees.

paper_title: Large Language Models: A Survey
original_question: How can hallucination in large language models be measured reliably when the same factual content can be expressed in different styles and even very small wording changes make false-information detection difficult?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a large language model viewed as a stochastic map from input prompts to output text strings, and let $\mathcal{F}$ denote a reference knowledge base specifying ground-truth facts. A response $y$ produced by $\mathcal{M}$ on a prompt $x$ is called a hallucination if the factual content of $y$ contradicts or is unsupported by $\mathcal{F}$. Define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on text strings such that $y_1 \sim y_2$ when $y_1$ and $y_2$ express the same factual content (possibly in different styles, paraphrases, or with minor wording changes).

Design a hallucination evaluation metric $H : (\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{D}) \mapsto [0,1]$, where $\mathcal{D}$ is an evaluation dataset of prompts together with reference factual content, that satisfies all of the following properties:

1. (Paraphrase invariance) $H$ depends only on the $\sim$-equivalence class of each generated response, so semantically equivalent outputs receive the same score regardless of stylistic or lexical variation.
2. (Sensitivity) $H$ detects factually incorrect outputs even when they differ from a correct reference by very small wording changes (e.g., a single negation, numeral, or entity substitution that flips truth value).
3. (Reliability) $H$ admits a quantifiable guarantee, such as a bound on false-positive and false-negative rates, when judged against $\mathcal{F}$.
4. (Operationality) $H$ is computable in practice without requiring human annotation at evaluation time.

Construct such a metric $H$, or prove that under reasonable formalizations of $\sim$ and $\mathcal{F}$ no metric simultaneously satisfies all four properties.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and methods (semantic entropy, multiple-testing frameworks, self-consistency over paraphrases, HaluEval and LLM-as-judge approaches) have made partial progress, but reliably evaluating hallucination under paraphrase invariance with formal guarantees and sensitivity to minimal wording changes remains an active open research problem identified in current surveys (2024–2025).

original_question: Find a square number such that subtracting 10 times its square root and 10 dirhams from it leaves a perfect square.
self_contained_problem: Find all positive rational (or, in the classical reading, positive integer) numbers $x$ such that $x^2$ is a perfect square and $x^2 - 10x - 10$ is also a perfect square. Equivalently, determine all pairs $(x,y)$ of positive integers satisfying $x^2 - 10x - 10 = y^2$, and exhibit at least one explicit solution.
status_search_result: The equation x² − 10x − 10 = y² is elementary: completing the square gives (x−5)² − y² = 35, so (x−5−y)(x−5+y) = 35. The factorizations 1·35 and 5·7 yield the positive integer solutions (x,y) = (23,17) and (11,1), verified directly (23² − 230 − 10 = 289 = 17²; 11² − 110 − 10 = 1 = 1²). The problem is a classical Diophantine exercise with a complete elementary solution.

Given a positive integer $n$, determine positive integers $a$ and $b$, together with positive integers $x$ and $y$, such that
\[ n = a + b, \qquad a = x^3, \qquad b = y^2. \]
Equivalently, characterize the positive integers $n$ that can be written in the form $n = x^3 + y^2$ with $x, y$ positive integers, and describe a general method for producing such a decomposition (or all such decompositions) for an arbitrary given $n$.

original_question: Find a square number such that when its square root is subtracted from it, and the remainder is multiplied by that square root, the result equals the original square number.
self_contained_problem:
Determine all positive rational (equivalently, positive integer) perfect squares $n$ with the following property. Let $r=\sqrt{n}$ denote the (positive) square root of $n$. Form the remainder $n-r$, and then multiply this remainder by $r$. The resulting product is required to equal the original square $n$; that is,
$$(n-r)\cdot r \;=\; n.$$
Equivalently, writing $n=x^{2}$ with $x>0$, find all $x$ for which
$$(x^{2}-x)\,x \;=\; x^{2}.$$
Describe the complete solution set, and in particular exhibit the (unique) nontrivial perfect square $n$ satisfying the condition.
status_search_result: The equation $(x^2-x)x=x^2$ simplifies to $x^3=2x^2$, whose unique nontrivial solution is $x=2$, giving the square $n=4$ (indeed $4-2=2$ and $2\cdot 2=4$). The problem is elementary and considered solved.

This is an elementary, fully resolved classical problem.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: Can large language models improve multi-step reasoning without human supervision by using fully automated process supervision methods that identify errors inside chain-of-thought traces, generate large amounts of supervision data, and reward intermediate progress in a scalable and computationally efficient way?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model M that produces, for an input prompt x, a chain-of-thought trace T(x) = (s_1, s_2, ..., s_n) consisting of intermediate reasoning steps s_i followed by a final answer a. A process supervision scheme is a procedure that, without access to any human-provided step-level labels, assigns to each intermediate step s_i a scalar reward r_i in [0,1] measuring the correctness or progress of that step, and uses the resulting (step, reward) pairs as training data to fine-tune M (for example via reinforcement learning or supervised learning on the generated labels).

Formally, design (or prove impossible) a fully automated supervision procedure S satisfying all of the following:

1. (No human labels) S takes as input only the model M, a distribution D over reasoning prompts, and access to a verifier V that judges only final-answer correctness on a subset of prompts; S uses no per-step human annotations.

2. (Error localization) For every trace T = (s_1,...,s_n) that leads to an incorrect final answer, S outputs an index i*(T) such that with probability at least 1 - delta over the randomness of S, s_{i*(T)} is a step where the reasoning first deviates from a correct solution path, for some specified delta > 0.

3. (Scalable data generation) The expected computational cost of producing one labeled trace is polynomial in n and in the inference cost of M, and the procedure can generate an arbitrarily large dataset of step-labeled traces.

4. (Intermediate progress reward) The reward signal r_i strictly distinguishes progress-making steps from non-progress steps in the sense that, on a held-out evaluation set, models fine-tuned on the rewards produced by S achieve strictly higher multi-step reasoning accuracy than the same models fine-tuned only on final-answer correctness.

The problem: prove or disprove the existence of such a procedure S, and if it exists, give explicit constructions and quantitative bounds relating delta, the computational cost, and the resulting improvement in reasoning accuracy.
category_tag: automated process supervision for LLM reasoning
status_search_result: Automated process supervision methods (e.g., Math-Shepherd, OmegaPRM, AutoPRM) have shown empirical progress on generating step-level rewards without human labels, but no formal proof or universally accepted construction satisfying scalable, computationally efficient error localization with provable progress rewards has been established. The problem is widely regarded as open in the LLM reasoning literature as of 2026.

self_contained_problem: Consider large language models (LLMs) evaluated on two classes of mathematical tasks: (i) isolated single-step problems, on which current models attain high accuracy, and (ii) chained, multi-hop, Olympiad-style composite problems whose solutions require composing several intermediate reasoning steps, on which current models exhibit a substantial accuracy drop ("reasoning gap"). Consider two training/inference interventions: (a) synthetic data generation, in which large quantities of artificially produced multi-step math problems and step-annotated solutions are used during training or fine-tuning, and (b) tool-integrated reasoning, in which the model can invoke external symbolic tools (e.g., computer algebra systems, code interpreters, calculators, theorem provers) during inference. Determine whether the combination of (a) and (b) is sufficient to close the reasoning gap, in the sense that an LLM achieving high accuracy on isolated math problems can be made to attain comparable accuracy on chained, multi-hop, Olympiad-style composite problems that lie outside the distribution of its training data. Formally: does there exist a training pipeline based on synthetic data generation together with tool-integrated reasoning such that, for every benchmark of Olympiad-style multi-hop problems, the resulting model's accuracy on that benchmark is within a small constant of its accuracy on a matched benchmark of isolated math problems?
status_search_result: This is an open empirical research direction in LLM mathematical reasoning. Recent work (e.g., AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, DeepSeek-Prover, ToRA, MathCoder, Numina, OpenMath) has shown substantial progress using synthetic data and tool integration on competition-level problems, but a persistent generalization gap on chained, out-of-distribution multi-hop Olympiad problems remains reported in surveys through 2025–2026. No published result establishes that the gap has been fully closed.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How critical is online, on-policy data for reinforcement learning from human feedback, compared with fixed offline preference datasets, when the goal is stable convergence and strong alignment performance on diverse tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of aligning a parametric stochastic policy $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ (with $x$ a prompt and $y$ a response) to human preferences. Let $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ be a fixed reference policy and let preference data consist of triples $(x, y^+, y^-)$ where $y^+$ is preferred to $y^-$ by a (latent) reward model $r^\star(x,y)$ under the Bradley-Terry model $\Pr(y^+\succ y^-\mid x) = \sigma\!\bigl(r^\star(x,y^+)-r^\star(x,y^-)\bigr)$.

Two training regimes are compared:
1. Offline preference optimization (e.g., Direct Preference Optimization): the dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}}=\{(x_i,y_i^+,y_i^-)\}$ is fixed in advance, with responses drawn from some behavior distribution $\mu$, and $\theta$ is optimized to minimize the DPO loss
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^+,y^-)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}}}\Bigl[\log\sigma\Bigl(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^+\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^+\mid x)}-\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^-\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^-\mid x)}\Bigr)\Bigr].$$
2. Online, on-policy reinforcement learning (e.g., PPO against a learned reward $\hat r$): at each iteration, fresh responses are sampled from the current policy $\pi_{\theta_t}$ and used to estimate gradients of the KL-regularized objective
$$J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[\hat r(x,y)\bigr]-\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\bigr].$$

Define the global coverage coefficient $C_{\mathrm{glob}}(\mu,\pi^\star)=\sup_{x,y}\pi^\star(y\mid x)/\mu(y\mid x)$ for a target optimal policy $\pi^\star$, and the partial coverage coefficient $C_{\mathrm{part}}(\mu,\pi^\star)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,y\sim\pi^\star}[\pi^\star(y\mid x)/\mu(y\mid x)]$.

Question: Quantify rigorously the extent to which access to online, on-policy samples from $\pi_{\theta_t}$ is necessary for stable convergence to a near-optimal aligned policy across a diverse family of prompt distributions, as compared to relying only on a fixed offline preference dataset. Specifically, characterize sample-complexity and convergence-rate separations between the two regimes as functions of $C_{\mathrm{glob}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{part}}$, and identify conditions on the data distribution $\mu$, the reward landscape $r^\star$, and the policy class $\{\pi_\theta\}$ under which offline preference optimization can match the alignment performance achievable by online RL.
status_search_result: The comparative criticality of online versus offline data in RLHF is an active research area. Theoretical work has established that offline methods like DPO require global coverage assumptions while online methods such as PPO need only partial coverage, but tight separations and the conditions under which offline matches online performance on diverse tasks remain open and are the subject of ongoing investigation.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: To what extent do reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback methods transfer across languages, and what mixture of English and multilingual preference data is needed to obtain strong alignment performance in languages beyond the ones used most heavily in training?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{L} = \{\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_K\}$ be a finite set of natural languages, and let $\pi_\theta$ denote an autoregressive language model with parameters $\theta$ that maps input token sequences to probability distributions over output token sequences. For each language $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$, suppose there is a preference dataset $\mathcal{D}_\ell = \{(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)\}_i$ in which $x_i$ is a prompt in language $\ell$ and $y_i^+, y_i^-$ are responses with $y_i^+$ preferred to $y_i^-$ by human annotators. Given a mixture distribution $\mu = (\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_K)$ with $\mu_k \ge 0$ and $\sum_k \mu_k = 1$, let $\pi_\theta^{\mu}$ denote the policy obtained by reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) training that draws training examples from $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_k}$ with probability $\mu_k$, using a standard objective such as KL-regularized reward maximization against a reward model fit to the same mixture.

For a held-out evaluation language $\ell^* \in \mathcal{L}$ (in particular, possibly one with $\mu_{\ell^*} = 0$), define the alignment performance $W(\mu, \ell^*)$ as the expected win rate of $\pi_\theta^{\mu}$ against a fixed reference policy on prompts drawn from $\ell^*$, as judged by an annotator (human or model) fluent in $\ell^*$.

Investigate the following:

(a) Cross-lingual transfer. Quantify $W(\mu, \ell^*) - W(\mathbf{0}_{\ell^*}, \ell^*)$ when $\mu$ places all mass on a single source language (e.g., English) different from $\ell^*$. In particular, characterize conditions on the source language, the base pretraining distribution, and the reward model under which English-only RLHF yields non-trivial gains in $\ell^*$.

(b) Optimal mixture. For a fixed total preference-data budget $N$, determine the mixture $\mu^*$ maximizing $\min_{\ell^* \in \mathcal{L}} W(\mu, \ell^*)$, or alternatively $\mathbb{E}_{\ell^* \sim \nu}[W(\mu, \ell^*)]$ for a target distribution $\nu$ over languages. Identify scaling laws relating the optimal proportion of non-source-language data to the number of languages $K$, the typological diversity of $\mathcal{L}$, and the multilingual coverage of the base model's pretraining corpus.

(c) Unseen languages. Extend the analysis to languages $\ell^* \notin \mathcal{L}$ (no preference data available), and characterize how multilingual mixing in $\mu$ affects generalization of alignment to such languages.

Provide either provable guarantees or empirically validated quantitative laws describing $W(\mu, \ell^*)$ as a function of $\mu$, $\ell^*$, and properties of the base model.
status_search_result: The question is framed as an open research direction in recent surveys on LLM alignment. While various empirical studies (e.g., on multilingual DPO/RLHF) report partial findings such as English-only RLHF transferring nontrivially to other languages and multilingual mixtures further improving unseen-language performance, no general theory or definitive optimal mixture is established. The problem appears open.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: Can Direct Preference Optimization improve large language models used as generative judges, so that they perform robust automatic evaluation across rating, pairwise comparison, and classification tasks while reducing common judge biases?
self_contained_problem:
Let a generative judge be a language model J that, given an input consisting of a prompt x together with one or more candidate responses, outputs a natural-language judgment together with a verdict belonging to one of the following task formats:
(i) single-response rating, where the verdict is a numeric score on a fixed scale;
(ii) pairwise comparison, where the verdict selects a preferred response from a pair;
(iii) classification, where the verdict assigns the response to one of finitely many labels.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is the training procedure that, given a reference model π_ref and a dataset D of preference triples (x, y_w, y_l) where y_w is preferred to y_l, fits a model π_θ by minimizing
  L_DPO(θ) = −E_{(x,y_w,y_l)∼D} [ log σ( β log(π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x)) − β log(π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l)) ) ],
where σ is the logistic function and β>0 a temperature parameter.

Common judge biases include: position bias (preference depending on the order of presented responses), length/verbosity bias (preferring longer responses independently of quality), self-preference bias (favoring responses generated by the judge's own family), and sentiment bias (preference based on tone rather than correctness).

Question: Does there exist a construction of preference data D (e.g., self-generated contrastive judgment pairs) and an application of DPO to a base language model π_ref such that the resulting model π_θ, used as a generative judge across all three task formats (i)–(iii), simultaneously (a) attains evaluation accuracy on standard judge benchmarks that is at least competitive with scalar reward models trained on comparable data, and (b) provably reduces the magnitudes of position, length, self-preference, and sentiment biases relative to π_ref?
status_search_result: Several recent works (e.g., "Learning LLM-as-a-Judge for Preference Alignment" at ICLR 2025, "Direct Judgement Preference Optimization", and "Improve LLM-as-a-Judge Ability as a General Ability" (arXiv:2502.11689)) report that DPO with self-generated contrastive judgment pairs trains generative judges that perform strongly on rating, pairwise, and classification tasks and are more robust to biases than scalar reward models. However, residual length, position, self-preference, and sentiment biases persist, so the broader question of fully eliminating common judge biases via DPO remains active research rather than fully resolved.

Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge", "url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02736v1", "snippet": "Documents persistent position, length, self-preference, and sentiment biases in LLM judges.", "claim": "Common judge biases are not fully eliminated by current preference-tuning methods."}]

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How should supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning be combined so that language models keep the formatting and instruction-following stability that supervised fine-tuning provides without falling into memorization that hurts out-of-domain generalization?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a pretrained autoregressive language model p_θ(y | x) with parameters θ ∈ Θ, trained on a base distribution D_pre over input–output sequences. Two standard post-training procedures are defined as follows.

(1) Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): given a labeled dataset S = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N drawn from an in-domain distribution D_in, minimize the negative log-likelihood loss
   L_SFT(θ) = -(1/N) Σ_i log p_θ(y_i | x_i).

(2) Reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RFT): given a (possibly learned) reward function r(x, y) ∈ ℝ on prompts x ~ D_in and model samples y ~ p_θ(· | x), maximize the expected reward (optionally with a KL penalty toward a reference model p_ref):
   J_RFT(θ) = E_{x ~ D_in, y ~ p_θ(·|x)} [ r(x, y) ] − β · KL( p_θ(· | x) ∥ p_ref(· | x) ).

Empirically, pure SFT yields strong instruction-following and formatting stability but tends to memorize training data, degrading performance on an out-of-domain test distribution D_out ≠ D_in. Pure RFT yields better out-of-domain generalization but can be unstable in formatting and instruction adherence.

Problem. Design and analyze a composite post-training procedure A that produces parameters θ_A = A(S, r, p_ref) such that, for a specified class 𝒟 of out-of-domain distributions D_out and a specified evaluation suite E = (E_format, E_instr, E_OOD) measuring formatting compliance, instruction-following, and out-of-domain task accuracy respectively, the following holds:

   (a) E_format(θ_A) ≥ E_format(θ_SFT) − ε_1,
   (b) E_instr(θ_A) ≥ E_instr(θ_SFT) − ε_2,
   (c) E_OOD(θ_A) ≥ E_RFT(θ_RFT) − ε_3,

for prescribed small tolerances ε_1, ε_2, ε_3 > 0, where θ_SFT and θ_RFT denote the parameters obtained by pure SFT and pure RFT respectively on the same data and reward.

Specifically, determine (i) the optimal scheduling, weighting, or interleaving of the SFT and RFT objectives (for example, a convex combination L(θ) = λ L_SFT(θ) − (1−λ) J_RFT(θ) with a schedule λ(t) ∈ [0,1], or a curriculum that alternates phases), and (ii) sufficient conditions on S, r, p_ref, and the schedule under which (a)–(c) provably hold. Quantify the trade-off between memorization (measured, e.g., by training-set memorization rate or by the gap E_in(θ) − E_OOD(θ)) and the generalization improvement contributed by the RFT phase.
status_search_result: This is an active open research question in LLM post-training. Recent works (e.g., "SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes" by Chu et al., 2025) document the trade-off and propose hybrid recipes (SFT warm-start followed by RL, mixed objectives, KL-regularized RLHF/DPO), but no canonical or theoretically optimal combination has been established. The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How much do rigid output formats such as JSON, XML, or YAML interfere with reasoning in large language models, and when does the gain in output consistency outweigh the loss in cognitive flexibility?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model (LLM) M that, given a natural-language prompt p, produces an output M(p). For a reasoning task T with input distribution D and a correctness indicator c(·) ∈ {0,1}, define the reasoning accuracy of a prompting scheme s as A(M, s, T) = E_{x∼D}[c(M(s(x)))], where s(x) augments the raw input x with formatting instructions. Consider two families of prompting schemes:

1. Free-form schemes s_free, which allow the model to produce unconstrained natural-language output.
2. Structured schemes s_struct(F), which require the output to conform to a fixed machine-readable schema F (e.g., JSON, XML, or YAML with a specified key/tag structure).

Also define an output-consistency measure C(M, s, T) ∈ [0,1] equal to the probability that two independent samples M(s(x)) and M'(s(x)) for x ∼ D are parseable under F and agree on a designated "answer" field (with F replaced by the trivial schema in the free-form case).

The problem is: quantitatively characterize the trade-off
   Δ_acc(F) := A(M, s_free, T) − A(M, s_struct(F), T),
   Δ_cons(F) := C(M, s_struct(F), T) − C(M, s_free, T),
as a function of (i) the schema F (including its depth, key count, and rigidity), (ii) the task T (e.g., arithmetic, multi-step deduction, code generation), and (iii) properties of the model M (scale, instruction tuning, decoding temperature). Specifically:

(a) Provide a model or formal framework predicting Δ_acc(F) and Δ_cons(F) for a given (M, T, F).
(b) Identify sufficient conditions on (M, T, F) under which the structured scheme is Pareto-improving, i.e., Δ_acc(F) ≤ 0 and Δ_cons(F) ≥ 0 simultaneously.
(c) Determine, for a given utility functional U(A, C) that is increasing in both arguments, the threshold(s) at which the structured scheme s_struct(F) becomes preferable to s_free, i.e., U(A(M, s_struct(F), T), C(M, s_struct(F), T)) ≥ U(A(M, s_free, T), C(M, s_free, T)).
status_search_result: This is an empirical/open research question in LLM evaluation. Recent empirical studies (e.g., "Let Me Speak Freely?" by Tam et al., 2024) report that rigid format constraints can degrade reasoning performance on some tasks while improving parseability, but no general theory or quantitative trade-off characterization has been established. The question therefore appears open.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How effective are large language models in retrieval-augmented generation when they must process very long contexts, what context lengths are actually optimal, and how can systems avoid failure modes such as degradation, repetition, copyright-related failures, and lost-in-the-middle effects beyond those thresholds?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language model $M$ with a maximum input context window of $N$ tokens, used in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Given a query $q$, a retriever returns an ordered set of passages $P = (p_1, \dots, p_k)$ whose total token length $L(P)$ may be varied up to $N$. Let $A(q, P)$ denote the answer produced by $M$ when conditioned on $q$ and $P$, and let $\mathrm{Acc}(L)$ denote the expected task accuracy of $A(q, P)$ over a distribution of queries when $L(P) = L$. Empirically, $\mathrm{Acc}(L)$ is observed to (i) increase with $L$ up to some task- and model-dependent threshold $L^\ast(M, \mathcal{T})$ and then decrease, and (ii) exhibit failure modes when $L > L^\ast$, including (a) degenerate repetition in the output, (b) verbatim regurgitation of copyrighted training data, and (c) the "lost-in-the-middle" effect in which relevant information located near the middle of $P$ is disproportionately ignored.

Provide:
(1) A quantitative characterization of $L^\ast(M, \mathcal{T})$ as a function of model architecture, scale, and post-training procedure, including conditions under which $L^\ast$ approaches the nominal context window $N$.
(2) A pipeline or training-time intervention (e.g., long-context post-training, retrieval ordering, or attention modification) that provably or empirically eliminates failure modes (a)–(c) for inputs with $L(P)$ up to a prescribed fraction of $N$, with measurable guarantees on accuracy retention.
(3) Theoretical or empirical lower and upper bounds relating $L^\ast$ to the model's pretraining context length and to the positional encoding scheme used.
status_search_result: Long-context RAG effectiveness, optimal context length, and mitigation of "lost-in-the-middle" and related long-context failure modes are active areas of investigation. Recent work (e.g., Liu et al. on lost-in-the-middle, Anthropic/Google long-context evaluations, NIAH and RULER benchmarks, and 2024–2025 long-context post-training studies) reports partial mitigations but no comprehensive solution; optimal context lengths remain strongly model- and task-dependent.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: How important is the choice and strength of the reference model in Direct Preference Optimization, including the KL-divergence setting and the compatibility between the policy and the reference model, for obtaining strong alignment performance?
self_contained_problem:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is an alignment method that fine-tunes a parametric policy $\pi_\theta$ (typically a large language model) from a dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(x, y_w, y_l)\}$ of prompts $x$ together with a preferred response $y_w$ and a dispreferred response $y_l$. Given a fixed reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and an inverse-temperature parameter $\beta>0$, DPO minimizes the loss
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\right)\right],$$
where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid. The parameter $\beta$ implicitly controls the strength of a KL-divergence regularizer $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ pulling $\pi_\theta$ toward $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

Develop a rigorous theoretical and empirical understanding of how the choice of reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and the KL-regularization strength $\beta$ affect the alignment quality of the learned policy $\pi_\theta$. In particular:
(a) Characterize the sense in which "stronger" or "more aligned" reference policies (for instance, a policy that has itself already been DPO-trained) lead to higher-quality DPO solutions, and quantify this advantage as a function of $\beta$ and of a suitable measure of distributional compatibility between $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and the policy class $\{\pi_\theta\}$.
(b) Determine conditions on $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, on the preference data distribution, and on $\beta$ under which DPO provably converges to an optimal aligned policy, and conversely identify regimes in which mismatch between $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and the target policy degrades performance.
(c) Propose and analyze principled procedures (e.g., iterative reference updating, KL-schedule selection) for choosing $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\beta$ that come with guarantees on alignment performance.
status_search_result: The role of the reference model and KL strength in DPO is an actively investigated open research direction. Recent works (e.g., iterative DPO, reference-free DPO variants such as SimPO and ORPO, and analyses of β-scheduling) provide partial insights but no complete theoretical characterization. No definitive resolution exists as of 2026.

paper_title: Reasoning Beyond Limits: Advances and Open Problems for LLMs
original_question: What is the right balance between online and offline alignment algorithms for large language models, given that online methods benefit from fresh on-policy data and stronger generative quality while offline methods can remain competitive on pairwise classification tasks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of aligning a large language model (LLM), modeled as a conditional distribution $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ over responses $y$ given prompts $x$, with human preferences encoded by a preference dataset or a reward model $r(x,y)$. Two broad families of alignment algorithms are studied:

1. Offline alignment: optimize $\pi_\theta$ using a fixed, pre-collected dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)\}$ of preference pairs, without ever sampling from the current policy. Representative methods include Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and its variants, which minimize a contrastive loss of the form
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{off}}(\theta)= -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^+,y^-)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Bigl[\log\sigma\bigl(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^+\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^+\mid x)} - \beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y^-\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^-\mid x)}\bigr)\Bigr].$$

2. Online alignment: iteratively draw fresh on-policy samples $y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)$, score them with a reward model or preference oracle, and update $\theta$ (e.g., via PPO/RLHF or online DPO).

Empirically, offline-trained policies tend to perform well on pairwise classification of preferences (i.e., predicting which of two responses is preferred) but worse on open-ended generative quality, whereas online-trained policies generate higher-quality responses but require costly on-policy sampling.

Problem. Develop a principled theoretical and algorithmic characterization of the optimal trade-off between online and offline preference-based alignment for LLMs. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a quantitative criterion (in terms of sample complexity, distribution shift between $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and $\pi_\theta$, reward-model accuracy, and a generation-quality metric) that determines when on-policy sampling is necessary, and when offline preference optimization suffices.

(b) Design a hybrid online/offline alignment algorithm whose generative-quality performance provably matches that of fully online methods while using only a controlled amount of on-policy data, and prove matching upper and lower bounds on the required online sample budget.

(c) Explain the observed gap between pairwise-classification performance and generative performance: identify conditions on the preference data distribution, the reward model, and the policy class under which optimizing a pairwise classification objective is (or is not) sufficient to guarantee high generative quality.
status_search_result: The question concerns the right balance between online and offline alignment algorithms for LLMs. Recent works (e.g., Tang et al., "Understanding the performance gap between online and offline alignment algorithms," 2024; subsequent hybrid-alignment papers in 2024–2025) characterize the gap empirically and propose hybrid methods, but no consensus theoretical optimum exists, and surveys continue to list this as an open research direction.
