paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Give a combinatorial proof of the q,t-symmetry of the Shuffle-Theorem summation by finding a bijection on word parking functions that interchanges the area and dinv statistics.
self_contained_problem:
A word parking function of length $n$ is a sequence $(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)$ of positive integers together with a labelling of an underlying Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$, defined as follows. Let $D$ be a Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ consisting of $n$ north steps $N_1,\dots,N_n$ (read from bottom to top) and $n$ east steps, staying weakly above the diagonal $y=x$. A word parking function $P=(D,w)$ assigns to each north step $N_i$ a positive-integer label $w_i$ such that, if two north steps $N_i$ and $N_{i+1}$ lie in the same column, then $w_i<w_{i+1}$.

Define two statistics on word parking functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathrm{area}(P)$ is the number of complete lattice squares strictly between the path $D$ and the diagonal $y=x$.
\item $\mathrm{dinv}(P)$ is the number of pairs $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ such that either
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_i=a_j$ and $w_i<w_j$, or
\item $a_i=a_j+1$ and $w_i>w_j$,
\end{itemize}
where $a_i$ denotes the number of complete squares in row $i$ between $D$ and the diagonal.
\end{itemize}

For a fixed composition (or weight) of the labels, the Shuffle Theorem expresses a certain symmetric-function evaluation as
$$\sum_{P} q^{\mathrm{dinv}(P)}\, t^{\mathrm{area}(P)}\, x^{w(P)},$$
where the sum ranges over all word parking functions of length $n$. This expression is known to be symmetric in $q$ and $t$.

Problem. Construct an explicit bijection $\varphi$ on the set of word parking functions of length $n$ (preserving the multiset of labels $w$) such that
$$\mathrm{area}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{dinv}(P) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{dinv}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{area}(P).$$
Equivalently, give a combinatorial proof, via such a bijection, of the $(q,t)$-symmetry of the above summation.
status_search_result: The problem of finding a bijection on (word) parking functions that swaps area and dinv, thereby giving a combinatorial proof of the q,t-symmetry in the Shuffle Theorem, is widely regarded as a long-standing open problem. Partial results exist, including the zeta map for the t=1 case (equidistribution of area and dinv) and bijections proving q,t-symmetry for the q,t-Catalan numbers in restricted cases (Lee-Li-Loehr for k≤9), as well as recent area-depth symmetric variants, but no full bijective proof of q,t-symmetry for word parking functions is known.

original_question: Give a combinatorial proof of the conjugate q,t-symmetry of the Macdonald-polynomial summation in equation (**) by explaining, via a bijection or equivalent combinatorial mechanism, why conjugating the partition interchanges the inv and maj statistics in the required way.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mu$ be a partition of $n$, and let $\mu^{*}$ denote its conjugate (transpose) partition. For a filling $\sigma : \mu \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ of the cells of the Young diagram of $\mu$ with positive integers, define the statistics $\mathrm{inv}(\sigma)$ and $\mathrm{maj}(\sigma)$ as in Haglund–Haiman–Loehr's combinatorial formula for the modified Macdonald polynomials, so that
$$\widetilde{H}_{\mu}(X; q, t) \;=\; \sum_{\sigma : \mu \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}} q^{\mathrm{inv}(\sigma)}\, t^{\mathrm{maj}(\sigma)}\, x^{\sigma} \qquad (**)$$
where $x^{\sigma} = \prod_{c \in \mu} x_{\sigma(c)}$. It is known (via symmetric function identities for $\widetilde{H}_{\mu}$) that
$$\widetilde{H}_{\mu}(X; q, t) \;=\; \widetilde{H}_{\mu^{*}}(X; t, q).$$
Provide a combinatorial proof of this conjugate $(q,t)$-symmetry directly from the right-hand side of $(**)$: exhibit an explicit bijection (or equivalent combinatorial mechanism) between fillings of $\mu$ and fillings of $\mu^{*}$ that preserves the content (multiset of entries) and interchanges the statistics $\mathrm{inv}$ and $\mathrm{maj}$, thereby explaining why conjugating the partition swaps these two statistics.
status_search_result: The general problem of giving a combinatorial bijection on fillings that interchanges inv and maj under partition conjugation is still open. Partial results include a bijective proof for hook-shaped partitions, the case of partitions with at most three rows for Hall-Littlewood (q=0) specialization, square-free monomial coefficients, and the specialization t=1 (Loehr–Niese and others, e.g., arXiv:1503.02109 and Electron. J. Combin. 23 (2016) #P2.38). A complete combinatorial explanation for arbitrary shapes remains elusive.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Classify central and internal graphical zonotopal algebras up to isomorphism; in particular, resolve the source's conjectural bridge-free-matroid criterion for central zonotopal algebras of connected graphs.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph with $V=\{1,\dots,n+1\}$ and edges $E=\{e_1,\dots,e_m\}$. For each subset $I\subseteq V$, let $d_I$ denote the number of edges of $G$ with exactly one endpoint in $I$ (the size of the cut determined by $I$). Working over a field of characteristic $0$, consider the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}]$ and define the linear forms $\ell_I=\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ for $I\subseteq V$.

Define two graded quotient algebras:
- The central zonotopal algebra $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G):=R/J^{(0)}_G$, where $J^{(0)}_G$ is the ideal generated by $\ell_I^{d_I}$ for all $\emptyset\neq I\subsetneq V$ (equivalently, defined via the standard kernel/Macaulay-inverse-system construction associated with the graphical matroid).
- The internal zonotopal algebra $\mathcal{C}^{(-1)}(G):=R/J^{(-1)}_G$, where $J^{(-1)}_G$ is generated by $\ell_I^{d_I-1}$ for all $\emptyset\neq I\subsetneq V$.

A bridge of $G$ is an edge whose removal disconnects $G$. The bridge-free matroid of $G$ is the matroid on the non-bridge edges obtained from the graphical matroid $M(G)$ by deleting all bridges.

Problem. Classify, up to graded $\mathbb{R}$-algebra isomorphism, the central zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G)$ and the internal zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(-1)}(G)$ as $G$ ranges over connected graphs. In particular, prove or disprove the following conjecture: for connected graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$, the central zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G_1)$ and $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G_2)$ are isomorphic as graded algebras if and only if the bridge-free matroids of $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic.
status_search_result: The external case was settled by Nenashev (2019), who showed that two external graphical zonotopal algebras are isomorphic iff their graphical matroids are isomorphic. The central and internal cases, including the conjectured bridge-free-matroid criterion, remain open according to the problem's blog post and subsequent literature (e.g., recent work on bizonotopal graphical algebras 2024 and the broken-wheel paper).

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Combinatorics
original_question: Let B be the class of Banff quivers and B' the subclass obtained using only covering pairs for which at least one endpoint is a source or a sink. Either find a quiver in B \ B', or prove that no such example exists.
self_contained_problem:
A quiver is a finite directed multigraph with no loops and no 2-cycles. Given a quiver $Q$, a covering pair is a pair of vertices $(u,v)$ such that there is at least one arrow from $u$ to $v$, the neighborhoods around $u$ and $v$ satisfy certain combinatorial conditions making $\{u,v\}$ "isolating," and removing $u$ and $v$ (together with any arrows incident to them) produces a quiver that, in turn, has its own covering pair or is empty. The class $\mathcal{B}$ of Banff quivers is the smallest class of quivers containing the empty quiver and closed under the following operation: a quiver $Q$ belongs to $\mathcal{B}$ if it has a covering pair $(u,v)$ such that the quiver obtained from $Q$ by deleting $u$ and $v$ belongs to $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $\mathcal{B}'$ denote the subclass of $\mathcal{B}$ defined analogously, but where at each step the covering pair $(u,v)$ used to certify membership is required to have at least one of $u,v$ being a source (a vertex with no incoming arrows) or a sink (a vertex with no outgoing arrows) of the current quiver.

Either exhibit a quiver belonging to $\mathcal{B} \setminus \mathcal{B}'$, or prove that no such quiver exists, i.e., $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}'$.
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved. Ervin and Jackson (arXiv:2305.17194, "Answering Two OPAC Problems Involving Banff Quivers," 2023) prove that every Banff quiver can be certified as Banff using only covering pairs that contain a source or a sink, so $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}'$. As a consequence every Banff quiver lies in the class $\mathcal{P}$.

original_question: Describe the Dedekind-MacNeille completion of the Type B Bruhat order B_n as a subset of the lattice ASM_{2n} of alternating sign matrices, equivalently characterize exactly which half-turn-symmetric alternating sign matrices arise from that completion.
self_contained_problem:
Let $B_n$ denote the hyperoctahedral group (the Weyl group of type $B_n$), realized as the group of signed permutations on $\{\pm 1, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n\}$, equipped with its Bruhat order. Embed $B_n$ into the symmetric group $S_{2n}$ by sending a signed permutation to the unique permutation matrix of size $2n \times 2n$ that is invariant under the half-turn (i.e., invariant under $180^\circ$ rotation: $M_{i,j} = M_{2n+1-i,\, 2n+1-j}$). This gives an order-preserving embedding of $B_n$ into $(S_{2n}, \leq_{\mathrm{Bruhat}})$, and hence into the lattice $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ of $2n \times 2n$ alternating sign matrices ordered by entry-wise comparison of their corner-sum (rank) matrices.

An alternating sign matrix (ASM) is a square matrix with entries in $\{0, 1, -1\}$ such that, in every row and every column, the nonzero entries alternate in sign and sum to $1$. The lattice $\mathrm{ASM}_N$ is the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of $(S_N, \leq_{\mathrm{Bruhat}})$, and is a distributive lattice under the order induced by corner sums. A matrix $M \in \mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ is called half-turn symmetric (HTSASM) if $M_{i,j} = M_{2n+1-i,\, 2n+1-j}$ for all $i, j$.

Recall that the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of a poset $P$ is the smallest complete lattice containing $P$ as a sub-order; concretely it is realized as the set of "cuts" of $P$.

Problem. Describe the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of the Bruhat order on $B_n$ as an explicit subset of $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$. Equivalently, give an exact combinatorial characterization of which half-turn-symmetric alternating sign matrices in $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ arise as elements of this completion. (Note: not every HTSASM arises; for $n=3$ the completion has cardinality $140$ while the number of HTSASMs is $132$, so a strictly intermediate subclass of HTSASMs must be identified.)

status_search_result: The problem (describing the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of type B Bruhat order inside ASM_{2n}) is listed as open. Blog comments indicate Paul Zinn-Justin has announced a characterization via a condition on rank matrices/HTSASMs, but the result is unpublished as of 2025. A related arXiv preprint (2604.26502) treats MacNeille completions of parabolic quotients of the symmetric group but does not explicitly resolve the type B case. Overall the problem appears partially solved, with no published solution.

original_question: Give a formula for the number of elements in the Dedekind-MacNeille completion of the Type B Bruhat order B_n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $B_n$ denote the hyperoctahedral group (signed permutation group of rank $n$), equipped with the (strong) Bruhat order, which is the partial order whose covering relations are given by left multiplication by reflections that increase Coxeter length. The Dedekind–MacNeille completion of a finite poset $P$ is the smallest lattice $\mathrm{DM}(P)$ containing $P$ as a sub-order; concretely, it can be realized as the set of order ideals $I \subseteq P$ satisfying $I = (I^u)^\ell$, where $I^u$ is the set of upper bounds of $I$ and $(\cdot)^\ell$ denotes the set of lower bounds. 

Find a closed-form formula (or explicit combinatorial enumeration) for $\lvert \mathrm{DM}(B_n) \rvert$, the number of elements in the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of the Type B Bruhat order on $B_n$, as a function of $n$. The first few values are $2, 10, 132, 4824$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to still be open. The known initial values are 2, 10, 132, 4824; the appearance of a large prime factor (67) in the fourth term suggests no simple closed formula. paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Combinatorics
context_brief: sign patterns in symmetric-group character tables
original_question: Prove that for all sufficiently large n, the row of the character table of the symmetric group S_n that contains the largest number of negative entries is the row corresponding to the sign representation.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Its complex irreducible representations are indexed by partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, and its conjugacy classes are indexed by partitions $\mu \vdash n$ (cycle types). The character table of $S_n$ is the square matrix whose entry in row $\lambda$ and column $\mu$ is the value $\chi^\lambda(\mu)$ of the irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ on the conjugacy class of cycle type $\mu$. The row indexed by the partition $(1^n)$ corresponds to the sign representation, whose character value on a permutation of cycle type $\mu$ equals $(-1)^{n - \ell(\mu)}$, where $\ell(\mu)$ is the number of parts of $\mu$.

For each partition $\lambda \vdash n$, let $N(\lambda) = \#\{\mu \vdash n : \chi^\lambda(\mu) < 0\}$ denote the number of conjugacy classes on which the irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ takes a strictly negative value.

Prove that for all sufficiently large $n$, the maximum of $N(\lambda)$ over all partitions $\lambda \vdash n$ is attained by, and only by, the partition $(1^n)$ corresponding to the sign representation.
status_search_result: The problem is posted as an open problem on the Open Problems in Algebraic Combinatorics blog (May 2025). No publication or preprint resolving it appears in available sources, and the problem is presented without indication of progress.

context_brief: Goldbach conjecture in additive number theory.
original_question: Does every even integer greater than 2 admit a representation as the sum of two prime numbers? Equivalently, is Goldbach's conjecture true for all even integers larger than 2, or does there exist at least one even integer greater than 2 that cannot be written as a sum of two primes?
self_contained_problem: Prove or disprove the following statement: for every even integer n > 2, there exist prime numbers p and q (not necessarily distinct) such that n = p + q. Equivalently, determine whether every even integer greater than 2 can be expressed as a sum of two primes, or exhibit an even integer greater than 2 that admits no such representation.
status_search_result: This is the classical (binary/strong) Goldbach conjecture, posed in 1742. It remains unresolved as of 2026. The ternary Goldbach conjecture was proved by Harald Helfgott (2013), and the binary version has been verified computationally up to roughly 4·10^18, but no proof or counterexample is known.

original_question: For the Collatz iteration defined by starting from a positive integer a0 and then setting an = 3a(n-1) + 1 when a(n-1) is odd and an = a(n-1) / 2 when a(n-1) is even, does every starting value eventually reach 1 after finitely many steps? Equivalently, is there any positive integer starting value whose Collatz trajectory never reaches 1?
self_contained_problem:
Define the Collatz function $T:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ by
\[ T(n) = \begin{cases} 3n+1 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd},\\ n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \]
For a positive integer $a_0$, define the Collatz trajectory by $a_n = T(a_{n-1})$ for $n \ge 1$. Prove or disprove the following: for every positive integer $a_0$, there exists a finite $n \ge 0$ such that $a_n = 1$. Equivalently, show that no positive integer starting value $a_0$ produces a trajectory $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ that never attains the value $1$.
status_search_result: The Collatz (3n+1) conjecture is a famous, long-standing open problem. The strongest known partial result is due to Terence Tao (2019/2022), showing that almost all Collatz orbits attain almost-bounded values, but the full conjecture remains unresolved. It has been verified computationally for all starting values up to roughly $2^{68}$.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For triangulations of the product polytope Δ_{n-1} × Δ_2 and of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3, where a flip changes one triangulation into another and the flip graph has triangulations as vertices and flips as edges, is each of these two flip graphs Hamiltonian?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Delta_{k}$ denote the standard $k$-dimensional simplex (the convex hull of $k+1$ affinely independent points). For positive integers $m,n$, consider the product polytope $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$, and let $\mathcal{T}(n,m)$ denote the set of all triangulations of this polytope (i.e., subdivisions into simplices whose vertices are vertices of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$, fitting together face-to-face and covering the polytope).

A flip is a minimal local modification that transforms one triangulation of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$ into another: it corresponds to a circuit of the point configuration, replacing one of its two triangulations by the other while leaving the rest of the triangulation unchanged. The flip graph $F(n,m)$ has $\mathcal{T}(n,m)$ as its vertex set, with an edge joining two triangulations whenever they differ by a single flip.

Question: For every $n\ge 1$, are the flip graphs $F(n,2)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{2}$) and $F(n,3)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{3}$) Hamiltonian, i.e., do they admit a Hamiltonian cycle visiting every triangulation exactly once?
status_search_result: Related work establishes flip-connectivity for triangulations of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3 (and disconnectedness for Δ_{n-1} × Δ_k with large k), but no result establishing or refuting Hamiltonicity of the flip graphs of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_2 or Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3 was found. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Let H_n be the subgraph of the associahedron graph G_n obtained from triangulations of a convex n-gon whose vertices are colored red and blue alternately, keeping only colorful triangulations with no monochromatic triangle. For odd n ≥ 7, does H_n contain a Hamilton path or a Hamilton cycle, and if so can such a structure be generated by an efficient algorithm?
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 4 and consider a convex n-gon whose vertices are labeled 1, 2, …, n around the boundary. A triangulation of the n-gon is a maximal set of non-crossing diagonals, which partitions the polygon into triangles. The associahedron graph G_n has as its vertex set all triangulations of the n-gon; two triangulations are adjacent in G_n if and only if they differ by a single flip, i.e. removing one diagonal shared by two triangles and replacing it by the other diagonal of the resulting quadrilateral.

Now suppose n is odd, n ≥ 7, and color the vertices of the n-gon alternately red and blue around the boundary (so that exactly one pair of adjacent vertices receives the same color). Call a triangulation colorful if no triangle of the triangulation is monochromatic, i.e. every triangle has vertices of both colors. Let H_n be the subgraph of G_n induced by the set of colorful triangulations.

Question: For every odd n ≥ 7, does H_n contain a Hamilton path, or a Hamilton cycle? If such paths/cycles exist, can they be generated by an algorithm whose amortized running time per produced triangulation is bounded by a small (e.g. constant or polylogarithmic) function of n?
status_search_result: For even n ≥ 8 (and more generally any color pattern with ≥10 color changes), Acharya, Mütze and Verciani (arXiv:2406.03783, J. Computational Geometry 2025) proved H_n has a Hamilton cycle and gave an algorithm producing each triangulation in O(1) amortized time. The odd-n case (which has exactly one pair of equally-colored adjacent vertices) is precisely the case left open in their setting, so the problem as stated for odd n ≥ 7 appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: How large can the chromatic number become for flip graphs of triangulations of a point set, for flip graphs of triangulations of a simple polygon, and for rotation graphs of elimination trees of a graph G, including natural structured families such as grids or trees?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions and setup.

(a) Let P be a finite point set in general position in the plane. A triangulation of P is a maximal planar straight-line graph on P. The flip graph F(P) has the triangulations of P as vertices, with two triangulations joined by an edge whenever they differ in exactly one diagonal (i.e., one is obtained from the other by replacing a diagonal e shared by two triangles forming a convex quadrilateral with the other diagonal of that quadrilateral).

(b) Let P be a simple polygon. A triangulation of P is a maximal set of non-crossing diagonals of P together with the boundary edges. The flip graph F(P) is defined analogously, with edges given by flips of a single diagonal between two triangulations.

(c) Let G = (V,E) be a connected graph on n vertices. An elimination tree of G is a rooted tree T on V defined recursively: choose a root r ∈ V; then for each connected component C of G − r, recursively form an elimination tree of G[C] and attach its root as a child of r. Two elimination trees of G are related by a rotation (tree rotation) if one is obtained from the other by a single local "edge rotation" operation on adjacent vertices, generalizing the rotation operation on binary search trees (the case G = Pn). The rotation graph R(G) has elimination trees of G as vertices and rotation moves as edges.

Problem. Determine, as a function of natural parameters of the underlying object (e.g., the number of points |P|, the size and structure of the polygon P, or the size and structural type of the graph G, including special structured families such as grids and trees), how large the chromatic number χ can be for:

1. the flip graph F(P) of triangulations of a finite planar point set P;
2. the flip graph F(P) of triangulations of a simple polygon P;
3. the rotation graph R(G) of elimination trees of a graph G.

Provide upper and lower bounds, in particular for the cases when G is a path Pn (recovering rotations of binary search trees), a grid graph, or a tree.
status_search_result: The chromatic number of flip graphs is an active research topic. Fabila-Monroy et al. obtained bounds for several flip graphs (matchings, triangulations of convex polygons, non-crossing Hamiltonian paths, triangles of convex point sets), but the general questions for arbitrary point sets, simple polygons, and rotation graphs of elimination trees (beyond binary search trees / G = Pn, and structured families like grids and trees) remain open with no tight answers in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: A cycle-plus-triangles graph on 3n vertices is the union of a Hamiltonian cycle of length 3n and n vertex-disjoint triangles. What is the largest constant α for which one can efficiently find an independent set of size αn in every such graph, improving on the simple α ≥ 3/5 bound and moving closer to the open target α = 1?
self_contained_problem:
A cycle-plus-triangles graph is a 4-regular graph on 3n vertices obtained as the edge-disjoint union of a Hamiltonian cycle C of length 3n and a set of n pairwise vertex-disjoint triangles whose vertex set is the same 3n vertices. It is known (non-constructively, via the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz) that every such graph has an independent set of size n, and in fact is n-colorable. A simple greedy/algorithmic argument shows that one can efficiently (in polynomial time) find an independent set of size at least 3n/5 in every cycle-plus-triangles graph.

Determine the largest constant α ∈ [3/5, 1] for which there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any cycle-plus-triangles graph on 3n vertices (with its Hamiltonian cycle and triangle decomposition as input), outputs an independent set of size at least αn. In particular, design an efficient algorithm achieving α strictly larger than 3/5, and ideally as close to 1 as possible.
status_search_result: The existence of an independent set of size n in every cycle-plus-triangles graph on 3n vertices is known non-constructively via Fleischner–Stiebitz (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz), but a polynomial-time algorithm achieving this bound is still open. Recent work (e.g., on constrained independent sets in cycles, ICALP 2023 / Algorithmica) makes partial progress but does not settle the algorithmic question of the optimal achievable constant α. No source found confirming an improved efficient bound beyond simple arguments.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: In the communication model where Alice knows an n-city traveling salesperson instance and can compute an optimal tour, while Bob is restricted to polynomial-time computation and must reconstruct the optimal tour from Alice’s message, can Alice use at most 0.4999·n log2 n bits of advice, or even o(n log n) bits? What stronger upper bounds become possible if the distance function is metric or Euclidean?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-party communication model for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP). An instance consists of n cities together with a distance function d : [n] × [n] → ℝ≥0 (not necessarily symmetric, not necessarily satisfying the triangle inequality). Alice receives the full instance and is computationally unbounded: in particular she can compute an optimal Hamiltonian tour. She then sends a single message (the "advice") to Bob, who also receives the same instance but is restricted to polynomial-time computation. Upon reading Alice's message together with the instance, Bob must output an optimal TSP tour (a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total length).

It is known that an advice length of n·log₂ n bits suffices (Alice can perturb distances so that an optimal tour becomes recoverable by Bob via a polynomial-time minimum-weight matching computation, encoding the perturbation in n·log₂ n bits).

(a) Does there exist a protocol in which Alice's advice uses at most 0.4999·n·log₂ n bits while Bob still recovers an optimal tour in polynomial time?

(b) More ambitiously, does there exist such a protocol with advice length o(n log n) bits?

(c) Do stronger upper bounds on the required advice length hold when the distance function d is restricted to be metric (symmetric and satisfying the triangle inequality), or Euclidean (cities are points in ℝ² with Euclidean distances)?
status_search_result: The n log₂ n upper bound on advice (via a matching-based reduction) is known and discussed in expository write-ups, but no source found reduces this bound to 0.4999·n log₂ n or to o(n log n), nor establishes corresponding stronger bounds in the metric or Euclidean cases. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For k ≤ 4, does there exist a pivot rule for the k-Opt local-search algorithm for the traveling salesperson problem such that, for every edge-weighted complete graph and every initial tour, repeated improving k-Opt steps are guaranteed to terminate in polynomial time? The question is especially interesting for k = 2 in the Euclidean setting.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a complete graph on $n$ vertices equipped with edge weights $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle in $G$, and its cost is the sum of the weights of its edges. For an integer $k\ge 2$, the k-Opt neighborhood of a tour $\tau$ consists of all tours $\tau'$ that can be obtained from $\tau$ by removing some $k$ edges of $\tau$ and reconnecting the resulting fragments into a single Hamiltonian cycle by adding $k$ new edges (so $\tau'$ differs from $\tau$ in at most $k$ edges). The k-Opt local-search algorithm starts from an initial tour and, at each step, replaces the current tour by a strictly cheaper tour in its k-Opt neighborhood, terminating at a k-Opt local optimum. A pivot rule is a (deterministic) procedure that, given the current tour, selects which improving k-Opt move to perform whenever such a move exists.

Question: For each $k\in\{2,3,4\}$, does there exist a pivot rule for the k-Opt algorithm such that, for every edge-weighted complete graph $G$ and every initial tour $\tau$, the number of improving k-Opt steps performed before termination is bounded by a polynomial in $n$? The case $k=2$ is of particular interest when the edge weights come from Euclidean distances between points in the plane.
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) established that for k≥3, the k-Opt algorithm has the "all-exp" property: even with an optimal pivot rule there exist instances and initial tours requiring exponentially many improving steps. In particular, no polynomial-time pivot rule exists for k=3 and k=4, settling those cases negatively. The case k=2 remains open in general (and is especially of interest in the Euclidean setting, where exponential lower-bound instances are known but a polynomial pivot rule has not been ruled out).

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Does there exist a value of k for which Euclidean TSP/k-Opt is PLS-complete?
self_contained_problem:
Background. The class PLS (Polynomial Local Search) consists of local search problems whose instances specify a finite set of feasible solutions, a polynomial-time-computable cost function, and a polynomial-time-computable neighborhood, such that for each solution one can in polynomial time either output a strictly better neighbor or certify that the current solution is locally optimal. A problem is PLS-complete if every problem in PLS reduces to it under PLS-reductions.

For an integer k ≥ 2, the k-Opt neighborhood for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is defined on the set of Hamiltonian tours of a complete weighted graph: two tours are neighbors if one can be obtained from the other by removing k edges and adding k other edges (so as to again form a Hamiltonian tour). The local search problem TSP/k-Opt asks, given an instance, to find a tour that is locally optimal with respect to this neighborhood (no k-Opt move strictly decreases the total length).

In the Euclidean version, the input consists of n points in the plane R^2 (or more generally R^d), and the cost of an edge between two points is their Euclidean (ℓ^2) distance; the tour length is the sum of edge costs along the cycle.

It is known that, for general (metric) TSP, the problem TSP/k-Opt is PLS-complete for sufficiently large k.

Question. Does there exist an integer k ≥ 2 for which the local search problem Euclidean TSP/k-Opt (points in the Euclidean plane, ℓ^2 distances, k-Opt neighborhood) is PLS-complete?
status_search_result: No source found establishing PLS-completeness of Euclidean TSP under the k-Opt neighborhood for any k. PLS-completeness is known for general/metric TSP under k-Opt (Krentel; later improved to smaller k by subsequent work), and recent work on Euclidean k-Opt has focused on approximation ratios and running-time lower bounds (e.g., exponential running time for k ≥ 5), but the PLS-completeness question for the Euclidean case appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Are there nontrivial permutation classes C ⊆ S_n for which the restricted determinant-like and permanent-like sums det_C(A) = Σ_{π∈C} sgn(π) Π_i A_{i,π(i)} and per_C(A) = Σ_{π∈C} Π_i A_{i,π(i)} can be computed efficiently, and can such permutation classes be classified? The same question is also posed for general immanants.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. For an $n\times n$ matrix $A=(A_{i,j})$ with entries in a commutative ring (e.g., $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$) and a subset $C\subseteq S_n$, define the restricted determinant and restricted permanent
$$\det\nolimits_C(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}, \qquad \operatorname{per}\nolimits_C(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.$$
More generally, for an irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ of $S_n$ associated with a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, define the restricted immanant
$$\operatorname{imm}\nolimits_C^{\lambda}(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\chi^\lambda(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.$$
A family $\mathcal C = (C_n)_{n\ge 1}$ with $C_n\subseteq S_n$ is called a permutation class. It is "trivial" in cases such as $C_n = S_n$ (giving the usual determinant, permanent, or immanant) or $C_n = \emptyset$.

Problem. Exhibit nontrivial permutation classes $\mathcal{C}=(C_n)_{n\ge 1}$ (for instance, classes defined by avoidance of fixed permutation patterns, or by other combinatorial restrictions) for which the maps $A\mapsto \det_{C_n}(A)$, $A\mapsto \operatorname{per}_{C_n}(A)$, and, more generally, $A\mapsto \operatorname{imm}_{C_n}^{\lambda}(A)$ can be evaluated in time polynomial in $n$ on arbitrary $n\times n$ input matrices. Furthermore, classify all permutation classes for which such polynomial-time algorithms exist.
status_search_result: Computational complexity of permanents and immanants is a long-studied area: Valiant established #P-hardness of the permanent, Ryser gave the best-known exact algorithm, and Curticapean and others have proved dichotomy results for families of immanants indexed by partitions. paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For 2-cut elimination trees on a tree G, where every rooted subtree T_v has boundary size at most 2 in the underlying graph, can the known 5n upper bound on rotation distance be improved?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a tree on $n$ vertices. An elimination tree of $G$ is a rooted tree $T$ on the same vertex set defined recursively: pick any vertex $r$ of $G$ as the root, and then for each connected component $C$ of $G - r$, recursively form an elimination tree of $G[C]$ and attach its root as a child of $r$. For a vertex $v$ in an elimination tree $T$, let $T_v$ denote the rooted subtree of $T$ at $v$, and define its boundary in $G$ as the set of vertices in $V(G)\setminus V(T_v)$ that are adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $V(T_v)$. An elimination tree $T$ of $G$ is called a 2-cut elimination tree if for every vertex $v$ of $T$ the boundary of $T_v$ in $G$ has size at most $2$. A rotation on an elimination tree of $G$ is the elementary move corresponding to an edge of the associated graph associahedron (equivalently, swapping the order of two consecutive vertices in a generating elimination ordering). The rotation distance between two elimination trees is the minimum number of such rotations needed to transform one into the other.

It is known that for any two 2-cut elimination trees of a tree $G$ on $n$ vertices, their rotation distance is at most $5n$. (For comparison, when $G$ is a path, the 2-cut elimination trees are exactly binary search trees on $n$ nodes, and the tight rotation distance bound is $2n-6$ for $n \ge 11$.)

Question: Can the upper bound of $5n$ on the rotation distance between two 2-cut elimination trees of an $n$-vertex tree $G$ be improved to a smaller function of $n$?
status_search_result: Recent literature on rotation distance in graph associahedra (e.g., the 2025 paper showing the problem is FPT and NP-hard in general) discusses bounds for elimination trees but does not report an improvement to the 5n upper bound for 2-cut elimination trees on trees. No source found claiming a better bound or a matching lower bound, so the problem appears to remain open.

The set of all elimination trees of G is connected by "tree rotations" (local moves that exchange a vertex with its parent in T, subject to the usual elimination-tree compatibility condition), and the rotation distance between two elimination trees is the minimum number of such rotations required to transform one into the other.

Question: Can the upper bound on the rotation distance between any two k-cut elimination trees of a tree on n vertices be improved to O(n log k)?

original_question: For k-cut elimination trees on general graphs of treewidth at most t, can the best known O(t·n log n) upper bound on rotation distance be improved to O(t·k·n), analogous to the O(k·n) bound known when the underlying graph is a tree?

original_question: Given a matroid M on m elements presented by an independence oracle, can the diameter δ(M) of its base polytope be computed faster than the current polynomial-time reduction to matroid intersection, or can one prove a superlinear conditional lower bound? What better algorithms are possible in other representations such as graphic, realizable, lattice-path, or transversal matroids?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be a matroid on a ground set of m elements, given via an independence oracle (a subroutine that, for any subset S of the ground set, reports whether S is independent in M). The base polytope of M is the convex hull in R^m of the indicator vectors of the bases of M. Its 1-skeleton (the graph whose vertices are the bases and whose edges connect pairs of bases that differ by a single element exchange) has a well-defined graph-theoretic diameter δ(M).

(a) In the independence-oracle model, design an algorithm that computes δ(M) strictly faster than the current best approach, which proceeds by a polynomial-time reduction to matroid intersection; alternatively, establish a superlinear (possibly conditional) lower bound on the number of oracle queries required to compute δ(M).

(b) Design improved algorithms for computing δ(M) when M is given in one of the following more structured representations:
   (i) graphic matroids (specified by a graph),
   (ii) realizable matroids (specified by a matrix over some field),
   (iii) lattice path matroids,
   (iv) transversal matroids (specified by a bipartite incidence structure).

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Diameter of implicit polytopes and polymatroids
original_question: Are there classes of polytopes given in implicit or partially implicit form whose graph diameter can nonetheless be computed in polynomial time, and are there classes of polymatroids whose diameter can be computed efficiently?
self_contained_problem:
A polytope P ⊂ ℝ^n is given in "implicit" or "partially implicit" form when it is not specified directly by an explicit list of all vertices or facets, but rather succinctly via some combinatorial or algebraic data (for example, by an oracle, by a small set of generators, or as the convex hull of objects parametrized by a graph, matroid, or other combinatorial structure). The graph (or 1-skeleton) of P has the vertices of P as nodes, with two vertices joined by an edge whenever they are connected by an edge of P; the diameter of P is the diameter of this graph.

A polymatroid is a polytope of the form
  P(f) = { x ∈ ℝ^E_{≥0} : x(S) ≤ f(S) for all S ⊆ E },
where E is a finite ground set and f : 2^E → ℝ_{≥0} is a nonnegative, nondecreasing, submodular set function with f(∅) = 0. Its diameter is defined as the diameter of its 1-skeleton.

Problems:

(a) Identify classes of polytopes presented in implicit or partially implicit form (other than already-known cases) for which the diameter of the polytope graph can be computed in time polynomial in the size of the implicit description.

(b) Identify nontrivial classes of polymatroids P(f) (specified, for instance, by an evaluation oracle for f, or by a succinct description of f) for which the diameter of P(f) can be computed efficiently, i.e., in polynomial time.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a vague open research direction. Known complexity results show that computing the combinatorial diameter of a polytope given by linear inequalities is hard (e.g., NP-/DP-hard in general), and only limited classes (such as 0/1 polytopes via specific combinatorial structure, or certain matroid polytopes) have efficient diameter algorithms. No source found that resolves the general question of identifying further implicit polytope classes or polymatroid classes with polynomial-time diameter computation; the problem appears open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Diameter of bipartite perfect matching polytope
original_question: What is the computational complexity of computing the diameter of the bipartite perfect matching polytope, whose vertices are perfect matchings and whose edges correspond to flips of alternating cycles?
self_contained_problem: Let $G = (U \cup V, E)$ be a balanced bipartite graph with $|U| = |V| = n$. A perfect matching of $G$ is a subset $M \subseteq E$ such that every vertex of $G$ is incident to exactly one edge of $M$. The bipartite perfect matching polytope $P(G)$ is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^E$ of the characteristic vectors of all perfect matchings of $G$. Two perfect matchings $M, M'$ correspond to adjacent vertices of $P(G)$ if and only if the symmetric difference $M \triangle M'$ is a single alternating cycle (equivalently, $M$ and $M'$ differ by a single cycle flip). The diameter of $P(G)$ is the maximum, over all pairs of perfect matchings $M, M'$ of $G$, of the minimum number of such cycle flips needed to transform $M$ into $M'$.\n\nDetermine the computational complexity of the following problem: given a balanced bipartite graph $G$ (and an integer $k$), compute (resp. decide whether the diameter of $P(G)$ is at most $k$).
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) resolves the complexity question: Nöbel and Steiner showed the diameter problem for the bipartite perfect matching polytope is NP-hard, and a 2025 result establishes that computing the diameter of the bipartite perfect matching polytope is $\Pi_2^p$-complete (i.e., complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy), also yielding inapproximability. This answers the open question.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For any integer k and any skew shape S, is the number of transversal fillings of S that avoid decreasing k-chains always at most the number of transversal fillings that avoid increasing k-chains?
self_contained_problem:
Let a skew shape $S = \lambda/\mu$ be the set of unit cells in the difference of two Young diagrams, where $\mu \subseteq \lambda$ are partitions; equivalently, $S$ is a finite region of the integer grid whose boundary consists of two monotone lattice paths sharing endpoints. A transversal of $S$ is a 0/1-filling of the cells of $S$ such that every row of $S$ contains exactly one 1 and every column of $S$ contains exactly one 1.

For an integer $k \geq 2$, an increasing $k$-chain (also called a north-east $k$-chain) in a 0/1-filling of $S$ is a sequence of $k$ cells containing 1, located at positions $(r_1,c_1),(r_2,c_2),\dots,(r_k,c_k)$ with $r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_k$ and $c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_k$, such that the bounding rectangle of every consecutive pair $(r_i,c_i),(r_{i+1},c_{i+1})$ is entirely contained in $S$. A decreasing $k$-chain (south-east $k$-chain) is defined analogously with $r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_k$ and $c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_k$, again with each bounding rectangle contained in $S$. A transversal is said to avoid increasing (respectively decreasing) $k$-chains if it contains no such chain.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $k \geq 2$ and every skew shape $S$,
$$\#\{\text{transversals of }S\text{ avoiding decreasing }k\text{-chains}\} \;\leq\; \#\{\text{transversals of }S\text{ avoiding increasing }k\text{-chains}\}.$$
category_tag: Pattern avoidance in fillings of skew shapes
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open in full generality. For the case k = 2, equality is known (proved by Jelínek and independently by Burstein–Pantone). A bijective equality has also been established for the hereditary subclass of "D-free" skew shapes (which contains Ferrers shapes), but the inequality is not known for arbitrary skew shapes and general k.

original_question: If H_0 is the ordered graph shown in Figure 7, is the chromatic number of the class of ordered graphs that avoid H_0 as an ordered subgraph bounded by a constant?
self_contained_problem:
An ordered graph is a pair (G,<) where G=(V,E) is a finite simple graph and < is a linear order on V. An ordered graph (H,<_H) is an ordered subgraph of (G,<_G) if there is an injection f:V(H)→V(G) that preserves both edges and the linear order (i.e. uv∈E(H) implies f(u)f(v)∈E(G), and u<_H v implies f(u)<_G f(v)).    E(H_0) = { v_1 v_4 ,  v_2 v_6 ,  v_3 v_5 ,  v_4 v_5 }.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Why does avoiding the two rectangulation patterns shown in Figure 9 produce Catalan-number many rectangulations, and can one give a formal bijection explaining this enumeration?
self_contained_problem:
A generic rectangulation of the unit square is a dissection of $[0,1]^2$ into finitely many axis-aligned rectangles by horizontal and vertical segments, such that no four rectangles share a common corner (equivalently, every interior wall meets the boundary or other walls only in T-junctions). Two generic rectangulations are considered equivalent if one can be deformed into the other by sliding segments while preserving the combinatorial adjacency structure; this gives the notion of a weak (generic) rectangulation with $n$ rectangles.

A pattern in a rectangulation is a small local configuration of rectangles meeting along walls in a prescribed way; a rectangulation $R$ is said to avoid a pattern $P$ if no subset of rectangles of $R$ forms a configuration equivalent to $P$.

Consider the following two specific T-junction patterns (a horizontal segment terminating on a vertical segment, in the two "windmill"-like orientations that together form a $\sqcap$-shape pattern):

- Pattern $P_1$: three rectangles $A, B, C$ where $A$ sits above the common top edges of $B$ and $C$, with $B$ to the left of $C$, and the vertical wall between $B$ and $C$ terminates strictly below the bottom edge of $A$;
- Pattern $P_2$: the left–right mirror image of $P_1$.

Let $f(n)$ denote the number of weak generic rectangulations of $[0,1]^2$ with $n$ rectangles that simultaneously avoid both $P_1$ and $P_2$. It is known that $f(n) = C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, the $n$-th Catalan number.

Provide a conceptual explanation of this enumeration by exhibiting an explicit, formal bijection between the set of such doubly-pattern-avoiding weak generic rectangulations with $n$ rectangles and a standard family of Catalan objects (for example, binary trees with $n$ nodes, Dyck paths of length $2n$, or $213$-avoiding permutations of length $n$).
status_search_result: Recent work on patterns in rectangulations (arXiv:2501.11781) explicitly addresses $\sqcap$-avoiding weak rectangulations and constructs formal bijections with several Catalan structures (binary trees, Dyck paths, 213-avoiding permutations, and (10)-avoiding inversion sequences), thereby providing the requested combinatorial explanation. A follow-up preprint (arXiv:2511.22015) further extends pattern-avoidance results in rectangulations. The enumeration question and the request for a formal bijection thus appear resolved.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Why does avoiding the three rectangulation patterns shown in Figure 10 produce Baxter-number many rectangulations, and can one give a formal bijection explaining this enumeration?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A generic rectangulation of the unit square is a partition of $[0,1]^2$ into finitely many axis-aligned rectangles, considered up to combinatorial equivalence (i.e., up to continuous deformations that preserve the contact structure between rectangles), with the further restriction that no four rectangles meet at a common point. Equivalently, every interior vertex has degree three (a T-junction), and edges may be "wall-slid" past each other.

A (rectangulation) pattern is a small generic rectangulation together with a specified contact configuration; a rectangulation $R$ is said to contain the pattern $P$ if some sub-collection of rectangles and walls of $R$ realises the same combinatorial contact structure as $P$. Otherwise $R$ avoids $P$.

Let $P_1, P_2, P_3$ be the following three specific generic-rectangulation patterns (each involving a small local configuration of three rectangles meeting in a particular T-junction arrangement, in the three "rotations" needed to exclude every direction of the offending local configuration). Let $\mathcal{R}_n$ denote the set of generic rectangulations with $n$ rectangles that simultaneously avoid $P_1$, $P_2$, and $P_3$.

The Baxter numbers are defined by
$$B_n \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1}}{\binom{n+1}{1}\binom{n+1}{2}}, \qquad n \ge 1,$$
giving the sequence $1,2,6,22,92,422,2074,\ldots$ (OEIS A001181), and also count, e.g., Baxter permutations of length $n$ (permutations avoiding the vincular patterns $2\,\underline{41}\,3$ and $3\,\underline{14}\,2$), as well as several other well-known combinatorial families (mosaic/diagonal rectangulations, pairs of non-crossing lattice paths, plane bipolar orientations, etc.).

Problem. It is observed that $|\mathcal{R}_n| = B_n$ for all $n \ge 1$. Provide a conceptual explanation for this equality, and in particular exhibit an explicit size-preserving bijection
$$\Phi : \mathcal{R}_n \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}_n$$
between $\mathcal{R}_n$ and some standard Baxter-counted family $\mathcal{B}_n$ (such as Baxter permutations of length $n$, mosaic rectangulations with $n$ rectangles, or plane bipolar orientations with $n+1$ edges) that explains the enumeration directly, ideally in a way that translates natural structural operations on one side (e.g., local flips, pattern containment) into natural operations on the other.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Is there a general bijection between rectangulations that avoid a rectangulation pattern P and permutations that avoid a corresponding mesh permutation pattern μ(P)?
self_contained_problem:
A (generic) rectangulation of the unit square is a partition of the square into finitely many axis-aligned rectangles such that no four rectangles share a corner. There is a classical mapping that associates to each rectangulation R on n rectangles a permutation π(R) in S_n (for instance, via the diagonal/labeling rule used in the bijections between rectangulations and Baxter or 2-clumped permutations).

A rectangulation pattern P is a small rectangulation that may "occur" inside a larger rectangulation R in a precise geometric/combinatorial sense (an occurrence is a sub-configuration of segments and rectangles of R isomorphic to P, possibly required to be contiguous in a prescribed way). We write Av(P) for the set of rectangulations that contain no occurrence of P.

A mesh permutation pattern μ is a pair (σ, M) consisting of a permutation σ ∈ S_k together with a set M ⊆ {0,1,…,k} × {0,1,…,k} of "shaded" cells of the k × k grid. A permutation τ contains μ if there exist indices i_1 < ⋯ < i_k such that τ(i_1)…τ(i_k) is order-isomorphic to σ and, for every shaded cell (a,b) ∈ M, no entry of τ lies strictly inside the corresponding region of the grid determined by these indices. Otherwise τ avoids μ. We write Av(μ) for the set of permutations avoiding μ.

Question: Does there exist a systematic construction P ↦ μ(P), assigning to every rectangulation pattern P a mesh permutation pattern μ(P), together with a bijection between Av(P) (rectangulations avoiding P) and Av(μ(P)) (permutations avoiding μ(P)), such that this bijection works uniformly across all rectangulation patterns P?
status_search_result: Recent work establishes such bijections for specific families—e.g., guillotine rectangulations correspond to avoidance of certain mesh patterns (windmills), and combining these with Baxter or 2-clumped patterns yields bijections for weak and strong guillotine rectangulations. Further bijections to inversion-sequence classes and Catalan-counted families have been obtained for various patterns. However, a fully general bijection P ↦ μ(P) covering all rectangulation patterns does not appear to be established; only case-by-case correspondences have been proven.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Is the wiggly flip graph WFG_n, whose vertices are wiggly pseudotriangulations and whose edges are flips between adjacent facets of the wiggly complex, Hamiltonian for every n?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $n\ge 1$ and consider $n+2$ collinear points $p_0,p_1,\dots,p_{n+1}$ in the plane. A wiggly arc on these points is a simple curve from $p_i$ to $p_j$ (with $0\le i<j\le n+1$) that wiggles above and/or below the horizontal line, allowed to pass arbitrarily often above and below each intermediate point $p_k$ with $i<k<j$, considered up to isotopy relative to the points. Two wiggly arcs are said to be compatible if they are pointed (no common endpoint at which they share a tangent direction on the same side) and non-crossing in their interiors. The wiggly complex is the simplicial complex whose faces are sets of pairwise compatible internal wiggly arcs; its facets are called wiggly pseudotriangulations, and each facet contains exactly $2n-1$ internal wiggly arcs.

In each wiggly pseudotriangulation, every internal arc can be flipped: replacing it with the unique other wiggly arc that, together with the remaining $2n-2$ arcs, again forms a wiggly pseudotriangulation. The wiggly flip graph $\mathrm{WFG}_n$ is the graph whose vertices are the wiggly pseudotriangulations on $n+2$ collinear points and whose edges connect two wiggly pseudotriangulations that differ by a single flip.

Question: Does $\mathrm{WFG}_n$ admit a Hamiltonian cycle for every positive integer $n$?

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For an arbitrary finite point set P in the plane equipped with the wiggly-arc construction defined in the booklet, is the reduced wiggly complex RWCP always the boundary complex of a simplicial polytope?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a finite point set in the plane in general position. A wiggly arc on $P$ is a simple curve in the plane whose two endpoints are two distinct points $p, q \in P$, which avoids all other points of $P$, and which crosses the open line segment $\overline{pq}$ transversally a finite number of times (so the arc "wiggles" above and below the chord, but never crosses any other chord through two points of $P$ in a degenerate way). Two wiggly arcs are called compatible (pointed and non-crossing) if they do not cross each other transversally in the plane (allowing only the prescribed touching behaviour at common endpoints, i.e., they are pointed at common endpoints). 

The wiggly complex $WC_P$ is the simplicial complex whose vertices are the wiggly arcs on $P$ (modulo isotopy fixing $P$) and whose faces are the sets of pairwise compatible wiggly arcs. After removing the "boundary" arcs that appear in every maximal face, one obtains the reduced wiggly complex $RWC_P$, an abstract simplicial complex which is a pseudomanifold without boundary.

Question: For every such finite point set $P$ in the plane, is $RWC_P$ isomorphic to the boundary complex of some simplicial convex polytope?
status_search_result: The wigglyhedron of Bapat and Pilaud (Mathematische Zeitschrift, 2025) realizes the wiggly complex as a simplicial polytope only in the case where the points lie on a line. The extension to arbitrary planar point sets is stated as a conjecture and is described as requiring connections with rigidity theory; no realization or disproof appears in the literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For an arbitrary finite point set P in the plane equipped with the wiggly-arc construction defined in the booklet, is the wiggly flip graph WFG_P Hamiltonian?
self_contained_problem:
Let P = {p_1, ..., p_n} be a finite set of points in the plane in general position. A wiggly arc on P is a simple curve that connects two points of P and "wiggles" around the remaining points: formally, it is determined by an ordered pair (p_i, p_j) of distinct points of P together with a partition of P \ {p_i, p_j} into two (possibly empty) subsets L and R, with the curve passing above the points of L and below the points of R relative to the line through p_i and p_j (up to ambient isotopy fixing P). Two wiggly arcs are said to be compatible if they are pointed (do not share an endpoint with one being a sub-arc of the other in a degenerate way) and non-crossing in the appropriate combinatorial sense; a wiggly pseudo-triangulation of P is an inclusion-maximal set of pairwise compatible wiggly arcs on P. Two wiggly pseudo-triangulations are related by a wiggly flip if they differ in exactly one wiggly arc. The wiggly flip graph WFG_P has the wiggly pseudo-triangulations of P as vertices and wiggly flips as edges.

Prove or disprove: for every finite point set P in the plane (in general position), the wiggly flip graph WFG_P admits a Hamiltonian cycle.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Can the construction that realizes the aligned-point wiggly complex as the boundary of the wigglyhedron be adapted to give a more combinatorial construction of the polytope of pseudotriangulations that depends only on the order type, equivalently the oriented matroid, of the point configuration?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A finite point configuration P in the plane gives rise to its set of pseudotriangulations: maximal collections of pairwise non-crossing pointed pseudo-edges whose union triangulates the convex hull of P into pseudo-triangles (regions bounded by three concave arcs meeting at three convex vertices). It is known (Rote–Santos–Streinu) that the set of pseudotriangulations of P is realized as the vertex set of a simple polytope, the pseudotriangulation polytope, whose construction uses metric data (specific coordinates and an expansion cone) of P.

In the special case in which P consists of n+2 collinear (aligned) points, the associated "aligned-point wiggly complex" of pointed non-crossing wiggly arcs has been realized as the boundary complex of a simplicial polytope, the wigglyhedron, by an explicit combinatorial construction (assigning to each wiggly pseudotriangulation a point in R^{2n+2} via simple integer-valued statistics on its arcs, and taking the convex hull).

The order type (equivalently, the chirotope of the oriented matroid) of a planar point configuration P records only the relative orientations of all triples of points in P, and does not depend on the metric coordinates.

Problem. Can the combinatorial construction that realizes the aligned-point wiggly complex as the boundary of the wigglyhedron be adapted to produce a construction of the pseudotriangulation polytope of an arbitrary planar point configuration P that depends only on the order type (oriented matroid) of P? Equivalently, does there exist a polytope, defined as the convex hull of points obtained from each pseudotriangulation of P by combinatorial statistics determined solely by the oriented matroid of P, whose boundary complex is the pseudotriangulation complex of P?
status_search_result: Recent work introducing the wigglyhedron (Mathematische Zeitschrift, 2025) realizes the aligned-point wiggly complex as a polytope boundary, but no published source indicates that the construction has been extended to give an oriented-matroid-only construction of the general pseudotriangulation polytope. The question appears to remain open.

original_question: What is the dual interpretation of wiggly pseudotriangulations in terms of pseudoline arrangements, and can that interpretation be extended to other finite Coxeter groups?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and consider n+2 points on a horizontal line in the plane. A wiggly arc is an isotopy class of simple curves that start at one of these points, end at another, and "wiggle" by passing above or below each intermediate point on the line. Two wiggly arcs are called pointed and non-crossing if they share endpoints only as common pointed endpoints and do not cross transversally. The wiggly complex is the simplicial complex whose vertices are wiggly arcs and whose faces are sets of pairwise pointed and non-crossing wiggly arcs; this complex is a (2n−1)-dimensional pseudomanifold, and its facets are called wiggly pseudotriangulations. Recall also that classical pseudotriangulations of a point configuration are known to be combinatorially dual to certain pseudoline arrangements in the Möbius strip (contact points of the arrangement correspond to edges of the pseudotriangulation), and that this duality admits generalizations to subword complexes attached to finite Coxeter groups.

(a) Describe a dual model for wiggly pseudotriangulations as arrangements of pseudolines (for instance in the Möbius strip or in another suitable surface), in which the wiggly arcs of a pseudotriangulation correspond to the contact points (or analogous combinatorial features) of the arrangement, in a way that recovers the flip structure on wiggly pseudotriangulations.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Construct a flip-Gray code for permutations of order n > 2 using only prefix reversals of sizes n−2, n−1, and n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_n$ denote the set of all permutations of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, written as sequences $\pi = \pi_1\pi_2\cdots\pi_n$. For an integer $k$ with $2\le k\le n$, the prefix reversal (or flip) of size $k$ applied to $\pi$ is the permutation $f_k(\pi) = \pi_k\pi_{k-1}\cdots\pi_1\pi_{k+1}\cdots\pi_n$ obtained by reversing the first $k$ entries.

A flip-Gray code for $S_n$ using a set $F\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n\}$ of allowed flip sizes is a cyclic (or linear) listing $\pi^{(1)},\pi^{(2)},\dots,\pi^{(n!)}$ of every permutation in $S_n$ exactly once such that for every consecutive pair (including the wrap-around pair in the cyclic case) one has $\pi^{(i+1)} = f_{k_i}(\pi^{(i)})$ for some $k_i\in F$.

Problem. For every integer $n > 2$, construct a flip-Gray code for $S_n$ using only the three flip sizes $F = \{n-2,\,n-1,\,n\}$, or prove that no such listing exists.
status_search_result: The problem appears in current compilations of open problems on combinatorial Gray codes (the "Big 3" pancake-flipping question). Searches surface related work on greedy pancake-flipping Gray codes (Sawada–Williams) and flip-swap languages, but no construction or impossibility proof restricted to flips of sizes n−2, n−1, n is reported. The status appears to be open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Construct a flip-Gray code for signed permutations of order n, representing burnt pancakes, using only prefix reversals of sizes n−2, n−1, and n.
self_contained_problem:
A signed permutation of order $n$ is a sequence $\pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots, \pi_n)$ where $(|\pi_1|, \ldots, |\pi_n|)$ is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ and each $\pi_i \in \{\pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots, \pm n\}$. Such objects model stacks of "burnt pancakes," where the sign of $\pi_i$ indicates which side faces up. For an integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le n$, the prefix reversal (flip) of size $k$ applied to $\pi$ produces the signed permutation $(-\pi_k, -\pi_{k-1}, \ldots, -\pi_1, \pi_{k+1}, \ldots, \pi_n)$.

A flip-Gray code of order $n$ is a cyclic listing of all $2^n \cdot n!$ signed permutations of order $n$ such that consecutive entries (including the last and the first) differ by a single prefix reversal.

Problem: For every sufficiently large $n$, construct a flip-Gray code for the signed permutations of order $n$ that uses only prefix reversals of sizes $n-2$, $n-1$, and $n$.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Let SP(n) be the shorthand permutations of order n and U*_n the lexicographically smallest universal cycle for SP(n). Is there an O(n)-time successor rule for generating successive symbols of U*_n, equivalently a simple parent rule for constructing a cycle-joining tree on the necklace representatives of SP(n)?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \geq 2$, let $\Pi(n)$ denote the set of all permutations of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ written as words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$. The shorthand encoding of $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Pi(n)$ is its length-$(n-1)$ prefix $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_{n-1}$, and the set of shorthand permutations of order $n$ is 
$$SP(n) = \{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_{n-1} : a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Pi(n)\}.$$
A universal cycle for $SP(n)$ is a circular string $U$ of length $n!$ over $\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that the $n!$ length-$(n-1)$ substrings of $U$ (read cyclically) are exactly the elements of $SP(n)$, each appearing once. Order such circular strings by the lexicographic order of their (unique) representative starting at the lexicographically smallest rotation, and let $U^*_n$ denote the lexicographically smallest universal cycle for $SP(n)$.

A necklace of length $m$ over an alphabet is the lexicographically smallest representative of its equivalence class under cyclic rotation. Let $\mathcal{N}(SP(n))$ denote the set of necklace representatives associated with the cycle structure underlying $SP(n)$ (so that universal cycles can be obtained by cycle-joining trees on $\mathcal{N}(SP(n))$).

Question: Does there exist a successor rule for $U^*_n$ that, given any length-$(n-1)$ window of $U^*_n$, computes the next symbol of $U^*_n$ in time $O(n)$? paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Does there exist a binary universal partial cycle for every length n = 2^j with j ≥ 2 in which wildcard symbols occur at every n-th position, and in particular can one construct such a cycle for n = 16?
self_contained_problem:
Let the alphabet be {0,1} together with a wildcard symbol ⋄, where ⋄ is regarded as matching either 0 or 1. A length-n binary word w ∈ {0,1}^n is said to be covered by a length-n partial word u ∈ {0,1,⋄}^n if w can be obtained from u by replacing each occurrence of ⋄ with some element of {0,1}. A binary universal partial cycle (UPC) for length n is a finite cyclic sequence C over the alphabet {0,1,⋄} such that every binary word w ∈ {0,1}^n is covered by exactly one of the |C| cyclic length-n contiguous substrings of C.

Question: For every integer j ≥ 2 (so n = 2^j), does there exist a binary universal partial cycle for length n in which the wildcard symbol ⋄ appears at exactly the positions that are multiples of n (i.e., at every n-th position of the cyclic sequence, and nowhere else)? In particular, does such a UPC exist for n = 16?
status_search_result: Universal partial cycles for n ≥ 5 are a recent and highly active area; existence for n = 8 has been shown, and constructions/structure theorems are being developed (e.g., arXiv:2310.13067, 2024–2025 work on UPCs and universal partial tori). No source found constructs a binary UPC for n = 16 with wildcards at every n-th position, and the problem appears to remain open as a research question.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Does there exist a constant-amortized-time algorithm that lists one representative from each k-ary unlabeled necklace class of length n? The question is already open and interesting for fixed alphabets k = 3 and k = 4, and if k is not fixed then an O(n)-amortized algorithm would already be notable.
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers $k\ge 2$ and $n\ge 1$. Consider the set $[k]^n$ of all strings of length $n$ over the alphabet $[k]=\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$. Two strings $u,v\in[k]^n$ are declared equivalent if there exist a cyclic rotation and a permutation $\pi\in S_k$ of the alphabet such that applying both to $u$ yields $v$. The equivalence classes under this action are called the $k$-ary unlabeled necklaces of length $n$; choose for each class a unique canonical representative (e.g.\ the lexicographically smallest string in the class).

A listing algorithm outputs one representative from each $k$-ary unlabeled necklace of length $n$. It is said to run in constant amortized time (CAT) if the total running time is $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of $k$-ary unlabeled necklaces of length $n$ produced.

Problem. Does there exist a CAT algorithm to list a representative of every $k$-ary unlabeled necklace of length $n$? The case is already of interest for the fixed values $k=3$ and $k=4$. When $k$ is part of the input (not fixed), does there at least exist an algorithm running in amortized time $O(n)$ per necklace?

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Is there a simple and efficient Gray-code algorithm to generate all bifurcated ordered trees of order n, and can the resulting ordering be ranked and unranked efficiently?
self_contained_problem:
A bifurcated ordered tree (BOT) is a rooted tree in which the children of every node are partitioned into a (possibly empty) ordered sequence of "left children" and a (possibly empty) ordered sequence of "right children"; thus a BOT carries strictly more structure than an ordered tree, because at each node one distinguishes the left subtrees (listed in order from first to last) from the right subtrees (listed in order from first to last). A BOT is said to be of order n if it has n nodes in total. Let B_n denote the set of all BOTs of order n.

(a) Design a simple and efficient combinatorial generation algorithm (ideally a Gray-code algorithm, in which any two consecutive BOTs in the listing differ by a small local modification) that produces every element of B_n exactly once, with small (preferably O(1) amortized or worst-case) delay per object.

(b) For the ordering produced in (a), describe efficient ranking and unranking procedures: given a BOT T ∈ B_n, compute its position (rank) in the listing in polynomial time in n, and given an integer r with 1 ≤ r ≤ |B_n|, construct in polynomial time in n the BOT T ∈ B_n of rank r.

The problem asks whether such a Gray-code generation algorithm together with efficient ranking/unranking procedures exists.

No source was found indicating a resolution.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Pivot Gray codes for spanning trees
original_question: Can one construct pivot Gray codes for spanning trees of broader classes of planar or other graphs, where consecutive spanning trees differ by exchanging two edges incident to the same vertex, and can such constructions be turned into efficient algorithms? What happens if the exchange condition is weakened so that the two exchanged edges need only be incident to the same face?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph, and let $\mathcal{T}(G)$ denote the set of spanning trees of $G$. For two spanning trees $T,T'\in\mathcal{T}(G)$, write $T\sim_{\mathrm{piv}}T'$ if $T'$ is obtained from $T$ by removing an edge $e\in T$ and adding an edge $f\in E\setminus T$ such that $e$ and $f$ share a common endpoint (a "pivot exchange"). When $G$ is a plane graph, write $T\sim_{\mathrm{face}}T'$ if $T$ and $T'$ differ by removing an edge $e\in T$ and adding an edge $f\in E\setminus T$ such that $e$ and $f$ lie on the boundary of a common face (a "face exchange"); equivalently this corresponds to a pivot exchange in the dual spanning tree.

A pivot (respectively face-exchange) Gray code for $\mathcal{T}(G)$ is a cyclic or linear ordering $T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_N$ of all spanning trees of $G$ such that consecutive trees $T_i,T_{i+1}$ satisfy $T_i\sim_{\mathrm{piv}}T_{i+1}$ (respectively $T_i\sim_{\mathrm{face}}T_{i+1}$).

(a) For which classes of planar graphs (beyond fans and outerplanar graphs) does a pivot Gray code for the spanning trees exist? In particular, identify broad subclasses of planar graphs, or other natural graph classes, for which such Gray codes can be constructed.

(b) Whenever such pivot Gray codes exist, can they be produced by an algorithm that generates each successive spanning tree in time polynomial (ideally polylogarithmic or amortized constant) in the size of $G$?

(c) For plane graphs, under the relaxed face-exchange closeness condition, for which classes of plane graphs does a face-exchange Gray code for the spanning trees exist, and can it be generated efficiently?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has established pivot Gray codes for further graph classes beyond fans: notably, outerplanar graphs admit a genlex pivot-or-face-exchange Gray code, with strict pivot Gray codes for outerplanar triangulations, and complete graphs $K_n$ admit a pivot Gray code generated in constant amortized time. The general question for arbitrary planar graphs and the full face-exchange relaxation remains open.

context_brief: Connectivity of plane perfect matching flip graph
original_question: For a set S of n = 2m points in the plane in general position, is the flip graph of all plane perfect matchings on S connected using only flips that change at most k edges for some fixed constant k, or at least for some sublinear k?
self_contained_problem:
Let S be a set of n = 2m points in the plane in general position (no three collinear). A plane perfect matching on S is a set of m straight-line segments with endpoints in S such that every point of S is an endpoint of exactly one segment and no two segments cross. Given two plane perfect matchings M and M' on S, a k-flip is a transformation from M to M' such that the symmetric difference M △ M' consists of at most k edges (equivalently, M and M' differ on at most k edges). The k-flip graph of plane perfect matchings on S has all plane perfect matchings on S as its vertices, with two matchings adjacent whenever one can be obtained from the other by a single k-flip.

Question: Does there exist a constant k (independent of n), or at least a function k = k(n) that is sublinear in n, such that for every set S of n = 2m points in general position the k-flip graph of plane perfect matchings on S is connected?

context_brief: Shortest always-available flip in plane matchings
original_question: What is the smallest value of k such that every plane perfect matching always admits at least one k-flip?
self_contained_problem:

For an integer $k \ge 2$, a *$k$-flip* on a plane perfect matching $M$ is an operation that selects $k$ edges $e_1,\dots,e_k$ of $M$, removes them, and replaces them with $k$ other straight-line segments $e'_1,\dots,e'_k$ on the same set of $2k$ endpoints, such that
(i) $\{e'_1,\dots,e'_k\} \ne \{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$, and
(ii) the resulting edge set $(M \setminus \{e_1,\dots,e_k\}) \cup \{e'_1,\dots,e'_k\}$ is again a plane perfect matching on $P$.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: If one generalizes the flip operation on plane perfect matchings by allowing the alternating cycle underlying a k-flip, for k ≥ 3, to have crossings among its own edges while the two participating matchings remain plane and no other edges are crossed, how does this affect the connectivity and shortest-flip questions above?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a set of $2m$ points in general position in the plane. A *plane perfect matching* on $P$ is a set of $m$ straight-line segments whose endpoints partition $P$ and such that no two segments cross.

Given two plane perfect matchings $M$ and $M'$ on $P$, their symmetric difference $M \triangle M'$ decomposes into edge-disjoint alternating cycles (cycles whose edges alternate between $M$ and $M'$). For an integer $k \ge 2$, a *$k$-flip* from $M$ to $M'$ is a transformation where $M \triangle M'$ consists of a single alternating cycle of length $2k$; that is, one removes $k$ edges of $M$ along this cycle and inserts the $k$ edges of $M'$ along it.

In the standard setting, both $M$ and $M'$ must be plane, and additionally the $2k$ edges of the alternating cycle must themselves form a non-crossing configuration. Define a *relaxed $k$-flip* (for $k \ge 3$) by weakening this requirement as follows: the edges of the alternating cycle of length $2k$ are allowed to cross each other, but no edge of the cycle is allowed to cross any edge of $M \cup M'$ that lies outside the cycle, and both $M$ and $M'$ must still be plane perfect matchings on $P$.

Let $G_k(P)$ be the graph whose vertices are the plane perfect matchings on $P$ and whose edges connect two matchings that differ by a relaxed $k$-flip (for some fixed $k \ge 3$, or alternatively by any relaxed $j$-flip with $3 \le j \le k$).

Determine:

(a) For which $k \ge 3$ and which classes of point sets $P$ is $G_k(P)$ connected?

(b) When $G_k(P)$ is connected, what are tight upper and lower bounds on its diameter, i.e., on the minimum number of relaxed flips needed to transform one plane perfect matching on $P$ into another?

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For token graphs T(G, a⃗) with a fixed number k of colors, what is the computational complexity of deciding whether the token graph is Hamiltonian, especially for intermediate values 3 ≤ k ≤ n−1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices and let $\vec a=(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k)$ be a tuple of positive integers with $a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_k=n$. The colored token graph $T(G,\vec a)$ is the graph whose vertices are the colorings of $V$ that use exactly $a_i$ vertices of color $i$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, where two such colorings are adjacent if one can be obtained from the other by swapping the colors of two adjacent vertices of $G$ that currently have different colors. Equivalently, $T(G,\vec a)$ has one vertex for each ordered partition $(V_1,\dots,V_k)$ of $V$ with $|V_i|=a_i$, with two partitions adjacent when they differ exactly by exchanging the parts of two endpoints of an edge of $G$.

It is known that deciding Hamiltonicity of $T(G,\vec a)$ is trivial for $k=1$, polynomial-time solvable for $k=n$ (i.e., when every $a_i=1$), and NP-complete for $k=2$ (since $T(G,(1,n-1))\cong G$).

Problem. For each fixed integer $k$ with $3\le k\le n-1$, determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem: given a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and a composition $\vec a=(a_1,\dots,a_k)$ of $n$ into $k$ positive parts, decide whether the token graph $T(G,\vec a)$ is Hamiltonian.
status_search_result: Literature on token graphs addresses Hamiltonicity for specific graph classes (e.g., join graphs) and the related but distinct colored token swapping problem (known NP-complete already for 3 colors), but no general complexity classification of Hamiltonicity of $T(G,\vec a)$ for intermediate fixed $k$ (with $3\le k\le n-1$) appears in the literature. The question is listed as an open problem.
