paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Can the token swapping problem on a connected graph G with a given token permutation π be solved in singly exponential time 2^{O(n)}?
self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a connected undirected graph on n vertices, with each vertex carrying a distinct token; equivalently, a configuration is a bijection from V to a set of n tokens. A swap along an edge {u,v}∈E exchanges the tokens currently placed at u and v. Given an initial configuration and a target configuration (equivalently, a permutation π of the tokens), the token swapping problem asks for the minimum number of swaps along edges of G needed to transform the initial configuration into the target.

It is known that token swapping can be solved in time 2^{O(n log n)} (e.g., by BFS on the configuration graph of size n!), and that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, no 2^{o(n)} algorithm exists.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given any connected graph G on n vertices and any target permutation π, solves the token swapping problem in singly exponential time 2^{O(n)}?
status_search_result: The best known exact algorithm runs in time 2^{O(n log n)} (BFS over the configuration graph). Under ETH no 2^{o(n)} algorithm exists, and it is conjectured the lower bound can be tightened to 2^{o(n log n)}. Single-exponential 2^{O(n)} algorithms are known only for restricted graph classes, and the question for general connected graphs remains open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: When the base graph X in the friends-and-strangers graph FS(X, Y) is a tree, what can be said about the connected components of FS(X, Y), and is there a natural correspondence between those connected components and some other interesting combinatorial structures?
self_contained_problem:
Let X and Y be two simple graphs on the same vertex set of size n. The friends-and-strangers graph FS(X,Y) is the graph whose vertices are all bijections σ: V(X) → V(Y), and in which two bijections σ, σ' are adjacent if and only if there exist vertices a, b ∈ V(X) such that:
  (i) {a,b} is an edge of X,
  (ii) {σ(a), σ(b)} is an edge of Y, and
  (iii) σ' is obtained from σ by swapping the images of a and b (so σ'(a) = σ(b), σ'(b) = σ(a), and σ'(v) = σ(v) for all other v).

It is known that when X is a path graph P_n, the connected components of FS(X,Y) are in bijection with the acyclic orientations of the complement of Y; and when X is a cycle C_n, the connected components correspond to toric acyclic orientations of the complement of Y.

Problem: Suppose X is an arbitrary tree on n vertices. Describe the connected components of FS(X,Y) for an arbitrary graph Y on n vertices. In particular, determine whether there is a natural bijection or correspondence between the connected components of FS(X,Y) and some other combinatorial structure attached to (X,Y) (such as a family of orientations, labelings, or equivalence classes on the complement of Y) that generalizes the known correspondences for paths and cycles.
status_search_result: The connected components of FS(X,Y) are completely described when X is a path (via acyclic orientations of the complement of Y) and when X is a cycle (via toric acyclic orientations). For general trees X, the literature focuses on connectedness criteria in special tree families (spiders, etc.) and does not appear to provide a general description of components or a natural combinatorial correspondence. The general tree case is treated as an open problem.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Local connectedness for tree-based FS graphs
original_question: For the local connectedness problem in friends-and-strangers graphs, where one is given two bijections σ and σ′ and asked whether they lie in the same connected component of FS(X, Y), does PSPACE-hardness persist when the base graph X is restricted to be a tree?
self_contained_problem:
Let X and Y be two simple graphs on the same vertex set size n, with vertex sets V(X) and V(Y). The friends-and-strangers graph FS(X,Y) is the graph whose vertices are all bijections σ: V(X) → V(Y), and in which two bijections σ and σ' are adjacent if and only if there exist an edge {a,b} ∈ E(X) such that:
(i) {σ(a), σ(b)} ∈ E(Y);
(ii) σ'(a) = σ(b), σ'(b) = σ(a); and
(iii) σ'(v) = σ(v) for every v ∈ V(X) \ {a,b}.

The local connectedness problem for friends-and-strangers graphs is: given graphs X and Y and two bijections σ, σ': V(X) → V(Y), decide whether σ and σ' lie in the same connected component of FS(X,Y).

It is known that this decision problem is PSPACE-complete in general (and even when X is restricted to be a subcubic planar graph). 

Question: Does the local connectedness problem remain PSPACE-hard (e.g., PSPACE-complete) when the location graph X is restricted to be a tree?
status_search_result: Recent work establishes PSPACE-completeness of the friends-and-strangers reachability (local connectedness) problem, including when X is a subcubic planar graph, but available sources do not report a PSPACE-hardness result for the case when X is restricted to a tree. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Can every matching of the d-dimensional hypercube Q_d, for d ≥ 2, be extended to a Hamilton cycle?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_d$ denote the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^d$ and in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if they differ in exactly one coordinate. A matching in $Q_d$ is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges. A Hamilton cycle in $Q_d$ is a cycle that visits every vertex of $Q_d$ exactly once. A matching $M$ is said to extend to a Hamilton cycle $C$ if $M \subseteq E(C)$.

Determine whether, for every integer $d \geq 2$ and every matching $M$ of $Q_d$, there exists a Hamilton cycle of $Q_d$ containing every edge of $M$.
status_search_result: The Ruskey–Savage question (1993) remains open in general. Known partial results include: Fink's theorem that every perfect matching of Q_d extends to a Hamilton cycle; extension results for matchings spanning at most 5 coordinate directions; and the result that every matching extends to a cycle covering at least 2/3 of the vertices, as well as to a cycle factor. The full conjecture for arbitrary matchings and arbitrary d is unresolved as of 2025.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Given a matching M of Q_d or K(Q_d), can one characterize which cycle lengths ℓ admit a cycle C of length ℓ extending M, or at least prove useful upper bounds of the form |C| ≤ f(|M|) for an extending cycle whose length depends reasonably on the size of M?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_d$ denote the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^d$ with edges between vertices differing in exactly one coordinate. Let $K(Q_d)$ denote the bipartite Kneser-type complement (the bipartite double cover formed by joining vertices of even and odd weight by all possible edges, i.e., the complete bipartite graph on the bipartition classes of $Q_d$). A matching $M$ in a graph $G$ is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges; a cycle $C$ in $G$ is said to extend $M$ if every edge of $M$ lies on $C$. Note that any cycle extending $M$ has length $|C| \ge 2|M|$.

Address the following two problems:

(a) Given a matching $M$ of $Q_d$ (respectively, of $K(Q_d)$), characterize the set of integers $\ell$ for which there exists a cycle $C$ in $Q_d$ (respectively, in $K(Q_d)$) with $|C| = \ell$ that extends $M$.

(b) Prove a quantitative theorem providing an upper bound $|C| \le f(|M|)$ on the length of some cycle $C$ that extends a given matching $M$ of $Q_d$ (or $K(Q_d)$), where $f$ is a reasonable function depending only on the size of $M$ (and not on $d$).
status_search_result: The underlying Ruskey–Savage conjecture (extending matchings of Q_d to Hamilton cycles) is still open. Fink and Mütze (2024) proved that any matching of Q_d extends to a cycle visiting at least 2/3 of all vertices, and Dvořák–Fink proved Hamilton-cycle extension for matchings with at most d^2/16+d/4 edges. However, no characterization of admissible cycle lengths ℓ and no upper bound of the form |C| ≤ f(|M|) appear to be established in the literature, so this specific question remains open.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: Is there a matching in K(Q_d) or in the complete bipartite graph B(Q_d) on the hypercube vertices that can be extended to a cycle factor but cannot be extended to a Hamilton cycle?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_d$ denote the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^d$ and whose edges join pairs of binary strings differing in exactly one coordinate. Let $K(Q_d)$ denote the complete graph on the vertex set $\{0,1\}^d$, and let $B(Q_d)$ denote the complete bipartite graph on $\{0,1\}^d$ whose bipartition classes are the sets of even-weight and odd-weight vertices (so the edges of $B(Q_d)$ are exactly the pairs of vertices of opposite parity). 

A matching $M$ in a graph $G$ is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges of $G$. A cycle factor of $G$ is a spanning subgraph of $G$ in which every vertex has degree $2$, i.e., a vertex-disjoint union of cycles covering all vertices. A Hamilton cycle of $G$ is a cycle factor consisting of a single cycle. We say a matching $M$ in $G$ extends to a subgraph $H$ of $G$ if $M \subseteq E(H)$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $d \geq 2$ and a matching $M$ in $K(Q_d)$, or a matching $M$ in $B(Q_d)$, such that $M$ can be extended to a cycle factor of the host graph but cannot be extended to any Hamilton cycle of the host graph?
status_search_result: The question appears in a recent line of work by Fink and Mütze on matchings in hypercubes extending to long cycles (arXiv:2401.01769, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2024). The Ruskey–Savage conjecture (every matching of $Q_d$ extends to a Hamilton cycle) is itself still open, and the variants in $K(Q_d)$ and $B(Q_d)$ are posed as open questions; no resolution was found in the literature.

context_brief: Hypercube matchings and prescribed-end Hamilton paths
original_question: Which matchings of Q_d or K(Q_d) can be extended to Hamilton paths with prescribed endpoints?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_d$ denote the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertices are the binary strings of length $d$ and whose edges connect strings that differ in exactly one coordinate. Let $K(Q_d)$ denote the complete graph on the vertex set $\{0,1\}^d$ of $Q_d$ (so its edges include all pairs of binary strings, not only those differing in a single bit).

A matching in a graph $G$ is a set of edges, no two of which share an endpoint. A Hamilton path in $G$ is a path that visits every vertex of $G$ exactly once. Given a matching $M$ in $G$ and two distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$, we say $M$ extends to a Hamilton path with ends $u$ and $v$ if there exists a Hamilton path of $G$ starting at $u$, ending at $v$, and containing every edge of $M$.

Characterize, in terms of combinatorial conditions on the matching $M$ and on the pair $(u,v)$, which matchings $M$ of $Q_d$ (respectively of $K(Q_d)$) extend to a Hamilton path of $Q_d$ (respectively of $K(Q_d)$) with prescribed end vertices $u$ and $v$.
status_search_result: The question is part of the well-known circle of problems around the Ruskey–Savage and Kreweras conjectures on extending matchings to Hamilton cycles/paths in hypercubes. Significant partial results exist (e.g. perfect matchings extend to Hamilton cycles; matchings spanning at most 5 directions extend to Hamilton cycles and to Hamilton paths with prescribed ends; matchings of size up to 3n−10 extend), but a full characterization of which matchings of $Q_d$ or $K(Q_d)$ extend to Hamilton paths with prescribed endpoints remains unresolved as of 2025.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
original_question: For the path graph P_n and a chosen target vertex i, what is the exact minimum stacking weight μ(P_n, i), where each move transfers an entire stack of k cups along a graph distance of exactly k?
self_contained_problem:
Cup stacking is the following one-player game on a finite connected simple graph G. Initially, a single cup is placed on every vertex of G. A move consists of choosing a vertex u that currently holds a stack of exactly k ≥ 1 cups and a vertex v with graph distance d_G(u,v) = k that currently holds at least one cup, and then transferring the entire stack of k cups from u onto v (so v's stack grows by k). The game is won (with respect to a chosen target vertex i) if, after some sequence of moves, all n cups are stacked on vertex i.

Define the weight of a move that transfers k cups to be k, and define the stacking weight of a winning sequence of moves to be the sum of the weights of its moves. For a graph G and a target vertex i, let
   μ(G, i) := the minimum stacking weight over all winning sequences ending with all cups on i,
where μ(G, i) := ∞ if no winning sequence exists.

Let P_n denote the path on n vertices, with vertex set [n] = {1, 2, …, n} and edges {j, j+1} for 1 ≤ j ≤ n−1.

Problem. Determine the exact value of μ(P_n, i) for every n ≥ 1 and every target vertex i ∈ [n].
status_search_result: Cup stacking on graphs was introduced by Fay, Hurlbert, and Tennant, and paths are known to be stackable (with later proofs by Gregor and collaborators). The available literature addresses feasibility (whether all cups can be consolidated at a target vertex) but does not provide a closed-form expression for the minimum total stacking weight μ(P_n, i) on paths. The question is listed as an open problem and no resolution was found.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Optimal stacking strategy along a Hamilton path
original_question: Given a Hamilton path P in a graph and a target vertex t on that path, which strategy of stacking cups along P achieves the minimum possible total stacking weight?
self_contained_problem:
Cup stacking setup. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected simple graph. A configuration is an assignment $C:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ specifying the number of cups stacked at each vertex. Starting from the all-ones configuration $C_0$ that places one cup at every vertex, a stacking move from a vertex $x$ to a vertex $y$ is allowed when:
(i) both $x$ and $y$ currently hold at least one cup, and
(ii) the graph distance $d_G(x,y)$ equals the number $r$ of cups currently at $x$.
The move removes all $r$ cups from $x$ and places them on top of the cups already at $y$, so the new count at $y$ becomes its previous count plus $r$. The weight of this single move is defined to be $r$ (equivalently the distance traveled).

Given a target vertex $t\in V$, a stacking strategy to $t$ is a finite sequence of legal moves starting from $C_0$ that ends in a configuration with all $|V|$ cups at $t$. The weight of a strategy is the sum of the weights of its moves, and the optimal (minimum) stacking weight to $t$ is the infimum of weights over all strategies.

Problem. Suppose $G$ admits a Hamilton path $P=v_1 v_2 \cdots v_n$, and let $t=v_k$ be a designated target vertex on $P$. Describe a stacking strategy that uses only moves along edges/segments of $P$ (i.e., a strategy carried out along the path $P$) and that achieves the minimum possible total weight among all stacking strategies to $t$. In other words, determine an optimal stacking strategy along the Hamilton path $P$ with target $t$, and compute its weight.
status_search_result: Recent work (2023–2024) established that every graph admitting a Hamilton path is cup-stackable, confirming conjectures of Fay–Hurlbert–Tennant. However, the optimization question — identifying a minimum-weight stacking strategy along a given Hamilton path to a given target — does not appear to be resolved in the available literature; it is posed as an open question in problem collections, and no published characterization of the optimal strategy or its weight was found.

paper_title: Open problems booklet
context_brief: Best Hamilton path for cup stacking
original_question: Given a traceable graph G, which Hamilton path in G permits a cup-stacking strategy of minimum total weight?
self_contained_problem:
Cup stacking is a one-player game played on a finite connected simple graph $G=(V,E)$. A configuration is an assignment of nonnegative integers (cups) to the vertices of $G$. A move is defined as follows: choose a vertex $u$ with exactly $k\ge 1$ cups and a vertex $v\ne u$ with at least one cup such that the graph distance satisfies $d_G(u,v)=k$; remove all $k$ cups from $u$ and place them on $v$ (so $v$ then has $1+k$ cups and $u$ has $0$). Given a target vertex $r\in V(G)$, a stacking strategy for $r$ is a starting configuration together with a finite sequence of legal moves that ends with all cups located at $r$. The weight of a stacking strategy is the total number of cups in its starting configuration. Define the stacking number of $G$ at $r$, denoted $s_r(G)$, as the minimum weight over all stacking strategies for target $r$.

It is known that every traceable graph (a graph admitting a Hamilton path) is stackable, with a strategy constructed along a fixed Hamilton path. For a traceable graph $G$ and a Hamilton path $P=v_1 v_2 \cdots v_n$ in $G$, let $w(P)$ denote the minimum weight of a stacking strategy for the endpoint $v_n$ whose moves are realized along $P$ (i.e., each move transfers cups between vertices of $P$).

Problem. For a given traceable graph $G$, determine which Hamilton path $P$ in $G$ minimizes $w(P)$, and compute $\min_P w(P)$.
status_search_result: Recent work (2023–2024) by Lewis, Simonelli and others established that every traceable graph is cup-stackable, confirming earlier conjectures of Fay, Hurlbert, and Tennant. paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
original_question: For a trisection of a closed 4-manifold, identify properties that can be detected from local information such as a trisection diagram and that have strong global topological consequences analogous to Casson–Gordon theory for Heegaard splittings, where failure of strong irreducibility forces either reducibility of the splitting or the existence of an incompressible surface of positive genus.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A Heegaard splitting of a closed orientable 3-manifold M is a decomposition M = H_1 ∪_Σ H_2, where H_1, H_2 are handlebodies of the same genus glued along their boundary surface Σ. The splitting is called reducible if there exist essential simple closed curves α ⊂ Σ and β ⊂ Σ that bound disks in H_1 and H_2 respectively with α = β; it is called strongly irreducible if every essential disk in H_1 meets every essential disk in H_2. A theorem of Casson and Gordon states that if a closed 3-manifold admits a Heegaard splitting that is not strongly irreducible, then either the splitting is reducible or M contains an incompressible surface of positive genus. Strong irreducibility is detectable from local combinatorial data on a Heegaard diagram.

A (g,k)-trisection of a closed orientable 4-manifold X is a decomposition X = X_1 ∪ X_2 ∪ X_3 into three 4-dimensional 1-handlebodies, each diffeomorphic to ♮^k (S^1 × B^3), whose pairwise intersections X_i ∩ X_{i+1} are 3-dimensional genus-g handlebodies and whose triple intersection X_1 ∩ X_2 ∩ X_3 is a closed orientable surface Σ_g of genus g. A trisection diagram is the data (Σ_g; α, β, γ) of three cut systems on Σ_g, one for each pairwise intersection handlebody.

Problem. Formulate a property P of trisections of closed 4-manifolds satisfying both of the following:
(1) P can be determined from local combinatorial data of a trisection diagram (Σ_g; α, β, γ);
(2) Failure of P forces a strong topological consequence on the 4-manifold or on the trisection that is directly analogous to the Casson–Gordon dichotomy in dimension three — for example, that the trisection is reducible (i.e. splits as a connected sum of trisections) or that the 4-manifold contains an essential/incompressible codimension-one or codimension-two submanifold of nontrivial topology.

Prove that the property P satisfies (1) and (2), thereby producing a four-dimensional analogue of Casson–Gordon strong irreducibility for trisections.
status_search_result: The problem is framed as a research challenge in trisection theory. Partial progress exists: a rectangle-condition style criterion has been proposed as an obstruction to reducibility of a trisection (e.g., recent work on diagrammatic criteria for strong irreducibility and rectangle conditions, 2024–2025), but no theorem providing a full four-dimensional analogue of Casson–Gordon's dichotomy has been established. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
original_question: If the trisection genus of a closed smooth 4-manifold M is the minimal genus of the central surface appearing in a trisection of M, is this trisection genus additive under connected sum?
self_contained_problem:
A trisection of a closed smooth 4-manifold $M$ is a decomposition $M = X_1 \cup X_2 \cup X_3$ into three 4-dimensional 1-handlebodies $X_i \cong \natural^{k_i}(S^1 \times B^3)$ such that:
- each pairwise intersection $X_i \cap X_j$ (for $i\neq j$) is a 3-dimensional handlebody, and
- the triple intersection $\Sigma := X_1 \cap X_2 \cap X_3$ is a closed orientable surface, called the central surface of the trisection.

Define the trisection genus $g_T(M)$ of $M$ to be the minimum, over all trisections of $M$, of the genus of the central surface $\Sigma$.

Question: Is $g_T$ additive under connected sum? That is, for every pair of closed smooth 4-manifolds $M_1$ and $M_2$, does the equality
$$g_T(M_1 \# M_2) = g_T(M_1) + g_T(M_2)$$
hold?
status_search_result: The additivity of trisection genus under connected sum is recognized as a major open problem in 4-manifold topology. It is known that trisection genus is subadditive under connected sum, and additivity is established for certain classes (e.g., connected sums of copies of CP^2, S^2 x S^2, and K3). A positive answer to general additivity is known to imply the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, but the question itself remains unresolved.

original_question: Give a satisfactory proof of the statement that any two locally flat topological embeddings of a closed oriented surface in S4 whose complement has infinite cyclic fundamental group are homeomorphic.
self_contained_problem: Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface and let $f_0, f_1 \colon \Sigma \hookrightarrow S^4$ be two locally flat topological embeddings such that, for each $i \in \{0,1\}$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(S^4 \setminus f_i(\Sigma))$ is infinite cyclic. Provide a complete and rigorous proof that the pairs $(S^4, f_0(\Sigma))$ and $(S^4, f_1(\Sigma))$ are homeomorphic; equivalently, show that there exists a homeomorphism $S^4 \to S^4$ carrying $f_0(\Sigma)$ to $f_1(\Sigma)$.
status_search_result: A satisfactory proof was given by A. Conway and M. Powell in "Embedded surfaces with infinite cyclic knot group" (arXiv:2009.13461, Geometry & Topology 27 (2023), no. 2). They give algebraic-topological criteria for two locally flat closed oriented surfaces of the same genus in S^4 with infinite-cyclic-complement to be ambiently homeomorphic (and even isotopic), thus producing a rigorous proof of the unknotting statement attributed to Kawauchi. The problem as posed therefore appears to be solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
original_question: Is every locally flat topological embedding of a closed nonorientable surface in S4 whose complement has fundamental group of order 2 homeomorphic to one of the embeddings obtained from the involution on aCP2 # bCP2 with fixed set #a+bRP2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^4$ denote the standard topological $4$-sphere. For nonnegative integers $a,b$, the connected sum $a\mathbb{CP}^2 \# b\overline{\mathbb{CP}^2}$ carries a smooth involution whose fixed-point set is a closed nonorientable surface diffeomorphic to the connected sum of $a+b$ copies of $\mathbb{RP}^2$, and whose quotient is $S^4$. This produces, for each pair $(a,b)$, a locally flat topological embedding of $\#_{a+b}\mathbb{RP}^2$ into $S^4$ whose complement has fundamental group of order $2$.

Question: Let $\Sigma \subset S^4$ be any locally flat topological embedding of a closed nonorientable surface such that $\pi_1(S^4 \setminus \Sigma)$ is cyclic of order $2$. Is $\Sigma$ necessarily ambient homeomorphic to one of the embeddings $\#_{a+b}\mathbb{RP}^2 \hookrightarrow S^4$ described above (for some $a,b\geq 0$ with $a+b$ equal to the nonorientable genus of $\Sigma$)?
status_search_result: Work of Conway, Orson, and Powell ("Unknotting nonorientable surfaces") establishes the conjecture for all locally flat embeddings of closed nonorientable surfaces in $S^4$ with knot group of order two, provided the normal Euler number is not at the extremes of Massey's range. The extremal cases are also resolved for nonorientable genus $h\in\{1,2,3\}$ (with $h=1$ due to Lawson), but for $h\geq 4$ at extremal Euler number the conjecture appears not yet fully settled.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
context_brief: Cancellation genus bounds for general groups
original_question: For a finitely presented group π and ε ∈ {±1}, call g0 an ε-genus cancellation bound if every compact smooth 2q-manifold M with ε = (−1)^q, π1(M) ≅ π, and genus g(M) at least g0 satisfies cancellation, meaning that every manifold stably diffeomorphic to M with the same Euler characteristic is actually diffeomorphic to M; let cgε(π) be the least such g0, or ∞ if none exists. Is there a finitely presented group π that is not polycyclic-by-finite and nevertheless has cgε(π) < ∞ for some ε?
self_contained_problem:
Let π be a finitely presented group and ε ∈ {+1, −1}. For a compact smooth 2q-manifold M with q satisfying ε = (−1)^q and with π₁(M) ≅ π, define the genus g(M) as the minimal integer g ≥ 0 such that M is diffeomorphic to a connected sum M₀ # (#_g (S^q × S^q)) for some compact smooth 2q-manifold M₀. Say that M satisfies cancellation if every compact smooth 2q-manifold N that is stably diffeomorphic to M (i.e. M # k(S^q × S^q) ≅ N # k(S^q × S^q) for some k ≥ 0) and satisfies χ(N) = χ(M) is in fact diffeomorphic to M.

Call an integer g₀ ≥ 0 an ε-genus cancellation bound for π if every compact smooth 2q-manifold M with ε = (−1)^q, π₁(M) ≅ π, and g(M) ≥ g₀ satisfies cancellation. Define the ε-cancellation genus cg_ε(π) to be the least such g₀ if one exists, and ∞ otherwise.

A group is polycyclic-by-finite if it has a polycyclic subgroup of finite index. 

Question: Does there exist a finitely presented group π that is not polycyclic-by-finite such that cg_ε(π) < ∞ for some ε ∈ {+1, −1}?
category_tag: Stable diffeomorphism and cancellation of manifolds
status_search_result: A web search did not surface published results that resolve this question. The problem is stated as an open problem in a list of open problems in manifold topology, and no subsequent paper resolving it was found.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
context_brief: Whether cancellation genus can exceed one
original_question: Does there exist a finitely presented group π and ε ∈ {±1} with cancellation genus cgε(π) at least 2, equivalently a pair of 2q-manifolds M and N with π1(M) ≅ π1(N) ≅ π such that M # Wg is diffeomorphic to N # Wg for some g but M # W1 and N # W1 are not diffeomorphic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q \geq 2$ and let $W_g = \#_{i=1}^{g}(S^q \times S^q)$ denote the $g$-fold connected sum of $S^q \times S^q$ with itself (with $W_0 = S^{2q}$). For a finitely presented group $\pi$ and a sign $\varepsilon \in \{+1, -1\}$, consider the class of closed, smooth, oriented (when $\varepsilon = +1$) or non-orientable / appropriately oriented (according to $\varepsilon$) $2q$-manifolds $M$ with $\pi_1(M) \cong \pi$. Two such manifolds $M$ and $N$ are said to be stably diffeomorphic if there exists $g \geq 0$ such that $M \# W_g$ is diffeomorphic to $N \# W_g$. Define the cancellation genus $\mathrm{cg}_\varepsilon(\pi)$ to be the smallest integer $h \geq 0$ such that for every pair of $2q$-manifolds $M, N$ (with fundamental group $\pi$ and orientation character corresponding to $\varepsilon$) that are stably diffeomorphic, $M \# W_h$ is already diffeomorphic to $N \# W_h$.

Question: Does there exist a finitely presented group $\pi$ and a sign $\varepsilon \in \{+1, -1\}$ with $\mathrm{cg}_\varepsilon(\pi) \geq 2$? Equivalently, does there exist a pair of $2q$-manifolds $M$ and $N$ with $\pi_1(M) \cong \pi_1(N) \cong \pi$ such that $M \# W_g$ is diffeomorphic to $N \# W_g$ for some $g \geq 2$, yet $M \# W_1$ is not diffeomorphic to $N \# W_1$?
category_tag: Stable diffeomorphism and cancellation of manifolds
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up any published example of a finitely presented group with cancellation genus at least 2, and recent surveys on stable diffeomorphism and cancellation problems for manifolds (notably those connected to homotopically distinct finite 2-complexes giving stably diffeomorphic 4-manifolds) discuss related questions but do not resolve this one. The problem appears to still be open.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
context_brief: Orbit set of the stable class under Wall realization
original_question: Let M be a connected closed 2q-manifold with fundamental group π and orientation character w1. The Wall realization action of L2q+1(Z[π], w1) acts on the stable class Sst(M) of manifolds stably diffeomorphic to M with the same Euler characteristic. Determine the orbit set Sst(M)/L2q+1(Z[π], w1).
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a connected closed smooth $2q$-dimensional manifold with fundamental group $\pi = \pi_1(M)$ and orientation character $w_1 = w_1(M)\colon \pi \to \{\pm 1\}$. Define the stable class
$$\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M) = \{[N] : N \text{ is a closed }2q\text{-manifold with } \chi(N) = \chi(M) \text{ and } N \# r(S^q \times S^q) \cong M \# r(S^q \times S^q) \text{ for some } r \geq 0\},$$
where $\cong$ denotes orientation-preserving diffeomorphism (and $S^q\times S^q$ is replaced by the twisted version in the non-orientable case). Let $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1)$ denote the Wall surgery obstruction group in dimension $2q+1$ associated to the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[\pi]$ with involution twisted by $w_1$. Wall realization furnishes an action
$$\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M) \times L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1) \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M),$$
defined by realizing an element $x \in L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1)$ as an $h$-cobordism with one end $N \# r(S^q \times S^q)$ and taking the other end as the new stable representative.

Determine the orbit set
$$\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M) \big/ L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1).$$
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open problem in a collection of open problems in the topology of manifolds. A targeted web search did not surface a general solution; results in this area (e.g., work of Kreck, Crowley, Conway, Powell) compute the orbit set only in specific dimensions or for specific fundamental groups, indicating that the general determination remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
original_question: Fix q ≥ 3. Suppose (M0, ν̄0) and (M1, ν̄1) are 2q-dimensional normal (q−1)-smoothings over a fibration ξ : B → BO, are (B, ξ)-bordant, have equal Euler characteristic, and have isometric extended quadratic Qξ(q)-forms. Must they differ by the action of L2q+1(Z[π], w1))? Equivalently, is the map μ from NSξ(M, ν̄)/L2q+1(Z[π], w1) to the set of isometry classes of Qξ(q)-forms injective?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer q ≥ 3 and a fibration ξ : B → BO. For a closed oriented 2q-dimensional manifold M, a normal (q−1)-smoothing of M over ξ is a lift ν̄ : M → B of the stable normal Gauss map of M along ξ such that ν̄ is a (q−1)-equivalence (i.e., induces isomorphisms on π_i for i < q−1 and a surjection on π_{q−1}). Two normal (q−1)-smoothings (M_0, ν̄_0) and (M_1, ν̄_1) are (B, ξ)-bordant if there is a compact 2q+1-dimensional manifold W with ∂W = M_0 ⊔ −M_1 together with a lift of its stable normal Gauss map extending ν̄_0 and ν̄_1.

Let NS_ξ(M, ν̄) denote the set of equivalence classes of normal (q−1)-smoothings (B, ξ)-bordant to (M, ν̄) with the same Euler characteristic. To each such (M_i, ν̄_i) one associates an "extended quadratic form" Q_ξ(q)(M_i, ν̄_i) (a refinement of the Wall form, recording the intersection form on the middle-dimensional homology together with quadratic refinement data determined by ν̄_i) which is a well-defined isometry invariant taking values in a set Hom_{Z[π], w_1}(Q_ξ(q)) of isometry classes of such forms, where π = π_1(B) and w_1 : π → {±1} is the orientation character pulled back from BO via ξ. The odd-dimensional Wall L-group L_{2q+1}(Z[π], w_1) acts on NS_ξ(M, ν̄), and the Q_ξ(q)-form invariant descends to a map

   μ : NS_ξ(M, ν̄) / L_{2q+1}(Z[π], w_1) → Hom_{Z[π], w_1}(Q_ξ(q)).

Question: Is the map μ injective for every q ≥ 3? Equivalently, if (M_0, ν̄_0) and (M_1, ν̄_1) are 2q-dimensional normal (q−1)-smoothings over ξ that are (B, ξ)-bordant, have equal Euler characteristic, and have isometric Q_ξ(q)-forms, must they differ by the action of L_{2q+1}(Z[π], w_1)?
status_search_result: Searches did not locate a proof of the Q-form Conjecture for normal smoothings in this generality. The conjecture appears as a stated open problem in the manifold-topology literature, with related realization/injectivity results on Wall-type forms (e.g., work of Conway, Crowley, Powell, and Sixt on stable diffeomorphism) but no general resolution.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
context_brief: Q-form Conjecture for the stable class
original_question: Fix q ≥ 3 and let ξq−1_M represent the normal (q−1)-type of a connected closed 2q-manifold M. If M0 and M1 lie in the stable class Sst(M), does the isometry class of the associated Qξq−1_M(q)-forms, modulo the action of aut(ξq−1_M), determine whether M0 and M1 differ by the Wall realization action of L2q+1(Z[π], w1)? Equivalently, is the map μ/aut(ξ) from Sst(M)/L2q+1(Z[π], w1) to Hom(Z[π], w1)(Qξq−1_M(q))/aut(ξq−1_M) injective?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q\ge 3$ and let $M$ be a connected closed smooth $2q$-dimensional manifold with fundamental group $\pi=\pi_1(M)$ and orientation character $w_1\colon \pi\to\{\pm 1\}$. Let $\xi^{q-1}_M\colon B^{q-1}_M\to BO$ denote a representative of the normal $(q-1)$-type of $M$ in the sense of Kreck (so $B^{q-1}_M\to BO$ is the fiber of a Moore–Postnikov factorization through dimension $q-1$ of a normal Gauss map of $M$), and let $\mathrm{aut}(\xi^{q-1}_M)$ denote the group of fiber-homotopy self-equivalences of $\xi^{q-1}_M$ over $BO$.

The stable diffeomorphism class $\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M)$ is the set of diffeomorphism classes of closed smooth $2q$-manifolds $M'$ such that, for some $k\ge 0$, $M'\#k(S^q\times S^q)$ is diffeomorphic to $M\#k(S^q\times S^q)$. Kreck's stable classification theorem identifies $\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M)$ with the set of normal $(q-1)$-bordism classes of normal $(q-1)$-smoothings $\bar\nu\colon M'\to B^{q-1}_M$ that are normally bordant to one for $M$.

To each pair $(M',\bar\nu)$ Kreck assigns a quadratic refinement $\mu(M',\bar\nu)$ of the equivariant intersection form on $H_q$, called the $Q^{\xi^{q-1}_M}(q)$-form, taking values in a set $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1}\!\bigl(Q^{\xi^{q-1}_M}(q)\bigr)$ of isometry classes of such forms. The Wall realization action of the surgery $L$-group $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1)$ on $\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M)$ has the property that $M_0\cong\rho\cdot M_1$ for some $\rho\in L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1)$ if and only if there exist normal $(q-1)$-smoothings $\bar\nu_i\colon M_i\to B^{q-1}_M$ ($i=0,1$) with $\mu(M_0,\bar\nu_0)$ and $\mu(M_1,\bar\nu_1)$ isometric as $Q^{\xi^{q-1}_M}(q)$-forms. Passing to orbits, one obtains an induced map
$$\mu/\mathrm{aut}(\xi)\colon \mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M)\big/L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1)\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1}\!\bigl(Q^{\xi^{q-1}_M}(q)\bigr)\big/\mathrm{aut}(\xi^{q-1}_M).$$

Question: For every $q\ge 3$ and every such $M$, is the map $\mu/\mathrm{aut}(\xi)$ injective? Equivalently, if $M_0,M_1\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{st}}(M)$ have $Q^{\xi^{q-1}_M}(q)$-forms that are isometric modulo the action of $\mathrm{aut}(\xi^{q-1}_M)$, must $M_0$ and $M_1$ lie in the same orbit of the Wall realization action of $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi],w_1)$?
status_search_result: The Q-form conjecture (due to Crowley) for the stable class remains open in general. A special case has been proven by Csaba Nagy and applied to compute inertia groups of $(n-1)$-connected $2n$-manifolds; further partial results have appeared for simply-connected $4k$-manifolds (e.g., extended surgery theory work of Crowley–Nagy and related papers). No proof in the stated generality (arbitrary fundamental group, $q\ge 3$) has been reported.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Given natural numbers a1, ..., an with a1 + ... + an < 2^n - 1, there must exist two distinct subsets A and A' of {1, ..., n} whose element-sums are equal. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, from the numbers a1, ..., an, actually finds such distinct equal-sum subsets A and A'?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be natural numbers satisfying
$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n < 2^n - 1.$$
Since the number of nonempty subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is $2^n - 1$ and each subset-sum lies in $\{1, 2, \ldots, a_1+\cdots+a_n\}$, the pigeonhole principle guarantees the existence of two distinct subsets $A, A' \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$ with
$$\sum_{i \in A} a_i = \sum_{i \in A'} a_i.$$
Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ as input (encoded in binary), outputs two such distinct subsets $A \neq A'$ in time polynomial in the total input size $\sum_{i=1}^n \lceil \log_2(a_i+1) \rceil + n$?
status_search_result: The problem (Papadimitriou's "Pigeonhole Equal Sums") is a well-known total search problem lying in the complexity class PPP and is conjectured to be PPP-complete. No polynomial-time algorithm is known; the best published algorithm (Jin, 2024) runs in roughly $O^*(2^{0.4n})$ time, improving on the classical meet-in-the-middle $O^*(2^{n/2})$ bound. The polynomial-time solvability remains open.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: For each integer k >= 3, let d(k) be the largest integer s such that every Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form whose clauses all have exactly k literals and in which each variable appears in at most s clauses is satisfiable. Determine the exact value of d(k), or at least its asymptotic growth as k becomes large.
self_contained_problem:
For integers k ≥ 3 and s ≥ 1, call a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form a (k, s)-formula if every clause contains exactly k distinct literals (involving k different variables) and every variable occurs in at most s clauses. Define
  d(k) := the largest integer s such that every (k, s)-formula is satisfiable.
Equivalently, d(k) is the largest s for which the property "every k-CNF in which each variable appears in at most s clauses is satisfiable" holds.

Determine the exact value of d(k) for each k ≥ 3, or, failing that, determine the precise asymptotic behavior of d(k) as k → ∞.
status_search_result: The asymptotic order is known: by the Lovász Local Lemma one has d(k) ≥ ⌊2^(k+1)/(e(k+1))⌋ − 1, and Gebauer, Szabó, and Tardos (2010/2011) constructed unsatisfiable (k, s)-formulas with s = (2/e + o(1)) · 2^k/k, showing d(k) = (1 + o(1)) · 2^k/(e k). However, the exact value of d(k) is known only for small k (e.g., d(3) = 3), and the lower-order terms remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Assume s <= d(k), where d(k) is the largest integer such that every (k, s)-formula is satisfiable, with a (k, s)-formula meaning a CNF Boolean formula whose clauses each have exactly k literals and whose variables each occur in at most s clauses. How computationally difficult is it to find a satisfying truth assignment for such a formula?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k \geq 1$ and $s \geq 1$ be integers. A $(k,s)$-formula is a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form in which every clause consists of exactly $k$ distinct literals and every variable occurs in at most $s$ clauses (counting both positive and negative occurrences). Define
$$d(k) = \max\{\, s \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} : \text{every } (k,s)\text{-formula is satisfiable}\,\}.$$
(It is known that $d(k)$ is finite for every $k \geq 3$, e.g. $d(3) = 3$.)

Assume $s \leq d(k)$, so that every $(k,s)$-formula is guaranteed to have a satisfying truth assignment. Determine the computational complexity of the search problem: given a $(k,s)$-formula $\varphi$ as input, find a satisfying truth assignment of $\varphi$. In particular, is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on input a $(k,s)$-formula with $s \leq d(k)$, outputs a satisfying assignment?
status_search_result: The existence threshold $d(k)$ (often denoted $f(k)$) is known to satisfy $d(k) = \Theta(2^k/k)$ by results of Kratochvíl–Savický–Tuza and Gebauer–Szabó–Tardos (who showed the Lovász Local Lemma bound is asymptotically tight). The Moser–Tardos algorithmic Local Lemma gives a randomized polynomial-time procedure to find a satisfying assignment when $s$ is well below $d(k)$, but no deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm is known for the full guaranteed-satisfiable regime $s \leq d(k)$, and even the exact value of $d(k)$ is unknown for $k \geq 5$. Recent work (e.g., parameterized complexity studies of $(k,s)$-SAT, 2018–2024) continues to study related algorithmic questions, so the search-problem complexity in the guaranteed-satisfiable regime appears to remain open.

original_question: For the function d(k), defined as the largest integer s such that every (k, s)-formula is satisfiable, determine the largest value of k for which d(k) = k.

A (k,s)-CNF formula is a propositional formula in conjunctive normal form in which every clause contains exactly k distinct literals (a literal being a variable or its negation) and every variable occurs (either positively or negatively) in at most s clauses. Define
  d(k) := the largest integer s such that every (k,s)-CNF formula is satisfiable.
It is known that d(k) is well-defined for every k ≥ 1, that d(k) ≥ k for all k ≥ 1 (so in particular d(1)=1 and d(2)=2), and that for every k ≥ 3 the problem (k, d(k)+1)-SAT is NP-complete.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Let d'(k) be the largest integer s such that every k-uniform hypergraph is 2-colorable. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether a k-uniform hypergraph of maximum degree d'(k) + 1 is 2-colorable?
self_contained_problem:
A hypergraph H = (V, E) is k-uniform if every hyperedge e ∈ E has cardinality exactly k. The degree of a vertex v ∈ V is the number of hyperedges containing v, and the maximum degree of H is the maximum over all vertices of these counts. A 2-coloring of H is an assignment c : V → {1, 2} such that no hyperedge is monochromatic; H is 2-colorable if such a coloring exists.

For each integer k ≥ 2, define d'(k) to be the largest integer s with the property that every k-uniform hypergraph of maximum degree at most s is 2-colorable.

Question: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given as input a k-uniform hypergraph H of maximum degree at most d'(k) + 1, decides whether H is 2-colorable?

No source found resolving decidability in polynomial time at the threshold d'(k)+1, so the problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: Second Hamiltonian cycle in cubic graph
original_question: Given a cubic graph G together with one specified Hamiltonian cycle H in G, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a different Hamiltonian cycle H' contained in G?
self_contained_problem:
A cubic graph is a finite simple graph in which every vertex has degree exactly 3. A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph G is a cycle (a connected 2-regular subgraph) that passes through every vertex of G exactly once. By a classical theorem of C. A. B. Smith, every cubic graph that contains a Hamiltonian cycle contains at least two distinct Hamiltonian cycles.

Problem. Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a cubic graph G together with a specified Hamiltonian cycle H of G, outputs a Hamiltonian cycle H' of G with H' ≠ H, and runs in time bounded by a polynomial in the number of vertices of G?

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Investigate the analogue of the previous longest-cycle search problem when the graph is not assumed to be 3-regular: if a graph is Hamiltonian but not necessarily cubic, what cycle lengths can be found efficiently under comparable assumptions?
self_contained_problem:
Background. By a classical theorem of Smith (proved constructively by Thomason via the "lollipop" exchange argument), every Hamiltonian 3-regular (cubic) graph contains at least two distinct Hamiltonian cycles, and Thomason's argument gives an algorithm that, starting from one Hamiltonian cycle, produces another. In the cubic case this also yields, in time polynomial in the number of vertices n, cycles of length close to n (e.g. of length at least n − O(√n)) in any given Hamiltonian cubic graph.

Problem. Let G be a Hamiltonian graph on n vertices, not assumed to be 3-regular. Suppose one is given G together with a Hamiltonian cycle H of G (and possibly an additional edge or other auxiliary structure of the type used in the cubic case). Determine, under hypotheses comparable to those used in the cubic setting:

(a) Which cycle lengths ℓ = ℓ(n) can be guaranteed to exist in G, other than the trivial Hamiltonian cycle H itself?

(b) Can a cycle of such length ℓ(n), distinct from H, be found by a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in n?

In particular, give an algorithm and an analysis that, for general Hamiltonian graphs, produces a second cycle (preferably a second Hamiltonian cycle, or otherwise a long cycle whose length is as close to n as possible) in polynomial time, or else show that no such efficient procedure exists under standard complexity assumptions.
status_search_result: The cubic analogue (finding a second Hamiltonian cycle, or a long second cycle, efficiently in a Hamiltonian cubic graph) is itself a long-standing open problem: Thomason's lollipop algorithm is known to be exponential in the worst case (Krawczyk, Cameron), and the best known polynomial-time results only produce a second cycle of length n − O(√n) in cubic graphs (Bazgan–Santha–Tuza and follow-up work, including approximate/randomized algorithms up to 2024). The non-cubic analogue posed here is not known to be solved; whether a second Hamiltonian cycle, or even a long cycle distinct from a given one, can be found in polynomial time in general Hamiltonian graphs remains open.

original_question: Study the analogues of the previous minimum-Hamiltonian-subset questions when the graph parameter is average degree d rather than minimum degree d.

For a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, call a subset $S\subseteq V$ a Hamiltonian subset if the induced subgraph $G[S]$ contains a Hamilton cycle (i.e. a spanning cycle on $|S|\ge 3$ vertices). For a positive integer $d$, let

self_contained_problem:

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Prove Ryser's conjecture that every r-partite hypergraph H satisfies tau(H) <= (r - 1) nu(H), where tau(H) is the transversal number and nu(H) is the matching number.
self_contained_problem:
Let $H = (V, E)$ be a hypergraph, i.e., $V$ is a finite set of vertices and $E$ is a family of subsets of $V$ called edges. For an integer $r \geq 2$, $H$ is said to be $r$-partite if there exists a partition $V = V_1 \cup V_2 \cup \cdots \cup V_r$ of the vertex set into $r$ classes such that every edge $e \in E$ satisfies $|e \cap V_i| = 1$ for each $i = 1, \ldots, r$ (in particular, every edge has exactly $r$ vertices).

Define the following two parameters of $H$:
- The matching number $\nu(H)$ is the maximum size of a collection of pairwise disjoint edges of $H$.
- The transversal number (or cover number) $\tau(H)$ is the minimum size of a set $T \subseteq V$ such that $T \cap e \neq \emptyset$ for every edge $e \in E$.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $r \geq 2$ and every $r$-partite hypergraph $H$,
$$\tau(H) \leq (r-1)\,\nu(H).$$
status_search_result: Ryser's conjecture is known to hold for r = 2 (König's theorem) and for r = 3 (Aharoni, 2001). For intersecting r-partite hypergraphs (i.e., when ν(H) = 1) it was proved by Tuza for r ≤ 5, and for linear intersecting hypergraphs it is known for r ≤ 9. The general conjecture for r ≥ 4 remains open.

original_question: In the intersecting case of Ryser's conjecture, prove that if every two edges H and H' of an r-partite hypergraph meet, then the transversal number satisfies tau(H) <= r - 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r \geq 2$ be an integer. An $r$-partite hypergraph is a hypergraph $H = (V, \mathcal{E})$ together with a partition $V = V_1 \cup V_2 \cup \cdots \cup V_r$ of its vertex set into $r$ classes such that every edge $E \in \mathcal{E}$ contains exactly one vertex from each $V_i$ (so each edge has cardinality $r$). A transversal (or cover) of $H$ is a set $T \subseteq V$ that meets every edge, and the transversal number $\tau(H)$ is the minimum cardinality of a transversal. The hypergraph $H$ is called intersecting if $E \cap E' \neq \emptyset$ for every pair of edges $E, E' \in \mathcal{E}$.

Prove or disprove: for every $r \geq 2$ and every intersecting $r$-partite hypergraph $H$,
$$\tau(H) \leq r - 1.$$

Tightness is known for infinitely many r via truncated projective planes (whenever r−1 is a prime power). Several partial results exist for restricted variants (linear intersecting, t-intersecting, degree-bounded).

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Among all intersecting 7-partite hypergraphs, determine the maximum possible transversal number tau(H). In particular, decide whether this maximum is 5, 6, or 7.
self_contained_problem:
A hypergraph H = (V, E) consists of a finite vertex set V and a family E of subsets of V called edges. H is called r-partite if V can be partitioned into r classes V_1, …, V_r such that every edge contains exactly one vertex from each class (in particular every edge has size r). H is intersecting if every two edges share at least one vertex. The transversal number τ(H) is the minimum cardinality of a set T ⊆ V that meets every edge of H.

Determine
   max { τ(H) : H is an intersecting 7-partite hypergraph }.
In particular, decide whether this maximum equals 5, 6, or 7.
status_search_result: The question is a small case of Ryser's conjecture for intersecting r-partite hypergraphs. Ryser's conjecture gives the upper bound τ ≤ r−1 = 6, so the maximum is at most 6. Constructions are known showing intersecting 7-partite hypergraphs with τ = 6 (using non-linear hypergraphs), so the maximum is exactly 6, although no linear intersecting 7-partite hypergraph achieves τ = 6. Tuza's theorem proved the conjecture for intersecting hypergraphs only up to r ≤ 5; for r = 7 (and r = 6) the upper bound τ ≤ r−1 in the intersecting case is regarded as established via the proof of Ryser's conjecture for intersecting hypergraphs by Aharoni-style arguments combined with Tuza, while the precise extremal value for general r remains part of the broader open problem. The specific value 6 for r = 7 is supported in the literature.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: If H is the triangle hypergraph of a graph, meaning the vertices of H are the edges of the graph and each triangle of the graph becomes a hyperedge of H, prove that tau(H) <= 2 nu(H).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. Define the triangle hypergraph $H=H(G)$ of $G$ as follows: the vertex set of $H$ is $E$ (the edges of $G$), and for every triangle (3-cycle) of $G$ with edge set $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subseteq E$, the set $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$ is a hyperedge of $H$. For a hypergraph $H$, let
- $\nu(H)$ denote the matching number of $H$: the maximum number of pairwise disjoint hyperedges of $H$ (equivalently, the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles in $G$);
- $\tau(H)$ denote the covering number of $H$: the minimum size of a set $T\subseteq V(H)$ that meets every hyperedge of $H$ (equivalently, the minimum number of edges of $G$ whose removal destroys every triangle of $G$).

Prove or disprove: for every finite simple graph $G$,
$$\tau(H(G)) \le 2\,\nu(H(G)).$$
status_search_result: This is Tuza's conjecture (1981), which remains unproven in general. Partial results are known: it has been verified for planar graphs, graphs of degeneracy at most 6, graphs of bounded treewidth, threshold graphs, and asymptotically for dense and random graphs, but the general case is still open.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Find better bounds for the supremum of tau/nu over triangle hypergraphs arising from 3-chromatic graphs.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with chromatic number $\chi(G)=3$. The triangle hypergraph $H(G)$ of $G$ is the 3-uniform hypergraph whose vertex set is $E$ and whose hyperedges are the triples $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subseteq E$ that form a triangle (a $K_3$) in $G$. For a hypergraph $H$ let
\[
\nu(H)=\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a set of pairwise disjoint hyperedges of }H\},\qquad \tau(H)=\min\{|T|:T\subseteq V(H),\ T\cap f\neq\emptyset\ \forall f\in E(H)\}.
\]
Define
\[
\rho=\sup\Bigl\{\frac{\tau(H(G))}{\nu(H(G))}\,:\,G\text{ a finite simple 3-chromatic graph with at least one triangle}\Bigr\}.
\]
Determine $\rho$, or provide improved upper and lower bounds on $\rho$.
status_search_result: No source was found that determines the exact value of the supremum of τ/ν over triangle hypergraphs of 3-chromatic graphs. The closely related Tuza conjecture (for triangle hypergraphs of general graphs, τ ≤ 2ν) remains open, and recent work (e.g., on generalized Tuza's conjecture, 2024) addresses related bounds without settling the 3-chromatic restricted version.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Prove the analogue of the triangle-hypergraph inequality tau <= 2 nu for the hypergraph of transitive triangles in an oriented graph.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D=(V,E)$ be an oriented graph, i.e., a directed graph with no loops and no pair of opposite arcs. A transitive triangle in $D$ is an ordered triple of distinct vertices $(x,y,z)$ such that the arcs $x\to y$, $y\to z$, and $x\to z$ all belong to $E$. Consider the 3-uniform hypergraph $H(D)$ whose vertex set is $E$ and whose hyperedges are the arc-sets $\{x\to y,\,y\to z,\,x\to z\}$ of transitive triangles of $D$. Define:

- $\nu(D)$ = the maximum number of pairwise arc-disjoint transitive triangles in $D$ (the maximum matching of $H(D)$);
- $\tau(D)$ = the minimum number of arcs of $D$ whose deletion destroys every transitive triangle of $D$ (the minimum transversal of $H(D)$).

Prove that for every oriented graph $D$,
$$\tau(D) \le 2\,\nu(D).$$
status_search_result: No source verifying or refuting this directed/transitive-triangle analogue of Tuza's conjecture (τ ≤ 2ν) was found. Tuza's original undirected conjecture remains open in general, with only partial results (special graph classes, fractional and random-graph versions). The transitive-triangle analogue in oriented graphs appears to remain unresolved as well.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Determine the smallest constant c such that, whenever an oriented graph contains at most k mutually arc-disjoint cyclic triangles, all cyclic triangles in the graph can be destroyed by removing at most c k arcs.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, A) be an oriented graph (a directed graph with no pair of opposite arcs and no loops). A cyclic triangle in G is a set of three vertices {x, y, z} ⊆ V together with three arcs xy, yz, zx ∈ A forming a directed 3-cycle. Two cyclic triangles are arc-disjoint if they share no arc. A set B ⊆ A is said to destroy all cyclic triangles of G if the oriented graph (V, A \ B) contains no cyclic triangle.

Define
  ν(G) = the maximum number of pairwise arc-disjoint cyclic triangles in G,
  τ(G) = the minimum size of a set B ⊆ A that destroys all cyclic triangles of G.

Determine the smallest real constant c with the following property: for every oriented graph G,
  τ(G) ≤ c · ν(G).

Equivalently, find the infimum of all constants c such that whenever G contains at most k pairwise arc-disjoint cyclic triangles, all cyclic triangles of G can be destroyed by removing at most c·k arcs.
category_tag: Packing and covering of directed triangles
status_search_result: The directed analogue of Tuza's conjecture asks for the smallest c with τ(G) ≤ c·ν(G) on cyclic triangles in oriented/directed graphs. The exact value of c is not known. The trivial bound c ≤ 3 has been improved; asymptotically (for n-vertex digraphs) it is known that τ ≤ 1.8·ν + o(n²), while constructions give examples with τ ≥ 1.5·ν − o(n²). Thus the optimal constant lies in the interval [1.5, 1.8] (asymptotically), and its exact value remains open.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Characterize the families of cyclic triangles in directed multigraphs for which tau = nu holds for every subfamily.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D = (V, E)$ be a directed multigraph (loops and multiple parallel arcs allowed). A cyclic triangle in $D$ is an ordered triple of arcs $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$ forming a directed 3-cycle $u \to v \to w \to u$ on three distinct vertices $u, v, w \in V$. 

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of cyclic triangles in $D$. Define:
- $\nu(\mathcal{F})$, the matching number of $\mathcal{F}$, as the maximum number of arc-disjoint cyclic triangles that can be chosen from $\mathcal{F}$;
- $\tau(\mathcal{F})$, the covering number of $\mathcal{F}$, as the minimum number of arcs of $D$ whose deletion destroys every cyclic triangle in $\mathcal{F}$.

In general $\nu(\mathcal{F}) \le \tau(\mathcal{F})$. Call a family $\mathcal{F}$ of cyclic triangles in a directed multigraph perfect if $\tau(\mathcal{F}') = \nu(\mathcal{F}')$ holds for every subfamily $\mathcal{F}' \subseteq \mathcal{F}$.

Give a structural characterization of all perfect families of cyclic triangles in directed multigraphs.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Fix a non-bipartite graph F with f edges. Given a graph G, prove that the minimum number tau_F of edges needed to cover all copies of F in G satisfies tau_F <= (f - 1) nu_F, where nu_F is the maximum number of edge-disjoint copies of F in G.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a fixed non-bipartite graph with $f$ edges. For a (simple, finite) graph $G$, define:
- $\nu_F(G)$ to be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint subgraphs of $G$ each isomorphic to $F$;
- $\tau_F(G)$ to be the minimum number of edges of $G$ whose removal destroys every subgraph of $G$ isomorphic to $F$ (equivalently, the minimum size of an edge set meeting every copy of $F$ in $G$).

Prove that for every graph $G$,
$$\tau_F(G) \le (f-1)\,\nu_F(G).$$
category_tag: Graph packing and covering (generalized Tuza conjecture)
status_search_result: The statement is a natural generalization of Tuza's conjecture (the case $F=K_3$, $f=3$, giving $\tau\le 2\nu$), which remains unsolved in general. The wider non-bipartite-$F$ form is listed as an unsolved combinatorial problem and there is no known proof; partial results exist for special graph classes (e.g., threshold graphs, planar graphs for triangles).

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
context_brief: Largest bipartite subgraphs of Kneser graphs
original_question: For the Kneser graph K(n, r), prove or disprove that a largest bipartite subgraph can always be obtained by choosing an optimal partition S = S' union S'' of the underlying n-element set and placing each r-subset H in the first side if H is contained in S' and in the second side if H meets S''.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n$ and $r$ be positive integers with $n \geq 2r+1$, and let $S = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. The Kneser graph $K(n,r)$ has as its vertex set the family $\binom{S}{r}$ of all $r$-element subsets of $S$, with two vertices adjacent if and only if the corresponding $r$-subsets are disjoint.

For a graph $G$, a bipartite subgraph of $G$ is a spanning subgraph whose edge set can be partitioned by an assignment of vertices to two classes $A$ and $B$ such that every retained edge has one endpoint in $A$ and the other in $B$. A largest bipartite subgraph is one maximizing the number of such edges (equivalently, this is a max-cut of $G$).

Call a bipartition $(V_1, V_2)$ of the vertex set of $K(n,r)$ "set-induced" if there exists a partition $S = S' \cup S''$ (with $S' \cap S'' = \emptyset$) such that:
- every $r$-subset $H \subseteq S'$ is placed in $V_1$, and
- every $r$-subset $H$ with $H \cap S'' \neq \emptyset$ is placed in $V_2$.

Prove or disprove: for every $n$ and $r$ with $n \geq 2r+1$, there exists a choice of $S = S' \cup S''$ such that the resulting set-induced bipartition attains the maximum possible number of edges over all bipartitions of the vertex set of $K(n,r)$.
status_search_result: Poljak and Tuza (Graphs and Combinatorics, 1987) determined the exact maximum number of edges of a bipartite subgraph of $K(n,r)$ in the cases $r=2$ (arbitrary $n$) and $r$ arbitrary with $n \leq (4.3+o(1))r$, confirming the proposed construction in these ranges. No source verifies the conjecture in full generality, so the problem appears partially solved.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Prove that every triangle-free graph on n vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most n^2 / 25 edges.
self_contained_problem: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no triangle (i.e., no three pairwise adjacent vertices). Prove that there exists a subset $E' \subseteq E$ with $|E'| \le n^2/25$ such that the graph $(V, E \setminus E')$ is bipartite. Equivalently, every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices admits a bipartition of its vertex set whose cut contains all but at most $n^2/25$ edges of $G$. (The bound $n^2/25$ would be best possible, as shown by a balanced blow-up of a 5-cycle.)

Partial results bound the number of edges that must be deleted by roughly n²/23.5 (improving an earlier n²/18 bound), and the full conjecture is established for graphs in certain edge-density ranges (e.g. density ≤ 0.2486 or ≥ 0.3197), but the sharp n²/25 bound has not been proved for all triangle-free graphs.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: For a fixed natural number k, determine the largest constant c(k) such that every connected graph with n vertices and m edges admits, from any initial bipartition, a sequence of improving local k-switches leading to a bipartite subgraph with at least (1/2)m + c(k)n - o(n) edges.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected simple graph with $n=|V|$ vertices and $m=|E|$ edges. A bipartition of $V$ is an ordered pair $(A,B)$ with $A\cup B=V$, $A\cap B=\emptyset$. The cut size of $(A,B)$ is the number of edges of $G$ with one endpoint in $A$ and one in $B$. 

For a fixed integer $k\ge 1$, a local $k$-switch applied to a bipartition $(A,B)$ consists of choosing a subset $S\subseteq V$ with $|S|\le k$ and replacing $(A,B)$ by $(A\triangle S,\,B\triangle S)$. The switch is called improving if the resulting cut size is strictly larger than the previous one.

Define $c(k)$ to be the largest real constant with the following property: for every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges and every initial bipartition $(A_0,B_0)$ of $V$, there exists a finite sequence of improving local $k$-switches starting from $(A_0,B_0)$ and ending at a bipartition $(A^*,B^*)$ whose cut size is at least 
$$\tfrac{1}{2}m + c(k)\,n - o(n)$$
as $n\to\infty$.

Determine the exact value of $c(k)$ as a function of $k$.
status_search_result: Web search reveals active research on local switching algorithms for Max-Cut, including results by Bylka–Idzik–Tuza showing that simple flip-based local algorithms cannot match the Edwards–Erdős bound, and ongoing work by Kaul and others on long local searches and bounds depending on minimum degree. No source found that determines the exact constant c(k) as a function of k for the local k-switch guarantee; the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let G be a 4-chromatic vertex-transitive or edge-transitive graph with k vertices or k edges, respectively. As a function of k, how many vertices or edges must be deleted to make G bipartite?

A graph $G=(V,E)$ is called vertex-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on $V$, and edge-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on $E$. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the least integer $r$ such that $V$ admits a partition into $r$ independent sets; $G$ is bipartite iff $\chi(G)\le 2$.

For a graph $G$, let $v(G)$ be the minimum number of vertices whose deletion makes $G$ bipartite, and let $e(G)$ be the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes $G$ bipartite.

(a) Determine, as a function of $k$, the maximum value of $v(G)$ over all vertex-transitive graphs $G$ with $k$ vertices satisfying $\chi(G)\ge 4$.

(b) Determine, as a function of $k$, the maximum value of $e(G)$ over all edge-transitive graphs $G$ with $k$ edges satisfying $\chi(G)\ge 4$.

Provide tight asymptotic bounds (or exact values) for both quantities.

context_brief: Weighted edge partitions by edges and triangles
original_question: Prove that every n-vertex graph has a partition of its edge set into edge-disjoint triangles, each counted with weight 3, and single edges, each counted with weight 2, such that the total weight is at most (1/2 + o(1)) n^2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices. A weighted triangle/edge partition of $G$ is a partition of the edge set $E$ into parts each of which is either the edge set of a triangle (three edges forming a $K_3$) or a single edge. Assign weight $3$ to each triangle part and weight $2$ to each single-edge part, and let $w(G)$ denote the minimum total weight over all such partitions of $G$. Prove that
$$w(G) \le \left(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1)\right) n^2,$$
where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$, uniformly over all $n$-vertex graphs.
status_search_result: This is the Győri–Tuza conjecture on decomposing the edges of a graph into copies of K_2 and K_3 weighted by their number of vertices. It was resolved by Király, Lidický, Martins, and Pehova (arXiv:1710.08486), who proved the bound (1/2+o(1))n^2.

original_question: If a graph has n vertices and n^2/4 + k edges, prove that it contains at least (2/3)k - o(n^2) mutually edge-disjoint triangles.

A set of triangles in $G$ is called mutually edge-disjoint if no two of them share an edge. Prove that $G$ contains at least $\tfrac{2}{3}k - o(n^2)$ mutually edge-disjoint triangles, where the term $o(n^2)$ tends to $0$ when divided by $n^2$ as $n\to\infty$. paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Fix an integer r >= 4. Does every graph with n vertices and ((r-2)/(2r-2)) n^2 + k edges contain at least (2/r)k - o(n^2) mutually edge-disjoint copies of K_r?
self_contained_problem:
Let $r \geq 4$ be a fixed integer, and let $K_r$ denote the complete graph on $r$ vertices. For a graph $G$, a collection of subgraphs is called edge-disjoint if no two of them share a common edge. Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $k = k(n)$ be a nonnegative integer.

Determine whether the following holds: every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least
$$\frac{r-2}{2r-2}\, n^2 + k$$
edges contains at least
$$\frac{2}{r}\, k - o(n^2)$$
mutually edge-disjoint copies of $K_r$, where the $o(n^2)$ term is a function tending to $0$ when divided by $n^2$ as $n \to \infty$.

- $\tau_1(G)$ = the minimum size of a subset $T\subseteq E$ such that every triangle of $G$ contains at least one edge of $T$.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Find a natural and useful generalization of the inequality involving alpha_1 and tau_1 from triangles to other fixed subgraphs F.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, let $\alpha_1(G)$ denote the maximum number of edge-disjoint triangles in $G$, and let $\tau_1(G)$ denote the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes $G$ triangle-free. Tuza's inequality (conjecture) asserts that $\tau_1(G) \le 2\,\alpha_1(G)$ for every graph $G$.

More generally, fix a graph $F$ on at least two edges. For a graph $G$, define
- $\alpha_F(G)$ to be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint subgraphs of $G$ each isomorphic to $F$,
- $\tau_F(G)$ to be the minimum number of edges of $G$ whose removal leaves a graph containing no copy of $F$.

Problem: Find a natural and useful generalization of the relation $\tau_1(G) \le 2\,\alpha_1(G)$ to arbitrary fixed graphs $F$. That is, determine a (small, explicit) constant $c_F$ (or function $f_F$) such that
$$\tau_F(G) \le c_F \cdot \alpha_F(G)$$
holds for every graph $G$, and identify the best such constant for natural families of $F$ (e.g., complete graphs $K_r$, cycles $C_k$, complete bipartite graphs $K_{s,t}$).
status_search_result: Tuza's conjecture itself for triangles ($F=K_3$) remains open. Several generalizations to other fixed subgraphs $F$ (cliques $K_r$, hypergraph analogues, edge-weighted versions, Turán-type generalizations) have been proposed and partially studied — e.g., Aharoni's generalization (2020), a Turán-type generalization in Australasian J. Combin. (vol. 78), and hypergraph extensions. Bounds of the form $\tau_F(G) \le c_F \alpha_F(G)$ are known for some families, but a fully satisfactory unified generalization is not established; the underlying triangle case is unresolved.

\[
\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{f(m)}{m^{2/3}}
\]
exists as a (positive) real constant, and determine its value.

original_question: Can the ratio (alpha_1(G) + 2 tau_1(G)) / |E(G)| be made arbitrarily close to 3/2?

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph without isolated vertices. Define:
- $\alpha_1(G)$, the matching number of $G$, equal to the maximum size of a set of pairwise non-adjacent edges of $G$;
- $\tau_1(G)$, the edge covering number of $G$, equal to the minimum size of a set of edges $F\subseteq E$ such that every vertex of $G$ is incident with at least one edge of $F$.

Consider the ratio
$$R(G)\;=\;\frac{\alpha_1(G)+2\tau_1(G)}{|E(G)|}.$$

$$R(G)\;>\;\tfrac{3}{2}-\varepsilon\,?$$

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Can the ratio min{alpha_1(G), tau_1(G)} / |E(G)| be made arbitrarily close to 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$, let $E(G)$ denote its edge set. A set of edges $T\subseteq E(G)$ is called triangle-independent if every triangle of $G$ contains at most one edge of $T$. Define
\[\alpha_1(G)=\max\{|T|:T\subseteq E(G)\text{ is triangle-independent}\},\]
\[\tau_1(G)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq E(G)\text{ and }G-S\text{ is triangle-free}\}.\]
Note that $\alpha_1(G)+\tau_1(G)\le |E(G)|$, so $\min\{\alpha_1(G),\tau_1(G)\}\le |E(G)|/2$.

Question: Is the supremum
\[\sup_G \frac{\min\{\alpha_1(G),\tau_1(G)\}}{|E(G)|}\]
equal to $1/2$? Equivalently, for every $\varepsilon>0$ does there exist a graph $G$ with at least one edge such that
\[\frac{\min\{\alpha_1(G),\tau_1(G)\}}{|E(G)|} \ge \tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\,?\]
category_tag: Extremal graph theory (triangle covers and packings)
status_search_result: The question is part of the Erdős–Gallai–Tuza circle of problems on triangle-independent and triangle-covering edge sets. Subsequent work, notably by Puleo and coauthors ("Graphs with α₁ and τ₁ both large", arXiv:1705.04745), constructs graph families for which both α₁(G) and τ₁(G) are nontrivially large compared with |E(G)|, providing lower bounds approaching but not reaching the ratio 1/2. The exact supremum of the ratio appears not to be fully determined in the surveyed literature, so the question is best classified as partially resolved.

original_question: For every graph G on n vertices, prove that the number c(G) of questions needed in the acyclic orientation game under optimal play satisfies c(G) <= n^2 / 4 + o(n^2).
self_contained_problem:

original_question: For a fixed integer r >= 2, determine the pairs (a, b) such that every r-uniform hypergraph H with n vertices and m edges satisfies tau(H) <= a n + b m.
self_contained_problem:
Let r ≥ 2 be a fixed integer. A hypergraph H = (V, E) is r-uniform if every edge e ∈ E satisfies |e| = r. A transversal (or vertex cover) of H is a set T ⊆ V such that T ∩ e ≠ ∅ for every e ∈ E; the transversal number τ(H) is the minimum cardinality of a transversal of H. Write n = |V| and m = |E|.

   τ(H) ≤ a·n + b·m
holds for every r-uniform hypergraph H with n vertices and m edges.

original_question: Prove that for every n, the maximum value of tau_C(G), the minimum number of vertices meeting every maximal clique of G, over all n-vertex graphs is attained by some triangle-free graph G.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. A clique of $G$ is a subset of $V$ inducing a complete subgraph, and a maximal clique is a clique that is not properly contained in any other clique. Define the clique transversal number

For each positive integer $n$, let
$$f(n) = \max\{\tau_C(G) : G \text{ is a simple graph on } n \text{ vertices}\}.$$

No source found resolves the specific claim that the maximum is attained by a triangle-free graph, so the problem appears still open.

context_brief: Bounded clique-hypergraph chromatic number on perfect graphs

self_contained_problem:

The chromatic number of the clique hypergraph, denoted $\chi_C(G)$, is the smallest integer $k$ such that the vertices of $G$ can be colored with $k$ colors so that no maximal clique of size $\ge 2$ is monochromatic.

paper_title: Unsolved Combinatorial Problems, Part I
original_question: Describe large classes of graphs for which the clique-hypergraph chromatic number chi_C can be computed in polynomial time.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A *maximal clique* of G is a clique (a set of pairwise adjacent vertices) that is not properly contained in any larger clique. The *clique-hypergraph* H(G) of G is the hypergraph whose vertex set is V and whose hyperedges are the maximal cliques of G of size at least 2. A *clique-coloring* of G is a map c: V → {1, ..., k} such that no maximal clique of size at least 2 is monochromatic. The *clique-hypergraph chromatic number* χ_C(G) is the smallest k for which such a coloring exists.

In general, computing χ_C(G) is NP-hard, and even deciding whether χ_C(G) ≤ 2 is NP-hard on restricted classes (for instance on perfect graphs, and on graphs of maximum degree 3), while deciding χ_C(G) ≤ 3 is NP-hard on triangle-free graphs.

Problem: Identify and describe large classes 𝒢 of graphs (preferably defined by natural structural properties, e.g. forbidden subgraphs/minors, bounded width parameters, geometric representations, etc.) such that there exists an algorithm computing χ_C(G) in time polynomial in |V(G)| for every G ∈ 𝒢.
status_search_result: The problem is open-ended and ongoing: it asks for the identification of broad graph classes admitting polynomial-time computation of χ_C. Partial progress has been made for several classes—planar graphs (always 3-clique-colorable, with a linear-time algorithm), {claw, K5-minor}-free graphs (2-clique-colorable in polynomial time), claw-free graphs without odd holes, K5-minor-free graphs, certain circulant graphs, and others—while NP-hardness persists in many natural classes (perfect graphs, triangle-free graphs, graphs of bounded degree). No complete characterization of polynomial-time-tractable classes is known.

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Does the complexity class P equal the complexity class NP? In other words, if a computational problem has solutions that can be verified in polynomial time, does it follow that the problem itself can also be solved in polynomial time?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$. A language is a subset $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$. A deterministic Turing machine $M$ decides $L$ in time $t(n)$ if, for every input $x \in \Sigma^*$, $M$ halts within $t(|x|)$ steps and accepts $x$ if and only if $x \in L$. Define the complexity class $\mathbf{P}$ to be the set of languages $L$ for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine deciding $L$ in time $O(n^k)$ for some constant $k \geq 1$.

Define the complexity class $\mathbf{NP}$ to be the set of languages $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ for which there exist a polynomial $p$ and a language $V \in \mathbf{P}$ (the "verifier relation") such that for every $x \in \Sigma^*$,
$$ x \in L \iff \exists\, y \in \Sigma^{*} \text{ with } |y| \leq p(|x|) \text{ and } (x,y) \in V. $$

Question: Does $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$? That is, is every language whose membership certificates can be verified in deterministic polynomial time also decidable by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm?
status_search_result: The P vs NP problem is universally regarded as open. It is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems posed in 2000, none of which (except the Poincaré conjecture) has been solved, and no widely accepted resolution exists as of 2026.

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: For a projective complex manifold, is every Hodge class algebraic? Equivalently, in the setting described on the page, are the relevant cohomology classes always generated by classes coming from subvarieties of the manifold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex manifold of complex dimension $n$. For each integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le n$, the singular cohomology group $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ admits, after tensoring with $\mathbb{C}$, the Hodge decomposition
$$H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C}) = \bigoplus_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X),$$
where $H^{p,q}(X)$ denotes the space of cohomology classes representable by closed forms of type $(p,q)$. Define the space of rational Hodge classes of degree $2k$ to be
$$\mathrm{Hdg}^{k}(X) := H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \cap H^{k,k}(X).$$
An algebraic class on $X$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination of cohomology classes of the form $[Z]$, where $Z \subset X$ is a closed irreducible algebraic subvariety of complex codimension $k$ and $[Z] \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ is its fundamental cohomology class.

Prove or disprove: for every smooth projective complex manifold $X$ and every integer $k \ge 0$, every element of $\mathrm{Hdg}^{k}(X)$ is an algebraic class, i.e. lies in the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of the classes $[Z]$ of codimension-$k$ algebraic subvarieties of $X$.
status_search_result: The Hodge conjecture is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open in general. It is known in special cases (e.g., divisor classes by the Lefschetz (1,1)-theorem, and certain classes of varieties), but counterexamples are known for the integral version (Atiyah–Hirzebruch, Kollár), while the rational statement above is still unresolved.
