paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Determine the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane: what is the smallest integer c such that every point of the plane can be assigned one of c colors with the property that any two points at Euclidean distance exactly 1 receive different colors? Equivalently, determine the maximum chromatic number possible for a unit-distance graph, meaning a graph whose vertices can be embedded as points in the plane with every edge represented by a unit-length segment. The source states that the answer is known to lie among 4, 5, 6, and 7, so the open task is to decide which value is correct; a closely related intermediate goal mentioned in the collection is to construct a 7-coloring of the plane, which would improve the stated 9-color upper-bound illustration to the best-known upper bound of 7.
self_contained_problem: Consider the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the standard Euclidean distance. A coloring of the plane with $c$ colors is a function $\chi:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \{1,2,\dots,c\}$ such that for every pair of points $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|x-y\|=1$ one has $\chi(x)\neq \chi(y)$. The chromatic number of the plane $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$ is the smallest positive integer $c$ for which such a coloring exists. Equivalently, a unit-distance graph is a graph $G=(V,E)$ admitting an injection $f:V\to\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\{u,v\}\in E$ if and only if $\|f(u)-f(v)\|=1$, and $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$ equals the supremum of the chromatic numbers of all finite unit-distance graphs. It is classically known that $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)\in\{4,5,6,7\}$ via a 7-coloring of the plane by a hexagonal tiling (upper bound) and a finite unit-distance graph with chromatic number 4 such as the Moser spindle (lower bound). Determine the exact value of $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$. As an explicit subtask, construct a coloring of the plane with $7$ colors witnessing the upper bound $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)\le 7$.
category_tag: Chromatic number of the plane / unit-distance graphs
status_search_result: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem remains open. In 2018, de Grey raised the lower bound to 5 by exhibiting a non-4-colorable unit-distance graph, so it is now known that the chromatic number of the plane lies in {5, 6, 7}. The upper bound of 7 (via a hexagonal tiling) and the new lower bound of 5 have not been improved as of 2025; the exact value is still undetermined.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: For unit-distance graphs that require 4 colors, determine how small such graphs can be when one also imposes large girth, and determine whether there exist 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth. The source records examples of girths 4 and 5 on 23 and 45 vertices respectively, and a non-3-colorable unit-distance graph of girth 12 with an extremely large number of vertices, so the open problem is to improve these constructions or prove existence for unbounded girth.
self_contained_problem:
A unit-distance graph is a graph G=(V,E) admitting an embedding f:V→ℝ² such that {u,v}∈E if and only if ‖f(u)−f(v)‖=1 (some authors require only the "only if" direction; here we adopt the same convention as in the source tradition: edges correspond exactly to pairs at Euclidean distance 1). The chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colors needed to properly color the vertices of G, and the girth g(G) is the length of a shortest cycle of G (∞ if G is a forest).

Currently known constructions include 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of girth 4 on 23 vertices and of girth 5 on 45 vertices, and a unit-distance graph of girth 12 with chromatic number at least 4 having an extremely large number of vertices.

(a) For each integer k≥4, determine the minimum number of vertices in a 4-chromatic unit-distance graph in the plane of girth at least k. In particular, improve the bounds 23 (for girth 4) and 45 (for girth 5).

(b) Decide whether, for every integer k, there exists a 4-chromatic unit-distance graph in the plane of girth at least k. Equivalently, do there exist 4-chromatic planar unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth?
status_search_result: The problem remains open for planar unit-distance graphs. A 21-vertex 4-chromatic unit-distance graph of girth 4 was found by Kitech and Payne, improving the original 23-vertex example. While there exist d-dimensional unit-distance graphs in ℝ^d with exponential chromatic number and arbitrarily large girth (Sagdeev et al.), the planar case—producing 4-chromatic planar unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth—remains unresolved.

original_question: Determine the crossing number of the complete bipartite graph K(9,9): among all plane drawings of K(9,9) in which edges are drawn as curves that meet vertices only at endpoints and no three curves pass through the same point, what is the minimum possible number of edge crossings? The source says 256 is conjectured, but unknown.
self_contained_problem:
A drawing of a graph in the plane assigns each vertex a distinct point and each edge a continuous simple curve joining its two endpoints, subject to the conditions that (i) the interior of any edge curve contains no vertex, (ii) any two edge curves meet in finitely many points, each of which is either a common endpoint or a transverse crossing, and (iii) no three edge curves pass through a common interior point. The crossing number cr(G) of a graph G is the minimum, over all such drawings of G in the plane, of the number of pairs of edges whose curves cross.

Let K_{9,9} denote the complete bipartite graph with parts of size 9 (so 18 vertices and 81 edges, each vertex of one part joined to every vertex of the other part). Determine cr(K_{9,9}).

(It is conjectured, in line with Zarankiewicz's general formula cr(K_{m,n}) = ⌊m/2⌋⌊(m-1)/2⌋⌊n/2⌋⌊(n-1)/2⌋, that cr(K_{9,9}) = 256; prove or disprove this value.)
status_search_result: The Zarankiewicz crossing number conjecture has been verified for K_{m,n} when min(m,n) ≤ 6 and for several additional cases up through K_{7,10} and K_{8,10}, but K_{9,9} remains among the smallest unresolved cases. Surveys (e.g., Székely's "Turán's Brick Factory Problem: The Status of the Conjectures of Zarankiewicz and Hill", 2016) and the Wikipedia article on Turán's brick factory problem list K_{9,9} as still open. The conjectured value is 256.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
context_brief: Cycles capturing independent vertices and neighbors
original_question: For an integer k greater than 1, does every k-connected graph that has no Hamiltonian cycle necessarily contain a cycle that includes k pairwise independent vertices together with all of their neighbors? The source says this statement is known for k = 2 and k = 3, and asks whether it continues to hold for all larger k.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. A graph $G$ is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $k$ vertices. A Hamiltonian cycle in $G$ is a cycle that passes through every vertex of $G$. A set of vertices is independent if no two of its members are adjacent. For a vertex $v$, let $N(v)$ denote the set of neighbors of $v$ in $G$.

Question: Is it true that every $k$-connected graph $G$ that does not contain a Hamiltonian cycle must contain a cycle $C$ and a set $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ of $k$ pairwise independent vertices such that $\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\} \cup N(v_1) \cup N(v_2) \cup \cdots \cup N(v_k) \subseteq V(C)$?
status_search_result: Web search did not return a definitive resolution of this conjecture for general k. The cases k = 2 and k = 3 are known to hold (the k = 2 case being a classical result attributed to Chvátal–Erdős–style arguments and the k = 3 case established later), but no source confirming or refuting it for all k ≥ 4 was located. Current status appears to remain open, but this could not be verified with certainty from the available search results.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Let D be an oriented graph, meaning a simple directed graph obtained from a simple undirected graph by orienting each edge so that no pair of opposite directed edges occurs. Form the square of D by keeping the same vertex set, keeping all existing arcs, and adding an arc (u,w) whenever D contains arcs (u,v) and (v,w) and the arc (u,w) is not already present. Must there always exist a vertex whose out-degree at least doubles when passing from D to its square?
self_contained_problem:
An oriented graph is a simple directed graph $D=(V,A)$ obtained from a simple undirected graph by assigning to each edge exactly one of the two possible orientations; equivalently, for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v$ at most one of the arcs $(u,v),(v,u)$ belongs to $A$. For a vertex $v\in V$, the out-degree $d^+_D(v)$ is the number of arcs of $D$ of the form $(v,w)$. Define the square $D^2$ of $D$ to be the directed graph on the same vertex set $V$ whose arc set consists of all arcs of $D$ together with every ordered pair $(u,w)$ with $u\neq w$ such that there exists a vertex $v$ with $(u,v),(v,w)\in A$ and $(u,w)\notin A$ (arcs are not repeated).

Prove or disprove: for every oriented graph $D$ there exists a vertex $v\in V$ such that
$$d^+_{D^2}(v)\;\ge\;2\,d^+_D(v).$$

Equivalently, every oriented graph contains a vertex whose second out-neighbourhood (the set of vertices at directed distance exactly two from $v$ in $D$) has cardinality at least that of its first out-neighbourhood.
status_search_result: This is Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture. It is established for tournaments (Fisher, and later Havet–Thomassé) and various special classes, but the general case remains open as of 2025. Recent work (2024–2025) has improved the constant factor (e.g., 0.715538 times the out-neighbourhood) and explored random and reduction-based approaches, but no accepted proof of the full conjecture exists.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Given N points in the plane in general position, meaning no three are collinear, draw the segment joining every pair of points. What lower bound must always hold on the size of a family of pairwise mutually crossing segments? More specifically, the source states that one can always guarantee a crossing family of size sqrt(N/12), and asks for the largest exponent t such that every such N-point set contains a crossing family of at least cN^t segments for some fixed positive constant c. In particular, any proof with t greater than 1/2 would improve the known exponent.
self_contained_problem:
Let N be a positive integer and let P be a set of N points in the plane in general position (no three collinear). Consider all closed line segments whose endpoints lie in P. Call a collection of such segments a crossing family if every two segments in the collection cross, i.e., share exactly one point lying in the relative interior of both. Let T(N) denote the maximum integer k such that every N-point set P in general position contains a crossing family of size at least k.

Determine the supremum of all real numbers t for which there exists a constant c=c(t)>0 with T(N) ≥ c N^t for all N. In particular, decide whether t can be taken strictly greater than 1/2, and identify the correct growth exponent of T(N).
status_search_result: The classical lower bound T(N) ≥ √(N/12) from 1994 stood for decades. In 2021, Pach, Rubin, and Tardos achieved a major breakthrough, proving T(N) ≥ N^{1−o(1)}, so the exponent t can be taken arbitrarily close to 1. The best known upper bound is T(N) ≤ ⌈8N/41⌉ (Aichholzer, Kynčl, Scheucher, Valtr, Vogtenhuber). Thus while the exponent question (whether t can exceed 1/2) is settled affirmatively, the exact asymptotic value of T(N) remains open.

original_question: Does there exist an integer N with the property that every set of at least N points in the plane in general position, meaning no three points lie on one line, must contain an empty hexagon: six points that are the vertices of a convex hexagon whose interior contains no point of the set?
self_contained_problem: A finite set of points in the Euclidean plane is said to be in general position if no three of its points are collinear. Given such a set S, an empty convex hexagon in S is a choice of six points of S that form the vertices of a convex hexagon whose (open) interior contains no point of S. Determine whether there exists a positive integer N with the following property: every set of at least N points in the plane in general position contains an empty convex hexagon.

Here an empty hexagon means six of the points form a convex hexagon whose interior contains no point of the set. The source presents this as a potentially easier restricted variant of the general empty-hexagon problem.
self_contained_problem: Call a finite planar point set $S$ (in general position, i.e., no three collinear) said to contain an "empty hexagon" if there exist six points of $S$ that form the vertices of a convex hexagon whose open interior contains no point of $S$. Prove or disprove the following statement: there exists an integer $K_0$ such that for every integer $K \ge K_0$, every set $S$ of $K^2$ points lying inside a $K \times K$ axis-aligned square and satisfying the separation condition $\|p - q\| \ge 1/10$ for all distinct $p,q \in S$ must contain an empty hexagon.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Let S be a set of N^2 points inside a disk whose boundary circle C has length N, and assume any two points of S are at distance at least 1/100. Let A be a set of N^2 points spaced equally along C. The source states that for at least c·N^4 ordered pairs a,b from A, some point of S lies within distance 1/N of the line through a and b, for a fixed positive constant c. Must there exist a positive constant d such that for at least d·N^4 pairs a,b from A, there are at least two points of S within distance 1/N of the line ab?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Let $C$ be a circle of length $N$ bounding a disk $D$. Let $S \subset D$ be a set of $N^2$ points such that any two distinct points of $S$ are at Euclidean distance at least $1/100$. Let $A \subset C$ be a set of $N^2$ points placed equidistantly along $C$. For an ordered pair $(a,b)$ of distinct points of $A$, let $\ell_{ab}$ denote the straight line through $a$ and $b$, and consider the strip of points of the plane at distance at most $1/N$ from $\ell_{ab}$.

It is known that there exists an absolute positive constant $c>0$ such that, for every choice of $S$ and $A$ as above, the number of ordered pairs $(a,b) \in A \times A$ with $a \ne b$ for which the strip around $\ell_{ab}$ contains at least one point of $S$ is at least $c \cdot N^4$.

Question: Does there exist an absolute positive constant $d>0$ such that, for every choice of $S$ and $A$ as above, the number of ordered pairs $(a,b) \in A \times A$ with $a \ne b$ for which the strip around $\ell_{ab}$ contains at least two distinct points of $S$ is at least $d \cdot N^4$?

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: How large can a finite set of points on the half-parabola y = x^2 with x > 0 be if every pairwise Euclidean distance among the chosen points is rational? The source says it is not even known whether more than five such points exist. It further asks whether there is an infinite family of points on this half-parabola with all pairwise distances rational, and notes that any configuration with rational pairwise distances can be converted into one with integer pairwise distances.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the half-parabola P = {(x, x^2) : x > 0} in the Euclidean plane. Call a finite set S ⊂ P a "rational distance set" if for every pair of distinct points p, q ∈ S the Euclidean distance |p - q| is a rational number.

(a) Determine the largest possible cardinality of a rational distance set S ⊂ P. In particular, decide whether there exists such a set with |S| ≥ 6.

(b) Decide whether there exists an infinite set S ⊂ P such that every pair of distinct points of S is at rational Euclidean distance.

(Remark: by clearing denominators via a suitable affine rescaling along the parabola, any finite configuration on P with pairwise rational distances can be transformed into one on P with pairwise integer distances, so the questions are equivalent to their integer-distance counterparts.)
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. A 2019 arXiv preprint claimed to construct infinite families of arbitrarily large pairwise-rational point sets on the parabola, but it has been withdrawn by the author. Related published work (e.g., Choudhry) constructs four-point and other configurations, but no verified result settles the existence of sets of size ≥ 6 or of infinite pairwise-rational-distance sets on y = x^2.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Is it possible to construct a Venn diagram using 6 triangles? In the source's terminology, a Venn diagram on n closed curves is one in which each of the 2^n subsets of the curves corresponds to a unique region lying inside exactly that subset. The page notes that diagrams with 5 triangles are possible, while the existence of one with 6 triangles is open.
self_contained_problem:
A Venn diagram on n closed curves in the plane is a collection of n simple closed curves C_1, ..., C_n such that the 2^n sets of the form A_1 ∩ A_2 ∩ ... ∩ A_n, where each A_i is either the interior or the exterior of C_i, are all nonempty and connected. Equivalently, each of the 2^n subsets S ⊆ {1, ..., n} corresponds to a unique nonempty connected region of the plane that lies inside C_i for i ∈ S and outside C_i for i ∉ S.

Does there exist a Venn diagram on 6 closed curves in which every curve C_i is the boundary of a triangle (i.e., each C_i consists of three line segments forming a triangle in the plane)?
status_search_result: The problem has been solved affirmatively. Jeremy Carroll constructed a Venn diagram of 6 triangles, and subsequent work has enumerated exactly 126 such diagrams. It is also known that no Venn diagram of 7 triangles exists, so 6 is the maximum.

paper_title: Open Problems for Undergraduates
original_question: Is every simple Venn diagram extendable to a larger simple Venn diagram by adding one more curve? Here 'simple' means that whenever curves meet they cross rather than being tangent, and no three curves meet at a single point. The source says this is Peter Winkler's conjecture and explains that, if one views the Venn diagram as a planar graph whose vertices are curve intersections and whose edges are curve-arcs between consecutive intersections, the conjecture is equivalent to asserting that the dual graph of any simple Venn diagram is Hamiltonian.
self_contained_problem:
A Venn diagram of n curves is a collection of n simple closed curves in the plane such that, for every subset S of the n curves, the region consisting of points lying inside every curve in S and outside every curve not in S is nonempty and connected. Such a Venn diagram is called simple if (i) whenever two curves meet, they cross transversally (no tangencies), and (ii) no three curves meet at a common point. A simple Venn diagram naturally gives rise to a planar graph whose vertices are the intersection points of the curves and whose edges are the arcs of curves between consecutive intersection points; the dual graph of the diagram is the dual of this plane graph.

Question: Is it true that every simple Venn diagram on n curves can be extended to a simple Venn diagram on n+1 curves by adding one additional simple closed curve? Equivalently, is the dual graph of every simple Venn diagram Hamiltonian?
status_search_result: Winkler's conjecture has been disproved. original_question: If a Noetherian local ring is weakly quasi-complete, must it already be quasi-complete?

Call $M$ weakly quasi-complete if the same property holds for every descending chain of cyclic $R$-submodules of $M$. The ring $R$ is called (weakly) quasi-complete if $R$ itself, viewed as an $R$-module, is (weakly) quasi-complete.

original_question: Does there exist an integrally closed reduced ring R such that for every maximal ideal M the localization R_M is an integrally closed McCoy ring, while R itself is not a McCoy ring and is not locally a domain?

A commutative ring R with identity is called a McCoy ring if for every finitely generated ideal I of R whose elements are all zero-divisors, there exists a nonzero element r in R such that rI = 0 (equivalently, the annihilator of I is nonzero). The ring R is said to be locally a domain if for every prime (equivalently, maximal) ideal P of R, the localization R_P is an integral domain. A ring R is integrally closed if R equals its integral closure in its total ring of quotients, and R is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

original_question: Do there exist reduced rings that satisfy both the annihilator condition (a.c.) and property (A_n) for some n at least 2, but are nevertheless not McCoy rings?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Recall the following definitions.

(i) An element of $R$ is a zero-divisor if it annihilates some nonzero element of $R$; write $Z(R)$ for the set of zero-divisors.

(ii) $R$ is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

(iii) For an integer $n \geq 1$, $R$ is said to satisfy property $(A_n)$ if every ideal of $R$ generated by at most $n$ elements and contained in $Z(R)$ has nonzero annihilator in $R$. (Property $(A)$ is the case where the bound on the number of generators is removed.)

(iv) $R$ satisfies the annihilator condition $(a.c.)$ if for every pair $a,b \in R$ there exists $c \in R$ such that $\operatorname{Ann}_R(a,b) = \operatorname{Ann}_R(c)$.

(v) $R$ is a McCoy ring if whenever a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ is a zero-divisor in $R[x]$, there exists a nonzero $r \in R$ with $rf(x) = 0$. Equivalently, $R$ has property $(A)$ together with the requirement that finite annihilators behave compatibly so that every zero-divisor polynomial has a nonzero constant annihilator.

Question: Does there exist a reduced commutative ring $R$ that satisfies both the annihilator condition $(a.c.)$ and the property $(A_n)$ for some integer $n \geq 2$, yet is not a McCoy ring?

original_question: Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. A prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$ is said to be divided if $\mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}} = \mathfrak{p}$, equivalently if $\mathfrak{p}$ is comparable (with respect to inclusion) to every principal ideal of $A$. The domain $A$ is called divided if every prime ideal of $A$ is divided, and $A$ is called locally divided if the localization $A_{\mathfrak{m}}$ is a divided domain for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of $A$. 

For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$, the CPI-extension of $A$ along $\mathfrak{p}$ is the subring $A + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ of $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$. The domain $A$ is called straight if for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$ and every overring $B$ of $A$ contained in $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$, the extension $A + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}} \subseteq B + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ has the going-down property (equivalently, the natural ring-theoretic condition characterizing straightness as introduced by Dobbs–Picavet).

Question: Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided?

$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{ f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D \},$$

For a nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$, define
$$\mathrm{Int}(I,D) = \{ f \in \mathrm{Int}(D) : f(D) \subseteq I \}.$$

The ring $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is said to satisfy the almost strong Skolem property if, for every pair of finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ such that $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ contain a nonzero constant from $D$, the equality $\mathfrak{A}(\alpha) = \mathfrak{B}(\alpha)$ for every $\alpha \in D$ (where $\mathfrak{A}(\alpha) = \{ f(\alpha) : f \in \mathfrak{A}\}$) implies $\mathfrak{A} = \mathfrak{B}$.

However, a full necessary-and-sufficient characterization for one-dimensional local Noetherian domains with finite residue field does not appear in the literature surveyed, and the question is still posed as open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Do there exist subsets E of the integers such that the associated sequence of Bhargava factorials (n!_E) is not ultimately strictly increasing?
self_contained_problem:
Let $E$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{Z}$. For each prime $p$, a $p$-ordering of $E$ is a sequence $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ of elements of $E$ defined recursively by choosing $a_0 \in E$ arbitrarily and, for $k \ge 1$, choosing $a_k \in E$ so as to minimize the $p$-adic valuation $v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right)$. The associated $p$-sequence of $E$ is $v_k(E,p) = v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right)$, which is independent of the choice of $p$-ordering. The Bhargava factorial of $E$ of order $n$ is defined by
$$ n!_E \; := \; \prod_{p \text{ prime}} p^{\,v_n(E,p)}. $$
(When $E = \mathbb{Z}$ one recovers the ordinary factorial $n!$.)

Question: Does there exist a subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that the sequence $\{n!_E\}_{n \ge 0}$ fails to be ultimately strictly increasing, i.e., such that for every integer $N$ there exist integers $n \ge N$ with $n!_E \ge (n+1)!_E$?
status_search_result: A web search did not produce a definitive resolution of this question. The theory of Bhargava factorials and $p$-orderings has been extended in several recent works (e.g., generalizations to $b$-orderings, polynomial maps, and Bhargava factorials of twin primes), but no source clearly confirms or refutes the existence of a subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ whose Bhargava factorial sequence is not ultimately strictly increasing. The status is therefore best described as unknown based on the available evidence.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: For which infinite subsets E of the integers is the generalized constant e_E associated to the Bhargava factorials of E a transcendental number?
self_contained_problem:
For a nonempty subset E of the integers Z and a prime p, a p-ordering of E is a sequence {a_0, a_1, a_2, ...} of elements of E defined recursively as follows: a_0 is chosen arbitrarily in E, and for k ≥ 1, a_k is chosen in E so as to minimize the p-adic valuation v_p( (a_k - a_0)(a_k - a_1) ⋯ (a_k - a_{k-1}) ). The associated p-sequence of E is v_k(E,p) = v_p( (a_k - a_0) ⋯ (a_k - a_{k-1}) ); this sequence depends only on E and p, not on the choice of p-ordering. The Bhargava factorial of order k of E is then defined by

  k!_E  =  ∏_{p prime} p^{v_k(E,p)}  ∈  Z_{>0},

and it agrees with the usual k! when E = Z. Associated to any infinite subset E ⊆ Z one defines the generalized constant

  e_E  =  ∑_{k=0}^{∞} 1 / k!_E.

Problem: Characterize the infinite subsets E ⊆ Z for which the real number e_E is transcendental. In particular, determine sufficient conditions on E (and, where possible, necessary conditions) that guarantee the transcendence of e_E.
status_search_result: A general transcendence criterion for the constants e_E associated to Bhargava factorials of arbitrary infinite subsets of Z does not appear in the literature. Bhargava's own surveys (including the extended 2023 version) treat e_E as an open-ended question and only mention transcendence of specific instances (e.g., when E equals the primes or the integers). No published characterization of all E for which e_E is transcendental was found.

original_question: For an arbitrary integral domain D, is Int(D) always a flat D-module?

$$\mathrm{Int}(D) \;=\; \{\, f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D \,\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$. Then $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is naturally a $D$-module (in fact a $D$-subalgebra of $K[X]$).

original_question: Let D be an integral domain. Is the canonical D-algebra homomorphism Int(D)^⊗n → Int(D^n) always injective, always surjective, or both?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$ in $m$ variables by
$$\operatorname{Int}(D^m) \;=\; \{\, f \in K[X_1,\dots,X_m] \;:\; f(D^m) \subseteq D \,\}.$$
For $m=1$ write $\operatorname{Int}(D) = \operatorname{Int}(D^1)$. For each integer $n \ge 2$, there is a canonical $D$-algebra homomorphism
$$\varphi_n \colon \underbrace{\operatorname{Int}(D) \otimes_D \operatorname{Int}(D) \otimes_D \cdots \otimes_D \operatorname{Int}(D)}_{n \text{ factors}} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Int}(D^n)$$
induced on simple tensors by
$$f_1(X_1) \otimes f_2(X_2) \otimes \cdots \otimes f_n(X_n) \;\longmapsto\; f_1(X_1)\, f_2(X_2)\cdots f_n(X_n).$$
Determine, for every integral domain $D$ and every $n \ge 2$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Is $\varphi_n$ always injective?
\item[(b)] Is $\varphi_n$ always surjective?
\item[(c)] Is $\varphi_n$ always an isomorphism?
\end{enumerate}
If not, characterize precisely those integral domains $D$ for which $\varphi_n$ is injective (respectively surjective, respectively bijective).
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not produce authoritative results indicating that this question about the canonical map $\operatorname{Int}(D)^{\otimes n} \to \operatorname{Int}(D^n)$ has been resolved in full generality. paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let D be an integral domain. Does Int(D) always admit a unique structure of a D-D-biring such that the inclusion D[X] → Int(D) is a homomorphism of D-D-birings?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$, and let 
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D\}$$
be the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$. Recall that a $D$-$D$-biring is a commutative $D$-algebra $B$ equipped with a lift of the covariant representable functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(B,-)$ from the category of commutative $D$-algebras to itself (equivalently, $B$ carries a cocommutative $D$-coalgebra structure in the category of commutative $D$-algebras, with comultiplication, counit, and co-inverse making $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(B,A)$ into a commutative $D$-algebra functorially in the $D$-algebra $A$). The polynomial ring $D[X]$ carries a canonical $D$-$D$-biring structure in which $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(D[X],A) \cong A$ as $D$-algebras. A homomorphism of $D$-$D$-birings is a $D$-algebra homomorphism that is compatible with the cobring structures.

Question: Does $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ always admit a (necessarily unique) structure of a $D$-$D$-biring such that the natural inclusion $D[X] \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Int}(D)$ is a homomorphism of $D$-$D$-birings?
status_search_result: The question has been studied by Elliott, who proved existence (and necessary uniqueness) of such a $D$-$D$-biring structure on $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ under hypotheses such as flatness of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ over $D$, or $D$-torsion-freeness of $\mathrm{Int}(D)^{\otimes n}$ for $n \leq 4$; this holds for Krull domains and more generally TV PVMDs. The general case (arbitrary integral domain $D$) does not appear to be resolved in the literature.

$$\mathrm{Int}(S, R) = \{ f \in K[X] : f(S) \subseteq R \},$$
and we write $\mathrm{Int}(R) = \mathrm{Int}(R, R)$. For a positive integer $n$, $\mathrm{Int}(R^n)$ denotes the ring of polynomials $f \in K[X_1, \dots, X_n]$ such that $f(R^n) \subseteq R$.

original_question: Let E be the set of values of a second-order recursive integer sequence u_{n+1} = a u_n + b u_{n-1} with given initial values u_0 and u_1. Compute a regular basis of the Z-module Int(E,Z), compute its characteristic sequence with respect to each prime p, and determine the asymptotic behavior of that characteristic sequence.
self_contained_problem:
Let $a,b,u_0,u_1\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $b\ne 0$, and define the second-order linear recurrence sequence $(u_n)_{n\ge 0}$ by $u_{n+1}=a\,u_n+b\,u_{n-1}$ for $n\ge 1$. Let $E=\{u_n : n\ge 0\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$, and consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-module of integer-valued polynomials on $E$:
$$\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z}) = \{\, f\in\mathbb{Q}[X] : f(E)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\,\}.$$
A regular basis of $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$ is a sequence $(f_n)_{n\ge 0}$ with $\deg f_n = n$ forming a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$. For each prime $p$, let $I_n^{(p)}(E)$ denote the fractional ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ generated by the leading coefficients of all polynomials in $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$ of degree $\le n$, and define the characteristic sequence at $p$ by
$$\alpha_p(n) = -v_p\bigl(I_n^{(p)}(E)\bigr),$$
where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation.

(a) Construct an explicit regular basis $(f_n)_{n\ge 0}$ of the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$.

(b) For every prime $p$, compute the characteristic sequence $(\alpha_p(n))_{n\ge 0}$ of $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$ at $p$.

(c) Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\alpha_p(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: For the ring Int_Q(M_n(Z)) of rational polynomials that are integer-valued on n × n integer matrices, compute a regular basis, compute the characteristic sequence with respect to each prime p, and determine the asymptotic behavior of that sequence.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Consider the ring of $n \times n$ matrices with integer entries, $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$, viewed as a subset of $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$. Define
$$\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z})) := \{\, f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(A) \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \text{ for every } A \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \,\},$$
i.e., the ring of polynomials with rational coefficients that take integer-matrix values on every integer matrix of size $n \times n$. This is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module graded by degree; a *regular basis* is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $\{f_k\}_{k \geq 0}$ with $\deg f_k = k$ for every $k$. For each prime $p$ and each integer $k \geq 0$, let $\alpha_p(k)$ denote the $p$-adic valuation of the denominator of the leading coefficient of $f_k$ (equivalently, $-v_p$ of the generator of the fractional ideal of leading coefficients of degree-$k$ elements). The sequence $(\alpha_p(k))_{k \geq 0}$ is called the *characteristic sequence* of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ at $p$.

(a) Construct an explicit regular basis of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$.

(b) For every prime $p$, compute the characteristic sequence $(\alpha_p(k))_{k \geq 0}$.

(c) Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\alpha_p(k)$ as $k \to \infty$.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let D be an integral domain, K its quotient field, and A a torsion-free D-algebra that is finitely generated as a D-module. Characterize those algebras A for which the inclusion ⋂_{a in A}(D[X] + μ_a(X)K[X]) ⊆ Int_K(A) is actually an equality.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $A$ be a torsion-free $D$-algebra that is finitely generated as a $D$-module. For each element $a \in A$, let $\mu_a(X) \in D[X]$ denote the minimal monic polynomial of $a$ over $D$ (equivalently, the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $a$ on $A \otimes_D K$, taken in a fixed normalization so that $\mu_a(a) = 0$). Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $A$ by
$$\mathrm{Int}_K(A) = \{\, f(X) \in K[X] : f(a) \in A \text{ for every } a \in A \,\}.$$
It is known that one always has the containment
$$\bigcap_{a \in A}\bigl(D[X] + \mu_a(X)\,K[X]\bigr) \;\subseteq\; \mathrm{Int}_K(A).$$
Characterize the $D$-algebras $A$ (within the class above) for which this containment is an equality, i.e.
$$\bigcap_{a \in A}\bigl(D[X] + \mu_a(X)\,K[X]\bigr) \;=\; \mathrm{Int}_K(A).$$

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Ring structure of Int(A) for noncommutative algebras
original_question: Give an example of a D-algebra A, possibly after relaxing some of the standing hypotheses such as finite generation as a D-module, for which the set Int(A) of polynomials over the total quotient algebra that are integer-valued on A is not a ring. Also determine whether the conjecture that Int(A) is always a ring when D has finite residue rings is true or false.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be a commutative integral domain with field of fractions $K$. Let $A$ be a torsion-free $D$-algebra (not necessarily commutative, and not necessarily finitely generated as a $D$-module) such that $A \cap K = D$, and let $B = K \otimes_D A$ denote the total quotient algebra of $A$. Define
$$\mathrm{Int}(A) = \{\, f \in B[x] : f(a) \in A \text{ for every } a \in A \,\}.$$
The set $\mathrm{Int}(A)$ is always a left $A$-module, but it is not known in general whether it is closed under multiplication, i.e. whether it forms a (sub)ring of $B[x]$.

(a) Exhibit an explicit $D$-algebra $A$ (possibly after relaxing standard hypotheses such as finite generation of $A$ as a $D$-module) for which $\mathrm{Int}(A)$ fails to be a ring.

(b) Decide the following conjecture: if $D$ has the property that every nonzero residue ring $D/\mathfrak{m}$ at a maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ is finite (equivalently, $D$ has finite residue fields at all maximal ideals), then $\mathrm{Int}(A)$ is a ring for every torsion-free $D$-algebra $A$ as above. Either prove this, or produce a counterexample in this setting.
status_search_result: Searches turned up active research by Frisch, Werner, Peruginelli, and others on integer-valued polynomials on (noncommutative) D-algebras, including sufficient conditions for Int(A) to be a ring (e.g. when every element of A is a sum of units and central elements, covering M_n(D)) and non-triviality results. No located source confirms either (i) a published counterexample of a D-algebra A with Int(A) not a ring under the stated hypotheses, nor (ii) a proof of the finite-residue-rings conjecture. The status appears to remain open or at most partially addressed, but available evidence is insufficient to assert this definitively.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Prüfer property for integral closures of Int_K(A)
original_question: Let D be an integral domain with quotient field K and A a D-algebra. Determine when the integral closure of Int_K(A) is a Prüfer domain.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $A$ be a $D$-algebra (for instance, torsion-free and finitely generated as a $D$-module, with $A \cap K = D$). Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $A$ by
$$\mathrm{Int}_K(A) = \{ f \in K[X] : f(a) \in A \text{ for every } a \in A \},$$
viewed as a subring of $K[X]$. Recall that an integral domain $R$ is called a Prüfer domain if every nonzero finitely generated ideal of $R$ is invertible (equivalently, $R_\mathfrak{p}$ is a valuation domain for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $R$).

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $D$ and $A$ under which the integral closure of $\mathrm{Int}_K(A)$ (in its quotient field) is a Prüfer domain.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. A 2026 Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society paper by Peruginelli provides a classification: assuming $D$ is semiprimitive (or under similar hypotheses) and $A$ torsion-free finitely generated, the integral closure of $\mathrm{Int}_K(A)$ is Prüfer iff $A$ is commutative and isomorphic to a finite direct product of almost Dedekind domains with finite residue fields satisfying a double-boundedness condition on ramification indices and residue degrees. Earlier work (Frisch, Loper–Werner, Peruginelli–Werner) addressed specific cases. The fully general problem (arbitrary $D$ and $A$) is not completely resolved.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let R be a ring and n a positive integer. If I is an n-absorbing ideal of R, must I be strongly n-absorbing? Must rad(I)^n be contained in I? And must I[X] be an n-absorbing ideal of the polynomial ring R[X]?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and let $n$ be a positive integer. A proper ideal $I$ of $R$ is called an $n$-absorbing ideal if whenever $x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}\in R$ satisfy $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_{n+1}\in I$, then there exist $n$ of the $x_i$ whose product lies in $I$. The ideal $I$ is called strongly $n$-absorbing if whenever $I_1,\dots,I_{n+1}$ are ideals of $R$ with $I_1 I_2 \cdots I_{n+1}\subseteq I$, then the product of some $n$ of the $I_j$'s is contained in $I$. Let $\mathrm{rad}(I)$ denote the radical of $I$, and let $R[X]$ denote the polynomial ring in one indeterminate over $R$, with $I[X]$ the ideal of polynomials with coefficients in $I$.

Answer the following three questions for every commutative ring $R$, every positive integer $n$, and every $n$-absorbing ideal $I$ of $R$:

(a) Must $I$ be a strongly $n$-absorbing ideal of $R$?

(b) Must $\mathrm{rad}(I)^n \subseteq I$?

(c) Must $I[X]$ be an $n$-absorbing ideal of the polynomial ring $R[X]$?
status_search_result: Parts (a) and (b) are reported as proved: a 2023 preprint claims that every $n$-absorbing ideal is strongly $n$-absorbing, and the formula $\mathrm{rad}(I)^n\subseteq I$ for $n$-absorbing ideals has been established (Proceedings — Mathematical Sciences, 2018). Part (c), asking whether $I[X]$ is $n$-absorbing in $R[X]$, is known only in special cases (Gaussian rings, pseudo-valuation domains, locally divided rings, Noetherian rings under conditions) and appears to remain open in general.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Is every stable Archimedean domain one-dimensional? If D is a one-dimensional Mori domain in which each divisorial ideal is 2-v-generated, must every divisorial ideal be stable? More generally, if D is a Mori domain in which each divisorial ideal is 2-v-generated, must D be v-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let D be an integral domain with quotient field K. For a nonzero fractional ideal I of D, set I^{-1} = (D : I) = { x in K : xI ⊆ D } and I_v = (I^{-1})^{-1}. An ideal I is called divisorial (or a v-ideal) if I = I_v. The endomorphism ring of I is E(I) = (I : I) = { x in K : xI ⊆ I }. A nonzero ideal I of D is said to be stable if I is invertible in E(I), i.e. I·(I^{-1}·I)·... — equivalently, I·(E(I) : I) = E(I). The domain D is called stable if every nonzero ideal of D is stable, and v-stable if every divisorial ideal of D is stable (i.e. invertible in its endomorphism ring).

The domain D is Archimedean if for every nonzero, noninvertible element a of D, ⋂_{n≥1} a^n D = 0. The domain D is a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial ideals. A divisorial ideal I is said to be 2-v-generated if there exist a, b ∈ I such that I = (a, b)_v.

Answer the following three questions:

(a) Must every stable Archimedean domain be one-dimensional (i.e. have Krull dimension one)?

(b) Let D be a one-dimensional Mori domain such that every divisorial ideal of D is 2-v-generated. Must every divisorial ideal of D be stable?

(c) Let D be a Mori domain such that every divisorial ideal of D is 2-v-generated. Must D be v-stable?
status_search_result: The questions appear in standard problem lists on commutative ring theory and remain open in general. Partial positive results are known: a stable Archimedean domain whose integral closure is local is one-dimensional and Mori, and there are characterizations of one-dimensional stable domains via finitely stable + Mori. No full resolution of (a), (b), or (c) was located.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Finite character of finitely stable LPI-domains
original_question: Assume that D is a finitely stable LPI-domain. Must D have finite character?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is called stable if $I$ is invertible in its endomorphism ring $(I:I) = \{x \in K : xI \subseteq I\}$, where $K$ is the quotient field of $D$. The domain $D$ is called finitely stable if every nonzero finitely generated ideal of $D$ is stable. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is locally principal if, for every maximal ideal $M$ of $D$, the localization $I_M$ is a principal ideal of $D_M$. The domain $D$ is called an LPI-domain (locally principal ideal domain) if every nonzero locally principal ideal of $D$ is invertible. The domain $D$ is said to have finite character if every nonzero element of $D$ belongs to only finitely many maximal ideals of $D$.

Question: If $D$ is a finitely stable LPI-domain, must $D$ have finite character?
category_tag: Commutative ring theory: stable domains and finite character
status_search_result: Related results are known: Bazzoni (2011) proved that a finitely stable domain has finite character if and only if it has the local stability property, and the Bazzoni conjecture for Prüfer domains (Prüfer LPI ⟹ finite character) was proved by Holland–Martinez–McGovern–Tesemma and independently by Halter-Koch. Subsequent work by Gabelli–Roitman ("On finitely stable domains, I, II") and others on LPI domains continues to address related characterizations, but I did not find a published resolution of the question of whether every finitely stable LPI-domain must have finite character. The problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: v-domains of D + X D_S[X] type
original_question: Find necessary and sufficient conditions for the ring R = D + X D_S[X] to be a v-domain, and determine whether R is a v-domain exactly when D is a v-domain and each ideal (d, X) is v-invertible for every nonzero d in D. More generally, for an extension of integral domains A ⊆ B, find necessary and sufficient conditions for A + X B[X] to be a v-domain.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $S$ be a (nonempty) multiplicatively closed subset of $D$. Denote by $D_S$ the localization of $D$ at $S$, and form the subring \[ R \;=\; D + X\,D_S[X] \;\subseteq\; D_S[X]. \]

A nonzero fractional ideal $I$ is called $v$-invertible if $(I\,I^{-1})_v = T$. The domain $T$ is called a $v$-domain if every nonzero finitely generated fractional ideal of $T$ is $v$-invertible.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let D be an almost GCD domain such that every nonzero t-locally principal ideal is t-invertible. Must D be of finite t-character?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$. For a nonzero fractional ideal $I$ of $D$, set $I^{-1}=\{x\in K : xI\subseteq D\}$, $I_v=(I^{-1})^{-1}$, and $I_t=\bigcup\{J_v : J\subseteq I \text{ is a nonzero finitely generated subideal}\}$. The ideal $I$ is called a $t$-ideal if $I=I_t$, and $I$ is $t$-invertible if $(II^{-1})_t=D$. A maximal $t$-ideal is an ideal maximal among proper integral $t$-ideals; every such ideal is prime. The domain $D$ is said to be of finite $t$-character if every nonzero nonunit of $D$ is contained in only finitely many maximal $t$-ideals. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is $t$-locally principal if, for every maximal $t$-ideal $M$ of $D$, the extension $ID_M$ is a principal ideal of $D_M$.

The domain $D$ is called an almost GCD domain (AGCD domain) if for every pair $x,y\in D\setminus\{0\}$ there exists a positive integer $n=n(x,y)$ such that $x^nD\cap y^nD$ is principal.

Question: Suppose $D$ is an almost GCD domain in which every nonzero $t$-locally principal ideal is $t$-invertible. Must $D$ be of finite $t$-character?

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Find conditions on a family 𝒯 of overrings and semistar operations {*_T} under which the induced semistar operation *_𝒯 on D is of finite type. Equivalently, find conditions on a family 𝒮 of semistar operations such that the intersection semistar operation ˆ𝒮 is of finite type.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$ denote the set of all nonzero $D$-submodules of $K$. A semistar operation on $D$ is a map $\star:\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)\to\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$, $E\mapsto E^\star$, such that for all $E,F\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$ and all $0\ne x\in K$:
(i) $(xE)^\star=xE^\star$;
(ii) $E\subseteq E^\star$;
(iii) $E\subseteq F\Rightarrow E^\star\subseteq F^\star$;
(iv) $(E^\star)^\star=E^\star$.

A semistar operation $\star$ is said to be of finite type if for every $E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$, $E^\star=\bigcup\{F^\star:F\subseteq E,\ F\text{ a finitely generated }D\text{-submodule of }K\}$.

Two constructions are considered:

(a) Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a family of overrings of $D$ (i.e.\ rings with $D\subseteq T\subseteq K$), and for each $T\in\mathcal{T}$ let $\star_T$ be a semistar operation on $T$. Define a semistar operation $\star_\mathcal{T}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\star_\mathcal{T}}:=\bigcap_{T\in\mathcal{T}}(ET)^{\star_T}\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

(b) Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of semistar operations on $D$. Define the intersection semistar operation $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\wedge_\mathcal{S}}:=\bigcap_{\star\in\mathcal{S}}E^\star\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

Problem: Determine necessary and sufficient conditions
(a) on the family $\mathcal{T}$ and the operations $\{\star_T\}_{T\in\mathcal{T}}$ under which $\star_\mathcal{T}$ is of finite type;
(b) on the family $\mathcal{S}$ under which $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ is of finite type.
status_search_result: The problem has been partially addressed via topological/spectral methods on the space of semistar operations of finite type. It is known that the infimum of a quasi-compact family of finite-type semistar operations is of finite type, and a converse holds when each operation is induced by a localization or a valuation overring; the general converse for arbitrary families of overrings remains conjectural. No complete characterization in the generality posed appears to have been established.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Is there a Krull domain, or even a factorial domain, D such that 1 + dim(D) is strictly less than dim(D[X])? Is David’s domain J locally Jaffard? More generally, if A ⊆ D is an extension of integral domains with A Noetherian and D a subalgebra of an affine domain over A, must D be locally Jaffard?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let D be an integral domain with field of fractions K. The Krull dimension dim(D) is the supremum of lengths of chains of prime ideals of D. The valuative dimension dim_v(D) is the supremum of the Krull dimensions of all valuation overrings of D (valuation rings V with D ⊆ V ⊆ K). For every integral domain D one has the inequalities

  dim(D) + 1 ≤ dim(D[X]) ≤ 2·dim(D) + 1, and dim(D[X]) ≤ dim(D) + dim_v(D) + 1.

D is called a Jaffard domain if dim(D) is finite and dim(D) = dim_v(D). D is locally Jaffard if D_P is a Jaffard domain for every prime ideal P of D (equivalently, every localization of D at a prime is Jaffard). Noetherian domains, Prüfer domains of finite dimension, and finite-dimensional universally catenary domains are all locally Jaffard. A Krull domain is an integral domain that is the intersection of a family of discrete valuation overrings with the finite-character property; a factorial (UFD) domain is in particular a Krull domain.

There is a known construction (referred to as "David's domain") of a three-dimensional non-Noetherian Krull domain J obtained by a pullback / D + M-type construction that exhibits anomalous polynomial-dimension behavior; let J denote such a domain.

Problems. 

(a) Does there exist a Krull domain D — or, more strongly, a factorial domain D — such that
  dim(D) + 1 < dim(D[X])?

(b) Is the domain J described above a locally Jaffard domain?

(c) Let A ⊆ D be an extension of integral domains in which A is Noetherian and D is an A-subalgebra of some affine A-domain T (i.e., T is a finitely generated A-algebra that is a domain, and D is a sub-A-algebra of T). Must D necessarily be a locally Jaffard domain?

No source found resolves whether a Krull/factorial domain D with dim(D)+1 < dim(D[X]) exists, whether David's domain J is locally Jaffard, or the affine-subalgebra question. Status appears open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: If R is a one-dimensional local Mori domain, is R necessarily locally tame?
self_contained_problem:
An integral domain $R$ is called a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial (i.e., $v$-) ideals. An atomic domain $R$ (every nonzero non-unit factors as a product of atoms/irreducibles) is said to be locally tame if for every atom $u \in R$ there exists a constant $\omega(R,u) \in \mathbb{N}_0 \cup \{\infty\}$, finite, such that whenever $u$ divides a product $a_1 \cdots a_n$ of atoms of $R$, there is a subproduct of length at most $\omega(R,u)$ which is divisible by $u$ (equivalently, the local tame degree at every atom is finite).

Let $R$ be a one-dimensional local Mori domain (i.e., a Mori domain with Krull dimension one and a unique maximal ideal). Must $R$ be locally tame?
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved affirmatively. Geroldinger, Kainrath, and Reinhart (and related work on strongly primary monoids and domains, arXiv:1807.10683, published in Comm. Algebra 2020) showed that every one-dimensional local Mori domain is strongly primary, and that every strongly primary domain is locally tame, thus answering this question in the affirmative.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Analyze and describe non-unique factorization in Int(D) when D is a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field, and let $K$ be its field of fractions. Consider the ring of integer-valued polynomials
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D\}.$$
It is known that $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is an atomic domain that is not a unique factorization domain: there exist nonzero non-unit elements admitting essentially distinct factorizations into irreducibles, and even into irreducibles of different lengths. Call an irreducible $f \in \mathrm{Int}(D)$ absolutely irreducible if every power $f^n$ factors uniquely (up to units and order) into irreducibles; otherwise call $f$ non-absolutely irreducible.

Provide a complete analysis and description of non-unique factorization in $\mathrm{Int}(D)$. In particular:
(a) Characterize, in terms of arithmetic data of $D$, the irreducible elements of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ and distinguish the absolutely irreducible ones from the non-absolutely irreducible ones.
(b) Determine, for each nonzero non-unit $f \in \mathrm{Int}(D)$, the set of factorization lengths $\mathcal{L}(f) = \{n : f = a_1 \cdots a_n \text{ with each } a_i \text{ irreducible}\}$, and describe which finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ arise as length sets of elements of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$.
(c) Describe the structure of the system of sets of lengths and other standard arithmetic invariants (elasticity, sets of distances, catenary and tame degrees) of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$.
category_tag: Non-unique factorization in integer-valued polynomial rings
status_search_result: A complete description of non-unique factorization in Int(D) for a DVR D with finite residue field is not known, but substantial partial progress has been made. Work by Frisch, Nakato, Rissner and others has produced characterizations of (absolutely) irreducible elements and realization theorems showing that essentially arbitrary finite multisets of factorization lengths can occur for integer-valued polynomials on valuation rings of global fields (e.g., Springer Archiv der Mathematik 2024 and Monatshefte für Mathematik 2023). A complete structural description (e.g., of all length sets and arithmetic invariants) remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Order types of spectra of polynomial rings
original_question: Find axioms characterizing the poset Spec(Q[x,y]). Determine whether Spec(Q[x,y]) and Spec(Q(√2)[x,y]) are order-isomorphic. More generally, for algebraic number fields F and K and a two-dimensional affine F-domain A, decide whether Spec(A) must be order-isomorphic to Spec(K[x,y]). Finally, if F and K are fields neither algebraic over a finite field and Spec(F[x,y]) and Spec(K[x,y]) are order-isomorphic, must F and K already be isomorphic fields?
self_contained_problem:
For a commutative ring R, let Spec(R) denote its prime spectrum, viewed as a partially ordered set under inclusion of prime ideals. Consider the following questions about order-types of spectra of two-dimensional polynomial rings.

(a) Find a list of axioms (in the language of partially ordered sets) that characterizes Spec(ℚ[x,y]) up to order-isomorphism, analogously to the known axiomatic characterization of Spec(ℤ[x]).

(b) Decide whether the posets Spec(ℚ[x,y]) and Spec(ℚ(√2)[x,y]) are order-isomorphic.

(c) More generally, let F and K be algebraic number fields (finite extensions of ℚ) and let A be a two-dimensional affine F-domain (i.e., an integral domain that is finitely generated as an F-algebra and has Krull dimension 2). Decide whether Spec(A) must be order-isomorphic, as a partially ordered set, to Spec(K[x,y]).

(d) Suppose F and K are fields, each of which is not algebraic over a finite field, and suppose Spec(F[x,y]) and Spec(K[x,y]) are order-isomorphic as partially ordered sets. Must F and K be isomorphic as fields?
status_search_result: The axiomatic characterization of Spec(ℤ[x]) by Roger Wiegand is well-known, but the analogous problem for Spec(ℚ[x,y]) and the order-isomorphism questions for two-dimensional affine domains over number fields are repeatedly listed as long-standing open problems in commutative ring theory, with only partial results (e.g., Arnavut's conjecture and related work on Proj(ℤ[h,k])). No resolution was found in the search.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let I be the integral closure of the ideal (x^a, y^b, z^c) in a polynomial ring in variables x, y, z over a field. Classify all triples (a,b,c) such that every power of I is integrally closed.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a field, let $R = k[x,y,z]$ be the polynomial ring in three variables over $k$, and let $a,b,c$ be positive integers. Consider the monomial ideal $J = (x^a, y^b, z^c) \subseteq R$, and let $I = \overline{J}$ denote the integral closure of $J$ in $R$. Recall that an ideal $L \subseteq R$ is called integrally closed if $L = \overline{L}$, where $\overline{L} = \{r \in R : r^n + a_1 r^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n = 0 \text{ for some } n \geq 1 \text{ and some } a_i \in L^i\}$, and that an ideal $L$ is called normal if every power $L^n$ ($n \geq 1$) is integrally closed.

Classify all triples of positive integers $(a,b,c)$ such that the ideal $I = \overline{(x^a, y^b, z^c)}$ is normal, i.e., such that $I^n$ is integrally closed for every positive integer $n$.
status_search_result: The classification of triples $(a,b,c)$ for which the integral closure of $(x^a,y^b,z^c)$ in $k[x,y,z]$ is normal is a well-known open problem in commutative algebra. Partial results exist (e.g., a recent result that every integrally closed monomial ideal in $k[x,y,z]$ with at most seven minimal monomial generators is normal, while $(x^7,y^3,z^2)$ produces a counterexample with eight generators), but no complete classification of the triples appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Algorithms for integral closure of ideals
original_question: Is there a more direct algorithm for computing the integral closure of a general ideal? In particular, can the Leonard–Pellikaan and Singh–Swanson algorithms be modified to compute integral closures of ideals?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and $I \subseteq R$ an ideal. The integral closure of $I$ is the ideal $\overline{I} = \{x \in R : x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n = 0 \text{ for some } n \geq 1 \text{ and } a_i \in I^i\}$. Two known algorithms for computing the integral closure of a reduced ring $R$ finitely generated over a finite field of characteristic $p>0$ are:

(i) The Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm, which applies to suitably weighted affine domains over finite fields and proceeds by iteratively constructing modules $V_{e+1} = \{f \in V_e : f^{p} \in V_e\}$ from an initial finite module $V_0$ containing the integral closure.

(ii) The Singh–Swanson algorithm, which is a generalization of (i) computing the integral closure of any reduced ring finitely generated over a finite field, also using the Frobenius/$p$-th power map.

Both algorithms compute the integral closure of the ambient ring rather than of an ideal.

Problem.
(a) Construct a direct algorithm for computing the integral closure $\overline{I}$ of a general ideal $I$ in a Noetherian commutative ring, more efficient or more direct than reducing to the integral closure of the Rees ring $R[It] = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} I^n t^n$.

(b) In particular, modify the Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm and/or the Singh–Swanson algorithm so that, given an ideal $I$ in an affine domain (or a reduced affine ring) over a finite field of characteristic $p > 0$, the algorithm directly outputs a presentation of the integral closure $\overline{I}$ (rather than the integral closure of a ring).
category_tag: Algorithms for integral closure of ideals
status_search_result: D. A. Leonard extended the Qth-power (Leonard–Pellikaan) algorithm to compute integral closures of ideals in affine domains over finite fields relative to a local monomial ordering (arXiv:1209.4070, 2012), and the corresponding routines (icFracP and ideal integral closure routines) are implemented in the Macaulay2 IntegralClosure package. Thus part (b) has been at least partially addressed in positive characteristic. A fully general "direct" algorithm for integral closure of arbitrary ideals in arbitrary Noetherian rings (part (a)) does not appear to be settled.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: How tight is the general Lipman–Sathaye theorem stated in the source? Relax some of its assumptions and either prove that the theorem still holds or produce a counterexample for the relaxed version.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $R$ be a Noetherian domain with field of fractions $K$, and let $S$ be a Noetherian extension domain of $R$ with field of fractions $L$, where $L/K$ is a finite separable field extension. Assume that:

(a) $R$ is universally catenary;
(b) for every prime ideal $Q$ of $S$ lying over a prime $P$ of $R$, the local ring $R_P$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\mathrm{ht}(Q)=\mathrm{ht}(P)$;
(c) $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra, generically étale over $R$, and the integral closure $\overline{S}$ of $S$ in $L$ is module-finite over $R$.

Let $J_{S/R}$ denote the Jacobian ideal of $S$ over $R$ (the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a Jacobian matrix coming from a presentation of $S$ as an $R$-algebra). The general Lipman–Sathaye theorem in this setting asserts the containment
$$ J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S} \;\subseteq\; (R : _{L}\, \overline{S})\, , $$
where $(R:_L \overline{S}) = \{x\in L : x\overline{S}\subseteq R\}$ is the conductor-type module, equivalently $J_{S/R}$ multiplies $\overline{S}$ into $R$ relative to the standard trace pairing.

Problem. Determine how sharp the hypotheses (a)–(c) are. Specifically, choose a proper relaxation of one of the assumptions — for example, dropping the Cohen–Macaulay hypothesis on $R_P$, weakening the equidimensionality condition $\mathrm{ht}(Q)=\mathrm{ht}(P)$, removing universal catenarity, weakening separability of $L/K$, or replacing module-finiteness of $\overline{S}$ over $R$ by a weaker finiteness condition — and either:

(i) prove that the conclusion $J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S}\subseteq (R:_L \overline{S})$ continues to hold under the relaxed hypotheses, or
(ii) construct an explicit example of $R\subseteq S$ satisfying the relaxed hypotheses for which the conclusion fails.
status_search_result: The problem, posed as a meta-question about relaxing the hypotheses of the general Lipman–Sathaye Jacobian theorem, is not a single precise statement with a recorded resolution. Refinements and reformulations exist (e.g., presentation-depth versions and Mather–Jacobian variants), but no comprehensive result determining the exact sharpness of the assumptions appears in the literature. The status is therefore taken to be open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Construction of rings with multiple Rees valuations
original_question: Construct a Noetherian, two-dimensional, complete, integrally closed local domain (R,m) in which every m-primary ideal has more than one Rees valuation, as in Cutkosky’s existence result.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ be a Noetherian local domain. Recall that for an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideal $I \subseteq R$, the Rees valuations of $I$ are the (finitely many) discrete valuations $v_1,\dots,v_r$ on the field of fractions of $R$ such that the integral closure of $I^n$ in $R$ equals $ igcap_{i=1}^r \{x \in R : v_i(x) \ge n\, v_i(I)\}$ for every $n \ge 1$, where $v_i(I) := \min\{v_i(x) : x \in I\}$. The set of Rees valuations of $I$ is the unique minimal such set.

It is known that there exists a Noetherian, two-dimensional, complete, integrally closed local domain $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ with the property that every $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideal of $R$ has more than one Rees valuation.

Problem: Give an explicit construction of such a ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$.
status_search_result: No explicit construction is known. Subsequent work (e.g., Heinzer–Swanson "Searching for Cutkosky's example") has ruled out broad classes of candidate rings (such as power series rings modulo quasi-homogeneous primes), but an explicit example has not been produced; the problem appears to remain open as of recent surveys.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a large positive integer N, determine the largest possible size of a subset of the interval [1,N] that contains no three-term arithmetic progression, and narrow the gap between the known Behrend lower bound and Bourgain upper bound.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r_3(N)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $A\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ that contains no nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression (i.e., no triple $(a,a+d,a+2d)$ with $a,a+d,a+2d\in A$ and $d\ne 0$). 

Behrend's construction shows that
$$r_3(N) \ge N\cdot \exp\!\bigl(-C\sqrt{\log N}\bigr)$$
for some constant $C>0$, while known upper bounds give
$$r_3(N) \le \frac{N}{(\log N)^{1+c}}$$
for some absolute constant $c>0$.

Determine the true asymptotic order of $r_3(N)$ as $N\to\infty$, and in particular close (or significantly narrow) the gap between the Behrend-type lower bound and the best available upper bound.
status_search_result: The problem remains open. The lower bound is still essentially Behrend's $N\exp(-C\sqrt{\log N})$. On the upper-bound side, the Bourgain bound $N/(\log N)^{1+c}$ has been dramatically improved: Kelley and Meka (2023) established a quasi-polynomial upper bound $r_3(N) \le N\exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})$, simplified/improved by Bloom–Sisask to exponent $1/9$, and further refined by Bloom–Sisask (2023). However, a substantial gap to Behrend's $\sqrt{\log N}$ exponent remains, so the asymptotic order of $r_3(N)$ is not known.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For the additive group of the finite field F_q with q = 3^r elements, determine the largest possible size of a subset that contains no three-term arithmetic progression, describe its asymptotic behavior as r grows, improve Meshulam’s O(3^r/r) upper bound, and decide whether an absolute constant c < 3 always bounds such a size by c^r.
self_contained_problem:
Let $q=3^r$ and consider the additive group of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ (equivalently, the vector space $\mathbb{F}_3^r$). A subset $A$ of this group is said to be free of three-term arithmetic progressions (or "progression-free") if there are no elements $x,y,z\in A$ with $x+z=2y$ and $\{x,y,z\}$ not all equal; equivalently, no solutions to $x+y+z=0$ with $x,y,z\in A$ other than $x=y=z$. Let $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r)$ denote the largest possible cardinality of such a subset.

(a) Determine $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r)$, and describe its asymptotic behavior as $r\to\infty$.

(b) Improve upon Meshulam's upper bound $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r) = O(3^r/r)$.

(c) Decide whether there exists an absolute constant $c<3$ such that $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r)\le c^r$ for all sufficiently large $r$.
category_tag: Cap sets / progression-free sets in finite fields
status_search_result: Parts (b) and (c) were resolved in 2016 by Croot–Lev–Pach and Ellenberg–Gijswijt, who used the polynomial/slice rank method to prove $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r) \le c^r$ with $c \approx 2.756 < 3$, a major exponential improvement over Meshulam's $O(3^r/r)$ bound. However, determining the exact value or the precise exponential growth rate of $r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^r)$ remains open: the best known lower bounds (Edel's construction) are about $2.217^r$, leaving a gap with the upper bound, and no exponential improvement to the Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound has been found as of 2026.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Arithmetic progressions from divergent reciprocal sums
original_question: If A is a subset of the natural numbers such that the reciprocal sum sum_{a in A} 1/a diverges, must A contain arithmetic progressions of every length k >= 3? In particular, must it contain a three-term arithmetic progression?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of positive integers such that
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a} = \infty.$$
A $k$-term arithmetic progression is a sequence of the form $n, n+d, n+2d, \dots, n+(k-1)d$ with $d \ge 1$ and all terms in $A$.

(a) Must $A$ contain a non-trivial $3$-term arithmetic progression?

(b) More generally, must $A$ contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression for every integer $k \ge 3$?

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Prove or disprove that for every epsilon > 0 there is a constant c > 0, depending on epsilon, such that every finite set A of integers satisfies max(|A + A|, |A · A|) > c |A|^{2 - epsilon}.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $A$ of integers, define the sumset and product set
$$A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\},\qquad A\cdot A=\{ab:a,b\in A\}.$$
Prove or disprove the following statement: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $c=c(\varepsilon)>0$ such that for every finite set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$,
$$\max\bigl(|A+A|,\,|A\cdot A|\bigr) > c\,|A|^{2-\varepsilon}.$$

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Find reasonable quantitative bounds for the Hales-Jewett theorem and for its density version.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer k ≥ 2 and a finite alphabet [k] = {1, 2, …, k}, a combinatorial line in [k]^n is a set of k points of the form {(w_1(i), w_2(i), …, w_n(i)) : i ∈ [k]}, where w_1, …, w_n ∈ [k] ∪ {∗}, at least one w_j equals the "wildcard" symbol ∗, and w_j(i) := w_j if w_j ∈ [k] while w_j(i) := i if w_j = ∗.

The Hales–Jewett theorem states that for every k ≥ 2 and every r ≥ 1 there exists an integer HJ(k, r) such that for every n ≥ HJ(k, r), every r-coloring of [k]^n contains a monochromatic combinatorial line.

The density Hales–Jewett theorem states that for every k ≥ 2 and every δ > 0 there exists an integer DHJ(k, δ) such that for every n ≥ DHJ(k, δ), every subset A ⊆ [k]^n with |A| ≥ δ k^n contains a combinatorial line.

Problem: Obtain reasonable quantitative upper bounds on the functions HJ(k, r) and DHJ(k, δ). In particular, determine the best possible growth rates (e.g., as a function of k, r, and 1/δ) for these quantities.
status_search_result: Shelah (1988) gave primitive recursive (tower-type) bounds for the Hales–Jewett theorem, removing the Ackermann-type bounds from Hales–Jewett's original proof. For the density version, Furstenberg–Katznelson's ergodic proof gave no effective bounds; the Polymath project (2009–2012) gave a combinatorial proof with explicit bounds — tower-type in 1/δ for k = 3 and Ackermann-type for k ≥ 4. Obtaining substantially better (e.g., primitive recursive or polynomial-tower) bounds, especially for the density version with k ≥ 4, remains open.

For an integer $k \ge 1$, let $W(k)$ denote the two-color van der Waerden number: the least positive integer $N$ such that every coloring of $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ with two colors contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$. Determine the order of growth of $W(k)$ as $k \to \infty$. In particular, decide whether
$$W(k) \le 2^{k^2}$$
holds for all sufficiently large $k$.

The best general upper bound is due to Gowers, of tower type derived from his proof of Szemerédi's theorem, far above 2^{k^2}. Graham offered a $1000 prize specifically for proving W(k) < 2^{k^2}, and this remains unclaimed. No recent work establishes such a bound for general k.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Does there exist a basis B of order 2 in the natural numbers, meaning every positive integer is a sum of two elements of B, such that the representation count nu_B(n) = |{(b1,b2) in B x B : b1 + b2 = n}| is bounded above by one constant independent of n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called a basis of order $2$ if every sufficiently large positive integer $n$ can be written as $n = b_1 + b_2$ with $b_1, b_2 \in B$ (equivalently, the representation function defined below is positive for all large $n$). For such a set $B$, define the representation function
$$\nu_B(n) = \#\{(b_1, b_2) \in B \times B : b_1 + b_2 = n\}.$$
Does there exist a basis $B$ of order $2$ in $\mathbb{N}$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that $\nu_B(n) \leq C$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$?
status_search_result: This is the classical Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases (1941), which conjectures the answer is "no" — every basis of order 2 must have an unbounded representation function. The problem remains open. Partial results give lower bounds on the limsup of the representation function (e.g., Grekos et al. proved limsup ≥ 6, later improved to ≥ 8 by Borwein–Choi–Chu), but no constant upper bound has been ruled out and no bounded example is known.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a prime p congruent to 1 modulo 4, determine the maximum size of a set A in F_p such that the difference between any two elements of A is a quadratic residue modulo p, equivalently determine the clique number of the Paley graph over F_p.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the finite field with $p$ elements. An element $x \in \mathbb{F}_p^*$ is called a quadratic residue modulo $p$ if there exists $y \in \mathbb{F}_p^*$ with $y^2 = x$. The Paley graph $G_p$ is the graph with vertex set $\mathbb{F}_p$ in which two distinct vertices $a, b$ are joined by an edge if and only if $a - b$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ (the condition $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ ensures $-1$ is a quadratic residue, so this relation is symmetric). 

Determine the maximum possible cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ such that for every pair of distinct elements $a, b \in A$, the difference $a - b$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. Equivalently, determine the clique number $\omega(G_p)$ of the Paley graph $G_p$, as a function of $p$.
status_search_result: The exact determination of the Paley graph clique number remains a well-known open problem. The best known upper bound, due to Hanson and Petridis (using Stepanov's method), is $\omega(G_p) \leq \sqrt{p/2}\,(1+o(1))$, far from the conjectured polylogarithmic order. Recent works (2020–2025) have extended these techniques to prime-power Paley and cyclotomic graphs but have not closed the gap for prime $p$.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Sumsets and difference sets in multiplicative subgroups
original_question: For a proper multiplicative subgroup H of F_q, determine the largest size of a subset A of F_p with A - A contained in H, and decide whether there is a set A with A + A = H or with A + A differing from H by only a small symmetric difference.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^n$ for some positive integer $n$. Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements, and let $H$ be a proper subgroup of the multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_q^* = \mathbb{F}_q \setminus \{0\}$ (so $1 < |H| < q-1$). For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$, define
$$A - A = \{a - a' : a, a' \in A\}, \qquad A + A = \{a + a' : a, a' \in A\}.$$

Address the following three questions:

(a) Determine (or give the best possible upper and lower bounds for) the largest possible size of a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ such that $A - A \subseteq H \cup \{0\}$.

(b) Decide whether there exists a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ with $A + A = H$ (as sets).

(c) Decide whether there exists a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ such that the symmetric difference $(A+A) \triangle H$ is "small" (e.g., of size $o(|H|)$ as $|H| \to \infty$ along a family of proper multiplicative subgroups).
category_tag: Sumsets in multiplicative subgroups of finite fields
status_search_result: Partial results exist: Shkredov and others have shown that small multiplicative subgroups of $\mathbb{F}_p$ cannot be written as a sumset $A+A$, and Alon–Bourgain and related work bound additive structure inside multiplicative subgroups. However, the precise extremal size of $A$ with $A-A \subseteq H$ and the existence/near-existence of $A$ with $A+A=H$ remain open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
context_brief: Large sum-free subsets of integer sets
original_question: Determine the largest constant c such that every sufficiently large finite set A of integers contains a sum-free subset of size at least c|A|, where sum-free means A has no solutions x + y = z within the subset.
self_contained_problem:
A subset S of an abelian group is called sum-free if there are no elements x, y, z ∈ S (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z. For a finite set A ⊂ ℤ, let s(A) denote the maximum size of a sum-free subset of A. Determine the largest constant c ∈ [0,1] such that for every sufficiently large finite set A ⊂ ℤ one has s(A) ≥ c·|A|. Equivalently, determine
   c* = liminf_{|A|→∞, A⊂ℤ finite}  s(A)/|A|.
status_search_result: Erdős (1965) proved c ≥ 1/3, and Bourgain improved the lower bound to s(A) ≥ (|A|+2)/3. In 2013, Eberhard, Green, and Manners proved a matching upper bound: for every ε > 0 there exist finite sets A ⊂ ℤ such that every sum-free subset has size at most (1/3 + ε)|A|. Together these results determine the constant: c = 1/3. (Refinements to the lower-order term remain of interest, but the value of the constant itself is settled.)
