$$E(\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}^r \oplus E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors}},$$
where the nonnegative integer $r$ is called the (algebraic) rank of $E$.

For each prime $p$ of good reduction, let $a_p = p + 1 - \#	ilde{E}(\mathbb{F}_p)$, where $	ilde{E}$ denotes the reduction of $E$ modulo $p$. Define the Hasse–Weil $L$-function of $E$ by the Euler product
$$L(E,s) = \prod_{p 	ext{ good}} \left(1 - a_p p^{-s} + p^{1-2s}ight)^{-1} \prod_{p 	ext{ bad}} \left(1 - a_p p^{-s}ight)^{-1},$$
which converges for $\Re(s) > 3/2$ and, by the modularity theorem, admits an analytic continuation to an entire function on $\mathbb{C}$.

Prove or disprove: for every elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ of rank $r$, the order of vanishing of $L(E,s)$ at $s = 1$ equals $r$, i.e.,
$$\mathrm{ord}_{s=1} L(E,s) = r.$$

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Let X be a non-singular complex projective variety. Determine whether every Hodge class on X, meaning a class in H^{2k}(X, Q) ∩ H^{k,k}(X), is a linear combination with rational coefficients of the cohomology classes of complex subvarieties of X.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a non-singular complex projective variety. For each non-negative integer k, the singular cohomology group H^{2k}(X, C) admits the Hodge decomposition H^{2k}(X, C) = ⊕_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X), and one defines the space of rational Hodge classes of degree 2k as Hdg^k(X) := H^{2k}(X, Q) ∩ H^{k,k}(X), where H^{2k}(X, Q) is viewed inside H^{2k}(X, C) via the natural inclusion. Every closed irreducible complex algebraic subvariety Z ⊂ X of complex codimension k determines a cohomology class [Z] ∈ H^{2k}(X, Q) (its Poincaré dual fundamental class), and such classes [Z] always lie in Hdg^k(X).

Prove or disprove the following statement: For every non-singular complex projective variety X and every non-negative integer k, every class α ∈ Hdg^k(X) can be written as a finite Q-linear combination α = Σ_i a_i [Z_i], where a_i ∈ Q and each Z_i is a closed complex algebraic subvariety of X of complex codimension k.
status_search_result: The Hodge conjecture is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open in general. It is known in low-degree cases (e.g., the Lefschetz (1,1)-theorem for k=1) and in some special classes of varieties, but the general statement is unresolved as of 2026.

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with given initial conditions, prove either that smooth, globally defined solutions satisfying the required conditions always exist, or that such smooth solutions do not always exist and the equations can break down.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $u:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}$:

$$\partial_t u_i + \sum_{j=1}^{3} u_j\,\partial_{x_j} u_i \;=\; \nu\,\Delta u_i - \partial_{x_i} p, \qquad i=1,2,3,$$

$$\nabla\cdot u \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{x_j} u_j \;=\; 0,$$

where $\nu>0$ is a fixed viscosity constant. Impose the initial condition $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$, where $u_0:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a prescribed divergence-free vector field that is $C^\infty$ and satisfies, for every multi-index $\alpha$ and every $K\ge 0$, a decay estimate of the form
$$|\partial^{\alpha} u_0(x)| \;\le\; C_{\alpha,K}\,(1+|x|)^{-K}.$$

Prove one of the following two statements:

(A) (Existence and smoothness) For every such initial datum $u_0$, there exist functions $u\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $p\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ solving the equations above on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$ with $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$ and satisfying the bounded-energy condition
$$\sup_{t\ge 0}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |u(x,t)|^2\,dx \;<\;\infty.$$

(B) (Breakdown) There exists an initial datum $u_0$ as above for which no pair $(u,p)$ with the smoothness and bounded-energy properties in (A) solves the equations on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$.
status_search_result: The Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open. No accepted proof of either global regularity or finite-time blow-up for the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exists as of 2026.

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Determine whether every problem for which a proposed solution can be verified quickly, meaning in polynomial time, also has an algorithm that can find a solution quickly; equivalently, determine whether every problem in NP is also in P.
self_contained_problem:
Let P denote the class of decision problems (languages L ⊆ {0,1}*) for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine that decides L in time polynomial in the length of its input. Let NP denote the class of decision problems L ⊆ {0,1}* for which there exists a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V(x, y) such that x ∈ L if and only if there exists a certificate y with |y| ≤ p(|x|) and V(x, y) = 1.

Determine whether P = NP. That is, prove that every language in NP can be decided by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time, or prove that there exists a language in NP that cannot be decided by any deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
status_search_result: The P versus NP problem is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems and is universally regarded as an open problem in theoretical computer science. No accepted proof of either P = NP or P ≠ NP exists as of 2026.

paper_title: Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Determine whether every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2.
self_contained_problem:
The Riemann zeta function is defined for complex numbers $s$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$ by the absolutely convergent series
$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s},$$
and is extended to a meromorphic function on the entire complex plane (with a single simple pole at $s = 1$) by analytic continuation. The functional equation
$$\zeta(s) = 2^{s}\pi^{s-1}\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi s}{2}\right)\Gamma(1-s)\,\zeta(1-s)$$
forces $\zeta(s) = 0$ at the negative even integers $s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots$; these are called the trivial zeros. All other zeros of $\zeta$ lie in the critical strip $\{s \in \mathbb{C} : 0 < \operatorname{Re}(s) < 1\}$ and are called nontrivial zeros.

Prove or disprove: every nontrivial zero $s$ of $\zeta(s)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(s) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis remains one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and is widely regarded as open. No accepted proof or disproof has been published; partial results include the proof that infinitely many nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line (Hardy, Selberg, Levinson, Conrey) and extensive numerical verification, but the full statement is unresolved as of 2026.

original_question: For any compact simple gauge group G, prove that a non-trivial quantum Yang-Mills theory exists on R^4 and has a positive mass gap Δ > 0, where the mass gap is the difference in energy between the vacuum and the next lowest energy state. The required existence result must establish axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in Streater and Wightman (1964) and Osterwalder and Schrader (1973, 1975).
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be an arbitrary compact, simple Lie group. Construct a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory on Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^4$ with gauge group $G$, satisfying a set of axiomatic properties at least as strong as the Wightman axioms for relativistic quantum field theory (alternatively, the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms in the Euclidean formulation, which guarantee reconstruction of a Wightman theory). The constructed theory must possess a positive mass gap: that is, there exists a constant $\Delta > 0$ such that every state in the Hilbert space (other than the vacuum) has energy at least $\Delta$ above the energy of the vacuum state. Equivalently, the spectrum of the Hamiltonian is contained in $\{0\} \cup [\Delta, \infty)$, with $0$ a simple eigenvalue corresponding to the vacuum. Prove the existence of such a theory and establish the mass gap property.

paper_title: The Top Unsolved Questions in Mathematics Remain Mostly Mysterious
original_question: Is every problem whose solution can be verified easily also a problem whose solution can be found easily? Using the terminology stated in the source, is the class P of questions with solutions that are easy to find the same as the class NP of questions with solutions that are easy to verify?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{0,1\}^*$ denote the set of finite binary strings. A language is a subset $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$. A deterministic Turing machine $M$ is said to decide $L$ in time $T(n)$ if, on every input $x \in \{0,1\}^*$ of length $n = |x|$, $M$ halts within $T(n)$ steps and accepts $x$ if and only if $x \in L$.

Define the complexity class $\mathrm{P}$ to be the set of all languages $L$ for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine $M$ and a polynomial $p$ such that $M$ decides $L$ in time $p(n)$.

Define the complexity class $\mathrm{NP}$ to be the set of all languages $L$ for which there exist a polynomial $q$ and a deterministic Turing machine $V$ (a verifier) running in time polynomial in $|x|$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$:
- if $x \in L$, then there exists a string $y \in \{0,1\}^*$ with $|y| \le q(|x|)$ such that $V$ accepts the pair $(x, y)$;
- if $x \notin L$, then for every string $y \in \{0,1\}^*$ with $|y| \le q(|x|)$, $V$ rejects $(x, y)$.

Question: Does $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$?
status_search_result: The P vs NP problem is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems and is universally regarded as a major open problem in mathematics and theoretical computer science. No accepted proof in either direction exists as of 2026.

original_question: Conjecture, 1947 ($100) The following limit exists: lim r(n, n)1/n = c n→∞
self_contained_problem:
For integers $s, t \geq 2$, the Ramsey number $r(s,t)$ is the smallest positive integer $N$ such that every 2-coloring of the edges of the complete graph $K_N$ with colors red and blue contains either a red clique on $s$ vertices or a blue clique on $t$ vertices. Write $r(n,n)$ for the diagonal Ramsey number. It is known that $\sqrt{2} \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} r(n,n)^{1/n} \leq \limsup_{n\to\infty} r(n,n)^{1/n} \leq 4$ (with recent improvements to the upper bound). Prove or disprove: the limit
$$c \;=\; \lim_{n \to \infty} r(n,n)^{1/n}$$
exists. If it does, determine its value.
status_search_result: The existence of $\lim_{n\to\infty} r(n,n)^{1/n}$ remains a famous open problem. Even with the recent exponential improvement on the upper bound for $r(n,n)$ by Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe (2023), the existence of the limit has not been established, and no nontrivial lower bound on $\liminf$ beyond $\sqrt 2$ is known.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on explicit constructions ($100) Give a constructive proof for r(n, n) > (1 + c)n for some constant c > 0. The best known constructive lower bound nc log n/ log log n is due to Frankl and Wilson [144]. 1 In this paper, by a graph we mean a simple loopless graph, unless otherwise specified.
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $s,t$, the diagonal Ramsey number $r(s,t)$ is the smallest integer $N$ such that every red/blue edge-coloring of the complete graph $K_N$ contains either a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$. Equivalently, $r(n,n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every simple graph on $N$ vertices contains either a clique of size $n$ or an independent set of size $n$.

A constructive lower bound for $r(n,n)$ means: an explicit deterministic algorithm that, given $n$, outputs a simple graph $G_n$ on $N$ vertices (in time polynomial in $N$) such that $G_n$ contains neither a clique of size $n$ nor an independent set of size $n$; this witnesses $r(n,n) > N$.

Problem: Exhibit such an explicit construction achieving an exponential lower bound. Concretely, find a constant $c > 0$ and an explicit (polynomial-time constructible) family of graphs $\{G_n\}$ on $N = N(n)$ vertices with no clique and no independent set of size $n$, such that
$$r(n,n) > (1+c)^n.$$
status_search_result: The best known explicit construction, due to Chattopadhyay and Zuckerman (2015) and subsequent improvements via two-source extractors, yields Ramsey graphs avoiding cliques/independent sets of size roughly $2^{(\log\log n)^c}$, i.e. lower bounds on $r(n,n)$ that are quasi-polynomial in $n$ but still far from exponential $(1+c)^n$. Recent (2025) exponential improvements by Ma–Shen–Xie are non-constructive. The explicit-construction problem of obtaining $r(n,n)>(1+c)^n$ remains open.

original_question: Problem (proposed by Burr, Erdo"s, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp [37]) Determine r(C4 , K1,n ).
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $H$ and an integer $n\ge 1$, let $r(H, K_{1,n})$ denote the Ramsey number, i.e., the least integer $N$ such that every red/blue edge-coloring of the complete graph $K_N$ contains either a red copy of $H$ or a blue copy of the star $K_{1,n}$ (equivalently, a vertex of blue-degree at least $n$). Let $C_4$ denote the cycle of length $4$.

It is known that
$$ n + \lceil \sqrt{n}\,\rceil + 1 \;\ge\; r(C_4, K_{1,n}) \;\ge\; n + \sqrt{n} - 6 n^{11/40}, $$
and that $r(C_4, K_{1,n}) = n + \lceil \sqrt{n}\,\rceil$ holds for infinitely many $n$.

Determine the value of $r(C_4, K_{1,n})$ for all positive integers $n$ (in particular, give an exact formula or sharp asymptotic expression).

original_question: Conjecture ($250, a very old problem of Erdo"s’) Determine lim (r(3, . . . , 3))1/k . k→∞    k This problem goes back essentially to Schur [200] who proved r(3, . . . , 3) < e k!    k It is known [45] that r(3, . . . , 3) is supermultiplicative so that the above    k limit exists.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $k\geq 1$, let $r_k = r(\underbrace{3,3,\dots,3}_{k})$ denote the $k$-color Ramsey number for triangles: the smallest integer $N$ such that every edge-coloring of the complete graph $K_N$ with $k$ colors contains a monochromatic triangle. It is known that the sequence $(r_k)$ is supermultiplicative, i.e. $r_{k+\ell}\geq r_k\, r_\ell$ for all $k,\ell\geq 1$, so by Fekete's lemma the limit 
$$L = \lim_{k\to\infty} r_k^{1/k}$$
exists in $(1,\infty]$. Schur's classical bound gives $r_k < e\cdot k!$ (in particular $L$ could a priori be infinite, although the upper bound $r_k \le \lfloor e\cdot k!\rfloor$ does not immediately yield finiteness via $k$-th roots). Determine the value of $L$.

Even basic values such as $r(3,3,3,3)$ are not known exactly (current bounds are $51\le r(3,3,3,3)\le 62$), and the asymptotic growth rate of multicolor triangle Ramsey numbers has not been resolved.

original_question: A size Ramsey problem for bounded degree graphs (proposed by Beck and Erdo"s [189]) For a graph G on n vertices with bounded degree, prove or disprove that r̂(G) ≤ cn. The case for paths was proved by Beck [19] and the case for cycles was proved by Haxell, Kohayakawa, and QLuczak [162]. Friedman and Pip- penger [145] settled the case for any bounded degree tree.

For a graph $G$, the size Ramsey number $\hat r(G)$ is the smallest integer $m$ such that there exists a graph $H$ with $m$ edges with the property that in every $2$-coloring of the edges of $H$ there is a monochromatic copy of $G$.

$$\hat r(G) \le c\, n.$$

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on the Turán number for complete bipartite graphs Prove that t(n, Kr,r ) > cn2−1/r where c is a constant depending on r (but independent of n). An upper bound for t(n, Kr,r ) of the same order was proved by Ko"vári, Sós and Turán [170] and Erdo"s independently. This long standing problem is well known as the problem of Zarankiewicz, first considered by Zarankiewicz [216] in 1951. However, it is included in the favorite problems of Erdo"s [79], who proposed many variations of this problem. The above conjecture is true for r = 2 and 3 (see [124]) and unsolved for r ≥ 4. The lower bound of t(n, Kr,r ) > cn2−2/(r+1) can be proved by probabilistic methods [131].
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $n$ and $r$, let $K_{r,r}$ denote the complete bipartite graph with $r$ vertices in each part, and let $t(n, K_{r,r})$ denote the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices that contains no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{r,r}$. The Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem gives
$$t(n, K_{r,r}) \le C_r \, n^{2 - 1/r}$$
for some constant $C_r > 0$ depending only on $r$.

Prove that for every integer $r \ge 2$ there exists a constant $c_r > 0$ (depending only on $r$) such that
$$t(n, K_{r,r}) > c_r \, n^{2 - 1/r}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Equivalently, show that the Kővári–Sós–Turán upper bound is tight in order of magnitude for every $r$.
status_search_result: The conjectured tight lower bound $t(n,K_{r,r}) \gtrsim n^{2-1/r}$ is known for $r=2$ (projective planes / Erdős–Rényi–Sós) and $r=3$ (via constructions of Brown). Kollár–Rónyai–Szabó (1996) and Alon–Rónyai–Szabó (1999) proved the bound for $K_{r,s}$ whenever $s \ge (r-1)!+1$ (and in particular $s \ge r!+1$), using norm and projective norm graphs. However, for the diagonal case $K_{r,r}$ with $r \ge 4$, the matching lower bound remains open; surveys continue to list it as a major open problem.

original_question: Conjecture (proposed by Erdo"s and Simonovits [129], 1984) If a bipartite graph H contains a subgraph H  with minimum degree greater than r, then t(n, H) ≥ cn2−1/r+ for some  > 0.
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $H$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ denote the Turán number of $H$: the maximum number of edges in an $H$-free graph on $n$ vertices. Prove or disprove the following statement.

Let $r \geq 2$ be an integer. Suppose $H$ is a bipartite graph that contains a subgraph $H'$ with minimum degree strictly greater than $r$. Then there exist constants $c > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ (depending only on $H$) such that
$$\mathrm{ex}(n,H) \;\geq\; c\, n^{\,2 - 1/r + \varepsilon}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.
status_search_result: The conjecture was disproved by Oliver Janzer (2021, published in IMRN 2023). For a finite simple graph $G$, call an induced subgraph $H$ of $G$ regular if every vertex of $H$ has the same degree within $H$ (this includes the empty graph and complete graphs as trivial regular subgraphs). By Ramsey's theorem one has $f(n) \geq c \log n$ for some absolute constant $c > 0$, since every $n$-vertex graph contains a clique or independent set of size at least $c \log n$, both of which are regular.

$$\frac{f(n)}{\log n} \longrightarrow \infty \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$

original_question: A problem on graphs covered by triangles (proposed by Erdo"s and Rothschild [86]) Suppose G is a graph of n vertices and e = cn2 edges. original_question: The problem of Erdo"s and Lovász [69] Suppose a graph G is k-chromatic and contains no Kk . Let a and b denote two integers satisfying a, b ≥ 2 and a+b = k+1. Do there exist two disjoint subgraphs of G of chromatic numbers a and b, respectively? The original question of Erdo"s is for the case k = 5, a = b = 3, which was proved aﬃrmatively by Brown and Jung [34]. Several small cases have been solved (for more discussion, see [158]). Of special interest is the following case for a = 2: Suppose the chromatic number of G decreases by 2 by removing any two vertices joining by an edge. Must G be the complete graph?

Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with chromatic number $\chi(G) = k$ that contains no clique on $k$ vertices (i.e., $K_k \not\subseteq G$). Let $a, b$ be integers with $a, b \geq 2$ and $a + b = k + 1$. 

Prove or disprove: there exist two vertex-disjoint subgraphs $G_1, G_2$ of $G$ with $\chi(G_1) = a$ and $\chi(G_2) = b$.

In particular, settle the following special case ($a = 2$): if $G$ is a graph such that for every edge $uv \in E(G)$ one has $\chi(G - \{u, v\}) = \chi(G) - 2$, must $G$ be a complete graph?

original_question: A problem on critical graphs (proposed by Erdo"s in 1949 [76]) A graph with chromatic number k is said to be edge critical or k-critical if the deletion of any edge decreases the chromatic number by 1. What is the largest number m, denoted by f (n, k), such that there is a k-critical graph on n vertices and m edges? In other words, determine f (n, k) lim = ck . n→∞ n2 Edge critical graphs were first introduced by Dirac [62] who answered a problem of Erdo"s from 1949 by showing f (n, k) > ck n2 for k ≥ 6 and, in particular, f (n, 6) > n2 /4 + cn. Erdo"s and Simonovits proved that f (n, 4) < n2 /4 + cn. Toft [212] showed that f (n, 4) > n2 /16 + cn by using a graph with many vertices of bounded degree. Erdo"s further raised the following questions:

original_question: Is it true that f (n, 6) = n2 /4 + n for n ≡ 2 modulo 4?
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ is called $k$-critical (more precisely, $k$-edge-critical) if $\chi(G) = k$ and $\chi(G - e) = k - 1$ for every edge $e$ of $G$. For integers $n \geq k \geq 4$, let 
$$f(n,k) = \max\{\,|E(G)| : G \text{ is a $k$-critical graph on } n \text{ vertices}\,\},$$
i.e. $f(n,k)$ is the largest possible number of edges in a $k$-critical graph with $n$ vertices.

Determine whether the following equality holds: for every integer $n$ with $n \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ (and $n$ sufficiently large),
$$f(n,6) \;=\; \frac{n^2}{4} + n.$$
status_search_result: The maximum number of edges in $k$-critical graphs has been studied since Dirac and Toft, with constructions giving roughly $n^2/4$ edges for $k \geq 6$. Pegden (2013) gave dense triangle-free critical constructions, and subsequent work (e.g. by Ma and others) addresses asymptotics, but no source located confirms the exact equality $f(n,6) = n^2/4 + n$ for $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$. The precise conjectured value appears still open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Is there a 4-chromatic critical graph on n vertices and cn2 edges which does not contain Kt,t for some large t?
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ is called $4$-chromatic critical (or $4$-critical) if its chromatic number is $\chi(G)=4$ and every proper subgraph $H \subsetneq G$ satisfies $\chi(H) < 4$. For positive integers $s,t$, let $K_{s,t}$ denote the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $s$ and $t$.

Does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that, for every sufficiently large integer $t$, there exist arbitrarily large $4$-chromatic critical graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $c n^{2}$ edges that contain no copy of $K_{t,t}$ as a subgraph?

(It is known that such graphs exist when $t$ is allowed to grow as slowly as $t \le c'\log n$; the question is whether $t$ can be taken to be an arbitrary large constant, independent of $n$.)
status_search_result: Web search did not locate a definitive resolution. Rödl (unpublished) is reported to have given a construction with t up to about c log n, but no source confirming a construction for arbitrary fixed large t, or a proof of impossibility, was found.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on critical graphs with large degree (proposed by Erdo"s [76, 73]) Let g(n, k) denote the maximum value m such that there exists a k-critical graph on n vertices with minimum degree at least m. What is the magnitude of g(n, k)? Is it true that g(n, 4) ≥ cn for some constant c? Simonovits [204] and Toft [213] proved that g(n, 4) ≥ cn1/3 .
self_contained_problem:
For integers $k\ge 4$ and $n\ge k$, a graph $G$ is called $k$-critical if its chromatic number is $\chi(G)=k$ but every proper subgraph $H\subsetneq G$ satisfies $\chi(H)<k$. Define
$$g(n,k) = \max\{\,m : \text{there exists a $k$-critical graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree at least } m\,\}.$$
It is known that $g(n,4) \ge c\, n^{1/3}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$.

(a) Determine the order of magnitude of $g(n,k)$ as $n\to\infty$ (for fixed $k\ge 4$).

(b) In particular, decide whether there exists a constant $c>0$ such that
$$g(n,4) \ge c\, n$$
for all sufficiently large $n$; that is, whether there exist $4$-critical graphs on $n$ vertices whose minimum degree is linear in $n$.
status_search_result: The question of the order of magnitude of g(n,k), and in particular whether g(n,4) ≥ cn, is listed as an open Erdős problem on the Erdős problems site. The best known lower bound remains the Simonovits/Toft result g(n,4) ≫ n^{1/3}; no construction giving linear minimum degree (or matching upper bound proving this is impossible) appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on vertex critical graphs (proposed by Erdo"s [73]) A graph with chromatic number k is said to be vertex critical or k-vertex- critical if the deletion of any vertex decreases the chromatic number by 1. Is there some positive function f (n) so that for every k ≥ 4 there exists a graph G on n vertices which is k-vertex-critical but χ(G − A) = k for any set A of at most f (n) edges? Brown [31] gave an example of a 5-vertex-critical graph with no critical edges.
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=k$ is called $k$-vertex-critical if $\chi(G-v) = k-1$ for every vertex $v$ of $G$. An edge $e$ of $G$ is called critical if $\chi(G-e) < \chi(G)$.

Question: Does there exist a positive function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $f(n)\to\infty$ such that for every integer $k\ge 4$ and for infinitely many $n$, there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with the property that $\chi(G-A)=k$ for every set $A$ of at most $f(n)$ edges of $G$?
status_search_result: Recent work (Skottova–Steiner, 2025) establishes for every k>4 that f_k(n) = Ω(n^{1/3}) (and Ω(√n) along an infinite subsequence), along with an upper bound f_k(n) = O(n/(log n)^{Ω(1)}) for k≥4. The case k=4 remains open and is tied to Dirac's 1970 conjecture on the existence of 4-vertex-critical graphs with no critical edges, which is still unresolved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on strong chromatic index (proposed by Erdo"s and Nešetřil [76] 1985) The strong chromatic index χ∗ (G) of a graph G is the least number r so that the edges of G can be colored in r colors in such a way that any two adjacent vertices in G are not incident to edges of the same color. Suppose G has maximum degree k. Is it true that χ∗ (G) ≤ 5k 2 /4 if k is even and χ∗ (G) ≤ 5k 2 /4 − k/2 + 1/4 if k is odd? This conjecture is open for k ≥ 4 while the cases of k ≤ 3 are solved by Anderson [13] and Horák, Qing and Trotter [156]. Chung, Gyárfás, Trotter and Tuza [56] proved that if G contains no induced 2K2 , then G has at most 5k 2 /4 edges.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a simple graph. The strong chromatic index χ'_s(G) is the smallest integer r such that the edges of G can be colored with r colors so that any two edges that are either adjacent or joined by an edge receive distinct colors (equivalently, every color class is an induced matching). Let k = Δ(G) be the maximum degree of G.

Prove or disprove: 
- If k is even, then χ'_s(G) ≤ 5k²/4.
- If k is odd, then χ'_s(G) ≤ (5k² − 2k + 1)/4.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Nešetřil strong chromatic index conjecture (1985) is verified only for maximum degree Δ ≤ 3 (Andersen; Horák, Qing, Trotter) and remains open for all Δ ≥ 4. Partial progress exists (e.g., Molloy–Reed bound ≤ 1.998Δ² for large Δ, results for claw-free and P5-free classes), but the conjectured bound is unproved in general.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on three-coloring (proposed by Erdo"s, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp [139]) Is it true that in every three-coloring of the edges of Kn there is a set of three vertices which are adjacent to at least two-third of all the vertices by edges of the same color? If true, it is the best possible as shown by an example given by Kierstead [139].
self_contained_problem:
Let $K_n$ denote the complete graph on $n$ vertices. Suppose the edges of $K_n$ are colored with three colors (arbitrarily). For a color $c$ and a set $S$ of vertices, say that a vertex $v \notin S$ is a $c$-neighbor of $S$ if there exists some $u \in S$ such that the edge $uv$ has color $c$.

Prove or disprove: for every three-coloring of the edges of $K_n$, there exist three vertices $v_1, v_2, v_3$ and a color $c \in \{1,2,3\}$ such that the number of vertices $v \in V(K_n) \setminus \{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ that are joined to at least one of $v_1, v_2, v_3$ by an edge of color $c$ is at least $\tfrac{2}{3} n$.

(The constant $2/3$ and the bound of three vertices cannot be improved, as shown by a known construction.)
status_search_result: The problem, known as the 2/3 conjecture of Erdős, Faudree, (Gould,) Gyárfás, Rousseau and Schelp, was solved by Haxell, Łuczak, Peng, Rödl, Ruciński and Skokan (and others), with a complete solution titled "A solution to the 2/3 conjecture" published in SIAM J. Discrete Math. (arXiv:1306.6202), proving that in every 3-edge-coloring of K_n there is a set of three vertices that monochromatically dominates at least 2n/3 vertices.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on anti-Ramsey graphs (proposed by Burr, Erdo"s, Graham and Sós [39]) For a graph G, determine the least integer r = f (n, e, G) so that there is some graph H on n vertices and e edges which can be r-edge-colored such that all edges of every copy of G in H have different colors. It seems to be a diﬃcult problem to get good bounds for f (n, e, G) for a general graph G (see [39]). Even for special cases, there are large gaps between known bounds. For example, it was shown in [39, 38] that f (n, e, C5 ) ≥ cn n for e = (1/4 + )n2 and f (n, e, C5 ) = O(n2 / log n) for e = (1/2 − )n2 . √ Also, f (n, e, P4 ) > cn n for e = n2 and f (n, e, P4 ) ≤ n for n = n / exp(c log n). Covering and packing
self_contained_problem:
For a fixed graph $G$ and positive integers $n,e$, let $f(n,e,G)$ denote the least integer $r$ such that there exists a graph $H$ on $n$ vertices and $e$ edges admitting an edge-coloring with $r$ colors in which every copy of $G$ in $H$ has all its edges colored with distinct colors (i.e., is rainbow). 

Determine good asymptotic bounds for $f(n,e,G)$ as a function of $n$, $e$, and $G$. In particular, close the gaps in the following special cases:

(a) For the 5-cycle $C_5$: it is known that $f(n,e,C_5) \ge c\sqrt{n}$ when $e = (1/4+\varepsilon)n^2$, while $f(n,e,C_5) = O(n^2/\log n)$ when $e = (1/2-\varepsilon)n^2$. Determine the true order of magnitude of $f(n,e,C_5)$ in these regimes.

(b) For the path $P_4$ on 4 vertices: it is known that $f(n,e,P_4) > c'\sqrt{n}$ when $e = \varepsilon n^2$, while $f(n,e,P_4) \le n'$ when $e = n^2/\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})$. Determine the true order of magnitude of $f(n,e,P_4)$ in these regimes.
status_search_result: Recent work has established the asymptotic formula f(n,e,C_{2k+1}) = e/2 + (n/2)√(e − n²/4) + o(n²) for odd cycles C_{2k+1} with k ≥ 4 over the full non-trivial range of e, confirming a related conjecture of Burr–Erdős–Graham–Sós. However, the specific gaps for C_5 and P_4 highlighted in the problem (between √n-type lower bounds and n²/log n or n/exp(c√log n) upper bounds) do not appear to have been closed; the general problem of determining f(n,e,G) remains open for many graphs G.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on covering by C4 ’s (proposed by Erdo"s and Faudree [88]) Suppose a graph G has 4n vertices with minimum degree at least 2n. Then G has n vertex-disjoint C4 ’s.
self_contained_problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $G$ be a graph on $4n$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta(G) \geq 2n$. Prove that $G$ contains $n$ pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles of length $4$ (i.e., $n$ vertex-disjoint copies of $C_4$ whose vertex sets together cover all $4n$ vertices of $G$).
status_search_result: The Erdős–Faudree conjecture on covering by C₄'s was proved by Hong Wang, "Proof of the Erdős–Faudree Conjecture on Quadrilaterals" (Graphs and Combinatorics, 2010), establishing that every graph on 4n vertices with minimum degree at least 2n contains n vertex-disjoint 4-cycles.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on clique covering and clique partition (proposed by Erdo"s, Faudree and Ordman [92]) The clique covering number cc(G) of G is the least number of cliques that covers the graph. The clique partition number cp(G) is the least number of cliques that partition the edge set of G. Here Gn denotes a graph on n vertices. Determine the largest value c such that cp(Gn ) > cn2 cc(Gn ) for an infinite family of graphs Gn . An example was given in [92] with c = 1/64. Is there a sequence of graphs Gn such that cp(Gn ) − cc(Gn ) = n2 /4 + O(n)? In [40] it was shown cp(Gn ) − cc(Gn ) = n2 /4 − n3/2 /2 + n/4 + O(1).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$, let the clique covering number $\mathrm{cc}(G)$ denote the minimum number of cliques of $G$ whose union covers every edge of $G$, and let the clique partition number $\mathrm{cp}(G)$ denote the minimum number of cliques that partition the edge set of $G$ (each edge in exactly one clique). Let $G_n$ denote a graph on $n$ vertices.

(a) Determine the largest constant $c > 0$ for which there exists an infinite family of graphs $\{G_n\}$ with
$$\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) > c\,n^2.$$
(It is known that this holds with $c = 1/64$, and that for every graph on $n$ vertices one has $\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) \le n^2/4 - n^{3/2}/2 + n/4 + O(1)$.)

(b) Does there exist an infinite sequence of graphs $\{G_n\}$ on $n$ vertices for which
$$\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) = \frac{n^2}{4} + O(n)?$$
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Erdős, Faudree, and Ordman (1988), asks for the largest constant c with cp(G_n) − cc(G_n) > c n² for an infinite family, and whether the difference can attain n²/4 + O(n). The best published lower-bound construction gives c = 1/64, and an upper bound of n²/4 − n^{3/2}/2 + n/4 + O(1) is known. Subsequent literature (e.g., Cavers' thesis, surveys of Erdős problems) still lists the gap as unresolved, with no source found establishing the optimal c or matching the n²/4 + O(n) lower bound.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: The ascending subgraph decomposition problem (proposed by Alavi, Boals, Erdo"s, Chartrand and Oellermann [5]) Suppose G is a graph with n(n + 1)/2 edges. Prove that G can be edge- partitioned into subgraphs Gi with i edges such that Gi is isomorphic to a subgraph of Gi+1 for i = 1, . . . , n − 1. A special case is the decomposition of star forests into stars (which is the so-called suitcase problem of partitioning integers 1, . . . , n into k parts with given sums a1 , . . . , ak for any ai ≤ n and ai = n(n + 1)/2). The suitcase problem was solved by Ma, Zhou and Zhou [185, 184]. General extremal problems
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer and let G be a (simple, finite) graph with exactly n(n+1)/2 edges. An ascending subgraph decomposition of G is a partition of the edge set E(G) into n edge-disjoint subgraphs G_1, G_2, ..., G_n such that:
(i) for each i = 1, ..., n, the subgraph G_i has exactly i edges, and
(ii) for each i = 1, ..., n-1, G_i is isomorphic to a subgraph of G_{i+1}.

Prove that every graph G with n(n+1)/2 edges admits an ascending subgraph decomposition.
status_search_result: The conjecture was posed in 1987 by Alavi, Boals, Chartrand, Erdős, and Oellermann. Many special cases (star forests, certain tournaments, regular graphs, etc.) have been resolved. A 2023 preprint by Katsamaktsis et al. (arXiv:2308.11613) proves the conjecture for all sufficiently large n, but the conjecture in full generality (all n) remains open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on trees 1962, (proposed by Erdo"s and Sós) Every graph on n vertices having at least n(k−1)/2+1 edges must contain as a subgraph every tree of k + 1 vertices, for n ≥ k + 1. This conjecture, if true, is best possible. Some asymptotic approximations of this conjecture were given by Komlós and Szemerédi (unpublished). Also, this conjecture is proved for some special families of trees such as caterpillars. Brandt and Dobson [30] have proved the conjecture for graphs with girth at least 5.
self_contained_problem: Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer and let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices with $n \ge k+1$. Prove or disprove the following statement: if $G$ has at least $\frac{n(k-1)}{2}+1$ edges, then $G$ contains, as a subgraph, every tree on $k+1$ vertices. (Equivalently, every graph with average degree greater than $k-1$ contains every tree with $k+1$ vertices as a subgraph.)
status_search_result: The Erdős–Sós conjecture (1962) remains open in general. It is known to hold in several special cases: for caterpillars, for graphs of girth at least 5 (Brandt–Dobson), and an announced proof by Ajtai, Komlós, Simonovits, and Szemerédi handles all sufficiently large $k$, but this proof has remained unpublished. Thus the conjecture is widely regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: The (n/2-n/2-n/2) conjecture (proposed by Erdo"s, Füredi, Loebl and Sós [99]) Let G be a graph with n vertices and suppose at least n/2 vertices have degree at least n/2. Then G contains any tree on at most n/2 vertices. Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi [4] proved the following asymptotic version: If G has n vertices and at least (1 + )n/2 vertices have degree at least (1 + )n/2, then G contains any tree on at most n/2 vertices if n is large enough (depending on ). Komlós and Sós conjectured [99]: Let G be a graph with n vertices and suppose at least n/2 vertices have degree at least k. Then G contains any tree with k vertices.
self_contained_problem:
Komlós–Sós conjecture (generalization of the (n/2, n/2, n/2) conjecture of Erdős, Füredi, Loebl and Sós):

Let k and n be positive integers. Let G = (V, E) be a simple finite graph with |V| = n vertices, and suppose that at least n/2 of its vertices have degree at least k. Prove that for every tree T on k vertices, G contains a subgraph isomorphic to T.

(Equivalently in the special case k = n/2: if at least n/2 vertices of an n-vertex graph have degree at least n/2, then G contains every tree on at most n/2 vertices.)
status_search_result: The Loebl–Komlós–Sós conjecture is known to be true asymptotically (Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi for the (n/2,n/2,n/2) case; Hladký–Komlós–Piguet–Simonovits–Stein–Szemerédi proved the approximate version for all k for large n). It is also known in special cases (e.g., trees of diameter at most 5, certain caterpillars, skewed trees). The exact conjecture in full generality remains open.

original_question: A conjecture of Erdo"s and Gallai, 1959 [100] Every connected graph on n vertices can be edge-partitioned into at most (n + 1)/2 paths. Lovász [179] showed that every graph on n vertices can be edge-partitioned into at most n/2 cycles and paths. self_contained_problem: Let G be a finite, simple, connected graph on n vertices. A path decomposition of G is a partition of the edge set E(G) into edge-disjoint subgraphs, each of which is a (simple) path. original_question: A problem on clique transversals (proposed by Erdo"s, Gallai and Tuza [101]) Estimate the cardinality, denoted by τ (G), of a smallest set that shares a vertex with every clique of G. Denote by R(n) the largest integer such that every triangle-free graph on n vertices contains an independent set of R(n) vertices. Is it true that τ (G) ≤ n − R(n) ? √ From the results √ on Ramsey numbers r(3, k), we know that c n log n < R(n) < c n log n. So far, the best known bound [101] is τ (G) ≤ n − √ 2n + c for a small constant c.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices. A clique of $G$ is a maximal complete subgraph. Define the clique transversal number $\tau(G)$ as the minimum cardinality of a set $S \subseteq V(G)$ such that $S \cap V(K) \neq \emptyset$ for every clique $K$ of $G$. Define $R(n)$ to be the largest integer $r$ such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set of size $r$ (equivalently, $R(n)$ is determined by the off-diagonal Ramsey number $r(3,k)$, and satisfies $c\sqrt{n\log n} < R(n) < c'\sqrt{n\log n}$ for absolute constants $c,c'>0$).

Prove or disprove: for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices,
$$\tau(G) \le n - R(n).$$
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. The best known bound stated in the literature is τ(G) ≤ n − √(2n) + c, which is significantly weaker than n − R(n) since R(n) is of order √(n log n). An Erdős problems database entry on "CliqueTransversalUpperBound" lists this question, and related papers on the Erdős–Gallai–Tuza conjecture address a different (edge-deletion) formulation, not this vertex bound.

original_question: A problem on the diameter of a Kr -free graph (proposed by Erdo"s, Pach, Pollack and Tuza [119]) Let G denote a connected graph on n vertices with minimum degree δ. Show that if G is K2r -free and δ is a multiple of (r − 1)(3r + 2), then the diameter of G, denoted by D(G), satisfies 2(r − 1)(3r + 2) D(G) ≤ n + O(1) (2r2 − 1)δ when n approaches infinity. If G is K2r+1 -free and δ is a multiple of 3r −1, then 3r − 1 D(G) ≤ n + O(1) rδ when n approaches infinity. In [119], bounds for the diameters of triangle-free or Ck -free graphs with given minimum degree were derived.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r \geq 2$ be an integer, and let $G$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta$. Denote by $D(G)$ the diameter of $G$.

(a) Suppose $G$ contains no clique on $2r$ vertices (i.e., $G$ is $K_{2r}$-free) and that $\delta$ is a multiple of $(r-1)(3r+2)$. Prove or disprove that, as $n \to \infty$,
$$D(G) \leq \frac{2(r-1)(3r+2)}{(2r^2-1)\,\delta}\, n + O(1).$$

(b) Suppose $G$ is $K_{2r+1}$-free and that $\delta$ is a multiple of $3r-1$. Prove or disprove that, as $n \to \infty$,
$$D(G) \leq \frac{3r-1}{r\,\delta}\, n + O(1).$$

Establish these bounds, or determine the correct asymptotic value of the supremum of $D(G)\,\delta/n$ over the respective classes.

Combin. Theory B, 2021), showing the conjectured constant is not correct for large δ. Sharp/refined results have since appeared (arXiv:2502.08626, 2025). paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem ($100, many years ago) Is there a sequence A of density 0 for which there is a constant c(A) so that for n > n0 (A), every graph on n vertices and c(A)n edges contains a cycle whose length is in A. Erdo"s said [81], “I am almost certain that if A is the sequence of powers of 2 then no such constant exists. What if A is the sequence of squares? I have no guess. Let f (n) be the smallest integer for which every graph on n vertices and f (n) edges contains a cycle of length 2k for some k. I think that f (n)/n → ∞ but that f (n) < n(log n)c for some c > 0.” Alon pointed out that f (n) ≤ cn log n using the fact [29] that graphs with n vertices and ck 1+1/k edges contain cycles of all even lengths between 2k and 2kn1/k (by taking k to be about log n/2).
self_contained_problem:
Call a set A of positive integers a "cycle-forcing density-zero set" if A has natural density 0 (i.e. |A ∩ [1,N]|/N → 0 as N → ∞) and there exist a constant c(A) > 0 and an integer n₀(A) such that for every n > n₀(A), every simple graph on n vertices with at least c(A)·n edges contains a cycle whose length belongs to A.

(a) Does there exist any cycle-forcing density-zero set A ⊆ ℕ?

(b) In particular, decide whether A = {2^k : k ≥ 1} (the powers of 2) and A = {k² : k ≥ 1} (the perfect squares) are cycle-forcing density-zero sets.

(c) Let f(n) denote the smallest integer such that every simple graph on n vertices with f(n) edges contains a cycle whose length is a power of 2. Determine the asymptotic growth of f(n); in particular, decide whether f(n)/n → ∞ and whether f(n) < n(log n)^c for some constant c > 0.
status_search_result: The variant for powers of 2 has been resolved in the positive direction by work of Liu and Montgomery (and Sudakov–Verstraëte), showing that there are density-zero sets (including the powers of 2, with appropriate edge bounds) for which every graph with sufficiently large average degree contains a cycle of length in the set—contrary to Erdős's original guess. The bound f(n) = O(n log n) was noted by Alon, and improved bounds on f(n) follow from these works. The case of squares and the precise asymptotics of f(n) appear to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A decomposition problem about odd cycles (proposed by Erdo"s and Graham [102])
self_contained_problem:
It is known that the complete graph $K_{2n}$ on $2n$ vertices can be edge-partitioned into $n$ bipartite graphs, and that this is impossible for $K_{2n+1}$. Consequently, in any decomposition of the edge set of $K_{2n+1}$ into $n$ subgraphs, at least one subgraph must contain an odd cycle. For each positive integer $n$, define
$$f(n) = \min_{\mathcal{D}} \; \max_{G \in \mathcal{D}} \; \mathrm{oddgirth}(G),$$
where the minimum is taken over all edge-decompositions $\mathcal{D} = \{G_1, \dots, G_n\}$ of $K_{2n+1}$ into $n$ subgraphs, and where, for a graph $G$ containing an odd cycle, $\mathrm{oddgirth}(G)$ is the length of a shortest odd cycle in $G$ (set to $0$ if $G$ has no odd cycle). Equivalently, $f(n)$ is the smallest integer $m$ such that in every decomposition of $K_{2n+1}$ into $n$ subgraphs, one of the subgraphs contains an odd cycle of length at most $m$.

Determine $f(n)$. In particular, decide whether $f(n)$ is bounded or unbounded as $n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up any published determination of f(n) or any proof that it is bounded/unbounded. The problem is listed among Erdős's open problems, and no resolution appears in the literature on cycle decompositions of complete graphs.

original_question: A problem on almost bipartite graphs (proposed by Erdo"s [82]) Suppose G has the property that for every m, every subgraph on m vertices contains an independent set of size m/2 − k. Let f (k) denote the smallest number such that G can be made bipartite by deleting f (k) vertices.
self_contained_problem:

Equivalently, $f(k)$ is the smallest integer such that every graph $G$ with property $P_k$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $f(k)$ vertices.

It is known that $f(k)$ is finite for every $k \geq 0$. Determine good upper and lower bounds on $f(k)$ as a function of $k$, and in particular improve the existing estimates for $f(k)$.

original_question: A problem of Erdo"s and Rado [122] What is the least number k = k(n, m) so that for every directed graph on k vertices, either there is an independent set of size n or the graph includes a directed path of size m (not necessarily induced)? Erdo"s and Rado [122] give an upper bound of [2m−1 (n−1)m +n−2]/(2n− 3). Mitchell and Larson [176] give a recurrence relation and obtain a bound of n2 for m = 3 and, more generally, of nm−1 for m > 3. Random graphs
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $n$ and $m$, let $k(n,m)$ denote the least positive integer $k$ such that every directed graph (digraph) on $k$ vertices either contains an independent set of size $n$ (i.e., a set of $n$ vertices with no directed edges among them in either direction) or contains a directed path of size $m$ (a sequence of $m$ distinct vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_m$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is a directed edge for each $i=1,\dots,m-1$; the path need not be induced). Determine the exact value, or improved bounds, for $k(n,m)$. Known bounds include the upper bound
$$k(n,m) \le \frac{2^{m-1}(n-1)^m + n - 2}{2n-3},$$
and the improved bound $k(n,3) \le n^2$, and more generally $k(n,m) \le n^{m-1}$ for $m > 3$.
status_search_result: The problem corresponds to digraph Ramsey-type numbers concerning independent sets versus directed paths (or transitive tournaments). Known upper bounds include the original Erdős–Rado bound and an improved $n^{m-1}$ bound by Mitchell and Larson, but no general exact determination of $k(n,m)$ was found in available sources, so the problem appears to remain open in general.

original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s, see [9]) Let G denote a random graph on n vertices and cn edges. What is the largest r, denoted by r(c), for which the probability that the chromatic number is r is at least some constant strictly greater than 0 (and indepen- dent of n)? This is open except for r = 3 (see [9]). QLuczak [182] gave an asymptotic estimate: c r(c) = (1 + o(1)) . 2 log c However, the exact values are not known.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a real number $c>0$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, let $G_n$ be a graph chosen uniformly at random from all graphs on the vertex set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ with exactly $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ edges. Let $\chi(G_n)$ denote the chromatic number of $G_n$.

Define
$$r(c) := \max\Bigl\{ r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} : \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\chi(G_n)=r] > 0 \Bigr\},$$
i.e., the largest integer $r$ such that the probability that $\chi(G_n)$ equals $r$ stays bounded below by a positive constant (independent of $n$) along the sequence.

Determine the exact value of $r(c)$ for every $c>0$. (It is known that $r(c) = (1+o(1))\,\dfrac{c}{2\log c}$ as $c\to\infty$, and that $r=3$ is understood; the problem is to find the exact values for all $c$.)
status_search_result: Literature on the chromatic number of sparse random graphs G(n, cn) provides asymptotic estimates (Łuczak's c/(2 log c) bound) and two-point concentration results, but no source gives exact values of r(c) for general c beyond the case r=3. The problem appears to still be open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s, see [9]) How accurately can one estimate the chromatic number of a random graph (with edge probability 1/2)? Prove or disprove that the error is more (much more) than O(1). Shamir and Spencer have an O(n1/2 ) upper bound [201]. An old problem raised by Erdo"s and Rényi [123] is to determine the chro- matic number of a random graph with given edge density. This problem has almost been completely resolved due to the work of Matula [186], Shamir and Spencer [201], and Bollobás [23]. The order of the chro- matic number for both sparse and dense random graphs have been deter- mined asymptotically. For random graphs with edge density p satisfying p ≤ n−5/6− , where  > 0, Shamir and Spencer showed that the chro- matic number almost surely takes on at most five different values. QLuczak later on [181] proved that for such sparse random graphs, the chromatic number is concentrated at two values.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(n,1/2)$ denote the Erdős–Rényi random graph on $n$ labeled vertices in which each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ possible edges is included independently with probability $1/2$. Let $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ denote its chromatic number, i.e., the minimum number of colors needed to properly color its vertices.

Shamir and Spencer proved that there exists a (deterministic) sequence of integers $a_n$ such that, with probability tending to $1$ as $n \to \infty$,
$$|\chi(G(n,1/2)) - a_n| = O(\sqrt{n}).$$
In other words, the chromatic number is concentrated in an interval of length $O(\sqrt{n})$.

Determine how accurately one can estimate $\chi(G(n,1/2))$. Specifically: prove or disprove that the error of any such estimate must grow faster than any constant, i.e., that $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ is not concentrated on $O(1)$ consecutive integers. More generally, identify the true order of magnitude of the smallest sequence of intervals $I_n$ such that $\chi(G(n,1/2)) \in I_n$ with high probability.
status_search_result: Major progress was made by Annika Heckel (2019, published in J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2021), who proved that $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ is not concentrated on any interval of length $n^{1/4-\varepsilon}$, thereby answering the qualitative form of the question (the error is much more than $O(1)$, in fact at least $n^{1/4-\varepsilon}$). Subsequent work by Heckel and Riordan further sharpened these non-concentration results. However, the exact order of the fluctuations of $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ — closing the gap between the $n^{1/4-\varepsilon}$ lower bound and the $O(\sqrt{n})$ Shamir–Spencer upper bound — remains open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on a spanning cube in a random graph (proposed by Erdo"s and Bollobás, see [88]) A random graph on n = 2d vertices with edge density 1/2 contains an d-cube.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d$ be a positive integer and set $n=2^d$. Let $G(n,1/2)$ denote the Erdős–Rényi random graph on $n$ labeled vertices in which each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ possible edges is included independently with probability $1/2$. The $d$-dimensional hypercube $Q_d$ is the graph whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^d$ and whose edges connect pairs of binary strings that differ in exactly one coordinate; in particular $Q_d$ has $2^d$ vertices and is $d$-regular.

Prove or disprove: as $d\to\infty$, with probability tending to $1$, the random graph $G(2^d,1/2)$ contains a spanning subgraph isomorphic to $Q_d$.
status_search_result: Alon and Füredi (1992) showed that for any fixed edge density p>1/2 the random graph on 2^d vertices contains a spanning d-cube with high probability, while for p≤1/4 it does not. Riordan (2000) strengthened this by proving that for any fixed p>1/4 the random graph G(2^d,p) almost surely contains a spanning d-cube. Since 1/2>1/4, Riordan's theorem resolves the Erdős–Bollobás conjecture affirmatively at edge density 1/2.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s and Spencer [9]) Start with n vertices and add edges at random one by one. If we stop when every vertex is contained in a triangle, is there a set of vertex disjoint triangles covering every vertex (except for at most two vertices)? The above question can be posed for other configurations as well [9]. In particular, Bollobás and Frieze [26] showed that stopping as soon as there is no isolated vertex, then there already almost surely is a perfect matching if the number of vertices is even. If we stop when every vertex has degree at least 2, Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi [3] and Bollobás [24] proved that there already almost surely is a Hamiltonian cycle.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the random graph process on $n$ labeled vertices: starting from the empty graph, edges are added one at a time, uniformly at random among all edges not yet present, producing a nested sequence of graphs $G_0 \subset G_1 \subset \cdots \subset G_{\binom{n}{2}}$. Let $\tau$ denote the stopping time

$$\tau = \min\{ m \ge 0 : \text{every vertex of } G_m \text{ is contained in a triangle}\}.$$

Prove or disprove: with probability tending to $1$ as $n \to \infty$, the graph $G_\tau$ contains a collection of pairwise vertex-disjoint triangles that covers all but at most two of the $n$ vertices.
status_search_result: Heckel, Kaufmann, Müller and Pasch (2023/2024, "The hitting time of clique factors", Random Structures & Algorithms) proved a hitting-time result showing that, in the random graph process, at the very moment the last vertex becomes contained in a triangle (more generally, in a copy of K_r), the graph already contains a triangle factor (clique factor), modulo divisibility. This affirmatively resolves the Erdős–Spencer question, which allowed for up to two uncovered vertices to deal with the divisibility issue.

original_question: Conjecture ($500) Is there an absolute constant c > 0 such that log log r3 (n, n) ≥ cn? This is true if four colors are allowed [110]. If just three colors are allowed, there is some improvement due to Erdo"s and Hajnal (unpublished). 2 2 r3 (n, n, n) > ecn log n .
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $N$, let $K_N^{(3)}$ denote the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $N$ vertices (whose edges are all $3$-element subsets of an $N$-vertex set). For a positive integer $n$, define the hypergraph Ramsey number $r_3(n,n)$ to be the least integer $N$ such that every $2$-coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_n^{(3)}$ (i.e., $n$ vertices all of whose $3$-element subsets receive the same color).

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\log \log r_3(n,n) \geq c\, n,$$
equivalently $r_3(n,n) \geq 2^{2^{cn}}$.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open. Erdős offered $500 for its resolution. The best known lower bound for the 2-color case is of the form $r_3(n,n) \geq 2^{n^{c\log n}}$ (so $\log\log r_3(n,n) \gtrsim (\log n)^2$), far from the conjectured $2^{2^{cn}}$. The analogous statement is known for 4 colors (Erdős–Hajnal–Rado), and for 3 colors there is a partial improvement by Erdős and Hajnal. Recent surveys and papers (e.g., Mubayi–Suk 2017 survey; Conlon–Fox–Sudakov work) still list it as open.

For an integer $t\ge 2$, a finite set $S$ of $n$ elements, and integers $u,v\ge t$, let $f_t(n,u,v)$ denote the largest integer $k$ such that for every 2-coloring of the $t$-element subsets of $S$ in blue and red, either there is a $k$-element subset of $S$ all of whose $t$-element subsets are blue, or there is a $u$-element subset of $S$ that contains at least $v$ red $t$-element subsets.

Define a function $g_t:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ recursively by:
- $g_t(k)=0$ for $k<t$,
- $g_t(t)=1$,
- for $k>t$, $g_t(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{t} g_t(u_i)+\prod_{i=1}^{t} u_i$, where $u_1,\dots,u_t$ are positive integers with $u_1+\cdots+u_t=k$ chosen to be as nearly equal as possible.

Prove or disprove the following: there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for every fixed $k\ge t$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$f_t(n,k,g_t(k)+1)\le (\log n)^{c}.$$

original_question: A conjecture for triple systems (proposed by Brown, Erdös and Sós [33, 78]) Let f (n, k, r) denote the least integer m such that every 3-graph on n vertices with more than m triples contains an induced subgraph on k vertices with at least r edges. Prove that f (n, k, k − 3) = o(n2 ).
self_contained_problem:
A 3-uniform hypergraph (3-graph) on a vertex set $V$ is a pair $(V,E)$ where $E$ is a collection of 3-element subsets ("triples" or "edges") of $V$. For positive integers $n$, $k$, and $r$, let $f(n,k,r)$ denote the least integer $m$ such that every 3-graph on $n$ vertices with more than $m$ triples contains a set $S$ of $k$ vertices for which the induced subhypergraph on $S$ has at least $r$ edges (i.e., at least $r$ triples of the hypergraph are subsets of $S$).

Prove (or disprove) that for every fixed integer $k \ge 3$,
$$f(n,k,k-3) = o(n^2)\qquad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$

Equivalently, show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every fixed $k\ge 3$, every sufficiently large 3-graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\varepsilon n^2$ triples contains $k$ vertices spanning at least $k-3$ triples. (The base case $k=6$, namely $f(n,6,3)=o(n^2)$, is known.)

Recent (2024–2025) preprints continue to attack the conjecture and confirm it is not yet fully resolved.

original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars (proposed by Erdo"s and Rado [120] in 1960) For given integers n and k, determine the smallest integer m, denoted by f (n, k), for which every family of sets Ai , i = 1, . . . , m, with |Ai | = n for all i, contains a k-star. Erdo"s and Rado [120, 121] proved that 2n < f (n, 3) ≤ 2n n!. Abbott and Hanson [1] proved f (n, 3) > 10n/2 . Spencer [208] showed f (n) < (1 + )n n!.

For positive integers n and k, let $f(n,k)$ denote the smallest integer m such that every family of m sets, each of cardinality exactly n, contains k members forming a k-star.

It is known that $f(n,3) > 10^{n/2}$ and $f(n,3) \le (1+\varepsilon)^n \, n!$ for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and sufficiently large n. The conjecture of Erdős and Rado asserts that for every fixed $k \ge 3$ there is a constant $C_k$ such that $f(n,k) \le C_k^n$.

Let f(n,k) denote the maximum possible cardinality of a family F of k-element sets that contains no Δ-system with n petals (i.e., no n members of F form a sunflower with n petals).

Prove or disprove the following: for every integer n ≥ 3 there exists a constant c_n, depending only on n, such that
    f(n, k) ≤ c_n^k
for every positive integer k.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture, asserting f(n,k) ≤ c_n^k, remains open. The best known bound, due to Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2019/2021) and subsequent refinements by Rao, Frankston–Kahn–Narayanan–Park, and Tao, is of the form (C n log k)^k, falling short of the conjectured (c_n)^k. Erdős offered $1000 for its resolution.

original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars of an n-set (proposed by Erdo"s and Szemerédi [136]) Determine the least integer m, denoted by f ∗ (n, k) such that for any family A of subsets of an n-set with |A| > f ∗ (n, k), A must contain a k-star. √ Erdo"s and Szemerédi [136] showed that f ∗ (n, 3) < 2(1−1/(10 n))n . Re- cently, Deuber, Erdo", Gunderson, Kostochka and Meyer [61] proved that f ∗ (n, r) > 2n(1−log log r/2r−O(1/r)) for every r ≥ 3 and infinitely many n. In particular, f ∗ (n, 3) > 1.551n−2 for infinitely many n.
self_contained_problem:
For integers $n\ge 1$ and $k\ge 3$, a $k$-star (also called a $k$-sunflower or $\Delta$-system of size $k$) is a family of $k$ distinct sets $A_1,\dots,A_k$ such that there exists a set $Y$ (the kernel) with $A_i\cap A_j = Y$ for all $1\le i<j\le k$. 

Let $f^*(n,k)$ be the least integer $m$ such that every family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of an $n$-element ground set with $|\mathcal{A}| > m$ contains a $k$-star.

Determine $f^*(n,k)$. In particular, determine the correct exponential order of growth: find the smallest constant $c_k$ (if it exists) such that $f^*(n,k) = c_k^{n(1+o(1))}$ as $n\to\infty$. The known bounds include
$$2^{n(1-\log\log r/(2r) - O(1/r))} < f^*(n,r) < 2^{n(1-1/(10\sqrt{n}))}\quad\text{(for }r=3\text{, infinitely many }n\text{)},$$
and in particular $f^*(n,3) > 1.551^{n-2}$ for infinitely many $n$.

status_search_result: The Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture, asserting $f^*(n,3) < c^n$ for some $c<2$, was confirmed in 2016 by Naslund and Sawin via the polynomial method, giving $f^*(n,3) \le (3/2^{2/3})^{n(1+o(1))}$. However, the exact value of $f^*(n,k)$ and the optimal exponential constant remain unknown, so the problem of fully determining $f^*(n,k)$ is still open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on weak ∆-systems (proposed by Erdo"s, Milner and Rado [118]) Let g(n, k) denote the least size for a family of n-sets forcing a weak ∆- system of k sets. Conjecture[118]: g(n, 3) < cnk .
self_contained_problem:
A family of three or more sets is called a weak Δ-system if all pairwise intersections among its members have the same cardinality (the cardinalities of the pairwise intersections agree, although the intersections themselves need not be equal). For integers $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 3$, let $g(n,k)$ denote the smallest integer $N$ such that every family of $N$ sets, each of cardinality $n$, contains a sub-family of $k$ sets forming a weak Δ-system.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture: there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that
$$g(n,3) < c^n \qquad \text{for all } n \ge 1.$$

(Equivalently, the maximum size of a family of $n$-element sets containing no three members that form a weak Δ-system grows at most exponentially in $n$.)
status_search_result: The conjecture, that the threshold $g(n,3)$ for forcing a weak Δ-system of 3 sets among families of $n$-sets is bounded by an exponential function $c^n$, appears to remain open. The best known upper bound for the uniform ($n$-set) version is still of the form $(n!)^{1/2+o(1)}$, established by Axenovich, Fon-Der-Flaass and Kostochka (1995) and not improved to exponential. Subsequent exponential bounds by Naslund–Sawin and Naslund concern a different (non-uniform) variant — families of subsets of an $n$-element ground set — and do not resolve the uniform conjecture.

self_contained_problem:
A family of sets $\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k\}$ is called a weak $\Delta$-system if there exists an integer $\lambda$ such that $|A_i \cap A_j| = \lambda$ for all $1 \le i < j \le k$ (the pairwise intersections all have the same size, but are not required to be equal as sets).

For integers $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 3$, define $g^*(n,k)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that every family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of an $n$-element set with $|\mathcal{A}| > m$ must contain $k$ members forming a weak $\Delta$-system.

Determine the value (or sharp asymptotic order) of $g^*(n,k)$. In particular, close the gap between the known lower bounds (such as $g^*(n,3) > n^{\log n / (4 \log \log n)}$ and $g^*(n,r) \ge 2^{(1+o(1))\, c_r n}$ type estimates) and the exponential upper bound $g^*(n,k) < (2 - \varepsilon_k)^n$ for some $\varepsilon_k > 0$ depending only on $k$.
status_search_result: The problem of determining $g^*(n,k)$ remains open. Recent work (e.g., Naslund 2022, "Upper Bounds For Families Without Weak Delta-Systems", arXiv:2203.13370) improves the upper bound to roughly $(1.8367...+o(1))^n$ using cap-set capacity techniques, but a substantial gap between lower and upper bounds persists. original_question: A problem of Erdo"s, Faber and Lovász ($500, 1972 [75]) Let G1 , . . . , Gn be n edge-disjoint complete graphs on n vertices. Then the chromatic number of ∪ni=1 Gi is n.
self_contained_problem: Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer, and let $G_1, G_2, \ldots, G_n$ be $n$ complete graphs, each on exactly $n$ vertices, such that any two distinct $G_i$ and $G_j$ share at most one common vertex (equivalently, $G_i$ and $G_j$ are edge-disjoint). Let $G = \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i$ be the graph on the union of the vertex sets whose edge set is the union of the edge sets of the $G_i$. Prove that the chromatic number $\chi(G)$ of $G$ is equal to $n$, i.e., the vertices of $G$ can be properly colored using exactly $n$ colors.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture was proved for all sufficiently large n by Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku, and Osthus (arXiv:2101.04698, 2021; published in Annals of Mathematics 198(2), 2023). The conjecture remains unverified for small values of n, so it is not yet fully resolved for every n, though the main asymptotic conjecture is considered established.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on property B (proposed by Erdo"s 1963, [66]) A family F of subsets is said to have property B if there is a subset S such that every subset in F contains an element in S and an element not in S. What is the minimum number f (n) of subsets in a family F of n-sets not having property B? Property B is named after Felix Bernstein who first introduced this prop- erty in 1908 [22]. The best known upper bound is due to Erdo"s [66, 67] and the following lower bound was given by Beck [20]. e log 2 2 n n1/3− 2n ≤ f (n) < (1 + ) n 2 for n ≥ n0 and n0 depends only on . This problem was extensively considered in [9, 158].
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 2, let an n-uniform family mean a finite collection F of sets, each of size exactly n. Say that F has property B (is 2-colorable) if there exists a set S such that every member of F contains at least one element of S and at least one element not in S; equivalently, the vertices of the hypergraph (V, F) (where V = ⋃F) admit a 2-coloring with no monochromatic edge. Define

  m(n) = min { |F| : F is an n-uniform family that does not have property B }.

Determine m(n), or equivalently determine its asymptotic growth as n → ∞. The currently known bounds are

  Ω( 2^n · √(n / log n) ) ≤ m(n) ≤ O( n^2 · 2^n ).

Close the gap between these lower and upper bounds (and ideally determine m(n) exactly).
status_search_result: The problem is open. The best known lower bound remains Ω(2^n √(n/log n)) due to Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan (2000), while the best known upper bound is the non-constructive O(n^2 · 2^n) due to Erdős. Recent work (e.g., 2016 and 2024 arXiv preprints) gives improvements only for small specific n or constant factors; exact values are known only for n ≤ 4 (m(4) = 23).

original_question: A conjecture on covering a hypergraph (proposed by Erdo"s and Lovász [117]) Let f (n) denote the smallest integer m such that for any n-element sets A1 , . . . , Am with Ai ∩ Aj = ∅ for i = j and for every set S with at most n − 1 elements, there is an Ai disjoint from S. Erdo"s and Lovász [117] proved that n − 3 ≤ f (n) ≤ cn3/2 log n.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, consider finite families $\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_m\}$ of $n$-element sets that are pairwise intersecting, i.e. $A_i \cap A_j 
eq \emptyset$ for all $i 
eq j$. Call such a family "uncoverable by small sets" if for every set $S$ with $|S| \leq n-1$ there exists some $A_i$ disjoint from $S$. Prove or disprove the following strengthened conjecture: for every constant $c > 0$ there exists $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(c) > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, whenever $\{A_i : 1 \leq i \leq cn\}$ is a collection of pairwise intersecting $n$-element sets, there exists a set $S$ with $|S| < n(1-\varepsilon)$ such that $A_i \cap S

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on unavoidable hypergraphs (proposed by Chung and Erdo"s [49]) A r-graph H is said to be (n, e)-unavoidable if H is contained in every r- graph on n vertices and e edges. Let fr (n, e) denote the largest integer m with the property that there exists an (n, e)-unavoidable r-graph having m edges. Determine fr (n, e). For the case of r = 2 and 3, the solutions can be found in [48, 49].
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $r\ge 2$, an $r$-uniform hypergraph (or $r$-graph) on a vertex set $V$ is a collection of $r$-element subsets of $V$ (the edges). Given positive integers $n$ and $e$ with $e\le \binom{n}{r}$, an $r$-graph $H$ is called $(n,e)$-unavoidable if every $r$-graph on $n$ vertices with $e$ edges contains a copy of $H$ as a subhypergraph. Define
$$f_r(n,e)\;=\;\max\{\,|E(H)|\;:\;H\text{ is an }(n,e)\text{-unavoidable }r\text{-graph}\,\}.$$
Determine the function $f_r(n,e)$ for all $r\ge 2$ and all admissible $n,e$. In particular, determine its order of magnitude in the ranges that remain open beyond the known cases $r=2$ and $r=3$.
status_search_result: The cases r=2 and r=3 were resolved (up to constant factors) by Chung and Erdős in the 1980s. Bucić, Draganić, and Sudakov (2020/2021) asymptotically resolved the r=4 case, describing this as the first progress in over 40 years, and noted that the general problem for r≥5 remains open. So the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars (proposed by Duke and Erdo"s [91]) Let f (n, r, k, t) denote the smallest integer m with the property that any r-graph on n vertices and m edges must contain a k-star with common intersection of size t. Determine f (n, r, k, t). Duke and Erdo"s proved that f (n, r, k, 1) ≤ cnr−2 where c depends only on r and k. For the case of r = 3, tight bounds are obtained by Chung and Frankl [54], also see [141, 47].
self_contained_problem:
An $r$-uniform hypergraph (or $r$-graph) on a vertex set $V$ is a collection of $r$-element subsets of $V$, called edges. Given integers $k\ge 2$ and $t\ge 1$, a $k$-star with common intersection of size $t$ is a family of $k$ distinct edges $E_1,\dots,E_k$ of an $r$-graph such that there exists a set $T\subseteq V$ with $|T|=t$ and $E_i\cap E_j=T$ for all $1\le i<j\le k$.

For integers $n\ge r\ge 2$, $k\ge 2$ and $1\le t\le r-1$, let $f(n,r,k,t)$ denote the smallest integer $m$ such that every $r$-graph on $n$ vertices with at least $m$ edges contains a $k$-star with common intersection of size exactly $t$.

Determine $f(n,r,k,t)$ for all admissible parameters $n,r,k,t$. In particular, determine the order of magnitude of $f(n,r,k,t)$ as $n\to\infty$ for each fixed $r,k,t$.

(Known partial information: it has been shown that $f(n,r,k,1)\le c\, n^{r-2}$ for a constant $c=c(r,k)$, and for $r=3$ asymptotically tight bounds for $f(n,3,k,t)$ are known.)
status_search_result: The problem of determining $f(n,r,k,t)$ in general remains open. The case $r=3$ has tight bounds (Chung–Frankl and related work), and a bound $f(n,r,k,1)\le cn^{r-2}$ is known due to Duke and Erdős, but the general determination for $r\ge 4$ and arbitrary $t$ has not been settled, and is listed among Erdős problems still being studied (e.g., recent work on unavoidable hypergraphs by Bucić–Draganić–Sudakov, 2020).

Let r ≥ 2 and k ≥ 2 be integers. An r-uniform hypergraph (r-graph) on a vertex set V is a pair (V, E) where E is a set of r-element subsets of V. Given r-graphs H_1, …, H_k with the same number of edges, a U-decomposition of (H_1, …, H_k) into t parts is a family of partitions

  E(H_i) = E_{i,1} ∪ E_{i,2} ∪ ⋯ ∪ E_{i,t}  (i = 1, …, k),

such that, for every j ∈ {1, …, t}, the r-graphs induced by E_{1,j}, E_{2,j}, …, E_{k,j} are pairwise isomorphic. Define

  U_k(n, r) = max over all k-tuples (H_1, …, H_k) of r-graphs on n vertices having the same number of edges, of the minimum number of parts t in any U-decomposition of (H_1, …, H_k).

It is known that for r = 2 (ordinary graphs),
  (2/3) n − 1/3 < U_2(n, 2) < (2/3) n + c,
and for k ≥ 3,
  (3/4) n − √n − 1 < U_k(n, 2) < (3/4) n + c_k.
For r = 3, it is known that
  c_1 n^{4/3} log log n / log n < U_2(n, 3) < c_2 n^{4/3},
and more generally, for every ε > 0,
  c_3 n^{2 − 2/k − ε} < U_k(n, 3) < c_4 n^{2 − 1/k}.

Determine the asymptotic behaviour of U_k(n, r) as n → ∞. In particular, determine U_2(n, 3) up to a constant factor and, more generally, close the gap between the known lower and upper bounds for U_k(n, r) when r ≥ 3.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on the product of the point and line covering numbers (proposed by Chung, Erdo"s and Graham [52]) In a hypergraph G with vertex set V and edge set E, the point covering number α0 (G) denotes the minimal cardinality of a subset of V which has non-empty intersection with every edge e in E. The line covering number α1 (G) denotes the minimal cardinality of a subset S of E such that every vertex is contained in some edge in S. The problem of interest is to characterize hypergraphs which achieve the maximum and minimum value of α0 (G)α1 (G). The case for graphs was solved in [52] and it was shown that n+1 n − 1 ≤ α0 (G)α1 (G) ≤ (n − 1)  which is asymptotically best possible. Infinite graphs Erdo"s wrote over a hundred papers on infinite graphs. In particular, the problem papers by Erdo"s and Hajnal [105, 106] contain 82 problems which have been the major driving force in this field. Many of the problems have been solved positively, negatively or proved to be undecidable. The problems here are mainly based on the survey papers [86, 155, 153]. Many comments to these problems were graciously provided by András Hajnal and Jean Larson. Here we use the following arrow notation, first introduced by Rado: κ → (λν )rγ which means that for any r-partition f : [κ]r → γ there are ν < γ and H ⊂ κ such that H has order type λν and f (Y ) = ν for all Y ∈ [H]r . If λν = λ for all ν < γ, then we write κ → (λ)rγ . In this language, Ramsey’s theorem can be written as ω → (ω)rk for 1 ≤ r, k < ω.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite hypergraph (a finite set V of vertices together with a family E of nonempty subsets of V called edges) with n vertices, having no isolated vertices. Define:

- the point covering number α₀(G) to be the smallest cardinality of a subset T ⊆ V such that T ∩ e ≠ ∅ for every edge e ∈ E;
- the line covering number α₁(G) to be the smallest cardinality of a subfamily S ⊆ E such that every vertex of V is contained in at least one edge of S.

For graphs (the 2-uniform case) it is known that
   n − 1 ≤ α₀(G) · α₁(G) ≤ ⌊(n+1)/2⌋ · ⌈(n−1)/2⌉ (or the analogous sharp bound),
and the extremal graphs are characterized.

Problem: Determine, for general finite hypergraphs on n vertices (with no isolated vertices), the maximum and the minimum possible value of the product α₀(G) · α₁(G), and characterize all hypergraphs attaining these extremal values.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not return a definitive resolution of the extremal problem for the product α₀(G)·α₁(G) over arbitrary hypergraphs. The graph case was settled by Chung, Erdős and Graham, but the hypergraph version does not appear to have a widely cited complete characterization.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: [105] Is it true that ω1 → (α, 4)3 for α < ω1 ? Milner and Prikry [188] gave an aﬃrmative answer for α ≤ ω2 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
For ordinals $\kappa, \alpha, \beta$ and a positive integer $n$, the partition relation $\kappa \to (\alpha, \beta)^n$ means: for every coloring $c : [\kappa]^n \to \{0, 1\}$ of the $n$-element subsets of $\kappa$ with two colors, either there exists $A \subseteq \kappa$ of order type $\alpha$ with $c$ constantly $0$ on $[A]^n$, or there exists $B \subseteq \kappa$ of order type $\beta$ with $c$ constantly $1$ on $[B]^n$.

Let $\omega_1$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Determine whether the following holds:
$$\omega_1 \to (\alpha, 4)^3 \quad \text{for every countable ordinal } \alpha < \omega_1.$$

That is, decide whether for every countable ordinal $\alpha$ and every 2-coloring of the 3-element subsets of $\omega_1$, there is either a subset of order type $\alpha$ all of whose triples receive color $0$, or a 4-element subset all of whose triples receive color $1$.
status_search_result: The problem is a longstanding question in the partition calculus of Erdős–Rado. Partial positive results have been established: Milner and Prikry handled countable ordinals up to about $\omega^2+1$; later Schipperus (1999 thesis, and subsequent work) and Jones extended this to countable ordinals whose Cantor normal form has at most two summands. The general case for all countable $\alpha < \omega_1$ does not appear to be settled, so the problem is partially solved.
