paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: [105] Is it true that ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 ? A. Hajnal [154] proved ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 under CH. Erdo"s and Hajnal [106] ask if MAℵ1 + 2ℵ0 = ℵ2 implies ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 ? Erdo", Hajnal and Larson [108] asked for the cardinals λ that λ2 → (λ2 , 3)2 holds. Hajnal [154] showed the relation failed at successors of regular cardinals under GCH. Baumgartner [15] showed that the relation failed at successors of singular cardinals under GCH.
self_contained_problem:
Using the Erdős–Rado partition arrow notation, for ordinals $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, write $\alpha \to (\beta, \gamma)^2$ to mean: for every coloring $c: [\alpha]^2 \to \{0,1\}$ of the unordered pairs of elements of $\alpha$ with two colors, either there is a subset $X \subseteq \alpha$ of order type $\beta$ with $c$ constantly $0$ on $[X]^2$, or there is a subset $Y \subseteq \alpha$ of order type $\gamma$ with $c$ constantly $1$ on $[Y]^2$. Here ordinal exponentiation is used, so $\omega_1^2$ denotes the ordinal product $\omega_1 \cdot \omega_1$ (where $\omega_1$ is the least uncountable ordinal).

(a) Decide whether the partition relation
$$\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1^2,\, 3)^2$$
holds in ZFC. It is known that under the Continuum Hypothesis this relation fails. Determine whether, under the axiom $\mathrm{MA}_{\aleph_1} + 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_2$ (Martin's Axiom at $\aleph_1$ together with the continuum being $\aleph_2$), the relation $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1^2, 3)^2$ holds.

(b) More generally, characterize the infinite cardinals $\lambda$ for which the partition relation
$$\lambda^2 \to (\lambda^2,\, 3)^2$$
holds. (It is known that under GCH this relation fails whenever $\lambda$ is the successor of a regular cardinal, and also whenever $\lambda$ is the successor of a singular cardinal.)

No published ZFC resolution of $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1^2, 3)^2$ or of the consistency consequence under $\mathrm{MA}_{\aleph_1} + 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_2$ was located. Known partial results: Hajnal's failure under CH, and failures at successors of regular cardinals (Hajnal) and singular cardinals (Baumgartner) under GCH. paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on graphs of infinite chromatic number ($250) (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Szemerédi, 1982, [114, 82]) Let f (n) → ∞ arbitrarily slowly. Is it true that there is a graph G of infinite chromatic number such that for every n, every subgraph of G of n vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most f (n) edges? Prove or disprove the existence of a graph G of infinite chromatic number for which f (n) = o(n ) or f (n) = o((log n)c ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be a function with $f(n)\to\infty$ that may grow arbitrarily slowly. Does there exist a (simple, undirected) graph $G$ of infinite chromatic number with the property that for every positive integer $n$, every subgraph of $G$ on $n$ vertices can be made bipartite by the deletion of at most $f(n)$ edges?

In addition, determine whether such a graph $G$ of infinite chromatic number exists when $f(n) = o(n^{\varepsilon})$ for some (every) $\varepsilon > 0$, and whether it exists when $f(n) = o((\log n)^{c})$ for some (every) constant $c > 0$.
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Erdős, Hajnal and Szemerédi in 1982, appears still open for graphs. Rödl resolved the analogous question for 3-uniform hypergraphs, and partial results are known (e.g., the existence is established when f(n) = εn). Listings on the Erdős problems database continue to mark the graph version with the stronger growth conditions as open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on the union of triangle-free graphs ($250) (proposed by Erdo"s and Hajnal [104]) Is there a graph G which contains no K4 and which is not the union of ℵ0 graphs which are triangle-free? Shelah [202] proved that the existence of such a graph is consistent but it is not known if this is provable in ZFC.
self_contained_problem:
Working in ZFC, does there exist a (simple, undirected) graph $G$ with the following two properties?

(1) $G$ contains no $K_4$ (i.e., no four pairwise adjacent vertices); and

(2) $G$ cannot be written as a union of countably many triangle-free spanning subgraphs; equivalently, there is no decomposition $E(G) = \bigcup_{n<\omega} E_n$ of the edge set such that each graph $(V(G), E_n)$ contains no triangle ($K_3$).

It is known that the existence of such a graph $G$ is consistent with ZFC (established by Shelah via a forcing/consistency argument). The problem asks whether the existence of such a $G$ can in fact be proved outright in ZFC.
status_search_result: Web searches indicate this Erdős–Hajnal problem on decomposing a $K_4$-free graph into countably many triangle-free subgraphs remains unresolved in ZFC. Shelah proved the consistency of the existence of such a graph, but no ZFC proof (or refutation) has been published. No source surfaced announcing a resolution.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on ℵ1 -chromatic graphs (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Szemerédi [114]) Is it true that if f (n) increases arbitrarily fast, then there is an ℵ1 - chromatic graph G so that if g(n) is the smallest integer for which G has an n-chromatic subgraph of g(n) vertices, then f (n)/g(n) → 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a (possibly infinite) simple graph. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least cardinal κ such that V admits a partition into κ independent sets. A graph G is called ℵ₁-chromatic if χ(G) = ℵ₁. For an ℵ₁-chromatic graph G and an integer n ≥ 2, define
  g_G(n) = min{ |V(H)| : H is a subgraph of G with χ(H) = n },
i.e., the smallest number of vertices of an n-chromatic subgraph of G.

Prove or disprove: for every function f : ℕ → ℕ (no matter how fast it tends to infinity), there exists an ℵ₁-chromatic graph G such that
  f(n) / g_G(n) → 0  as n → ∞.
status_search_result: The problem is listed in the Erdős problems database (proposed by Erdős, Hajnal and Szemerédi) on ℵ₁-chromatic graphs and the size of their smallest n-chromatic subgraphs. No resolution is reported; it appears to remain open. Related conjectures (e.g., Taylor's, and the Erdős–Hajnal–Shelah strengthening) are known to have been refuted/independent, but the specific question about the growth rate of g(n) for some ℵ₁-chromatic graph is not reported as solved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on odd cycles (proposed by Erdo"s and Hajnal [87]) Let G be a graph of infinite chromatic number and let n1 < n2 < . . . be the sequence consisting of lengths of odd cycles in G. Is it true that = ∞? ni Gyárfás, Komlós and Szemerédi [151] proved that the set of all cycle lengths has positive upper density.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a (simple) graph with infinite chromatic number, and suppose that $G$ contains odd cycles of lengths $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$ (listed without repetition). Must it be the case that
$$\sum_{i \ge 1} \frac{1}{n_i} = \infty?$$
Equivalently, does every graph of infinite chromatic number contain odd cycles whose lengths form a set with divergent reciprocal sum?
status_search_result: The problem was resolved affirmatively by Hong Liu and Richard Montgomery (arXiv:2010.15802, 2020). They proved that for a graph of chromatic number k, the sum of reciprocals of its odd cycle lengths is at least (1/2 - o(1)) log k, which is asymptotically tight. This implies the Erdős–Hajnal odd cycle conjecture.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on ordinal graphs and infinite paths (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Milner [109]) For which limit ordinals α is it true that if G is a graph whose vertices form a set of type α then either G has an infinite path or contains an independent set of type α. In other words, determine the limit α for which α → (α, infinite path)2 . Erdo"s, Hajnal and Milner [109] proved that the positive relation is true for all limit α < ω ω+2 . Baumgartner and Larson [17] showed that if Jensen’s Diamond Principle holds, then α → (α, infinite path)2 for all α with ω1ω+2 ≤ α < ω2 . Larson [175] obtained further results under the assumption of GCH.
self_contained_problem:
For an ordinal $\alpha$, write $\alpha \to (\alpha, \text{infinite path})^2$ to mean: for every graph $G$ whose vertex set is a set of order type $\alpha$ (with edges an arbitrary symmetric irreflexive relation on that set), either $G$ contains an infinite path, or $G$ contains an independent set whose order type (as a suborder of $\alpha$) is $\alpha$.

Determine, in ZFC, the class of all limit ordinals $\alpha$ for which the relation $\alpha \to (\alpha, \text{infinite path})^2$ holds. In particular, characterize precisely those limit ordinals $\alpha$ with $\omega^{\omega+2} \le \alpha$ for which the positive partition relation is provable, and identify those for which the relation fails.
status_search_result: Partial results are known: Erdős–Hajnal–Milner proved the positive relation for all limit α < ω^{ω+2}; Baumgartner–Larson showed that under Jensen's Diamond there are counterexamples for ω_1^{ω+2} ≤ α < ω_2, while Larson obtained further positive results under GCH and MA. A complete ZFC characterization of the limit ordinals α for which α → (α, infinite path)² holds does not appear to be established, and recent work (e.g., on formalizing ordinal partition relations and studies of countable partition ordinals) continues to address such questions, indicating the problem remains open in general.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on ordinal graphs and down-up matchings (proposed by Erdo"s and Larson [116]) A down-up matching in an ordinal graph is a matching of a set A with a set B where every element of A is less than all elements of B, denoted by A < B. Suppose for every graph on an ordinal α there is either an independent set of type β or a down-up matching from a A to a set B. If A has order type γ, then we write α → (β, γ − matching)2 . Suppose that j and k are positive integers with k ≥ 2 and η is a limit ordinal. Is it true that ω η+jk → (ω η+j , ω k − matching)2 ? If j and k ≥ 2 are positive integers and η a countable limit ordinal, then Erdo"s and Larson have shown that ω η+jk+1 → (ω η+j , γ − matching)2 but ω η+jk−1 → (ω η+j , γ − matching)2 .

Setup. An ordinal graph is a simple graph whose vertex set is an ordinal (with the natural well-order). For subsets A, B of an ordinal, write A < B to mean that every element of A is strictly less than every element of B. A down-up matching in an ordinal graph G is a perfect matching between two disjoint vertex sets A and B of G such that A < B and every matched pair {a, m(a)} (with a ∈ A and m(a) ∈ B) is an edge of G.

Partition notation. For ordinals α, β, γ, write
  α → (β, γ-matching)²
to mean: for every graph G on the ordinal α, either G contains an independent set of order type β, or G contains a down-up matching between some sets A and B with A of order type γ (and A < B).

Known facts. Let j, k be positive integers with k ≥ 2 and let η be a countable limit ordinal. Then
  ω^{η+jk+1} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)²,
while
  ω^{η+jk−1} ↛ (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)².

Question. Under the same hypotheses (j, k positive integers with k ≥ 2 and η a countable limit ordinal), is it true that
  ω^{η+jk} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)²?

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let pi(x) denote the number of primes at most x. For sufficiently large x it is known that pi(2x) < 2pi(x). Is it true for all positive x and y that pi(x+y) <= pi(x)+pi(y)? More weakly, for each epsilon > 0, does there exist y_e such that for all y > y_e one has pi(x+y)-pi(y) < (1+epsilon)y/log y? Erdos also records that it has not been disproved that the Hardy-Littlewood quantity rho(y)=lim sup_{x->infinity}[pi(x+y)-pi(x)] equals 1 for all y.
self_contained_problem:
Let π(x) denote the number of primes not exceeding x. Consider the following three questions:

(a) Is it true that for all real x, y ≥ 2,
   π(x + y) ≤ π(x) + π(y) ?

(b) (A weaker form.) Prove or disprove: for every ε > 0 there exists y_ε such that, for all y > y_ε and all x ≥ 0,
   π(x + y) − π(x) < (1 + ε) y / log y .

(c) Define ρ(y) = limsup_{x → ∞} [π(x + y) − π(x)]. Is it true that ρ(y) = 1 for every integer y ≥ 2 (equivalently, is the bound π(x+y) − π(x) ≤ 1 attained infinitely often, but never exceeded asymptotically, for each fixed y)?

Determine the truth of (a), (b), and (c).
status_search_result: The inequality π(x+y) ≤ π(x)+π(y) is the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, generally regarded as still open. Hensley and Richards (1973) showed it is incompatible with the first Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuples conjecture, so at most one of the two can hold; most number theorists believe (a) is false but no explicit counterexample is known. The weaker form (b) and the assertion ρ(y)=1 also remain unresolved. A 2021 preprint by Visser claims a proof, but it has not been accepted by the mainstream community, and subsequent papers (e.g., 2025) continue to treat the conjecture as open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: If p_n is the nth prime, determine the true order of the prime gap p_{n+1}-p_n. In particular, is Piltz's conjecture p_{n+1}-p_n = O(n^epsilon) for every epsilon > 0 true, and is Cramer's stronger conjecture p_{n+1}-p_n = O((log n)^2) correct? A related old question asks whether there is always a prime between two consecutive squares.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p_n$ denote the $n$-th prime number, so that $p_1=2, p_2=3, p_3=5,\ldots$, and let $g_n = p_{n+1}-p_n$ denote the $n$-th prime gap.

(a) (Piltz's conjecture) Prove or disprove: for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$p_{n+1}-p_n = O(n^{\varepsilon}),$$
i.e., there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon > 0$ such that $p_{n+1}-p_n \le C_\varepsilon\, n^{\varepsilon}$ for all $n \ge 1$.

(b) (Cramér's conjecture) Prove or disprove the stronger assertion
$$p_{n+1}-p_n = O\!\left((\log n)^2\right).$$

(c) (Primes between consecutive squares) Prove or disprove: for every integer $m \ge 1$, there exists a prime $p$ with $m^2 < p < (m+1)^2$.

Determine, more generally, the true order of magnitude of $p_{n+1}-p_n$.
status_search_result: All three questions remain open. Cramér's conjecture $p_{n+1}-p_n = O((\log n)^2)$ is unproven, and probabilistic refinements by Granville and others suggest the constant may need adjustment, but no proof or counterexample exists. Piltz's weaker $O(n^\varepsilon)$ bound is also open: the best unconditional results give $p_{n+1}-p_n \ll p_n^{0.525}$ (Baker–Harman–Pintz), still far from $n^\varepsilon$. Legendre's conjecture that there is a prime between $m^2$ and $(m+1)^2$ remains open and is known to lie beyond the Riemann hypothesis.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let d_n = p_{n+1}-p_n be the nth prime gap. Do the sets of integers n for which d_{n+1} > d_n and d_{n+1} < d_n each have asymptotic density 1/2, and does d_{n+1} = d_n occur for infinitely many n? More strongly, do strictly increasing triples d_{n+2} > d_{n+1} > d_n or strictly decreasing triples d_{n+2} < d_{n+1} < d_n occur infinitely often?
self_contained_problem:
Let p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < ... denote the sequence of prime numbers, and for each positive integer n define the nth prime gap by d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n. Consider the following questions.

(a) Density question. Do the two sets
   A = { n ∈ ℕ : d_{n+1} > d_n }  and  B = { n ∈ ℕ : d_{n+1} < d_n }
each have asymptotic density 1/2, i.e.
   lim_{N→∞} |A ∩ [1,N]| / N = lim_{N→∞} |B ∩ [1,N]| / N = 1/2 ?

(b) Equality question. Are there infinitely many positive integers n such that d_{n+1} = d_n ?

(c) Monotone triples. Are there infinitely many positive integers n such that
   d_{n+2} > d_{n+1} > d_n ,
and are there infinitely many positive integers n such that
   d_{n+2} < d_{n+1} < d_n ?
status_search_result: The existence of infinitely many strictly increasing and strictly decreasing runs of any fixed length m (in particular triples) among consecutive prime gaps was proved by Banks, Freiberg, and Turnage-Butterbaugh using the Maynard–Tao machinery on bounded gaps between primes, settling part (c). The density-1/2 conjecture in part (a) and the question of whether d_{n+1} = d_n holds infinitely often (part (b)) appear to remain open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Consider the normalized prime-gap sequence (p_{n+1}-p_n)/log p_n. Although the set of its limit points has positive measure, no finite limit point was known in the source. Is this sequence dense on the positive real axis, and does it possess a distribution function?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p_n$ denote the $n$-th prime number, and consider the sequence of normalized prime gaps
$$d_n := \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\dots.$$
Let $L \subseteq [0,\infty]$ be the set of limit points of $(d_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in the extended real line.

(a) Is $L = [0,\infty]$? Equivalently, is the sequence $(d_n)$ dense in the positive real axis $[0,\infty)$?

(b) Does $(d_n)$ possess a limiting distribution function? That is, does there exist a non-decreasing right-continuous function $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ such that for every continuity point $x\ge 0$ of $F$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\,\#\{n\le N : d_n \le x\} = F(x)?$$
status_search_result: Partial progress has been obtained but the full questions remain open. Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım (2005) showed $0\in L$; Banks–Freiberg–Maynard (2016) proved that at least 12.5% of $[0,\infty)$ lies in $L$, and subsequent refinements (Pintz; Merikoski) raised this to at least one-third and showed $L$ has bounded gaps. However, density of $(d_n)$ in $[0,\infty)$ (i.e. $L=[0,\infty]$) and existence of a limiting distribution function are still unresolved.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Do there exist arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of prime numbers? Erdos also records the stronger old conjecture that there exist arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions consisting of consecutive primes.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P} = \{2,3,5,7,11,\dots\}$ denote the set of prime numbers, and let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ be the increasing enumeration of $\mathbb{P}$. A finite arithmetic progression of length $k$ is a sequence $a, a+d, a+2d, \dots, a+(k-1)d$ with $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ and $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every integer $k \ge 3$, there exist positive integers $a, d$ such that $a, a+d, a+2d, \dots, a+(k-1)d$ are all prime.

(b) Prove or disprove the stronger assertion: for every integer $k \ge 3$, there exists an index $n$ such that the $k$ consecutive primes $p_n, p_{n+1}, \dots, p_{n+k-1}$ form an arithmetic progression (i.e., $p_{n+i+1} - p_{n+i}$ is the same for $i = 0, 1, \dots, k-2$).
status_search_result: Part (a) was resolved affirmatively by Ben Green and Terence Tao (2004, published Annals of Math. 2008), who proved that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. Part (b), the stronger conjecture about arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes, remains open; the longest known such progression has length 10, and no proof of existence for all $k$ is known.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let f(k) be the least integer such that every 2-coloring of {1,...,f(k)} contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k. Determine substantially better upper bounds for f(k), in particular a useful majorant for the least possible such function.
self_contained_problem: For every integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(k)$ denote the least positive integer $N$ with the following property: whenever the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ is partitioned into two classes, at least one class contains an arithmetic progression of length $k$ (i.e., $k$ integers of the form $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+(k-1)d$ with $d \geq 1$). The existence of $f(k)$ is guaranteed by van der Waerden's theorem. Establish substantially improved (in particular, as small as possible) explicit upper bounds for $f(k)$ as a function of $k$; equivalently, exhibit a useful majorant for $f$.
status_search_result: Major progress exists but the problem of determining the true order of $f(k)$ remains open. Shelah (1988) gave the first primitive-recursive upper bound (in the wowzer/tower hierarchy). Gowers (2001), as a consequence of his quantitative Szemerédi theorem, proved $f(k) \le 2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}$, a vast improvement. The gap to the best known lower bounds (essentially $2^k/k$-type, due to Berlekamp and improvements) is still enormous, and finding the true growth rate of $f(k)$ is widely regarded as open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, Cramer showed that the sum of squared prime gaps up to x satisfies sum_{p_n < x}(p_{n+1}-p_n)^2 < c_e x(log x)^{3+e}. Can the exponent 3+epsilon be reduced to 1? Erdos also asks for the analogous bound that if 1=a_1<...<a_{phi(n)}=n-1 are the integers less than n that are coprime to n, then sum_{k=1}^{phi(n)-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)^2 < c n^2/phi(n) for an absolute constant c.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers, and let $\varphi$ denote Euler's totient function.

(a) Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, it is known that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a constant $c_\varepsilon$ such that
$$\sum_{p_n < x} (p_{n+1} - p_n)^2 \;<\; c_\varepsilon \, x (\log x)^{3+\varepsilon}$$
for all $x \ge 2$. Determine whether the exponent $3+\varepsilon$ on $\log x$ can be reduced to $1$; that is, prove or disprove the existence of an absolute constant $C$ such that
$$\sum_{p_n < x} (p_{n+1} - p_n)^2 \;<\; C \, x \log x \qquad \text{for all } x \ge 2.$$

(b) For each integer $n \ge 2$, let $1 = a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_{\varphi(n)} = n-1$ be the integers in $\{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ that are coprime to $n$. Prove or disprove that there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\varphi(n)-1} (a_{k+1} - a_k)^2 \;<\; \frac{c \, n^2}{\varphi(n)}$$
holds for every integer $n \ge 2$.
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a definitive resolution of either question. The conditional Cramér-type bound on the sum of squared prime gaps remains the standard reference, and known second-moment improvements have not been shown to reach the $x\log x$ exponent. The totative analogue (a conjecture of Erdős) is referenced in lists of Erdős problems on gaps between integers coprime to $n$, but no proof of the absolute constant bound $c\,n^2/\varphi(n)$ was found in the search. Status is therefore taken as unknown.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: For prime gaps d_n = p_{n+1}-p_n, is lim inf d_n = 2, as predicted by the twin-prime conjecture? Is lim inf d_n/log n equal to 0? Erdos also asks whether lim sup min(d_n,d_{n+1},d_{n+2})/log n = infinity and whether lim inf max(d_n,d_{n+1})/log n < 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers, and for each $n \ge 1$ set $d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. Resolve the following four questions:

(a) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} d_n = 2$ (the twin-prime conjecture)?

(b) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{d_n}{\log n} = 0$?

(c) Is $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\min(d_n,\, d_{n+1},\, d_{n+2})}{\log n} = \infty$?

(d) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\max(d_n,\, d_{n+1})}{\log n} < 1$?
status_search_result: The four sub-questions have different statuses. (a) The twin-prime conjecture $\liminf d_n = 2$ remains open, though Zhang (2013) and Maynard (2013) established that $\liminf d_n$ is finite. (b) $\liminf d_n/\log n = 0$ was proved by Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım (2009). (c) Large gaps results of Ford–Green–Konyagin–Tao and Maynard (2014/2016), combined with chain-of-large-gaps results (Banks–Freiberg–Maynard and related work), give $\limsup \min(d_n,d_{n+1},d_{n+2})/\log n = \infty$. (d) The question of whether $\liminf \max(d_n,d_{n+1})/\log n < 1$ appears to remain open. Overall the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let f(n) take only the values +1 and -1. Is it true that for every constant C there exist integers d and m such that |f(d)+f(2d)+...+f(md)| > C? In the multiplicative case, if f is multiplicative and f(n)=+/-1, must the Cesaro mean (1/n)sum_{k=1}^n f(k) always converge?
self_contained_problem:
Consider functions f : ℕ → {+1, −1}.

(a) (Discrepancy form.) Prove or disprove: for every such function f and every constant C > 0, there exist positive integers d and m such that
   | f(d) + f(2d) + f(3d) + ⋯ + f(md) | > C.

(b) (Multiplicative mean.) Suppose in addition that f is multiplicative, i.e. f(mn) = f(m)f(n) whenever gcd(m,n) = 1, and still takes only the values +1 and −1. Must the Cesàro mean
   M(f) := lim_{n → ∞} (1/n) ∑_{k=1}^{n} f(k)
exist?
status_search_result: Part (a), the Erdős discrepancy problem, was resolved affirmatively by Terence Tao in 2015 (published in Discrete Analysis, 2016), who proved that for every ±1-valued sequence the discrepancy sup_{d,m} |∑_{k≤m} f(kd)| is infinite. Part (b), on the existence of the Cesàro mean of a ±1-valued multiplicative function, is a long-standing conjecture (in the spirit of Chudakov/Erdős): Tao established a logarithmically averaged version via the Elliott conjecture, but the existence of the ordinary natural-density mean for arbitrary ±1-valued multiplicative functions appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let r_k(n) be the largest size of a subset of {1,...,n-1} containing no arithmetic progression of length k. Determine the true order of magnitude of r_3(n), and more generally of r_k(n), as n grows. Erdos also records the conjecture that lim r_k(n)/n = 0.
self_contained_problem:
For integers $k \geq 3$ and $n \geq 2$, let $r_k(n)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ that contains no arithmetic progression of length $k$ (i.e., no $k$ distinct elements $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+(k-1)d$ all belonging to $A$, with $d \geq 1$).

(a) Determine the true order of magnitude of $r_3(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

(b) More generally, determine the true order of magnitude of $r_k(n)$ as $n \to \infty$, for each fixed $k \geq 3$.

(c) Prove the conjecture that 
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{r_k(n)}{n} = 0$$
for every fixed integer $k \geq 3$.
status_search_result: Part (c), namely $r_k(n)/n \to 0$, was established by Szemerédi's theorem (1975), resolving the qualitative density conjecture. The exact order of magnitude in parts (a) and (b) remains open. For $k=3$, the best known upper bound is due to Kelley–Meka (2023), $r_3(n) \leq 2^{-\Omega((\log n)^{1/12})} n$, subsequently improved by Bloom–Sisask to exponent $1/9$; the best known lower bound is Behrend's $r_3(n) \geq n \cdot 2^{-O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. A gap remains, so the precise order is not determined. For $k \geq 4$, quantitative bounds are weaker and far from tight.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Choose distinct positive integers a_i <= x so that every subset sum sum epsilon_i a_i is different. If h(x) denotes the maximum possible number of chosen integers, is h(x) = (log x)/(log 2) + O(1)? Equivalently, is it possible to choose k+2 integers a_i with 1 <= a_i <= 2^k such that all 2^k subset sums are distinct?
self_contained_problem:
For a positive real number x, let h(x) denote the maximum integer n for which there exist distinct positive integers a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_n with a_i ≤ x such that all 2^n subset sums ∑_{i=1}^n ε_i a_i (ε_i ∈ {0,1}) are pairwise distinct.

(a) Determine whether h(x) = (log x)/(log 2) + O(1) as x → ∞.

Equivalently:

(b) Does there exist an integer k and a choice of k+2 distinct positive integers a_1, ..., a_{k+2} with 1 ≤ a_i ≤ 2^k such that all 2^{k+2} subset sums ∑ ε_i a_i (ε_i ∈ {0,1}) are distinct? More generally, can one always find k+c integers in [1, 2^k] with distinct subset sums for arbitrarily large constants c?

(Note: the geometric progression 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^{k-1} gives k integers in [1, 2^k] with distinct subset sums, so h(2^k) ≥ k; the question asks whether the constant O(1) error is sharp, equivalently h(x) − ⌊log_2 x⌋ is bounded.)
status_search_result: The Erdős distinct subset sums problem is widely regarded as still open. The best known lower bounds for the largest element in a Sidon-type distinct-subset-sum set in {1,...,N} of size n give N ≥ √(2/(πn))·2^n (Elkies–Gleason, with subsequent refinements), but the conjectured bound N ≫ 2^n (equivalently h(x) = log_2 x + O(1)) has not been established. Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2208.12182, arXiv:2006.12988, arXiv:2308.03748) continues to refine bounds without resolving the conjecture.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let A={a_i} be a set of nonnegative integers such that every natural number n can be written as n=a_i+2^j, and let k(x) count elements of A below x. If there exists such a set with k(x) < c x(log log x)/log x, can the factor log log x be removed? More generally, if every natural number can be written as n=a_i+p_j with p_j prime and k(x) < c(log x)^2, can this bound be improved? Erdos also asks whether for two increasing sequences {a_i} and {b_i} with every n=a_i+b_j one must have lim sup a(x)b(x)/x > 1.
self_contained_problem:
For a set $A=\{a_i\}$ of nonnegative integers, let $k_A(x)=|\{i:a_i\le x\}|$ denote its counting function.

(a) Suppose $A$ has the property that every natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+2^j$ for some $a_i\in A$ and some nonnegative integer $j$. It is known that there exists such a set with $k_A(x)<c\,x(\log\log x)/\log x$ for some constant $c>0$. Can the factor $\log\log x$ be removed, i.e., does there exist such a set with $k_A(x)=O(x/\log x)$?

(b) Suppose $A$ has the property that every natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+p_j$ where $a_i\in A$ and $p_j$ is prime. It is known that there exists such a set with $k_A(x)<c(\log x)^2$. Can this bound be improved; in particular, can one achieve $k_A(x)=O(\log x)$?

(c) Let $\{a_i\}$ and $\{b_i\}$ be two infinite increasing sequences of nonnegative integers such that every sufficiently large natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+b_j$. Let $A(x)$ and $B(x)$ be the corresponding counting functions. Is it true that
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}>1?$$
status_search_result: Part (b) has seen substantial progress: Wolke, Kolountzakis, and Ruzsa successively improved the upper bound, with Ruzsa achieving $\ll \omega(N)\log N$ for any $\omega\to\infty$, and a lower bound $\liminf A(x)/\log x\ge e^\gamma$ is known; whether $O(\log N)$ is attainable remains open (Erdős offered $50). Part (c) is the Erdős–Danzer conjecture, which was confirmed by Sárközy and Szemerédi (1994), who proved that for infinite additive complements with $\limsup A(x)B(x)/x\le 1$ one must have $A(x)B(x)-x\to\infty$. Part (a) about removing the $\log\log x$ factor for powers of 2 appears still open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let {a_i} be an increasing sequence of natural numbers and let f(n) count the number of representations n=a_i+a_j. If f(n) > 0 for every n, must lim sup f(n) be infinite? More generally, if a_k < c k^2 for all k, must lim sup f(n) be infinite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a_1<a_2<a_3<\cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers, and for every nonnegative integer $n$ define
$$f(n) = \#\{(i,j) : i \le j,\ a_i + a_j = n\},$$
the number of representations of $n$ as an (unordered) sum of two terms of the sequence.

(a) Suppose $f(n) > 0$ for every sufficiently large natural number $n$ (i.e., the sequence is an additive basis of order $2$). Must
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} f(n) = \infty\,?$$

(b) More generally, suppose there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $a_k < c\,k^2$ for all $k\ge 1$. Must
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} f(n) = \infty\,?$$
status_search_result: The Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases (1941) is widely regarded as still open. Partial results exist: it is known that if f(n) ≥ 1 for all large n then lim sup f(n) ≥ 6, later improved to ≥ 8, but the full conjecture (and the stronger version with a_k < c k^2) remains unresolved. It is listed as an open problem on Open Problem Garden and Wikipedia.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Fix a positive integer n_0. Does there exist an integer k and a covering system of congruences x ≡ a_i (mod n_i) with n_0 < n_1 < ... < n_k such that every integer satisfies at least one of the congruences? Erdos also asks whether such a covering system can be found with all moduli n_i odd.
self_contained_problem:
A covering system of congruences is a finite collection of congruences x ≡ a_i (mod n_i), i = 1, …, k, with positive integer moduli n_i, such that every integer x ∈ ℤ satisfies at least one of the congruences.

(a) Let n_0 be a fixed positive integer. Does there exist an integer k ≥ 1 and a covering system of congruences x ≡ a_i (mod n_i) for i = 1, …, k with strictly increasing moduli

   n_0 < n_1 < n_2 < ⋯ < n_k ?

Equivalently, can the minimum modulus of a covering system (with distinct moduli) be made arbitrarily large?

(b) Does there exist a covering system of congruences x ≡ a_i (mod n_i), i = 1, …, k, with distinct moduli n_1 < n_2 < ⋯ < n_k all of which are odd integers greater than 1?
status_search_result: Part (a), the minimum modulus problem, was solved negatively by R. Hough (2015), who proved that the minimum modulus of a covering system with distinct moduli is bounded by an absolute constant (originally ≤ 10^16, later improved to 616000 by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba); thus for sufficiently large n_0 no such covering exists. Part (b), the odd covering problem, remains open, although Hough–Nielsen (2019) and subsequent work by Balister et al. show that any distinct covering system must contain a modulus divisible by 2 or 3 (and in the odd case, by 9 or 15).

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let a_1<a_2<... be the increasing sequence of all natural numbers of the form x^2+y^2. Estimate the gap a_{k+1}-a_k. In particular, although a_{k+1}-a_k = O(a_k^{1/4}) was known, can that big-O be improved to little-o?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots$ be the strictly increasing enumeration of all natural numbers that can be represented in the form $x^2 + y^2$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. It is classically known (Bambah–Chowla) that 
$$a_{k+1} - a_k = O\!\left(a_k^{1/4}\right) \qquad (k \to \infty).$$
Determine whether this upper bound can be sharpened to a little-$o$ estimate; that is, decide whether
$$a_{k+1} - a_k = o\!\left(a_k^{1/4}\right) \qquad (k \to \infty),$$
and more generally give the best possible upper estimate for the gap $a_{k+1} - a_k$ in terms of $a_k$.
category_tag: Gaps between sums of two squares
status_search_result: A search shows that the Bambah–Chowla bound $a_{k+1}-a_k\ll a_k^{1/4}$ remains the standard pointwise upper bound, with refinements only to the implicit constant by Uchiyama, Shiu, and Jameson. Hooley and others obtained results on moments and on short-interval behavior for almost all intervals, and recent work by Dietmann–Elsholtz and Kalmynin–Konyagin has improved lower bounds for the largest gap up to $X$ (now of order $\log X$). No source found establishes the pointwise improvement to $o(a_k^{1/4})$, so the question as posed appears to still be open.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: For a finite set S={p_1,...,p_n} of n points in the plane, let N(S) be the number of distinct pairwise distances and let f(n) be the least possible value of N(S). Determine the true lower growth of f(n); Erdos conjectures that for every epsilon > 0 and all sufficiently large n one has f(n) > n^{1-epsilon}. He also asks, for convex n-gons, whether every convex n-gon has a vertex from which no three vertices are equidistant.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set S = {p_1, ..., p_n} of n points in the Euclidean plane, let N(S) denote the number of distinct values that occur among the pairwise distances |p_i p_j| (1 ≤ i < j ≤ n), and define
   f(n) = min { N(S) : |S| = n }.
(a) Determine the asymptotic growth of f(n). In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that for every ε > 0 there exists n_0 = n_0(ε) such that for all n ≥ n_0,
   f(n) > n^{1-ε}.
(b) Strengthening (a): prove or disprove that for every ε > 0 and all sufficiently large n, every n-point set S in the plane contains a point p_j ∈ S from which more than n^{1-ε} distinct distances to the other points of S occur, i.e.
   |{ |p_i p_j| : i ≠ j }| > n^{1-ε}.
(c) Prove or disprove the following stronger geometric conjecture: every convex n-gon in the plane has a vertex v such that no three of the remaining vertices are equidistant from v.
status_search_result: Part (a), the original Erdős distinct distances conjecture, was essentially settled by Guth and Katz (Annals of Math., 2015), who proved f(n) ≥ c·n/log n, far exceeding the n^{1-ε} bound. The pointwise strengthening (b) — that some point sees at least n^{1-ε} distinct distances — remains open in this strong form; the best known bound is roughly n/log n by Katz–Tardos and subsequent work, which is weaker than n^{1-ε} only by a logarithmic factor and is widely viewed as still partially open at the conjectured level. The convex-polygon conjecture (c), that every convex n-gon has a vertex from which no three vertices are equidistant, does not appear to have been resolved in the literature and is generally listed among unresolved Erdős-type problems.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Borsuk's partition problem asks whether every subset of Euclidean n-space of diameter 1 can be written as the union of n+1 subsets of smaller diameter. The source reports this as open for n > 3.
self_contained_problem: For an integer n ≥ 1, let a "set of diameter 1" in Euclidean n-space ℝⁿ be a bounded subset S ⊆ ℝⁿ with sup{‖x − y‖ : x, y ∈ S} = 1, where ‖·‖ denotes the Euclidean norm. Borsuk's partition problem asks: for which integers n ≥ 1 is it true that every subset S ⊆ ℝⁿ of diameter 1 can be written as a union S = S₁ ∪ S₂ ∪ ⋯ ∪ S_{n+1} of n+1 subsets, each having diameter strictly less than 1? Determine, for every n ≥ 4, whether such a partition into n+1 pieces of strictly smaller diameter exists for every bounded subset of ℝⁿ.
status_search_result: Borsuk's conjecture is known to be true for n ≤ 3 and was disproved by Kahn and Kalai (1993) in high dimensions. The currently smallest known counterexample dimension is 64 (Jenrich, building on Bondarenko 2013). The conjecture remains open for 4 ≤ n ≤ 63.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: If S is a set of n points in Euclidean n-space, all at diameter 1, how many times can the distance 1 occur? The planar bound is at most n and the 3-dimensional bound at most 2n-2 are recorded, but Erdos states that the problem remains open in dimensions higher than 3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d \geq 4$ be an integer, and let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points whose diameter equals $1$, i.e. $\max_{x,y \in S} \|x-y\|_2 = 1$. A pair $\{x,y\} \subseteq S$ is called a diameter pair if $\|x-y\|_2 = 1$. Determine, as a function of $n$ and $d$, the maximum possible number of diameter pairs $f_d(n)$ over all such configurations $S$.

For context, the analogous quantities in low dimensions are known: $f_2(n) = n$ (planar case) and $f_3(n) = 2n-2$ (three-dimensional case). The problem asks for the exact value of $f_d(n)$ when $d \geq 4$.
status_search_result: The maximum number of diameters among n points in d-dimensional Euclidean space has been exactly determined for every d ≥ 4 (for n sufficiently large depending on d), with extremal configurations characterized as Lenz constructions. The result is due to work of Swanepoel and collaborators (Kupitz–Martini–Perles for d=4 originally), so the problem in dimensions d > 3, stated as open by Erdős, is now considered solved.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: If S is a set of 2^k+1 points in k-dimensional Euclidean space, must some three points determine an obtuse angle? Erdos also asks whether there exists a set of six or seven points in 3-space such that every plane angle determined by those points is acute.
self_contained_problem:
Let k ≥ 1 be an integer and let S be a finite set of points in Euclidean space ℝ^k. The plane angle determined by an ordered triple of distinct points (A,B,C) in S is the angle ∠ABC at the vertex B; this angle is called acute if it is strictly less than π/2, and obtuse if it is strictly greater than π/2.

(a) Prove or disprove: every set S ⊂ ℝ^k of 2^k + 1 points contains three points that determine an obtuse angle.

(b) Does there exist a set of six points in ℝ^3 such that every plane angle determined by three of the points is acute? Does there exist such a set of seven points?
category_tag: Acute and obtuse angles in point configurations
status_search_result: Part (a) is the Danzer–Grünbaum theorem (1962): any set of 2^k+1 points in ℝ^k determines an obtuse angle, with at most 2^k points possible if all angles are required to be at most π/2. The proof is reproduced in Aigner–Ziegler's "Proofs from THE BOOK" ("Every large point set has an obtuse angle"). Part (b) is also resolved affirmatively: explicit constructions of acute sets of 6, 7, and even 8 points in ℝ^3 are known (Grünbaum, Croft, and later authors), and the maximum size of an acute set in ℝ^3 is known to be 8. Thus both questions are solved.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let f(theta) be a trigonometric polynomial all of whose roots are real and whose maximum absolute value on [0,2pi] equals 1. Is it always true that integral_0^{2pi} |f(theta)| dtheta <= 4?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a trigonometric polynomial, i.e. a finite linear combination
$$f(\theta) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(a_k\cos(k\theta) + b_k\sin(k\theta)\bigr)$$
with real coefficients. Assume that:
(i) every zero of $f$ (in $\mathbb{C}$) is real, and
(ii) $\max_{\theta\in[0,2\pi]}|f(\theta)| = 1$.

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses one always has
$$\int_0^{2\pi}|f(\theta)|\,d\theta \;\le\; 4.$$
(Equality is attained for $f(\theta)=\cos\theta$.)
status_search_result: The conjectured bound $\int_0^{2\pi}|f|\,d\theta\le 4$ for trigonometric polynomials with all real zeros and sup norm $1$ has been established. It was proved by Kristiansen in the real-coefficient case and by Saff and Sheil-Small in the general (complex-coefficient) case, as recorded in the Erdős problems database.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let z_k lie on the unit circle and define f_n(z)=product_{k=1}^n (z-z_k). Can the sequence {f_n(z)} ever remain uniformly bounded on |z|=1? Erdos also asks for an infinite sequence of points on the unit circle whose discrepancy on every fixed arc (a,b) stays bounded by a constant c(a,b) independent of n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{z_k\}_{k\ge 1}$ be a sequence of points on the unit circle $\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\}$, and for each $n\ge 1$ define the monic polynomial
$$f_n(z)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}(z-z_k).$$

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists a choice of $\{z_k\}$ such that the sequence of functions $\{f_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ is uniformly bounded on $|z|=1$; equivalently, there exists a constant $C$ with
$$\sup_{|z|=1}|f_n(z)|\le C\qquad\text{for all }n\ge 1.$$

(b) Does there exist an infinite sequence $\{z_k\}$ on the unit circle with the following local discrepancy property: for every arc $(a,b)\subseteq[0,2\pi)$ on $|z|=1$ there is a constant $c(a,b)$ (depending only on the arc) such that, writing $N_n(a,b)$ for the number of indices $1\le k\le n$ with $z_k=e^{i\theta}$, $\theta\in(a,b)$,
$$\left|N_n(a,b)-\frac{b-a}{2\pi}\,n\right|<c(a,b)\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1?$$
category_tag: Polynomials on the unit circle and discrepancy
status_search_result: Part (a) — Erdős's conjecture that $\max_{|z|=1}|f_n(z)|$ cannot remain bounded — was resolved affirmatively by J. Beck, "The modulus of polynomials with zeros on the unit circle: a problem of Erdős," Annals of Mathematics 134 (1991), 609–651, where in fact a lower bound tending to infinity is established. The companion discrepancy formulation in (b) is closely related and is generally believed to admit no such sequence; available sources point to Beck's work as the source of the resolution but do not give a single explicit citation for the precise arc-discrepancy statement, so its status is reported here as partially solved.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: If P(z)=sum_{k=1}^n a_k z^k with |a_k|=1 for every k, Parseval gives max_{|z|=1}|P(z)| >= sqrt(n). Does there exist a universal constant c>0 such that for every n>=2 one always has max_{|z|=1}|P(z)| >= (1+c)sqrt(n)?
self_contained_problem:
Consider polynomials with unimodular coefficients on the unit circle. For each integer n ≥ 2, let
   P(z) = a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + ... + a_n z^n,
where a_k ∈ ℂ and |a_k| = 1 for every k = 1, ..., n. By Parseval's identity one has
   max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| ≥ √n.
Question: Does there exist a universal constant c > 0, independent of n and of the choice of coefficients, such that for every n ≥ 2 and every choice of unimodular coefficients a_1, ..., a_n one has
   max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| ≥ (1 + c) √n ?
status_search_result: The question (originally asked in Erdős's spirit) is resolved in the negative. Kahane (1980) constructed "ultraflat" unimodular polynomials P_n of degree n with max_{|z|=1}|P_n(z)| = (1+o(1))√n, so no such universal constant c > 0 exists. Let $\{S_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of subsets of the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, each of which has no finite limit point (equivalently, each $S_n$ is at most countable and discrete in $\mathbb{C}$). Does there always exist a (transcendental) entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ and a sequence of nonnegative integers $\{k_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ such that, for every $n\ge 1$, the $k_n$-th derivative satisfies
$$f^{(k_n)}(z)=0\quad\text{for every } z\in S_n?$$

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Does there exist a nonlinear entire function f, meaning not of the form a_0+a_1 z, such that f(x) is rational exactly when x is rational and irrational exactly when x is irrational? More generally, if A and B are two countable dense subsets of the complex plane, does there exist an entire function mapping A onto B?
self_contained_problem:
(a) Does there exist a transcendental entire function f : ℂ → ℂ (i.e. an entire function not of the form f(z) = a_0 + a_1 z) with the property that, for every real number x, f(x) is rational if and only if x is rational (equivalently, f(x) is irrational if and only if x is irrational)?

(b) More generally, given any two countable dense subsets A and B of the complex plane ℂ, does there exist an entire function f : ℂ → ℂ such that f(A) = B?

original_question: For an entire function f(z)=sum a_n z^n, let M(r)=max_theta |f(re^{i theta})| and mu(r)=max_n |a_n|r^n. It is always true, except for trivial cases, that mu(r) < M(r). If the limit of mu(r)/M(r) as r tends to infinity exists, must that limit equal 0?

\[ L = \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} \]

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: For each positive integer n, does there exist a polynomial f_n(z)=sum_{k=1}^n epsilon_{nk} z^k with coefficients epsilon_{nk} in {+1,-1} such that on the whole unit circle one has c_1 sqrt(n) < |f_n(e^{i theta})| < c_2 sqrt(n), where c_1 and c_2 are positive constants independent of both theta and n?
self_contained_problem:
Do there exist absolute positive constants c_1 and c_2 such that for every positive integer n there is a polynomial
  f_n(z) = sum_{k=1}^{n} epsilon_{n,k} z^k,
with each coefficient epsilon_{n,k} in {+1, -1}, satisfying
  c_1 sqrt(n) < |f_n(e^{i theta})| < c_2 sqrt(n)
for every real theta? In other words, does there exist a sequence of Littlewood polynomials (coefficients in {-1,+1}) of every degree n whose modulus on the unit circle is uniformly comparable to sqrt(n) from both above and below, with constants independent of n and of theta?
status_search_result: The problem was resolved affirmatively by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba in their 2019 preprint "Flat Littlewood Polynomials Exist," published in the Annals of Mathematics (Vol. 192, Issue 3, 2020, pp. 977–1004). They proved the existence of absolute constants δ, Δ > 0 such that for every n ≥ 2 there is a {-1,+1}-polynomial of degree n satisfying δ√n ≤ |P(z)| ≤ Δ√n on the unit circle, confirming the conjecture.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let z_1=1 and let z_2,...,z_n satisfy |z_i|<=1. For the power sums s_k=sum_{i=1}^n z_i^k, does there exist an absolute constant c, independent of n, k, and the chosen complex numbers z_i, such that max_{1<k<n}|s_k| > c?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n$ be complex numbers with $z_1 = 1$ and $|z_i| \leq 1$ for $i = 2, 3, \ldots, n$. For each positive integer $k$, define the power sum $s_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i^k$. Does there exist an absolute constant $c > 0$, independent of $n$, of $k$, and of the chosen complex numbers $z_2, \ldots, z_n$, such that
$$\max_{1 \leq k \leq n} |s_k| > c\,?$$
status_search_result: The existence of such an absolute constant is known: this is Turán's second main problem on power sums, and Atkinson proved a lower bound $R_n > 1/6$ (later improved to $1/5$ and beyond), confirming the existence of an absolute constant $c > 0$. The determination of the optimal value of the constant remains an active problem, with bounds refined by Biró and others to roughly $[1/2 + q, 5/6]$ for large $n$.

paper_title: Some Unsolved Problems
original_question: Let N(k) be the least integer N such that every length-N sequence over the alphabet {1,2,...,k} contains two adjacent blocks that are rearrangements of one another. Erdos notes that the conjecture N(k)=2k-1 is false, and asks in particular whether N(4) is finite.
self_contained_problem: For an integer k ≥ 1, let N(k) denote the least positive integer N such that every finite sequence s_1, s_2, …, s_N with entries from {1, 2, …, k} contains two adjacent blocks of equal length that are rearrangements (permutations) of one another; that is, there exist indices 1 ≤ i ≤ j < j + (j - i + 1) ≤ N such that the block s_i, s_{i+1}, …, s_j and the block s_{j+1}, s_{j+2}, …, s_{2j-i+1} have the same multiset of entries. If no such N exists, set N(k) = ∞. Determine whether N(4) is finite.
status_search_result: Keränen (1992, "Abelian squares are avoidable on 4 letters") constructed an infinite word over a 4-letter alphabet containing no two adjacent blocks that are permutations of each other. Hence N(4) is infinite, settling Erdős's question.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: Why do the elementary particles have the particular masses they have, when the standard model contains many free parameters whose values cannot be calculated or predicted theoretically, and why do there exist heavier second- and third-generation copies of the first-generation matter particles that appear identical except for mass even though ordinary matter consists only of first-generation particles?
self_contained_problem:
The Standard Model of particle physics is a quantum field theory with gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, coupled to three generations of chiral fermions (each generation containing a charged lepton, a neutrino, an up-type quark, and a down-type quark) together with a complex scalar Higgs doublet that breaks the electroweak symmetry SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y down to U(1)_EM via a nonzero vacuum expectation value. The Lagrangian of this theory contains a set of free dimensionless parameters that are not fixed by its internal consistency: the three gauge couplings, the Higgs self-coupling and mass parameter, and the Yukawa couplings of the Higgs to the fermions, which after electroweak symmetry breaking determine the masses of the charged leptons, the quarks, and (together with possible Majorana terms) the neutrinos, as well as the CKM (and PMNS) mixing parameters.

Address the following two questions within this framework:

(a) Provide a theoretical principle, derivation, or first-principles mechanism that determines the observed values of the elementary fermion masses (equivalently, the Yukawa couplings) of the Standard Model, rather than treating them as independent free parameters whose numerical values must be measured experimentally.

(b) Explain why the chiral fermion content of nature consists of exactly three generations, each an apparent replica of the first under the gauge group and differing only in mass, and account for the existence and role of the heavier second and third generations given that stable ordinary matter is composed only of first-generation fermions (electron, electron neutrino, up quark, down quark).
category_tag: Standard Model parameters and fermion generations
status_search_result: The flavor puzzle—why the Standard Model has the specific Yukawa couplings/fermion masses it does and why there are three generations of fermions—remains an unsolved problem in theoretical particle physics. Proposed frameworks such as Froggatt–Nielsen models, family symmetries, anarchy in the neutrino sector, and string-theoretic constructions provide partial ideas but no accepted derivation of the parameters or of the number three. The status is widely recognized as open in review literature and Standard Model overviews.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: How and why does a quantum measurement make a particle's wave function collapse to a single definite outcome, and how does the definite macroscopic world we observe arise from a microscopic quantum description in which many states coexist in superposition and linear evolution alone would allow those coexisting states to persist forever?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system whose state is described by a vector $|\psi\rangle$ in a complex separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, evolving in time according to the linear Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t|\psi\rangle = H|\psi\rangle$ for a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$. Because the evolution is linear and unitary, any superposition $|\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n|\phi_n\rangle$ of eigenstates of an observable $A = \sum_n a_n |\phi_n\rangle\langle\phi_n|$ remains a superposition for all time. The standard measurement postulate, however, asserts that upon measurement of $A$ the state discontinuously "collapses" to a single eigenstate $|\phi_n\rangle$ with probability $|c_n|^2$ (the Born rule), yielding a definite outcome $a_n$.

Couple such a microscopic system to a macroscopic apparatus (and possibly an environment), modeled as a larger quantum system on $\mathcal{H}_{\text{sys}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\text{app}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\text{env}}$ evolving under a global self-adjoint Hamiltonian and hence linearly and unitarily. The problem is the following:

Provide a mathematically precise dynamical mechanism, derivable from (or consistent with) the linear unitary quantum dynamics of the composite system alone — i.e., without invoking the collapse postulate as an additional axiom — that
(i) explains why and how a single definite outcome $a_n$ is realized in any individual measurement,
(ii) reproduces the Born rule probabilities $|c_n|^2$,
(iii) accounts for the absence of observable macroscopic superpositions of distinguishable pointer states, and
(iv) is compatible with the empirical fact that classical, definite macroscopic configurations emerge from the underlying quantum description.

Equivalently: identify and justify the precise mathematical modification, interpretation, or derivation (e.g., a nonlinear stochastic extension of the Schrödinger equation, a decoherence-plus-branching account, a hidden-variable completion, or another scheme) that resolves the tension between linear unitary evolution and the occurrence of definite measurement outcomes.
status_search_result: The quantum measurement problem remains a widely acknowledged open foundational problem. No proposed resolution (Copenhagen, many-worlds, GRW/CSL spontaneous collapse models, Bohmian mechanics, decoherence-based approaches, QBism, etc.) is universally accepted, and experimental tests of collapse models continue but have not settled the issue as of 2026.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: Do general solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluids exist, and if they do, are they free of singularities and sufficient to describe turbulent fluid motion; more broadly, is turbulence ultimately understandable within human mathematical and physical methods or not?
self_contained_problem:
Let $u_0 : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a divergence-free, infinitely differentiable vector field, all of whose derivatives decay rapidly at infinity (a Schwartz-class solenoidal field). Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,\infty)$:
\[
\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u = -\nabla p + \nu \,\Delta u, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0,
\]
with viscosity $\nu > 0$, unknown velocity field $u(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and unknown pressure $p(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}$, subject to the initial condition $u(x,0) = u_0(x)$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every such initial datum $u_0$, there exist functions $u \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $p \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ that solve the above system, satisfy the bounded-energy condition
\[
\sup_{t \ge 0} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |u(x,t)|^2 \, dx < \infty,
\]
and for which no finite-time singularities occur. Equivalently: do globally defined, smooth, energy-bounded solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exist for all such initial data?
status_search_result: The global existence and smoothness of solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains unsolved as of 2026. While partial results exist (e.g., Leray–Hopf weak solutions, conditional regularity criteria, Tao's averaged Navier–Stokes blowup, and recent non-uniqueness results for weak solutions), the central regularity/existence question is still open.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: What is the dark matter whose existence has been inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation, and cosmic structure formation, if it exists at all, and can it be directly detected or identified among candidate forms such as weakly interacting massive particles or massive compact halo objects?
self_contained_problem: Cosmological and astrophysical observations — including galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background, and large-scale structure formation — indicate that the gravitational dynamics of the universe cannot be accounted for by visible (baryonic, electromagnetically interacting) matter alone, and suggest that the dominant matter component is a non-luminous, non-absorbing form of matter commonly called dark matter. Determine the physical nature of this dark matter, if it indeed exists as a material constituent rather than as a manifestation of modified gravitational laws. In particular, decide whether dark matter can be directly detected in terrestrial or astrophysical experiments, and identify the correct candidate (or combination of candidates) among possibilities such as weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) — hypothetical particles that interact only via gravity and the weak nuclear force — and massive compact halo objects (MACHOs) — compact baryonic or otherwise dark astrophysical bodies (e.g. brown dwarfs, neutron stars, primordial black holes) populating galactic halos, or some other class of candidates (e.g. axions, sterile neutrinos).

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: Can the behavior of even mildly complex systems be derived in detail from the four known fundamental forces alone, or must physics be supplemented by additional principles at larger scales; in particular, how should one explain self-organization, the origin of life, what life is, and how consciousness can arise from matter if reduction to fundamental laws is not by itself enough?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the four fundamental interactions currently recognized in physics — gravitation, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force, and the weak nuclear force — together with the established laws (quantum field theory and general relativity) that govern them. Call a description of nature "constructionist" if the qualitative and quantitative behavior of every physical system, at every scale, can in principle be derived from these fundamental laws alone (without introducing further independent organizing principles). Determine whether the constructionist hypothesis holds. Specifically:

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: What physical mechanism produced the small excess of matter over antimatter in the early universe, given the expectation that the Big Bang should have produced matter and antimatter symmetrically and given that the known CP-violation is far too weak to explain the matter-dominated universe observed today?
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of the Standard Model of particle physics together with standard Big Bang cosmology, an initially hot, dense, and approximately symmetric early universe is expected to produce baryons and antibaryons in equal abundance. Observationally, however, the present universe contains a small but nonzero baryon-to-photon ratio η = (n_B − n_{B̄})/n_γ ≈ 6 × 10^{−10}, with no significant primordial antimatter component. Sakharov's conditions (baryon number violation, C and CP violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium) are necessary for any dynamical mechanism that generates such an asymmetry, but the CP violation present in the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa quark mixing matrix of the Standard Model is quantitatively far too small to account for the observed value of η.

Problem: Identify and describe a physical mechanism — specifying the underlying microscopic dynamics, the new sources of CP violation (if any), the relevant out-of-equilibrium process, and the baryon-number-violating interactions — that can, starting from a matter–antimatter symmetric initial state in the early universe, dynamically generate the observed baryon asymmetry η ≈ 6 × 10^{−10}, in quantitative agreement with cosmological and laboratory constraints.
status_search_result: The baryon asymmetry / baryogenesis problem remains one of the major unsolved problems in modern physics. Standard Model CP violation is known to be insufficient, and although LHCb reported in 2025 the first observation of CP asymmetry in baryon decays, this does not resolve the mechanism that produced the cosmological matter excess. Leptogenesis, electroweak baryogenesis, and other extensions of the Standard Model remain competing but unverified hypotheses.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: How does macroscopic friction arise in a world made entirely of atoms when the microscopic quantum description itself contains no friction, and why do frictional macroscopic processes display an obvious preferred direction of time even though microscopic frictionless interactions can be run equally well forward or backward?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an isolated physical system composed of N atoms whose microscopic time evolution is governed by the Schrödinger equation
  i ℏ ∂_t |ψ(t)⟩ = H |ψ(t)⟩,
with a self-adjoint Hamiltonian H on a Hilbert space ℋ. This microscopic dynamics is unitary and time-reversal symmetric: if t ↦ |ψ(t)⟩ is a solution and T denotes the antiunitary time-reversal operator (assuming [H,T]=0 up to complex conjugation), then t ↦ T|ψ(−t)⟩ is also a solution, so no dissipation or friction is present at the microscopic level.

At the macroscopic level, however, one observes phenomena such as a hockey puck sliding on ice and coming to rest: a kinetic-energy-bearing degree of freedom is irreversibly damped, and the time-reversed process (the puck spontaneously starting to move) is never observed.

Provide a rigorous derivation, starting from the unitary quantum dynamics above (possibly together with a precisely specified prescription such as a partition of degrees of freedom into "macroscopic" and "microscopic / environmental" variables, a coarse-graining map Π: ℋ → ℳ onto a space of macroscopic observables, an initial-state assumption, and a thermodynamic / large-N limit), that yields:

(a) An effective macroscopic equation of motion for a selected macroscopic degree of freedom (e.g. the center-of-mass momentum P(t) of a solid body in contact with another) of the form
  dP/dt = F_ext − γ(P) + ξ(t),
with a strictly positive friction coefficient γ > 0 and noise ξ obeying a fluctuation–dissipation relation; and

(b) A proof that the resulting macroscopic evolution is not invariant under t ↦ −t, i.e. it generates a semigroup rather than a group, thereby establishing a thermodynamic arrow of time as an emergent consequence of the time-reversal-symmetric microscopic Schrödinger dynamics.

The problem is to give such a derivation under physically natural and minimal assumptions, and to characterize precisely which assumptions (e.g. typicality of initial states, locality of H, ergodicity, finite observational time resolution) are necessary for friction and macroscopic irreversibility to emerge.
category_tag: Emergence of irreversibility and friction from unitary quantum dynamics
status_search_result: The reconciliation of reversible microscopic (quantum) dynamics with irreversible macroscopic friction and a thermodynamic arrow of time is widely regarded as a long-standing open foundational problem. Recent works (2025–2026) propose partial mechanisms — e.g. temporal coarse-graining as the origin of friction in quantum spin chains, semigroup-vs-group obstructions, and open-system formulations — but no universally accepted first-principles derivation exists. The problem remains active and open.

paper_title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics
original_question: What explains the arrow of time, namely the fact that time appears to move forward for macroscopic systems, and more specifically why was the entropy of the universe so low in the past so that the universe began in such an ordered state; relatedly, is time as represented in current physical theories perhaps not fundamental but an illusion?
self_contained_problem: Within the framework of modern physics, the second law of thermodynamics asserts that the entropy (a measure of disorder) of an isolated macroscopic system is non-decreasing in time, which is commonly invoked to explain the thermodynamic "arrow of time" — the empirical asymmetry that macroscopic processes proceed in one temporal direction. This explanation, however, requires that the entropy of the universe was extraordinarily low at early times (the "past hypothesis"). Provide a fundamental physical explanation for the arrow of time, and in particular give a principled account of why the early universe was in such an exceptionally low-entropy, highly ordered macrostate. As part of the analysis, address the question of whether time, as it currently appears in physical theories (classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, general relativity, quantum field theory, and candidate theories of quantum gravity), is a fundamental feature of reality or instead an emergent, effective, or illusory notion arising from more basic timeless structure.
category_tag: arrow of time and low-entropy past
status_search_result: The origin of the arrow of time and the low-entropy initial state of the universe (the "past hypothesis") remains a widely acknowledged open problem in physics and cosmology, with active proposals (Penrose's Weyl Curvature Hypothesis, Carroll–Chen eternal inflation models, Barbour's timeless approaches, etc.) but no consensus solution. The question of whether time is fundamental or emergent is likewise still open, with ongoing work in quantum gravity (Wheeler–DeWitt, loop quantum gravity, causal set theory).

original_question: Is the group SLn(Z), for n≥3, uniform Kazhdan ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a discrete group with Kazhdan's property (T). For a finite generating subset $Q \subset G$ and a unitary representation $\pi$ of $G$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\pi$ without nonzero invariant vectors, define the Kazhdan constant
$$\kappa(G,Q,\pi) \;=\; \inf_{v \in \mathcal{H}_\pi,\, \|v\|=1}\ \max_{q \in Q}\ \|\pi(q)v - v\|,$$
and set $\kappa(G,Q) = \inf_\pi \kappa(G,Q,\pi)$, where the infimum is taken over all unitary representations of $G$ without nonzero invariant vectors. The group $G$ is said to be \emph{uniform Kazhdan} if
$$\kappa(G) \;:=\; \inf_{Q}\, \kappa(G,Q) \;>\; 0,$$
where the infimum is taken over all finite generating subsets $Q$ of $G$.

For an integer $n \geq 3$, is the group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ uniform Kazhdan?

original_question: Let B be a suitably finite K(n)-local commutative S-algebra (for example LK(n)S→B could be a G-Galois extension). Then the map V∧KB→T∧KB induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups in suﬃciently high de- grees.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a prime $p$ and a chromatic height $n\ge 0$. Let $K(n+1)$ denote the $(n+1)$-st Morava $K$-theory spectrum at $p$, and let $T(n+1)$ denote the telescope on a $v_{n+1}$-self map of a finite type-$(n+1)$ complex (so the natural map $T(n+1) \to K(n+1)$ identifies $K(n+1)$-localization with a smashing localization of $T(n+1)$-localization). For a connective $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectrum $A$, let $K(A)$ denote its algebraic $K$-theory spectrum.

Let $B$ be a "suitably finite" $K(n)$-local commutative $S$-algebra; for example, $B$ may be obtained as a $G$-Galois extension $L_{K(n)} S \to B$ in the sense of Rognes for a finite group $G$. 

Prove or disprove: the natural comparison map
$$ T(n+1) \wedge K(B) \;\longrightarrow\; K(n+1) \wedge K(B) $$
induces an isomorphism on stable homotopy groups in all sufficiently high degrees. Equivalently, the $T(n+1)$-local and $K(n+1)$-local algebraic $K$-theory of $B$ agree in sufficiently high degrees.
status_search_result: This is a form of the Ausoni–Rognes "higher chromatic Quillen–Lichtenbaum" / redshift conjecture, closely tied to the telescope conjecture for K(B). Several cases of the Ausoni–Rognes Galois-descent and redshift conjectures have been verified (Clausen–Mathew–Naumann–Noel; Hahn–Wilson; Yuan; Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank). However, Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank (2023) disproved the general telescope conjecture, showing that $T(n+1)$- and $K(n+1)$-localizations differ in general; consequently the precise form of this statement is now known to fail for some $B$, while it remains established in a range of explicit cases. original_question: Is FW equivalant to (T), or 13 does there exist a group G such that G does not have property (T), but G and all its finite index subgroups have property FW?
self_contained_problem:
A discrete group $G$ is said to have Kazhdan's property (T) if every continuous unitary representation of $G$ that has almost invariant vectors has a non-zero invariant vector. The group $G$ is said to have property FW if every isometric action of $G$ on a (discrete) CAT(0) cube complex has a global fixed point; equivalently, every cofinite action of $G$ on a set with a commensurated subset stabilizes some subset within the commensuration class. It is known that property (T) implies property FW, and that property FW is inherited by finite-index subgroups.

Question: Is property FW equivalent to property (T)? More precisely, does there exist a discrete group $G$ such that $G$ does not have property (T), yet $G$ and every finite-index subgroup of $G$ have property FW?

status_search_result: The literature (notably Cornulier's work on property FW and commensurated subsets) introduced property FW as a strict weakening of property (T) in formulation. While various concrete groups (e.g. Thompson-type groups, certain piecewise groups) have been investigated with respect to FW versus (T), web search did not surface a definitive published resolution stating that FW for a group together with all its finite-index subgroups is equivalent to property (T), nor a counterexample explicitly recognized as such. The status therefore appears unresolved based on available sources.

original_question: As proved recently, the outer automorphism group of any polycyclic by finite group, and, hence, also the group of homotopy equivalences of any aspherical space with a polycyclic by finite fundamental group is an arithmetic group. Hence, we ask: Does Sullivan 's arithmeticity result for nilpotent spaces carry over to a (suitable) more general class of polycyclic spaces ?
self_contained_problem:
A group is called polycyclic-by-finite (or virtually polycyclic) if it has a subgroup of finite index that admits a finite subnormal series with cyclic factors. An aspherical space is a CW-complex whose higher homotopy groups vanish. For a connected CW-complex X, let aut(X) denote the group of homotopy classes of self-homotopy equivalences of X. It is known that for any polycyclic-by-finite group G, the outer automorphism group Out(G) is an arithmetic group, and consequently if X is an aspherical CW-complex with fundamental group polycyclic-by-finite then aut(X) is an arithmetic group.

A nilpotent space is a connected CW-complex X whose fundamental group π₁(X) is nilpotent and acts nilpotently on each higher homotopy group π_n(X). Sullivan's arithmeticity theorem states that for a simply connected (or, more generally, nilpotent) CW-complex X of finite type, the group aut(X) of homotopy classes of self-homotopy equivalences is commensurable with an arithmetic group.

Problem: Define a suitable class of "polycyclic spaces" extending the class of nilpotent spaces of finite type — for instance, finite-type CW-complexes X whose fundamental group is polycyclic-by-finite and whose higher homotopy groups carry compatible polycyclic-by-finite structures — and prove that for every X in this class the group aut(X) of self-homotopy equivalences is an arithmetic group (or at least commensurable with one). In other words, extend Sullivan's arithmeticity theorem from nilpotent spaces to a class of spaces that simultaneously generalizes nilpotent spaces of finite type and aspherical spaces with polycyclic-by-finite fundamental group.
status_search_result: No definitive source was located confirming or refuting an extension of Sullivan's arithmeticity theorem for self-homotopy equivalences from nilpotent spaces to a general class of polycyclic spaces. The arithmeticity of Out(G) for polycyclic-by-finite G is established, but the proposed unified extension to a class of "polycyclic spaces" appears to remain a programmatic question without a verified general solution.

$$\mathrm{Reg}(M) = \max_i \{\,a_i(M) + i\,\},$$
where $a_i(M) = \max\{\,n : H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M)_n \neq 0\,\}$ (with $a_i(M) = -\infty$ if $H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M)=0$) and $H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}$ denotes local cohomology with respect to the maximal homogeneous ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of positive-degree elements.

original_question: Is it true that any infinite amenable group contains an infinite abelian subgroup (this is of course of interest only for torsion groups)?

original_question: For solvable non-virtually nilpotent groups, is there a canonical way of constructing a Følner sequence ?
self_contained_problem:
A discrete countable group $G$ is amenable if and only if it admits a Følner sequence, i.e., a sequence $(F_n)_{n\ge 1}$ of finite nonempty subsets of $G$ such that for every $g \in G$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{|gF_n \triangle F_n|}{|F_n|} = 0.$$
Recall that $G$ is solvable if its derived series terminates at the trivial subgroup, and $G$ is virtually nilpotent if it has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index.

Question: For every finitely generated solvable group $G$ that is not virtually nilpotent, is there a canonical (i.e., systematic and uniform) way of constructing an explicit Følner sequence in $G$?
status_search_result: Weiss showed that any solvable group admits a Følner monotile sequence, and explicit Følner sequences are known in many specific examples of non-virtually-nilpotent solvable groups (e.g., lamplighter groups, Baumslag–Solitar groups BS(1,m)). However, whether there is a single canonical construction covering all solvable non-virtually-nilpotent groups in a uniform way does not appear to be settled by a clearly identifiable theorem, so the status is best reported as unknown.

The group multiplication on $G$ extends to a semigroup operation on $\beta G$ which makes $\beta G$ a compact right-topological semigroup: for each $q \in \beta G$ the map $p \mapsto p \cdot q$ is continuous, and for each $g \in G$ the map $p \mapsto g \cdot p$ is continuous. Recall that $G$ is said to be amenable if there exists a finitely additive left-invariant probability measure on the power set of $G$ (equivalently, a left-invariant mean on $\ell^\infty(G)$).

Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. A subset $R \subseteq G$ is called a set of measurable recurrence (property MR) if for every measure-preserving action of $G$ on a probability space $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ and every $A \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, there exists $g \in R \setminus \{e\}$ such that $\mu(A \cap g^{-1}A) > 0$. A subset $R \subseteq G$ is called a set of topological recurrence (property TR) if for every minimal action of $G$ by homeomorphisms on a compact metric space $X$ and every nonempty open set $U \subseteq X$, there exists $g \in R \setminus \{e\}$ such that $U \cap g^{-1}U \neq \emptyset$.

Every set of topological recurrence is a set of measurable recurrence. Prove or disprove the following: $G$ is amenable if and only if every set of measurable recurrence in $G$ is a set of topological recurrence.
