paper_title: THE HODGE CONJECTURE
context_brief: Field of definition of the Hodge locus
original_question: In the same setting of a smooth projective family f : X → S defined over Q̄, the Hodge conjecture predicts that the locus in S where a fixed integral cohomology class becomes of type (p,p) is a denumerable union of algebraic subvarieties. Must that Hodge locus in fact be defined over Q̄?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f: \mathcal{X} \to S$ be a smooth projective morphism of smooth complex algebraic varieties defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. For an integer $p \geq 0$, the local system $R^{2p} f_* \mathbb{Z}$ underlies a polarizable variation of Hodge structure of weight $2p$ on $S$. Given a point $s_0 \in S(\mathbb{C})$ and an integral cohomology class $\gamma_0 \in H^{2p}(\mathcal{X}_{s_0}, \mathbb{Z})$ that is of Hodge type $(p,p)$, the associated Hodge locus is the set of points $s \in S(\mathbb{C})$ such that, after parallel transport along some path from $s_0$ to $s$, the class $\gamma_0$ becomes a class of type $(p,p)$ on the fiber $\mathcal{X}_s$. More intrinsically, one defines the Hodge locus $\mathrm{HL}(S, \gamma_0) \subseteq S$ as the union of all components of the locus of Hodge classes (in the relative de Rham bundle) that pass through $(s_0, \gamma_0)$, projected to $S$.

It is known that $\mathrm{HL}(S, \gamma_0)$ is a countable union of closed algebraic subvarieties of $S$ (theorem of Cattani–Deligne–Kaplan). The question is: must every irreducible component of $\mathrm{HL}(S, \gamma_0)$ be defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ as a subvariety of $S$?
category_tag: Hodge loci and variations of Hodge structure
status_search_result: The question of whether the Hodge locus, known to be a countable union of algebraic subvarieties by Cattani–Deligne–Kaplan, is necessarily defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ when the family is, remains open in general. Partial results exist (e.g., the locus of Hodge classes in the de Rham bundle has good algebraicity/field-of-definition properties in certain settings, and recent work by Baldi–Klingler–Ullmo and others addresses the structure of the Hodge locus), but the general conjecture that components are defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ has not been established.

paper_title: THE HODGE CONJECTURE
original_question: Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension N, and let Δ ⊂ X × X be the diagonal. The Künneth decomposition of the cohomology class cl(Δ) gives components cl(Δ)_{a,b} in H^a(X) ⊗ H^b(X) for a + b = 2N, and each of these components is a Hodge class. Are these Künneth components of the diagonal algebraic cycles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety of complex dimension $N$, and let $\Delta \subset X \times X$ denote the diagonal, which is an algebraic cycle of codimension $N$. Consider its cohomology class $\mathrm{cl}(\Delta) \in H^{2N}(X \times X, \mathbb{Q})$. By the Künneth formula
$$H^{2N}(X \times X, \mathbb{Q}) = \bigoplus_{a+b=2N} H^a(X, \mathbb{Q}) \otimes H^b(X, \mathbb{Q}),$$
the class decomposes as $\mathrm{cl}(\Delta) = \sum_{a+b=2N} \mathrm{cl}(\Delta)_{a,b}$ with $\mathrm{cl}(\Delta)_{a,b} \in H^a(X, \mathbb{Q}) \otimes H^b(X, \mathbb{Q})$. Since the Hodge decomposition is compatible with the Künneth decomposition, each component $\mathrm{cl}(\Delta)_{a,b}$ is a rational Hodge class on $X \times X$.

Question: Is each Künneth component $\mathrm{cl}(\Delta)_{a,b}$ the cohomology class of an algebraic cycle on $X \times X$ with rational coefficients?
status_search_result: This is Grothendieck's Künneth-type standard conjecture (Conjecture C). It remains open in general; it is implied by the Hodge conjecture in characteristic zero. Known cases include abelian varieties (Šermenev 1974; Deninger–Murre 1991), surfaces, curves, and Hilbert schemes of points on smooth surfaces (de Cataldo–Migliorini 2002).

paper_title: THE HODGE CONJECTURE
context_brief: Algebraicity of the inverse hard Lefschetz correspondence
original_question: Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension N, let η ∈ H^2(X, Z) be the class of a hyperplane section, and for p ≥ 0 let η^p : H^{N-p}(X, C) → H^{N+p}(X, C) be the hard Lefschetz isomorphism. If z ∈ H^{N-p}(X, C) ⊗ H^{N-p}(X, C) is the Hodge class that represents the inverse map (η^p)^{-1}, is the class z algebraic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety of complex dimension $N$. Fix an ample line bundle on $X$ and let $\eta \in H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$ be the cohomology class of a hyperplane section. For each integer $p \geq 0$, the iterated cup product with $\eta^p$ gives the hard Lefschetz isomorphism
$$\eta^p \,:\, H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C}) \longrightarrow H^{N+p}(X,\mathbb{C}).$$
By the Künneth formula, $H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C}) \otimes H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C})$ embeds in $H^{2N-2p}(X \times X, \mathbb{C})$. Let $z \in H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C}) \otimes H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C}) \subset H^{2N-2p}(X \times X, \mathbb{C})$ be the unique class such that the inverse isomorphism $(\eta^p)^{-1} \,:\, H^{N+p}(X,\mathbb{C}) \to H^{N-p}(X,\mathbb{C})$ is given by the correspondence
$$c \;\longmapsto\; \mathrm{pr}_{1\,!}\bigl(z \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^{*}\, c\bigr),$$
where $\mathrm{pr}_1, \mathrm{pr}_2 : X \times X \to X$ are the two projections. One checks that $z$ is a Hodge class on $X \times X$, i.e. it lies in $H^{2N-2p}(X\times X, \mathbb{Q}) \cap H^{N-p,N-p}(X\times X)$.

Question: Is the class $z$ algebraic? Equivalently, is $z$ a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination of cohomology classes of algebraic subvarieties of $X \times X$ of codimension $N-p$?
status_search_result: This is precisely Grothendieck's Lefschetz standard conjecture B (algebraicity of the inverse of the hard Lefschetz operator), which is a special case of the Hodge conjecture. It remains open in general over $\mathbb{C}$. It is known in some cases: for varieties over finite fields (Katz–Messing, via the Weil conjectures), for abelian varieties (Lieberman), for surfaces, and recently for various hyper-Kähler varieties (e.g. OG10-type, certain generalized Kummer deformation types). The general case is widely regarded as still open.

paper_title: THE HODGE CONJECTURE
context_brief: Rationality of intersections of reduced Hodge classes
original_question: Let A be an abelian variety over the algebraic closure F of a finite field F_q. Suppose A is lifted in two different ways to characteristic 0, giving complex abelian varieties A_1 and A_2 defined over Q̄, and choose Hodge classes z_1 on A_1 and z_2 on A_2 of complementary dimension. After interpreting z_1 and z_2 as ℓ-adic cohomology classes and reducing them over F, is their intersection number κ always a rational number?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}$ be the algebraic closure of a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}$. Suppose $A$ admits two liftings to characteristic $0$: complex abelian varieties $A_1$ and $A_2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, each equipped with an isomorphism whose reduction recovers $A$. Recall that a Hodge class on a smooth projective complex variety $X$ of dimension $n$ is a class in $H^{2p}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \cap H^{p,p}(X)$ for some $0 \le p \le n$. Choose Hodge classes $z_1$ on $A_1$ of degree $2p$ and $z_2$ on $A_2$ of complementary degree $2(\dim A - p)$. Fix a prime $\ell$ different from the characteristic of $\mathbb{F}$, and view $z_1$ and $z_2$ as classes in $\ell$-adic cohomology $H^{2p}_{\text{ét}}(A_1,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(p))$ and $H^{2(\dim A - p)}_{\text{ét}}(A_2,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(\dim A - p))$ via the comparison isomorphism with Betti cohomology. Using the smooth and proper reduction maps, transport these classes to $\ell$-adic cohomology classes on $A$, and define $\kappa \in \mathbb{Q}_\ell$ to be their cup-product pushed forward to $H^0$, i.e. the intersection number of the reductions of $z_1$ and $z_2$ over $\mathbb{F}$.

Question: Is $\kappa$ necessarily a rational number, independent of the choices of liftings $A_1, A_2$ and of $\ell$?
status_search_result: This rationality question is a well-known consequence that would follow from the Hodge conjecture (or even from the conjecture that Hodge classes on abelian varieties reduce to algebraic classes in positive characteristic). Although Deligne proved that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are absolute Hodge, this does not allow reduction mod p, and the question of rationality of such intersection numbers κ remains open. No published resolution appears in the literature.

paper_title: THE HODGE CONJECTURE
context_brief: Rationality of intersections with algebraic cycles after reduction
original_question: In the same finite-field lifting setup, fix a Hodge class z_1 on one characteristic-0 lift of an abelian variety A over the algebraic closure F of F_q, reduce z_1 over F, and pair it with the cohomology class of an algebraic cycle on A itself. Must the resulting intersection number always be a rational number?

Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}$ of dimension $g$, and let $\tilde{A}$ be a lift of $A$ to characteristic zero: that is, a smooth projective abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}$ over the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}$ of some number field (or over a complete discrete valuation ring with residue field contained in $\mathbb{F}$), together with an isomorphism of the special fiber with $A$, and with generic fiber $\tilde{A}$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (embedded in $\mathbb{C}$). $$\kappa := \langle \bar{z}_1, \mathrm{cl}(Z) \rangle \in \mathbb{Q}_\ell.$$

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Does there exist a composite integer n such that Euler's totient φ(n), meaning the number of positive integers at most n that are coprime to n, divides n − 1? Equivalently, is the set of composite integers n satisfying φ(n) | (n − 1) actually empty?
self_contained_problem: For a positive integer n, let φ(n) denote Euler's totient function, i.e., the number of integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and gcd(k, n) = 1. It is well known that if n is prime then φ(n) = n − 1, so φ(n) divides n − 1. Determine whether there exists a composite integer n > 1 such that φ(n) divides n − 1. Equivalently, prove that the set S = { n composite : φ(n) ∣ (n − 1) } is empty, or exhibit an element of S.
status_search_result: Lehmer's totient problem, posed in 1932, remains open. No composite n with φ(n) | (n−1) is known, and any such n must be a squarefree product of at least 15 distinct primes and exceed 10^22, with stronger lower bounds in later work. No proof of nonexistence has been found.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let d1, ..., dk be distinct integers, and for each prime p let b(p) be the number of distinct residue classes modulo p represented by d1, ..., dk. If b(p) < p for every prime p, must there exist infinitely many positive integers n such that all k numbers n + d1, ..., n + dk are prime?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer and let $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$ be distinct integers. For each prime $p$, let $b(p)$ denote the number of distinct residue classes modulo $p$ represented by $d_1, \dots, d_k$. Call the tuple $(d_1, \dots, d_k)$ admissible if $b(p) < p$ for every prime $p$.

Prove or disprove: for every admissible tuple $(d_1, \dots, d_k)$, there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that all of $n + d_1, n + d_2, \dots, n + d_k$ are prime.
status_search_result: The prime k-tuples conjecture remains a famous open problem in analytic number theory. The case k=2 (twin primes and related) is unresolved. Significant progress on bounded gaps between primes (Zhang, Maynard, Tao, Polymath) implies that for any admissible k-tuple, some specific linear forms infinitely often produce primes at bounded positions, but the full conjecture is not proven.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: If χ is a non-principal Dirichlet character modulo q, is every short character sum of the form ∑_{n=M+1}^{M+N} χ(n) bounded by Oε(N^{1/2} q^ε) for every ε > 0, uniformly in the starting point M and length N?

Let $q\ge 2$ be an integer and let $\chi$ be a non-principal Dirichlet character modulo $q$ (that is, a group homomorphism $\chi:(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^\times\to\mathbb{C}^\times$, extended to $\mathbb{Z}$ by setting $\chi(n)=0$ when $\gcd(n,q)>1$, and not identically $1$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^\times$). For integers $M\ge 0$ and $N\ge 1$, consider the short character sum
$$ S_\chi(M,N) \;=\; \sum_{n=M+1}^{M+N}\chi(n). $$
Prove or disprove the following: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$ |S_\chi(M,N)| \;\le\; C_\varepsilon\, N^{1/2}\, q^{\varepsilon} $$
holds uniformly for all $q\ge 2$, all non-principal Dirichlet characters $\chi$ modulo $q$, all $M\ge 0$, and all $N\ge 1$.

The best unconditional results remain those of Burgess type, which give nontrivial bounds only for $N\gg q^{1/4+\delta}$ (with improvements in special cases), and even under GRH the full conjectured range is not known. Recent surveys and papers (e.g., on "three conjectures about character sums" and Shparlinski's open problem list) explicitly list this as an open conjecture.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Does the Riemann zeta function satisfy the Lindelöf hypothesis, namely that ζ(1/2 + it) ≪ε (|t| + 4)^ε for every ε > 0? Equivalently, is the Lindelöf μ-function equal to 0 at σ = 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for $\Re(s) > 1$ by $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ and continued meromorphically to the complex plane with its only pole a simple pole at $s = 1$. For a real number $\sigma$, define the Lindelöf $\mu$-function by
$$\mu(\sigma) = \inf\{\, c \ge 0 : \zeta(\sigma + it) \ll_c (|t|+4)^{c} \text{ as } |t|\to\infty \,\}.$$
It is known that $\mu(\sigma) = 0$ for $\sigma \ge 1$, that $\mu(\sigma) = 1/2 - \sigma$ for $\sigma \le 0$, and that $\mu$ is a non-increasing, convex function of $\sigma$. In particular $0 \le \mu(1/2) \le 1/4$ from the classical convexity bound.

Prove or disprove the Lindelöf hypothesis: for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} + it\right) \ll_{\varepsilon} (|t|+4)^{\varepsilon},$$
equivalently, $\mu(1/2) = 0$.
status_search_result: The Lindelöf hypothesis is a long-standing open problem in analytic number theory. It is implied by the Riemann Hypothesis but remains unproved. The current best unconditional subconvexity bound on the critical line is $\mu(1/2) \le 13/84$ due to Bourgain (2017), improving on the Weyl-type exponent $1/6$ and later refinements; no proof of $\mu(1/2)=0$ is known.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: For a primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q > 1, do all non-trivial zeros ρ = β + iγ of the Dirichlet L-function L(s, χ) lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let q > 1 be an integer and let χ be a primitive Dirichlet character modulo q, i.e., a completely multiplicative function χ : ℤ → ℂ of period q with χ(n) = 0 whenever gcd(n, q) > 1, which does not arise from any character of smaller modulus dividing q. Define the associated Dirichlet L-function by

  L(s, χ) = ∑_{n=1}^{∞} χ(n) n^{-s}    for Re(s) > 1,

and extend L(s, χ) to an entire function on ℂ via analytic continuation (which exists since χ is non-principal). The completed L-function satisfies a functional equation relating L(s, χ) to L(1-s, χ̄), and L(s, χ) has so-called "trivial" zeros at the non-positive integers s = 0, -2, -4, … or s = -1, -3, -5, … (depending on whether χ(-1) = 1 or χ(-1) = -1). All other zeros, called non-trivial, lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1.

Problem: Prove or disprove that for every integer q > 1 and every primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q, every non-trivial zero ρ = β + iγ of L(s, χ) satisfies Re(ρ) = 1/2.
status_search_result: The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions remains a famous open problem; it is one of the central unsolved conjectures in analytic number theory and is widely cited as open in current literature.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let ψ(x) = ∑_{n≤x} Λ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. Is it true that for every pair of real numbers h and x with 2 ≤ h ≤ x, one has ψ(x + h) − ψ(x) = h + Oε(h^{1/2} x^ε) for every ε > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ denote the von Mangoldt function, defined by $\Lambda(n) = \log p$ if $n = p^k$ for some prime $p$ and integer $k \geq 1$, and $\Lambda(n) = 0$ otherwise. Define the Chebyshev function $\psi(x) = \sum_{n \leq x} \Lambda(n)$ for $x \geq 1$.

Determine whether the following statement holds: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon > 0$ such that, for all real numbers $h$ and $x$ with $2 \leq h \leq x$,
$$\bigl|\psi(x+h) - \psi(x) - h\bigr| \leq C_\varepsilon\, h^{1/2} x^{\varepsilon}.$$

Equivalently, prove or disprove the asymptotic $\psi(x+h) - \psi(x) = h + O_\varepsilon\bigl(h^{1/2} x^{\varepsilon}\bigr)$ uniformly in $2 \le h \le x$.
status_search_result: This is a well-known conjecture on primes in short intervals, generally attributed to Montgomery (and related to a conjecture of Selberg under RH). It implies the Riemann Hypothesis and remains unproven; the best unconditional and conditional (under RH) results give substantially weaker error terms.

paper_title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
original_question: Let ψ(x; q, a) = ∑_{n≤x, n≡a mod q} Λ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. When (a, q) = 1 and q ≤ x, is it true that ψ(x; q, a) = x/ϕ(q) + Oε(x^{1/2+ε} / q^{1/2}) for every ε > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ denote the von Mangoldt function, defined by $\Lambda(n)=\log p$ if $n=p^k$ for some prime $p$ and integer $k\ge 1$, and $\Lambda(n)=0$ otherwise. For positive integers $q$ and $a$ with $(a,q)=1$, and for a real number $x\ge 2$, define
$$\psi(x;q,a)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x \\ n\equiv a\,(\mathrm{mod}\,q)}}\Lambda(n),$$
and let $\varphi$ denote Euler's totient function.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon>0$ such that, uniformly for all integers $q,a$ with $(a,q)=1$ and $1\le q\le x$,
$$\psi(x;q,a)=\frac{x}{\varphi(q)}+O_\varepsilon\!\left(\frac{x^{1/2+\varepsilon}}{q^{1/2}}\right),$$
i.e. the error term is bounded in absolute value by $C_\varepsilon\, x^{1/2+\varepsilon}/q^{1/2}$.

It is widely regarded as open: it lies beyond what GRH alone gives (GRH yields only $O(x^{1/2}\log^2 x)$ uniformly), and current results (e.g., Bombieri–Vinogradov, large-moduli work, and recent 2024–2025 papers on primes in APs to large moduli) fall short of this pointwise bound. original_question: For a Prüfer ring R, is the finitistic projective dimension fp.dim R always at most 1?

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. Recall that $R$ is called a Prüfer ring if every finitely generated regular ideal of $R$ is invertible (equivalently, projective). The (small) finitistic projective dimension of $R$ is defined as
$$\mathrm{fp.dim}\, R = \sup\{\mathrm{pd}_R M : M \text{ is a finitely generated } R\text{-module with finite projective dimension}\},$$
where $\mathrm{pd}_R M$ denotes the projective dimension of $M$.

Question: Is it true that for every Prüfer ring $R$, $\mathrm{fp.dim}\, R \le 1$?

original_question: For a total ring of quotients R, is the finitistic projective dimension fp.dim R always equal to 0?

Let R be a commutative ring. Recall that R is called a total ring of quotients if every element of R is either a unit or a zero-divisor (equivalently, R equals its own total quotient ring). For a commutative ring R, define the finitistic projective dimension by
  fp.dim R = sup { proj.dim_R M : M is a finitely generated R-module with proj.dim_R M < ∞ }.

Question: Is it true that for every total ring of quotients R, one has fp.dim R = 0?

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Gaussian rings and weak global dimension
original_question: If R is a Gaussian ring, must its weak global dimension w.dim R be 0, 1, or infinite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. For a polynomial $f = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n \in R[x]$, denote by $c(f)$ the content of $f$, i.e., the ideal of $R$ generated by the coefficients $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$. The ring $R$ is called Gaussian if $c(fg) = c(f)c(g)$ for every pair of polynomials $f, g \in R[x]$. The weak global dimension $\mathrm{w.dim}\, R$ of $R$ is defined as the supremum of the flat dimensions of all $R$-modules (equivalently, the supremum over all pairs of $R$-modules $M, N$ of the largest $n$ with $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N) \neq 0$).

Prove or disprove: if $R$ is a Gaussian ring, then $\mathrm{w.dim}\, R \in \{0, 1, \infty\}$.

status_search_result: The problem is the Bazzoni–Glaz conjecture (2007). A 2011 paper resolved it in all cases except when R is a non-reduced local Gaussian ring whose nilradical N satisfies N² = 0. A subsequent 2014 paper published in the Journal of Algebra reportedly handles the remaining case, completing the proof. The conjecture is therefore considered solved, with the weak global dimension of a Gaussian ring being 0, 1, or ∞.

original_question: If R is a total ring of quotients, must its weak global dimension w.dim R be 0, 1, or infinite?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a commutative ring with identity. Recall that R is called a total ring of quotients if every non-zero-divisor of R is a unit (equivalently, R equals its own classical ring of quotients). The weak global dimension of R, denoted w.dim R, is defined as the supremum over all R-modules M of the flat dimension of M, i.e.

  w.dim R = sup { fd_R(M) : M is an R-module },

where fd_R(M) is the smallest integer n ≥ 0 such that M admits a flat resolution of length n (or ∞ if no such n exists).

Question: Must every total ring of quotients R satisfy w.dim R ∈ {0, 1, ∞}? That is, is it true that if R is a total ring of quotients then w.dim R is either 0, 1, or infinite?
category_tag: Weak global dimension of commutative rings
status_search_result: This is a special case of the Bazzoni–Glaz conjecture, which posits that the weak global dimension of a Gaussian ring is 0, 1, or ∞ (every total ring of quotients of relevance here is connected to this framework). The conjecture has been verified in many cases, including the reduced case, but remains generally open in the non-reduced local case with nilradical N satisfying N² = 0. Recent preprints by Donadze and Thomas claim a full resolution but verification in the literature is not yet conclusive.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Prüfer rings and weak global dimension
original_question: What values can the weak global dimension w.dim R take when R is a Prüfer ring?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. The weak global dimension of $R$, denoted $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R$, is defined as
$$\mathrm{w.dim}\,R = \sup\{\mathrm{fd}_R(M) : M \text{ is an } R\text{-module}\},$$
where $\mathrm{fd}_R(M)$ denotes the flat dimension of $M$ (the length of the shortest flat resolution of $M$, or $\infty$ if none is finite).

A commutative ring $R$ is called a Prüfer ring if every finitely generated regular ideal of $R$ is invertible (equivalently, every finitely generated ideal containing a non-zero-divisor is projective). Note that a Prüfer ring need not be a domain and may have zero divisors.

Problem. Determine the set of values that $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R$ can take as $R$ ranges over all Prüfer rings. In particular, decide whether $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R \in \{0, 1, \infty\}$ for every Prüfer ring $R$, or characterize which other values $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R$ may attain.
status_search_result: The question is fully resolved for several subclasses of Prüfer-like rings: Osofsky (1969) showed arithmetical rings have weak global dimension 0, 1, or ∞; Bazzoni–Glaz (2007) extended this to coherent Gaussian rings; Abuhlail–Jarrar–Kabbaj (2011) to fqp-rings. The general Bazzoni–Glaz conjecture for Gaussian rings (and hence the broader Prüfer ring question) remains open, with a 2010 example showing the situation outside the arithmetical/coherent case is subtle. Thus the problem is partially solved.

Recall that $D$ is coherent if every finitely generated ideal of $D$ is finitely presented (equivalently, the intersection of any two finitely generated ideals is finitely generated and the annihilator of every element is finitely generated). The Krull dimension of $D$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of prime ideals. The integral closure $\overline{D}$ of $D$ in $K$ is the set of elements of $K$ that satisfy a monic polynomial equation with coefficients in $D$. A domain is called Prüfer if every nonzero finitely generated ideal is invertible (equivalently, every localization at a prime ideal is a valuation domain).

original_question: Assume that R is a G-GCD ring and G is a finitely generated abelian group. Do the finite conductor property and the quasi coherent property both ascend from R to the group ring RG?

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. Recall the following definitions:

- $R$ is a *finite conductor ring* if for every pair of elements $a,b \in R$, the ideal $aR \cap bR$ is finitely generated.
- $R$ is a *quasi-coherent ring* if for every element $a \in R$ and every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$, the ideal $aR \cap I$ is finitely generated.
- $R$ is a *G-GCD ring* (generalized GCD ring) if every principal ideal of $R$ is projective and the intersection of any two finitely generated flat ideals of $R$ is again a finitely generated flat ideal.

Let $G$ be a finitely generated abelian group, and let $RG$ denote the group ring of $G$ over $R$.

Question: If $R$ is a G-GCD ring, does the finite conductor property ascend from $R$ to $RG$ (i.e., is $RG$ necessarily a finite conductor ring)? Likewise, does the quasi-coherent property ascend from $R$ to $RG$ (i.e., is $RG$ necessarily quasi-coherent)?

The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Are the finite conductor property and the quasi coherent property genuinely different properties for commutative rings, or do they coincide?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a commutative ring with identity. Recall the following definitions:

(i) R is said to have the finite conductor property if for every a, b, c ∈ R, the ideals aR ∩ bR and (0 : c) = {x ∈ R : xc = 0} are finitely generated.

(ii) R is said to have the quasi coherent property if for every finite collection of non-nilpotent elements a₁, …, aₙ ∈ R and every c ∈ R, the ideals a₁R ∩ a₂R ∩ ⋯ ∩ aₙR and (0 : c) are finitely generated.

Clearly every quasi coherent ring (in this sense) shares much in common with the finite conductor condition, and in many natural classes (e.g. rings of weak dimension at most one) the two properties are known to agree.

Question: Do the finite conductor property and the quasi coherent property define genuinely distinct classes of commutative rings? Equivalently, does there exist a commutative ring with identity that has the finite conductor property but is not quasi coherent (or vice versa), or do the two properties coincide for all commutative rings?

status_search_result: A web search returned only the original problem list and related surveys on finite conductor and coherence-type properties (Glaz, Zafrullah, and related work). No source explicitly constructs a commutative ring distinguishing the finite conductor property from the quasi coherent property, and the question continues to be cited as an open problem in the literature on commutative coherent-like rings.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Find characterizations of commutative group rings that are semisimple and of commutative group rings that are hereditary.
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a commutative ring with identity and let G be an abelian group. Consider the group ring R[G], which is the free R-module with basis G, equipped with multiplication extending that of G linearly over R. Recall:
(i) R[G] is called semisimple if every R[G]-module is a direct sum of simple R[G]-modules, equivalently if R[G] is a direct sum of minimal ideals.
(ii) R[G] is called (left) hereditary if every submodule of a projective R[G]-module is projective, equivalently if every ideal of R[G] is projective.

(a) the commutative group ring R[G] is semisimple;
(b) the commutative group ring R[G] is hereditary.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Non-Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein group rings
original_question: Determine when a commutative group ring RG, with R a commutative ring and G an abelian group, is Cohen–Macaulay or Gorenstein in the non-Noetherian sense introduced in the cited literature.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let R be a commutative ring (not assumed Noetherian) and let G be an abelian group (written multiplicatively). The group ring RG is the free R-module with basis G endowed with the multiplication extending that of G R-bilinearly.

For Noetherian commutative rings the Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein properties have classical definitions in terms of regular sequences, depth versus Krull dimension, and finiteness of injective dimension. In the non-Noetherian setting these notions admit extensions: a commutative ring A is called (non-Noetherian) Cohen–Macaulay in the sense of Hamilton–Marley if every strong parameter sequence of A is a regular sequence (equivalently, formulated via Čech cohomology), and A is called (non-Noetherian) Gorenstein in the sense of, e.g., the Hamilton–Marley/Miller framework, where the definition agrees with the classical one in the Noetherian case, every regular ring is Gorenstein, and every coherent Gorenstein ring is Cohen–Macaulay.

Problem. Characterize, in terms of ring-theoretic properties of R and group-theoretic properties of the abelian group G, precisely when the commutative group ring RG is:
(a) Cohen–Macaulay in the non-Noetherian (Hamilton–Marley) sense;
(b) Gorenstein in the corresponding non-Noetherian sense.

In particular, give necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair (R, G) for each of these properties to hold, without any Noetherian hypothesis on R or finite generation hypothesis on G.
status_search_result: Literature on non-Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay (Hamilton–Marley) and non-Noetherian Gorenstein (Miller) rings exists, and surveys on finiteness/homological conditions in commutative group rings explicitly note that determining when RG (R commutative, G abelian) is Cohen–Macaulay or Gorenstein in these senses remains to be investigated. No characterization theorem was located, so the question appears to still be open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Find a non-Noetherian characterization of local complete intersection rings that is compatible with the coherent setting in the sense that coherent local Gorenstein rings are complete intersections and coherent local complete intersection rings are Cohen–Macaulay.
self_contained_problem:
Background. In the Noetherian setting a local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ is called a complete intersection if its $\mathfrak{m}$-adic completion $\widehat{R}$ is isomorphic to a quotient of a regular local ring by an ideal generated by a regular sequence. For Noetherian local rings one has the chain of implications: regular $\Rightarrow$ complete intersection $\Rightarrow$ Gorenstein $\Rightarrow$ Cohen–Macaulay.

In the non-Noetherian setting, the following analogues exist for a commutative ring $R$ that need not be Noetherian:
- $R$ is coherent if every finitely generated ideal of $R$ is finitely presented.
- A notion of "non-Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay ring" has been defined (via, e.g., the theory of Hamilton–Marley using a homological/regular-sequence approach) that agrees with the classical definition when $R$ is Noetherian.
- A notion of "non-Noetherian Gorenstein ring" has been defined such that, when $R$ is coherent and local, $R$ Gorenstein in this generalized sense implies $R$ is Cohen–Macaulay in the above generalized sense.

Problem. Formulate a definition of "local complete intersection ring" for (not necessarily Noetherian) commutative local rings such that:
(i) the new definition agrees with the classical one when the ring is Noetherian;
(ii) every coherent local Gorenstein ring (in the established non-Noetherian sense above) is a local complete intersection in the new sense;
(iii) every coherent local complete intersection ring (in the new sense) is Cohen–Macaulay in the above generalized non-Noetherian sense.
status_search_result: Web searches reveal active work on non-Noetherian/coherent analogues of Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein rings (Hamilton–Marley, Glaz, Bertin), but no published characterization of local complete intersection rings in the non-Noetherian/coherent setting satisfying the requested compatibilities was found. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Is every weakly quasi-complete Noetherian local ring quasi-complete?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ be a commutative Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ (the Jacobson radical of $R$). 

Call $R$ quasi-complete if for every descending chain of ideals 
$$A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq A_3 \supseteq \cdots$$
of $R$ and for every integer $k \geq 1$, there exists an index $s = s(k)$ such that
$$A_s \;\subseteq\; \Big(\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\Big) + \mathfrak{m}^k.$$

Call $R$ weakly quasi-complete if for every descending chain of ideals $A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ of $R$ satisfying $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n = (0)$, and for every integer $k \geq 1$, there exists an index $s = s(k)$ such that
$$A_s \;\subseteq\; \mathfrak{m}^k.$$

Quasi-completeness clearly implies weak quasi-completeness. The problem is to determine whether the converse holds:

Is every weakly quasi-complete Noetherian local ring quasi-complete?

original_question: Let k be a field and let R = k[X1, …, Xn] localized at the maximal ideal (X1, …, Xn) with n ≥ 2. Is R weakly quasi-complete, and in particular is it quasi-complete?

The ring $R$ is called (weakly) quasi-complete if $R$, viewed as a module over itself, has the corresponding property.

Determine whether $R$ is weakly quasi-complete, and in particular whether $R$ is quasi-complete.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Does there exist an integrally closed reduced ring R such that for every maximal ideal M the localization RM is an integrally closed McCoy ring, while R itself is not a McCoy ring and is not locally a domain?
self_contained_problem:
A commutative ring $R$ (with identity) is called a McCoy ring if, for every finitely generated ideal $I \subseteq R$ whose annihilator $\mathrm{ann}_R(I) = \{r \in R : rI = 0\}$ is zero, there exists no nonzero element $r \in R$ such that $rI = 0$; equivalently, whenever two polynomials $f(x), g(x) \in R[x]$ satisfy $f(x)g(x) = 0$ with $g(x) \neq 0$, there exists a nonzero element $c \in R$ with $cf(x) = 0$. The ring $R$ is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotents, and integrally closed if it is integrally closed in its total ring of quotients. Say that $R$ is locally a domain if $R_M$ is an integral domain for every maximal ideal $M$ of $R$.

original_question: Do there exist reduced rings that satisfy both property (a.c.) and property (An) for some n ≥ 2, but are nevertheless not McCoy rings?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a commutative ring with identity, and let Z(R) denote the set of zero-divisors of R. For an element or subset S ⊆ R, write Ann(S) = {r ∈ R : rs = 0 for all s ∈ S}.

Define the following properties of R:
- (a.c.) (the annihilator condition): for every pair of elements r, s ∈ R there exists t ∈ R such that Ann({r, s}) = Ann(t).
- (A_n), where n ≥ 1 is an integer: every ideal I ⊆ Z(R) that can be generated by at most n elements has nonzero annihilator, i.e. Ann(I) ≠ 0.
- McCoy: every finitely generated ideal I ⊆ Z(R) has nonzero annihilator.

Recall that R is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements; equivalently, the only element x ∈ R with x^2 = 0 is x = 0.

Question. Does there exist a reduced commutative ring R that satisfies property (a.c.) and property (A_n) for some integer n ≥ 2, but is not a McCoy ring?

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Straight domains vs locally divided domains
original_question: Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$.

(i) A prime ideal $P$ of $R$ is called divided if $P$ is comparable (under inclusion) with every principal ideal of $R$; equivalently, $PR_P = P$. The domain $R$ is called divided if every prime ideal of $R$ is divided, and $R$ is called locally divided if $R_M$ is a divided domain for every maximal ideal $M$ of $R$ (equivalently, $R_P$ is divided for every prime $P$).

(ii) The domain $R$ is called straight if, for every overring $T$ of $R$ (i.e., a ring with $R \subseteq T \subseteq K$) and every prime ideal $Q$ of $T$, the canonical extension $R/(Q\cap R) \hookrightarrow T/Q$ makes $T/Q$ a flat $R/(Q\cap R)$-module.

It is known that every locally divided domain is straight. 

Question. Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided?
category_tag: commutative ring theory: straight and divided domains
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved in the negative: every straight domain is locally divided. A proof appeared on arXiv in 2023 (arXiv:2305.01809, "Straight Domains are Locally Divided") and was published in Communications in Algebra, Vol. 52, No. 7 (2024). The stronger statement that a prime ideal is straight if and only if it is locally divided is established there.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let D be a one-dimensional local Noetherian domain with finite residue field. Give necessary and sufficient conditions for Int(D) to satisfy the almost strong Skolem property.
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be a one-dimensional local Noetherian integral domain with finite residue field, and let $K$ be its field of fractions. Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D\}.$$
For a nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ and $f \in \mathrm{Int}(D)$, let $f(I) = \{f(a) : a \in I\}$ and let $\mathfrak{I}_f$ denote the ideal of $D$ generated by $f(I)$. The ring $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is said to have the strong Skolem property if for any two finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ with the property that $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{m}) = \mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{m})$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of $D$ of finite residue field (where $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{m})$ denotes the ideal of $D/\mathfrak{m}$ generated by the residues $f(a) + \mathfrak{m}$ for $f \in \mathfrak{A}$ and $a \in D$), one has $\mathfrak{A} = \mathfrak{B}$. The ring $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is said to have the almost strong Skolem property if the same conclusion holds under the additional assumption that the ideals $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are unitary (i.e., contain elements with constant terms generating $D$).

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $D$ for $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ to satisfy the almost strong Skolem property.
status_search_result: The problem is widely cited as open. Partial results are known: the almost strong Skolem property for Int(D) implies D is unibranched, and a sufficient condition is that Int(D) be dense in the ring of m-adically continuous functions on the completion. R. Rissner's dissertation on integer-valued polynomials surveys progress, but no complete characterization has been established.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Besides the known examples coming from iterates of nonconstant integer polynomials and affine transformations of the three displayed examples in the paper, are there any other natural self-ordered sequences of integers?
self_contained_problem:
A sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ of distinct integers is called self-ordered if, for every prime $p$, the sequence itself is a $p$-ordering of the set $S=\{a_n : n\ge 0\}$ in the sense of Bhargava. That is, for every prime $p$ and every $n\ge 1$,
$$v_p\!\left(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(a_n-a_k)\right)=\min_{a\in S}\, v_p\!\left(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(a-a_k)\right),$$
where $v_p$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation.

Two classes of examples are known:

(1) Dynamical examples: sequences obtained by iterating a nonconstant polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, i.e. $a_n=f^{\circ n}(a_0)$.

(2) Affine images of the three classical examples
$\;a_n=n,\quad a_n=q^n\text{ (for a fixed integer }q\ge 2),\quad a_n=\binom{2n}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{n+1}\text{ (or another specified classical sequence)},$
i.e. sequences of the form $\alpha a_n+\beta$ with $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\alpha\ne 0$, where $(a_n)$ is one of the three known basic self-ordered sequences.

Question: Does there exist a "natural" self-ordered sequence of integers that neither arises from a dynamical construction as in (1) nor is an affine image of one of the three classical examples as in (2)?
status_search_result: A direct search for additional natural classes of self-ordered integer sequences beyond dynamical (polynomial iteration) examples and affine images of the three classical examples did not produce evidence of a resolution. The literature on Bhargava's p-orderings and self-ordered sequences continues to develop, but no publication confirming new natural classes or a proof of non-existence was located.

The Bhargava factorial of $E$ at $n$ is defined by
$$ n!_E \;=\; \prod_{p \text{ prime}} p^{\,v_p(n,E)}. $$

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Transcendence of constants from abstract factorials
original_question: For which infinite subsets E of the integers is the constant eE obtained from the Bhargava-factorial construction transcendental?
self_contained_problem:
Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ be an infinite subset. For each prime $p$ and each non-negative integer $k$, define a $p$-ordering of $E$ to be a sequence $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ of elements of $E$ chosen as follows: $a_0 \in E$ is arbitrary, and for $k \geq 1$, $a_k \in E$ is chosen to minimize the $p$-adic valuation $v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right)$. Set
\[ w_k(E,p) \;=\; v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right), \]
which is independent of the choice of $p$-ordering, and define the Bhargava factorial of $E$ at $k$ by
\[ k!_E \;=\; \prod_{p \text{ prime}} p^{\,w_k(E,p)}. \]
Define the associated constant
\[ e_E \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!_E}. \]
For which infinite subsets $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ is the real number $e_E$ transcendental?
status_search_result: The question of characterizing those infinite subsets $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ for which the associated Bhargava-factorial constant $e_E = \sum 1/k!_E$ is transcendental appears in lists of open problems in commutative ring theory. paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: For an integral domain D, does Int(D) always admit a unique D–D-biring structure for which the inclusion D[X] → Int(D) is a homomorphism of D–D-birings?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain. For any commutative ring $R$, let $\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D\}$, where $K$ is the field of fractions of $D$; this is the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$, and it contains $D[X]$ as a subring.

Recall that an $A$–$B$-biring is an $A$-algebra $S$ together with a lift of the representable functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{A\text{-alg}}(S, -)$ from $A$-algebras to sets to a functor from $A$-algebras to $B$-algebras. Equivalently, it is an $A$-algebra $S$ equipped with $A$-algebra co-operations (comultiplication, coaddition, co-unit, co-zero, co-negation, and a $B$-action via co-scalar multiplications) satisfying the co-axioms dual to those of a commutative $B$-algebra. The polynomial ring $D[X]$ has a canonical $D$–$D$-biring structure, where the coaddition and comultiplication are determined by $X \mapsto X \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes X$ and $X \mapsto X \otimes X$, respectively.

Question: Does $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ always admit a unique $D$–$D$-biring structure such that the inclusion $D[X] \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Int}(D)$ is a homomorphism of $D$–$D$-birings?
status_search_result: Elliott (2011, "Birings and plethories of integer-valued polynomials") showed that if $D$ is an integral domain such that $\mathrm{Int}(D)^{\otimes n}$ (tensor power over $D$) is $D$-torsion-free for $n \le 4$ — in particular if $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is $D$-flat — then $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ carries a unique $D$–$D$-biring structure compatible with $D[X] \to \mathrm{Int}(D)$. The general case (arbitrary integral domain $D$) does not appear to be resolved in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let K be a number field with ring of integers OK. Prove or disprove that the natural density δ(Int(OK)) of the non-negative integers n for which Intn(OK) is a free OK-module exists, is rational, and is at least 1 divided by the cardinality of the Pólya group of OK; then compute that density.
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. For each non-negative integer $n$, let
$$\mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K) = \{f \in K[X] : \deg f \le n,\ f(\mathcal{O}_K) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_K\},$$
the $\mathcal{O}_K$-module of integer-valued polynomials of degree at most $n$. It is known that $\mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ is a finitely generated projective $\mathcal{O}_K$-module of rank $n+1$. For each $n \ge 0$ there is a "characteristic ideal" $\mathfrak{I}_n(\mathcal{O}_K) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_K$ (generated by the leading coefficients of polynomials in $\mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ together with $0$), and $\mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ is a free $\mathcal{O}_K$-module if and only if all the ideals $\mathfrak{I}_0(\mathcal{O}_K), \dots, \mathfrak{I}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ are principal. The Pólya group $\mathrm{Po}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ of $K$ is the subgroup of the ideal class group of $\mathcal{O}_K$ generated by the classes of the ideals $\mathfrak{I}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ for $n \ge 0$. Define
$$\delta(\mathrm{Int}(\mathcal{O}_K)) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N+1} \#\{0 \le n \le N : \mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K) \text{ is a free } \mathcal{O}_K\text{-module}\},$$
the natural density of the set of indices $n$ for which $\mathrm{Int}_n(\mathcal{O}_K)$ is free.

Prove or disprove the following: $\delta(\mathrm{Int}(\mathcal{O}_K))$ exists, is a rational number, and satisfies
$$\delta(\mathrm{Int}(\mathcal{O}_K)) \ge \frac{1}{\#\mathrm{Po}(\mathcal{O}_K)}.$$
If the conjecture holds, compute $\delta(\mathrm{Int}(\mathcal{O}_K))$ explicitly in terms of arithmetic invariants of $K$.
status_search_result: The conjecture is listed in a collection of open problems in commutative ring theory. Recent works on Pólya groups and integer-valued polynomials (e.g., 2023–2024 arXiv papers on Pólya groups of number fields) continue to investigate related questions but do not appear to resolve the density conjecture for δ(Int(O_K)). No published proof or disproof was found.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Let E be the set of values of a second-order recursive integer sequence un+1 = a un + b un−1 with initial values u0 and u1. Compute a regular basis, meaning a basis whose nth term has degree n, for the Z-module Int(E; Z).

Let $a, b, u_0, u_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ and define the second-order linear recursive integer sequence $(u_n)_{n\ge 0}$ by
$$u_{n+1} = a\, u_n + b\, u_{n-1}, \qquad n \ge 1,$$
with initial values $u_0$ and $u_1$. Let
$$E = \{u_n : n \ge 0\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$$
denote the set of values taken by this sequence, and consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-module of integer-valued polynomials on $E$,
$$\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z}) = \{ f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(E) \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \}.$$
A sequence of polynomials $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ in $\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z})$ is called a regular basis of this $\mathbb{Z}$-module if it is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis and $\deg f_n = n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

Construct an explicit regular basis of the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z})$ in terms of the parameters $a, b, u_0, u_1$.

original_question: For the same recursive set E, compute for each prime p the characteristic sequence of Int(E; Z), namely the sequence αp(n) given by the p-adic valuation of the fractional ideal of leading coefficients of elements of Int(E; Z) of degree at most n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $E$ be a recursive (i.e., computable) subset of $\mathbb{Z}$. Define
$$\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z}) \;=\; \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(a) \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ for every } a \in E \,\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $E$. For each integer $n \ge 0$, let $\mathcal{I}_n(E)$ denote the fractional ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ consisting of $0$ together with the leading coefficients of those elements of $\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z})$ that have degree at most $n$.

Fix a prime $p$ and write $v_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation, extended to nonzero fractional ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$ in the natural way (so $v_p(\mathcal{I}_n(E))$ is the unique integer $k$ with $\mathcal{I}_n(E) \otimes \mathbb{Z}_{(p)} = p^{k}\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$). The characteristic sequence of $\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z})$ at $p$ is the sequence
$$\alpha_p(n) \;=\; -\,v_p\!\bigl(\mathcal{I}_n(E)\bigr), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots .$$

Problem. Give an effective procedure (e.g., a recursive description, closed form, or algorithm) that, given the recursive set $E$ and the prime $p$, computes the characteristic sequence $\bigl(\alpha_p(n)\bigr)_{n \ge 0}$.
status_search_result: The problem appears in a published list of open problems in commutative ring theory. Recursive formulas for characteristic sequences of Int(E;Z) are known for specific families (e.g., E equal to the set of d-th powers, primes, or other structured sets), via Bhargava's p-orderings, but no general computational procedure for an arbitrary recursive E appears to have been established. Recent literature continues to study such characteristic sequences case by case, suggesting the general problem remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: For the same recursive set E, determine the asymptotic behavior of the characteristic sequence, in particular compute the limit of α(n)/n as n tends to infinity.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a prime number p and an integer d ≥ 2. Let E denote the subset of nonnegative integers consisting of all d-th powers,
   E = { k^d : k ∈ ℤ_{≥0} } ⊂ ℤ.
For each integer n ≥ 0, consider the fractional ideal
   I_n(E) = { leading coefficient of f : f ∈ ℚ[X], deg f ≤ n, and f(E) ⊆ ℤ } ∪ {0} ⊂ ℚ,
i.e. the ideal of leading coefficients of integer-valued polynomials on E of degree at most n. Define the p-adic characteristic sequence of E by
   α(n) = α_{p,d}(n) := − v_p( I_n(E) ),
where v_p is the p-adic valuation (and v_p of a fractional ideal is the minimum of v_p over its nonzero elements). The sequence (α(n))_{n ≥ 0} is known to be superadditive (α(m+n) ≥ α(m) + α(n)) and bounded by a linear function of n, so by Fekete's subadditive lemma the limit
   L(p,d) := lim_{n → ∞} α(n)/n
exists in [0, ∞).

Determine, as a function of the prime p and the exponent d, the value of L(p,d). In particular, give a closed-form expression (or explicit formula) for lim_{n → ∞} α(n)/n.
status_search_result: The problem is listed (as Problem 24c, contributed by K. Johnson) in the 2014 collection "Open Problems in Commutative Ring Theory." Existence of the limit follows from Fekete's lemma, but computing it explicitly is left open. Subsequent literature (Fares–Johnson 2012 on d-th powers; Johnson 2009 on homogeneous sets; Boulanger–Chabert 2000) provides recursive formulas and partial results in special cases, but no general closed-form value for lim α(n)/n appears to be known.

original_question: Compute a regular basis of the ring IntQ(Mn(Z)) of rational-coefficient polynomials that are integer-valued on n×n integer matrices.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ denote the ring of $n\times n$ matrices with integer entries, and let $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$ denote the ring of $n\times n$ matrices with rational entries. Define
$$\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z})) = \{\, f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(A) \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \text{ for every } A \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \,\},$$
where $f(A)$ is computed by substituting the matrix $A$ into the polynomial $f$ (with the constant term multiplied by the identity matrix). This is a $\mathbb{Z}$-subalgebra of $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ which is free as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module. A regular basis of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module basis $\{f_0, f_1, f_2, \dots\}$ consisting of exactly one polynomial $f_k$ of each degree $k \geq 0$.

Explicitly compute (i.e., give a closed-form description of) a regular basis of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ for general $n \geq 2$.

However, an explicit closed-form description of a regular basis for general n appears not to have been achieved; surveys on regular bases for integer-valued polynomials continue to list it as an open problem.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Compute the characteristic sequence of IntQ(Mn(Z)) with respect to each prime p.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ be an integer and let $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ denote the ring of $n\times n$ matrices with integer entries, viewed inside $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$. Define
$$\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z})) \;=\; \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}[x] \;:\; f(M)\in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \text{ for every } M\in M_n(\mathbb{Z})\,\}.$$
For each positive integer $k$, let
$$\mathfrak{I}_k \;=\; \{\, \text{leading coefficients of } f \;:\; f\in \operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z})),\ \deg f \le k\,\}\cup\{0\},$$
the $k$-th characteristic ideal of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ (a fractional ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$). For a prime number $p$, define the characteristic sequence of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ with respect to $p$ by

original_question: Let D be an integral domain with quotient field K, and let A be a torsion-free D-algebra that is finitely generated as a D-module. Determine for which such algebras A the inclusion ⋂a∈A (D[X] + μa(X)K[X]) ⊆ IntK(A) is actually an equality.

$$\bigcap_{a \in A} \bigl( D[X] + \mu_a(X) K[X] \bigr) \;\subseteq\; \operatorname{Int}_K(A).$$

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: If I is an n-absorbing ideal of a commutative ring R, must I also be strongly n-absorbing?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and let $n$ be a positive integer. A proper ideal $I$ of $R$ is called $n$-absorbing if whenever $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1} \in R$ satisfy $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_{n+1} \in I$, then there exist $n$ of these elements whose product lies in $I$. A proper ideal $I$ of $R$ is called strongly $n$-absorbing if whenever $I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_{n+1}$ are ideals of $R$ with $I_1 I_2 \cdots I_{n+1} \subseteq I$, then there exist $n$ of these ideals whose product is contained in $I$.

Every strongly $n$-absorbing ideal is clearly $n$-absorbing. Determine whether the converse holds: must every $n$-absorbing ideal of an arbitrary commutative ring $R$ be strongly $n$-absorbing?
status_search_result: The equivalence was known in special cases (e.g., Prüfer domains, and for n=2 by Anderson–Badawi). A 2023 arXiv preprint by Spencer Secord (arXiv:2305.03878) claims a proof that every n-absorbing ideal of a commutative ring is strongly n-absorbing, resolving the first of the Anderson–Badawi conjectures. As this result is a recent preprint and its peer-reviewed status is unclear, the problem is best classified as partially solved pending verification.

self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$. original_question: Let T be a non-empty collection of overrings of an integral domain D, and for each T in that collection let ?T be a semistar operation on T. Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $\overline{F}(D)$ denote the set of all non-zero $D$-submodules of $K$. (i) $(xE)^{\star} = x E^{\star}$;
(ii) $E \subseteq F$ implies $E^{\star} \subseteq F^{\star}$;
(iii) $E \subseteq E^{\star}$ and $(E^{\star})^{\star} = E^{\star}$.
A semistar operation $\star$ on $D$ is said to be of finite type if for every $E \in \overline{F}(D)$,
$$E^{\star} = \bigcup\{F^{\star} : F \subseteq E,\ F \text{ a non-zero finitely generated } D\text{-submodule of } K\}.$$

$$\star_{\mathcal{T}} : E \longmapsto \bigcap_{T \in \mathcal{T}} (ET)^{\star_T}.$$
Then $\star_{\mathcal{T}}$ is a semistar operation on $D$.

original_question: Is there a Krull domain, or even a factorial domain, D such that the polynomial ring D[X] has dimension strictly larger than 1 + dim(D)?

For a commutative ring R with finite Krull dimension, let dim(R) denote its Krull dimension and let R[X] denote the polynomial ring in one indeterminate over R. Recall:
- An integral domain D is a Krull domain if there is a family {V_i}_{i∈I} of discrete valuation rings of the field of fractions of D such that D = ∩_i V_i, and every nonzero element of D is a non-unit in only finitely many V_i.
- An integral domain D is a factorial domain (unique factorization domain) if every nonzero non-unit factors uniquely (up to units and order) into irreducible elements.

It is known that for any integral domain D of finite Krull dimension, 1 + dim(D) ≤ dim(D[X]) ≤ 1 + 2·dim(D).

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: If R is a one-dimensional local Mori domain, must R be locally tame?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be an integral domain. Recall:

- R is a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial (i.e., v-)ideals; equivalently, every nonzero ideal of R contains a divisorial ideal and the divisorial ideals satisfy ACC.
- R is local if it has a unique maximal ideal.
- R is one-dimensional if its Krull dimension equals 1.
- For the multiplicative monoid R• = R \ {0} of nonzero elements (or equivalently the reduced monoid R•/R^×), an atom (irreducible element) is a non-unit that cannot be written as a product of two non-units. For a nonzero non-unit a ∈ R, the set of lengths L(a) is the set of all positive integers n such that a = u_1 ··· u_n for some atoms u_1, …, u_n.
- For a non-unit a, the local tame degree t(a) is the smallest N ∈ ℕ ∪ {∞} with the following property: for every factorization a = u_1 ··· u_n into atoms and every factorization a · b = v_1 ··· v_m into atoms (where b ∈ R), there exist an atom factorization a · b = u_1 · w_2 ··· w_k · z_1 ··· z_ℓ and a subproduct of v_1 ··· v_m of length at most N whose product equals u_1 · w_2 ··· w_k (in the standard sense of local tameness from factorization theory). R is called locally tame if t(a) < ∞ for every nonzero non-unit a ∈ R.

Question: Must every one-dimensional local Mori domain R be locally tame?
status_search_result: The question was answered affirmatively by Geroldinger, Kainrath, and Reinhart (and collaborators) in "On strongly primary monoids and domains" (arXiv:1807.10683, published in Comm. Algebra 2020). They prove that every strongly primary domain is locally tame, and since every one-dimensional local Mori domain is strongly primary, it follows that every one-dimensional local Mori domain is locally tame. The authors explicitly state that this resolves the problem.

original_question: Let I be the integral closure of the monomial ideal (x^a, y^b, z^c) in a polynomial ring over a field. Classify all triples (a, b, c) for which every power of I is integrally closed.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a field and let $R = k[x,y,z]$ be the polynomial ring in three variables. For positive integers $a,b,c$, let $J = (x^a, y^b, z^c) \subset R$ and let $I = \overline{J}$ denote the integral closure of $J$ in $R$. Recall that for a monomial ideal $M \subset R$, the integral closure $\overline{M}$ is again a monomial ideal, and it equals the monomial ideal generated by all monomials $x^{\alpha} y^{\beta} z^{\gamma}$ whose exponent vector $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^3$ lies in the convex hull (Newton polyhedron) of the exponent vectors of the monomials in $M$, together with $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^3$. A monomial ideal $M$ is called normal if every power $M^n$ ($n \geq 1$) is integrally closed (equivalently, $M^n = \overline{M^n}$ for all $n \geq 1$).

Classify all triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers for which the ideal $I = \overline{(x^a, y^b, z^c)}$ is normal, i.e., every power $I^n$ is integrally closed.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
context_brief: Algorithms for integral closure of ideals
original_question: Is there a more direct algorithm for computing the integral closure of a general ideal than the standard approach of computing the integral closure of the entire Rees algebra?
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring and let $I \subseteq R$ be an ideal. An element $x \in R$ is called integral over $I$ if it satisfies an equation of the form
$$x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + a_2 x^{n-2} + \cdots + a_n = 0$$
with $a_i \in I^i$ for each $i = 1, \dots, n$. The set of all such elements forms an ideal $\overline{I}$, the integral closure of $I$. Equivalently, $\overline{I}$ can be recovered from the integral closure of the Rees algebra $R[It] = \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} I^n t^n$ inside $R[t]$, since this integral closure is $\bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \overline{I^n}\, t^n$.

The standard algorithmic approach to computing $\overline{I}$ proceeds by first computing the integral closure (normalization) of the entire Rees algebra $R[It]$ and then extracting the degree-one piece.

Problem. Does there exist an algorithm that computes the integral closure $\overline{I}$ of a general ideal $I$ in a more direct fashion than by first computing the integral closure of the whole Rees algebra $R[It]$?
category_tag: Computational commutative algebra: integral closure of ideals
status_search_result: Current algorithms (Vasconcelos, Singh–Swanson, and implementations in Macaulay2 and Singular) still proceed via the Rees algebra / normalization route, possibly with improvements such as using Jacobian ideals, but no fundamentally more direct general algorithm appears in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Can the Leonard–Pellikaan and Singh–Swanson algorithms be modified to compute the integral closure of ideals?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let R be a reduced commutative Noetherian ring that is finitely generated over a finite field of prime characteristic p, and let R̄ denote its integral closure in its total ring of fractions. The Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm (originally for weighted affine rings finitely generated over a finite field) and its Singh–Swanson generalization compute R̄ as follows: choose a nonzerodivisor D in the conductor of R, set V₀ = (1/D)·R, and inductively define
   V_{e+1} = { f ∈ V_e : f^p ∈ V_e }.
Then the descending chain V₀ ⊇ V₁ ⊇ V₂ ⊇ ⋯ stabilizes at R̄. The key feature is that the algorithm starts from a finitely generated R-module containing R̄ and successively cuts down to R̄ using the Frobenius map.

Recall that for an ideal I of a commutative ring R, the integral closure Ī of I is the set of all elements x ∈ R that satisfy an equation of the form
   x^n + a₁ x^{n-1} + a₂ x^{n-2} + ⋯ + a_n = 0,    with a_k ∈ I^k for k = 1, …, n.

Problem. Can the Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm and the Singh–Swanson algorithm be modified to give an effective algorithm that, given a finitely generated ideal I in a reduced ring R finitely generated over a finite field of characteristic p, computes the integral closure Ī of I (rather than the integral closure of the ring)?

status_search_result: Web searches surface the original Leonard–Pellikaan and Singh–Swanson algorithms for the integral closure of rings (and their Macaulay2 implementation icFracP) but do not turn up a published modification of either algorithm that computes the integral closure of ideals. The current status of this specific question could not be conclusively determined from accessible sources.

paper_title: Open problems in commutative ring theory
original_question: Determine how tight the general Lipman–Sathaye theorem stated in the paper is by relaxing one or more assumptions and either proving the resulting statement or producing a counterexample.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $R \subseteq S$ be an extension of Noetherian integral domains satisfying the following hypotheses:
(a) $R$ is normal (integrally closed in its field of fractions $K = \mathrm{Frac}(R)$);
(b) $S$ is a domain with field of fractions $L$, and $L/K$ is a finite separable field extension;
(c) $S$ is essentially of finite type over $R$, and the integral closure $\overline{S}$ of $S$ in $L$ is module-finite over $S$;
(d) for every height-one prime $Q$ of $\overline{S}$, the localization $\overline{S}_Q$ is flat over $R_{Q\cap R}$ (equivalently, the going-down property holds along these primes).

Let $J_{S/R}$ denote the Jacobian ideal of $S$ over $R$, defined as the $0$-th Fitting ideal of the module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{S/R}$ (for $S = R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_n)$, this is the ideal generated by the $n \times n$ minors of the Jacobian matrix $(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)$).

The Lipman–Sathaye theorem under these hypotheses asserts the containment
$$ J_{S/R} \cdot \overline{S} \;\subseteq\; \mathfrak{c}_{\overline{S}/S}, $$
where $\mathfrak{c}_{\overline{S}/S} = \{ s \in S : s\,\overline{S} \subseteq S\}$ is the conductor of $S$ in $\overline{S}$.

Problem. Investigate the sharpness of this theorem by selecting one or more of the hypotheses (a)–(d) (for instance, dropping the normality of $R$, dropping separability of $L/K$, replacing the integral-domain hypothesis on $S$ by reducedness, weakening the going-down/flatness condition at height-one primes, or replacing finite separable by generically étale in mixed or positive characteristic) and either:
(i) prove that the conclusion $J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S} \subseteq \mathfrak{c}_{\overline{S}/S}$ continues to hold under the relaxed hypotheses, or
(ii) exhibit an explicit counterexample, i.e. a ring extension $R \subseteq S$ satisfying the relaxed hypotheses for which $J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S} \not\subseteq \mathfrak{c}_{\overline{S}/S}$.
status_search_result: Hochster's work "Presentation depth and the Lipman–Sathaye Jacobian theorem" provides versions with substantially weakened hypotheses (allowing $S$ to be reduced rather than a domain and weakening regularity/Cohen–Macaulay assumptions, replaced by a relative $S_2$-type condition). However, a definitive determination of which assumptions can be dropped, with matching counterexamples, does not appear to be settled in the literature; the problem of fully characterizing the sharpness of the Lipman–Sathaye theorem appears to remain open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Let X1, X2, and X3 be observed random variables that each take four states, and let Y be a hidden four-state random variable, so that the joint distribution of (X1, X2, X3) is represented by a 4×4×4 table (p_ijk) lying in the 64-dimensional tensor space C^4 ⊗ C^4 ⊗ C^4. Equivalently, this is the variety of 4×4×4 tensors of rank at most 4, also described as the naive Bayes model, the conditional independence model [X1 ⟂⟂ X2 ⟂⟂ X3 | Y], or the third secant variety of P^3 × P^3 × P^3. Do the known polynomial invariants of degrees 5 and 9 suffice to cut out this variety set-theoretically or ideally?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Segre variety $\mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^4 \otimes \mathbb{C}^4 \otimes \mathbb{C}^4) = \mathbb{P}^{63}$, embedded by sending $([u],[v],[w])$ to $[u\otimes v\otimes w]$. Let $\sigma_4 = \sigma_4(\mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3)$ denote its fourth secant variety, i.e. the Zariski closure of the set of tensors in $\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4$ of tensor rank at most $4$. Statistically, $\sigma_4$ is the model of joint distributions $(p_{ijk})_{i,j,k=1}^{4}$ of three observed four-state random variables $X_1,X_2,X_3$ that are conditionally independent given a hidden four-state random variable $Y$ (the naive Bayes model $[X_1 \perp\!\!\!\perp X_2 \perp\!\!\!\perp X_3 \mid Y]$).

Two families of $\mathrm{GL}_4 \times \mathrm{GL}_4 \times \mathrm{GL}_4$-invariant polynomials are known to vanish on $\sigma_4$: certain degree-$5$ invariants coming from Strassen-type commutation conditions, and certain degree-$9$ invariants coming from symmetrization (Strassen/Landsberg–Manivel-type) conditions.

Questions:
(a) Do the degree-$5$ and degree-$9$ invariants together cut out $\sigma_4$ set-theoretically as a subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^{63}$?
(b) Do they generate the homogeneous prime ideal of $\sigma_4$?
category_tag: Secant varieties of Segre products (Salmon conjecture)
status_search_result: The set-theoretic version (the "Salmon Conjecture") was established by Friedland and Gross, who proved that $\sigma_4(\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3)$ is cut out set-theoretically by polynomial equations of degrees $5$, $6$, and $9$ (with the degree-$6$ Landsberg–Manivel polynomials needed in addition to the degree $5$ and $9$ invariants originally proposed). Thus the degree-$5$ and degree-$9$ invariants alone are not known to suffice set-theoretically. The ideal-theoretic version (the original "Salmon Prize" problem of E. Allman) remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: For the 4×4×4 hidden-variable model whose coordinates are p_ijk with i, j, k ∈ {A, C, G, T} and whose parametrization is p_ijk = ρ_Ai σ_Aj θ_Ak + ρ_Ci σ_Cj θ_Ck + ρ_Gi σ_Gj θ_Gk + ρ_Ti σ_Tj θ_Tk, determine the homogeneous prime ideal I of polynomial relations among the 64 coordinates in the ring Q[p_AAA, p_AAC, p_AAT, ..., p_TTG, p_TTT].
self_contained_problem:
Let the index set be $\Sigma=\{A,C,G,T\}$. Consider the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb{Q}[p_{ijk} : i,j,k\in\Sigma]$ in $64$ indeterminates. Introduce $48$ additional parameters $ho_{ai},\sigma_{aj},	heta_{ak}$ for $a\in\Sigma$ and $i,j,k\in\Sigma$, and define the polynomial map $\varphi:\mathbb{Q}[p_{ijk}]	o\mathbb{Q}[ho,\sigma,	heta]$ by
$$\varphi(p_{ijk})=\sum_{a\in\Sigma}ho_{ai}\,\sigma_{aj}\,	heta_{ak}, \qquad i,j,k\in\Sigma.$$
Geometrically, the image of the corresponding morphism is (the affine cone over) the fourth secant variety of the Segre variety $\mathbb{P}^3	imes\mathbb{P}^3	imes\mathbb{P}^3 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{63}$, equivalently the variety of $4	imes 4	imes 4$ tensors of rank $\leq 4$.

Determine explicit generators for the homogeneous prime ideal
$$I=\ker(\varphi)\subset R,$$
i.e., find a finite set of homogeneous polynomial relations among the $64$ coordinates $p_{ijk}$ that generate $I$.
status_search_result: This is the ideal-theoretic "Salmon Conjecture/Prize" question on the defining prime ideal of the fourth secant variety of $\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3$. The set-theoretic version was resolved (Friedland–Gross 2011, with computational work by Bates–Oeding), showing the variety is cut out by certain degree 5, 6, and 9 equations. The full ideal-theoretic version — finding generators of the prime ideal itself — is generally reported as still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Develop the geometry and commutative algebra of graphical models with hidden random variables by constructing the associated varieties from familiar secant varieties and by using representation-theoretic methods. In particular, the task is to understand these hidden-variable graphical-model varieties as algebraic varieties assembled from known secant constructions and then analyzed with tools from representation theory.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a directed acyclic graph whose vertex set V is partitioned into a set of observed vertices O and a set of hidden vertices H. To each vertex v ∈ V associate a discrete random variable X_v taking finitely many values (or a Gaussian random variable). The graphical model M(G) associated to G is the set of joint probability distributions on (X_v)_{v∈V} that factorize as p(x) = ∏_{v∈V} p(x_v | x_{pa(v)}), where pa(v) denotes the parents of v in G. The hidden-variable model M(G,O) is the image of M(G) under the marginalization map that integrates out the variables X_h, h ∈ H. The Zariski closure of M(G,O) inside the probability simplex (or the corresponding tensor space) is an algebraic variety V(G,O).

Problem: Develop the geometry and commutative algebra of the varieties V(G,O) arising from directed acyclic graphical models with hidden variables. Specifically:

(a) Express V(G,O) as a variety obtained by "gluing" classical secant varieties — for example, higher secant varieties of Segre varieties P^{n_1} × ⋯ × P^{n_k} (in the discrete case) or secant varieties of varieties of bounded-rank symmetric tensors (in the Gaussian case) — corresponding to the marginalization over each hidden node.

(b) Using the natural action of the product of general linear / symmetric groups arising from relabelings of the states of each observed variable, apply representation-theoretic decompositions of the coordinate ring of the ambient tensor space to determine generators (and, ideally, a minimal generating set or a Gröbner basis) of the prime ideal I(V(G,O)), together with its dimension, degree, and singular locus.

Provide such a description that is uniform in the underlying graph G and the partition (O,H).
status_search_result: Substantial partial progress exists. The connection between hidden-variable Bayesian networks on small graphs and secant varieties of Segre varieties is established (e.g., Garcia–Stillman–Sturmfels; Allman–Rhodes; Landsberg–Manivel on equations for secant varieties via representation theory), and Gaussian Bayesian networks have been studied algebraically (Sullivant et al., 2007). Later work on hidden Markov models and on the geometry of Bayesian graphical models with hidden variables (e.g., arXiv:1301.7411) extends the program. However, a uniform structural description (defining ideals, dimension, singularities) for arbitrary DAGs with hidden nodes remains open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Characterize all projective varieties M for which the maximum likelihood degree equals 1, where the maximum likelihood degree is the number of critical points, for generic data, of the likelihood function restricted to M after excluding poles and zeros. Equivalently, determine exactly which algebraic statistical models have a rational maximum likelihood estimator in this sense.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ be an irreducible complex projective variety with homogeneous coordinates $(p_0:p_1:\cdots:p_n)$, viewed as a statistical model on the probability simplex via the affine chart $p_0+p_1+\cdots+p_n=1$. For generic integers (data) $u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_n$, consider the rational likelihood function
$$L_u \;=\; \frac{p_0^{u_0}\,p_1^{u_1}\cdots p_n^{u_n}}{(p_0+p_1+\cdots+p_n)^{u_0+u_1+\cdots+u_n}}$$
on $\mathbb{P}^n$. The maximum likelihood degree $\mathrm{mldeg}(M)$ is defined to be the number of critical points of $L_u|_M$ lying in the smooth locus of $M$ and outside the divisor $\{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_n (p_0+\cdots+p_n)=0\}$, for generic $u$.

Characterize precisely those irreducible projective varieties $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ for which $\mathrm{mldeg}(M)=1$. Equivalently, characterize the algebraic statistical models that admit a rational maximum likelihood estimator (a rational function from data $u$ to the unique critical point of $L_u|_M$).
status_search_result: June Huh resolved this characterization: a projective variety has maximum likelihood degree one if and only if it is the image, under a monomial map with finite fibers, of the reduced A-discriminantal variety of Gelfand–Kapranov–Zelevinsky, with the MLE given explicitly by Kapranov's Horn uniformization. This appears in Huh, "Varieties with maximum likelihood degree one" (arXiv:1301.2732, 2014). Follow-up work has further classified subclasses (e.g. quasi-independence models with rational MLE).

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: For the determinantal variety consisting of m×n matrices of rank at most r, determine its maximum likelihood degree, meaning the number of nonzero, nonpole critical points of the likelihood function on that model for generic data.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m,n,r$ be positive integers with $r \le \min(m,n)$, and let $V_r \subset \mathbb{P}^{mn-1}$ denote the projective determinantal variety of $m\times n$ matrices $P=(p_{ij})$ of rank at most $r$, viewed as a statistical model for the joint distribution of two discrete random variables with $m$ and $n$ states respectively (so the entries $p_{ij}$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$). For a data vector $u=(u_{ij})\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{mn}$ of observed counts, define the likelihood function
$$L_u(P) \;=\; \frac{\prod_{i,j} p_{ij}^{u_{ij}}}{\Bigl(\sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\Bigr)^{\sum_{i,j} u_{ij}}}.$$
The maximum likelihood (ML) degree of $V_r$ is defined as the number of critical points of $L_u$ on the smooth locus of $V_r$ (i.e. the number of complex critical points $P$ with all $p_{ij}\ne 0$ and $\sum p_{ij}\ne 0$) for generic data $u$.

Problem: Determine, as a function of $m$, $n$, and $r$, the ML degree of the determinantal variety $V_r$ of $m\times n$ matrices of rank at most $r$.
status_search_result: A general closed-form formula for the ML degree of the rank-$r$ determinantal variety of $m\times n$ matrices remains unknown. Substantial partial results exist: Hauenstein–Rodriguez–Sturmfels (2012) computed many cases numerically and conjectured an ML-duality between ranks $r$ and $\min(m,n)-r+1$; this duality was subsequently proved by Draisma and Rodriguez. A closed-form formula for the rank-2 case with $m=3$ is known, and recursive/Euler-characteristic formulas for rank-2 $m\times n$ matrices were obtained (Manivel–Michałek and others). No general closed formula for arbitrary $(m,n,r)$ has been established.
