paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Which collections of almost-principal minors [i ⟂⟂ j | K] can simultaneously vanish for a positive definite symmetric 5×5 covariance matrix Σ? Here [i ⟂⟂ j | K] denotes the determinant of the submatrix with row indices {i} ∪ K and column indices {j} ∪ K, and its vanishing is equivalent to conditional independence of variable i and variable j given the joint variable K in a multivariate Gaussian model.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = (\sigma_{ij})$ be a $5 \times 5$ real symmetric positive definite matrix, regarded as the covariance matrix of a centered multivariate Gaussian random vector $(X_1, \ldots, X_5)$. For disjoint $K \subset \{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $i, j \in \{1,2,3,4,5\} \setminus K$ with $i \ne j$, the almost-principal minor $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K]$ is defined as the determinant of the submatrix of $\Sigma$ with row index set $\{i\} \cup K$ and column index set $\{j\} \cup K$. It is known that $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] = 0$ if and only if $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given the random vector $(X_k)_{k \in K}$. 

Determine, combinatorially, all subsets $\mathcal{S}$ of the set of triples $\{(i,j \mid K) : i \ne j,\ K \subseteq \{1,\ldots,5\} \setminus \{i,j\}\}$ for which there exists a positive definite symmetric $5 \times 5$ matrix $\Sigma$ such that $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] = 0$ if and only if $(i,j \mid K) \in \mathcal{S}$. In other words, classify all realizable conditional independence patterns (zero sets of almost-principal minors) for $5 \times 5$ Gaussian covariance matrices.
status_search_result: The problem of classifying zero patterns of almost-principal minors of 5×5 positive definite covariance matrices is closely related to the realizability problem for gaussoids on 5 elements. Boege, D'Alì, Kahle and Sturmfels (FoCM 2019, "The Geometry of Gaussoids") gave a census of gaussoids for n=5 via SAT computations and classified small realizable and non-realizable gaussoids, but gaussoids are only a combinatorial axiomatization (they coincide with realizable patterns for n ≤ 4 but not in general), and a complete intrinsic characterization of realizable patterns for n=5 has not been established. The problem remains partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Determine which semigraphoids are realizable by multivariate Gaussian random variables, equivalently which conditional-independence structures can occur for Gaussian conditional independence models inside the cone of positive semidefinite covariance matrices.
status_search_result: The problem has motivated the theory of gaussoids (Lněnička–Matúš) and its geometry (Boege–D'Alì–Kahle–Sturmfels). For $n=4$, realizable Gaussian CI structures coincide with structural semigraphoids/gaussoids. For general $n$, no finite axiomatization exists: it has been shown that the conditional independence implications of Gaussians cannot be captured by any finite list of inference rules, and recent work using selfadhesivity yields new necessary axioms but no full characterization. The problem remains open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Characterize the image of the entropy map H: SDP_n → SubMod_n that sends a positive definite matrix to the logarithms of all 2^n principal minors. Here SubMod_n is the polyhedral cone of vectors satisfying the submodular inequalities H_{ {i}∪K } + H_{ {j}∪K } ≤ H_{ {i,j}∪K } + H_K.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $\mathrm{SDP}_n$ denote the cone of real symmetric positive definite $n\times n$ matrices. For any subset $I\subseteq [n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ and any matrix $\Sigma\in\mathrm{SDP}_n$, let $\Sigma_I$ denote the principal submatrix of $\Sigma$ indexed by rows and columns in $I$, with the convention $\det(\Sigma_\emptyset)=1$.

Define the entropy map
$$H:\mathrm{SDP}_n\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2^n},\qquad \Sigma\mapsto \bigl(H_I(\Sigma)\bigr)_{I\subseteq[n]},\qquad H_I(\Sigma):=\log\det(\Sigma_I).$$

Let $\mathrm{SubMod}_n\subset\mathbb{R}^{2^n}$ denote the polyhedral cone of vectors $(h_I)_{I\subseteq[n]}$ satisfying $h_\emptyset=0$ and the submodular inequalities
$$h_{\{i\}\cup K}+h_{\{j\}\cup K}\;\le\;h_{\{i,j\}\cup K}+h_K$$
for all $K\subseteq[n]$ and all distinct $i,j\in[n]\setminus K$. It is known that $H(\mathrm{SDP}_n)\subseteq\mathrm{SubMod}_n$.

Problem: Give an explicit characterization (for example, as a semialgebraic subset described by equalities and inequalities) of the image $H(\mathrm{SDP}_n)\subseteq\mathrm{SubMod}_n$.
category_tag: Principal minors of positive definite matrices
status_search_result: The exact characterization of the image of the entropy map remains open in general. Recent work (Tropicalizing Principal Minors of Positive Definite Matrices, arXiv:2410.11220, 2024) provides a partial answer at the tropical level: the tropicalization of the image of $\mathrm{SDP}_n$ under the principal minors map equals the intersection of the submodular cone with an affine tropical flag variety, and this yields new algebraic inequalities among principal minors. A full description of $H(\mathrm{SDP}_n)$ itself has not been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
context_brief: Rational points on strict CI varieties
original_question: Let X1, X2, ..., Xn be discrete random variables with d1, d2, ..., dn states, and let a chosen collection of conditional-independence statements define a determinantal variety in C^{d1} ⊗ C^{d2} ⊗ ··· ⊗ C^{dn}. The corresponding strict conditional-independence variety consists of those tables for which exactly the chosen conditional-independence statements hold and all other conditional-independence statements fail. Does every such strict conditional-independence variety have a Q-rational point? What can be said in the regime where d1, d2, ..., dn are all sufficiently large?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be discrete random variables, where $X_i$ takes values in a finite set of cardinality $d_i$. A joint probability distribution on $(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$ may be represented as a tensor (table) $P \in \mathbb{C}^{d_1} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_n}$. For disjoint subsets $A, B, C \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$, the conditional independence (CI) statement $X_A \perp\!\!\!\perp X_B \mid X_C$ is the polynomial condition on $P$ that all $2\times 2$ minors of certain flattenings of $P$ (obtained by fixing values of $X_C$ and marginalizing over the remaining variables outside $A\cup B\cup C$) vanish; thus any collection $\mathcal{C}$ of CI statements cuts out a determinantal variety $V_\mathcal{C}$ in the tensor space.

Given a chosen collection $\mathcal{C}$ of CI statements, define the strict conditional independence variety associated to $\mathcal{C}$ as
$$V_\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{strict}} = V_\mathcal{C} \setminus \bigcup_{\sigma \notin \mathcal{C}} V_{\{\sigma\}},$$
that is, the set of tables $P$ for which exactly the CI statements in $\mathcal{C}$ hold while every CI statement not in $\mathcal{C}$ fails.

Question: Does every nonempty strict conditional independence variety $V_\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{strict}}$ contain a $\mathbb{Q}$-rational point? In particular, what is the answer when the state sizes $d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n$ are all sufficiently large?
status_search_result: No source addressing the existence of $\mathbb{Q}$-rational points on strict conditional-independence varieties in general was located. The problem appears in a list of open problems in algebraic statistics and no resolution is indicated in the literature reachable by search.

paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: For complete noncompact Riemannian manifolds, especially negatively curved ones, what general results should hold about bounded harmonic functions and harmonic functions of polynomial growth? In particular, can the Dirichlet problem at infinity for bounded harmonic functions on negatively curved manifolds be characterized in a satisfactory way, and how should one understand the existence and structure of harmonic functions of polynomial growth on such manifolds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M^n, g)$ be a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. A function $u:M\to\mathbb{R}$ is harmonic if $\Delta_g u = 0$, where $\Delta_g$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator. For a fixed basepoint $p\in M$ and $d\geq 0$, let $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$ denote the space of harmonic functions $u$ on $M$ satisfying $|u(x)|\leq C(1+\operatorname{dist}(x,p))^d$ for some constant $C=C(u)$.

Address the following two questions:

(A) Bounded harmonic functions / Dirichlet problem at infinity. Suppose $M$ is simply connected with sectional curvature bounded between two negative constants, $-b^2 \leq \mathrm{Sec}_M \leq -a^2 < 0$. The geometric boundary at infinity $\partial_\infty M$ is defined as equivalence classes of geodesic rays under the relation of being asymptotic, equipped with the cone topology so that $\overline{M} = M \cup \partial_\infty M$ becomes a compact topological space homeomorphic to a closed ball. The Dirichlet problem at infinity asks: for every continuous function $f:\partial_\infty M\to\mathbb{R}$, does there exist a unique harmonic function $u\in C^\infty(M)\cap C^0(\overline{M})$ with $u|_{\partial_\infty M}=f$? Characterize, in geometric terms, the classes of complete noncompact negatively curved manifolds for which this Dirichlet problem at infinity is solvable, and describe the structure of the space of bounded harmonic functions on such manifolds.

(B) Harmonic functions of polynomial growth. Suppose $M$ has nonnegative Ricci curvature (or, more generally, satisfies appropriate volume-doubling and Poincaré-type hypotheses). Determine the dimension and structure of $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$: in particular, establish whether $\dim \mathcal{H}_d(M) < \infty$ for every $d\geq 0$, give sharp dimension bounds in terms of $n$ and $d$, and describe the asymptotic structure of elements of $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$ (for instance via separation-of-variables-type expansions on asymptotic cones).
status_search_result: Substantial parts of these problems are resolved. Yau's conjecture on finite dimensionality of spaces of polynomial-growth harmonic functions on manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature was proved by Colding and Minicozzi (1997), with subsequent sharp bounds and structural results. The Dirichlet problem at infinity on simply connected manifolds with pinched negative sectional curvature was solved by Anderson and Sullivan in the 1980s. However, a fully satisfactory geometric characterization of solvability of the Dirichlet problem at infinity in greater generality, and a complete description of the structure of polynomial-growth harmonic functions in broader settings, remain active areas of research, so the overall program is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: Can one define a notion of rank for general Riemannian manifolds that extends the classical rank notion for locally symmetric spaces, and then prove corresponding rigidity theorems for manifolds with higher-rank metrics? More specifically, what rigidity and classification results should hold for higher-rank nonpositively curved manifolds, and how should the still poorly understood rank-1 manifolds of non-positive curvature be characterized?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. Recall that for a locally symmetric space of noncompact type, the rank is the maximal dimension of a flat totally geodesic subspace of its universal cover, and that for a nonpositively curved manifold the rank of a geodesic c in the universal cover is defined as the dimension of the space of parallel Jacobi fields along c, with the rank of the manifold being the minimum of these ranks over all geodesics. A manifold is said to have higher rank if its rank is at least 2, and rank one otherwise.

(a) Formulate a notion of rank for general Riemannian manifolds (not assumed to be of nonpositive curvature or locally symmetric) that specializes to the classical rank for symmetric spaces of noncompact type, and prove rigidity theorems analogous to Mostow strong rigidity: namely, that closed manifolds of higher rank are, up to suitable equivalence, locally symmetric.

(b) Provide a complete classification, up to isometry, of closed irreducible Riemannian manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature having higher rank, beyond the known case where such manifolds are locally symmetric spaces of noncompact type.

(c) Give a structural characterization of closed rank-one Riemannian manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature, describing their geometric, dynamical, and topological properties in a way that parallels what is known for manifolds of strictly negative curvature.
status_search_result: The higher-rank case for closed nonpositively curved manifolds was resolved by Ballmann and independently by Burns–Spatzier, showing such irreducible manifolds are locally symmetric. Further partial extensions exist (e.g., to manifolds without focal points and to convex real projective structures, 2023). However, defining a general notion of rank for arbitrary Riemannian manifolds and proving full rigidity, as well as a complete structural characterization of rank-one nonpositively curved manifolds, remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: For a complex Kähler manifold, what is the precise relationship between the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric and algebro-geometric stability of the manifold? In particular, under what hypotheses does the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric force the tangent bundle or the manifold itself to be stable, and conversely when does stability guarantee the existence of such a special metric?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact complex Kähler manifold, and let $L \to X$ be an ample line bundle (a polarization). Recall the following notions:

(a) A Kähler metric $\omega$ on $X$ is called Kähler–Einstein if $\mathrm{Ric}(\omega) = \lambda\,\omega$ for some real constant $\lambda$; more generally, a Kähler metric $\omega \in c_1(L)$ is said to have constant scalar curvature (cscK) if its scalar curvature is constant.

(b) A holomorphic vector bundle $E \to X$ is slope-stable (with respect to $L$) if for every coherent subsheaf $\mathcal{F} \subset E$ with $0 < \mathrm{rank}(\mathcal{F}) < \mathrm{rank}(E)$ one has $\mu_L(\mathcal{F}) < \mu_L(E)$, where $\mu_L(\cdot) = \deg_L(\cdot)/\mathrm{rank}(\cdot)$.

(c) The polarized manifold $(X,L)$ is K-stable if for every nontrivial test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ for $(X,L)$ the Donaldson–Futaki invariant satisfies $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) > 0$ (with appropriate normalizations such as uniform or reduced K-stability when automorphisms are present).

Problem. Determine the precise relationship between the existence of canonical Kähler metrics and algebro-geometric stability:

(1) Prove that if $X$ admits a Kähler–Einstein metric, then its holomorphic tangent bundle $T_X$ is slope-polystable with respect to the relevant polarization, and identify the sharpest hypotheses under which this implication and its variants hold.

(2) For an arbitrary polarized Kähler manifold $(X,L)$, establish the equivalence
$$(X,L)\ \text{admits a cscK metric in } c_1(L) \iff (X,L)\ \text{is K-stable (in a suitable uniform/reduced sense)},$$
specializing to: $X$ Fano admits a Kähler–Einstein metric iff $(X,-K_X)$ is K-stable.

Provide a complete characterization, including necessary and sufficient conditions linking existence of Kähler–Einstein / cscK metrics to stability of $(X,L)$ and of $T_X$.
status_search_result: The Fano case of the Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture (existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric on a Fano manifold is equivalent to K-stability of $(X,-K_X)$) was resolved by Chen–Donaldson–Sun (2012–2015), and the implication "KE metric ⇒ polystability of the tangent bundle" is classical (Kobayashi, Lübke, Donaldson, Yau). The general polarized YTD conjecture for cscK metrics on arbitrary $(X,L)$ remains open, with substantial progress: it is known for cohomogeneity one manifolds, for general polarizations under uniform/strong K-stability assumptions, and the "cscK ⇒ uniform K-stability" direction has been established in considerable generality, but the full equivalence in the polarized cscK setting is not yet proved.

paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: Can mirror manifolds be constructed explicitly for the relevant classes of Kähler or Calabi–Yau manifolds predicted by mirror symmetry? In particular, can the Strominger–Yau–Zaslow program be carried out in a concrete way that produces explicit mirror manifolds and clarifies the geometric mechanism behind mirror symmetry?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a Calabi–Yau $n$-fold, i.e. a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$ with trivial canonical bundle and a Ricci-flat Kähler metric. Mirror symmetry predicts the existence of a "mirror" Calabi–Yau $n$-fold $X^\vee$ such that the complex geometry of $X$ is exchanged with the symplectic geometry of $X^\vee$ (in particular, the Hodge numbers satisfy $h^{p,q}(X) = h^{n-p,q}(X^\vee)$, and the A-model on $X$ is equivalent to the B-model on $X^\vee$).

The Strominger–Yau–Zaslow (SYZ) proposal asserts that, near a large complex structure limit point in the moduli space, $X$ admits a special Lagrangian torus fibration $\pi : X \to B$ over a real $n$-dimensional base $B$ (with singular fibers over a discriminant locus), and that the mirror $X^\vee$ can be constructed as the fiberwise dual fibration $\pi^\vee : X^\vee \to B$, obtained by replacing each smooth special Lagrangian torus fiber $T \subset X$ with its dual torus $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(T), U(1))$, with suitable instanton corrections accounting for the singular fibers.

Problem. Carry out the SYZ program rigorously and explicitly for the relevant classes of Calabi–Yau manifolds. Specifically:

(a) Prove that a Calabi–Yau $n$-fold $X$ near a large complex structure limit admits a special Lagrangian torus fibration $\pi: X \to B$, and describe the structure of its discriminant locus and singular fibers.

(b) Give an explicit construction of the mirror manifold $X^\vee$ as a (suitably corrected) dual special Lagrangian torus fibration over the same base $B$, and prove that the result is a Calabi–Yau manifold mirror to $X$ in the sense of mirror symmetry (e.g., matching Hodge numbers, Yukawa couplings, or yielding a derived equivalence of categories).

(c) Use the construction to clarify the geometric mechanism underlying mirror symmetry.
category_tag: SYZ mirror symmetry for Calabi–Yau manifolds
status_search_result: The SYZ conjecture is widely regarded as open in general. Major partial progress exists (e.g., topological/affine-geometric versions by Gross–Siebert via degenerations, Kontsevich–Soibelman's non-archimedean approach, and metric SYZ results by Li, Collins–Jacob–Lin, and others near the large complex structure limit), but a complete construction of special Lagrangian torus fibrations and explicit mirrors for general Calabi–Yau manifolds has not been achieved. Recent surveys (2022–) list it among the central open problems in mirror symmetry.

original_question: For a subset S of R^n and an integer p >= 1, define S_p to be the set of all convex combinations of at most p points of S. Since S_1 = S and S_{n+1} is the full convex hull co(S), what topological properties are shared by the intermediate partial convexifications S_p?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty set. For each integer $p \geq 1$, define the $p$-th partial convexification of $S$ by
$$S_p \;=\; \Bigl\{ \sum_{i=1}^{p} \lambda_i x_i \;:\; x_i \in S,\ \lambda_i \geq 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{p} \lambda_i = 1 \Bigr\},$$
i.e., the set of all convex combinations of at most $p$ points of $S$. Then $S_1 = S$ and, by Carathéodory's theorem, $S_{n+1} = \operatorname{co}(S)$, the convex hull of $S$. The intermediate sets $S_2, S_3, \dots, S_n$ are "partially convexified" versions of $S$.

Determine what topological properties (such as openness, closedness, connectedness, local connectedness, compactness, contractibility, Borel/measurability class, dimension, etc.) are necessarily shared by all of the sets $S_p$ for $1 \leq p \leq n+1$, and how these properties depend on the corresponding properties of $S$ and on the parameter $p$.

status_search_result: A targeted web search did not locate a definitive resolution or systematic study of the topological properties shared by all partial convexifications $S_p$ in the sense above. Standard references on convex sets discuss only $S$ and its full convex hull $\operatorname{co}(S)$, leaving the intermediate $S_p$ apparently not comprehensively treated. The status is therefore unclear from public sources.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Let k > 2, let H be a symmetric k-linear form on R^n, and let A be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix such that |H(x, ..., x)| <= <Ax, x>^(k/2) for every x in R^n. Can the resulting inequality |H(x_1, ..., x_k)|^2 <= product_i <Ax_i, x_i> be proved by optimization methods, such as higher-order optimality conditions, rather than by the existing inductive or algebraic proofs?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k>2$ be an integer and let $H:\mathbb{R}^n\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ ($k$ copies) be a symmetric $k$-linear form. Let $A$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $n\times n$ real matrix such that
\[
|H(x,x,\ldots,x)| \le \langle Ax,x\rangle^{k/2} \qquad \text{for every } x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
It is known (via inductive/algebraic arguments) that this hypothesis implies the multilinear Cauchy–Schwarz-type inequality
\[
|H(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)|^2 \le \prod_{i=1}^k \langle Ax_i,x_i\rangle \qquad \text{for all } x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Provide a proof of this implication using only methods of optimization theory — for example, first-, second-, or higher-order optimality conditions applied to a suitable extremal problem — rather than inductive or purely algebraic manipulations.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any published optimization-based proof (via higher-order optimality conditions) of this multilinear Cauchy–Schwarz-type inequality for symmetric k-linear forms dominated by a positive semidefinite quadratic form. Existing multilinear Cauchy–Schwarz generalizations in the literature use inductive/algebraic arguments. The status of an optimization-theoretic proof appears unverified.

original_question: Among all continuous rectifiable plane curves that start at the center of the unit circle and are guaranteed to touch every tangent line to that circle, give a proof—using calculus of variations or optimal control—that the optimal curve has length 7π/6 + √3 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ denote the unit circle in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, centered at the origin $O$. Call a continuous rectifiable curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ a "search curve" if $\gamma(0)=O$ and, for every line $\ell$ that is tangent to $C$, the image $\gamma([0,1])$ has nonempty intersection with $\ell$. Let $L(\gamma)$ denote the arc length of $\gamma$.

Using methods from the calculus of variations or optimal control, prove that
$$\inf_{\gamma} L(\gamma) \;=\; \frac{7\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3} + 1,$$
where the infimum is taken over all search curves, and exhibit (and verify the optimality of) a minimizer that attains this length.
category_tag: Calculus of variations / optimal search curves
status_search_result: The exact value 7π/6 + √3 + 1 ≈ 6.3972 for the shortest curve from the center of the unit disk meeting every tangent line is established: Joris (1980, "Le chasseur perdu dans la forêt") gave a complete proof, with the result earlier indicated by Isbell (1957). Thus the length is known. The specific request to obtain this via a calculus-of-variations / optimal-control argument is a methodological reformulation; the underlying value is solved, but a uniformly accepted derivation strictly within the optimal-control framework is less standard.

original_question: Determine the minimal possible length and the geometric structure of a curve in R^3 that starts at the center of the unit sphere and intersects every tangent plane to that sphere.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere centered at the origin $O$, and for each unit vector $p \in S^2$ let $\Pi_p = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \langle x, p \rangle = 1\}$ be the tangent plane to $S^2$ at $p$. Consider rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,L] \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\gamma(0) = O$ that meet every tangent plane to $S^2$, i.e. for each $p \in S^2$ there exists $t \in [0,L]$ with $\langle \gamma(t), p \rangle = 1$ (equivalently, the closed convex hull of the image of $\gamma$ contains the closed unit ball). 

Determine the infimum 
$$\ell^* = \inf\{\,\mathrm{length}(\gamma) : \gamma(0)=O,\ \gamma \text{ meets every tangent plane to } S^2\,\},$$
decide whether this infimum is attained, and describe the geometric structure (shape, smoothness, number of pieces, curvature properties) of any optimal curve.
status_search_result: The closely related problem of the shortest closed curve whose convex hull contains the unit sphere was resolved by Ghomi and Wenk (Zalgaller's "baseball seam" conjecture, length 4π). However, the variant considered here — an open curve starting at the center of the sphere and required to meet every tangent plane — appears not to have been resolved; no source identifying the minimal length or the structure of an optimal such curve was found, and the original formulation explicitly states that nothing is known about the optimal path's structure.

context_brief: Curve visible from every point on a sphere
original_question: Determine the minimal possible length and shape of a curve in space that can be seen from every point on a sphere.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ be the unit sphere and let $B$ denote the closed unit ball it bounds. Say that a (rectifiable) curve $\gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\mathrm{int}(B)$ "inspects" $S$ if for every point $p\in S$ there exists a point $q\in\gamma$ such that the open line segment from $p$ to $q$ does not meet the interior of $B$ (equivalently, $q$ is visible from $p$ from outside the sphere). 

Determine
$$L^{*}=\inf\bigl\{\operatorname{length}(\gamma):\gamma\text{ inspects }S\bigr\},$$
and describe the shape(s) of the minimizing curve(s). The same question is to be answered both in the class of all rectifiable curves and in the class of closed rectifiable curves.
status_search_result: The problem (often called the "sphere inspection" or "opaque set for a sphere" problem) remains an active area. Ghomi and Wenk (Crelles J., 2021; arXiv:2010.15204) proved that any closed curve whose convex hull contains the unit sphere has length at least 4π, with equality only for a baseball-seam shape, settling Zalgaller's 1996 conjecture for that class. However, the general inspection problem (curves merely visible from every point of the sphere, not necessarily closed or convex-hull-containing) is not fully resolved; sharp lower bounds and minimizers in the broader setting remain open.

original_question: Let F_N be the sum of cosines of all angles determined by N distinct points in R^3, and let (P_N) be the problem of maximizing F_N subject to the triangle-angle consistency constraints. Determine the maximizing configurations for larger values of N and decide whether the conjectured optimal configurations for N = 5, 6, and 8 are correct.
self_contained_problem:
Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer and let $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ be $N$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^3$. For each ordered triple $(i,j,k)$ with $i,j,k$ pairwise distinct, let $\theta_{jik} \in [0,\pi]$ denote the angle at vertex $x_i$ in the (possibly degenerate) triangle $x_j x_i x_k$, that is, the angle between the vectors $x_j - x_i$ and $x_k - x_i$. Define the total angle energy
$$F_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{\substack{j<k \\ j,k\neq i}} \cos\theta_{jik}.$$
Consider the problem $(P_N)$ of maximizing $F_N$ over all configurations of $N$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (equivalently, over all collections of angles satisfying the consistency constraints imposed by triangles in $\mathbb{R}^3$).

(a) Determine, for each $N \ge 3$, the maximum value of $F_N$ and the configurations that achieve it.

(b) In particular, prove or disprove the following conjectured optimal configurations:
  - For $N = 5$: the optimum is attained by a configuration consisting of the four vertices of a regular tetrahedron together with its center.
  - For $N = 6$: the optimum is attained by the six vertices of a regular octahedron.
  - For $N = 8$: the optimum is attained by the eight vertices of a regular cube (or, alternatively, of a square antiprism / specified configuration), in the sense made precise by the conjecture.

Give exact maximizers and the value of $F_N$ at the maximum.
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The problem is stated as a challenge ("solving (P_N) with accuracy seems out of reach for larger N"), and web search returned only the original conjecture list and related copositivity work, with no source claiming a proof of the N=5,6,8 cases or a general solution. Status appears open.

original_question: For the same optimization problem (P_N) that maximizes the angle-based energy F_N over configurations of N points in R^3, determine whether, as N tends to infinity, the maximizing configurations become uniformly distributed on a sphere and whether sup F_N = (2/9)N^3 + o(N^3).
self_contained_problem:
Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer. For a configuration of $N$ points $M_1,\dots,M_N$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (assumed pairwise distinct and in general position), define the angle-based ("Coulombian-type") energy
\[
F_N(M_1,\dots,M_N)\;=\;\sum_{\substack{(i,j,k)\\ i,j,k\text{ pairwise distinct}}}\widehat{M_i M_j M_k},
\]
where $\widehat{M_i M_j M_k}\in[0,\pi]$ denotes the (non-oriented) angle at vertex $M_j$ in the triangle with vertices $M_i,M_j,M_k$. Consider the maximization problem
\[
(P_N)\qquad \sup\bigl\{F_N(M_1,\dots,M_N)\ :\ M_1,\dots,M_N\in\mathbb{R}^3\bigr\}.
\]
Establish (or refute) the following two assertions:

(a) As $N\to\infty$, every sequence of (almost) maximizing configurations of $(P_N)$, after suitable normalization, has its empirical distribution converging weakly to the uniform probability measure on some sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

(b) The optimal value satisfies the asymptotic
\[
\sup(P_N)\;=\;\tfrac{2}{9}\,N^{3}+o(N^{3})\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty.
\]

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
context_brief: Optimization proof for Van der Waerden inequality
original_question: Find a proof, based entirely on constrained-optimization ideas such as higher-order optimality conditions, that every doubly stochastic n x n matrix A satisfies per(A) >= n!/n^n, with equality only at the matrix whose entries are all 1/n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrix; that is, $a_{ij}\ge 0$ for all $i,j$, and every row sum and every column sum of $A$ equals $1$. The permanent of $A$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. It is known that
$$\operatorname{per}(A)\ \ge\ \frac{n!}{n^{n}},$$
with equality if and only if $A=J_n$, the matrix all of whose entries are $1/n$.

Provide a proof of this inequality (including the equality case) that is carried out entirely within the framework of constrained optimization. More precisely, view the problem as minimizing the multilinear objective $A\mapsto\operatorname{per}(A)$ over the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices, and derive both the lower bound $n!/n^n$ and the uniqueness of the minimizer $J_n$ by invoking only optimality conditions (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions and, if necessary, higher-order — e.g.\ second-order or beyond — optimality conditions for constrained extrema), without recourse to algebraic, combinatorial, or analytic-inequality arguments external to optimization theory.
status_search_result: The Van der Waerden conjecture itself was proved in 1981 by Egorychev and Falikman, and alternative proofs (including geometric-programming-based ones by Bapat and others) have appeared. However, the specific request — a proof carried out purely through constrained-optimization machinery such as higher-order optimality conditions on the Birkhoff polytope — does not appear to be settled in the literature; existing "optimization" proofs rely on additional analytic or algebraic tools rather than higher-order KKT-type conditions alone.

original_question: Let B_n be the set of doubly stochastic n x n matrices. Determine whether the permanent function on B_n intersected with the trace-zero constraint {A : tr(A) = 0} attains its minimum uniquely at the matrix with every off-diagonal entry equal to 1/(n - 1) and every diagonal entry equal to 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ be an integer, and let $B_n$ denote the set of $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrices, i.e. real $n\times n$ matrices with nonnegative entries whose every row sum and every column sum is equal to $1$. For a matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in B_n$, recall that the permanent of $A$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Consider the convex subset
$$T_n=\{A\in B_n:\operatorname{tr}(A)=0\}=\{A\in B_n: a_{ii}=0\text{ for all }i\}.$$
Let $A^\star\in T_n$ be the matrix with $a^\star_{ii}=0$ for all $i$ and $a^\star_{ij}=\tfrac{1}{n-1}$ for all $i\ne j$. Decide whether
$$\min_{A\in T_n}\operatorname{per}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A^\star),$$
and whether the minimum is attained uniquely at $A^\star$.
status_search_result: Searches turned up the classical Van der Waerden conjecture (proved by Egorychev and Falikman in 1980–81) and various related conjectures (e.g. Brualdi, Holens–Đoković, and minimum-permanent problems on faces of the Birkhoff polytope) but no clear resolution of the specific minimization problem over doubly stochastic matrices with zero diagonal. The problem appears to remain open in general; partial results exist for restricted classes of faces of the Birkhoff polytope.

paper_title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
original_question: Are Large Reasoning Models capable of generalizable reasoning, or are their apparent reasoning gains mainly another form of pattern matching rather than a robust ability to reason across problems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a class of neural sequence models, referred to as Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), which are trained on large text corpora and additionally optimized to produce intermediate step-by-step "reasoning traces" (e.g., chain-of-thought or scratchpad outputs) before emitting a final answer. Let a problem family be specified by a parameter (such as instance size, recursion depth, or compositional structure) that controls its intrinsic complexity, and let an LRM's performance on the family be measured by its accuracy as a function of this complexity parameter, evaluated on instances drawn from distributions that may differ from the training distribution.

Determine whether such LRMs exhibit genuinely generalizable reasoning — meaning that they implement procedures whose accuracy remains robust as problem complexity grows and as instances move out of the training distribution — or whether their apparent reasoning improvements over standard language models are explained instead by sophisticated pattern matching, in which performance degrades systematically with increased complexity or distribution shift. Provide either: (a) a precise definition of generalizable reasoning together with theoretical or empirical demonstrations that current LRMs satisfy it across problem families of unbounded complexity; or (b) a demonstration that for every current LRM there exist problem families on which accuracy collapses as complexity increases, in a manner consistent with pattern matching rather than algorithmic reasoning.
category_tag: reasoning generalization in large language models
status_search_result: The question of whether large reasoning models perform generalizable reasoning versus pattern matching is an active open research debate as of 2026. Multiple recent studies report systematic accuracy collapse on sufficiently complex or out-of-distribution problem instances, but no consensus definition or resolution has been established, and counter-arguments dispute the interpretation of these failures.

paper_title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
original_question: How does the performance of Large Reasoning Models change as problem complexity increases, especially when the task requires longer sequential reasoning chains and greater compositional depth?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a class of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs): autoregressive language models that, prior to producing a final answer, generate an extended internal "thinking" trace (chain-of-thought, self-reflection, or search-like steps). Fix a family of controllable reasoning tasks parametrized by a complexity parameter N (for example, the number of disks in Tower of Hanoi, the number of blocks in a Blocks-World plan, the number of segments in a River-Crossing puzzle, or the depth of a compositional logical derivation), so that larger N forces longer sequential reasoning chains and greater compositional depth, while keeping the rule set of the task fixed.

For each task family, let Acc(N) denote the final-answer accuracy of a given LRM on instances of complexity N (averaged over a representative distribution of instances), and let T(N) denote the average number of thinking tokens the model expends on such instances before producing its final answer.

Characterize, both empirically and theoretically, the joint scaling behavior of Acc(N) and T(N) as N increases. In particular:

(a) Determine whether there exists, for each task family and model, a critical complexity N* beyond which Acc(N) collapses to near zero, and describe how N* depends on model size, training compute, and the availability of an explicit "thinking" mode versus a matched non-thinking baseline.

(b) Describe the behavior of the reasoning-effort curve T(N): does T(N) grow monotonically with N up to the model's context limit, or does it exhibit a counter-intuitive decrease near N*, indicating that the model reduces its reasoning effort precisely when the task becomes hardest?

(c) Identify and formalize the three regimes suggested by such experiments: (i) a low-complexity regime in which non-thinking models match or outperform thinking models, (ii) a medium-complexity regime in which extended thinking provides a clear advantage, and (iii) a high-complexity regime in which both thinking and non-thinking variants collapse to zero accuracy.

(d) Provide a quantitative model (e.g., a scaling law of the form Acc(N) ≈ f(N/N*) with explicit dependence on model and task parameters) that predicts the location of these transitions and the collapse of reasoning effort, and prove or disprove the conjecture that current LRMs fail to develop generalizable algorithmic reasoning, in the sense that no finite increase in inference-time compute suffices to push N* to infinity for the above task families.
status_search_result: The qualitative empirical findings — accuracy collapse beyond a task-dependent complexity threshold, a counter-intuitive decrease in reasoning tokens near that threshold, and three distinct complexity regimes — have been reported and partially replicated for current Large Reasoning Models (e.g., Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking, DeepSeek-R1, o1/o3-style models). However, a rigorous quantitative scaling law and a definitive theoretical explanation for the collapse remain open, and follow-up work has contested whether the collapse reflects fundamental reasoning limits or evaluation/context-length artifacts. The problem is therefore partially solved at the empirical level and open at the theoretical level.

original_question: When Large Reasoning Models and their non-thinking Large Language Model counterparts are given the same inference token budget, how do their capabilities compare, and when does explicit reasoning provide a genuine advantage over standard generation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two classes of autoregressive language models operating over a shared vocabulary and tokenizer:

(1) A "Large Reasoning Model" (LRM), which, given an input prompt, first generates an internal chain-of-thought sequence of tokens before producing a final answer, and is trained (e.g., via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards or supervised fine-tuning on long reasoning traces) to use such intermediate tokens.

(2) A "standard Large Language Model" (LLM), of comparable parameter count and pretraining, which generates a response directly without an explicitly trained thinking phase, though it may use prompt-elicited chain-of-thought.

Fix an inference-time token budget B (the maximum total number of tokens that may be generated, including any internal reasoning tokens and the final answer). For a family of evaluation tasks T parameterized by a measurable notion of problem complexity c (for instance, problem size, search depth, or compositional length), let

  A_LRM(c, B) = expected task-success rate of the LRM on tasks of complexity c under budget B,
  A_LLM(c, B) = expected task-success rate of the matched standard LLM on tasks of complexity c under budget B.

Investigate the following:

(a) Characterize, as a function of complexity c and budget B, the sign and magnitude of the gap Δ(c, B) = A_LRM(c, B) − A_LLM(c, B).

(b) Identify the regimes (c, B) in which Δ(c, B) > 0 (explicit reasoning helps), Δ(c, B) ≈ 0 (no benefit), and Δ(c, B) < 0 (explicit reasoning hurts under matched compute).

(c) Determine whether there exists a complexity threshold c*(B) above which both models collapse to near-zero accuracy, and below which the standard LLM matches or exceeds the LRM at equal token budget.
status_search_result: Empirical studies comparing reasoning-trained models (e.g., o1-style, DeepSeek-R1, Claude thinking models) with their non-thinking counterparts under matched inference token budgets report a three-regime pattern: standard LLMs match or exceed LRMs on low-complexity tasks, LRMs show clear advantages at medium complexity, and both collapse at high complexity. These findings are partial and contested across benchmarks; a full theoretical characterization remains open.

original_question: What inherent limitations do current reasoning approaches have, and what changes or improvements would be necessary to produce more robust reasoning capabilities in language models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of large language models augmented with explicit chain-of-thought or "thinking" mechanisms (so-called large reasoning models), which generate intermediate token sequences before producing a final answer. Empirically, the accuracy of such models on families of controllable reasoning tasks (e.g., compositional puzzles parameterized by a complexity parameter n such as Tower of Hanoi, blocks-world planning, river-crossing, and checker-jumping) exhibits three regimes as n grows: (i) a low-complexity regime where non-reasoning models match or outperform reasoning models, (ii) a medium-complexity regime where explicit reasoning yields improvement, and (iii) a high-complexity regime in which both approaches collapse to near-zero accuracy, and where the length of generated reasoning traces paradoxically decreases as problems become harder, despite available token budget.

Determine what algorithmic, architectural, training-objective, or inference-time modifications would be necessary and sufficient to overcome these limitations and yield reasoning capabilities that remain robust as problem complexity increases.

paper_title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
original_question: When thinking models outperform non-thinking models more strongly on newer math benchmarks such as AIME24 and AIME25, is that widening gap caused by genuinely greater problem complexity that rewards more sophisticated reasoning, or by reduced data contamination that makes the newer benchmarks a cleaner test of model ability?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two families of large language models evaluated on competition mathematics benchmarks: "thinking" models, which produce explicit intermediate chain-of-thought reasoning before answering, and "non-thinking" models, which produce direct answers without an extended deliberation phase. Empirically, on older mathematical olympiad-style benchmarks (such as the 2024 AIME problem set, AIME24) the average accuracy gap between thinking and non-thinking models is comparatively small, while on the newer 2025 AIME problem set (AIME25) this gap is substantially larger.

Two competing explanations are proposed for this widening performance gap:

(H1) Complexity hypothesis: The newer benchmark contains problems that are intrinsically more complex and demand more sophisticated multi-step reasoning, so that thinking models, by virtue of their extended deliberation, gain a real advantage that non-thinking models cannot match.

(H2) Contamination hypothesis: The newer benchmark was released after most pretraining corpora were collected, so its problems and solutions are less likely to appear in training data; the apparent advantage of thinking models on AIME25 therefore reflects reduced memorization on the part of non-thinking models rather than improved reasoning by thinking models.

Design and carry out an empirical or theoretical analysis that determines which of (H1) and (H2) — or what quantitative mixture of the two — accounts for the observed widening gap between thinking and non-thinking model accuracies when moving from AIME24 to AIME25. The analysis should control for problem difficulty (for example via human solver statistics or per-problem solve rates) and for training-data contamination (for example via membership-inference style tests, n-gram overlap with known corpora, or release-date cutoffs), and should produce a defensible attribution of the gap to complexity versus contamination.

(a) the model is asked to produce a full valid move sequence for the n-disk instance from scratch;
(b) the model is given, as part of its prompt, a complete and correct step-by-step algorithm (e.g., the recursive solver) that it is instructed to execute, so that the task reduces to faithful symbolic execution rather than search or discovery.

What does this phenomenon imply, in a precise and quantifiable sense, about such a model's capabilities for (i) exact stepwise computation on long deterministic procedures, (ii) logical verification of intermediate states against rule constraints, and (iii) reliable symbolic manipulation of structured representations?

context_brief: cross-puzzle inconsistency in exact step execution
original_question: What explains the strong cross-puzzle inconsistency in current reasoning models, where the same model can execute about 100 correct moves in a Tower of Hanoi instance with 10 disks and solve a 5-disk Tower of Hanoi puzzle that needs 31 moves, yet fails to produce more than about 4 or 5 correct moves in River Crossing and cannot solve a River Crossing instance with 3 actor-agent pairs that has a solution of only 11 moves?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a large language "reasoning" model evaluated on two classical planning puzzles, treated as sequential move-generation tasks:

1. Tower of Hanoi with N disks: starting from N disks stacked in decreasing size on peg A, transfer all disks to peg C using peg B, moving one disk at a time and never placing a larger disk on a smaller one. The unique optimal solution requires 2^N − 1 moves.

2. River Crossing with N actor–agent pairs: N actors and their N respective agents must cross a river using a boat of capacity at most 2 (or 3 for large N). The boat cannot move empty, and no actor may be on the same bank (or in the boat) as another actor's agent unless that actor's own agent is also present. The task is to produce a valid sequence of boat trips transporting everyone from the left bank to the right bank.

Empirically, the same model can execute approximately 100 consecutive correct moves on a Tower of Hanoi instance with N = 10 disks and solves Tower of Hanoi with N = 5 (which needs 31 moves) with near-perfect accuracy, yet on the River Crossing puzzle it produces only about 4–5 correct moves before erring and fails to solve the instance with N = 3 actor–agent pairs (whose optimal solution has only 11 moves).

Specifically, identify and justify properties of the two puzzles (e.g., constraint structure, branching factor, frequency of legal-move types in training data, recursive vs. constraint-satisfaction nature, search-space topology) that account for the disparity, and formulate a model-agnostic measure of "executional difficulty per move" under which Tower of Hanoi instances with hundreds of optimal moves are easier than River Crossing instances with about 11 optimal moves, consistent with the observed behavior.

original_question: Riemann's hypothesis asks whether every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2; equivalently, whether all zeros other than the negative even integers are of the form s = 1/2 + iτ.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for complex $s$ with $\Re(s) > 1$ by the convergent Dirichlet series
$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s},$$
and extended to a meromorphic function on the entire complex plane (with a single simple pole at $s=1$) via analytic continuation. The function $\zeta(s)$ vanishes at the negative even integers $s = -2, -4, -6, \dots$; these are called the trivial zeros. All other zeros of $\zeta(s)$ are called nontrivial zeros, and it is known that they lie in the critical strip $0 < \Re(s) < 1$.

Prove or disprove: every nontrivial zero $s$ of $\zeta(s)$ satisfies $\Re(s) = 1/2$; equivalently, every zero of $\zeta(s)$ other than the negative even integers is of the form $s = \tfrac{1}{2} + i\tau$ for some real number $\tau$.
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis remains one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems and has not been resolved as of 2026.

For each integer $n \geq 1$, consider packings of congruent closed balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, i.e., collections of balls of equal radius whose interiors are pairwise disjoint. The density of such a packing is defined as
$$\Delta = \limsup_{R\to\infty} \frac{\mathrm{vol}\bigl(B_R(0) \cap \bigcup_i B_i\bigr)}{\mathrm{vol}(B_R(0))},$$

original_question: Can a minimum weight triangulation of a planar point set be found in polynomial time? Theweightof a triangulation is its total edge length.
self_contained_problem:
Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane. A triangulation of $P$ is a maximal set $T$ of straight-line edges with endpoints in $P$ such that no two edges of $T$ cross in their interiors; equivalently, $T$ subdivides the convex hull of $P$ into triangles whose vertices lie in $P$ and which meet edge-to-edge. The weight of a triangulation $T$ is
$$w(T) = \sum_{e \in T} \|e\|_2,$$
the total Euclidean length of its edges. A minimum weight triangulation of $P$ is a triangulation minimizing $w(T)$ over all triangulations of $P$.

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given $P$, computes a minimum weight triangulation of $P$ in time polynomial in $|P|$?
status_search_result: Mulzer and Rote (2006, published JACM 2008) proved that the minimum weight triangulation problem for planar point sets is NP-hard via a reduction from PLANAR-1-IN-3-SAT, ruling out a polynomial-time algorithm unless P = NP. (A subtlety: NP-completeness of the decision version depends on the sum-of-square-roots problem, but Mulzer–Rote settles the polynomial-time question modulo P ≠ NP.)

original_question: What is the combinatorial complexity of the Voronoi diagram of a set of lines (or line segments) in three dimensions?

original_question: What is the complexity of the union of “fat” objects inR 3?
self_contained_problem:
A compact set $O \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is called $\alpha$-fat (for some constant $\alpha > 0$) if there exist concentric balls $B_{\text{in}} \subseteq O \subseteq B_{\text{out}}$ with $\operatorname{radius}(B_{\text{in}})/\operatorname{radius}(B_{\text{out}}) \geq \alpha$. Given a collection of $n$ such $\alpha$-fat objects in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (where $\alpha$ is treated as a fixed positive constant), the combinatorial complexity of their union $\bigcup_{i=1}^n O_i$ is the total number of faces of all dimensions on the boundary of the union (assuming the objects are semi-algebraic of constant description complexity).

Determine the worst-case combinatorial complexity, as a function of $n$, of the union of $n$ $\alpha$-fat objects in $\mathbb{R}^3$. In particular, is this complexity $O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$?
status_search_result: The problem is listed as open on The Open Problems Project, with the conjecture that the union complexity should be nearly quadratic ($O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$). Partial results are known for special cases: the union of $n$ fat tetrahedra in 3-space has complexity $O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$, and the same bound is known for Minkowski sums of polyhedra with a ball and for unions of congruent cubes. The general fat-object case in $\mathbb{R}^3$ remains unresolved.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Can the Euclideanminimum spanning tree(MST) ofnpoints in Rd be computed in time close to the lower bound of Ω(nlogn) [GKFS96]?
self_contained_problem:
Let d ≥ 3 be a fixed integer and let P ⊂ ℝ^d be a set of n points. The Euclidean minimum spanning tree of P, denoted EMST(P), is a spanning tree of the complete weighted graph on P in which the weight of every edge {p,q} equals the Euclidean distance ‖p−q‖₂, having minimum total edge weight among all such spanning trees. Any algorithm that computes EMST(P) in the algebraic decision tree model requires Ω(n log n) time in the worst case.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that, given any finite set P ⊂ ℝ^d of n points (with d ≥ 3 fixed), computes EMST(P) in time n·(log n)^{O(1)}, i.e., within a polylogarithmic factor of the Ω(n log n) lower bound?
status_search_result: For d = 2, an O(n log n) algorithm has long been known via the Delaunay triangulation. For fixed d ≥ 3, the best known deterministic worst-case complexity remains super-linear by more than a polylog factor (closely tied to the bichromatic closest-pair problem). Recent works (e.g., 2023 massively parallel algorithms; 2024–2025 high-dimensional approximation algorithms) address approximations or models of computation but do not close the gap to near-linear in the standard sequential model, so the problem appears to still be open.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: What is the complexity of computing a minimum-cost Euclidean matching for 2npoints in the plane? Thecostof a matching is the total length of the edges in the matching.
self_contained_problem:
Let $P=\{p_1,\dots,p_{2n}\}$ be a set of $2n$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A perfect matching $M$ of $P$ is a partition of $P$ into $n$ unordered pairs. Define the cost of $M$ to be
$$\mathrm{cost}(M)=\sum_{\{p_i,p_j\}\in M}\|p_i-p_j\|_2,$$
the total Euclidean length of the edges in $M$. A minimum-cost Euclidean matching of $P$ is a perfect matching that minimizes $\mathrm{cost}(M)$ over all perfect matchings of $P$.

Determine the computational complexity of the following problem: given $P$, compute a minimum-cost Euclidean matching of $P$. In particular, can it be solved in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$, or is there a matching lower bound? Pin down the exact polynomial-time complexity (best achievable running time) of this problem.
status_search_result: The exact complexity of computing a minimum-cost Euclidean perfect matching of 2n points in the plane is still open. The best known exact algorithms run in roughly O(n^{2+ε}) time (Varadarajan; Agarwal et al.), and faster (1+ε)-approximation algorithms are known, but no matching lower bound or substantially faster exact algorithm has been established.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: What is the maximum number ofk-sets? (Equivalently, what is the maximum complexity of ak-level in an arrangement of hyperplanes?) 15
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a set of $n$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $k$ be an integer with $1 \le k < n$. A $k$-set of $S$ is a subset $T \subseteq S$ with $|T|=k$ such that there exists an open halfspace $H$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $T = S \cap H$. Let $f_d(n,k)$ denote the maximum, over all such point sets $S$ of size $n$ in general position, of the number of $k$-sets of $S$.

Equivalently, given an arrangement of $n$ hyperplanes in general position in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the $k$-level is the closure of the set of points lying on some hyperplane and having exactly $k$ hyperplanes strictly below them; $f_d(n,k)$ equals the maximum combinatorial complexity (number of vertices, or equivalently number of faces) of the $k$-level over all such arrangements.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of $f_d(n,k)$. In particular:
(a) For $d = 2$, determine sharp asymptotics for $f_2(n,k)$. The best known bounds are $n \cdot 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})} \le f_2(n,k) \le O(n\, k^{1/3})$.
(b) For $d = 3$, determine sharp asymptotics for $f_3(n,k)$, where the best known bounds are $n k \cdot 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})} \le f_3(n,k) \le O(n\, k^{3/2})$.
(c) More generally, for each fixed $d \ge 2$, determine the maximum asymptotic order of $f_d(n,k)$.
status_search_result: The k-set / k-level problem remains open in all dimensions $d \ge 2$. In the plane, the best known upper bound $O(n k^{1/3})$ is due to Dey (1998) and the best known lower bound is $n \cdot 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})}$ due to Tóth (1999); there is still a substantial gap between these bounds. In three dimensions, the best known bounds are $n k \cdot 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})}$ and $O(n k^{3/2})$ (Sharir–Smorodinsky–Tardos and others). Recent work (e.g., on pseudoplanes, SoCG 2019) has refined related bounds but has not closed the gap.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Is linear programming strongly polynomial?
self_contained_problem:
A linear programming problem is the optimization problem of maximizing (or minimizing) a linear objective function $c^	op x$ over $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ subject to finitely many linear inequality constraints $Ax \le b$, where $A \in \mathbb{Q}^{m 	imes n}$, $b \in \mathbb{Q}^m$, and $c \in \mathbb{Q}^n$. An algorithm for linear programming is said to be strongly polynomial if it satisfies the following two conditions:

1. The number of elementary arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and comparison) performed by the algorithm on the input $(A, b, c)$ is bounded by a polynomial in the dimensions $m$ and $n$ only (independent of the bit-sizes of the numerical entries of $A$, $b$, $c$).

2. The algorithm runs in polynomial space; equivalently, the bit-size of every number occurring in any intermediate computation, when the input is rational, is bounded by a polynomial in the total bit-size of the input.

Decide the following question: Does there exist a strongly polynomial algorithm that, given any instance $(A, b, c)$ of a linear program, correctly solves it (i.e., either finds an optimal solution, reports unboundedness, or reports infeasibility)?
status_search_result: This is a well-known long-standing open problem, listed by Smale (1998) as one of the mathematical problems for the 21st century. No strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programming is known as of 2026; known polynomial algorithms (ellipsoid, interior point) depend on the bit-size of the input. Recent progress (e.g., Tardos's strongly polynomial algorithm for combinatorial LPs, and works by Allamigeon, Dadush, Huiberts, Vegh and others) addresses special cases but the general problem remains open.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Can every convex polyhedron be cut along its edges and unfolded flat to a single, nonoverlapping, simple polygon?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a convex polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space, that is, the boundary of the convex hull of a finite set of points with non-empty interior. The edges and faces of P form its (1- and 2-dimensional) skeleton. An edge unfolding of P is obtained by choosing a spanning tree T of the 1-skeleton of P, cutting P along the edges in T, and then continuously unfolding the resulting development by rotating adjacent faces about their shared (uncut) edges until all faces lie isometrically in a common plane. The unfolding is called a valid net if the images of the faces tile, without overlap, a single simple (connected, non-self-intersecting, simply connected) polygon in the plane.

Question: Does every convex polyhedron admit such a valid edge unfolding? Equivalently, for every convex polyhedron P does there exist a spanning tree of its edges along which P can be cut and unfolded into a single nonoverlapping simple planar polygon?
status_search_result: The question is the classical Dürer unfolding problem, dating back to 1525. As of recent surveys (Ghomi, AMS Notices 2018; "Unfolding Polyhedra," arXiv:1908.07152) and the Open Problem Garden / TOPP entries, it remains open. Partial results are known: every convex polyhedron admits a non-overlapping edge unfolding after a suitable affine transformation, but Dürer's conjecture in its original form is unresolved. A pseudo-edge analogue is known to be false.

original_question: Is there a deterministic, linear-time polygon triangulation algorithm significantly simpler than that of Chazelle [Cha91]? 18

A simple polygon is a closed planar region whose boundary is a simple (non-self-intersecting) closed polygonal curve with n vertices. A triangulation of a simple polygon P is a partition of P into triangles whose vertices are vertices of P. It is known that there exists a deterministic algorithm that, given any simple polygon with n vertices, computes a triangulation of it in O(n) time; however, this algorithm is extremely intricate.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Can the class of3SUM hardproblems be solved in subquadratic time? These problems can be reduced from the problem of determining whether, given three sets of integers,A,B, andCwith total sizen, there are elementsa∈A,b∈B, andc∈Csuch thata+b=c.
self_contained_problem: The 3SUM problem is defined as follows: given three sets of integers $A$, $B$, and $C$ with $|A|+|B|+|C|=n$, decide whether there exist $a\in A$, $b\in B$, $c\in C$ with $a+b=c$. A problem is called 3SUM-hard if 3SUM admits a subquadratic-time reduction to it. The question is: does there exist an algorithm solving 3SUM (and hence the entire class of 3SUM-hard problems) in truly subquadratic time, i.e., in time $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ for some constant $\varepsilon>0$, in the standard (real or word) RAM model?
status_search_result: Grønlund and Pettie (2014) refuted the strict form of the 3SUM conjecture by giving a deterministic $O(n^2/(\log n/\log\log n)^{2/3})$ algorithm, later improved to $O(n^2 (\log\log n)^{O(1)}/\log^2 n)$. They also obtained an $O(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\log n})$ 4-linear decision tree bound. However, whether 3SUM admits a truly subquadratic $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm remains open and is the basis of the modern 3SUM hardness hypothesis in fine-grained complexity. Some special cases (Chan–Lewenstein) are truly subquadratic.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Can a planar convex hull be maintained to support both dynamic updates and queries in logarithmic time? More precisely, is there a data structure supporting insertions and deletions of points and supporting various queries about the convex hull of the current set ofnpoints, all inO(logn) time per operation? Anextreme-point queryasks to find the vertex of the convex hull that is extreme in a given direction. Atangent queryasks to determine whether a given point is interior to the convex hull, and if not, to find the two tangent lines of the convex hull that passes through the given point. Agift-wrapping queryasks to find the two vertices of the convex hull adjacent to a given vertex of the convex hull. Aline-stabbing queryasks to find the two edges of the convex hull (if any) that intersect a given line. (Note that two extreme-point queries suffice to determine whether a line intersects the convex hull, while a linestabbing query determines where exactly the line intersects the convex hull if it does.)
self_contained_problem:
Design a data structure that maintains a dynamic set S of points in the Euclidean plane R^2 under insertions and deletions, while supporting queries on the convex hull conv(S) of the current set. Let n denote the current size of S. The structure must support each of the following operations in O(log n) time per operation (worst-case or amortized):

1. Insert(p): add a point p in R^2 to S.
2. Delete(p): remove a point p from S.
3. Extreme-point query: given a direction vector d in R^2, return the vertex of conv(S) that maximizes the inner product with d.
4. Tangent query: given a query point q in R^2, decide whether q lies in the interior of conv(S); if not, return the two tangent lines to conv(S) through q (equivalently, the two vertices of conv(S) at which these tangents touch).
5. Gift-wrapping query: given a vertex v of conv(S), return the two vertices of conv(S) adjacent to v on the boundary of conv(S).
6. Line-stabbing query: given a line L in R^2, return the (at most two) edges of conv(S) that intersect L, or report that none exist.

Does such a data structure exist, achieving O(log n) time for both updates and all queries?
status_search_result: Brodal and Jacob (FOCS 2002, journal version on arXiv 1902.11169) gave a linear-space data structure maintaining the planar convex hull under insertions and deletions in O(log n) amortized time per update and supporting the listed queries (extreme-point, tangent, neighbor/gift-wrapping, line-stabbing) in O(log n) worst-case time. This matches the lower bound and resolves the question in the amortized setting; achieving fully worst-case O(log n) updates remains a related refinement, but the question as posed (logarithmic per operation) is answered affirmatively.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: Is it possible to construct abinary space partition(BSP) forn disjoint line segments in the plane of size less than Θ(nlogn)?
self_contained_problem:
A binary space partition (BSP) for a set S of n pairwise disjoint (open) line segments in the plane is a recursively defined subdivision of the plane produced as follows. If |S| ≤ 1, the BSP is a single region containing the (at most one) segment. Otherwise, choose a line ℓ that splits the plane into two open half-planes H⁺ and H⁻; the segments of S are clipped by ℓ, producing two new sets S⁺ and S⁻ of segments contained in H⁺ and H⁻ respectively (a segment that crosses ℓ is split into two pieces, while pieces lying on ℓ may be discarded). The BSP is then formed recursively on (H⁺, S⁺) and (H⁻, S⁻). The size of the BSP is the total number of segment pieces produced, equivalently the number of leaves of the recursion tree.

Let f(n) denote the maximum, over all sets S of n disjoint line segments in the plane, of the minimum size of a BSP for S. It is classical that f(n) = O(n log n) and f(n) = Ω(n). Determine the asymptotic growth rate of f(n); in particular, decide whether f(n) = o(n log n), and if so identify the correct order of magnitude.
status_search_result: The problem is resolved. Tóth proved a lower bound of Ω(n log n / log log n) on the worst-case BSP size for n disjoint segments in the plane, and subsequently (in "Binary Plane Partitions for Disjoint Line Segments", Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2011) established a matching upper bound O(n log n / log log n). Thus the answer is yes: one can do strictly better than Θ(n log n), with the tight bound Θ(n log n / log log n).

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: What is the best output-sensitive convex hull algorithm fornpoints inR d?
self_contained_problem:
For a fixed integer dimension $d \geq 2$, consider the problem of computing the convex hull of a set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Let $h$ denote the combinatorial complexity (e.g., total number of faces, or number of vertices) of the convex hull $\mathrm{conv}(S)$. An algorithm is called output-sensitive if its running time is expressed as a function of both the input size $n$ and the output size $h$.

Determine the optimal worst-case time complexity, as a function of $n$ and $h$, of an output-sensitive algorithm that computes the convex hull of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Let $d \geq 5$ be an integer, and let $\mathcal{S} = \{S_1, \dots, S_n\}$ be a collection of $n$ algebraic surfaces (or surface patches) of constant description complexity in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (i.e., each $S_i$ is a semi-algebraic set defined by a bounded number of polynomial equations and inequalities of bounded degree). The vertical decomposition $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{S})$ of $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})$ is the refinement of $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})$ obtained by the following recursive process. In $\mathbb{R}^2$, each cell of the arrangement is decomposed into pseudo-trapezoids by erecting vertical segments (in the $x_2$-direction) from each vertex and from each locally $x_1$-extremal point of the bounding arcs until they hit another arc or extend to infinity. In $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \geq 3$, for each $d$-dimensional cell $C$ of $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})$ and for each point $p$ in the projection of $C$ to the hyperplane $x_d = 0$, one erects the maximal vertical segment in the $x_d$-direction through $p$ contained in $C$; the cell $C$ is partitioned into the pseudo-prisms swept by such segments over each cell of the $(d-1)$-dimensional vertical decomposition of the arrangement induced on $\{x_d = 0\}$ by the projections of the boundary features of $C$. The complexity of $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{S})$ is the total number of cells (of all dimensions) in this decomposition.

Define the flip graph $\mathcal{F}(P)$ to have one node for each tetrahedralization of $P$, with an edge between two nodes whenever the corresponding tetrahedralizations differ by a single bistellar flip.

self_contained_problem:

original_question: What is the maximum number of edges in a thrackle? Athrackleis a planar drawing of a graph ofnvertices by edges which are smooth curves between vertices, with the condition that each pair of edges intersect at exactly one point, and have distinct tangents there. A thrackle is a drawing of a finite simple graph in the plane in which every vertex is represented by a distinct point and every edge is represented by a smooth simple curve joining its two endpoints, such that:
(i) any two edges that share an endpoint have no other point in common (in particular they do not share an interior point), and
(ii) any two edges that do not share an endpoint meet at exactly one point, where they cross transversally (i.e., have distinct tangent lines at the intersection).

Determine the maximum possible number of edges of a thrackle on n vertices. In particular, decide Conway's thrackle conjecture: is it true that every thrackle on n vertices has at most n edges?
status_search_result: Conway's thrackle conjecture (that an n-vertex thrackle has at most n edges) remains open. The known upper bound has been progressively improved from 2n−3 to 3(n−1)/2, then to roughly 1.428n (Fulek–Pach), and most recently to about 1.393n (Xu, 2021). No proof or disproof of the full conjecture is known.

original_question: Which polyhedra are bar-magnet polyhedra? Call a vertexvofPto bealternatingunder mappings of its edges to bar magnets if the incident edges assigns alternating magnetic poles tov in the cyclic order of those edges on the surface aroundv: (N, S, N, S,...). Thus if deg(v) is even, the poles alternate, and if deg(v) is odd, at most two like poles are adjacent in the circular sequence. self_contained_problem:
Let P be a convex polyhedron with vertex set V and edge set E; equivalently, regard P as a 3-connected planar graph together with its planar (spherical) embedding, which determines a cyclic order of the edges incident to each vertex v.

A bar-magnet assignment is a function that assigns to each edge e ∈ E one of the two ordered labelings of its endpoints, either (N, S) or (S, N) (so each edge becomes a "bar magnet" with a North pole at one endpoint and a South pole at the other; equivalently, an orientation of e).

For a vertex v of degree d, read off the labels N or S contributed at v by its incident edges in the cyclic order determined by the embedding around v. Call v alternating if this cyclic sequence of d symbols in {N, S} alternates as much as possible:
 • if d is even, the sequence is strictly alternating (N, S, N, S, ..., N, S);
 • if d is odd, at most one pair of consecutive equal symbols occurs in the cyclic sequence (so there is exactly one position where two like poles are adjacent).

Call P a bar-magnet polyhedron if there exists a bar-magnet assignment under which every vertex of P is alternating.

Problem: Characterize exactly which polyhedra (equivalently, which 3-connected planar embedded graphs) are bar-magnet polyhedra.

original_question: What is the minimum nonzero difference between two sums of square roots of integers? More precisely, find tight upper and lower bounds onr(n, k), the minimum positive value of kX i=1 √ai − kX i=1 p bi 44 wherea i andb i are integers no larger thann. Bounds should be expressed as a function ofnandk. Examples: r(20,2)≈.0002 = √ 10 + √ 11− √ 5− √ 18 r(20,3)≈.000005 = √ 5 + √ 6 + √ 18− √ 4− √ 12− √ 12

For positive integers $n$ and $k$, let
$$r(n,k) = \min\left\{ \left| \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sqrt{a_i} - \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sqrt{b_i} \right| : a_i, b_i \in \{1,2,\dots,n\},\ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sqrt{a_i} \neq \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sqrt{b_i} \right\}.$$
That is, $r(n,k)$ is the smallest possible positive difference between two sums of $k$ square roots of positive integers each bounded by $n$.

Determine tight upper and lower bounds on $r(n,k)$ as a function of $n$ and $k$. In particular, decide whether $\log(1/r(n,k))$ can be bounded above by a polynomial in $k$ and $\log n$.

paper_title: The Open Problems Project
original_question: How many intersections among an arrangement of pseudosegments in the plane must be added as vertices to allow the pseudosegment arrangment to be extended to a pseudoline arrangement? Anarrangement of pseudosegmentsin the plane is a family of finite-length planar curves such that every two curves intersect in at most one point. Anarrangement of pseudolinesin the plane is a family of planar curves that extend to infinity on both ends such that every two curves intersect in at most one point. Only some pseudosegment arrangements can be extendedto pseudoline arrangements. However, if we allow turning intersection points into vertices of the arrangement, thereby subdividing the segments, then it is always possible to make a pseudosegment arrangement extendible. self_contained_problem:
An arrangement of pseudosegments in the plane is a finite family of simple finite-length planar curves such that any two of them intersect in at most one point (and when they meet, they cross transversally). An arrangement of pseudolines in the plane is a finite family of simple planar curves, each unbounded on both ends, such that any two of them intersect in exactly one point (or at most one point, in the non-simple setting). A pseudosegment arrangement is said to be extendible if each pseudosegment can be prolonged at both ends so that the resulting family is a pseudoline arrangement.

Not every pseudosegment arrangement is extendible. However, given any pseudosegment arrangement, one may select a subset S of its intersection points and declare them to be vertices, thereby subdividing each pseudosegment at each chosen intersection into shorter sub-pseudosegments; the resulting refined arrangement (whose pseudosegments are the maximal pieces obtained by this subdivision) is then a new pseudosegment arrangement. It is known that for every pseudosegment arrangement there exists a choice of such S that makes the refined arrangement extendible to a pseudoline arrangement.

Let f(n) denote the smallest integer such that for every arrangement of n pseudosegments in the plane there exists a set of at most f(n) intersection points whose promotion to vertices yields an extendible arrangement. Determine the worst-case asymptotic behavior of f(n) as a function of n.
status_search_result: The problem remains listed in the Open Problems Project as Problem 34. Related work (Arroyo–Bensmail–Richter on extendibility obstructions; results on monotone pseudosegment extension; NP-hardness for cylindrically monotone pseudosegments) addresses adjacent questions but does not establish the worst-case number of vertices that must be added by subdivision to ensure extendibility. No source found resolving the asymptotic bound on f(n).
