paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: Can one define a notion of rank for general Riemannian manifolds that extends the classical rank notion for locally symmetric spaces, and then prove corresponding rigidity theorems for manifolds with higher-rank metrics? More specifically, what rigidity and classification results should hold for higher-rank nonpositively curved manifolds, and how should the still poorly understood rank-1 manifolds of non-positive curvature be characterized?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a complete Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature. For a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ in $M$, define the rank of $\gamma$ to be the dimension of the space of parallel Jacobi fields along $\gamma$, and define the rank of $M$ to be the minimum of the ranks of all of its geodesics. Thus $M$ has rank at least $2$ ("higher rank") if and only if every geodesic in the universal cover lies in a flat totally geodesic strip isometric to a Euclidean half-plane of dimension $\ge 2$; otherwise $M$ is said to have rank $1$.

The following intertwined problems are posed:

(a) Formulate a notion of "rank" for general (not necessarily nonpositively curved) Riemannian manifolds that specializes, on closed locally symmetric spaces of noncompact type, to the classical algebraic rank (the real rank of the isometry group), and prove rigidity theorems characterizing closed Riemannian manifolds of "higher rank" in this generalized sense.

(b) For closed Riemannian manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature: classify, up to isometry, those of higher rank beyond the known irreducible case (where, by the higher rank rigidity theorem, any closed irreducible nonpositively curved manifold of rank $\ge 2$ is locally symmetric of noncompact type).

(c) Provide a structural characterization of closed rank-$1$ manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature, describing the extent to which their geometry, dynamics of the geodesic flow, and topology resemble those of strictly negatively curved manifolds.
status_search_result: The higher-rank rigidity theorem for closed irreducible nonpositively curved manifolds (Ballmann; Burns–Spatzier) resolves part (b) in the irreducible case, and various extensions (foliations, no focal points, convex real projective manifolds, hyperbolic rank rigidity) have been proved. However, Yau's broader call for a general notion of rank and corresponding rigidity, as well as a structural classification of rank-$1$ nonpositively curved manifolds, remains an active and largely open research program.

paper_title: Open Problems list
original_question: For a complex Kähler manifold, what is the precise relationship between the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric and algebro-geometric stability of the manifold? In particular, under what hypotheses does the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric force the tangent bundle or the manifold itself to be stable, and conversely when does stability guarantee the existence of such a special metric?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact complex Kähler manifold. A Kähler metric $\omega$ on $X$ is called Kähler–Einstein if its Ricci form satisfies $\mathrm{Ric}(\omega) = \lambda\,\omega$ for some real constant $\lambda$. When $X$ is polarised by an ample line bundle $L$, one has the algebro-geometric notion of K-(poly/uniform)stability of the pair $(X,L)$, defined via the sign of the Donaldson–Futaki invariant (or, equivalently in the uniform setting, via the non-Archimedean Mabuchi functional) on all test configurations for $(X,L)$. A holomorphic vector bundle $E\to X$ is said to be slope-stable (with respect to a Kähler class) if for every coherent subsheaf $F\subset E$ with $0<\mathrm{rank}(F)<\mathrm{rank}(E)$ one has $\mu(F)<\mu(E)$, where $\mu(\cdot)$ denotes the slope.

Determine the precise relationship between the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric on $X$ and the algebro-geometric stability of $X$. Specifically:

(a) Under what hypotheses on $X$ does the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric imply that the tangent bundle $T_X$ is slope-stable, or that $X$ itself (with a suitable polarisation) is K-stable (resp. K-polystable, resp. uniformly K-stable)?

(b) Conversely, under what hypotheses does an algebro-geometric stability condition on $(X,L)$ guarantee the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric (or, more generally, a constant scalar curvature Kähler metric) in the class $c_1(L)$?

Formulate and prove a sharp equivalence (the Yau–Tian–Donaldson correspondence) between such metric and stability conditions for general polarised Kähler manifolds.
status_search_result: The Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture has been fully resolved in the Fano setting: Chen–Donaldson–Sun (and subsequent proofs by Datar–Székelyhidi, Chen–Sun–Wang, Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson) proved that a smooth Fano manifold admits a Kähler–Einstein metric iff it is K-polystable, and the uniform version is known for Q-Fano varieties. For general polarised manifolds (the cscK version), one direction is known (Stoppa: existence of cscK implies K-polystability), but the reverse implication — that an algebraic stability condition implies existence of a cscK/Kähler–Einstein metric — remains open in general.

original_question: Does the smooth 4-sphere S^4 admit any exotic smooth structure; equivalently, is there a smooth manifold homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to S^4?
self_contained_problem:
A smooth structure on a topological manifold $M$ is a maximal atlas of charts whose transition maps are $C^\infty$. Two smooth manifolds are said to be diffeomorphic if there exists a bijection between them that is $C^\infty$ in both directions with respect to their smooth structures. Let $S^4 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^5 : \|x\| = 1\}$ denote the standard 4-sphere with its standard smooth structure inherited from $\mathbb{R}^5$. An exotic smooth structure on $S^4$ is a smooth structure on the topological manifold $S^4$ that is not diffeomorphic to the standard one. Equivalently, an exotic $S^4$ is a smooth 4-manifold that is homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to the standard $S^4$.

Question: Does there exist a smooth 4-manifold that is homeomorphic to $S^4$ but not diffeomorphic to the standard smooth $S^4$?
status_search_result: The smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4 — equivalently, the question of whether $S^4$ admits an exotic smooth structure — is widely regarded as one of the major open problems in geometric topology. As of 2026, no exotic smooth structure on $S^4$ has been confirmed, and no proof of its nonexistence is known; several candidate exotic 4-spheres have been proposed and subsequently shown to be standard or remain undetermined.

original_question: Is Thompson group F amenable?
self_contained_problem:
Thompson's group $F$ is the group of orientation-preserving piecewise-linear homeomorphisms of the closed interval $[0,1]$ such that each homeomorphism is differentiable except at finitely many dyadic rational numbers (numbers of the form $p/2^q$ with $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$), and on each maximal subinterval of differentiability the slope is an integer power of $2$. Equivalently, $F$ admits the finite presentation
$$F=\langle A,B \mid [AB^{-1},A^{-1}BA]=1,\ [AB^{-1},A^{-2}BA^{2}]=1\rangle.$$
A discrete group $G$ is called amenable if there exists a finitely additive probability measure $\mu$ on the power set of $G$ that is invariant under left translation, i.e. $\mu(gE)=\mu(E)$ for every $g\in G$ and every $E\subseteq G$. Equivalently (by Kesten's criterion), $G$ generated by a finite symmetric set $S$ is amenable iff the norm of $\sum_{s\in S} \lambda(s)$ in $B(\ell^2(G))$ (where $\lambda$ is the left regular representation) equals $|S|$.

Question: Is Thompson's group $F$ amenable?
status_search_result: The amenability of Thompson's group F is a well-known long-standing open problem. Several claimed proofs (both for amenability and non-amenability) have appeared but have been found to contain errors. Recent surveys (e.g., a 2023 state-of-the-art arXiv survey) still describe the problem as open, with computational evidence inconclusive.

original_question: If S is a subset of the natural numbers and the harmonic sum over S, namely sum_{s in S} 1/s, diverges, must S contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length?
self_contained_problem: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of positive integers such that the series $\sum_{s \in S} \frac{1}{s}$ diverges. Must $S$ necessarily contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length? That is, for every positive integer $k$, do there exist $a, d \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d \geq 1$ such that $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+(k-1)d$ all belong to $S$?
status_search_result: This is the well-known Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions. It remains open in general. The case k=3 was proved by Bloom and Sisask (2020), giving the first nontrivial case. The general conjecture for arbitrary k is still unresolved. The celebrated Green–Tao theorem (2004) establishes the conclusion for the specific set of primes, but does not resolve the conjecture.

original_question: Is there an algorithm that, given finitely many polynomial equations with rational coefficients, decides whether those equations have a rational solution?

original_question: Does a Moore graph of degree 57 and diameter 2 exist?
self_contained_problem:
A Moore graph is a regular graph that achieves the Moore bound: for a graph of maximum degree $k$ and diameter $d$, the number of vertices is at most
$$1 + k\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}(k-1)^i.$$
Equivalently, a Moore graph of degree $k$ and diameter $2$ is a $k$-regular graph on $k^2+1$ vertices with girth $5$ (every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbor, and every two adjacent vertices have no common neighbor).

It is known that a Moore graph of diameter $2$ can exist only for degree $k \in \{2, 3, 7, 57\}$. Examples are known for $k=2$ (the $5$-cycle), $k=3$ (the Petersen graph), and $k=7$ (the Hoffman–Singleton graph).

Question: Does there exist a Moore graph of degree $57$ and diameter $2$, i.e., a $57$-regular graph on $3250$ vertices with girth $5$?
status_search_result: The existence of a Moore graph of degree 57 and diameter 2 (on 3250 vertices) remains a famous open problem, unresolved for over 60 years. A 2020 arXiv preprint claiming non-existence was shown to be incorrect, and a 2022 note explicitly affirms the problem is still open. Recent works (2024–2025) continue partial investigations, e.g., ruling out certain cyclic constructions and enumerating potential subgraphs, but neither existence nor non-existence is established.

original_question: Are the Mordell-Weil ranks of elliptic curves over Q uniformly bounded; that is, does there exist a constant R such that every elliptic curve E over Q satisfies rank(E) <= R?
self_contained_problem:
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e., a smooth projective curve of genus one with a specified $\mathbb{Q}$-rational point, given (after a change of variables) by a Weierstrass equation $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$ and nonzero discriminant. original_question: A problem on explicit constructions ($100) Give a constructive proof for r(n, n) > (1 + c)n for some constant c > 0. The best known constructive lower bound nc log n/ log log n is due to Frankl and Wilson [144]. 1 In this paper, by a graph we mean a simple loopless graph, unless otherwise specified.
self_contained_problem:
For integers $s, t \geq 2$, let $r(s,t)$ denote the diagonal Ramsey number, defined as the smallest integer $N$ such that every red/blue edge-coloring of the complete graph $K_N$ contains a monochromatic clique on $s$ red-colored edges or $t$ blue-colored edges; in particular $r(n,n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every graph on $N$ vertices contains either a clique of size $n$ or an independent set of size $n$.

It is known by a probabilistic argument of Erdős that $r(n,n) > (\sqrt{2})^{n}$, and more generally that $r(n,n) \geq (1+c_0)^{n}$ for some absolute constant $c_0 > 0$. However, the probabilistic proof gives no explicit graph achieving this bound.

Problem. Exhibit a deterministic, explicit construction of a sequence of graphs $G_n$ on $N_n$ vertices, together with a constant $c > 0$, such that:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $G_n$ contains neither a clique of size $n$ nor an independent set of size $n$, and
  \item $N_n \geq (1+c)^{n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$,
\end{enumerate}
so that the explicit construction certifies $r(n,n) > (1+c)^{n}$. Here "explicit" means the adjacency relation of $G_n$ is computable by an algorithm running in time polynomial in $N_n$.

Equivalently, give an explicit construction of a graph $G$ on $N$ vertices whose largest clique and largest independent set both have size $O(\log N)$.
status_search_result: The problem remains open in its strict exponential form. The Frankl–Wilson construction gave explicit Ramsey graphs avoiding cliques and independent sets of size $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt{\log N \log\log N}))$. This was improved by Barak–Rao–Shaltiel–Wigderson, Cohen, Chattopadhyay–Zuckerman, and most notably by Xin Li (2023), who achieved explicit $N$-vertex graphs with clique/independent number $(\log N)^{O(1)}$. These advances yield $r(n,n) > 2^{n^{1/C}}$ explicitly for some constant $C \geq 1$, which is super-polynomial but still falls short of the exponential bound $(1+c)^n$ required by Erdős's question. Thus the original $\$100$ problem is partially solved but not fully resolved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Linear Ramsey bounds (proposed by Burr, Erdo"s, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp [37]) Suppose a graph G satisfies the property that every subgraph of G on p vertices has at most 2p − 3 edges. Is it true that r(G, G) ≤ cn? In general, the problem of interest is to characterize graphs whose Ramsey number r(G, G) is linear.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite simple graph on n vertices such that every subgraph of G on p vertices has at most 2p − 3 edges (in particular, G is 2-degenerate). The diagonal Ramsey number r(G,G) is the smallest integer N such that every 2-coloring of the edges of the complete graph K_N contains a monochromatic copy of G.

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every graph G satisfying the above sparsity condition, r(G,G) ≤ c·n.

(b) More generally, characterize the classes of graphs G for which the Ramsey number r(G,G) is linear in the number of vertices of G.
status_search_result: Part (a) is a special case of the Burr–Erdős conjecture that every d-degenerate graph on n vertices has Ramsey number linear in n. The conjecture was proved by Choongbum Lee in "Ramsey numbers of degenerate graphs" (Annals of Mathematics, 2017), establishing that r(G,G) ≤ c_d · n for every d-degenerate graph G on n vertices. Since the hypothesis "every p-vertex subgraph has ≤ 2p−3 edges" implies 2-degeneracy, Lee's theorem resolves (a) affirmatively. The more general characterization problem in (b) — exactly which graph classes have linear Ramsey numbers — remains an active topic, but the principal conjectured sufficient condition (bounded degeneracy) is now a theorem.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A size Ramsey problem for bounded degree graphs (proposed by Beck and Erdo"s [189]) For a graph G on n vertices with bounded degree, prove or disprove that r̂(G) ≤ cn. The case for paths was proved by Beck [19] and the case for cycles was proved by Haxell, Kohayakawa, and QLuczak [162]. Friedman and Pip- penger [145] settled the case for any bounded degree tree.
self_contained_problem:
For a graph H, the size-Ramsey number r̂(H) is the smallest integer m such that there exists a graph G with m edges with the property that every 2-coloring of the edges of G contains a monochromatic copy of H.

Question: Does there exist a constant c > 0 (possibly depending on the degree bound Δ) such that for every positive integer n and every graph H on n vertices with maximum degree at most Δ, one has
   r̂(H) ≤ c·n ?

Equivalently, prove or disprove that the size-Ramsey number of every bounded-degree graph on n vertices is linear in n.
status_search_result: The question, posed by Beck and Erdős, was answered negatively by Rödl and Szemerédi, who constructed graphs of maximum degree 3 on n vertices with size-Ramsey number at least c·n·(log n)^{1/60}, showing that the linear upper bound fails. Subsequent works (e.g., Tikhomirov 2022) have strengthened the lower bound to c·n·exp(c√(log n)). Thus the conjectured linear bound is disproved, though determining the correct order of magnitude remains open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on the Turán number for complete bipartite graphs Prove that t(n, Kr,r ) > cn2−1/r where c is a constant depending on r (but independent of n). An upper bound for t(n, Kr,r ) of the same order was proved by Ko"vári, Sós and Turán [170] and Erdo"s independently. This long standing problem is well known as the problem of Zarankiewicz, first considered by Zarankiewicz [216] in 1951. However, it is included in the favorite problems of Erdo"s [79], who proposed many variations of this problem. The above conjecture is true for r = 2 and 3 (see [124]) and unsolved for r ≥ 4. The lower bound of t(n, Kr,r ) > cn2−2/(r+1) can be proved by probabilistic methods [131].
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers n and r, let t(n, K_{r,r}) denote the Zarankiewicz extremal number: the maximum number of edges in a simple graph on n vertices that contains no copy of the complete bipartite graph K_{r,r} as a subgraph. The Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem provides the upper bound t(n, K_{r,r}) ≤ C_r · n^{2 - 1/r} for some constant C_r > 0 depending only on r.

Prove or disprove the following matching lower bound: for every integer r ≥ 2 there exists a constant c_r > 0 (depending only on r) such that for all sufficiently large n,
    t(n, K_{r,r}) ≥ c_r · n^{2 - 1/r}.

The cases r = 2 and r = 3 are known. Establish the conjecture (or refute it) for all r ≥ 4.
status_search_result: The Zarankiewicz problem for K_{r,r} with r ≥ 4 remains open. The tight bound is known only for r = 2 (Reiman/Kővári–Sós–Turán) and r = 3 (Brown 1966). Kollár–Rónyai–Szabó (1996) and Alon–Rónyai–Szabó (1999) achieve the tight order n^{2−1/r} only for K_{r,s} with s ≥ (r−1)!+1. Matching the upper bound for K_{r,r}, r ≥ 4, is a well-known open problem.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Conjecture (proposed by Erdo"s and Simonovits [129], 1984) If a bipartite graph H contains a subgraph H  with minimum degree greater than r, then t(n, H) ≥ cn2−1/r+ for some  > 0.
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $H$, let $t(n,H)$ (also denoted $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$) denote the Turán number of $H$, i.e., the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices that does not contain $H$ as a subgraph.

Conjecture: Let $r \ge 1$ be an integer. If $H$ is a bipartite graph that contains a subgraph $H'$ with minimum degree strictly greater than $r$, then there exist constants $c > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
$$t(n,H) \;\ge\; c\, n^{2 - 1/r + \varepsilon}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Determine whether this conjecture is true.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on the exponent of a bipartite graph (proposed by Erdo"s and Simonovits [129], 1984) For all rationals 1 < p/q < 2, there exists a bipartite graph G such t(n, G) = Θ(np/q ).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph H, let ex(n, H) denote the Turán number of H, i.e., the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex simple graph that contains no copy of H as a subgraph. A real number r is called a Turán exponent if there exists a graph H such that ex(n, H) = Θ(n^r), meaning there exist positive constants c_1, c_2 and an integer n_0 such that c_1 n^r ≤ ex(n, H) ≤ c_2 n^r for all n ≥ n_0.

Prove or disprove: for every rational number p/q with 1 < p/q < 2, there exists a bipartite graph G such that ex(n, G) = Θ(n^{p/q}).
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in its original single-graph form. Bukh and Conlon (2018) proved a family version: for every rational r ∈ [1,2) there is a finite family of bipartite graphs with Turán number Θ(n^r). For individual bipartite graphs, only special families of rationals are known to be realized (e.g., 1+1/k, 2-1/k, 2-2/(2k+1), and rationals 1+p/q with q > p^2 by Jiang–Qiu, plus further classes obtained via subdivisions and related constructions). No full resolution has been announced.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Conversely, is it true that for every bipartite graph G there is a rational exponent r = r(G) such that t(n, G) = Θ(nr )?
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $G$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n,G)$ denote the Turán number of $G$, i.e., the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices that contains no copy of $G$ as a subgraph. It is known that if $G$ is not bipartite then $\mathrm{ex}(n,G) = \Theta(n^2)$, while if $G$ is bipartite then $\mathrm{ex}(n,G) = o(n^2)$.

Prove or disprove the following: for every bipartite graph $G$ (with at least one cycle), there exists a rational number $r = r(G) \in [1,2)$ such that
$$\mathrm{ex}(n,G) = \Theta(n^{r}).$$
status_search_result: The rational exponents conjecture of Erdős and Simonovits remains open. Bukh and Conlon (2018) made major progress by showing that every rational in (1,2) is realized as a Turán exponent of a finite family of graphs, and Kang–Kim–Liu (2018, 2020) and others have established new individual rational exponents, but the conjecture for single bipartite graphs is not resolved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A Turán problem for even cycles (Proposed by Erdo"s [70]) Prove that t(n, C2k ) ≥ cn1+1/k . A lower bound of order n1+1/(2k−1) can be proved by probabilistic methods [131]. The bipartite Ramanujan graph [180, 186] gives t(n, C2k ) ≥ n1+2/3k .
self_contained_problem:
For integers $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 2$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k})$ denote the Turán number of the cycle $C_{2k}$, that is, the maximum number of edges in a simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no cycle of length $2k$ as a subgraph. It is known (Bondy–Simonovits) that 
$$\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) \leq c_k\, n^{1+1/k}$$
for some constant $c_k > 0$ depending only on $k$. Matching lower bounds of the form 
$$\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) \geq c\, n^{1+1/k}$$
(for some absolute constant $c > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$) are known only for $k = 2, 3, 5$, via explicit algebraic/geometric constructions (generalized quadrangles, hexagons, and Ramanujan/incidence-type graphs).

Prove (or disprove) that for every integer $k \geq 2$ there exists a constant $c = c(k) > 0$ such that 
$$\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) \geq c\, n^{1+1/k}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Equivalently, settle the conjecture for all $k \notin \{2,3,5\}$ (the first open case being $k = 4$, i.e.\ the Turán number of $C_8$).
status_search_result: The conjectured lower bound $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_{2k}) \geq c\, n^{1+1/k}$ is known to hold only for $k=2,3,5$ (via generalized polygons / Benson-type constructions). For all other $k$, including $k=4$, the best known lower bounds remain of weaker order such as $n^{1+2/(3k-3)}$ (Lazebnik–Ustimenko–Woldar) or $n^{1+1/(2k-1)}$ (probabilistic). Current surveys and recent literature continue to list the problem as open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on Turán numbers for an n-cube (proposed by Erdo"s and Simonovits [130], 1970) Let Qk denote an k-cube on 2k vertices. Determine t(n, Qk ). In particular, determine t(n, Q3 ). Erdo"s and Simonovits [130] proved that t(n, Q3 ) ≤ cn8/5 . No better lower bound than cn3/2 is known.
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $H$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n, H)$ (the Turán number of $H$) denote the maximum number of edges in a simple graph on $n$ vertices that does not contain $H$ as a subgraph. For an integer $k \ge 1$, let $Q_k$ denote the $k$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^k$ and in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if they differ in exactly one coordinate; thus $Q_k$ has $2^k$ vertices and $k\,2^{k-1}$ edges.

(a) Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\mathrm{ex}(n, Q_k)$ as $n \to \infty$ for each fixed $k \ge 3$.

(b) In particular, determine the asymptotic order of $\mathrm{ex}(n, Q_3)$. It is known that 
$$c_1 n^{3/2} \le \mathrm{ex}(n, Q_3) \le c_2 n^{8/5}$$
for some positive constants $c_1, c_2$ and all sufficiently large $n$. Close the gap between these bounds, or determine the correct exponent $\alpha$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n, Q_3) = \Theta(n^\alpha)$ (or more refined asymptotics if possible).

The upper bound $\mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)=O(n^{8/5})$ from 1970 is still the best known, and the best known lower bound is $\Omega(n^{3/2})$. Recent work (Janzer, and Sudakov–Tomon, ca. 2020–2023) gave the first power-type improvement of the bound $O(n^{2-1/d})$ for $Q_d$ with $d \ge 4$, but for $Q_3$ the 8/5 bound has not been improved and the exact exponent is still unknown.

For a graph $H$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ denote the Turán number of $H$, i.e., the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices that contains no copy of $H$ as a subgraph. Prove or disprove the following statement: there exists a constant $c=c(H)>0$ such that 
$$\mathrm{ex}(n,H) < c\,n^{3/2}$$
for all $n$, if and only if $H$ does not contain any subgraph in which every vertex has degree at least $3$ (equivalently, $H$ is $2$-degenerate).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Turán numbers in an n-cube ($100, from the 70’s, see [84]) Let f2k (n) denote the maximum number of edges in a subgraph of Qn containing no C2k . Prove or disprove f4 (n) = ( + o(1))n2n−1 .
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_n$ denote the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^n$ with two vertices adjacent if and only if they differ in exactly one coordinate; thus $Q_n$ has $2^n$ vertices and $n\,2^{n-1}$ edges. For an integer $k \ge 2$, let $f_{2k}(n)$ denote the maximum number of edges in a subgraph of $Q_n$ that contains no cycle of length $2k$ as a subgraph.

Prove or disprove the following statement:
$$f_4(n) = \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + o(1)\right) n\, 2^{n-1} \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$

Equivalently, show that $\sigma_4 := \lim_{n \to \infty} f_4(n) / (n\,2^{n-1})$ equals $\tfrac{1}{2}$ (the existence of this limit being known).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on the octahedron graph (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal, Sós and Szemerédi [113]) Let G be a graph on n vertices which contains no K2,2,2 and whose largest independent set has o(n) vertices. Is it true that the number of edges of G is o(n2 )? Erdo"s and Simonovits [127] determined the Turán number for the octahe- dron graph K2,2,2 as well as other Platonic graphs [206, 203].
self_contained_problem:
Let $K_{2,2,2}$ denote the octahedron graph, i.e. the complete tripartite graph with three parts of size $2$. For a graph $G$, let $\alpha(G)$ denote the size of a largest independent set in $G$.

original_question: A problem on regular induced subgraphs (Proposed by Erdo"s, Fajtlowicz and Staton [82]) Let f (n) be the largest integer for which every graph of n vertices contains a regular induced subgraph of ≥ f (n) vertices. Ramsey’s theorem implies that a graph of n vertices contains a trivial subgraph, i.e., a complete or empty subgraph of c log n vertices. Conjecture: f (n)/ log n → ∞. Note that f (5) = 3 (since if a graph on 5 vertices contains no trivial subgraph of 3 vertices then it must be a pentagon). f (7) = 4 was proved by Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton [137] and also by Erdo"s and Kohayakawa (unpublished). McKay (personal communication) found that f (16) = 5 and f (17) = 6. Bollobás observed that f (n) < n1/2+ for n suﬃciently large (unpublished).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$, an induced subgraph $H$ of $G$ is called regular if every vertex of $H$ has the same degree in $H$ (this includes complete and empty induced subgraphs as trivial examples). For each positive integer $n$, define
$$ f(n) = \min_{|V(G)|=n} \, \max\{\, |V(H)| : H \text{ is a regular induced subgraph of } G \,\}, $$
that is, $f(n)$ is the largest integer such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $f(n)$ vertices. By Ramsey's theorem one has $f(n) \ge c \log n$ for some absolute constant $c>0$.

Prove or disprove the conjecture: 
$$\frac{f(n)}{\log n} \longrightarrow \infty \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture of Erdős, Fajtlowicz, and Staton that f(n)/log n → ∞ remains open. Known upper bounds have improved over time: Bollobás observed f(n) ≤ n^{1/2+o(1)}, Alon–Krivelevich–Sudakov improved this to n^{1/2}(log n)^{O(1)}, and further refinements give f(n) ≪ n^{1/2}; however, no lower bound asymptotically larger than the Ramsey bound c log n is known.

original_question: A problem of Erdo"s and McKay [82], 1994 ($100) Let f (n, c) denote the largest integer m such that a graph G on n vertices containing no clique or independent set of size c log n must contain an induced subgraph with exactly i edges for each i, 0 < i ≤ m. Prove or disprove that f (n, c) ≥ n2 . McKay wrote, “It is easy to get bounds of the form f (n, c) ≥ c log n, and Paul had a more complicated way to prove a bound f (n) ≥ c (log n)2 , but I cannot remember it.” Calkin, Frieze and McKay [42] proved that a random graph with pn2 edges, for a constant p, contains an induced subgraph with exactly i edges for each i, for i ranging from 0 up to (1 − )pn2 .
self_contained_problem:
For a graph $G$, let $\omega(G)$ denote the clique number and $\alpha(G)$ the independence number. For constants $c>0$ and integers $n\ge 2$, define $f(n,c)$ to be the largest integer $m$ such that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices satisfying $\omega(G) < c\log n$ and $\alpha(G) < c\log n$ contains, for each integer $i$ with $0 \le i \le m$, an induced subgraph having exactly $i$ edges.

Prove or disprove the following: for every $c>0$ there exists $\delta = \delta(c) > 0$ such that
$$f(n,c) \ge \delta\, n^2$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Equivalently, show that for every constant $C>0$ there exists $\delta_C>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph $G$ with no clique or independent set of size $C\log n$ contains, for every integer $x$ with $0\le x\le \delta_C n^2$, an induced subgraph with exactly $x$ edges.
status_search_result: Recent work on anticoncentration in Ramsey graphs by Kwan, Sah, Sauermann and Sawhney resolves the Erdős–McKay conjecture, establishing the conjectured lower bound $f(n,c)\ge \delta_c n^2$. A bipartite version was also proved by Long and Ploscaru. The problem is therefore reported as solved.

Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices. Suppose that for every subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ with $|S| = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, the induced subgraph $G[S]$ has more than $n^2/50$ edges. Prove (or disprove) that $G$ must contain a triangle.

status_search_result: The conjecture appears to still be open in its original form. Krivelevich established the weaker bound $n^2/36$ (with $n/2$ vertices). paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: The problem of Erdo"s and Lovász [69] Suppose a graph G is k-chromatic and contains no Kk . Let a and b denote two integers satisfying a, b ≥ 2 and a+b = k+1. Do there exist two disjoint subgraphs of G of chromatic numbers a and b, respectively? The original question of Erdo"s is for the case k = 5, a = b = 3, which was proved aﬃrmatively by Brown and Jung [34]. Several small cases have been solved (for more discussion, see [158]). Of special interest is the following case for a = 2: Suppose the chromatic number of G decreases by 2 by removing any two vertices joining by an edge. Must G be the complete graph?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with chromatic number $\chi(G) = k$, and suppose $G$ contains no clique on $k$ vertices (i.e., $K_k \not\subseteq G$). Let $a, b$ be integers with $a, b \geq 2$ and $a + b = k + 1$. 

Question: Must there exist two vertex-disjoint subgraphs $G_1, G_2$ of $G$ with $\chi(G_1) = a$ and $\chi(G_2) = b$?

In addition, consider the following special case (corresponding to $a = 2$): suppose $G$ is a graph such that for every edge $uv$ of $G$, the chromatic number satisfies $\chi(G - \{u, v\}) \leq \chi(G) - 2$. Must $G$ be a complete graph?
status_search_result: The general conjecture (the Erdős–Lovász Tihany conjecture) remains open. For arbitrary graphs it is known only for the pairs (a,b) ∈ {(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5)}: (2,3) and (3,3) by Brown–Jung (1969), (2,4) by Mozhan and Stiebitz independently (1987), and (3,4) and (3,5) by Stiebitz (1988). It has also been confirmed for restricted graph classes, including line graphs, quasi-line graphs, graphs with independence number 2, and certain claw-free graphs (e.g., for the pair (3,10)).

original_question: A conjecture on strong chromatic index (proposed by Erdo"s and Nešetřil [76] 1985) The strong chromatic index χ∗ (G) of a graph G is the least number r so that the edges of G can be colored in r colors in such a way that any two adjacent vertices in G are not incident to edges of the same color. Suppose G has maximum degree k. Is it true that χ∗ (G) ≤ 5k 2 /4 if k is even and χ∗ (G) ≤ 5k 2 /4 − k/2 + 1/4 if k is odd? This conjecture is open for k ≥ 4 while the cases of k ≤ 3 are solved by Anderson [13] and Horák, Qing and Trotter [156]. Chung, Gyárfás, Trotter and Tuza [56] proved that if G contains no induced 2K2 , then G has at most 5k 2 /4 edges.

For a simple graph $G$, the strong chromatic index $\chi'_s(G)$ is the least integer $r$ such that the edges of $G$ admit a proper edge coloring with $r$ colors in which any two edges that are either adjacent or joined by an edge receive distinct colors (equivalently, every color class is an induced matching of $G$). $$\chi'_s(G) \le \tfrac{5k^2}{4} \quad \text{if } k \text{ is even}, \qquad \chi'_s(G) \le \tfrac{5k^2}{4} - \tfrac{k}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4} \quad \text{if } k \text{ is odd}.$$
The cases $k \le 3$ are known to hold; the problem is to settle all remaining cases $k \ge 4$.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Nešetřil strong chromatic index conjecture remains open for maximum degree k ≥ 4. Known unconditional progress includes asymptotic upper bounds of the form cΔ² with c < 5/4 (Molloy–Reed and subsequent improvements down to roughly 1.772Δ²), and bounds for specific small degrees (e.g., 21 colors suffice for Δ = 4 by Huang–Santana–Yu), as well as confirmations for restricted classes like K₁,ₜ-free graphs with Δ ≥ 12. The full conjecture has not been resolved.

original_question: A problem on anti-Ramsey graphs (proposed by Burr, Erdo"s, Graham and Sós [39]) For a graph G, determine the least integer r = f (n, e, G) so that there is some graph H on n vertices and e edges which can be r-edge-colored such that all edges of every copy of G in H have different colors. It seems to be a diﬃcult problem to get good bounds for f (n, e, G) for a general graph G (see [39]). Even for special cases, there are large gaps between known bounds. For example, it was shown in [39, 38] that f (n, e, C5 ) ≥ cn n for e = (1/4 + )n2 and f (n, e, C5 ) = O(n2 / log n) for e = (1/2 − )n2 . √ Also, f (n, e, P4 ) > cn n for e = n2 and f (n, e, P4 ) ≤ n for n = n / exp(c log n). Covering and packing
self_contained_problem:
For a fixed graph $G$ and positive integers $n,e$, let $f(n,e,G)$ denote the least integer $r$ such that there exists a graph $H$ on $n$ vertices with $e$ edges admitting an edge-coloring using $r$ colors in which every copy of $G$ in $H$ is rainbow (i.e., all of its edges receive pairwise distinct colors).

Determine, or give matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds for, $f(n,e,G)$. In particular, close the gaps in the following two cases:

(a) For $G = C_5$ (the 5-cycle): it is known that $f(n,e,C_5) \ge c\, n\sqrt{n}$ when $e = (\tfrac14+\varepsilon)n^2$, and $f(n,e,C_5) = O(n^2/\log n)$ when $e = (\tfrac12-\varepsilon)n^2$. Determine the correct order of magnitude of $f(n,e,C_5)$ across this range.

(b) For $G = P_4$ (the path on $4$ vertices): it is known that $f(n,e,P_4) > c'\, n\sqrt{n}$ when $e = \varepsilon n^2$, and $f(n,e,P_4) \le n$ when $e = n^2/\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})$. Determine the correct order of magnitude of $f(n,e,P_4)$.
status_search_result: Recent work has resolved the asymptotic behavior of $f(n,e,C_{2k+1})$ for odd cycles with $k \ge 4$ (and more generally established the asymptotic $f(n,e,C_{2k+1}) = e/2 + (n/2)\sqrt{e - n^2/4} + o(n^2)$ in the dense regime), confirming a conjecture of Burr–Erdős–Graham–Sós. However, the specific cases $G=C_5$ and $G=P_4$ across the full edge ranges described above, and the general problem for arbitrary $G$, still exhibit substantial gaps between known upper and lower bounds, so the problem remains only partially solved.

original_question: A conjecture on covering by C4 ’s (proposed by Erdo"s and Faudree [88]) Suppose a graph G has 4n vertices with minimum degree at least 2n. Then G has n vertex-disjoint C4 ’s.
self_contained_problem: Let n be a positive integer and let G be a simple graph on 4n vertices such that every vertex of G has degree at least 2n. Prove or disprove: G contains n pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles of length 4 (i.e., n vertex-disjoint copies of C_4 whose vertex sets partition the vertex set of G).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on clique covering and clique partition (proposed by Erdo"s, Faudree and Ordman [92]) The clique covering number cc(G) of G is the least number of cliques that covers the graph. The clique partition number cp(G) is the least number of cliques that partition the edge set of G. Here Gn denotes a graph on n vertices. Determine the largest value c such that cp(Gn ) > cn2 cc(Gn ) for an infinite family of graphs Gn . An example was given in [92] with c = 1/64. Is there a sequence of graphs Gn such that cp(Gn ) − cc(Gn ) = n2 /4 + O(n)? In [40] it was shown cp(Gn ) − cc(Gn ) = n2 /4 − n3/2 /2 + n/4 + O(1).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A clique covering of $G$ is a collection of cliques of $G$ whose union contains every edge of $G$ at least once; the clique covering number $\mathrm{cc}(G)$ is the minimum cardinality of such a collection. A clique partition of $G$ is a collection of cliques of $G$ such that every edge of $G$ lies in exactly one clique; the clique partition number $\mathrm{cp}(G)$ is the minimum cardinality of such a collection. Always $\mathrm{cc}(G) \le \mathrm{cp}(G)$, and for any graph on $n$ vertices $\mathrm{cp}(G) \le \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$.

Let $G_n$ denote a graph on $n$ vertices.

(a) Determine the largest constant $c$ with the property that there exists an infinite family of graphs $\{G_n\}$ satisfying
$$\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) > c\, n^2$$
for all $n$ in the family. (A construction is known achieving $c = 1/64$.)

(b) Does there exist a sequence of graphs $\{G_n\}$ such that
$$\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) = \frac{n^2}{4} + O(n)\,? $$
(A known construction achieves $\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) = \frac{n^2}{4} - \frac{n^{3/2}}{2} + \frac{n}{4} + O(1)$.)
status_search_result: The problem originates from work of Erdős, Faudree, and Ordman on clique partitions and clique coverings. Subsequent work, including a thesis by Cavers on clique partitions and coverings of graphs, discusses constructions yielding gaps of order $n^2/4 - n^{3/2}/2 + n/4 + O(1)$, but no source found establishes the exact optimal constant $c$ or resolves whether $\mathrm{cp}(G_n) - \mathrm{cc}(G_n) = n^2/4 + O(n)$ is attainable. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: The ascending subgraph decomposition problem (proposed by Alavi, Boals, Erdo"s, Chartrand and Oellermann [5]) Suppose G is a graph with n(n + 1)/2 edges. Prove that G can be edge- partitioned into subgraphs Gi with i edges such that Gi is isomorphic to a subgraph of Gi+1 for i = 1, . . . , n − 1. A special case is the decomposition of star forests into stars (which is the so-called suitcase problem of partitioning integers 1, . . . , n into k parts with given sums a1 , . . . , ak for any ai ≤ n and ai = n(n + 1)/2). The suitcase problem was solved by Ma, Zhou and Zhou [185, 184]. General extremal problems
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer and let G be a (simple) graph with exactly n(n+1)/2 edges. Prove that the edge set of G can be partitioned into n subgraphs G_1, G_2, ..., G_n such that:
(i) for each i = 1, ..., n, the subgraph G_i has exactly i edges; and
(ii) for each i = 1, ..., n-1, G_i is isomorphic to a subgraph of G_{i+1}.

Equivalently, show that every graph whose number of edges is a triangular number admits an "ascending subgraph decomposition": an edge-decomposition into an ascending chain (under subgraph isomorphism) of subgraphs with 1, 2, ..., n edges.
status_search_result: The Ascending Subgraph Decomposition Conjecture (Alavi, Boals, Chartrand, Erdős, Oellermann, 1987) remains open in full generality. It has been verified for many classes (regular bipartite graphs, star forests, certain tournaments, etc.), and a 2023 arXiv preprint establishes the conjecture for all sufficiently large n, but a complete proof for all n is not yet available.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on trees 1962, (proposed by Erdo"s and Sós) Every graph on n vertices having at least n(k−1)/2+1 edges must contain as a subgraph every tree of k + 1 vertices, for n ≥ k + 1. This conjecture, if true, is best possible. Some asymptotic approximations of this conjecture were given by Komlós and Szemerédi (unpublished). Also, this conjecture is proved for some special families of trees such as caterpillars. Brandt and Dobson [30] have proved the conjecture for graphs with girth at least 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer and let $G$ be a finite simple graph on $n \ge k+1$ vertices. Prove or disprove: if $G$ has at least $\frac{n(k-1)}{2} + 1$ edges, then $G$ contains, as a subgraph, every tree $T$ on $k+1$ vertices.

(Equivalently, every graph with average degree greater than $k-1$ contains every tree on $k+1$ vertices as a subgraph.) The bound on the number of edges, if the statement holds, is best possible.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Sós conjecture (1962) remains open in general. A proof for sufficiently large k was announced by Ajtai, Komlós, Simonovits, and Szemerédi but has not been published in full. Numerous partial results exist (caterpillars, spiders, graphs of girth ≥ 5, etc.).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: The (n/2-n/2-n/2) conjecture (proposed by Erdo"s, Füredi, Loebl and Sós [99]) Let G be a graph with n vertices and suppose at least n/2 vertices have degree at least n/2. Then G contains any tree on at most n/2 vertices. Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi [4] proved the following asymptotic version: If G has n vertices and at least (1 + )n/2 vertices have degree at least (1 + )n/2, then G contains any tree on at most n/2 vertices if n is large enough (depending on ). Komlós and Sós conjectured [99]: Let G be a graph with n vertices and suppose at least n/2 vertices have degree at least k. Then G contains any tree with k vertices.
self_contained_problem: Komlós–Sós conjecture (a generalization of the (n/2, n/2, n/2) conjecture): Let G be a finite simple graph on n vertices, and let k be a positive integer. Suppose that at least n/2 of the vertices of G have degree at least k. Prove or disprove that for every tree T on k vertices, G contains T as a subgraph.
status_search_result: The exact Loebl–Komlós–Sós conjecture remains open in general. An approximate (asymptotic) version has been proved by Hladký, Komlós, Piguet, Simonovits, Stein, and Szemerédi in a series of papers, and the exact conjecture has been confirmed in several special cases (e.g., dense graphs, trees of small diameter), but the general exact statement is not resolved.

original_question: A conjecture of Erdo"s and Gallai, 1959 [100] Every connected graph on n vertices can be edge-partitioned into at most (n + 1)/2 paths. Lovász [179] showed that every graph on n vertices can be edge-partitioned into at most n/2 cycles and paths. Pyber [190] showed that every con- nected graph on n vertices can be covered by at most n/2 + O(n3/4 ) paths.
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a connected simple graph on $n$ vertices. A path decomposition of $G$ is a partition of the edge set $E(G)$ into subsets, each of which forms the edge set of a simple path in $G$. Prove or disprove: every connected simple graph on $n$ vertices admits a path decomposition consisting of at most $\lceil (n+1)/2 \rceil$ paths.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Gallai (Gallai) path decomposition conjecture remains open in general. It has been verified for several classes (graphs of maximum degree at most 5, planar graphs, 2-degenerate graphs, graphs with forest-like E-subgraphs, etc.), and the best general bound is roughly ⌊3n/4⌋ paths (Dean–Kouider, Yan).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on clique transversals (proposed by Erdo"s, Gallai and Tuza [101]) Estimate the cardinality, denoted by τ (G), of a smallest set that shares a vertex with every clique of G. Denote by R(n) the largest integer such that every triangle-free graph on n vertices contains an independent set of R(n) vertices. Is it true that τ (G) ≤ n − R(n) ? √ From the results √ on Ramsey numbers r(3, k), we know that c n log n < R(n) < c n log n. So far, the best known bound [101] is τ (G) ≤ n − √ 2n + c for a small constant c.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices. A clique of $G$ is a maximal complete subgraph (a maximal set of pairwise adjacent vertices). A clique transversal of $G$ is a set $T \subseteq V$ such that $T \cap K \neq \emptyset$ for every clique $K$ of $G$. Let $\tau(G)$ denote the minimum cardinality of a clique transversal of $G$.

For a positive integer $n$, let $R(n)$ denote the largest integer such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set of size at least $R(n)$. (It is known from bounds on the Ramsey numbers $r(3,k)$ that $c\sqrt{n\log n} \le R(n) \le c'\sqrt{n\log n}$ for some absolute constants $c,c' > 0$.)

Prove or disprove: for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices,
$$\tau(G) \le n - R(n).$$

(The best bound currently established in this direction is $\tau(G) \le n - \sqrt{2n} + c$ for some small absolute constant $c$.)
status_search_result: The conjecture of Erdős, Gallai and Tuza on clique transversals appears to remain open. The best known upper bound in the literature is still τ(G) ≤ n − √(2n) + c, far from the conjectured n − R(n) with R(n) of order √(n log n). Related work (e.g., on the Erdős–Gallai–Tuza conjecture) addresses different formulations, and recent problem listings continue to record this as an unsolved problem.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on the diameter of a Kr -free graph (proposed by Erdo"s, Pach, Pollack and Tuza [119]) Let G denote a connected graph on n vertices with minimum degree δ. Show that if G is K2r -free and δ is a multiple of (r − 1)(3r + 2), then the diameter of G, denoted by D(G), satisfies 2(r − 1)(3r + 2) D(G) ≤ n + O(1) (2r2 − 1)δ when n approaches infinity. If G is K2r+1 -free and δ is a multiple of 3r −1, then 3r − 1 D(G) ≤ n + O(1) rδ when n approaches infinity. In [119], bounds for the diameters of triangle-free or Ck -free graphs with given minimum degree were derived.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r \geq 2$ be an integer and let $G$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta$. Denote the diameter of $G$ by $D(G)$. Prove or disprove the following asymptotic bounds as $n \to \infty$:

(a) If $G$ contains no clique on $2r$ vertices (i.e. $G$ is $K_{2r}$-free) and $\delta$ is a multiple of $(r-1)(3r+2)$, then
$$D(G) \;\leq\; \frac{2(r-1)(3r+2)}{(2r^{2}-1)\,\delta}\, n + O(1).$$

(b) If $G$ is $K_{2r+1}$-free and $\delta$ is a multiple of $3r-1$, then
$$D(G) \;\leq\; \frac{3r-1}{r\,\delta}\, n + O(1).$$

Here $O(1)$ denotes a quantity bounded by a constant depending only on $r$ as $n \to \infty$.
category_tag: Extremal graph theory: diameter vs. minimum degree
status_search_result: The conjecture has been disproved. Counterexamples to the Erdős–Pach–Pollack–Tuza conjecture were published in the Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (2021), constructing $K_{2r}$-free graphs with diameter larger than the conjectured bound for all r > 1 and sufficiently large δ. Subsequent work (2025) gave sharp results refining the correct asymptotics. The original conjectured bounds are therefore false in general.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem ($100, many years ago) Is there a sequence A of density 0 for which there is a constant c(A) so that for n > n0 (A), every graph on n vertices and c(A)n edges contains a cycle whose length is in A. Erdo"s said [81], “I am almost certain that if A is the sequence of powers of 2 then no such constant exists. What if A is the sequence of squares? I have no guess. Let f (n) be the smallest integer for which every graph on n vertices and f (n) edges contains a cycle of length 2k for some k. I think that f (n)/n → ∞ but that f (n) < n(log n)c for some c > 0.” Alon pointed out that f (n) ≤ cn log n using the fact [29] that graphs with n vertices and ck 1+1/k edges contain cycles of all even lengths between 2k and 2kn1/k (by taking k to be about log n/2).
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of positive integers. We say $A$ has density $0$ if $|A \cap \{1,2,\dots,N\}|/N \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. For a (simple, undirected) graph $G$, let $v(G)$ and $e(G)$ denote the number of vertices and edges of $G$, and let $\mathcal{L}(G) = \{\ell \geq 3 : G \text{ contains a cycle of length } \ell\}$.

(a) Does there exist an infinite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of density $0$ and constants $c(A) > 0$ and $n_0(A)$ such that every graph $G$ with $v(G) = n \geq n_0(A)$ and $e(G) \geq c(A)\, n$ satisfies $\mathcal{L}(G) \cap A \neq \emptyset$?

(b) In particular, does such a constant $c(A)$ exist when $A = \{k^2 : k \geq 2\}$ is the set of perfect squares?

(c) Define $f(n)$ to be the smallest integer such that every graph on $n$ vertices and $f(n)$ edges contains a cycle of length $2^k$ for some positive integer $k$. Prove or disprove that $f(n)/n \to \infty$ and that there exists a constant $c > 0$ with $f(n) < n(\log n)^c$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
status_search_result: Liu and Montgomery (2020) resolved the powers-of-2 case affirmatively: there exists a constant $c$ such that every graph with average degree at least $(\log n)^C$ (for some absolute $C$) contains a cycle of length a power of $2$, contrary to Erdős's expectation. More generally they showed many density-zero sets $A$ (of even integers not growing too quickly) admit such a constant. The case of $A$ being the squares appears to remain open, as does the general characterization of which density-zero sets work. The bound $f(n) \le c n \log n$ noted by Alon is classical; the precise growth rate of $f(n)$ is not fully settled.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A decomposition problem about odd cycles (proposed by Erdo"s and Graham [102])
self_contained_problem:
It is a classical fact that the edges of the complete graph $K_{2^k}$ on $2^k$ vertices can be partitioned into $k$ bipartite (spanning) subgraphs, while the edges of $K_{2^k+1}$ cannot be partitioned into $k$ bipartite subgraphs; equivalently, in every decomposition of the edge set of $K_{2^k+1}$ into $k$ subgraphs, at least one of the subgraphs contains an odd cycle.

For each integer $k \geq 1$, let
$$f(k) = \min_{\mathcal{D}} \; \max_{G \in \mathcal{D}} \; \big(\text{length of a shortest odd cycle in } G\big),$$
where the minimum is taken over all edge-decompositions $\mathcal{D} = \{G_1, \dots, G_k\}$ of $K_{2^k+1}$ into $k$ spanning subgraphs, and where the length of a shortest odd cycle in $G$ is taken to be $+\infty$ if $G$ contains no odd cycle. Equivalently, $f(k)$ is the smallest integer $m$ such that in every decomposition of the edge set of $K_{2^k+1}$ into $k$ subgraphs, some subgraph contains an odd cycle of length at most $m$.

Determine $f(k)$. In particular, is the sequence $\{f(k)\}_{k \geq 1}$ unbounded, and if so, what is its asymptotic behaviour as $k \to \infty$?
status_search_result: The problem is the 1973 Erdős–Graham question on the shortest monochromatic odd cycle forced in a $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2^k+1}$. It is known that $f(k)$ is unbounded (indeed grows exponentially). Recent work by Girão–Hunter (2024) gave the first nontrivial upper bound $L(k)=O(2^k/k^{1-o(1)})$, and a 2025 preprint (“Short monochromatic odd cycles”) improved this exponentially to $L(k)=O(k^{3/2} 2^{k/2})$. The exact value of $f(k)$ remains unknown, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on almost bipartite graphs (proposed by Erdo"s [82]) Suppose G has the property that for every m, every subgraph on m vertices contains an independent set of size m/2 − k. Let f (k) denote the smallest number such that G can be made bipartite by deleting f (k) vertices.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$ and a nonnegative integer $k$, say that $G$ has property $P(k)$ if for every positive integer $m$ and every subgraph $H$ of $G$ on $m$ vertices, $H$ contains an independent set of size at least $m/2 - k$. Define
$$f(k) = \sup \{\, t : \text{there exists a finite graph } G \text{ with property } P(k) \text{ that cannot be made bipartite by deleting fewer than } t \text{ vertices} \,\},$$
i.e., $f(k)$ is the smallest number such that every finite graph $G$ with property $P(k)$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $f(k)$ vertices. It is known that $f(k)$ is finite for every $k$. Determine good upper and lower bound estimates for $f(k)$ as a function of $k$.
status_search_result: The existence of f(k) was proved by Reed (unpublished) via graph minors, but improved estimates for f(k) are still sought. No published bounds resolving the problem appear to be available; the problem is listed as an open Erdős problem.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem of Erdo"s and Rado [122] What is the least number k = k(n, m) so that for every directed graph on k vertices, either there is an independent set of size n or the graph includes a directed path of size m (not necessarily induced)? Erdo"s and Rado [122] give an upper bound of [2m−1 (n−1)m +n−2]/(2n− 3). Mitchell and Larson [176] give a recurrence relation and obtain a bound of n2 for m = 3 and, more generally, of nm−1 for m > 3. Random graphs
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $n, m \geq 2$, let $k(n,m)$ denote the least positive integer $k$ such that every directed graph (digraph) on $k$ vertices either contains an independent set of size $n$ (a set of vertices with no directed edge between any two of them in either direction) or contains a directed path of length $m$ (a sequence of $m$ vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$, not required to be induced, with $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ an arc for every $1 \le i \le m-1$).

Determine $k(n,m)$, or determine its asymptotic growth. It is known that
$$k(n,m) \le \frac{2^{m-1}(n-1)^m + n - 2}{2n-3},$$
and that $k(n,3) \le n^2$ and more generally $k(n,m) \le n^{m-1}$ for $m > 3$. Improve these bounds, or give exact values.
status_search_result: Searches reveal that this Erdős–Rado problem about digraph Ramsey numbers k(n,m) for independent sets versus directed paths has received attention (e.g., a paper "On a problem of Erdős and Rado" in Annals of Combinatorics, and earlier work by Mitchell and Larson giving the n^{m-1} bound), but no exact formula for general n and m was located. The current best bounds remain polynomial in n for fixed m, and the precise value/asymptotics appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s, see [9]) Let G denote a random graph on n vertices and cn edges. What is the largest r, denoted by r(c), for which the probability that the chromatic number is r is at least some constant strictly greater than 0 (and indepen- dent of n)? This is open except for r = 3 (see [9]). QLuczak [182] gave an asymptotic estimate: c r(c) = (1 + o(1)) . 2 log c However, the exact values are not known.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(n,m)$ denote the uniform random graph on the vertex set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ with exactly $m$ edges, chosen uniformly among all such graphs. Fix a real constant $c>0$ and set $m=\lfloor cn\rfloor$. Let $\chi(G)$ denote the chromatic number of a graph $G$.

Define
$$r(c) \;=\; \max\Big\{\, r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \;:\; \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr\big[\chi(G(n,\lfloor cn\rfloor))=r\big] \;>\; 0 \,\Big\}.$$

In other words, $r(c)$ is the largest integer $r$ such that, for some constant $\delta>0$ independent of $n$, the probability that $G(n,\lfloor cn\rfloor)$ has chromatic number exactly $r$ is at least $\delta$ for infinitely many $n$.

It is known that $r(c) = (1+o(1))\,\dfrac{c}{2\log c}$ as $c\to\infty$, and that the value $r(c)$ is determined for the regime corresponding to $r=3$.

Determine the exact value of $r(c)$ as a function of $c$ for all $c>0$ (equivalently, identify, for each integer $r\ge 2$, the precise set of $c>0$ for which $r(c)=r$).
status_search_result: The Achlioptas–Naor "two-value" theorem (2005) shows that for fixed average degree d, χ(G(n,d/n)) concentrates a.s. on one of two consecutive integers k_d, k_d+1, and pins down the exact value for roughly half of all d (those in [(2k−1)log k, 2k log k)). The general exact value remains undetermined for the remaining values of c, and recent work (e.g., Heckel and others) continues to refine bounds rather than provide exact answers. The exact-value problem is therefore still open in general.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s, see [9]) How accurately can one estimate the chromatic number of a random graph (with edge probability 1/2)? Prove or disprove that the error is more (much more) than O(1). Shamir and Spencer have an O(n1/2 ) upper bound [201]. An old problem raised by Erdo"s and Rényi [123] is to determine the chro- matic number of a random graph with given edge density. This problem has almost been completely resolved due to the work of Matula [186], Shamir and Spencer [201], and Bollobás [23]. The order of the chro- matic number for both sparse and dense random graphs have been deter- mined asymptotically. For random graphs with edge density p satisfying p ≤ n−5/6− , where  > 0, Shamir and Spencer showed that the chro- matic number almost surely takes on at most five different values. QLuczak later on [181] proved that for such sparse random graphs, the chromatic number is concentrated at two values.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(n,1/2)$ denote the Erdős–Rényi random graph on $n$ labeled vertices in which each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ possible edges is included independently with probability $1/2$. Let $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ denote its chromatic number (a random variable).

Shamir and Spencer proved that there exists a sequence of intervals $I_n$ of length $O(\sqrt{n})$ such that $\chi(G(n,1/2)) \in I_n$ asymptotically almost surely. The question is to determine the true concentration width of $\chi(G(n,1/2))$.

Specifically: prove or disprove that the "error" in estimating $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ is more than $O(1)$ — that is, decide whether there exist (deterministic) integers $a_n$ such that $\chi(G(n,1/2)) \in \{a_n, a_n+1, \dots, a_n + C\}$ asymptotically almost surely for some constant $C$, and more generally determine the smallest $f(n)$ such that $\chi(G(n,1/2))$ is concentrated on an interval of length $f(n)$.
status_search_result: The problem is partially resolved. Heckel (and later Heckel–Riordan) proved non-concentration of $\chi(G(n,1/2))$: it is not concentrated on any interval of length $n^{1/4-\varepsilon}$, and subsequent work strengthened this toward $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. The Shamir–Spencer $O(\sqrt{n})$ upper bound remains the best known, so the exact concentration width is not yet determined.

original_question: A conjecture on a spanning cube in a random graph (proposed by Erdo"s and Bollobás, see [88]) A random graph on n = 2d vertices with edge density 1/2 contains an d-cube.

The d-dimensional hypercube Q_d is the graph whose vertex set is {0,1}^d and whose edges join pairs of vertices differing in exactly one coordinate; in particular Q_d has 2^d vertices and is d-regular. original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s and Bollobás, see [9]) In a random graph (with edge probability 1/2), find the best possible c such that every subgraph on nα vertices will almost surely contain an independent set of size c log n (where c depends on α).

Let $G = G(n, 1/2)$ be the Erdős–Rényi random graph on $n$ labeled vertices in which each pair of vertices is joined by an edge independently with probability $1/2$. For a real number $\alpha \in (0,1]$, define
$$f(\alpha) = \sup\{c > 0 : \text{with probability tending to } 1 \text{ as } n \to \infty, \text{ every induced subgraph of } G(n,1/2) \text{ on } \lceil n^{\alpha} \rceil \text{ vertices contains an independent set of size at least } c \log n\}.$$
Determine the best possible constant $f(\alpha)$ (as a function of $\alpha$). That is, find the largest constant $c = c(\alpha)$ such that asymptotically almost surely every subset of $\lceil n^{\alpha} \rceil$ vertices of $G(n,1/2)$ induces a subgraph containing an independent set of size at least $c \log n$.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Problem (proposed by Erdo"s and Spencer [9]) Start with n vertices and add edges at random one by one. If we stop when every vertex is contained in a triangle, is there a set of vertex disjoint triangles covering every vertex (except for at most two vertices)? The above question can be posed for other configurations as well [9]. In particular, Bollobás and Frieze [26] showed that stopping as soon as there is no isolated vertex, then there already almost surely is a perfect matching if the number of vertices is even. If we stop when every vertex has degree at least 2, Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi [3] and Bollobás [24] proved that there already almost surely is a Hamiltonian cycle.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the random graph process on a vertex set V of size n: starting from the empty graph, edges of the complete graph K_n are added one at a time in a uniformly random order, producing a nested sequence of graphs G_0 ⊂ G_1 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ G_{\binom{n}{2}}. Let τ_△ denote the first time t at which every vertex of G_t is contained in at least one triangle (a copy of K_3).

Prove or disprove: asymptotically almost surely (i.e., with probability tending to 1 as n → ∞), the graph G_{τ_△} contains a collection of pairwise vertex-disjoint triangles that together cover all but at most two vertices of V.
category_tag: Random graph processes and triangle factors
status_search_result: Recent work on hitting times for clique factors in the random graph process (building on Johansson–Kahn–Vu and Kahn's resolution of Shamir's problem) shows that in the random graph process the K_r-factor appears at the very moment the last vertex joins a copy of K_r. For r=3 this implies that as soon as every vertex is contained in a triangle, a (near-)perfect triangle factor exists a.a.s., resolving the Erdős–Spencer question in the affirmative (in fact in a stronger form, with at most two uncovered vertices being necessary only due to divisibility).

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on monotone graph properties (proposed by Erdo"s, Suen and Winkler [133]) A graph property P is said to be monotone if every subgraph of a graph with property P also has property P . Start with n vertices and add edges one by one at random, subject to the condition that property P continues to hold. Stop when no more edges can be added. How many edges can such a graph have? The cases when P denotes “triangle-free”, “bipartite”, or “disconnected” were considered by Erdo"s, Suen and Winkler [133]. The property “max- imum degree bounded by k” was examined by Ruciński and Wormald [197]. Many interesting cases are still open, including “C4 -free”, “Kr -free” (for r ≥ 4), “k-colorable” (for k ≥ 3), “planar” and “girth > k”. Hypergraphs Ramsey theory for hypergraphs A t-graph has a vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of some prescribed set of t-subsets of V . For t-graphs Gi , i = 1, . . . , k, let rt (G1 , . . . , Gk ) denote the smallest integer m satisfying the property that if the edges of the complete t-graph on m vertices are colored in k-colors, then for some i, 1 ≤ i ≤ k, there is a t-subgraph isomorphic to Gi with all t-edges in the i-th color. We denote rt (n1 , . . . , nk ) = rt (Kn1 , . . . , Knk ). Clearly r2 (n1 , . . . , nk ) = r(n1 , . . . , nk ).

status_search_result: The C_4-free random greedy process has been resolved: the final graph has Θ(n^{4/3}(log n)^{1/3}) edges with high probability (Picollelli, building on Bohman–Keevash and Osthus–Taraz). The H-free process is well-studied for general H including K_r (Bohman–Keevash give n^{2-1/(r-1)+o(1)} lower bounds, with matching upper bounds known for small r) and the girth case is partially understood, but sharp two-sided results for K_r-free (r ≥ 4), k-colorable (k ≥ 3), planar, and girth > k random greedy processes are not all known. Hence the collective problem is only partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: Conjecture ($500) Is there an absolute constant c > 0 such that log log r3 (n, n) ≥ cn? This is true if four colors are allowed [110]. If just three colors are allowed, there is some improvement due to Erdo"s and Hajnal (unpublished). 2 2 r3 (n, n, n) > ecn log n .
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \ge 2$, let $r_3(n,n)$ denote the smallest integer $N$ such that every 2-coloring of the 3-element subsets of an $N$-element set contains a monochromatic subset of size $n$ (that is, an $n$-element subset all of whose 3-subsets receive the same color). It is known that there exist absolute constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ such that
$$2^{c_1 n^2} \;<\; r_3(n,n) \;<\; 2^{2^{c_2 n}}.$$
Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\log \log r_3(n,n) \;\ge\; c\,n,$$
equivalently $r_3(n,n) \ge 2^{2^{cn}}$.
status_search_result: The conjecture that $r_3(n,n) \ge 2^{2^{cn}}$ for the 2-color 3-uniform hypergraph Ramsey number remains open. A double-exponential lower bound is known when 4 colors are used (via the Erdős–Hajnal stepping-up lemma), and there have been small improvements for 3 colors, but for 2 colors the best lower bound is still of the form $2^{c n^2}$. Recent surveys (Mubayi) and papers (Conlon–Fox–Sudakov, Mubayi–Suk) continue to list this as a central open problem.

original_question: Turán’s conjecture for 3-graphs For an r-uniform hypergraph (or r-graph, for short) H, we denote by tr (n, H) the smallest integer m such that every r-graph on n vertices with m + 1 edges must contain H as a subgraph. When H is a complete graph on k vertices, we write tr (n, k) = tr (n, H). In memory of Turán, Erdo"s offered $1000 for the following conjecture: Conjecture [214] t3 (n, 4) 5 lim n = . n→∞ There are many  different extremal constructions [32, 169] which show t3 (n, 4) ≥ 59 n3 (1 + o(n−1 )). The best upper bound for t3 (n, 4)/ n3 is √ (−1 + 21)/6 = .5971 . . . due to Giraud (unpublished, mentioned in [41]). An excellent survey on this problem can be found in Füredi [149].
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $r\ge 2$, an $r$-uniform hypergraph (or $r$-graph) on a vertex set $V$ is a collection of $r$-element subsets of $V$, called edges. For a fixed $r$-graph $H$ and an integer $n$, let $t_r(n,H)$ denote the largest integer $m$ such that there exists an $r$-graph on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges that does not contain $H$ as a subgraph. When $H = K_k^{(r)}$ is the complete $r$-graph on $k$ vertices (all $\binom{k}{r}$ possible edges), write $t_r(n,k) := t_r(n,K_k^{(r)})$.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture of Turán: for the complete 3-uniform hypergraph on 4 vertices,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{t_3(n,4)}{\binom{n}{3}} \;=\; \frac{5}{9}.$$

It is known that the limit exists, that the lower bound $t_3(n,4) \ge \frac{5}{9}\binom{n}{3}(1+o(1))$ holds via several extremal constructions, and that the corresponding upper bound is strictly larger than $5/9$.
status_search_result: The Turán density conjecture for the tetrahedron $K_4^{(3)}$ remains a central open problem in extremal combinatorics. The best known upper bound on $t_3(n,4)/\binom{n}{3}$ is approximately 0.5616 (Razborov, via flag algebras), still strictly above the conjectured $5/9 \approx 0.5556$. Numerous non-isomorphic extremal constructions achieving density $5/9$ are known, but no proof of the upper bound has been found.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture for triple systems (proposed by Brown, Erdös and Sós [33, 78]) Let f (n, k, r) denote the least integer m such that every 3-graph on n vertices with more than m triples contains an induced subgraph on k vertices with at least r edges. Prove that f (n, k, k − 3) = o(n2 ).
self_contained_problem:
A 3-uniform hypergraph (or 3-graph) on a vertex set V is a collection of 3-element subsets of V, called triples (or edges). For positive integers n, k, r, let f(n,k,r) denote the least integer m such that every 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with more than m triples contains an induced sub-3-graph on some k vertices that has at least r edges (i.e., there exist k vertices spanning at least r triples of the hypergraph).

Prove that for every fixed integer k ≥ 3,
    f(n, k, k − 3) = o(n²)
as n → ∞.

(Equivalently, for every ε > 0 and every fixed k ≥ 3, every 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with more than εn² edges contains, for sufficiently large n, a set of k vertices spanning at least k − 3 edges.)
status_search_result: This is the classical Brown–Erdős–Sós conjecture (in the equivalent (k+3, k)-formulation), known only for k = 3 by Ruzsa–Szemerédi's theorem (f(n,6,3) = o(n²)). The general case for k ≥ 4 remains open as of 2025; recent research (e.g., arXiv:2508.09841, arXiv:2506.01739) addresses only partial cases such as the quadratic 8-edge case or related (k+2, k) and dense variants, but the full conjecture f(n, k, k−3) = o(n²) is not yet established.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars (proposed by Erdo"s and Rado [120] in 1960) For given integers n and k, determine the smallest integer m, denoted by f (n, k), for which every family of sets Ai , i = 1, . . . , m, with |Ai | = n for all i, contains a k-star. Erdo"s and Rado [120, 121] proved that 2n < f (n, 3) ≤ 2n n!. Abbott and Hanson [1] proved f (n, 3) > 10n/2 . Spencer [208] showed f (n) < (1 + )n n!.
self_contained_problem:
A k-star (or sunflower with k petals) is a family of sets A_1, ..., A_k such that there exists a set Y (the kernel) with A_i ∩ A_j = Y for all 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k, and such that the sets A_i \ Y are nonempty and pairwise disjoint.

For positive integers n and k, let f(n, k) denote the smallest integer m with the following property: every family {A_1, A_2, ..., A_m} of m sets, each of cardinality exactly n, contains k members forming a k-star.

It is classical that f(n, k) is finite, with the bounds
   2^n < f(n, 3) ≤ 2^n · n!,
and more generally f(n, k) ≤ (k-1)^n · n! (with refinements giving f(n,3) > 10^{n/2} and f(n,k) ≤ (1+ε)^n · n! type improvements).

Problem: Determine the exact growth rate of f(n, k). In particular, prove or disprove that there exists a constant C = C(k) (depending only on k) such that
   f(n, k) ≤ C^n
for all n ≥ 1.
status_search_result: The Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture (existence of C(k)^n upper bound) remains open. Major progress was made by Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2019/2021) and subsequently sharpened by Rao, giving bounds of the form (C log n)^n · poly(k), but no C^n bound is known. The conjecture is widely cited as one of the central open problems in extremal set theory.

original_question: Conjecture ($1000): f (n, 3) ≤ cn for some absolute constant c.
self_contained_problem:
Let f(n, r) denote the following extremal hypergraph Turán-type function introduced in the study of intersecting r-uniform hypergraphs with large cover number: f(n, r) is the minimum possible number of edges in an n-uniform hypergraph H on a finite vertex set such that

(i) every two edges of H have non-empty intersection (H is intersecting), and
(ii) H has cover number equal to r, meaning that the minimum size of a set of vertices meeting every edge of H equals r.

(Equivalently, in the convention used in compilations of Erdős's problems, f(n, r) is the minimum number of edges in an n-uniform, intersecting hypergraph whose covering number is r.)

                 f(n, 3) ≤ c · n
for every sufficiently large positive integer n.

The currently known upper bound is of the form
                 f(n, 3) < n! · (c · log log n / log n)^n,
which is dramatically larger than the conjectured linear bound.

Problem: Prove or disprove the conjecture that f(n, 3) = O(n), i.e., that f(n, 3) is bounded above by an absolute constant times n.

original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars of an n-set (proposed by Erdo"s and Szemerédi [136]) Determine the least integer m, denoted by f ∗ (n, k) such that for any family A of subsets of an n-set with |A| > f ∗ (n, k), A must contain a k-star. √ Erdo"s and Szemerédi [136] showed that f ∗ (n, 3) < 2(1−1/(10 n))n . Re- cently, Deuber, Erdo", Gunderson, Kostochka and Meyer [61] proved that f ∗ (n, r) > 2n(1−log log r/2r−O(1/r)) for every r ≥ 3 and infinitely many n. In particular, f ∗ (n, 3) > 1.551n−2 for infinitely many n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. A family $\mathcal{S}=\{S_1,S_2,\dots,S_k\}$ of distinct subsets of $[n]$ is called a $k$-star (or $k$-sunflower, $\Delta$-system of size $k$) if there exists a set $K\subseteq[n]$ (the kernel) such that $S_i\cap S_j=K$ for all $1\le i<j\le k$, and the sets $S_i\setminus K$ are nonempty and pairwise disjoint.

For integers $n\ge 1$ and $k\ge 3$, define $f^{*}(n,k)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that every family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $[n]$ with $|\mathcal{A}|>m$ contains a $k$-star.

Determine the function $f^{*}(n,k)$, or more modestly, determine the exponential growth rate
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} f^{*}(n,k)^{1/n}$$
for each fixed $k\ge 3$. It is known that
$$2^{n\left(1-\frac{\log\log r}{2r}-O(1/r)\right)} < f^{*}(n,r) < 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{10\sqrt{n}}\right)}$$
(the lower bound holding for infinitely many $n$ and every $r\ge 3$, the upper bound stated for $r=3$); in particular $f^{*}(n,3)>1.551^{n-2}$ for infinitely many $n$. Close the gap between these bounds.
status_search_result: The problem of determining f*(n,k), the threshold for unavoidable k-sunflowers in families of subsets of an n-set, remains open. The best known bounds remain those of Erdős–Szemerédi (1978) from above and Deuber–Erdős–Gunderson–Kostochka–Meyer (1997) from below, with a substantial gap. No more recent work appears to have closed the gap, although the related Erdős–Rado sunflower lemma (different parameter regime) has seen breakthroughs.

original_question: A problem on weak ∆-systems (proposed by Erdo"s, Milner and Rado [118]) Let g(n, k) denote the least size for a family of n-sets forcing a weak ∆- system of k sets. Conjecture[118]: g(n, 3) < cnk .
self_contained_problem:
A family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite sets is called a weak $\Delta$-system of size $k$ if it consists of $k$ distinct sets $A_1,\dots,A_k$ such that all pairwise intersections have the same cardinality, i.e. $|A_i\cap A_j|$ is the same integer for every pair $i\ne j$ (note that, unlike a sunflower / strong $\Delta$-system, the pairwise intersections need not coincide as sets).

For positive integers $n$ and $k$, let $g(n,k)$ denote the least integer $N$ with the following property: every family of $N$ distinct $n$-element sets contains a subfamily of $k$ sets forming a weak $\Delta$-system.

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that
$$ g(n,3) < c^{\,n} \quad\text{for all } n\ge 1. $$

A family of k ≥ 3 sets {A_1, ..., A_k} is called a weak Δ-system if there exists an integer t such that |A_i ∩ A_j| = t for every pair of distinct indices i, j ∈ {1, ..., k} (note that, unlike a strong Δ-system or sunflower, the pairwise intersections are not required to all be equal as sets, only to have the same cardinality).

(i) g*(n, 3) ≥ n^{(log n)/(4 log log n)};
(ii) for r ≥ 3, g*(n, r) ≥ 2^{(1/3) n^{1/5} log^{4/5}(r−1)};
(iii) there exists ε = ε(k) > 0 with g*(n, k) < (2 − ε)^n.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem of Erdo"s, Faber and Lovász ($500, 1972 [75]) Let G1 , . . . , Gn be n edge-disjoint complete graphs on n vertices. Then the chromatic number of ∪ni=1 Gi is n.
self_contained_problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $G_1, G_2, \ldots, G_n$ be $n$ complete graphs, each on exactly $n$ vertices, such that any two of them share at most edges of a graph with no common edge (i.e., they are pairwise edge-disjoint). Form the graph $G = \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i$ on the union of their vertex sets, whose edge set is the union of the edge sets of the $G_i$. Prove that the chromatic number $\chi(G)$ of $G$ equals $n$; that is, the vertices of $G$ can be properly colored with $n$ colors (and not fewer).
