paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on property B (proposed by Erdo"s 1963, [66]) A family F of subsets is said to have property B if there is a subset S such that every subset in F contains an element in S and an element not in S. What is the minimum number f (n) of subsets in a family F of n-sets not having property B? Property B is named after Felix Bernstein who first introduced this prop- erty in 1908 [22]. The best known upper bound is due to Erdo"s [66, 67] and the following lower bound was given by Beck [20]. e log 2 2 n n1/3− 2n ≤ f (n) < (1 + ) n 2 for n ≥ n0 and n0 depends only on . This problem was extensively considered in [9, 158].
self_contained_problem:
A family $\mathcal{F}$ of sets is said to have **property B** if there exists a set $S$ such that, for every $A \in \mathcal{F}$, the intersection $A \cap S$ is a proper, nonempty subset of $A$ (equivalently, $\mathcal{F}$ is 2-colorable as a hypergraph: the underlying vertex set admits a 2-coloring with no $A \in \mathcal{F}$ monochromatic).

For a positive integer $n$, let
$$m(n) = \min\{|\mathcal{F}| : \mathcal{F} \text{ is a family of }n\text{-element sets that does not have property B}\}.$$

Determine $m(n)$, or its asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$. In particular, close the gap between the known bounds
$$c \cdot 2^{n}\sqrt{\tfrac{n}{\log n}} \;\le\; m(n) \;\le\; (1+o(1))\,\tfrac{e \ln 2}{4}\, n^{2}\, 2^{n},$$
where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant.
status_search_result: The exact value of m(n) is known only for very small n (m(2)=3, m(3)=7, m(4)=23) and the asymptotic order of magnitude remains open. The best known bounds — Erdős's upper bound of order n² 2^n and Radhakrishnan–Srinivasan's lower bound of order 2^n √(n/log n) — leave a substantial gap that has not been closed despite recent improvements for small n.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A conjecture on covering a hypergraph (proposed by Erdo"s and Lovász [117]) Let f (n) denote the smallest integer m such that for any n-element sets A1 , . . . , Am with Ai ∩ Aj = ∅ for i = j and for every set S with at most n − 1 elements, there is an Ai disjoint from S. Erdo"s and Lovász [117] proved that n − 3 ≤ f (n) ≤ cn3/2 log n.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n\ge 1$, an $n$-set means a set of cardinality $n$. A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_m\}$ of $n$-sets is called intersecting if $A_i\cap A_j\neq\emptyset$ for all $i\neq j$. A set $S$ is said to cover the family if $S\cap A_i\neq\emptyset$ for every $i$.

Prove or disprove the following strengthened form of an Erdős–Lovász covering conjecture: for every constant $c>0$ there exists $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(c)>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every intersecting family $\{A_i:1\le i\le cn\}$ of $n$-sets admits a covering set $S$ with $|S|<n(1-\varepsilon)$ and $A_i\cap S\neq\emptyset$ for all $1\le i\le cn$.

(Equivalently: any intersecting family of $cn$ many $n$-sets has cover number strictly less than $(1-\varepsilon)n$.)
status_search_result: The original Erdős–Lovász question on the minimum number of edges in an $n$-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number $n$ was resolved by Kahn, who proved a linear bound. The strengthened version asking for a cover of size at most $(1-\varepsilon)n$ for any intersecting family of $cn$ many $n$-sets does not appear to be reported as settled in recent surveys or follow-up work (e.g., Barát–Király–Tóthmérész and related papers on the Erdős–Lovász theme), so its current status could not be verified.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on unavoidable hypergraphs (proposed by Chung and Erdo"s [49]) A r-graph H is said to be (n, e)-unavoidable if H is contained in every r- graph on n vertices and e edges. Let fr (n, e) denote the largest integer m with the property that there exists an (n, e)-unavoidable r-graph having m edges. Determine fr (n, e). For the case of r = 2 and 3, the solutions can be found in [48, 49].
self_contained_problem:
For an integer r ≥ 2, an r-uniform hypergraph (r-graph) is a pair (V, E) where E is a collection of r-element subsets of V. Given positive integers n and e, an r-graph H is called (n, e)-unavoidable if every r-graph on n vertices having exactly e edges contains a copy of H as a subhypergraph. Define
  f_r(n, e) = max{ |E(H)| : H is an (n, e)-unavoidable r-graph }.
Determine f_r(n, e) (exactly, or up to its order of magnitude) for all integers r ≥ 2 and all admissible pairs (n, e) with 1 ≤ e ≤ C(n, r). In particular, resolve the cases r ≥ 4.
status_search_result: Chung and Erdős determined f_2(n,e) up to a multiplicative factor and later identified the order of magnitude of f_3(n,e). Bucić, Draganić, and Sudakov (2020/2021) asymptotically resolved the 4-uniform case and made progress for higher r, but the problem of determining f_r(n,e) in general remains open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on unavoidable stars (proposed by Duke and Erdo"s [91]) Let f (n, r, k, t) denote the smallest integer m with the property that any r-graph on n vertices and m edges must contain a k-star with common intersection of size t. Determine f (n, r, k, t). Duke and Erdo"s proved that f (n, r, k, 1) ≤ cnr−2 where c depends only on r and k. For the case of r = 3, tight bounds are obtained by Chung and Frankl [54], also see [141, 47].
self_contained_problem:
For integers $r \ge 2$, $k \ge 2$, $n \ge 1$ and $1 \le t \le r-1$, let an $r$-graph denote an $r$-uniform hypergraph, i.e. a family of $r$-element subsets ($r$-edges) of a vertex set. A $k$-star with common intersection of size $t$ is a collection of $k$ distinct $r$-edges $E_1, \dots, E_k$ such that there exists a set $T$ of exactly $t$ vertices with $E_i \cap E_j = T$ for all $i \ne j$ (equivalently, a sunflower with $k$ petals and a core of size $t$).

Define $f(n, r, k, t)$ to be the smallest integer $m$ such that every $r$-graph on $n$ vertices having at least $m$ edges must contain a $k$-star with common intersection of size $t$.

It is known (Duke–Erdős) that $f(n, r, k, 1) \le c\, n^{r-2}$ for a constant $c$ depending only on $r$ and $k$, and tight asymptotic bounds are known when $r = 3$.

Problem: Determine the function $f(n, r, k, t)$ for all admissible parameters $n, r, k, t$ (in particular, obtain tight asymptotic bounds as $n \to \infty$ for all $r \ge 4$, all $k \ge 2$, and all $1 \le t \le r-1$).
status_search_result: The problem of determining the Turán number for sunflowers (k-stars with prescribed core size t) in r-uniform hypergraphs, posed by Duke and Erdős in 1977, remains open in general. Tight bounds are known for r = 3 (Chung–Frankl and follow-ups), and partial progress for general r has appeared in recent works on Turán numbers of sunflowers (e.g., arXiv:2110.11319, 2021), but the complete determination of f(n,r,k,t) for r ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ t ≤ r−1 has not been achieved.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on decompositions of hypergraphs (proposed by Chung, Erdo"s and Graham [51]) For r-graphs H1 , . . . , Hk with the same number of edges, a U -decomposition (first suggested by Ulam) is a family of partitions of each of the edge sets E(Hi ) into t mutually isomorphic sets, i.e., say E(Hi ) = ∪tj=1 Eij , where for each j, all the Eij are isomorphic. Let Uk (n, r) denote the least possible value m such that all families of k r-graphs must have a U -decompositions into t isomorphic sets. For graphs, it was shown [53, 50] that 2 1 2 n − < U2 (n, 2) < n + c 3 3 3 and for k ≥ 3, 3 √ 3 n − n − 1 < Uk (n, 2) < n + ck . 4 4 There is still room for improvement. For hypergraphs, it is of interest to determine U2 (n, 3), for example. It is known (see [51]) that c1 n4/3 log log n/ log n < U2 (n, 3) < c2 n4/3 . Also, for  > 0, c3 n2−2/k− < Uk (n, 3) < c4 n2−1/k .
self_contained_problem:
Let $r\ge 2$ and let $H_1,\dots,H_k$ be $r$-uniform hypergraphs on vertex set $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ all having the same number of edges. A $U$-decomposition (in the sense of Ulam) of $H_1,\dots,H_k$ into $t$ parts is a collection of partitions
$$E(H_i)=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{t}E_{ij}\qquad (i=1,\dots,k)$$
such that for every fixed $j\in\{1,\dots,t\}$ the $k$ hypergraphs $(V,E_{1j}),\dots,(V,E_{kj})$ are pairwise isomorphic. Define
$$U_k(n,r)=\max_{H_1,\dots,H_k}\;\min_{\text{$U$-decompositions}} t,$$
where the maximum is over all $k$-tuples of $r$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices having a common edge count, and the minimum is over all $U$-decompositions of that $k$-tuple.

It is known that for some absolute constants $c_1,c_2>0$,
$$c_1\,\frac{n^{4/3}\log\log n}{\log n}\;<\;U_2(n,3)\;<\;c_2\,n^{4/3},$$
and for every $k\ge 2$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist constants $c_3,c_4>0$ such that
$$c_3\,n^{\,2-2/k-\varepsilon}\;<\;U_k(n,3)\;<\;c_4\,n^{\,2-1/k}.$$

Determine the asymptotic behaviour of $U_2(n,3)$ as $n\to\infty$, and more generally of $U_k(n,3)$ for $k\ge 3$. In particular, close the gap between the known lower and upper bounds for $U_2(n,3)$.
status_search_result: The problem of determining the order of magnitude of U_2(n,3) and U_k(n,3) for U-decompositions of 3-uniform hypergraphs, posed by Chung, Erdős, and Graham, appears still open. Existing literature (Chung–Erdős–Graham 1982, Graham's 2018 survey on Ulam-type decompositions, and the Erdős problems collection) reports the same gap between the n^{4/3} log log n/log n lower bound and the n^{4/3} upper bound, with no resolution found in recent search results.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on the product of the point and line covering numbers (proposed by Chung, Erdo"s and Graham [52]) In a hypergraph G with vertex set V and edge set E, the point covering number α0 (G) denotes the minimal cardinality of a subset of V which has non-empty intersection with every edge e in E. The line covering number α1 (G) denotes the minimal cardinality of a subset S of E such that every vertex is contained in some edge in S. The problem of interest is to characterize hypergraphs which achieve the maximum and minimum value of α0 (G)α1 (G). The case for graphs was solved in [52] and it was shown that n+1 n − 1 ≤ α0 (G)α1 (G) ≤ (n − 1)  which is asymptotically best possible. Infinite graphs Erdo"s wrote over a hundred papers on infinite graphs. In particular, the problem papers by Erdo"s and Hajnal [105, 106] contain 82 problems which have been the major driving force in this field. Many of the problems have been solved positively, negatively or proved to be undecidable. The problems here are mainly based on the survey papers [86, 155, 153]. Many comments to these problems were graciously provided by András Hajnal and Jean Larson. Here we use the following arrow notation, first introduced by Rado: κ → (λν )rγ which means that for any r-partition f : [κ]r → γ there are ν < γ and H ⊂ κ such that H has order type λν and f (Y ) = ν for all Y ∈ [H]r . If λν = λ for all ν < γ, then we write κ → (λ)rγ . In this language, Ramsey’s theorem can be written as ω → (ω)rk for 1 ≤ r, k < ω.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite hypergraph on n vertices with no isolated vertices. Define:

- The point covering number α₀(G) as the minimum cardinality of a subset T ⊆ V such that T ∩ e ≠ ∅ for every e ∈ E.
- The line covering number α₁(G) as the minimum cardinality of a subset S ⊆ E such that every vertex v ∈ V is contained in some edge of S.

For ordinary graphs on n vertices it is known that
   n − 1 ≤ α₀(G) · α₁(G) ≤ ⌊(n+1)²/4⌋,
and the extremal graphs achieving the upper and lower bounds have been characterized; the bounds are asymptotically best possible.

Problem. Characterize the hypergraphs G on n vertices (without isolated vertices) that attain the maximum value, and those that attain the minimum value, of the product α₀(G) · α₁(G). In particular, determine the sharp upper and lower bounds for α₀(G) · α₁(G) over all such hypergraphs on n vertices, and describe the extremal hypergraphs.
status_search_result: A brief search did not reveal a complete characterization of the extremal hypergraphs achieving the maximum and minimum of α₀(G)α₁(G); the problem of Chung, Erdős, and Graham appears to remain open for general hypergraphs, with only the graph case fully resolved.

original_question: [105] Is it true that ω1 → (α, 4)3 for α < ω1 ? Milner and Prikry [188] gave an aﬃrmative answer for α ≤ ω2 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Use the Erdős–Rado partition notation: for ordinals κ, α, β and a positive integer r, write κ → (α, β)^r to mean that for every coloring f : [κ]^r → {0,1} of the r-element subsets of κ with two colors, either there exists a subset A ⊆ κ of order type α such that f is identically 0 on [A]^r, or there exists a subset B ⊆ κ of order type β such that f is identically 1 on [B]^r.

Let ω₁ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Determine whether the partition relation
   ω₁ → (α, 4)^3
holds for every countable ordinal α (i.e. for every α < ω₁).

(It is known that the relation holds for all α ≤ ω² + 1; the question is whether it holds for all α < ω₁.)
status_search_result: Web searches did not locate a definitive resolution of the relation ω₁ → (α, 4)^3 for all countable α. Partial results (such as the case α ≤ ω² + 1 by Milner and Prikry) are documented, and surveys of Erdős-style partition problems indicate that many such ordinal partition relations involving triples remain unresolved, but no source confirming a full solution was found.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: [105] Is it true that ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 ? A. Hajnal [154] proved ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 under CH. Erdo"s and Hajnal [106] ask if MAℵ1 + 2ℵ0 = ℵ2 implies ω1 2 → (ω1 2 , 3)2 ? Erdo", Hajnal and Larson [108] asked for the cardinals λ that λ2 → (λ2 , 3)2 holds. Hajnal [154] showed the relation failed at successors of regular cardinals under GCH. Baumgartner [15] showed that the relation failed at successors of singular cardinals under GCH.
self_contained_problem:
Work in ZFC. For ordinals (or order types) α, β, γ and a positive integer n, the partition relation
  α → (β, γ)²
means: for every coloring f : [α]² → {0,1} of the unordered pairs of α with two colors, either there exists a subset H ⊆ α of order type β with f(H)² = {0} (i.e., all pairs in H are colored 0), or there exists a subset K ⊆ α of order type γ with f(K)² = {1}.

Let ω₁ denote the first uncountable ordinal, and let ω₁·2 denote the ordinal sum, i.e., the order type obtained by concatenating two copies of ω₁ (so a well-ordered set of order type ω₁·2 consists of two consecutive blocks each of order type ω₁).

Question: Is it consistent (in particular, does the assumption MA_{ℵ₁} together with 2^{ℵ₀} = ℵ₂ imply) that
  ω₁·2 → (ω₁·2, 3)²
holds? More generally, characterize the cardinals (or initial ordinals) λ for which λ·2 → (λ·2, 3)² holds.

(Known facts to be respected: under the Continuum Hypothesis, ω₁·2 ↛ (ω₁·2, 3)²; under GCH, λ·2 ↛ (λ·2, 3)² whenever λ is the successor of a regular cardinal, and also whenever λ is the successor of a singular cardinal.)

original_question: Is it true that ω3 → (ω2 + 2)3ω ? Baumgartner, Hajnal and Todorčević [16] showed that GCH implies ω3 → (ω2 + χ)3k for χ < ω1 and k < ω.
self_contained_problem:
Using the Erdős–Rado partition arrow notation, for ordinals α, β and cardinals/ordinals γ, k, the relation α → (β)^n_k means: for every coloring f : [α]^n → k of the n-element subsets of α with k colors, there exists a subset H ⊆ α of order type β such that f is constant on [H]^n.

    ω_3 → (ω_2 + 2)^3_ω
hold? That is, is it true that for every coloring f : [ω_3]^3 → ω, there exists H ⊆ ω_3 with order type ω_2 + 2 such that f is constant on [H]^3?

(It is known that, assuming the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, ω_3 → (ω_2 + χ)^3_k holds whenever χ < ω_1 and k < ω.)

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on graphs of infinite chromatic number ($250) (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Szemerédi, 1982, [114, 82]) Let f (n) → ∞ arbitrarily slowly. Is it true that there is a graph G of infinite chromatic number such that for every n, every subgraph of G of n vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most f (n) edges? Prove or disprove the existence of a graph G of infinite chromatic number for which f (n) = o(n ) or f (n) = o((log n)c ).
self_contained_problem: Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be a function with $f(n)\to\infty$ arbitrarily slowly. Determine whether there exists a (simple, undirected) graph $G$ of infinite chromatic number with the following property: for every positive integer $n$, every subgraph of $G$ on $n$ vertices can be made bipartite by the deletion of at most $f(n)$ edges. original_question: A problem on the union of triangle-free graphs ($250) (proposed by Erdo"s and Hajnal [104]) Is there a graph G which contains no K4 and which is not the union of ℵ0 graphs which are triangle-free? self_contained_problem:
A graph $G = (V, E)$ is called triangle-free if it contains no three pairwise adjacent vertices, and $K_4$-free if it contains no four pairwise adjacent vertices. Given a graph $G$, one says that $G$ is the union of a family $\{G_i\}_{i \in I}$ of subgraphs (on the same vertex set $V$) if $E(G) = \bigcup_{i \in I} E(G_i)$.

Question: Does there exist a graph $G$ (possibly infinite) which contains no $K_4$ and which cannot be written as the union of countably many (i.e., $\aleph_0$-many) triangle-free graphs? In other words, must every $K_4$-free graph admit a decomposition of its edge set into countably many triangle-free subgraphs, or can the contrary be proved in ZFC?
status_search_result: The existence of such a $K_4$-free graph not expressible as a countable union of triangle-free graphs was shown by Shelah to be consistent with ZFC, but as of recent surveys of Erdős's open problems and work on uncountable graphs, whether such a graph exists provably in ZFC remains open.

paper_title: Open problems of Paul Erdős in graph theory
original_question: A problem on ℵ1 -chromatic graphs (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Szemerédi [114]) Is it true that if f (n) increases arbitrarily fast, then there is an ℵ1 - chromatic graph G so that if g(n) is the smallest integer for which G has an n-chromatic subgraph of g(n) vertices, then f (n)/g(n) → 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a (simple, undirected) graph, possibly with infinite vertex set. Its chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the least cardinal $\kappa$ such that there exists a map $c:V\to\kappa$ with $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $\{u,v\}\in E$. A graph $G$ is called $\aleph_1$-chromatic if $\chi(G)=\aleph_1$.

For a graph $G$ and an integer $n\ge 1$, define
$$g_G(n)=\min\{|V(H)| : H\subseteq G,\ \chi(H)\ge n\},$$
with $g_G(n)=\infty$ if $G$ contains no $n$-chromatic subgraph.

Prove or disprove: for every function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, no matter how rapidly increasing, there exists an $\aleph_1$-chromatic graph $G$ such that $g_G(n)<\infty$ for all $n$ and
$$\frac{f(n)}{g_G(n)}\;\longrightarrow\;0\qquad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$
status_search_result: Chris Lambie-Hanson proved in ZFC that for every function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a graph $G$ of uncountable chromatic number such that every subgraph of $G$ with fewer than $f(k)$ vertices has chromatic number less than $k$. Applied with a sufficiently fast-growing $f$ (e.g. replacing $f$ by $n\cdot f(n)$), this yields the desired $\aleph_1$-chromatic graph with $f(n)/g_G(n)\to 0$, so the question is answered affirmatively.

original_question: A problem on ordinal graphs and infinite paths (proposed by Erdo"s, Hajnal and Milner [109]) For which limit ordinals α is it true that if G is a graph whose vertices form a set of type α then either G has an infinite path or contains an independent set of type α. Baumgartner and Larson [17] showed that if Jensen’s Diamond Principle holds, then α → (α, infinite path)2 for all α with ω1ω+2 ≤ α < ω2 . Larson [175] obtained further results under the assumption of GCH.

For an ordinal α, write α → (α, infinite path)² to mean: for every (simple, undirected) graph G whose vertex set has order type α, either G contains an infinite path or G contains an independent set whose vertex set (under the induced order) has order type α.

Determine, in ZFC, exactly the class of limit ordinals α for which the partition relation
   α → (α, infinite path)²
holds. In particular, characterize the limit ordinals α ≥ ω^(ω+2) for which this relation is true.

Known partial information: the relation holds for all limit ordinals α < ω^(ω+2); under Jensen's Diamond Principle, the relation fails for all α with ω^(ω+2) ≤ α < ω₂; further partial results are known under GCH and under Martin's Axiom. The problem is to give a complete characterization.

original_question: A problem on ordinal graphs and down-up matchings (proposed by Erdo"s and Larson [116]) A down-up matching in an ordinal graph is a matching of a set A with a set B where every element of A is less than all elements of B, denoted by A < B. Suppose for every graph on an ordinal α there is either an independent set of type β or a down-up matching from a A to a set B. If A has order type γ, then we write α → (β, γ − matching)2 . Suppose that j and k are positive integers with k ≥ 2 and η is a limit ordinal. Is it true that ω η+jk → (ω η+j , ω k − matching)2 ? If j and k ≥ 2 are positive integers and η a countable limit ordinal, then Erdo"s and Larson have shown that ω η+jk+1 → (ω η+j , γ − matching)2 but ω η+jk−1 → (ω η+j , γ − matching)2 .

Definitions. An ordinal graph is a graph whose vertex set is (an initial segment of) the ordinals, so that any subset of vertices inherits a linear order. For subsets A, B of vertices we write A < B to mean that every element of A is strictly less than every element of B. A down-up matching in an ordinal graph is a perfect matching between two disjoint vertex sets A and B such that A < B and every matched pair {a, m(a)} (with a ∈ A) is an edge of the graph. For an ordinal A, the order type of A is denoted tp(A).

For ordinals α, β and γ, write
   α → (β, γ-matching)^2
to mean: for every graph G whose vertex set is α, either G contains an independent set of order type β, or G contains a down-up matching from a set A to a set B with tp(A) = γ.

   ω^{η+jk+1} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^{k}-matching)^2,
while
   ω^{η+jk-1} ↛ (ω^{η+j}, ω^{k}-matching)^2.

Question. Let j and k be positive integers with k ≥ 2 and let η be a (countable) limit ordinal. Determine whether
   ω^{η+jk} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^{k}-matching)^2.

original_question: Let an ordinate of an L-function mean the positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of that L-function. Prove that the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) has at least one positive ordinate that is irrational.
self_contained_problem:
Let ζ(s) denote the Riemann zeta function, the meromorphic continuation to the complex plane of the Dirichlet series ∑_{n≥1} n^{-s} (Re(s) > 1). A nontrivial zero of ζ(s) is a zero ρ = β + iγ lying in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1. Call a positive real number γ an "ordinate" of ζ if there exists a nontrivial zero ρ = β + iγ with γ > 0.

Prove that at least one positive ordinate of ζ(s) is irrational. Equivalently, show that it is not the case that every positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of ζ(s) is a rational number.
status_search_result: This is a well-known long-standing open problem in analytic number theory; no proof is known that even a single nontrivial zero of ζ(s) has irrational imaginary part. original_question: Let the positive ordinates of ζ(s) denote the positive imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Prove that these positive ordinates are not all rational multiples of one another.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, and consider its nontrivial zeros (those zeros lying in the critical strip $0 < \operatorname{Re}(s) < 1$). Let $\Gamma^+ = \{\gamma > 0 : \zeta(\beta + i\gamma) = 0 \text{ for some } \beta \in (0,1)\}$ denote the set of positive imaginary parts of these nontrivial zeros.

Prove that the elements of $\Gamma^+$ are not all rational multiples of one another. Equivalently, show that there do not exist a real number $\alpha > 0$ and, for every $\gamma \in \Gamma^+$, a rational number $q_\gamma \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $\gamma = q_\gamma \alpha$ for all $\gamma \in \Gamma^+$.

original_question: For nontrivial zeros ρ of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s), obtain upper bounds for the quantity 1/|ζ′(ρ)| as ρ ranges over those zeros.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, viewed as a meromorphic function on the complex plane, and let $\zeta'(s)$ denote its derivative. A nontrivial zero of $\zeta$ is any zero $\rho$ lying in the critical strip $0 < \mathrm{Re}(s) < 1$. Assume that all nontrivial zeros are simple (so $\zeta'(\rho) \neq 0$).

Obtain nontrivial upper bounds for the quantity
$$\frac{1}{|\zeta'(\rho)|}$$
as $\rho$ ranges over the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$. More precisely, find an explicit function $f(T)$, as small as possible, such that
$$\frac{1}{|\zeta'(\rho)|} \ll f(|\mathrm{Im}(\rho)|)$$
holds for all nontrivial zeros $\rho$ with $|\mathrm{Im}(\rho)|$ sufficiently large (either unconditionally, or under the Riemann Hypothesis).
status_search_result: Obtaining nontrivial upper bounds for $1/|\zeta'(\rho)|$ is widely regarded as a longstanding open problem, intimately tied to the Gonek–Hejhal conjecture on negative moments of $\zeta'(\rho)$. Recent work (e.g., a 2024 arXiv preprint on multiplicative function anticorrelation and bounds on $1/\zeta'(\rho)$, and conditional results giving lower bounds for the second negative moment) addresses related questions but does not resolve the basic pointwise upper bound problem. No general unconditional or RH-conditional sharp upper bound is known.

original_question: Assume the simple zeros conjecture for ζ(s) and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble conjecture for nearest-neighbour spacing of its zeros. Using formula (1) in the paper for 1/ζ′(ρ), compute an upper bound for the moment sum Σ_{0<γ<T} 1/|ζ′(ρ)|^{2k} for positive real k, with special interest in k = 1/2 and k = 1, where ρ = 1/2 + iγ runs over nontrivial zeros of ζ(s).

Let ζ(s) denote the Riemann zeta-function and write its nontrivial zeros as ρ = 1/2 + iγ (assuming the Riemann Hypothesis). Assume in addition:

(SZ) The Simple Zeros Conjecture: every nontrivial zero of ζ(s) is simple, so ζ′(ρ) ≠ 0 for every nontrivial zero ρ.

(GUE) The Gaussian Unitary Ensemble conjecture for the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution of the nontrivial zeros of ζ(s): when the zeros 1/2 + iγ are normalized so that their mean spacing near height T is 1 (i.e., γ̃ = γ · (log γ)/(2π)), the distribution of consecutive spacings γ̃_{n+1} − γ̃_n agrees, in the limit T → ∞, with the limiting nearest-neighbour spacing distribution of eigenvalues of random matrices drawn from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble.

For a nontrivial simple zero ρ = 1/2 + iγ of ζ(s), the explicit-formula representation expresses 1/ζ′(ρ) as a (suitably truncated/limited) sum over the primes involving the Möbius function and the values n^{−ρ}.

Problem. Using this representation of 1/ζ′(ρ), and assuming SZ and GUE, determine an upper bound, as T → ∞, for the discrete moment
   J_{−k}(T) := Σ_{0 < γ ≤ T} 1/|ζ′(ρ)|^{2k}
for each positive real number k. In particular, give as sharp an upper bound as the hypotheses allow in the cases k = 1/2 and k = 1.

original_question: Let m(ρ) denote the multiplicity of a nontrivial zero ρ of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s). Improve the known upper bounds for m(ρ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, and for a nontrivial zero $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ of $\zeta$, let $m(\rho)$ denote its multiplicity (the order of vanishing of $\zeta$ at $\rho$). The classical unconditional bound asserts that
$$m(\beta + i\gamma) \ll \log|\gamma| \qquad \text{as } |\gamma| \to \infty,$$
and under the Lindelöf hypothesis this can be improved to $m(\beta + i\gamma) = o(\log|\gamma|)$. The problem is to establish an unconditional improvement of the upper bound $m(\rho) \ll \log|\gamma|$ for the multiplicity of nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$, i.e. to prove $m(\beta + i\gamma) = o(\log|\gamma|)$ (or any sharper bound) without assuming unproven hypotheses.
category_tag: Multiplicity of zeros of the Riemann zeta function

paper_title: COMPARATIVE PRIME NUMBER THEORY PROBLEM LIST
context_brief: Skewes numbers for highly biased races
original_question: In highly biased prime number races, such as the appropriately normalized race between quadratic residues and nonresidues for composite moduli q, bound the associated Skewes numbers in terms of the parameters defining the race, either conjecturally or with proofs.
self_contained_problem:
For a modulus $q\ge 3$ and a reduced residue class $a\pmod q$, let $\pi(x;q,a)=\#\{p\le x:\ p\text{ prime},\ p\equiv a\pmod q\}$. A "prime race" compares two or more such counting functions (or weighted/normalized linear combinations of them, e.g. comparing the count of primes in the set of quadratic nonresidues against the count in the set of quadratic residues mod $q$, possibly with appropriate normalizations to account for differing sizes of the two sets). For a race between two such normalized functions $F_1(x)$ and $F_2(x)$ with $F_1(x)\ge F_2(x)$ holding for all small $x$, the associated Skewes number is defined as the least $x_0$ at which the inequality first reverses, i.e.\ $x_0=\inf\{x\ge 2: F_1(x)<F_2(x)\}$ (assuming such a crossover exists).

Certain races are known to be "highly biased": one side leads for an extraordinarily long range. A prototypical example is, for composite moduli $q$, the suitably normalized race between primes lying in quadratic nonresidue classes mod $q$ and primes lying in quadratic residue classes mod $q$.

Problem: For such highly biased prime races, give bounds (either conjectural or unconditionally proved) for the associated Skewes number $x_0$ in terms of the parameters defining the race (such as the modulus $q$, the residue classes or character data involved, and the normalization). Equivalently, quantify how large the first sign-change must be as an explicit function of these parameters.
status_search_result: The problem of bounding Skewes-type numbers for highly biased prime races (for example the quadratic nonresidues vs. residues race for composite moduli) is an active topic in comparative prime number theory. While Skewes-type bounds are known for the classical $\pi(x)$ vs. $\mathrm{li}(x)$ problem and for some specific races (work of Rubinstein–Sarnak, Martin, Lamzouri, Fiorilli, and others), a general framework giving conjectural or unconditional bounds on Skewes numbers for arbitrary highly biased races in terms of the defining parameters does not appear to have been established, and the problem is listed as open in current problem lists in this area.

paper_title: COMPARATIVE PRIME NUMBER THEORY PROBLEM LIST
context_brief: function-field bias and linear independence with pi
original_question: In the function-field setting for Chebyshev’s bias, one often assumes both linear independence over Q of the relevant zero arguments and linear independence of those arguments together with π. Show that whenever linear independence with π fails, that failure always has a geometric explanation.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $K/\mathbb{F}_q(T)$ be a finite Galois extension with Galois group $G$. For a nontrivial irreducible representation $\rho$ of $G$, let $L(s,\rho)$ denote the associated Artin $L$-function, which is a polynomial in $q^{-s}$; write its inverse zeros as $\sqrt{q}\,e^{i\gamma}$, so that the "zero arguments" $\gamma \in (-\pi,\pi]$ are the real numbers attached to the nontrivial zeros of $L(s,\rho)$ on the critical line.

In the study of Chebyshev's bias in this function-field setting, one customarily invokes two hypotheses:

(LI) The multiset of all positive zero arguments $\gamma$ arising from all nontrivial irreducible $\rho$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

(LI$_\pi$) The above multiset of zero arguments, together with $\pi$, is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Problem. Prove that whenever (LI$_\pi$) fails — that is, whenever there exists a nontrivial $\mathbb{Q}$-linear relation among $\pi$ and the zero arguments of the Artin $L$-functions $L(s,\rho)$ attached to the nontrivial irreducible representations of $G$ — this failure admits a geometric explanation. More precisely, show that any such linear relation involving $\pi$ must arise from the geometry of the cover of curves underlying the extension $K/\mathbb{F}_q(T)$ (for instance, from the action of Frobenius on cohomology, from multiplicities or symmetries among the inverse zeros forced by the geometry, or from factorizations and isogeny relations among the relevant $L$-functions), rather than from a purely arithmetic coincidence.
category_tag: Comparative prime number theory in function fields
status_search_result: The literature on Chebyshev's bias in function fields (work of Cha, Cha–Fiorilli–Jouve, Devin, Perret-Gentil, and others) describes the linear independence hypothesis and notes that, contrary to the number-field setting, it can be proved or violated in concrete cases, with biases in "unexpected directions" arising from linear relations among zeros. However, no source found establishes that every failure of linear independence involving $\pi$ has a geometric origin; this remains a guiding problem in the area.

context_brief: compare two formulations of Chebyshev bias
original_question: A new formulation of Chebyshev’s bias considers the weighted prime-counting difference Σ_{p≤x, p≡3 (mod 4)} 1/√p − Σ_{p≤x, p≡1 (mod 4)} 1/√p ∼ (1/2) log log x as x → ∞. Determine the logical inclusion or precise relation between this weighted formulation and the conventional formulation of Chebyshev’s bias in which the set of x satisfying π(x;4,3) > π(x;4,1) has logarithmic density very close to 1.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $a$ coprime to $4$, let $\pi(x;4,a)$ denote the number of primes $p\le x$ with $p\equiv a\pmod 4$. Two formulations of "Chebyshev's bias" toward the residue class $3\pmod 4$ are considered.

(A) Conventional formulation. The set
$$E := \{ x\ge 2 : \pi(x;4,3) > \pi(x;4,1)\}$$
has logarithmic density very close to $1$; equivalently,
$$\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log X}\int_{[2,X]\cap E}\frac{dt}{t}$$
is close to $1$ (Rubinstein–Sarnak type statement, conditional on the relevant hypotheses).

(B) Weighted formulation. As $x\to\infty$,
$$\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\ p\equiv 3\,(4)}}\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\;-\;\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\ p\equiv 1\,(4)}}\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\;\sim\;\frac{1}{2}\log\log x.$$

Determine the precise logical relation between (A) and (B): does either statement imply the other, are they equivalent, or are they logically independent? In particular, establish (or disprove) any implication between the asymptotic (B) and the statement that the logarithmic density of $E$ is close to $1$.

status_search_result: Recent literature (Aoki–Koyama and subsequent works on weighted prime-counting and Chebyshev bias, 2022–2025) introduces the weighted asymptotic at $w=1/2$ as a new formulation of Chebyshev's bias under the Deep Riemann Hypothesis, but does not establish a logical equivalence or implication with the Rubinstein–Sarnak logarithmic-density formulation. original_question: Let q be a modulus and let a and b be distinct reduced residue classes modulo q. Prove unconditionally that the set of real numbers x for which π(x; q, a) = π(x; q, b), meaning the ties in this prime number race, has natural density 0 or logarithmic density 0.

$$\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{X}\int_{1}^{X}\mathbf{1}_{E}(t)\,dt,$$

$$\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log X}\int_{1}^{X}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{E}(t)}{t}\,dt,$$

$$|M(x)| \le K\, x \exp\!\bigl(-C (\log x)^{3/5} (\log\log x)^{-1/5}\bigr)$$

original_question: Let W_ψ(T) be the sign-change counting function associated with the error term ψ(x) − x. Improve the known lower bound for lim inf W_ψ(T)/log T, even under RH if needed, and make progress on understanding sign changes beyond repeated-averaging techniques. The source suggests targets such as 1.01·γ₁/π, 2·γ₁/π, or even an unbounded lim inf.
self_contained_problem:
Let ψ(x) = ∑_{p^k ≤ x} log p denote the second Chebyshev function. For T > 0, let W_ψ(T) be the number of sign changes of the function ψ(x) − x on the interval [1, T] (i.e., the number of points x ∈ [1, T] at which ψ(x) − x changes sign). Let γ₁ = 14.13472514… denote the ordinate of the lowest-lying nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) in the upper half-plane.

It is known (by repeated-averaging techniques originating with Pólya and refined by Kaczorowski and others) that
    liminf_{T→∞} W_ψ(T)/log T ≥ γ₁/π,
with subsequent work improving this by a tiny additive constant.

Problem: Improve this lower bound, possibly under the Riemann Hypothesis. In particular, establish any one of the following:
(a) liminf_{T→∞} W_ψ(T)/log T ≥ 1.01·γ₁/π;
(b) liminf_{T→∞} W_ψ(T)/log T ≥ 2·γ₁/π;
(c) liminf_{T→∞} W_ψ(T)/log T = ∞.

More generally, develop techniques for studying sign changes of ψ(x) − x that go essentially beyond the repeated-averaging method.
category_tag: Sign changes in prime number theorem
status_search_result: The best known lower bound, due to recent work (Ramanujan Journal, 2022), improves Kaczorowski's bound only by an additive constant of order 10^(-30), giving liminf W_ψ(T)/log T ≥ γ₁/π + 1.867·10^(-30). No proof of the stronger targets (1.01·γ₁/π, 2·γ₁/π, or ∞), nor any technique substantively beyond repeated averaging, is known. The problem remains open.

$$ S(x) \;=\; \sum_{2 \le n \le x} \chi_{-4}\!\left(P^{+}(n)\right). $$

original_question: For prime number races with three or more competitors, numerically compute additional three-way or higher-order race densities, and determine a list such as the 100 most biased three-way races.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer modulus $q \ge 3$ and distinct reduced residue classes $a_1,\dots,a_r$ modulo $q$ (with $r \ge 3$), the prime number race $(q;a_1,\dots,a_r)$ studies the asymptotic behavior of the vector
$$\bigl(\pi(x;q,a_1),\pi(x;q,a_2),\dots,\pi(x;q,a_r)\bigr),$$
where $\pi(x;q,a) := \#\{p \le x : p \text{ prime},\ p \equiv a \pmod q\}$. Assume the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet $L$-functions modulo $q$ and the Linear Independence Hypothesis (i.e., the imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of those $L$-functions with positive imaginary part are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$). Under these hypotheses, for any permutation $\sigma \in S_r$ the logarithmic density
$$\delta_{q;a_{\sigma(1)},\dots,a_{\sigma(r)}} := \lim_{X\to\infty} \frac{1}{\log X}\int_{[2,X]} \mathbf{1}\bigl[\pi(t;q,a_{\sigma(1)}) > \pi(t;q,a_{\sigma(2)}) > \cdots > \pi(t;q,a_{\sigma(r)})\bigr]\,\frac{dt}{t}$$
exists and is strictly positive.

(a) Develop and carry out numerical computations of these $r$-way race densities $\delta_{q;a_1,\dots,a_r}$ for $r \ge 3$ across a broad collection of moduli $q$ and ordered tuples $(a_1,\dots,a_r)$, extending the known catalogue of computed values.

(b) Using such computations, produce a ranked list of the $100$ most biased three-way prime number races, where the "bias" of an ordered triple $(q;a_1,a_2,a_3)$ is measured by how far $\delta_{q;a_1,a_2,a_3}$ deviates from the unbiased value $1/6$ (equivalently, identify the $100$ ordered triples achieving the largest values of $\delta_{q;a_1,a_2,a_3}$).
status_search_result: The literature on prime number races (Rubinstein–Sarnak, Feuerverger–Martin, Lamzouri, Fiorilli–Martin, Harper–Lamzouri) provides methods to compute $r$-way race densities under GRH and LI, with several explicit computations for small moduli and for two-way races. However, no comprehensive ranked list of the most biased three-way races nor a substantially extended table of higher-order race densities appears in the published literature; the computational problem remains an open task.

original_question: Assuming GRH and LI, compute the logarithmic densities in the five-way prime race among the quadratic residues {1,3,4,5,9} modulo 11 and likewise among the quadratic nonresidues {2,6,7,8,10} modulo 11. The source notes that symmetry reduces the computation to eight representative densities of the form δ_{11;a1,a2,a3,a4,a5}.
self_contained_problem:
For a modulus q and distinct reduced residues a_1,...,a_r modulo q, let π(x;q,a) denote the number of primes p ≤ x with p ≡ a (mod q). Under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet L-functions modulo q, and the Linear Independence hypothesis (LI) — namely, that the nonnegative imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of all Dirichlet L-functions modulo q are linearly independent over the rationals — the logarithmic density

  δ_{q;a_1,...,a_r} := lim_{X→∞} (1/log X) ∫_{[2,X] : π(x;q,a_1) > π(x;q,a_2) > ... > π(x;q,a_r)} dx/x

original_question: Investigate additional numerical examples of prime number races arising from Chebotarev’s density theorem, and determine which two-way Chebotarev races are the most biased.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $L/K$ be a Galois extension of number fields with Galois group $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. For each prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ that is unramified in $L$, let $\mathrm{Frob}_\mathfrak{p}\subset G$ denote its Frobenius conjugacy class. For two distinct conjugacy classes $C_1,C_2\subset G$ of equal cardinality, and for $x>0$, define the prime-counting functions
$$\pi(x;L/K,C_i)=\#\{\mathfrak{p}\text{ unramified}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\mathfrak{p}\le x,\ \mathrm{Frob}_\mathfrak{p}=C_i\},\quad i=1,2.$$
Under the assumption of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and a linear-independence hypothesis for the imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of the Artin $L$-functions attached to $L/K$, the logarithmic density
$$\delta(L/K;C_1,C_2)=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log X}\int_2^X \mathbf{1}\bigl[\pi(t;L/K,C_1)>\pi(t;L/K,C_2)\bigr]\,\frac{dt}{t}$$
exists, and a "two-way Chebotarev race" between $C_1$ and $C_2$ is said to be biased toward $C_1$ when $\delta(L/K;C_1,C_2)>\tfrac12$.

Problem. Among all triples $(L/K,C_1,C_2)$ with $L/K$ a Galois extension of number fields and $C_1,C_2$ distinct conjugacy classes in $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ of equal size, compute and exhibit further numerical examples of the densities $\delta(L/K;C_1,C_2)$, and determine the supremum
$$\delta^*=\sup_{L/K,\,C_1,C_2}\delta(L/K;C_1,C_2),$$
i.e., identify (or characterize) the most biased two-way Chebotarev prime races, and decide whether this supremum is attained.
category_tag: Comparative prime number theory / Chebotarev races
status_search_result: Web searches return general background on Chebyshev's bias and Chebotarev density, plus recent works (e.g., on bias against splitting/principal primes, 2022) studying particular families, but no source identifies "the most biased" two-way Chebotarev race or computes a sharp supremum of two-way densities. The problem appears to remain open, with only partial numerical and theoretical progress for specific extensions.

original_question: Assuming GRH and LI, calculate the logarithmic densities of the sets {n ≥ 1 : (−1)^{Ω(n)}χ_{−4}(n) = 1} and {n ≥ 1 : (−1)^{Ω(n)}χ_{−4}(n) = −1}, where Ω(n) is the number of prime factors of n counted with multiplicity and χ_{−4} is the nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo 4.
self_contained_problem:

$$\delta(S)=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log X}\sum_{\substack{n\le X\\ n\in S}}\frac{1}{n}.$$
Assume the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for all Dirichlet $L$-functions, and the Linear Independence hypothesis (LI), which asserts that the nonnegative imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of these $L$-functions are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Determine the logarithmic densities of the two sets
$$A_+=\{n\ge 1:(-1)^{\Omega(n)}\chi_{-4}(n)=1\}\quad\text{and}\quad A_-=\{n\ge 1:(-1)^{\Omega(n)}\chi_{-4}(n)=-1\}.$$

$$A^{1}_{\pi}(x;q,a) \;=\; \int_0^x\bigl(\varphi(q)\,\pi(t;q,a)-\operatorname{li}(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
Assume the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for all Dirichlet $L$-functions modulo $q$. Classify completely those pairs $(q,a)$, with $1\le a\le q$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$, for which
$$A^{1}_{\pi}(x;q,a) < 0 \qquad \text{for all sufficiently large } x.$$

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: For a subset S of R^n and an integer p >= 1, define S_p to be the set of all convex combinations of at most p points of S. Since S_1 = S and S_{n+1} is the full convex hull co(S), what topological properties are shared by the intermediate partial convexifications S_p?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty subset. For each integer $p \geq 1$, define the $p$-th partial convexification of $S$ by
$$S_p = \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i x_i : 1 \leq k \leq p,\ x_i \in S,\ \lambda_i \geq 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i = 1 \right\},$$
that is, the set of all convex combinations of at most $p$ points of $S$. Then $S_1 = S$, the sets $S_p$ form a nondecreasing chain $S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \cdots$, and by Carathéodory's theorem $S_{n+1} = \operatorname{co}(S)$, the convex hull of $S$.

Determine what topological properties are necessarily shared by the intermediate partial convexifications $S_p$ for $1 \leq p \leq n+1$. In particular, identify and prove the strongest statements that can be made about properties such as closedness, openness, compactness, connectedness, arcwise connectedness, contractibility, simple connectedness, and Borel/measurability class of $S_p$ in terms of corresponding properties of $S$ (and of $n$ and $p$).
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any published resolution of the question of which topological properties are shared by the partial convexifications $S_p$ in the sense above. The question is posed as an open problem in the listing of conjectures on partial convexification, and no follow-up work providing a complete characterization was found. Some related facts (e.g. compactness of $S_p$ when $S$ is compact, via continuity of the convex-combination map on a compact simplex times $S^p$) are folklore, but a full description of preserved topological properties does not appear to be established.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Let k > 2, let H be a symmetric k-linear form on R^n, and let A be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix such that |H(x, ..., x)| <= <Ax, x>^(k/2) for every x in R^n. Can the resulting inequality |H(x_1, ..., x_k)|^2 <= product_i <Ax_i, x_i> be proved by optimization methods, such as higher-order optimality conditions, rather than by the existing inductive or algebraic proofs?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k > 2$ be an integer and let $H : (\mathbb{R}^n)^k \to \mathbb{R}$ be a symmetric $k$-linear form (i.e., $H(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ is linear in each argument and invariant under permutations of its arguments). Let $A$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $n \times n$ matrix, and suppose that
$$|H(x,x,\dots,x)| \le \langle Ax, x\rangle^{k/2} \quad \text{for every } x \in \mathbb{R}^n.$$
Prove, using methods from optimization theory (for example, first-, second-, or higher-order optimality conditions for a suitably formulated extremal problem), the following multilinear Cauchy–Schwarz-type inequality:
$$|H(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k)|^2 \le \prod_{i=1}^{k} \langle Ax_i, x_i\rangle \quad \text{for all } x_1,\dots,x_k \in \mathbb{R}^n.$$
The challenge is to give a proof that proceeds via optimization-theoretic arguments rather than the known inductive or purely algebraic proofs.
status_search_result: The inequality itself is known and has been proved by inductive and algebraic methods. The specific question of whether it can be derived purely from optimization techniques (such as higher-order optimality conditions) does not appear to have a definitive published resolution that web search could surface; status is therefore unclear.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Among all continuous rectifiable plane curves that start at the center of the unit circle and are guaranteed to touch every tangent line to that circle, give a proof—using calculus of variations or optimal control—that the optimal curve has length 7π/6 + √3 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ denote the unit circle in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, centered at the origin $O$. A "tangent line to $C$" means any straight line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that meets $C$ in exactly one point. Consider all continuous, rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ such that:
(i) $\gamma(0)=O$, and
(ii) for every tangent line $\ell$ to $C$, there exists $t\in[0,1]$ with $\gamma(t)\in\ell$.

Let $L(\gamma)$ denote the arclength of $\gamma$, and let
$$L^* = \inf\{\,L(\gamma) : \gamma \text{ satisfies (i) and (ii)}\,\}.$$
Using techniques from the calculus of variations or optimal control theory, prove that
$$L^* = \frac{7\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3} + 1,$$
and that this infimum is attained by an explicit minimizing curve.
status_search_result: The geometric optimization problem of finding the shortest plane curve starting at the center of the unit disk that meets every tangent to the unit circle was solved by Henri Joris in his 1980 paper "Le chasseur perdu dans la forêt" (Elemente der Mathematik 35), where he established the optimal length 7π/6 + √3 + 1 via geometric arguments. A proof specifically based on calculus of variations / optimal control techniques (as requested) does not appear to be standard in the literature, though Joris's geometric solution is well known. The value itself is verified; a variational/control-theoretic proof has been sought as a separate problem.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Determine the minimal possible length and the geometric structure of a curve in R^3 that starts at the center of the unit sphere and intersects every tangent plane to that sphere.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere centered at the origin $O$, and for each point $p \in S^2$ let $T_p$ denote the affine tangent plane to $S^2$ at $p$. Consider the class $\mathcal{C}$ of all rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,L]\to\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\gamma(0)=O$ such that for every $p\in S^2$ the image of $\gamma$ has nonempty intersection with $T_p$ (equivalently, $\sup_{t\in[0,L]} \langle \gamma(t), p\rangle \ge 1$ for every unit vector $p$). Determine
$$\ell^* = \inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal{C}}\, \mathrm{length}(\gamma),$$
and describe the geometric structure of any curve $\gamma\in\mathcal{C}$ that attains (or approaches) this infimum.
status_search_result: Web searches turn up the closely related Zalgaller-type "shortest closed inspection curve" problem (closed curve outside the sphere whose convex hull contains it), recently resolved by Ghomi and Wenk with the baseball-seam curve of length 4π. However, the variant asked here — an open curve emanating from the center of the sphere and meeting every tangent plane — does not appear to have a known optimal length or known structure of the minimizer, and the original formulation explicitly states that nothing is known about the optimal path. No subsequent resolution was located.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: Let F_N be the sum of cosines of all angles determined by N distinct points in R^3, and let (P_N) be the problem of maximizing F_N subject to the triangle-angle consistency constraints. Determine the maximizing configurations for larger values of N and decide whether the conjectured optimal configurations for N = 5, 6, and 8 are correct.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer N ≥ 3, consider N distinct points P_1, ..., P_N in ℝ³ in general position (no three collinear). For each ordered triple of distinct indices (i, j, k), let θ_{ijk} ∈ [0, π] denote the angle at vertex P_j in the triangle P_i P_j P_k, i.e., the angle between the vectors P_i − P_j and P_k − P_j. Define

  F_N(P_1, ..., P_N) = Σ cos(θ_{ijk}),

where the sum is taken over all unordered selections of a vertex P_j together with an unordered pair {P_i, P_k} of the remaining points (so that each planar angle of each triangle determined by the configuration is counted exactly once). Equivalently, the angles satisfy, for every triangle P_i P_j P_k, the consistency constraint θ_{ijk} + θ_{jki} + θ_{kij} = π with each angle in (0, π).

Problem (P_N): determine

  sup F_N(P_1, ..., P_N)

over all such configurations of N points in ℝ³, and characterize all maximizing configurations.

(a) For N = 5, it is conjectured that the maximum is attained by the configuration whose points are the vertices of a regular triangular bipyramid (two regular tetrahedra glued along a face). Prove or disprove this.

(b) For N = 6, it is conjectured that the maximum is attained by the vertices of a regular octahedron. Prove or disprove this.

(c) For N = 8, it is conjectured that the maximum is attained by a specific highly symmetric configuration (the vertices of a square antiprism / regular cross-polytope-like arrangement). Prove or disprove this.

(d) For general N ≥ 5, describe the maximizing configurations of (P_N).
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a published resolution of the conjectured optimal configurations for N = 5, 6, 8 or a general solution for larger N of this Coulombian-type angle-energy maximization problem. The problem appears to remain open; the original formulation itself notes that solving it accurately for larger N seems out of reach.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: For the same optimization problem (P_N) that maximizes the angle-based energy F_N over configurations of N points in R^3, determine whether, as N tends to infinity, the maximizing configurations become uniformly distributed on a sphere and whether sup F_N = (2/9)N^3 + o(N^3).
self_contained_problem:
For an integer N ≥ 3 and a configuration of N distinct points x_1, …, x_N in R^3, define the angle-based ("Coulombian-angle") energy

  F_N(x_1, …, x_N) = ∑_{(i,j,k)} θ_{ijk},

where the sum is taken over ordered triples (i, j, k) of distinct indices in {1, …, N} and θ_{ijk} ∈ [0, π] denotes the (unsigned) angle at the vertex x_j of the triangle with vertices x_i, x_j, x_k (with the convention that θ_{ijk} is undefined and excluded only when two of the three points coincide). Consider the maximization problem

  (P_N):  maximize F_N(x_1, …, x_N) over all N-tuples of distinct points in R^3, subject to a fixed normalization (e.g. constraining the points to a ball of fixed radius, or fixing the diameter of the configuration).

Prove or disprove the following two assertions:

(a) As N → ∞, every sequence of maximizing configurations of (P_N), after suitable rescaling to fit a fixed ball, becomes uniformly distributed on a 2-sphere (in the sense of weak-* convergence of the empirical measures to the normalized surface measure of that sphere).

(b) The supremum of F_N satisfies the asymptotic

  sup F_N = (2/9) N^3 + o(N^3) as N → ∞.

Related literature (Thomson problem, Riesz/log-energy asymptotics by Hardin–Saff–Brauchart, Smale's 7th problem) addresses different functionals and does not appear to settle this specific conjecture, so its status is best classified as unknown / open.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
context_brief: Optimization proof for Van der Waerden inequality
original_question: Find a proof, based entirely on constrained-optimization ideas such as higher-order optimality conditions, that every doubly stochastic n x n matrix A satisfies per(A) >= n!/n^n, with equality only at the matrix whose entries are all 1/n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and let $\Omega_n$ denote the set of $n \times n$ doubly stochastic matrices, i.e., matrices $A = (a_{ij})$ with nonnegative real entries such that $\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij} = 1$ for every $j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} = 1$ for every $i$. The permanent of $A$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{per}(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. It is known that
$$\operatorname{per}(A) \geq \frac{n!}{n^n} \quad \text{for all } A \in \Omega_n,$$
with equality if and only if $A = J_n$, the matrix all of whose entries equal $1/n$.

Provide a proof of this inequality and the equality case which belongs entirely to the framework of constrained optimization, viewing the problem as minimizing the multilinear functional $A \mapsto \operatorname{per}(A)$ over the polytope $\Omega_n$, and using only optimization tools such as first-order, second-order, or higher-order optimality conditions (e.g., Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions and higher-order tangent/normal cone analysis), without recourse to the algebraic or analytic arguments (such as those of Egorychev, Falikman, or geometric programming) traditionally employed.
status_search_result: The van der Waerden inequality itself was proved by Egorychev (1980) and Falikman (1981), and alternative proofs include a geometric-programming approach by Gurvits-type methods and an elementary proof. However, the specific request for a proof based entirely on constrained-optimization techniques using higher-order optimality conditions does not appear to be addressed in the available literature; no such optimization-only derivation is reported.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: If A and B are Hermitian n x n matrices and B is positive semidefinite, is the function λ ↦ tr(exp(A - λB)) the Laplace transform of a positive measure on [0, +∞)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian $n\times n$ complex matrices, and assume that $B$ is positive semidefinite. Consider the real-valued function
$$f(\lambda) = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\exp(A - \lambda B)\bigr), \qquad \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.$$
Decide whether there always exists a positive (nonnegative) Borel measure $\mu$ supported on $[0,+\infty)$ such that
$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\exp(A - \lambda B)\bigr) = \int_{0}^{+\infty} e^{-\lambda t}\, d\mu(t)$$
for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ (equivalently, for $\lambda$ in some right half-line). In other words, is $\lambda \mapsto \operatorname{tr}(\exp(A-\lambda B))$ the Laplace transform of a positive measure on $[0,+\infty)$ for every such pair $(A,B)$?
status_search_result: The statement is the Bessis–Moussa–Villani (BMV) conjecture (1975). It was proved by Herbert Stahl in 2011 (arXiv:1107.4875), with the full proof published in Acta Mathematica 211 (2013), 255–290. A simplified version of the proof was given by Eremenko (arXiv:1312.6003).

original_question: For Hermitian positive semidefinite n x n matrices A and B, a positive integer p, and 1 <= m <= n, let S_{m,p}(M) denote the sum of the principal minors of order m of M^p. Does the polynomial λ ↦ S_{m,p}(A + λB) always have only nonnegative coefficients?

Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite $n\times n$ complex matrices, and let $p$ be a positive integer. For an integer $1\le m\le n$ and an $n\times n$ matrix $M$, define
$$S_{m,p}(M) := \sum_{|I|=m}\det\bigl((M^{p})_{I,I}\bigr),$$
i.e., the sum of all principal minors of order $m$ of the matrix $M^{p}$ (where the sum runs over all subsets $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ of size $m$, and $(M^{p})_{I,I}$ denotes the principal submatrix of $M^p$ with rows and columns indexed by $I$).

Consider the real polynomial
$$g_{m,p}(\lambda) := S_{m,p}(A+\lambda B), \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb{R}.$$

Prove or disprove: for all Hermitian positive semidefinite $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$, all positive integers $p$, and all $1\le m\le n$, the polynomial $\lambda\mapsto g_{m,p}(\lambda)$ has only nonnegative coefficients.

Let n be a positive integer and let a = (a_1, ..., a_n) be a unit vector in R^n, i.e., a_1^2 + ... + a_n^2 = 1. Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent Rademacher random variables, i.e., P(X_i = +1) = P(X_i = -1) = 1/2 for each i. Prove or disprove: 
P(|Σ_{i=1}^n X_i a_i| ≤ 1) ≥ 1/2. 
Equivalently, show that for every such unit vector a, at least half of the 2^n sign patterns ε = (ε_1, ..., ε_n) ∈ {-1, +1}^n satisfy |Σ_{i=1}^n ε_i a_i| ≤ 1.

paper_title: A New Series of Conjectures and Open Questions in Optimization and Matrix Analysis
original_question: If A and B are normal n x n matrices with eigenvalues a_1, ..., a_n and b_1, ..., b_n respectively, must det(A - B) belong to the convex hull of the n! products Π_i (a_i - b_{σ(i)}) over all permutations σ of {1, ..., n}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be normal $n \times n$ complex matrices with eigenvalues $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$ respectively (each list including multiplicities). Recall that a matrix $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ is normal if $MM^* = M^*M$. For each permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, define
$$P_\sigma \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)}\bigr) \in \mathbb{C},$$
and let $\mathrm{co}\{P_\sigma : \sigma \in S_n\}$ denote the convex hull in $\mathbb{C}$ of these $n!$ complex numbers.

Determine whether the following inclusion always holds:
$$\det(A - B) \;\in\; \mathrm{co}\bigl\{\,\textstyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)}) \,:\, \sigma \in S_n\,\bigr\}.$$

Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every pair of normal $n \times n$ matrices $A, B$ with the prescribed eigenvalues, $\det(A-B)$ lies in this convex polygon.
status_search_result: The Marcus–de Oliveira determinantal conjecture remains open in general. It is known to hold in several special cases, including when both matrices are Hermitian, when one is positive definite Hermitian and the other skew-Hermitian, and various other restricted settings, but no proof or counterexample is known in the general normal case. Recent surveys and articles (e.g., a 2019 Springer survey and a 2025 MDPI Mathematics paper) continue to treat it as an open problem.

original_question: Does there exist a Hadamard matrix for every positive integer that is a multiple of 4?
self_contained_problem:
A Hadamard matrix of order n is an n×n matrix H with entries in {+1, -1} satisfying H Hᵀ = n I_n, where I_n denotes the n×n identity matrix. It is known that if a Hadamard matrix of order n>2 exists, then n must be a multiple of 4.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems
original_question: Are there infinitely many twin primes, that is, infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by 2?
self_contained_problem: A prime number is a positive integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. A pair of primes (p, q) with q = p + 2 is called a twin prime pair (for example, (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31), ...). Prove or disprove: there exist infinitely many twin prime pairs, i.e., infinitely many primes p such that p + 2 is also prime.
status_search_result: The twin prime conjecture remains open. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine how a finite subtraction set controls the length and structure of the resulting nim-sequence period, extend that analysis to partizan subtraction games with separate subtraction sets for the two players, and resolve the related open questions about complete analysis of three-member subtraction sets, superpolynomial versus polynomial period growth, characterization of purely periodic subtraction sets, and periodicity behavior for infinite subtraction games and aperiodic subtraction/division variants.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A (finite, impartial) subtraction game is determined by a finite set S = {s_1, s_2, …, s_k} of positive integers, called the subtraction set. From a position of n ≥ 0 chips, a player may remove s chips for any s ∈ S with s ≤ n; the player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy value (nim-value) G_S(n) is defined recursively by G_S(n) = mex{ G_S(n − s) : s ∈ S, s ≤ n }, where mex denotes the minimum excludant. The sequence (G_S(0), G_S(1), G_S(2), …) is called the nim-sequence of S; it is known to be ultimately periodic, and is called purely periodic if it is periodic from index 0.

A partizan subtraction game is specified by two finite sets S_L, S_R ⊆ ℤ_{>0}: from n chips, Left may subtract any element of S_L (provided it is ≤ n), and Right any element of S_R. Sprague–Grundy theory is replaced by partizan game values.

An infinite subtraction game allows S ⊆ ℤ_{>0} to be infinite; the nim-sequence is still defined by the same recursion.

Problems.
(a) Determine, as a function of the finite subtraction set S, the (eventual) period length p(S) and the structure (preperiod, transient, period word) of the nim-sequence of S.
(b) Give a complete analysis of subtraction games whose subtraction set S has exactly three elements: describe p(S) and the nim-sequence of S = {a, b, c} for all choices of 1 ≤ a < b < c.
(c) Decide whether the period length p(S) can grow faster than any polynomial in max(S), or whether p(S) is always bounded by a polynomial in max(S) (and if so, determine the optimal polynomial bound).
(d) Characterize the finite subtraction sets S whose nim-sequence is purely periodic (i.e. for which the preperiod has length 0).
(e) Extend (a)–(d) to partizan subtraction games (S_L, S_R): establish a periodicity theorem, and describe period length and structure in terms of (S_L, S_R).
(f) For infinite subtraction sets S, and for natural aperiodic variants such as "division" games (where moves remove a divisor of the current position from a prescribed set), determine when the nim-sequence is ultimately periodic, and analyze its period length and purity.
status_search_result: Recent literature confirms these questions remain largely open. Although nim-sequences of finite subtraction games are known to be ultimately periodic, a complete analysis is not known even for three-element subtraction sets; partial results (e.g., the (s,4s,12s+1,16s+1) family with cubic period, and recent work on linearity of periods and two-element partizan cases) address special families but do not resolve general period-length growth, pure-periodicity characterization, or the partizan/infinite variants.

original_question: Decide whether every finite octal game is ultimately periodic, resolve the many listed outstanding octal codes and related splitting games such as Treblecross and Couples-Are-Forever, determine whether large nim-values such as 2048 occur in Treblecross, explain the structure of periods in those octal games already known to be periodic, and clarify the computational complexity of octal, partizan octal, and related poset-style heap games.
self_contained_problem:
An octal game is a two-player impartial combinatorial game played on heaps of tokens, specified by a code of octal digits d_1 d_2 d_3 ... with each d_k in {0,1,...,7}. On a single heap of size n a legal move removes k>=1 tokens (for some k with d_k != 0) and replaces the heap by 0, 1, or 2 nonempty heaps according to which of the bits 1, 2, 4 of d_k are set: bit 1 allows removing the whole heap, bit 2 allows leaving one nonempty heap, bit 4 allows splitting the remainder into two nonempty heaps. The last player to move wins, and the position on disjoint heaps is the disjunctive sum, with Sprague–Grundy (nim) values G(n) defined recursively by G(n)=mex of the nim-values of options. A "finite" octal game is one whose code has only finitely many nonzero digits.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every finite octal game the sequence (G(n))_{n>=0} is ultimately periodic.

(b) For the specific octal game 0.007 (Treblecross), decide whether (G(n)) is ultimately periodic, and determine whether arbitrarily large nim-values such as 2048 occur in this sequence.

(c) For those finite octal games already proved to have ultimately periodic nim-sequences, give a structural explanation of the observed periods (and preperiods) in terms of the code.

(d) Determine the computational complexity of deciding the outcome (or computing the nim-value) of a position in a general octal game, in a partizan octal game (where Left and Right have possibly distinct octal codes), and in related poset-style heap games.
status_search_result: Guy's conjecture that every finite octal game has an ultimately periodic nim-sequence remains open. The specific octal game 0.007 (Treblecross) is the most notorious open case: Flammenkamp and others have computed millions of nim-values without detecting periodicity, and the question of whether large nim-values (e.g. 2048) occur is unresolved. The complexity of general octal and partizan octal games is also not settled.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Complete the analysis of unsolved hexadecimal heap games by establishing periodicity or arithmetic periodicity where suspected, and resolve the explicitly listed outstanding hexadecimal codes whose full behavior remains unknown.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Given a code $d_0 . d_1 d_2 d_3 \cdots$ in hexadecimal (each $d_i \in \{0,1,\ldots,15\}$, written in binary as $d_i = \sum_{k} 2^{k} \varepsilon_{i,k}$ with $\varepsilon_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$), the associated heap game is played on heaps of counters as follows. A single move on a heap of size $n$ consists of choosing some $i\ge 1$ with $i\le n$, removing $i$ counters from the heap, and then splitting the remaining $n-i$ counters into exactly $k$ nonempty heaps, where $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and $\varepsilon_{i,k}=1$. (The digit $d_0$ governs the analogous moves that take no counters but split a heap; usually $d_0=0$.) Players alternate moves and the player who cannot move loses. By the Sprague–Grundy theorem each heap of size $n$ has a Grundy value $G(n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, and the game is called ultimately periodic if there exist $n_0,p$ with $G(n+p)=G(n)$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and arithmetically periodic (with saltus $s$) if there exist $n_0,p,s$ with $G(n+p)=G(n)+s$ for all $n\ge n_0$.

Problem. For each hexadecimal code whose Grundy sequence has not been shown to be ultimately periodic or arithmetically periodic, decide whether such (arithmetic) periodicity holds and, when it does, determine the eventual period $p$, preperiod $n_0$, and (where relevant) saltus $s$. In particular, carry out this analysis for the hexadecimal game with code $\cdot 9$ (i.e. $d_1 = 9 = 1001_2$, so a move on a heap of size $i$ either removes the whole heap when $i$ counters are taken with no split, or removes $i$ counters and splits the remainder into three nonempty heaps), and resolve the corresponding question for every other hexadecimal heap code whose Grundy-value behavior is not yet fully determined.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: For N-heap Wythoff Game with N at least 3, prove or disprove Fraenkel’s two conjectures describing the eventual structure of P-positions when N−2 heaps are fixed, including the mex-plus-shift description and the eventual golden-ratio asymptotic formula.
self_contained_problem:
N-heap Wythoff's game is played as follows. Fix an integer N ≥ 3. A position is an N-tuple (a_1, a_2, …, a_N) of nonnegative integers, viewed as the sizes of N heaps of tokens. Two players alternate moves; a legal move either (i) removes a positive number of tokens from exactly one heap, or (ii) removes positive numbers of tokens from two or more heaps simultaneously, subject to the constraint that the multiset of removed amounts equals a "losing Nim position" for ordinary Nim on those heaps (equivalently, in the original two-heap Wythoff game one removes equal amounts from both heaps; the N-heap version generalises this by allowing simultaneous removals constrained by Nim-losing patterns). The player unable to move loses. A position is a P-position if the Previous player (the one who just moved) can force a win.

For each fixed (N−2)-tuple of nonnegative integers (a_1, …, a_{N−2}), order the P-positions (a_1, …, a_{N−2}, x_n, y_n) with x_n ≤ y_n by the n-th smallest value of x_n. Let φ = (1+√5)/2.

Prove or disprove the following two conjectures:

(1) (Mex-plus-shift description.) There exist nonnegative integers A and B, depending on (a_1, …, a_{N−2}), and a finite "exceptional" set, such that for all sufficiently large n,
   x_n = mex{ x_i, y_i : i < n } + A,   y_n = x_n + n + B,
where mex denotes the minimum excludant of a set of nonnegative integers.

(2) (Golden-ratio asymptotics.) There exist integers A, B (depending on (a_1, …, a_{N−2})) such that for all sufficiently large n,
   x_n = ⌊n φ⌋ + A + ε_n,   y_n = ⌊n φ^2⌋ + B + ε'_n,
with bounded error terms ε_n, ε'_n ∈ {−1, 0, 1}.
status_search_result: The conjectures appear still open in full generality. Sun and Zeilberger gave a sufficient condition and verified the three-heap case for small initial heap sizes (up to 10 tokens), and later work has extended partial results, but no complete proof for all N ≥ 3 or arbitrary fixed heaps is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine the actual game values in End-Nim, analyze impartial and partizan End-Wythoff and Fraenkel’s generalized end-heap Wythoff variant, analyze Hub-and-Spoke Nim and the natural forest generalization, and decide how broadly integer-valued behavior fails or holds in Red-Blue Cherries positions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following combinatorial games played between two players who alternate moves, with the player unable to move losing (normal play convention).

(1) End-Nim. A position is a finite sequence (h_1, h_2, …, h_n) of positive integers (heap sizes arranged in a row). A move consists of removing any positive number of tokens from either the leftmost heap h_1 or the rightmost heap h_n (a heap that becomes empty is removed from the row). Determine the Sprague–Grundy values G(h_1,…,h_n) of all positions.

(2) End-Wythoff (impartial version). A position is a sequence (h_1,…,h_n) of positive integers. A move is either (a) an End-Nim move as above, or (b) a simultaneous removal of equal positive numbers of tokens from the two end heaps h_1 and h_n (provided n ≥ 2). Determine the Sprague–Grundy values; in particular, characterize the P-positions.

(3) Partizan End-Wythoff. As in (2) but with Left and Right restricted to different end heaps (Left may only act on the leftmost heap or take equally from both, Right only on the rightmost heap or take equally from both). Determine the game values in the partizan sense.

(4) Generalized end-heap Wythoff. Same as (2)/(3) but the equal-removal move may take any equal positive number of tokens from h_1 and h_n with the constraint generalized so that the two end heaps need not be the only heaps affected in a prescribed way (treat the position as a row of heaps, where a Wythoff-style move acts on the two extreme heaps). Analyze the P-positions and Sprague–Grundy values.

(5) Hub-and-Spoke Nim. A position is a "hub" heap together with several "spoke" heaps each attached to the hub. A move removes a positive number of tokens from any single heap, subject to the rule that the hub heap may only be reduced if all spoke heaps adjacent to it are empty (or some analogous spoke restriction). Determine the Sprague–Grundy theory of this game, and analyze the natural generalization in which the underlying graph is a forest and a move removes tokens from a leaf heap only.

(6) Red-Blue Cherries. A position is a finite collection of "cherries" each colored red or blue and attached by stems in a prescribed combinatorial structure; Left removes blue cherries (with the prescribed local rules of the game) and Right removes red ones. Decide whether every Red-Blue Cherries position has an integer game value, and characterize precisely when integer-valued behavior fails.
status_search_result: These problems are posed as unsolved problems in a recent compendium of open problems in combinatorial game theory; no published resolution of the Sprague–Grundy theory of End-Nim, the partizan or generalized End-Wythoff variants, Hub-and-Spoke Nim, or the integer-value question for Red-Blue Cherries was found. They appear to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Kotzig’s Nim by deciding whether every finite move set yields eventual periodicity as the circle length grows, analyzing the misère version, and resolving the stated conjectures for specific move sets such as {1,4} and {3,5}.
self_contained_problem:
Kotzig's Nim is played on a directed cycle of length $n$ as follows. A token is placed at a fixed vertex of the cycle $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, and the players alternately move the token clockwise by a number of steps chosen from a fixed finite set $M \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ of allowed moves. A vertex, once visited (including the starting vertex), may not be revisited; a player who cannot move loses (normal play convention). For each $n$, let $O_M(n) \in \{\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{P}\}$ denote the outcome of the game (first-player win or second-player win) under optimal play.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every finite move set $M \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, the sequence $\{O_M(n)\}_{n \geq 1}$ is eventually periodic in $n$.

(b) Carry out the analogous analysis for the misère version of Kotzig's Nim, in which a player unable to move wins.

(c) Resolve the eventual-periodicity question (and determine the eventual period and outcome pattern) for the specific move sets $M = \{1,4\}$ and $M = \{3,5\}$.
status_search_result: Recent work (Arun, "Geography, Kotzig's Nim, and Variants", published in Theoretical Computer Science 2024 and presented as an RSI 2023 project) reports a proof that for every fixed finite move set $M$, the outcome sequence of Kotzig's Nim is eventually periodic in $n$, resolving the main conjecture in the normal-play case. The misère version and complete explicit periods/outcomes for specific move sets such as $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,5\}$ do not appear to be fully settled in the published literature, so the overall problem is partially solved.
