paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Obtain asymptotic estimates for the proportions of N-, O-, and P-positions in Epstein’s Put-or-Take-a-Square game.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the impartial combinatorial game "Put-or-Take-a-Square" (due to Richard Epstein), played with a single pile of nonnegative integer size. From a position with $n \geq 1$ chips, the player to move chooses either to remove a positive perfect square $s^2 \leq n$ (so the new position is $n - s^2$), or to add a positive perfect square $s^2$ with $s^2 \leq n$ (so the new position is $n + s^2$). The position $0$ is terminal and the player who cannot move (faced with $n=0$) loses; positions from which infinite play is optimal for one side are classified as O-positions (drawn under optimal play). Under normal play, classify each positive integer $n$ as 
- an N-position (the Next player to move wins), 
- a P-position (the Previous player wins, i.e., the player to move loses), or 
- an O-position (optimal play leads to a draw / infinite game). 

For $N \geq 1$, let $\mathcal{N}(N)$, $\mathcal{P}(N)$, $\mathcal{O}(N)$ denote the number of integers $1 \leq n \leq N$ that are N-, P-, and O-positions respectively. Determine the asymptotic behavior, as $N \to \infty$, of the proportions
$$\frac{\mathcal{N}(N)}{N}, \quad \frac{\mathcal{P}(N)}{N}, \quad \frac{\mathcal{O}(N)}{N},$$
i.e., find asymptotic estimates (limits or sharp growth rates) for the densities of N-, O-, and P-positions in this game.
status_search_result: The problem of obtaining asymptotic densities of N-, O-, and P-positions in Epstein's Put-or-Take-a-Square game is listed among unsolved problems in combinatorial game theory in the Games of No Chance 5 volume (2017). Empirical computations exist, but no rigorous asymptotic estimates have been established, and no later paper resolving this density question was located.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Analyze the still-open four-heap case of Gale’s Nim when all heap sizes are distinct and greater than 2, and extend the analysis to the natural generalization with h heaps where play ends once k heaps have vanished.
self_contained_problem:
Gale's Nim is the following impartial combinatorial game. There are four heaps of tokens. On each move, a player chooses one heap and removes any positive number of tokens from it (possibly the entire heap). The game ends as soon as three of the four heaps have been emptied, leaving only one nonempty heap; the player who makes the move that causes the third heap to vanish wins (normal play convention).

(a) Determine the P-positions (previous-player winning positions) for Gale's Nim restricted to starting configurations in which the four heap sizes are pairwise distinct and each is strictly greater than 2.

(b) For integers h > k ≥ 1, consider the generalization in which the game is played with h heaps under the same move rule, with play terminating as soon as k of the heaps have vanished. Determine the P-positions, or give a structural characterization of the winning strategy, for this (h,k) family of games.
status_search_result: Gale's Nim has only a partial analysis (due to Brouwer and Guy independently); the four-heap case with distinct heap sizes all greater than 2 is listed as still open in the most recent compilation of unsolved problems in combinatorial games (Games of No Chance 5, 2017). No subsequent resolution was found in the search.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the known analysis of Euclid’s Nim from two integers to broader settings, including the partially solved three-integer case, and determine values or at least atomic weights for Partizan Euclid positions.
self_contained_problem:
Euclid's Nim is the following combinatorial game on an ordered tuple of positive integers. In the two-pile version, a position is a pair (a,b) of positive integers; a legal move replaces (a,b) by (a, b - k a) for some positive integer k with b - k a > 0, or symmetrically by (a - k b, b). The player unable to move loses (normal play). The two-pile game is fully understood: the first player has a winning strategy from (a,b) with a ≤ b iff b/a ≥ φ = (1+√5)/2, and the Sprague–Grundy values are known.

(a) (Three-integer Euclid's Nim.) Extend the analysis to positions consisting of triples (a,b,c) of positive integers, where a legal move subtracts a positive integer multiple of one entry from another entry, subject to the result remaining positive. Determine the P-positions and, more generally, the Sprague–Grundy function of this game for arbitrary triples (only special cases are currently known).

(b) (Partizan Euclid.) Consider the partizan version in which Left and Right have differing move options on a position (a,b) (for instance, Left may only subtract multiples from one specified coordinate and Right from the other, or analogous restrictions). Determine the combinatorial game values of Partizan Euclid positions; failing that, determine their atomic weights (in the sense of combinatorial game theory, governing the all-small / infinitesimal behavior of positions).
status_search_result: The three-integer Euclid's Nim has been investigated by Collins and Lengyel ("The game of 3-Euclid", Discrete Mathematics 308 (2008), 1130–1136) and by Ho ("Variations of the Game 3-Euclid", 2012), who solve special cases and certain restricted variants, but no complete description of the Sprague–Grundy function for general triples is known. No published complete determination of values or atomic weights for Partizan Euclid was located. The problem therefore appears partially solved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Complete the odd-parameter analysis of Dudeney, explain the evidence suggesting arbitrarily long pearl-string periods and possibly incompletable behavior, and determine the structure underlying the unresolved odd-Y cases.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the impartial combinatorial game DUDENEY, defined as follows. Fix a positive integer Y (the upper bound). A position consists of a single heap of n ≥ 0 beans together with a record of the opponent's most recent move (an integer in {1, 2, …, Y}, or "none" at the start). On a turn a player removes between 1 and Y beans from the heap, subject to the restriction that the number removed must differ from the number the opponent removed on the immediately preceding move. A player unable to move loses (normal play convention).

For each Y, the sequence (G_Y(n))_{n≥0} of Sprague–Grundy (Nim) values of the positions with heap size n (after a generic opening) is eventually periodic; the structural patterns of these sequences are called "pearl-strings", with a well-defined period associated to each Y.

(a) Complete the analysis of the Nim-value sequence G_Y for every odd Y, classifying the pearl-string structure in all remaining unresolved odd-Y cases.

(b) Determine whether the pearl-string periods for odd Y are bounded, or whether they become arbitrarily large as Y → ∞ through odd values.

(c) Decide whether there exist odd values of Y for which the analysis is "incompletable" in the sense that no finite description of the Nim-value sequence exists (i.e., G_Y fails to be eventually periodic, or no algorithm computes its structure), and identify the underlying combinatorial structure governing the odd-Y cases.
status_search_result: The DUDENEY game appears in the "Unsolved Problems in Combinatorial Games" updates (Games of No Chance volumes). The even-Y case is straightforward, while the odd-Y analysis remains incomplete despite partial progress by Wallace, Fink, and Saff. Observed pearl-string periods are reported to grow without apparent bound, and the source explicitly states the analysis may never be complete. No subsequent resolution has been located.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine whether Schuhstrings can have arbitrarily many simultaneous string terminations, extending the known example with three simultaneous terminations.
self_contained_problem:
Schuhstring is a combinatorial game played with a finite collection of "strings," each of which is a positive integer. On a turn, a player chooses one string of length n and replaces it by a string of length n − d for some allowed deduction d (with 1 ≤ d ≤ Y for a fixed maximum deduction Y); when a string is reduced to length 0 it terminates and is removed. A position is said to exhibit k simultaneous string terminations if there exists a single move (in some play of the game) that causes exactly k strings to reach length 0 at the same time (equivalently, the game-theoretic analysis forces k strings to terminate simultaneously at one move).

It is known that there exist Schuhstring positions in which three strings terminate simultaneously (for example, with maximum deduction Y = 3430). Determine whether, for every positive integer k, there exists a Schuhstring position in which k strings terminate simultaneously. Equivalently, can the number of simultaneous string terminations in Schuhstring be made arbitrarily large?
status_search_result: The problem appears in a standard list of unsolved problems in combinatorial games, where it is recorded that Kevin Saff found an example with three simultaneous terminations and conjectured that arbitrarily many are possible. No published resolution of this conjecture was located; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Analyze DUDE, the unbounded Dudeney game, and explain the apparent lack of a simple pattern in its nim-values.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following take-away game, called DUDE (the unbounded version of Dudeney's game). A position consists of a finite multiset of heaps of nonnegative integer sizes together with a "forbidden move" m ≥ 0, written [h_1, h_2, …, h_k; m]. A move consists of choosing one heap and removing a positive integer number r of tokens from it, with the single restriction r ≠ m (where m is the size of the removal performed by the opponent on the previous turn; at the start of play m = 0, which imposes no restriction, and any positive r is allowed since heaps are unbounded). The position then becomes the resulting multiset of heaps together with the new forbidden value m' = r. The player who cannot move loses (normal play convention).

Define the Sprague–Grundy (nim) value G([h_1, …, h_k; m]) of every such position via the usual recursion 
G(P) = mex { G(P') : P' is a position reachable from P by a legal move }, 
with G of a terminal position equal to 0.

Problem: Carry out a complete analysis of DUDE. In particular, determine a closed-form description (or a structural characterization) of the nim-values G([h_1, …, h_k; m]) as a function of the heap sizes h_1, …, h_k and the forbidden move m, and explain whether the apparent lack of a simple pattern observed in computed values can be replaced by an explicit formula or proven to follow no such pattern.
status_search_result: DUDE (unbounded Dudeney) appears as a listed unsolved problem in the standard compendium of unsolved problems in combinatorial games. While the P-positions are known in some cases, no simple description of the full nim-value table has been established, and the problem is still considered open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Develop fuller analyses of games with pass moves, including complete or improved solutions for Nim with a pass, Chocolate Bar with a pass when s is even, regularity questions for octal games with a pass, the case of more than one pass, and structural questions about Oslo versions of games.
self_contained_problem:
Background. In an impartial combinatorial game under the normal play convention, every position has a Sprague–Grundy value (SG-value), defined recursively by G(x) = mex{ G(y) : y is an option of x }, where mex denotes the minimum excludant. A position is a P-position (previous-player winning) iff its SG-value is 0. A "game with a pass" is the variant obtained from a base game G by giving each player, once during the whole play, the option of making a single pass move instead of a legal move (the pass is consumed once it is used; if a player cannot move and the pass has been used, that player loses).

(a) Nim with a pass. In ordinary Nim, there are k piles of sizes n_1,…,n_k and a move removes a positive number of tokens from a single pile; the player unable to move loses. Augment Nim with one global pass move (available once to whichever player chooses to use it). Determine the P-positions (and, more generally, the Sprague–Grundy values) of Nim-with-a-pass for k ≥ 3, in particular giving a closed-form characterization or proving that none of a given complexity exists.

(b) Chocolate Bar with a pass. Consider the Chocolate Bar game parameterized by integers t, s, k: a position is a triple (x,y,z) of nonnegative integers, and a move replaces (x,y,z) by (x',y,z) with 0 ≤ x' < x, or (x, y', z) with 0 ≤ y' < y, or (x, y, z') with 0 ≤ z' < z, subject to the constraint y ≤ ⌊z/s⌋ (chocolate cannot exceed the bar). Augment this game with a single global pass. For odd s, the P-positions are known; provide a complete analysis (P-positions and SG-values) for the case when s is even.

(c) Octal games with a pass. An octal game is specified by a code 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 … with each d_i ∈ {0,…,7}, defining a heap game in the standard way. It is known that many octal games have eventually periodic Grundy sequences (the so-called regularity). When one global pass is added to an octal game, determine which octal games have eventually periodic (regular) Grundy sequences, and classify the kinds of regularity that can occur.

(d) Multiple passes. For each of the above games, extend the analysis to the variant in which each player is allowed p ≥ 2 passes during the whole play (or in which a total of p passes is shared). Describe how the P-positions and SG-values depend on p.

(e) Oslo versions. Define the "Oslo version" of an impartial game G to be the variant in which a player, on their turn, may either make a legal move of G or declare "Oslo," after which the roles of the players are exchanged for the remainder of the play (the Oslo declaration may be used at most once in the entire game). For natural families of games G (e.g., Nim, Wythoff, Chocolate Bar, octal games), determine the P-positions and Sprague–Grundy theory of their Oslo versions, and identify structural relationships between G and its Oslo variant.

Provide, where possible, complete solutions; otherwise, give the strongest partial structural results.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Advance misère analysis of octal and quaternary games by deciding whether the Dawson’s Kayles quotient becomes infinite at heap 34, producing presentations and detection algorithms for infinite misère quotients, and defining and detecting algebraic periodicity well enough to solve the listed periodic octal examples.
self_contained_problem:
Background. An impartial combinatorial game under the misère convention is one in which the last player to move loses. To each finite set A of impartial games one associates its misère quotient Q(A): the commutative monoid obtained by quotienting the free commutative monoid generated by the positions reachable from A (under disjunctive sum) by the indistinguishability congruence ≡, where G ≡ H iff for every game X, G+X is a previous-player win (under misère play) precisely when H+X is. Octal games are coded by a string ·d₁d₂d₃… with digits dᵢ ∈ {0,…,7}; quaternary games use digits in {0,1,2,3}. Dawson's Kayles is the octal game ·07. For a single octal/quaternary game Γ let Qₙ(Γ) denote the misère quotient of the set {Γ-heap of size k : 1 ≤ k ≤ n}. It is known that Q₃₃(·07) is finite, of order 638. A game Γ is said to exhibit algebraic periodicity in misère play if, informally, the sequence of partial quotients Qₙ(Γ) stabilizes in a structural (algebraic) sense beyond ordinary periodicity of Grundy values.

Problems. 
(a) Decide whether Q₃₄(·07), the misère quotient of Dawson's Kayles taken through heap size 34, is infinite.
(b) Provide a general method that, given a finite set A of impartial games (specified, e.g., by their game graphs), produces a presentation of Q(A) when it is finite and otherwise produces a finite presentation or other certificate establishing that Q(A) is infinite; in particular, give an algorithm that decides whether Q(A) is infinite.
(c) Give a precise mathematical definition of "algebraic periodicity" for misère play of an octal (or quaternary) game, give an algorithm that detects it from finite data, and use it to produce complete misère analyses of those octal games whose normal-play Grundy sequences are periodic and which empirically display algebraic periodicity in misère play.
status_search_result: Published work computes the partial misère quotient of Dawson's Kayles up to heap 33 (order 638), but no source reports a determination of finiteness at heap 34 or a general algorithm for detecting infinite misère quotients. Algebraic periodicity in misère play remains informally described in the literature without a generally accepted definition or detection algorithm, indicating the questions remain open.

original_question: Prove or refute the conjecture that every MNEM position has finite nim-value, and prove or refute the claimed formula that in MEM and MNEM one has value floor(n/k) whenever k squared is at least n.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two impartial combinatorial games played on a single heap of tokens. A position is a pair (n, k) of nonnegative integers, where n is the current heap size and k records how many tokens were removed on the immediately preceding move (with the convention that the initial position can be written (n, 1), allowing the first player any legal move).

(MEM) From the position (n, k), a legal move consists of removing i tokens, where k ≤ i ≤ n, producing the new position (n − i, i). If no such i exists (i.e. n < k), the player to move loses (normal play convention).

(MNEM) From the position (n, k), in addition to the moves allowed in MEM, the moving player may also add tokens: for each i with 1 ≤ i < k they may move to (n + i, i). (Thus MNEM differs from MEM only in permitting "negative-progress" moves that increase the heap while reducing the memory.)

Let G(n, k) denote the Sprague–Grundy (nim) value of position (n, k) in the relevant game.

(a) Prove or disprove: in MNEM, every position (n, k) has finite nim value.

(b) Prove or disprove: in both MEM and MNEM, whenever k² ≥ n one has
        G(n, k) = ⌊ n / k ⌋.
status_search_result: The games MEM and MNEM were introduced by Larsson, Rubinstein-Salzedo, and Siegel (2019, "Memgames"), where these conjectures were formulated and reported as verified experimentally for small n but with no known proof. original_question: Extend Fibonacci Nim beyond the solved cases by analyzing the multiheap game for values of α other than 2 and for larger numbers of heaps.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a real or integer parameter α ≥ 1. The single-heap α-Fibonacci Nim is played as follows: there is one heap of n tokens; on the first move a player may remove any positive number of tokens strictly fewer than n; on each subsequent move a player may remove between 1 and ⌊α·k⌋ tokens, where k is the number of tokens removed by the opponent on the previous move. The player who removes the last token wins. The classical case α = 2 on a single heap is solved via the Zeckendorf (Fibonacci) representation.

Consider the multiheap extension: the position consists of h heaps of sizes (n₁, …, n_h), together with a record of the number k of tokens removed on the previous move (or "free" if it is the first move). A move selects one heap and removes between 1 and ⌊α·k⌋ tokens from it (any positive number on the first move). The last player to move wins.

Problem. For each integer h ≥ 2 and each parameter α (in particular, for α ≠ 2 with h = 2, and for h ≥ 3 with arbitrary α including α = 2):

(a) Characterize the P-positions (previous-player-winning positions) of the multiheap α-Fibonacci Nim.

(b) Determine the Sprague–Grundy values of single-heap positions in a form that allows the multiheap game to be analyzed by XOR (or otherwise give a complete description of optimal play).
status_search_result: The single-pile Fibonacci Nim (α = 2) is fully solved via Zeckendorf representations, and a two-heap variant has been characterized in special cases ("Global Fibonacci Nim" and related work). original_question: Extend the analysis of self-referential subtraction games by solving SUSEN for more than three heaps and solving the still-unsolved two-heap case of ALBUS.
self_contained_problem:
Consider impartial combinatorial games played on a finite multiset of heaps of nonnegative integer counters under normal play convention (the player unable to move loses). For a position with nonzero heaps of sizes $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k$, let $S = \{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$ denote the set of distinct nonzero heap sizes currently present.

Define two self-referential subtraction games:

(i) SUSEN ("SUbtraction Set ENcoded"). A legal move from a position is to choose one heap of size $a_i$ and remove from it exactly $s$ counters, where $s \in S$ and $1 \le s \le a_i$. (Thus the subtraction set used at each turn is the set of currently present nonzero heap sizes.)

(ii) ALBUS. A legal move from a position is to choose one heap of size $a_i$ and remove from it exactly $s$ counters with $1 \le s \le a_i$ and $s \notin S$. (Thus the currently present nonzero heap sizes are precisely the forbidden subtraction amounts.) For a single heap, the only legal move is to reduce it to $1$ counter.

Solve the following:

(a) For SUSEN, determine all P-positions (i.e., previous-player winning positions) for arbitrary number of heaps $k \ge 4$. (The three-heap case is known.)

(b) For ALBUS, determine all P-positions in the two-heap case $(a,b)$ with $a, b \ge 1$.

Available sources describe the three-heap case of SUSEN as solved (proof by Alex Fink) and explicitly state that the two-heap case of ALBUS remains unsolved. No subsequent publication resolving SUSEN for four or more heaps or solving two-heap ALBUS was found.

original_question: Resolve the specific ko-temperature problem at N4 in the Jiang–Rui position, and more broadly unify or sharply distinguish atomic weight theory from Nakamura’s liberty theory while extending liberty theory to practical Go complications such as internal and external kos.
self_contained_problem:
Consider combinatorial game theory applied to the game of Go. Two principal frameworks are available for analyzing capturing races (semeai) and related positions:

(i) Atomic weight theory (the all-small / infinitesimal theory developed within combinatorial game theory), which assigns to a position an integer-valued "atomic weight" that governs the outcome of sums of infinitesimal Go games.

(ii) Nakamura's theory of liberties, which assigns numerical liberty counts to groups in a capturing race and predicts the winner of the race via arithmetic on these counts.

Consider also the specific "Jiang–Rui position," a Go endgame/semeai position in which, after Black takes a ko at the point L6 on move 85, the local hot region includes the intersection N4.

Solve the following:

(a) Determine, in closed form, the temperature of the local game at the intersection N4 in the Jiang–Rui position immediately after Black takes the ko at L6.

(b) Either produce a single combinatorial-game-theoretic formulation that subsumes both atomic weight theory and Nakamura's liberty theory (so that each is recovered as a specialization), or exhibit a precise position or class of positions on which the two theories give provably different predictions, thereby sharply distinguishing them.

(c) Extend Nakamura's theory of liberties so that it correctly handles capturing races complicated by simple kos, including both internal kos (kos located within the contested groups) and external kos (kos elsewhere on the board whose ko threats interact with the race).
status_search_result: No published resolution of the N4 ko-temperature question in the Jiang–Rui position, nor a unification (or sharp separation) of atomic weight theory with Nakamura's liberty theory, nor an extension of liberty theory to internal/external kos, could be located. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend current analyses of Woodpush from three-piece positions to positions with more pieces and understand draw behavior under superko.
self_contained_problem:
Woodpush is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite one-dimensional strip of squares. Each square is either empty or occupied by a Left (L) or Right (R) piece. On their turn, a player must move one of their own pieces according to the following rule: a Left piece normally retreats one square to the left (and a Right piece one square to the right) into the adjacent empty square, or off the board if there is no square in that direction; however, if the adjacent square in the retreating direction is occupied by a contiguous string of pieces that contains at least one opposing piece, then the player may instead move the piece in the opposite direction, pushing the entire contiguous string one square ahead (pieces pushed off the end of the board are removed). Standard play convention applies: a player unable to move loses. The superko rule forbids any move that recreates a previously seen global board position; positions in which optimal play forces infinite repetition under superko are declared draws.

(a) Extend the use of top-down thermography (a thermographic technique that handles loopy/ko-like positions) beyond Woodpush positions with three pieces, and determine the temperatures and mean values of Woodpush positions containing four or more pieces.

(b) Identify and rigorously prove which classes of multi-piece Woodpush positions are draws under the superko rule (for example, positions of the form L□L□…□R□R with various numbers of empty squares between the inner pieces).

original_question: Make progress on Elkies’s conjecture that values ∗k occur for all k in sufficiently large pawn endings, analyze Impartial Chess, and determine larger transfinite or multidimensional values in Infinite Chess and 3-dimensional Chess.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, the Nimber (or star value) ∗k is the value of a single Nim heap of size k, and a position has value ∗k if and only if it is equivalent under disjunctive sum to such a heap. Consider chess played on an m×n board (with m, n allowed to be arbitrarily large), under standard chess rules restricted to pawn endings (positions containing only kings and pawns, or — in the simplest model — only pawns moving according to standard chess rules, treated as a loopfree combinatorial game where the players Left and Right move the White and Black pawns respectively, with a player who cannot move losing).

(a) Prove or disprove the conjecture that for every nonnegative integer k there exists a pawn ending on some sufficiently large board whose combinatorial game value is ∗k.

(b) Formulate and analyze "Impartial Chess," the impartial variant in which either player on their turn may move any piece (of either color) according to the usual chess movement rules, under normal play convention; determine the Sprague–Grundy values of natural classes of positions.

(c) For Infinite Chess (chess played on the infinite board ℤ×ℤ) and for 3-dimensional Chess (chess generalized to a 3-dimensional board with naturally extended piece movement rules), determine whether arbitrarily large transfinite ordinal game values and/or multidimensional surreal-number values can be realized by legal positions, and exhibit explicit positions achieving such values.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Improve the king-and-rook versus king analysis and determine whether the boiling point of Entrepreneurial Chess is 55/8.
self_contained_problem:
Entrepreneurial Chess (ECHESS) is a combinatorial game played on the quarter-infinite board {(x,y) : x,y ≥ 1}. The initial position has a Black king together with a White king and a White rook. The usual rules of chess apply, with the following modifications:
- The board is the first quadrant (no upper or right boundary; the left and bottom edges act as the edges of an ordinary chessboard).
- On any of his turns, in lieu of making a chess move, Black may "cash out": the game ends and Black receives a payoff equal to x+y, where (x,y) are the coordinates of his king at that moment.
- If Black is checkmated or stalemated by the White pieces in the ordinary chess sense, the game terminates with payoff 0.
- White's objective is to minimize the eventual payoff, Black's to maximize it.

For a position G in this loopy combinatorial game, the temperature t(G) is defined in the usual sense of combinatorial game theory (via cooling by t until the position becomes infinitesimally close to a number). The boiling point of ECHESS is the supremum of the temperatures of all positions reachable from king-and-rook versus king starting configurations.

Problem: Refine the analysis of the king-and-rook versus king endgame on the quarter-infinite board for ECHESS, and determine whether the boiling point of ECHESS equals 55/8.
status_search_result: The value 55/8 for the boiling point of Entrepreneurial Chess remains a conjecture by Berlekamp and Low. original_question: Determine whether natural stopper positions with wild cycles exist in Phutball-like games, whether noncollusive draws or P-positions occur in standard Phutball, analyze PHLAG Phutball boards, and give a complete analysis of 2×n Directional Phutball.
self_contained_problem:
Phutball (Philosopher's Football) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a rectangular board (traditionally 19×15). A single "ball" stone sits on a board intersection and either player may, on a turn, either (a) place a "man" on any empty point, or (b) make a (possibly compound) jump: the ball hops over one or more contiguous lines of men in any of the eight orthogonal/diagonal directions, with each jumped group of men being removed after the jump; consecutive jumps in a single turn may change direction. One player wins by ending a turn with the ball on or past their goal line. In the language of loopy combinatorial game theory, a position is called a stopper if it has no infinite alternating play; a wild cycle is an alternating cycle in the canonical-form game graph of length greater than three (it is known that 2-cycles and 3-cycles cannot occur in stoppers, but longer cycles are a priori possible). A P-position is one from which the Previous player (the player who just moved) has a winning strategy. The "PHLAG Phutball" variants are versions of Phutball played on alternative boards (such as hexagonal or otherwise non-standard tilings). "Directional Phutball" is the variant in which each player is restricted to jumping the ball only in their own designated direction toward their own goal.

Solve the following:

(a) Exhibit, or prove the nonexistence of, a Phutball-like position whose canonical form is a stopper that contains a wild cycle (an alternating cycle of length at least 4), arising in actual play rather than by collusion of the players.

(b) Determine whether standard Phutball admits any noncollusive draw, and more specifically whether it admits any P-position.

(c) Carry out the loopy game-theoretic analysis of PHLAG Phutball boards, classifying positions up to canonical form.

(d) Give a complete combinatorial-game-theoretic analysis of Directional Phutball played on a 2×n board for all n ≥ 1, determining the outcome class (and where possible, the canonical form or game value) of every reachable position.

The existence of a non-collusive position in an actual combinatorial game whose canonical form is a stopper containing a wild cycle is listed as unsolved; all Phutball positions studied so far are equivalent to stoppers, but the wild-cycle question is unresolved. P-positions / non-collusive draws in standard Phutball and the complete analysis of 2×n Directional Phutball also appear to remain open, while general Phutball is known to be PSPACE-hard and its immediate-win problem NP-complete.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Quantify first-player winning efficiency in Hex by finding the shortest guaranteed winning path on an n×n board and the minimum number of moves that guarantees a first-player win.
self_contained_problem:
The game of Hex is played on an n×n rhombus-shaped board of hexagonal cells. Two players, conventionally called the first player (who owns two opposite sides of the rhombus) and the second player (who owns the other two opposite sides), alternately place stones of their color on empty cells. The first player moves first. A player wins as soon as the cells occupied by their stones contain a connected chain (through hexagonal adjacency) linking their two opposite sides of the board. It is known (by a strategy-stealing argument) that for every n the first player has a winning strategy.

Define:
(a) f(n) = the minimum, over all first-player winning strategies S, of the maximum over all second-player replies of the length (number of stones) of the first player's connecting chain at the moment the game is won.
(b) g(n) = the minimum, over all first-player winning strategies S, of the maximum over all second-player replies of the total number of moves made in the game until the first player wins.

Problem: For each positive integer n, determine f(n) and g(n).
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open in general. Only the trivial lower bound f(n) ≥ n is known, and exact first-player winning strategies have been computed only for small boards (up to 8×8 fully, and many 9×9 openings); no closed-form or general quantitative answer for f(n) or g(n) is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Formalize and prove the listed large-board escape, critical-rank, retreat-rule, and board-width/board-count assertions for Fox and Geese, including the explicit thesis conjectures for special n×4, n×6, and Ceylonese-rule positions.
self_contained_problem:
Fox and Geese is the following two-player combinatorial game. Consider an n×k board (n,k ≥ 4) of squares colored as a checkerboard, with k Geese (Left's pieces) initially placed on the k dark squares of one short edge and a single Fox (Right's piece) initially placed on some dark square. Players alternate moves. A Goose moves one square diagonally forward (toward the Fox's starting edge) onto an empty dark square; the Fox moves one square diagonally in any of the four diagonal directions onto an empty dark square. There are no captures. Left ("the Geese") wins if the Fox is trapped with no legal move; Right ("the Fox") wins if the Fox reaches the Geese's starting edge.

For a position P, define its span to be a numerical measure of how far the Fox is from escape (for example, the minimum number of Fox-moves to a winning configuration in optimal play, or a related rank in the loopy game value).

Establish the following:

(a) (Large-board escape.) Prove that for every k ≥ 4, there exists N(k) such that on every n×k board with n ≥ N(k), every initial Fox position results, under optimal play, in a Fox win; quantify N(k) explicitly for k = 4 and k = 6.

(b) (Critical rank.) Show that any formation of three Geese in suitable configuration on a sufficiently large board admits a critical span/rank value, and determine that value.

(c) (Retreat rule.) Determine the outcome and game-theoretic value when the Fox is empowered to retreat in the manner of a bishop, sliding backward any number of squares in a straight diagonal line; analyze the variants in which the allowed retreat step-lengths are restricted to the set {1,2} versus {1,3}.

(d) (Board width and Geese count.) For every pair (k, g) with k ≥ 4 and g ≥ 2, determine, as a function of n, the outcome of n×k Fox and Geese with g Geese.

(e) (Ceylonese rule variant.) Under the Ceylonese rule (in which a Goose may also move one square sideways but never backward), prove the analogous escape/trap thesis for the standard initial position.

Provide rigorous proofs (or explicit counterexamples) for each assertion.
status_search_result: The collection of Fox-and-Geese questions (span, three-Geese formations, retreat rules, varying widths and counts of Geese, Ceylonese rule) is listed in the standing "Unsolved problems in combinatorial games" compendium, and remains posed as open in the most recent (Games of No Chance 5) update. Parallel computations have strongly solved the standard 8×8 instance, but the general thesis-style conjectures for arbitrary n×4, n×6, varying Geese counts, retreat-empowered Fox, and Ceylonese rules remain unresolved.

original_question: Decide whether the displayed sequences of Hare and Hounds positions become increasingly hot or have arbitrarily large negative atomic weight, and prove or disprove the explicit value conjecture for the starting position on a 6n+5 by 3 board.
self_contained_problem:
Hare and Hounds is a two-player combinatorial game played on a rectangular grid graph of dimensions m × 3 (m columns, 3 rows). One player controls three Hounds, initially placed on the three leftmost squares (one in each row), and the other player controls a single Hare, initially placed on the rightmost middle square. Players alternate moves: the Hounds player moves one Hound one step horizontally forward (rightward) or vertically (up/down), but never backward; the Hare may move one step in any of the four orthogonal directions. The Hounds win if they trap the Hare so it cannot move; the Hare wins if it slips past all Hounds (reaches a column strictly to the left of every Hound) or if the Hounds player cannot move. Treating the game using combinatorial game theory (so that positions have well-defined game-theoretic values, temperatures, and atomic weights), consider the sequence of starting positions indexed by the board length m = 5, 11, 17, …, i.e. m = 6n + 5 for n = 0, 1, 2, ….

(a) Determine whether the temperatures of these starting positions tend to infinity (i.e. whether the sequence of positions is "increasingly hot").

(b) Determine whether the atomic weights of these positions are unbounded below (i.e. whether arbitrarily large negative atomic weights occur in the sequence).

(c) Prove or disprove the conjecture that gives an explicit closed-form game-theoretic value for the starting position on every 6n + 5 by 3 board (n ≥ 0).

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend Domineering analysis by resolving open rectangular-board values, especially on 2×n, 3×n, and 4×n boards, characterizing hot positions up to infinitesimal shift, finding new temperatures, and pushing the partial analysis of Tromineering.
self_contained_problem:
Domineering is a two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice. Two players, Left (Vertical) and Right (Horizontal), alternate moves; on his turn, Left places a 1×2 vertical domino covering two empty adjacent cells, while Right places a 2×1 horizontal domino covering two empty adjacent cells. A player who cannot move loses (normal play convention). Each Domineering position has a well-defined game value in the sense of Combinatorial Game Theory (Conway), and to each hot position one can associate a temperature.

Resolve the following open questions about Domineering on rectangular m×n boards:

(a) Determine the exact combinatorial-game value (not merely up to "ish", i.e., up to addition of an infinitesimal) of the 2×n board for every even n; currently the value is only known up to infinitesimal shift.

(b) Determine the exact game values of the 3×n and 4×n boards for all n for which they are currently unknown.

(c) Characterize, up to infinitesimal shift, all hot Domineering positions (i.e., positions whose temperature is strictly positive).

(d) Exhibit a Domineering position whose temperature is a value not previously realized as the temperature of any known Domineering position (a "new temperature").

(e) For the variant Tromineering, in which the dominoes are replaced by straight trominoes (Left places vertical 1×3 trominoes, Right places horizontal 3×1 trominoes) and play is otherwise identical, extend the partial analysis to obtain values for further rectangular boards.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., endgame database studies and Tromping/Tromineering analyses by Blanco–Fraenkel) has extended Domineering analysis to larger boards and computed winners or values for additional cases, but exact values for general 2×n (even n), 3×n, and 4×n boards remain incomplete, and Berlekamp's questions on characterizing all hot positions and finding a new temperature are not reported as resolved. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine the nim-dimension of one-dimensional and two-dimensional NoGo, and decide whether there is a bound on the denominators of fractions that occur on the two-dimensional board.
self_contained_problem:
NoGo is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite graph (typically a strip of n vertices for the "one-dimensional" version, or an m × n rectangular grid for the "two-dimensional" version). Players, Left (Black) and Right (White), alternately place a stone of their own color on an empty vertex, subject to the rule that after the move, every maximal monochromatic connected component of stones must be adjacent to at least one empty vertex (i.e., must retain a "liberty"). A player who cannot make a legal move loses (normal play convention).

Each position decomposes under disjunctive sum into a value in the universe of partizan combinatorial games. The nim-dimension of a class of games is the smallest k ≥ 0 such that every value arising from positions in that class can be written as a sum of a number (a surreal of the form p/2^q) and an "atomic" infinitesimal part lying in the additive subgroup generated by ↑, * , *2, …, *2^k (so nim-dimension 0 means only nimbers * and *2 are needed, etc.); if no such finite k exists, the nim-dimension is infinite.

(a) Determine the nim-dimension of one-dimensional NoGo, i.e., the class of all positions arising on the 1 × n strip for n ≥ 1.

(b) Determine the nim-dimension of two-dimensional NoGo, i.e., the class of all positions arising on m × n rectangular boards.

(c) Decide whether there exists a uniform upper bound on the denominators (when written in lowest terms as dyadic rationals p/2^q) of the number-parts of values that occur among positions of two-dimensional NoGo boards.
status_search_result: Linear (one-dimensional) NoGo has been the subject of recent computational study (e.g., a 2024 paper "Solving Linear NoGo with Combinatorial Game Theory" extending solved boards up to 1 × 39 using CGT-based search), but no source found explicitly determines the nim-dimension of one- or two-dimensional NoGo, nor settles the boundedness of denominators on the 2D board. The questions appear to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Resolve the listed narrow-board Dots-and-Boxes conjectures, including the Faroese and Icelandic one-dimensional cases, eventual periodicity in misère Swedish 1×n Dots-and-Boxes, and a complete impartial theory for the Icelandic 1×n game.
self_contained_problem:
Dots-and-Boxes is a classical combinatorial game played on an array of dots. Two players alternately draw a single horizontal or vertical unit edge between adjacent dots; whenever a player completes the fourth side of a unit square (a "box"), that player claims the box and must move again. When all edges have been drawn, the player who has claimed more boxes wins (in normal play); in the misère convention, the player who has claimed fewer boxes wins.

Several board variants differ only in which boundary edges are pre-drawn at the start of play:
- American board: no boundary edges are pre-drawn.
- Swedish board: the entire outer rectangular boundary is pre-drawn.
- Icelandic board: only the left and bottom boundary edges are pre-drawn.
- Faroese board: only the bottom boundary edge is pre-drawn.

For a positive integer n, the 1×n board has 2 rows and n+1 columns of dots, forming n unit squares in a single row.

Resolve the following:

(a) (Faroese 1×n) Determine the outcome class (and Sprague–Grundy / game value structure as appropriate) for Faroese 1×n Dots-and-Boxes for all n, confirming or refuting the conjectured pattern that completely characterizes who wins.

(b) (Icelandic 1×n, partizan) Determine the outcome class for Icelandic 1×n Dots-and-Boxes for all n, confirming or refuting the conjectured characterization.

(c) (Misère Swedish 1×n) Prove or disprove that the outcome of misère Swedish 1×n Dots-and-Boxes is eventually periodic in n.

(d) (Impartial Icelandic 1×n) Provide a complete theory of the impartial version of Icelandic 1×n Dots-and-Boxes: compute its Sprague–Grundy values for all n and describe their structure.
status_search_result: These narrow-board Dots-and-Boxes conjectures (Faroese and Icelandic 1×n outcome conjectures, eventual periodicity of misère Swedish 1×n, and a complete impartial theory of Icelandic 1×n requested by Berlekamp) are listed among unsolved problems in combinatorial games. A targeted web search did not surface any publication resolving these specific conjectures, so they appear to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Sprouts in either normal or misère play.
self_contained_problem:
The game of Sprouts is a two-player combinatorial game defined as follows. The initial position consists of n spots drawn in the plane. A move consists of drawing a new curve in the plane that:
  (i) joins two existing spots, or starts and ends at the same existing spot,
  (ii) does not cross itself or any previously drawn curve, and does not pass through any existing spot, and
  (iii) after which a new spot is placed somewhere along the newly drawn curve.
At every moment each spot may have at most three incident curve-ends (a spot becomes "dead" when it has three incident ends). Players alternate moves and a player who cannot move loses (normal play convention) or wins (misère play convention).

Let N(n) ∈ {1, 2} denote the index of the winning player (1 = first player, 2 = second player) in the normal-play n-spot Sprouts game under optimal play, and let M(n) denote the same for the misère-play version.

Problem: Extend the analysis of Sprouts. Specifically:
  (a) Determine N(n) for as large a range of n as possible, and prove or disprove the conjecture that N(n) = 1 (first-player win) if and only if n ≡ 3, 4, or 5 (mod 6).
  (b) Determine M(n) for as large a range of n as possible, and prove or disprove the conjecture that, except for n = 1 (first-player win) and n = 4 (second-player win), M(n) = 1 if and only if n ≡ 0, 4, or 5 (mod 6).
status_search_result: The Sprouts conjectures remain unproven in general, but computer-assisted analysis has steadily extended the known outcomes. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Sylver Coinage.
self_contained_problem:
Sylver Coinage is a two-player combinatorial game played as follows. The set of positive integers $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ is fixed. Players alternate turns; on each turn the current player names a positive integer that is not expressible as a nonnegative-integer linear combination of the previously named integers. A player who names $1$ loses (equivalently, the game ends when the set of allowed moves becomes empty after $1$ is named). 

It is known (Hutchings's theorem) that every prime $p \geq 5$ is a winning opening move, although no explicit winning strategy following such an opening is known. The status of the opening moves $2^i 3^j$ with $(i,j) \neq (0,0)$ (the nontrivial 3-smooth openings) is essentially open; in particular, it is unknown who wins after the opening move $16$, and more generally who wins from arbitrary positions generated by 3-smooth numbers.

Problem: Extend the analysis of Sylver Coinage. Specifically, determine, for each opening move $n \in \{2,3,4,6,8,9,12,16,\dots\}$ (the 3-smooth numbers other than $1$), whether the first player wins or loses, and where the first player wins, provide an explicit winning strategy. More generally, classify positions (finite sets $S \subset \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ of previously-named integers with $1 \notin \langle S\rangle$) as P-positions or N-positions and, for N-positions, exhibit a winning move.
status_search_result: Sylver Coinage remains substantially unsolved. While Hutchings's theorem proves that every prime $\geq 5$ is a winning first move, no explicit winning strategies are known, and the status of 3-smooth opening moves (including $16$, for which Conway reportedly offered a prize) is still open as of recent expositions.

original_question: Extend the analysis of Von Neumann’s Game from directed forests to directed acyclic graphs.

Von Neumann's Game is the following two-player combinatorial game. A position is a finite directed forest (later, a finite directed acyclic graph) with a single token placed on one of its vertices. original_question: Push further analysis of Inverting Hackenbush and Reversing Hackenbush.
self_contained_problem:
Blue-Red Hackenbush is the two-player combinatorial game played on a finite graph whose edges are colored blue or red and in which certain vertices are designated as ground. On a turn, Left removes a blue edge and Right removes a red edge; after the removal, every edge no longer connected to the ground is also deleted. A player unable to move loses.

Define two variants:

(a) Inverting Hackenbush: the game is played as in Blue-Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (and the resulting disconnected edges fall), every remaining edge in the graph has its color inverted (blue↔red).

(b) Reversing Hackenbush: the game is played as in Blue-Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (and the resulting disconnected edges fall), every remaining edge has its color reversed (blue↔red) only within the connected component(s) containing the removed edge's former endpoints (or, equivalently, along an analogous local rule).

original_question: Determine whether Beanstalk has any O-positions, meaning positions of infinite remoteness.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the two-player combinatorial game Beanstalk, defined as follows. The Giant chooses a positive integer $n_0$. Then Jack and the Giant alternate moves, producing a sequence $n_0, n_1, n_2, \dots$ of positive integers according to the rule: if $n_i$ is even, then $n_{i+1} = n_i/2$; if $n_i$ is odd, then the player to move chooses $n_{i+1} = 3n_i + 1$ or $n_{i+1} = 3n_i - 1$. The player who moves to $1$ wins.

For a position $n$, define the remoteness in the usual way for combinatorial games with last-player-winning convention: positions from which a player can win have remoteness equal to $1$ plus the minimum remoteness of an option leading to a losing position, and positions from which a player must lose have remoteness equal to $1$ plus the maximum remoteness of any option. A position is called an O-position if it has infinite remoteness (equivalently, optimal play from that position never terminates).

Determine whether the Beanstalk game admits any O-positions; that is, decide whether there exists a starting integer $n_0$ such that, under optimal play, the sequence $n_0, n_1, n_2, \dots$ never reaches $1$.
status_search_result: The question of whether Beanstalk (a game of Isbell/Conway closely related to the Collatz-type 3n±1 dynamics) has any O-positions appears to remain open; published unsolved-problem compilations in combinatorial game theory still list it as unresolved, and no resolution was located in the search.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Prove or disprove the conjecture that for a at least d at least 3 and all sufficiently large n the Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is a first-player win in normal and misère play, extend the rational-number variant, and analyze the permutation-graph variant.
self_contained_problem:
Let a, d ≥ 2 be integers and let n ≥ (a−1)(d−1)+1. The Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is played as follows. Two players, I and II, alternately choose distinct real numbers (initially from {1,2,…,n}), with I moving first. Each chosen number is appended to a sequence in the order it is played. The game ends as soon as the sequence so far contains an increasing subsequence of length a or a decreasing subsequence of length d (by the Erdős–Szekeres theorem this must occur within (a−1)(d−1)+1 moves).

(a) Normal play: the player whose move first creates such a monotone subsequence wins. 
(b) Misère play: the player whose move first creates such a monotone subsequence loses.

A position is called an N-position if the Next player (the one to move) has a winning strategy; the game is a "first-player win" when the empty starting position is an N-position.

Tasks:
1. Prove or disprove: for all integers a ≥ d ≥ 3 and all sufficiently large n, the Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game on {1,…,n} is a first-player win under normal play and also under misère play.
2. Consider the rational-number variant, in which on each turn a player names any rational number not previously named (so the resulting sequence is an arbitrary finite sequence of distinct rationals), with the same winning conditions. Determine, for a ≥ d ≥ 3, the outcome of this variant under normal play (and extend the analysis to misère play).
3. Consider the permutation-graph variant, in which on each turn a player names a pair (i, π_i) with i ∈ {1,…,n} distinct from previously chosen indices and π_i a real value distinct from previously chosen values, thereby building a partial permutation; the game ends when the values, read in order of increasing i, contain a monotone subsequence of length a or d. Analyze who wins this variant under normal and misère play.
status_search_result: The conjecture (originally by Harary, Sagan, and West) that the Erdős–Szekeres sequence game is a first-player win for a ≥ d ≥ 3 and all sufficiently large n remains open in general. Recent work by Pudwell (2024–2025) determines the winner and a winning strategy when a ≥ b and b ∈ {2,3,4,5}, settling several cases but leaving the general conjecture for arbitrary a ≥ d ≥ 3 unresolved. The rational and permutation-graph variants are also not fully analyzed in the literature.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Thinning Thickets from very thin trees to general trees.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the partizan combinatorial game "Thinning Thickets" played on a finite directed graph called a thicket, defined as follows. A thicket is a finite directed graph with a distinguished nonempty set of vertices called roots, such that every arc lies on a directed path to some root. Each arc of the thicket is colored blue, red, or green. Two players, Left and Right, move alternately. On Left's turn she deletes a blue or green arc; on Right's turn he deletes a red or green arc. After deletion, every arc that no longer lies on a directed path to some root is also removed. The player unable to move loses (normal play convention).

A cordon is a thicket whose underlying undirected graph is a "very thin" tree — a singly rooted path-like tree in which every non-root vertex has out-degree exactly one and in-degree at most one (i.e., the underlying graph is a simple path with a single root endpoint). The game values, canonical forms, and Nim-dimension of Thinning Thickets are known for cordons (in particular it is known that green cordons have infinite Nim-dimension).

Problem: Determine the game-theoretic values (canonical forms, temperatures, atomic weights, and/or Nim-values where applicable) of Thinning Thickets positions whose underlying thickets are general finite rooted trees, extending the known analysis from cordons (very thin trees) to arbitrary rooted trees with arbitrary branching, with each arc colored blue, red, or green.
status_search_result: The Thinning Thickets game was introduced and analyzed for cordons (very thin singly-rooted trees) by Huggan and Nowakowski (Integers 18, 2018). They explicitly leave the extension of the analysis to general trees as an open problem, and no subsequent published resolution was found in a search.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Extend the analysis of Chomp by solving the infinite three-dimensional game, proving or disproving uniqueness of the winning move from a 3×n rectangle, computing the nim-value of transfinite Chomp position ω×4, and resolving the transfinite stratification conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Chomp is the two-player impartial game played on a (possibly infinite) poset of "cookies." On a move, a player selects a remaining cookie c and removes c together with every cookie c' ≥ c; the player who is forced to take the bottom (minimum) cookie loses. The standard d-dimensional finite Chomp is played on the poset {1,...,n_1} × ... × {1,...,n_d} ordered componentwise, and transfinite Chomp allows the coordinate sets to be arbitrary ordinals.

Resolve the following four problems about Chomp.

(a) (Infinite three-dimensional Chomp.) Determine the outcome (first-player win or second-player win) and a winning strategy for Chomp played on the poset ω × ω × ω.

(b) (Uniqueness of the winning move in 3 × n.) For every integer n ≥ 1, prove or disprove that the starting position {1,2,3} × {1,...,n} of Chomp admits exactly one winning first move, and provide a deterministic (non-strategy-stealing) proof of this fact.

(c) (Nim-value of ω × 4.) Compute the Sprague–Grundy value G(ω × 4) of the transfinite Chomp position whose underlying poset is ω × {1,2,3,4}.

(d) (Stratification conjecture.) For transfinite Chomp positions, the "stratification" phenomenon asserts that the leading (highest) term of the Cantor normal form of the Sprague–Grundy value of a position is determined by the leading term of the ordinal "size" of the position; more precisely, in dimension d, for any finite Chomp position A and any ordinal h with Cantor normal form h = ω^i · a_i + (lower terms), 0 < a_i < ω, one has
   G(A + (1^{d-1} × h)) = ω^i · a_i + (lower terms),
i.e. the highest term of the Grundy value equals the highest term of h. Prove or disprove this stratification conjecture in full generality.
status_search_result: Standard references on Chomp (including the Huddleston–Shurman treatment of transfinite Chomp and survey/encyclopedia pages) discuss these questions as open: no explicit winning strategy is known for infinite 3D Chomp, no deterministic proof of uniqueness of the winning move from a 3×n rectangle is known (only strategy-stealing existence), G(ω × 4) has not been computed, and the stratification conjecture for transfinite Chomp remains unresolved.

original_question: Determine the remaining structure of (n;k) Subset Take-Away after the original broad conjectures were disproved.
self_contained_problem: Subset Take-Away on a truncated Boolean lattice. Fix integers n ≥ k ≥ 1 and let [n] = {1, 2, …, n}. Define the poset P_{n,k} to consist of all non-empty subsets of [n] of cardinality at most k, ordered by inclusion. Two players play the impartial game (n;k) on P_{n,k} as follows. On a move a player chooses an element S of P_{n,k} that has not yet been removed and removes S together with every T in the current position that contains S (i.e. an order filter generated by S, intersected with the remaining poset). Players alternate; the player who cannot move (the poset is empty) loses. Under normal play convention, determine, for every pair (n,k) with 1 ≤ k ≤ n, which player has a winning strategy in the game (n;k), and describe the structure of the set of P-positions (previous-player wins). In particular, classify all pairs (n,k) for which the second player wins (n;k), and provide a closed-form description or a complete combinatorial characterization of the outcome function (n,k) ↦ {first-player-win, second-player-win}.
status_search_result: The Subset Take-Away game introduced by Gale, and its (n;k) variant studied by Gale and Neyman, remains unresolved in general. Gale's conjecture that the second player always wins is verified for n ≤ 6, and computer-aided work has disproved certain broader conjectures about the (n;k) version (e.g. exhibiting that the second player wins (7;3) although natural divisibility conditions fail). No complete classification of P-positions for the (n;k) family is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Make substantial progress on sowing or Mancala games, which the paper identifies as a still-fruitful and largely untouched field of investigation.
self_contained_problem:
A sowing game (Mancala-type game) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite row or ring of pits, each pit containing a nonnegative number of stones. A move consists of selecting a nonempty pit, removing all its stones, and "sowing" them one by one into successive pits according to a fixed rule (typically moving in a fixed direction around the board, possibly with capture rules depending on the variant). The terminal condition and winning condition are specified by the particular variant (for example, the player unable to move loses, or the player capturing the most stones wins).

Develop a substantive combinatorial-game-theoretic analysis of sowing/Mancala games. Concretely, address one or more of the following:

1. For a natural infinite family of sowing games (parametrized by the number of pits n and/or the number of stones s), determine the Sprague–Grundy values of positions, or prove structural results (e.g., periodicity, polynomial-time computability) about these values.

2. Identify nontrivial classes of sowing positions whose game-theoretic outcome (first-player win, second-player win, or draw) can be determined in closed form or by an efficient algorithm.

3. Provide a rigorous classification of which sowing variants are tractable (e.g., polynomial-time solvable) versus intractable (e.g., PSPACE-hard) as combinatorial games, beyond the small finite instances already settled by computer search.

Any such result, supported by proof, would constitute substantial progress on the combinatorial theory of sowing games.
status_search_result: Sowing/Mancala games remain a largely open area in combinatorial game theory. Small variants (Awari, Kalah for some sizes, MiniMancala, Ohvalhu) have been solved by computer search, but more complex variants such as Bao and Omweso are unsolved, and no general combinatorial-game-theoretic framework giving Sprague–Grundy values or structural results for natural infinite families is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether there is a polynomial-time algorithm for k-Annihilation when k is greater than 1.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called the k-Annihilation game (for a fixed positive integer k). The board is a finite strip of squares labelled 0, 1, 2, …, n. A finite set of indistinguishable tokens ("coins") is placed on distinct squares of the strip. The two players move alternately. A legal move consists of selecting one coin on some square s > 0 and shifting it to an unoccupied square s' with 0 ≤ s' < s and s - s' ≤ k. A player who cannot move loses (normal play convention).

The decision problem k-Annihilation is: given an initial position (the strip length n and the set of occupied squares), determine whether the player to move has a winning strategy.

Question: For every fixed integer k > 1, does there exist an algorithm that decides k-Annihilation in time polynomial in the size of the input (i.e., polynomial in n and the number of coins)?
status_search_result: The question, posed by Fraenkel, asks whether k-Annihilation admits a polynomial-time algorithm for k > 1. Partial results are known: polynomial strategies have been given for the three-coin case for any k, and for the subcase k = 2m - 2 the Sprague-Grundy function can be computed in polynomial time. The general case for k > 1 does not appear to have been resolved in the literature surveyed; it is listed among Fraenkel's unsolved problems on combinatorial games.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether palindromic positions in Toppling Dominoes have uniquely occurring values, determine actual values in Timber and Partizan Timber more systematically, and characterize whether some values never occur in the partizan setting.
self_contained_problem:
Toppling Dominoes is a partizan combinatorial game played on a finite row (string) of dominoes, where each domino is colored Left (L), Right (R), or grey (g). On Left's turn, Left chooses an L-domino or a g-domino and topples it either leftward or rightward; toppling a domino in a given direction removes that domino together with every domino on the chosen side of it. Right plays analogously on R- or g-dominoes. The player who cannot move loses (normal play). Each position has a well-defined game value in the partizan universe (a surreal number, a switch, or a more general game). A position is called a palindrome if its color string reads the same left-to-right as right-to-left.

Timber is the impartial variant in which all dominoes are grey and either player may topple any domino in either direction (with the same chain-removal rule); Partizan Timber is the partizan variant in which each domino is colored L or R and is toppleable only by its owner in either direction, again with chain removal.

Settle the following questions:

(a) (Palindromic uniqueness in Toppling Dominoes.) Prove or disprove: if G is a Toppling Dominoes position whose color string is a palindrome, then no other Toppling Dominoes position (palindromic or not) has the same game value as G. Equivalently, does each game value arising from a palindromic position arise from a unique Toppling Dominoes position?

(b) (Systematic value computation.) Give a systematic method (e.g., a closed-form rule, recursion, or polynomial-time algorithm) for computing the game values of arbitrary Timber positions and of arbitrary Partizan Timber positions.

(c) (Missing values.) In Partizan Timber, characterize which game values can occur as values of positions, and in particular determine whether there exist surreal numbers, or more general partizan game values, that never occur as the value of any Partizan Timber position.
status_search_result: Subsequent work on "Toppling Conjectures" (Games of No Chance 4) established that for each number x there is exactly one Toppling Dominoes position with value x, and that position is necessarily a palindrome, resolving the numeric case of the palindrome-uniqueness conjecture; the full conjecture for arbitrary game values, together with the systematic determination of Timber/Partizan Timber values and the characterization of values that never occur, does not appear to have been fully settled in the literature.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Find second-player-win scoring variations of two-player Tower of Hanoi if any exist, and extend the still-incomplete analysis of Hanoi Stick-Up beyond the cases already solved.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two combinatorial-game settings built on the classical Tower of Hanoi.

(A) Two-player scoring Tower of Hanoi. Take the standard Tower of Hanoi with three pegs and n disks of distinct sizes, where a legal move transfers the top disk of one peg onto another peg subject to the rule that no disk may be placed on a smaller disk. Two players alternate making legal moves. A scoring variation is specified by assigning, to each ordered pair (i,j) of distinct pegs, a real-valued weight w(i,j); the score of a play is the sum (with appropriate sign convention for the two players, or with each player accumulating the weights of their own moves) of the weights of the moves performed. Termination is governed by reaching a designated target configuration, or by a no-legal-move/normal-play convention. Determine whether there exists any choice of disk number n, peg-pair weights w(i,j), starting position, and termination/scoring rule for which the resulting two-player Tower of Hanoi scoring game is a second-player win under optimal play, and if so exhibit such a variation.

(B) Hanoi Stick-Up. Played with several stacks of disks of distinct sizes; on a turn a player moves a top disk from one stack onto another stack subject to the Hanoi rule (a disk may only be placed on a strictly larger disk, or on an empty position). Play ends when no legal move remains; both the normal convention (last player to move wins) and the misère convention (last player to move loses) are considered. The outcome of every starting position with at most six stacks is known. Extend the determination of the normal-play outcome class and the misère-play outcome class to all starting positions with seven or more stacks.
status_search_result: Published work on two-player Tower of Hanoi (Chappelon, Larsson, Matsuura) analyzes scoring and last-move variants and reports that the known variants are first-player wins, leaving the existence of second-player-win scoring variations as an open question. No source found resolving the Hanoi Stick-Up analysis beyond six stacks.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether full-deck Beggar-My-Neighbor has any draws or cycles.
self_contained_problem:
Beggar-My-Neighbor is a two-player deterministic card game played with a standard 52-card deck consisting of 12 "court" cards (4 Aces, 4 Kings, 4 Queens, 4 Jacks) and 40 plain cards. The deck is shuffled and dealt entirely between two players, each receiving a face-down pile. Players alternate turns, each turn playing the top card of their pile face-up onto a central pile. If the played card is a plain card and no court card is currently "active," play passes to the opponent. If a court card is played, the opponent must "pay" by playing cards from the top of their pile: 4 cards for an Ace, 3 for a King, 2 for a Queen, 1 for a Jack. During payment, if the paying player plays another court card, the obligation transfers and the original player must now pay. When a payment is completed with only plain cards, the player who last played a court card collects the entire central pile (placing it on the bottom of their face-down pile, in order). The game ends when one player holds all 52 cards.

Question: Does there exist an initial deal of the full 52-card deck such that play proceeds forever without termination (equivalently, enters a cycle)? In other words, decide whether full-deck Beggar-My-Neighbor admits any non-terminating (drawn or cyclic) game.
status_search_result: In February 2024, Brayden Casella (with coauthors) constructed an explicit deal of the full 52-card deck that produces a non-terminating, cyclic game of Beggar-My-Neighbor (a 62-trick cycle reached by 30 distinct starting hands). The result has been posted on arXiv (2403.13855) and published in the American Mathematical Monthly (2025), resolving the existence question affirmatively.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Construct a game with simple playable rules, finitely many options per move, a simple explicit strategy, play length at most exponential in the input, and NP-hard-or-harder decision complexity.
self_contained_problem:
Exhibit a two-player combinatorial game G satisfying all of the following conditions simultaneously:

1. (Simple, playable rules.) The rules of G can be described concisely and the game is humanly playable.
2. (Bounded branching.) From every position, each player has only finitely many legal moves.
3. (Simple explicit strategy.) There is an explicitly described strategy (i.e., a function from positions to moves) that one of the players can follow.
4. (Bounded play length.) The number of moves in any play of G, as a function of the size n of the input position, is at most exponential in n (i.e., bounded by 2^{p(n)} for some polynomial p).
5. (High decision complexity.) The decision problem "Given an instance/position of G, does the first player have a winning strategy?" is NP-hard, or harder (e.g., PSPACE-hard, EXPTIME-hard).

Construct such a game G, or prove that no such game exists.
status_search_result: This is a reformulation of a question raised by Berlekamp concerning the existence of games with simple rules and explicit strategies yet high computational complexity. No widely cited resolution appears in standard surveys of unsolved problems in combinatorial game theory; the problem is generally treated as open/folklore in the combinatorial games community.

original_question: Determine whether the winner of a sum of switch games of the form a k b | c or a | b k c can be decided in polynomial time or is NP-hard.
self_contained_problem:
Consider combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway) of the following form. A "switch" position is denoted {x | y} with x > y, meaning that the Left player can move to a position of value x and the Right player can move to a position of value y (no further moves available after that). More generally, write a position "a k b | c" to denote the game {a, {b | c} | ... } where Left has options to numbers a and to the switch {b | c}, and "a | b k c" to denote the game with Left option a and Right option to the switch {b | c}; here a, b, c are dyadic rationals (or integers) with a > b > c, and k indicates the switch component on the indicated side.

Given a finite multiset G = G_1 + G_2 + ... + G_n (disjunctive sum) where each G_i is a game of one of the two forms

    a_i k b_i | c_i    or    a_i | b_i k c_i,

with rational numerical parameters specified in the input, determine the computational complexity of deciding the winner of G under normal play convention (last player to move wins) with Left to move.

Question: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm (in the size of the description of G) to decide the winner of such a sum, or is this decision problem NP-hard?

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Give formal and algorithmic foundations for sentestrat and top-down thermography, compute or characterize dogmatic thermographs of double kos, build a temperature theory for all loopy games, and characterize natural conditions under which the overheating homomorphism is uniquely determined.
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of combinatorial game theory (in the sense of Berlekamp–Conway–Guy), where games are recursively defined positions G = {G^L | G^R} with Left and Right options, and where one studies invariants such as the mean value, temperature, and thermograph of a game, address the following collection of open foundational problems concerning thermography and the heating/overheating operators:

1. (Sentestrat.) Sentestrat is a heuristic strategy defined as follows: when it is your turn to move in a sum of games, play in the component whose thermograph indicates the largest loss were the opponent to move there first (i.e., respond in the "hottest" component according to a defensive rule based on thermographs). Provide a formal definition and a rigorous proof of correctness for sentestrat, establishing under what hypotheses it achieves optimal or near-optimal play in sums of games.

2. (Top-down thermography.) Give an explicit algorithmic procedure for constructing thermographs in a "top-down" manner (working from the root of a game tree using bounds derived from ancestors, rather than purely bottom-up from terminal positions), together with a proof of its correctness and an analysis of its complexity.

3. (Dogmatic thermographs of double kos.) For loopy games of the type known as "double kos" (positions arising in Go that contain two interacting repetition cycles), develop the machinery needed to compute their dogmatic thermographs (thermographs defined under a fixed convention for resolving loops), and characterize these thermographs explicitly.

4. (Temperature theory for loopy games.) Construct a general temperature theory — including well-defined notions of mean value, temperature, cooling, heating, and thermograph — that applies to all loopy games (partizan games that need not satisfy the ending condition), extending the classical theory for short games.

5. (Uniqueness of the overheating-type homomorphism.) The map G ↦ *G (sending a game G to its nim-sum with the star game *) annihilates all infinitesimals. Identify a natural set of axiomatic conditions on a homomorphism on (an appropriate class of) games under which G ↦ *G is the unique homomorphism satisfying those conditions and annihilating all infinitesimals.
