paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Find a notion of simplest form that works for all finite loopy games including Carousel, detect natural wild cycles in playable games such as Phutball, and characterize when infinitesimal stoppers have well-defined atomic weight together with an algorithm to compute it.
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of loopy combinatorial games (two-player perfect-information games in which positions may recur, so that game graphs need not be acyclic), address the following three problems.

(1) Simplest form for finite loopy games. The standard theory of stoppers (loopy games with no infinite alternating play) provides each stopper with a unique canonical "simplest form" obtained by removing dominated options and bypassing reversible ones. However, the known notion of simplest form is known to fail to give a canonical representative for certain finite loopy games, in particular for the game Carousel (a specific small loopy game defined by the standard recursion arising in the loopy theory). Find an alternative notion of "simplest form" that applies to every finite loopy game (including Carousel) so that two such games are equal (in the sense of equality of game values) if and only if they have the same simplest form.

(2) Wild cycles in playable games. A loopy game-graph is said to contain a "wild cycle" if it contains a cycle that cannot be eliminated under any of the standard reductions used in the loopy theory. Although wild cycles are known to exist abstractly, no example has been identified in a naturally arising combinatorial game. Exhibit a wild cycle occurring in a playable game such as Phutball (Conway's Philosopher's Football), or prove no such cycle can occur.

(3) Atomic weight of infinitesimal stoppers. The atomic weight of an infinitesimal game (a game whose value is bounded in absolute value by every positive number of the form 1/n) is, when defined, an integer-valued (more generally, number-valued) measurement of how "all-small" the game is. For infinitesimal stoppers (loopy infinitesimals with no infinite alternating play), give necessary and sufficient conditions under which a well-defined atomic weight exists, and provide an algorithm that computes the atomic weight of any infinitesimal stopper g for which it is defined.
status_search_result: The three questions appear in standard problem lists on loopy combinatorial games attributed to A. N. Siegel. Subsequent work by Siegel (e.g. "New results in loopy games" and his GSM monograph) has refined the theory of stoppers and simplest forms, but no published resolution is found for (i) a unified simplest form covering Carousel, (ii) a natural wild cycle in a playable game such as Phutball, or (iii) a characterization plus algorithm for atomic weights of infinitesimal stoppers. They are still presented as open in the relevant literature.

original_question: Characterize where the nimber ∗2 can occur in natural games and, more generally, determine the smallest exponent bound controlling which nimbers ∗k can appear in a given game.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (loopfree, short) combinatorial game has a Sprague–Grundy value that, for an impartial position, is a nimber ∗k for some nonnegative integer k (with ∗0 = 0). For a given ruleset (a class of games), one may ask which nimbers ∗k actually arise as values of positions of that ruleset.

(a) Characterize the rulesets ("natural games") in which a position of value ∗2 can occur; in particular, give a structural description of the "habitat" of ∗2, i.e., the family of natural game rulesets that admit a position with Grundy value exactly 2.

(b) More generally, for a given ruleset G, define
   n(G) = the smallest nonnegative integer n such that every position of G has nimber value ∗k with k < 2^n
(set n(G) = ∞ if no such bound exists). Determine n(G), or sharp bounds on n(G), for natural rulesets, and characterize which sequences of nimbers ∗k (k < 2^n) can be realized as the set of nimber values of positions of some ruleset with parameter n.
status_search_result: Berlekamp's question about the "habitat of *2" — which natural rulesets contain a position of nimber value *2 — is recognized in the combinatorial game theory community as an open-ended problem. Partial results exist (e.g., explicit *2 positions found in Domineering, and an algorithm by Carlos dos Santos producing *k positions in Konane), but no general characterization or sharp bound on the exponent n controlling which nimbers can appear in an arbitrary ruleset is known.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Tighten the growth bounds for numbers of games born by day n, determine structural properties of games born by day 3 and of alternative birthday partial orders, describe the exact structure and parameters of the lattices L3 and L4, characterize which seed sets generate distributive or modular lattices, understand handedness in all-small lattices, count option-closed games, and find other natural planar lattice families.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A short combinatorial game is defined recursively as an ordered pair G = {G^L | G^R}, where G^L and G^R are finite sets of previously defined short games, called the Left and Right options of G. The unique game born by day 0 is 0 = {∅ | ∅}. The set of games born by day n, denoted B_n, consists of all games G such that every Left and Right option of G lies in B_{n-1}. Two games are identified when they have equal value under the usual equivalence G = H ⇔ G − H is a second-player win, where −G = {−G^R | −G^L} and G + H is defined by componentwise option addition.

The partial order on games is given by G ≥ H ⇔ G − H ≥ 0 (Left wins moving second). Under this order, the set of (equivalence classes of) games born by day n forms a lattice L_n with the further property that L_n is distributive when n ≤ 2. A game is all-small if every position reachable from it has at least one Left option and one Right option whenever it is nonzero; let L^0_n denote the lattice of all-small games born by day n. A game is option-closed if every option of every position is itself an option of the game.

Problems. Provide complete and rigorous answers to each of the following.

1. Tighten the known upper and lower bounds for |B_n|, the number of distinct games born by day n, improving the currently known doubly-exponential growth estimates.

2. Describe explicitly the partial order (lattice) structure of B_3 — its covering relations, rank/height function, atoms and coatoms, and any self-dualities or symmetry groups it admits.

3. For alternative recursive notions of "birthday" (for example, defining birthday as the maximum depth of a position, the length of a longest play, or the maximum over Left/Right option subgames of one plus the option's birthday), describe the structure of the resulting partial orders on games and compare them to the standard birthday ordering.

4. Determine the exact lattice structure of L_3 and L_4: their cardinalities, order dimensions, maximum longitudes (length of the longest chain), join- and meet-irreducible elements, and whether they are graded.

5. Characterize the sets S of seed games such that the smallest lattice (under the game order) generated by S is (a) distributive, (b) modular but not distributive. Exhibit, if possible, an explicit seed set producing a modular non-distributive lattice.

6. For the all-small lattices L^0_n, decide whether the elements possess an intrinsic notion of "handedness" — a canonical Z/2-action or sign — and if so describe its lattice-theoretic characterization.

7. Compute (or give exact asymptotics for) the number of option-closed games born by day n.

8. Identify additional natural families of combinatorial games whose value-lattices are planar (i.e., have order dimension at most 2), beyond the families already known.

original_question: Given a group or monoid of games, develop a general method for calculating the simplest game in each equivalence class modulo that structure.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game G is defined recursively by a pair of finite sets of games G = {G^L | G^R}, called the left and right options. Games form a partially ordered commutative monoid under disjunctive sum +, with the zero game 0 = {|} as identity, and a notion of equality where G = H iff G + H' = 0 for every K in some class, where H' is the conjugate (negative) of H. Given a submonoid (or subgroup) K of the universe of games, define the K-equivalence relation by: G ≡_K H iff G + X has the same outcome as H + X for every X in K. This partitions games into K-equivalence classes. Within each equivalence class one may seek a canonical "simplest" representative (for instance, one minimizing birthday, formal complexity, or having no dominated or reversible options relative to K).

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Develop a misère theory for unions of partizan games.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) partizan game is defined recursively by $G = \{G^L \mid G^R\}$, where $G^L$ and $G^R$ are finite sets of partizan games called the Left and Right options of $G$. The disjunctive sum (also called the union) of two games $G$ and $H$ is the game $G + H$ in which a player on their turn chooses one of the two component games and makes a legal move in it. In the normal-play convention, a player who cannot move loses; in the misère-play convention, a player who cannot move wins. Two games $G$ and $H$ are said to be equivalent (in a given convention and a given universe $\mathcal{U}$ of games closed under disjunctive sum and taking options) if for every $X \in \mathcal{U}$, the outcomes of $G + X$ and $H + X$ coincide.

Whereas the normal-play theory of disjunctive sums of partizan games is well developed (with a canonical-form theorem, an abelian group structure on equivalence classes, and the surreal-number embedding), the corresponding misère theory is far less complete: under misère play the class of partizan games does not form a group under disjunctive sum, equivalence is much coarser to detect, and few general structural simplification or comparison theorems are available.

Problem. Develop a misère theory for disjunctive sums (unions) of partizan games: namely, produce a general framework that provides canonical forms (or suitable equivalence/comparison invariants) for partizan games under misère disjunctive sum, identifies the algebraic structure of equivalence classes, and yields effective methods for determining the outcome of arbitrary disjunctive sums of partizan games in the misère convention.
status_search_result: A general misère theory for disjunctive sums of partizan games remains unresolved, but substantial partial progress has been achieved through the framework of "restricted" misère play, in which equivalence is defined within structured universes (e.g., dicot, dead-ending, alternating). Surveys and recent papers (e.g., Milley–Renault's survey, the "Restricted developments in partizan misère game theory" paper, and Milley's thesis "Restricted Universes of Partizan Misère Games") establish canonical forms and indistinguishability quotients in such universes, but no fully general theory comparable to normal play exists.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Resolve the open structural questions about impartial misère quotients, including faithfulness of quotient maps, subgroup intersections with P, classification growth, existence of quotient elements of specific periods such as 5 or 8, and smallest quotients containing specified periods.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{I}$ denote the class of impartial combinatorial games played under the misère convention (the last player to move loses). For a fixed set $\Gamma$ of impartial game positions closed under taking options, let $\equiv$ be the indistinguishability congruence: $G \equiv H$ iff for every position $X$ formed from $\Gamma$, the disjunctive sum $G+X$ has the same misère outcome as $H+X$. The quotient monoid $Q(\Gamma) = \langle \Gamma \rangle/\!\equiv$ together with the distinguished subset $P \subseteq Q(\Gamma)$ of $\equiv$-classes of previous-player-win positions is called the misère quotient of $\Gamma$. A surjective monoid homomorphism $\varphi : Q(\Gamma_1) \to Q(\Gamma_2)$ that arises from inclusion of game sets and respects the distinguished $P$-sets is called a quotient map; $\varphi$ is faithful if for all $a,b \in Q(\Gamma_1)$, $\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)$ implies that $a$ and $b$ are indistinguishable with respect to $P$ in $Q(\Gamma_1)$. An element $x$ of a misère quotient has period $n$ if $n$ is the smallest positive integer with $x^{k+n}=x^k$ for some $k\ge 1$.

Resolve the following structural questions about finite impartial misère quotients $(Q,P)$:

(1) Is every quotient map between impartial misère quotients faithful?

(2) For every finite impartial misère quotient $(Q,P)$ and every submonoid $S \subseteq Q$ that arises as a sub-quotient, must $S \cap P$ be nonempty?

(3) Extend the existing classification of finite impartial misère quotients to higher orders (i.e., describe all finite impartial misère quotients of order up to a prescribed bound).

(4) Does there exist an impartial misère quotient containing an element of period $5$? Does there exist one containing an element of period $8$?

(5) For each $n \in \{3,4,6\}$, determine the smallest (by monoid order) impartial misère quotient that contains an element of period $n$.
status_search_result: These structural questions on impartial misère quotients are listed among the open problems in the misère quotient theory developed by Plambeck and Siegel. Available surveys and the miseregames.org problem list still pose faithfulness of quotient maps, nonempty intersection with P, and the existence/minimality of quotients with elements of various periods as open; partial results (e.g., absence of odd-order quotients) restrict but do not resolve the period questions. No published resolution was located.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Characterize inverses in partizan misère universes by determining when G plus its conjugate is equivalent to zero in dicotic settings, whether every inverse must be the conjugate in suitably closed universes, and which universes forbid nonconjugate inverses.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A partizan combinatorial game is a finite game tree in which each non-terminal position has a set of Left options and a set of Right options; the disjunctive sum G+H and the conjugate (or "negative") -G obtained by swapping the roles of Left and Right are defined recursively in the usual way. Under the misère convention, the player who cannot move on their turn wins. A game G is dicotic if every non-terminal subposition has at least one Left option and at least one Right option; the class D of all dicotic games is closed under disjunctive sum and conjugation.

Given a class (universe) U of partizan games that is closed under disjunctive sum, taking options, and conjugation, two games G and H are equivalent modulo U, written G ≡ H (mod U), if for every X ∈ U the misère outcomes of G+X and H+X coincide. A game G is invertible in U if there exists H ∈ U with G+H ≡ 0 (mod U); the universe U is said to have the conjugate property if every invertible G has G + (-G) ≡ 0 (mod U), and to have no nonconjugate inverses if whenever G+H ≡ 0 (mod U) then H = -G (equivalently up to equivalence in U).

Problems.
(1) Characterize the games G ∈ D for which G + (-G) ≡ 0 (mod D), i.e., describe the invertible elements of the misère dicotic universe.
(2) Determine, for a given universe U of partizan misère games closed under sum, options, and conjugation, whether G+H ≡ 0 (mod U) forces H = -G.
(3) Classify the universes U of partizan misère games that admit no nonconjugate inverses.

More recently, Davies and Yadav ("Invertibility in the misère multiverse", 2024) proved that every universe (in the sense considered) has the conjugate property and gave a characterization of invertibility in each universe, addressing problems (2) and (3) in broad generality. The full classification questions in arbitrary universes are still an active area, so the problem is best described as partially solved rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Determine whether guaranteed scoring games are the largest conjugation- and disjunctive-sum-closed scoring universe into which normal-play games order-embed, and solve the game of Brushes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider combinatorial scoring games: two-player games of perfect information without chance in which each terminal position is assigned a real-valued final score (Left maximizes, Right minimizes). For such games one defines a disjunctive sum (players choose, on their turn, one component in which to move) and a conjugate (swap the roles of Left and Right and negate scores). A scoring universe U is a class of scoring games closed under taking options, under disjunctive sum, and under conjugation. The class of guaranteed scoring games consists of those scoring games G in which, for every position, the Left-stop is at least the Right-stop (so that an extra pass move can never harm its owner); this class is a scoring universe, and Conway's normal-play games admit an order-embedding into it (preserving disjunctive sum, conjugation, and the order ≥ defined via outcomes against all disjunctive-sum opponents).

(b) Solve the scoring game Brushes: provide a complete analysis (game values and/or optimal strategies determining the outcome from arbitrary starting positions) of this combinatorial scoring game.

A position in the game of Nim is a finite multiset $\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$ of nonnegative integers (the pile sizes); two players alternate moves, and a move consists of choosing one pile and replacing its size $a_i$ by any strictly smaller nonnegative integer. paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: For square-free lattice games and related lattice-point rulesets, determine whether winning moves from any N-position can be computed efficiently.
self_contained_problem:
A lattice game is specified by the following data: a pointed rational convex polyhedral cone $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a finite set of "move" vectors $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ (the ruleset), and a finite set of "defeated" positions $D \subset C \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$. From a position $p \in C \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, a player may move to $p - \gamma$ for any $\gamma \in \Gamma$ such that $p - \gamma \in C \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$; a player who cannot move (because the current position lies in $D$ or has no legal move) loses under normal play. Positions are classified recursively as P-positions (previous-player wins; equivalently, every move leads to an N-position) or N-positions (next-player wins; some move leads to a P-position). A lattice game is called squarefree if its ruleset can be encoded by a squarefree monomial structure generalizing the encoding of octal games.

Question: For squarefree lattice games (and the related class of lattice-point rulesets), does there exist an algorithm that, given any N-position $p$, computes in time polynomial in the bit-length of $p$ (together with the fixed game data) a legal move from $p$ to some P-position?
status_search_result: Guo and Miller proved their rational-strategy conjecture for squarefree lattice games under normal play, providing an algorithm for computing winning positions in that case; this yields a procedure for finding winning moves from N-positions. However, the broader conjecture that every lattice game has a rational strategy was disproved by Alex Fink (lattice games support universal computation), so an efficient general algorithm is impossible. The precise complexity (polynomial-time efficiency) of finding winning moves for the squarefree case does not appear to be fully resolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Decide whether every game with bounded nim-dimension has only finitely many exceptional cases in its atomic-weight calculations.
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of combinatorial games under normal-play convention, every short game G has a Grundy/nim-value and, for all-small games, an atomic weight (Conway–Berlekamp–Guy "uppitiness") aw(G), an integer-valued invariant defined recursively by aw(G) = "the value obtained by playing the atomic-weight calculus on options of G", with the property that aw behaves additively up to bounded perturbation. For a class C of games (closed under disjunctive sum and option-taking) the nim-dimension is the supremum, over G ∈ C, of the number of distinct nim-values appearing among the positions reachable from G; C is said to have bounded nim-dimension if this supremum is finite.

In computing atomic weights within such a class, one typically obtains a "generic" formula valid for all but finitely many positions, together with a list of "exceptional" positions where the generic formula fails and the atomic weight must be computed individually.

Question: Is it true that for every class of all-small combinatorial games with bounded nim-dimension, the atomic-weight calculation has only finitely many exceptional cases?

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Find other universal partizan games besides Generalized Konane, and develop general techniques for proving that certain game values cannot occur in a given ruleset.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A short partizan combinatorial game is defined recursively as a pair G = {G^L | G^R}, where G^L and G^R are finite sets of previously constructed short partizan games (the Left and Right options of G). Two such games are equal if they have the same canonical form; the class of equivalence classes forms the universe of short partizan game values, denoted U.

A ruleset R (a set of rules defining legal moves for Left and Right on positions of some combinatorial game) is called a universal partizan ruleset if, for every short partizan game value v ∈ U, there exists a position P in R whose canonical game value equals v. It is known that a certain ruleset called Generalized Konane is universal in this sense.

Problem.
(a) Exhibit additional universal partizan rulesets that are not equivalent to (and do not directly simulate) Generalized Konane.
(b) Develop general techniques that, given a ruleset R and a short partizan game value v, can prove that no position of R has value v (i.e., methods establishing that specified values cannot occur within a given ruleset).

status_search_result: Part (a) has seen significant progress: beyond Generalized (Portuguese) Konane, several additional rulesets have since been proven universal, including Turning Tiles and new rulesets introduced in recent works on universal partizan and universal dicotic rulesets. original_question: Determine boiling points of specific rulesets such as Domineering and develop feasible methods for obtaining strong upper bounds on temperatures.
self_contained_problem:
Domineering is a two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice. Players, conventionally called Left (Vertical) and Right (Horizontal), alternate moves; on each turn Left places a 1×2 vertical domino covering two adjacent empty cells, and Right places a 1×2 horizontal domino covering two adjacent empty cells. A player who cannot move loses. Each Domineering position G has a well-defined combinatorial game value, and an associated temperature t(G), defined as the smallest real number t such that the cooled game G_t is infinitesimally close to a number (equivalently, the highest critical temperature in the thermograph of G). The boiling point of Domineering is defined as the supremum of t(G) over all finite Domineering positions G.

(a) Determine the boiling point of Domineering. In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that this boiling point equals 2.

(b) Develop feasible general methods that yield strong (provably correct) upper bounds on the temperature t(G) of an arbitrary Domineering position G, and more generally for positions in other concrete rulesets of combinatorial games.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in combinatorial games
original_question: Develop a clearer theory of joins of games, including compatibility and switching mechanisms among normal, misère, and nearly disjunctive compositions.
self_contained_problem:
In combinatorial game theory, a position in a two-player game is identified with its set of options for the Left and Right players, and the disjunctive sum G + H of two games is defined as the game in which a player, on his or her turn, chooses one of the components and makes a legal move there. Outcomes of a game are determined either by the normal convention (the player unable to move loses) or by the misère convention (the player unable to move wins). Beyond the disjunctive sum, several other "joins" of games have been considered, including:
  - the conjunctive sum (each player must move in every component simultaneously),
  - the selective (or shortened) sum (a player may move in any nonempty collection of components),
  - "nearly disjunctive" compositions, in which the components are not fully independent but interact through some auxiliary mechanism, and
  - WHIM-type joins, in which on each turn a player must choose whether to play under the normal or misère convention, or in which a move may switch which component, or which convention, is currently active.

Develop a coherent theory of such joins of games that:
  (a) gives a precise formal definition of "compatibility" between two component games that is needed for the join to be well-defined and well-behaved;
  (b) treats uniformly the normal-play, misère-play, and mixed conventions, including joins in which a player may, as an option of a move, switch the current convention or the current active component;
  (c) classifies the algebraic structure (e.g., monoid, partial order, equivalence under the join) of games modulo such compositions, in analogy with the Sprague–Grundy theory for the disjunctive sum under normal play;
  (d) in particular formalizes and analyzes the "nearly disjunctive" joins, identifying invariants that determine outcomes of joined positions from invariants of the components.

State and prove a structural theorem that unifies these compositions and clarifies precisely which compatibility and switching mechanisms admit a tractable solution theory.
category_tag: Combinatorial game theory: joins of games
status_search_result: The problem is a longstanding research direction in combinatorial game theory. While Sprague–Grundy theory completely solves the disjunctive sum of impartial games under normal play, misère and "nearly disjunctive" joins remain only partially understood, and no unifying theory of compatibility and convention-switching joins (such as WHIM-type joins) appears to exist in the literature. Recent Games of No Chance volumes continue to list related questions, and surveys note that misère sums lack a general combination theory. No source found that resolves the problem.

original_question: Analyze multiplayer game behavior under different preference systems, especially the remaining open cases of misère three-player Nim and broader recursive/canonical-form questions for cooperative multiplayer sums.
self_contained_problem:
Consider three-player impartial combinatorial games played as disjunctive sums, where on each move the player whose turn it comes must move in exactly one component, players alternate in a fixed cyclic order, and a player who cannot move is eliminated (or, depending on convention, loses or wins). To resolve coalition ambiguities, a "preference system" is fixed: each player has a strict preference ordering on the possible final rankings of the three players, and each player plays optimally with respect to this ordering.

A central instance is misère three-player Nim: positions are triples (or tuples) of nonempty heaps of tokens, a move removes any positive number of tokens from a single heap, and under misère convention the player who takes the last token loses. Under the "podium rule" preference (each player most prefers to win; failing that, prefers to finish second rather than last), Li's analysis characterizes the P-positions of normal-play three-player Nim, but the misère version is only partially understood.

(a) Give a complete characterization of the outcome classes (i.e., for each starting position, determine which player wins under optimal play) for misère three-player Nim under the podium-rule preference system.

(b) For other natural preference systems on the set of finishing orders of three players, determine the outcome classes of misère three-player Nim.

(c) Develop a theory of canonical forms for cooperative/competitive multiplayer disjunctive sums: define and establish a recursive construction of game values, a comparison procedure between game forms, and canonical (reduced) representatives modulo game equivalence, analogous to the Conway canonical form for two-player partizan games but adapted to three or more players with prescribed preference systems.

original_question: For an elliptic curve C over Q, is the Tate-Shafarevich group X_C finite? The refined Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture involves |X_C|, but the source states that this group is not known in general to be finite, although it is conjectured to be so.

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$. For each place $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ (including the archimedean place), let $\mathbb{Q}_v$ denote the corresponding completion, and consider the Galois cohomology groups $H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}))$ and $H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}/\mathbb{Q}_v), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}))$. The Tate–Shafarevich group of $E$ is defined by
$$\mathrm{Sha}(E/\mathbb{Q}) \;=\; \ker\!\left(H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})) \;\longrightarrow\; \prod_{v} H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}/\mathbb{Q}_v), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}))\right),$$
where the map is induced by the restriction maps for each place $v$. Equivalently, $\mathrm{Sha}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ classifies isomorphism classes of principal homogeneous spaces (torsors) for $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that have a $\mathbb{Q}_v$-rational point for every place $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$.

status_search_result: The finiteness of the Tate–Shafarevich group for elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ remains open in general. It is known to be finite for elliptic curves of analytic rank 0 or 1 (work of Kolyvagin, Gross–Zagier, et al.), but the general case is widely regarded as an open conjecture, and is implicit in the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (a Millennium Prize Problem).

Let $W := V \setminus \overline{S}$ be the open complement of the closure of this union. Must the set $W(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points of $W$ be finite for every such $V$?
status_search_result: This is a form of Lang's conjecture on rational points (the "geometric/arithmetic" Lang conjecture), which predicts that rational points concentrate on the special/exceptional locus swept out by images of $\mathbb{P}^1$ and abelian varieties. It remains an open conjecture in general; only partial results are known (e.g., Faltings' theorem on subvarieties of abelian varieties, and various cases for specific classes of varieties).

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: If X is a projective nonsingular algebraic variety over C, is every Hodge class on X a rational linear combination of classes cl(Z) of algebraic cycles Z on X?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective algebraic variety over the field $\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers. Its singular cohomology with rational coefficients admits, for each integer $k \ge 0$, a Hodge decomposition

$$H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathbb{C} \;=\; \bigoplus_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X),$$

where $H^{p,q}(X)$ is the space of cohomology classes representable by closed differential forms of type $(p,q)$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}(X)} = H^{q,p}(X)$. A rational cohomology class $\alpha \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ is called a Hodge class of degree $2k$ if its image in $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C})$ lies in the subspace $H^{k,k}(X)$.

For any closed irreducible algebraic subvariety $Z \subset X$ of complex codimension $k$ (more generally, for any algebraic cycle, i.e., a finite formal $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination of such subvarieties), one has an associated cohomology class $\mathrm{cl}(Z) \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$, and $\mathrm{cl}(Z)$ is a Hodge class.

Question: Is it true that for every smooth projective complex algebraic variety $X$ and every integer $k \ge 0$, every Hodge class of degree $2k$ on $X$ can be written as a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination
$$\alpha \;=\; \sum_i q_i \, \mathrm{cl}(Z_i),$$
where $q_i \in \mathbb{Q}$ and each $Z_i$ is an algebraic cycle of codimension $k$ on $X$?
status_search_result: The Hodge conjecture is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open in full generality. It is known in special cases (e.g., degree 2 by the Lefschetz (1,1)-theorem, abelian varieties of certain types, and other partial results), but no general proof or disproof exists as of 2026.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Let X be a projective nonsingular variety and let J_p(X) be the extension involving the intermediate Jacobian that receives codimension-p algebraic cycles. If A_p(X) denotes the subgroup of J_p(X) generated by algebraic cycles, which subgroup of J_p(X) is A_p(X)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex variety, and fix an integer $p$ with $1 \le p \le \dim X$. Let $H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb{C})$ carry its Hodge decomposition, and define the $p$-th intermediate Jacobian
$$J^p(X) \;=\; \frac{H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb{C})}{F^p H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb{C}) + H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb{Z})},$$
where $F^\bullet$ denotes the Hodge filtration. Let $Z^p_{\mathrm{hom}}(X)$ denote the group of codimension-$p$ algebraic cycles on $X$ that are homologically equivalent to zero, and let
$$\mathrm{AJ}_p : Z^p_{\mathrm{hom}}(X) \longrightarrow J^p(X)$$
be the Griffiths Abel–Jacobi map. Let $A^p(X) \subseteq J^p(X)$ be the image of $\mathrm{AJ}_p$, that is, the subgroup of $J^p(X)$ generated by classes of algebraic cycles.

Problem: Give an intrinsic Hodge-theoretic (or otherwise structural) characterization of the subgroup $A^p(X) \subseteq J^p(X)$. Equivalently, formulate and establish a conjectural description that predicts, for every smooth projective $X$ and every $p$, exactly which subgroup of $J^p(X)$ coincides with $A^p(X)$.
status_search_result: No general conjecture is known that characterizes the subgroup of the intermediate Jacobian $J^p(X)$ generated by algebraic cycles via the Abel–Jacobi map. The problem is part of the broader open landscape surrounding the Hodge conjecture and Griffiths' work on intermediate Jacobians; standard references confirm only partial results (e.g., for $p=1$ where $A^1(X)=J^1(X)$, and isolated cases in higher codimension), with no predictive conjecture in general.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Given an algebraic family of projective nonsingular algebraic varieties (X_s) over a parameter space S defined over the algebraic closure of Q in C, is there an algorithm that decides whether a given integral cohomology class of a typical fiber X_0 becomes of Hodge type (p,p) somewhere on S?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\pi: \mathcal{X} \to S$ be a smooth projective morphism of complex algebraic varieties, defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subset \mathbb{C}$, whose fibers $X_s = \pi^{-1}(s)$ are projective nonsingular algebraic varieties. Fix a base point $0 \in S$ and an integer $p \geq 0$. For each $s \in S$, the singular cohomology $H^{2p}(X_s, \mathbb{C})$ carries a Hodge decomposition $H^{2p}(X_s, \mathbb{C}) = \bigoplus_{i+j=2p} H^{i,j}(X_s)$, and the local system $R^{2p}\pi_* \mathbb{Z}$ allows us to transport an integral class $\alpha \in H^{2p}(X_0, \mathbb{Z})$ to a (multi-valued) integral class $\alpha_s \in H^{2p}(X_s, \mathbb{Z})$ along paths in $S$. Say that $\alpha$ becomes of Hodge type $(p,p)$ somewhere on $S$ if there exist $s \in S$ and a flat transport of $\alpha$ to $X_s$ whose image in $H^{2p}(X_s, \mathbb{C})$ lies in $H^{p,p}(X_s)$.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input such a family $\pi: \mathcal{X} \to S$ (encoded by polynomial equations with coefficients in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$), an integer $p$, and an integral cohomology class $\alpha \in H^{2p}(X_0, \mathbb{Z})$, decides whether $\alpha$ becomes of Hodge type $(p,p)$ at some point of $S$?
status_search_result: This is the well-known algorithmic question raised in the Clay Millennium description of the Hodge conjecture. It remains open: no decision algorithm is known, and the broader Hodge conjecture itself is unresolved.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Let A be an abelian variety over the algebraic closure F of a finite field F_q. Lift A in two different ways to characteristic 0, obtaining complex abelian varieties A1 and A2 defined over Q̄, and choose complementary-dimensional Hodge classes z1 and z2 on A1 and A2. After interpreting z1 and z2 as l-adic cohomology classes and reducing them over F, is the resulting intersection number κ always a rational number?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}$ denote the algebraic closure of a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}$. Choose two liftings of $A$ to characteristic $0$: that is, two abelian schemes whose special fibers are isomorphic to $A$ and whose generic fibers, base-changed to $\mathbb{C}$ via embeddings of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ into $\mathbb{C}$, yield complex abelian varieties $A_1$ and $A_2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Choose Hodge classes $z_1$ on $A_1$ and $z_2$ on $A_2$ of complementary (real) codimension, where a Hodge class on a smooth complex projective variety $X$ of dimension $d$ is a rational cohomology class in $H^{2p}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \cap H^{p,p}(X)$ for some $p$. Fix a prime $\ell$ different from the characteristic of $\mathbb{F}$. Via the comparison isomorphism between singular and $\ell$-adic étale cohomology, interpret $z_1$ and $z_2$ as $\ell$-adic étale cohomology classes on $A_1$ and $A_2$. Using smooth and proper base change, specialize these classes to $\ell$-adic étale cohomology classes $\bar z_1$ and $\bar z_2$ on $A$ over $\mathbb{F}$, and form the intersection number
$$\kappa = \langle \bar z_1, \bar z_2 \rangle \in \mathbb{Q}_\ell.$$
Question: must $\kappa$ always be a rational number, i.e., does $\kappa \in \mathbb{Q}$ hold for every choice of $A$, of the two liftings, and of the complementary-dimensional Hodge classes $z_1, z_2$?
status_search_result: This rationality question on the intersection of reductions of complementary Hodge classes coming from distinct liftings of an abelian variety over a finite field is a known test problem on the way to the Hodge conjecture, surveyed alongside Deligne's theorem that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are absolute. No proof of the general rationality statement appears in the literature; the question remains open.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with viscosity ν > 0, must one of the standard global regularity statements hold: either smooth physically reasonable solutions always exist globally on R^3 or on the periodic domain R^3/Z^3 for smooth divergence-free initial data, or else there exist smooth data for which no such global smooth solution exists on one of those domains?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on three-dimensional space, governing the velocity field u(x,t) = (u_1, u_2, u_3) and pressure p(x,t):

  ∂_t u_i + Σ_{j=1}^3 u_j ∂_{x_j} u_i = ν Δ u_i − ∂_{x_i} p + f_i(x,t),   (x ∈ R^3, t ≥ 0, i=1,2,3),
  div u := Σ_{j=1}^3 ∂_{x_j} u_j = 0,
  u(x,0) = u^0(x),

where ν > 0 is a fixed viscosity constant, Δ is the Laplacian in the spatial variables, and f is a prescribed external force.

A solution (u,p) is called physically reasonable if u ∈ C^∞(R^3 × [0,∞)), p ∈ C^∞(R^3 × [0,∞)), and the bounded-energy condition

  ∫_{R^3} |u(x,t)|^2 dx ≤ C for all t ≥ 0

holds. The initial datum u^0 is assumed to be a C^∞ divergence-free vector field on R^3 satisfying, for any multi-index α and any K, an estimate of the form

  |∂^α_x u^0(x)| ≤ C_{α,K} (1+|x|)^{−K}.

The forcing f is similarly assumed to be smooth and rapidly decreasing in space.

Analogously, on the periodic torus T^3 = R^3 / Z^3, consider the same system with periodic boundary conditions and smooth periodic divergence-free initial data and forcing.

Prove one of the following four statements:

(A) (Existence and smoothness on R^3.) For ν > 0, f ≡ 0, and any smooth divergence-free u^0 on R^3 satisfying the above decay conditions, there exist smooth functions (u,p) on R^3 × [0,∞) solving the Navier–Stokes system with finite global energy bound.

(B) (Existence and smoothness on T^3.) The analogous global existence and smoothness statement holds on R^3/Z^3 with smooth periodic divergence-free initial data and f ≡ 0.

(C) (Breakdown on R^3.) There exist ν > 0, a smooth divergence-free u^0 on R^3 with the above decay, and a smooth f with appropriate decay in space and time, such that no smooth solution (u,p) on R^3 × [0,∞) of the Navier–Stokes system with the bounded-energy condition exists.

(D) (Breakdown on T^3.) The analogous breakdown statement holds on R^3/Z^3 with smooth periodic data and forcing.
status_search_result: This is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. No accepted proof of global regularity or of finite-time blow-up for the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations under the Clay formulation has appeared. Significant partial results exist (e.g., Tao's averaged Navier–Stokes blow-up, conditional regularity criteria), but none resolve the official problem.

original_question: If a compact three-dimensional manifold M^3 has the property that every simple closed curve in M^3 can be continuously deformed to a point within M^3, must M^3 be homeomorphic to the 3-sphere S^3?

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Is every decision problem whose proposed solutions can be checked in polynomial time also solvable in polynomial time; equivalently, does P = NP?
self_contained_problem: Let a decision problem be a language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$. Define the complexity class $\mathrm{P}$ as the set of languages $L$ for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine $M$ and a polynomial $p$ such that, on every input $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $M$ halts within $p(|x|)$ steps and accepts if and only if $x \in L$. Define the complexity class $\mathrm{NP}$ as the set of languages $L$ for which there exists a polynomial $q$ and a language $V \in \mathrm{P}$ (the verifier) such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $x \in L$ if and only if there exists a certificate $y \in \{0,1\}^*$ with $|y| \le q(|x|)$ and $(x,y) \in V$.\n\nQuestion: Is $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$? Equivalently, is every decision problem whose candidate solutions can be verified in deterministic polynomial time also decidable in deterministic polynomial time?
status_search_result: The P vs NP problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains a famous open problem in mathematics and theoretical computer science as of 2026. No accepted proof in either direction exists.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Do all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) have real part equal to 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
The Riemann zeta function is defined for complex numbers s with real part greater than 1 by the absolutely convergent series ζ(s) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^s, and is extended to a meromorphic function on the entire complex plane with a single simple pole at s = 1 via analytic continuation. This continued function satisfies the functional equation relating ζ(s) and ζ(1 − s), and vanishes at the negative even integers s = −2, −4, −6, …; these are called the trivial zeros. All other zeros of ζ(s) are called nontrivial zeros, and they are known to lie in the critical strip {s ∈ ℂ : 0 < Re(s) < 1}.

Prove or disprove: every nontrivial zero s of ζ(s) satisfies Re(s) = 1/2.
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains unsolved. Extensive numerical verification has confirmed that the first many trillions of nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2, but no proof or disproof is known.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Is there, for the classical global setting of the Riemann zeta function and related L-functions, a theory that plays the same role that cohomology plays for zeta functions of varieties over a field of positive characteristic?
self_contained_problem:
For a smooth projective variety $X$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the Hasse–Weil zeta function $\zeta(X,s) = \prod_{x \in |X|}(1 - N(x)^{-s})^{-1}$ admits a cohomological interpretation: by the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula, it can be expressed as an alternating product $\zeta(X,s) = \prod_{i=0}^{2\dim X} \det\!\big(1 - q^{-s}\,\mathrm{Frob} \mid H^i_{\ell}(X)\big)^{(-1)^{i+1}}$ where $H^i_\ell(X)$ are the $\ell$-adic étale cohomology groups, and the Riemann Hypothesis for $\zeta(X,s)$ (Deligne's theorem) is a consequence of the existence of a suitable Weil cohomology theory together with the Riemann Hypothesis–type bounds on Frobenius eigenvalues.

Construct, for the classical global setting of the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n^{-s}$ (and more generally Dirichlet, Hecke, and automorphic $L$-functions over number fields), a cohomological formalism that plays the same role as $\ell$-adic (or other Weil) cohomology plays for zeta functions of varieties over fields of positive characteristic. Concretely: produce a category of "motivic" or geometric objects attached to $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$ and number rings, together with cohomology functors $H^i$ valued in vector spaces over some coefficient field, equipped with an endomorphism (analogue of Frobenius) whose characteristic polynomials yield the completed zeta/$L$-functions as an alternating product, and from which the Riemann Hypothesis for $\zeta(s)$ and related $L$-functions would follow by an analogue of Deligne's positivity/purity argument.
category_tag: Cohomological approach to the Riemann Hypothesis
status_search_result: No such cohomology theory in the global (number field) setting is known. There are influential programs aiming at this — Deninger's conjectural infinite-dimensional cohomology and dynamical-system framework, Connes–Consani's work on the adele class space and the "arithmetic site," and various approaches via $\mathbb{F}_1$-geometry and condensed/topos-theoretic methods — but none has produced a Weil-style cohomological proof of RH or an established formalism playing the role analogous to $\ell$-adic cohomology in positive characteristic. The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: In the classical setting of the Riemann zeta function, is there an analogue of the Frobenius automorphism that would play the corresponding role it plays for varieties over finite fields?
self_contained_problem:
For a smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the geometric Frobenius endomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}_q$ acts on the $\ell$-adic étale cohomology groups $H^i_{\mathrm{ét}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_q}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)$, and the zeta function $Z(X,t)$ of $X$ can be expressed in terms of characteristic polynomials of this action. Deligne's theorem (the Weil conjectures) shows that the eigenvalues of $\mathrm{Frob}_q$ on $H^i$ are algebraic numbers all of whose conjugates have absolute value $q^{i/2}$, which yields the Riemann hypothesis for $Z(X,t)$.

Now consider the classical Riemann zeta function
$$\zeta(s) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s}, \qquad \Re(s) > 1,$$
extended meromorphically to $\mathbb{C}$, whose nontrivial zeros are conjectured (the Riemann hypothesis) to lie on the line $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

Problem. Construct, in a mathematically meaningful sense, an object playing the role of $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ as a variety over a hypothetical "absolute base," together with a cohomology theory and an endomorphism that plays for $\zeta(s)$ the role that the geometric Frobenius plays for zeta functions of varieties over finite fields. More precisely: does there exist a natural operator (a "Frobenius analogue in the classical case") acting on a suitable cohomology of $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ (or a suitable completion thereof) whose characteristic-polynomial-type data recovers the completed Riemann zeta function $\xi(s) = \tfrac{1}{2} s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$, and whose eigenvalue distribution would directly account for the location of the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ on the critical line?
status_search_result: The question of finding a Frobenius/cohomological analogue in the classical Riemann zeta setting is widely regarded as open. Multiple programs (Deninger's conjectural cohomology, Connes' noncommutative-geometry/adelic approach, the field-with-one-element $\mathbb{F}_1$ program, arithmetic topology) propose partial frameworks but no construction yields a Frobenius-like operator whose spectrum is proven to give the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$. No proof of RH or of such an analogue has been accepted.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: Is there a general index theorem that could be used to prove the classical Riemann hypothesis?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ for $\Re(s) > 1$, extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a unique simple pole at $s=1$. The classical Riemann Hypothesis (RH) asserts that every non-trivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ (i.e., every zero not at $s = -2, -4, -6, \dots$) lies on the critical line $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

Recall that an index theorem (in the sense of Atiyah–Singer and its generalizations) equates the analytic index of an elliptic (or suitably Fredholm) operator $D$ acting on sections of a vector bundle over a manifold (or a more general geometric/noncommutative space) with a topological index defined in terms of characteristic classes (or K-theoretic data) of the underlying space. A typical use of such a theorem is to express the dimension of an obstruction space, or the signature of a quadratic form, in manifestly non-negative or topologically constrained terms.

Question: Does there exist a general index theorem—that is, an identification of an analytic index of some naturally constructed (possibly Hilbert space, possibly noncommutative geometric) operator with a topological/cohomological invariant—from which the classical Riemann Hypothesis can be deduced? More precisely, exhibit a geometric or noncommutative-geometric framework together with a self-adjoint (or otherwise spectrally constrained) operator $D$ whose spectrum encodes the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ via the relation $s = 1/2 + it$ with $t$ ranging over $\mathrm{Spec}(D) \subset \mathbb{R}$, and a corresponding index-theoretic identity that forces the reality of this spectrum, thereby proving RH.
status_search_result: The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. Various approaches (Connes' noncommutative geometry / trace formula, Hilbert–Pólya conjecture, Berry–Keating Hamiltonian) seek to interpret RH spectrally or via index-theoretic methods, but no such proof has been achieved.

paper_title: The Millennium Prize Problems
original_question: For any compact simple gauge group G, does there exist a non-trivial quantum Yang-Mills theory on R^4 with a positive mass gap Δ > 0, with existence understood as establishing axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in the source?
self_contained_problem: Let G be a compact simple Lie group. Construct a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills gauge theory with gauge group G on four-dimensional Euclidean space R^4 satisfying a system of Wightman-type (or Osterwalder–Schrader) axioms for a relativistic quantum field theory at least as strong as the standard axiomatic formulations used for constructive quantum field theory (existence of a Hilbert space of states carrying a unitary representation of the Poincaré group, a unique Poincaré-invariant vacuum, local gauge-invariant field operators or correlation functions satisfying the appropriate locality/clustering/positivity conditions, and so on). Prove furthermore that the resulting theory has a positive mass gap: there exists a constant Δ > 0 such that every state in the Hilbert space, other than the vacuum, has energy at least Δ above the vacuum energy. paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Number-theoretic and zero-spacing questions about the Riemann xi-function and partial Fourier integrals
original_question: Let Phi(t) = 2 * sum_{n=1}^{infinity} (2n^4 pi^2 e^{9t/2} - 3n^2 pi e^{5t/2}) e^{-n^2 pi e^{2t}} and Xi(z) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} Phi(t) e^{izt} dt (the completed Riemann xi-function). (i) What number-theoretic information is encoded in integral_0^{infinity} Phi(x) cos(zx) dx? In particular, can the Prime Number Theorem — equivalent to this function having no zeros in {z in C : Im(z) >= 1/2} — be proved using only this integral expression? (ii) Which multiplier sequences (real sequences {gamma_k} such that applying the diagonal operator sum gamma_k a_k x^k to any hyperbolic polynomial sum a_k x^k yields a hyperbolic polynomial) even out the zero spacings of the Xi function? (iii) Does there exist R > 0 such that integral_0^R Phi(x) cos(zx) dx has more than one pair of complex conjugate zeros? (iv) Is differentiation a more effective method than the midpoint method for evening out the spacings of zeros of real entire functions of order 1 with all real zeros?
self_contained_problem:
Define
\[\Phi(t) \;=\; 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\Bigl(2n^{4}\pi^{2}e^{9t/2} \;-\; 3n^{2}\pi e^{5t/2}\Bigr) e^{-n^{2}\pi e^{2t}}, \qquad t\in\mathbb R,\]
and the completed Riemann xi-function
\[\Xi(z) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\,e^{izt}\,dt \;=\; 2\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\cos(zt)\,dt.\]
A real sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 0}$ is called a multiplier sequence if for every hyperbolic polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{k}a_k x^k$ (a polynomial with only real zeros) the polynomial $\sum_{k}\gamma_k a_k x^k$ is again hyperbolic. Address the following:

(i) What number-theoretic information is encoded in $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi(x)\cos(zx)\,dx$? In particular, is it possible to prove the Prime Number Theorem — which is equivalent to the statement that this function of $z$ has no zeros in the half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb C : \operatorname{Im} z \ge 1/2\}$ — using only this integral representation?

(ii) Characterize the multiplier sequences $\{\gamma_k\}$ whose associated diagonal action evens out the spacings between consecutive real zeros of $\Xi$.

(iii) Does there exist $R>0$ such that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{R}\Phi(x)\cos(zx)\,dx$ has more than one pair of complex conjugate (non-real) zeros?

(iv) For real entire functions of order $1$ all of whose zeros are real, is differentiation a more effective method for evening out the spacings between consecutive zeros than the midpoint method (the operation that replaces consecutive zeros by their pairwise midpoints)?
status_search_result: The questions appear on a published list of open problems on Polya–Schur–Lax type hyperbolicity and stability preservers, and there is no indication in the literature that any of them have been resolved. They appear to remain open.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Converse characterization of determinantal stable polynomials from skew-symmetric and positive definite matrices
original_question: Let A be a skew-symmetric n x n real matrix and B_1, B_2 positive definite real matrices. It is known that det(A + i(x B_1 + y B_2)) is a stable polynomial (nonzero whenever Im(x) > 0 and Im(y) > 0), with all terms of even degree if n is even and odd degree if n is odd. Is the converse true: if a polynomial in x, y has all terms of even (resp. odd) degree according to n, must it equal det(A + i(x B_1 + y B_2)) for some such A, B_1, B_2?
self_contained_problem:
A polynomial p(x,y) in two complex variables is called stable if p(x,y) ≠ 0 whenever Im(x) > 0 and Im(y) > 0. Fix a positive integer n. If A is a real skew-symmetric n×n matrix and B₁, B₂ are real positive definite n×n matrices, then the polynomial

  p(x,y) := det(A + i(xB₁ + yB₂))

is stable, and moreover every monomial appearing in p has total degree of the same parity as n (all monomials of even total degree when n is even, all monomials of odd total degree when n is odd).

Question: Is the converse true? That is, suppose p(x,y) is a polynomial of total degree n in which every monomial has total degree of the same parity as n, and suppose p is stable in the sense above. Must there exist a real skew-symmetric n×n matrix A and real positive definite n×n matrices B₁, B₂ such that

  p(x,y) = det(A + i(xB₁ + yB₂)) ?

Determine whether this characterization holds, or exhibit a stable polynomial of the indicated parity that admits no such determinantal representation.
status_search_result: Related results exist on determinantal representations of stable/real-stable polynomials (e.g., Helton–Vinnikov theorem for real zero polynomials in two variables, and Borcea–Brändén type representations), and there is work on definite symmetric determinantal representations. However, no direct confirmation or refutation of this specific converse — requiring the matrix A to be real skew-symmetric and B₁, B₂ real positive definite with the exact form det(A + i(xB₁ + yB₂)) — was located in the search.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Polynomial analogue of the additive Horn problem via homogeneous stable polynomials
original_question: Polynomial analogue of the additive Horn problem: Given n and vectors alpha, beta, gamma in R^n, when does there exist a triple (f, g, h) of real-rooted polynomials with roots alpha, beta, gamma respectively, and a homogeneous stable polynomial F(x, y, z) (stable meaning F(x,y,z) != 0 whenever Im(x), Im(y), Im(z) > 0) such that f = F(x, 1, 0), g = F(0, x, 1), h = F(1, 0, x)? It is known that Horn's problem is solvable if and only if (alpha, beta, gamma) is the boundary of a hive, and that the logs of the coefficients of F determine a hive, but this condition is not sufficient. What are necessary and sufficient conditions on f, g, h guaranteeing the existence of such F?
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer. A polynomial F(x,y,z) in three complex variables is called stable if F(x,y,z) ≠ 0 whenever Im(x) > 0, Im(y) > 0, and Im(z) > 0. A univariate polynomial is called real-rooted if all its roots are real.

Given vectors α, β, γ ∈ ℝⁿ, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on α, β, γ (equivalently, on the real-rooted polynomials f, g, h ∈ ℝ[x] of degree n whose roots are α, β, γ respectively) such that there exists a homogeneous stable polynomial F(x,y,z) of degree n with

  f(x) = F(x, 1, 0),  g(x) = F(0, x, 1),  h(x) = F(1, 0, x).

Background: The classical additive Horn problem (existence of Hermitian matrices A, B, C with A + B + C = 0 having prescribed real spectra α, β, γ) is known to be solvable if and only if the triple (α, β, γ) forms the boundary of a hive (a real-valued function on the triangular grid satisfying certain rhombus concavity inequalities). The logarithms of the coefficients of any such F necessarily determine a hive, but this hive condition alone is not known to be sufficient. Find the precise characterization.
status_search_result: The problem appears on an AIM workshop open problems list on hyperbolicity and stability preservers, and web searches turn up no published resolution providing necessary and sufficient conditions on (f, g, h) for the existence of such a homogeneous stable polynomial F. The hive condition is known to be necessary but not sufficient, and no later paper claiming a full characterization was located.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Fischer-Fock inner product lower bound via capacity for homogeneous polynomials
original_question: In the Fischer-Fock space F_k with inner product <f,g>_{F_k} = sum_{alpha in N^k} alpha! a(alpha) b(alpha) (where a(alpha), b(alpha) are Taylor coefficients of f and g respectively), define for a real homogeneous polynomial p(z_1,...,z_k) of degree n the capacity Cap(p) = inf_{z_1>0,...,z_k>0} [p(z_1,...,z_k) / (z_1 ... z_k)^{n/k}] * (n! / k^n). For real homogeneous degree-n polynomials p, q in k variables, is it true that <p, q>_{F_k} >= Cap(p) Cap(q) (n! / k^n)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k,n\geq 1$ be integers. The Fischer–Fock space $F_k$ is the Hilbert space of polynomials in $k$ complex variables equipped with the inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{F_k}=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^k}\alpha!\,a(\alpha)\,\overline{b(\alpha)},$$
where $f(z)=\sum_\alpha a(\alpha)z^\alpha$ and $g(z)=\sum_\alpha b(\alpha)z^\alpha$ are the Taylor expansions of $f$ and $g$, and $\alpha!=\alpha_1!\cdots\alpha_k!$. For a real homogeneous polynomial $p(z_1,\dots,z_k)$ of degree $n$, define its capacity by
$$\mathrm{Cap}(p)=\inf_{z_1,\dots,z_k>0}\frac{p(z_1,\dots,z_k)}{(z_1z_2\cdots z_k)^{n/k}}.$$
Determine whether the following inequality holds for every pair $p,q$ of real homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ in $k$ variables:
$$\langle p,q\rangle_{F_k}\;\geq\;\mathrm{Cap}(p)\,\mathrm{Cap}(q)\,\frac{n!}{k^n}.$$
status_search_result: The inequality is posed as an open problem in the AIM Polya–Schur–Lax workshop problem list (Gurvits). Searches turn up related work by Gurvits on capacity-based lower bounds (van der Waerden / Schrijver–Valiant generalizations) but no publication establishing or refuting this specific Fischer–Fock inner-product capacity bound, so it appears still open.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Whether a quadratic growth condition on a positive sequence implies it is a CZDS
original_question: A sequence {gamma_k}_{k in N} of positive reals is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if for every real polynomial sum a_k x^k, the number of non-real zeros of sum gamma_k a_k x^k is at most the number of non-real zeros of sum a_k x^k. Let {gamma_k}_{k in N} be a sequence of positive reals satisfying gamma_k^2 >= 4 gamma_{k+1} gamma_{k-1} for all k. Is {gamma_k} necessarily a CZDS?
self_contained_problem:
A sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive real numbers is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if, for every real polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_k x^k$, the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^n \gamma_k a_k x^k$ has at most as many non-real zeros (counted with multiplicity) as $p(x)$.

Suppose $\{\gamma_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of positive real numbers satisfying
$$\gamma_k^2 \;\ge\; 4\,\gamma_{k+1}\,\gamma_{k-1} \qquad \text{for all } k \ge 1.$$
Must $\{\gamma_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a CZDS?
status_search_result: The question appears as a listed open problem in the AIM workshop problem list on Pólya–Schur–Lax problems, and the survey paper of Craven and Csordas on CZDS discusses related sufficient conditions but does not resolve it. No publication has been found that affirms or refutes the conjecture under the quadratic-growth hypothesis $\gamma_k^2 \ge 4\gamma_{k+1}\gamma_{k-1}$.

context_brief: Zeros of xi-function deformations and entire functions under heat-operator perturbation; connection to Riemann Hypothesis
original_question: Let Xi(z) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} Phi(t) e^{izt} dt where Phi(t) = 2 sum_{n=1}^{infinity} (2n^4 pi^2 e^{9t/2} - 3n^2 pi e^{5t/2}) e^{-n^2 pi e^{2t}} (related to the Riemann xi-function). Define Xi_lambda(z) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} Phi(t) e^{lambda t^2} e^{izt} dt. (i) Is it true that for any lambda < 0, almost all zeros of Xi_lambda(z) are real? An affirmative answer would imply that almost all complex zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line. (ii) Suppose f is a real entire function of order 1 and maximal type, even, with all zeros in the strip {z : |Im(z)| <= Delta}. Is it true that for every lambda > 0, all but finitely many zeros of e^{-lambda D^2} f (where D = d/dx) are real and simple? Note: the source confirms an affirmative answer to (ii) for the specific functions Xi, Phi, H (defined via the Riemann zeta and Dirichlet L-functions); the general question for arbitrary f remains open.
self_contained_problem:
Define
\[
\Phi(t) \;=\; 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(2n^{4}\pi^{2}e^{9t/2} - 3n^{2}\pi e^{5t/2}\bigr)e^{-n^{2}\pi e^{2t}}, \qquad t\in\mathbb{R},
\]
and
\[
\Xi(z) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\,e^{izt}\,dt.
\]
For a real parameter $\lambda$ set
\[
\Xi_{\lambda}(z) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\,e^{\lambda t^{2}}\,e^{izt}\,dt.
\]

(i) Is it true that for every $\lambda<0$, almost all (i.e. all but a density-zero subset of the) zeros of $\Xi_{\lambda}(z)$ are real?

(ii) Let $f$ be a real entire function of order $1$ and maximal type that is even and whose zeros all lie in the horizontal strip $\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|\operatorname{Im} z|\le \Delta\}$ for some $\Delta>0$. Writing $D=d/dx$, is it true that for every $\lambda>0$ all but finitely many zeros of the entire function $e^{-\lambda D^{2}}f$ are real and simple?

status_search_result: Both questions concern the heat-flow deformation of the Riemann xi-function and the closely related de Bruijn–Newman framework. Part (i) would imply that almost all zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line, and remains open: the exact value of the de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ is unknown, with only the bounds 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.22 established (Rodgers–Tao 2018 lower bound, Polymath15 upper bound 2019). Part (ii), in its stated generality for arbitrary even real entire functions of order 1 and maximal type with zeros in a horizontal strip, is not known; only the special case of the Riemann xi-function and related L-functions has affirmative partial information.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Characterization of linear zero-preserving operators on polynomials with zeros in a region
original_question: Let Omega be a subset of C and pi(Omega) the class of all univariate polynomials (with complex coefficients) whose zeros all lie in Omega. Characterize all linear operators T : pi(Omega) -> pi(Omega) union {0}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a subset of the complex plane, and let $\pi(\Omega)$ denote the class of all univariate polynomials with complex coefficients whose zeros all lie in $\Omega$ (the zero polynomial is excluded from $\pi(\Omega)$). Give an explicit characterization (in terms of suitable symbols, transforms, or generating functions) of all linear operators
$$T : \pi(\Omega) \to \pi(\Omega) \cup \{0\},$$
that is, all $\mathbb{C}$-linear maps defined on the linear span of $\pi(\Omega)$ (or on the space of all univariate polynomials) which send every element of $\pi(\Omega)$ either to a polynomial whose zeros all lie in $\Omega$ or to the zero polynomial.
status_search_result: For $\Omega$ a closed circular domain (image of the closed unit disk under a Möbius transformation) or its boundary, and in particular for $\Omega = \mathbb{R}$ or a half-plane, the characterization was obtained by Borcea and Brändén (2009), resolving long-standing questions of Laguerre and Pólya–Schur. Extensions to intervals/rays and representation-theoretic reformulations have been given subsequently. However, for general subsets $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ (e.g., arbitrary strips, sectors, or more exotic regions), a complete classification of zero-preserving linear operators remains open.

original_question: Let Omega be a subset of C, pi_n the vector space of polynomials of degree at most n, and pi_n(Omega) the subclass of pi_n whose zeros all lie in Omega. Describe all linear operators T : pi_n(Omega) -> pi(Omega) union {0} for each n in N.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a given subset of the complex plane. For each nonnegative integer $n$, let $\pi_n$ denote the complex vector space of univariate polynomials of degree at most $n$, and let $\pi = \bigcup_{n\ge 0}\pi_n$. Define
$$\pi_n(\Omega) = \{p \in \pi_n : \text{every zero of } p \text{ lies in } \Omega\}, \qquad \pi(\Omega) = \{p \in \pi : \text{every zero of } p \text{ lies in } \Omega\}.$$
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, give an explicit characterization (description) of all linear operators
$$T : \pi_n(\Omega) \longrightarrow \pi(\Omega) \cup \{0\},$$
i.e. all linear maps that send each polynomial of degree at most $n$ with zeros in $\Omega$ either to the zero polynomial or to a polynomial all of whose zeros lie in $\Omega$.

Math. 2009, and subsequent works) gave complete characterizations of such zero-preserving linear operators when Ω is a closed circular domain (image of the closed disk under a Möbius transformation) or its boundary, in particular for Ω = ℝ, the upper half-plane, and disks, settling classical Pólya–Schur–Laguerre questions. Further classification theorems were obtained for strips and Bargmann–Fock-type settings, and a representation-theoretic explanation was given by Leake–Ryder (2018). For general subsets Ω ⊆ ℂ the problem remains open.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Settling the linear zero-preserver characterization for specific open domains: circular, sector, strip, half-line
original_question: Problems 7 and 8 ask to characterize all linear operators T : pi(Omega) -> pi(Omega) union {0} (respectively T : pi_n(Omega) -> pi(Omega) union {0}) where pi(Omega) is the class of polynomials with all zeros in Omega and pi_n(Omega) is its degree-at-most-n subclass. The cases where Omega is a closed circular domain or its boundary are completely solved. Settle these problems for each of the following remaining cases: (a) Omega is an open circular domain (open disk, half-plane, or complement of a closed disk); (b) Omega is a sector or double sector; (c) Omega is a strip; (d) Omega is a half-line.
status_search_result: The closed circular domain and boundary cases were settled by Borcea–Brändén's Pólya–Schur master theorems. The strip case (c) has been addressed by classification theorems for operators preserving zeros in a strip (Brändén–Chasse–Visontai-type results, published in J. d'Analyse Math. 2017). The sector/double-sector and half-line cases, as well as the general open circular domain setting beyond stability, do not appear to have a full published characterization, so the problem as a whole is only partially solved.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Characterization of coefficient polynomials Q_k in the differential representation of a linear zero-preserver
original_question: Every linear operator T on C[z] has a unique formal differential representation T = sum_{k=0}^{infinity} Q_k(z) (d^k/dz^k) where Q_k are polynomials in C[z]. For a given region Omega subset C, characterize the sequences of polynomials (Q_k) such that T maps pi_n(Omega) into pi(Omega) union {0} for every n in N, where pi_n(Omega) is the class of polynomials of degree at most n with all zeros in Omega.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{C}[z]$ denote the algebra of complex polynomials in one variable. Every $\mathbb{C}$-linear operator $T\colon \mathbb{C}[z]\to \mathbb{C}[z]$ admits a unique formal differential representation
$$T \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q_k(z)\,\frac{d^k}{dz^k},\qquad Q_k\in\mathbb{C}[z],$$
in the sense that for every $p\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ only finitely many terms $Q_k(z)\,p^{(k)}(z)$ are nonzero and their sum equals $T(p)$.

For a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, let $\pi_n(\Omega)$ denote the set of polynomials of degree at most $n$ whose zeros all lie in $\Omega$, and let $\pi(\Omega)=\bigcup_{n\ge 0}\pi_n(\Omega)$.

Problem. Given a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, characterize all sequences of polynomials $(Q_k)_{k\ge 0}$ in $\mathbb{C}[z]$ such that the associated operator $T=\sum_{k\ge 0} Q_k(z)\,\dfrac{d^k}{dz^k}$ satisfies
$$T\bigl(\pi_n(\Omega)\bigr)\subseteq \pi(\Omega)\cup\{0\}\qquad\text{for every } n\in\mathbb{N}.$$
status_search_result: Borcea and Brändén (2009) gave a complete characterization of linear operators preserving stability/non-vanishing on products of prescribed open circular regions, which solves the problem for circular regions Ω and yields the classification of the coefficient polynomials Q_k in those cases. For general regions Ω (e.g. arbitrary open or closed sets in C), no full characterization is known, and subsequent works (e.g., interlacing/real-root preserving results, representation-theoretic explanations) extend but do not fully resolve the general problem.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Characterization of linear operators on real polynomials that do not increase the count of non-real zeros
original_question: Let pi_n denote the space of real polynomials of degree at most n, and for a real polynomial p let Z_c(p) denote the number of non-real zeros of p counted with multiplicity. Characterize all linear operators T : pi_n -> pi_n such that Z_c(T[p(x)]) <= Z_c(p(x)) for every real polynomial p in pi_n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\pi_n$ denote the real vector space of polynomials in one variable $x$ with real coefficients and degree at most $n$. For a real polynomial $p(x)$, let $Z_c(p)$ denote the number of non-real zeros of $p$, counted with multiplicity (so that $Z_c(p) = \deg p - (\text{number of real zeros of } p \text{ counted with multiplicity})$ when $p \not\equiv 0$).

Give a complete characterization of all linear operators $T : \pi_n \to \pi_n$ with the property that
$$Z_c\bigl(T[p](x)\bigr) \le Z_c\bigl(p(x)\bigr)$$
for every $p \in \pi_n$. Equivalently, describe explicitly the set of all linear maps on $\pi_n$ that do not increase the number of non-real zeros of any real polynomial of degree at most $n$.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing linear operators on real polynomials that do not increase the number of non-real zeros (so-called complex zero decreasing operators / sequences) is a classical long-standing open problem, sometimes referred to as the Karlin–Laguerre problem. While Borcea–Brändén (Annals of Math., 2009) characterized the stronger class of stability/hyperbolicity preservers (the case $Z_c(Tp)=0$ whenever $Z_c(p)=0$), and various partial results, new examples, and sub-classes (e.g. zero-sector and zero-strip reducing operators, CZDS in orthogonal polynomial bases) have been obtained by Craven–Csordas, Bakan–Golub–Csordas, Forgács and others, no complete characterization of complex zero decreasing operators on $\pi_n$ is known.

paper_title: Polya-Schur-Lax Problems: Hyperbolicity and Stability Preservers — A List of Open Problems
context_brief: Characterization of linear operators preserving hyperbolicity with respect to a cone
original_question: Let V be a cone in R^n and H_n(V) the set of real homogeneous polynomials in n variables that are hyperbolic with respect to every direction e in V (meaning f(e) != 0 and the univariate polynomial t -> f(alpha + te) has only real zeros for every alpha in R^n). Describe all linear operators T on R[z_1,...,z_n] such that T maps H_n(V) into H_n(V) union {0}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be an open convex cone. A real homogeneous polynomial $f \in \mathbb{R}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ is said to be hyperbolic with respect to a direction $e \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if $f(e) \neq 0$ and, for every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the univariate polynomial $t \mapsto f(\alpha + te)$ has only real zeros. Denote by $H_n(V)$ the set of real homogeneous polynomials in $z_1,\dots,z_n$ that are hyperbolic with respect to every $e \in V$.

Characterize all linear operators $T \colon \mathbb{R}[z_1,\dots,z_n] \to \mathbb{R}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ such that
$$T\bigl(H_n(V)\bigr) \subseteq H_n(V) \cup \{0\}.$$

That is, give an explicit description (for instance, in terms of a symbol or transform of $T$) of the linear operators on $\mathbb{R}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ that preserve hyperbolicity with respect to the cone $V$.
status_search_result: Borcea and Brändén (2009) characterized linear operators preserving stability (non-vanishing on products of open half-planes) for complex multivariate polynomials, and there are related results on majorization and hyperbolicity preservers in one variable. A full characterization of linear operators preserving hyperbolicity of homogeneous real polynomials with respect to a general open cone $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ does not appear in the literature; subsequent work (e.g., representation-theoretic extensions and notes on hyperbolicity cones) treats special cases or related preservation properties but does not resolve the general cone version. The problem appears to remain open.
